Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Dīghanikāye

The Long Discourses

Sīlakkhandhavaggaabhinavaṭīkā

The New Sub-commentary on the Division of Morality

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Yo [M 1.0001][V 1.0001] desetvāna saddhammaṃ, gambhīraṃ duddasaṃ varaṃ;

Dīghadassī ciraṃ kālaṃ, patiṭṭhāpesi sāsanaṃ.1.

That Lord, the Far-seeing One, having taught the good Dhamma—profound, difficult to see, and excellent—for a long time established the Dispensation.

Vineyyajjhāsaye chekaṃ, mahāmatiṃ mahādayaṃ;

Natvāna taṃ sasaddhammagaṇaṃ gāravabhājanaṃ.2.

Having paid homage to that Lord—who is skilled in the dispositions of those to be trained, of great wisdom, of great compassion, a recipient of reverence—together with his assembly of the good Dhamma.

Saṅgītittayamāruḷhā, dīghāgamavarassa yā;

Saṃvaṇṇanā yā ca tassā, vaṇṇanā sādhuvaṇṇitā. 3.

The commentary on the excellent Dīgha Nikāya that was brought to the three Councils by the Arahant Elders, and the explanation of that commentary that is praised by the virtuous,

Ācariyadhammapāla- [V 1.0002] ttherenevābhisaṅkhatā;

Sammā nipuṇagambhīra-duddasatthappakāsanā.4.

Was composed by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla himself, rightly making clear the meaning that is subtle, profound, and difficult to see.

Kāmañca sā tathābhūtā, paramparābhatā pana;

Pāṭhato atthato cāpi, bahuppamādalekhanā.5.

Although that explanation is indeed so, yet, having been handed down through succession, there is much negligent copying regarding both the text and the meaning.

Saṅkhepattā ca sotūhi, sammā ñātuṃ sudukkarā;

Tasmā sabrahmacārīnaṃ, yācanaṃ samanussaraṃ.6.

And being concise, it is very difficult for listeners to understand correctly; therefore, repeatedly remembering the request of my fellow practitioners,

Yo’nekasetanāgindo, rājā nānāraṭṭhissaro;

Sāsanasodhane daḷhaṃ, sadā ussāhamānaso.7.

That king, lord of many white elephants, who is always firm with a striving mind in the purification of the Dispensation,

Taṃ nissāya “mamesopi, satthusāsanajotane;

Appeva nāmupatthambho, bhaveyyā”ti vicintayaṃ.8.

Relying on him, and considering thus: “Perhaps this one of mine might also become a support in the illumination of the Teacher’s Dispensation,”

Vaṇṇanaṃ [M 1.0002] ārabhissāmi, sādhippāyamahāpayaṃ;

Atthaṃ tamupanissāya, aññañcāpi yathārahaṃ.9.

Relying on that method of the commentary and also on others as is appropriate, without omitting the meaning together with its intention, I will begin this explanation.

Cakkābhivuḍḍhikāmānaṃ, dhīrānaṃ cittatosanaṃ;

Sādhuvilāsiniṃ nāma, taṃ suṇātha samāhitāti. 10.

Listen with concentrated minds to this explanation named Sādhuvilāsinī, which delights the minds of the wise who desire the growth of the Wheel.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

Nānānayanipuṇagambhīravicitrasikkhattayasaṅgahassa buddhānubuddhasaṃvaṇṇitassa saddhāvahaguṇasampannassa dīghāgamavarassa gambhīraduranubodhatthadīpakaṃ saṃvaṇṇanamimaṃ karonto sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhanasamattho mahāveyyākaraṇoyamācariyo saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayapaṇāmapayojanādividhānāni karonto paṭhamaṃ tāva ratanattayapaṇāmaṃ kātuṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādimāha. Ettha ca saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇappayojanaṃ tattha tattha bahudhā papañcenti ācariyā. Tathā hi vaṇṇayanti –

Desiring to compose this commentary which illuminates the profound and hard-to-realize meaning of the excellent Dīgha Nikāya—which is included in the collection of the three trainings that are various, subtle, profound, and wonderful, was explained by the Buddha and the Anubuddhas, and is endowed with qualities that bring forth faith—this teacher, a great grammarian capable of penetrating the thicket of his own and other doctrines, wishing to set forth at the beginning of the commentary the homage to the Triple Gem, its purpose, and so on, first spoke the verse beginning “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ” in order to pay homage to the Triple Gem. And in this connection, at the beginning of a commentary, the teachers explain in detail and in many ways in various places the purpose of paying homage to the Triple Gem. For thus they explain:

“Saṃvaṇṇanārambhe [V 1.0003] satthari paṇāmakaraṇaṃ dhammassa svākkhātabhāvena satthari pasādajananatthaṃ, satthu ca avitathadesanabhāvappakāsanena dhamme pasādajananatthaṃ. Tadubhayappasādā hi mahato atthassa siddhi hotī”ti (dha. sa. ṭī. 1-1).

“At the beginning of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Teacher is for the purpose of generating confidence in the Teacher because of the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and for the purpose of generating confidence in the Dhamma by showing the Teacher’s nature of having taught without error. For through confidence in both of these, the accomplishment of great benefit occurs.”

Atha vā “ratanattayapaṇāmavacanaṃ attano ratanattayappasādassa viññāpanatthaṃ, taṃ pana viññūnaṃ cittārādhanatthaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya gāhaṇatthaṃ, taṃ sabbasampattinipphādanattha”nti. Atha vā “saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayavandanā saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa pabhavanissayavisuddhipaṭivedanatthaṃ, taṃ pana dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāsu viññūnaṃ bahumānuppādanatthaṃ, taṃ sammadeva tesaṃ uggahaṇadhāraṇādikkamaladdhabbāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbahitasukhanipphādanattha”nti. Atha vā “maṅgalabhāvato, sabbakiriyāsu pubbakiccabhāvato, paṇḍitehi samācaritabhāvato, āyatiṃ paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanato ca saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmakiriyā”ti. Atha vā “catugambhīrabhāvayuttaṃ dhammavinayaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmassa mahāsamuddaṃ ogāhantassa viya paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatassāpi mahantaṃ bhayaṃ sambhavati, bhayakkhayāvahañcetaṃ ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇajanitaṃ [M 1.0003] paṇāmapūjāvidhānaṃ, tato ca saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmakiriyā”ti. Atha vā “asattharipi satthābhinivesassa lokassa yathābhūtaṃ satthari eva sammāsambuddhe satthusambhāvanatthaṃ, asatthari ca satthusambhāvanapariccajāpanatthaṃ, ‘tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī’ti (pārā. 195) ca vuttadosapariharaṇatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ paṇāmakiriyā”ti. Atha vā “buddhassa bhagavato paṇāmavidhānena sammāsambuddhabhāvādhigamāya buddhayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ, saddhammassa ca paṇāmavidhānena paccekabuddhabhāvādhigamāya paccekabuddhayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ, saṅghassa ca paṇāmavidhānena paramatthasaṅghabhāvādhigamāya sāvakayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ paṇāmakiriyā”ti. Atha vā “maṅgalādikāni satthāni anantarāyāni, ciraṭṭhitikāni, bahumatāni ca bhavantīti evaṃladdhikānaṃ cittaparitosanatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ paṇāmakiriyā”ti. Atha vā “sotujanānaṃ yathāvuttapaṇāmena anantarāyena uggahaṇadhāraṇādinipphādanatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ paṇāmakiriyā. Sotujanānuggahameva hi padhānaṃ katvā ācariyehi saṃvaṇṇanārambhe thutipaṇāmaparidīpakāni vākyāni nikkhipīyanti, itarathā vināpi taṃ nikkhepaṃ kāyamanopaṇāmeneva yathādhippetappayojanasiddhito kimetena ganthagāravakaraṇenā”ti ca evamādinā. Mayaṃ pana idhādhippetameva payojanaṃ dassayissāma, tasmā saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇaṃ yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Idameva ca payojanaṃ ācariyena idhādhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “iti me pasannamatino [V 1.0004] …pe… tassānubhāvenā”ti. Ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇañhi yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanatthaṃ ratanattayapūjāya paññāpāṭavabhāvato, tāya ca paññāpāṭavaṃ rāgādimalavidhamanato. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Alternatively, ‘The utterance of homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of declaring one’s confidence in the Triple Gem; that, in turn, is for the sake of delighting the discerning; that, for the sake of grasping the commentary; and that, for the accomplishment of all prosperity.’ Alternatively, ‘At the commencement of an exposition, homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of realizing the purity of the origin and basis of the Dhamma to be expounded; that, in turn, is for the sake of arousing great esteem in the discerning for the expositions of the Dhamma; and that, through right practice which is to be obtained by the sequence of learning, retention, and so on, is for the sake of accomplishing all welfare and happiness for them.’ Alternatively, ‘Homage to the Triple Gem is performed in the exposition because of its being auspicious, because of its being a preliminary duty in all activities, because of its being practiced by the wise, and because of leading others in the future to follow the example seen.’ Alternatively, ‘For one who wishes to expound the Dhamma and Vinaya, which is endowed with the four profundities, great fear arises even for one endowed with skill in wisdom, like one entering the great ocean. This act of paying homage and offering reverence, born of recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, brings about the destruction of fear. Therefore, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is performed in the exposition.’ Alternatively, ‘For a world that adheres to a non-teacher as the Teacher, it is for the purpose of esteeming, in accordance with reality, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone as the Teacher, and for the purpose of causing the abandonment of esteeming a non-teacher as the Teacher; and to avoid the fault spoken of thus: “Having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, one places it as one’s own”—for this purpose the act of homage is performed in the exposition.’ Alternatively, ‘By the act of paying homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, it is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the Buddha-vehicle for the attainment of the state of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; and by the act of paying homage to the Good Dhamma, it is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the Paccekabuddha-vehicle for the attainment of the state of a Paccekabuddha; and by the act of paying homage to the Sangha, it is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the disciple-vehicle for the attainment of the state of the ultimate Sangha—for this purpose the act of homage is performed in the exposition.’ Alternatively, ‘The act of homage is performed in the exposition for the purpose of gladdening the minds of those who hold the view that: “Auspicious and fruitful undertakings are free from obstacles, long-lasting, and highly esteemed.”’ Alternatively, ‘The act of homage is performed in the exposition for the purpose of accomplishing, without obstacle, the learning, retention, and so on, for the listeners through the aforesaid homage. For it is by making the support of the listeners primary that the teachers place sentences indicating praise and homage at the commencement of the exposition. Otherwise, even without that placement, since the desired purpose is accomplished by physical and mental homage alone, what is the use of this homage which makes the text heavy?’ and so on. We, however, shall show here only the intended purpose. Therefore, it should be understood that the performance of homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the exposition is for the purpose of completing the exposition as promised, without obstacle. This is the very purpose intended by the Teacher here. For he will say: “Thus I, with a clear mind… by the power of that…” Indeed, the performance of homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the exposition as promised, without obstacle, due to the proficiency of wisdom arising from the worship of the Triple Gem, and that proficiency of wisdom is from the dispelling of the stains of lust and so on. As it is stated—

“Yasmiṃ mahānāma samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; a. ni. 11.11).

“Mahānāma, at a time when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not overcome by lust, his mind is not overcome by hatred, his mind is not overcome by delusion. At that time, his mind becomes upright.”

Tasmā [M 1.0004] ratanattayapūjāya vikkhālitamalāya paññāya pāṭavasiddhi. Atha vā ratanattayapūjāya paññāpadaṭṭhānasamādhihetuttā paññāpāṭavaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Therefore, through the worship of the Triple Gem, there is the accomplishment of proficiency for a wisdom that has its stains washed away. Alternatively, because the worship of the Triple Gem is a cause for concentration, which is the proximate cause of wisdom, there is proficiency of wisdom. As it is stated—

“Ujugatacitto kho pana mahānāma ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammopasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (a. ni. 6.10; a. ni. 11.11).

“Moreover, Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind attains understanding of the meaning, attains understanding of the Dhamma, attains joy connected with the Dhamma. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.”

Samādhissa ca paññāya padaṭṭhānabhāvo “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071; netti. 40; peṭako. 66; mi. pa. 14) vuttoyeva. Tato evaṃ paṭubhūtāya paññāya khedamabhibhuyya paṭiññātaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ samāpayissati. Tena vuttaṃ “ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇañhi…pe… paññāpāṭavabhāvato”ti. Atha vā ratanattayapūjāya āyuvaṇṇasukhabalavaḍḍhanato anantarāyena parisamāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ratanattayapaṇāmena hi āyuvaṇṇasukhabalāni vaḍḍhanti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

And that concentration is the proximate cause of wisdom has indeed been stated: “One who is concentrated understands in accordance with reality.” Therefore, with wisdom thus sharpened, having overcome weariness, one will complete the promised exposition. For that reason it was said: “Indeed, the performance of homage to the Triple Gem… due to the proficiency of wisdom.” Alternatively, the completion without obstacle should be understood as resulting from the increase of life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength through the worship of the Triple Gem. For by homage to the Triple Gem, life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. As it is stated—

“Abhivādanasīlissa, niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino;

Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti, āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ bala”nti. (dha. pa. 109);

“For one who is habitually respectful, who constantly reveres the worthy, four things increase: life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength.”

Tato āyuvaṇṇasukhabalavuddhiyā hotveva kāriyaniṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “ratanattayapūjāya āyu…pe… veditabba”nti. Atha vā ratanattayapūjāya paṭibhānāparihānāvahattā anantarāyena parisamāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aparihānāvahā hi ratanattayapūjā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Therefore, due to that increase of life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength, the completion of the treatise to be made is indeed certain; thus it was said by me: 'By worship of the Triple Gem, life-span... should be understood.' Alternatively, it should be understood that the completion is without obstacle because worship of the Triple Gem is conducive to the non-decline of ready wit. For indeed, worship of the Triple Gem is conducive to non-decline. And this was said:

“Sattime [V 1.0005] bhikkhave, aparihānīyā dhammā, katame satta? Satthugāravatā, dhammagāravatā, saṅghagāravatā, sikkhāgāravatā, samādhigāravatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sovacassatā”ti (a. ni. 7.34) tato paṭibhānāparihānena hotveva yathāpaṭiññātaparisamāpananti vuttaṃ “ratanattaya…pe… veditabba”nti. Atha vā pasādavatthūsu pūjāya puññātisayabhāvato anantarāyena parisamāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Puññātisayā hi pasādavatthūsu pūjā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Monks, these are seven principles of non-decline. What seven? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, having good friends, and being easy to admonish.’ Therefore, due to the non-decline of ready wit, the completion as was promised is indeed certain; thus it was said: ‘The Triple Gem... should be understood.’ Alternatively, it should be understood that the completion is without obstacle due to the state of surpassing merit in worship towards the objects of faith. For indeed, worship towards the objects of faith is surpassing merit. And this was said:

“Pūjārahe [M 1.0005] pūjayato, buddhe yadiva sāvake;

Papañcasamatikkante, tiṇṇasokapariddave.

To one who worships those worthy of worship, whether Buddhas or their disciples, who have overcome proliferation and crossed over sorrow and lamentation,

Te tādise pūjayato, nibbute akutobhaye;

Na sakkā puññaṃ saṅkhātuṃ, imettamapi kenacī”ti. (khu. pā. 196; apa. 1.10.2);

worshipping such as these, the extinguished, the fearless from any quarter; it is not possible for anyone to measure that merit, saying, ‘It is this much.’

Puññātisayo ca yathādhippetaparisamāpanupāyo. Yathāha –

And surpassing merit is the means for accomplishing the completion as desired. As was said:

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhi;

Yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti. (khu. pā. 8.10);

‘This is a treasure for devas and humans that bestows all that is wished for; whatever they may long for, all that is obtained by this.’

Upāyesu ca paṭipannassa hotveva kāriyaniṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “pasādavatthūsu…pe… veditabba”nti. Evaṃ ratanattayapūjā niratisayapuññakkhettasambuddhiyā aparimeyyappabhāvo puññātisayoti bahuvidhantarāyepi lokasannivāse antarāyanibandhanasakalasaṃkilesaviddhaṃsanāya pahoti, bhayādiupaddavañca nivāreti. Tasmā suvuttaṃ “saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇaṃ yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanatthanti veditabba”nti.

And for one who is practicing the means, the completion of the treatise to be made is indeed certain; thus it was said: ‘Regarding the objects of faith... should be understood.’ In this way, worship of the Triple Gem—because of the fruitfulness of that unsurpassed field of merit—is a surpassing merit of immeasurable power. Thus, even in this worldly abode with its many various dangers, it is able to destroy all defilements that are the cause of obstacles, and it wards off calamities such as fear. Therefore, it was well said: ‘It should be understood that at the commencement of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the commentary as promised, without obstacle.’

Evaṃ pana sapayojanaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmaṃ kattukāmo buddharatanamūlakattā sesaratanānaṃ paṭhamaṃ tassa paṇāmaṃ kātumāha – “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ…pe… gativimutta”nti. Buddharatanamūlakāni hi dhammasaṅgharatanāni, tesu ca dhammaratanamūlakaṃ saṅgharatanaṃ, tathābhāvo ca “puṇṇacando viya bhagavā, candakiraṇanikaro viya tena desito dhammo, candakiraṇasamuppāditapīṇito loko viya saṅgho”ti evamādīhi aṭṭhakathāyamāgataupamāhi vibhāvetabbo. Atha vā sabbasattānaṃ aggoti katvā paṭhamaṃ buddho, tappabhavato, tadupadesitato ca tadanantaraṃ dhammo, tassa dhammassa sādhāraṇato[V 1.0006], tadāsevanato ca tadanantaraṃ saṅgho vutto. “Sabbasattānaṃ vā hite viniyojakoti katvā paṭhamaṃ buddho, sabbasattahitattā tadanantaraṃ dhammo, hitādhigamāya paṭipanno adhigatahito cāti katvā tadanantaraṃ saṅgho vutto”ti aṭṭhakathāgatanayena anupubbatā veditabbā.

Thus, wishing to pay homage with purpose to the Triple Gem, and because the Buddha Gem is the root of the other gems, he first speaks to pay homage to it, saying: ‘With a heart cooled by compassion... liberated from all destinations.’ For the Dhamma Gem and the Saṅgha Gem are rooted in the Buddha Gem, and of these, the Saṅgha Gem is rooted in the Dhamma Gem. This state of being should be clarified by the similes found in the commentary, such as: ‘The Blessed One is like the full moon, the Dhamma taught by him is like the host of moonbeams, and the Saṅgha is like the world gladdened by the arising of the moonbeams.’ Alternatively, the Buddha is mentioned first because he is the foremost of all beings; then the Dhamma, because it originates from him and was taught by him; and then the Saṅgha, because they are partakers in that Dhamma and practice it. Or, the sequence should be understood according to the method found in the commentary: ‘The Buddha is mentioned first because he engages all beings in their welfare; then the Dhamma, because it is for the welfare of all beings; and then the Saṅgha, because it has attained welfare and is practicing for the attainment of welfare.’

Buddharatanapaṇāmañca [M 1.0006] karonto kevalapaṇāmato thomanāpubbaṅgamovasātisayoti “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādipadehi thomanāpubbaṅgamataṃ dasseti. Thomanāpubbaṅgamena hi paṇāmena satthu guṇātisayayogo, tato cassa anuttaravandanīyabhāvo, tena ca attano paṇāmassa khettaṅgatabhāvo, tena cassa khettaṅgatassa paṇāmassa yathādhippetanipphattihetubhāvo dassitoti. Thomanāpubbaṅgamatañca dassento yassā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā suttantadesanā karuṇāpaññāppadhānāyeva, na vinayadesanā viya karuṇāppadhānā, nāpi abhidhammadesanā viya paññāppadhānāti tadubhayappadhānameva thomanamārabhati. Esā hi ācariyassa pakati, yadidaṃ ārambhānurūpathomanā. Teneva ca vinayadesanāya saṃvaṇṇanārambhe “yo kappakoṭīhipi…pe… mahākāruṇikassa tassā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) karuṇāppadhānaṃ, abhidhammadesanāya saṃvaṇṇanārambhe “karuṇā viya…pe… yathārucī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1) paññāppadhānañca thomanamāraddhaṃ. Vinayadesanā hi āsayādinirapekkhakevalakaruṇāya pākatikasattenāpi asotabbārahaṃ suṇanto, apucchitabbārahaṃ pucchanto, avattabbārahañca vadanto sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesīti karuṇāppadhānā. Tathā hi ukkaṃsapariyantagatahirottappopi bhagavā lokiyasādhujanehipi pariharitabbāni “sikharaṇī, sambhinnā”tiādivacanāni, (pārā. 185) yathāparādhañca garahavacanāni mahākaruṇāsañcoditamānaso mahāparisamajjhe abhāsi, taṃtaṃsikkhāpadapaññatti kāraṇāpekkhāya ca verañjādīsu sārīrikaṃ khedamanubhosi. Tasmā kiñcāpi bhūmantarapaccayākārasamayantarakathānaṃ viya vinayapaññattiyāpi samuṭṭhāpikā paññā anaññasādhāraṇatāya atisayakiccavatī, karuṇāya kiccaṃ pana tatopi adhikanti vinayadesanāya karuṇāppadhānatā vuttā. Karuṇābyāpārādhikatāya hi desanāya karuṇāpadhānatā, abhidhammadesanā pana kevalapaññāppadhānā paramatthadhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhasamatthāya paññāya tattha sātisayappavattito. Suttantadesanā pana karuṇāpaññāppadhānā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayādhimutticaritādibhedaparicchindanasamatthāya paññāya sattesu ca mahākaruṇāya tattha sātisayappavattito. Suttantadesanāya hi mahākaruṇāya samāpattibahulo vineyyasantāne tadajjhāsayānulomena [M 1.0007] gambhīramatthapadaṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Tasmā ārambhānurūpaṃ karuṇāpaññāppadhānameva thomanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ, ayamettha samudāyattho.

The Commentator, wishing to make the homage to the Buddha-jewel, shows that homage preceded by praise is superior to mere homage. Therefore, with verses such as “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ,” he demonstrates the state of homage being preceded by praise. Indeed, by homage preceded by praise, the connection with the Teacher's superior qualities is shown; and from that, His state of being unsurpassably worthy of veneration is shown; and by that, the state of one's own homage having reached a fertile field is shown; and by that, the state of this homage, which has reached a field, being a cause for the accomplishment of what is desired is shown. And in demonstrating that homage is preceded by praise, the Suttanta discourse for which he wishes to compose the commentary is one where compassion and wisdom are predominant. It is not like the Vinaya discourse, where compassion is predominant, nor is it like the Abhidhamma discourse, where wisdom is predominant. Therefore, he begins a praise where both are predominant. For this is the Teacher's custom, that is, a praise that is appropriate to the undertaking. For that very reason, at the beginning of the commentary on the Vinaya discourse, a praise where compassion is predominant was undertaken: “yo kappakoṭīhipi…pe… mahākāruṇikassa tassā”ti; and at the beginning of the commentary on the Abhidhamma discourse, a praise where wisdom is predominant was undertaken: “karuṇā viya…pe… yathārucī”ti. Indeed, the Vinaya discourse is predominant in compassion because the Blessed One, with mere compassion that is independent of the disciples' disposition and so on, laid down the training rules while listening to what should not be listened to even by an ordinary being, asking what should not be asked, and speaking what should not be spoken. Thus indeed, the Blessed One, though he had reached the highest limit of moral shame and fear, with a mind impelled by great compassion, spoke in the midst of the great assembly words that should be avoided even by virtuous worldly people, such as “sikharaṇī, sambhinnā,” and words of censure according to the offense. And out of consideration for the reason for laying down each training rule, he endured physical fatigue in Verañjā and other places. Therefore, although the wisdom that originates the Vinaya rules—like the discourses on different planes of existence, causal conditions, and different views—has a function of superior importance due to its being unique to the Buddha, the function of compassion is even greater than that. Thus, the Vinaya discourse is said to be predominant in compassion. For a discourse is predominant in compassion due to the predominance of the activity of compassion. The Abhidhamma discourse, however, is predominant in mere wisdom, due to the exceedingly powerful operation therein of the wisdom that is capable of penetrating the true nature of ultimate realities. The Suttanta discourse, on the other hand, is predominant in compassion and wisdom, due to the exceedingly powerful operation therein of the wisdom that is capable of discerning the differences in the disposition, latent tendencies, inclinations, character, and so on of various beings, and of great compassion towards those beings. For in the Suttanta discourse, the Blessed One, abounding in absorption in great compassion, established profound meaning and text in the mental continuity of the disciples in accordance with their dispositions. Therefore, it should be understood that a praise where compassion and wisdom are predominant, appropriate to the undertaking, was made. This is the collective meaning here.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0007] pana avayavattho – kiratīti karuṇā, paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati paccayavekallakaraṇena apanetīti attho. Dukkhitesu vā kiriyati pasāriyatīti karuṇā. Atha vā kiṇātīti karuṇā, paradukkhe sati kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsati vibādhati, paradukkhaṃ vā vināsetīti attho. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ kampanaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti vā karuṇā. Atha vā kamiti sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Esā hi paradukkhāpanayanakāmatālakkhaṇā attasukhanirapekkhatāya kāruṇikānaṃ sukhaṃ rundhati vibandhatīti, sabbattha saddasatthānusārena padanipphatti veditabbā. Uṇhābhitattehi sevīyatīti sītaṃ, uṇhābhisamanaṃ. Taṃ lāti gaṇhātīti sītalaṃ, “cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṃ vā te phālessāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. āḷavakasutta) ettha uro “hadaya”nti vuttaṃ, “vakkaṃ hadaya”nti (ma. ni. 1.110; 2.114; 3.154) ettha hadayavatthu, “hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.63) ettha cittaṃ, idhāpi cittameva abbhantaraṭṭhena hadayaṃ. Attano sabhāvaṃ vā haratīti hadayaṃ, ra-kārassa da-kāraṃ katvāti neruttikā. Karuṇāya sītalaṃ hadayamassāti karuṇāsītalahadayo, taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

This, however, is the meaning of the component words. It dispels (kirati), thus it is compassion (karuṇā); the meaning is that it scatters away the suffering of others, it removes it by causing a deficiency in its causes. Or, it is spread out (kiriyati/pasāriyati) towards those who are suffering, thus it is compassion (karuṇā). Alternatively, it afflicts (kiṇāti), thus it is compassion (karuṇā); the meaning is that when there is the suffering of others, it harms or oppresses the compassionate person, or it destroys the suffering of others. Or, when there is the suffering of others, it causes trembling and mental pain for the virtuous, thus it is compassion (karuṇā). Alternatively, ‘kaṃ’ is happiness (sukha); it obstructs (rundhati) that, thus it is compassion (karuṇā). For this compassion, which is characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others, obstructs and hinders the happiness of the compassionate due to their indifference to their own happiness. In all cases, the derivation of the word should be understood according to the science of grammar. It is served by those afflicted by heat, thus it is cool (sītaṃ), a pacifier of heat. It takes (lāti) or grasps that, thus it is cooling (sītalaṃ). In the passage, “cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṃ vā te phālessāmī” (“I will cast down your mind, or I will split your heart”), the chest (uro) is called ‘heart’ (hadayaṃ). In “vakkaṃ hadayaṃ” (“the kidney is the heart”), the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is called ‘heart’ (hadayaṃ). In “hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī” (“I think he knows heart with heart...”), the mind (cittaṃ) is called ‘heart’ (hadayaṃ). Here too, it is the mind (cittaṃ) that is the ‘heart’ (hadayaṃ) in the sense of being internal. Or, it carries (harati) its own nature, thus it is ‘hadayaṃ’, having changed the letter ‘ra’ to the letter ‘da’; so say the etymologists. He is ‘one with a heart cooled by compassion’ (karuṇāsītalahadayo) because for him there is a heart (hadayaṃ) that is cool (sītalaṃ) through compassion (karuṇāya). Him, the one with a heart cooled by compassion (taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ).

Kāmañcettha paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānijjhānasabhāvatāya, byāpādādīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya ca sattasantānagatasantāpavicchedanākārappavattiyā mettāmuditānampi cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā upalabbhati, tathāpi paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattiyā parūpatāpāsahanarasā avihiṃsābhūtā karuṇāva visesena bhagavato cittassa cittapassaddhi viya sītibhāvanimittanti tassāyeva cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttā. Karuṇāmukhena vā mettāmuditānampi hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi sabbattha niravasesattho upadisīyati, padhānasahacaraṇāvinābhāvādinayehipi yathālabbhamānaṃ gayhamānattā. Apicettha taṃsampayuttañāṇassa chaasādhāraṇañāṇapariyāpannatāya asādhāraṇañāṇavisesanibandhanabhūtā sātisayaṃ, niravasesañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [M 1.0008] viya savisayabyāpitāya mahākaruṇābhāvamupagatā anaññasādhāraṇasātisayabhāvappattā karuṇāva hadayasītalattahetubhāvena vuttā. Atha vā satipi mettāmuditānaṃ paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānijjhānasabhāvatāya sātisaye hadayasītalabhāvanibandhanatte sakalabuddhaguṇavisesakāraṇatāya tāsampi kāraṇanti karuṇāya eva hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttā. Karuṇānidānā hi sabbepi buddhaguṇā. Karuṇānubhāvanibbāpiyamānasaṃsāradukkhasantāpassa hi bhagavato paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāya anekānipi kappānamasaṅkhyeyyāni akilantarūpasseva niravasesabuddhakaradhammasambharaṇaniratassa samadhigatadhammādhipateyyassa ca sannihitesupi sattasaṅghātasamupanītahadayūpatāpanimittesu na īsakampi [V 1.0008] cittasītibhāvassa aññathattamahosīti. Tīsu cettha vikappesu paṭhame vikappe avisesabhūtā buddhabhūmigatā, dutiye tatheva mahākaruṇābhāvūpagatā, tatiye paṭhamābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya tīsupi avatthāsu pavattā bhagavato karuṇā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, although for loving-kindness and sympathetic joy the state of being a cause for the coolness of the mind is indeed obtained—due to their nature of contemplating the non-diminution of such things as the welfare and happiness of others, their being the direct opposite of ill-will and so on, and their proceeding in the manner of cutting off the torment that has arisen in the mental continuum of beings—nevertheless, because compassion proceeds in the manner of removing the suffering of others, has the function of not being able to endure the mental torment of others, and is of a non-harming nature, it alone is especially the cause of the coolness of the Blessed One's mind, like the tranquility of mind itself. Therefore, its state of being a cause for the coolness of the mind is stated. Or, it should be seen that with compassion as the principal means, the state of being a cause for the coolness of the heart is also stated for loving-kindness and sympathetic joy. For the meaning is not taught without remainder in every case, as it is to be grasped as it is obtained also by methods such as the principal factor, concomitance, and inseparability. Moreover, here, because the knowledge associated with it is included among the six uncommon knowledges, and because it is connected to the special uncommon knowledge, compassion—which is excellent and without remainder, and, like the knowledge of omniscience, pervades its own object, having reached the state of great compassion and attained a state of excellence not shared by others—is alone stated as being a cause for the coolness of the heart. Or else, even though for loving-kindness and sympathetic joy there is an excellent connection to the state of coolness of the heart due to their nature of contemplating the non-diminution of such things as the welfare and happiness of others, because compassion is the cause of all the special qualities of a Buddha and is thus also the cause of them, the state of being a cause for the coolness of the heart is stated of compassion alone. For all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source. Indeed, for the Blessed One—whose torment of the suffering of saṃsāra was being extinguished by the power of compassion, who, due to the wish to remove the suffering of others, for many incalculable aeons, with an untiring form, delighted in the accumulation of all the Buddha-making qualities without remainder, and who had well attained mastery over the Dhamma—even when the signs of heart-torment brought about by multitudes of beings were present, there was not even the slightest alteration of the coolness of his mind. And here, among these three alternatives, it should be seen that in the first alternative, the compassion included is that which has reached the Buddha-stage, being undifferentiated; in the second, likewise, it is that which has reached the state of great compassion; and in the third, it is the Blessed One's compassion which has proceeded in all three stages, beginning from the first aspiration.

Pajānātīti paññā, yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi paṭivijjhatīti attho. Paññapetīti vā paññā, taṃ tadatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti attho. Sāyeva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānato pakārehi dhammasabhāvajotanaṭṭhena pajjototi paññāpajjoto. Paññavato hi ekapallaṅkenapi nisinnassa dasasahassilokadhātu ekapajjotā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “cattārome bhikkhave, pajjotā. Katame cattāro? Candapajjoto, sūriyapajjoto, aggipajjoto, paññāpajjoto, ime kho bhikkhave, cattāro pajjotā. Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave, imesaṃ catunnaṃ pajjotānaṃ yadidaṃ paññāpajjoto”ti (a. ni. 4.145). Tena vihato visesena samugghāṭitoti paññāpajjotavihato, visesatā cettha upari āvi bhavissati. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho, avijjā. Sveva visayasabhāvapaṭicchādanato andhakārasarikkhatāya tamo viyāti mohatamo. Satipi tamasaddassa sadisakappanamantarena avijjāvācakatte mohasaddasannidhānena tabbisesakatāvettha yuttāti sadisakappanā. Paññāpajjotavihato mohatamo [M 1.0009] yassāti paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo, taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ.

‘It knows distinctly’ (pajānāti), therefore it is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that it penetrates things according to their true nature in various ways. Or, ‘it makes known’ (paññapeti), therefore it is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that it makes that particular meaning manifest. That same wisdom, because it abandons the obstruction to the knowable and has the function of illuminating the nature of phenomena in various ways, is a light (pajjoto); thus, it is the ‘light of wisdom’ (paññāpajjoto). For, to one with wisdom seated even with a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world-system becomes a single light. And this was stated by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these four lights. What four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. Monks, these are the four lights. Of these four lights, monks, this is the foremost, that is, the light of wisdom.’ By that it is dispelled (tena vihato) means it is especially uprooted (visesena samugghāṭito); thus, it is ‘dispelled by the light of wisdom’ (paññāpajjotavihato). And the special nature here will become manifest later on. ‘One is deluded by it’ (muyhanti tena), or ‘it itself is deluded’ (sayaṃ vā muyhati), or ‘it is mere delusion’ (muyhanamattameva vā taṃ), thus it is delusion (moho), which is ignorance (avijjā). That same delusion, because it conceals the nature of its object and is similar to darkness, is like darkness (tamo viya); thus, it is the ‘darkness of delusion’ (mohatamo). Although the word ‘darkness’ (tamo) can denote ignorance without a comparison, here, due to its proximity to the word ‘delusion’ (moha), it is fitting that it is only its qualifier; thus, a comparison is stated. ‘He for whom the darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom’ is one who is ‘paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo’. The text refers to ‘him whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom’ (taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ).

Nanu ca sabbesampi khīṇāsavānaṃ paññāpajjotena avijjandhakārahatatā sambhavati, atha kasmā aññasādhāraṇāvisesaguṇena bhagavato thomanā vuttāti? Savāsanappahānena anaññasādhāraṇavisesatāsambhavato. Sabbesampi hi khīṇāsavānaṃ paññāpajjotahatāvijjandhakārattepi sati saddhādhimuttehi viya diṭṭhippattānaṃ sāvakapaccekabuddhehi sammāsambuddhānaṃ savāsanappahānena kilesappahānassa viseso vijjatevāti. Atha vā paropadesamantarena attano santāne accantaṃ avijjandhakāravigamassa nipphāditattā (nibbattitattā ma. ni. ṭī. 1.1), tattha ca sabbaññutāya balesu ca vasībhāvassa samadhigatattā, parasantatiyañca dhammadesanātisayānubhāvena sammadeva tassa pavattitattā, bhagavāyeva visesato paññāpajjotavihatamohatamabhāvena thometabboti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe paññāpajjotapadena sasantānagatamohavidhamanā paṭivedhapaññā ceva parasantānagatamohavidhamanā desanāpaññā ca sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā saṅgahitā. Na tu purimasmiṃ atthavikappe viya paṭivedhapaññāyevāti veditabbaṃ.

Is it not so that for all those whose cankers are destroyed, the state of having the darkness of ignorance destroyed by the light of wisdom is possible? Then why is the praise of the Blessed One stated with a non-special quality common to others? Because of the possibility of a special quality not common to others, through the abandonment together with latent tendencies. For, although for all those whose cankers are destroyed there is the state of having the darkness of ignorance destroyed by the light of wisdom, just as there is a distinction in the abandonment of defilements for those who have attained to the view as compared to those liberated by faith, so too there is indeed a distinction in the abandonment of defilements for the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas as compared to the disciples and Paccekabuddhas, through the abandonment together with latent tendencies. Or alternatively, because he has accomplished the complete removal of the darkness of ignorance in his own continuum without the instruction of another, and because mastery over omniscience and the powers has been well attained therein, and because that removal of darkness has been rightly set in motion in the continuum of others through the power of the excellence of his Dhamma teaching, the Blessed One alone is especially to be praised as one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom. And in this alternative explanation of the meaning, by the term ‘light of wisdom,’ both the wisdom of penetration that destroys the delusion that has arisen in one's own continuum and the wisdom of teaching that destroys the delusion that has arisen in the continuum of others are included, either by way of a general designation or by the method of ekasesa. It should be understood that it is not, as in the previous alternative explanation, only the wisdom of penetration that is included.

Aparo [V 1.0009] nayo – bhagavato ñāṇassa ñeyyapariyantikattā sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvāvabodhanasamatthena anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena paññāpajjotena sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvacchādakamohatamassa vihatattā anāvaraṇañāṇabhūtena anaññasādhāraṇapaññāpajjotavihatamohatamabhāvena bhagavato thomanā veditabbā. Imasmiṃ pana atthavikappe mohatamavidhamanante adhigatattā anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ kāraṇūpacārena sakasantāne mohatamavidhamananti veditabbaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā savāsanappahānameva hi kilesānaṃ ñeyyāvaraṇappahānanti, parasantāne pana mohatamavidhamanassa kāraṇabhāvato phalūpacārena anāvaraṇañāṇameva mohatamavidhamananti vuccati. Anāvaraṇañāṇanti ca sabbaññutaññāṇameva, yena dhammadesanāpaccavekkhaṇāni karoti. Tadidañhi ñāṇadvayaṃ atthato ekameva. Anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammārammaṇatāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [M 1.0010] tatthāvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgacāramupādāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti, visayappavattimukhena pana aññehi asādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ dvidhā katvā chaḷāsādhāraṇañāṇabhede vuttaṃ.

Another method: Praise of the Blessed One is to be known through the state of having the darkness of delusion dispelled by the radiance of wisdom—a state not shared with others and which has become the Unobstructed Knowledge. This is so because, as the Blessed One's knowledge has the knowable as its limit, the darkness of delusion which conceals the nature of all knowable phenomena has been dispelled by the radiance of wisdom called the Unobstructed Knowledge, which is capable of penetrating and knowing the nature of all knowable phenomena. Furthermore, in this alternative meaning, because it is attained at the end of dispelling the darkness of delusion, the Unobstructed Knowledge, by way of causal metaphor, is to be known as 'the dispelling of the darkness of delusion' in one's own mental continuum. Indeed, by the perfection of the aspiration, the abandoning of defilements together with their latent tendencies is itself the abandoning of the obstruction to the knowable. Furthermore, in the mental continuum of others, because it is the cause for dispelling the darkness of delusion, by way of resultant metaphor, the Unobstructed Knowledge itself is called 'the dispelling of the darkness of delusion'. And 'Unobstructed Knowledge' is indeed Omniscient Knowledge, by which He performs the teaching of the Dhamma and reflection. Indeed, these two knowledges are one in essence. Due to having as its object all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional phenomena without remainder, it is called Omniscient Knowledge; because there is no obstruction therein, based on its unimpeded functioning, it is called Unobstructed Knowledge. Furthermore, for the purpose of showing its unshared nature with others by way of its operation in its domain, having been made twofold, it is spoken of in the section on the six unshared knowledges.

Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ avijjāsamugghātoyeveko pahānasampattivasena bhagavato thomanāya gayhati, na pana sātisayaṃ niravasesakilesappahānanti? Vuccate – tappahānavacaneneva hi tadekaṭṭhatāya sakalasaṃkilesasamugghātassa jotitabhāvato niravasesakilesappahānamettha gayhati. Na hi so saṃkileso atthi, yo niravasesāvijjāsamugghātanena na pahīyatīti. Atha vā sakalakusaladhammuppattiyā, saṃsāranivattiyā ca vijjā viya niravasesākusaladhammuppattiyā, saṃsārappavattiyā ca avijjāyeva padhānakāraṇanti tabbighātavacaneneva sakalasaṃkilesasamugghātavacanasiddhito soyeveko gayhatīti. Atha vā sakalasaṃkilesadhammānaṃ muddhabhūtattā avijjāya taṃ samugghātoyeveko gayhati. Yathāha –

What is the reason here that only the one uprooting of ignorance is taken by way of the perfection of abandoning for the praise of the Blessed One, and not the excellent, complete abandoning of all defilements? It is said: Indeed, by the very statement of its (ignorance's) abandonment, because the uprooting of all corruptions is illuminated due to their common basis, the complete abandoning of defilements is taken here. For there is no corruption that is not abandoned by the complete uprooting of ignorance. Or alternatively, just as knowledge is the principal cause for the arising of all wholesome phenomena and for the cessation of saṃsāra, so too ignorance itself is the principal cause for the arising of all unwholesome phenomena and for the continuation of saṃsāra. Therefore, by the very statement of its destruction, because the statement of the uprooting of all corruptions is accomplished, that one alone is taken. Or alternatively, because ignorance is the head of all corrupting phenomena, the uprooting of it alone is taken. As it was said:

“Avijjā muddhāti jānāhi, vijjā muddhādhipātinī;

Saddhāsatisamādhīhi, chandavīriyena saṃyutā”ti. (su. ni. 1032; cūḷa. ni. 51);

“Know ignorance as the head; know knowledge—conjoined with faith, mindfulness, and concentration, and with wholesome zeal and energy—as that which tramples upon the head.”

Sanarāmaralokagarunti ettha pana paṭhamapakatiyā avibhāgena sattopi naroti vuccati, idha pana dutiyapakatiyā manujapurisoyeva, itarathā lokasaddassa avattabbatā siyā. “Yathā hi paṭhamapakatibhūto satto itarāya pakatiyā seṭṭhaṭṭhena pure uccaṭṭhāne seti pavattatīti purisoti vuccati, evaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ netīti naroti. Puttabhātubhūtopi hi puggalo mātujeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ pituṭṭhāne [V 1.0010] tiṭṭhati, pageva bhattubhūto itarāsa”nti (vi. aṭṭha. 43-46) nāvāvimānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekasesappakappanena puthuvacanantaviggahena vā narā, maraṇaṃ maro, so natthi yesanti amarā, saha narehi, amarehi cāti sanarāmaro.Garati uggacchati uggato pākaṭo bhavatīti garu, garasaddo hi uggame. Apica pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya bhāriyaṭṭhena “garū”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, in the phrase 'sanarāmaralokagaruṃ': by its primary nature, without distinction, even a being is called 'nara'. But here, by its secondary nature, only a human male is meant; otherwise, the meaning of the word 'loka' (as 'being') would be unstatable. As was stated in the commentary on the Nāva-vimāna: 'Just as a being of a primary nature, by another nature, is called 'purisa' because he lies or exists (seti) in a high place (pure) due to being excellent, so too he is called 'nara' because he leads (neti) to a state of seniority (jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ). Indeed, a person who is a son or brother stands in the place of a father to his mother, elder sister, and younger sister; how much more so a person who is a supporter to the others.' Or, 'narā' (humans) by the method of ekasesa or by a dissolution ending in the plural. Death is 'mara'; those for whom that is not are 'amarā' (deathless). 'Sanarāmaro' means 'together with humans and the deathless'. 'Garu' means one who is eminent (uggacchati), becomes renowned (uggato), becomes manifest (pākaṭo); for the word 'gara' is in the sense of eminence. Moreover, like a stone umbrella, due to the meaning of 'heavy' or 'worthy of respect', he is called 'garu'.

Mātāpitācariyesu[M 1.0011], dujjare alahumhi ca;

Mahante cuggate ceva, nichekādikaresu ca;

Tathā vaṇṇavisesesu, garusaddo pavattati.

The word 'garu' occurs in the context of mother, father, and teacher; in the context of that which is difficult to destroy; in the context of that which is heavy; in the context of that which is great; and in the context of eminence; in the context of meanings such as subtle skillfulness; and likewise in the context of distinctions of letters.

Idha pana sabbalokācariye tathāgate. Keci pana “garu, gurūti ca dvidhā gahetvā bhāriyavācakatte garusaddo, ācariyavācakatte tu gurusaddo”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Pāḷivisaye hi sabbesampi yathāvuttānamatthānaṃ vācakatte garusaddoyevicchitabbo akārassa ākārabhāvena “gārava”nti taddhitantapadassa savuddhikassa dassanato. Sakkatabhāsāvisaye pana gurusaddoyevicchitabbo ukārassa vuddhibhāvena aññathā taddhitantapadassa dassanatoti. Sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko, tassa garūti tathā, taṃ sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. “Sanaramarūlokagaru”ntipi paṭhanti, tadapi ariyāgāthattā vuttilakkhaṇato, atthato ca yuttameva. Atthato hi dīghāyukāpi samānā yathāparicchedaṃ maraṇasabhāvattā marūti devā vuccanti. Etena devamanussānaṃ viya tadavasiṭṭhasattānampi yathārahaṃ guṇavisesāvahatāya bhagavato upakārakataṃ dasseti. Nanu cettha devamanussā padhānabhūtā, atha kasmā tesaṃ appadhānatā niddisīyatīti? Atthato padhānatāya gahetabbattā. Añño hi saddakkamo, añño atthakkamoti saddakkamānusārena padhānāpadhānabhāvo na codetabbo. Edisesu hi samāsapadesu padhānampi appadhānaṃ viya niddisīyati yathā taṃ “sarājikāya parisāyā”ti, tasmā sabbattha atthatova adhippāyo gavesitabbo, na byañjanamattena. Yathāhu porāṇā –

But here, it applies to the Tathāgata, the teacher of the whole world. Some, however, taking it in two ways as 'garu' and 'gurū', say that the word 'garu' is used when it means 'heavy', but the word 'guru' is used when it means 'teacher'. That should not be accepted. For in the domain of Pāli, the word 'garu' itself should be desired as the signifier of all the aforementioned meanings, because the derivative word 'gārava', which has a strengthened vowel, is seen due to the 'a' becoming 'ā'. But in the domain of Sanskrit, the word 'guru' itself should be desired, because otherwise the derivative word is seen with the strengthening of the 'u' vowel. 'The world with its humans and devas' is 'sanarāmaraloko'; he is the 'garu' of that; thus, the accusative is 'sanarāmaralokagaruṃ'. Some also recite it as 'sanaramarūlokagaru'. That too is suitable on account of being an Āriyā verse, from the perspective of meter, and from the perspective of meaning. For in terms of meaning, the devas are called 'marū' (mortal) because, although they are long-lived, they have the nature of dying according to their limit. By this, he shows the helpfulness of the Blessed One in bringing about special qualities for the remaining beings as is fit, just as for devas and humans. But are not devas and humans primary here? Then why is their non-primacy indicated? Because they are to be taken as primary in meaning. For the word-order is one thing, and the meaning-order is another; therefore, the state of being primary or non-primary should not be questioned according to the word-order. For in such compound words, even what is primary is indicated as if it were non-primary, as in 'sarājikāya parisāya' (with the assembly including the king). Therefore, in all cases, the intention should be sought only from the meaning, not by the mere letter. As the ancients have said:

“Atthañhi nātho saraṇaṃ avoca,

Na byañjanaṃ lokahito mahesi.

Tasmā akatvā ratimakkharesu,

Atthe niveseyya matiṃ matimā”ti. (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikakaṇḍavaṇṇanā);

“Indeed, the Lord, the great seer, benefactor of the world, declared the meaning to be the refuge, not the letter. Therefore, the wise one, not delighting in letters, should place their intellect in the meaning.”

Kāmañcettha [V 1.0011] sattasaṅkhārabhājanavasena tividho loko, garubhāvassa pana adhippetattā garukaraṇasamatthasseva yujjanato sattalokavasena attho gahetabbo. So hi lokīyanti ettha puññāpuññāni[M 1.0012], tabbipāko cāti loko, dassanatthe ca lokasaddamicchanti saddavidū. Amaraggahaṇena cettha upapattidevā adhippetā. Aparo nayo – samūhattho ettha lokasaddo samudāyavasena lokīyati paññāpīyatīti katvā. Saha narehīti sanarā, teyeva amarāti sanarāmarā, tesaṃ loko tathā, purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Amarasaddena cettha upapattidevā viya visuddhidevāpi saṅgayhanti. Tepi hi paramatthato maraṇābhāvato amarā. Imasmiṃ pana atthavikappe narāmarānameva gahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157, 255). Tathā hi sabbānatthaparihānapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā, sadevamanussāya pajāya accantamupakāritāya aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamamanaññasādhāraṇaṃ gāravaṭṭhānanti. Kāmañca itthīnampi tathāupakārattā bhagavā garuyeva, padhānabhūtaṃ pana lokaṃ dassetuṃ purisaliṅgena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Neruttikā pana avisesanicchitaṭṭhāne tathā niddiṭṭhamicchanti yathā “narā nāgā ca gandhabbā, abhivādetvāna pakkamu”nti (apa. 1.1.48). Tathā cāhu –

Although here the world is threefold—by way of the world of beings, the world of formations, and the world of location—nevertheless, because the state of being a teacher is intended, and because it is fitting only for the world of beings which is capable of showing reverence, the meaning should be taken by way of the world of beings. For that world is called ‘loka’ because herein meritorious and demeritorious actions and their results are observed. And those skilled in grammar desire the word ‘loka’ in the sense of seeing. And here, by the term ‘amara’, deities by rebirth are intended. Another method: here the word ‘loka’ has the meaning of a collection, because it is known or designated by way of a collection. Those who are ‘with men’ (saha narehi) are ‘sanarā’; they themselves are ‘deathless’ (amarā), thus they are ‘sanarāmarā’. Their collection (loko) is thus, and it should be connected with the word ‘garu’ as in the previous method. And here by the word ‘amara’, just as deities by rebirth, deities by purity are also included. For they too, in the ultimate sense, are ‘amarā’ due to the absence of death. In this alternative meaning, however, the taking of only ‘narāmarā’ (men and the deathless) is done by way of indicating excellence, just as in ‘the Teacher of devas and men’. For indeed, the Blessed One, being the supreme among all beings, is the supreme and unshared basis for reverence for countless beings in countless world-systems, due to his unsurpassed perfection of effort, which is preceded by the abandoning of all that is not of benefit and is devoted to arranging welfare and happiness without remainder; and due to being extremely beneficial to the populace of beings together with its devas and men; and due to being endowed with immeasurable, incomparable qualities of power and majesty. And although the Blessed One is indeed a teacher for women too, due to being beneficial in the same way, it should be understood that it is stated in the masculine gender in order to show the primary world. Grammarians, however, desire such an indication in a place where the meaning is decided without distinction, as in ‘Men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.’ And thus they have said:

“Napuṃsakena liṅgena, saddodāhu pumena vā;

Niddissatīti ñātabbamavisesavinicchite”ti.

“It should be known that in a context where the meaning is decided without distinction, a word is indicated by the neuter gender, or else by the masculine.”

Vandeti ettha pana –

Now, regarding the word ‘vande’:

Vattamānāya pañcamyaṃ, sattamyañca vibhattiyaṃ;

Etesu tīsu ṭhānesu, vandesaddo pavattati.

The word ‘vande’ occurs with the present tense ending, with the fifth ending, and with the seventh ending; in these three instances.

Idha pana vattamānāyaṃ aññāsamasambhavato. Tattha ca uttamapurisavasenattho gahetabbo “ahaṃ vandāmī”ti. Namanathutiyatthesu ca vandasaddamicchanti ācariyā, tena ca sugatapadaṃ, nāthapadaṃ vā ajjhāharitvā yojetabbaṃ. Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Gamanañcettha kāyagamanaṃ, ñāṇagamanañca, kāyagamanampi vineyyajanopasaṅkamanaṃ, pakatigamanañcāti dubbidhaṃ. Bhagavato hi vineyyajanopasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato [M 1.0013] sobhanaṃ, tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dutavilambitakhalitānukaḍḍhananippīḷanukkuṭika-kuṭilākulatādidosarahita- mavahasitarājahaṃsa- [V 1.0012] vasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ pakatigamanañca, vimalavipulakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasahitampi ñāṇagamanaṃ abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva mahābodhi, tāva niravajjatāya sobhanamevāti. Atha vā “sayambhūñāṇena sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto sammā gato avagatoti sugato. Yo hi gatyattho, so buddhayattho. Yo ca buddhayattho, so gatyatthoti. Tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammatamāpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato. Lokanirodhaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato paṭipannoti sugato, ayañcattho ‘sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatī’ti (mahāni. 38; cūḷani. 27) sugatotiādinā niddesanayena vibhāvetabbo.

Here, however, it occurs in the present tense because of the impossibility of the others. And there, the meaning should be taken by way of the first person as ‘I pay homage’. The teachers desire the word ‘vanda’ in the meanings of bowing and praising, and therefore, it should be connected by supplying the word ‘Sugata’ or the word ‘Nātha’. ‘His going is excellent’, thus he is Sugata. And here ‘going’ is twofold: bodily going and the going of knowledge. Bodily going is also twofold: approaching those to be trained and natural going. For the Blessed One’s approaching those to be trained is excellent because it certainly accomplishes their welfare and happiness. Likewise, his natural going—due to his physical body being adorned with the major and minor characteristics—is free from faults such as being too fast, too slow, stumbling, dragging the feet, being impeded, stooping, crookedness, or agitation, and it surpasses the gait of a king of swans, a bull, an elephant, or a king of beasts. And the going of knowledge, accompanied by special qualities such as pure and vast compassion, mindfulness, and energy, is also excellent due to its faultlessness from the time of the aspiration up until the great awakening. Alternatively, ‘one who, having fully known the entire world by way of the breakthrough of full understanding with self-originating knowledge, has gone well or understood’, thus he is Sugata. For that which has the meaning of ‘going’, that has the meaning of ‘understanding’. And that which has the meaning of ‘understanding’, that has the meaning of ‘going’. Similarly, ‘one who, abandoning the origin of the world by way of the breakthrough of relinquishment, bringing about the state of non-rearising, has gone well or surpassed’, thus he is Sugata. ‘One who, by way of the breakthrough of realization, has gone well or attained the cessation of the world’, thus he is Sugata. ‘One who, by way of the breakthrough of cultivation, has gone well or practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world’, thus he is Sugata. And this meaning should be clarified by the method of the Niddesa beginning with: ‘Because with regard to those defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, he does not return, does not go back, does not come back again, he is called Sugata’.

Aparo nayo – sundaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ, nibbānameva vā gato adhigatoti sugato. Bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva vācaṃ vineyyānaṃ sammā gadatīti vā sugato, da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā, taṃ sugataṃ. Puññāpuññakammehi upapajjanavasena gantabbāti gatiyo, upapattibhavavisesā. Tā pana nirayādibhedena pañcavidhā, sakalassāpi bhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggādhigamena avipākārahabhāvakaraṇena nivattitattā pañcahipi tāhi visaṃyutto hutvā muttoti gativimutto. Uddhamuddhabhavagāmino hi devā taṃtaṃkammavipākadānakālānurūpena tato tato bhavato muttāpi muttamattāva, na pana visaññogavasena muttā, gatipariyāpannā ca taṃtaṃbhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggena anivattitattā, na tathā bhagavā. Bhagavā pana yathāvuttappakārena visaṃyutto hutvā muttoti. Tasmā anena bhagavato katthacipi gatiyā apariyāpannataṃ dasseti. Yato ca bhagavā “devātidevo”ti vuccati. Tenevāha –

Another method: ‘one who has gone to or attained beautiful perfect self-awakening, or Nibbāna itself’, thus he is Sugata. Or, ‘one who speaks well to those to be trained speech that is true, factual, beneficial, appropriate, and timely’, thus he is Sugata, having changed the letter ‘d’ to ‘t’. To that Sugata. ‘Destinations’ are so called because they are to be gone to by way of arising through meritorious and demeritorious kamma; they are particular kinds of rebirth-existence. They, however, are fivefold by the distinction of hell, etc. He is ‘Gativimutto’ (freed from destinations) because, all kamma leading to existence having been turned back by the attainment of the noble path which renders it incapable of producing a result, he is liberated, having become dissociated from all five of them. For devas who go to ever higher existences, although freed from this or that existence in accordance with the time for the respective kamma to give its result, are merely freed. But they are not freed by way of dissociation, and they are included in the destinations because their respective kamma leading to existence has not been turned back by the noble path. The Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One, however, is liberated, having become dissociated in the way described. Therefore, by this word, it shows the Blessed One’s non-inclusion in any destination whatsoever. And since the Blessed One is called ‘the deva surpassing devas’, for that reason he said:

“Yena [M 1.0014] devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

“By which influx a rebirth as a deva might be for me, or as a gandhabba that travels through the sky; by which I might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state—those influxes of mine are destroyed, shattered, and made free of ties.”

Taṃtaṃgatisaṃvattanakānañhi kammakilesānaṃ mahābodhimūleyeva aggamaggena pahīnattā natthi bhagavato taṃtaṃgatipariyāpannatāti accantameva bhagavā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyehi parimuttoti. Atha vā kāmaṃ saupādisesāyapi nibbānadhātuyā tāhi gatīhi [V 1.0013] vimutto, esā pana “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etthevantogadhāti iminā padena anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyāva thometīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Indeed, because the kamma and defilements that lead to various destinies were abandoned by the supreme path at the very foot of the great Bodhi tree, there is for the Blessed One no inclusion in those various destinies. Therefore, the Blessed One is utterly liberated from all existences, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings. Alternatively, although he is liberated from those destinies by the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining, this liberation from destinies is included within the phrase 'dispelled the darkness of delusion by the light of wisdom'; therefore, it should be understood that by this term ['freed from destinies'], he extols him with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

Ettha pana attahitasampattiparahitapaṭipattivasena dvīhākārehi bhagavato thomanā katā hoti. Tesu anāvaraṇañāṇādhigamo, saha vāsanāya kilesānamaccantappahānaṃ, anupādisesanibbānappatti ca attahitasampatti nāma, lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa pana sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammadesanāpayogato devadattādīsupi viruddhasattesu niccaṃ hitajjhāsayatā, vinītabbasattānaṃ ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanañca āsayato parahitapaṭipatti nāma. Sā pana āsayapayogato duvidhā, parahitapaṭipatti tividhā ca attahitasampatti imāya gāthāya yathārahaṃ pakāsitā hoti. “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti hi etena āsayato parahitapaṭipatti, sammā gadanatthena sugatasaddena payogato parahitapaṭipatti. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ gativimutta”nti etehi, catusaccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugatasaddena tividhāpi attahitasampatti, avasiṭṭhaṭṭhena pana tena, “sanarāmaralokagaru”nti ca etena sabbāpi attahitasampatti, parahitapaṭipatti ca pakāsitā hoti.

Here, praise of the Blessed One is made in two ways: by way of the accomplishment of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others. Among these, the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the utter abandonment of defilements together with their latent tendencies, and the attainment of Nibbāna without residue are called the accomplishment of his own welfare. On the other hand, the teaching of the Dhamma that leads to escape from all suffering—by one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and so on—by way of application; the state of always having a benevolent disposition even towards hostile beings such as Devadatta; and awaiting the time of the maturing of the knowledge-faculty of beings to be trained, by way of intention, are called the practice for the welfare of others. That practice for the welfare of others is twofold by way of intention and application, and the accomplishment of his own welfare is threefold; these are shown fittingly in this verse. For by 'with a heart cooled by compassion', the practice for the welfare of others by way of intention is shown. By the word 'Sugata' in the sense of 'one who speaks well', the practice for the welfare of others by way of application is shown. By these phrases, 'dispelled the darkness of delusion by the light of wisdom' and 'freed from destinies', and by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of having penetrated the four truths, the threefold accomplishment of his own welfare is shown. Furthermore, by the remaining phrase, that is, by 'a teacher for the world with its humans and devas', all of the accomplishment of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others are shown.

Atha vā hetuphalasattūpakāravasena tīhākārehi thomanā katā. Tattha hetu nāma mahākaruṇāsamāyogo, bodhisambhārasambharaṇañca, tadubhayampi paṭhamapadena yathārutato, sāmatthiyato ca pakāsitaṃ. Phalaṃ pana ñāṇappahānaānubhāvarūpakāyasampadāvasena catubbidhaṃ[M 1.0015]. Tattha sabbaññutañāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ maggañāṇaṃ, tammūlakāni ca dasabalādiñāṇāni ñāṇasampadā, savāsanasakalasaṃkilesānamaccantamanuppādadhammatāpādanaṃ pahānasampadā, yathicchitanipphādane ādhipaccaṃ ānubhāvasampadā, sakalalokanayanābhisekabhūtā pana lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitā attabhāvasampatti rūpakāyasampadā. Tāsu ñāṇappahānasampadā dutiyapadena, saccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugatasaddena pakāsitā, ānubhāvasampadā tatiyapadena, rūpakāyasampadā sobhanakāyagamanatthena sugatasaddena lakkhaṇānubyañjanapāripūriyā vinā tadabhāvato. Yathāvuttā duvidhāpi parahitapaṭipatti sattūpakārasampadā, sā pana sammā gadanatthena sugatasaddena pakāsitāti veditabbā.

Alternatively, praise is made in three ways: by way of the perfection of cause, the perfection of fruit, and the perfection of benefiting beings. Therein, being endowed with great compassion and the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment are called the perfection of cause; both of these are shown by the first phrase, both literally and by its capacity. The perfection of fruit, however, is fourfold: by way of the perfection of knowledge, abandonment, power, and physical form. Therein, the knowledge of the path which is the proximate cause for omniscience, and the knowledges rooted in it such as the ten powers, are the perfection of knowledge. Bringing all defilements together with their latent tendencies to a state of utter non-arising again is the perfection of abandonment. Sovereignty in accomplishing whatever is desired is the perfection of power. The perfection of the personage, adorned with the major and minor characteristics, which is like an anointing for the eyes of the entire world, is the perfection of the physical form. Among these, the perfections of knowledge and abandonment are shown by the second phrase, and by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of having penetrated the truths. The perfection of power is shown by the third phrase. The perfection of the physical form is shown by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of a beautiful gait, because without the fulfillment of the major and minor characteristics, that perfection does not exist. The aforementioned twofold practice for the welfare of others is the perfection of benefiting beings, and it should be known that this is shown by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of 'one who speaks well'.

Apica imāya gāthāya sammāsambodhi tammūla – tappaṭipattiyādayo aneke buddhaguṇā ācariyena pakāsitā honti. Esā hi ācariyānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ yena kenaci pakārena atthantaraviññāpanaṃ. Kathaṃ? “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti hi etena sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ dasseti[V 1.0014]. Mahākaruṇāsañcoditamānaso hi bhagavā saṃsārapaṅkato sattānaṃ samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhāro anupubbena pāramiyo pūretvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhimadhigatoti karuṇā sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena sammāsambodhiṃ dasseti. Sabbaññutañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi aggamaggañāṇaṃ, aggamaggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ “sammāsambodhī”ti vuccati. Sammā gamanatthena sugatasaddena sammāsambodhiyā paṭipattiṃ dasseti līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyogasassatucchedābhinivesādiantadvayarahitāya karuṇāpaññāpariggahitāya majjhimāya paṭipattiyā pakāsanato, itarehi sammāsambodhiyā padhānāppadhānappabhedaṃ payojanaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇañhettha padhānaṃ, tadaññamappadhānaṃ. Tesu ca padhānena payojanena parahitapaṭipattiṃ dasseti, itarena attahitasampattiṃ, tadubhayena ca attahitapaṭipannādīsu catūsu puggalesu bhagavato catutthapuggalabhāvaṃ pakāseti. Tena ca anuttaraṃ dakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ, uttamañca vandanīyabhāvaṃ, attano ca vandanāya khettaṅgatabhāvaṃ vibhāveti.

Furthermore, by this verse, the teacher has shown perfect self-enlightenment, its root, its practice, and so on—many qualities of the Buddha. For this is the nature of teachers: making known a different meaning by some means or other. How so? By the phrase 'with a heart cooled by compassion', he shows the root of perfect self-enlightenment. For the Blessed One, his mind urged on by great compassion, having made the aspiration to rescue beings from the mire of saṃsāra, and having sequentially fulfilled the perfections, attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. Therefore, compassion is the root of perfect self-enlightenment. By the phrase 'dispelled the darkness of delusion by the light of wisdom', he shows perfect self-enlightenment. For the knowledge of the supreme path, which has omniscience as its proximate cause, and omniscience, which has the knowledge of the supreme path as its proximate cause, are called 'perfect self-enlightenment'. By the word 'Sugata' in the sense of 'one who has gone well', he shows the practice for perfect self-enlightenment, because it shows the middle practice—embraced by compassion and wisdom, and free from the two extremes such as exertion established in sloth and restlessness, indulgence in sensual pleasures, self-mortification, and adherence to eternalism and annihilationism. By the other phrases, he shows the purpose of perfect self-enlightenment, with its distinction of principal and non-principal. Herein, the ferrying of beings across the great flood of saṃsāra is the principal purpose; what is other than that is non-principal. Among these, by the principal purpose he shows the practice for the welfare of others; by the other, the accomplishment of his own welfare. And by both of these, he shows the Blessed One's state as the fourth person among the four types of persons, such as one who practices for their own welfare. And by that, he makes clear the unsurpassed state of being worthy of offerings, the supreme state of being worthy of veneration, and his own act of veneration's having reached its proper field.

Apica karuṇāggahaṇena lokiyesu mahaggatabhāvappattāsādhāraṇaguṇadīpanato sabbalokiyaguṇasampatti dassitā, paññāggahaṇena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānamaggañāṇadīpanato [M 1.0016] sabbalokuttaraguṇasampatti. Tadubhayaggahaṇasiddho hi attho “sanarāmaralokagaru”ntiādinā vipañcīyatīti. Karuṇāggahaṇena ca nirupakkilesamupagamanaṃ dasseti, paññāggahaṇena apagamanaṃ. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena lokasamaññānurūpaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ dasseti lokavohāravisayattā karuṇāya, paññāggahaṇena lokasamaññāya anatidhāvanaṃ. Sabhāvānavabodhena hi dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ atidhāvitvā sattādiparāmasanaṃ hoti. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattivihāraṃ dasseti, paññāggahaṇena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ, catusaccañāṇaṃ, catupaṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ, karuṇāggahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa gahitattā sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, cha abhiññā, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇāni, dasa balāni, cuddasa buddhaguṇā, soḷasa ñāṇacariyā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, catucattārīsa ñāṇavatthūni, sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnīti evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paññāpabhedānaṃ vasena ñāṇacāraṃ dasseti. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena caraṇasampattiṃ, paññāggahaṇena vijjāsampattiṃ. Karuṇāggahaṇena attādhipatitā, paññāggahaṇena dhammādhipatitā. Karuṇāggahaṇena lokanāthabhāvo, paññāggahaṇena attanāthabhāvo. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena pubbakārībhāvo, paññāggahaṇena kataññutā. Karuṇāggahaṇena aparantapatā, paññāggahaṇena anattantapatā. Karuṇāggahaṇena vā buddhakaradhammasiddhi, paññāggahaṇena buddhabhāvasiddhi. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena parasantāraṇaṃ, paññāggahaṇena [V 1.0015] attasantāraṇaṃ. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena sabbasattesu anuggahacittatā, paññāggahaṇena sabbadhammesu virattacittatā dassitā hoti sabbesañca buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi tannidānabhāvato, paññā pariyosānaṃ tato uttari karaṇīyābhāvato. Iti ādipariyosānadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo samādhikkhandho dassito hoti. Karuṇānidānañhi sīlaṃ tato pāṇātipātādiviratippavattito, sā ca jhānattayasampayoginīti, paññāvacanena paññākkhandho. Sīlañca sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti evampi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti nayato dassitattā. Eso eva hi niravasesato buddhaguṇānaṃ dassanupāyo, yadidaṃ nayaggāhaṇaṃ, aññathā ko [M 1.0017] nāma samattho bhagavato guṇe anupadaṃ niravasesato dassetuṃ. Tenevāha –

Furthermore, by taking up compassion, the perfection of all worldly qualities is shown, for it reveals the quality of great compassion, which is uncommon among those who have attained a sublime state. By taking up wisdom, the perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown, for it reveals the path-knowledge that is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience. Indeed, the meaning established by taking up both is elaborated by such phrases as, “venerable one for the world with its humans and gods.” And by taking up compassion, an approach free from defilements is shown; by taking up wisdom, a departure from them is shown. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the Blessed One’s conduct in accordance with worldly convention is shown, since compassion has worldly discourse as its domain; by taking up wisdom, the non-transgression of worldly convention is shown. For it is through not understanding the intrinsic nature of phenomena that one transgresses their intrinsic nature, and the misapprehension of a ‘being,’ and so on, occurs. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the abiding in the attainment of great compassion is shown. By taking up wisdom, the course of knowledge is shown through its numerous divisions, such as: the unimpeded knowledge in the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, the four analytical knowledges, and the four fearlessnesses. And since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by taking up compassion, the remaining uncommon knowledges are also shown: the six direct knowledges, the unshaken knowledges in the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the fourteen Buddha-qualities, the sixteen courses of knowledge, the eighteen Buddha-dharmas, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the perfection of conduct is shown; by taking up wisdom, the perfection of higher knowledge. By taking up compassion, having oneself as master is shown; by taking up wisdom, having the Dhamma as master. By taking up compassion, the state of being a refuge for the world is shown; by taking up wisdom, the state of being a refuge for oneself. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the state of being a prior benefactor is shown; by taking up wisdom, gratitude. By taking up compassion, not tormenting others is shown; by taking up wisdom, not tormenting oneself. Alternatively, by taking up compassion, the accomplishment of the dhammas that make a Buddha is shown; by taking up wisdom, the accomplishment of Buddhahood. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the saving of others is shown; by taking up wisdom, the saving of oneself. Likewise, by taking up compassion, a mind of helpfulness towards all beings is shown; by taking up wisdom, a mind of detachment from all phenomena. And of all the Buddha-qualities, compassion is the beginning, because it is their root cause, and wisdom is the end, because beyond it there is nothing further to be done. Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the Buddha-qualities are shown. Likewise, by taking up compassion, the aggregate of concentration, which is preceded by the aggregate of virtue, is shown. For virtue has compassion as its cause, because from it arises abstinence from killing living beings and so on; and that compassion is associated with the three jhānas. By the word ‘wisdom,’ the aggregate of wisdom is shown. And virtue is the beginning of all Buddha-qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end. In this way also, all the Buddha-qualities, being good in the beginning, middle, and end, are shown, because they are shown by way of a method. Indeed, this grasping by way of a method is the very means for showing the Buddha-qualities without remainder. Otherwise, who indeed would be able to show the qualities of the Blessed One word by word without remainder? Therefore, he said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno.

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti.

‘Even a Buddha, speaking of nothing else, might speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon. The eon would be exhausted in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.’

Teneva ca āyasmatā sāriputtattherenāpi buddhaguṇaparicchedanaṃ pati bhagavatā anuyuttena “no hetaṃ bhante”ti paṭikkhipitvā “api ca me bhante dhammanvayo vidito”ti sampasādanīyasutte vuttaṃ.

For that very reason, when questioned by the Blessed One concerning the limit of the Buddha’s qualities, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta rejected it, saying, “This is not so, venerable sir,” and declared, “But, venerable sir, the causal sequence of the Dhamma is known to me,” as was said in the Sampasādanīya Sutta.

Evaṃ saṅkhepena sakalasabbaññuguṇehi bhagavato thomanāpubbaṅgamaṃ paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni saddhammassāpi thomanāpubbaṅgamaṃ paṇāmaṃ karonto “buddhopī”tiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ saha padasambandhena saṅkhepattho – yathāvuttavividhaguṇagaṇasamannāgato buddhopi yaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ, saha pubbabhāgapaṭipattidhammena vā ariyamaggabhūtaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā ceva yaṃ phalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ, pariyattidhammapaṭipattidhammehi vā saha phalanibbānabhūtaṃ dhammaṃ sacchikatvā ca sammāsambodhisaṅkhātaṃ buddhabhāvamupagato, vītamalamanuttaraṃ taṃ dhammampi vandeti.

Thus, having briefly made a salutation to the Blessed One, preceded by praise of all the qualities of the Omniscient One, now, wishing to make a salutation to the good Dhamma as well, preceded by praise, he uttered the verse beginning, “Even a Buddha…” Therein, this is the concise meaning together with the syntactical connection: The Buddha, endowed with the collection of various qualities as described, attained the state of a Buddha, called perfect self-enlightenment, by having developed the Dhamma called the noble path (or the Dhamma that is the noble path together with the practice-Dhamma of the preliminary part), and by having realized the Dhamma called fruit and Nibbāna (or the Dhamma that is fruit and Nibbāna together with the Dhamma of the scriptures and the Dhamma of practice); to that very Dhamma, stainless and unsurpassed, I pay homage.

Tattha buddhasaddassa tāva “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho. Bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā niddesanayena attho veditabbo. Atha vā aggamaggañāṇādhigamena savāsanāya sammohaniddāya accantavigamanato, aparimitaguṇagaṇālaṅkatasabbaññutaññāṇappattiyā vikasitabhāvato [V 1.0016] ca buddhavāti buddho jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena.
