Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena ñeyyavisesassa kammabhāvāgahaṇato kammavacanicchāyābhāvena avagamanatthavasena kattuniddesova labbhati, tasmā buddhavāti buddhotipi vattabbo. Padesaggahaṇe hi asati gahetabbassa nippadesatāva viññāyati yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Evañca katvā kammavisesānapekkhā kattari eva buddhasaddasiddhi veditabbā, atthato [M 1.0018] pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhuñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhastaniravasesakilesomahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho, yathāha –

In this context, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should first be understood according to the method of the Niddesa, such as: 'Because he has understood the truths, he is a Buddha; because he causes the populace to understand, he is a Buddha.' Or alternatively, because of the complete departure from the sleep of delusion together with its latent tendencies through the attainment of the supreme path-knowledge, and because of having blossomed through the attainment of omniscience-knowledge adorned with a collection of immeasurable virtues, he is a 'Buddha' because he has awakened (buddhavā), this being by way of the meaning of 'awakening' and 'blossoming'. Or alternatively, because there is no knowable phenomenon whatsoever that is not understood by him, because a particular knowable is not taken in the sense of an object, and because there is no desire to express it in the objective case, only the designation of the agent is obtained by way of the meaning of 'understanding'; therefore, it is also a valid etymology that because 'he has understood' (buddhavā), he is a 'Buddha'. For when a part is not taken, what is to be taken is understood as being without remainder, just as in 'the initiated one does not give'. And thus, the establishment of the word 'Buddha' should be understood as being in the agent alone, without regard for a particular object. In terms of meaning, however, the continuum of aggregates—imbued by the perfections, who with self-originated knowledge has destroyed and shattered without remainder the defilements together with their latent tendencies, and is the basis for a collection of immeasurable virtues such as great compassion and omniscience-knowledge—is the Buddha. As it is said:

“Buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 97; paṭi. ma. 161).

He is called ‘Buddha’—that Blessed One, the Self-Arisen One, without a teacher, who by himself fully understood the truths in regard to things unheard of before, attained omniscience therein, and mastery over the powers.”

Apisaddo sambhāvane, tena evaṃ guṇavisesayutto sopi nāma bhagavā īdisaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā, sacchikatvā ca buddhabhāvamupagato, kā nāma kathā aññesaṃ sāvakādibhāvamupagamaneti dhamme sambhāvanaṃ dīpeti. Buddhabhāvanti sammāsambodhiṃ. Yena hi nimittabhūtena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānena aggamaggañāṇena, aggamaggañāṇapadaṭṭhānena ca sabbaññutaññāṇena bhagavati “buddho”ti nāmaṃ, tadārammaṇañca ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tamevidha “bhāvo”ti vuccati. Bhavanti buddhisaddā etenāti hi bhāvo. Tathā hi vadanti –

The particle `api` is used in the sense of esteem. By this, he shows high regard for the Dhamma, thus: 'Endowed with such special qualities, even that Blessed One attained the state of a Buddha by having developed and realized such a Dhamma; what then is to be said of others attaining the state of disciples and so forth?' 'The state of a Buddha' means perfect self-enlightenment. For by that supreme path-knowledge—which is the sign and has omniscience-knowledge as its proximate cause—and by that omniscience-knowledge—which has the supreme path-knowledge as its proximate cause—the name 'Buddha' and the knowledge that has that as its object arise in the Blessed One; that very thing is here called 'bhāva' (state). For cognitions and words arise by this, therefore it is 'bhāva'. Thus they say:

“Yena yena nimittena, buddhi saddo ca vattate;

Taṃtaṃnimittakaṃ bhāvapaccayehi udīrita”nti.

By whatever sign cognition and word occur, that very sign is expressed by the suffixes indicating 'state' (`bhāva`).

Bhāvetvāti uppādetvā, vaḍḍhetvā vā. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Ceva-saddo ca-saddo ca tadubhayattha samuccaye. Tena hi saddadvayena na kevalaṃ bhagavā dhammassa bhāvanāmattena buddhabhāvamupagato, nāpi sacchikiriyāmattena, atha kho tadubhayenevāti samuccinoti. Upagatoti patto, adhigatoti attho. Etassa “buddhabhāva”nti padena sambandho. Vītamalanti ettha virahavasena eti pavattatīti vīto, malato vīto, vītaṃ vā malaṃ yassāti vītamalo, taṃ vītamalaṃ. “Gatamala”ntipi pāṭho dissati, evaṃ sati saupasaggo viya anupasaggopi gatasaddo virahatthavācako veditabbo dhātūnamanekatthattā. Gacchati apagacchatīti hi gato, dhammo[V 1.0017]. Gataṃ vā malaṃ, purimanayena samāso. Anuttaranti uttaravirahitaṃ. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyato, saṃsārato ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo, navavidho lokuttaradhammo. Tappakāsanattā, sacchikiriyāsammasanapariyāyassa ca labbhamānattā pariyattidhammopi idha saṅgahito[M 1.0019]. Tathā hi “abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ adhigacchi, tīṇi piṭakāni sammasī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā sacchikatvā”ti ca vuttattā bhāvanāsacchikiriyāyogyatāya buddhakaradhammabhūtāhi pāramitāhi saha pubbabhāgaadhisīlasikkhādayopi idha saṅgahitāti veditabbā. Tāpi hi vigatapaṭipakkhatāya vītamalā, anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarā ca. Kathaṃ pana tā bhāvetvā, sacchikatvā ca bhagavā buddhabhāvamupagatoti? Vuccate – sattānañhi saṃsāravaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇāya [nissaraṇatthāya (paṇṇāsa ṭī.) nissaraṇe (katthaci)] katamahābhinīhāro mahākaruṇādhivāsanapesalajjhāsayo paññāvisesapariyodātanimmalānaṃ dānadamasaññamādīnaṃ uttamadhammānaṃ kappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ niravasesaṃ bhāvanāsacchikiriyāhi kammādīsu adhigatavasībhāvo acchariyācinteyyamahānubhāvo adhisīlādhicittānaṃ paramukkaṃsapāramippatto bhagavā paccayākāre catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pesetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhisaṅkhātaṃ buddhabhāvamupagatoti.

`Bhāvetvā` means having produced, or having developed. `Sacchikatvā` means having made it directly present. The particle `ceva` and the particle `ca` both serve a conjunctive purpose. Thus, by these two words, he indicates a conjunction: it is not merely that the Blessed One attained the state of a Buddha through the mere cultivation of the Dhamma, nor through mere realization alone, but through both together. `Upagato` means reached, attained; this is the meaning. Its connection is with the word `buddhabhāvaṃ`. Regarding `vītamalaṃ`: `vīto` means 'gone' or 'departed' in the sense of being separated from; free from defilement (`malato vīto`); or one whose defilement is gone (`vītaṃ malaṃ yassa`), thus `vītamalo`. The reading `gatamalaṃ` is also seen; in that case, the word `gata`, even without a prefix like `vi-`, should be understood as meaning 'separated from', because verbal roots have many meanings. For `gato` is from `gacchati` (goes) or `apagacchati` (goes away). Or, `gataṃ malaṃ` is a compound in the same way as before. `Anuttaraṃ` means that which has no superior. Because it upholds (`dhāreti`) those who practice as instructed, causing them not to fall into states of loss and the cycle of samsara, it is called `dhammo`; this is the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Because it makes that manifest, and because the method for realization and comprehension is obtained, the textual Dhamma is also included here. For it is said in the commentary: 'He penetrated the ocean of the Abhidhamma method; he comprehended the three Piṭakas.' Likewise, because it is said 'having cultivated and realized which Dhamma', the preliminary trainings in higher virtue, etc., together with the perfections which are the dhammas that make one a Buddha and are suitable for cultivation and realization, should be understood as included here. For these too are `vītamalā` because their opposites are gone, and `anuttarā` because they are not shared by others. But how is it that the Blessed One, having cultivated and realized these, attained the state of a Buddha? It is said: The Blessed One—who had made the great aspiration for the liberation of beings from the suffering of the cycle of samsara; whose gentle disposition was inclined to great forbearance through great compassion; who, by diligently, continuously, and completely cultivating and realizing for four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand more the supreme dhammas such as giving, self-control, and restraint, which are purified and stainless through special wisdom, had attained mastery in actions and so forth; who possessed marvelous, inconceivable great power; and who had reached the highest, most excellent perfection in higher virtue and higher mind—attained the unsurpassed state of a Buddha, known as perfect self-enlightenment, by directing the great diamond-like knowledge through the twenty-four hundred-thousand koṭis of aspects of dependent origination.

Imāya pana gāthāya vijjāvimuttisampadādīhi anekehi guṇehi yathārahaṃ saddhammaṃ thometi. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi “bhāvetvā”ti etena vijjāsampadāya thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena vimuttisampadāya. Tathā paṭhamena jhānasampadāya, dutiyena vimokkhasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā samādhisampadāya, dutiyena samāpattisampadāya. Atha vā paṭhamena khayañāṇabhāvena, dutiyena anuppādañāṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā vijjūpamatāya, dutiyena vajirūpamatāya. Paṭhamena vā virāgasampattiyā, dutiyena nirodhasampattiyā. Tathā paṭhamena niyyānabhāvena, dutiyena nissaraṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā hetubhāvena, dutiyena asaṅkhatabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā dassanabhāvena, dutiyena vivekabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā adhipatibhāvena, dutiyena amatabhāvena dhammaṃ thometi. Atha vā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā buddhabhāvaṃ upagato”ti etena svākkhātatāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena sandiṭṭhikatāya. Tathā paṭhamena akālikatāya, dutiyena ehipassikatāya. Paṭhamena vā opaneyyikatāya, dutiyena paccattaṃveditabbatāya. Paṭhamena vā saha pubbabhāgasīlādīhi sekkhehi sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhehi[M 1.0020], dutiyena saha asaṅkhatadhātuyā asekkhehi dhammaṃ thometi.

Now, by this verse, he praises the good Dhamma in a fitting manner with many qualities, such as the accomplishment of knowledge and liberation. How so? Herein, by 'having developed,' he praises it for the accomplishment of knowledge; by 'having realized,' for the accomplishment of liberation. Likewise, by the first, for the accomplishment of jhāna; by the second, for the accomplishment of deliverance. Or, by the first, for the accomplishment of concentration; by the second, for the accomplishment of attainment. Alternatively, by the first, for the state of the knowledge of destruction; by the second, for the state of the knowledge of non-arising. Or, by the first, for its likeness to lightning; by the second, for its likeness to a thunderbolt. Or, by the first, for the accomplishment of dispassion; by the second, for the accomplishment of cessation. Likewise, by the first, for the state of leading out; by the second, for the state of escape. Or, by the first, for the state of being a cause; by the second, for the state of being unconditioned. Or, by the first, for the state of vision; by the second, for the state of seclusion. Or, by the first, for the state of sovereignty; by the second, for the state of being deathless, he praises the Dhamma. Alternatively, by the phrase 'the Dhamma having developed which he attained Buddhahood,' he praises the Dhamma for its quality of being well-proclaimed; by 'having realized,' for its quality of being directly visible. Likewise, by the first, for its quality of being timeless; by the second, for its quality of inviting inspection. Or, by the first, for its quality of leading onward; by the second, for its quality of being personally experienced by the wise. Or, by the first, he praises the Dhamma through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to the trainees, together with the preliminary virtues and so on; by the second, through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to the adepts, together with the unconditioned element.

“Vītamala”nti [V 1.0018] iminā pana saṃkilesābhāvadīpanena visuddhatāya dhammaṃ thometi, “anuttara”nti etena aññassa visiṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena paripuṇṇatāya. Paṭhamena vā pahānasampadāya, dutiyena sabhāvasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā bhāvanāphalayogyatāya. Bhāvanāguṇena hi so saṃkilesamalasamugghātako, tasmānena bhāvanākiriyāya phalamāha. Dutiyena sacchikiriyāphalayogyatāya. Taduttarikaraṇīyābhāvato hi anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarabhāvo sacchikiriyānibbattito, tasmānena sacchikiriyāphalamāhāti.

Now, by the word 'stainless,' showing the absence of defilements, he praises the Dhamma for its purity. By the word 'unsurpassed,' showing the absence of any other more excellent thing, he praises it for its completeness. Or, by the first, for the accomplishment of abandonment; by the second, for the accomplishment of its own-nature. Or, by the first, for its suitability for the fruit of development. For, through the quality of development, it eradicates the stain of defilements; therefore, by this word, he speaks of the fruit of the act of development. By the second, for its suitability for the fruit of the act of realization. For, because there is nothing further to be done beyond it and because it is not shared with anything else, its unsurpassed nature is produced from the act of realization; therefore, by this word, he speaks of the fruit of the act of realization.

Evaṃ saṅkhepeneva sabbasaddhammaguṇehi saddhammassāpi thomanāpubbaṅgamaṃ paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni ariyasaṅghassāpi thomanāpubbaṅgamaṃ paṇāmaṃ karonto “sugatassa orasāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha sugatassāti sambandhaniddeso, “puttāna”nti etena sambajjhitabbo. Urasi bhavā, jātā, saṃvuddhā vā orasā, attajo khettajo antevāsiko dinnakoti catubbidhesu puttesu attajā, taṃsarikkhatāya pana ariyapuggalā “orasā”ti vuccanti. Yathā hi manussānaṃ orasaputtā attajātatāya pitusantakassa dāyajjassa visesabhāgino honti, evametepi saddhammasavanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya bhagavato santakassa vimuttisukhassa dhammaratanassa ca dāyajjassa visesabhāginoti. Atha vā bhagavato dhammadesanānubhāvena ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānā, okkantā ca ariyasāvakā bhagavato ure vāyāmajanitābhijātatāya sadisakappanamantarena nippariyāyeneva “orasā”ti vattabbatamarahanti. Tathā hi te bhagavatā āsayānusayacariyādhimuttiādiolokanena, vajjānucintanena ca hadaye katvā vajjato nivāretvā anavajje patiṭṭhāpentena sīlādidhammasarīraposanena saṃvaḍḍhāpitā. Yathāha bhagavā itivuttake “ahamasmi bhikkhave brāhmaṇo…pe… tassa me tumhe puttā orasā mukhato jātā”tiādi (itivu. 100). Nanu sāvakadesitāpi desanā ariyabhāvāvahāti? Saccaṃ, sā pana tammūlikattā, lakkhaṇādivisesābhāvato ca “bhagavato dhammadesanā” [M 1.0021] icceva saṅkhyaṃ gatā, tasmā bhagavato orasaputtabhāvoyeva tesaṃ vattabboti, etena catubbidhesu puttesu ariyasaṅghassa attajaputtabhāvaṃ dasseti. Attano kulaṃ punenti sodhenti, mātāpitūnaṃ vā hadayaṃ pūrentīti puttā, attajādayo. Ariyā pana dhammatantivisodhanena, dhammānudhammapaṭipattiyā cittārādhanena ca tappaṭibhāgatāya bhagavato puttā nāma, tesaṃ. Tassa “samūha”nti padena sambandho.

Thus, having made homage preceded by praise to the good Dhamma with all its qualities, albeit only in brief, now, wishing to make homage preceded by praise to the noble Saṅgha as well, he says, 'of the Sugata’s breast-born sons,' and so on. Therein, 'of the Sugata' indicates a relationship; it is to be connected with the word 'of the sons.' Those born, produced, or nurtured in the breast are 'breast-born sons' (orasā). Among the four kinds of sons—the one born of oneself (attaja), the one born in the field (khettaja), the pupil (antevāsika), and the adopted one (dinnaka)—are those born of oneself. But noble individuals are called 'breast-born sons' because of their resemblance to a son born of oneself. For just as the breast-born sons of humans, because they are born of oneself, are special heirs to the inheritance belonging to their father, so too these noble disciples, at the conclusion of hearing the good Dhamma, because they are born into the noble birth, are special heirs to the inheritance belonging to the Blessed One—the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the Dhamma. Alternatively, the noble disciples who are entering the noble plane and those who have entered it, through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, because they are born in the Blessed One’s breast into the supreme birth produced by effort, are worthy of being called 'breast-born sons' in a direct sense, without recourse to figurative comparison. For indeed, they were made to grow by the Blessed One, who, having taken them to heart by observing their disposition, latent tendencies, conduct, resolve, and so on, and by reflecting on their faults, restrained them from fault, established them in what is faultless, and nourished their Dhamma-body of virtue and so on. As the Blessed One said in the Itivuttaka: 'I, monks, am a brahmin… you are my sons, breast-born, born from my mouth,' and so on. But is it not so that a teaching given by a disciple also leads to the noble state? True, but that teaching, because its root is in him and because it lacks special characteristics, is counted only as 'the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.' Therefore, their state as the Blessed One’s breast-born sons is indeed to be spoken of. By this, he shows the noble Saṅgha’s state as sons born of oneself among the four kinds of sons. They are called 'sons' (puttā) because they purify (punenti) and cleanse their own clan, or because they fulfill (pūrenti) the hearts of their parents; these are sons born of oneself and so on. But the noble ones, by purifying the lineage of the Dhamma, by the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, and by pleasing his mind, are named the Blessed One’s sons due to their resemblance to him. Of these sons, the word for them (puttānaṃ) is to be connected with the word 'assembly' (samūhaṃ).

Saṃkilesanimittaṃ hutvā guṇaṃ māreti vibādhatīti māro, devaputtamāro. Sināti pare bandhati etāyāti senā, mārassa senā tathā, mārañca mārasenañca mathenti vilothentīti mārasenamathanā[V 1.0019], tesaṃ. “Māramārasenamathanāna”nti hi vattabbepi ekadesasarūpekasesavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Mārasaddasannidhānena vā senāsaddena mārasenā gahetabbā, gāthābandhavasena cettha rasso. “Mārasenamaddanāna”ntipi katthaci pāṭho, so ayuttova ariyājātikattā imissā gāthāya. Nanu ca ariyasāvakānaṃ maggādhigamasamaye bhagavato viya tadantarāyakaraṇatthaṃ devaputtamāro vā mārasenā vā na apasādeti, atha kasmā evaṃ vuttanti? Apasādetabbabhāvakāraṇassa vimathitattā. Tesañhi apasādetabbatāya kāraṇe saṃkilese vimathite tepi vimathitā nāma hontīti. Atha vā khandhābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ viya devaputtamārassāpi guṇamāraṇe sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kilesabalakāyo idha “mārasenā”ti vuccati yathāha bhagavā –

Having become a cause of defilement, it obstructs and hinders virtue; therefore, it is Māra, the devaputta-Māra. With this army, one binds others; therefore, it is a senā, the army of Māra. They crush and destroy Māra and Māra's army; therefore, they are 'crushers of Māra's army' (mārasenamathanā). Although it should be said 'of the crushers of Māra and Māra's army' (Māramārasenamathanānaṃ), it is stated thus by means of ellipsis where one of two similar parts remains. Alternatively, by the proximity of the word 'Māra', the word 'army' should be understood as 'Māra's army'; and here the short vowel is due to the verse construction. Elsewhere there is also the reading 'Mārasenamaddanānaṃ', but that is incorrect because this verse is of the Ariyā metre. Is it not the case that at the time of attaining the path, for the noble disciples, devaputta-Māra or Māra's army does not intimidate them for the purpose of creating an obstacle, as they did for the Blessed One? Why then is it stated thus? Because the cause for being intimidated has been crushed. For when the defilement, which is the cause for their being intimidated, is crushed, then they—Māra and his army—too are indeed called 'crushed'. Alternatively, because devaputta-Māra also acts as an ally in the destruction of virtue, just like the Māras of the aggregates and formations, the host of the forces of defilement is here called 'Māra's army', as the Blessed One said:

“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;

Tatiyā khuppipāsā te, catutthī taṇhā pavuccati.

“Your first army is sensual pleasures; the second is called discontent. Your third is hunger and thirst; the fourth is called craving.

Pañcamaṃ thinamiddhaṃ te, chaṭṭhā bhīrū pavuccati;

Sattamī vicikicchā te, makkho thambho te aṭṭhamo.

Your fifth is sloth and torpor; the sixth is called fear. Your seventh is doubt; your eighth is hypocrisy and obstinacy.

Lābho siloko sakkāro,

Micchāladdho ca yo yaso;

Yo cattānaṃ samukkaṃse,

Pare ca avajānati.

Gain, renown, honour, and whatever fame is wrongly gained; whoever extols oneself and disparages others—

Esā [M 1.0022] namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī;

Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvā ca labhate sukha”nti. (su. ni. 438; mahāni. 28; cūḷani. 47);

This, Namuci, is your army, the striking force of the Dark One. One who is not a hero does not conquer it, but having conquered it, one obtains happiness.”

Sā ca tehi ariyasāvakehi diyaḍḍhasahassabhedā, anantabhedā vā kilesavāhinī satidhammavicayavīriyasamathādiguṇapaharaṇīhi odhiso mathitā, viddhaṃsitā, vihatā ca, tasmā “mārasenamathanā”ti vuccanti. Vilothanañcettha viddhaṃsanaṃ, vihananaṃ vā. Apica khandhābhisaṅkhāramaccudevaputtamārānaṃ tesaṃ sahāyabhāvūpagamanatāya senāsaṅkhātassa kilesamārassa ca mathanato “mārasenamathanā”tipi attho gahetabbo. Evañca sati pañcamāranimmathanabhāvena attho paripuṇṇo hoti. Ariyasāvakāpi hi samudayappahānapariññāvasena khandhamāraṃ, sahāyavekallakaraṇena [V 1.0020] sabbathā, appavattikaraṇena ca abhisaṅkhāramāraṃ, balavidhamanavisayātikkamanavasena maccumāraṃ, devaputtamārañca samucchedappahānavasena sabbaso appavattikaraṇena kilesamāraṃ mathentīti, iminā pana tesaṃ orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaṃ, tīsu puttesu ca anujātataṃ dasseti. Mārasenamathanatāya hi te bhagavato orasaputtā, anujātā cāti.

And that army of defilements, which has one and a half thousand divisions or infinite divisions, has been crushed, destroyed, and annihilated in part by those noble disciples with the weapons of such qualities as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, and calm. Therefore, they are called 'crushers of Māra's army'. And here, 'vilothana' means destruction or slaying. Moreover, the meaning 'crushers of Māra's army' should also be understood from the crushing of the Māra of defilements, which is reckoned as an army because it acts as an ally to the Māras of the aggregates, formations, death, and the devaputta. And this being so, the meaning becomes complete through the crushing of the five Māras. For the noble disciples crush: the aggregate-Māra by means of abandoning its origin and through full understanding; the formation-Māra by completely making its ally deficient and by preventing its arising; the death-Māra and the devaputta-Māra by means of destroying their forces and transcending their domain; and the defilement-Māra by means of eradication through cutting off and by completely preventing its recurrence. By this, it shows the reason for their being true-born sons and their being 'born-in-conformity' among the three kinds of sons. For by virtue of crushing Māra's army, they are the Blessed One's true-born sons and are 'born-in-conformity'.

Aṭṭhannanti gaṇanaparicchedo, tenasatipi tesaṃ taṃtaṃbhedena anekasatasahassasaṅkhyābhede ariyabhāvakaramaggaphaladhammabhedena imaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ nātivattanti maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvānativattanatoti dasseti. Pi-saddo, api-saddo vā padalīḷādinā kāraṇena aṭṭhāne payutto, so “ariyasaṅgha”nti ettha yojetabbo, tena na kevalaṃ buddhadhammeyeva, atha kho ariyasaṅghampīti sampiṇḍeti. Yadipi avayavavinimutto samudāyo nāma koci natthi avayavaṃ upādāya samudāyassa vattabbattā, aviññāyamānasamudāyaṃ pana viññāyamānasamudāyena visesitumarahatīti āha “aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti, etena “ariyasaṅgha”nti ettha na yena kenaci saṇṭhānādinā, kāyasāmaggiyā vā samudāyabhāvo, api tu maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvenevāti viseseti. Avayavameva sampiṇḍetvā ūhitabbo vitakketabbo, saṃūhanitabbo vā saṅghaṭitabboti samūho, soyeva samoho vacanasiliṭṭhatādinā. Dvidhāpi hi pāṭho yujjati. Ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye ca iriyanato ariyā niruttinayena[M 1.0023]. Atha vā sadevakena lokena saraṇanti araṇīyato upagantabbato, upagatānañca tadatthasiddhito ariyā, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhato, samaggaṃ vā kammaṃ samudāyavasena samupagatoti saṅgho, ariyānaṃ saṅgho, ariyo ca so saṅgho ca yathāvuttanayenāti vā ariyasaṅgho, taṃ ariyasaṅghaṃ. Bhagavato aparabhāge buddhadhammaratanānampi samadhigamo saṅgharatanādhīnoti ariyasaṅghassa bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ idheva “sirasā vande”ti vuttaṃ. Avassañcāyamattho sampaṭicchitabbo vinayaṭṭhakathādīsupi (pārā. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) tathā vuttattā. Keci pana purimagāthāsupi taṃ padamānetvā yojenti, tadayuttameva ratanattayassa asādhāraṇaguṇappakāsanaṭṭhānattā, yathāvuttakāraṇassa ca sabbesampi saṃvaṇṇanākārānamadhippetattāti.

‘Of the eight’ is a numerical definition. By this it is shown that although there are many hundreds of thousands of them according to their various distinctions, they do not go beyond this numerical definition in terms of the distinction of the path-and-fruit states that make one a noble being, because they do not go beyond the state of being established in the path and established in the fruit. The particle ‘pi’, or ‘api’, is used out of place for reasons such as stylistic elegance, and it should be connected here with ‘the noble Saṅgha’. By this, it summarizes that homage is paid not only to the Buddha and the Dhamma, but also to the noble Saṅgha. Although there is no such thing as a collection apart from its components—since a collection is spoken of with reference to its components—it is nevertheless proper to specify an unperceived collection by means of a perceived collection. Therefore, he said ‘the group of the eight’. By this, he specifies that here, in ‘the noble Saṅgha’, the state of being a collection is not due to some form or other or to physical togetherness, but rather solely to the state of being established in the path and established in the fruit. The components themselves, having been gathered, are to be inferred or considered; or they are to be grouped or assembled; therefore, it is a ‘group’ (samūho). That very word becomes ‘samoho’ due to euphonic smoothness, etc. For the reading is suitable in both ways. According to the etymological method, they are ‘noble’ (ariyā) because they are far from defilements, because they do not go into what is unprofitable, and because they go into what is profitable. Alternatively, they are ‘noble’ because they are to be gone to or approached as a refuge by the world with its devas, and because for those who have approached them, their purpose is accomplished. It is a ‘Saṅgha’ because it is bound together by commonality of view and virtue, or because it comes together harmoniously as a group for formal acts. The Saṅgha of the noble ones is the ‘Ariyasaṅgha’. Or, it is the ‘Ariyasaṅgha’ because it is both noble and a Saṅgha in the way described. To that Ariyasaṅgha. To show the great helpfulness of the noble Saṅgha—in that after the Blessed One, the attainment of even the Buddha-gem and the Dhamma-gem is dependent on the Saṅgha-gem—it is said right here ‘I pay homage with my head’. And this meaning must certainly be accepted, because it is stated thus in the Vinaya commentaries and so on. Some, however, bring that phrase and apply it even to the preceding verses. That is quite inappropriate, because this is the place for proclaiming the unique qualities of the Triple Gem, and because the aforementioned reason is intended by all commentators.

Imāya pana gāthāya ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadā pahānasampadādayo aneke guṇā dassitā honti. Kathaṃ? “Sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti hi etena ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti sammāsambuddhapabhavatādīpanato. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti etena pahānasampadaṃ sakalasaṃkilesappahānadīpanato. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena ñāṇasampadaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvadīpanato[V 1.0021]. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena sabhāvasampadaṃ sabbasaṅghānaṃ aggabhāvadīpanato. Atha vā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti ariyasaṅghassa visuddhanissayabhāvadīpanaṃ. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti sammāujuñāyasāmīcipaṭipannabhāvadīpanaṃ. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti āhuneyyādibhāvadīpanaṃ. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti anuttarapuññakkhettabhāvadīpanaṃ. Tathā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa lokuttarasaraṇagamanasabbhāvaṃ dasseti. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanena hi te bhagavato orasaputtā jātā. “Mārasenamathanāna’nti etena abhinīhārasampadāsiddhaṃ pubbabhāgasammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Katābhinīhārā hi sammāpaṭipannā māraṃ, mārasenaṃ vā abhivijinanti. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena viddhastavipakkhe sekkhāsekkhadhamme dasseti puggalādhiṭṭhānena maggaphaladhammānaṃ dassitattā. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ dasseti anuttarapuññakkhettabhāvassa dassitattā. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakānaṃ sabbaguṇassa ādi, sapubbabhāgapaṭipadā sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo majjhe, asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo [M 1.0024] pariyosānantiādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā saṅkhepato sabbepi ariyasaṅghaguṇā dassitā hontīti.

Moreover, by this verse, many qualities of the Noble Sangha—such as the excellence of origin, the excellence of abandonment, and so on—are shown. How? By the phrase 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata,' the excellence of origin of the Noble Sangha is shown, because it indicates their origin from the Sammāsambuddha. By the phrase 'crushers of Māra’s army,' the excellence of abandonment is shown, because it indicates the abandonment of all defilements. By the phrase 'the group of the eight,' the excellence of knowledge is shown, because it indicates the state of being established in the path and established in the fruition. By the term 'Noble Sangha,' the excellence of nature is shown, because it indicates their state of being the highest of all Saṅghas. Alternatively, 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata' indicates the state of having a thoroughly purified support. 'Crushers of Māra’s army' indicates the state of having practiced rightly, straightly, properly, and correctly. 'The group of the eight' indicates the state of being worthy of offerings, and so on. 'Noble Sangha' indicates the state of being an unsurpassed field of merit. Likewise, by the phrase 'the legitimate sons of the Sugata,' it shows the existence of the supramundane going for refuge for the Noble Sangha. For it is through the supramundane going for refuge that they are born as the Blessed One’s legitimate sons. 'Crushers of Māra’s army' shows the preliminary right practice accomplished through the perfection of aspiration. For those who have made the aspiration and practice rightly conquer Māra or his army. 'The group of the eight' shows the qualities of learners and non-learners, whose opposing forces have been destroyed, because the path and fruition states are shown by way of reference to individuals. 'Noble Sangha' shows their supreme worthiness of offerings, as their state of being an unsurpassed field of merit is shown. And for the disciples, going for refuge is the beginning of all virtues; the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the learners, along with the preliminary practice, are the middle; and the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the non-learners are the end. Thus, in brief, all the qualities of the Noble Sangha—good in the beginning, middle, and end—are shown.

Evaṃ gāthāttayena saṅkhepato sakalaguṇasaṃkittanamukhena ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni taṃ nipaccakāraṃ yathādhippetapayojane pariṇāmento “iti me”tiādimāha. Tattha iti-saddo nidassane. Tena gāthāttayena yathāvuttanayaṃ nidasseti. Meti attānaṃ karaṇavacanena kattubhāvena niddisati. Tassa “yaṃ puññaṃ mayā laddha”nti pāṭhasesena sambandho, sampadānaniddeso vā eso, “atthī”ti pāṭhaseso, sāminiddeso vā “yaṃ mama puññaṃ vandanāmaya”nti. Pasīdīyate pasannā, tādisā mati paññā, cittaṃ vā yassāti pasannamati, aññapadaliṅgappadhānattā imassa samāsapadassa “pasannamatino”ti vuttaṃ. Ratiṃ nayati, janeti, vahatīti vā ratanaṃ, sattavidhaṃ, dasavidhaṃ vā ratanaṃ, tamiva imānīti neruttikā. Sadisakappanamaññatra pana yathāvuttavacanattheneva buddhādīnaṃ ratanabhāvo yujjati. Tesañhi “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.157, 255) yathābhūtaguṇe āvajjantassa amatādhigamahetubhūtaṃ anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

Thus, with these three verses, having briefly paid homage to the Triple Gem by means of praising all their qualities, now, directing that act of reverence toward the intended purpose, he says, 'Iti me,' and so on. Therein, the word 'iti' is in the sense of indication. By that, he indicates the method as stated with the three verses. By 'me', he indicates himself as the agent with the instrumental case. Its connection is with the elliptical phrase 'whatever merit has been obtained by me.' Or, this is an indication of the dative, the ellipsis being 'there is.' Or, it is an indication of the genitive, as in 'whatever merit of mine consists of veneration.' Pasīdīyate means pasannā (serene). One who has such a mati (intention) or citta (mind) is pasannamati. Because the gender of the external referent is predominant for this compound word, it is said as 'pasannamatino.' Because it leads to (nayati), generates (janeti), or brings (vahati) delight (ratiṃ), it is a 'ratana' (gem). There is the sevenfold or tenfold gem. The etymologists say: 'These (imāni) are like that (tamiva).' However, setting aside the metaphorical comparison, the nature of the Buddha and so on as gems is justified precisely by the meaning of the word as stated. For, to one reflecting on their true qualities, beginning with 'Iti’pi so Bhagavā...', immeasurable joy and gladness arises, which is a cause for attaining the deathless. As he said:

“Yasmiṃ mahānāma samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na moha…pe… ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Ujugatacitto kho pana mahānāma ariyasāvako [V 1.0022] labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not assailed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time his mind becomes straight, taking the Tathāgata as its object. With a straight mind, Mahānāma, a noble disciple gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises,” and so on.

Cittīkatādibhāvo vā ratanaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu –

Alternatively, the meaning of 'ratana' is the state of being esteemed, and so on. For this has been said in the commentaries:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; udāna. aṭṭha. 47; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; su. ni. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 1.226);

“Because it is esteemed and of great price, incomparable, rare to see, and fit for the use of superior beings, for that reason it is called a 'ratana'.”

Cittīkatabhāvādayo ca anaññasādhāraṇā sātisayato buddhādīsuyeva labbhantīti. Vitthāro ratanasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226) gahetabbo. Ayamattho [M 1.0025] pana nibbacanatthavasena na vutto, atha kenāti ce? Loke ratanasammatassa vatthuno garukātabbatādiatthavasenāti saddavidū. Sādhūnañca ramanato, saṃsāraṇṇavā ca taraṇato, sugatinibbānañca nayanato ratanaṃ tulyatthasamāsavasena, alamatipapañcena. Ekasesapakappanena, puthuvacananibbacanena vā ratanāni. Tiṇṇaṃ samūho, tīṇi vā samāhaṭāni, tayo vā avayavā assāti tayaṃ, ratanānameva tayaṃ, nāññesanti ratanattayaṃ. Avayavavinimuttassa pana samudāyassa abhāvato tīṇi eva ratanāni tathā vuccanti, na samudāyamattaṃ, samudāyāpekkhāya pana ekavacanaṃ kataṃ. Vandīyate vandanā, sāva vandanāmayaṃ yathā “dānamayaṃ sīlamaya”nti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60; netti. 33). Vandanā cettha kāyavācācittehi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaninnatā, thomanā vā. Apica tassā cetanāya sahajātādopakāreko saddhāpaññāsativīriyādisampayuttadhammo vandanā, tāya pakatanti vandanāmayaṃ yathā “sovaṇṇamayaṃ rūpiyamaya”nti, atthato pana yathāvuttacetanāva. Ratanattaye, ratanattayassa vā vandanāmayaṃ ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ. Pujjabhavaphalanibbattanato puññaṃ niruttinayena, attano kārakaṃ, santānaṃ vā punāti visodhetīti puññaṃ, sakammakattā dhātussa kāritavasena atthavivaraṇaṃ labbhati, saddanipphatti pana suddhavasenevāti saddavidū.

And the qualities of being revered, etc., being uncommon and preeminent, are found only in the Buddha and others. The detailed explanation should be taken from the commentary on the Ratanasutta. This meaning, however, is not stated by way of etymological analysis. If it is asked, 'Then by what is it stated?' It is by way of the meaning of being worthy of high esteem, etc., of an object conventionally known as a jewel in the world—so say the experts in grammar. And because it delights the virtuous, because it enables one to cross over from the ocean of saṃsāra, and because it leads to a good destination and Nibbāna, it is called 'ratana' (jewel) by way of a compound of similar meaning; enough with excessive elaboration. By applying the ekasesa method, or by an explanation in the plural, they are called ratanāni (jewels). A collection of three, or three brought together, or that which has three parts, is tayaṃ (a triad). It is the triad of the jewels only, not of others; hence, ratanattayaṃ (the Triple Gem). However, due to the non-existence of a collection separate from its components, the three jewels themselves are so called, not the mere collection. But with reference to the collection, the singular is used. It is venerated (vandīyate), which is veneration (vandanā). That veneration itself is vandanāmayaṃ (consisting of veneration), just as in 'consisting of giving, consisting of virtue'. And here, vandanā is the inclination towards the qualities of the Three Jewels with body, speech, and mind, or it is praise. Moreover, the associated states such as faith, wisdom, mindfulness, and energy, which are helpful to that volition by way of co-nascence, etc., are vandanā. 'Made by that' (tāya pakataṃ) is vandanāmayaṃ, just as in 'made of gold' (sovaṇṇamayaṃ), 'made of silver' (rūpiyamayaṃ). But in terms of meaning, it is just the aforesaid volition. In the Triple Gem, or of the Triple Gem, the act of veneration is ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ. Because it produces a state of existence and a result that are worthy of veneration, it is called puññaṃ (merit) by way of etymology. Or, because it purifies, cleanses, the doer himself or his mental continuity, it is called puññaṃ. The explanation of the meaning is obtained by way of the causative form of the root, but the derivation of the word is obtained by way of the simple agent alone—so say the experts in grammar.

Taṃtaṃsampattiyā vibandhanavasena sattasantānassa antare vemajjhe eti āgacchatīti antarāyo, diṭṭhadhammikādianattho. Paṇāmapayojane vuttavidhinā suṭṭhu vihato viddhasto antarāyo assāti suvihatantarāyo. Vihananañcettha taduppādakahetupariharaṇavasena tesaṃ antarāyānamanuppattikaraṇanti [V 1.0023] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Hutvāti pubbakālakiriyā, tassa “atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena sambandho. Tassāti yaṃ-saddena uddiṭṭhassa vandanāmayapuññassa. Ānubhāvenāti balena.

Because it comes or arrives in the middle of the continuity of beings by way of obstructing this or that accomplishment, it is called an obstacle (antarāyo); it is a disadvantage concerning the present life and so on. He for whom obstacles are well destroyed and vanquished is one with obstacles well destroyed (suvihatantarāyo). And here, 'destroying' (vihananaṃ) should be understood as the act of preventing the arising of those obstacles by way of removing their generative causes. Hutvā ('having been') is a verb of prior action; its connection is with 'I will explain the meaning'. Tassa ('of that') refers to the merit consisting of veneration which was indicated by the word yaṃ. Ānubhāvena ('by the power') means by strength.

“Tejo ussāhamantā ca, pabhū sattīti pañcime;

‘Ānubhāvo’ti vuccanti, ‘pabhāvo’ti ca te vade”ti. –

“Majesty, effort and counsel, mastery, and strength—these five are called 'power' (ānubhāva); and they may also be called 'influence' (pabhāva).”

Vuttesu hi atthesu idha sattiyaṃ vattati. Anu punappunaṃ taṃsamaṅgiṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti hi anubhāvo, soyeva ānubhāvoti udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ[M 1.0026], atthato pana yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa purimakammassa balānuppadānavasasaṅkhātā vandanāmayapuññassa sattiyeva, sā ca suvihatantarāyatāya karaṇaṃ, hetu vā sambhavati.

Indeed, among the meanings stated, here it occurs in the sense of strength. Indeed, because it repeatedly develops and increases one who is endowed with it, it is called anubhāva; that very thing is ānubhāva—so it is said in the Udāna commentary. But in terms of its intrinsic nature, it is indeed the strength of the merit produced by the volition of veneration, which is described as the power that gives support to previous kamma that is the cause for whatever prosperity has been obtained. And that becomes an instrument, or a cause, for the state of having obstacles well destroyed.

Ettha pana “pasannamatino”ti etena attano pasādasampattiṃ dasseti. “Ratanattayavandanāmaya”nti etena ratanattayassa khettabhāvasampattiṃ, tato ca tassa puññassa attano pasādasampattiyā, ratanattayassa ca khettabhāvasampattiyāti dvīhi aṅgehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāya upaghātakaupaddavānaṃ vihanane samatthataṃ dīpeti. Caturaṅgasampattiyā dānacetanā viya hi dvayaṅgasampattiyā paṇāmacetanāpi antarāyavihananena diṭṭhadhammikāti.

Here, by the phrase 'of one with a clear mind' (pasannamatino), he shows his own accomplishment in faith. By the phrase 'consisting of veneration for the Triple Gem' (ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ), he shows the Triple Gem's accomplishment of being a field of merit. And thereby, he reveals the capability of that merit—through two factors, namely his own accomplishment in faith and the Triple Gem's accomplishment of being a field of merit—to destroy the destructive dangers and adversities for the explanation of the meaning. For just as the volition of giving, through the accomplishment of four factors, can bear fruit in the present life, so too the volition of homage, through the accomplishment of two factors, by destroying obstacles, bears fruit in the present life.

Evaṃ ratanattayassa nipaccakārakaraṇe payojanaṃ dassetvā idāni yassā dhammadesanāya atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmo, tadapi saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammabhāvena dassetvā guṇābhitthavanavisesena abhitthavetuṃ “dīghassā”tiādimāha. Ayañhi ācariyassa pakati, yadidaṃ taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu ādito tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammassa visesaguṇakittanena thomanā. Tathā hi tesu tesu papañcasūdanīsāratthapakāsanīmanorathapūraṇīaṭṭhasālinīādīsu yathākkamaṃ “paravādamathanassa, ñāṇappabhedajananassa, dhammakathikapuṅgavānaṃ vicittapaṭibhānajananassa,

Thus, having shown the benefit in the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem, now, desiring to explain the meaning of that Dhamma discourse, and having shown that also as a teaching to be explained, in order to praise it with a special extolling of its qualities, the author spoke the words beginning with 'Of the Dīgha...' For this is the author's custom: namely, the praise at the beginning of his various commentaries by proclaiming the special qualities of the particular teaching to be explained. For so it is that in those respective works, such as the Papañcasūdanī, Sāratthappakāsinī, Manorathapūraṇī, Aṭṭhasālinī, and so forth, he says, in due order: 'for the crushing of others’ views, for the generation of varied sagacity in the foremost Dhamma speakers,

Tassa gambhīrañāṇehi, ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso;

Nānānayavicittassa, abhidhammassa ādito”ti. ādinā –

'...of that Abhidhamma, repeatedly penetrated by profound knowledges, and wonderful with its various methods, at the beginning,' and so on.

Thomanā katā. Tattha dīghassāti dīghanāmakassa. Dīghasuttaṅkitassāti dīghehi abhiāyatavacanappabandhavantehi suttehi lakkhitassa, anena “dīgho”ti ayaṃ imassa āgamassa [V 1.0024] atthānugatā samaññāti dasseti. Nanu ca suttāniyeva āgamo, kathaṃ so tehi aṅkīyatīti? Saccametaṃ paramatthato, paññattito pana suttāni upādāya āgamabhāvassa paññattattā avayavehi suttehi avayavībhūto āgamo aṅkīyati. Yatheva hi atthabyañjanasamudāye “sutta”nti vohāro, evaṃ suttasamudāye āgamavohāroti. Paṭiccasamuppādādinipuṇatthabhāvato nipuṇassa. Āgacchanti attatthaparatthādayo ettha, etena, etasmāti vā āgamo, uttamaṭṭhena, patthanīyaṭṭhena ca so varoti [M 1.0027] āgamavaro. Apica āgamasammatehi bāhirakapaveditehi bhāratapurāṇakathānarasīhapurāṇakathādīhi varotipi āgamavaro, tassa. Buddhānamanubuddhā buddhānubuddhā, buddhānaṃ saccapaṭivedhaṃ anugamma paṭividdhasaccā aggasāvakādayo ariyā, tehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena, guṇasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena ca saṃvaṇṇitoti tathā. Atha vā buddhā ca anubuddhā ca, tehi saṃvaṇṇito yathāvuttanayenāti tathā, tassa. Sammāsambuddheneva hi tiṇṇampi piṭakānaṃ atthasaṃvaṇṇanākkamo bhāsito, tato paraṃ saṅgāyanādivasena sāvakehīti ācariyā vadanti. Vuttañca majjhimāgamaṭṭhakathāya upālisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ “veyyākaraṇassāti vitthāretvā atthadīpakassa. Bhagavatā hi abyākataṃ tantipadaṃ nāma natthi, sabbesaṃyeva attho kathito”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.76). Saddhāvahaguṇassāti buddhādīsu pasādāvahaguṇassa. Nanu ca sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ tepiṭakaṃ saddhāvahaguṇameva, atha kasmā ayamaññasādhāraṇaguṇena thomitoti? Sātisayato imassa tagguṇasampannattā. Ayañhi āgamo brahmajālādīsu sīladiṭṭhādīnaṃ anavasesaniddesādivasena, mahāpadānādīsu (dī. ni. 2.3) purimabuddhānampi guṇaniddesādivasena, pāthikasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 3.1.4) titthiye madditvā appaṭivattiyasīhanādanadanādivasena, anuttariyasuttādīsu visesato buddhaguṇavibhāvanena ratanattaye sātisayaṃ saddhaṃ āvahatīti.

Praise has been made. Therein, ‘Dīghassa’ means ‘of the one named Dīgha.’ ‘Marked by long discourses’ (dīghasuttaṅkitassa) means marked by discourses that have very long series of words and sentences. By this, it shows that this name ‘Dīgha’ is a designation for this collection that follows its meaning. An objection is raised: Are not the discourses themselves the collection (āgamo)? How then is that collection marked by them? In terms of ultimate reality, this is true. However, in terms of convention, because the state of being a collection is designated based on the discourses, the collection, which is the whole possessing parts, is marked by the discourses, which are its parts. Just as the term ‘sutta’ is used for a collection of meaning and text, so the term ‘āgama’ is used for a collection of suttas. It is subtle because of having subtle meanings such as dependent origination. One's own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., come (āgacchanti) herein, or by this, or from this; therefore, it is an ‘āgama.’ And that is excellent (varo) because of its supreme meaning and its desirable meaning; therefore, it is the ‘excellent collection’ (āgamavaro). Moreover, it is also excellent in comparison to those proclaimed by outsiders and considered āgamas, such as the Bhārata-purāṇa-kathā, Narasiha-purāṇa-kathā, etc.; therefore, it is the ‘excellent collection.’ ‘Buddhānubuddhā’ are those enlightened following the Buddhas; they are the noble ones, such as the chief disciples, who have penetrated the truths by following the Buddhas' penetration of the truths. By them, it was explained by way of explaining the meaning and by way of explaining the qualities; therefore, it is so called. Alternatively, it was explained by the Buddhas and the Anubuddhas in the aforementioned manner; therefore, it is so called. Indeed, the sequence of the explanation of the meaning of all three Piṭakas was spoken by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One himself. After that, it was explained by the disciples by way of the Councils, etc.—so the teachers say. And it is stated in the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, in the explanation of the Upāli Sutta: ‘Of an exposition’ (veyyākaraṇassa) means ‘of that which illuminates the meaning by elaborating. Indeed, there is no textual passage that was not declared by the Blessed One; the meaning of all of them was taught.’ ‘Of that which has the quality of bringing forth faith’ means of that which has the quality of bringing forth confidence in the Buddha, etc. An objection is raised: Is not all the Buddha's word, the Tipiṭaka, possessed of the quality that brings forth faith? Why then is this one praised with a quality common to others? Because this collection is endowed with that quality to an exceptional degree. For this collection, by way of the exhaustive exposition of moralities, views, and so forth in discourses like the Brahmajāla Sutta; by way of the exposition of the qualities of even past Buddhas in discourses like the Mahāpadāna Sutta; by way of crushing the sectarians and roaring an irresistible lion's roar in discourses like the Pāthika Sutta; and by way of especially revealing the Buddha's qualities in discourses like the Anuttariya Sutta, brings forth exceptional faith in the Triple Gem.

Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammassa abhitthavanampi katvā idāni saṃvaṇṇanāya sampati vakkhamānāya āgamanavisuddhiṃ dassetuṃ “atthappakāsanattha”ntiādimāha. Imāya hi gāthāya saṅgītittayamāruḷhadīghāgamaṭṭhakathātova sīhaḷabhāsāmattaṃ vinā ayaṃ vakkhamānasaṃvaṇṇanā āgatā, nāññato, tadeva kāraṇaṃ katvā vattabbā, nāññanti attano saṃvaṇṇanāya āgamanavisuddhiṃ dasseti. Aparo nayo – paramanipuṇagambhīraṃ buddhavisayamāgamavaraṃ attano baleneva vaṇṇayissāmīti aññehi vattumpi asakkuṇeyyattā saṃvaṇṇanānissayaṃ dassetumāha “atthappakāsanattha”ntiādi. Imāya hi pubbācariyānubhāvaṃ nissāyeva tassa atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāmīti attano saṃvaṇṇanānissayaṃ dasseti. Tattha “atthappakāsanattha”nti pāṭhattho, sabhāvattho, ñeyyattho, pāṭhānurūpattho, tadanurūpattho, sāvasesattho, nivarasesattho, nītattho, neyyatthotiādinā [M 1.0028][V 1.0025] anekappakārassa atthassa pakāsanatthāya, pakāsanāya vā. Gāthābandhasampattiyā dvibhāvo. Attho kathīyati etāyāti atthakathā, sāyeva aṭṭhakathā ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā yathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.17; 2.8), ayañca sasaññogavidhi ariyājātibhāvato. Akkharacintakāpi hi “tathānaṃṭṭha yuga”nti lakkhaṇaṃ vatvā idamevudāharanti.

Having thus also made a eulogy of the Dhamma that is to be explained, the commentator now, in order to show the purity of the origin of the explanation that is about to be spoken, says, ‘for the purpose of clarifying the meaning,’ etc. For by this verse, this explanation that is about to be spoken has come only from the old commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya that was established in the three Councils, with the exception of the mere Sinhala language; it has not come from another source. It should be spoken for that very reason and not for another; thus, he shows the purity of the origin of his own explanation. Another method: Because others would be unable even to say, ‘I will explain the excellent collection, which is the domain of the Buddha and is supremely subtle and profound, by my own power alone,’ the commentator, in order to show the basis of the explanation, says, ‘for the purpose of clarifying the meaning,’ etc. For by this verse, he shows the basis of his own explanation, stating, ‘Relying only on the power of the ancient teachers, I will explain its meaning.’ Therein, ‘for the purpose of clarifying the meaning’ is for the purpose of clarifying, or for the clarification of, the meaning which is of many kinds, such as: the textual meaning, the intrinsic meaning, the meaning to be known, the meaning corresponding to the text, the meaning in accordance with that, the meaning with a remainder, the meaning without a remainder, the direct meaning, the meaning to be inferred, etc. The duplication is for the perfection of the verse composition. The meaning is explained by this, thus it is an `atthakathā`. That very `atthakathā` becomes `aṭṭhakathā` by making the letter `ṭṭha` from the letter `ttha`, just as in ‘suffering has the meaning of oppression.’ And this rule of conjunction is due to its being of the Āriyā meter. For even the grammarians, having stated the rule ‘tathānaṃ ṭṭha yugaṃ,’ cite this very word as an example.

Yāya’tthamabhivaṇṇenti, byañjanatthapadānugaṃ;

Nidānavatthusambandhaṃ, esā aṭṭhakathā matā.

That by which they explain the meaning—which follows the phrasing, meaning, and words, and is connected with the introductory story—is known by the wise as the commentary (aṭṭhakathā).

Āditotiādimhi paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ. Chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittavasībhāvena samannāgatattā, jhānādīsu pañcavasitā sabbhāvato ca vasino, therā mahākassapādayo, tesaṃ satehi pañcahi. Yā saṅgītāti yā aṭṭhakathā atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne “ayametassa attho, ayametassa attho”ti saṅgahetvā vuttā. Anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpīti na kevalaṃ paṭhamasaṅgītiyameva, atha kho pacchā dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsupi. Na ca pañcahi vasisatehi ādito saṅgītāyeva, api tu yasattherādīhi anusaṅgītā cāti saha samuccayena attho veditabbo. Samuccayadvayañhi paccekaṃ kiriyākālaṃ samuccinoti.

‘Ādito’ means: at the beginning, in the First Council. Because they were endowed with the six supernormal knowledges and the supreme mastery of mind, and because they were masters due to the existence of the five masteries in the jhānas, etc., they were the elders, such as Mahākassapa. By five hundred of them. ‘That which was recited’ (yā saṅgītā) means: the commentary which was spoken, having been compiled in suitable places in order to clarify the meaning, as ‘This is the meaning of this.’ ‘And subsequently recited also’ (anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi) means: it was not recited only in the First Council, but rather it was also subsequently recited in the Second and Third Councils. And it was not only recited from the beginning by the five hundred masters, but it was also subsequently recited by the elders such as Yasa, etc. Thus, the meaning should be understood together with the conjunction. For the twofold conjunction combines each action and time.

Atha porāṇaṭṭhakathāya vijjamānāya kimetāya adhunā puna katāya saṃvaṇṇanāyāti punaruttiyā, niratthakatāya ca dosaṃ samanussaritvā taṃ pariharanto “sīhaḷadīpa”ntiādimāha. Taṃ pariharaṇeneva hi imissā saṃvaṇṇanāya nimittaṃ dasseti. Tattha sīhaṃ lāti gaṇhātīti sīhaḷo la-kārassa ḷa-kāraṃ katvā yathā “garuḷo”ti. Tasmiṃ vaṃse ādipuriso sīhakumāro, tabbaṃsajātā pana tambapaṇṇidīpe khattiyā, sabbepi ca janā taddhitavasena, sadisavohārena vā sīhaḷā, tesaṃ nivāsadīpopi taddhitavasena, ṭhānīnāmena vā “sīhaḷo”ti veditabbo. Jalamajjhe dippati, dvidhā vā āpo ettha sandatīti dipo, soyeva dīpo, bhedāpekkhāya tesaṃ dīpoti tathā. Panasaddo arucisaṃsūcane, tena kāmañca sā saṅgītittayamāruḷhā, tathāpi puna evaṃbhūtāti aruciyabhāvaṃ saṃsūceti. Tadatthasambandhatāya pana purimagāthāya “kāmañca saṅgītā [M 1.0029] anusaṅgītā cā”ti sānuggahatthayojanā sambhavati. Aññatthāpi hi tathā dissatīti. Ābhatāti jambudīpato ānītā. Athāti saṅgītikālato pacchā, evaṃ sati ābhatapadena sambandho. Athāti vā mahāmahindattherenābhatakālato pacchā, evaṃ sati ṭhapitapadena sambandho. Sā hi dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi paṭhamaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni saṅgāyitvā tassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanānurūpeneva vācanāmaggaṃ [V 1.0026] āropitattā tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhāyeva, tato pacchā ca mahāmahindattherena tambapaṇṇidīpamābhatā, pacchā pana tambapaṇṇiyehi mahātherehi nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti. Ācariyadhammapālatthero pana pacchimasambandhameva duddasattā pakāseti. Tathā “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti idampi “ṭhapitā”ti ca “apanetvā āropento”ti ca etehi padehi sambajjhitabbaṃ. Ekapadampi hi āvuttiyādinayehi anekatthasambandhamupagacchati. Purimasambandhena cettha sīhaḷadīpavāsīnamatthāya nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkarapariharaṇena sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti tambapaṇṇiyattherehi ṭhapanapayojanaṃ dasseti. Pacchimasambandhena pana imāya saṃvaṇṇanāya jambudīpavāsīnaṃ, aññadīpavāsīnañca atthāya sīhaḷabhāsāpanayanassa, tantinayānucchavikabhāsāropanassa ca payojananti. Mahāissariyattā mahindoti rājakumārakāle nāmaṃ, pacchā pana guṇamahantatāya mahāmahindoti vuccati. Sīhaḷabhāsā nāma anekakkharehi ekatthassāpi voharaṇato paresaṃ voharituṃ atidukkarā kañcukasadisā sīhaḷānaṃ samudāciṇṇā bhāsā.

If the ancient commentary exists, what is the use of this commentary being made again now? Thus, wishing to avoid the fault of repetition and of being useless, he said the words beginning with “Sīhaḷadīpaṃ.” Indeed, by the very act of dispelling that fault, he shows the reason for this commentary. Therein, “he is able to seize a lion (sīhaṃ lāti)” is Sīhaḷa, having changed the letter ‘la’ to the letter ‘ḷa,’ just as in ‘garuḷa.’ In that lineage, the first man was Prince Sīha. Furthermore, the Khattiyas born in that lineage on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, and all the people, are called Sīhaḷas, either by way of a taddhita derivative or by similar designation. Their island of residence should also be known as “Sīhaḷa,” either by way of a taddhita derivative or by the name of the location. “It shines (dippati) in the middle of the water,” or “water (āpo) flows here in two ways (dvidhā),” therefore it is called ‘dipa.’ That very ‘dipa’ is ‘dīpa.’ With regard to the distinction, it is their island (dīpo); thus it is so called. The word ‘pana’ is used to indicate displeasure. By that, it indicates the state of displeasure thus: “Although it was indeed included in the three Councils, nevertheless, it has again become like this.” Due to the connection of that meaning, in the previous verse, “Though it was recited and re-recited,” a construction with a supportive meaning is possible. Indeed, it is seen so in other places as well. “Ābhatā” means brought from Jambudīpa. “Atha” means after the time of the Council; this being so, it connects with the word ‘ābhatā.’ Or, “atha” means after the time it was brought by the Elder Mahāmahinda; this being so, it connects with the word ‘ṭhapitā.’ Indeed, that commentary, because it was established in its mode of recitation by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma after first chanting the three Piṭakas in accordance with the explanation of their meaning, was certainly included in the three Councils. And after that, it was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahāmahinda. Later, however, it was established in the Sīhaḷa language by the great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding the admixture of the views of other schools. The teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, however, clarifies only the latter connection because it is difficult to see. Likewise, this phrase “for the benefit of the island-dwellers” should be connected with these words: “ṭhapitā” and “apanetvā āropento.” Indeed, even a single word, by methods such as repetition, attains connection with many meanings. With the former connection, it shows the purpose of the establishment by the Elders of Tambapaṇṇi: it was established in the Sīhaḷa language for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island of Sīhaḷa by avoiding the admixture of the views of other schools. With the latter connection, however, it shows the purpose of this commentary: for the benefit of the inhabitants of Jambudīpa and of other islands, the purpose of removing the Sīhaḷa language and of establishing a language suitable to the method of the canon. Due to his great sovereignty, ‘Mahinda’ was his name during the time he was a prince. Later, however, due to the greatness of his virtues, he is called ‘Mahāmahinda.’ The Sīhaḷa language is a language that, because it expresses even a single meaning with many letters, is extremely difficult for others to use, is like a tunic, and is the customary language of the Sīhaḷas.

Evaṃ hotu porāṇaṭṭhakathāya, adhunā kariyamānā pana aṭṭhakathā kathaṃ karīyatīti anuyoge sati imissā aṭṭhakathāya karaṇappakāraṃ dassetumāha “apanetvānā”tiādi. Tattha tato mūlaṭṭhakathāto sīhaḷabhāsaṃ apanetvā potthake anāropitabhāvena niraṅkaritvāti sambandho, etena ayaṃ vakkhamānā aṭṭhakathā saṅgītittayamāropitāya mūlaṭṭhakathāya sīhaḷabhāsāpanayanamattamaññatra atthato saṃsandati ceva sameti ca yathā “gaṅgodakena yamunodaka”nti dasseti. “Manorama” miccādīni “bhāsa”nti etassa sabhāvaniruttibhāvadīpakāni visesanāni. Sabhāvaniruttibhāvena hi paṇḍitānaṃ manaṃ ramayatīti manoramā. Tanoti atthametāya, tanīyati vā atthavasena vivarīyati, vaṭṭato vā satte tāreti[M 1.0030], nānātthavisayaṃ vā kaṅkhaṃ taranti etāyāti tanti, pāḷi. Tassā nayasaṅkhātāya gatiyā chaviṃ chāyaṃ anugatāti tantinayānucchavikā. Asabhāvaniruttibhāsantarasaṃkiṇṇadosavirahitatāya vigatadosā, tādisaṃ sabhāvaniruttibhūtaṃ –

Let it be so regarding the ancient commentary. But when there is the question, “How is the commentary that is now being made, being made?” in order to show the method of this commentary’s creation, the author says, “Having removed,” and so on. Therein, the connection is: “having removed the Sīhaḷa language from that original commentary, and having rejected it by not including it in the book.” By this, he shows that this commentary which is about to be spoken, apart from the mere removal of the Sīhaḷa language, corresponds and agrees in meaning with the original commentary that was included in the three Councils, just as the water of the Yamunā with the water of the Gaṅgā. “Manoramā” and so on are qualifying words that illuminate the state of being the natural language for this word “bhāsaṃ.” Indeed, because it delights the minds of the wise through its nature as the natural language, it is called ‘manoramā.’ “By this, the meaning is expanded (tanoti),” or “it is explained (tanīyati) by way of its meaning,” or “it saves (tāreti) beings from the round of existence,” or “by this, they cross over (taranti) doubt concerning various meanings”—therefore, it is ‘tanti,’ the Pāḷi. Because it follows the style and character of that Pāḷi’s course, which is called ‘naya,’ it is ‘tantinayānucchavikā’ (suitable to the method of the canon). Because it is free from the fault of being mixed with another language that is not the natural language, it is ‘vigatadosā’ (faultless). Such, being the natural language—

“Sā māgadhī mūlabhāsā, narā yāyā’dikappikā;

Brahmāno cassutālāpā, sambuddhā cāpi bhāsare”ti. –

“That Māgadhī is the root language, which men of the beginning of the aeon, and Brahmās who have not heard the speech of others, and also the Perfectly Enlightened Ones speak.”

Vuttaṃ pāḷigatibhāsaṃ potthake likhanavasena āropentoti attho, iminā saddadosābhāvamāha.

The meaning is: placing the language that follows the method of the Pāḷi, as spoken of, into the book by way of writing. By this, he states the absence of faults in wording.

Samayaṃ [V 1.0027] avilomentoti siddhantamavirodhento, iminā pana atthadosābhāvamāha. Aviruddhattā eva hi te theravādāpi idha pakāsayissanti. Kesaṃ pana samayanti āha “therāna”ntiādi, etena rāhulācariyādīnaṃ jetavanavāsīabhayagirivāsīnikāyānaṃ samayaṃ nivatteti. Thirehi sīlasutajhānavimuttisaṅkhātehi guṇehi samannāgatāti therā. Yathāha “cattārome bhikkhave therakaraṇā dhammā. Katame cattāro? Idha bhikkhave bhikkhu sīlavā hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.22). Apica saccadhammādīhi thirakaraṇehi samannāgatattā therā. Yathāha dhammarājā dhammapade –

“Not violating the doctrine” means not contradicting the established tenet. By this, however, he states the absence of faults in meaning. Indeed, precisely because they are not contradictory, the doctrines of those Elders will also be explained here. But whose doctrine? To answer this, he says “therānaṃ” (“of the Elders”), and so on. By this, he refutes the doctrine of the schools of the Jetavanavāsins and Abhayagirivāsins, such as the teacher Rāhula. Because they are endowed with the steadfast qualities called virtue, learning, jhāna, and liberation, they are ‘theras’ (Elders). As was said: “Monks, there are these four qualities that make one an Elder. What four? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous,” and so on. Moreover, because they are endowed with things that make one steadfast, such as truth and Dhamma, they are ‘theras.’ As the King of Dhamma said in the Dhammapada—

“Yamhi saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Sa ve vantamalo dhīro, ‘thero’iti pavuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 260);

“He in whom there is truth and Dhamma, harmlessness, restraint, and self-control; he, indeed, who has cast out defilements and is steadfast, is called an ‘Elder.’”

Tesaṃ. Mahākassapattherādīhi āgatā ācariyaparamparā theravaṃso, tappariyāpannā hutvā āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa samujjalanato taṃ pakārena dīpenti, tasmiṃ vā padīpasadisāti theravaṃsapadipā. Vividhena ākārena nicchīyatīti vinicchayo, gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khīlamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedanīkathā, suṭṭhu nipuṇo saṇho vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Atha vā vinicchinotīti vinicchayo, yathāvuttavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ, suṭṭhu nipuṇo cheko vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Mahāmeghavane ṭhito vihāro mahāvihāro, yo satthu mahābodhinā virocati, tasmiṃ vasanasīlā mahāvihāravāsino[M 1.0031], tādisānaṃ samayaṃ avilomentoti attho, etena mahākassapāditheraparamparāgato, tatoyeva aviparito saṇhasukhumo vinicchayoti mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ samayassa pamāṇabhūtataṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānavasena dasseti.

Of them. The succession of teachers, having come from the great elders beginning with Mahākassapa, is the Theravaṃsa. Being included in that lineage and endowed with scripture and realization, they illuminate that lineage in detail by the radiance of wisdom. Or, in that lineage, they are like lamps; therefore, they are the Theravaṃsapadīpā (Lamps of the Elders' Lineage). Because it is decided upon in various ways, it is a Vinicchaya (decision). It is a discourse that cuts through doubt, which proceeds in the manner of extracting a stake in knotted points. For them, there is a very skillful and subtle decision; therefore, they are the Sunipuṇavinicchayā (those of very skillful decision). Alternatively, because it decides, it is a Vinicchaya; it is the knowledge that has the aforementioned subject as its object. For them, there is a very skillful and adept deciding knowledge; therefore, they are the Sunipuṇavinicchayā. The monastery situated in the Mahāmeghavana (Great Cloud Forest) is the Mahāvihāra, which is splendid with the Teacher's great Bodhi tree. Those who are accustomed to dwelling there are the Mahāvihāravāsins (Dwellers of the Great Monastery). The meaning is: not contradicting the doctrine of such ones. By this, it shows, by way of personal authority, that the decision—which has come down through the succession of elders beginning with Mahākassapa and is therefore unerring, fine, and subtle—of the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins is the standard.

Hitvā punappunabhatamatthanti ekattha vutampi puna aññattha ābhatamatthaṃ punaruttibhāvato, ganthagarukabhāvato ca cajitvā tassa āgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmīti attho.

‘Having abandoned the meaning brought again and again’ means: having abandoned the meaning which, though stated in one place, is brought again to another place—both because of its repetitiveness and because of the heaviness of the text—I will explain the meaning of that excellent scripture. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ karaṇappakārampi dassetvā “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti vuttappayojanato aññampi saṃvaṇṇanāya payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “sujanassa cā”tiādimāha. Tattha sujanassa cāti ca-saddo samuccayattho, tena na kevalaṃ jambudīpavāsīnameva atthāya, atha kho sādhujanatosanatthañcāti samuccinoti. Teneva ca tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnampi atthāyāti ayamattho siddho hoti uggahaṇādisukaratāya tesampi bahūpakārattā. Ciraṭṭhitatthañcāti etthāpi ca-saddo na kevalaṃ tadubhayatthameva, api tu tividhassāpi sāsanadhammassa, pariyattidhammassa vā pañcavassasahassaparimāṇaṃ [V 1.0028] cirakālaṃ ṭhitatthañcāti samuccayatthameva dasseti. Pariyattidhammassa hi ṭhitiyā paṭipattidhammapaṭivedhadhammānampi ṭhiti hoti tasseva tesaṃ mūlabhāvato. Pariyattidhammo pana sunikkhittena padabyañjanena, tadatthena ca ciraṃ sammā patiṭṭhāti, saṃvaṇṇanāya ca padabyañjanaṃ aviparītaṃ sunikkhittaṃ, tadatthopi aviparīto sunikkhitto hoti, tasmā saṃvaṇṇanāya aviparītassa padabyañjanassa, tadatthassa ca sunikkhittassa upāyabhāvamupādāya vuttaṃ “ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Thus, having also shown the manner of composition, in order to show another purpose of the commentary, different from the stated purpose ‘for the benefit of the island-dwellers,’ the author said the words beginning with ‘sujanassa ca’ (and for a good person). Therein, in ‘sujanassa ca,’ the particle ‘ca’ has the meaning of conjunction. By that, it is not merely for the benefit of the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, but indeed it is also for the purpose of delighting good people; it thus conjoins this meaning. And precisely because of that, the meaning that it is also for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island of Tambapaṇṇi is established, because of the ease of learning, etc., and because it is of great benefit to them as well. Also in ‘ciraṭṭhitatthañca’ (and for long-lasting establishment), the particle ‘ca’ shows only the meaning of conjunction: it is not merely for those two benefits, but indeed it is also for the purpose of the long-lasting establishment—for a long period of time, for the measure of five thousand years—of the Dhamma of the Dispensation, which has three aspects, or of the Dhamma of the scriptures. Indeed, because of the stability of the Dhamma of the scriptures, there is also stability of the Dhamma of practice and the Dhamma of penetration, because the former is their root. Furthermore, the Dhamma of the scriptures, through well-placed phrases and sentences and their meaning, is correctly established for a long time. And through the commentary, the phrases and sentences are well-placed and unerring, and their meaning is also well-placed and unerring. Therefore, on account of the commentary being the means for the well-placed and unerring phrases and sentences and their well-placed meaning, it was said, ‘and for the long-lasting establishment of the Dhamma.’ Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:

“Dveme bhikkhave dhammā saddhammassa ṭhitiyā asammosāya anantaradhānāya saṃvattanti. Katame dve? Sunikkhittañca padabyañjanaṃ, attho ca sunīto, ime kho…pe… saṃvattantī”tiādi (a. ni. 2.21).

‘Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma. What two? Well-placed phrases and sentences, and a well-understood meaning. These, Bhikkhus, ... lead to it.’

Evaṃ payojanampi dassetvā vakkhamānāya saṃvaṇṇanāya mahattapariccāgena ganthagarukabhāvaṃ pariharitumāha “sīlakathā”tiādi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “na taṃ vicarayissāmī”ti. Aparo nayo – yadaṭṭhakathaṃ kattukāmo, tadekadesabhāvena visuddhimaggo gahetabboti kathikānaṃ upadesaṃ karonto [M 1.0032] tattha vicāritadhamme uddesavasena dassetumāha “sīlakathā”tiādi. Tattha sīlakathāti cārittavārittādivasena sīlavitthārakathā. Dhutadhammāti piṇḍapātikaṅgādayo terasa kilesadhunanakadhammā. Kammaṭṭhānānīti bhāvanāsaṅkhātassa yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānattā kammaṭṭhānanāmāni dhammajātāni. Tāni pana pāḷiyamāgatāni aṭṭhatiṃ seva na gahetabbāni, atha kho aṭṭhakathāyamāgatānipi dveti ñāpetuṃ “sabbānipī”ti vuttaṃ. Cari yāvidhānasahitoti rāgacaritādīnaṃ sabhāvādividhānena saha pavatto, idaṃ pana “jhānasamāpattivitthāro”ti imassa visesanaṃ. Ettha ca rūpāvacarajjhānāni jhānaṃ, arūpāvacarajjhānāni samāpatti. Tadubhayampi vā paṭiladdhamattaṃ jhānaṃ, samāpajjanavasībhāvappattaṃ samāpatti. Apica tadapi ubhayaṃ jhānameva, phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyo pana samāpatti, tāsaṃ vitthāroti attho.

Thus, having also shown the purpose, in order to avoid the heaviness of the text by abandoning the great extent of the commentary that is about to be spoken, the author said the words beginning with ‘sīlakathā’ (discourse on virtue). For so it was said: ‘I will not elaborate on that.’ Another way: when one wishes to compose a certain commentary, the Visuddhimagga should be taken as a part of it. Thus, giving instruction to speakers, in order to show the dhammas investigated therein by way of a summary, he said the words beginning with ‘sīlakathā.’ Therein, ‘sīlakathā’ is the detailed discourse on virtue by way of virtue as conduct, virtue as restraint, etc. ‘Dhutadhammā’ (ascetic practices) are the thirteen practices that shake off defilements, beginning with the alms-food-eater's practice. ‘Kammaṭṭhānāni’ (meditation subjects) are the collections of dhammas so named because they are the place of occurrence for the yogic work called ‘bhāvanā’ (mental development). Furthermore, not only the thirty-eight that have come in the Pāḷi are to be taken, but indeed also the two that have come in the commentary. In order to make this known, ‘sabbānipi’ (all of them) was said. ‘Cariyāvidhānasahito’ (together with the arrangement of temperaments) means that which proceeds together with the arrangement of the nature, etc., of those with a lustful temperament, etc. This word, however, is a qualifier of ‘jhānasamāpattivitthāro’ (the detailed explanation of jhāna and samāpatti). And herein, the fine-material absorptions are ‘jhāna’; the immaterial absorptions are ‘samāpatti.’ Alternatively, both of them, when merely attained, are ‘jhāna’; when mastery in entering has been reached, they are ‘samāpatti.’ Moreover, both of those are just ‘jhāna,’ but the fruition attainment and the cessation attainment are ‘samāpatti.’ The detailed explanation of these is the meaning.

Lokiyalokuttarabhedānaṃ channampi abhiññānaṃ gahaṇatthaṃ “sabbā ca abhiññāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 751) āgatanayena ekavidhādinā bhedena paññāya saṅkalayitvā sampiṇḍetvā, gaṇetvā vā vinicchayanaṃ paññāsaṅkalanavinicchayo. Ariyānīti buddhādīhi ariyehi paṭivijjhitabbattā, ariyabhāvasādhakattā vā ariyāni uttarapadalopena. Avitathabhāvena vā araṇīyattā, avagantabbattā ariyāni, “saccānī”timassa visesanaṃ.

For the purpose of including all six supernormal knowledges, which are divided into mundane and supramundane, it was said, ‘sabbā ca abhiññāyo’ (and all the supernormal knowledges). Paññāsaṅkalanavinicchayo (the decision by collecting and enumerating wisdom) is the decision made by collecting, combining, or enumerating wisdom according to the method of division into one kind, etc., that has come in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts. As for ‘ariyāni’ (noble): because they are to be penetrated by the noble ones beginning with the Buddha, or because they accomplish the state of being noble, they are called ‘ariyāni’ with the elision of the final word. Alternatively, because they are to be approached or understood on account of their unfailing nature, they are ‘ariyāni.’ It is a qualifier of this word ‘saccāni’ (truths).

Hetādipaccayadhammānaṃ [V 1.0029] hetupaccayādibhāvena paccayuppannadhammānamupakārakatā paccayākāro, tassa desanā tathā, paṭiccasamuppādakathāti attho. Sā pana nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkararahitatāya suṭṭhu parisuddhā, ghanavinibbhogassa ca sudukkaratāya nipuṇā, ekattādinayasahitā ca tattha vicāritāti āha “suparisuddhanipuṇanayā”ti. Padattayampi hetaṃ paccayākāradesanāya visesanaṃ. Paṭisambhidādīsu āgatanayaṃ avissajjitvāva vicāritattā avimutto tantimaggo yassāti avimuttatanti maggā. Maggoti cettha pāḷisaṅkhāto upāyo taṃtadatthānaṃ avabodhassa, saccapaṭivedhassa vā upāyabhāvato. Pabandho vā dīghabhāvena pakatimaggasadisattā, idaṃ pana “vipassanā, bhāvanā”ti padadvayassa visesanaṃ.

The mode of conditionality (paccayākāro) is the state of being supportive of conditioning phenomena, such as hetu, to conditioned phenomena by way of being the hetu-condition and so on. The teaching of that is thus; this is the meaning of 'the discourse on dependent origination'. Moreover, that teaching is well-purified because it is free from admixture with the views of other schools, and it is subtle because of the great difficulty in analyzing a dense mass. And because it was investigated there, in the Visuddhimagga, accompanied by the method of unity and so on, the commentator said it is 'of well-purified, subtle method'. Indeed, this triad of words is a qualifier of the teaching on the mode of conditionality. Because it is investigated without abandoning the method that has come down in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and so on, it is called avimuttatantimaggā, meaning 'that for which the textual lineage is not abandoned'. And here, 'magga' is the means designated as Pāḷi, because it is the means for understanding those various meanings or for penetrating the truths. Or, it is a continuous discourse (pabandho), called magga because of its similarity to an ordinary path due to its length. This word, however, is a qualifier for the pair of words 'insight, development'.

Iti [M 1.0033] pana sabbanti ettha iti-saddo parisamāpane yathāuddiṭṭhauddesassa pariniṭṭhitattā, ettakaṃ sabbanti attho. Panāti vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ visuṃ atthābhāvato. Padatthasaṃkiṇṇassa, vattabbassa ca avuttassa avasesassa abhāvato suviññeyyabhāvena suparisuddhaṃ, “sabba”nti iminā sambandho, bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ vā etaṃ “vutta”nti iminā sambajjhanato. Bhiyyoti atirekaṃ, ativitthāranti attho, etena padatthamattameva vicārayissāmīti dasseti. Etaṃ sabbaṃ idha aṭṭhakathāya na vicārayissāmi punaruttibhāvato, ganthagarukabhāvato cāti adhippāyo. Vicarayissāmīti ca gāthābhāvato na vuddhibhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, in 'iti pana sabbaṃ', the particle 'iti' occurs in the sense of conclusion, because the stated theme is completely finished; the meaning is: 'all this is just this much'. The word 'pana' is merely an embellishment of speech, as it has no separate meaning. Because of the absence of any confusion of word-meanings, of anything yet to be said, of anything left unsaid, or of any remainder, it is thoroughly pure by being easy to understand; it is connected with this word 'sabbaṃ'. Or, because this word 'suparisuddhaṃ' is connected with 'vuttaṃ', it is a neuter of abstract state (bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ). 'Bhiyyo' means 'exceedingly' or 'very extensively'; by this word, he shows the meaning: 'I will investigate only the mere meaning of the words'. The intention is: 'I will not investigate all this here in the commentary because of it being a repetition and because of textual heaviness'. And in 'vicārayissāmi', it should be understood that there is no vṛddhi strengthening of the vowel because it is in a verse.

Evampi esa visuddhimaggo āgamānamatthaṃ na pakāseyya, atha sabbopeso idha vicāritabboyevāti codanāya tathā avicāraṇassa ekantakāraṇaṃ niddhāretvā taṃ pariharanto “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādimāha. Tattha majjheti khuddakato aññesaṃ catunnampi āgamānaṃ abbhantare. Hi-saddo kāraṇe, tena yathāvuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ joteti. Tatthāti tesu catūsu āgamesu. Yathābhāsitanti bhagavatā yaṃ yaṃ desitaṃ, desitānurūpaṃ vā. Api ca saṃvaṇṇakehi saṃvaṇṇanāvasena yaṃ yaṃ bhāsitaṃ, bhāsitānurūpantipi attho. Iccevāti ettha iti-saddena yathāvuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ nidasseti, imināva kāraṇena, idameva vā kāraṇaṃ manasi sannidhāyāti attho. Katoti etthāpi “visuddhimaggo esā”ti padaṃ kammabhāvena sambajjhati āvuttiyādinayenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tampīti taṃ visuddhimaggampi ñāṇena gahetvāna. Etāyāti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā nāma etāya aṭṭhakathāya. Ettha ca “majjhe ṭhatvā”ti etena majjhattabhāvadīpanena visesato catunnampi āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā visuddhimaggo, na sumaṅgalavilāsinīādayo viya asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathāti dasseti. Avisesato pana vinayābhidhammānampi yathārahaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā hotiyeva, tehi sammissatāya ca tadavasesassa khuddakāgamassa [V 1.0030] visesato sādhāraṇā samānāpi taṃ ṭhapetvā catunnameva āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇātveva vuttāti.
