In order to refute the objection—'Even so, this Visuddhimagga would not reveal the meaning of the Āgamas; then all of it must certainly be investigated here'—by determining the definite reason for not investigating it all, he said, 'majjhe visuddhimaggo' and so on. Therein, 'majjhe' means within the four Āgamas other than the Khuddaka Nikāya. The particle 'hi' is in the sense of reason; by it, he illuminates the aforesaid reason. 'Tattha' means in those four Āgamas. 'Yathābhāsitaṃ' means whatever was taught by the Blessed One, or in accordance with what was taught. Moreover, the meaning can also be: whatever was stated by the commentators by way of commentary, or in accordance with what was stated. Here in 'icceva', by the word 'iti' he indicates the aforesaid reason; the meaning is 'by this very reason', or 'having placed this very reason in the mind'. Here too in 'kato', it should be understood that the phrase 'visuddhimaggo eso' is connected in the accusative sense by the method of repetition and so on. 'Tampi' means having grasped that Visuddhimagga too with knowledge. 'Etāya' means by this commentary called the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. And here, by the phrase 'majjhe ṭhatvā', through this indication of its central nature, he shows that the Visuddhimagga is, in particular, a common commentary for all four Āgamas, and not an uncommon commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. However, in a general sense, it is indeed a common commentary for the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as well, as is appropriate. And although, due to its being mixed with them, it is especially common to the remaining Khuddaka Āgama, having set that aside, it is said to be common only to the four Āgamas.

Iti soḷasagāthāvaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the sixteen verses.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the beginning of the book is concluded.

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Origin

Evaṃ [V 1.0031][M 1.0034] yathāvuttena vividhena nayena paṇāmādikaṃ pakaraṇārambhavidhānaṃ katvā idāni vibhāgavantānaṃ sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanavaseneva suvibhāvitaṃ, suviññāpitañca hotīti paṭhamaṃ tāva vaggasuttavasena vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha dīghāgamo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti “dīghassa āgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti yadidaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ vacane. “Yassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti paṭiññātaṃ, so dīghāgamo nāma vaggasuttavasena evaṃ veditabbo, evaṃ vibhāgoti vā attho. Atha vā tatthāti “dīghāgamanissita”nti yaṃ vuttaṃ, etasmiṃ vacane. Yo dīghāgamo vutto, so dīghāgamo nāma vaggasuttavasena. Evaṃ vibhajitabbo, edisoti vā attho. “Dīghassā”tiādinā hi vuttaṃ dūravacanaṃ taṃ-saddena paṭiniddisati viya “dīghāgamanissita”nti vuttaṃ āsannavacanampi taṃ-saddena paṭiniddisati attano buddhiyaṃ parammukhaṃ viya parivattamānaṃ hutvā pavattanato. Edisesu hi ṭhānesu attano buddhiyaṃ sammukhaṃ vā parammukhaṃ vā parivattamānaṃ yathā tathā vā paṭiniddisituṃ vaṭṭati saddamattapaṭiniddesena atthassāvirodhanato. Vaggasuttādīnaṃ nibbacanaṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Tayo vaggā yassāti tivaggo. Catuttiṃsa suttāni ettha saṅgayhanti, tesaṃ vā saṅgaho gaṇanā etthāti catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho.

Having thus, by the various aforesaid methods, performed the procedure for commencing the treatise, such as paying homage, now, because the explanation of the nature of things that have divisions is well explained and well made known only by way of showing the division, therefore, in order to first show the division by way of vaggas and suttas, he said the words beginning with 'tattha dīghāgamo nāma'. Therein, 'tattha' refers to the statement that was made: 'I will explain the meaning of the excellent Dīgha Āgama'. In that statement, the meaning is: that Dīgha Āgama, about which it was pledged, 'whose meaning I will explain', is to be known thus by way of vaggas and suttas; or, such is the division. Alternatively, 'tattha' refers to the statement that was made: 'relying on the Dīgha Āgama'. In that statement, the meaning is: that Dīgha Āgama which was mentioned is to be divided thus by way of vaggas and suttas; or, such is the division. For, by the word 'taṃ', he refers back to the distant statement made with 'dīghassa' and so on, just as by the word 'taṃ' he also refers back to the nearby statement made as 'dīghāgamanissitaṃ', because it proceeds as if turning out of sight in one's own intellect. For in such places, it is proper to refer back in whatever way to something that is turning in one's own intellect, whether it is present or out of sight, because there is no contradiction to the meaning by a mere verbal reference. The derivation of 'vagga', 'sutta', and so on will become clear later. It is 'tivaggo' because it has three vaggas. Thirty-four suttas are compiled in it, or the compilation, the counting of them, is in it; therefore, it is 'catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho'.

Attano saṃvaṇṇanāya paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkameneva pavattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tassa…pe… nidānamādī”ti vuttaṃ. Ādibhāvo hettha saṅgītikkameneva veditabbo. Kasmā pana catūsu āgamesu dīghāgamo paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto, tattha ca sīlakkhandhavaggo paṭhamaṃ nikkhitto, tasmiñca brahmajālasuttaṃ, tatthāpi nidānanti? Nāyamanuyogo katthacipi na pavattati sabbattheva vacanakkamamattaṃ paṭicca anuyuñjitabbato. Apica saddhāvahaguṇattā dīghāgamova paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto. Saddhā hi kusaladhammānaṃ bījaṃ. Yathāha “saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.197; su. ni. 77). Saddhāvahaguṇatā cassa heṭṭhā dassitāyeva. Kiñca bhiyyo – katipayasuttasaṅgahatāya [V 1.0032] ceva appaparimāṇatāya ca uggahaṇadhāraṇādisukhato paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto. Tathā hesa catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho, catusaṭṭhibhāṇavāraparimāṇo ca. Sīlakathābāhullato pana sīlakkhandhavaggo paṭhamaṃ nikkhitto. Sīlañhi sāsanassa ādi sīlapatiṭṭhānattā sabbaguṇānaṃ[M 1.0035]. Tenevāha “tasmā tiha tvaṃ bhikkhu ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.469). Sīlakkhandhakathābāhullato hi so “sīlakkhandhavaggo”ti vutto. Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathābhāvato pana suttantapiṭakassa niravasesadiṭṭhivibhajanaṃ brahmajālasuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhittanti veditabbaṃ. Tepiṭake hi buddhavacane brahmajālasadisaṃ diṭṭhigatāni niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā vibhattasuttaṃ natthi. Nidānaṃ pana paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ mahākassapattherena puṭṭhena āyasmatā ānandena desakālādinidassanatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhittanti. Tenāha “brahmajālassāpī”tiādi. Tattha ca “āyasmatā”tiādinā desakaṃ niyameti, paṭhamasaṅgītikāleti pana kālanti, ayamattho upari āvi bhavissati.

To show that its own commentary proceeds in the very same sequence as that which was laid down in the First Council, it was said by the commentator: “Of that… (etc.)… the introduction is the beginning.” Here, the state of being the beginning should be understood only by the sequence of the council. But why, among the four Āgamas, was the Dīgha Āgama recited first, and within it, the Sīlakkhandhavagga placed first, and within that, the Brahmajāla Sutta, and within that, the introduction? This inquiry is not one that does not occur anywhere, for it is to be pursued everywhere based on the mere sequence of the words. Moreover, the Dīgha Āgama itself was recited first because of its quality of inspiring faith. For faith is the seed of wholesome states. As it is said: “Faith is the seed, austerity the rain.” And its quality of inspiring faith has already been shown below. Furthermore, it was recited first because it is a collection of a few suttas, is of small extent, and is thus easy to learn, memorize, and so on. Thus, it is a collection of thirty-four suttas and is sixty-four recitation sections in extent. However, due to the abundance of discourses on morality, the Sīlakkhandhavagga was placed first. For morality is the beginning of the Dispensation, being the foundation for all good qualities. Therefore, He said: “Therefore, monk, here you should first purify the very beginning in wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Morality, well purified,” and so on. Indeed, because of the abundance of discourses on the section on morality, it is called the “Sīlakkhandhavagga.” However, it should be understood that the Brahmajāla Sutta, which is the analysis of views without remainder in the Suttanta Piṭaka, was placed first because it is a discourse on the disentangling of views. Indeed, in the Tipiṭaka, the Word of the Buddha, there is no other sutta like the Brahmajāla Sutta that analyzes the types of views, having made them free of thickets and free of tangles. The introduction, however, was placed first in the First Council by the Venerable Ānanda, when asked by the Elder Mahākassapa, in order to indicate the speaker, time, and so on. Therefore, he said: “Of the Brahmajāla Sutta too,” and so on. Therein, by “by the Venerable,” and so on, he specifies the speaker, and by “at the time of the First Council,” the time. This meaning will become clear later on.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the First Great Council

Idāni “paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle”ti vacanappasaṅgena taṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiṃ dassento, yassaṃ vā paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkamena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmattā taṃ vibhāvento tassā tantiyā āruḷhāyapi idha vacane kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma cesā”tiādimāha. Ettha hi kiñcāpi…pe… māruḷhāti etena nanu sā saṅgītikkhandhake tantimāruḷhā, kasmā idha puna vuttā, yadi ca vuttā assa niratthakatā, ganthagarutā ca siyāti codanālesaṃ dasseti. “Nidāna…pe… veditabbā”ti pana etena nidānakosallatthabhāvato yathāvuttadosatā na siyāti visesakāraṇadassanena pariharati. “Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma cesā”ti ettha ca-saddo īdisesu ṭhānesu vattabbasampiṇḍanattho. Tena hi paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānañca ādi, esā ca paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma evaṃ veditabbāti imamatthaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Upaññāsattho vā ca-saddo, upaññāsoti ca vākyārambho vuccati. Esā hi ganthakārānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ kiñci vatvā puna aparaṃ vattumārabhantānaṃ ca-saddapayogo. Yaṃ pana vajirabuddhittherena vuttaṃ “ettha ca-saddo atirekattho, tena aññāpi atthīti dīpetī”ti (vajira ṭī. bāhiranidānakathāvaṇṇanā), tadayuttameva. Na hettha ca-saddena tadattho viññāyati. Yadi cettha tadatthadassanatthameva ca-kāro adhippeto siyā, evaṃ sati so na kattabboyeva paṭhamasaddeneva aññāsaṃ dutiyādisaṅgītīnampi [M 1.0036] atthibhāvassa dassitattā. Dutiyādimupādāya hi paṭhamasaddapayogo [V 1.0033] dīghādimupādāya rassādisaddapayogo viya. Yathāpaccayaṃ tattha tattha desitattā, paññattattā ca vippakiṇṇānaṃ dhammavinayānaṃ saṅgahetvā gāyanaṃ kathanaṃ saṅgīti, etena taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ, taṃtaṃsuttānañca ādipariyosānesu, antarantarā ca sambandhavasena ṭhapitaṃ saṅgītikārakavacanaṃ saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Mahāvisayattā, pūjitattā ca mahatī saṅgīti mahāsaṅgīti, paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti. Kiñcāpīti anuggahattho, tena pāḷiyampi sā saṅgītimāruḷhāvāti anuggahaṃ karoti, evampi tatthāruḷhamattena idha sotūnaṃ nidānakosallaṃ na hotīti pana-saddena aruciyatthaṃ dasseti. Nidadāti desanaṃ desakālādivasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ, tasmiṃ kosallaṃ, tadatthāyāti attho.

Now, in connection with the phrase “at the time of the First Great Council,” showing that First Great Council; or, because of the desire to compose the commentary according to the sequence laid down in that First Great Council, and thus clarifying it, in order to show the reason for its mention here in this commentary even though it is already included in the canon, he said: “This is called the First Great Council,” and so on. Here, by the phrase “Although… (etc.)… has ascended,” he shows a hint of an objection: “Has not that council already ascended into the canon in the Saṅgītikkhandhaka? Why is it mentioned again here? And if it is mentioned, this would be pointless and make the book cumbersome.” However, by the phrase “The introduction… (etc.)… should be understood,” he refutes this by showing a special reason, namely: because its purpose is skill in the introduction, the aforementioned fault would not arise. In the phrase “This is called the First Great Council,” the particle “ca” has the meaning of summarizing what is to be said in such places. By it, he summarizes this meaning: “The introduction spoken at the time of the First Great Council is the beginning, and this is called the First Great Council; thus it should be understood.” Alternatively, the particle “ca” has the meaning of introduction (upaññāsa); and upaññāsa is said to be the beginning of a sentence. For this is the nature of authors: when, having said something, they begin to say something else, there is the use of the particle “ca”. However, what was said by the Elder Vajirabuddhi, “Here the particle ‘ca’ has an additional meaning, thereby indicating that others also exist,” is indeed inappropriate. For that meaning is not understood here by the particle “ca”. And if the particle “ca” were intended here only to show that meaning, in that case it should not have been used at all, since the existence of other councils, the second and so on, is already shown by the word “first” itself. For the use of the word “first” is made in relation to a second, etc., just as the use of the word “short”, etc., is made in relation to “long”, etc. Saṅgīti (council) is the chanting or recitation, having collected the scattered Dhamma and Vinaya that were taught and laid down here and there according to conditions. By this term, the words of the council-makers, placed at the beginning and end of each training rule and each sutta, and also in between, by way of connection, are included. Because of its vast scope and because it is honored, a great council is a mahāsaṅgīti (Great Council). The first great council is the paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti (First Great Council). The word kiñcāpi (although) has the meaning of concession. By this, he makes the concession that “that Council has indeed ascended into the Pāḷi.” Even so, by the word pana (however), he shows a sense of disinclination, stating that “merely by its having ascended there, skill in the introduction does not arise for the listeners here.” It is called nidāna (introduction) because it lays down (nidadāti), that is, it points out the teaching in terms of speaker, time, etc., making the unknown known. Skill in that is for the sake of that; this is the meaning.

Idāni taṃ vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “dhammacakkapavattanañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sattānaṃ dassanānuttariyasaraṇādipaṭilābhahetubhūtāsu vijjamānāsupi aññāsu bhagavato kiriyāsu “buddho bodheyya”nti (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. abbhantaranidāna 1; cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathā; udāna aṭṭha. 18) paṭiññāya anulomanato vineyyānaṃ maggaphaluppattihetubhūtā kiriyāva nippariyāyena buddhakiccaṃ nāmāti taṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “dhammacakkappavattanañhi…pe… vinayanā”ti vuttaṃ. Dhammacakkappavattanato pana pubbabhāge bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ suṇantānampi vāsanābhāgiyameva jātaṃ, na sekkhabhāgiyaṃ, na nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ tapussabhallikānaṃ saraṇadānaṃ viya. Esā hi dhammatā, tasmā tameva mariyādabhāvena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Saddhindriyādi dhammoyeva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Atha vā cakkanti āṇā, dhammato anapetattā dhammañca taṃ cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Dhammena ñāyena cakkantipi dhammacakkaṃ. Vuttañhi paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

Now, to show that introduction in detail, the phrase beginning with 'For the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma...' was stated. Therein, although there were other actions of the Blessed One that were the cause for beings to attain the unsurpassed vision, refuge, and so on, in accordance with the pledge, 'A Buddha should awaken others,' only that action which is the cause for the arising of the path and its fruit for those to be trained is, unequivocally, called the Buddha's duty. Therefore, to show that in its essential nature, the phrase 'For the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma... up to... the training' was stated. However, what was spoken by the Blessed One in the period before the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma became, even for those who heard it, only conducive to wholesome dispositions, not conducive to the learner's training, nor conducive to disenchantment, like the giving of refuge to Tapussa and Bhallika. For this is the nature of things; therefore, it should be known that this very thing was spoken of as the limit. The Dhamma itself, such as the faculty of faith and so on, is a wheel in the sense of causing to turn; thus, it is the Wheel of Dhamma. Alternatively, 'wheel' means 'command'; and because it is not separate from the Dhamma, it is both Dhamma and that wheel—hence, the Wheel of Dhamma. It is also the Wheel of Dhamma because it is a wheel turned by the Dhamma, by right method. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Dhammañca pavatteti cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Cakkañca pavatteti dhammañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena pavattetīti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammacariyāya pavattetīti dhammacakka”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 2.40, 41).

'It sets the Dhamma in motion and the wheel, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma. It sets the wheel in motion and the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma. It sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma. It sets it in motion by means of Dhamma-conduct,' and so on.

Tassa pavattanaṃ tathā. Pavattananti ca pavattayamānaṃ, pavattitanti paccuppannātītavasena dvidhā attho. Yaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ “dhammacakkapavattanasuttantaṃ [M 1.0037] desento dhammacakkaṃ pavatteti nāma, aññāsikoṇḍaññattherassa maggaphalādhigatato paṭṭhāya pavattitaṃ nāmā”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.1081-1088; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.40). Idha pana paccuppannavaseneva attho yutto. Yāvāti paricchedatthe nipāto, subhaddassa nāma paribbājakassa vinayanaṃ [V 1.0034] antoparicchedaṃ katvāti abhividhivasena attho veditabbo. Tañhi bhagavā parinibbānamañce nipannoyeva vinesīti. Kataṃ pariniṭṭhāpitaṃ buddhakiccaṃ yenāti tathā, tasmiṃ. Katabuddhakicce bhagavati lokanāthe parinibbuteti sambandho, etena buddhakattabbassa kiccassa kassacipi asesitabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tatoyeva hi bhagavā parinibbutoti. Nanu ca sāvakehi vinītāpi vineyyā bhagavatāyeva vinītā nāma. Tathā hi sāvakabhāsitaṃ suttaṃ “buddhabhāsita”nti vuccati. Sāvakavineyyā ca na tāva vinītā, tasmā “katabuddhakicce”ti na vattabbanti? Nāyaṃ doso tesaṃ vinayanupāyassa sāvakesu ṭhapitattā. Tenevāha –

The turning of that Dhamma is thus called the Wheel of Dhamma. And 'turning' (pavattanaṃ) has a twofold meaning by way of the present and the past: 'setting in motion' (pavattayamānaṃ) and 'having been set in motion' (pavattitaṃ). With reference to this, it is said in the commentaries: 'While teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he is said to be setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; from the attainment of the path and fruit by the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña onwards, it is said to have been set in motion.' Here, however, the meaning is appropriate only by way of the present. The word 'yāva' is a particle in the sense of limitation. The meaning should be understood by way of an inclusive limit (abhividhi), as in 'having made the training of the wanderer named Subhadda the inner limit.' For the Blessed One trained him while lying on his Parinibbāna-couch. He is so-called because the Buddha's duty was done and completed by him. The connection is: 'when the Blessed One, the Protector of the World, who had completed the Buddha's duty, attained Parinibbāna.' By this, it shows the state of there being no remainder whatsoever of the duty to be done by a Buddha. For it is precisely for that reason that the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. Is it not so that even those to be trained who were trained by disciples are said to be trained by the Blessed One himself? For indeed, a sutta spoken by a disciple is called 'spoken by the Buddha.' And those to be trained by disciples have not yet been trained; therefore, 'having completed the Buddha's duty' should not be said. This is not a fault, because the method for their training was established among the disciples. For that reason, he said:

“Na tāvāhaṃ pāpima parinibbāyissāmi, yāva me bhikkhū na sāvakā bhavissanti viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā…pe… uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ saha dhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessantī”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.168; udā. 51).

'Evil One, I will not yet attain Parinibbāna so long as my bhikkhu disciples will not be accomplished, trained, confident, of great learning, bearers of the Dhamma... so long as they will not, having thoroughly refuted an opposing doctrine that has arisen in accordance with the Dhamma, teach the Dhamma that leads to deliverance,' and so on.

“Kusinārāya”ntiādinā bhagavato parinibbutadesakālavisesavacanaṃ “aparinibbuto bhagavā”ti gāhassa micchābhāvadassanatthaṃ, loke jātasaṃvaddhādibhāvadassanatthañca. Tathā hi manussabhāvassa supākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ mahābodhisattā carimabhave dārapariggahādīnipi karontīti. Kusinārāyanti evaṃ nāmake nagare. Tañhi nagaraṃ kusahatthaṃ purisaṃ dassanaṭṭhāne māpitattā “kusināra”nti vuccati, samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Upavattane mallānaṃ sālavaneti tassa nagarassa upavattanabhūte mallarājūnaṃ sālavane. Tañhi sālavanaṃ nagaraṃ pavisitukāmā uyyānato upacca vattanti gacchanti etenāti upavattanaṃ. Yathā hi anurādhapurassa dakkhiṇapacchimadisāyaṃ thūpārāmo, evaṃ taṃ uyyānaṃ kusinārāya dakkhiṇapacchimadisāyaṃ hoti. Yathā ca thūpārāmato dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisanamaggo pācīnamukho gantvā uttarena nivattati, evaṃ uyyānato sālapanti pācīnamukhā gantvā uttarena nivattā, tasmā taṃ “upavattana”nti vuccati. Apare pana [M 1.0038] “taṃ sālavanamupagantvā mittasuhajje apaloketvā nivattanato upavattananti pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ kirā”ti vadanti. Yamakasālānamantareti yamakasālānaṃ vemajjhe. Tattha kira bhagavato paññattassa parinibbānamañcassa sīsabhāge ekā sālapanti hoti, pādabhāge ekā. Tatrāpi eko taruṇasālo sīsabhāgassa āsanno hoti, eko pādabhāgassa. Tasmā “yamakasālānamantare”ti vuttaṃ. Apica “yamakasālā nāma mūlakkhandhaviṭapapattehi aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbetvā ṭhitasālā”tipi mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mā iti cando vuccati tassa gatiyā divasassa [V 1.0035] minitabbato, tadā sabbakalāpāripūriyā puṇṇo eva māti puṇṇamā. Saddavidū pana “mo sivo candimā cevā”ti vuttaṃ sakkatabhāsānayaṃ gahetvā okārantampi candimavācaka ma-saddamicchanti. Visākhāya yutto puṇṇamā yatthāti visākhāpuṇṇamo, soyeva divaso tathā, tasmiṃ. Paccūsati timiraṃ vināsetīti paccūso, pati-pubbo usa-saddo rujāyanti hi neruttikā, soyeva samayoti rattiyā pacchimayāmapariyāpanno kālaviseso vuccati, tasmiṃ. Visākhāpuṇṇamadivase īdise rattiyā pacchimasamayeti vuttaṃ hoti.

The statement specifying the place and time of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, beginning with the words 'At Kusinārā,' is for the purpose of showing the falsity of the wrong view that 'the Blessed One has not attained Parinibbāna,' and for showing the state of being born, growing up, and so on, in the world. Indeed, for the purpose of making the human state well-manifest, it should be known that the great Bodhisattas, in their final existence, also perform such acts as taking a wife and so on. 'At Kusinārā' means in a city of that name. That city is called 'Kusinārā' because it was created in a place where a man with kusa grass in his hand was seen. This is a locative case in the sense of proximity. 'At Upavattana, the sāla grove of the Mallās' means in the sāla grove of the Mallā kings, which was the Upavattana of that city. Indeed, it is called 'Upavattana' because those wishing to enter the city go by way of it, turning aside from the grove. Just as the Thūpārāma is in the south-west direction of Anurādhapura, so that grove is in the south-west direction of Kusinārā. And just as the path for entering the city from the Thūpārāma through the southern gate, having gone facing east, turns by the north, so from the grove, the row of sāla trees, having gone facing east, turns by the north; therefore, it is called 'Upavattana.' Others, however, say: 'It is said that it became known as "Upavattana" from turning back after having approached that sāla grove and taken leave of friends and companions.' 'Between the twin sāla trees' means in the middle of the twin sāla trees. There, it is said, at the head-part of the Parinibbāna-couch prepared for the Blessed One, there was one row of sāla trees, and at the foot-part, one row. Therein also, one young sāla tree was near the head-part, and one was near the foot-part. Therefore, it was said, 'between the twin sāla trees.' Furthermore, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā it is also said: 'Twin sāla trees, namely, are sāla trees standing intertwined with one another by root, trunk, branches, and leaves.' The moon is called 'mā' because the day is measured by its movement. At that time, the 'mā' (moon) was indeed full with the completion of all its phases; hence, 'puṇṇamā' (full moon). Grammarians, however, taking the Sanskrit usage stated as 'mo sivo candimā cevā,' also accept the 'ma'-sound ending in 'o' as a word denoting the moon. 'Visākhāpuṇṇamo' is so called because it is the day on which the full moon is conjoined with the Visākhā constellation; that very day is meant. 'Tasmiṃ' means 'on that day.' 'Paccūso' (dawn) is so called because it destroys the darkness. Indeed, etymologists say that the root 'usa' preceded by 'pati' is in the sense of 'destroying'. That very 'samayo' (time) is said to be the specific time included in the last watch of the night. 'Tasmiṃ' means 'at that time.' Thus, it is said to be: 'on the Visākhā full moon day, at such a last period of the night'.

Upādīyate kammakilesehīti upādi, vipākakkhandhā, kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ. So pana upādi kilesābhisaṅkhāramāranimmathane anossaṭṭho, idha khandhamaccumāranimmathane ossaṭṭhona sesito, tasmā natthi etissā upādisaṅkhāto seso, upādissa vā sesoti katvā “anupādisesā”ti vuccati. Nibbānadhātūti cettha nibbutimattaṃ adhippetaṃ, nibbānañca taṃ sabhāvadhāraṇato dhātu cāti katvā. Nibbutiyā hi kāraṇapariyāyena asaṅkhatadhātu tathā vuccati. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cāyaṃ karaṇaniddeso. Anupādisesatāsaṅkhātaṃ imaṃ pakāraṃ bhūtassa pattassa parinibbutassa bhagavato lakkhaṇe nibbānadhātusaṅkhāte atthe tatiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nanu ca “anupādisesāyā”ti nibbānadhātuyāva visesanaṃ hoti, na parinibbutassa bhagavato, atha kasmā taṃ bhagavā pattoti vuttoti? Nibbānadhātuyā sahacaraṇato. Taṃsahacaraṇena hi bhagavāpi anupādisesabhāvaṃ pattoti vuccati. Atha vā anupādisesabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ imaṃ pakāraṃ pattāya nibbānadhātuyā lakkhaṇe sañjānanakiriyāya tatiyātipi vattuṃ yujjati. Anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyāti ca anupādisesanibbānadhātu [M 1.0039] hutvāti attho. “Ūnapañcabandhanena pattenā”ti (pārā. 612). Ettha hi ūnapañcabandhanapatto hutvāti atthaṃ vadanti. Apica nibbānadhātuyā anupādisesāya anupādisesā hutvā bhūtāyātipi yujjati. Vuttañhi udānaṭṭhakathāya nandasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ “upaḍḍhullikhitehi kesehīti itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ vippakatullikhitehi kesehi upalakkhitāti attho”ti (udā. aṭṭha. 22) esanayo īdisesu. Dhātubhājanadivaseti jeṭṭhamāsassa sukkapakkhapañcamīdivasaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tañca na “sannipatitāna”nti etassa visesanaṃ, “ussāhaṃ janesī”ti etassa pana visesanaṃ “dhātubhājanadivase bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesī”ti ussāhajananassa kālavasena bhinnādhikaraṇavisesanabhāvato. Dhātubhājanadivasato hi purimataradivasesupi bhikkhū sannipatitāti. Atha vā “sannipatitāna”nti idaṃ kāyasāmaggivasena sannipatanameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, na samāgamanamattena. Tasmā “dhātubhājanadivase”ti idaṃ “sannipatitāna”nti etassa visesanaṃ sambhavati, idañca bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesīti ettha “bhikkhūna”nti etenapi sambajjhanīyaṃ[V 1.0036]. Saṅghassa thero saṅghatthero. So pana saṅgho kiṃ parimāṇoti āha “sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassāna”nti. Saṅghasaddena hi aviññāyamānassa parimāṇassa viññāpanatthamevetaṃ puna vuttaṃ. Saddavidū pana vadanti –

Because it is grasped by kamma and the defilements, it is called 'upādi'; this refers to the resultant aggregates and form produced by kamma. Furthermore, that upādi, not having been abandoned in the crushing of the Defilement-Māra and the Formation-Māra, is here, in the crushing of the Aggregate-Māra and the Death-Māra, abandoned, made without remainder. Therefore, for this Nibbāna element, there is no remainder called 'upādi', or there is no remainder of 'upādi'; for this reason, it is called 'anupādisesā' (with no remainder of upādi). Here, by 'Nibbāna element', merely the quenching is intended; and it is Nibbāna and, because of bearing its own nature, it is also an element. Indeed, the unconditioned element is so called by way of being a cause for quenching. And this is an indication of the instrumental case in the sense of 'itthambhūtalakkhaṇa' (a characteristic of being in a certain state). It is said that the third case ending is used in the sense of the Nibbāna element, which is the characteristic of the Blessed One who has become, has attained, has fully passed away into this state called 'the state of having no remainder of upādi'. Is it not so that 'anupādisesāya' is a qualifier of the Nibbāna element only, and not of the Blessed One who has fully passed away? If so, why is it said that the Blessed One has attained it? Because of association with the Nibbāna element. Indeed, through association with it, the Blessed One is also said to have attained the state of having no remainder of upādi. Alternatively, it is also suitable to say that the third case ending is used for the action of knowing the characteristic of the Nibbāna element which has attained this state called 'the state of having no remainder of upādi'. And 'anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā' means 'having become the Nibbāna element with no remainder of upādi'. In the phrase 'ūnapañcabandhanena pattena', the teachers say the meaning is 'having a bowl with less than five bindings'. Moreover, it is also suitable to say 'by means of the Nibbāna element which is without remainder, having become without remainder'. Indeed, it is stated in the commentary to the Udāna, in the explanation of the Nanda Sutta: 'The phrase "upaḍḍhullikhitehi kesehi" (by the half-shaven hair) is an instrumental expression in the sense of itthambhūtalakkhaṇa; the meaning is "marked by the incompletely shaven hair"'. This is the method in such cases. The phrase 'dhātubhājanadivase' (on the day of the relic distribution) is said with reference to the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Jeṭṭha. And that is not a qualifier of 'sannipatitānaṃ' (of the assembled), but rather a qualifier of 'ussāhaṃ janesi' (he aroused effort). The connection should be understood as: 'On the day of the relic distribution, he aroused effort in the monks', because it is a qualifier with a different locus by way of time for the arousing of effort. For, the monks had assembled even on days much earlier than the day of the relic distribution. Alternatively, the term 'sannipatitānaṃ' is said with reference to the assembly itself in the sense of physical unity, not merely coming together. Therefore, 'dhātubhājanadivase' can be a qualifier of 'sannipatitānaṃ', and this phrase should also be connected with 'bhikkhūnaṃ' in the clause 'bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesi'. The elder of the Sangha is the saṅghatthera. But what was the size of that Sangha? He said, 'of seven hundred thousand monks.' For this was said again for the very purpose of making known the quantity which was not specified by the word 'saṅgha'. But the experts in grammar say—

“Samāso ca taddhito ca, vākyatthesu visesakā;

Pasiddhiyantu sāmaññaṃ, telaṃ sugatacīvaraṃ.

Compounds and derivatives are specifiers in the meanings of sentences; but in established usage, the meaning is general, like 'oil', 'the Sugata's robe'.

Tasmā nāmamattabhūtassa saṅghattherassa visesanatthamevetaṃ puna vuttanti, niccasāpekkhatāya ca edisesu samāso yathā “devadattassa garukula”nti. Niccasāpekkhatā cettha saṅghasaddassa bhikkhusatasahassasaddaṃ sāpekkhattepi aññapadantarābhāvena vākye viya apekkhitabbatthassa gamakattā. “Sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassāna”nti hi etassa saṅghasadde avayavībhāvena sambandho, tassāpi sāmibhāvena therasaddeti. “Sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassāna”nti ca gaṇapāmokkhabhikkhūyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadā hi sannipatitā bhikkhū ettakāti gaṇanapathamatikkantā. Tathā hi veḷuvagāme vedanāvikkhambhanato paṭṭhāya “nacireneva bhagavā parinibbāyissatī”ti sutvā tato tato āgatesu bhikkhūsu ekabhikkhupi pakkanto nāma natthi. Yathāhu –

Therefore, [the grammarians] say, 'This was said again for the very purpose of qualifying the saṅghatthera, who is so just in name.' And in such cases, a compound is formed due to constant expectancy, as in 'devadattassa gurukulaṃ' (the family of Devadatta's teacher). And here, there is constant expectancy because, even though the word 'saṅgha' has expectancy for the word 'bhikkhusatasahassa', due to the absence of any other intervening word, it makes known the expected meaning, just as in a sentence. Indeed, 'of seven hundred thousand monks' is related to the word 'saṅgha' by way of the latter being the whole of which the monks are the parts. And that word 'saṅgha' is related to the word 'thera' by way of the former being the master. And 'of seven hundred thousand monks' was said referring only to the monks who were the leaders of the groups. For at that time, the assembled monks surpassed any path of counting. Indeed, it was so: from the time of suppressing the feeling at Veḷuvagāma onwards, having heard, 'The Blessed One will attain final Nibbāna very soon,' among the monks who had come from here and there, there was not a single one who departed. As it was said:

“Sattasatasahassāni[M 1.0040], tesu pāmokkhabhikkhavo;

Thero mahākassapova, saṅghatthero tadā ahū”ti.

The leading monks among them were seven hundred thousand; the Elder Mahākassapa himself was the saṅghatthera at that time.

Āyasmā mahākassapo anussaranto maññamāno cintayanto hutvā ussāhaṃ janesi, anussaranto maññamāno cintayanto āyasmā mahākassapo ussāhaṃ janesīti vā sambandho. Mahantehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā mahanto kassapoti mahākassapo. Apica “mahākassapo”ti uruvelakassapo nadīkassapo gayākassapo kumārakassapoti ime khuddānukhuddake there upādāya vuccati. Kasmā panāyasmā mahākassapo ussāhaṃ janesīti anuyoge sati taṃ kāraṇaṃ vibhāvento āha “sattāhaparinibbute”tiādi. Satta ahāni samāhaṭāni sattāhaṃ. Sattāhaṃ parinibbutassa assāti tathā yathā “acirapakkanto, māsajāto”ti, antatthaaññapadasamāsoyaṃ, tasmiṃ. Bhagavato parinibbānadivasato paṭṭhāya sattāhe vītivatteti vuttaṃ hoti, etassa “vuttavacana”nti padena sambandho, tathā “subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitenā”ti etassapi. Tattha subhaddoti tassa nāmamattaṃ, vuḍḍhakāle pana pabbajitattā “vuḍḍhapabbajitenā”ti vuttaṃ, etena subhaddaparibbājakādīhi taṃ visesaṃ karoti. “Alaṃ āvuso”tiādinā [V 1.0037] tena vuttavacanaṃ nidasseti. So hi sattāhaparinibbute bhagavati āyasmatā mahākassapattherena saddhiṃ pāvāya kusināraṃ addhānamaggapaṭipannesu pañcamattesu bhikkhusatesu avītarāge bhikkhū antarāmagge diṭṭhaājīvakassa santikā bhagavato parinibbānaṃ sutvā pattacīvarāni chaḍḍetvā bāhā paggayhaṃ nānappakāraṃ paridevante disvā evamāha.

Venerable Mahākassapa, recollecting, considering, and thinking, generated the effort. Or, the connection is thus: recollecting, considering, and thinking, Venerable Mahākassapa generated the effort. Because he was endowed with the great qualities of the aggregates of virtue and so forth, he was the great Kassapa; thus, he was Mahākassapa. Moreover, he is called ‘Mahākassapa’ with reference to these lesser elders: Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, Gayākassapa, and Kumārakassapa. When the question is posed, “But why did Venerable Mahākassapa generate the effort?”—wishing to clarify that reason, the author said, “When it was seven days since the Parinibbāna,” and so on. Seven days brought together are a week (sattāhaṃ). ‘For whom it has been seven days since attaining Parinibbāna’ is like ‘recently departed’ or ‘born a month ago.’ This is an antatthaaññapadasamāsa compound. In that case, it is meant that seven days had passed since the day of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna. The connection of this phrase is with the word vuttavacanaṃ (the words spoken), and likewise for the phrase ‘by Subhadda, the one who went forth in old age.’ Therein, ‘Subhadda’ is merely his name; but because he had gone forth in old age, it is said, ‘by the one who went forth in old age.’ By this, he is distinguished from the wanderer Subhadda and others. With “Enough, sirs,” and so on, the author indicates the words spoken by that one. For when it was seven days since the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, among the five hundred monks who were traveling the long road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa, he saw the monks who were not free from passion, upon hearing of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna from an Ājīvaka who was seen on the way, throw down their bowls and robes, raise their arms, and lament in various ways, and he spoke thus.

Kasmā pana so evamāhāti? Bhagavati āghātena. Ayaṃ kireso khandhake āgate ātumāvatthusmiṃ (mahāva. 303) nahāpitapubbako vuḍḍhapabbajito bhagavati kusinārato nikkhamitvā aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ ātumaṃ gacchante “bhagavā āgacchatī”ti sutvā “āgatakāleyāgudānaṃ karissāmī”ti sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhite dve putte etadavoca “bhagavā kira tātā ātumaṃ āgacchati mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi, gacchatha tumhe tātā, khurabhaṇḍaṃ ādāya nāḷiyā vā pasibbakena vā anugharakaṃ āhiṇḍatha, loṇampi telampi taṇḍulampi khādanīyampi [M 1.0041] saṃharatha, bhagavato āgatassa yāgudānaṃ karissāmī”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Atha bhagavati ātumaṃ āgantvā bhusāgārakaṃ paviṭṭhe subhaddo sāyanhasamayaṃ gāmadvāraṃ gantvā manusse āmantetvā “hatthakammamattaṃ me dethā”ti hatthakammaṃ yācitvā “kiṃ bhante karomā”ti vutte “idañcidañca gaṇhathā”ti sabbūpakaraṇāni gāhāpetvā vihāre uddhanāni kāretvā ekaṃ kāḷakaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā tādisameva pārupitvā “idaṃ karotha, idaṃ karothā”ti sabbarattiṃ vicārento satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā bhojjayāguñca madhugoḷakañca paṭiyādāpesi. Bhojjayāgu nāma bhuñjitvā pātabbayāgu, tattha sappimadhuphāṇitamacchamaṃsapupphaphalarasādi yaṃ kiñci khādanīyaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ pavisati. Kīḷitukāmānaṃ sīsamakkhanayoggā hoti sugandhagandhā.

But why did he speak thus? Because of a grudge against the Blessed One. Indeed, this is the story: This one, who was formerly a barber and had gone forth in old age—as related in the story of the Ātumā affair in the Khandhaka—when the Blessed One was departing from Kusinārā and going to Ātumā with twelve hundred and fifty monks, heard, “The Blessed One is coming,” and said this to his two sons who were in the state of novices, “I will make an offering of gruel when he arrives.” He said: “My dears, the Blessed One, it is said, is coming to Ātumā with a great Saṅgha of monks, with twelve hundred and fifty monks. Go, my dears, take the barber’s equipment and wander from house to house with a tube or a bag. Collect salt, oil, rice, and edibles. I will make an offering of gruel for the Blessed One when he arrives.” They did so. Then, when the Blessed One had arrived at Ātumā and entered the straw hut, Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, called the people, and having requested manual labor, saying, “Give me just a little manual labor,” and being asked, “What shall we do, venerable sir?” he had them take this and that, getting all the utensils. He had fireplaces made in the monastery, and having put on one black robe and draped himself in a similar one, he went about all night arranging things, saying, “Do this, do this.” Having spent one hundred thousand, he had a rich gruel and honey-balls prepared. A rich gruel (bhojjayāgu) is a gruel that is to be drunk after eating. Therein, whatever is called an edible—ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flower essence, fruit juice, and so on—all of that is included. It is suitable for anointing the heads of those who wish to amuse themselves, and it is very fragrant.

Atha bhagavā kālasseva sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto piṇḍāya carituṃ ātumābhimukho pāyāsi. Atha tassa ārocesuṃ “bhagavā piṇḍāya gāmaṃ pavisati, tayā kassa yāgu paṭiyāditā”ti. So yathānivatthapāruteheva tehi kāḷakakāsāvehi ekena hatthena dabbiñca kaṭacchuñca gahetvā brahmā viya dakkhiṇaṃ jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā vanditvā “paṭiggaṇhātu me bhante bhagavā yāgu”nti āha. Tato “jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchantī”ti khandhake (mahāva. 304) āgatanayena bhagavā pucchitvā ca sutvā ca taṃ vuḍḍhapabbajitaṃ vigarahitvā tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ akappiyasamādānasikkhāpadaṃ, khurabhaṇḍapariharaṇasikkhāpadañcāti dve sikkhāpadāni paññapetvā “anekakappakoṭiyo bhikkhave bhojanaṃ pariyesanteheva vītināmitā[V 1.0038], idaṃ pana tumhākaṃ akappiyaṃ, adhammena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ imaṃ paribhuñjitvā anekāni attabhāvasahassāni apāyesveva nibbattissanti, apetha mā gaṇhathā”ti vatvā bhikkhācārābhimukho agamāsi, ekabhikkhunāpi na kiñci gahitaṃ. Subhaddo anattamano hutvā “ayaṃ sabbaṃ jānāmī”ti āhiṇḍati, sace na gahetukāmo pesetvā ārocetabbaṃ assa, pakkāhāro nāma sabbaciraṃ tiṭṭhanto sattāhamattaṃ tiṭṭheyya, idañca mama yāvajīvaṃ pariyattaṃ assa, sabbaṃ tena nāsitaṃ, ahitakāmo ayaṃ mayha”nti bhagavati āghātaṃ bandhitvā dasabale dharamāne kiñci vattuṃ [M 1.0042] nāsakkhi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “ayaṃ uccā kulā pabbajito mahāpuriso, sace kiñci dharantassa vakkhāmi, mamaṃyeva santajjessatī”ti.

Then the Blessed One, having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, set out towards Ātumā to walk for alms. Then they informed him: “The Blessed One is entering the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the gruel?” Just as he was dressed and robed in those black garments, holding a ladle and a dipper in one hand, like Brahmā, he placed his right knee on the ground, paid homage, and said: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my gruel.” Then, in accordance with the method from the Khandhaka, “Tathāgatas ask, even though they know,” the Blessed One, having questioned and heard him, rebuked that one who had gone forth in old age. In that matter, he laid down two training rules: the training rule on undertaking what is improper and the training rule on carrying barber’s equipment. He said: “Monks, many crores of aeons have been passed by you just in seeking food. But this is improper for you, this food obtained unrighteously. Having consumed this, you will be reborn in the woeful states for many thousands of existences. Depart! Do not accept it!” Having said this, he proceeded on his alms-round, and not even a single monk took anything. Subhadda, being displeased, thought: “This one wanders about claiming, ‘I know everything.’ If he did not wish to accept it, he should have sent someone to inform me. Cooked food, if it lasts for the longest time, would last for about seven days. And this would have been sufficient for me for my whole life. It has all been destroyed by him. This one desires my harm!” Having thus formed a grudge against the Blessed One, he was unable to say anything while the one with Ten Powers was still present. Indeed, it is said this thought occurred to him: “This one is a great man, gone forth from a high family. If I say anything to him while he is present, he will just threaten me.”

Svāyaṃ ajja mahākassapattherena saddhiṃ gacchanto “parinibbuto bhagavā”ti sutvā laddhassāso viya haṭṭhatuṭṭho evamāha. Thero pana taṃ sutvā hadaye pahāraṃ viya, matthake patitasukkhāsaniṃ viya (sukkhāsani viya dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.232) maññi, dhammasaṃvego cassa uppajji “sattāhamattaparinibbuto bhagavā, ajjāpissa suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ dharatiyeva, dukkhena bhagavatā ārādhitasāsane nāma evaṃ lahuṃ mahantaṃ pāpaṃ kasaṭaṃ kaṇṭako uppanno, alaṃ kho panesa pāpo vaḍḍhamāno aññepi evarūpe sahāye labhitvā sāsanaṃ osakkāpetu”nti.

Today, while traveling with the Elder Mahākassapa, this Subhadda heard the words, “The Blessed One has attained parinibbāna,” and, as if having gained relief, he became joyful and delighted and spoke thus. The Elder, however, upon hearing that word, considered it as though a blow to the heart, as if a dry thunderbolt had fallen upon his head. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him: “The Blessed One attained parinibbāna just seven days ago, and even today His golden-hued body still remains. In the Dispensation, which the Blessed One established with difficulty, such a great evil, a worthless thing, a thorn has arisen so quickly. Indeed, this evil one, if allowed to grow, having obtained other such companions, is certainly capable of causing the Dispensation to decline.”

Tato thero cintesi “sace kho panāhaṃ imaṃ mahallakaṃ idheva pilotikaṃ nivāsetvā chārikāya okirāpetvā nīharāpessāmi, manussā ‘samaṇassa gotamassa sarīre dharamāneyeva sāvakā vivadantī’ti amhākaṃ dosaṃ dassessanti, adhivāsemi tāva. Bhagavatā hi desitadhammo asaṅgahitapuppharāsisadiso, tattha yathā vātena pahaṭapupphāni yato vā tato vā gacchanti, evameva evarūpānaṃ vasena gacchante gacchante kāle vinaye ekaṃ dve sikkhāpadāni nassissanti, sutte eko dve pañhāvārā nassissanti, abhidhamme ekaṃ dve bhūmantarāni nassissanti, evaṃ anukkamena mūle naṭṭhe pisācasadisā bhavissāma, tasmā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ karissāmi, evaṃ sati daḷhasuttena saṅgahitapupphāni viya ayaṃ dhammavinayo niccalo bhavissati. Etadatthañhi bhagavā mayhaṃ tīṇi gāvutāni paccuggamanaṃ akāsi, tīhi ovādehi (saṃ. ni. 2.149, 150, 151) upasampadaṃ akāsi, kāyato cīvaraparivattanaṃ akāsi, ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvā candopamapaṭipadaṃ kathento maññeva sakkhiṃ katvā kathesi, tikkhattuṃ sakalasāsanaratanaṃ paṭicchāpesi, mādise bhikkhumhi tiṭṭhamāne ayaṃ pāpo sāsane vaḍḍhiṃ mā alattha, yāva adhammo na dippati, dhammo na paṭibāhiyyati, avinayo na dippati, vinayo na paṭibāhiyyati, adhammavādino na balavanto honti, dhammavādino [V 1.0039] na dubbalā honti, avinayavādino na balavanto honti, vinayavādino na dubbalā honti, tāva dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmi, tato bhikkhū attano attano pahonakaṃ [M 1.0043] gahetvā kappiyākappiye kathessanti, athāyaṃ pāpo sayameva niggahaṃ pāpuṇissati, puna sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkhissati, sāsanaṃ iddhañceva phīttañca bhavissatī”ti cintetvā so “evaṃ nāma mayhaṃ cittaṃ uppanna”nti kassacipi anārocetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ samassāsetvā atha pacchā dhātubhājanadivase dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesi. Tena vuttaṃ “āyasmā mahākassapo sattāhaparinibbute…pe… dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesī”ti.

Then the Elder thought: “If I were to have this old man wear a worn-out cloth right here, be sprinkled with ash, and then be expelled, people would find fault with us, saying, ‘While the body of the ascetic Gotama is still present, his disciples are quarreling.’ I will endure for now. For the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of unstrung flowers. Just as flowers scattered by the wind go here and there, so too, through the influence of such people, as time goes on, one or two training rules in the Vinaya will be lost, one or two question-sections in the Sutta will be lost, and one or two sections in the Abhidhamma will be lost. Gradually, when the root is lost, we will become like demons. Therefore, I will make a compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. When this is done, this Dhamma and Vinaya will be unshaken, like flowers strung with a strong thread. It is for this purpose that the Blessed One came three gāvutas to meet me, gave me ordination with three exhortations, exchanged robes with me, and, moving His hand in the sky while teaching the practice likened to the moon, He spoke taking me as His witness. Three times He entrusted the entire jewel of the Dispensation to me. While a monk like me is present, may this evil one not find growth in the Dispensation. As long as the non-Dhamma does not shine and the Dhamma is not suppressed, as long as the non-Vinaya does not shine and the Vinaya is not suppressed, as long as those who speak non-Dhamma are not strong and those who speak Dhamma are not weak, as long as those who speak non-Vinaya are not strong and those who speak Vinaya are not weak, for so long I will chant the Dhamma and Vinaya together. Then the monks, each according to his own capacity, will discuss what is allowable and what is not. And this evil one will automatically meet his downfall—he will never again be able to raise his head. The Dispensation will flourish and prosper.” Having reflected thus, without informing anyone of what had arisen in his mind, he consoled the Saṅgha of monks. Later, on the day of distributing the relics, he inspired the monks to undertake the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. Hence it is said: “The Venerable Mahākassapa, seven days after the parinibbāna... inspired the monks to undertake the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.”

Tattha alanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ, na yuttanti attho. Āvusoti paridevante bhikkhū ālapati. Mā socitthāti citte uppannabalavasokena mā sokamakattha. Mā paridevitthāti vācāya mā vilāpamakattha. “Paridevanaṃ vilāpo”ti hi vuttaṃ. Asocanādīnaṃ kāraṇamāha “sumuttā”tiādinā. Tena mahāsamaṇenāti nissakke karaṇavacanaṃ, smāvacanassa vā nābyappadeso. “Upaddutā”ti pade pana kattari tatiyāvasena sambandho. Ubhayāpekkhañhetaṃ padaṃ. Upaddutā ca homāti taṃkālāpekkhavattamānavacanaṃ, “tadā”ti seso. Atītatthe vā vattamānavacanaṃ, ahumhāti attho. Anussaranto dhammasaṃvegavaseneva, na pana kodhādivasena. Dhammasabhāvacintāvasena hi pavattaṃ sahottappañāṇaṃ dhammasaṃvego. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, ‘alaṃ’ is a word of rejection, meaning ‘it is not proper.’ With ‘āvuso,’ he addresses the lamenting monks. ‘Mā socittha’ means ‘do not create sorrow with the strong sorrow that has arisen in the mind.’ ‘Mā paridevittha’ means ‘do not make lamentation with speech.’ For it is said, ‘Lamentation is wailing.’ He states the reason for not grieving and so on with ‘sumuttā,’ etc. The phrase ‘by that great ascetic’ is an instrumental case in the sense of the ablative, or it is a substitution of the instrumental for the ablative case. In the word ‘upaddutā,’ however, the connection is by means of the instrumental case in the agentive sense. This word refers to both. ‘Upaddutā ca homa’ is a present tense statement referring to that time, with ‘tadā’ implied. Or it may be a present tense statement in the sense of the past, meaning ‘we were.’ One recollects only through the power of spiritual urgency, not through anger or the like. For spiritual urgency is the knowledge accompanied by moral dread that arises through reflection on the nature of phenomena. As it is said—

“Sabbasaṅkhatadhammesu, ottappākārasaṇṭhitaṃ;

Ñāṇamohitabhārānaṃ, dhammasaṃvegasaññita”nti. (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā);

“That knowledge of those who have laid down the burden, which is established in the manner of moral dread regarding all conditioned phenomena, is designated as spiritual urgency.”

Aññaṃ ussāhajananakāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “īdisassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha īdisassa ca saṅghasannipātassāti sattasatasahassagaṇapāmokkhattherappamukhagaṇanapathātikkantasaṅghasannipātaṃ sandhāya vadati. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjatī”tiādināpi aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, hetu. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Panāti vacanālaṅkāre, etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjateva, no na vijjatīti attho. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “yaṃ pāpabhikkhū”tiādi. Yanti nipātamattaṃ, kāraṇaniddeso vā, yena ṭhānena antaradhāpeyyuṃ, tadetaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatiyevāti. Pāpena lāmakena icchāvacarena samannāgatā bhikkhū pāpabhikkhū[M 1.0044]. Atīto satthā ettha, etassāti vā atītasatthukaṃ yathā “bahukattuko”ti. Padhānaṃ vacanaṃ pāvacanaṃ. Pā-saddo [V 1.0040] cettha nipāto “pā eva vutyassā”tiādīsu viya. Upasaggapadaṃ vā etaṃ, dīghaṃ katvā pana tathā vuttaṃ yathā “pāvadatī”tipi vadanti. Pakkhanti alajjipakkhaṃ. “Yāva cā”tiādinā saṅgītiyā sāsanaciraṭṭhitikabhāve kāraṇaṃ, sādhakañca dasseti. “Tasmā”ti hi padamajjhāharitvā “saṅgāyeyya”nti padena sambandhanīyaṃ.

To show another reason for generating effort, it is said, 'such a one,' etc. Herein, 'such a gathering of the Sangha' refers to a gathering of the Sangha, led by chief elders of a group of seven hundred thousand, which surpasses calculation. By 'And indeed, this cause exists,' etc., he also shows another reason. A 'ṭhāna' is so called because the result stands therein, its occurrence being dependent on that; it means a cause. 'Kho' is for emphasis. 'Pana' is for verbal embellishment; the meaning is that this cause certainly exists, not that it does not exist. To the question, 'But what is that?' he says, 'that the wicked monks,' etc. 'Yaṃ' is merely a particle, or it is an indication of the cause, meaning: by which cause they might cause disappearance, that cause certainly exists. Monks endowed with evil, base, and corrupt desires are wicked monks. 'Atītasatthukaṃ' (having a past Teacher) means the Teacher is past in this Dispensation, or this Dispensation has a past Teacher, just as 'bahukattuko' (having many agents). 'Pāvacana' is the chief utterance. Herein, the word 'pā' is a particle, as in 'pā eva vutyassā,' etc. Or, it is a prefix, but having been lengthened, it is said thus, just as in 'pāvadati,' so they say. 'Faction' means the shameless faction. By 'And as long as,' etc., he shows the recitation to be the reason and the means of accomplishment for the long-lasting state of the Dispensation. Indeed, the word 'tasmā' (therefore), having been supplied, should be connected with the word 'saṅgāyeyya' (they should recite).

Tattha yāva ca dhammavinayo tiṭṭhatīti yattakaṃ kālaṃ dhammo ca vinayo ca lajjipuggalesu tiṭṭhati. Parinibbānamañcake nipannena bhagavatā mahāparinibbānasutte (dī. ni. 2.216) vuttaṃ sandhāya “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Hi-saddo āgamavasena daḷhijotako. Desito paññattoti dhammopi desito ceva paññatto ca. Suttābhidhammasaṅgahitassa hi dhammassa atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanā, tasseva pakārato ñāpanaṃ vineyyasantāne ṭhapanaṃ paññāpanaṃ. Vinayopi desito ceva paññatto ca. Vinayatantisaṅgahitassa hi atthassa atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanā, tasseva pakārato ñāpanaṃ asaṅkarato ṭhapanaṃ paññāpanaṃ, tasmā kammadvayampi kiriyādvayena sambajjhanaṃ yujjatīti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, 'as long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure' means for as long as the Dhamma and the Vinaya remain among conscientious people. This refers to what was said by the Blessed One lying on the couch of final Nibbāna in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta; hence, it is said, 'for it was said.' The particle 'hi' is a strengthener based on tradition. 'Taught and prescribed'—the Dhamma is both taught and prescribed. For the Dhamma included in the Suttas and Abhidhamma, teaching is elucidation and awakening, while prescribing is making it known in various ways and establishing it in the mental continuum of those to be trained. The Vinaya, too, is both taught and prescribed. For the meaning included in the Vinaya texts, teaching is elucidation and awakening, while prescribing is making it known in various ways and establishing it without confusion. Therefore, it should be understood that the connection of both objects with the two actions is fitting.

Soti so dhammo ca vinayo ca. Mamaccayenāti mama accayakāle. “Bhummatthe karaṇaniddeso”ti hi akkharacintakā vadanti. Hetvatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ, mama accayahetu tumhākaṃ satthā nāma bhavissatīti attho. Vuttañhi mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ “mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessatī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.216). Lakkhaṇavacanañhettha hetvatthasādhakaṃ yathā “nette ujuṃ gate satī”ti (a. ni. 4.70; netti. 10.90, 93). Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mayā vo ṭhiteneva “idaṃ lahukaṃ, idaṃ garukaṃ, idaṃ satekicchaṃ, idaṃ atekicchaṃ, idaṃ lokavajjaṃ, idaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ, ayaṃ āpatti puggalassa santike vuṭṭhāti, ayaṃ gaṇassa, ayaṃ saṅghassa santike vuṭṭhātī”ti sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamanīyatāvasena otiṇṇavatthusmiṃ sakhandhakaparivāro ubhatovibhaṅgo mahāvinayo nāma desito, taṃ sakalampi vinayapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati “idaṃ vo kattabbaṃ, idaṃ vo na kattabba”nti kattabbākattabbassa vibhāgena [M 1.0045] anusāsanato. Ṭhiteneva ca mayā “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti tena tena vineyyānaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpena pakārena ime sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme vibhajitvā vibhajitvā suttantapiṭakaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ sakalampi suttantapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati taṃtaṃcariyānurūpaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā anusāsanato, ṭhiteneva ca mayā “ime [V 1.0041] pañcakkhandhā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.216), dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, cattāri saccāni, bāvīsatindriyāni, nava hetū, cattāro āhārā, satta phassā, satta vedanā, satta saññā, satta cetanā, satta cittāni. Tatrāpi ettakā dhammā kāmāvacarā, ettakā rūpāvacarā, ettakā arūpāvacarā, ettakā pariyāpannā, ettakā apariyāpannā, ettakā lokiyā, ettakā lokuttarā”ti ime dhamme vibhajitvā vibhajitvā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ sakalampi abhidhammapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati khandhādivibhāgena ñāyamānaṃ catusaccasambodhāvahattā. Iti sabbampetaṃ abhisambodhito yāva parinibbānā pañcacattālīsa vassāni bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ “tīṇi piṭakāni, pañca nikāyā, navaṅgāni, caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti evaṃ mahappabhedaṃ hoti. Imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni tiṭṭhanti, ahaṃ ekova parinibbāyissāmi, ahañca panidāni ekova ovadāmi anusāsāmi, mayi parinibbute imāni caturāsīti buddhasahassāni tumhe ovadissanti anusāsissanti ovādānusāsanakiccassa nipphādanatoti.

That is the Dhamma and the Vinaya. ‘After my passing’ means ‘at the time of my passing.’ For grammarians say: ‘The instrumental designation is in the locative sense.’ Or the instrumental case is in the sense of cause, meaning: ‘Because of my passing, you will have a Teacher.’ For it is said in the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta: ‘When I have attained Parinibbāna, it will accomplish the duty of a Teacher for you.’ Here, the expression of circumstance accomplishes the causal sense, as in: ‘When the lead bull goes straight.’ This is what is meant: While I am still present, I have taught the great Vinaya, called the Ubhatovibhaṅga, together with its Khandhakas and Parivāra, by explaining the seven classes of offenses—this is light, this is grave, this is curable, this is incurable, this is blameworthy by the world, this is blameworthy by convention, this offense is resolved in the presence of an individual, this in the presence of a group, this in the presence of the Saṅgha—according to the un-transgressable nature of the matter that has been entered upon. When I have attained Parinibbāna, this entire Vinaya Piṭaka will accomplish the duty of a Teacher for you, because it instructs by distinguishing what should be done and what should not be done. And while I am still present, I have taught the Suttanta Piṭaka by analyzing and re-analyzing these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven enlightenment factors, and the Noble Eightfold Path—in various ways suited to the dispositions of those to be trained. When I have attained Parinibbāna, this entire Suttanta Piṭaka will accomplish the duty of a Teacher for you, because it instructs in right practice in accordance with each one's temperament. And while I am still present, I have taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka by analyzing and re-analyzing these phenomena—the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, and the seven consciousnesses; and among them, so many phenomena are of the sense-sphere, so many of the form-sphere, so many of the formless-sphere, so many are included, so many are not included, so many are worldly, so many are supramundane. When I have attained Parinibbāna, this entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka will accomplish the duty of a Teacher for you, because it brings about the full understanding of the Four Noble Truths, which are known through the analysis of the aggregates and so on. Thus, all this that was spoken and uttered for forty-five years from my full awakening until my Parinibbāna is of great variety: the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine Aṅgas, and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. These eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma remain; I alone will attain Parinibbāna. And now I alone advise and instruct you. When I have attained Parinibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddhas will advise and instruct you, because they accomplish the duty of advice and instruction.

Sāsananti pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhavasena tividhampi sāsanaṃ, nippariyāyato pana sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā. Addhānaṃ gamitumalanti addhaniyaṃ, addhānagāmi addhānakkhamanti attho. Ciraṃ ṭhiti etassāti ciraṭṭhitikaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena pakārena idaṃ sāsanaṃ addhaniyaṃ, tatoyeva ca ciraṭṭhitikaṃ bhaveyya, tena pakārena dhammañca vinayañca yadi panāhaṃ saṅgāyeyyaṃ, sādhu vatāti.

By 'the Teaching' is meant the threefold Teaching by way of study, practice, and penetration; but in the direct sense, it is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. It is 'long-lasting' because it is able to last for a long time; the meaning is 'lasting for a long time' and 'enduring for a long time.' It is 'of long duration' because its stability is for a long time. This is what is meant: 'In whatever way this Teaching would be long-lasting, and for that very reason would be of long duration, if I were to rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya in that way, it would indeed be good!'

Idāni sammāsambuddhena attano kataṃ anuggahavisesaṃ samanussaritvā cintanākārampi dassento “yañcāhaṃ bhagavatā”tiādimāha. Tattha “yañcāha”nti etassa “anuggahito, pasaṃsito”ti etehi sambandho. Yanti [M 1.0046] yasmā, kiriyāparāmasanaṃ vā etaṃ, tena “anuggahito, pasaṃsito”ti ettha anuggahaṇaṃ, pasaṃsanañca parāmasati. “Dhāressasī”tiādikaṃ pana vacanaṃ bhagavā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle mahākassapattherena paññattasaṅghāṭiyaṃ nisinno taṃ saṅghāṭiṃ padumapupphavaṇṇena pāṇinā antantena parāmasanto āha. Vuttañhetaṃ kassapasaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 2.154) mahākassapatthereneva ānandattheraṃ āmantetvā kathentena –

Now, repeatedly recollecting the special favor done for him by the Perfectly Enlightened One, and also showing the manner of his thought, the Elder said, ‘And in that I was favored by the Blessed One…’ and so on. Therein, ‘And in that I’ is to be connected with ‘favored’ and ‘praised.’ ‘Yaṃ’ means ‘since,’ or it is a word referring to the action; by it, in the phrase ‘favored, praised,’ it refers to the action of favoring and praising. However, the statement ‘You will wear…’ and so on, was spoken by the Blessed One while seated at the foot of a certain tree on a robe arranged by the Elder Mahā Kassapa, stroking that robe at the very edge with his hand, which was the color of a lotus flower. For this is stated in the Kassapa Saṃyutta, as spoken by the Elder Mahā Kassapa himself when he addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:

“Atha kho āvuso bhagavā maggā okkamma yena aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ tenupasaṅkami, atha khvāhaṃ āvuso paṭapilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ catugguṇaṃ paññapetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavocaṃ ‘idha bhante bhagavā nisīdatu, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’ti[V 1.0042]. Nisīdi kho āvuso bhagavā paññatte āsane, nisajja kho maṃ āvuso bhagavā etadavoca ‘mudukā kho tyāyaṃ kassapa paṭapilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭī’ti. Paṭiggaṇhātu me bhante bhagavā paṭapilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ anukampaṃ upādāyāti. Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ kassapa sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānīti. Dhāressāmahaṃ bhante bhagavato sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānīti. So khvāhaṃ āvuso paṭapilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ bhagavato pādāsiṃ, ahaṃ pana bhagavato sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanāni paṭipajji”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154).

‘Then, friend, the Blessed One stepped off the road and approached a certain tree. Then, friend, having folded the outer robe made of worn-out cloth fourfold, I spread it out and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One sit here, that it may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.” The Blessed One, friend, sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, friend, the Blessed One said this to me: “Soft, Kassapa, is this outer robe of yours made of worn-out cloth.” “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my outer robe made of worn-out cloth, out of compassion.” “But will you, Kassapa, wear these worn-out hempen rag-robes of mine?” “I will wear, Venerable sir, the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag-robes.” So, friend, I gave the outer robe made of worn-out cloth to the Blessed One, and I myself undertook to wear the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag-robes.’

Tattha mudukā kho tyāyanti mudukā kho te ayaṃ. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamāhāti? Therena saha cīvaraṃ parivattetukāmatāya. Kasmā parivattetukāmo jātoti? Theraṃ attano ṭhāne ṭhapetukāmatāya. Kiṃ sāriputtamoggallānā natthīti? Atthi, evaṃ panassa ahosi “ime na ciraṃ ṭhassanti, ‘kassapo pana vīsavassasatāyuko, so mayi parinibbute sattapaṇṇiguhāyaṃ vasitvā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ katvā mama sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇakālaṃ pavattanakaṃ karissatī”ti attano naṃ ṭhāne ṭhapesi, evaṃ bhikkhū kassapassa sussusitabbaṃ maññissantī”ti tasmā evamāha. Thero pana yasmā cīvarassa vā pattassa vā vaṇṇe kathite “imaṃ tumhe gaṇhathā”ti vacanaṃ cārittameva, tasmā “paṭiggaṇhātu me bhante bhagavā”ti āha.

Herein, for the phrase ‘mudukā kho tyāyaṃ,’ the division of words should be made as ‘mudukā kho te ayaṃ’ (soft indeed is this of yours). But why did the Blessed One speak thus? Because of the desire to exchange robes with the Elder. Why did the desire to exchange arise? Because of the desire to establish the Elder in His own position. Are Sāriputta and Moggallāna not present? They are present. However, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: “These two will not last long. But Kassapa has a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years. After I have attained Parinibbāna, he, dwelling in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave and making a compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, will cause my Dispensation to last for a period of five thousand years.” Thus, He established him in His own position, thinking: ‘In this way, the bhikkhus will think Kassapa’s word should be well-heeded.’ Therefore, He spoke thus. As for the Elder, because it is the custom, when the quality of a robe or a bowl is praised, to say, “You may take this,” he therefore said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept it from me.”

Dhāressasi [M 1.0047] pana me tvaṃ kassapāti kassapa tvaṃ imāni paribhogajiṇṇāni paṃsukūlāni pārupituṃ sakkhissasīti vadati. Tañca kho na kāyabalaṃ sandhāya, paṭipattipūraṇaṃ pana sandhāya evamāha. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – ahaṃ imaṃ cīvaraṃ puṇṇaṃ nāma dāsiṃ pārupitvā āmakasusāne chaḍḍitaṃ susānaṃ pavisitvā tumbamattehi pāṇakehi samparikiṇṇaṃ te pāṇake vidhunitvā mahāariyavaṃse ṭhatvā aggahesiṃ, tassa me imaṃ cīvaraṃ gahitadivase dasasahassacakkavāḷe mahāpathavī mahāviravaṃ viravamānā kampittha, ākāsaṃ taṭataṭāyi, cakkavāḷe devatā sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu, imaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhantena bhikkhunā jātipaṃsukūlikena jātiāraññikena jātiekāsanikena jātisapadānacārikena bhavituṃ vaṭṭati, tvaṃ imassa cīvarassa anucchavikaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasīti. Theropi attanā pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti, so taṃ atakkayitvā “ahametaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūressāmī”ti ussāhena sugatacīvarassa anucchavikaṃ kātukāmo “dhāressāmahaṃ bhante”ti āha. Paṭipajjinti paṭipannosiṃ. Evaṃ pana cīvaraparivattanaṃ [V 1.0043] katvā therena pārupitacīvaraṃ bhagavā pārupi, satthu cīvaraṃ thero. Tasmiṃ samaye mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā unnadantī kampittha.

The phrase ‘Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ kassapa’ means: ‘Kassapa, will you be able to wear these rag-robes that are worn out from use?’ And He said this not with reference to physical strength, but rather with reference to the fulfillment of the practice. Herein, this is the intended meaning: ‘I, having entered a charnel ground, took this robe, which had been worn by a female slave named Puṇṇā and discarded in that charnel ground, a robe swarming with worms the size of a tumba. Shaking off those worms and standing in the great lineage of the Noble Ones, I picked it up. On the day I took this robe, the great earth in the ten-thousand world-system trembled, making a great roar; the sky resounded thunderously; the deities in the world-system gave cries of approval. A bhikkhu who takes this robe ought to be one who by nature undertakes the practice of wearing rag-robes, who by nature undertakes the practice of dwelling in the forest, who by nature undertakes the practice of eating in one session, and who by nature undertakes the practice of eating alms-food in sequence. Will you be able to act in a manner befitting this robe?’ The Elder, too, possessed the strength of five elephants. Not considering that physical strength, he thought, “I will fulfill this practice.” With effort, desiring to act in a manner befitting the Sugata’s robe, he said, “Venerable sir, I will wear it.” The word ‘paṭipajjiṃ’ means ‘I undertook.’ Thus, having made the exchange of robes, the Blessed One wore the robe that had been worn by the Elder, and the Elder wore the Teacher’s robe. At that moment, the great earth, up to its water-boundary, trembled, roaring and echoing.

Sāṇāni paṃsukūlānīti matakaḷevaraṃ pariveṭhetvā chaḍḍitāni tumbamatte kimī papphoṭetvā gahitāni sāṇavākamayāni paṃsukūlacīvarāni. Nibbasanānīti niṭṭhitavasanakiccāni, paribhogajiṇṇānīti attho. Ettha ca kiñcāpi ekameva taṃ cīvaraṃ, anekāvayavattā pana bahuvacanaṃ katanti majjhimagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogenāti ettha attanā sādhāraṇaparibhogenāti atthassa viññāyamānattā, viññāyamānatthassa ca saddassa payoge kāmācārattā “attanā”ti na vuttaṃ. “Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ kassapa sāṇāni paṃsukūlānī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) hi vuttattā “attanāva sādhāraṇaparibhogenā”ti viññāyati, nāññena. Na hi kevalaṃ saddatoyeva sabbattha atthanicchayo, atthapakaraṇādināpi yebhuyyena atthassa niyamitattā. Ācariyadhammapālattherena panettha evaṃ vuttaṃ “cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogenāti ettha ‘attanā samasamaṭṭhapanenā’ti idha vuttaṃ attanā – saddamānetvā ‘cīvare attanā sādhāraṇaparibhogenā’ti yojetabbaṃ.

‘Sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni’ (hempen rag-robes) refers to rag-robes made of hemp fiber, which were taken after shaking off worms the size of a tumba, having been discarded after wrapping a corpse. ‘Nibbasanāni’ means that their function of being worn is finished; the meaning is that they are worn out from use. And herein, although it is a single robe, the plural is used because it is composed of many parts; so it is said in the Majjhima Gaṇṭhipada. Here, in the phrase ‘cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena’ (by common use of the robe), because the meaning ‘attanā sādhāraṇaparibhogena’ (by common use with oneself) is understood, and because the use of a word whose meaning is understood is at the discretion of the speaker, the word ‘attanā’ (by oneself) is not stated. For since it is said, “Will you, Kassapa, wear my hempen rag-robes?” it is understood as “by shared use with myself alone,” not with another. Indeed, the determination of meaning is not everywhere made from the word alone, since the meaning is for the most part determined by the context of the meaning and other factors. Herein, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has said thus: “In the phrase ‘cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena,’ one should bring the word ‘attanā’ stated here in ‘attanā samasamaṭṭhapanena’ (by establishing as equal to oneself) and construe it as: ‘cīvare attanā sādhāraṇaparibhogena’ (by common use of the robe with oneself).”

Yassa [M 1.0048] yena hi sambandho, dūraṭṭhampi ca tassa taṃ;

Atthato hyasamānānaṃ, āsannattamakāraṇanti.

Indeed, whatever word has a connection with another, that word should be connected to it, even if it stands far away. For, regarding words that are dissimilar in meaning, their proximity is not a reason for connection.

Atha vā bhagavatā cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena bhagavatā anuggahitoti yojanīyaṃ. Ekassāpi hi karaṇaniddesassa sahādiyogakattutthajotakattasambhavato”ti. Samānaṃ dhāraṇametassāti sādhāraṇo, tādiso paribhogoti sādhāraṇaparibhogo, tena. Sādhāraṇaparibhogena ca samasamaṭṭhapanena ca anuggahitoti sambandho.

Alternatively, it should be construed thus: ‘He was favored by the Blessed One through the shared use of the robe.’ For it is possible for even a single term in the instrumental case to express the meaning of companionship, etc., and the meaning of agent. The word ‘sādhāraṇa’ (shared) is so called because ‘it has a similar wearing’ (samānaṃ dhāraṇaṃ etassa). Such use is ‘sādhāraṇaparibhoga’ (shared use); by means of that. The connection is: ‘He was favored by that shared use and by being established as an equal.’

Idāni –

Now—

“Ahaṃ bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharāmi, kassapopi bhikkhave yāvade ākaṅkhati vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.152) –

“Bhikkhus, for as long as I wish, secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness. Bhikkhus, for as long as Kassapa wishes, secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness,” and so on.

Navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāpabhede [V 1.0044] uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhapanatthāya bhagavatā vuttaṃ kassapasaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 2.151) āgataṃ pāḷimimaṃ peyyālamukhena, ādiggahaṇena ca saṅkhipitvā dassento āha “ahaṃ bhikkhave”tiādi.

Wishing to show, by abbreviating it through the elision formula and by taking the beginning, this Pāḷi text that comes in the Kassapa Saṃyutta, spoken by the Blessed One for the purpose of establishing Kassapa as exactly equal to himself in the superhuman states distinguished by the nine successive abidings and the six supernormal knowledges, the commentator said: “Ahaṃ bhikkhave,” and so on.

Tattha yāvadeti yāvadeva, yattakaṃ kālaṃ ākaṅkhāmi, tattakaṃ kālaṃ viharāmīti attho. Tatoyeva hi majjhimagaṇṭhipade, cūḷagaṇṭhipade ca “yāvadeti yāvadevāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti likhitaṃ. Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyampi “yāvade ākaṅkhāmīti yāvadeva icchāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2.152) attho vutto. Tathā hi tattha līnatthapakāsaniyaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherena “yāvadevāti iminā samānatthaṃ ‘yāvade’ti idaṃ pada”nti vuttaṃ. Potthakesu pana katthaci “yāvadevā”ti ayameva pāṭho dissati. Api ca yāvadeti yattakaṃ samāpattivihāraṃ viharituṃ ākaṅkhāmi, tattakaṃ samāpattivihāraṃ viharāmīti samāpattiṭṭhāne, yattakaṃ abhiññāvohāraṃ voharituṃ [M 1.0049] ākaṅkhāmi, tattakaṃ abhiññāvohāraṃ voharāmīti abhiññāṭhāne ca saha pāṭhasesena attho veditabbo. Ācariyadhammapālattherenāpi tadevatthaṃ yathālābhanayena dassetuṃ “yattake samāpattivihāre, abhiññāvohāre vā ākaṅkhanto vihārāmi ceva voharāmi ca, tathā kassapopīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Apare pana “yāvadeti ‘yaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ ākaṅkhāmi, taṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja vihārāmī’tiādinā samāpattiṭṭhāne, iddhividhābhiññāṭhāne ca ajjhāharitassa ta-saddassa kammavasena ‘yaṃ dibbasotaṃ ākaṅkhāmi, tena dibbasotena sadde suṇāmī’tiādinā sesābhiññāṭhāne karaṇavasena yojanā vattabbā”ti vadanti. Vivicceva kāmehīti ettha eva-saddo niyamattho, ubhayattha yojetabbo. Yamettha vattabbaṃ, tadupari āvi bhavissati.

Therein, 'yāvade' means 'yāvadeva'; the meaning is: 'For whatever length of time I wish, for that length of time I dwell.' For this very reason, in the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada and the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada it is written: "'Yāvade' means 'yāvadeva.'" In the Saṃyutta Commentary as well, the meaning is stated: "'Yāvade ākaṅkhāmi' means 'yāvadeva icchāmi' (just as much as I desire)." Indeed, in the Līnatthapakāsanī commentary on that text, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has said: "This word 'yāvade' has the same meaning as 'yāvadeva.'" In some manuscripts, however, this very reading 'yāvadevā' is found. Furthermore, 'yāvade' should be understood with the rest of the text as follows: in the context of attainments (samāpatti), it means, 'Whatever abiding in attainment I wish to dwell in, that abiding in attainment I dwell in'; and in the context of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), 'Whatever engagement with supernormal knowledge I wish to engage in, that engagement with supernormal knowledge I engage in.' The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla also, in order to show that very meaning according to the context, has said: "The meaning is: 'Whatever abidings in attainment or engagements with supernormal knowledge I, wishing for, dwell in and engage with, so too does Kassapa.'" Other teachers, however, say: "The connection should be stated as follows: in the context of attainments and in the context of the supernormal knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha), by way of the object case (kamma) for the supplied pronoun 'ta', as in, 'Whatever first jhāna I wish for, that first jhāna I, having attained, dwell in,' and so on; and in the context of the remaining supernormal knowledges, by way of the instrumental case (karaṇa), as in, 'Whatever divine ear I wish for, with that divine ear I hear sounds,' and so on." Herein, in 'vivicceva kāmehi', the word 'eva' has the meaning of determination and should be connected in both places. Whatever is to be said about this will become clear later on.

Navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhedeti ettha navānupubbavihārā nāma anupaṭipāṭiyā samāpajjitabbattā evaṃsaññitā nirodhasamāpattiyā saha aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Chaḷabhiññā nāma āsavakkhayañāṇena saha pañcābhiññāyo. Katthaci potthake cettha ādisaddo dissati. So anadhippeto yathāvuttāya pāḷiyā gahetabbassa atthassa anavasesattā. Manussesu, manussānaṃ vā uttaribhūtānaṃ, uttarīnaṃ vā manussānaṃ jhāyīnañceva ariyānañca dhammoti uttarimanussadhammo, manussadhammā vā uttarīti uttarimanussadhammo. Dasa kusalakammapathā cettha vinā bhāvanāmanasikārena pakatiyāva manussehi nibbattetabbato, manussattabhāvāvahanato ca manussadhammo nāma, tato uttari pana jhānādi uttarimanussadhammoti veditabbo. Samasamaṭṭhapanenāti “ahaṃ yattakaṃ kālaṃ, yattake vā samāpattivihāre, yattakā abhiññāyo ca vaḷañjemi[V 1.0045], tathā kassapopī”ti evaṃ samasamaṃ katvā ṭhapanena. Anekaṭṭhānesu ṭhapanaṃ, kassacipi uttarimanussadhammassa asesabhāvena ekantasamaṭṭhapanaṃ vā sandhāya “samasamaṭṭhapanenā”ti vuttaṃ, idañca navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññābhāvasāmaññena pasaṃsāmattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi āyasmā mahākassapo bhagavā viya devasikaṃ catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā samāpattiyo samāpajjati, yamakapāṭihāriyādivasena ca abhiññāyo vaḷañjetīti. Ettha ca uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhapanenā”ti idaṃ nidassanamattanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi –

Herein, in 'the distinctions of the nine successive abidings and the six supernormal knowledges': the 'nine successive abidings' are so-called because they are to be attained in sequence; they are the eight attainments together with the attainment of cessation. The 'six supernormal knowledges' are the five supernormal knowledges together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. In some manuscripts, the word 'etc.' (ādi) is found here. That is not intended, because there is no remainder of the meaning to be taken from the Pāḷi as stated. A 'superhuman state' (uttarimanussadhamma) is a state of meditators and noble ones, who are superior among humans or superior to humans. Or, it is a state superior to human states. Herein, the ten wholesome courses of action are called 'human states' (manussadhamma) because they are to be accomplished by humans naturally, without the mental application of cultivation, and because they lead to the state of a human being. But a state superior to that, such as jhāna and so on, should be understood as a 'superhuman state'. 'By establishing as exactly equal' means establishing as exactly equal thus: 'For whatever length of time, or whatever abidings in attainment, and whatever supernormal knowledges I make use of, so too does Kassapa.'
