The phrase 'by establishing as exactly equal' is said with reference to establishing equality in many instances, or to establishing someone as completely equal in every respect of any superhuman state. And this should be seen as mere praise on account of the commonality of possessing the nine successive abidings and the six supernormal knowledges. For indeed, the Venerable Mahākassapa does not attain attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand koṭis daily as the Blessed One does, nor does he make use of the supernormal knowledges by way of the twin miracle and so on. And herein, this statement 'by establishing as equal to himself in the superhuman states' should be known as a mere illustration. For indeed—

“Ovada [M 1.0050] kassapa bhikkhū, karohi kassapa bhikkhūnaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ, ahaṃ vā kassapa bhikkhū ovadeyyaṃ, tvaṃ vā. Ahaṃ vā kassapa bhikkhūnaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kareyyaṃ, tvaṃ vā”ti –

“Kassapa, admonish the bhikkhus; Kassapa, give the bhikkhus a talk on the Dhamma. Either I, Kassapa, should admonish the bhikkhus, or you. Either I, Kassapa, should give the bhikkhus a talk on the Dhamma, or you.”

Evampi attanā samasamaṭṭhapanamakāsiyevāti.

In this way also, he did indeed establish him as equal to himself.

Tathāti rūpūpasaṃhāro yathā anuggahito, tathā pasaṃsitoti. Ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvāti bhagavatā attanoyeva pāṇiṃ ākāse cāletvā kulesu alaggacittatāya ceva karaṇabhūtāya pasaṃsitoti sambandho. Alaggacittatāyāti vā ādhāre bhummaṃ, ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvā kulūpakassa bhikkhuno alaggacittatāya kulesu alagganacittena bhavituṃ yuttatāya ceva maññeva sakkhiṃ katvā pasaṃsitoti attho. Yathāha –

'Tathā' (Thus) means: just as he was favored by the presentation of a form, so was he praised. 'Waving his hand in the air'—the connection is that the Blessed One, having waved his own hand in the air, praised him on account of his state of mind being unattached to families, which was the cause. Alternatively, 'alaggacittatāya' (on account of the unattached state of mind) is a locative in the sense of a basis. The meaning is: having waved his hand in the air, he praised him in the matter of the unattached state of mind of a bhikkhu who frequents families, and on account of the suitability of being one with a mind unattached to families, having made me (Kassapa) indeed the witness. As it is said—

“Atha kho bhagavā ākāse pāṇiṃ cālesi seyyathāpi bhikkhave, ayaṃ ākāse pāṇi na sajjati na gayhati na bajjhati, evameva kho bhikkhave yassa kassaci bhikkhuno kulāni upasaṅkamato kulesu cittaṃ na sajjati na gayhati na bajjhati ‘labhantu lābhakāmā, puññakāmā karontu puññānī’ti. Yathā sakena lābhena attamano hoti sumano, evaṃ paresaṃ lābhena attamano hoti sumano. Evarūpo kho bhikkhave bhikkhu arahati kulāni upasaṅkamituṃ. Kassapassa bhikkhave kulāni upasaṅkamato kulesu cittaṃ na sajjati na gayhati na bajjhati ‘labhantu lābhakāmā, puññakāmā karontu puññānī’ti. Yathā sakena lābhena attamano hoti sumano, evaṃ paresaṃ lābhena attamano hoti sumano”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.146).

Then the Blessed One moved his hand in the air. ‘Just as, monks, this hand does not stick, is not caught, and is not bound in the air, even so, monks, for any monk who approaches families, his mind does not stick, is not caught, and is not bound in regard to families, thinking: “Let those who desire gain obtain gain; let those who desire merit make merit.” Just as he is pleased and joyful with his own gain, so too is he pleased and joyful with the gain of others. A monk of such a nature, monks, is worthy to approach families. When Kassapa approaches families, monks, his mind does not stick, is not caught, and is not bound in regard to families, thinking: “Let those who desire gain obtain gain; let those who desire merit make merit.” Just as he is pleased and joyful with his own gain, so too is he pleased and joyful with the gain of others.’”

Tattha ākāse pāṇiṃ cālesīti nīle gaganantare yamakavijjukaṃ sañcālayamāno viya heṭṭhābhāge[V 1.0046], uparibhāge, ubhato ca passesu pāṇiṃ sañcālesi, idañca pana tepiṭake buddhavacane asambhinnapadaṃ nāma. Attamanoti sakamano, na domanassena pacchinditvā gahitamano. Sumanoti tuṭṭhamano, idāni yo hīnādhimuttiko micchāpaṭipanno evaṃ [M 1.0051] vadeyya “sammāsambuddho ‘alaggacittatāya ākāse cālitapāṇūpamā kulāni upasaṅkamathā’ti vadanto aṭṭhāne ṭhapeti, asayhabhāraṃ āropeti, yaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ, taṃ kārehī”ti, tassa vādapathaṃ pacchinditvā “sakkā ca kho evaṃ kātuṃ, atthi evarūpo bhikkhū”ti āyasmantaṃ mahākassapattherameva sakkhiṃ katvā dassento “kassapassa bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

Herein, ‘moved his hand in the air’ means that in the middle of the dark blue sky, as if brandishing a twin flash of lightning, he moved his hand well in the lower region, the upper region, and on both sides. And this word sañcālesi is what is called in the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, an asambhinnapada, a word not different in meaning from cālesi. ‘Pleased’ means having one’s own mind, not a mind seized and overcome by displeasure. ‘Joyful’ means having a delighted mind. Now, if some person of inferior inclination and wrong practice were to say: ‘The Perfectly Enlightened One, in saying, “Approach families with a mind unattached, like a hand moved in the air,” sets an impossible standard, imposes an unbearable burden, and makes one do what cannot be done,’ then, to cut off that line of argument and to show that it is indeed possible to act in this way and that such a monk exists, the Blessed One, making the Venerable Mahākassapa himself the witness, spoke the words beginning, ‘For Kassapa, monks...’

Aññampi pasaṃsanamāha “candopamapaṭipadāya cā”ti, candapaṭibhāgāya paṭipadāya ca karaṇabhūtāya pasaṃsito, tassaṃ vā ādhārabhūtāya maññeva sakkhiṃ katvā pasaṃsitoti attho. Yathāha –

He spoke of another praise with the words, ‘and by the practice comparable to the moon.’ The meaning is that he was praised by means of this practice comparable to the moon, which is the instrument. Or alternatively, that he was praised by the Blessed One making me [Kassapa] the witness in that practice, which is the basis. As it is said:

“Candūpamā bhikkhave kulāni upasaṅkamatha apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittaṃ niccanavakā kulesu appagabbhā. Seyyathāpi bhikkhave puriso jarudapānaṃ vā olokeyya pabbatavisamaṃ vā nadīviduggaṃ vā apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittaṃ, evameva kho bhikkhave candūpamā kulāni upasaṅkamatha apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittaṃ niccanavakā kulesu appagabbhā. Kassapo bhikkhave candūpamo kulāni upasaṅkamati apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittaṃ niccanavako kulesu appagabbho”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.146).

‘Monks, approach families like the moon: keeping the body withdrawn, keeping the mind withdrawn, always as if a newcomer among families, and without being forward. Just as, monks, a person might look into an old, dilapidated well, or a mountain precipice, or a treacherous river crossing, keeping the body withdrawn and keeping the mind withdrawn, even so, monks, approach families like the moon: keeping the body withdrawn, keeping the mind withdrawn, always as if a newcomer among families, and without being forward. Kassapa, monks, approaches families like the moon: keeping his body withdrawn, keeping his mind withdrawn, always as if a newcomer among families, and without being forward.’”

Tattha candūpamāti candasadisā hutvā. Kiṃ parimaṇḍalatāya sadisāti? No, apica kho yathā cando gaganatalaṃ pakkhandamāno na kenaci saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā sinehaṃ vā ālayaṃ vā nikantiṃ vā patthanaṃ vā pariyuṭṭhānaṃ vā karoti, na ca na hoti mahājanassa piyo manāpo, tumhepi evaṃ kenaci saddhiṃ santhavādīnaṃ akaraṇena bahujanassa piyā manāpā candūpamā hutvā khattiyakulādīni cattāri kulāni upasaṅkamathāti attho. Apica yathā cando andhakāraṃ vidhamati, ālokaṃ pharati, evaṃ kilesandhakāravidhamanena, ñāṇālokapharaṇena ca candūpamā hutvāti evamādīhipi nayehi attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, ‘like the moon’ means being similar to the moon. Is it similar in respect to its roundness? No. Rather, just as the moon, when ascending into the sky, does not form any intimacy, affection, attachment, fondness, longing, or obsession with anyone, and yet it is indeed dear and pleasing to the great populace; so too should you, by not forming intimacy and the like with anyone, become dear and pleasing to the many people and, being like the moon, approach the four kinds of families, starting with the warrior class. This is the meaning. Furthermore, just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, so too one is ‘like the moon’ by dispelling the darkness of the defilements and spreading the light of wisdom. The meaning should be understood according to these and other similar methods.

Apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittanti teneva santhavādīnamakaraṇena kāyañca cittañca apakassitvā, akaḍḍhitvā apanetvāti attho. Niccanavakāti niccaṃ navikāva, āgantukasadisā [V 1.0047] eva hutvāti attho. Āgantuko [M 1.0052] hi paṭipāṭiyā sampattagehaṃ pavisitvā sace naṃ gharasāmikā disvā “amhākaṃ puttabhātaropi vippavāsagatā evaṃ vicariṃsū”ti anukampamānā nisīdāpetvā bhojenti, bhuttamattoyeva “tumhākaṃ bhājanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti uṭṭhāya pakkamati, na tehi saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā karoti, kiccakaraṇīyāni vā saṃvidahati, evaṃ tumhepi paṭipāṭiyā sampattagharaṃ pavisitvā yaṃ iriyāpathesu pasannā manussā denti, taṃ gahetvā pacchinnasanthavā tesaṃ kiccakaraṇīye abyāvaṭā hutvā nikkhamathāti dīpeti. Appagabbhāti na pagabbhā, aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena, catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena, anekaṭṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca virahitā kulāni upasaṅkamathāti attho.

The phrase ‘keeping the body withdrawn, keeping the mind withdrawn’ means having withdrawn, not dragged, and removed both body and mind by that very act of not forming intimacy and the like. The phrase ‘always as if a newcomer’ means always being like a new arrival, just like a guest. For a guest, having entered a house he has come to in due course, if the householders see him and, feeling compassion, think, ‘Our own sons and brothers have gone abroad and wander just like this,’ they have him sit down and they feed him. As soon as he has eaten, he says, ‘Please take your bowl,’ and then gets up and departs. He does not form intimacy with them, nor does he get involved in their affairs. In the same way, this passage shows that you too, having entered a house you have come to in due course, should accept whatever the people, being pleased with your deportment, may give. Then, with intimacy severed and being uninvolved in their affairs, you should depart. The phrase ‘without being forward’ means not being bold. The meaning is that you should approach families while being devoid of the eight kinds of bodily forwardness, the four kinds of verbal forwardness, and the many kinds of mental forwardness.

Jarudapānanti jiṇṇakūpaṃ. Pabbatavisamanti pabbate visamaṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ. Nadīvidugganti nadiyā viduggaṃ chinnataṭaṭṭhānaṃ. Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – jarudapānādayo viya hi cattāri kulāni, olokanapuriso viya bhikkhu, yathā pana anapakaṭṭhakāyacitto tāni olokento puriso tattha patati, evaṃ arakkhitehi kāyādīhi kulāni upasaṅkamanto bhikkhu kulesu bajjhati, tato nānappakāraṃ sīlapādabhañjanādikaṃ anatthaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yathā pana apakaṭṭhakāyacitto puriso tattha na patati, evaṃ rakkhiteneva kāyena, rakkhitāya vācāya, rakkhitehi cittehi, sūpaṭṭhitāya satiyā apakaṭṭhakāyacitto hutvā kulāni upasaṅkamanto bhikkhu kulesu na bajjhati, athassa sīlasaddhāsamādhipaññāsaṅkhātāni pādahatthakucchisīsāni na bhañjanti, rāgakaṇṭakādayo na vijjhanti, sukhito yenakāmaṃ agatapubbaṃ nibbānadisaṃ gacchati, evarūpo ayaṃ mahākassapoti hīnādhimuttikassa micchāpaṭipannassa vādapathapacchindanatthaṃ mahākassapattheraṃ eva sakkhiṃ katvā dassento “kassapo bhikkhave”tiādimāhāti. Evampettha atthamicchantialaggacittatāsaṅkhātāya candopamapaṭipadāya karaṇabhūtāya pasaṃsito, tassaṃ vā ādhārabhūtāya maññeva sakkhiṃ katvā pasaṃsitoti, evaṃ sati ceva-saddo, ca-saddo ca na payujjitabbo dvinnaṃ padānaṃ tulyādhikaraṇattā, ayameva attho pāṭho ca yuttataro viya dissati parinibbānasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ “ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvā candūpamaṃ paṭipadaṃ kathento maṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā kathesī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.232) vuttattāti.

`Jarudapāna` means an old, ruined well. `Pabbatavisama` means an uneven place on a mountain, a precipice. `Nadīvidugga` means a difficult passage in a river, a place with a collapsed bank. Herein, the phrase `evameva kho` serves to connect the analogy. Indeed, the four families are to be seen as like the ruined well and so on, and the bhikkhu as like the man looking down. To explain further: just as a man with an unwithdrawn body and mind, looking down at those places, falls therein, so too a bhikkhu who approaches families with unguarded body, speech, and mind becomes bound in those families. From that, he comes to various kinds of harm, such as the breaking of the leg of virtue. But just as a man with a withdrawn body and mind does not fall therein, so too a bhikkhu who approaches families with a guarded body, guarded speech, guarded mind, and well-established mindfulness—having become withdrawn in body and mind—is not bound in those families. Then for him, his feet, hands, belly, and head—known as virtue, faith, concentration, and wisdom—are not broken. The thorns of lust and so on do not pierce him. Happy, he goes wherever he wishes to the destination of Nibbāna, never reached before. This Mahākassapa is of such a nature. Thus, in order to cut off the path of argument of one with inferior resolve and wrong practice, the Blessed One, making the Elder Mahākassapa himself the witness, showed this, saying, “Kassapa, monks…” and so on. Thus also, herein the teachers desire this meaning: he was praised by means of the moon-like practice, which is instrumental, known as the state of having an unattached mind. Or alternatively, in that moon-like practice, which is the basis, he was praised by making me (Kassapa) the witness. This being the case, the words ‘ceva’ and ‘ca’ should not be used, because the two terms have the same referent. This very meaning and this very reading seem more suitable, because in the commentary on the Parinibbāna Sutta it is said: “Waving his hand in the air, while speaking of the moon-like practice, he spoke making me his physical witness.”

Tassa [M 1.0053] kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissati, aññatra dhammavinayasaṅgāyanāti adhippāyo. Tattha tassāti yaṃ-saddassa kāraṇanidassane “tasmā”ti ajjhāharitvā tassa meti attho, kiriyāparāmasane pana tassa anuggahaṇassa, pasaṃsanassa cāti. Potthakesupi katthaci “tassa me”ti pāṭho dissati, evaṃ sati kiriyāparāmasane “tassā”ti aparaṃ padamajjhāharitabbaṃ. Natthi [V 1.0048] iṇaṃ yassāti aṇaṇo, tassa bhāvo āṇaṇyaṃ. Dhammavinayasaṅgāyanaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kiṃ nāma tassa iṇavirahitattaṃ bhavissati, na bhavissati evāti attho. “Nanu maṃ bhagavā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ upamāvasena vibhāveti. Sakakavacaissariyānuppadānenāti ettha kavaco nāma uracchado, yena uro chādīyate, tassa ca cīvaranidassanena gahaṇaṃ, issariyassa pana abhiññāsamāpattinidassanenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakanti kulavaṃsassa kulapaveṇiyā patiṭṭhāpakaṃ. “Me”ti padassa niccasāpekkhattā saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakoti samāso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sattusaṅghanimmaddanena attano kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ sakakavacaissariyānuppadānena kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ puttaṃ rājā viya bhagavāpi maṃ dīghadassī “saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako me ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti mantvā sāsanapaccatthikagaṇanimmaddanena saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ cīvaradānasamasamaṭṭhapanasaṅkhātena iminā asādhāraṇānuggahena anuggahesi nanu, imāya ca uḷārāya pasaṃsāya pasaṃsi nanūti. Iti cintayantoti ettha itisaddena “antaradhāpeyyuṃ, saṅgāyeyyaṃ, kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissatī”ti vacanapubbaṅgamaṃ, “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjatī”tiādi vākyattayaṃ nidasseti.

The intention is this: ‘What other freedom from debt will there be for me, besides the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya?’ Therein, regarding the word `tassa`, when indicating the reason for the relative pronoun, one should supply `tasmā` and understand the meaning as `tassa me` (for me, that one). However, when considering the action, the connection should be understood as ‘of that support’ and ‘of that praise.’ In some manuscripts, the reading `tassa me` is found; this being the case, when considering the action, another word `tassa` should be supplied. One for whom there is no debt (`iṇaṃ`) is called ‘debt-free’ (`aṇaṇo`); his state is ‘freedom from debt’ (`āṇaṇyaṃ`). Besides the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, what other state of being free from debt will there be for him? There will be none at all. This is the meaning. He clarifies this very meaning that was stated, beginning with ‘Did not the Blessed One…,’ by means of a simile. Herein, in the phrase ‘by granting his own armor and sovereignty,’ ‘armor’ (`kavaca`) is a breastplate, by which the chest is covered; its taking should be understood by the indication of the robe. And the taking of ‘sovereignty’ (`issariya`) should be understood by the indication of the supernormal knowledges and attainments. `Kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ` means ‘establisher of the family lineage.’ Because the word `me` has a constant requirement, the compound should be understood as `saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako` (establisher of the lineage of the good Dhamma). This is what is said: Just as a king, for the sake of establishing his own lineage by crushing the host of enemies, supports a son who establishes the lineage by granting his own armor and sovereignty, so too the far-seeing Blessed One, thinking, ‘This one will be the establisher of my lineage of the good Dhamma,’ surely supported me with this uncommon favor—namely, the gift of the robe and placing me on an equal footing—for the sake of establishing the lineage of the good Dhamma by crushing the host of adversaries of the Sāsana, did he not? And surely he praised me with this lofty praise, did he not? In the phrase ‘thus reflecting,’ the word `iti` indicates the triad of sentences beginning with `ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati`, which are preceded by the words: ‘they might disappear,’ ‘I should recite,’ and ‘what other freedom from debt will there be?’

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ saṅgītikkhandhakapāḷiyā sādhento āha “yathāhā”tiādi. Tattha yathāhāti kiṃ āha, mayā vuttassa atthassa sādhakaṃ kiṃ āhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā vā yena pakārena mayā vuttaṃ, tathā tena pakārena pāḷiyampi āhāti attho. Yathā vā yaṃ vacanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āha, tathā tena vacanena mayā vuttavacanaṃ saṃsandati ceva sameti ca yathā taṃ gaṅgodakena yamunodakantipi vattabbo pāḷiyā sādhanatthaṃ udāharitabhāvassa paccakkhato viññāyamānattā, viññāyamānatthassa ca saddassa payoge kāmācārattā. Adhippāyavibhāvanatthā hi atthayojanā. Yathā vā yena pakārena dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [M 1.0054] ussāhaṃ janesi, tathā tena pakārena pāḷiyampi āhāti attho. Evamīdisesu.

Now, wishing to establish the aforesaid meaning with the Pāli of the Saṅgītikhandhaka, he said, ‘as it was said,’ and so on. Therein, ‘as it was said’ means: ‘What did he say? What statement did he make that establishes the meaning I have stated?’ This is what is meant. Or alternatively, the meaning is: in whatever way I have spoken, in that same way he also spoke in the Pāli. Or alternatively, it can also be said thus: Whatever statement he made in the Pāli, with that statement the statement I have made connects and agrees, just as the water of the Yamunā connects and agrees with the water of the Ganges. This is because the fact of it being cited to establish something with the Pāli is directly evident, and because there is freedom of choice in the use of a word whose meaning is evident. Indeed, the application of meaning is for the purpose of clarifying the intention. Or alternatively, the meaning is: in whatever way he generated enthusiasm in the bhikkhus for the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, in that same way he also spoke in the Pāli. Thus it should be understood in such cases.

Ekamidāhanti ettha idanti nipātamattaṃ. Ekaṃ samayanti ca bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ, ekasmiṃ samayeti attho. Pāvāyāti pāvānagarato, tattha piṇḍāya caritvā “kusināraṃ gamissāmī”ti addhānamaggappaṭipannoti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhānamaggoti ca dīghamaggo vuccati, dīghapariyāyo hettha addhānasaddo. Mahatāti guṇamahattenapi saṅkhyāmahattenapi mahatā. “Pañcamattehī”tiādinā saṅkhyāmahattaṃ dasseti, mattasaddo ca pamāṇavacano “bhojane mattaññutā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.16) viya. “Dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ janesī”ti etassatthassa sādhanatthaṃ āhatā “atha kho”tiādikā pāḷi yathāvuttamatthaṃ na sādheti[V 1.0049]. Na hettha ussāhajananappakāro āgatoti codanaṃ pariharitumāha “sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthārato veditabba”nti. Evampesā codanā tadavatthāyevāti vuttaṃ “tato paraṃ āhā”tiādi. Apica yathāvuttatthasādhikā pāḷi mahatarāti ganthagarutāpariharaṇatthaṃ majjhe peyyālamukhena ādiantameva pāḷiṃ dassento “sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthārato veditabba”nti āha. Tena hi “atha khvāhaṃ āvuso maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdī”ti (cūḷava. 437) vuttapāḷito paṭṭhāya “yaṃ na icchissāma, na taṃ karissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 437) vuttapāḷipariyosānaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ dasseti.

In 'Ekamidāhaṃ,' the word 'idaṃ' is merely a particle. The phrase 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' is an accusative expression in the locative sense; the meaning is 'on one occasion.' 'Pāvāya' means from the city of Pāvā; having wandered there for alms, he set out on the long road, thinking 'I will go to Kusinārā.' This is the intended meaning. A long road is also called 'addhānamagga'; here, the word 'addhāna' is a synonym for 'long'. 'Mahatā' means great, both by greatness of quality and by greatness of number. By 'pañcamattehi,' etc., it shows greatness of number, and the word 'matta' denotes measure, as in 'knowledge of the measure in food,' etc. The Pāḷi which was brought, beginning with 'atha kho,' etc., to establish the meaning 'he aroused effort for the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya,' does not establish the meaning as stated. To refute the objection that 'the manner of arousing effort has not come here,' he said, 'the entire Subhaddakaṇḍa should be understood in detail.' Even so, this objection remains in that very state; therefore, the commentator said 'tato paraṃ āha,' etc. Furthermore, because the Pāḷi that establishes the aforesaid meaning is very extensive, therefore, to avoid the heaviness of the text, showing only the beginning and the end of that Pāḷi by means of an ellipsis in the middle, he said, 'the entire Subhaddakaṇḍa should be understood in detail.' By that, he indicates the Subhaddakaṇḍa, starting from the Pāḷi passage spoken, 'Then, friends, having stepped off the road, I sat down at the foot of a certain tree,' up to the end of the Pāḷi passage spoken, 'What we shall not wish for, that we shall not do.'

“Tato para”ntiādinā pana tadavasesaṃ “handa mayaṃ āvuso”tiādikaṃ ussāhajananappakāradassanapāḷiṃ. Tasmā tato paraṃ āhāti ettha subhaddakaṇḍato paraṃ ussāhajananappakāradassanavacanamāhāti attho veditabbo. Mahāgaṇṭhipadepi hi soyevattho vutto. Ācariyasāriputtattherenāpi (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) tatheva adhippeto. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana “tato paranti tato bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananato parato”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, tadetaṃ vicāretabbaṃ heṭṭhā ussāhajananappakārassa pāḷiyaṃ avuttattā. Ayameva hi ussāhajananappakāro yadidaṃ “handa mayaṃ āvuso dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma, pure adhammo dippatī”tiādi. Yadi [M 1.0055] pana subhaddakaṇḍameva ussāhajananahetubhūtassa subhaddena vuttavacanassa pakāsanattā ussāhajanananti vadeyya, natthevettha vicāretabbatāti. Pure adhammo dippatīti ettha adhammo nāma dasakusalakammapathapaṭipakkhabhūto adhammo. Dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ ussāhajananappasaṅgattā vā tadasaṅgāyanahetuko dosagaṇopi sambhavati, “adhammavādino balavanto honti, dhammavādino dubbalā hontī”ti vuttattā sīlavipattiādihetuko pāpicchatādidosagaṇo adhammotipi vadanti. Pure dippatīti api nāma dippati. Saṃsayatthe hi pure-saddo. Atha vā yāva adhammo dhammaṃ paṭibāhituṃ samattho hoti, tato puretaramevāti attho. Āsanne hi anadhippete ayaṃ pure-saddo. Dippatīti dippissati, pure-saddayogena hi anāgatatthe ayaṃ vattamānapayogo yathā “purā vassati devo”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, by 'Tato paraṃ,' etc., he indicates the remaining Pāḷi that shows the manner of arousing effort, beginning with 'handa mayaṃ āvuso.' Therefore, here in 'tato paraṃ āha,' the meaning should be understood as: after the Subhaddakaṇḍa, he spoke the words showing the manner of arousing effort. Indeed, the same meaning is stated in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada. The teacher, the Elder Sāriputta, also intended it thus. However, the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, has said: '“tato paraṃ” means after the arousing of effort in the monks.' This should be investigated, because the manner of arousing effort was not spoken in the Pāḷi before. For this itself is the manner of arousing effort, that is: 'Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, before what is not-Dhamma shines forth,' etc. However, if one were to say that the Subhaddakaṇḍa itself is the 'arousing of effort' because it proclaims the words spoken by Subhadda which were the cause for arousing effort, in that case, there is nothing here that needs to be investigated. Here in 'pure adhammo dippati,' 'adhammo' means that which is the opposite of the ten wholesome courses of action. Or, due to the context of arousing effort for the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, a collection of faults caused by not reciting it is also possible; because it is said, 'Speakers of not-Dhamma become powerful, speakers of Dhamma become weak,' the teachers also say that 'adhammo' is the collection of faults, such as evil desire, which has the corruption of virtue, etc., as its cause. 'Pure dippati' means 'might it shine forth?'. For the word 'pure' is in the sense of doubt. Alternatively, the meaning is: even before the not-Dhamma is able to obstruct the Dhamma. The word 'pure' here is not intended to mean 'near'. 'Dippati' means 'it will shine forth'; due to the connection with the word 'pure', this present tense form is in the future sense, as in 'purā vassati devo' (the sky will rain before long). For thus it has been said:

“Anāgate sannicchaye, tathātīte ciratane;

Kāladvayepi kavīhi, puresaddo payujjate”ti. (vajira. ṭī. bāhiranidānakathāvaṇṇanā);

'In the determined future, and likewise in the distant past; in both periods of time, the word 'pure' is used by the wise.'

“Pureyāvapurāyoge[V 1.0050], niccaṃ vā karahi kadā;

Lacchāyamapi kiṃ vutte, vattamānā bhavissatī”ti ca.

And: 'In connection with the words `pure`, `yāva`, and `purā`, or always, and when one asks, “When? When? What shall I obtain?,” the present tense is used for the future.'

Keci panettha evaṃ vaṇṇayanti – pureti pacchā anāgate, yathā addhānaṃ gacchantassa gantabbamaggo “pure”ti vuccati, tathā idhāpi maggagamananayena anāgatakālo “pure”ti vuccatīti. Evaṃ sati taṃkālāpekkhāya cettha vattamānapayogo sambhavati. Dhammo paṭibāhiyyatīti etthāpi pure-saddena yojetvā vuttanayena attho veditabbo, tathā dhammopi adhammaviparītavasena, ito parampi eseva nayo. Avinayoti pahānavinayasaṃvaravinayānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūto avinayo. Vinayavādino dubbalā hontīti evaṃ iti-saddena pāṭho, so “tato paraṃ āhā”ti ettha āha-saddena sambajjhitabbo.

Some, however, explain it thus: 'pure' means in the future, later. Just as for one traveling a long road, the road to be traveled is called 'ahead' (`pure`), so too here, by the analogy of traveling a road, the future time is called 'pure.' Thus they explain. This being so, with reference to that time, the use of the present tense here is possible. Also in 'the Dhamma is obstructed' (`dhammo paṭibāhiyyatī`), the meaning should be understood in the aforesaid manner by connecting it with the word 'pure'. Likewise, 'Dhamma' should be understood as the opposite of 'not-Dhamma'. From here on, this is the same method. 'Avinayo' (not-discipline) is that which is the opposite of the discipline of abandoning and the discipline of restraint. The reading should be seen together with the word 'iti', thus: 'vinayavādino dubbalā honti iti' (speakers of Vinaya become weak). That 'iti' should be connected with the word 'āha' in 'tato paraṃ āha'.

Tena hīti uyyojanatthe nipāto. Uccinane uyyojentā hi mahākassapattheraṃ evamāhaṃsu “bhikkhū uccinatū”ti, saṅgītiyā anurūpe bhikkhū uccinitvā upadhāretvā gaṇhātūti attho. “Sakala…pe… pariggahesī”ti etena sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavapariyantānaṃ yathāvuttapuggalānaṃ satipi [M 1.0056] āgamādhigamasambhave saha paṭisambhidāhi pana tevijjādiguṇayuttānaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiyā ukkaṃsagatattā saṅgītiyā bahūpakārataṃ dasseti. Sakalaṃ suttageyyādikaṃ navaṅgaṃ ettha, etassāti vā sakalanavaṅgaṃ, satthu bhagavato sāsanaṃ satthusāsanaṃ sāsīyati etenāti katvā, tadeva satthusāsananti sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanaṃ. Nava vā suttageyyādīni aṅgāni ettha, etassāti vā navaṅgaṃ, tameva satthusāsanaṃ, tañca sakalameva, na ekadesanti tathā. Atthakāmena pariyāpuṇitabbā sikkhitabbā, diṭṭhadhammikādipurisatthaṃ vā nipphādetuṃ pariyattā samatthāti pariyatti, tīṇi piṭakāni, sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanasaṅkhātā pariyatti, taṃ dhārentīti tathā, tādiseti attho. Puthujjana…pe… sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavabhikkhūti ettha –

The term 'Tena hi' is a particle in the sense of urging. Indeed, in urging the selection, they spoke thus to the Elder Mahākassapa: 'Select the monks.' The meaning is: 'Having selected, having examined, may he take the monks suitable for the council.' By this phrase 'Sakala…pe… pariggahesī,' it is shown that there is great benefit to the council because, although there is the possibility of attaining scripture and realization for the aforementioned persons up to the dry-insight arahants, the accomplishment of scripture and realization for those endowed with qualities such as the three knowledges along with the analytical knowledges has reached excellence. The entire ninefold [teaching] such as suttas, geyyas, etc., is in this [dispensation] (ettha), or belongs to this (etassa), therefore it is the 'entire ninefold' (sakalanavaṅgaṃ). The teaching (sāsanaṃ) of the Teacher (satthu), the Blessed One, is the 'Teacher's Dispensation' (satthusāsanaṃ) because one is instructed (sāsīyati) by it (etena). That very thing is the Teacher's Dispensation, therefore it is the 'entire ninefold Teacher's Dispensation' (sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanaṃ). Alternatively, nine divisions such as suttas, geyyas, etc., are in this [dispensation], or belong to this, therefore it is 'ninefold' (navaṅgaṃ). That very thing is the Teacher's Dispensation, and it is entire, not a part; therefore, it is so [called]. It is 'pariyatti' (scripture) because it is to be learned (pariyāpuṇitabbā) and studied (sikkhitabbā) by one who desires benefit; or because it is sufficient (pariyattā) and able (samatthā) to accomplish the welfare of persons in this visible life and beyond. The three Piṭakas are the scripture (pariyatti) designated as the entire ninefold Teacher's Dispensation. Because they bear (dhārenti) it (taṃ), they are so [called 'bearers of the entire ninefold Teacher's Dispensation']. 'Tādise' (of such a kind) is the meaning. Herein, in the phrase 'Puthujjana…pe… sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavabhikkhū'—

“Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.61; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.51; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 88; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.130); –

'Two worldlings are spoken of by the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun: one worldling is blind, one is a virtuous worldling.'

Vuttesu kalyāṇaputhujjanāva adhippetā saddantarasannidhānenapi atthavisesassa viññātabbattā. Samathabhāvanāsinehābhāvena [V 1.0051] sukkhā lūkhā asiniddhā vipassanā etesanti sukkhavipassakā, teyeva khīṇāsavāti tathā. “Bhikkhū”ti pana sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Vuttañhi –

Among those spoken of, only the virtuous worldlings are intended, because the specific meaning is to be understood also by the proximity of the other word. Because for them, due to the absence of the moisture of serenity meditation, insight is dry, rough, and unlubricated, they are 'dry-insight practitioners' (sukkhavipassakā). They themselves are the ones with cankers destroyed (khīṇāsavā), therefore they are so called. Furthermore, the word 'bhikkhu' should be connected everywhere. For it has been said—

“Yañcatthavato saddekasesato vāpi suyyate;

Taṃ sambajjhate paccekaṃ, yathālābhaṃ kadācipī”ti.

And whatever word is heard after a meaningful word or after an elliptical compound, that word is connected with each individually; or sometimes it is connected according to what is appropriate.

Tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhareti ettha tiṇṇaṃ piṭakānaṃ samāhāro tipiṭakaṃ, taṃsaṅkhātaṃ navaṅgādivasena anekabhedabhinnaṃ sabbaṃ pariyattippabhedaṃ dhārentīti tathā, tādise. Anu anu taṃ samaṅginaṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti anubhāvo, soyeva ānubhāvo, pabhāvo, mahanto ānubhāvo yesaṃ te mahānubhāvā. “Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave”ti bhagavatā vuttavacanamupādāya pavattattā “etadagga”nti padaṃ anukaraṇajanāmaṃ nāma yathā “yevāpanaka”nti, tabbasena vuttaṭṭhānantaramidha etadaggaṃ, tamāropiteti attho. Etadaggaṃ eso bhikkhu aggoti vā āropitepi vaṭṭati. Tadanāropitāpi avasesaguṇasampannattā uccinitā tattha santīti dassetuṃ “yebhuyyenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tisso vijjā tevijjā, tā [M 1.0057] ādi yesaṃ chaḷabhiññādīnanti tevijjādayo, te bhedā anekappakārā yesanti tevijjādibhedā. Atha vā tisso vijjā assa khīṇāsavassāti tevijjo, so ādi yesaṃ chaḷabhiññādīnanti tevijjādayo, teyeva bhedā yesanti tevijjādibhedā. Tevijjachaḷabhiññādivasena anekabhedabhinne khīṇāsavabhikkhūyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ye sandhāya vuttanti ye bhikkhū sandhāya idaṃ “atha kho”tiādivacanaṃ saṅgītikkhandhake vuttaṃ. Iminā kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ avisesatova vuttaṃ, tathāpi visesena yathāvuttakhīṇāsavabhikkhūyeva sandhāya vuttanti pāḷiyā saṃsandanaṃ karoti.

Herein, regarding 'Tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhare' (bearers of all the divisions of the Tipiṭaka scripture): the collection of the three Piṭakas is the Tipiṭaka. Because they bear all the divisions of the scripture—which is designated as that [Tipiṭaka] and is divided into many divisions by way of the ninefold division, etc.—they are so called; 'tādise' means 'of such a kind'. 'Anubhāva' (power) is so called because it repeatedly (anu anu) develops and increases [that power] for one endowed with it. That very word becomes 'ānubhāvo' by vowel lengthening; it means 'pabhāvo' (influence). Those for whom there is great power (mahanto ānubhāvo) are 'mahānubhāvā' (of great power). Because the word 'etadaggaṃ' occurs in dependence on the words spoken by the Blessed One, 'Bhikkhus, this is the foremost,' it is a name born of imitation, like 'yevāpanakaṃ'. By the power of that [name], the position spoken of is here 'etadaggaṃ'. The meaning is 'appointed to that [position]'. Alternatively, the meaning 'this monk is the foremost' (eso bhikkhu aggo), thus being appointed, is also suitable. To show that even those not appointed to that [position] are selected there because they are endowed with the remaining qualities, 'yebhuyyena' (for the most part) is said. The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) are 'tevijjā'. Those for whom these are the beginning (ādi) of the six supernormal knowledges, etc., are 'tevijjādayo'. Those for whom there are these divisions of many kinds are 'tevijjādibhedā'. Alternatively, an arahant who has the three knowledges is a 'tevijjo'. He is the beginning (ādi) of those with the six supernormal knowledges, etc., hence they are 'tevijjādayo'. Those for whom these very things are the divisions are 'tevijjādibhedā'. Thus, it is said that they are indeed arahant bhikkhus, distinguished by many divisions by way of the three knowledges, six supernormal knowledges, etc. 'Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ' (referring to whom it was said) means: referring to which monks this statement beginning 'atha kho' was spoken in the Saṅgīti Khandhaka. By this, he makes a connection with the Pāḷi, saying: 'Although in the Pāḷi it was spoken without distinction, nevertheless it was spoken specifically with reference to the aforementioned arahant bhikkhus.'

Nanu ca sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanapariyattidharā khīṇāsavā anekasatā, anekasahassā ca, kasmā thero ekenūnamakāsīti codanaṃ uddharitvā visesakāraṇadassanena taṃ pariharituṃ “kissa panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kissāti kasmā. Pakkhantarajotako pana-saddo. Okāsakaraṇatthanti okāsakaraṇanimittaṃ okāsakaraṇahetu. Attha-saddo hi “chaṇatthañca nagarato nikkhamitvā missakapabbataṃ abhiruhatū”tiādīsu viya kāraṇavacano, “kissa hetū”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.238) viya ca hetvatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Tathā hi vaṇṇayanti “chaṇatthanti chaṇanimittaṃ chaṇahetūti attho”ti. Evañca sati pucchāsabhāgatāvissajjanāya hoti, esa nayo īdisesu.

Having raised the objection: 'Is it not so that there are many hundreds and many thousands of arahants who are bearers of the entire ninefold Teacher's Dispensation scripture? Why then did the Elder make it one less?'—to refute that objection by showing a special reason, the passage beginning 'kissa pana' was spoken. Therein, 'kissa' means 'why'. The word 'pana' indicates another side of the matter. 'Okāsakaraṇatthaṃ' means for the purpose of making an opportunity, for the reason of making an opportunity. Indeed, the word 'attha' denotes a reason, as in 'let him leave the city and climb Missaka mountain for the festival's sake'; and it is a nominative word in the sense of cause, as in 'for what reason?'. For thus the teachers explain: 'chaṇatthaṃ' means 'for the purpose of the festival, for the reason of the festival'. This being so, the answer has the quality of a question. This is the method to be understood in such instances.

Kasmā panassa okāsamakāsīti āha “tenā”tiādi. Hi-saddo kāraṇatthe. “So hāyasmā”tiādinā [V 1.0052] “sahāpi vināpi na sakkā”ti vuttavacane paccekaṃ kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Keci pana “tamatthaṃ vivaratī”ti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ “tasmā”ti kāraṇavacanadassanato. “Tasmā”tiādinā hi kāraṇadassanaṭṭhāne kāraṇajotakoyeva hi-saddo. Saññāṇamattajotakā sākhābhaṅgopamā hi nipātāti, evamīdisesu. Sikkhatīti sekkho, sikkhanaṃ vā sikkhā, sāyeva tassa sīlanti sekkho. So hi apariyositasikkhattā, tadadhimuttattā ca ekantena sikkhanasīlo, na asekkho viya pariniṭṭhitasikkho tattha paṭippassaddhussāho, nāpi vissaṭṭhasikkho pacurajano viya tattha anadhimutto, kitavasena viya ca taddhitavasenidha tappakatiyattho gayhati yathā “kāruṇiko”ti. Atha vā ariyāya jātiyā tīsupi sikkhāsu jāto, tattha vā bhavoti [M 1.0058] sekkho. Apica ikkhati etāyāti ikkhā, maggaphalasammādiṭṭhi, saha ikkhāyāti sekkho. Uparimaggattayakiccassa apariyositattā saha karaṇīyenāti sakaraṇīyo. Assāti anena, “appaccakkhaṃ nāmā”ti etena sambandho. Assāti vā “natthī”ti ettha kiriyāpaṭiggahakavacanaṃ. Paguṇappavattibhāvato appaccakkhaṃ nāma natthi. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, taṃ” dve sahassāni bhikkhuto”ti vuttampi bhagavato santike paṭiggahitameva nāmāti katvā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi sāvakabhāsitampi suttaṃ “buddhabhāsita”nti vuccatīti.

In response to the question, 'Why did he give him the opportunity?' he said, 'tena,' etc. The word 'hi' is in the sense of a reason. With 'So hāyasmā,' etc., he shows the respective reason for the statement, 'It is not possible either with him or without him.' Some, however, say, 'He explains that meaning,' but that is incorrect because of the showing of the word for reason, 'tasmā.' Indeed, in a place where a reason is shown with 'tasmā,' etc., the word 'hi' is merely an illuminator of the reason. Indeed, particles are merely illuminators of a sign, like a broken branch on a path; thus it should be understood in such instances. 'He trains' (sikkhati), therefore he is a trainee (sekkho); or, training (sikkhanaṃ) is sikkhā, and that very thing is his nature (sīla), therefore he is a sekkho. Indeed, because his training is unfinished and because he is intent on it, he is one whose nature is to train completely. He is not like one beyond training (asekkho) whose training is completed and whose effort therein has been calmed, nor is he like an indolent person (pacurajano) who has abandoned the training and is not intent on it. And here, the meaning of 'that nature' is taken by way of taddhita derivation, and also as it were by way of kita derivation, as in 'kāruṇiko' (compassionate). Alternatively, he is born in the three trainings by noble birth, or he exists therein, therefore he is a sekkho. Furthermore, 'one sees (ikkhati) with this (etāya),' thus it is 'ikkhā,' which is the right view of the path and fruit; 'with (saha) ikkhā,' thus he is a 'sekkho.' Because the task of the three higher paths is unfinished, he is 'sakaraṇīyo,' meaning 'with (saha) what is to be done (karaṇīyena).' 'Assa' is connected with 'appaccakkhaṃ nāma.' Or, 'assa' is in the dative case (kiriyāpaṭiggahaka) here with 'natthī.' Because of its state of being well-practiced, there is nothing that is not directly perceived. But in the Vinaya Commentary, it is said, 'There is nothing that was received not in the presence [of the Buddha].' That was said having considered that even what was stated as 'two thousand from the bhikkhus' was indeed received in the presence of the Blessed One. Indeed, even a sutta spoken by a disciple is called 'spoken by the Buddha.'

“Yathāhā”tiādinā āyasmatā ānandena vuttagāthameva sādhakabhāvena dasseti. Ayañhi gāthā gopakamoggallānena nāma brāhmaṇena “buddhasāsane tvaṃ bahussutoti pākaṭo, kittakā dhammā te satthārā bhāsitā, tayā ca dhāritā”ti pucchitena tassa paṭivacanaṃ dentena āyasmatā ānandeneva gopakamoggallānasutte, attano guṇadassanavasena vā theragāthāyampi bhāsitā. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – buddhato satthu santikā dvāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni ahaṃ gaṇhiṃ adhigaṇhiṃ, dve dhammakkhandhasahassāni bhikkhuto dhammasenāpatiādīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santikā gaṇhiṃ. Ye dhammā me jivhāgge, hadaye vā pavattino paguṇā vācuggatā, te dhammā tadubhayaṃ sampiṇḍetvā caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānīti. Keci pana “yemeti ettha ‘ye ime’ti padacchedaṃ katvā ye ime dhammā buddhassa, bhikkhūnañca pavattino pavattitā, tesu dhammesu buddhato dvāsīti sahassāni ahaṃ gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto gaṇhiṃ, evaṃ caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti sambandhaṃ vadanti, ayañca sambandho “ettakāyeva dhammakkhandhā”ti sanniṭṭhānassa aviññāyamānattā kecivādo nāma kato.

With 'Yathāha,' etc., he presents the very verse spoken by the Venerable Ānanda as proof. Indeed, this verse was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda himself in the Gopakamoggallānasutta—when asked by a brahmin named Gopakamoggallāna, 'You are renowned as very learned in the Buddha’s Dispensation; how many teachings were spoken by the Teacher, and how many were retained by you?' and while giving his reply—and also in the Theragāthā, by way of showing his own quality. Therein, this is the brief meaning: From the Buddha, from the Teacher's presence, I received and mastered eighty-two thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. From the bhikkhus, from the presence of bhikkhus such as the General of the Dhamma, I received two thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. Those teachings which are proceeding on the tip of my tongue or in my heart, are well-practiced, and have come to my lips—those teachings, combining both these, are eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. Some, however, making the word division of 'yeme' as 'ye ime,' state the connection thus: 'Of these teachings that arose from the Buddha and the bhikkhus, I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha and two thousand from the bhikkhus; thus there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.' And this connection, because the conclusion 'there are only this many aggregates of the Dhamma' is not ascertained, is called a 'keci' opinion.

“Sahāpi [V 1.0053] na sakkā”ti vattabbahetuto “vināpi na sakkā”ti vattabbahetuyeva balavataro saṅgītiyā bahukārattā. Tasmā tattha codanaṃ dassetvā pariharituṃ “yadi eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yadi evanti evaṃ vinā yadi na sakkā, tathā satīti attho. Sekkhopi samānoti sekkhapuggalo samānopi. Māna-saddo hettha lakkhaṇe. Bahukārattāti bahūpakārattā. Upakāravacano hi kāra-saddo “appakampi [M 1.0059] kataṃ kāraṃ, puññaṃ hoti mahapphala”ntiādīsu viya. Assāti bhaveyya. Atha-saddo pucchāyaṃ. Pañhe “atha tvaṃ kena vaṇṇenā”ti hi payogamudāharanti. “Evaṃ sante”ti pana attho vattabbo. Parūpavādavivajjanatoti yathāvuttakāraṇaṃ ajānantānaṃ paresaṃ āropitaupavādato vivajjitukāmattā. Taṃ vivarati “thero hī”tiādinā. Ativiya vissatthoti atirekaṃ vissāsiko. Kena viññāyatīti āha “tathā hī”tiādi. Daḷhīkaraṇaṃ vā etaṃ vacanaṃ. “Vuttañhi, tathā hi iccete daḷhīkaraṇatthe”ti hi vadanti saddavidū. Nanti ānandattheraṃ. “Ovadatī”ti iminā sambandho. Ānandattherassa yebhuyyena navakāya parisāya vibbhamane mahākassapatthero “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) āha. Tathā hi parinibbute bhagavati mahākassapatthero bhagavato parinibbāne sannipatitassa bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisīditvā dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ pañcasate bhikkhū uccinitvā “rājagahe āvuso vassaṃ vasantā dhammavinayaṃ saṅgāyissāma, tumhe pure vassūpanāyikāya attano attano palibodhaṃ pacchinditvā rājagahe sannipatathā”ti vatvā attanā rājagahaṃ gato.

The reason for saying 'it is not possible without him' is stronger than the reason for saying 'it is not possible even with him,' because of his great service to the council. Therefore, to present and resolve the objection there, 'yadi evaṃ,' etc., was said. Therein, 'yadi evaṃ' means: 'if it is thus not possible without him, that being the case.' 'Sekkhopi samāno' means 'although being a trainee-person.' Here, the suffix '-māna' is in the sense of a characteristic. 'Bahukārattā' means 'because of being of great help.' Indeed, the word 'kāra' is a term for service, as in 'even a little service done, being merit, is of great fruit.' 'Assa' means 'it would be.' The word 'atha' is in the sense of a question. In a question, they cite the usage 'atha tvaṃ kena vaṇṇena' (Now, by what quality do you...?). However, the meaning 'this being the case' should be stated. 'Parūpavādavivajjanato' means 'because of the desire to avoid the blame imputed by others who do not know the aforementioned reason.' He explains that with 'thero hi,' etc. 'Ativiya vissattho' means 'excessively familiar.' In response to 'How is this known?' he says, 'tathā hi,' etc. Or, this statement is a confirmation. Indeed, scholars of grammar say, 'It is said that "vuttañhi" and "tathā hi" are in the sense of confirmation.' 'Naṃ' refers to the Elder Ānanda. It is connected with 'ovadati.' When the new assembly of the Elder Ānanda was, for the most part, going astray, the Elder Mahākassapa said, 'This boy did not know his measure.' Indeed, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, seated amidst the community of bhikkhus gathered at the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, selected five hundred bhikkhus for the purpose of rehearsing the Dhamma and Vinaya. Having said, 'Friends, residing for the rains in Rājagaha, we shall rehearse the Dhamma and Vinaya. Before the commencement of the rains-residence, you should cut off your respective impediments and assemble in Rājagaha,' he himself went to Rājagaha.

Ānandattheropi bhagavato pattacīvaramādāya mahājanaṃ saññāpento sāvatthiṃ gantvā tato nikkhamma rājagahaṃ gacchanto dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ cārikaṃ cari. Tasmiṃ samaye ānandattherassa tiṃsamattā saddhivihārikā yebhuyyena kumārakā ekavassikaduvassikabhikkhū ceva anupasampannā ca vibbhamiṃsu. Kasmā panete pabbajitā, kasmā ca vibbhamiṃsūti? Tesaṃ kira mātāpitaro cintesuṃ “ānandatthero satthuvissāsiko aṭṭha vare yācitvā upaṭṭhahati, icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ satthāraṃ gahetvā gantuṃ sakkoti, amhākaṃ dārake etassa santike pabbajeyyāma, evaṃ so satthāraṃ gahetvā āgamissati, tasmiṃ āgate mayaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ kātuṃ labhissāmā”ti. Iminā tāva kāraṇena nesaṃ ñātakā te pabbājesuṃ, satthari pana parinibbute tesaṃ sā patthanā upacchinnā, atha ne ekadivaseneva uppabbājesuṃ. Atha ānandattheraṃ dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ cārikaṃ caritvā rājagahamāgataṃ disvā mahākassapatthero evamāhāti. Vuttañhetaṃ kassapasaṃyutte –

The Venerable Ānanda, taking the Blessed One's bowl and robe and informing the great multitude of the Buddha's final passing, went to Sāvatthī. After departing from there and going to Rājagaha, he wandered in the Southern Hills. At that time, about thirty of the Venerable Ānanda’s resident pupils—mostly young boys, monks of one or two years' standing, and novices—left the monastic order. Why, then, did they go forth, and why did they leave the monastic order? It is said that their parents had thought: “The Venerable Ānanda is intimate with the Teacher. Having requested eight boons, he attends upon him. He is able to take the Teacher to any place he wishes. Let us have our sons ordained in his presence; in that way, he will bring the Teacher to us. When he has come, we will be able to make a great offering.” For this reason, their relatives had them ordained. But when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, that aspiration of theirs was cut off. Then, they had them disrobed in a single day. Then, seeing that the Venerable Ānanda had come to Rājagaha after wandering in the Southern Hills, the Venerable Mahākassapa spoke thus. And this was stated in the Kassapa Saṃyutta:

“Atha [M 1.0060] kiñcarahi tvaṃ āvuso ānanda imehi navehi bhikkhūhi indriyesu aguttadvārehi [V 1.0054] bhojane amattaññūhi jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttehi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ carasi, sassaghātaṃ maññe carasi, kulūpaghātaṃ maññe carasi, olujjati kho te āvuso ānanda parisā, palujjanti kho te āvuso navappāyā, na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsīti.

“Then why is it, friend Ānanda, that you now wander on tour with these junior monks who are unguarded in their sense faculties, do not know the measure in eating, and are not devoted to wakefulness? It seems to me you wander about as if destroying crops. It seems to me you wander about as if destroying families. Your assembly, friend Ānanda, is breaking up. These who are mostly juniors, friend Ānanda, are falling away. This young boy does not know the measure.”

Api me bhante kassapa sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha ca pana mayaṃ ajjāpi āyasmato mahākassapassa kumārakavādā na muccāmāti. Tathā hi pana tvaṃ āvuso ānanda imehi navehi bhikkhūhi indriyesu aguttadvārehi bhojane amattaññūhi jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttehi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ carasi, sassaghātaṃ maññe carasi, kulūpaghātaṃ maññe carasi, olujjati kho te āvuso ānanda parisā, palujjanti kho te āvuso navappāyā, na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154).

“Venerable Kassapa, grey hairs have appeared on my head, yet even today we are not freed from being called a 'young boy' by the Venerable Mahākassapa.” “Indeed it is so, friend Ānanda, for you wander on tour with these junior monks who are unguarded in their sense faculties, do not know the measure in eating, and are not devoted to wakefulness. It seems to me you wander about as if destroying crops. It seems to me you wander about as if destroying families. Your assembly, friend Ānanda, is breaking up. These who are mostly juniors, friend Ānanda, are falling away. This young boy does not know the measure.”

Tattha sassaghātaṃ maññe carasīti sassaṃ ghātento viya āhiṇḍasi. Kulūpaghātaṃ maññe carasīti kulāni upaghātento viya āhiṇḍasi. Olujjatīti palujjati bhijjati. Palujjanti kho te āvuso navappāyāti āvuso ānanda ete tuyhaṃ pāyena yebhuyyena navakā ekavassikaduvassikadaharā ceva sāmaṇerā ca palujjanti. Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsīti ayaṃ kumārako attano pamāṇaṃ na vata jānātīti theraṃ tajjento āha. Kumārakavādā na muccāmāti kumārakavādato na muccāma. Tathā hi pana tvanti idamassa evaṃ vattabbatāya kāraṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – yasmā tvaṃ imehi navehi indriyasaṃvaravirahitehi bhojane amattaññūhi saddhiṃ vicarasi, tasmā kumārakehi saddhiṃ vicaranto “kumārako”ti vattabbataṃ arahasīti.

Therein, ‘It seems to me you wander about as if destroying crops’ means you wander about as if destroying crops. ‘It seems to me you wander about as if destroying families’ means you wander about as if destroying families. ‘Is breaking up’ means it is perishing, it is shattering. ‘These who are mostly juniors, friend Ānanda, are falling away’ means, ‘Friend Ānanda, these of yours, who are mostly juniors—youngsters of one or two years' standing and novices—are falling away.’ ‘This young boy does not know the measure’ means ‘This young boy truly does not know his own limit,’ he spoke, admonishing the elder. ‘We are not freed from being called a 'young boy'’ means we are not freed from the address 'young boy'. ‘Indeed it is so, for you...’—this was said to show the reason why he should be addressed thus. Herein, this is the intended meaning: Because you wander about with these juniors who are devoid of sense restraint and do not know the measure in eating, therefore, by wandering with young boys, you deserve to be called a ‘young boy.’”

Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsīti ettha vā-saddo padapūraṇe. Vā-saddo hi upamānasamuccayasaṃsayavissaggavikappapadapūraṇādīsu bahūsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hesa “paṇḍito vāpi tena so”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 63) upamāne [M 1.0061] dissati, sadisabhāveti attho. “Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 213) samuccaye. “Ke vā ime kassa vā”tiādīsu (pārā. 296) saṃsaye. “Ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 181) vavassagge. “Ye hi keci bhikkhave samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā”tiādīsupi (ma. ni. 1.170; saṃ. ni. 2.13) vikappe. “Na vāhaṃ paṇṇaṃ bhuñjāmi, na hetaṃ mayha bhojana”ntiādīsu padapūraṇe. Idhāpi padapūraṇe [V 1.0055] daṭṭhabbo. Teneva ca ācariyadhammapālattherena vā-saddassa atthuddhāraṃ karontena vuttaṃ “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”tiādīsu padapūraṇe”ti. Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyampi idameva vuttaṃ “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsīti ayaṃ kumārako attano pamāṇaṃ na vata jānāsīti theraṃ tajjento āhā”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.154). Etthāpi “vatā”ti vacanasiliṭṭhatāya vuttaṃ. “Na vāya”nti etassa vā “na ve aya”nti padacchedaṃ katvā ve-saddassatthaṃ dassentena “vatā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi ve-saddassa ekaṃsatthabhāve tadeva pāḷiṃ payogaṃ katvā udāharanti neruttikā. Vajirabuddhitthero pana evaṃ vadati “na vāyanti ettha ca vāti vibhāsā, aññāsipi na aññāsipī”ti, (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) taṃ tassa matimattaṃ saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāya tathā avuttattā. Idamekaṃ parūpavādasambhavakāraṇaṃ “tattha kecī”tiādinā sambajjhitabbaṃ.

In ‘Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsi,’ the word ‘vā’ is a particle for filling out the phrase. Indeed, the word ‘vā’ is seen in many senses, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, exclusion, alternative, and filling out a phrase. Thus, in ‘paṇḍito vāpi tena so’ (‘thereby he is like a wise one’), etc., it is seen in the sense of comparison, meaning in the sense of similarity. In ‘Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti’ (‘That, too, the wise know as a sage’), etc., it is in the sense of conjunction. In ‘Ke vā ime kassa vā’ (‘Who might these be, or whose might they be?’), etc., it is in the sense of doubt. In ‘Ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho’ (‘This one, among these ascetics and brahmins, is the most foolish, the most deluded’), etc., it is in the sense of exclusion. In ‘Ye hi keci bhikkhave samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā’ (‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus’), etc., it is also in the sense of alternative. In ‘Na vāhaṃ paṇṇaṃ bhuñjāmi, na hetaṃ mayha bhojanaṃ’ (‘I do not eat leaves, for that is not my food’), etc., it is in the sense of filling out the phrase. Here too, it should be understood as filling out the phrase. For that very reason, the teacher, the Venerable Dhammapāla, in explaining the meaning of the word ‘vā,’ said: “In ‘na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsi,’ etc., it is for filling out the phrase.” In the Saṃyutta Commentary as well, this very thing was said: “‘Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsi’ means ‘This young boy truly does not know his own limit,’ he spoke, admonishing the elder.” There too, ‘vata’ is stated for the sake of verbal elegance. Or, having parsed ‘na vāyaṃ’ as ‘na ve ayaṃ,’ ‘vata’ is stated by one showing the meaning of the word ‘ve.’ Thus, when the word ‘ve’ has the sense of certainty, grammarians cite that very Pāli passage as an example. The Venerable Vajirabuddhi, however, says this: “And here in ‘na vāyaṃ,’ ‘vā’ is optional (vibhāsā), meaning ‘he might know or he might not know.’” That is merely his own opinion, because it is not stated thus in the Saṃyutta Commentary. This is one cause for the arising of reproach from others, to be connected with ‘Therein, some...’ etc.

Aññampi kāraṇamāha “sakyakulappasuto cāyasmā”ti. Sākiyakule jāto, sākiyakulabhāvena vā pākaṭo ca āyasmā ānando. Tattha…pe… upavadeyyunti sambandho. Aññampi kāraṇaṃ vadati “tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto”ti. Bhātāti cettha kaniṭṭhabhātā cūḷapituputtabhāvena, na pana vayasā sahajātabhāvato.

He stated another reason: ‘And the venerable one is born of the Sakyan clan.’ The venerable Ānanda was born in the Sākiya clan, or alternatively, he is well-known for being of the Sākiya clan. Therein… the connection is ‘…might reproach.’ He states another reason: ‘He is the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of his younger paternal uncle.’ Here, ‘brother’ means the younger brother by virtue of being the son of the younger paternal uncle, but not a brother on account of being co-born in age.

“Suddhodano dhotodano, sakkasukkāmitodanā;

Amitā pālitā cāti, ime pañca imā duve”ti.

“Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, and Amitodana; and Amitā and Pālitā—these five brothers and these two sisters.”

Vuttesu hi sabbakaniṭṭhassa amitodanasakkassa putto āyasmā ānando. Vuttañhi manorathapūraṇiyaṃ –

Indeed, among those mentioned, the venerable Ānanda was the son of Amitodana the Sakyan, who was the youngest of all. For it is stated in the Manorathapūraṇī:

“Kappasatasahassaṃ [M 1.0062] pana dānaṃ dadamāno amhākaṃ bodhisattena saddhiṃ tusitapure nibbattitvā tato cuto amitodanasakkassa gehe nibbatti, athassa sabbe ñātake ānandite pamodite karonto jātoti ‘ānando’tveva nāmamakaṃsū”ti.

“Having given gifts for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita realm together with our Bodhisatta. After passing away from there, he was reborn in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. Then, because he was born making all his relatives delighted and gladdened, they gave him the name ‘Ānanda’.”

Tathāyeva vuttaṃ papañcasūdaniyampi –

In the same way, it is also stated in the Papañcasūdanī:

“Aññe pana vadanti – nāyasmā ānando bhagavatā sahajāto, vayasā ca cūḷapituputtatāya [V 1.0056] ca bhagavato kaniṭṭhabhātāyeva. Tathā hi manorathapūraṇiyaṃ ekanipātavaṇṇanāyaṃ sahajātagaṇane so na vuto”ti.

“Others, however, say: ‘The venerable Ānanda was not co-born with the Blessed One; both by age and by being the son of the Blessed One’s younger paternal uncle, he was indeed His younger brother. For it is so that in the Manorathapūraṇī, in the commentary on the Ekanipāta, he is not mentioned in the enumeration of those who were co-born.’”

Yaṃ vuccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ vissatthādibhāve sati. Ativissatthasakyakulappasutatathāgatabhātubhāvatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe hi katthaci hetvattho sampajjati. Tathā hi ācariyadhammapālattherena nettiṭṭhakathāyaṃ “gunnañce taramānāna”nti gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ –

What is said, that should be accepted. ‘Therein’ means: when there is that state of intimacy and so on. This is said to mean: on account of the state of extreme intimacy, of being born of the Sakyan clan, and of being the Tathāgata’s brother. For indeed, in the locative absolute construction (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa), the meaning of cause sometimes arises. Thus, by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, in the commentary on the Netti, in the explanation of the verse ‘gunnañce taramānāna,’ it was said:

“Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchantīti sabbā tā gāviyo kuṭilameva gacchanti, kasmā? Nette jimhagate sati nette kuṭilaṃ gate sati, nettassa kuṭilaṃ gatattāti attho”ti.

“‘Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti’ means: all those cows go crookedly. Why? When the leader goes crookedly; that is, when the leader has gone crookedly, it is because of the leader’s going crookedly. This is the meaning.”

Udānaṭṭhakathāyampi “iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti suttapadavaṇṇanāyaṃ “hetuatthatā bhummavacanassa kāraṇassa bhāvena tadavinābhāvī phalassa bhāvo lakkhīyatīti veditabbā”ti (udā. aṭṭha. 1.1). Tatthāti vā nimittabhūte vissatthādimhīti attho, tasmiṃ uccinanetipi vadanti. Chandāgamanaṃ viyāti ettha chandā āgamanaṃ viyāti padacchedo. Chandāti ca hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ, chandena āgamanaṃ pavattanaṃ viyāti attho, chandena akattabbakaraṇamivāti vuttaṃ hoti, chandaṃ vā āgacchati sampayogavasenāti chandāgamanaṃ, tathā pavatto apāyagamanīyo akusalacittuppādo. Atha vā ananurūpaṃ gamanaṃ agamanaṃ. Chandena agamanaṃ chandāgamanaṃ, chandena sinehena ananurūpaṃ gamanaṃ pavattanaṃ viya akattabbakaraṇaṃ viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Asekkhabhūtā paṭisambhidā, taṃpattāti [M 1.0063] tathā, asekkhā ca te paṭisambhidāppattā cāti vā tathā, tādise. Sekkhapaṭisambhidāppattanti etthāpi esa nayo. Parivajjentoti hetvatthe antasaddo, parivajjanahetūti attho. Anumatiyāti anuññāya, yācanāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Also in the Udāna Commentary, in the explanation of the sutta phrase ‘When this is, that is,’ it is stated: ‘The fact that the locative case has the meaning of cause should be known thus: by the existence of the cause, the existence of the result, which is inseparable from it, is indicated.’ Or, ‘Therein’ (tatthāti) means in that which has become a sign, i.e., in intimacy and so on. Some also say this refers to that selection. In ‘chandāgamanaṃ viya,’ the division of words is ‘chandā āgamanaṃ viya.’ Here, ‘chandā’ is an ablative in the sense of cause; the meaning is ‘like the arising or proceeding from desire,’ which is to say, like doing what should not be done out of desire. Or, ‘chandaṃ āgacchati sampayogavasena’ means sensual desire arises by way of association; thus ‘chandāgamanaṃ’ is an unwholesome thought-process that leads to a state of loss. Alternatively, ‘agamanaṃ’ is improper conduct. ‘Chandena agamanaṃ’ is ‘chandāgamanaṃ,’ meaning like improper conduct or proceeding out of desire or affection, like doing what should not be done. ‘Asekkhapaṭisambhidā’ means the analytical knowledge that is of a non-learner; ‘tathā’ means those who have attained it. Or, they are both non-learners (asekkhā) and attainers of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidāppattā); thus they are called ‘tathā’ (such). This same method applies to ‘sekkhapaṭisambhidāppatta.’ In ‘parivajjento,’ the ‘-anta’ suffix is in the sense of cause; the meaning is ‘because of avoiding.’ ‘Anumatiyā’ means by permission, which is to say, by request.

“Kiñcāpi sekkho”ti idaṃ asekkhānaṃyeva uccinitattā vuttaṃ, na sekkhānaṃ agatigamanasambhavena. Paṭhamamaggeneva hi cattāri agatigamanāni pahīyanti, tasmā kiñcāpi sekkho, tathāpi thero āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ uccinatūti sambandho. Na pana kiñcāpi sekkho, tathāpi abhabbo agatiṃ gantunti. “Abhabbo”tiādinā pana dhammasaṅgītiyā tassa arahabhāvaṃ dassento vijjamānaguṇe katheti, tena saṅgītiyā dhammavinayavinicchaye sampatte chandādivasena aññathā [V 1.0057] akathetvā yathābhūtameva kathessatīti dasseti. Na gantabbā, ananurūpā vā gatīti agati, taṃ. Pariyattoti adhigato uggahito.

‘Although he is a learner’: this was said because only non-learners were being chosen, not because of the possibility of a learner going on an improper course. For the four improper courses of action are indeed abandoned by the first path itself. Therefore, the connection should be made thus: ‘Although he is a learner, still the Elder should choose the venerable Ānanda.’ The connection should not be made thus: ‘Although he is a learner, still he is incapable of going on an improper course.’ Furthermore, with the words beginning ‘incapable,’ while indicating his worthiness for the recitation of the Dhamma, he speaks of his existing virtues. By this, he shows that when a decision on the Dhamma and Vinaya is reached during the recitation, he will not speak otherwise due to desire and so on, but will speak only in accordance with reality. ‘Agati’ means a course that should not be gone upon, or an unsuitable course. ‘Pariyatta’ means mastered, learned.

“Eva”ntiādinā sanniṭṭhānagaṇanaṃ dasseti. Uccinitenāti uccinitvā gahitena. Apica evaṃ…pe… uccinīti nigamanaṃ, “tenāyasmatā”tiādi pana sanniṭṭhānagaṇanadassanantipi vadanti.

With the words beginning ‘Evaṃ,’ he shows the concluding enumeration. ‘Uccinitena’ means: having been chosen and accepted. Moreover, ‘evaṃ…pe…uccini’ is the conclusion. But some also say that the words beginning ‘tenāyasmatā’ are for the purpose of showing the concluding enumeration.

Evaṃ saṅgāyakavicinanappakāraṃ dassetvā aññampi saṅgāyanatthaṃ desavicinanādippakāraṃ dassento “atha kho”tiādimāha. Tattha etadahosīti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi. Nu-saddena hi parivitakkanaṃ dasseti. Rājagahanti “rājagahasāmantaṃ gahetvā vutta”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vadanti. Gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, gunnaṃ caraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, so viyāti gocaro, bhikkhūnaṃ caraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, mahanto so assa, etthāti vā mahāgocaraṃ. Aṭṭhārasannaṃ mahāvihārānampi atthitāya pahūtasenāsanaṃ.

Having thus shown the manner of selecting the reciters, and now showing another manner, that of selecting a location and so on for the purpose of the recitation, he said the words beginning ‘Atha kho.’ Therein, ‘etadahosi’ means: this reflection occurred. Indeed, the particle ‘nu’ indicates reflection. Regarding ‘Rājagaha,’ in the glosses they say: ‘it is spoken of by referring to the vicinity of Rājagaha.’ ‘Gocara’ is so called because ‘cows (gāvo) wander (caranti) here (ettha)’; it is a pasture for cattle. Similar to that, ‘gocara’ is a place where bhikkhus wander for alms. Or, because that alms-resort is vast (mahanto) there (ettha), it is called ‘mahāgocara.’ Due to the existence of eighteen great monasteries, it had abundant lodgings.

Thāvarakammanti ciraṭṭhāyikammaṃ. Visabhāgapuggalo subhaddasadiso. Ukkoṭeyyāti nivāreyya. Iti-saddo idamatthe, iminā manasikārena hetubhūtena etadahosīti attho. Garubhāvajananatthaṃ ñattidutiyena kammena saṅghaṃ sāvesi, na apalokanañattikammamattenāti adhippāyo.

‘Thāvarakammaṃ’ means a long-lasting act. A ‘visabhāgapuggalo’ is a person of a different character, like Subhadda. ‘Ukkoṭeyyāti’ means one might obstruct. The particle ‘iti’ is in the sense of ‘this’; the meaning is that this reflection occurred with this consideration as its cause. The intention is that, in order to generate a sense of gravity, he announced it to the Saṅgha by means of an act preceded by a motion (ñattidutiyakamma), and not merely by an act of seeking consent or an act consisting of a motion alone.

Kadā panāyaṃ katāti āha “ayaṃ panā”tiādi. Evaṃ katabhāvo ca imāya gaṇanāya viññāyatīti dasseti “bhagavā hī”tiādinā. Athāti anantaratthe nipāto, parinibbānantaramevāti attho. Sattāhanti [M 1.0064] hi parinibbānadivasampi saṅgaṇhitvā vuttaṃ. Assāti bhagavato, “sarīra”nti iminā sambandho. Saṃvegavatthuṃ kittetvā kittetvā aniccatāpaṭisaññuttāni gītāni gāyitvā pūjāvasena kīḷanato sundaraṃ kīḷanadivasā sādhukīḷanadivasā nāma, saparahitasādhanaṭṭhena vā sādhūti vuttānaṃ sappurisānaṃ saṃvegavatthuṃ kittetvā kittetvā kīḷanadivasātipi yujjati. Imasmiñca purimasattāhe ekadeseneva sādhukīḷanamakaṃsu. Visesato pana dhātupūjādivasesuyeva. Tathā hi vuttaṃ mahāparinibbānasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.235) –

To the question, 'But when was this formal act performed?', he says, 'ayaṃ pana,' and so on. And he shows that the fact of its being performed thus is known by this reckoning, with 'bhagavā hi,' and so on. 'Atha' is a particle in the sense of 'immediately after,' meaning 'right after the Parinibbāna.' For 'seven days' is stated including even the day of the Parinibbāna in its count. 'Assa' means 'of the Blessed One'; this connects with 'sarīra' (body). Having repeatedly proclaimed the grounds for spiritual urgency, and having sung songs connected with the perception of impermanence, through acts of veneration, they engaged in festive celebration; because of this beautiful celebration, these are called 'sādhukīḷanadivasā' (days of excellent festive celebration). Alternatively, it is also fitting to call them 'days of festive celebration' because the virtuous ones, who are called 'sādhu' (good) by virtue of accomplishing good for themselves and others, having repeatedly proclaimed the grounds for spiritual urgency, engaged in festive celebration. And in this first week, they performed the excellent festive celebration only in part. But especially on the days of relic veneration and so on. For so it is said in the commentary to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta:

“Ito purimesu hi dvīsu sattāhesu te bhikkhū saṅghassa ṭhānanisajjokāsaṃ karontā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ saṃvidahantā sādhukīḷikāya okāsaṃ na labhiṃsu, tato nesaṃ [V 1.0058] ahosi ‘imaṃ sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷissāma, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ amhākaṃ pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā kocideva āgantvā dhātuyo gaṇheyya, tasmā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā kīḷissāmā’ti, tena te evamakaṃsū”ti.

For in the two weeks prior to this, those people, while preparing a place for the Saṅgha to stay and sit and arranging food, did not get the opportunity for the excellent festive celebration. Then a thought occurred to them: 'This week we will engage in the excellent festive celebration. But the possibility exists that someone, knowing our negligence, might come and take the relics. Therefore, having set a guard, we will celebrate.' For that reason, they did so.

Tathāpi te dhātupūjāyapi katattā dhātupūjādivasā nāma. Imeyeva visesena bhagavati kattabbassa aññassa abhāvato ekadesena katampi sādhukīḷanaṃ upādāya “sādhukīḷanadivasā”ti pākaṭā jātāti āha “evaṃ sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷanadivasā nāma ahesu”nti.

Nevertheless, because relic veneration was also performed, they were called 'Relic Veneration Days'. And since these very people, especially as there was no other duty to be performed for the Blessed One, became known as 'sādhukīḷanadivasā' on account of the excellent festive celebration, though performed only in part, he said: 'Thus, for a week they were called Days of Excellent Festive Celebration'.

Citakāyāti vīsasataratanuccāya candanadārucitakāya, padhānakiccavaseneva ca sattāhaṃ citakāyaṃ agginā jhāyīti vuttaṃ. Na hi accantasaṃyogavasena nirantaraṃ sattāhameva agginā jhāyi tattha pacchimadivaseyeva jhāyitattā, tasmā sattāhasminti attho veditabbo. Purimapacchimānañhi dvinnaṃ sattāhānamantare sattāhe yattha katthacipi divase jhāyamāne sati “sattāhe jhāyī”ti vattuṃ yujjati. Yathāha –

'On the pyre' means on the pyre of sandalwood, one hundred and twenty cubits high. And it is said that the pyre burned with fire for seven days only by way of the principal affair. For it did not burn continuously with fire for seven days without interruption, because it burned only on the last day; therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'within the seven days'. For in the week between the former and the latter weeks, if it burned on any day whatsoever, it is appropriate to say 'it burned in that week'. As he says:

“Tena kho pana samayena cattāro mallapāmokkhā sīsaṃ nhātā ahatāni vatthāni nivatthā ‘mayaṃ bhagavato citakaṃ āḷimpessāmā’ti na sakkonti āḷimpetu”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.233).

'At that time, four Malla chieftains, having bathed their heads and dressed in new clothes, intending, "We will light the Blessed One's pyre," were unable to light it,' and so on.

Sattipañjaraṃ [M 1.0065] katvāti sattikhaggādihatthehi purisehi mallarājūnaṃ bhagavato dhātuārakkhakaraṇaṃ upalakkhaṇavasenāha. Sattihatthā purisā hi sattiyo yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti, tāhi samantato rakkhāpanavasena pañjarapaṭibhāgattā sattipañjaraṃ. Sandhāgāraṃ nāma rājūnaṃ ekā mahāsālā. Uyyogakālādīsu hi rājāno tattha ṭhatvā “ettakā purato gacchantu, ettakā pacchato, ettakā ubhohi passehi, ettakā hatthīsu abhiruhantu, ettakā assesu, ettakā rathesū”ti evaṃ sandhiṃ karonti mariyādaṃ bandhanti, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ “sandhāgāra”nti vuccati. Apica uyyogaṭṭhānato āgantvāpi yāva gehesu allagomayaparibhaṇḍādīni karonti, tāva dve tīṇi divasāni rājāno tattha santhambhanti vissamanti parissayaṃ vinodentītipi sandhāgāraṃ, rājūnaṃ vā saha atthānusāsanaṃ agārantipi sandhāgāraṃ ha-kārassa dha-kāraṃ, anusarāgamañca katvā, yasmā vā rājāno tattha sannipatitvā “imasmiṃ kāle kasituṃ vaṭṭati, imasmiṃ kāle vapitu”nti evamādinā nayena gharāvāsakiccāni sammantayanti, tasmā chinnavicchinnaṃ gharāvāsaṃ tattha sandhārentītipi sandhāgāraṃ. Visākhapuṇṇamito [V 1.0059] paṭṭhāya yāva visākhamāsassa amāvāsī, tāva soḷasa divasā sīhaḷavohāravasena gahitattā, jeṭṭhamūlamāsassa sukkapakkhe ca pañca divasāti āha “iti ekavīsati divasā gatā”ti. Tattha carimadivaseyeva dhātuyo bhājayiṃsu, tasmiṃyeva ca divase ayaṃ kammavācā katā. Tena vuttaṃ “jeṭṭhamūlasukkapakkhapañcamiya”ntiādi. Tattha jeṭṭhanakkhattaṃ vā mūlanakkhattaṃ vā tassa māsassa puṇṇamiyaṃ candena yuttaṃ, tasmā so māso “jeṭṭhamūlamāso”ti vuccati. Anācāranti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ anācāraṃ.

'Having made a spear-cage'—this he says by way of illustration of the Malla kings' protection of the Blessed One's relics with men holding spears, swords, and so on. For men with spears in hand are called 'spears,' just as in the expression 'lances are moving about'; because of its resemblance to a cage, by means of them providing protection all around, it is a 'spear-cage.' 'Sandhāgāra' is a great hall of the kings. For at times of war and so on, the kings would stand there and make arrangements, saying, 'Let so many go in front, so many behind, so many on both sides, so many mount elephants, so many horses, so many chariots.' Thus they make an agreement and set a boundary, so that place is called the 'Sandhāgāra' (Assembly Hall). Moreover, even after returning from the battlefield, for as long as they are performing tasks in their homes like smearing with wet cow-dung, for that period of two or three days, the kings stay there, rest, and dispel their weariness—for this reason also it is a 'Sandhāgāra.' Or, it is a 'Sandhāgāra' as it is a house for the kings' joint instruction on affairs, by changing the letter 'h' to 'dh' and inserting an anusvāra. Or, because the kings assemble there and deliberate on household duties with such reasoning as, 'At this time it is suitable to plow, at this time to sow,' and so on, and thereby maintain their interrupted household life—for this reason also it is a 'Sandhāgāra.' From the full moon of Visākha until the new moon of the month of Visākha is sixteen days, this being taken according to Sinhalese reckoning, and five days in the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla—thus he said, 'In this way, twenty-one days passed.' There, on the very last day, they distributed the relics, and on that very same day, this formal act was performed. Therefore, it is said, 'on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Jeṭṭhamūla,' and so on. In this context, either the Jeṭṭha or the Mūla lunar mansion is in conjunction with the moon on the full moon day of that month, therefore that month is called 'Jeṭṭhamūlamāsa.' 'Improper conduct' refers to the improper conduct mentioned before.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) maṅgalasuttaṭṭhakathāyañca (khu. pā. aṭṭha. maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā) “sattasu sādhukīḷanadivasesu, sattasu ca dhātupūjādivasesu vītivattesū”ti vuttanti? Sattasu dhātupūjādivasesu gahitesu tadavinābhāvato majjhe citakāya jhāyanasattāhampi gahitamevāti katvā visuṃ na vuttaṃ viya dissati. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “aḍḍhamāso atikkanto, diyaḍḍhamāso seso”ti ca vuttanti? Nāyaṃ doso. Appakañhi ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hoti, tasmā appakena adhikopi samudāyo anadhiko viya hotīti katvā aḍḍhamāsato adhikepi pañcadivase “aḍḍhamāso atikkanto”ti vuttaṃ dvāsītikhandhakavattānaṃ katthaci “asīti khandhakavattānī”ti vacanaṃ viya, tathā appakena ūnopi samudāyo anūno viya hotīti [M 1.0066] katvā diyaḍḍhamāsato ūnepi pañcadivase “diyaḍḍhamāso seso”ti vuttaṃ satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. 356) chamāsato ūnepi aḍḍhamāse “chamāsaṃ sajjhāyo kātabbo”ti vacanaṃ viya, aññathā aṭṭhakathānaṃ aññamaññavirodho siyā. Apica dīghabhāṇakānaṃ matena tiṇṇaṃ sattāhānaṃ vasena “ekavīsati divasā gatā”ti idha vuttaṃ. Vinayasuttanipātakhuddakapāṭhaṭṭhakathāsu pana khuddakabhāṇakānaṃ matena ekameva jhāyanadivasaṃ katvā tadavasesānaṃ dvinnaṃ sattāhānaṃ vasena “aḍḍhamāso atikkanto, diyaḍḍhamāso seso”ti ca vuttaṃ. Paṭhamabuddhavacanādīsu viya taṃ taṃ bhāṇakānaṃ matena aṭṭhakathāsupi vacanabhedo hotīti gahetabbaṃ. Evampettha vadanti – parinibbānadivasato paṭṭhāya ādimhi cattāro sādhukīḷanadivasāyeva, tato paraṃ tayo sādhukīḷanadivasā ceva citakajhāyanadivasā ca, tato paraṃ eko citakajhāyanadivasoyeva, tato paraṃ tayo citakajhāyanadivasā ceva dhātupūjādivasā ca, tato paraṃ cattāro dhātupūjādivasāyeva, iti taṃ taṃ kiccānurūpagaṇanavasena tīṇi sattāhāni paripūrenti, agahitaggahaṇena pana aḍḍhamāsova hoti. “Ekavīsati divasā gatā”ti idha vuttavacanañca taṃ taṃ kiccānurūpagaṇaneneva. Evañhi catūsupi aṭṭhakathāsu vuttavacanaṃ sametīti vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. Vajirabuddhittherena pana vuttaṃ “aḍḍhamāso atikkantoti ettha eko divaso naṭṭho, so pāṭipadadivaso, kolāhaladivaso [V 1.0060] nāma so, tasmā idha na gahito”ti, (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) taṃ na sundaraṃ parinibbānasuttantapāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 2.227) pāṭipadadivasatoyeva paṭṭhāya sattāhassa vuttattā, aṭṭhakathāyañca parinibbānadivasena saddhiṃ tiṇṇaṃ sattāhānaṃ gaṇitattā. Tathā hi parinibbānadivasena saddhiṃ tiṇṇaṃ sattāhānaṃ gaṇaneneva jeṭṭhamūlasukkapakkhapañcamī ekavīsatimo divaso hoti.

If so, why is it stated in the Vinaya Commentary and the Maṅgalasutta Commentary: “When seven days of joyful celebration and seven days of relic veneration had passed”? When the seven days of relic veneration are included, because of their inseparability, the week of the pyre's burning in the middle is also considered included; thus, it appears as if it is not mentioned separately. If so, why is it also said: “Half a month has passed, one and a half months remain”? This is not a fault. For a small amount, whether deficient or in excess, does not enter into the reckoning. Therefore, because a total that is slightly in excess is like one that is not in excess, even when it was five days more than half a month, it was said, “Half a month has passed,” just like the statement in some places, “eighty Khandhaka observances,” regarding the eighty-two Khandhaka observances. Similarly, because a total that is slightly deficient is like one that is not deficient, even when it was five days less than one and a half months, it was said, “One and a half months remain,” just like the statement in the Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga Commentary, “The recitation should be done for six months,” even when it was half a month less than six months. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction among the commentaries. Moreover, according to the view of the Dīghabhāṇakas, based on three weeks, it is said here: “Twenty-one days have passed.” But in the Vinaya, Suttanipāta, and Khuddakapāṭha commentaries, according to the view of the Khuddakabhāṇakas, having counted only one day of the pyre's burning, and based on the remaining two weeks, it is said: “Half a month has passed, one and a half months remain.” It should be understood that just as in the first words of the Buddha and so on, there are differences in statements in the commentaries according to the views of the respective reciters. In this matter, some also say thus: starting from the day of the Parinibbāna, the first four days were only days of joyful celebration; after that, three days were both days of joyful celebration and days of the pyre's burning; after that, one day was only a day of the pyre's burning; after that, three days were both days of the pyre's burning and days of relic veneration; after that, four days were only days of relic veneration. In this way, by means of counting according to the respective activities, three weeks are completed. By another reckoning, however, it is only half a month.
