The statement here, “Twenty-one days have passed,” is also by means of counting according to the respective activities. For in this way, the statements in all four commentaries are reconciled. This should be understood after due consideration. Venerable Vajirabuddhi, however, said: “In the phrase ‘half a month has passed,’ one day is lost; that is the first day of the lunar fortnight. It is called the day of commotion; therefore, it is not included here.” That is not sound, because in the Pāli of the Parinibbāna Suttanta, the week is stated as beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight itself, and also because in the commentary, the three weeks are counted together with the day of the Parinibbāna. Indeed, it is by counting the three weeks together with the day of the Parinibbāna that the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha becomes the twenty-first day.

Cattālīsa divasāti jeṭṭhamūlasukkapakkhachaṭṭhadivasato yāva āsaḷhī puṇṇamī, tāva gaṇetvā vuttaṃ. Etthantareti cattālīsadivasabbhantare. Rogo eva rogapalibodho. Ācariyupajjhāyesu kattabbakiccameva ācariyupajjhāyapalibodho[M 1.0067], tathā mātāpitupalibodho. Yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ, kammaṃ vā paribundheti uparodheti pavattituṃ na detīti palibodho ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā. Taṃ palibodhaṃ chinditvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ karotūti saṅgāhakena chinditabbaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ palibodhaṃ chinditvā dhammavinayasaṅgāyanasaṅkhātaṃ tadeva karaṇīyaṃ karotu.

The phrase 'forty days' is stated by counting from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha up to the full moon day of Āsāḷha. 'Within this interval' means within the forty days. Illness itself is the 'impediment of illness.' The duties to be performed for teachers and preceptors are the 'impediment of teachers and preceptors,' and similarly for the 'impediment of mother and father.' It is called 'palibodha' because it hinders or obstructs a desired purpose or action, not allowing it to proceed; this is formed by changing the letter 'r' of 'pari-' to 'l'. The phrase 'Having cut off that impediment, let him do what should be done' means: the rehearsing monk, having cut off every such impediment that should be cut off, should perform that very duty, namely, the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

Aññepi mahātherāti anuruddhattherādayo. Sokasallasamappitanti sokasaṅkhātena sallena anupaviṭṭhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ. Asamucchinnaavijjātaṇhānusayattā avijjātaṇhābhisaṅkhātena kammunā bhavayonigatiṭṭhitisattāvāsesu khandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ attabhāvaṃ janeti abhinibbattetīti jano. Kilese janeti, ajani, janissatīti vā jano, mahanto jano tathā, taṃ. Āgatāgatanti āgatamāgataṃ yathā “ekeko”ti. Ettha siyā – “thero attano pañcasatāya parisāya parivutto rājagahaṃ gato, aññepi mahātherā attano attano parivāre gahetvā sokasallasamappitaṃ mahājanaṃ assāsetukāmā taṃ taṃ disaṃ pakkantā”ti idha vuttavacanaṃ samantapāsādikāya “mahākassapatthero ‘rājagahaṃ āvuso gacchāmā’ti upaḍḍhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato, anuruddhattheropi upaḍḍhaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttavacanañca aññamaññaṃ viruddhaṃ hoti. Idha hi mahākassapattherādayo attano attano parivārabhikkhūhiyeva saddhiṃ taṃ taṃ disaṃ gatāti attho āpajjati, tattha pana mahākassapattheraanuruddhattherāyeva paccekamupaḍḍhasaṅghena saddhiṃ ekekaṃ maggaṃ gatāti? Vuccate – tadubhayampi hi vacanaṃ na virujjhati atthato saṃsandanattā. Idha hi niravasesena therānaṃ paccekagamanavacanameva tattha nayavasena dasseti, idha attano attano parisāya gamanavacanañca tattha upaḍḍhasaṅghena saddhiṃ gamanavacanena. Upaḍḍhasaṅghoti hi sakasakaparisābhūto bhikkhugaṇo gayhati upaḍḍhasaddassa asamepi bhāge pavattattā. Yadi hi sannipatite saṅghe upaḍḍhasaṅghena saddhinti atthaṃ gaṇheyya, tadā saṅghassa gaṇanapathamatītattā na yujjateva[V 1.0061], yadi ca saṅgāyanatthaṃ uccinitānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ majjhe upaḍḍhasaṅghena saddhinti atthaṃ gaṇheyya, evampi tesaṃ gaṇapāmokkhānaṃyeva uccinitattā na yujjateva. Paccekagaṇino hete. Vuttañhi “sattasatasahassāni, tesu pāmokkhabhikkhavo”ti[M 1.0068], iti atthato saṃsandanattā tadetaṃ ubhayampi vacanaṃ aññamaññaṃ na virujjhatīti. Taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ matenevaṃ vuttantipi vadanti.

Other great elders (aññepi mahātherā): this refers to Elder Anuruddha and others. Pierced by the dart of sorrow (sokasallasamappitaṃ): this means pierced and penetrated by the dart called sorrow. Because the underlying tendencies of ignorance and craving are not eradicated, a being (jano) generates and brings forth personal existence—which is the fivefold aggregate—in the realms of existence, wombs, destinations, states of being, and abodes of beings, through actions conditioned by ignorance and craving. Alternatively, one is called a 'being' (jano) because one generates, has generated, or will generate defilements. A great multitude (mahanto jano) is likewise; that (taṃ) refers to the great multitude. Coming one after another (āgatāgataṃ): this means each and every one who came, just as in “ekeko” (one by one). Here, an objection might be raised: “The Elder went to Rājagaha surrounded by his five hundred followers, and other great elders, each taking their own retinue and desiring to console the great multitude afflicted by the dart of sorrow, departed in various directions.” This statement here and the account in the Samantapāsādikā— “The Elder Mahākassapa, saying, ‘Friends, let us go to Rājagaha,’ took half the Saṅgha of monks and went one way; the Elder Anuruddha also took half and went another way”—appear contradictory. For here, the meaning is that the Elders Mahākassapa and others each went in different directions with their own monastic followers. But there, it is said that only the Elders Mahākassapa and Anuruddha each went separately with half the Saṅgha. The reply is: Both statements are not contradictory, for they are reconciled in meaning. For here, the statement about the individual departure of all the elders without exception is simply shown there by way of method. And the statement here about going with one's own retinue is shown there by the statement about going with half the Saṅgha. For “half the Saṅgha” (upaḍḍhasaṅgha) refers to the group of monks who constituted their own respective retinues, since the term “half” (upaḍḍha) is used for a portion even when it is unequal. If one were to take it to mean “with half of the assembled Saṅgha,” it would not be valid, for the Saṅgha was beyond counting. And if one were to take it to mean “with half the Saṅgha among the five hundred monks selected for the recitation,” even then, it would not be valid, for they were chosen as the leaders of groups. For these were leaders of individual groups. As it is said: “There were seven hundred thousand; among them were the leading monks.” Thus, because the meaning is reconciled, these two statements do not contradict each other. Some also say that it was stated thus according to the view of the respective reciters.

“Aparinibbutassa bhagavato”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Pattacīvaramādāyāti ettha catumahārājadattiyaselamayapattaṃ, sugatacīvarañca gaṇhitvāti attho. Soyeva hi patto bhagavatā sadā paribhutto. Vuttañhi samacittapaṭipadāsuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vassaṃvutthānusārena atirekavīsativassakālepi tasseva paribhuttabhāvaṃ dīpetukāmena pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā sunivatthanivāsano sugatacīvaraṃ pārupitvā selamayapattamādāya bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā piṇḍāya caranto”ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.37) gandhamālādayo nesaṃ hattheti gandhamālādihatthā.

This should be connected with “of the Blessed One who had not yet attained Parinibbāna” (aparinibbutassa bhagavato) and so forth. In the phrase “taking the bowl and robe” (pattacīvaramādāya), the meaning is: having taken the bowl made of sapphire-stone given by the Four Great Kings and the Sugata’s robe. Indeed, that very bowl was always used by the Blessed One. For it is stated in the commentary to the Samacittapaṭipadā Sutta: “Wishing to show that it was still in use even after more than twenty years, following his emergence from the rains retreat, in the early morning, having attended to his body, having properly worn his under-robe and donned the Sugata’s robe, he would take the stone bowl and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, enter the city by the southern gate, wandering for alms.” Because perfumes, garlands, and so on were in their hands (gandhamālādayo nesaṃ hatthe), they were called 'those with perfumes, garlands, etc., in hand' (gandhamālādihatthā).

Tatrāti tissaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāyāti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā (dha. pa. 277) aniccasabhāvapaṭisaññuttāya. Dhammena yuttā, dhammassa vā patirūpāti dhammī, tādisāya. Saññāpetvāti suṭṭhu jānāpetvā, samassāsetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vasitagandhakuṭinti niccasāpekkhattā samāso. Paribhogacetiyabhāvato “gandhakuṭiṃ vanditvā”ti vuttaṃ. “Vanditvā”ti ca “vivaritvā”ti ettha pubbakālakiriyā. Tathā hi ācariyasāriputtattherena vuttaṃ “gandhakuṭiyā dvāraṃ vivaritvāti paribhogacetiyabhāvato gandhakuṭiṃ vanditvā gandhakuṭiyā dvāraṃ vivarīti veditabba”nti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) milātā mālā, sāyeva kacavaraṃ, milātaṃ vā mālāsaṅkhātaṃ kacavaraṃ tathā. Atiharitvāti paṭhamaṃ ṭhapitaṭṭhānamabhimukhaṃ haritvā. Yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvāti paṭhamaṃ ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ anatikkamitvā yathāṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapetvā. Bhagavato ṭhitakāle karaṇīyaṃ vattaṃ sabbamakāsīti senāsane kattabbavattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kurumāno cāti taṃ sabbaṃ vattaṃ karonto ca. Lakkhaṇe hi ayaṃ māna-saddo. Nhānakoṭṭhakassa sammajjanañca tasmiṃ udakassa upaṭṭhāpanañca, tāni ādīni yesaṃ dhammadesanāovādādīnanti tathā, tesaṃ kālesūti attho. Sīhassa migarājassa seyyā sīhaseyyā, taddhitavasena, sadisavohārena vā bhagavato seyyāpi “sīhaseyyā”ti vuccati. Tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā vā, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ [V 1.0062] kappesi [M 1.0069] pāde pādaṃ accādhāya sato sampajāno”ti, (dī. ni. 2.198) taṃ. Kappanakālo karaṇakālo nanūti yojetabbaṃ.

There (tatrā) means: in that Sāvatthī. The word 'sudaṃ' is merely a particle. Connected with impermanence, etc. (aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāya): this means connected with the nature of impermanence, as in “All conditioned things are impermanent,” and so on. It is called 'dhammī' because it is endowed with the Dhamma, or alternatively, because it is befitting of the Dhamma; of such a kind. Having made them understand (saññāpetvā): this means having made them know well; it is said to mean 'having consoled them.' The perfumed chamber where he dwelt (vasitagandhakuṭi): this is a compound formed because of the constant connection. Because it is a cetiya of use, it is said, “having paid homage to the perfumed chamber.” And “having paid homage” (vanditvā) is a prior action in relation to “having opened” (vivaritvā). For it was said by the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta: “Regarding the phrase ‘having opened the door of the perfumed chamber,’ it should be understood thus: because it is a cetiya of use, having first paid homage to the perfumed chamber, he opened the door of the perfumed chamber.” A withered garland (milātā mālā); that very thing is rubbish (kacavaraṃ). Or, it is the rubbish called a withered garland. Having removed it (atiharitvā): having carried it towards the place where it was first put. Having placed it in its proper place (yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā): having placed it in the very same place where it was, without moving it from where it was first put. The statement, “he performed all the duties that were to be done while the Blessed One was present,” was said in reference to the duties to be performed in the dwelling. And while performing (kurumāno ca): this means while performing all those duties. For this '-māna' suffix is in the sense of a characteristic. Sweeping the bathing enclosure and setting up water in it—these are the first of such duties as giving Dhamma talks and admonitions; hence the name. The meaning is 'at the times for these things.' The posture of the lion, the king of beasts, is the lion's posture (sīhaseyyā). By way of derivation or by similar designation, the Blessed One's posture is also called the 'lion's posture.' Alternatively, because it is a posture of great power, the supreme posture is called the 'lion's posture.' It is in reference to this that it was said: “Then the Blessed One lay down in the lion's posture on his right side, placing one foot on the other, mindful and fully aware.” That (taṃ) should be connected thus: “Is it not the time for arranging, the time for doing?” (kappanakālo karaṇakālo nanu).

“Yathā ta”ntiādinā yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāya āvi karoti. Tattha yathā aññopi bhagavato…pe… patiṭṭhitapemo ceva akhīṇāsavo ca anekesu…pe… upakārasañjanitacittamaddavo ca akāsi, evaṃ āyasmāpi ānando bhagavato guṇa…pe… maddavo ca hutvā akāsīti yojanā. Nti nipātamattaṃ. Apica etena tathākaraṇahetuṃ dasseti, yathā aññepi yathāvuttasabhāvā akaṃsu, tathā āyasmāpi ānando bhagavato…pe… patiṭṭhitapemattā ceva akhīṇāsavattā ca anekesu…pe… upakārasañjanitacittamaddavattā cāti hetuatthassa labbhamānattā. Hetugabbhāni hi etāni padāni tadatthasseva tathākaraṇahetubhāvato. Dhanapāladamana (cūḷava. 342), suvaṇṇakakkaṭa (jā. 1.5.94), cūḷahaṃsa (jā. 1.15.133) -mahāhaṃsajātakādīhi (jā. 2.21.89) cettha vibhāvetabbo. Guṇānaṃ gaṇo, soyeva amatanipphādakarasasadisatāya amataraso. Taṃ jānanapakatitāyāti patiṭṭhitapade hetu. Upakāra…pe… maddavoti upakārapubbabhāvena sammājanitacittamuduko. Evampi so iminā kāraṇena adhivāsesīti dassento “tamena”ntiādimāha. Tattha tamenanti taṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ. Eta-saddo hi padālaṅkāramattaṃ. Ayañhi saddapakati, yadidaṃ dvīsu sabbanāmesu pubbapadasseva atthapadatā. Saṃvejesīti “nanu bhagavatā paṭikacceva akkhātaṃ ‘sabbeheva piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo’tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.183; saṃ. ni. 5.379; a. ni. 10.48) saṃvegaṃ janesī”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati “bhante…pe… assāsessathāti paṭhamaṃ vatvā”ti saha pāṭhasesena yojanā assa. Yathārutato pana ādyatthena iti-saddena “evamādinā saṃvejesī”ti yojanāpi yujjateva. Yena kenaci hi vacanena saṃvegaṃ janesi, taṃ sabbampi saṃvejanassa karaṇaṃ sambhavatīti. Santhambhitvāti paridevanādivirahena attānaṃ paṭibandhetvā patiṭṭhāpetvā. Ussannadhātukanti upacitapittasemhādidosaṃ. Pittasemhavātavasena hi tisso dhātuyo idha bhesajjakaraṇayogyatāya [M 1.0070] adhippetā, yā “dosā, malā”ti ca loke vuccanti, pathavī āpo tejo vāyo ākāsoti ca bhedena paccekaṃ pañcavidhā. Vuttañhi –

By “Yathā taṃ,” etc., he makes clear the aforesaid meaning with a simile. Therein, just as another person, having established love for the Blessed One and with unexhausted taints, and in many hundreds of thousands of existences having a tenderness of mind well-produced by benefits rendered to one another, acted, so too did the Venerable Ānanda, because of knowing the ambrosial taste which is the collection of the Blessed One's qualities, and having a tenderness of mind, act. Thus the construction should be made. The word “taṃ” is merely a particle. Furthermore, by this he shows the reason for acting thus. Just as others of the aforesaid nature acted, so too did the Venerable Ānanda act because of having established love for the Blessed One, because of having unexhausted taints, and because of having a tenderness of mind well-produced by benefits rendered in many existences; thus, the meaning of a reason is obtained. For indeed, these words contain a reason within, because their very meaning is the reason for acting thus. And here, this should be clarified by the Dhanapāladamana, Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa, Cūḷahaṃsa, and Mahāhaṃsa Jātakas, etc. A collection of qualities. That very collection is the ambrosial taste because of its similarity to the taste that produces the deathless. “Because of having the nature of knowing that” is the reason in the word “established.” “Softened by benefit…” means having a tender mind well-produced through the state of having rendered prior benefit. To show, “Even so, he endured for this reason,” he said “tamenaṃ,” etc. Therein, “tamenaṃ” means that Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, the word “eta” is merely an embellishment of the phrase. For this is the nature of the word: that in two pronouns, the first word alone has the meaning. “He stirred up” means: “He produced a sense of urgency by means of ‘Was it not declared by the Blessed One from the very beginning, “There is separation and parting from all who are dear and beloved”?’ etc.” Thus it was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla. This being so, the construction should be with the remainder of the text, “having first said, ‘Venerable sir… you will console…’” However, according to the literal text, a construction such as “he stirred up with such as this,” with the word “iti” having the meaning of “etc.,” is also suitable. For by whatever speech he produced a sense of urgency, all of that can possibly be the cause of the sense of urgency. “Having composed himself” means having restrained and established oneself, being free from lamentation and the like. “With aggravated humors” means having the disorder of accumulated bile, phlegm, and the like. For here, by way of bile, phlegm, and wind, three elements are intended due to their suitability for being treated by medicine, which are called “disorders” and “impurities” in the world, and by the division of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, they are each of five kinds. For it is said:

“Vāyupittakaphā dosā, dhātavo ca malā tathā;

Tatthāpi pañcadhākhyātā, paccekaṃ dehadhāraṇā.

“Wind, bile, and phlegm are disorders; they are also elements and likewise impurities. Therein, they are also declared to be fivefold, each individually sustaining the body.

Sarīradūsanā [V 1.0063] dosā, malīnakaraṇā malā;

Dhāraṇā dhātavo te tu, itthamanvatthasaññakā”ti.

Because they corrupt the body, they are disorders (dosa); because they cause impurity, they are impurities (mala). Furthermore, because they sustain, they are elements (dhātu). In this way, they have names that follow their meaning.”

Samassāsetunti santappetuṃ. Devatāya saṃvejitadivasato, jetavanavihāraṃ paviṭṭhadivasato vā dutiyadivase. Viriccati etenāti virecanaṃ, osadhaparibhāvitaṃ khīrameva virecanaṃ tathā. Yaṃ sandhāyāti yaṃ bhesajjapānaṃ sandhāya. Aṅgapaccaṅgena sobhatīti subho, manuno apaccaṃ mānavo, na-kārassa pana ṇa-kāre kate māṇavo. Manūti hi paṭhamakappikakāle manussānaṃ mātāpituṭṭhāne ṭhito puriso, yo sāsane “mahāsammatarājā”ti vutto. So hi sakalalokassa hitaṃ manabhi jānātīti manūti vuccati. Evampettha vadanti “dantaja na-kārasahito mānavasaddo sabbasattasādhāraṇavacano, muddhaja ṇa-kārasahito pana māṇavasaddo kucchitamūḷhāpaccavacano”ti. Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttaṭṭhakathāyampi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 4.289) hi muddhaja ṇa-kārasahitasseva māṇavasaddassa attho vaṇṇito. Taṭṭīkāyampi “yaṃ apaccaṃ kucchitaṃ mūḷhaṃ vā, tattha loke māṇavavohāro, yebhuyyena ca sattā daharakāle mūḷhadhātukā hontīti tassevattho pakāsito”ti vadanti ācariyā. Aññattha ca vīsativassabbhantaro yuvā māṇavo, idha pana tabbohārena mahallakopi. Vuttañhi cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ “māṇavoti pana taṃ taruṇakāle vohariṃsu, so mahallakakālepi teneva vohārena voharīyatī”ti, (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 4.289) subhanāmakena laddhamāṇavavohārenāti attho. So pana “satthā parinibbuto, ānandatthero kirassa pattacīvaramādāya āgato, mahājano taṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamatī”ti sutvā “vihāraṃ kho pana gantvā mahājanamajjhe na sakkā sukhena paṭisanthāraṃ vā kātuṃ, dhammakathaṃ vā sotuṃ, gehamāgataṃyeva naṃ disvā sukhena paṭisanthāraṃ karissāmi[M 1.0071], ekā ca me kaṅkhā atthi, tampi naṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā ekaṃ māṇavakaṃ pesesi, taṃ sandhāyāha “pahitaṃ māṇavaka”nti khuddake cettha kapaccayo. Etadavocāti etaṃ “akālo”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ ānandatthero avoca.

“To comfort” means to appease. On the second day from the day he was stirred by the deity, or on the second day from the day he entered the Jetavana monastery. “It purges by means of this,” thus it is a purgative; a purgative is indeed milk infused with medicinal herbs. “Referring to which” means referring to which medicinal drink. “He is beautiful in major and minor limbs,” thus he is Subha. The offspring of Manu is a mānava; however, when the letter 'na' is made into 'ṇa', it becomes māṇava. For 'Manu' refers to the man who stood in the place of mother and father for humans in the primordial age, who is called “King Mahāsammata” in the Dispensation. He is called 'Manu' because he knows the welfare of the entire world. Thus the teachers also say here: “The word 'mānava' with the dental 'na' is a term common to all beings, but the word 'māṇava' with the cerebral 'ṇa' signifies something contemptible, deluded, or an offspring.” Indeed, in the commentary to the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta, the meaning of the word 'māṇava' with the cerebral 'ṇa' is explained. In its subcommentary also, the teachers say: “Where there is an offspring that is contemptible or deluded, the term 'māṇava' is used in the world, and since beings are for the most part of a deluded nature in their youth, that very meaning is clarified.” Elsewhere, a youth under twenty years of age is a māṇava, but here, by that designation, even an elder is so called. For it is said in the explanation of the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta: “They called him 'māṇava' in his youth, and even in his old age he is referred to by that same designation,” the meaning being, by the one named Subha who had received the designation 'māṇava'. Hearing that “The Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, the Elder Ānanda has reportedly come with his bowl and robe, and a great crowd is approaching to see him,” he thought: “Having gone to the monastery, it is not possible to comfortably exchange greetings or listen to a Dhamma talk amidst the great crowd. Having seen him only when he has come to my home, I will comfortably exchange greetings; and I have one doubt, which I will also ask him.” Having thought thus, he sent a young man. Referring to that, he said, “the sent young man.” Here, the suffix 'ka' is in the sense of 'small'. “He said this” means the Elder Ānanda said these words, “It is not the time,” etc.

Akāloti ajja gantuṃ ayuttakālo. Kasmāti ce “atthi me”tiādimāha. Bhesajjamattāti appakaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Appattho hettha mattāsaddo “mattā sukhapariccāgā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 290) viya. Pītāti pivitā. Svepīti ettha “api-saddo apekkho mantā nuññāyā”ti (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vajirabuddhittherena vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana tassādhippāyo – “appeva nāmā”ti saṃsayamatte vutte anuññātabhāvo na siddho, tasmā taṃ sādhanatthaṃ [V 1.0064] “apī”ti vuttaṃ, tena imamatthaṃ dīpeti “appeva nāma sve mayaṃ upasaṅkameyyāma, upasaṅkamituṃ paṭibalā samānā upasaṅkamissāma cā”ti.

‘Akāla’ means: it is an unsuitable time to go today. If it is asked, ‘Why?’, he says the words beginning with ‘atthi me’. ‘Bhesajjamattā’ means: a small amount of medicine. Herein, the word ‘mattā’ has the meaning of ‘a little’, as in ‘mattā sukhapariccāgā’ and so on. ‘Pītā’ means: having been drunk. In ‘svepi’, it was said by the Elder Vajirabuddhi: ‘The word “api” has the meaning of expectation, with slight permission.’ But this is his intention: when mere doubt is expressed by ‘appeva nāma’, the state of being permitted is not established. Therefore, to establish that, ‘api’ is said. By that, it reveals this meaning: ‘Perhaps we might approach tomorrow; being able to approach, we will indeed approach.’

Dutiyadivaseti khīravirecanapītadivasato dutiyadivase. Cetakattherenāti cetiyaraṭṭhe jātattā cetakoti evaṃ laddhanāmena therena. Pacchāsamaṇenāti pacchānugatena samaṇena. Sahatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Subhena māṇavena puṭṭhoti “yesu dhammesu bhavaṃ gotamo imaṃ lokaṃ patiṭṭhapesi, te tassa accayena naṭṭhā nu kho, dharanti nu kho, sace dharanti, bhavaṃ (natthi dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.448) ānando jānissati, handa naṃ pucchāmī”ti evaṃ cintetvā “yesaṃ so bhavaṃ gotamo dhammānaṃ vaṇṇavādī ahosi, yattha ca imaṃ janataṃ samādapesi nivesesi patiṭṭhāpesi, katamesānaṃ kho bho ānanda dhammānaṃ so bhavaṃ gotamo vaṇṇavādī ahosī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.448) puṭṭho, athassa thero tīṇi piṭakāni sīlakkhandhādīhi tīhi khandhehi saṅgahetvā dassento “tiṇṇaṃ kho māṇava khandhānaṃ so bhagavā vaṇṇavādī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.449) idha sīlakkhandhavagge dasamaṃ suttamabhāsi, taṃ sandhāyāha “imasmiṃ…pe… mabhāsī”ti.

‘Dutiyadivase’ means: on the second day from the day of drinking the milk-purgative. ‘Cetakattherena’ means: by the Elder who had received the name ‘Cetaka’ because he was born in the Cetiya country. ‘Pacchāsamaṇena’ means: by the monk who followed behind. And this is an instrumental case in the sense of ‘with’. ‘Puṭṭho subhena māṇavena’ means: having been asked by the young man Subha, who, having thought thus: “Regarding those teachings by which the venerable Gotama established this world, have they perished after his passing away, or do they still exist? If they exist, the venerable Ānanda will know. Well then, I shall ask him,” then asked: “Venerable Ānanda, of which teachings was the venerable Gotama a speaker in praise, and in which did he guide, settle, and establish this populace?” When asked thus, the Elder, wishing to show the three Piṭakas by summarizing them with the three aggregates—the aggregate of virtue and so on—spoke the tenth sutta in this Sīlakkhandhavagga, beginning with: “Young man, the Blessed One was a speaker in praise of the three aggregates.” Referring to that sutta, the commentator said: ‘imasmiṃ…pe… mabhāsi’.

Khaṇḍanti chinnaṃ. Phullanti bhinnaṃ, sevālāhichattakādivikassanaṃ vā, tesaṃ paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ sammā pākatikakaraṇaṃ, abhinavapaṭikaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Upakaṭṭhāyāti āsannāya. Vassaṃ upanenti upagacchanti etthāti vassūpanāyikā, vassūpagatakālo, tāya. Saṅgītipāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 440) sāmaññena vuttampi vacanaṃ [M 1.0072] evaṃ gateyeva sandhāya vuttanti saṃsandetuṃ sādhetuṃ vā āha “evañhī”tiādi.

‘Khaṇḍa’ means: broken. ‘Phulla’ means: split, or the blooming of things like moss and mushrooms. The repairing of these—properly restoring them to their original state, repairing them anew—is what is meant. ‘Upakaṭṭhāya’ means: when it is near. Because they approach (upanenti), they go to (upagacchanti) the Rains-residence at this time (ettha), it is called ‘vassūpanāyikā’; it refers to the time of entering the Rains-residence; by that time. To connect or to establish that even the statement spoken generally in the Saṅgīti Pāḷi was said referring only to those who had gone thus, he says the words beginning with ‘evañhi’.

Rājagahaṃ parivāretvāti bahinagare ṭhitabhāvena vuttaṃ. Chaḍḍitapatitauklāpāti chaḍḍitā ca patitā ca uklāpā ca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhagavato parinibbānaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantehi bhikkhūhi chaḍḍitā vissaṭṭhā, tatoyeva ca upacikādīhi khāditattā ito cito ca patitā, sammajjanābhāvena ākiṇṇakacavarattā uklāpā cāti. Tadevatthaṃ “bhagavato hī”tiādinā vibhāveti. Avakuthi pūtibhāvamagamāsīti uklāpo tha-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā, ujjhiṭṭho vā kalāposamūhoti uklāpo, vaṇṇasaṅgamanavasenevaṃ vuttaṃ yathā “upakleso, sneho” – iccādi, tena yuttāti tathā. Paricchedavasena veṇīyanti dissantīti pariveṇā. Kurumānāti kattukāmā. Senāsanavattānaṃ paññattattā, senāsanakkhandhake ca senāsanapaṭibaddhānaṃ bahūnampi vacanānaṃ vuttattā senāsanapaṭisaṅkharaṇampi tassa pūjāyeva nāmāti āha “bhagavato vacanapūjanattha”nti. Paṭhamaṃ māsanti [V 1.0065] vassānassa paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. “Titthiyavādaparimocanatthañcā”ti vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “titthiyā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Rājagahaṃ parivāretvā’ was said in the sense of being situated outside the city. ‘Chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā’ means: discarded, fallen, and rubbish. This is the intended meaning: because they were discarded and abandoned by the monks going to the place of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, and because of that, having been eaten by termites and so on, they were also fallen here and there, and because of the absence of sweeping, being filled with refuse, they were also rubbish. He clarifies that very meaning with the words beginning ‘bhagavato hi’. Because it reached a state of decay and rottenness (avakuthi pūtibhāvaṃ agamāsi), by changing the letter ‘tha’ to ‘la’, it is called ‘uklāpa’. Or, because it is a discarded heap of refuse (ujjhiṭṭho kalāposamūho), it is called ‘uklāpa’; it is said thus by way of phonetic assimilation, as in ‘upakleso, sneho’, and so on. Because they are joined with that refuse, they are so-called. Because they are seen by way of demarcation, they are called ‘pariveṇā’. ‘Kurumānā’ means: desiring to do. Because the duties concerning lodgings were prescribed, and because in the Senāsanakkhandhaka many statements connected with lodgings were spoken, even the repairing of lodgings is indeed a form of veneration to him; therefore, the commentator said: ‘bhagavato vacanapūjanatthaṃ’. ‘Paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ’ means: for the first month of the rainy season. And this is an accusative case in the sense of continuous connection. To make clear the meaning of what was said as ‘titthiyavādaparimocanatthañca’, the words beginning ‘titthiyā hi’ are stated.

Yanti katikavattakaraṇaṃ. Edisesu hi ṭhānesu yaṃ-saddo taṃ-saddānapekkho teneva atthassa paripuṇṇattā. Yaṃ vā katikavattaṃ sandhāya “atha kho”tiādi vuttaṃ, tadeva mayāpi vuttanti attho. Esa nayo īdisesu bhagavatā…pe… vaṇṇitanti senāsanavattaṃ paññapentena senāsanakkhandhake (cūḷava. 308) ca senāsanapaṭibaddhavacanaṃ kathentena vaṇṇitaṃ. Saṅgāyissāmāti ettha iti-saddassa “vuttaṃ ahosī”ti ca ubhayattha sambandho, ekassa vā iti-saddassa lopo.

‘Yaṃ’ means: the making of an agreement. For in such instances, the word ‘yaṃ’ does not expect the word ‘taṃ’, because the meaning is complete with that word alone. Or, the meaning is: that very agreement, referring to which the words beginning ‘atha kho’ were said, was also stated by me. This is the method in such instances. ‘Praised by the Blessed One…’ means: it was praised by him who was prescribing the duties concerning lodgings and who was speaking words connected with lodgings in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. Here in ‘saṅgāyissāma’, the word ‘iti’ should be connected with both ‘vuttaṃ’ and ‘ahosi’, or the elision of one ‘iti’ should be understood.

Dutiyadivaseti evaṃ cintitadivasato dutiyadivase, so ca kho vassūpanāyikadivasato dutiyadivasova. Therā hi āsaḷhipuṇṇamito pāṭipadadivaseyeva sannipatitvā vassamupagantvā evaṃ cintesunti. Rājadvāreti rājagehadvāre. Hatthakammanti hatthakiriyaṃ, hatthakammassa karaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭivedesunti jānāpesuṃ. Visaṭṭhāti nirāsaṅkacittā. Āṇāyeva [M 1.0073] appaṭihatavuttiyā pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti āṇācakkaṃ. Tathā dhammoyeva cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ, taṃ panidha desanāñāṇapaṭivedhañāṇavasena duvidhampi yujjati tadubhayeneva saṅgītiyā pavattanato. “Dhammacakkanti cetaṃ desanāñāṇassāpi nāmaṃ, paṭivedhañāṇassāpī”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78) hi aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Sannisajjaṭṭhānanti sannipatitvā nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ. Satta paṇṇāni yassāti sattapaṇṇī, yo “chattapaṇṇo, visamacchado” tipi vuccati, tassa jātaguhadvāreti attho.

On the second day: that is, on the second day from the day of deliberation; and it is indeed also the second day from the day of entering the rains retreat. For the elders, having gathered on the very first day after the full moon of Āsāḷhī and entered the rains retreat, deliberated thus. At the king’s gate means at the door of the king’s house. Hand-work means manual action; it is said to be the doing of hand-work. They informed means they made known. Free from apprehension means with a mind free from apprehension. The wheel of command: Command itself, because of its nature of proceeding with unimpeded occurrence, is called a wheel; therefore, it is the wheel of command. Similarly, the wheel of Dhamma: Dhamma itself is the wheel; therefore, it is the wheel of Dhamma. And here, that wheel of Dhamma is also suitable in two ways—by way of the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration—because the council proceeded by means of both. For it is said in the commentaries: “And this name ‘wheel of Dhamma’ is a name for the knowledge of teaching as well as for the knowledge of penetration.” The place of assembly means the place for gathering and sitting. That which has seven leaves is a Sattapaṇṇī tree, which is also called “umbrella-leaf” and “uneven-shade”; the meaning is: at the entrance of the cave where it grew.

Vissakammunāti sakkassa devānamindassa kammākammavidhāyakaṃ devaputtaṃ sandhāyāha. Suvibhattabhittithambhasopānanti ettha suvibhattapadassa dvandato pubbe suyyamānattā sabbehi dvandapadehi sambandho, tathā “nānāvidha…pe… vicitta”ntiādīsupi. Rājabhavanavibhūtinti rājabhavanasampattiṃ, rājabhavanasobhaṃ vā. Avahasantamivāti avahāsaṃ kurumānaṃ viya. Siriyāti sobhāsaṅkhātāya lakkhiyā. Niketanamivāti vasanaṭṭhānamiva, “jalantamivā”tipi pāṭho. Ekasmiṃyeva pānīyatitthe nipatantā pakkhino viya sabbesampi janānaṃ cakkhūni maṇḍapeyeva nipatantīti vuttaṃ “ekanipāta…pe… vihaṅgāna”nti. Nayanavihaṅgānanti nayanasaṅkhātavihaṅgānaṃ. Lokarāmaṇeyyakamiva sampiṇḍitanti yadi loke vijjamānaṃ rāmaṇeyyakaṃ sabbameva ānetvā ekattha sampiṇḍitaṃ siyā, taṃ viyāti vuttaṃ hoti, yaṃ yaṃ vā loke ramitumarahati, taṃ sabbaṃ sampiṇḍitamivātipi [V 1.0066] attho. Daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍanti pheggurahitaṃ sāraṃ viya, kasaṭavinimuttaṃ pasannaṃ viya ca daṭṭhumaraharūpesu sārabhūtaṃ, pasannabhūtañca. Apica daṭṭhabbo dassanīyo sārabhūto visiṭṭhataro maṇḍo maṇḍanaṃ alaṅkāro etassāti daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍo, taṃ. Maṇḍaṃ sūriyarasmiṃ pāti nivāreti, sabbesaṃ vā janānaṃ maṇḍaṃ pasannaṃ pāti rakkhati, maṇḍanamalaṅkāraṃ vā pāti pivati alaṅkarituṃ yuttabhāvenāti maṇḍapo, taṃ.

By Vissakamma: this refers to the devaputta who arranges the tasks great and small for Sakka, the lord of the devas. In “with well-divided walls, pillars, and staircases”: here, because the word “well-divided” is heard before the dvanda compound, it should be connected with all the words of that compound; similarly in phrases like “of various kinds… variegated.” The splendor of a royal palace means the opulence of a royal palace, or the beauty of a royal palace. As if mocking means like one who is making a mockery. By Sirī means by the splendor known as beauty. Like a dwelling means like a place of residence; there is also the reading “as if blazing.” Just as birds descend on a single watering place, so too do the eyes of all people descend only upon the pavilion; therefore it is said, “a single descent… of birds.” Of eye-birds means of the birds known as eyes. As if the world’s delightfulness were gathered together: this means it is said to be as if all the delightfulness existing in the world were brought and gathered together in one place; or, that whatever in the world is fit to be delighted in is as if gathered together. Worthy of being seen, the essential and the choice: like heartwood devoid of sapwood, and like clarified butter free from dregs, it is that which has become the essence and that which has become clear among forms worthy of being seen. Furthermore, another method: It has an ornament that is worthy of being seen, sightly, essential, and most excellent; therefore, it is called `daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍo`. A pavilion (maṇḍapo) is so called because it wards off the sun's rays; or, it protects (pāti) the clear delight (maṇḍaṃ) of all people; or, because it is suitable for being adorned, it 'drinks' (pāti) adornment (maṇḍanaṃ).

Kusumadāmāni ca tāni olambakāni ceti kusumadāmolambakāni. Visesanassa cettha paranipāto yathā “agyāhito”ti. Vividhāniyeva kusumadāmolambakāni tathā, tāni viniggalantaṃ visesena vamentaṃ nikkhāmentamiva cāru sobhanaṃ vitānaṃ etthāti tathā. Kuṭṭena gahito samaṃ katoti kuṭṭimo, koṭṭimo vā, tādisoyeva maṇīti maṇikoṭṭimo[M 1.0074], nānāratanehi vicitto maṇikoṭṭimo, tassa talaṃ tathā. Atha vā maṇiyo koṭṭetvā katatalattā maṇikoṭṭena nipphattanti maṇikoṭṭimaṃ, tameva talaṃ, nānāratanavicittaṃ maṇikoṭṭimatalaṃ tathā. Tamiva ca nānāpupphūpahāravicittaṃ supariniṭṭhitabhūmikammanti sambandho. Pupphapūjā pupphūpahāro. Ettha hi nānāratanavicittaggahaṇaṃ nānāpupphūpahāravicittatāyanidassanaṃ, maṇikoṭṭimatalaggahaṇaṃ supariniṭṭhitabhūmikammatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanti maṇḍapaṃ. Brahmavimānasadisanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, yathā brahmavimānaṃ sobhati, tathā alaṅkaritvāti attho. Visesena mānetabbanti vimānaṃ. Saddavidū pana “vihe ākāse māyanti gacchanti devā yenāti vimāna”nti vadanti. Visesena vā sucaritakammunā mīyati nimmīyatīti vimānaṃ, vīti vā sakuṇo vuccati, taṃ saṇṭhānena mīyati nimmīyatīti vimānantiādināpi vattabbo. Vimānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ekayojanadviyojanādibhāvena pamāṇavisesayuttatāya, sobhātisayayogena ca visesato mānanīyatāya vimāna”nti (vi. va. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) vuttaṃ. Natthi agghametesanti anagghāni, aparimāṇagghāni agghitumasakkuṇeyyānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Patirūpaṃ, paccekaṃ vā attharitabbānīti paccattharaṇāni, tesaṃ satāni tathā. Uttarābhimukhanti uttaradisābhimukhaṃ. Dhammopi satthāyeva satthukiccanipphādanatoti vuttaṃ “buddhassa bhagavato āsanārahaṃ dhammāsanaṃ paññapetvā”ti. Yathāha “yo kho…pe… mamaccayena satthā”tiādi, (dī. ni. 2.216) tathāgatappaveditadhammadesakassa vā satthukiccāvahattā tathārūpe āsane nisīditumarahatīti dassetumpi evaṃ vuttaṃ. Āsanārahanti nisīdanārahaṃ. Dhammāsananti dhammadesakāsanaṃ, dhammaṃ vā kathetuṃ yuttāsanaṃ. Dantakhacitanti dantehi khacitaṃ, hatthidantehi katanti vuttaṃ hoti. “Danto nāma hatthidanto vuccatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ dhammāsane. Mama kiccanti mama kammaṃ, mayā vā karaṇīyaṃ.

Garlands of flowers that are also hanging down are `kusumadāmolambakāni`. Herein, the adjective is placed after the noun, as in `agyāhito`. Various indeed are the hanging flower garlands; a beautiful, splendid canopy issuing forth from them is in this place, thus it is so-called. Struck with a hammer, taken, and made even is `kuṭṭimo`, or `koṭṭimo`; a gem of such a nature is `maṇikoṭṭimo`. A `maṇikoṭṭimo` variegated with various jewels, its surface is likewise. Alternatively, because its surface is made by cutting gems, it is accomplished with a slab of gems, hence it is called `maṇikoṭṭimaṃ`; that very surface, variegated with various jewels, is a surface made of a slab of gems, thus it is so-called. And like that surface, it is variegated with various flower offerings and has perfectly finished groundwork—this is how the connection should be made. The offering of flowers is `pupphūpahāro`. Herein, it should be understood that the inclusion of 'variegated with various jewels' is an illustration of being variegated with various flower offerings, and the inclusion of 'a surface of `maṇikoṭṭima`' is an illustration of having perfectly finished groundwork. `Naṃ` refers to the pavilion. `Brahmavimānasadisaṃ` is a neuter noun indicating an action; the meaning is 'having adorned it so that it is splendid like Brahma's celestial mansion'. It is especially to be revered, hence it is a `vimāna`. Experts in grammar, however, say: 'By which the devas go (`māyanti`) in the sky (`vihe`), that is a `vimāna`.' Alternatively, it is especially created by wholesome kamma, hence it is a `vimāna`; or, `vī` is said to be a bird, and it is created in its shape, hence it is a `vimāna`—it can also be explained in these and other ways. In the commentary on the Vimānavatthu, however, it is said: 'It is called a `vimāna` because of possessing a special measure of one yojana, two yojanas, and so on, and because of its supreme splendor, it is especially to be honored.' Their price does not exist, hence they are priceless (`anagghāni`); this means they are of immeasurable value, impossible to appraise. They are to be spread suitably, or individually, hence they are `paccattharaṇāni`; hundreds of them are likewise. `Uttarābhimukhaṃ` means facing the northern direction. The Dhamma itself is the Teacher because it accomplishes the Teacher's task, thus it is said: 'having prepared a Dhamma seat worthy of the Blessed One, the Buddha.' As he said: 'Who, after my passing, will be the Teacher...' and so on. Alternatively, it is also said thus to show that one who teaches the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata is worthy to sit on such a seat because he carries out the Teacher's task. `Āsanārahaṃ` means worthy to sit on. `Dhammāsanaṃ` means the seat of one who teaches the Dhamma, or a suitable seat for speaking the Dhamma. `Dantakhacitaṃ` means inlaid with tusks; this means it is made with elephant tusks. For it is said: '`Danto` is the word for an elephant's tusk.' `Ettha` means on this Dhamma seat. `Mama kiccaṃ` means my kamma, or the duty to be done by me.

Idāni [V 1.0067] āyasmato ānandassa asekkhabhūmisamāpajjanaṃ dassento “tasmiñca panā”tiādimāha. Tattha tasmiñca pana divasaeti tathā raññā ārocāpitadivase, sāvaṇamāsassa kāḷapakkhacatutthadivaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Anatthajananato visasaṅkāsatāya kileso visaṃ, tassa khīṇāsavabhāvato aññathābhāvasaṅkhātā satti gandho. Tathā hi so [M 1.0075] bhagavato parinibbānādīsu vilāpādimakāsi. Apica visajananakapupphādigandhapaṭibhāgatāya nānāvidhadukkhahetukiriyājananako kilesova “visagandho”ti vuccati. Tathā hi so “visaṃ haratīti visattikā, visamūlāti visattikā, visaphalāti visattikā, visaparibhogāti visattikā”tiādinā (mahāni. 3) vuttoti. Apica visagandhonāma virūpo maṃsādigandho, taṃsadisatāya pana kileso. “Vissasaddo hi virūpe”ti (dha. sa. ṭī. 624) abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃvuttaṃ. Addhāti ekaṃsato. Saṃveganti dhammasaṃvegaṃ. “Ohitabhārāna”nti hi yebhuyyena, padhānena ca vuttaṃ. Edisesu pana ṭhānesu tadaññesampi dhammasaṃvegoyeva adhippeto. Tathā hi “saṃvego nāma sahottappaṃ ñāṇaṃ, so tassā bhagavato dassane uppajjī”ti (vi. va. aṭṭha. 838) rajjumālāvimānavaṇṇanāyaṃvuttaṃ, sā ca tadā aviññātasāsanā anāgataphalāti. Itarathā hi cittutrāsavasena dosoyeva saṃvegoti āpajjati, evañca sati so tassa asekkhabhūmisamāpajjanassa ekaṃsakāraṇaṃ na siyā. Evamabhūto ca so idha na vattabboyevāti alamatipapañcena. Tenāti tasmā sve saṅghasannipātassa vattamānattā, sekkhasakaraṇīyattā vā. Te na yuttanti tava na yuttaṃ, tayā vā sannipātaṃ gantuṃ na patirūpaṃ.

Now, wishing to show the Venerable Ānanda's attainment of the non-learner's stage, the author spoke the words beginning with `tasmiñca pana`. Herein, `tasmiñca pana divase` means on that very day when the king had it announced; that is to say, the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa. Because it generates what is unbeneficial and is to be suspected like poison, defilement is called `visaṃ` (poison). For him, the potential (`satti`), described as the state of being otherwise than one whose taints are destroyed, is the `gandho` (scent). For indeed, on the occasion of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna and so on, he engaged in lamentation and the like. Furthermore, because of its similarity to the scent of poison-producing flowers and so on, and because it generates actions that are the cause of various kinds of suffering, defilement itself is called `visagandho` (scent of poison). For it is said: 'It carries poison, thus it is `visattikā`; its root is poison, thus it is `visattikā`; its fruit is poison, thus it is `visattikā`; its enjoyment is poison, thus it is `visattikā`,' and so on. Furthermore, `vissagandho` means a foul smell, such as that of meat. Because of its similarity to this, defilement is also called `vissagandho`. For it is said in the Abhidhammaṭīkā: 'The word `vissa` is used in the sense of "foul".' `Addhā` means certainly. `Saṃvegaṃ` means `dhammasaṃvegaṃ` (spiritual urgency). The phrase 'of those who have laid down the burden' is spoken generally and primarily. But in such instances, `dhammasaṃvega` is also intended for others besides them. For it is stated in the commentary on the Rajjumālāvimāna: '`Saṃvega` is knowledge accompanied by moral dread, and it arose in her upon seeing the Blessed One.' And at that time, she had not understood the teaching and had not attained the fruit. Otherwise, `saṃvega` would amount to mere aversion (`dosa`) arising from mental terror. And if that were the case, that `saṃvega` could not be the decisive cause for his attainment of the non-learner's stage. And being such, it should not be spoken of here at all. Enough with this excessive elaboration. `Tena` means: therefore, because the Saṅgha assembly is tomorrow, or because it is a duty for a learner. `Te na yuttaṃ` means: it is not proper for you; or, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly.

Metanti mama etaṃ gamanaṃ. Yvāhanti yo ahaṃ, yanti vā kiriyāparāmasanaṃ, tena “gaccheyya”nti ettha gamanakiriyaṃ parāmasati, kiriyāparāmasanassa ca yaṃ taṃ-saddassa ayaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgena, ekavacanena ca yogyatā tathāyeva tattha tattha dassanato. Kiriyāya hi sabhāvato napuṃsakattamekattañca icchanti saddavidū. Āvajjesīti upanāmesi. Muttāti muccitā. Appattañcāti agatañca, bimbohane na tāva ṭhapitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Etasmiṃ antareti etthantare, iminā padadvayena dassitakālānaṃ vemajjhakkhaṇe, tathādassitakāladvayassa vā vivareti vuttaṃ hoti.

`Metanti` means `mama etaṃ gamanaṃ`: 'this going of mine.' `Yvāhanti` means `yo ahaṃ`: 'who I am.' Alternatively, by the word `yanti`, there is a reference to the action. By that, here in `gaccheyya`, it refers to the action of going. And this is the nature of the words `yaṃ` and `taṃ` when referring to an action: that is, their suitability for the neuter gender and singular number, because it is seen thus in various places. Indeed, experts in grammar desire for an action, by its nature, to have neuter gender and singular number. `Āvajjesīti` means `upanāmesi`: 'he inclined.' `Muttāti` means `muccitā`: 'they were released.' `Appattañcāti` means `agatañca`: 'and not yet arrived'; it means not yet placed on the pillow. `Etasmiṃ antareti` means `etthantare`: 'in this interval'; it means at the intermediate moment of the times indicated by these two words, or in the interval between the two times thus indicated.

“Kāraṇe ceva citte ca, khaṇasmiṃ vivarepi ca;

Vemajjhādīsu atthesu ‘antarā’ti ravo gato”ti.

In cause and in mind, in a moment and also in an interval, and in the meanings of intermediate and so on, the word `antarā` is used.

Hi [V 1.0068] vuttaṃ. Anupādāyāti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena kañci dhammaṃ aggahetvā, yehi vā kilesehi muccati, tesaṃ lesamattampi aggahetvā. Āsavehīti [M 1.0076] bhavato ā bhavaggaṃ, dhammato ca ā gotrabhuṃ savanato pavattanato āsavasaññitehi kilesehi. Upalakkhaṇavacanamattañcetaṃ. Tadekaṭṭhatāya hi sabbehipi kilesehi sabbehipi pāpadhammehi cittaṃ vimuccatiyeva. Cittaṃ vimuccīti cittaṃ arahattamaggakkhaṇe āsavehi vimuccamānaṃ hutvā arahattaphalakkhaṇe vimucci. Tadatthaṃ vivarati “ayañhī”tiādinā. Caṅkamenāti caṅkamanakiriyāya. Visesanti attanā laddhamaggaphalato visesamaggaphalaṃ. Vivaṭṭūpanissayabhūtaṃ kataṃ upacitaṃ puññaṃ yenāti katapuñño, arahattādhigamāya katādhikāroti attho. Padhānamanuyuñjāti vīriyamanuyuñjāhi, arahattasamāpattiyā anuyogaṃ karohīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hohisīti bhavissasi. Kathādosoti kathāya doso vitathabhāvo. Accāraddhanti ativiya āraddhaṃ. Uddhaccāyāti uddhatabhāvāya. Handāti vossaggavacanaṃ. Tena hi adhunāyeva yojemi, na panāhaṃ papañcaṃ karomīti vossaggaṃ karoti. Vīriyasamataṃ yojemīti caṅkamanavīriyassa adhimattattā tassa hāpanavasena samādhinā samatāpādanena vīriyassa samataṃ samabhāvaṃ yojemi, vīriyena vā samathasaṅkhātaṃ samādhiṃ yojemītipi attho. Dvidhāpi hi pāṭho dissati. Vissamissāmīti assasissāmi. Idāni tassa visesato pasaṃsanārahabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāti catuiriyāpathavirahitatākāraṇena. “Anipanno”tiādīni paccuppannavacanāneva. Parinibbutopi so ākāseyeva parinibbāyi. Tasmā therassa kilesaparinibbānaṃ, khandhaparinibbānañca visesena pasaṃsārahaṃ acchariyabbhutamevāti.

`Anupādāya`: 'Without clinging' means not grasping any object by way of craving or wrong view, or not grasping even a trace of the defilements from which one is freed. `Āsavehī`: 'From the taints' means from the defilements designated as `āsava` because they flow and proceed from existence up to the highest existence, and from phenomena up to the change-of-lineage. This is merely an illustrative term. Indeed, because of their co-existence with the taints in a single mind-moment, the mind is certainly freed from all defilements and all evil states. `Cittaṃ vimucci`: 'The mind was freed' means the mind, being in the process of being freed from the taints at the moment of the path of Arahantship, became fully freed at the moment of the fruition of Arahantship. That meaning is clarified by `ayañhī`, and so on. `Caṅkamena`: 'By walking meditation' means by the act of walking meditation. `Visesaṃ`: 'Distinction' refers to a more distinguished path and fruition than the one already attained by oneself. `Katapuñño`: 'one who has made merit' means one by whom merit has been made and accumulated that serves as a strong supporting condition for Nibbāna (the turning away from saṃsāra); the meaning is one who has made the preparations for the attainment of Arahantship. `Padhānamanuyuñja`: 'Apply yourself to striving' means exert energy, engage in the practice for attaining Arahantship, is what is meant. `Hohisi`: 'You will be' means `bhavissasi`, 'you will become.' `Kathādosoti`: 'Fault in the statement' means the falsehood or fault in the statement. `Accāraddhaṃ`: 'Overly exerted' means excessively exerted. `Uddhaccāyāti`: 'For restlessness' means for a state of agitation. `Handā`: 'Very well' is a term of relinquishment. 'Then, I will now apply myself; I will not create proliferation'—thus he makes a resolution. `Vīriyasamataṃ yojemi`: 'I will balance the energy' means, due to the excessive energy in walking meditation, I will balance the energy by reducing it and making it equal with concentration. Alternatively, it means I will yoke concentration, which is called serenity, with energy. For indeed, the reading is seen in two ways. `Vissamissāmīti`: 'I will rest' means `assasissāmi`, 'I will find relief.' Now, to show his special worthiness of praise, it is said, `tenā`, and so on. `Tenā`: 'Therefore' means because of being devoid of the four postures. The words `anipanno`, and so on, are indeed present-tense statements. Even when attaining final Nibbāna, that elder attained final Nibbāna in mid-air. Therefore, the elder's Nibbāna of defilements and the Nibbāna of the aggregates are especially worthy of praise, truly wonderful and marvelous.

Dutiyadivaseti therena arahattapattadivasato dutiyadivase. Pañcamiyanti tithīpekkhāya vuttaṃ, “dutiyadivase”ti iminā tulyādhikaraṇaṃ. Bhinnaliṅgampi hi tulyatthapadaṃ dissati yathā “guṇo pamāṇaṃ, vīsati cittāni” iccādi. Kāḷapakkhassāti sāvaṇamāsakāḷapakkhassa. Paṭhamañhi māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇamakaṃsu, paṭhamamāsabhāvo ca majjhimappadesavohārena. Tattha hi purimapuṇṇamito yāva aparā puṇṇamī, tāva eko māsoti voharanti. Tato tīṇi divasāni rājā maṇḍapamakāsi, tato dutiyadivase thero arahattaṃ sacchākāsi, tatiyadivase pana sannipatitvā therā saṅgītimakaṃsu, tasmā āsaḷhimāsakāḷapakkhapāṭipadato yāva sāvaṇamāsakāḷapakkhapañcamī[M 1.0077], tāva pañcadivasādhiko ekamāso hoti. Samānoti uppajjamāno. Haṭṭhatuṭṭhacittoti ativiya somanassacitto, pāmojjena vā haṭṭhacitto pītiyā tuṭṭhacitto. Ekaṃsanti ekasmiṃ aṃse, vāmaṃseti attho. Tathā hi vaṅgīsasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ –

`Dutiyadivase`: 'On the second day' means on the second day from the day the elder attained Arahantship. `Pañcamiyaṃ`: 'On the fifth' is said with reference to the lunar date; it is in apposition with `dutiyadivase`. Indeed, a word with the same meaning is seen even though it has a different gender, for example: `guṇo pamāṇaṃ`, `vīsati cittāni`, and so on. `Kāḷapakkhassa`: 'Of the dark fortnight' means of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa. For indeed, during the first month they carried out repairs of what was broken and dilapidated; and the 'first month' is according to the convention of the Middle Country. There, they reckon from the previous full moon up to the next full moon as one month. After that, for three days the king had a pavilion made. After that, on the second day, the elder realized Arahantship. Then, on the third day, the elders assembled and held the council. Therefore, from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī up to the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa is one month plus five days. `Samāno`: 'being' means `uppajjamāno`, 'arising.' `Haṭṭhatuṭṭhacitto`: 'with a gladdened and delighted mind' means with an exceedingly joyful mind; or, with a mind gladdened by joy and a mind delighted by rapture. `Ekaṃsaṃ`: 'on one shoulder' means on one shoulder, that is, on the left shoulder. For so it is said in the commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta:

“Ekaṃsaṃ [V 1.0069] cīvaranti ettha puna saṇṭhāpanavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ, ekaṃsanti ca vāmaṃsaṃ pārupitvā ṭhitassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yato yathā vāmaṃsaṃ pārupitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, tathā cīvaraṃ katvāti evamassattho veditabbo”ti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.345).

'Here, in `ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ`, it is said thus again by way of proper arrangement. And `ekaṃsaṃ` is a designation for the robe of one who stands having draped it over the left shoulder. Therefore, the meaning should be understood in this way: having arranged the robe in such a manner that it is draped over the left shoulder.'

Bandha…pe… viyāti vaṇṭato pavuttasuparipakkatālaphalamiva. Paṇḍu…pe… viyāti sitapītapabhāyuttapaṇḍuromajakambale ṭhapito jātimā maṇi viya, jātivacanena cettha kuttimaṃ nivatteti. Samuggatapuṇṇacando viyāti juṇhapakkhapannarasuposathe samuggato soḷasakalāparipuṇṇo cando viya. Bālā…pe… viyāti taruṇasūriyapabhāsamphassena phullitasuvaṇṇavaṇṇaparāgagabbhaṃ satapattapaddhaṃ viya. “Piñjarasaddo hi hemavaṇṇapariyāyo”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.22) sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vutto. Pariyodātenāti pabhassarena. Sappabhenāti vaṇṇappabhāya, sīlappabhāya ca samannāgatena. Sassirikenāti sarīrasobhaggādisaṅkhātāya siriyā ativiya sirimatā. Mukhavarenāti yathāvuttasobhāsamalaṅkatattā uttamamukhena. Kāmaṃ “ahamasmi arahattaṃ patto”ti nārocesi, tathārūpāya pana uttamalīḷāya gamanato passantā sabbepi tamatthaṃ jānanti, tasmā ārocento viya hotīti āha “attano arahattappattiṃ ārocayamāno viya agamāsī”ti.

The phrase beginning 'From bonds...' means: like a perfectly ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk. The phrase beginning 'Pale...' means: like a gem of high quality placed on a woolen blanket from Paṇḍu and Roma, endowed with a white and yellow luster; and here, by the word 'high quality,' the artificial is excluded. The phrase 'Like the full moon risen' means: like the moon risen on the fifteenth Uposatha of the waxing fortnight, complete with all sixteen digits. The phrase beginning 'Young...' means: like a hundred-petaled lotus, its golden-colored, pollen-filled interior opened by the touch of the young sun's rays. 'For the word 'piñjara' is a synonym for the color of gold,' as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. 'With pure radiance' means with brilliant radiance. 'With splendor' means endowed with the splendor of complexion and the splendor of virtue. 'With great splendor' means exceedingly splendid with the splendor consisting of bodily grace and so on. 'With a sublime countenance' means with an excellent face, being adorned with the aforementioned beauty. Although he did not declare, 'I have attained Arahantship,' yet by his supreme demeanor as he walked, all who saw him understood that fact. Therefore, the commentator said that he went as if declaring his attainment of Arahantship.

Kimatthaṃ panāyaṃ evamārocayamāno viya agamāsīti? Vuccate – so hi “attupanāyikaṃ akatvā aññabyākaraṇaṃ bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇita”nti manasi karitvā “sekkhatāya dhammavinayasaṅgītiyā gahetumayuttampi bahussutattā gaṇhissāmā”ti nisinnānaṃ therānaṃ arahattappattivijānanena somanassuppādanatthaṃ, “appamatto hohī”ti bhagavatā dinnaovādassa ca saphalatādīpanatthaṃ evamārocayamāno viya agamāsīti. Āyasmato mahākassapassa [M 1.0078] etadahosi samasamaṭṭhapanādinā yathāvuttakāraṇena satthukappattā. Dhareyyāti vijjamāno bhaveyya. “Sobhati vata te āvuso ānanda arahattasamadhigamatā”tiādinā sādhukāramadāsi. Ayamidha dīghabhāṇakānaṃ vādo. Khuddakabhāṇakesu ca suttanipātakhuddakapāṭhabhāṇakānaṃ vādotipi yujjati tadaṭṭhakathāsupi tathā vuttattā.

Why, then, did he go as if declaring it thus? It is said: He, having reflected, 'The declaration of final knowledge without making it a personal claim was praised by the Blessed One,' went as if declaring it thus for the purpose of causing joy in the elders seated there—who were thinking, 'Although it is not proper to choose him for the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya on account of his being a learner, we shall choose him because of his great learning'—through their knowing of his attainment of Arahantship, and also for the purpose of showing the fruitfulness of the admonition given by the Blessed One: 'Be heedful.' This thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa because he had attained the Teacher's position through the aforementioned reasons, such as placing Ānanda on an equal footing. 'Dhareyya' means 'may he exist.' He gave his approval, saying, 'Friend Ānanda, your attainment of Arahantship is truly splendid,' and so on. This, here, is the view of the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya. And it is also fitting as the view of the reciters of the Suttanipāta and Khuddakapāṭha among the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya, because it is said so in their commentaries as well.

Majjhimaṃ nikāyaṃ bhaṇanti sīlenāti majjhimabhāṇakā, tappaguṇā ācariyā. Yathāvuḍḍhanti vuḍḍhapaṭipāṭiṃ, tadanatikkamitvā vā. Tatthāti tasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe. Ānandassa etamāsananti sambandho. Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ evaṃkathanasamaye. Thero cintesi “kuhiṃ gato”ti pucchantānaṃ attānaṃ dassente ativiya pākaṭabhāvena bhavissamānattā, ayampi majjhimabhāṇakesveva ekaccānaṃ vādo, tasmā itipi eke vadantīti sambandho. Ākāsena āgantvā attano āsaneyeva [V 1.0070] attānaṃ dassesītipi tesameva ekacce vadanti. Pulliṅgavisaye hi “eke”ti vutte sabbattha “ekacce”ti attho veditabbo. Tīsupi cettha vādesu tesaṃ tesaṃ bhāṇakānaṃ tena tenākārena āgatamattaṃ ṭhapetvā visuṃ visuṃ vacane aññaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ natthi. Sattamāsaṃ katāya hi dhammavinayasaṅgītiyā kadāci pakatiyāva, kadāci pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā, kadāci ākāsena āgatattā taṃ tadāgamanamupādāya tathā tathā vadanti. Apica saṅgītiyā ādidivaseyeva paṭhamaṃ pakatiyā āgantvā tato paraṃ ākāsamabbhuggantvā parisaṃ pattakāle tato otaritvā bhikkhupantiṃ apīḷento pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā āsane attānaṃ dassesītipi vadanti. Yathā vā tathā vā āgacchatu, āgamanākāramattaṃ na pamāṇaṃ, āgantvā gatakāle āyasmato mahākassapassa sādhukāradānameva pamāṇaṃ satthārā dātabbasādhukāradāneneva arahattappattiyā aññesampi ñāpitattā, bhagavati dharamāne paṭiggahetabbāya ca pasaṃsāya therassa paṭiggahitattā. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “yathā vā”tiādimāha. Sabbatthāpīti sabbesupi tīsu vādesu.

'Majjhimabhāṇakas' (Middle Reciters) are those who habitually recite the Majjhima Nikāya; they are teachers endowed with that quality. 'Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ' (according to seniority) means according to the order of seniority, or without transgressing it. 'Tattha' (there) means in that community of monks. The connection is: 'This seat is for Ānanda.' 'Tasmiṃ samaye' (at that time) means at that very moment of speaking thus. The Elder thought that if he were to show himself to those asking, 'Where has he gone?', he would become excessively conspicuous. This, too, is the view of some among the Middle Reciters; therefore, the connection is made: 'Thus, some say.' Some of those same reciters also say that he came through the sky and revealed himself right on his own seat. Indeed, in the masculine gender, when 'eke' is said, the meaning 'ekacce' (some) should be understood everywhere. And here, in these three views, apart from the mere fact of his arrival in this or that manner according to those respective reciters, there is no other special reason in their separate statements. Indeed, during the seven months that the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya was being done, because he sometimes came in the ordinary way, sometimes by diving into the earth, and sometimes through the sky, they speak in this or that way depending on that particular arrival. Moreover, some also say that on the very first day of the recitation, he first came in the ordinary way, then rose into the sky, and when it was time to reach the assembly, he descended from there and, without disturbing the row of monks, dived into the earth and showed himself in his seat. However he may have come, the mere manner of arrival is not the measure. The true measure is the approval given by the Venerable Mahākassapa when he had arrived, for his attainment of Arahantship was made known to others by the very approval that would have been given by the Teacher, and because the Elder accepted the praise that ought to have been received while the Blessed One was alive. Therefore, the commentator, wishing to show this meaning, said, 'Yathā vā...' ('However it may be...'). 'Sabbatthāpi' (in all cases) means in all three views.

Bhikkhū āmantesīti bhikkhū ālapīti ayamettha attho, aññatra pana ñāpanepi dissati yathā “āmantayāmi vo bhikkhave, (dī. ni. 2.218) paṭivedayāmi vo bhikkhave”ti [M 1.0079] (a. ni. 7.72) pakkosanepi dissati yathā “ehi tvaṃ bhikkhu mama vacanena sāriputtaṃ āmantehī”ti (a. ni. 9.11) ālapanepi dissati yathā “tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi ‘bhikkhavo’ti” (saṃ. ni. 1.249), idhāpi ālapaneti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Ālapanamattassa pana abhāvato “kiṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāmā”tiādinā vuttena viññāpiyamānatthantarena ca sahacaraṇato ñāpaneva vaṭṭati, tasmā āmantesīti paṭivedesi viññāpesīti attho vattabbo. “Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi ‘bhikkhavo’ti, ‘bhaddante’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.249) hi ālapanamattameva dissati, na viññāpiyamānatthantaraṃ, taṃ pana “bhūtapubbaṃ bhikkhave”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 1.249) paccekameva āraddhaṃ. Tasmā tādisesveva ālapane vaṭṭatīti no takko. Saddavidū pana vadanti “āmantayitvā devindo, vissakammaṃ mahiddhika’ntiādīsu (cariyā. 107) viya mantasaddo guttabhāsane. Tasmā ‘āmantesī’ti etassa sammantayīti attho”ti. “Āvuso”tiādi āmantanākāradīpanaṃ. Dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vāti ettha vā-saddo vikappane, tena “kimekaṃ tesu paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti dasseti. Kasmā āyūti āha “vinaye ṭhite”tiādi. “Yasmā, tasmā”ti ca ajjhāharitvā yojetabbaṃ. Tasmāti tāya āyusarikkhatāya[V 1.0071]. Dhuranti jeṭṭhakaṃ. No nappahotīti pahotiyeva. Dvipaṭisedho hi saha atisayena pakatyatthadīpako.

“He addressed the bhikkhus” (bhikkhū āmantesi) means “he called the bhikkhus” (bhikkhū ālapi); this is the meaning here. Elsewhere, however, it is also seen in the sense of informing, as in “I inform you, bhikkhus,” “I announce to you, bhikkhus.” It is also seen in the sense of summoning, as in “Come, bhikkhu, by my word, summon Sāriputta.” It is also seen in the sense of addressing, as in “There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying, ‘Bhikkhus.’” Here too, it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī that it is in the sense of addressing. However, because it is not a mere addressing, and because it is accompanied by another meaning to be made known, stated in “What should we recite first?” etc., it is appropriate only in the sense of informing. Therefore, it is said that the meaning of “āmantesi” is “he informed” (paṭivedesi), “he made known” (viññāpesi). Indeed, in passages such as “There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying, ‘Bhikkhus.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One,” it is seen only in the sense of mere addressing; another meaning to be made known is not seen. But that is begun separately with “Once upon a time, bhikkhus,” etc. Therefore, it is appropriate in the sense of addressing only in such instances; this is our (the sub-commentators’) reasoning. Grammarians, however, say: “Just as in ‘Having consulted Vissakamma of great psychic power, Devinda...’, the word ‘manta’ occurs in the sense of secret speech. Therefore, the meaning of ‘āmantesi’ is ‘he consulted.’” “Āvuso,” etc., indicates the manner of addressing, or consulting, or informing. In “Dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā” (the Dhamma or the Vinaya), the word “vā” is in the sense of an alternative; by it, it shows, “Which of these should we recite first?” Why is it the lifespan (of the teaching)? He said, “When the Vinaya is established,” etc. And “yasmā” (because) and “tasmā” (therefore) should be supplied and connected. “Tasmā” means “because of its being like that lifespan.” “Dhuraṃ” means “the foremost.” “No nappahoti” means “it is indeed capable.” For a double negation indicates the natural meaning with emphasis.

Etadagganti eso aggo. Liṅgavipallāsena hi ayaṃ niddeso. Yadidanti ca yo ayaṃ, yadidaṃ khandhapañcakanti vā yojetabbaṃ. Evañhi sati “etadagga”nti yathārutaliṅgameva. “Yadida”nti padassa ca ayaṃ sabhāvo, yā tassa tassa atthassa vattabbassa liṅgānurūpena “yo aya”nti vā “yā aya”nti vā “yaṃ ida”nti vā yojetabbatā tathāyevassa tattha tattha dassitattā. Bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānanti niddhāraṇachaṭṭhīniddeso.

“This is the foremost” means “this one is the foremost.” Indeed, this explanation is by way of gender inversion. And “namely this” should be construed as “he who is this” or “that which is this fivefold aggregate.” For in this way, “this is the foremost” remains in the neuter gender, just as it is written. And this is the nature of the word “namely this”: its construability as “he who is this,” or “she who is this,” or “that which is this,” according to the gender of the particular meaning to be expressed, has been shown in various places just so. “Among the bhikkhus who are upholders of the Discipline” is an explanation of the sixth (genitive) case in the sense of specification.

Attanāva attānaṃ sammannīti sayameva attānaṃ sammataṃ akāsi. “Attanā”ti hi idaṃ tatiyāvisesanaṃ bhavati, tañca parehi sammannanaṃ nivatteti, “attanā”ti vā ayaṃ vibhatyantapatirūpako abyayasaddo[M 1.0080]. Keci pana “liṅgatthe tatiyā abhihitakattubhāvato”ti vadanti. Tadayuttameva “thero”ti kattuno vijjamānattā. Vissajjanatthāya attanāva attānaṃ sammannīti yojetabbaṃ. Pucchadhātussa dvikammikattā “upāliṃ vinaya”nti kammadvayaṃ vuttaṃ.

“By himself alone he appointed himself” means he made himself appointed by himself. Indeed, this “attanā” (by himself) is a qualifier in the third case, and it excludes appointment by others. Alternatively, this “attanā” is an indeclinable particle that resembles a word with a case ending. Some, however, say, “The third case is in the sense of the agent, because the agent has been expressed.” That is inappropriate, because the agent, “thero” (the elder), is present. For the purpose of answering, it should be construed as: “by himself alone, he appointed himself.” Because the root “pucch” (to ask) is di-transitive, the two objects, “Upāliṃ vinayaṃ” (Upāli regarding the Vinaya), are stated.

Bījaniṃ gahetvāti ettha bījanīgahaṇaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ dhammatāti veditabbaṃ. Tāya hi dhammakathikānaṃ parisāya hatthakukkuccamukhavikārādi paṭicchādīyati. Bhagavā ca dhammakathikānaṃ dhammatādassanatthameva vicitrabījaniṃ gaṇhāti. Aññathā hi sabbassapi lokassa alaṅkārabhūtaṃ paramukkaṃsagatasikkhāsaṃyamānaṃ buddhānaṃ mukhacandamaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetabbaṃ na siyā. “Paṭhamaṃ āvuso upāli pārājikaṃ kattha paññatta”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu tassa saṅgītiyā purimakāle paṭhamabhāvo na yuttoti? No na yutto bhagavatā paññattānukkamena, pātimokkhuddesānukkamena ca paṭhamabhāvassa siddhattā. Yebhuyyena hi tīṇi piṭakāni bhagavato dharamānakāle ṭhitānukkameneva saṅgītāni, visesato vinayābhidhammapiṭakānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kismiṃ vatthusminti, methunadhammeti ca nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ. “Kattha paññatta”ntiādinā dassitena saha tadavasiṭṭhampi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “vatthumpi pucchī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

In “Having taken a fan,” it should be understood that the taking of a fan is the custom of Dhamma-preachers. For by it, a Dhamma-preacher’s fidgeting of hands, distortion of the face, and so on, are concealed in the midst of the assembly. And the Blessed One takes an ornate fan solely for the purpose of showing the custom of Dhamma-preachers. Otherwise, it would not be fitting to conceal the moon-like face-disc of the Buddhas, who are an ornament to the entire world and possess the training and restraint that have reached the highest excellence. Why was it said, “Friend Upāli, where was the first pārājika laid down?” Surely, is it not inappropriate for it to be first at a time before its recitation? It is not that it is inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. Why? Because its firstness is established by the sequence of its being laid down by the Blessed One and by the sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation. Indeed, for the most part, the three Piṭakas were recited in the very sequence they existed during the Blessed One’s lifetime; this should be understood especially of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas. In “kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ” (in what matter?) and “methunadhamme” (in the matter of sexual intercourse), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause. The statement “he also asked about the story,” etc., was said in order to show, by including the remainder, together with what was indicated by “Where was it laid down?”, etc.

Saṅgītikārakavacanasammissaṃ vā nu kho, suddhaṃ vā buddhavacananti āsaṅkāpariharaṇatthaṃ, yathāsaṅgītasseva pamāṇabhāvaṃ dassanatthañca pucchaṃ samuddharitvā vissajjento “kiṃ panetthā”tiādimāha. Ettha paṭhamapārājiketi etissaṃ tathāsaṅgītāya paṭhamapārājikapāḷiyaṃ. Tenevāha “na hi tathāgatā ekabyañjanampi niratthakaṃ vadantī”ti. Apanetabbanti atirekabhāvena [V 1.0072] niratthakatāya, vitathabhāvena vā ayuttatāya chaḍḍetabbavacanaṃ. Pakkhipitabbanti asampuṇṇatāya upanetabbavacanaṃ. Kasmāti āha “na hī”tiādi. Sāvakānaṃ pana devatānaṃ vā bhāsiteti bhagavato pucchāthomanādivasena bhāsitaṃ sandhāyāha. Sabbatthāpīti bhagavato sāvakānaṃ devatānañca bhāsitepi. Taṃ pana pakkhipanaṃ sambandhavacanamattasseva, na sabhāvāyuttiyā atthassāti dasseti “kiṃ pana ta”ntiādinā sambandhavacanamattanti pubbāparasambandhavacanameva. Idaṃ paṭhamapārājikanti vavatthapetvā ṭhapesuṃ imināva vācanāmaggena uggahaṇadhāraṇādikiccanipphādanatthaṃ, tadatthameva ca gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsu “tena…pe… viharatī”ti. Sajjhāyārambhakāleyeva pathavī akampitthāti vadanti, tadidaṃ pana pathavīkampanaṃ therānaṃ dhammasajjhāyānubhāvenāti [M 1.0081] ñāpetuṃ “sādhukāraṃ dadamānā viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Udakapariyantanti pathavīsandhārakaudakapariyantaṃ. Tasmiñhi caliteyeva sāpi calati, etena ca padesapathavīkampanaṃ nivatteti.

To dispel the doubt, “Is the word of the Buddha mixed with the words of the reciters, or is it pure?” and to show that only what was recited is the standard, having raised the question, he answers by saying, “But what is here?” and so on. Here, “the first pārājika” refers to this first Pārājika text as it was recited. Therefore, he says, “For the Tathāgatas do not speak even a single syllable without meaning.” “What should be removed” refers to a statement that should be discarded due to being excessive, meaningless, false, or inappropriate. “What should be included” refers to a statement that should be added due to incompleteness. Why? He says, “For indeed…” and so on. “But spoken by disciples or deities” refers to what was spoken based on the Blessed One’s questioning, praising, and so on. “In all cases” means even when spoken by the Blessed One, disciples, or deities. However, that inclusion is only for the sake of connecting words, not for the sake of the meaning's inherent logic; this is shown by saying, “But what is that?” and so on. “Only words that connect” means only words that connect the preceding and following. Having defined this as the first Pārājika, they established it for the purpose of accomplishing the tasks of learning, retention, and so on through this very method of recitation, and for that very purpose, they also performed a group recitation: “Therefore… he dwells.” They say that the earth shook at the very moment they began the recitation. This shaking of the earth, however, was to make known the power of the elders’ Dhamma recitation, hence it is said, “as if giving applause.” “To the water’s limit” means to the limit of the earth-supporting water. For indeed, only when that moves, does the earth also move. And by this, he excludes a merely localized shaking of the earth.

Kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ gaṇanā natthi, saṅgītimāropitāni pana ettakānevāti dīpetuṃ “pañcasattati sikkhāpadānī”ti vuttaṃ “purimanayenevā”ti etena sādhukāraṃ dadamānā viyāti atthamāha. Na kevalaṃ sikkhāpadakaṇḍavibhaṅganiyameneva, atha kho pamāṇaniyamenāpīti dassetuṃ “catusaṭṭhibhāṇavārā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca bhāṇavāroti –

Although there is no numerical count in the Pāḷi, to indicate that just this many were included in the recitation, it is said, “seventy-five training rules.” By “in the former manner,” he states the meaning “as if giving applause.” To show that it was not only by the principle of the section-by-section division of the training rules, but also by the principle of measurement, it is stated, “sixty-four recitation sections.” And here, a recitation section is—

“Aṭṭhakkharā ekapadaṃ, ekagāthā catuppadaṃ;

Gāthā cekā mato gantho, gantho bāttiṃsatakkharo.

“Eight syllables are one line, one verse has four lines; a single verse is considered a text, and a text has thirty-two syllables.

Bāttiṃsakkharaganthānaṃ, paññāsadvisataṃ pana;

Bhāṇavāro mato eko, svaṭṭhakkharasahassako”ti.

Furthermore, two hundred and fifty texts of thirty-two syllables are considered one recitation section; it has eight thousand syllables.”

Evaṃ aṭṭhakkharasahassaparimāṇo pāṭho vuccati. Bhaṇitabbo vāro yassāti hi bhāṇavāro, ekena sajjhāyanamaggena kathetabbavāroti attho. Khandhakanti mahāvaggacūḷavaggaṃ. Khandhānaṃ samūhato, pakāsanato vā khandhakoti hi vuccati, khandhāti cettha pabbajjūpasampadādivinayakammasaṅkhātā, cārittavārittasikkhāpadasaṅkhātā ca paññattiyo adhippetā. Pabbajjādīni hi bhagavatā paññattattā paññattiyoti vuccanti. Paññattiyañca khandhasaddo dissati “dārukkhandho, (a. ni. 6.41) aggikkhandho (a. ni. 7.72), udakakkhandho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.45; 6.37) viya. Apica bhāgarāsaṭṭhatāpi [V 1.0073] yujjatiyeva tāsaṃ paññattīnaṃ bhāgato, rāsito ca vibhattattā, taṃ pana vinayapiṭakaṃ bhāṇakehi rakkhitaṃ gopitaṃ saṅgahāruḷhanayeneva cirakālaṃ anassamānaṃ hutvā patiṭṭhahissatīti āyasmantaṃ upālittheraṃ paṭicchāpesuṃ “āvuso imaṃ tuyhaṃ nissitake vācehī”ti.

Thus, a text with the measure of eight thousand syllables is called a recitation section. Indeed, it is called a bhāṇavāra because it is a section (vāra) to be recited (bhaṇitabba); the meaning is a section to be spoken in a single course of recitation. “Khandhaka” refers to the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. Indeed, it is called “Khandhaka” because it is a collection (samūha) or an exposition (pakāsana) of khandhas. Here, khandhas are understood as the regulations designated as disciplinary procedures—such as going forth and full admission—and the training rules designated as matters of conduct and avoidance. Indeed, since matters such as going forth were regulated by the Blessed One, they are called regulations. And the word khandha is seen in the sense of a mass or aggregate, as in “a mass of wood,” “a mass of fire,” and “a mass of water,” and so on. Moreover, the meaning of “portion” and “group” is also fitting, because those regulations are divided by portion and by group. Thinking that this Vinaya Piṭaka, protected and guarded by the reciters, would be established for a long time without being lost through the very method of inclusion in the council, they entrusted it to the Venerable Upāli, saying, “Friend, teach this to your dependents.”

Dhammaṃ saṅgāyitukāmoti suttantābhidhammasaṅgītiṃ kattukāmo “dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.216) viya pārisesanayena dhammasaddassa suttantābhidhammesveva pavattanato. Ayamattho upari āvi bhavissati.

“Desiring to recite the Dhamma” means desiring to perform the recitation of the Suttanta and Abhidhamma. This is because, by the method of remainder, the term ‘Dhamma’ applies only to the Suttanta and Abhidhamma, as in passages like, “The Dhamma has been taught and the Vinaya laid down,” and so on. This meaning will become clear later on.

Saṅghaṃ ñāpesīti ettha heṭṭhā vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Kataraṃ āvuso piṭakanti vinayāvasesesu dvīsu piṭakesu kataraṃ piṭakaṃ. Vinayābhidhammānampi [M 1.0082] khuddakasaṅgītipariyāpannattā tamantarena vuttaṃ “suttantapiṭake catasso saṅgītiyo”ti. Saṅgītiyoti ca saṅgāyanakāle dīghādivasena visuṃ visuṃ niyametvā saṅgayhamānattā nikāyāva vuccanti. Tenāha “dīghasaṅgīti”ntiādi. Suttāneva sampiṇḍetvā vaggakaraṇavasena tayo vaggā, nāññānīti dassetuṃ “catuttiṃsa suttāni tayo vaggā”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā catuttisaṃ suttāni tayo vaggā honti, suttāni vā catuttiṃsa, tesaṃ vaggakaraṇavasena tayo vaggā, tesu tīsu vaggesūti yojetabbaṃ. “Brahmajālasuttaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti vutte kasmāti codanāsambhavato “tividhasīlālaṅkata”ntiādimāha. Hetugabbhāni hi etāni. Cūḷamajjhimamahāsīlavasena tividhassāpi sīlassa pakāsanattā tena alaṅkataṃ vibhūsitaṃ tathā nānāvidhe micchājīvabhūte kuhanalapanādayo viddhaṃsetīti nānāvidhamicchājīvakuhanalapanādividdhaṃsanaṃ. Tattha kuhanāti kuhāyanā, paccayapaṭisevanasāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitasaṅkhātena tividhena vatthunā vimhāpanāti attho. Lapanāti vihāraṃ āgate manusse disvā “kimatthāya bhonto āgatā, kiṃ bhikkhū nimantetuṃ. Yadi evaṃ gacchatha, ahaṃ pacchato bhikkhū gahetvā āgacchāmī”ti evamādinā bhāsanā. Ādisaddena pupphadānādayo, nemittikatādayo ca saṅgaṇhāti. Apicettha micchājīvasaddena kuhanalapanāhi sesaṃ anesanaṃ gaṇhāti. Ādisaddena pana tadavasesaṃ mahicchatādikaṃ dussilyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo eva paliveṭhanaṭṭhena jālasarikkhatāya jālaṃ, tassa viniveṭhanaṃ apaliveṭhakaraṇaṃ tathā.

Saṅghaṃ ñāpesi.—Here the meaning is to be understood according to the method explained below. 'Which Piṭaka, friend?'—among the two remaining Piṭakas apart from the Vinaya, which Piṭaka? Because the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are also included in the Khuddaka Saṅgīti, it is said, excluding them, 'In the Suttanta Piṭaka there are four saṅgītis.' And by 'saṅgīti' are meant the Nikāyas themselves, because at the time of the recitation they were compiled by being separately determined according to the Dīgha, etc. Hence he said, 'the Dīgha Saṅgīti,' etc. To show that by compiling only the suttas and arranging them into sections there are three sections and no others, it is said, 'thirty-four suttas, three sections.' Therefore, thirty-four suttas are three sections; or, there are thirty-four suttas, and by arranging them into sections, there are three sections; it should be construed as 'in those three sections.' When it is said, 'There is a sutta named the Brahmajāla Sutta; let us recite it first,' because of the possibility of the objection 'Why?' arising, he said 'adorned with threefold virtue,' etc. For these terms contain the reason within them. Because it proclaims the threefold virtue—by way of the minor, intermediate, and major virtues—it is adorned and embellished by that. Likewise, because it destroys various kinds of wrong livelihood such as scheming and talkativeness, it is called 'the destroyer of various wrong livelihoods, scheming, talkativeness, etc.' Therein, 'scheming' (kuhanā) is deception; the meaning is causing astonishment through the threefold ground comprised of exploiting requisites, hinting, and artificial posture. 'Talkativeness' (lapanā) is speaking in such ways as, upon seeing people who have come to the monastery, saying, 'For what purpose have you come, sirs? Is it to invite the monks? If so, you go on; I will bring the monks and come later.' By the term 'etc.' it includes giving hints (such as with flowers) and the like, as well as making signs and so on. Moreover, here, by the term 'wrong livelihood,' it takes the remaining improper seeking apart from scheming and talkativeness. But by the term 'etc.,' it should be understood that it takes the remaining immorality such as great ambition, etc. The sixty-two views themselves, because of their similarity to a net in the sense of enveloping, are the 'net.' Its disentanglement is the act of un-enveloping; likewise.
