Antarā ca bhante rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandanti ettha antarāsaddo vivare “apicāyaṃ bhikkhave [V 1.0074] tapodādvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 231) viya. Tasmā rājagahassa ca nāḷandassa ca vivareti attho daṭṭhabbo. Antarāsaddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Īdisesu ṭhānesu akkharacintakā “antarā gāmañca nadiñca yātī”ti evaṃ ekameva antarāsaddaṃ payujjanti, so dutiyapadenapi yojetabbo hoti. Ayojiyamāne hi upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti sāmivacanassa pasaṅge antarāsaddayogena upayogavacanassa icchitattā. Tattha rañño kīḷanatthaṃ paṭibhānacittavicitraagāramakaṃsu, taṃ “rājāgāraka”nti vuccati, tasmiṃ. Ambalaṭṭhikāti rañño [M 1.0083] uyyānaṃ. Tassa kira dvārasamīpe taruṇo ambarukkho atthi, taṃ “ambalaṭṭhikā”ti vadanti, tassa samīpe pavattattā uyyānampi “ambalaṭṭhikā” tveva saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ yathā “varuṇanagara”nti, tasmā ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ nāma uyyāne rājāgāraketi attho. Aviññāyamānassa hi viññāpanatthaṃ etaṃ ādhāradvayaṃ vuttaṃ rājāgārametassāti vā rājāgārakaṃ, uyyānaṃ, rājāgāravati ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ nāma uyyāneti attho. Bhinnaliṅgampi hi visesanapadamatthī”ti keci vadanti, evaṃ sati rājāgāraṃ ādhāro na siyā. “Rājāgāraketi evaṃnāmake uyyāne abhiramanārahaṃ kira rājāgārampi. Tattha, yassa vasenetaṃ evaṃ nāmaṃ labhatī”ti (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vajirabuddhitthero. Evaṃ sati “ambalaṭṭhikāya”nti āsannataruṇambarukkhena visesetvā “rājāgārake”ti uyyānameva nāmavasena vuttanti attho āpajjati, tathā ca vuttadosova siyā. Suppiyañca paribbājakanti suppiyaṃ nāma sañcayassa antevāsiṃ channaparibbājakañca. Brahmadattañca māṇavanti ettha taruṇo “māṇavo”ti vutto “ambaṭṭho māṇavo, aṅgako māṇavo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.259, 211) viya, tasmā brahmadattaṃ nāma taruṇapurisañca ārabbhāti attho. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇeti pasaṃsāya ceva garahāya ca. Atha vā guṇo vaṇṇo, aguṇo avaṇṇo, tesaṃ bhāsanaṃ uttarapadalopena tathā vuttaṃ yathā “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti.

`Antarā ca bhante rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ`—here the word `antarā` (between) signifies an interval, just as in such passages as, “Moreover, monks, this Tapodā river comes from the interval between the two great hells.” Therefore, the meaning is to be understood as “the interval between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda.” However, because it is connected with the word `antarā`, the accusative case is used. In such instances, grammarians use the word `antarā` only once, as in “He travels between the village and the river,” and it should also be connected to the second term. Indeed, if it is not connected, the accusative case would not apply, since the accusative case is intended through the connection with `antarā` in contexts where the genitive case would otherwise apply. There, for the king’s amusement, they built a splendid and intricate house, which is called `rājāgāraka` (the king's house); in that... `Ambalaṭṭhikā` refers to the king’s park. Near its entrance, it is said, there was a young mango tree, which they called `Ambalaṭṭhikā`. Because the park was located near it, the park too came to be known as `Ambalaṭṭhikā`, just like `Varuṇanagara`. Therefore, the meaning is “in the park named Ambalaṭṭhikā, at the king’s house.” Indeed, this pair of locatives is stated to clarify what is not understood. Alternatively, `rājāgārakaṃ` is derived from `rājāgāram etassa atthi` ('this has a king's house'), referring to the park; the meaning is: 'in the park named Ambalaṭṭhikā, which possesses a king's house.' Some say that even if the genders differ, an adjective can still apply; if so, `rājāgāra` would not be the location. Venerable Vajirabuddhi says: '`Rājāgārake` means in the park so named. It is said that a place worthy of delight is also a `rājāgāra` (king's house). Therein, it is by virtue of that `rājāgāra` that this park obtains such a name.' If so, the meaning would be that `ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ` qualifies it by the nearby young mango tree, and `rājāgārake` refers to the park itself by way of its name, and thus the aforementioned fault would occur. `Suppiyañca paribbājakaṃ`—Suppiya by name, the pupil of Sañcaya, and the wanderer Channa. `Brahmadattañca māṇavaṃ`—here, `māṇava` (young man) refers to a youth, as in “Ambaṭṭha the young man, Aṅgaka the young man.” Therefore, the meaning is “concerning Brahmadatta by name, a young man.” `Vaṇṇāvaṇṇe`—both praise and blame. Alternatively, virtue is `vaṇṇa`, and non-virtue is `avaṇṇa`; their utterance is stated thus with the latter term elided, as in “form-becoming is form.”

“Tato para”ntiādimhi ayaṃ vacanakkamo – sāmaññaphalaṃ panāvuso ānanda kattha bhāsitanti? Rājagahe bhante jīvakambavaneti. Kena saddhinti? Ajātasattunā vedehiputtena saddhinti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sāmaññaphalassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchīti. Ettha hi “kaṃ ārabbhā”ti avatvā “kena saddhi”nti vattabbaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Na bhagavatā eva etaṃ suttaṃ bhāsitaṃ, raññāpi “yathā nu kho imāni puthusippāyatanānī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.163) kiñci kiñci vuttamatthi, tasmā evameva vattabbanti. Imināva nayena sabbattha “kaṃ ārabbhā”ti vā “kena saddhi”nti vā yathārahaṃ vatvā saṅgītimakāsīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tantinti suttavaggasamudāyavasena vavatthitaṃ pāḷiṃ. Evañca [V 1.0075] katvā “tivaggasaṅgahaṃ catuttiṃsasuttapaṭimaṇḍita”nti vacanaṃ upapannaṃ hoti. Pariharathāti uggahaṇavācanādivasena dhāretha. Tato anantaraṃ saṅgāyitvāti sambandho.

“After that”—in this context, the sequence of statements is as follows: “But, friend Ānanda, where was the Sāmaññaphala Sutta spoken?” “At Rājagaha, venerable sir, in Jīvaka’s mango grove.” “With whom?” “With Ajātasattu, the son of the Vedehī queen.” Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda about the introduction of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and also about the person involved. Here, instead of saying “concerning whom,” it should be said “with whom.” Why is that? Because this sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One alone; the king also said something, beginning with “yathā nu kho imāni puthusippāyatanāni…” Therefore, it should be stated just so. It should be understood that by this very method, everywhere he performed the recitation by saying either “concerning whom” or “with whom,” as was appropriate. “Tantī” refers to the Pāḷi text, established by way of the collection of suttas and divisions. And having done so, the statement “compiled into three divisions, adorned with thirty-four suttas” becomes fitting. “Pariharatha” means “you should bear it in mind” by way of learning, reciting, and so on. After that, the connection is to be made with “having recited”.

“Dhammasaṅgaho [M 1.0084] cā”tiādinā samāso. Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇitaṃ porāṇakehīti attho. Etena “mahādhammahadayena, mahādhātukathāya vā saddhiṃ sattappakaraṇaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ vitaṇḍavādimataṃ paṭikkhipitvā “kathāvatthunāva saddhi”nti vuttaṃ samānavādimataṃ dasseti. Saṇhañāṇassa, saṇhañāṇavantānaṃ vā visayabhāvato sukhumañāṇagocaraṃ.

“The compilation of the Dhamma,” and so on, is a compound. 'Thus it was explained by the ancients'—this is the meaning. By this, having rejected the view of the sophists which states, “The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is the seven treatises together with the Mahādhammahadaya or the Mahādhātukathā,” it shows the view of those with a similar view, which states, “The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is the seven treatises together with the Kathāvatthu only.” Because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, or of those possessing subtle knowledge, it is the sphere of subtle knowledge.

Cūḷaniddesamahāniddesavasena duvidhopi niddeso. Jātakādike khuddakanikāyapariyāpanne, yebhuyyena ca dhammaniddesabhūte tādise abhidhammapiṭakeva saṅgaṇhituṃ yuttaṃ, na pana dīghanikāyādippakāre suttantapiṭake, nāpi paññattiniddesabhūte vinayapiṭaketi dīghabhāṇakā jātakādīnaṃ abhidhammapiṭake saṅgahaṃ vadanti. Cariyāpiṭakabuddhavaṃsānañcettha aggahaṇaṃ jātakagatikattā, nettipeṭakopadesādīnañca niddesapaṭisambhidāmaggagatikattā. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana aṭṭhuppattivasena desitānaṃ jātakādīnaṃ yathānulomadesanābhāvato tādise suttantapiṭake saṅgaho yutto, na pana sabhāvadhammaniddesabhūte yathādhammasāsane abhidhammapiṭake, nāpi paññattiniddesabhūte yathāparādhasāsane vinayapiṭaketi jātakādīnaṃ suttantapiṭakapariyāpannataṃ vadanti. Yuttamettha vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

The Niddesa is also twofold: the Cūḷaniddesa and the Mahāniddesa. The Dīghabhāṇakas say that the Jātakas and similar texts, which are included in the Khuddaka Nikāya and are for the most part expositions of the Dhamma, should properly be included in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka alone; not in the Suttanta Piṭaka, which is of the type of the Dīgha Nikāya and others, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is an exposition of rules. The Cariyāpiṭaka and the Buddhavaṃsa are not included here because they have the nature of the Jātakas, and the Netti, Peṭakopadesa, and others are not included because they have the nature of the Niddesa and Paṭisambhidāmagga. The Majjhimabhāṇakas, however, say that since the Jātakas and similar texts were taught by way of narrative occasion and are of the nature of conventional teaching, their inclusion in the Suttanta Piṭaka is fitting. But their inclusion is not fitting in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which is an exposition of intrinsic natures, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is an exposition of rules according to the offense committed. Thus, they state that the Jātakas and so on are included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Here, what is suitable should be considered and adopted.

Evaṃ nimittapayojanakāladesakārakakaraṇappakārehi paṭhamaṃ saṅgītiṃ dassetvā idāni tattha vavatthāpitesu dhammavinayesu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ ekavidhādibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “evameta”ntiādimāha. Tattha “eva”nti iminā etasaddena parāmasitabbaṃ yathāvuttasaṅgītippakāraṃ nidasseti. “Yañhī”tiādi vitthāro. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ. Etthantareti abhisambujjhanassa, parinibbāyanassa ca vivare. Tadetaṃ pañcacattālīsa vassānīti kālavasena niyameti. Paccavekkhantena vāti udānādivasena pavattadhammaṃ sandhāyāha. Yaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ tanti sambandho. Kiṃ panetanti āha “vimuttirasamevā”ti, na tadaññarasanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vimuccitthāti vimutti, rasitabbaṃ assādetabbanti rasaṃ, vimuttisaṅkhātaṃ rasametassāti vimuttirasaṃ, arahattaphalassādanti attho. Ayaṃ ācariyasāriputtattherassa mati (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā). Ācariyadhammapālatthero pana taṃ kecivādaṃ katvā imamatthamāha [M 1.0085] “vimuccati vimuccitthāti vimutti, yathārahaṃ maggo phalañca. Rasanti guṇo, sampattikiccaṃ vā[V 1.0076], vuttanayena samāso. Vimuttānisaṃsaṃ, vimuttisampattikaṃ vā maggaphalanipphādanato, vimuttikiccaṃ vā kilesānamaccantavimuttisampādanatoti attho”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā). Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “attharasassādīsu attharaso nāma cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, dhammaraso nāma cattāro maggā, vimuttiraso nāma amatanibbāna”nti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.335) vuttaṃ.

Having thus first shown the First Council by way of its sign, purpose, time, place, agent, instrument, and manner, now, in order to show the divisions beginning with the onefold for the sake of various kinds of skill in the Dhamma and Vinaya established there, he said, 'evametaṃ' and so on. Therein, by 'evaṃ', he indicates the manner of the recitation as stated, which is to be referred to by the word 'etaṃ'. 'Yañhi' and so on is an elaboration. 'Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment' means the path-knowledge which has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and the unobstructed knowledge which has path-knowledge as its proximate cause. 'Etthantare' means in the interval between his full awakening and his final passing away. 'Tadetaṃ pañcacattālīsa vassāni' defines it by way of time. 'Paccavekkhantena vā' is said with reference to the Dhamma that arose by way of inspired utterances and so forth. Whatever was spoken, all of that is the Tanti; this is the connection. To the question 'What is this?' he said, 'It is the taste of liberation alone,' meaning that no other taste is spoken of. 'Vimuccittha' (it was liberated), thus 'vimutti' (liberation); 'rasitabbaṃ assādetabbaṃ' (to be savored, to be enjoyed), thus 'rasaṃ' (taste); 'this has the taste designated as liberation,' thus 'vimuttirasaṃ' (the taste of liberation). The meaning is the enjoyment of the fruit of Arahantship. This is the view of the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta. The teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, however, making that a 'certain view,' stated this meaning: ''Vimuccati, vimuccittha' (is being liberated, was liberated), thus 'vimutti,' meaning the path and fruit, as appropriate. 'Rasaṃ' means quality, or the function of accomplishment; the compound is formed as stated. The meaning is: having the benefit of liberation, or the accomplishment of liberation, because it brings about the path and fruit; or having the function of liberation because it brings about the complete liberation from defilements.' In the Aṅguttara commentary, however, it is said: 'Among the tastes of meaning and so on, the taste of meaning means the four fruits of recluseship, the taste of Dhamma means the four paths, and the taste of liberation means the deathless Nibbāna.'

Kiñcāpi avisesena sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ kilesavinayanena vinayo, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyapatanādito dhāraṇena dhammo ca hoti, tathāpi idhādhippeteyeva dhammavinaye vatticchāvasena sarūpato niddhāretuṃ “tattha vinayapiṭaka”ntiādimāha. Avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ dhammo khandhādivasena sabhāvadhammadesanābāhullato. Atha vā yadipi vinayo ca dhammoyeva pariyattiyādibhāvato, tathāpi vinayasaddasannidhāne bhinnādhikaraṇabhāvena payutto dhammasaddo vinayatanti viparītaṃ tantimeva dīpeti yathā “puññañāṇasambhārā, gobalībadda”nti. Payogavasena taṃ dassentena “tenevāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yena vinaya…pe… dhammo, teneva tesaṃ tathābhāvaṃ saṅgītikkhandhake (cūḷava. 347) āhāti attho.

Although all the words of the Buddha, without distinction, are Vinaya because they subdue the defilements, and are Dhamma because they protect beings who practice as instructed from falling into the states of woe, etc., nevertheless, here, in order to determine the intended Dhamma and Vinaya according to their own nature by way of the desire to express them, he said, “Therein, the Vinayapiṭaka,” and so on. The remaining word of the Buddha is Dhamma because of the abundance of teachings on intrinsic realities by way of the aggregates, etc. Or, although the Vinaya is also Dhamma because it is scripture, etc., nevertheless, when used in the proximity of the word ‘Vinaya’, the word ‘Dhamma’, being employed with a different referent, indicates only the text that is the opposite of the Vinaya text, just as in “the accumulations of merit and knowledge,” or “oxen and bulls.” It was to show this by way of usage that the commentator said, “Therefore he said,” and so on. The meaning is that for the reason that the Vinaya… and the Dhamma…, the Blessed One spoke of their being so in the Saṅgīti Khandhaka.

“Anekajātisaṃsāra”nti ayaṃ gāthā bhagavatā attano sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ arahattappattiṃ paccavekkhantena ekūnavīsatimassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa anantaraṃ bhāsitā, tasmā “paṭhamabuddhavacana”nti vuttā. Idaṃ kira sabbabuddhehi avijahitaṃ udānaṃ. Ayamassa saṅkhepattho – ahaṃ imassa attabhāvasaṅkhātassa gehassa kārakaṃ taṇhāvaḍḍhakiṃ gavesanto yena ñāṇena taṃ daṭṭhuṃ sakkā, tassa bodhiñāṇassatthāya dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhāro ettakaṃ kālaṃ anekajātisaṃsāraṃ anekajātisatasahassasaṅkhyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ anibbisaṃ anibbisanto taṃ ñāṇaṃ avindanto alabhantoyeva sandhāvissaṃ saṃsariṃ. Yasmā jarābyādhimaraṇamissatāya jāti nāmesā punappunaṃ upagantuṃ dukkhā, na ca sā tasmiṃ adiṭṭhe nivattati, tasmā taṃ gavesanto sandhāvissanti attho. Idāni bho attabhāvasaṅkhātassa gehassa kāraka taṇhāvaḍḍhaki tvaṃ mayā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhantena diṭṭho asi. Puna imaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ mama gehaṃ na kāhasi na karissasi. Tava sabbā avasesakilesa phāsukā mayā bhaggā bhañjitā[M 1.0086]. Imassa tayā katassa attabhāvasaṅkhātassa gehassa kūṭaṃ avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ kaṇṇikamaṇḍalaṃ visaṅkhataṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ. Idāni mama cittaṃ visaṅkhāraṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena gataṃ anupaviṭṭhaṃ. Ahañca taṇhānaṃ khaya saṅkhātaṃ arahattamaggaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ vā ajjhagā adhigato pattosmīti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana visaṅkhāragataṃ [V 1.0077] cittameva taṇhānaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattamaggaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ vā ajjhagā adhigatanti attho vutto.

This verse, “Through many a birth in saṃsāra,” was spoken by the Blessed One immediately after the nineteenth knowledge of review, while He was reviewing His attainment of Arahantship, which has omniscience as its proximate cause. Therefore, it is called “the first utterance of the Buddha.” This, it seems, is the inspired utterance not abandoned by all Buddhas. This is its concise meaning: ‘I, seeking the craving-carpenter, the maker of this house called the personal existence, having made the aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara for the sake of that knowledge of enlightenment by which it is possible to see that carpenter, for such a long time, through the cycle of saṃsāra numbering hundreds of thousands of births, not discovering, not finding, and not obtaining that knowledge, I have transmigrated. Because this thing called birth, being mixed with aging, sickness, and death, is suffering to undergo again and again, and it does not cease as long as that carpenter is unseen, therefore, seeking him, I have transmigrated.’ This is the meaning. ‘Now, O craving-carpenter, maker of this house called the personal existence, you have been seen by me, who has penetrated omniscience. You shall not build this house of mine again. All your rafters—the remaining defilements—have been shattered by me. The ridgepole of this house made by you, this pinnacle-circlet called ignorance, has been dismantled. Now my mind has gone to and entered Nibbāna, the unconditioned, by way of making it an object. And I have reached and attained the path of Arahantship, or the fruit of Arahantship, called the destruction of cravings.’ In the Ganthipadas, however, the meaning is stated that the mind itself, having gone to the unconditioned, has attained the path of Arahantship, or the fruit of Arahantship, called the destruction of cravings.

“Sandhāvissa”nti ettha ca “gāthāyamatītatthe imissa”nti neruttikā. “Taṃkālavacanicchāyamatītepi bhavissantī”ti keci. Punappunanti abhiṇhatthe nipāto. Pātabbā rakkhitabbāti phāsu pa-kārassa pha-kāraṃ katvā, phusitabbāti vā phāsu, sāyeva phāsukā. Ajjhagāti ca “ajjataniyamāttamiṃ vā aṃ vā”ti vadanti. Yadi pana cittameva kattā, tadā parokkhāyeva. Antojappanavasena kira bhagavā “anekajātisaṃsāra”nti gāthādvayamāha, tasmā esā manasā pavattitadhammānamādi. “Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”ti ayaṃ pana vācāya pavattitadhammānanti vadanti.

Regarding “sandhāvissaṃ,” the grammarians say, “In a verse, for the past tense, the aorist ending ‘iṃ’ becomes ‘issaṃ’.” Some say, “When there is a desire to express past time, a future tense ending can also occur for the past.” The word “punappunaṃ” is an indeclinable particle used in the sense of “repeatedly.” Because it is to be protected (pātabbā, rakkhitabbā), by changing the letter ‘pa’ to ‘pha’, it becomes ‘phāsu’; or, because it is to be touched (phusitabbā), it is ‘phāsu’; that very ‘phāsu’ is ‘phāsukā’ (rafter). Regarding “ajjhagā,” they say, “In the aorist, the ending ‘iṃ’ or ‘aṃ’ becomes ‘ā’.” However, if the mind itself is the agent, then it is in the perfect tense. It is said that the Blessed One uttered the two verses beginning “Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ” by way of internal recitation; therefore, these verses are the beginning of the Dhammas that arose in the mind. But this, “Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,” is the beginning of the Dhammas that arose through speech, they say.

Kecīti khandhakabhāṇakā. Paṭhamaṃ vutto pana dhammapadabhāṇakānaṃ vādo. Yadā…pe… dhammāti ettha nidassanattho, ādyattho ca iti-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho. Nidassanena hi mariyādavacanena vinā padatthavipallāsakārināva attho paripuṇṇo na hoti. Tattha ādyatthameva iti-saddaṃ gahetvā iti-saddo ādiattho, “tena ātāpino…pe… sahetudhamma’ntiādigāthāttayaṃ saṅgaṇhātī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) ācariyasāriputtattherena vuttaṃ. Khandhaketi mahāvagge. Udānagāthanti jātiyā ekavacanaṃ, tatthāpi vā paṭhamagāthameva gahetvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Some” refers to the reciters of the Khandhakas. But the view stated first is that of the reciters of the Dhammapada. Here in the text “Yadā…pe…dhammā,” the word ‘iti’, having the sense of “for example” and “beginning with,” is indicated as elided. Indeed, without an ‘iti’ for illustration and for setting a limit, the meaning is not complete. There, taking the word ‘iti’ as having only the sense of “beginning with,” the Elder, the teacher Sāriputta, has said: “The word ‘iti’ has the sense of ‘beginning’. By it, the three verses beginning ‘Ātāpino…pe…sahetudhammaṃ’ are included.” “In the Khandhaka” means in the Mahāvagga. “Udānagāthaṃ” is a generic singular. Or, it should be understood that even there, it is stated in the singular because only the first verse is taken.

Ettha ca khandhakabhāṇakā evaṃ vadanti “dhammapadabhāṇakānaṃ gāthā manasāva desitattā tadā mahato janassa upakārāya nāhosi, amhākaṃ pana gāthā vacībhedaṃ katvā desitattā tadā suṇantānaṃ devabrahmānaṃ upakārāya ahosi, tasmā idameva paṭhamabuddhavacana”nti. Dhammapadabhāṇakā pana “desanāya janassa upakārānupakārabhāvo paṭhamabhāve lakkhaṇaṃ na hoti, bhagavatā manasā paṭhamaṃ desitattā idameva paṭhamabuddhavacana”nti vadanti[M 1.0087]. Tasmā ubhayampi ubhayathā yujjatīti veditabbaṃ. Nanu ca yadi “anekajātisaṃsāra”nti gāthā manasāva desitā, atha kasmā dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “anekajātisaṃsāra’nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ satthā bodhirukkhamūle nisinno udānavasena udānetvā aparabhāge ānandattherena puṭṭho kathesī”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.152 udānavatthu) vuttanti? Atthavasena tathāyeva gahetabbattā. Tatthāpi hi manasā udānetvāti atthoyeva gahetabbo. Desanā viya hi udānampi manasā udānaṃ, vacasā udānanti dvidhā viññāyati. Yadi cāyaṃ vacasā udānaṃ siyā, udānapāḷiyamāruḷhā bhaveyya[V 1.0078], tasmā udānapāḷiyamanāruḷhabhāvoyeva vacasā anudānetvā manasā udānabhāve kāraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Pāṭipadadivase”ti idaṃ “sabbaññubhāvappattassā”ti etena na sambajjhitabbaṃ, “paccavekkhantassa uppannā”ti etena pana sambajjhitabbaṃ. Visākhapuṇṇamāyameva hi bhagavā paccūsasamaye sabbaññutaṃ patto. Lokiyasamaye pana evampi sambajjhanaṃ bhavati, tathāpi nesa sāsanasamayoti na gahetabbaṃ. Somanassameva somanassamayaṃ yathā “dānamayaṃ, sīlamaya”nti, (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60; netti. 34) taṃsampayuttañāṇenāti attho. Somanassena vā sahajātādisattiyā pakataṃ, tādisena ñāṇenātipi vaṭṭati.

Here, the reciters of the Khandhaka say thus: 'Because the verse of the reciters of the Dhammapada was taught only by mind, it was not for the benefit of the great multitude of people at that time. Our verse, however, having been taught with vocal utterance, was for the benefit of the devas and brahmās who were listening at that time. Therefore, this alone is the first utterance of the Buddha.' The reciters of the Dhammapada, however, say: 'The state of being beneficial or not beneficial to people by the teaching is not a characteristic mark of being the first. Because it was first taught by the Blessed One with the mind, this alone is the first utterance of the Buddha.' Therefore, it should be known that both are suitable in their own way. But if the verse 'anekajātisaṃsāraṃ' was taught only by mind, then why is it said in the Dhammapada Commentary: 'The Teacher, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having uttered this Dhamma teaching as an inspired utterance, later, when questioned by the Venerable Ānanda, explained it'? Because it is to be taken in that very way according to the meaning. For even there, the meaning 'having uttered an inspired utterance with the mind' is indeed to be taken. For, like a teaching, an inspired utterance is also known in two ways: as a mental inspired utterance and a verbal inspired utterance. And if this were a verbal inspired utterance, it would have been included in the Udāna Pāḷi. Therefore, the very fact of its not being included in the Udāna Pāḷi should be seen as the reason for its being an inspired utterance by mind, not uttered verbally. This phrase 'on the first day of the lunar fortnight' should not be connected with 'having attained the state of omniscience,' but it should be connected with 'arose while reflecting.' For indeed, the Blessed One attained omniscience on the full moon day of Visākha itself, at the time of dawn. However, in worldly convention, such a connection is also possible; even so, as that is not the convention of the Dispensation, it should not be taken as such. Joy itself is 'somanassamayaṃ,' just as in 'dānamayaṃ' (consisting of generosity) and 'sīlamayaṃ' (consisting of virtue); the meaning is: with the knowledge associated with that joy. Or, it is also suitable to say: with such knowledge produced by joy through the power of co-arising and so on.

Handāti codanatthe nipāto. Iṅgha sampādethāti hi codeti. Āmantayāmīti paṭivedayāmi, bodhemīti attho. Voti pana “āmantayāmī”ti etassa kammapadaṃ. “Āmantanatthe dutiyāyeva, na catutthī”ti hi vatvā tamevudāharanti akkharacintakā. Vayadhammāti aniccalakkhaṇamukhena saṅkhārānaṃ dukkhānattalakkhaṇampi vibhāveti “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15, 45, 76, 77; 2.3.1, 4; paṭi. ma. 2.10) vacanato. Lakkhaṇattayavibhāvananayeneva ca tadārammaṇaṃ vipassanaṃ dassento sabbatitthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ buddhāveṇikaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānaṃ aviparītaṃ nibbānagāminipaṭipadaṃ pakāsetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idāni tattha sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ niyojeti “appamādena sampādethā”ti, tāya catusaccakammaṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānāya aviparītanibbānagāminipaṭipadāya appamādena sampādethāti attho. Apica “vayadhammā saṅkhārā”ti etena saṅkhepena saṃvejetvā “appamādena sampādethā”ti saṅkhepeneva niravasesaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti[M 1.0088]. Appamādapadañhi sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ sāsanaṃ pariyādiyitvā tiṭṭhati, sikkhattayasaṅgahitāya kevalaparipuṇṇāya sāsanasaṅkhātāya sammāpaṭipattiyā appamādena sampādethāti attho. Ubhinnamantareti dvinnaṃ vacanānamantarāḷe vemajjhe. Ettha hi kālavatā kālopi nidassito tadavinābhāvittāti veditabbo.

The word 'handa' is a particle that occurs in the sense of urging. Indeed, it urges thus: 'Come, strive to accomplish this!' 'Āmantayāmi' means 'I shall make known,' 'I shall make understand.' The word 'vo,' however, is the object of 'āmantayāmi.' For, having said, 'In the sense of addressing, only the second case occurs, not the fourth,' the grammarians cite that very example. 'Vayadhammā' (subject to decay) reveals, by way of the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristics of suffering and non-self of conditioned things as well, because of the teaching: 'Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Whatever is suffering, that is non-self.' And it should be understood that, by this very method of revealing the three characteristics, while showing insight that has them as its object, he proclaims the unerring path leading to Nibbāna, which is founded on the meditation subject of the Four Truths, is exclusive to the Buddhas, and is beyond the sphere of all sectarians. Now, he urges them towards right practice therein, saying, 'Strive with heedfulness!' The meaning is: 'Strive with heedfulness in that unerring path leading to Nibbāna which is founded on the meditation subject of the Four Truths.' Furthermore, having stirred a sense of urgency concisely with 'conditioned things are subject to decay,' with 'strive with heedfulness,' he shows concisely the complete right practice without remainder. Indeed, the term 'heedfulness' stands, having encompassed the entire, complete Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training. The meaning is: 'Strive with heedfulness in the right practice called the Dispensation, which is entirely complete and comprised of the threefold training.' 'Ubhinnamantare' (between both) means: in the interval, in the middle of the two utterances. For herein, both the temporal event and time itself are indicated, because of their inseparability; thus it should be understood.

Suttantapiṭakanti ettha suttameva suttantaṃ yathā “kammantaṃ, vananta”nti. Saṅgītañca asaṅgītañcāti sabbasarūpamāha. “Asaṅgītanti ca saṅgītikkhandhakakathāvatthuppakaraṇādi. Keci pana ‘subhasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 1.444) paṭhamasaṅgītiyamasaṅgīta’nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Paṭhamasaṅgītito puretarameva hi āyasmatā ānandattherena jetavane viharantena subhassa māṇavassa bhāsita”nti (dī. ni. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Subhasuttaṃ pana “evaṃ me suttaṃ ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ānando sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa [V 1.0079] ārāme aciraparinibbute bhagavatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.444) āgataṃ. Tattha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādivacanaṃ paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ āyasmatā ānandatthereneva vattuṃ yuttarūpaṃ na hoti. Na hi ānandatthero sayameva subhasuttaṃ desetvā “evaṃ me suta”ntiādīni vadati. Evaṃ pana vattabbaṃ siyā “ekamidāhaṃ bhante samayaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ viharāmi jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”tiādi. Tasmā dutiyatatiyasaṅgītikārakehi “evaṃ me suta”ntiādinā subhasuttaṃ saṅgītimāropitaṃ viya dissati. Athācariyadhammapālattherassa evamadhippāyo siyā “ānandatthereneva vuttampi subhasuttaṃ paṭhamasaṅgītimāropetvā tantiṃ ṭhapetukāmehi mahākassapattherādīhi aññesu suttesu āgatanayeneva ‘evaṃ me suta’ntiādinā tanti ṭhapitā”ti. Evaṃ sati yujjeyya. Atha vā āyasmā ānando subhasuttaṃ sayaṃ desentopi sāmaññaphalādīsu bhagavatā desitanayeneva desesīti bhagavato sammukhā laddhanaye ṭhatvā desitattā bhagavatā desitaṃ dhammaṃ attani adahanto “evaṃ me suta”ntiādimāhāti evamadhippāyepi sati yujjateva. “Anusaṅgītañcā”tipi pāṭho. Dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsu puna saṅgītañcāti atthavasena ninnānākaraṇameva. Samodhānetvā vinayapiṭakaṃ nāma veditabbaṃ, sutta…pe… abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāma veditabbanti yojanā.

In the term Suttantapiṭaka, the sutta itself is the suttanta, just as in ‘kammantaṃ’ and ‘vanantaṃ’. By ‘recited and not recited,’ he states its entire scope. And ‘not recited’ refers to the Saṅgītikkhandhaka, Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa, and so on. Some, however, say that the Subhasutta was not recited at the First Council, but that is not correct. For, as stated by Ācariya Dhammapālatthera, ‘it was spoken by the Venerable Ānandatthera to the young man Subha while dwelling in Jetavana even before the First Council.’ The Subhasutta, however, is transmitted beginning with: ‘Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling in Sāvatthī at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, not long after the Blessed One had passed into final Nibbāna...’ Therein, for the Venerable Ānandatthera himself to utter the words ‘Thus have I heard,’ etc., at the First Council would not be suitable. For Ānandatthera, having taught the Subhasutta himself, would not say ‘Thus have I heard,’ etc. Rather, it should have been said thus: ‘Venerable sir, at one time I was dwelling in Sāvatthī at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park...’ and so on. Therefore, it appears as if the Subhasutta was included in the council by the compilers of the Second and Third Councils with the introduction ‘Thus have I heard,’ etc. Or, this might be Ācariya Dhammapālatthera's intention: ‘Although the Subhasutta was spoken by Ānandatthera himself, when Mahākassapatthera and others, desiring to establish the canon by including it in the First Council, established the text with “Thus have I heard,” etc., following the same method found in other suttas.’ If this is so, it would be acceptable. Alternatively, even though the Venerable Ānanda taught the Subhasutta himself, he taught it in the same way the Blessed One taught in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and others. Therefore, because he taught while abiding in the method received in the Blessed One's presence, not attributing the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to himself, he said ‘Thus have I heard,’ etc. If this is the intention, it is also quite acceptable. There is also the reading ‘Anusaṅgītañca’. In the Second and Third Councils, that it was recited again is, by way of meaning, without distinction. Having combined them, it should be known as the Vinayapiṭaka, the Suttantapiṭaka... and the Abhidhammapiṭaka; this is how the connection should be made.

Bhikkhubhikkhunīpātimokkhavasena [M 1.0089] ubhayāni pātimokkhāni. Bhikkhubhikkhunīvibhaṅgavasena dve vibhaṅgā. Mahāvaggacūḷavaggesu āgatā dvāvīsati khandhakā. Paccekaṃ soḷasahi vārehi upalakkhitattā soḷasa parivārāti vuttaṃ. Parivārapāḷiyañhi mahāvibhaṅge soḷasa vārā, bhikkhunīvibhaṅge soḷasa vārā cāti bāttiṃsa vārā āgatā. Potthakesu pana katthaci “parivārā”ti ettakameva dissati, bahūsu pana potthakesu vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyañca “soḷasa parivārā”ti evameva dissamānattā ayampi pāṭho na sakkā paṭibāhitunti tassevattho vutto. “Itī”ti yathāvuttaṃ buddhavacanaṃ nidassetvā “ida”nti taṃ parāmasati. Iti-saddo vā idamatthe, idanti vacanasiliṭṭhatāmattaṃ, iti idanti vā pariyāyadvayaṃ idamattheyeva vattati “idānetarahi vijjatī”tiādīsu viya. Esa nayo īdisesu. Brahmajālādīni catuttiṃsa suttāni saṅgayhanti ettha, etena vā, tesaṃ vā saṅgaho gaṇanā etassāti brahmajālādicatuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho. Evamitaresupi. Heṭṭhā vuttesu dīghabhāṇakamajjhimabhāṇakānaṃ vādesu majjhimabhāṇakānaññeva vādassa yuttatarattā khuddakapāṭhādayopi suttantapiṭakeyeva saṅgahetvā dassento “khuddaka…pe… suttantapiṭakaṃ nāmā”ti āha. Tattha “suṇātha bhāvitattānaṃ, gāthā atthūpanāyikāti (theragā. nidānagāthā) vuttattā “theragāthā therīgāthā”ti ca pāṭho yutto.

The two Pātimokkhas, by way of the Bhikkhu- and Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha. The two Vibhaṅgas, by way of the Bhikkhu- and Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga. The twenty-two Khandhakas are those transmitted in the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. It is said ‘sixteen Parivāras’ because each is marked by sixteen sections (vāra). For in the Parivārapāḷi, sixteen sections are transmitted in the Mahāvibhaṅga, and sixteen sections in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, thus thirty-two sections are transmitted. In some manuscripts, however, only ‘Parivārā’ is seen, but since in many manuscripts, and in the Vinayaṭṭhakathā and Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā, ‘sixteen Parivārā’ is seen just so, this reading cannot be rejected, and so the meaning of that very reading is stated. ‘Iti’ indicates the aforesaid word of the Buddha, and ‘idaṃ’ refers to it. Alternatively, the word ‘iti’ is in the sense of ‘idaṃ’; ‘idaṃ’ is merely for elegance of speech; or the pair of synonyms ‘iti idaṃ’ occurs only in the sense of ‘idaṃ’, as in ‘idāni etarahi vijjati’ and so on. This is the method in such cases. ‘The collection of the thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla’ is so called because herein the thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla are collected, or by this Nikāya they are collected, or the collection and enumeration of them belongs to this Nikāya. Likewise in the other Nikāyas. Among the views of the Dīghabhāṇakas and Majjhimabhāṇakas mentioned below, because the view of the Majjhimabhāṇakas is more suitable, the commentator, wishing to show that the Khuddakapāṭha and others are included only in the Suttantapiṭaka, said: ‘Khuddaka… is called the Suttantapiṭaka.’ Therein, because it is said: ‘Listen to the verses of those with developed selves, which bring benefit,’ the readings ‘Theragāthā’ and ‘Therīgāthā’ are suitable.

Evaṃ [V 1.0080] sarūpato piṭakattayaṃ niyametvā idāni nibbacanaṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu tibbidhesu piṭakesu. Vividhavisesanayattāti vividhanayattā, visesanayattā ca. Vinayanatoti vinayanabhāvato, bhāvappadhānaniddesoyaṃ, bhāvalopo vā, itarathā dabbameva padhānaṃ siyā, tathā ca sati vinayanatāguṇasamaṅginā vinayadabbeneva hetubhūtena vinayoti akkhāto, na pana vinayanatāguṇenāti anadhippetatthappasaṅgo bhaveyya. Ayaṃ nayo edisesu. Vinīyate vā vinayanaṃ, tatoti attho. Ayaṃ vinayoti atthapaññattibhūto saññīsaṅkhāto ayaṃ tanti vinayo. Vinayoti akkhātoti saddapaññattibhūto saññāsaṅkhāto vinayo nāmāti kathito. Atthapaññattiyā hi nāmapaññattivibhāvanaṃ nibbacananti.

Having thus defined the threefold Piṭaka according to its nature, now, to show its etymological explanation, the passage beginning ‘therein’ was stated. ‘Therein’ refers to those three kinds of Piṭakas. ‘Due to various and special methods’ means due to having various methods and due to having special methods. ‘Due to disciplining’ means due to the state of disciplining. This is a designation where the state is primary, or it is an elision of the word for ‘state’; otherwise, the substance alone would be primary. And if that were so, ‘Vinaya’ would be so called because of the substance of Vinaya, which is endowed with the quality of disciplining, being the cause, but not because of the quality of disciplining itself. Thus, the unwanted consequence of an unintended meaning would arise. This method should be applied in such cases. Alternatively, ‘disciplining’ (vinayanaṃ) is that by which one is disciplined (vinīyate); because of that (tato), it is called Vinaya. This is the meaning. This Vinaya refers to the Vinaya of the canon, which is the conceptual meaning, known as the ‘thing that is named’. That which is called ‘Vinaya’ is the conceptual name, known as a ‘name’, and is spoken of as the Vinaya by name. For indeed, the clarification of a conceptual name by means of a conceptual meaning is called an ‘etymological explanation’.

Idāni [M 1.0090] imissā gāthāya atthaṃ vibhāvento āha “vividhā hī”tiādi. “Vividhā ettha nayā, tasmā vividhanayattā vinayoti akkhāto”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Vividhattaṃ sarūpato dasseti “pañcavidhā”tiādinā, tathā visesattampi “daḷhīkammā”tiādinā. Lokavajjesu sikkhāpadesu daḷhīkammapayojanā, paṇṇattivajjesu sithilakaraṇapayojanā. Saññamavelaṃ abhibhavitvā pavatto ācāro ajjhācāro, vītikkamo, kāye, vācāya ca pavatto so, tassa nisedhanaṃ tathā, tena tathānisedhanameva pariyāyena kāyavācāvinayanaṃ nāmāti dasseti. “Tasmā”ti vatvā tassānekadhā parāmasanamāha “vividhanayattā”tiādi. Yathāvuttā ca gāthā īdisassa nibbacanassa pakāsanatthaṃ vuttāti dassetuṃ “tenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāti vividhanayattādihetunā karaṇabhūtenāti vadanti. Apica “vividhā hī”tiādivākyassa yathāvuttassa guṇaṃ dassento “tenā”tiādimāhātipi sambandhaṃ vadanti. Evaṃ sati tenāti vividhanayattādinā hetubhūtenāti attho. Atha vā yathāvuttavacanameva sandhāya porāṇehi ayaṃ gāthā vuttāti saṃsandetuṃ “tenā”tiādi vuttantipi vadanti, dutiyanaye viya “tenā”ti padassa attho. Etanti gāthāvacanaṃ. Etassāti vinayasaddassa, “vacanatthā”ti padena sambandho. “Vacanassa attho”ti hi sambandhe vuttepi tassa vacanasāmaññato visesaṃ dassetuṃ “etassā”ti puna vuttaṃ. Neruttikā pana samāsataddhitesu siddhesu sāmaññattā, nāmasaddattā ca edisesu saddantarena visesitabhāvaṃ icchanti.

Now, wishing to elucidate the meaning of this verse, he said what begins with 'vividhā hi'. It should be connected with what begins thus: 'Here, there are various methods; therefore, because of having various methods, it is called Vinaya'. He shows its variedness in its own form with what begins with 'fivefold', and likewise its specialness with what begins with 'making firm'. In the training rules that are worldly faults, there is the purpose of making firm; in the training rules that are faults by stipulation, there is the purpose of making lax. Conduct that occurs having overcome the boundary of restraint is ajjhācāra, a transgression; it occurs in the body and in speech. He shows that its prevention—that very prevention by that means—is figuratively called the disciplining of body and speech. Having said 'tasmā' (therefore), he stated its manifold consideration with what begins with 'vividhanayattā' (because of having various methods). And to show that the verse as stated was spoken for the purpose of clarifying such a derivation, what begins with 'tena' was said. They say: 'tena' means 'by the reason beginning with "vividhanayattā", which has become the instrument'. Furthermore, the teachers also state the connection thus: 'Wishing to show the quality of the aforementioned sentence beginning with "vividhā hi", he said what begins with "tena"'. This being so, the meaning is: 'tena' means 'by what begins with "vividhanayattā", which has become the cause'. Alternatively, they also say that what begins with 'tena' was said in order to connect it thus: 'This verse was spoken by the ancients with reference to the very statement as it was said'; the meaning of the word 'tena' is as in the second method. 'Etaṃ' (this) means the words of the verse. The connection of 'etassa' (of this) is with the word 'vacanattha' (meaning of the word) of the word 'vinaya'. For even when the connection is stated as 'the meaning of the word', 'etassa' was said again to show the specific meaning, due to its being a general word. Indeed, etymologists desire that in such cases, when words are established in compounds and derivatives, they be specified by another word, due to their generality and their being a noun.

“Atthāna”nti padaṃ “sūcanato…pe… suttāṇā”ti padehi yathārahaṃ kammasambandhavasena yojetabbaṃ. Tamatthaṃ vivarati “tañhī”tiādinā. Attatthaparatthādibhede attheti yo taṃ suttaṃ sajjhāyati, suṇāti, vāceti, cinteti, deseti ca, suttena saṅgahito sīlādiattho tassapi hoti, tena parassa sādhetabbato parassapīti tadubhayaṃ taṃ suttaṃ sūceti dīpeti, tathā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthe [V 1.0081] lokiyalokuttaratthe cāti evamādibhede atthe ādi-saddena saṅgaṇhāti. Atthasaddo cāyaṃ hitapariyāyo, na bhāsitatthavacano. Yadi siyā, suttaṃ attanopi bhāsitatthaṃ sūceti, parassapīti ayamanadhippetattho vutto siyā. Suttena hi yo attho pakāsito, so tasseva pakāsakassa [M 1.0091] suttassa hoti, tasmā na tena parattho sūcito, tena sūcetabbassa paratthassa nivattetabbassa abhāvā attatthaggahaṇañca na kattabbaṃ. Attatthaparatthavinimuttassa bhāsitatthassa abhāvā ādiggahaṇañca na kattabbaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttassa hitapariyāyassa atthassa sutte asambhavato suttādhārassa puggalassa vasena attatthaparatthā vuttā.

The word 'atthānaṃ' should be connected with the words 'sūcanato…pe… suttāṇā' as appropriate, by way of the objective relation. He explains that meaning with what begins with 'tañhi'. Regarding the meanings with distinctions such as one's own welfare and others' welfare: for whichever person recites, hears, teaches, reflects upon, and preaches that sutta, the meaning, such as virtue, etc., which is comprised by the sutta, is also for him; because it is to be accomplished for another, it is also for another. Therefore, that sutta indicates and illuminates both of these. Likewise, with the word 'ādi', he includes meanings with such distinctions as these: benefits in the present life and in the future, and worldly and supramundane benefits. And this word 'attha' is a synonym for 'hita' (welfare), not a word expressing the meaning of what is spoken. If it were, the sutta would indicate its own spoken meaning and also that of another, and thus this unintended meaning would be stated. For whatever meaning is clarified by a sutta, that meaning belongs only to that very sutta which clarifies it. Therefore, the meaning of another is not indicated by it. Because there is no meaning of another to be indicated by it, the taking of 'own meaning' should not be done. And because there is no spoken meaning that is separate from one's own meaning and others' meaning, the taking of 'ādi' should not be done. Therefore, because the aforesaid meaning, which is a synonym for 'hita', is impossible in the sutta itself, one's own welfare and others' welfare are spoken of by way of the person who is the receptacle of the sutta.

Atha vā suttaṃ anapekkhitvā ye attatthādayo atthappabhedā “na ha’ññadattha’tthi pasaṃsalābhā”ti etassa padassa niddese (mahāni. 63) vuttā “attattho, parattho, ubhayattho, diṭṭhadhammiko attho, samparāyiko attho, uttāno attho, gambhīro attho, gūḷho attho, paṭicchanno attho, neyyo attho, nīto attho, anavajjo attho, nikkileso attho, vodāno attho, paramattho”ti, (mahāni. 63) te atthappabhede sūcetīti attho gahetabbo. Kiñcāpi hi suttanirapekkhaṃ attatthādayo vuttā suttatthabhāvena aniddiṭṭhattā, tesu pana ekopi atthappabhedo suttena dīpetabbataṃ nātivattatīti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe atthasaddo bhāsitatthapariyāyopi hoti. Ettha hi purimakā pañca atthappabhedā hitapariyāyā, tato pare cha bhāsitatthappabhedā, pacchimakā cattāro ubhayasabhāvā. Tattha suviññeyyatāya vibhāvena anagādhabhāvo uttāno. Duradhigamatāya vibhāvena agādhabhāvo gambhīro. Avivaṭo gūḷho. Mūludakādayo viya paṃsunā akkharasannivesādinā tirohito paṭicchanno. Niddhāretvā ñāpetabbo neyyo. Yathārutavasena veditabbo nīto. Anavajjanikkilesavodānā pariyāyavasena vuttā, kusalavipākakiriyādhammavasena vā yathākkamaṃ yojetabbā. Paramattho nibbānaṃ, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo eva vā.

Alternatively, without regard to the Sutta, the meaning should be taken as: it indicates those distinctions of meaning, beginning with one's own welfare, which are spoken of in the explanation of the phrase 'There is no other welfare than praise and gain', namely: 'one's own welfare, others' welfare, the welfare of both; welfare in the present life, welfare in a future life; an obvious meaning, a profound meaning, a concealed meaning, a hidden meaning, a meaning requiring guidance, a direct meaning; a blameless welfare, a stainless welfare, a pure welfare, the ultimate welfare'. For although those beginning with one's own welfare were spoken without reference to a sutta, because they were not designated as the meaning of a sutta, yet not even one of those distinctions of meaning surpasses being that which is to be illuminated by a sutta. And in this alternative of meaning, the word 'attha' is also a synonym for 'bhāsitattha' (spoken meaning). Here, the first five distinctions of meaning are synonyms for 'hita' (welfare), the next six are distinctions of spoken meaning, and the last four have a dual nature. Therein, 'obvious' is the state of not being deep in elucidation, due to being easily understood. 'Profound' is the state of being deep in elucidation, due to being difficult to attain. 'Concealed' is the unrevealed meaning. 'Hidden' is that which is obscured by the arrangement of letters, etc., like roots, water, and so on are by dust. 'Requiring guidance' is that which should be made known by extracting it. 'Direct' is that which should be understood according to the way it was uttered. 'Blameless', 'stainless', and 'pure' are spoken of by way of synonyms, or they should be connected respectively by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional dhammas. The 'ultimate welfare' is Nibbāna, or it is simply the undistorted nature of dhammas.

Atha vā “attanā ca appiccho hotī”ti attatthaṃ, “appicchakathañca paresaṃ kattā hotī”ti paratthaṃ sūceti. Evaṃ “attanā ca pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, parañca pāṇātipātā veramaṇiyā samādapetī”tiādisuttāni (a. ni. 4.99, 265) yojetabbāni. Apare pana “yathāsabhāvaṃ bhāsitaṃ attatthaṃ, pūraṇakassapādīnamaññatitthiyānaṃ samayabhūtaṃ paratthaṃ sūceti, suttena vā saṅgahitaṃ attatthaṃ, suttānulomabhūtaṃ paratthaṃ, suttantanayabhūtaṃ vā attatthaṃ, vinayābhidhammanayabhūtaṃ paratthaṃ [M 1.0092] sūcetī”tipi vadanti. Vinayābhidhammehi ca visesetvā suttasaddassa attho vattabbo, tasmā veneyyajjhāsayavasappavattāya desanāya sātisayaṃ attahitaparahitādīni [V 1.0082] pakāsitāni honti tappadhānabhāvato, na pana āṇādhammasabhāva-vasappavattāyāti idameva “atthānaṃ sūcanato sutta”nti vuttaṃ. Sūca-saddassa cettha rasso. “Evañca katvā ‘ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpanna’nti (pāci. 655, 1242) ca sakavāde pañca suttasatānī’ti (aṭṭhasā. nidānakathā, kathā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) ca evamādīsu suttasaddo upacaritoti gahetabbo”ti (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) ācariyasāriputtattherena vuttaṃ. Aññe pana yathāvuttasadiseneva nibbacanena suttasaddassa vinayābhidhammānampi vācakattaṃ vadanti.

Alternatively: because it is said, 'oneself is of few desires,' it indicates one's own benefit; because it is said, 'one makes for others a talk on few desires,' it indicates the benefit of others. In this way, suttas such as, 'oneself abstains from killing living beings, and one encourages another to undertake abstinence from killing,' should be connected. Other teachers, however, say that it indicates one's own benefit, which is what is spoken according to its own nature, and the benefit of others, which is the doctrine of other sectarians like Pūraṇa Kassapa. Or, it indicates one's own benefit, which is what is included by the sutta, and the other's benefit, which is what is in accordance with the sutta; or, one's own benefit, which is the Suttanta method, and the other's benefit, which is the Vinaya and Abhidhamma method. And the meaning of the word 'sutta' should be stated by distinguishing it from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. Therefore, because in a teaching that proceeds according to the disposition of the trainable, one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so on, are exceedingly proclaimed due to that being its primary nature—but not so in a teaching that proceeds according to the nature of command and ultimate reality—this very Sutta Piṭaka is called a 'sutta' because it indicates meanings. And here, the vowel of the word 'sūca' is short. 'And having done so, in such cases as, "So much of the Blessed One's teaching has come down in the suttas, is included in the suttas," and, "In our own doctrine, there are five hundred suttas," the word "sutta" should be understood as used figuratively.' Thus it was said by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta. Other teachers, however, say that by a derivation just like the one stated, the word 'sutta' is also a designator of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.

Sutte ca āṇādhammasabhāvo veneyyajjhāsayamanuvattati, na vinayābhidhammesu viya veneyyajjhāsayo āṇādhammasabhāve, tasmā veneyyānaṃ ekantahitapaṭilābhasaṃvattanikā suttantadesanāti āha “suvuttā cettha atthā”tiādi. “Ekantahitapaṭilābhasaṃvattanikā suttantadesanā”ti idampi veneyyānaṃ hitasampādane suttantadesanāya tapparabhāvameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tapparabhāvo ca veneyyajjhāsayānulomato daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha “veneyyajjhāsayānulomena vuttattā”ti. Etena ca hetunā nanu vinayābhidhammāpi suvuttā, atha kasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti anuyogaṃ pariharati.

And in the Sutta, the nature of command and ultimate reality conforms to the disposition of the trainable, unlike in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, where the disposition of the trainable conforms to the nature of command and ultimate reality. Therefore, the Suttanta teaching brings about the certain attainment of welfare for the trainable. Thus, the commentator said, 'Well-spoken are the meanings here,' and so on. This statement, 'The Suttanta teaching brings about the certain attainment of welfare,' was also said with reference only to the Suttanta teaching's quality of being devoted to accomplishing the welfare of the trainable. And that quality of being devoted should be understood from its conformity to the disposition of the trainable. For that very reason, he said, 'because it is spoken in accordance with the disposition of the trainable.' And by this reason, he refutes the objection: 'Are not the Vinaya and Abhidhamma also well-spoken? Then why is this very teaching spoken of thus?'

Anupubbasikkhādivasena kālantarena atthābhinipphattiṃ dassetuṃ “sassamiva phala”nti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā sassaṃ nāma vapanaropanādikkhaṇeyeva phalaṃ na pasavati, anupubbajagganādivasena kālantareneva pasavati, tathā idampi savanadhāraṇādikkhaṇeyeva atthe na pasavati, anupubbasikkhādivasena kālantareneva pasavatīti. Pasavatīti ca phalati, abhinipphādetīti attho. Abhinipphādanameva hi phalanaṃ. Upāyasamaṅgīnaññeva atthābhinipphattiṃ dassento “dhenu viya khīra”nti āha. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yathā dhenu nāma kāle jātavacchā thanaṃ gahetvā duhataṃ upāyavantānameva khīraṃ paggharāpeti, na akāle ajātavacchā. Kālepi vā visāṇādikaṃ gahetvā duhataṃ anupāyavantānaṃ, tathā idampi nissaraṇādinā savanadhāraṇādīni kurutaṃ upāyavantānameva [M 1.0093] sīlādiatthe paggharāpeti, na alagaddūpamāya savanadhāraṇādīni kurutaṃ anupāyavantānanti. Yadipi “sūdatī”ti etassa gharati siñcatīti attho, tathāpi sakammikadhātuttā paggharāpetīti kāritavasena attho vutto yathā “taratī”ti etassa nipātetīti attho”ti. “Suttāṇā”ti etassa atthamāha “suṭṭhu ca ne tāyatī”ti. Neti atthe.

To show the accomplishment of the benefit after some time through progressive training, it is said, 'like a crop, it bears fruit.' This is what is meant: just as a crop does not bear fruit at the very moment of sowing and planting, but bears fruit only after some time through progressive tending, so too this sutta does not produce its benefits at the very moment of hearing and memorizing, but produces them only after some time through progressive training. And 'pasavati' means 'it bears fruit,' that is, 'it accomplishes.' For accomplishment itself is fruition. To show that the accomplishment of the benefit occurs only for those endowed with the right method, he said, 'like a cow, milk.' This is the intention here: just as a cow that has given birth, at the proper time, yields milk only to those with the right method who milk her by taking the udder—not at the wrong time, or if she has not given birth, nor even at the right time for those without the right method who try to milk her by taking the horns—so too this teaching causes the benefits of virtue and so on to flow only for those with the right method who practice hearing, memorizing, and so on, beginning with renunciation, not for those without the right method who practice these things like one wrongly grasping a snake. Although the meaning of 'sūdati' is 'it flows, it sprinkles,' nevertheless, because it is a transitive verb, the meaning 'causes to flow' is stated in the causative sense, just as the meaning of 'tarati' is stated as 'causes to fall.' He states the meaning of 'suttāṇa' as 'and it protects them well.' Here, 'ne' refers to the benefits.

Suttasabhāganti [V 1.0083] suttasadisaṃ. Tabbhāvaṃ dasseti “yathā hī”tiādinā. Tacchakānaṃ suttanti vaḍḍhakīnaṃ kāḷasuttaṃ. Pamāṇaṃ hoti tadanusārena tacchanato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā kāḷasuttaṃ pasāretvā saññāṇe kate gahetabbaṃ, vissajjetabbañca paññāyati, tasmā taṃ tacchakānaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ vivādesu uppannesu sutte ānītamatte “idaṃ gahetabbaṃ, idaṃ vissajjetabba”nti pākaṭattā vivādo vūpasammati, tasmā etaṃ viññūnaṃ pamāṇanti. Idāni aññathāpi suttasabhāgataṃ vibhāvento “yathā cā”tiādimāha. Suttenāti pupphāvutena yena kenaci thirasuttena. Saṅgahitānīti suṭṭhu, samaṃ vā gahitāni, āvutānīti attho. Na vikiriyantīti ito cito ca vippakiṇṇābhāvamāha, na viddhaṃsīyantīti chejjabhejjābhāvaṃ. Ayametthādhippāyo – yathā thirasuttena saṅgahitāni pupphāni vātena na vikiriyanti na viddhaṃsīyanti, evaṃ suttena saṅgahitā atthā micchāvādena na vikiriyanti na viddhaṃsīyantīti. Veneyyajjhāsayavasappavattāya ca desanāya attatthaparatthādīnaṃ sātisayappakāsanato āṇādhammasabhāvehi vinayābhidhammehi visesetvā imasseva suttasabhāgatā vuttā. “Tenā”tiādīsu vuttanayānusārena sambandho ceva attho ca yathārahaṃ vattabbo. Ettha ca “suttantapiṭaka”nti heṭṭhā vuttepi antasaddassa avacanaṃ tassa visuṃ atthābhāvadassanatthaṃ tabbhāvavuttito. Sahayogassa hi saddassa avacanena sesatā tassa tulyādhikaraṇataṃ, anatthakataṃ vā ñāpeti.

“Suttasabhāga” means similar to a thread. Its nature is shown by the phrase “just as,” and so forth. The “thread of carpenters” refers to the black thread of woodworkers. It serves as a standard because of planing according to it. This is what is meant: just as, when a black thread is stretched out and a mark is made, what should be taken and what should be discarded becomes apparent, and therefore it is a standard for woodworkers; so too, when disputes arise, as soon as a sutta is brought forth, it becomes clear that “this should be taken, this should be discarded,” and thus the dispute is settled. Therefore, this is a standard for the wise. Now, explaining the similarity to a thread in another way, the author says, “just as,” and so forth. “By a thread” means by any strong thread used for stringing flowers. “Gathered together” means well or evenly taken, that is, strung. “They are not scattered” indicates the state of not being dispersed here and there; “they are not destroyed” indicates the state of not being cut or broken. The intended meaning here is this: just as flowers strung by a strong thread are not scattered or destroyed by the wind, so too are the meanings gathered by the sutta not scattered or destroyed by wrong views. And because the teaching proceeds according to the dispositions of those to be trained, and because it reveals the benefits for oneself and others in an exceptional way, this similarity to a thread is stated specifically for the Sutta Piṭaka, distinguishing it from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, which have the nature of command and ultimate phenomena. In the phrases beginning with “Therefore,” and so forth, the connection and meaning should be stated appropriately according to the method already explained. Here, even though “Suttanta Piṭaka” is mentioned below, the word “anta” is not explained in order to show that it has no separate meaning, because it is spoken of as being of that very nature. For the non-explanation of a connected word indicates that the remainder either shares the same grammatical basis or is meaningless.

Yanti esa nipāto kāraṇe, yenāti attho. Ettha abhidhamme vuḍḍhimanto dhammā yena vuttā, tena abhidhammo nāma akkhātoti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Abhi-saddassa atthavasenāyaṃ pabhedoti tassa tadatthappavattatādassanena tamatthaṃ sādhento “ayañhī”tiādimāha. Abhi-saddo [M 1.0094] kamanakiriyāya vuḍḍhibhāvasaṅkhātamatirekatthaṃ dīpetīti vuttaṃ “abhikkamantītiādīsu vuḍḍhiyaṃ āgato”ti. Abhiññātāti aḍḍhacandādinā kenaci saññāṇena ñātā, paññātā pākaṭāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aḍḍhacandādibhāvo hi rattiyā upalakkhaṇavasena paññāṇaṃ hoti “yasmā aḍḍho, tasmā aṭṭhamī. Yasmā ūno, tasmā cātuddasī. Yasmā puṇṇo, tasmā pannarasī”ti. Abhilakkhitāti etthāpi ayamevattho veditabbo, idaṃ pana mūlapaṇṇāsake bhayabheravasutte (ma. ni. 1.34) abhilakkhitasaddapariyāyo abhiññātasaddoti āha “abhiññātā abhilakkhitātiādīsu lakkhaṇe”ti. Yajjevaṃ lakkhitasaddasseva lakkhaṇatthadīpanato abhi-saddo anatthakova siyāti? Nevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tassāpi tadatthajotanato. Vācakasaddasannidhāne hi upasagganipātā tadatthajotakamattāti lakkhitasaddena vācakabhāvena pakāsitassa lakkhaṇatthasseva jotakabhāvena pakāsanato abhi-saddopi lakkhaṇe pavattatīti vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rājābhirājāti parehi [V 1.0084] rājūhi pūjitumaraho rājā. Pūjiteti pūjārahe. Idaṃ pana suttanipāte selasutte (su. ni. 553 ādayo).

The word “yaṃ” is a particle in the sense of cause; the meaning is “for which reason.” Here, it should be connected individually: “Because in this Abhidhamma, teachings endowed with growth are spoken of, for that reason it is called Abhidhamma.” This distinction is by way of the meaning of the prefix “abhi.” To establish that meaning by showing its occurrence in that sense, the author says, “For this…” and so forth. The prefix “abhi” indicates the meaning of excess, which is designated as the state of increase in the action of going; thus it is said, “in ‘abhikkamanti,’ etc., it has come in the sense of growth.” “Abhiññātā” means known by some sign such as a half-moon, recognized, and manifest; this is what is meant. For the state of the half-moon and so forth is a sign by way of indicating the night: “Because it is half, it is the eighth day. Because it is diminished, it is the fourteenth day. Because it is full, it is the fifteenth day.” In “abhilakkhitā” also, this same meaning should be understood. Furthermore, this statement is from the Bhayabheravasutta in the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka (ma. ni. 1.34). The word “abhiññāta” is a synonym for the word “abhilakkhita”; therefore, regarding “abhiññātā,” “abhilakkhitā,” and so on, the author says it is in the sense of “characteristic.” If so, since the meaning of “characteristic” is indicated by the word “lakkhita” itself, would the prefix “abhi” not be meaningless? It should not be seen thus, because it too illuminates that meaning. For when in proximity to a signifying word, prefixes and particles are mere illuminators of its meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that it is said the prefix “abhi” also occurs in the sense of “characteristic” because it illuminates, in its capacity as an illuminator, the very meaning of “characteristic” which was expressed by the word “lakkhita” in its capacity as a signifier. “Rājābhirājā” means a king worthy of being honored by other kings. “Pūjite” is in the sense of “worthy of honor.” This, moreover, is in the Selasutta of the Suttanipāta (su. ni. 553 ādayo).

Abhidhammeti “supinantena sukkavisaṭṭhiyā anāpattibhāvepi akusalacetanā upalabbhatī”tiādinā (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vinayapaññattiyā saṅkaravirahite dhamme. Pubbāparavirodhābhāvena yathāvuttadhammānameva aññamaññasaṅkaravirahato aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhammetipi vadanti. “Pāṇātipāto akusala”nti (ma. ni. 2.192) evamādīsu vā maraṇādhippāyassa jīvitindriyupacchedakapayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā akusalo, na pāṇasaṅkhātajīvitindriyassa upacchedasaṅkhāto atipāto. Tathā “adinnassa parasantakassa ādānasaṅkhātā viññatti abyākato dhammo, taṃviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā akusalo dhammo”ti evamādināpi aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhammeti attho veditabbo. Abhivinayeti ettha pana “jātarūparajataṃ na paṭiggahetabba”nti vadanto vinaye vineti nāma. Ettha ca “evaṃ paṭiggaṇhato pācittiyaṃ, evaṃ pana dukkaṭa”nti vadanto abhivinaye vineti nāmāti vadanti. Tasmā jātarūparajataṃ parasantakaṃ theyyacittena gaṇhantassa yathāvatthuṃ [M 1.0095] pārājikathullaccayadukkaṭesu aññataraṃ, bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena gaṇhantassa pācittiyaṃ, attano atthāya gaṇhantassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, kevalaṃ lolatāya gaṇhantassa anāmāsadukkaṭaṃ, rūpiyachaḍḍakasammatassa anāpattīti evaṃ aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite vinayepi paṭibalo vinetunti attho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ pana paricchinnataṃ sarūpato saṅkhepeneva dassento “aññamañña…pe… hotī”ti āha.

“Abhidhamma” refers to the Dhamma that is free from confusion with the Vinaya's ordinances, as in the statement: “Even though there is no offense for a seminal emission during a dream, an unwholesome intention is found,” and so forth (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā). Because there is no contradiction between what comes before and after, and because the aforementioned dhammas themselves are free from mutual confusion, the teachers also speak of it as “the Dhamma free from mutual confusion.” Or, in statements such as, “Destroying life is unwholesome” (ma. ni. 2.192), the intention—originating the effort that cuts off the life faculty with the purpose of killing—is unwholesome; the striking down, designated as the cutting off of the life faculty called “a living being,” is not itself unwholesome. Similarly, in statements such as, “The intimation, designated as taking what is not given and belongs to another, is an indeterminate dhamma, whereas the thieving intention that originates that intimation is an unwholesome dhamma,” the meaning should also be understood as “the Dhamma free from mutual confusion.” As for “Abhivinaya,” one who says, “Gold and silver should not be accepted,” is called one who trains in the Vinaya. But the teachers say that one who explains, “For accepting in this way there is a pācittiya offense, but for accepting in that way there is a dukkaṭa offense,” is called one who trains in the Abhivinaya. Therefore, the meaning should be understood that one is capable of training even in the Vinaya that is free from mutual confusion, as follows: for one who takes gold and silver belonging to another with a thieving mind, there is one of the pārājika, thullaccaya, or dukkaṭa offenses, according to the value; for one who takes it on the basis of being a treasurer, there is a pācittiya offense; for one who takes it for one's own benefit, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense; for one who takes it merely out of fickleness, there is an anāmāsa dukkaṭa offense; for one designated as a “discarder of money,” there is no offense. Thus, showing its distinctness in its own nature and only concisely, the author says, “mutual… and so on… is.”

Abhikkantenāti ettha kantiyā adhikattaṃ abhi-saddo dīpetīti vuttaṃ “adhike”ti. Nanu ca “abhikkamantī”ti ettha abhi-saddo kamanakiriyāya vuḍḍhibhāvaṃ atirekattaṃ dīpeti, “abhiññātā abhilakkhitā”ti ettha ñāṇalakkhaṇakiriyānaṃ supākaṭataṃ visesaṃ, “abhikkantenā”ti ettha kantiyā adhikattaṃ visiṭṭhabhāvaṃ dīpetīti idaṃ tāva yuttaṃ kiriyāvisesakattā upasaggassa. “Pādayo kiriyāyoge upasaggā”ti hi saddasatthe vuttaṃ. “Abhirājā, abhivinaye”ti pana pūjitaparicchinnesu rājavinayesu abhi-saddo vattatīti kathametaṃ yujjeyya. Na hi asatvavācī saddo satvavācako sambhavatīti? Natthi atra doso pūjanaparicchedanakiriyānampi dīpanato, tāhi ca kiriyāhi yuttesu rājavinayesupi pavattattā. Abhipūjito rājāti hi atthena kiriyākārakasambandhaṃ nimittaṃ katvā kammasādhanabhūtaṃ rājadabbaṃ abhi-saddo padhānato vadati, pūjanakiriyaṃ pana appadhānato. Tathā abhiparicchinno vinayoti [V 1.0085] atthena kiriyākārakasambandhaṃ nimittaṃ katvā kammasādhanabhūtaṃ vinayadabbaṃ abhi-saddo padhānato vadati, paricchindanakiriyaṃ pana appadhānato. Tasmā atimālādīsu ati-saddo viya abhi-saddo ettha saha sādhanena kiriyaṃ vadatīti abhirājaabhivinayasaddā sopasaggāva siddhā. Evaṃ abhidhammasaddepi abhisaddo saha sādhanena vuḍḍhiyādikiriyaṃ vadatīti ayamattho dassitoti veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase `abhikkantena`, the prefix `abhi-` indicates an excellence of delightfulness; therefore, it is said by the commentator to be in the sense of 'excellent'. Now then, in `abhikkamanti`, the prefix `abhi-` indicates growth and excellence in the action of going; in `abhiññātā abhilakkhitā`, it indicates a special distinction of being very clear in the actions of knowing and marking; and in `abhikkantena`, it indicates an excellence and distinction of delightfulness. This is indeed appropriate because a prefix specifies an action. For in the grammatical texts it is said: 'The `pa`-group are prefixes when in conjunction with a verb.' However, in `abhirājā` and `abhivinaye`, the prefix `abhi-` applies to honored kings and delimited disciplines. How can this be suitable? For a word that denotes a substance cannot denote an action, can it? There is no fault here, because it also indicates the actions of honoring and delimiting, and because it applies to kings and disciplines that are connected with those actions. For, in the sense of 'a king who is honored,' taking the connection between action and agent as the basis, the prefix `abhi-` primarily denotes the substance 'king,' which is formed with the objective derivation, while it denotes the action of honoring secondarily. Similarly, in the sense of 'a discipline that is delimited,' taking the connection between action and agent as the basis, the prefix `abhi-` primarily denotes the substance 'discipline,' which is formed with the objective derivation, while it denotes the action of delimiting secondarily. Therefore, just as the prefix `ati-` in words like `atimāla`, here too the prefix `abhi-` denotes the action together with the derived object. Thus, the words `abhirāja` and `abhivinaya` are established as having prefixes. Likewise, in the word `abhidhamma` too, it should be understood that this meaning is shown: the prefix `abhi-` denotes the action of growth, etc., together with the derived agent.

Hotu abhi-saddo yathāvuttesu atthesu, tappayogena pana dhammasaddena dīpitā vuḍḍhimantādayo dhammā ettha vuttā na bhaveyyuṃ, kathaṃ ayamattho yujjeyyāti anuyoge sati taṃ pariharanto “ettha cā”tiādimāha. Tattha etthāti etasmiṃ abhidhamme. Upanyāse ca-saddo. Bhāvetīti cittassa vaḍḍhanaṃ vuttaṃ, pharitvāti ārammaṇassa vaḍḍhanaṃ, tasmā tāhi bhāvanāpharaṇavuḍḍhīhi vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttāti attho[M 1.0096]. Ārammaṇādīhīti ārammaṇasampayuttakammadvārapaṭipadādīhi. Ekantato lokuttaradhammānaññeva pūjārahattā “sekkhā dhammā”tiādinā teyeva pūjitāti dassitā. “Pūjārahā”ti etena kattādisādhanaṃ, atītādikālaṃ, sakkuṇeyyatthaṃ vā nivatteti. Pūjitabbāyeva hi dhammā kālavisesaniyamarahitā pūjārahā ettha vuttāti adhippāyo dassito. Sabhāvaparicchinnattāti phusanādisabhāvena paricchinnattā. Kāmāvacarehi mahantabhāvato mahaggatā dhammā adhikā, tatopi uttaravirahato anuttarā dhammāti dasseti “mahaggatā”tiādinā. Tenāti “vuḍḍhimanto”tiādinā vacanena karaṇabhūtena, hetubhūtena vā.

Let the prefix `abhi-` have the meanings as stated. However, through its conjunction with the word `dhamma`, the dhammas possessing growth, etc., indicated thereby would not be spoken of here. How could this meaning be suitable? When this inquiry is made, the commentator, refuting it, said, `ettha ca`, etc. Therein, `ettha` means 'in this Abhidhamma.' The particle `ca` is in the sense of introduction. By `bhāveti` (develops), the growth of the mind is stated; by `pharitvā` (pervading), the growth of the object. Therefore, the meaning is that by those growths of development and pervasion, dhammas possessing growth are also spoken of. `Ārammaṇādīhi` (by objects, etc.) means by objects, associated states, kamma, doors, practice, etc. Because supramundane dhammas alone are exclusively worthy of honor, it is shown by `sekkhā dhammā` (dhammas of the trainee), etc., that they alone are honored. By `pūjārahā` (worthy of honor), he excludes agent derivation, etc., past time, etc., or the meaning of capability. For the intended meaning shown is this: dhammas that are simply to be honored, free from the limitation of a specific time, are spoken of here as 'worthy of honor.' `Sabhāvaparicchinnattā` (because of being delimited by their intrinsic nature) means because of being delimited by their intrinsic nature of contact, etc. The sublime dhammas are superior because of their greatness in comparison to the sense-sphere dhammas; even more superior than those are the unsurpassed dhammas, because they are without a superior—this is what he shows by `mahaggatā`, etc. `Tena` (by that) means by the statement `vuḍḍhimanto`, etc., which is either instrumental or causal.

Yaṃ panetthāti etesu vinayādīsu tīsu aññamaññavisiṭṭhesu yaṃ avisiṭṭhaṃ samānaṃ, taṃ piṭakanti attho. Vinayādayo hi tayo saddā aññamaññāsādhāraṇattā visiṭṭhā nāma, piṭakasaddo pana tehi tīhipi sādhāraṇattā “avisiṭṭho”ti vuccati. Pariyattibbhājanatthatoti pariyāpuṇitabbatthapatiṭṭhānatthehi karaṇabhūtehi, visesanabhūtehi vā. Apica pariyattibbhājanatthato pariyattibhājanatthanti āhūti attho daṭṭhabbo. Paccattatthe hi to-saddo iti-saddena niddisitabbattā. Itinā niddisitabbehito – saddamicchanti neruttikā yathā “aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassantī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.406, 408, 411) etena pariyāpuṇitabbato, taṃtadatthānaṃ bhājanato ca piṭakaṃ nāmāti dasseti. Anipphannapāṭipadikapadañhetaṃ. Saddavidū pana “piṭa saddasaṅghāṭesū”ti vatvā idha vuttameva payogamudāharanti, tasmā tesaṃ matena piṭīyati saddīyati pariyāpuṇīyatīti piṭakaṃ, piṭīyati vā saṅghāṭīyati taṃtadattho etthāti piṭakanti nibbacanaṃ kātabbaṃ. “Tenā”tiādinā samāsaṃ dasseti.

As for `yaṃ panettha`: among these three—Vinaya, etc.—which are distinct from one another, that which is common and not distinct, that is the meaning of `piṭaka`. For the three terms, Vinaya, etc., are called 'distinct' because they are not common to one another, but the term `piṭaka` is called 'not distinct' because it is common to all three of them. `Pariyattibbhājanatthatoti` means in the senses of being the foundation for the meaning to be learned, either as instrumental or as qualifying. Furthermore, the meaning should be seen as: they say `pariyattibhājanatthaṃ` (it has the meaning of being a receptacle for what is to be learned). For the suffix `-to` is in the nominative sense, because it is to be indicated by the word `iti`. Grammarians desire the `-to` suffix to be indicated by `iti`, as in `aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassanti` (they see as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self). By this, he shows that it is called `piṭaka` because it is to be learned and because it is a receptacle for the various meanings. And this is an underived nominal stem. Experts in grammar, however, saying, 'The root `piṭa` is in the senses of "sound" and "collecting,"' cite only the usage mentioned here. Therefore, according to their view, the etymological analysis should be made thus: it is `piṭaka` because it is sounded out and learned; or, it is `piṭaka` because the various meanings are collected or combined therein. By `tena`, etc., he shows the compound.

Mā [V 1.0086] piṭakasampadānenāti kālāmasutte, (a. ni. 3.66) sāḷhasutte (a. ni. 3.67) ca āgataṃ pāḷimāha. Tadaṭṭhakathāyañca “amhākaṃ piṭakatantiyā saddhiṃ sametīti mā gaṇhitthā”ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.66) attho vutto. Ācariyasāriputtattherena pana “pāḷisampadānavasena mā gaṇhathā”ti (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Kudālapiṭakamādāyāti kudālañca [M 1.0097] piṭakañca ādāya. Ku vuccati pathavī, tassā dālanato vidālanato ayomayaupakaraṇaviseso kudālaṃ nāma. Tesaṃ tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ bhājanabhāvato tālapaṇṇavettalatādīhi kato bhājanaviseso piṭakaṃ nāma. Idaṃ pana mūlapaṇṇāsake kakacūpamasutte (ma. ni. 1.227).

He cites the Pāḷi passage `Mā piṭakasampadānena` (Do not go by the authority of the Piṭaka), which comes in the Kālāma Sutta and the Sāḷha Sutta. And in the commentary on those suttas, the meaning is given as: 'Do not accept it just because it agrees with our textual tradition of the Piṭaka.' The venerable Ācariya Sāriputta, however, has said: 'Do not accept it on the basis of textual transmission.' `Kudālapiṭakamādāya` means 'having taken a spade and a basket.' `Ku` is said of the earth; because it splits or breaks it, a particular iron implement is called `kudāla`. Because it is a receptacle for various things, a particular container made from palm leaves, cane, etc., is called `piṭaka`. This, however, is in the Kakacūpama Sutta in the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka.

“Tena…pe… ñeyyā”ti gāthāpadaṃ ulliṅgetvā “tenā”tiādinā vivarati. Sabbādīhi sabbanāmehi vuttassa vā liṅgamādiyate, vuccamānassa vā, idha pana vatticchāya vuttassevāti katvā “vinayo ca so piṭakañcā”ti vuttaṃ. “Yathāvutteneva nayenā”ti iminā “evaṃ duvidhatthena…pe… katvā”ti ca “pariyattibhāvato, tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato cā”ti ca vuttaṃ sabbamatidisati. Tayopīti ettha apisaddo, pi-saddo vā avayavasampiṇḍanattho. “Apī”ti avatvā “pī”ti vadanto hi api-saddo viya pi-saddopi visuṃ nipāto atthīti dasseti.

Having skipped over the verse-phrase 'Tena…pe… ñeyyā,' he explains it with 'tenā,' etc. By pronouns beginning with 'sabba,' the gender of what has been said or of what is being said is taken. Here, however, due to the speaker's intention, because the gender of only what has been stated is taken, it is said, 'vinayo ca so piṭakañca.' By this phrase, 'Yathāvutteneva nayenā,' he makes an extended application of all that was said in the phrases 'evaṃ duvidhatthena…pe… katvā' and 'pariyattibhāvato, tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato cā.' In 'Tayopī,' the word 'api,' or 'pi,' has the meaning of combining the parts. Indeed, by not saying 'api' but saying 'pi,' he shows that just like the word 'api,' the word 'pi' also exists as a separate particle.

Kathetabbānaṃ atthānaṃ desakāyattena āṇādividhinā atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanā. Sāsitabbapuggalagatena yathāparādhādisāsitabbabhāvena anusāsanaṃ vinayanaṃ sāsanaṃ. Kathetabbassa saṃvarāsaṃvarādino atthassa kathanaṃ vacanapaṭibaddhatākaraṇaṃ kathā, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – desitāraṃ bhagavantamapekkhitvā desanā, sāsitabbapuggalavasena sāsanaṃ, kathetabbassa atthassa vasena kathāti evamimesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ veditabbanti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi desanādayo desetabbādinirapekkhā na honti, āṇādayo pana visesato desakādiadhīnāti taṃ taṃ visesayogavasena desanādīnaṃ bhedo vutto. Yathā hi āṇāvidhānaṃ visesato āṇārahādhīnaṃ tattha kosallayogato, evaṃ vohāraparamatthavidhānāni ca vidhāyakādhīnānīti āṇādividhino desakāyattatā vuttā. Aparādhajjhāsayānurūpaṃ viya ca dhammānurūpampi sāsanaṃ visesato, tathā vinetabbapuggalāpekkhanti sāsitabbapuggalavasena sāsanaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṃvarāsaṃvaranāmarūpānaṃ viya ca vinibbeṭhetabbāya diṭṭhiyā kathanaṃ sati vācāvatthusmiṃ, nāsatīti visesato tadadhīnaṃ, tasmā kathetabbassa atthassa vasena kathā vuttā. Honti cettha –

The making known and awakening to meanings that are to be spoken, by way of the method of command and so on, which is dependent on the teacher, is desanā (teaching). The admonishing and training, by way of the state of being one who is to be disciplined according to offense and so on, which pertains to the person to be disciplined, is sāsana (discipline). The speaking on a meaning to be spoken, such as restraint and non-restraint, which is the act of making it bound to speech, is kathā (discourse). This is what is meant: with reference to the Blessed One, the teacher, it is desanā; by way of the person to be disciplined, it is sāsana; by way of the meaning to be spoken, it is kathā. Thus, the distinction between these should be known. And here, although teaching and so on are not independent of what is to be taught, etc., commands and so on are, however, especially dependent on the teacher, etc. Therefore, the distinction of teaching and so on is stated by way of connection with this or that particularity. For just as the ordaining of a command is especially dependent on one who is worthy of commanding, due to the skill therein, so too are the applications of conventional and ultimate realities dependent on the one who establishes them; thus, the dependence of the method of command and so on upon the teacher is stated. And just as discipline is in accordance with offense and disposition, so too is discipline in accordance with the Dhamma especially dependent on the person to be trained in such a way; thus, discipline is stated by way of the person to be disciplined. And just as there is speaking on restraint, non-restraint, and name-and-form, so too is there speaking for the unraveling of a view that is to be unraveled when there is a basis for speech, but not when there is not; thus, it is especially dependent on that. Therefore, discourse is stated by way of the meaning to be spoken. And here there are these [verses]:

“Desakassa [V 1.0087][M 1.0098] vasenettha, desanā piṭakattayaṃ;

Sāsitabbavasenetaṃ, sāsananti pavuccati.

Herein, by way of the teacher, the three Piṭakas are called desanā (teaching); by way of the one to be disciplined, this is called sāsana (discipline).

Kathetabbassa atthassa, vasenāpi kathāti ca;

Desanāsāsanakathā-bhedampevaṃ pakāsaye”ti.

And by way of the meaning to be spoken, it is also called kathā (discourse); thus should one explain the distinction between desanā, sāsana, and kathā.

Padattayampetaṃ samodhānetvā tāsaṃ bhedoti katvā bhedasaddo visuṃ visuṃ yojetabbo dvandapadato paraṃ suyyamānattā “desanābhedaṃ, sāsanabhedaṃ, kathābhedañca yathārahaṃ paridīpaye”ti. Bhedanti ca nānattaṃ, visesaṃ vā. Tesu piṭakesu. Sikkhā ca pahānañca gambhīrabhāvo ca, tañca yathārahaṃ paridīpaye.

Having combined this triad of terms, and because it means 'their distinction,' the word 'bheda' (distinction) should be applied to each separately, as it is heard after the dvandva compound. Thus: 'one should explain the distinction of desanā, the distinction of sāsana, and the distinction of kathā, as is appropriate.' And 'bheda' means difference, or particularity. In those Piṭakas, one should also explain, as is appropriate, the training, the abandoning, and the state of profundity.

Dutiyagāthāya pariyattibhedaṃ pariyāpuṇanassa pakāraṃ, visesañca vibhāvaye. Yahiṃ vinayādike piṭake. Yaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñca yathā bhikkhu pāpuṇāti, tathā tampi sabbaṃ tahiṃ vibhāvayeti sambandho. Atha vā yaṃ pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñca yahiṃ yathā bhikkhu pāpuṇāti, tathā tampi sabbaṃ tahiṃ vibhāvayeti yojetabbaṃ. Yathāti ca yehi upārambhādihetupariyāpuṇanādippakārehi, upārambhanissaraṇadhammakosarakkhaṇahetupariyāpuṇanaṃ suppaṭipattiduppaṭipattīti etehi pakārehīti vuttaṃ hoti.
