Santesupi ca aññesu tathā pāpuṇantesu jeṭṭhaseṭṭhāsannasadāsannihitabhāvato, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ sammāpaṭipajjanena dhammādhiṭṭhānabhāvato ca bhikkhūti vuttaṃ.

In the second verse, one should explain the distinction of learning, the manner of mastering, and its particularity. The connection is as follows: in which Piṭaka, such as the Vinaya, and in what way a bhikkhu attains a certain attainment or failure, all that too should be explained therein. Alternatively, it should be connected thus: whatever distinction of learning, attainment, or failure a bhikkhu attains, in whichever Piṭaka and in whatever way, all that too should be explained therein. And 'yathā' (in what way) means: by which manners, such as mastering for reasons like refutation. It is meant that these are the manners: mastering for the sake of refutation, for liberation, for protecting the treasury of the Dhamma; and good practice and bad practice. And although there are others who attain similarly, 'bhikkhu' is mentioned because of their being senior, foremost, near, and always present, and because they are a foundation for the Dhamma through right practice as instructed.

Tatrāti tāsu gāthāsu. Ayanti adhunā vakkhamānā kathā. Paridīpanāti samantato pakāsanā, kiñcimattampi asesetvā vibhajanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vibhāvanāti evaṃ paridīpanāyapi sati gūḷhaṃ paṭicchannamakatvā sotūnaṃ suviññeyyabhāvena āvibhāvanā. Saṅkhepena paridīpanā, vitthārena vibhāvanātipi vadanti. Apica etaṃ padadvayaṃ heṭṭhā vuttānurūpato kathitaṃ, atthato pana ekameva. Tasmā paridīpanā paṭhamagāthāya, vibhāvanā dutiyagāthāyāti yojetabbaṃ. Ca-saddena ubhayatthaṃ aññamaññaṃ samucceti. Kasmā, vuccantīti āha “ettha hī”tiādi. Hīti kāraṇe nipāto “akkharavipattiyaṃ hī”tiādīsu viya. Yasmā, kasmāti vā attho. Āṇaṃ paṇetuṃ [ṭhapetuṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā)] arahatīti āṇāraho, sammāsambuddhattā, mahākāruṇikatāya [M 1.0099] ca aviparītahitopadesakabhāvena pamāṇavacanattā āṇārahena bhagavatāti attho. Vohāraparamatthadhammānampi tattha sabbhāvato “āṇābāhullato”ti [V 1.0088] vuttaṃ, tena yebhuyyanayaṃ dasseti. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Visesena sattānaṃ manaṃ avaharatīti vohāro, paññatti, tasmiṃ kusalo, tena.

'Tatra' means in those verses. 'Ayaṃ' is the discourse about to be spoken. 'Paridīpanā' is clarification from all sides, meaning analysis without leaving even a little bit out. 'Vibhāvanā' is, even when there is such a clarification, making what is profound and hidden manifest by way of being easily understood by the listeners, without making it obscure. Some also say that 'paridīpanā' is a brief explanation and 'vibhāvanā' is a detailed one. Furthermore, this pair of terms is spoken of in accordance with what was said previously; in meaning, however, they are one and the same. Therefore, it should be connected thus: 'paridīpanā' is for the first verse, 'vibhāvanā' is for the second verse. By the word 'ca,' he connects the meaning in both places to each other. To the question, 'Why are they spoken of?' he says, 'ettha hī,' etc. 'Hī' is a particle in the sense of 'reason,' as in 'akkharavipattiyaṃ hī,' etc. The meaning is 'because' or 'for what reason.' He is 'āṇāraho' (worthy of command) because he is worthy to issue a command. The meaning is: by the Blessed One, who is worthy of command because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One, has great compassion, and because his speech is authoritative as he is an instructor in unerring welfare. Because conventional and ultimate dhammas are also found therein, it is said 'due to the abundance of command'; by this, he shows the principle of prevalence. This same method is to be known in the subsequent cases as well. 'Vohāra' (convention) is so called because it especially carries away the minds of beings; it is a designation. He is skilled in that; by him [who is skilled in convention].

Pacuro bahulo aparādho doso vītikkamo yesaṃ te pacurāparādhā, seyyasakattherādayo. Yathāparādhanti dosānurūpaṃ. “Anekajjhāsayā”tiādīsu āsayova ajjhāsayo, so atthato diṭṭhi, ñāṇañca, pabhedato pana catubbidho hoti. Vuttañca –

They are 'pacurāparādhā' (of many offenses) for whom there is much, abundant offense, fault, transgression; such as the Elder Seyyasaka and others. 'Yathāparādhaṃ' means according to the offense. In 'anekajjhāsayā,' etc., 'āsaya' itself is 'ajjhāsaya' (disposition). In essence, it is view and knowledge, but by way of division, it is fourfold. And it is said:

“Sassatucchedadiṭṭhī ca, khanti cevānulomikā;

Yathābhūtañca yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, etaṃ āsayasaddita”nti.

The eternalist and annihilationist views, the conforming acceptance, and that which is knowledge of things as they truly are—this is called 'āsaya' (disposition).

Tattha sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhīhi saṅgahitattā sabbepi diṭṭhigatikā sattā imā eva dve diṭṭhiyo sannissitā. Yathāha “dvayanissito kho panāyaṃ kaccāna loko yebhuyyena atthitañca natthitañcā”ti, (saṃ. ni. 2.15) atthitāti hi sassataggāho adhippeto, natthitāti ucchedaggāho. Ayaṃ tāva vaṭṭanissitānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ āsayo. Vivaṭṭanissitānaṃ pana suddhasattānaṃ anulomikā khanti, yathābhūtañāṇanti duvidho āsayo. Tattha ca anulomikā khanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Yathābhūtañāṇaṃ pana kammasakatāñāṇaṃ. Catubbidho peso āsayanti sattā ettha nivasanti, cittaṃ vā āgamma seti etthāti āsayo migāsayo viya. Yathā migo gocarāya gantvāpi paccāgantvā tattheva vanagahane sayatīti taṃ tassa “āsayo”ti vuccati, tathā cittaṃ aññathāpi pavattitvā yattha paccāgamma seti, tassa so “āsayo”ti. Kāmarāgādayo satta anusayā. Mūsikavisaṃ viya kāraṇalābhe uppajjamānārahā anāgatā, atītā, paccuppannā ca taṃsabhāvattā tathā vuccanti. Na hi dhammānaṃ kālabhedena sabhāvabhedoti. Cariyāti rāgacariyādikā cha mūlacariyā, antarabhedena anekavidhā, saṃsaggavasena pana tesaṭṭhi honti. Atha vā cariyāti sucaritaduccaritavasena duvidhaṃ caritaṃ. Tañhi vibhaṅge caritaniddese niddiṭṭhaṃ.

Herein, since all views are included under the eternalist and annihilationist views, all beings who hold views rely only on these two views. As it was said: 'This world, Kaccāna, for the most part, relies on a duality: on existence and on non-existence' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.15). For by 'existence' the grasp of eternalism is intended, and by 'non-existence' the grasp of annihilationism. This, firstly, is the disposition of ordinary people who rely on the round of existence. But for pure beings who rely on that which is unbound from the round, there are two kinds of disposition: conforming acceptance and knowledge of things as they truly are. Therein, conforming acceptance is insight-knowledge, while knowledge of things as they truly are is the knowledge of kamma as one's own property. This disposition is fourfold. Because beings dwell (āsenti) herein, or because the mind, having approached, lies down (seti) herein, it is called an 'āsaya' (disposition), like a deer's lair (migāsayo). Just as a deer, even after going out to graze, returns and lies down in that very forest thicket, so that is called its 'āsaya' (lair); in the same way, that wherein the mind, even after proceeding otherwise, returns and lies down, is called its 'āsaya'. The seven latent tendencies, such as sensual lust, are the 'anusayas'. Like the poison of a mouse, being fit to arise when a cause is obtained, the future, past, and present defilements are called thus because they have that nature. For the nature of phenomena does not differ according to a difference in time. 'Cariyā' (conduct) refers to the six root conducts, such as conduct rooted in lust; by way of internal divisions, they are of many kinds, but by way of combination, they become sixty-three. Alternatively, 'cariyā' is conduct of two kinds: good conduct and bad conduct. For that is explained in the Vibhaṅga, in the exposition on conduct.

“Adhimutti [M 1.0100] nāma ‘ajjeva pabbajissāmi, ajjeva arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmī’tiādinā tanninnabhāvena pavattamānaṃ sanniṭṭhāna”nti (sārattha. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana “adhimutti nāma sattānaṃ pubbacariyavasena abhiruci, sā duvidhā hīnapaṇītabhedenā’ti (dī. ni. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Tathā hi yāya hīnādhimuttikā sattā hīnādhimuttikeyeva satte sevanti, paṇītādhimuttikā paṇītādhimuttikeyeva[V 1.0089]. Sace hi ācariyupajjhāyā sīlavanto na honti, saddhivihārikā sīlavanto, te attano ācariyupajjhāyepi na upasaṅkamanti, attanā sadise sāruppabhikkhūyeva upasaṅkamanti. Sace ācariyupajjhāyā sāruppabhikkhū, itare asāruppā, tepi na ācariyupajjhāye upasaṅkamanti, attanā sadise asāruppabhikkhūyeva upasaṅkamanti. Dhātusaṃyuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 2.85 ādayo) cesa attho dīpetabbo. Evamayaṃ hīnādhimuttikādīnaṃ aññamañño pasevanādiniyamitā abhiruci ajjhāsayadhātu “adhimuttī”ti veditabbā. Anekā ajjhāsayādayo te yesaṃ atthi, anekā vā ajjhāsayādayo yesanti tathā yathā “bahukattuko, bahunadiko”ti. Yathānulomanti ajjhāsayādīnaṃ anulomaṃ anatikkamma, ye ye vā ajjhāsayādayo anulomā, tehi tehīti attho. Āsayādīnaṃ anulomassa vā anurūpantipi vadanti. Ghanavinibbhogābhāvato diṭṭhimānataṇhāvasena “ahaṃ mama santaka”nti evaṃ pavattasaññino. Yathādhammanti “natthettha attā, attaniyaṃ vā, kevalaṃ dhammamattameveta”nti evamādinā dhammasabhāvānurūpanti attho.

'Adhimutti' (resolve), it is said in the glossaries (gaṇṭhipadas), 'is the conclusion that proceeds with an inclination towards that, by way of such thoughts as, “Today I will go forth, today I will attain Arahantship.”' But the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has said: ''Adhimutti' is the inclination of beings by way of their former practice; it is twofold through the distinction of inferior and superior.' And so it is, for by means of it, beings of inferior disposition associate only with beings of inferior disposition, and those of superior disposition only with those of superior disposition. Indeed, if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, but the co-residents are virtuous, they do not approach their own teachers and preceptors, but approach only suitable monks who are like themselves. If the teachers and preceptors are suitable monks, but the others are unsuitable, they too do not approach the teachers and preceptors, but approach only unsuitable monks who are like themselves. And this meaning should be illustrated by way of the Dhātusaṃyutta (Saṃ. Ni. 2.85 ff.). Thus, this inclination—this element of disposition (ajjhāsayadhātu)—which is determined by the mutual association of those with inferior dispositions and so on, should be known as 'adhimutti'. They are called 'those of many and various dispositions, etc.' (anekajjhāsayādayo) because they have many dispositions, etc., or because their dispositions, etc., are many, just as in 'one who has many agents' (bahukattuko) and 'one who has many rivers' (bahunadiko). 'Yathānulomaṃ' (in conformity with) means: without transgressing what is conformable to their dispositions, etc., or by means of whatever dispositions, etc., are conformable. They also say it means 'in accordance with' their dispositions, etc. Due to the absence of breaking up the compact mass, they are those who have perceptions that proceed by way of view, conceit, and craving, thus: 'I,' 'my property.' 'Yathādhammaṃ' (in accordance with the Dhamma) means: in accordance with the nature of phenomena, by way of such thoughts as, 'There is no self or what belongs to a self herein; this is merely phenomena.'

Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro, kāyavācāhi avītikkamo. Mahanto saṃvaro asaṃvaro. Vuḍḍhiattho hi ayaṃ a-kāro yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 21) taṃyogatāya ca khuddako saṃvaro pārisesādinayena saṃvaro, tasmā khuddako, mahanto ca saṃvaroti attho. Tenāha “saṃvarā saṃvaro”tiādi. Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanāti diṭṭhiyā vimocanaṃ, atthato pana tassa ujuvipaccanikā sammādiṭṭhiādayo dhammā. Tathā cāha “dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhipaṭipakkhabhūtā”ti. Nāmassa, rūpassa, nāmarūpassa ca paricchindanaṃ nāmarūpaparicchedo, so pana “rāgādipaṭipakkhabhūto”ti vacanato tathāpavattameva ñāṇaṃ.

Restraining is 'saṃvara' (restraint); it is non-transgression by body and speech. Great restraint is 'asaṃvara'. For this prefix 'a-' has the meaning of augmentation, as in 'asekkhā dhammā' (dhammas of one beyond training) (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Tikamātikā 21). And in connection with that, by the principle of remainder and so on, small restraint is 'saṃvarā'. Therefore, the meaning is small restraint and great restraint. For that reason, he said 'saṃvarāsaṃvaro' (small and great restraint), etc. 'Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanā' (dispelling of views) is liberation from view. But in terms of its essence, it is the dhammas that are its direct opposite, such as right view and so on. And thus he said, 'that which is the opponent of the sixty-two views.' The defining of name, of form, and of name-and-form is 'nāmarūpapariccheda' (the defining of name-and-form). And that, because it is said to be 'the opponent of lust, etc.', is the knowledge that proceeds in just that way.

“Tīsupī”tiādinā [M 1.0101] aparaḍḍhaṃ vivarati. Tīsupi tāsaṃ vacanasambhavato “visesenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tadetaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Tatra “yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti vacanato āha “vinayapiṭake adhisīlasikkhā”ti. Suttantapāḷiyaṃ “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 1.152; a. ni. 4.123) samādhidesanābāhullato “suttanta piṭake adhicittasikkhā”ti vuttaṃ. Nāmarūpaparicchedassa adhipaññāpadaṭṭhānato, adhipaññāya ca atthāya tadavasesanāmarūpadhammakathanato āha “abhidhammapiṭake adhipaññāsikkhā”ti.

By 'In the three' (tīsupi), etc., he explains the latter half of the verse. Because the teaching of them is found in all three Piṭakas, it is said 'especially' (visesena). This should be applied in all instances. Therein, based on the statement, 'That which is the higher training in virtue, this is the training intended in this context,' he said, 'in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the higher training in virtue.' In the Suttanta Piṭaka, because of the abundance of teachings on concentration beginning with 'secluded from sensual pleasures,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.226; etc.), it is said, 'in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the higher training in mind.' Because the defining of name-and-form has higher wisdom as its proximate cause, and because the remaining name-and-form dhammas are taught for the sake of higher wisdom, he said, 'in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the higher training in wisdom.'

Kilesānanti saṃklesadhammānaṃ, kammakilesānaṃ vā, ubhayāpekkhañcetaṃ “yo kāyavacīdvārehi [V 1.0090] kilesānaṃ vītikkamo, tassa pahānaṃ, tassa paṭipakkhattā”ti ca. “Vītikkamo”ti ayaṃ “paṭipakkha”nti bhāvayoge sambandho, “sīlassā”ti pana bhāvapaccaye. Evaṃ sabbattha. Anusayavasena santāne anuvattantā kilesā kāraṇalābhe pariyuṭṭhitāpi sīlabhedabhayavasena vītikkamituṃ na labhantīti āha “vītikkamapaṭipakkhattā sīlassā”ti. Okāsādānavasena kilesānaṃ citte kusalappavattiṃ pariyādiyitvā uṭṭhānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ, tassa pahānaṃ, cittasantāne uppattivasena kilesānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānassa pahānanti vuttaṃ hoti. “Kilesāna”nti hi adhikāro, taṃ pana pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ cittasamādahanavasena bhavatīti āha “pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkhattā samādhissā”ti. Appahīnabhāvena santāne anu anu sayanakā anurūpakāraṇalābhe uppajjanārahā thāmagatā kāmarāgādayo satta kilesā anusayā, tesaṃ pahānaṃ, te pana sabbaso ariyamaggapaññāya pahīyantīti āha “anusayapaṭipakkhattā paññāyā”ti.

Of defilements (kilesānaṃ) means of the afflicting states (saṃklesadhammānaṃ), or of kamma and defilements (kammakilesānaṃ); and this has reference to both. It is also said: 'That transgression of the defilements through the doors of body and speech—the abandoning of that is spoken of because it is the counteraction.' Here, this word 'vītikkamo' (transgression) is connected with 'paṭipakkha' (counteraction) in the sense of a state (bhāvayoga); furthermore, the word 'sīlassa' (of virtue) is connected to the suffix indicating a state (bhāvapaccaye). So it is in all cases. Defilements that follow along in the continuum by way of latent tendencies, even when they have arisen upon obtaining a cause, do not get to transgress due to fear of breaking virtue; thus, it is said, 'because virtue is the counteraction to transgression.' By way of not giving an opportunity, the arising of defilements, having taken over the occurrence of the wholesome in the mind, is obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna); the abandoning of that, that is, the abandoning of the obsession of defilements by way of their arising in the mental continuum, is what is meant. Indeed, 'of the defilements' is the topic. Furthermore, that abandoning of obsession occurs by means of composing the mind; thus, it is said, 'because concentration is the counteraction to obsession.' The seven defilements, such as sensual desire (kāmarāga), which, due to not being abandoned, are apt to lie dormant again and again in the continuum, are fit to arise upon obtaining a suitable cause, and have reached a state of strength, are the latent tendencies (anusayā). Their abandoning is spoken of. And they are abandoned in all respects by the wisdom of the noble path; thus, it is said, 'because wisdom is the counteraction to the latent tendencies.'

Dīpālokena viya tamassa dānādipuññakiriyavatthugatena tena tena kusalaṅgena tassa tassa akusalassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ. Idha pana adhisīlasikkhāya vuttaṭṭhānattā tena tena susīlyaṅgena tassa tassa dussīlyaṅgassa pahānaṃ “tadaṅgappahāna”nti gahetabbaṃ. Upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattinivāraṇena ghaṭappahārena viya jalatale sevālassa tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ vikkhambhanavasena pahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ. Catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃ taṃ maggavato santāne samudayapakkhikassa [M 1.0102] kilesagaṇassa accantamappavattisaṅkhāta samucchindanavasena pahānaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ. Duṭṭhu caritaṃ, saṃkilesehi vā dūsitaṃ caritaṃ duccaritaṃ. Tadeva yattha uppannaṃ, taṃ santānaṃ sammā kilisati vibādhati, upatāpeti cāti saṃkileso, tassa pahānaṃ. Kāyavacīduccaritavasena pavattasaṃkilesassa tadaṅgavasena pahānaṃ vuttaṃ sīlassa duccaritapaṭipakkhattā. Sikkhattayānusārena hi attho veditabbo. Tasatīti taṇhā, sāva vuttanayena saṃkileso, tassa vikkhambhanavasena pahānaṃ vuttaṃ samādhissa kāmacchandapaṭipakkhattā. Diṭṭhiyeva yathāvuttanayena saṃkileso, tassa samucchedavasena pahānaṃ vuttaṃ paññāya attādivinimuttasabhāva dhammappakāsanato.

Like the abandoning of darkness by the light of a lamp, the abandoning of each particular unwholesome state by each particular wholesome factor comprised in the grounds for meritorious action, such as giving, is abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna). But here, because it is the place where the higher training in virtue is spoken of, the abandoning of each particular factor of bad virtue by each particular factor of good virtue should be taken as 'abandonment by substitution of opposites.' By means of concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—which prevents their occurrence, the abandoning of those various hindrances and other states by way of suppression, like the removal of moss on the surface of water by a blow from a pot, is abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna). Because the four noble paths have been developed, the abandoning of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of the origin of suffering in the continuum of one who possesses each respective path, by way of cutting off, which is described as complete non-occurrence, is abandonment by cutting off (samucchedappahāna). Badly practiced conduct is misconduct (duccarita); or, conduct corrupted by afflicting states is misconduct. That very thing, where it has arisen, thoroughly defiles, afflicts, and torments that continuum; therefore, it is an affliction (saṃkileso). The abandoning of this is spoken of. The abandoning by substitution of opposites of the affliction that occurs by way of misconduct of body and speech is spoken of, because virtue is the counteraction to misconduct. Indeed, the meaning should be understood in accordance with the threefold training. That which is anxious or attached (tasati) is craving (taṇhā). That very craving, in the way explained, is an affliction. Its abandoning by way of suppression is spoken of because concentration is the counteraction to sensual desire. Views themselves, in the way explained, are an affliction. Their abandoning by way of cutting off is spoken of because wisdom reveals the nature of phenomena as being devoid of a self and so on.

Ekamekasmiñcetthāti etesu tīsu piṭakesu ekamekasmiṃ piṭake, ca-saddo vākyārambhe, pakkhantare vā. Pi-saddo, api-saddo vā avayavasampiṇḍane, tena na kevalaṃ catubbidhasseva gambhīrabhāvo, atha kho paccekaṃ tadavayavānampīti sampiṇḍanaṃ karoti. Esa nayo īdisesu. Idāni te sarūpato dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tantīti pāḷi. Sā hi ukkaṭṭhānaṃ sīlādiatthānaṃ [V 1.0091] bodhanato, sabhāvaniruttibhāvato, buddhādīhi bhāsitattā ca pakaṭṭhānaṃ vacanānaṃ āḷi pantīti “pāḷī”ti vuccati.

“In each of these” means: in these three Piṭakas, in each single Piṭaka. The word “ca” occurs at the beginning of a sentence, or in an alternative sense. The word “pi,” or “api,” occurs in the sense of combining components; by this, it effects a combination thus: it is not merely the fourfold division that has profundity, but rather that each of its individual components also has profundity. This is the method to be seen in such cases. Now, in order to show them according to their intrinsic nature, the phrase beginning with “tattha” is stated. Therein, “tantī” means Pāḷi. For it is called “Pāḷi” because it makes known excellent meanings such as virtue, because of its nature as an unchanging term, and because it was spoken by the Buddha and others, being a row (āḷi) or line (panti) of excellent words.

Idha pana vinayagaṇṭhipadakārādīnaṃ saddavādīnaṃ matena pubbe vavatthāpitā paramatthasaddappabandhabhūtā tanti dhammo nāma. Iti-saddo hi nāmatthe, “dhammo”ti vā vuccati. Tassāyevāti tassā yathāvuttāya eva tantiyā attho. Manasā vavatthāpitāyāti uggahaṇa-dhāraṇādivasappavattena manasā pubbe vavatthāpitāya yathāvuttāya paramatthasaddappabandhabhūtāya tassā tantiyā. Desanāti pacchā paresamavabodhanatthaṃ desanāsaṅkhātā paramatthasaddappabandhabhūtā tantiyeva. Apica yathāvuttatanti saṅkhātasaddasamuṭṭhāpako cittuppādo desanā. Tantiyā, tantiatthassa cāti yathāvuttāya duvidhāyapi tantiyā, tadatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodhoti attho veditabbo. Te hi bhagavatā vuccamānassa atthassa, vohārassa ca dīpako saddoyeva tanti nāmāti vadanti. Tesaṃ pana vāde dhammassāpi saddasabhāvattā dhammadesanānaṃ ko visesoti ce? Tesaṃ tesaṃ atthānaṃ bodhakabhāvena ñāto, uggahaṇādivasena [M 1.0103] ca pubbe vavatthāpito paramatthasaddappabandho dhammo, pacchā paresaṃ avabodhanatthaṃ pavattito taṃ tadatthappakāsako saddo desanāti ayamimesaṃ visesoti. Atha vā yathāvuttasaddasamuṭṭhāpako cittuppādo desanā desīyati samuṭṭhāpīyati saddo etenāti katvā musāvādādayo viya tatthāpi hi musāvādādisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādādisaddehi voharīyatīti. Kiñcāpi akkharāvalibhūto paññattisaddoyeva atthassa ñāpako, tathāpi mūlakāraṇabhāvato “akkharasaññāto”tiādīsu viya tassāyeva atthoti paramatthasaddoyeva atthassa ñāpakabhāvena vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Tassā tantiyā desanā”ti ca sadisavohārena vuttaṃ yathā “uppannā ca kusalādhammā bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya saṃvattantī”ti.

Here, however, according to the view of the authors of the Vinaya glossaries and others who are proponents of the sound theory, the text (tanti), which is a series of ultimate sounds previously determined, is called 'Dhamma'. For the word 'iti' occurs in the sense of a name; or, it is called 'Dhamma'. 'Of that very text' means the meaning of that very text as stated above. 'Determined by the mind' means: of that text, which is a series of ultimate sounds as stated above, previously determined by the mind through the power of learning, retaining, and so on. 'Teaching' (desanā) is that very text, which is a series of ultimate sounds, designated as 'teaching' for the purpose of making others understand afterwards. Furthermore, as another method, the thought-moment (cittuppāda) that produces the sound designated as the aforementioned text is the teaching. 'Of the text and the meaning of the text' means: the comprehension, as it really is, of both kinds of text as stated above and of their meaning; this is the meaning that should be understood. For those teachers say that the sound itself, which illuminates both the meaning and the usage spoken by the Blessed One, is called the text (tanti). But in their view, if it is said, 'Since the Dhamma also has the nature of sound, what is the distinction between the Dhamma and the teaching?' The distinction for them is this: the Dhamma is the series of ultimate sounds, known as that which makes known various meanings and previously determined through learning and so on; the teaching is the sound that clarifies those meanings, put forth afterwards for the purpose of making others understand. This is their distinction. Alternatively, the thought-moment that produces the aforementioned sound is the teaching, because 'the sound is taught (desīyati) or produced by it,' just as in the case of false speech and so on. For there too, the volition (cetanā) that produces false speech and so on is expressed by the sounds of false speech and so on. Although it is only the conceptual sound (paññattisadda), which is a series of letters, that makes the meaning known, nevertheless, because it is the root cause, it should be understood that the ultimate sound (paramatthasadda) itself is said to be that which makes the meaning known, just as in phrases like 'perceived as letters' and so on, it is the meaning of that very thing. And the phrase 'the teaching of that text' is stated by way of similar usage, just as it is said: 'Arisen wholesome states lead to increase and abundance.'

Abhidhammagaṇṭhipadakārādīnaṃ pana paṇṇattivādīnaṃ matena sammutiparamatthabhedassa atthassa anurūpavācakabhāvena paramatthasaddesu ekantena bhagavatā manasā vavatthāpitā nāmapaññattipabandhabhūtā tanti dhammo nāma, “dhammo”ti vā vuccati. Tassāyevāti tassā nāmapaññattibhūtāya tantiyā eva attho. Manasā vavatthāpitāyāti sammutiparamatthabhedassa atthassānurūpavācakabhāvena paramatthasaddesu bhagavatā manasā vavatthāpitāya nāmapaṇṇattipabandhabhūtāya tassā tantiyā. Desanāti paresaṃ pabodhanena atisajjanā vācāya pakāsanā vacībhedabhūtā paramatthasaddappabandhasaṅkhātā tanti. Tantiyā, tantiatthassa cāti yathāvuttāya dubbidhāyapi tantiyā, tadatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodhoti attho. Te hi evaṃ vadanti – sabhāvatthassa, sabhāvavohārassa ca anurūpavaseneva bhagavatā manasā vavatthāpitā paṇṇatti [V 1.0092] idha “tantī”ti vuccati. Yadi ca saddavādīnaṃ matena saddoyeva idha tanti nāma siyā. Tantiyā, desanāya ca nānattena bhavitabbaṃ, manasā vavatthāpitāya ca tantiyā vacībhedakaraṇamattaṃ ṭhapetvā desanāya nānattaṃ natthi. Tathā hi desanaṃ dassentena manasā vavatthāpitāya tantiyā desanāti vacībhedakaraṇamattaṃ vinā tantiyā saha desanāya anaññatā vuttā. Tathā ca upari “desanāti paññattī”ti vuttattā desanāya anaññabhāvena tantiyāpi paṇṇattibhāvo kathito hoti.

However, according to the view of the authors of the Abhidhamma glossaries and others who are proponents of the concept theory, the text (tanti), which is a series of name-concepts entirely determined by the Blessed One by mind among ultimate sounds as a suitable expression for the meaning distinguished as conventional and ultimate, is called 'Dhamma', or it is called 'Dhamma'. 'Of that very text' means the meaning of that very text, which is a name-concept. 'Determined by the mind' means: of that text, which is a series of name-concepts, determined by the Blessed One by mind among ultimate sounds as a suitable expression for the meaning distinguished as conventional and ultimate. 'Teaching' (desanā) is the text, designated as a series of ultimate sounds, which is a manifestation of speech, a declaration by voice that makes things known to others and causes a deep impression. 'Of the text and the meaning of the text' means: the comprehension, as it really is, of both kinds of text as stated above—distinguished as conventional and ultimate—and of their meaning. This is the meaning. For those teachers say thus: 'Here, the concept (paññatti) determined by the mind by the Blessed One only in a manner suitable for the real meaning and the real usage is called the 'text' (tanti).' And if, according to the view of the proponents of the sound theory, sound itself were to be called the text here, there would have to be a difference between the text and the teaching. But, apart from the mere act of verbal utterance, there is no difference between the mentally determined text and the teaching. For thus, when the teaching is shown by the commentator, the non-difference of the teaching from the text is stated by the phrase 'the teaching of the mentally determined text', apart from the mere act of verbal utterance. And so, since it is stated later on that 'teaching is concept', the status of the text as a concept is also explained by its non-difference from the teaching.

Apica [M 1.0104] yadi tantiyā aññāyeva desanā siyā, “tantiyā ca tantiatthassa ca desanāya ca yathābhūtāvabodho”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Evaṃ pana avatvā “tantiyā ca tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho”ti vuttattā tantiyā, desanāya ca anaññabhāvo dassito hoti. Evañca katvā upari “desanā nāma paññattī”ti dassentena desanāya anaññabhāvato tantiyā paṇṇattibhāvo kathito hotīti. Tadubhayampi pana paramatthato saddoyeva paramatthavinimuttāya sammutiyā abhāvā, imameva ca nayaṃ gahetvā keci ācariyā “dhammo ca desanā ca paramatthato saddo evā”ti voharanti, tepi anupavajjāyeva. Yathā kāmāvacarapaṭisandhivipākā “parittārammaṇā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi kāmāvacarapaṭisandhivipākā “nibbattitaparamatthavisayāyevā”ti sakkā vattuṃ itthipurisādiākāraparivitakkapubbakānaṃ rāgādiakusalānaṃ, mettādikusalānañca ārammaṇaṃ gahetvāpi samuppajjanato. Paramatthadhammamūlakattā panassa parikappassa paramatthavisayatā sakkā paññapetuṃ, evamidhāpi daṭṭhabbanti ca. Evampi paṇṇattivādīnaṃ mataṃ hotu, saddavādīnaṃ matepi dhammadesanānaṃ nānattaṃ vuttanayeneva ācariyadhammapālattherā dīhi pakāsitanti. Hoti cettha –

Furthermore, if the teaching were different from the text, it would have been necessary to say, 'the comprehension, as it really is, of the text, the meaning of the text, and the teaching.' However, by not saying so, and since it was said, 'the comprehension, as it really is, of the text and the meaning of the text,' the non-difference of the text and the teaching is shown. And for this reason, when it is shown later on that 'teaching is a name-concept,' the status of the text as a concept is explained due to its non-difference from the teaching; thus they also say. However, both of them are, in an ultimate sense, just sound, because of the absence of a conceptual convention apart from ultimate reality. And some teachers, taking this very method, declare, 'Both the Dhamma and the teaching are ultimately just sound,' and they too are blameless. Just as sense-sphere rebirth-linking resultants are called 'having a sense-sphere object,' so should this case be understood. For it cannot be said that sense-sphere rebirth-linking resultants have only a produced ultimate reality as their object, since they arise even by taking as their object unwholesome states like lust, etc., which are preceded by thoughts about the forms of women, men, etc., and wholesome states like loving-kindness. However, because this conceptualization has an ultimate phenomenon as its root, its status as having an ultimate object can be designated; so it should be understood here also, they say. Even so, let this be the view of the proponents of the concept theory; even in the view of the proponents of the sound theory, the difference between the Dhamma and the teaching has been explained by teachers such as the Elder Dhammapāla in accordance with the stated method. And here there is the following:

“Saddo dhammo desanā ca, iccāhu apare garū;

Dhammo paṇṇatti saddo tu, desanā vāti cāpare”ti.

Some venerable teachers say: 'Sound is Dhamma and also teaching.' Yet others say: 'The sound that is a concept, however, is Dhamma and only teaching.'

Tīsupi cetesu ete dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhāti ettha tantiattho, tantidesanā, tantiatthapaṭivedho cāti ime tayo tantivisayā hontīti vinayapiṭakādīnaṃ atthadesanāpaṭivedhādhārabhāvo yutto, piṭakāni pana tantiyevāti tesaṃ dhammādhārabhāvo kathaṃ yujjeyyāti? Tantisamudāyassa avayavatantiyā ādhārabhāvato. Samudāyo hi avayavassa parikappanāmattasiddhena ādhārabhāvena vuccati yathā “rukkhe sākhā”ti. Ettha ca dhammādīnaṃ dukkhogāhabhāvato tehi dhammādīhi vinayādayo gambhīrāti vinayādīnampi catubbidho gambhīrabhāvo [V 1.0093] vuttoyeva, tasmā dhammādayo eva dukkhogāhattā gambhīrā, na vinayādayoti na codetabbametaṃ samukhena, visayavisayīmukhena ca vinayādīnaññeva gambhīrabhāvassa vuttattā. Dhammo hi vinayādayo eva abhinnattā. Tesaṃ visayo attho vācakabhūtānaṃ tesameva vāccabhāvato, visayino desanāpaṭivedhā [M 1.0105] dhammatthavisayabhāvatoti. Tattha paṭivedhassa dukkarabhāvato dhammatthānaṃ, desanāñāṇassa dukkarabhāvato desanāya ca dukkhogāhabhāvo veditabbo, paṭivedhassa pana uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, tabbisayañāṇuppattiyā ca dukkarabhāvato dukkhogāhatā veditabbā. Dhammatthadesanānaṃ gambhīrabhāvato tabbisayo paṭivedhopi gambhīro yathā taṃ gambhīrassa udakassa pamāṇaggahaṇe dīghena pamāṇena bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃsampadamidanti (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vajirabuddhitthero. Piṭakāvayavānaṃ dhammādīnaṃ vuccamāno gambhīrabhāvo taṃsamudāyassa piṭakassāpi vuttoyeva, tasmā tathā na codetabbantipi vadanti, vicāretabbametaṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ piṭakāvayavāsambhavato. Mahāsamuddo dukkhogāho, alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho viya cāti sambandho. Atthavasā hi vibhattivacanaliṅgapariṇāmoti. Dukkhena ogayhanti, dukkho vā ogāho anto pavisanametesūti dukkhogāhā. Na labhitabboti alabbhanīyo, soyeva alabbhaneyyo, labhīyate vā labbhanaṃ, taṃ nārahatīti alabbhaneyyo. Patiṭṭhahanti ettha okāseti patiṭṭho, patiṭṭhahanaṃ vā patiṭṭho, alabbhaneyyo so yesu te alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā. Ekadesena ogāhantehipi mandabuddhīhi patiṭṭhā laddhuṃ na sakkāyevāti dassetuṃ etaṃ puna vuttaṃ. “Eva”ntiādi nigamanaṃ.

Herein, regarding the statement concerning these three [Piṭakas], 'these are the Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration,' the meaning of the text, the teaching of the text, and the penetration of the meaning of the text—these three are subjects of the text. Thus, it is appropriate that the Vinaya Piṭaka and others serve as the basis for the meaning, teaching, and penetration. But since the Piṭakas themselves are the texts, how can they be the basis for the Dhamma? Because the collection of texts is the basis for its constituent texts. For a collection is said to be the basis of its parts merely by conceptual designation, just as in 'branches on a tree.' And here, because the Dhamma and the others are difficult to fathom, the Vinaya and the others are profound due to this Dhamma and the others. Thus, the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and the others has indeed been stated. Therefore, it should not be objected that only the Dhamma and the others are profound because they are difficult to fathom, and not the Vinaya and the others, for the profundity of the Vinaya and the others has been stated both directly and through the perspective of object and subject. For the Dhamma is indeed the Vinaya and the others, being not different. Their object is the meaning, because it is the expressed content of those very texts which are the expressers. The subjects are the teaching and the penetration, because they have the Dhamma and the meaning as their domain. Therein, the Dhamma and the meaning are to be understood as difficult to fathom due to the difficulty of penetration, and the teaching also, due to the difficulty of the knowledge of teaching. As for penetration, its being difficult to fathom should be understood from the inability to produce it and from the difficulty in the arising of knowledge concerning its object. Because the Dhamma, the meaning, and the teaching are profound, the penetration that has them as its object is also profound. Just as in taking the measure of deep water, there must be a long measure, so should the aptness of this simile be understood. Thus says the Elder Vajirabuddhi. Some also say that the profundity spoken of the Dhamma and the others, which are parts of the Piṭakas, is also stated for their collection, the Piṭaka itself; therefore, it should not be objected in that way. This should be investigated, because not all of them are components of the Piṭaka. The connection should be made thus: 'like the great ocean, difficult to fathom and having an unobtainable footing.' For the transformation of case, number, and gender occurs according to the power of the meaning. They are 'difficult to fathom' (dukkhogāhā) because they are entered with difficulty, or because the entering, the penetration into them, is difficult. It is 'unobtainable' (alabbhaneyyo) because it is not to be obtained (alabbhanīyo); or, obtaining (labbhanaṃ) is obtained (labhīyate), but it does not merit that, thus it is 'unobtainable' (alabbhaneyyo). One stands (patiṭṭhahanti) in this place (ettha okāse), therefore it is a 'footing' (patiṭṭho); or, the standing (patiṭṭhahanaṃ) itself is a footing (patiṭṭho). Those in which that footing is unobtainable are 'of unobtainable footing' (alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā). This is stated again to show that even for those of dull intellect who fathom it only in part, a footing cannot possibly be found. The words beginning with 'Thus' (Evaṃ) are the conclusion.

Idāni hetuhetuphalādīnampi vasena gambhīrabhāvaṃ dassento “aparo nayo”tiādimāha. Tattha hetūti paccayo. So ca attano phalaṃ dahati vidahatīti dhammo da-kārassa dha-kāraṃ katvā. Dhammasaddassa cettha hetupariyāyatā kathaṃ viññāyatīti āha “vuttañheta”ntiādi. Vuttaṃ paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge (vibha. 718). Nanu ca “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti etena vacanena dhammassa hetubhāvo kathaṃ viññāyatīti? “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti etassa samāsapadassa avayavapadatthaṃ dassentena “hetumhi ñāṇa”nti vuttattā. “Dhamme paṭisambhidā dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti ettha hi “dhamme”ti etassa atthaṃ dassentena “hetumhī”ti vuttaṃ, “paṭisambhidā”ti etassa atthaṃ dassentena “ñāṇa”nti. Tasmā hetudhammasaddā ekatthā, ñāṇapaṭisambhidā saddā cāti imamatthaṃ vadantena sādhito dhammassa hetubhāvoti. Tathā “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti etena vacanena sādhito atthassa hetuphalabhāvoti [M 1.0106] daṭṭhabbo. Hetuno phalaṃ hetuphalaṃ, tañca hetuanusārena arīyati adhigamīyatīti atthoti vuccati.

Now, showing the profound nature also by way of cause, the fruit of the cause, and so on, he begins with 'another method.' Herein, 'cause' (hetu) means condition (paccayo). And that, because it bears or establishes its own fruit, is a 'dhamma', by changing the letter 'da' to 'dha'. But how is it understood here that the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for 'cause'? He says, 'for it has been said,' and so forth. It has been stated in the Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga. Indeed, how is the nature of 'dhamma' as a cause understood through the statement, 'Knowledge in the cause is analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā)'? Because in explaining the meaning of the constituent words of the compound 'dhammapaṭisambhidā,' it is said, 'knowledge in the cause.' For here, in 'analytical knowledge in the Dhamma is analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhamme paṭisambhidā dhammapaṭisambhidā),' in showing the meaning of 'in the Dhamma (dhamme),' it is said 'in the cause (hetumhi),' and in showing the meaning of 'analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā),' it is said 'knowledge (ñāṇa).' Therefore, by stating that the words 'cause' (hetu) and 'dhamma' have the same meaning, and the words 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) and 'analytical knowledge' (paṭisambhidā) are also synonymous, the nature of 'dhamma' as a cause is established. Similarly, through the statement, 'Knowledge of the fruit of the cause is analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā),' the nature of 'meaning' (attha) as the fruit of the cause should be understood. The fruit of a cause is 'the fruit of the cause' (hetuphalaṃ), and it is called 'meaning' (attha) because it is known (ariyati) or attained (adhigamīyati) in accordance with the cause.

Desanāti [V 1.0094] paññattīti ettha saddavādīnaṃ vāde atthabyañjanakā aviparītābhilāpadhammaniruttibhūtā paramatthasaddappabandhasaṅkhātā tanti “desanā”ti vuccati, desanā nāmāti vā attho. Desīyati attho etāyāti hi desanā. Pakārena ñāpīyati attho etāya, pakārato vā ñāpetīti paññatti. Tameva sarūpato dassetuṃ “yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Yathādhammanti ettha pana dhammasaddo hetuṃ, hetuphalañca sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sabhāvavācako hesa dhammasaddo, na pariyattihetuādivācako, tasmā yo yo avijjāsaṅkhārādidhammo, tasmiṃ tasminti attho. Tesaṃ tesaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārādidhammānaṃ anurūpaṃ vā yathādhammaṃ. Desanāpi hi paṭivedho viya aviparītasavisayavibhāvanato dhammānurūpaṃ pavattati, tatoyeva ca aviparītābhilāpoti vuccati. Dhammābhilāpoti hi atthabyañjanako aviparītābhilāpo dhammaniruttibhūto tantisaṅkhāto paramatthasaddappabandho. So hi abhilappati uccārīyatīti abhilāpo, dhammo aviparīto sabhāvabhūto abhilāpo dhammābhilāpoti vuccati, etena “tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 718) ettha vuttaṃ dhammaniruttiṃ dasseti saddasabhāvattā desanāya. Tathā hi niruttipaṭisambhidāya parittārammaṇādibhāvo paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 718) vutto. Tadaṭṭhakathāya ca “taṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā”tiādinā (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) tassā saddārammaṇatā dassitā. “Imassa atthassa ayaṃ saddo vācako”ti hi vacanavacanatthe vavatthapetvā taṃ taṃ vacanatthavibhāvanavasena pavattito saddo “desanā”ti vuccati. “Adhippāyo”ti etena “desanāti paññattī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ dhammaniruttābhilāpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na tato vinimuttaṃ paññattiṃ sandhāyāti dasseti anekadhā atthasambhave attanā adhippetatthasseva vuttattāti ayaṃ saddavādīnaṃ vādato vinicchayo.

Here, in the view of the sound-theorists, regarding the phrase 'Teaching is designation,' the Pāḷi text (tanti)—which indicates the meaning, is the unerringly recited Dhamma-expression, and is known as the sequence of ultimate sounds—is called 'teaching' (desanā); or, this is the meaning of 'teaching.' For, the meaning is taught (desīyati) by this; hence, it is 'teaching' (desanā). The meaning is made known (ñāpīyati) by this in a particular way (pakārena), or it makes known (ñāpeti) in a particular way; hence, it is 'designation' (paññatti). To show that very designation in its own nature, it was said, 'The intention is: an expression of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.' Here, in 'in accordance with the Dhamma,' the word 'Dhamma' includes the cause, the fruit of the cause, and everything. For this word 'Dhamma' denotes intrinsic nature; it does not denote the scriptures, cause, and so on. Therefore, the meaning is: in whatever phenomenon there is, such as ignorance, formations, etc.; or, 'in accordance with the Dhamma' means in accordance with those very phenomena such as ignorance, formations, etc. For the teaching, like penetration, proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma because it unerringly clarifies its own object. For that very reason, it is called 'unerring expression.' For 'expression of the Dhamma' is the sequence of ultimate sounds, known as the Pāḷi text, which indicates the meaning, is an unerring utterance, and is the Dhamma-expression. For it is expressed (abhilappati) or uttered, thus it is an 'expression' (abhilāpa). The expression (abhilāpa) that is the Dhamma—unerring and of intrinsic nature—is called 'expression of the Dhamma' (dhammābhilāpa). By this, it shows the 'Dhamma-expression' mentioned in the passage, 'Therein, knowledge in the expression of the Dhamma-expression is the analytical knowledge of language' (Vibh. 718), because teaching has the nature of sound. Thus, the state of the analytical knowledge of language having a limited object, etc., is stated in the Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga Pāḷi. And in its commentary, its having sound as its object is shown by the passage beginning, 'having made that sound, which is the natural expression, its object.' For when it has been determined regarding the expression and its meaning that 'this sound expresses this meaning,' the sound that proceeds by way of clarifying the meaning of each expression is called 'teaching.' By the word 'intention,' it is shown that the statement 'Teaching is designation' was said with reference to the expression of the Dhamma-expression, and not with reference to a designation separate from that, because when there is a possibility of many meanings, only the intended meaning is stated. This is the determination according to the view of the sound-theorists.

Paññattivādīnaṃ vāde pana sammutiparamatthabhedassa atthassānurūpavācakabhāvena paramatthasaddesu bhagavatā manasā vavatthāpitā tantisaṅkhātā nāmapaññatti desanā nāma, “desanā”ti vā vuccatīti attho. Tadeva mūlakāraṇabhūtassa [M 1.0107] saddassa dassanavasena kāraṇūpacārena dassetuṃ “yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi “dhammābhilāpo”ti ettha abhilappati uccārīyatīti abhilāpoti saddo vuccati, na paṇṇatti, tathāpi sadde vuccamāne tadanurūpaṃ vohāraṃ gahetvā tena vohārena dīpitassa atthassa jānanato sadde kathite tadanurūpā paṇṇattipi kāraṇūpacārena kathitāyeva hoti. Apica “dhammābhilāpoti attho”ti avatvā “dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo”ti vuttattā desanā nāma saddo na hotīti dīpitameva. Tena hi adhippāyamattameva mūlakāraṇasaddavasena kathitaṃ, na idha gahetabbo “desanā”ti etassa atthoti [V 1.0095] ayaṃ paññattivādīnaṃ vādato vinicchayo. Atthantaramāha “anuloma…pe… kathana”nti, etena heṭṭhā vuttaṃ desanāsamuṭṭhāpakaṃ cittuppādaṃ dasseti. Kathīyati attho etenāti hi kathanaṃ. Ādisaddena nītaneyyādikā pāḷigatiyo, ekattādinandiyāvattādikā pāḷinissitā ca nayā saṅgahitā.

However, in the view of the designation-theorists, the name-designation (nāmapaññatti), known as the Pāḷi text, established by the Blessed One by mind among the ultimate sounds as a suitable expression for the meaning differentiated as conventional and ultimate, is named 'teaching' (desanā), or it is called 'teaching'; this is the meaning. To show that very thing by way of a figurative expression of cause (kāraṇūpacāra), by indicating the sound which is the root cause, it was said, 'The intention is: an expression of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.' For although here, in 'expression of the Dhamma,' 'expression' (abhilāpa) refers to the sound that is expressed or uttered, not to the designation (paññatti), nevertheless, when the sound is spoken, by taking up the corresponding conventional usage (vohāra) and knowing the meaning clarified by that usage, when the sound is stated, the corresponding designation is also considered stated by a figurative expression of cause. Moreover, because it was not said, 'The meaning is: an expression of the Dhamma,' but rather, 'The intention is: an expression of the Dhamma,' it is indeed shown that what is called 'teaching' is not the sound. For by that, only the intention is stated by way of the sound which is the root cause; the meaning of 'teaching' is not to be taken here. This is the determination according to the view of the designation-theorists. He states another meaning: 'conformable... statement.' By this, he shows the thought-process that originates the teaching, which was mentioned below. For the meaning is stated by this, hence it is a 'statement' (kathanaṃ). By the word 'etc.,' the Pāḷi styles such as those of explicit and implicit meaning (nīta-neyya), and the methods based on the Pāḷi such as unity (ekatta), repetition (nandiyāvatta), etc., are included.

Sayameva paṭivijjhati, etena vā paṭivijjhantīti paṭivedho, ñāṇaṃ. Tadeva abhisameti, etena vā abhisamentīti abhisamayotipi vuccati. Idāni taṃ paṭivedhaṃ abhisamayappabhedato, abhisamayākārato, ārammaṇato, sabhāvato ca pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “so cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hi lokiyalokuttaroti pabhedato, visayato, asammohatoti ākārato, dhammesu, atthesu, paññattīsūti ārammaṇato, atthānurūpaṃ, dhammānurūpaṃ, paññattipathānurūpanti sabhāvato ca pākaṭaṃ karoti. Tattha visayato atthādianurūpaṃ dhammādīsu avabodho nāma avijjādidhammārammaṇo, saṅkhārādiatthārammaṇo, tadubhayapaññāpanārammaṇo ca lokiyo abhisamayo. Asammohato atthādianurūpaṃ dhammādīsu avabodho nāma nibbānārammaṇo maggasampayutto yathāvuttadhammatthapaññattīsu sammohaviddhaṃsano lokuttaro abhisamayo. Tathā hi “ayaṃ hetu, idamassa phalaṃ, ayaṃ tadubhayānurūpo vohāro”ti evaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena lokiyañāṇaṃ visayato paṭivijjhati, lokuttarañāṇaṃ pana tesu hetuhetuphalādīsu sammohassañāṇena samucchinnattā asammohato paṭivijjhati. Lokuttaro pana paṭivedho [M 1.0108] visayato nibbānassa, asammohato ca itarassātipi vadanti eke.

It penetrates by itself, or that by which associated states penetrate—this is penetration (paṭivedha), which is knowledge (ñāṇa). That very thing it fully understands, or that by which associated states fully understand—this is also called full understanding (abhisamaya). Now, to make that penetration clear in terms of division, mode, object, and nature, the passage beginning 'And that...' was stated. Therein, he makes it clear: by 'mundane and supramundane' in terms of division; by 'from the standpoint of the object' and 'from the standpoint of non-delusion' in terms of mode; by 'in the dhammas, in the meanings, in the designations' in terms of object; and by 'in accordance with the meaning,' 'in accordance with the dhamma,' and 'in accordance with the path of designation' in terms of nature. Therein, the understanding in dhammas, etc., in accordance with meaning, etc., from the standpoint of the object, is the mundane full understanding, which has as its object the dhammas beginning with ignorance, the meanings beginning with formations, and the designation of both. The understanding in dhammas, etc., in accordance with meaning, etc., from the standpoint of non-delusion, is the supramundane full understanding, which has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the path, and destroys delusion regarding the aforesaid dhammas, meanings, and designations. Thus, mundane knowledge penetrates from the standpoint of the object by way of taking as its object: 'This is the cause, this is its fruit, this is the conventional expression in accordance with both.' Supramundane knowledge, however, penetrates from the standpoint of non-delusion because delusion regarding those causes, fruits of causes, etc., has been utterly cut off by knowledge. But some say that supramundane penetration penetrates Nibbāna from the standpoint of the object, and the remaining things from the standpoint of non-delusion.

Atthānurūpaṃ dhammesūti “avijjā hetu, saṅkhārā hetusamuppannā, saṅkhāre uppādeti avijjā”ti evaṃ kāriyānurūpaṃ kāraṇesūti attho. Atha vā “puññābhisaṅkhāraapuññābhisaṅkhāraāneñjābhisaṅkhāresu tīsu apuññābhisaṅkhārassa avijjā sampayuttapaccayo, itaresaṃ yathānurūpa”ntiādinā kāriyānurūpaṃ kāraṇesu paṭivedhotipi attho. Dhammānurūpaṃ atthesūti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1; vibha. 225) kāraṇānurūpaṃ kāriyesu. Chabbidhāya paññattiyā patho paññattipatho, tassa anurūpaṃ tathā, paññattiyā vuccamānadhammānurūpaṃ paññattīsu avabodhoti attho. Abhisamayato aññampi paṭivedhatthaṃ dassetuṃ “tesa”ntiādimāha. Paṭivijjhīyatīti paṭivedhoti hi taṃtaṃrūpādidhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo vuccati. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ piṭake, pāḷipadese vā. Salakkhaṇasaṅkhātoti ruppananamanaphusanādisakasakalakkhaṇasaṅkhāto.

‘In accordance with meaning in the dhammas’ means: ‘Ignorance is a cause; formations are arisen from a cause; ignorance produces formations’—thus, the meaning is penetration into causes in accordance with the effect. Alternatively, the meaning is also penetration into causes in accordance with the effect, as in ‘among the three kinds of formations—meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations—ignorance is a conjoined condition for demeritorious formations, and for the others, it is a condition in a suitable manner,’ and so on. ‘In accordance with dhamma in the meanings’ means: ‘Dependent on ignorance, formations arise,’ and so on—thus, it is the understanding of effects in accordance with their causes. In accordance with the path of the sixfold designation; thus, the meaning is the understanding of designations in accordance with the dhamma being spoken of by designation. To show the meaning of penetration, which is also different from full understanding, he says 'of these,' and so on. Indeed, because of the etymological meaning 'it is penetrated' (paṭivijjhīyati), it is called 'penetration' (paṭivedho); it is said to be the undistorted nature of those respective dhammas such as form and so on. 'Here and there' means in this or that Piṭaka, or in a Pāli passage. 'Known by its own characteristic' means known by its own respective characteristic such as being afflicted (ruppana), bending (namana), touching (phusana), and so on.

Yathāvuttehi [V 1.0096] dhammādīhi piṭakānaṃ gambhīrabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “idānī”tiādimāha. Dhammajātanti kāraṇappabhedo, kāraṇameva vā. Atthajātanti kāriyappabhedo, kāriyameva vā. Yā cāyaṃ desanāti sambandho. Tadatthavijānanavasena abhimukho hoti. Yo cetthāti yo etāsu taṃ taṃ piṭakāgatāsu dhammatthadesanāsu paṭivedho, yo ca etesu piṭakesu tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvoti attho. Sambharitabbato kusalameva sambhāro, so sammā anupacito yehi te anupacitakusalasambhārā, tatova duppaññehi, nippaññehīti attho. Na hi paññavato, paññāya vā duṭṭhubhāvo dūsitabhāvo ca sambhavatīti nippaññattāyeva duppaññā yathā “dussīlo”ti (a. ni. 5.213; 10.75; pārā. 295; dha. pa. 308). Ettha ca avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ dhammatthānaṃ duppaṭivijjhatāya dukkhogāhatā, tesaṃ paññāpanassa dukkarabhāvato taṃdesanāya, abhisamayasaṅkhātassa paṭivedhassa uppādanavisayīkaraṇānaṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, aviparītasabhāvasaṅkhātassa paṭivedhassa dubbiññeyyatāya dukkhogāhatā veditabbā. Evampīti pi-saddo pubbe [M 1.0109] vuttaṃ pakārantaraṃ sampiṇḍeti. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya anūnaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ paridīpitatthabhāvaṃ dassento “ettāvatā”tiādimāha. “Siddhe hi satyārambho atthantaraviññāpanāya vā hoti, niyamāya vā”ti iminā punārambhavacanena anūnaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ paridīpitatthabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ettāvatāti paricchedatthe nipāto, ettakena vacanakkamenāti attho. Etaṃ vā parimāṇaṃ yassāti ettāvaṃ, tena, etaparimāṇavatā saddatthakkamenāti attho. “Sadde hi vutte tadatthopi vuttoyeva nāmā”ti vadanti. Vutto saṃvaṇṇito attho yassāti vuttatthā.

To show the profundity of the Piṭakas through the aforementioned dhammas and so on, he says 'now,' and so on. 'A type of dhamma' means a classification of causes, or the cause itself. 'A type of meaning' means a classification of effects, or the effect itself. The connection is: 'And this discourse'. By means of knowing its meaning, it is directed towards the knowledge of the listeners. As for 'And whatever is here', the meaning is: whatever penetration there is in these discourses on dhamma and meaning found in the various Piṭakas, and whatever undistorted nature of those respective dhammas there is in these Piṭakas. From what should be accumulated, only the wholesome is an accumulation. Those by whom it is not rightly accumulated are 'those who have not accumulated wholesome provisions'; precisely because of that, the meaning is 'by those of little wisdom', 'by those without wisdom'. Indeed, for one with wisdom or for wisdom, a bad state or a corrupted state is not possible; therefore, precisely because of the state of being without wisdom, they are called 'of little wisdom' (duppañña), just as in 'unvirtuous' (dussīla). And here, the difficulty of fathoming the dhammas and meanings of ignorance, formations, and so on, should be known from their being difficult to penetrate; the difficulty of fathoming that discourse, from the difficulty of explaining them; and the difficulty of fathoming should be known from the inability to cause the arising of the penetration called full understanding and to make it an object, and from the penetration called the undistorted nature being difficult to discern. In 'Even so', the particle 'pi' consolidates the other aspect spoken of previously. Thus, showing that the meaning of the first verse has been fully and completely illuminated, he says 'thus far,' and so on. By this renewed statement, 'For when a matter is accomplished, a new undertaking is for making known another meaning or for establishing a rule,' he shows that the meaning has been fully and completely illuminated. 'Ettāvatā' is a particle in the sense of limitation; the meaning is 'by this much in the sequence of words.' Or, 'ettāvaṃ' is that which has this measure; by that, the meaning is 'by this sequence of word and meaning which has this measure.' They say, 'Indeed, when the word is spoken, its meaning is also spoken.' 'Vuttatthā' is that of which the meaning has been spoken, has been explained.

Etthāti etissā gāthāya. Evaṃ attho, vinicchayoti vā seso. Tīsu piṭakesūti ettha “ekekasmi”nti adhikārato, pakaraṇato vā veditabbaṃ. “Ekamekasmiñcetthā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) hi heṭṭhā vuttaṃ. Atha vā vatticchānupubbikattā saddapaṭipattiyā niddhāraṇamidha avattukāmena ādhāroyeva vutto. Na cettha codetabbaṃ “tīsuyeva piṭakesu tividho pariyattibhedo daṭṭhabbo siyā”ti samudāyavasena vuttassāpi vākyassa avayavādhippāyasambhavato. Dissati hi avayavavākyanipphatti “brāhmaṇādayo bhuñjantū”tiādīsu, tasmā alamatipapañcena. Yathā attho na virujjhati, tathāyeva gahetabboti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Pariyattibhedoti pariyāpuṇanaṃ pariyatti. Pariyāpuṇanavācako hettha pariyattisaddo, na pana pāḷipariyāyo, tasmā pariyāpuṇanappakāroti attho. Atha vā tīhi pakārehi pariyāpuṇitabbā pāḷiyo eva “pariyattī”ti vuccanti. Tathā ceva abhidhammaṭṭhakathāya sīhaḷagaṇṭhipade vuttanti vadanti. Evampi hi alagaddūpamāpariyāpuṇanayogato “alagaddūpamā pariyattī”ti pāḷipi sakkā vattuṃ. Evañca katvā “duggahitā upārambhādihetu [V 1.0097] pariyāpuṭā alagaddūpamā”ti parato niddesavacanampi upapannaṃ hoti. Tattha hi pāḷiyeva “duggahitā, pariyāpuṭā”ti ca vattuṃ yuttā.

'Ettha' means 'in this verse'. The remainder of the sentence to be supplied is 'thus the meaning should be understood', or 'the decision should be understood'. In 'in the three Piṭakas', the word 'in each one' should be understood from the governing context or from the general context. For it was said below, 'And in each one of these'. Alternatively, because the production of words follows the speaker's intention, one who did not wish to state a specification here has stated only the locative basis. And here one should not object, 'The threefold division of learning should be seen only in the three Piṭakas,' because even for a sentence spoken in a collective sense, the possibility of an intention referring to its parts exists. For the formation of a partial sentence is seen in cases like 'Let brahmins and others eat.' Therefore, enough with excessive elaboration. It should be taken in such a way that the meaning is not contradicted. This applies everywhere. 'Division of learning' (pariyattibhedo): 'pariyatti' is learning (pariyāpuṇana). Here the word 'pariyatti' denotes the act of learning, not a synonym for the Pāli texts. Therefore, the meaning is 'the mode of learning'. Alternatively, the Pāli texts themselves, which are to be learned in three ways, are called 'pariyatti'. And they say it is stated similarly in the Sīhaḷa-gaṇṭhipada of the Abhidhamma commentary. Indeed, even so, because of its connection with the learning that is like the water-snake simile, it is possible to call the Pāli text itself 'the learning like the water-snake simile' (alagaddūpamā pariyatti). And having done so, the subsequent explanatory statement—'Poorly grasped, mastered for the sake of reproach, etc., it is like the water-snake'—also becomes appropriate. For there it is fitting to say of the Pāli text itself that it is 'poorly grasped' and 'mastered'.

Alagaddo alagaddaggahaṇaṃ upamā etissāti alagaddūpamā. Alagaddassa gahaṇañhettha alagaddasaddena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āpūpikoti ettha āpūpa-saddena āpūpakhādanaṃ viya, veṇikoti ettha vīṇāsaddena vīṇāvādanaggahaṇaṃ viya ca. Alagaddaggahaṇena hi pariyatti upamīyati[M 1.0110], na alagaddena. “Alagaddaggahaṇūpamā”ti vā vattabbe majjhepadalopaṃ katvā “alagaddūpamā”ti vuttaṃ “oṭṭhamukho”tiādīsu viya. Alagaddoti ca āsīviso vuccati. Gadoti hi visassa nāmaṃ, tañca tassa alaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ atthi, tasmā alaṃ pariyatto paripuṇṇo gado assāti alagaddo anunāsikalopaṃ, da-kārāgamañca katvā, alaṃ vā jīvitaharaṇe samattho gado yassāti alagaddo vuttanayena. Vaṭṭadukkhato nissaraṇaṃ attho payojanametissāti nissaraṇatthā. Bhaṇḍāgāre niyutto bhaṇḍāgāriko, rājaratanānupālako, so viyāti tathā, dhammaratanānupālako khīṇāsavo. Aññamatthamanapekkhitvā bhaṇḍāgārikasseva sato pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti.

For this learning, the grasping of a snake is the simile; therefore, it is called alagaddūpamā. Herein, it should be understood that the grasping of the snake is expressed by the word alagadda. This is just as in the word āpūpika, the eating of cakes is expressed by the word āpūpa, and in the word veṇika, the playing of the lute is expressed by the word vīṇā. For the learning is compared to the grasping of a snake, not to the snake itself. Alternatively, when it should be said as alagaddaggahaṇūpamā, having elided the middle word, it is said as alagaddūpamā, just as in words like oṭṭhamukha. And a venomous snake is called alagadda. For gada is a name for poison, and for this snake, that poison is sufficient and complete. Therefore, because 'for it there is a sufficient, complete poison,' it is called alagadda, after eliding the nasal consonant and inserting the letter 'd'. Alternatively, it is called alagadda by the aforementioned method because its poison is capable of taking life. For this learning, the meaning and purpose is escape from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths; therefore, it is called nissaraṇatthā. One appointed in a treasury is a treasurer, a guardian of the king's jewels; the learning is like him, and so it is called thus. A guardian of the jewels of the Dhamma is an Arahant, one whose cankers are destroyed. Without regard for any other purpose, the learning of one who is just like a treasurer is bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti.

Duggahitāti duṭṭhu gahitā. Tadeva sarūpato niyametuṃ “upārambhādihetu pariyāpuṭā”ti āha, upārambhaitivādappamokkhādihetu uggahitāti attho. Lābhasakkārādihetu pariyāpuṇanampi ettheva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ alagaddasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Duggahitā means wrongly grasped. To define that very thing in its essence, he said, 'mastered for reasons such as reproach.' The meaning is: wrongly learned for reasons such as the desire to censure others and the desire to be free from such talk and blame. It should be understood that learning for reasons such as gain, honor, and so on is also included herein. For this is stated in the commentary to the Alagaddūpama Sutta:

“Yo buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā ‘evaṃ cīvarādīni vā labhissāmi, catuparisamajjhe vā maṃ jānissantī’ti lābhasakkārahetu pariyāpuṇāti, tassa sā pariyatti alagaddapariyatti nāma. Evaṃ pariyāpuṇanato hi buddhavacanaṃ apariyāpuṇitvā niddokkamanaṃ varatara”nti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.239).

Whatever person, having learned the Buddha's word, studies it for the sake of gain and honor, thinking, 'Thus I will receive robes and so forth, or they will know me in the midst of the fourfold assembly'—for that person, that learning is called alagaddapariyatti. Indeed, rather than learning in this way, it would be far better not to learn the Buddha's word and to fall asleep.

Nanu ca alagaddaggahaṇūpamā pariyatti “alagaddūpamā”ti vuccati, evañca sati suggahitāpi pariyatti “alagaddūpamā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati tatthāpi alagaddaggahaṇassa upamābhāvena pāḷiyaṃ vuttattā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But surely, the learning that has the simile of grasping a snake is called alagaddūpamā. This being so, it is also fitting to call even well-grasped learning alagaddūpamā, because even in that case, it is stated in the Pāḷi text as being a simile for grasping a snake. For this has been said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno, so passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ, tamenaṃ ajapadena daṇḍena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇheyya[V 1.0098], ajapadena daṇḍena suniggahitaṃ niggahitvā gīvāya suggahitaṃ gaṇheyya. Kiñcāpi so bhikkhave, alagaddo tassa purisassa hatthaṃ vā bāhaṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ bhogehi paliveṭheyya[M 1.0111]. Atha kho so neva tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu, suggahitattā bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho bhikkhave, idhekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ geyya”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.239).

Bhikkhus, it is as if a man needing a snake, seeking a snake, wandering in search of a snake, should see a large snake. He should press it down firmly with a forked stick; having pressed it down firmly with a forked stick, he should grasp it securely by the neck. Bhikkhus, even if that snake were to wrap its coils around that man's hand or arm or any of his major or minor limbs, still, he would not on that account come to death or deadly suffering. For what reason? Because, Bhikkhus, of the snake's being well-grasped. So too, Bhikkhus, some clansmen here master the Dhamma—the discourses, the mixed prose and verse, and so on.

Tasmā idha duggahitā eva pariyatti alagaddūpamāti ayaṃ viseso kuto viññāyati, yena duggahitā upārambhādihetu pariyāpuṭā “alagaddūpamā”ti vuccatīti? Saccametaṃ, idaṃ pana pārisesañāyena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi nissaraṇatthabhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīnaṃ visuṃ gahitattā pārisesato alagaddassa duggahaṇūpamāyeva pariyatti “alagaddūpamā”ti viññāyati. Alagaddassa suggahaṇūpamā hi pariyatti nissaraṇatthā vā hoti, bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti vā. Tasmā suvuttametaṃ “duggahitā…pe… pariyattī”ti. Idāni tamatthaṃ pāḷiyā sādhento “yaṃ sandhāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha yanti yaṃ pariyattiduggahaṇaṃ. Majjhimanikāye mūlapaṇṇāsake alagaddasutte (ma. ni. 1.239) bhagavatā vuttaṃ.

Therefore, whence is this distinction understood here, that only wrongly grasped learning is alagaddūpamā, such that the wrongly grasped learning, mastered for reasons such as reproach, is called alagaddūpamā? This is true. However, it should be understood that this was stated by the Commentator by the method of elimination. Indeed, since the learning for the purpose of escape and the treasurer-like learning have been taken separately, by elimination it is understood that only the learning that is a simile of wrongly grasping a snake is alagaddūpamā. For the learning that is a simile of well-grasping a snake is either for the purpose of escape or is treasurer-like learning. Therefore, it was well said: 'wrongly grasped... learning.' Now, establishing that meaning with the Pāḷi text, he said, 'With reference to which...,' and so on. Therein, 'which' refers to that wrong grasping of the learning spoken of by the Blessed One in the Alagaddasutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka in the Majjhima Nikāya.

Alagaddatthikoti āsīvisena, āsīvisaṃ vā atthiko, alagaddaṃ gavesati pariyesati sīlenāti alagaddagavesī. Alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramānoti āsīvisapariyesanatthaṃ caramāno. Tadatthe hetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, upayogavacanaṃ vā, alagaddapariyesanaṭṭhānaṃ vā caramāno. Alagaddaṃ pariyesanti etthāti hi alagaddapariyesanaṃ. Tamenanti taṃ alagaddaṃ. Bhogeti sarīre. “Bhogo tu phaṇino tanū”ti hi vuttaṃ. Bhujīyati kuṭilaṃ karīyatīti bhogo. Tassāti purisassa. Hatthe vā bāhāya vāti sambandho. Maṇibandhato paṭṭhāya yāva agganakhā hattho. Saddhiṃ aggabāhāya avasesā bāhā, katthaci pana kapparato paṭṭhāya yāva agganakhā “hattho”ti vuttaṃ bāhāya visuṃ anāgatattā. Vuttalakkhaṇaṃ hatthañca bāhañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ sarīraṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ. Tatonidānanti tannidānaṃ, taṃkāraṇāti attho. Taṃ hatthādīsu ḍaṃsanaṃ nidānaṃ kāraṇaṃ etassāti “tannidāna”nti hi vattabbe “tatonidāna”nti purimapade paccattatthe nissakkavacanaṃ katvā, tassa ca lopamakatvā niddeso, hetvatthe ca paccattavacanaṃ. Kāraṇatthe nipātapadametantipi vadanti. Apica “tatonidāna”nti etaṃ “maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti ettha vuttanayena visesanaṃ. Taṃ [M 1.0112] kissa hetūti yaṃ vuttaṃ hatthādīsu ḍaṃsanaṃ, tannidānañca maraṇādiupagamanaṃ[V 1.0099], taṃ kissa hetu kena kāraṇenāti ce? Tassa purisassa alagaddassa duggahitattā.

'One who wants a snake' (Alagaddatthiko): this means one who is desirous of a venomous snake. 'A snake-searcher' (alagaddagavesī): this is because that person habitually (sīlena) searches for and seeks out a snake. 'Going about searching for a snake' (Alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno) means going about for the purpose of searching for a venomous snake. This expression is a nominative in the sense of 'for that purpose', or an accusative. Alternatively, it means going about to a place for searching for a snake. For it is called 'a place for searching for a snake' (alagaddapariyesanaṃ) because 'here they search for a snake'. 'That one' (Tamenaṃ) means that snake. 'On its coil' (Bhoge) means on its body. For it is said: "The coil (bhogo) of a snake is its body (tanu)." It is called bhogo because it is bent (bhujīyati) or made crooked. 'Of that one' (Tassa) means of the person. The connection is to be made with 'on the hand or on the arm'. The hand (hattho) is from the wrist up to the fingertips. The arm (bāhā) is the remainder together with the upper arm. In some cases, however, 'hand' is said to be from the elbow up to the fingertips, because the arm is not mentioned separately. Excluding the hand and arm with the characteristics mentioned, the remaining body is the major and minor limbs (aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ). 'From that as cause' (Tatonidānaṃ) means having that as its cause (tannidānaṃ); the meaning is 'that cause'. For when it should be said tannidānaṃ—meaning "that biting on the hand, etc., is the cause for this suffering"—tatonidānaṃ is said, having formed an ablative expression in the preceding word in the nominative sense, and this reference is made without elision; and it is a nominative expression in the sense of cause. Some also say this is an indeclinable particle in the sense of cause. Furthermore, this term tatonidānaṃ is an adjective for 'death or suffering equivalent to death', in the way previously stated. 'For what reason is that?' (Taṃ kissa hetū): If it is asked, "That which was spoken of—the biting on the hand, etc., and the consequent undergoing of death and so on—for what reason, for what cause does this occur?" It is because of that person's wrong grasping of the snake.

Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Moghapurisāti guṇasārarahitatāya tucchapurisā. Dhammanti pāḷidhammaṃ. Pariyāpuṇantīti uggaṇhanti, sajjhāyanti ceva vācuggataṃ karontā dhārenti cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Dhamma”nti sāmaññato vuttameva sarūpena dasseti “sutta”ntiādinā. Na hi suttādinavaṅgato añño dhammo nāma atthi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “tesaṃ dhammāna”nti. Atthanti cettha sambandhīniddeso eso, atthanti ca yathābhūtaṃ bhāsitatthaṃ, payojanatthañca sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā vuttaṃ. Yañhi padaṃ sutisāmaññena anekadhā atthaṃ dīpeti, taṃ sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vāti sabbattha veditabbaṃ. Na upaparikkhantīti na pariggaṇhanti na vicārenti. Ikkhasaddassa hi dassanaṅkesu idha dassanameva attho, tassa ca pariggaṇhanacakkhulocanesu pariggaṇhanameva, tañca vicāraṇā pariyādānavasena dubbidhesu vicāraṇāyeva, sā ca vīmaṃsāyeva, na vicāro, vīmaṃsā ca nāmesā bhāsitatthavīmaṃsā, payojanatthavīmaṃsā cāti idha dubbidhāva adhippetā, tāsu “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, imasmiṃ samādhi, imasmiṃ paññā, mayañca taṃ pūressāmā”ti evaṃ bhāsitatthavīmaṃsañceva “sīlaṃ samādhissa kāraṇaṃ, samādhi vipassanāyā”tiādinā payojanatthavīmaṃsañca na karontīti attho. Anupaparikkhatanti anupaparikkhantānaṃ tesaṃ moghapurisānaṃ. Na nijjhānakkhamantīti nijjhānaṃ nissesena pekkhanaṃ paññaṃ na khamanti. Jhe-saddo hi idha pekkhaneyeva, na cintanajhāpanesu, tañca ñāṇapekkhanameva, na cakkhupekkhanaṃ, ārammaṇūpanijjhānameva vā, na lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, tasmā paññāya disvā rocetvā gahetabbā na hontīti adhippāyo veditabbo. Nissesena jhāyate pekkhateti hi nijjhānaṃ. Sandhivasena anusvāralopo nijjhānakkhamantīti, “nijjhānaṃ khamantī”tipi pāṭho, tena imamatthaṃ dīpeti “tesaṃ paññāya atthassa anupaparikkhanato te dhammā na upaṭṭhahanti, imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ, samādhi, vipassanā, maggo, vaṭṭaṃ, vivaṭṭhaṃ kathitanti evaṃ jānituṃ na sakkā hontī”ti.

'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'Worthless persons' means empty persons, due to being devoid of the essence of virtues. 'The Dhamma' means the Dhamma in Pāḷi. 'They master it' means they learn it, recite it, and, making it come to the tip of the tongue, they bear it in mind; this is the intended meaning. What was spoken of generally as 'Dhamma', the Blessed One shows in its specific form with 'sutta', and so on. For there is no other Dhamma apart from the ninefold division beginning with 'sutta'. That is why it was said, "of those Dhammas". Here, this indication 'meaning' (atthaṃ) is an indication of what is related. And 'meaning' refers to both the meaning of what was spoken as it really is and the meaning as purpose, spoken of either by general indication or by the method of single remainder. For whatever word reveals its meaning in many ways through general hearing, it should be understood everywhere as being spoken of by general indication or by the method of single remainder. 'They do not investigate' means they do not grasp with wisdom, they do not scrutinize. For of the meanings of the root ikkha, which are seeing and marking, here the meaning is just seeing. And of that seeing, which can be grasping with wisdom or seeing with the eye, it is just grasping with wisdom. And that grasping, which can be of two kinds, investigation and taking up, is just investigation. And that investigation is inquiry (vīmaṃsā), not discursive thought (vicāro). This inquiry is twofold: inquiry into the meaning of what was spoken and inquiry into the purpose. Here, both kinds are intended. The meaning is: they do not perform either the inquiry into the meaning of what was spoken, such as: "In this place, virtue was taught; in this place, concentration; in this place, wisdom; and we shall fulfill them," or the inquiry into the purpose, such as: "Virtue is the cause for concentration, concentration is the cause for insight," and so on. 'Of those who do not investigate' refers to those worthless persons. 'They do not tolerate contemplation' means they do not tolerate the wisdom that is contemplation, that is, seeing without remainder. For the root jhe here is used only in the sense of seeing, not in the senses of thinking or burning. And that seeing is only seeing with knowledge, not seeing with the eye. Or, it is only close contemplation of the object, not close contemplation of the characteristics. Therefore, the intended meaning to be understood is: they are not ones to be taken up after seeing with wisdom and approving. For nijjhānaṃ is so called because one contemplates or sees without remainder. Due to euphonic combination, the nasal consonant is elided, resulting in nijjhānakkhamanti. There is also the reading nijjhānaṃ khamantī. This reading shows the following meaning: "Because they do not investigate the meaning of those Dhammas with wisdom, those Dhammas do not become clear to them. They are unable to know thus: 'In this place virtue is taught, concentration, insight, the path, the round of rebirth, and that which is free from the round.'"

Upārambhānisaṃsā cevāti paresaṃ vāde dosāropanānisaṃsā ca hutvā. Bhuso ārambhanañhi paresaṃ vāde dosāropanaṃ upārambho, pariyattiṃ [M 1.0113] nissāya paravambhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hesa “paravajjānupanayanalakkhaṇo”ti vutto. Iti vādappamokkhānisaṃsā cāti iti evaṃ etāya pariyattiyā vādappamokkhānisaṃsā attano upari parehi āropitassa vādassa niggahassa attato, sakavādato vā pamokkhapayojanā ca hutvā. Iti saddo idamatthe, tena “pariyāpuṇantī”ti [V 1.0100] ettha pariyāpuṇanaṃ parāmasati. Vadanti niggaṇhanti etenāti vādo, doso, pamuccanaṃ, pamuccāpanaṃ vā pamokkho, attano upari āropitassa pamokkho ānisaṃso yesaṃ tathā. Āropitavādo hi “vādo”ti vutto yathā “devena datto datto”ti. Vādoti vā upavādonindā yathāvuttanayeneva samāso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – parehi sakavāde dose āropite, nindāya vā āropitāya taṃ dosaṃ, nindaṃ vā evañca evañca mocessāmāti iminā ca kāraṇena pariyāpuṇantīti. Atha vā so so vādo iti vādo iti-saddassa saha vicchāya ta-saddatthe pavattattā. Itivādasa pamokkho yathāvuttanayena, so ānisaṃso yesaṃ tathā, taṃ taṃ vādapamocanānisaṃsā hutvāti attho. Yassa catthāyāti yassa ca sīlādipūraṇassa, maggaphalanibbānabhūtassa vā anupādāvimokkhassa atthāya. Abhedepi bhedavohāro eso yathā “paṭimāya sarīra”nti, bhedyabhedakaṃ vā etaṃ yathā “kathinassatthāya ābhataṃ dussa”nti. “Tañcassa attha”nti hi vuttaṃ. Ca-saddo avadhāraṇe, tena tadatthāya eva pariyāpuṇanaṃ sambhavati, nāññatthāyāti vinicchinoti. Dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantīti hi jātiācāravasena duvidhāpi kulaputtā ñāyena dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantīti attho. Tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhontīti assa dhammassa sīlādipūraṇasaṅkhātaṃ, maggaphalanibbānabhūtaṃ vā anupādāvimokkhasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ ete duggahitagāhino nānubhonti na vindantiyeva.

The benefits of rebuke, that is, having the benefit of placing blame on the views of others. For 'rebuke' (upārambha) is indeed the intense placing of blame on the views of others; it is said to be the crushing of others based on scriptural learning. Thus it is called 'characterized by suitably bringing forward others' faults.' And 'the benefits of being freed from disputes' means that by this learning, one has the benefit of being freed from the censure, the fault imputed upon oneself by others, or from one's own view. The word 'iti' is in the sense of 'this,' and by it, the learning in 'they learn' is referred to. That by which they speak or censure is a 'dispute' (vādo), a fault. 'Pamokkho' is being freed or causing freedom. For whom the benefit is the freedom from what has been imputed upon oneself, they are so-called. For an imputed censure is called a 'censure' (vādo), just as 'Devenadatta' is called 'Datta.' Alternatively, 'dispute' (vādo) means blame or censure; the compound is formed in the way already stated. This is what is said: when others impute a fault to one's own view, or when censure is imputed, they learn for this reason: 'We shall free ourselves from that fault or that censure in this way and that.' Or alternatively, 'this and that censure' is 'itivādo', because the word 'iti', with its separation, occurs in the sense of the word 'ta' (that). The freedom from this and that censure, as explained, is the benefit for those who are so-called. The meaning is: having the benefit of being freed from this and that censure. And 'for whose purpose?' means for the purpose of fulfilling virtue and so on, or for the purpose of liberation through non-clinging, which is the path, fruition, and Nibbāna. Even when there is no distinction, this is a conventional expression of distinction, as in 'the body of an image.' Or it may be the qualified and the qualifier, as in 'cloth brought for the purpose of the kathina.' For it is said, 'And that is its purpose.' The particle 'ca' is for emphasis; by it, it is determined that learning is possible only for that purpose, not for any other. For 'they learn the Dhamma' means that clansmen, of both kinds by birth and by conduct, learn the Dhamma according to the method. But 'they do not experience its purpose' means that these who grasp wrongly do not experience, do not indeed find, the purpose of that Dhamma, which is designated as the fulfillment of virtue and so on, or as liberation through non-clinging, which is the path, fruition, and Nibbāna.
