Aparo nayo – yassa upārambhassa, itivādappamokkhassa vā atthāya ye moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, te parehi “ayamattho na hotī”ti vutte duggahitattāyeva “tadatthova hotī”ti paṭipādanakkhamā na honti, tasmā parassa vāde upārambhaṃ āropetuṃ attano vādaṃ pamocetuñca asakkontāpi taṃ atthaṃ nānubhonti ca na vindantiyevāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Idhāpi hi ca-saddo avadhāraṇatthova. “Tesa”ntiādīsu [M 1.0114] tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitattā upārambhamānadabbamakkhapalāsādihetubhāvena dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattantīti attho. Duggahitāti hi hetugabbhavacanaṃ. Tenāha “duggahitattā bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.238). Ettha ca kāraṇe phalavohāravasena “te dhammā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattantī’ti vuttaṃ yathā “ghatamāyu, dadhi bala”nti. Tathā hi kiñcāpi na te dhammā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, tathāpi vuttanayena pariyāpuṇantānaṃ sajjhāyanakāle, vivādakāle ca tammūlakānaṃ upārambhādīnaṃ anekesaṃ akusalānaṃ uppattisambhavato “te…pe… saṃvattantī”ti vuccati. Taṃ kissa hetūti ettha nti yathāvuttassatthassa ananubhavanaṃ, tesañca dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanaṃ parāmasati. Kissāti sāmivacanaṃ hetvatthe, tathā hetūti paccattavacanañca.

Another method: For whatever purpose of rebuke or of being freed from this and that censure those foolish persons learn the Dhamma, when it is said by others, 'This is not the meaning,' they are not capable of establishing, 'That is indeed the meaning,' precisely because of their wrong grasp. Therefore, being unable to place blame on another's view and to free their own view, they do not experience and do not indeed find that purpose. The meaning here should also be understood in this way. Here too, indeed, the particle 'ca' is for emphasis. In 'For them,' etc., the meaning is: for those foolish persons, those teachings, because they are wrongly grasped, conduce to what is not for their welfare and to their suffering for a long time, by being a cause for rebuke, conceit, hypocrisy, rivalry, and so on. For 'wrongly grasped' is a word containing a cause. Therefore, He said, 'Because of the wrong grasp of the teachings, O bhikkhus...' And here, by way of the convention of referring to the cause by the name of its effect, it is said, 'those teachings conduce to what is not for their welfare and to their suffering,' just as in 'ghee is long life, curd is strength.' For although those teachings do not in themselves conduce to what is not for one's welfare and to suffering, nevertheless, because of the possible arising of many unwholesome states rooted in them—such as rebuke and so on—for those who learn in the aforesaid manner at the time of recitation and at the time of dispute, it is said, 'those... conduce to...' Here, in 'What is the reason for that?', the word 'that' refers to the non-experiencing of the aforesaid purpose and to those teachings conducing to what is not for one's welfare and to suffering. 'Kissa' is a genitive word in the sense of cause, and likewise 'hetu' is a nominative word.

Yā [V 1.0101] panāti ettha kiriyā pāḷivasena vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Tattha kiriyāpakkhe yā suggahitāti abhedepi bhedavohāro “cārikaṃ pakkamati, cārikaṃ caramāno”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.254, 300) viya. Tadevatthaṃ vivarati “sīlakkhandhādī”tiādinā, ādisaddena cettha samādhivipassanādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Yo hi buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā sīlassa āgataṭṭhāne sīlaṃ pūretvā, samādhino āgataṭṭhāne samādhiṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā, vipassanāya āgataṭṭhāne vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā, maggaphalānaṃ āgataṭṭhāne “maggaṃ bhāvessāmi, phalaṃ sacchikarissāmī”ti uggaṇhāti, tasseva sā pariyatti nissaraṇatthā nāma hoti. Yanti yaṃ pariyattisuggahaṇaṃ. Vuttaṃ alagaddasutte. Dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattantīti sīlādīnaṃ āgataṭṭhāne sīlādīni pūrentānampi arahattaṃ patvā parisamajjhe dhammaṃ desetvā dhammadesanāya pasannehi upanīte cattāro paccaye paribhuñjantānampi paresaṃ vāde sahadhammena upārambhaṃ āropentānampi sakavādato parehi āropitadosaṃ pariharantānampi dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattantīti attho. Tathā hi na kevalaṃ suggahitapariyattiṃ nissāya maggabhāvanāphalasacchikiriyādīniyeva, api tu paravādaniggahasakavādapatiṭṭhāpanānipi ijjhanti. Tathā ca vuttaṃ parinibbānasuttā dīsu “uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessantī”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.68).

In the phrase 'Yā pana,' the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated, by way of the Pāḷi of the action. Therein, in the action-aspect, 'that which is well-grasped' is a conventional expression of division even when there is no division, just as in 'he sets out on a journey, while walking on a journey.' The Blessed One explains that very meaning by 'the aggregate of virtue, etc.' And here, by the word 'etc.', concentration, insight, and so on are included. For whichever person, having learned the Buddha's word, fulfills virtue where virtue is mentioned, causes the chamber of concentration to be taken up where concentration is mentioned, establishes insight where insight is mentioned, and learns where the paths and fruits are mentioned, thinking, 'I shall develop the path, I shall realize the fruit'—for that very person, that learning is called 'for the purpose of liberation.' 'That' means that well-grasping of the scriptural study. It is stated in the Alagaddasutta. The meaning of 'it leads to welfare and happiness for a long time' is this: it leads to welfare and happiness for a long time for those who fulfill virtue and so on where virtue and so on are mentioned; for those who, having attained Arahantship and taught the Dhamma in the midst of an assembly, partake of the four requisites offered by those pleased with the Dhamma teaching; for those who, in accordance with the Dhamma, lay blame on the views of others; and for those who refute the faults imputed by others to their own view. For, by relying on well-grasped scriptural study, not only are the cultivation of the path, the realization of the fruit, and so on accomplished, but also the refutation of others' views and the establishment of one's own view are accomplished. And so it was said by the Blessed One in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and others: 'Having thoroughly refuted with reason the arisen wrong views of others, they will teach the Dhamma with its marvels,' and so on.

Yaṃ [M 1.0115] panāti etthāpi vuttanayena duvidhena attho. Dukkhaparijānena pariññātakkhandho. Samudayappahānena pahīnakileso. Paṭividdhārahattaphalatāya paṭividdhākuppo. Akuppanti ca arahattaphalassetaṃ nāma. Satipi hi cattunnaṃ maggānaṃ, catunnañca phalānaṃ avinassanabhāve sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ sakasakanāmapariccāgena uparūpari nāmantarappattito tesaṃ maggaphalāti “akuppāmi”ti na vuccanti. Arahā pana sabbadāpi arahāyeva nāmāti tasseva phalaṃ puggalanāmavasena “akuppa”nti vuttaṃ, iminā ca imamatthaṃ dasseti “khīṇāsavasseva pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti nāmā”ti. Tassa hi apariññātaṃ, appahīnaṃ abhāvitaṃ, asacchikataṃ vā natthi, tasmā so buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇantopi tantidhārako paveṇīpālako vaṃsānurakkhakova hutvā pariyāpuṇāti, tenevāha “paveṇīpālanatthāyā”tiādi. Paveṇī cettha dhammasantati dhammassa avicchedena pavatti. Buddhassa bhagavato vaṃsoti ca yathāvuttapaveṇīyeva.

In the phrase 'Yaṃ pana' also, the meaning should be understood in two ways according to the method already stated. One whose aggregates are fully understood through the full understanding of suffering. One whose defilements are abandoned through the abandonment of the origin. One who has penetrated the unshakeable through the penetration of the fruit of Arahantship. And 'unshakeable' is a name for the fruit of Arahantship. For although the four paths and four fruits are imperishable, the paths and fruits of the seven trainees are not called 'unshakeable' because they attain different names one after another by abandoning their respective names. But an Arahant is always called an Arahant; thus, the fruit of that one alone is called 'unshakeable' by way of the person's name. And by this, it shows this meaning: 'The scriptural study of one whose taints are destroyed is called the treasurer's scriptural study.' For that one, there is nothing not fully understood, not abandoned, not developed, or not realized. Therefore, even when learning the Buddha's word, they learn it only as a custodian of the texts, a preserver of the tradition, and a protector of the lineage. Hence it is said, 'for the sake of preserving the tradition,' etc. And here, 'tradition' (paveṇī) is the continuity of the Dhamma, the proceeding of the Dhamma without interruption. And 'the lineage (vaṃsa) of the Blessed One, the Buddha' is just that tradition as explained.

Nanu ca yadi paveṇīpālanatthāya buddhavacanassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti, atha kasmā “khīṇāsavo”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Ekaccassa hi puthujjanassāpi ayaṃ nayo labbhati. Tathā hi ekacco puthujjano bhikkhu chātakabhayādinā ganthadhuresu ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasitumasakkontesu [V 1.0102] sayaṃ bhikkhācārena atikilamamāno “atimadhuraṃ buddhavacanaṃ mā nassatu, tantiṃ dhāressāmi, vaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmi, paveṇiṃ pālessāmī”ti pariyāpuṇāti. Tasmā tassāpi pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti nāma kasmā na hotīti? Vuccate – evaṃ santepi hi puthujjanassa pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti nāma na hoti. Kiñcāpi hi puthujjano “paveṇiṃ pālessāmī”ti ajjhāsayena pariyāpuṇāti, attano pana bhavakantārato avitiṇṇattā tassa sā pariyatti nissaraṇatthāyeva nāma hoti, tasmā puthujjanassa pariyatti alagaddupamā vā hoti, nissaraṇatthā vā. Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ nissaraṇatthāva. Khīṇāsavānaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattiyevāti veditabbaṃ. Khīṇāsavo hi bhaṇḍāgārika sadisattā “bhaṇḍāgāriko”ti vuccati. Yathā hi bhaṇḍāgāriko alaṅkārabhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā pasādhanakāle tadupiyaṃ alaṅkārabhaṇḍaṃ rañño upanāmetvā taṃ alaṅkaroti, evaṃ khīṇāsavopi dhammaratanabhaṇḍaṃ sampaṭicchitvā mokkhādhigamāya [M 1.0116] bhabbarūpe sahetuke satte passitvā tadanurūpaṃ dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggaṅgabojjhaṅgādisaṅkhātena lokuttarena alaṅkārena alaṅkarotīti.

Now, if the learning of the Buddha's word for the purpose of preserving the tradition is the treasurer's scriptural study, then why is it specifically stated as 'one whose taints are destroyed'? For this method is found even in the case of some worldlings. Indeed, some worldling monk—when those engaged in the duty of studying the scriptures are unable to stay in one place due to the fear of famine and so on—though greatly exhausted by going on alms-round himself, learns with the thought, 'May the exceedingly sweet word of the Buddha not be lost! I will uphold the texts, establish the lineage, and preserve the tradition.' Therefore, why is his scriptural study also not called the treasurer's scriptural study? It is said: Even so, a worldling's scriptural study is not called the treasurer's scriptural study. For although a worldling learns with the intention, 'I will preserve the tradition,' because he himself has not crossed over the wilderness of existence, his scriptural study is only for the purpose of liberation. Therefore, a worldling's scriptural study is either like the water-snake simile or for the purpose of liberation. For the seven trainees, it is only for the purpose of liberation. It should be understood that for those whose taints are destroyed, it is only the treasurer's scriptural study. For one whose taints are destroyed is called a 'treasurer' because he is like a treasurer. Just as a treasurer, having stored away ornaments, presents suitable ornaments to the king at the time of adornment and adorns him, so too, one whose taints are destroyed, having received the treasure of the Dhamma, sees beings who are capable and have the necessary conditions for the attainment of liberation, and then, having expanded on a Dhamma teaching suitable for them, adorns them with the supramundane adornment known as the path factors, enlightenment factors, and so on.

Evaṃ tisso pariyattiyo vibhajitvā idāni tīsupi piṭakesu yathārahaṃ sampattivipattiyo niddhāretvā vibhajanto “vinaye panā”tiādimāha. “Sīlasampadaṃ nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇātī”tiādīsu yasmā sīlaṃ visujjhamānaṃ satisampajaññabalena, kammassakatāñāṇabalena ca saṃkilesamalato visujjhati, pāripūriñca gacchati, tasmā sīlasampadā sijjhamānā upanissayasampattibhāvena satibalaṃ, ñāṇabalañca paccupaṭṭhapetīti tassā vijjattayūpanissayatā veditabbā sabhāgahetusampādanato. Satibalena hi pubbenivāsavijjāsiddhi. Sampajaññabalena sabbakiccesu sudiṭṭhakāritāparicayena cutūpapātañāṇānubaddhāya dutiyavijjāya siddhi. Vītikkamābhāvena saṃkilesappahānasabbhāvato vivaṭṭūpanissayatāvasena ajjhāsayasuddhiyā tatiyavijjāsiddhi. Puretarasiddhānaṃ samādhipaññānaṃ pāripūriṃ vinā sīlassa āsavakkhayañāṇūpanissayatā sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavehi dīpetabbā. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 5.1071; netti. 40; mi. pa. 14) vacanato samādhisampadā chaḷabhiññatāya upanissayo. “Yogā ve jāyate bhūrī”ti (dha. pa. 282) vacanato pubbayogena garuvāsadesabhāsākosallauggahaṇaparipucchādīhi ca paribhāvitā paññāsampadā paṭisambhidāppabhedassa upanissayo. Ettha ca “sīlasampadaṃ nissāyā”ti vuttattā yassa samādhivijambhanabhūtā anavasesā cha abhiññā na ijjhanti, tassa ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena na samādhisampadā atthīti satipi vijjānaṃ abhiññekadesabhāve sīlasampadāsamudāgatā eva tisso vijjā gahitā, yathā ca paññāsampadāsamudāgatā catasso paṭisambhidā upanissayasampannassa [V 1.0103] maggeneva ijjhanti maggakkhaṇeyeva tāsaṃ paṭiladdhattā. Evaṃ sīlasampadāsamudāgatā tisso vijjā, samādhisampadāsamudāgatā ca cha abhiññā upanissayasampannassa maggeneva ijjhantīti maggādhigameneva tāsaṃ adhigamo veditabbo. Paccekabuddhānaṃ, sammāsambuddhānañca paccekabodhisammāsambodhisamadhigamasadisā hi imesaṃ ariyānaṃ ime visesādhigamāti.

Having thus analyzed the three kinds of learning, now, after appropriately determining the accomplishments and failures in each of the three Piṭakas, the commentator, wishing to analyze them, said the words beginning with, “But in the Vinaya…”. In such passages as, “Relying on the accomplishment in virtue, one attains the three knowledges,” the meaning should be understood in the following way. Because virtue, being purified by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension and by the power of the knowledge of kamma as one’s own property, is purified from the stain of defilements and reaches fulfillment, therefore the accomplishment in virtue, being achieved, due to being an accomplishment of the supporting condition, brings forth the power of mindfulness and the power of knowledge. Thus, its state of being a supporting condition for the three knowledges should be known because of the accomplishment of a homogeneous cause. For, by the power of mindfulness, the accomplishment of the knowledge of previous existences occurs. By the power of clear comprehension, through the practice of acting on what is well-seen in all activities, the accomplishment of the second knowledge, which is connected with the knowledge of passing away and reappearance, occurs. Due to the absence of transgression, due to the nature of having abandoned defilements, and by the power of being a supporting condition for the Unbinding, through purity of disposition, the accomplishment of the third knowledge occurs. The state of virtue being a supporting condition for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, without the fulfillment of concentration and wisdom accomplished previously, should be explained by the taint-destroyed ones who are dry-insight meditators. In accordance with the saying, “One who is concentrated knows things as they really are,” the accomplishment in concentration is a supporting condition for the six higher knowledges. In accordance with the saying, “Truly, from exertion wisdom arises,” the accomplishment in wisdom, cultivated by previous exertion and by residing with a teacher, skill in the local language, learning, questioning, and so on, is a supporting condition for the varieties of analytical knowledge. And here, because it is said, “relying on the accomplishment in virtue,” for a person for whom the six higher knowledges without remainder, which are a manifestation of concentration, do not succeed, for that person, in the sense of the highest limit, there is no accomplishment in concentration. Thus, even though the knowledges are a part of the higher knowledges, the three knowledges are taken as having arisen only from the accomplishment in virtue. And just as the four analytical knowledges, having arisen from the accomplishment in wisdom, succeed for one endowed with the supporting condition through the path itself—because they are obtained at the very moment of the path—so too, the three knowledges, having arisen from the accomplishment in virtue, and the six higher knowledges, having arisen from the accomplishment in concentration, succeed for one endowed with the supporting condition through the path itself. Thus, their attainment should be understood as being through the attainment of the path itself. For these special attainments of these noble ones are similar to the attainment of the enlightenment of Paccekabuddhas and the full enlightenment of Sammāsambuddhas.

Tāsaṃyeva [M 1.0117] ca tattha pabhedavacanatoti ettha “tāsaṃyevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ pāpuṇitabbānaṃ chaḷabhiññācatupaṭisambhidānaṃ vinaye pabhedavacanābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Verañjakaṇḍe (pārā. 12) hi tisso vijjāva vibhattāti. Casaddena samuccinanañca tāsaṃ ettha ekadesavacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ abhiññāpaṭisambhidānampi ekadesānaṃ tattha vuttattā. Dutiye “tāsaṃyevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ catasso paṭisambhidā apekkhitvā kataṃ, na tisso vijjā. Tā hi chasu abhiññāsu antogadhattā sutte vibhattāyevāti. Ca-saddena ca paṭisambhidānamekadesavacanaṃ samuccinoti. Tatiye “tāsañcā”ti ca-saddena sesānampi tattha atthibhāvaṃ dīpeti. Abhidhamme hi tisso vijjā, cha abhiññā, catasso ca paṭisambhidā vuttāyeva. Paṭisambhidānaṃ pana aññattha pabhedavacanābhāvaṃ, tattheva ca sammā vibhattabhāvaṃ dīpetukāmo heṭṭhā vuttanayena avadhāraṇamakatvā “tatthevā”ti parivattetvā avadhāraṇaṃ ṭhapeti. “Abhidhamme pana tisso vijjā, cha abhiññā, catasso ca paṭisambhidā aññe ca sammappadhānādayo guṇavisesā vibhattā. Kiñcāpi vibhattā, visesato pana paññājātikattā catassova paṭisambhidā pāpuṇātīti dassanatthaṃ ‘tāsañca tatthevā’ti avadhāraṇavipallāso kato”ti vajirabuddhitthero. “Eva”ntiādi nigamanaṃ.

Here, the emphasis in `tāsaṃyeva` ('of those very ones') is stated with reference to the absence in the Vinaya of a detailed explanation of the six higher knowledges and four analytical knowledges that are to be attained. For in the Verañja chapter, only the three knowledges are analyzed. And the word 'ca' (and) refers to a partial mention of those, since some aspects of the higher knowledges and analytical knowledges are also stated there. In the second [Piṭaka], the emphasis `tāsaṃyeva` is made with reference to the four analytical knowledges, not the three knowledges. For those (three knowledges) are indeed analyzed in the Sutta, being included within the six higher knowledges. And the word 'ca' also includes a partial mention of the analytical knowledges. In the third [Piṭaka], in `tāsañca` ('and of those'), the word 'ca' indicates the presence of the remaining ones there as well. For in the Abhidhamma, the three knowledges, the six higher knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges are indeed stated. However, wishing to show that for the analytical knowledges there is no detailed statement elsewhere, and that only there are they properly analyzed, the author, instead of making the emphasis in the manner stated previously, reverses it to 'there indeed' (`tatthevā`) and places the emphasis. 'In the Abhidhamma, however, the three knowledges, the six higher knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and other special qualities such as the right exertions are classified. Although they are classified, especially because they are of the nature of wisdom, this pertains only to the four analytical knowledges. To show this, the reversal of emphasis in "and of those, there indeed" was made,' says the Elder Vajirabuddhi. The words beginning with 'Thus' are the conclusion.

Sukho samphasso etesanti sukhasamphassāni, anuññātāniyeva tādisāni attharaṇapāvuraṇādīni, tesaṃ phassasāmaññato sukho vā samphasso tathā, anuññāto so yesanti anuññātasukhasamphassāni, tādisāni attharaṇapāvuraṇādīni tesaṃ phassena samānatāya. Upādinnakaphasso itthiphasso, methunadhammoyeva. Vuttaṃ ariṭṭhena nāma gaddhabādhipubbena bhikkhunā (ma. ni. 234; pāci. 417). So hi bahussuto dhammakathiko kammakilesavipākaupavādaāṇāvītikkamavasena pañcavidhesu antarāyikesu āṇāvītikkamantarāyikaṃ na jānāti, sesantarāyikeyeva jānāti, tasmā so rahogato evaṃ cintesi “ime agārikā pañca kāmaguṇe paribhuñjantā sotāpannāpi sakadāgāminopi anāgāminopi honti, bhikkhūpi manāpikāni cakkhuviññeyyāni rūpāni passanti [M 1.0118] …pe… kāyaviññeyye [V 1.0104] phoṭṭhabbe phusanti, mudukāni attharaṇapāvuraṇāni paribhuñjanti, etaṃ sabbampi vaṭṭati, kasmā itthīnaṃyeva rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā na vaṭṭanti, etepi vaṭṭantiyevā”ti anavajjena paccayaparibhogarasena sāvajjaṃ kāmaguṇaparibhogarasaṃ saṃsanditvā sachandarāgaparibhogañca nicchandarāgaparibhogañca ekaṃ katvā thullavākehi saddhiṃ atisukhumasuttaṃ ghaṭento viya, sāsapena saddhiṃ sineruno sadisataṃ upasaṃharanto viya ca pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppādetvā “kiṃ bhagavatā mahāsamuddaṃ bandhantena viya mahatā ussāhena paṭhamapārājikaṃ paññattaṃ, natthi ettha doso”ti sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhanto vesārajjañāṇaṃ paṭibāhanto ariyamagge khāṇukaṇṭakādīni pakkhipanto “methunadhamme doso natthī”ti jinacakke pahāramadāsi, tenāha “tathāha”ntiādi.

They are called 'having pleasant contact' (sukhasamphassāni) because 'for these, there is a pleasant contact.' Such things as bedding and coverings are indeed allowed, being similar in contact to that of women. Or, they are called 'having an allowed pleasant contact' (anuññātasukhasamphassāni) because 'for them, a pleasant contact is thus allowed,' referring to such things as bedding and coverings, due to the similarity with their contact. Contact that is clung to is female contact, namely, the sexual act. This was stated by the monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly of a vulture-killer clan (MN 234; Pāc. 417). He was learned, a preacher of the Dhamma, but regarding the five kinds of obstacles—those of kamma, defilement, result, censure, and transgression of the command—he did not know the obstacle of transgression of the command, only knowing the other obstacles. Therefore, he thought in private: 'These householders, enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, are stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. Monks also see pleasing forms cognizable by the eye, … touch agreeable tangibles cognizable by the body, use soft bedding and coverings—all this is permissible. Why then are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of women not permissible? These too should be permissible!' Mixing the blameless enjoyment of requisites with the blameworthy enjoyment of sensual pleasures, and equating enjoyment with lust with enjoyment without lust, he was like one trying to join an extremely fine thread with coarse hemp, like one comparing a mustard seed to Mount Sineru. Generating a wicked wrong view, he said, 'Why did the Blessed One, with great effort as if binding the great ocean, lay down the first pārājika? There is no fault in this.' Thus, opposing the knowledge of omniscience, obstructing the knowledge of fearlessness, and inserting stumps and thorns into the Noble Path, he struck a blow against the Conqueror's Wheel, declaring, 'There is no fault in sexual intercourse.' Therefore, he said the words beginning, 'Thus I...'

Anatikkamanatthena antarāye niyuttā, antarāyaṃ vā phalaṃ arahanti, antarāyassa vā karaṇasīlāti antarāyikā, saggamokkhānaṃ antarāyakarāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te ca kammakilesavipākaupavādaāṇāvītikkamavasena pañcavidhā. Vitthāro ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanādīsu (pāci. aṭṭha. 417) gahetabbo. Ayaṃ panettha padatthasambandho – ye ime dhammā antarāyikā iti bhagavatā vuttā desitā ceva paññattā ca, te dhamme paṭisevato paṭisevantassa yathā yena pakārena te dhammā antarāyāya saggamokkhānaṃ antarāyakaraṇatthaṃ nālaṃ samatthā na honti, tathā tena pakārena ahaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ dhammaṃ ājānāmīti. Tato dussīlabhāvaṃ pāpuṇātīti tato anavajjasaññibhāvahetuto vītikkamitvā dussīlabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti.

They are called 'obstructive' (antarāyikā) because of the meaning 'not to be transgressed'; or, they are worthy of an obstructive result; or, they are of a nature to create an obstacle. This means they are said to create obstacles to heaven and liberation. And these are of five kinds by way of kamma, defilement, result, censure, and transgression of the command. The detailed explanation should be taken from the commentary on the Ariṭṭha training rule and other texts (Pāc.A. 417). Here, this is the connection of the meaning of the words: 'I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that, for one who partakes of those things spoken of, taught, and laid down by the Blessed One as obstructive, those things are not able or capable of being an obstacle to heaven and liberation.' The phrase 'From that, he attains a state of immorality' means that from that cause, which is the state of perceiving them as blameless, he transgresses and attains a state of immorality.

Cattāro…pe…ādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena –

In the text beginning 'Four...' and so on, here by the word 'ādi' is indicated—

“Cattārome bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame cattāro? Attahitāya paṭipanno no parahitāya, parahitāya paṭipanno no attahitāya, nevattahitāya paṭipanno no parahitāya, attahitāya ceva paṭipanno parahitāya ca…pe… ime kho bhikkhave…pe… lokasmi”nti (a. ni. 4.96) –

“Monks, these four types of individuals are found existing in the world. Which four? One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit; one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others… These, monks, are the four types of individuals found existing in the world.” (AN 4.96)

Evamādinā [M 1.0119] puggaladesanāpaṭisaññuttasuttantapāḷiṃ nidasseti. Adhippāyanti “ayaṃ puggaladesanāvohāravasena, na paramatthato”ti evaṃ bhagavato adhippāyaṃ. Vuttañhi –

By this, he points to the Suttanta Pāḷi connected with the exposition of individuals. The intention is this: 'This teaching is by way of the conventional designation of individuals, not in the ultimate sense'—this is the Blessed One’s intention. For it was said:

“Duve [V 1.0105] saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nūpalabbhati.

“The Sambuddha, the best of speakers, declared two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth; a third is not found.

Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇā;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtakāraṇā.

The conventional expression is true, because of worldly convention; the ultimate expression is true, because of the real nature of phenomena.

Tasmā vohārakusalassa, lokanāthassa satthuno;

Sammutiṃ voharantassa, musāvādo na jāyatī”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.57; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170; itivu. aṭṭha. 24);

Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, skilled in conventional speech, when speaking in accordance with convention, no false speech arises.” (MA 1.57; AA 1.1.170; ItvA 24)

Na hi lokasammutiṃ buddhā bhagavanto vijahanti, lokasamaññāya lokaniruttiyā lokābhilāpe ṭhitāyeva dhammaṃ desenti. Apica “hirottappadīpanatthaṃ, kammassakatādīpanattha”nti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.57; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.202; itivu. aṭṭha. 24; kathā. anuṭī. 1) evamādīhipi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā puggalakathaṃ kathetī”ti evaṃ adhippāyamajānanto. Ayamattho upari āvi bhavissati. Duggahitaṃ gaṇhātīti “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati anañña”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.144) duggahitaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, viparītaṃ gaṇhātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Duggahitanti hi bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso kiriyāyavisesanabhāvena napuṃsakaliṅgena niddisitabbattā. Ayañhi bhāvanapuṃsakapadassa pakati, yadidaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgena niddisitabbattā, bhāvappaṭṭhānatā, sakammākammakiriyānuyogaṃ paccattopayogavacanatā ca. Tena vuttaṃ “duggahitaṃ katvā”ti. Yanti duggahitagāhaṃ. Majjhimanikāye mūlapaṇṇāsake mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutte (ma. ni. 1.144) tathāvādīnaṃ sādhināmakaṃ kevaṭṭaputtaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Attanā duggahitena dhammenāti pāṭhaseso, micchāsabhāvenāti attho. Atha vā duggahaṇaṃ duggahitaṃ, attanāti ca sāmiatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, vibhattiyantapatirūpakaṃ vā abyayapadaṃ, tasmā attano duggahaṇena viparītagāhenāti attho. Abbhācikkhatīti abbhakkhānaṃ karoti. Attano kusalamūlāni khananto attānaṃ khanati nāma. Tatoti duggahitabhāvahetuto.

Indeed, the Blessed Buddhas do not abandon worldly conventions; they teach the Dhamma while remaining established in worldly designations, worldly expressions, and worldly language. Moreover, not knowing this intention of the Buddha—that 'the Blessed One speaks of individuals for eight reasons, such as “for the purpose of showing moral shame and moral dread, for the purpose of showing ownership of kamma,” and so on'—[one grasps wrongly]. This meaning will become clear later. 'He grasps wrongly' (duggahitaṃ gaṇhāti) means that he grasps it wrongly, having made it so, as in: 'I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way: that it is this very consciousness that runs on and transmigrates, not another,' and so on. It is said that he grasps it perversely. For 'wrongly grasped' (duggahitaṃ) is a neuter-gender term indicating an abstract state, because it must be indicated in the neuter gender as it modifies an action. This, indeed, is the nature of a neuter term indicating an abstract state: namely, that it must be indicated in the neuter gender, its being the basis of an abstract state, its connection with transitive and intransitive verbs, and its having nominative and accusative endings. Therefore, it is said, 'having grasped it wrongly.' As for 'yaṃ,' it means 'the wrongly grasped view.' In the Majjhima Nikāya, in the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka, in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, this was spoken by the Blessed One concerning the monk named Sāti, the son of a fisherman, who held such a view. The remainder of the text is to be understood as 'through the teaching wrongly grasped by himself,' which means 'through its false nature.' Alternatively, 'wrong grasping' (duggahaṇaṃ) is 'duggahitaṃ.' And 'attanā' is an instrumental case word in the sense of ownership, or it is an indeclinable resembling a word with a case ending. Therefore, the meaning is 'by one's own wrong grasping, by a perverse grasp.' 'He slanders' (abbhācikkhati) means he makes an accusation. Digging up his own roots of merit, he is said to 'dig up' himself. As for 'tato' (from that), it means 'from the cause of being wrongly grasped.'

Dhammacintanti [M 1.0120] dhammasabhāvavicāraṃ. Atidhāvantoti ṭhātabbamariyādāyaṃ aṭṭhatvā “cittuppādamattenapi dānaṃ hoti, sayameva cittaṃ attano ārammaṇaṃ hoti, sabbampi cittaṃ sabhāvadhammārammaṇameva hotī”ti ca evamādinā atikkamitvā pavattayamāno. Cintetumasakkuṇeyyāni[V 1.0106], anaraharūpāni vā acinteyyāni nāma, tāni dassento “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Tattha acinteyyānīti tesaṃ sabhāvadassanaṃ. Na cintetabbānīti tattha kattabbakiccadassanaṃ. “Yānī”tiādi tassa hetudassanaṃ. Yāni cintento ummādassa cittakkhepassa, vighātassa vihesassa ca bhāgī assa, acinteyyāni imāni cattāri na cintetabbāni, imāni vā cattāri acinteyyāni nāma na cintetabbāni, yāni vā…pe… assa, tasmā na cintetabbāni acintetabbabhūtāni imāni cattāri acinteyyāni nāmāti yojanā. Iti-saddena pana –

'Contemplating the Dhamma' (dhammacintaṃ) means the investigation of the nature of phenomena. 'Exceeding the bounds' (atidhāvanto) means, not standing within the boundary where one should stand, but transgressing and proceeding with such ideas as: 'Giving occurs even by the mere arising of a thought,' 'The mind itself is its own object,' and 'All mind has only the nature of phenomena as its object,' and so on. Things that are impossible to contemplate, or are unsuitable, are called 'unthinkables' (acinteyyāni). Showing these, he said, 'For it has been said,' and so on. Therein, 'acinteyyāni' (unthinkables) shows their nature. 'Na cintetabbāni' (they should not be contemplated) shows the duty to be performed in their regard. 'Yāni' (which), etc., shows the reason for that. The construction (yojanā) is as follows: 'Which things a person contemplating would become a partaker of madness, mental distraction, distress, and vexation; these four are unthinkables and should not be contemplated.' Or: 'These four are called unthinkables; they should not be contemplated.' Or: 'Which things... would become a partaker... therefore, they should not be contemplated. Having become things that should not be contemplated, these four are called unthinkables.' By the word 'iti,' however—

“Katamāni cattāri? Buddhānaṃ bhikkhave buddhavisayo acinteyyo na cintetabbo, yaṃ cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assa. Jhāyissa bhikkhave jhānavisayo acinteyyo…pe… kammavipāko bhikkhave acinteyyo…pe… lokacintā bhikkhave acinteyyā…pe… imāni…pe… assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77) –

“What are the four? Monks, the Buddha-range of the Buddhas is unthinkable, not to be thought about; one who thinks about it would become a partaker of madness and distress. Monks, the jhāna-range of one who practices jhāna is unthinkable… Monks, the result of kamma is unthinkable… Monks, speculation about the world is unthinkable… these… would become…” (A.N. 4.77)

Caturaṅguttare vuttaṃ acinteyyasuttaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ acinteyyabhāvadīpakaṃ pāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Kāmaṃ acinteyyāni cha asādhāraṇañāṇādīni, tāni pana anussarantassa kusaluppattihetubhāvato cintetabbāni, imāni pana evaṃ na honti aphalabhāvato, tasmā na cintetabbāni. “Dussīlya…pe… pabheda”nti iminā vipattiṃ sarūpato dasseti. “Kathaṃ? Piṭakavasenā”tiādivacanasambajjhanena pubbāparasambandhaṃ dassento “evaṃ nānappakārato”tiādimāha. Pubbāparasambandhavirahitañhi vacanaṃ byākulaṃ. Sotūnañca atthaviññāpakaṃ na hoti, pubbāparaññūnameva ca tathāvicāritavacanaṃ visayo. Yathāha –

He includes all the Pāḷi text that explains the state of being unthinkable, beginning with the Acinteyya Sutta spoken in the Catukka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. Granted, the six unique knowledges and so on are unthinkable; however, since they are a cause for the arising of the wholesome for one who recollects them, they should be contemplated. But these four are not like that, due to their fruitlessness; therefore, they should not be contemplated. By 'immorality... division,' he shows failure in its own nature. Showing the connection between what comes before and after by connecting the words 'How? By way of the Piṭaka,' and so on, he said, 'Thus, in various ways,' and so on. For speech devoid of connection between what comes before and after is confused and does not make the meaning known to the listeners. And such well-examined speech is the domain only of those who know what comes before and after. As it is said—

“Pubbāparaññū atthaññū, niruttipadakovido;

Suggahītañca gaṇhāti, atthañco’ paparikkhatī”ti. (theragā. 1031);

“One who knows what comes before and after, who knows the meaning, skilled in expression and words; he grasps what is well-grasped, and closely investigates the meaning.” (Thag. 1031)

Tesanti piṭakānaṃ. Etanti buddhavacanaṃ.

As for 'tesaṃ' (of them), it means 'of the Piṭakas.' As for 'etaṃ' (this), it means 'the word of the Buddha.'

Sīlakkhandhavaggamahāvaggapāthikavaggasaṅkhātehi [M 1.0121] tīhi vaggehi saṅgaho etesanti tivaggasaṅgahāni. Gāthāya pana yassa nikāyassa suttagaṇanato catuttiṃseva suttantā. Vaggasaṅgahavasena tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassāti tivaggo saṅgaho. Paṭhamo esa nikāyo dīghanikāyoti [V 1.0107] anulomiko apaccanīko, atthānulomanato atthānulomanāmiko vā, anvatthanāmoti attho. Tattha “tivaggo saṅgaho”ti etaṃ “yassā”ti antarikepi samāsoyeva hoti, na vākyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ “navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhenā”ti (pāci. 368) ettha “navaṃcīvaralābhenā”ti padaṃ viya. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyā vaṇṇayanti “alabbhīti labho, labho eva lābho. Kiṃ alabbhi? Cīvaraṃ. Kīdisaṃ? Navaṃ, iti ‘navacīvaralābhenā’ti vattabbe anunāsikalopaṃ akatvā ‘navaṃcīvaralābhenā’ti vuttaṃ, paṭiladdhanavacīvarenāti attho. Majjhe ṭhitapadadvaye panāti nipāto. Bhikkhunāti yena laddhaṃ, tassa nidassana”nti (pāci. aṭṭha. 368). Idhāpi saddato, atthato ca vākye yuttiyāabhāvato samāsoyeva sambhavati. “Tivaggo”ti padañhi “saṅgaho”ti ettha yadi karaṇaṃ, evaṃ sati karaṇavacanantameva siyā. Yadi ca padadvayametaṃ tulyādhikaraṇaṃ, tathā ca sati napuṃsakaliṅgameva siyā “tiloka”ntiādipadaṃ viya. Tathā “tivaggo”ti etassa “saṅgaho”ti padamantarena aññatthāsambandho na sambhavati, tattha ca tādisena vākyena sambajjhanaṃ na yuttaṃ, tasmā samānepi padantarantarike saddatthāvirodhabhāvoyeva samāsatākāraṇanti samāso eva yutto. Tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassāti hi tivaggosaṅgaho akārassa okārādesaṃ, okārāgamaṃ vā katvā yathā “sattāhaparinibbuto, acirapakkanto, māsajāto”tiādi, assa saṅgahassāti ca saṅgahitassa assa nikāyassāti attho. Apare pana “tayo vaggā yassāti katvā ‘saṅgaho’ti padena tulyādhikaraṇameva sambhavati, saṅgahoti ca gaṇanā. Ṭīkācariyehi (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) pana ‘tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassā’ti padadvayassa tulyādhikaraṇatāyeva dassitā”ti vadanti, tadayuttameva saṅkhyāsaṅkhyeyyānaṃ missakattā, apākaṭattā ca.

For these suttas, there is a collection by three divisions called the Sīlakkhandhavagga, the Mahāvagga, and the Pāthikavagga; therefore, they are called `tivaggasaṅgahāni` (those having a collection of three divisions). Furthermore, in the verse, according to the count of suttas, this Nikāya has only thirty-four suttas. By way of the collection of divisions, there are three divisions for this collection; hence, it is a `tivaggo saṅgaho` (threefold collection). This first Nikāya is called the Dīgha Nikāya; it is non-contradictory, or has a name in accordance with the meaning (`atthānulomanāmiko`) because it follows the meaning; that is, it is a name that follows the meaning (`anvatthanāmo`). Therein, the phrase `tivaggo saṅgaho` should be understood as a compound, even with the intervening word `yassā`, and not as a sentence, just like the phrase `navaṃcīvaralābhenā` in the passage `navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhenā`. Indeed, the commentary teachers explain: '`Alabbhī` means "was obtained," hence `labho`, "obtainment"; `labho` itself is `lābho`. What was obtained? A robe. What kind? New. Thus, while it should be said `navacīvaralābhenā`, without eliding the nasal sound, it was said by the Blessed One as `navaṃcīvaralābhenā`, meaning "by one who has obtained a new robe." In the two words standing in the middle, `pana` is a particle. `Bhikkhunā` indicates the one by whom it was obtained.' Here too, a compound is possible because of the lack of suitability in the sentence, both in terms of sound and meaning. For if the word `tivaggo` were the instrument for `saṅgaho`, it would have to end in the instrumental case-ending. And if this pair of words were in apposition, it would have to be in the neuter gender, like the word `tilokaṃ`, etc. Likewise, the word `tivaggo` cannot be connected elsewhere without the word `saṅgaho`, and a connection with such a sentence is not suitable there. Therefore, even with an intervening word, a compound is indeed suitable because the absence of contradiction between sound and meaning is the reason for being a compound. For `tivaggosaṅgaho` is from `tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassa` (three divisions of this collection), by changing the letter 'a' to 'o' or by the addition of 'o', just as in `sattāhaparinibbuto`, `acirapakkanto`, `māsajāto`, etc. And `assa saṅgahassa` means 'of this collected Nikāya'. Others, however, say: 'Having formed the compound `tayo vaggā yassa`, it is possible only in apposition with the word `saṅgaho`, and `saṅgaho` means "counting." The subcommentary teachers, however, have shown that the two words in `tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassa` are indeed in apposition.' That is indeed unsuitable because of the mixing of the number and the numbered, and because of the lack of clarity.

Atthānulomikattaṃ vibhāvetumāha “kasmā”tiādi. Guṇopacārena, taddhitavasena vā dīgha-saddena dīghappamāṇāni suttāniyeva gahitāni[M 1.0122], nikāyasaddo ca ruḷhivasena samūhanivāsatthesu vattatīti dasseti “dīghappamāṇāna”ntiādinā. Saṅketasiddhattā vacanīyavācakānaṃ payogato tadatthesu tassa saṅketasiddhataṃ ñāpento “nāha”ntiādimāha. Ekanikāyampīti ekasamūhampi. Evaṃ cittanti evaṃ vicittaṃ. Yathayidanti yathā ime tiracchānagatā pāṇā. Poṇikā, cikkhallikā ca khattiyā, tesaṃ nivāso “poṇikanikāyo cikkhallikanikāyo”ti vuccati. Etthāti nikāyasaddassa samūhanivāsānaṃ vācakabhāve. Sādhakānīti adhippetassatthassa sādhanato udāharaṇāni vuccanti. “Samānītānī”ti pāṭhasesena cetassa sambandho, sakkhīni vā yathāvuttanayena sādhakāni. Yañhi niddhāretvā adhippetatthaṃ sādhenti[V 1.0108], taṃ “sakkhī”ti vadanti. Tathā hi manorathapūraṇiyaṃ vuttaṃ “pañcagarujātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.132) pana sakkhibhāvatthāya āharitvā kathetabba”nti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.5) sāsanatoti sāsanapayogato, sāsane vā. Lokatoti lokiyapayogato, loke vā. Idaṃ pana piṭakattaye na vijjati, tasmā evaṃ vuttanti vadanti. Ettha ca paṭhamamudāharaṇaṃ sāsanato sādhakavacanaṃ, dutiyaṃ lokatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

To clarify its accordance with the meaning, the commentary teacher said, 'kasmā,' etc. By way of figurative use based on quality, or by way of a taddhita derivative, by the word `dīgha` only suttas of long measure are taken; and it is shown by `dīghappamāṇānaṃ`, etc., that the word `nikāya` occurs, by way of convention, in the meanings of 'collection' and 'abode'. Wishing to make known its establishment by convention in those meanings through usage—because of the established convention of what is expressed and the words that express it—he said, 'nāhaṃ,' etc. `Ekanikāyampi` means 'even one collection.' `Evaṃ cittaṃ` means 'thus variegated.' `Yathayidaṃ` means 'just as these animal beings are variegated.' The Poṇika and Cikkhallika are Khattiyas, and their abode is called `poṇikanikāyo` and `cikkhallikanikāyo`. Herein, this refers to the word `nikāya` being a term for 'collections' and 'abodes.' `Sādhakāni` means the examples are called 'proofs' because they accomplish the intended meaning. And its connection is to be made with the remaining part of the text, `samānītāni`; or, they are witnesses that prove in the aforementioned manner. For whatever example is singled out to accomplish the intended meaning, that the teachers call a 'witness.' Indeed, it is said in the Manorathapūraṇī: 'The Pañcagaru Jātaka should be brought forth and related for the purpose of being a witness.' `Sāsanato` means 'by way of usage in the Teaching,' or 'in the Teaching.' `Lokatoti` means 'by way of worldly usage,' or 'in the world.' Some say that this usage, however, is not found in the three Piṭakas; therefore, it was stated thus. And herein, it should be understood that the first example is a proving statement from the Teaching, and the second is from the world.

Mūlapariyāya vaggādivasena pañcadasavaggasaṅgahāni. Aḍḍhena dutiyaṃ diyaḍḍhaṃ, tadeva sataṃ, ekasataṃ, paññāsa ca suttānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ nikāye. Pañcadasavaggapariggahoti pañcadasahi vaggehi pariggahito saṅgahito.

It is a collection of fifteen divisions, by way of the Mūlapariyāyavagga, etc. It is said that there are one hundred and fifty suttas (`diyaḍḍhasataṃ`), which is to say, one hundred suttas and fifty suttas. `Yatthā` means 'in which Nikāya.' `Pañcadasavaggapariggaho` means encompassed and collected by fifteen divisions.

Saṃyujjanti etthāti saṃyuttaṃ, kesaṃ saṃyuttaṃ? Suttavaggānaṃ. Yathā hi byañjanasamudāye padaṃ, padasamudāye ca vākyaṃ, vākyasamudāye suttaṃ, suttasamudāye vaggoti samaññā, evaṃ vaggasamudāye saṃyuttasamaññā. Devatāya pucchitena kathitasuttavaggādīnaṃ saṃyuttattā devatāsaṃyuttādibhāvo (saṃ. ni. 1.1), tenāha “devatāsaṃyuttādivasenā”tiādi. “Suttantānaṃ sahassāni satta suttasatāni cā”ti pāṭhe suttantānaṃ satta sahassāni, satta suttasatāni cāti yojetabbaṃ. “Satta suttasahassāni, satta suttasatāni cā”tipi pāṭho. Saṃyuttasaṅgahoti saṃyuttanikāyassa saṅgaho gaṇanā.

They are connected herein, thus it is called 'Saṃyutta' (Connected). A connection of what? Of suttas and divisions. For just as in a collection of letters there is a word, in a collection of words a sentence, in a collection of sentences a sutta, and in a collection of suttas there is the designation 'vagga' (division), so too in a collection of divisions there is the designation 'Saṃyutta'. Because the suttas, divisions, etc., spoken in response to what was asked by a devatā are connected, there arises the state of being Devatāsaṃyutta, etc. Hence, the teacher said, 'by way of Devatāsaṃyutta, etc.' In the reading 'Suttantānaṃ sahassāni satta suttasatāni cā', it should be construed as 'of the suttas, seven thousand and seven hundred suttas'. There is also the reading: 'Satta suttasahassāni, satta suttasatāni cā'. 'Saṃyuttasaṅgaho' means the collection or enumeration of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Ekekehi [M 1.0123] aṅgehi uparūpari uttaro adhiko etthāti aṅguttaroti āha “ekekaaṅgātirekavasenā”tiādi. Tattha hi ekekato paṭṭhāya yāva ekādasa aṅgāni kathitāni. Aṅganti ca dhammakoṭṭhāso.

Because here, by each successive factor, it is progressively higher and superior, it is called 'Aṅguttara.' He said, 'by way of the excess of each successive factor,' and so on. For therein, starting from one factor up to eleven factors are taught. And 'aṅga' is a division of the Dhamma.

Pubbeti suttantapiṭakaniddese. Vuttameva pakārantarena saṅkhipitvā avisesetvā dassetuṃ “ṭhapetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Sakalaṃ vinayapiṭaka”ntiādinā vuttameva hi iminā pakārantarena saṅkhipitvā dasseti. Apica yathāvuttato avasiṭṭhaṃ yaṃ kiñci bhagavatā dinnanaye ṭhatvā desitaṃ, bhagavatā ca anumoditaṃ nettipeṭakopadesādikaṃ, taṃ sabbampi ettheva pariyāpannanti anavasesapariyādānavasena dassetuṃ evaṃ vuttantipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Siddhepi hi sati ārambho atthantaraviññāpanāya vā hoti, niyamāya vāti. Ettha ca yathā “dīghappamāṇāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ, evaṃ “khuddakappamāṇāna”ntiādimavatvā sarūpasseva kathanaṃ vinayābhidhammādīnaṃ dīghappamāṇānampi tadantogadhatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena ca viññāyati “na sabbattha khuddakapariyāpannesu [V 1.0109] tassa anvatthasamaññatā, dīghanikāyādisabhāvaviparītabhāvasāmaññena pana katthaci tabbohāratā”ti. Tadaññanti tehi catūhi nikāyehi aññaṃ, avasesanti attho.

'Pubbe' refers to the exposition of the Suttantapiṭaka. What has already been said is stated as 'ṭhapetvā,' and so on, in order to show it concisely and without distinction in another way. For indeed, what has been stated beginning with 'the entire Vinayapiṭaka' is shown concisely by this in another manner. Moreover, it should also be understood that it is stated thus in order to show, by way of including everything without remainder, that whatever remains from what has been stated—anything taught abiding in the method given by the Blessed One, and approved by the Blessed One, such as the Netti, the Peṭakopadesa, and so on—all of that is included right here. For even when something is established, a statement is made either for making known another meaning or for confirmation. And here, it should be understood that just as 'of long measure,' and so on, is stated, similarly, without stating 'of short measure,' and so on, the statement is of its essential nature alone because of the inclusion therein of the Vinaya, Abhidhamma, and so on, even though they are of long measure. And by that it is understood that 'its name corresponding to the meaning is not found everywhere among those included in the Khuddaka, but in some cases, its usage is by way of the general state of being contrary to the nature of the Dīgha Nikāya, and so on.' 'Tadaññaṃ' means other than those four Nikāyas; the meaning is 'the remainder.'

Navappabhedanti ettha kathaṃ panetaṃ navappabhedaṃ hoti. Tathā hi navahi aṅgehi vavatthitehi aññamaññasaṅkararahitehi bhavitabbaṃ, tathā ca sati asuttasabhāvāneva geyyaṅgādīni siyuṃ, atha suttasabhāvāneva geyyaṅgādīni, evaṃ sati suttanti visuṃ suttaṅgameva na siyā, evaṃ sante aṭṭhaṅgaṃ sāsananti āpajjati. Apica “sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti (dī. ni. aṭṭha., pārā. aṭṭha. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Suttañca nāma sagāthakaṃ vā siyā, niggāthakaṃ vā, tasmā aṅgadvayeneva tadubhayaṃ saṅgahitanti tadubhayavinimuttaṃ suttaṃ udānādivisesasaññārahitaṃ natthi, yaṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā, athāpi kathañci visuṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā, maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ (khu. pā. 1; su. ni. 261) suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā gāthābhāvato dhammapadādīnaṃ viya. Geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā sagāthakattā sagāthāvaggassa viya. Tathā ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānanti? Vuccate –

'Navappabhedaṃ'—here, how then does this become a ninefold division? For it must be established by nine factors that are free from mutual confusion. That being so, the Geyyaṅga and so on would be of a non-sutta nature. Or if the Geyyaṅga and so on were of a sutta nature, in that case, 'sutta' as a separate Suttaṅga would not exist. In that case, the fault arises that the teaching would be eightfold. Moreover, it is stated in the commentary: 'A sutta with verses is Geyya; a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa.' And a sutta may be with verses or without verses; therefore, both are included by just those two factors. Thus, there is no sutta, free from both of these and devoid of specific designations like Udāna, and so on, which could be the Suttaṅga. Even if there were somehow a separate Suttaṅga, the inclusion of the Maṅgalasutta and so on would not be in the Suttaṅga because of their nature as verses, like the Dhammapada and so on. Or their inclusion would be in the Geyyaṅga because of having verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. Similarly for the sections with verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and so on? The reply is spoken:

Suttanti [M 1.0124] sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare;

Sanimittā niruḷhattā, sahatāññena nāññato. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā);

Sutta is the general method; the others are specific methods with defining marks. The classification is made because of being established as such, because of being conjoined with another, and because of being from another source.

Yathāvuttassa dosassa, natthi etthāvagāhaṇaṃ;

Tasmā asaṅkaraṃyeva, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ. (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā);

Of the fault as stated, there is no entry here. Therefore, the Teacher's Dispensation is indeed unconfused and ninefold.

Sabbassāpi hi buddhavacanassa suttanti ayaṃ sāmaññavidhi. Tathā hi “ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpannaṃ, (pāci. aṭṭha. 655, 1242) sāvatthiyā suttavibhaṅge, (cūḷava. 456) sakavāde pañca suttasatānī”tiādi (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) vacanato vinayābhidhammapariyatti visesesupi suttavohāro dissati. Teneva ca āyasmā mahākaccāyano nettiyaṃ āha “navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti (netti. saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā) tattha hi suttādivasena navaṅgassa sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhi pariyesanā atthavicāraṇā “navavidha suttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti vuttā. Tadekadesesu pana pare geyyādayo sanimittā visesavidhayo tena tena nimittena patiṭṭhitā. Tathā hi geyyassa sagāthakattaṃ tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Lokepi hi sasilokaṃ sagāthakaṃ cuṇṇiyaganthaṃ “geyya”nti [V 1.0110] vadanti, gāthāvirahe pana sati pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Pucchāvissajjanañhi “byākaraṇa”nti vuccati, byākaraṇameva veyyākaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sante sagāthakādīnampi pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanavasena pavattānaṃ veyyākaraṇabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati geyyādisaññānaṃ anokāsabhāvato. Saokāsavidhito hi anokāsavidhi balavā. Apica “gāthāvirahe satī”ti visesitattā. Yathādhippetassa hi atthassa anadhippetato byavacchedakaṃ visesanaṃ. Tathā hi dhammapadādīsu kevalagāthābandhesu, sagāthakattepi somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaññuttesu, “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādivacana sambandhesu, abbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttesu ca suttavisesesu yathākkamaṃ gāthāudānaitivuttaka abbhutadhammasaññā patiṭṭhitā. Ettha hi satipi saññāntaranimittayoge anokāsasaññānaṃ balavabhāveneva gāthādisaññā patiṭṭhitā, tathā satipi gāthābandhabhāve bhagavato atītāsu jātīsu cariyānubhāvappakāsakesu jātakasaññā patiṭṭhitā, satipi pañhāvissajjanabhāve[M 1.0125], sagāthakatte ca kesuci suttantesu vedassa labhāpanato vedallasaññā patiṭṭhitā, evaṃ tena tena sagāthakattādinā nimittena tesu tesu suttavisesesu geyyādisaññā patiṭṭhitāti visesavidhayo suttaṅgato pare geyyādayo, yaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādinimittarahitaṃ, taṃ suttaṅgameva visesasaññāparihārena sāmaññasaññāya pavattanato. Nanu ca evaṃ santepi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇanti tadubhayavinimuttassa suttassa abhāvato visuṃ suttaṅgameva na siyāti codanā tadavatthā evāti? Na tadavatthā sodhitattā. Sodhitañhi pubbe gāthāvirahe sati pucchāvissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittanti.

For all of the Buddha's Word, this is the general rule: it is sutta. Indeed, it is said: “So much of the Blessed One’s teaching is included in the suttas, is comprised in the suttas,” “the sutta analysis in Sāvatthī,” “five hundred suttas in one’s own doctrine,” and so on. From this, it is seen that even in the special scriptural traditions of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, the term 'sutta' is used. For that very reason, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said in the Netti: “the ninefold search for the suttanta.” There, the search, investigation, and examination of the meaning of the nine-limbed Dispensation by way of sutta, etc., is called the “ninefold search for the suttanta.” However, in some portions of these, other divisions such as geyya, possessing their own characteristic marks, are special rules established by those respective marks. Indeed, for geyya, the state of being accompanied by verses is the characteristic mark of its being so. Even in the world, a prose text accompanied by verses is called geyya. However, in the absence of verses, the state of asking a question and giving an answer is the characteristic mark of veyyākaraṇa being so. Indeed, questioning and answering is called byākaraṇa, and byākaraṇa itself is veyyākaraṇa. This being so, would even those texts accompanied by verses, etc., which proceed by way of asking a question and giving an answer, attain the state of being veyyākaraṇa? They would not, because the designations geyya, etc., have a specific scope. Indeed, a rule with a specific scope is stronger than one with a general scope. Moreover, it is specified by the phrase “in the absence of verses.” A qualifier is what distinguishes the intended meaning from the unintended. Thus, in the Dhammapada and other compositions of mere verses; in special suttas connected with verses born of knowledge accompanied by joy, even though they are accompanied by verses; in those connected with sayings like “It was said by the Blessed One”; and in special suttas connected with marvelous phenomena, the designations gāthā (verse), udāna (inspired utterance), itivuttaka (as-it-was-said discourses), and abbhutadhamma (marvelous phenomena) are respectively established. Here, indeed, even when there is a connection with the characteristic mark of another designation, it is precisely because of the strength of the designations with a specific scope that the designations gāthā, etc., are established. Likewise, although there is the state of being a verse composition, in those texts that reveal the power of the Blessed One's conduct in past lives, the designation jātaka is established. And although there is the state of question-and-answer and the state of being accompanied by verses, in certain suttas, because they bring about veda (joyful wisdom), the designation vedalla is established. Thus, by this or that characteristic mark, such as being accompanied by verses, etc., the designations geyya, etc., are established in those respective special suttas. Therefore, geyya, etc., which are other than the sutta component, are special rules. Whatever herein is devoid of the characteristic marks of the geyya component, etc., that is the sutta component itself, because it proceeds by the general designation, through the exclusion of a special designation. But surely, this being so, a sutta with verses is geyya, and a sutta without verses is veyyākaraṇa; thus, due to the absence of a sutta free from both of these, would there not be a separate sutta component? Is this objection not still standing? It is not still standing, because it has been refuted. Indeed, it was previously refuted by the statement: “In the absence of verses, the state of asking a question and giving an answer is the characteristic mark of veyyākaraṇa being so.”

Yañca vuttaṃ “gāthābhāvato maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ (khu. pā. 1; su. ni. 261) suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā”ti, tampi na, niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttabhāvo. Na hi tāni dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādayo viya gāthābhāvena saññitāni, atha kho suttabhāveneva. Teneva hi akathāyaṃ “suttanāmaka”nti nāmaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Yañca pana vuttaṃ “sagāthakattā geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā”ti, tampi natthi. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā sahatāññena, tasmā. Sahabhāvo hi nāma attato aññena hoti. Saha gāthāhīti ca sagāthakaṃ, na ca maṅgalasuttādīsu gāthāvinimutto koci suttapadeso atthi, yo “saha gāthāhī”ti vucceyya, nanu ca gāthāsamudāyo tadekadesāhi gāthāhi añño hoti, yassa vasena “saha gāthāhī”ti sakkā vattunti? Taṃ na. Na hi avayavavinimutto samudāyo nāma koci atthi, yo tadekadesehi saha bhaveyya. Katthaci pana “dīghasuttaṅkitassā”tiādīsu samudāyekadesānaṃ vibhāgavacanaṃ vohāramattaṃ pati pariyāyavacanameva, ayañca nippariyāyena pabhedavibhāgadassanakathāti[V 1.0111]. Yampi vuttaṃ “ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānaṃ geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tampi na, aññato. Aññāyeva hi tā gāthā jātakādipariyāpannattā. Tādisāyeva hi kāraṇānurūpena tattha desitā, ato na tāhi ubhatovibhaṅgādīnaṃ geyyaṅgabhāvoti. Evaṃ suttādinavaṅgānaṃ aññamaññasaṅkarābhāvo veditabboti.

And as to what was said, “Due to being composed of verses, the inclusion of suttas like the Maṅgala Sutta under the sutta component would not be possible,” that too is not correct, because of their being well-established. Indeed, the status of the Maṅgala Sutta and others as sutta is well-established. They are not designated by their nature as verses, like the Dhammapada or the Buddhavaṃsa, but rather, they are designated precisely by their nature as sutta. For that very reason, in the commentary, the term 'nāma' was used in the phrase 'suttanāmakaṃ' (named sutta). And as to what was said, “Or, because they are accompanied by verses, they might be included under the geyya component,” that too is not the case. If one asks why, it is because the term sagāthaka means 'together with another'. Indeed, the state of 'being together' is with something other than oneself. And sagāthakaṃ means 'together with verses', but in the Maṅgala Sutta and others, there is no portion of the sutta text whatsoever that is separate from the verses, which could be said to be 'together with verses'. But surely, is not a collection of verses something other than the individual verses that are its parts, by reason of which one could say 'together with verses'? That is not so. Indeed, there is no such thing as a collection separate from its parts, which could exist together with those parts. However, elsewhere, in expressions like 'marked by a long sutta,' the statement dividing a collection and its parts is merely a figurative expression depending on conventional usage. But this discussion here is a statement showing a division and distinction in a literal sense. And as to what was said, “In the Ubhatovibhaṅga and similar texts, the portions containing verses might be included under the geyya component,” that too is not so, because they are from another category. Indeed, those verses are entirely different, as they are included within the Jātaka and other categories. For only such verses were taught there in accordance with the context. Therefore, because of those verses, the Ubhatovibhaṅga and similar texts do not attain the state of being the geyya component. Thus, it should be understood that there is no intermingling among the nine components, sutta, etc.

Idāni [M 1.0126] etāni navaṅgāni vibhajitvā dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Niddeso nāma suttanipāte –

Now, showing these nine components by dividing them, the commentator says, beginning with “Therein.” The Niddesa is in the Suttanipāta:

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa ce taṃ samijjhati;

Addhā pītimano hoti, laddhā macco yadicchatī”tiādinā. (su. ni. 772); –

“When one desires sensual pleasures, if that is fulfilled for him, he is surely gladdened in mind, the mortal, having obtained what he wishes,” and so on.

Āgatassa aṭṭhakavaggassa;

of the Aṭṭhakavagga that has come;

“Kenassu nivuto loko, (iccāyasmā ajito);

Kenassu na pakāsati;

Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi,

Kiṃsu tassa mahabbhaya”ntiādinā. (su. ni. 1038); –

“By what is the world shrouded, (so said the Venerable Ajita), by what does it not shine forth? What do you say is its defilement? What is its great fear?” and so on.

Āgatassa pārāyanavaggassa;

of the Pārāyanavagga that has come;

“Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

Aviheṭhayaṃ aññatarampi tesaṃ;

Na puttamiccheyya kuto sahāyaṃ,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”tiādinā. (su. ni. 35); –

“Having laid down the rod with regard to all beings, not harming any one of them, one should not wish for a son, how then a companion? One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn,” and so on.

Āgatassa khaggavisāṇasuttassa ca atthavibhāgavasena satthukappena āyasmatā dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherena kato niddeso, yo “mahāniddeso, cūḷaniddeso”ti vuccati. Evamidha niddesassa suttaṅgasaṅgaho bhadantabuddhadhosācariyena dassito, tathā aññatthāpi vinayaṭṭhakathādīsu[V 1.0112], ācariyadhammapālattherenāpi nettippakaraṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Apare pana niddesassa gāthāveyyākaraṇaṅgesu dvīsu saṅgahaṃ vadanti. Vuttañhetaṃ niddesaṭṭhakathāyaṃ upasenattherena –

The Niddesa, which is called the “Mahāniddesa” and the “Cūḷaniddesa,” was made by the venerable Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, who is like the Teacher, by way of analyzing the meaning of the Khaggavisāṇasutta that has come down. Thus, here, the inclusion of the Niddesa in the Sutta-aṅga was shown by the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa, and likewise elsewhere in the Vinaya commentaries and so on, and also by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, in the commentary on the Nettippakaraṇa. But other teachers state the inclusion of the Niddesa in the two aṅgas of Gāthā and Veyyākaraṇa. This was stated in the Niddesa commentary by the Elder Upasena:

“So panesa vinayapiṭakaṃ…pe… abhidhammapiṭakanti tīsu piṭakesu suttantapiṭakapariyāpanno, dīghanikāyo…pe… khuddakanikāyoti pañcasu nikāyesu khuddakamahānikāyapariyāpanno, suttaṃ…pe… vedallanti navasu satthusāsanaṅgesu yathāsambhavaṃ gāthaṅgaveyyākaraṇaṅgadvayasaṅgahito”ti (mahāni. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā).

“This Niddesa, however, among the three Piṭakas—the Vinayapiṭaka… and the Abhidhammapiṭaka—is included in the Suttantapiṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas—the Dīghanikāya… and the Khuddakanikāya—it is included in the Khuddakanikāya. Among the nine aṅgas of the Teacher’s Dispensation—Sutta… and Vedalla—it is, as is appropriate, included in the two aṅgas of Gāthā and Veyyākaraṇa.”

Ettha [M 1.0127] tāva katthaci pucchāvissajjanasabbhāvato niddesekadesassa veyyākaraṇaṅgasaṅgaho yujjatu, agāthābhāvato gāthaṅgasaṅgaho kathaṃ yujjeyyāti vīmaṃsitabbametaṃ. Dhammāpadādīnaṃ viya hi kevalaṃ gāthābandhabhāvo gāthaṅgassa tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Dhammapadādīsu hi kevalaṃ gāthābandhesu gāthāsamaññā patiṭṭhitā, niddese ca na koci kevalo gāthābandappadeso upalabbhati. Sammāsambuddhena bhāsitānaṃyeva hi aṭṭhakavaggādisaṅgahitānaṃ gāthānaṃ niddesamattaṃ dhammasenāpatinā kataṃ. Atthavibhajanatthaṃ ānītāpi hi tā aṭṭhakavaggādisaṅgahitā niddisitabbā mūlagāthāyo suttanipātapariyāpannattā aññāyevāti na niddesasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu āgatāpi taṃ vohāramalabhamānā jātakādipariyāpannā gāthāyo viya, tasmā kāraṇantaramettha gavesitabbaṃ, yuttataraṃ vā gahetabbaṃ.

In this statement, let the inclusion of a part of the Niddesa in the Veyyākaraṇa-aṅga be appropriate, due to the existence of question and answer in some places; but due to the absence of gāthā, how could its inclusion in the Gāthā-aṅga be appropriate? This should be investigated. For, as in the Dhammapada and so on, the state of being merely a verse composition is the cause for its being a Gāthā-aṅga. Indeed, in the Dhammapada and so on, which are mere verse compositions, the designation ‘gāthā’ is established. But in the Niddesa, no passage that is merely a verse composition is found. For only an exposition of the gāthās included in the Aṭṭhakavagga and so on, which were spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One, was made by the General of the Dhamma. For although those root gāthās to be expounded, included in the Aṭṭhakavagga and so on, are brought for the purpose of analyzing the meaning, because they are included in the Suttanipāta, they are indeed something else and therefore do not come under the count of ‘Niddesa,’ like the gāthās included in the Jātaka and so on, which, although they appear in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and so on, do not receive that designation. Therefore, another reason should be sought here, or a more suitable one should be accepted.

Nālakasuttaṃ nāma dhammacakkappavattita divasato sattame divase nālakattherassa “moneyyaṃ te upaññissa”ntiādinā (su. ni. 706) bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ moneyya paṭipadāparidīpakaṃ suttaṃ. Tuvaṭṭakasuttaṃ nāma mahāsamayasuttantadesanāya sannipatitesu devesu “kā nu kho arahattappattiyā paṭipattī”ti uppannacittānaṃ ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā “mūlaṃ papañcasaṅkhāyā”tiādinā (su. ni. 922) bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ suttaṃ. Evamidha suttanipāte āgatānaṃ maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttaṅgasaṅgaho dassito, tattheva āgatānaṃ asuttanāmikānaṃ suddhikagāthānaṃ gāthaṅgasaṅgahañca dassayissati, evaṃ sati suttanipātaṭṭhakathārambhe –

The Nālaka Sutta is the discourse that illuminates the practice of the sage (moneyyapaṭipadā), spoken by the Blessed One to the Elder Nālaka on the seventh day from the day of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, beginning with, “I will proclaim to you the state of a sage.” The Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta is the discourse spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with, “The root of the proliferation of reckoning…,” after having had himself questioned by a created Buddha in order to explain the matter to certain deities among the devas assembled for the teaching of the Mahāsamaya Sutta, in whose minds the thought had arisen, “What, indeed, is the practice for the attainment of Arahantship?” Thus, here, the inclusion in the Sutta-aṅga of the Maṅgala Sutta and so forth, which appear in the Suttanipāta, has been shown; and the inclusion in the Gāthā-aṅga of the verses without sutta names that also appear there will be shown. This being so, at the beginning of the Suttanipāta commentary—

“Gāthāsatasamākiṇṇo, geyyabyākaraṇaṅkito;

Kasmā suttanipātoti, saṅkhamesa gatoti ce”ti. (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā); –

“Filled with hundreds of verses, marked by the Geyya and Byākaraṇa aṅgas; why has this come to be reckoned as ‘Suttanipāta’?”

Sakalassāpi [V 1.0113] suttanipātassa geyyaveyyākaraṇaṅgasaṅgaho kasmā coditoti? Nāyaṃ virodho. Kevalañhi tattha codakena sagāthakattaṃ, katthaci pucchāvissajjanattañca gahetvā codanāmattaṃ kataṃ, aññathā suttanipāte niggāthakassa suttasseva abhāvato veyyākaraṇaṅgasaṅgaho na codetabbo siyā, tasmā codakassa vacanametaṃ appamāṇanti idha, aññāsu ca vinayaṭṭhakathādīsu vuttanayeneva tassa [M 1.0128] suttaṅgagāthaṅgasaṅgaho dassitoti. Suttanti cuṇṇiyasuttaṃ. Visesenāti rāsibhāvena ṭhitaṃ sandhāyāha. Sagāthāvaggo geyyanti sambandho.

Why is the inclusion of the entire Suttanipāta in the Geyya and Veyyākaraṇa aṅgas challenged? This is not a contradiction. For the challenger there, having taken into account its having verses and, in some places, its being question-and-answer, made a mere challenge. Otherwise, since there is no sutta without verses in the Suttanipāta, its inclusion in the Veyyākaraṇa-aṅga should not be challenged. Therefore, this statement of the challenger is without authority. Thus, its inclusion in the Sutta-aṅga and Gāthā-aṅga is shown in the very way stated here and in other commentaries like the Vinaya Aṭṭhakathā. ‘Sutta’ means a prose discourse (cuṇṇiyasutta). ‘Especially’ (visesena) is said referring to that which stands as a collection. The Sagāthāvagga is to be connected as ‘Geyya’.

“Aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ nāma paṭisambhidādī”ti tīsupi kira gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Apare pana paṭisambhidāmaggassa geyyaveyyākaraṇaṅgadvayasaṅgahaṃ vadanti. Vuttañhetaṃ tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “navasu satthusāsanaṅgesu yathāsambhavaṃ geyyaveyyākaraṇaṅgadvayasaṅgahita”nti (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā), etthāpi geyyaṅgasaṅgahitabhāvo vuttanayena vīmaṃsitabbo. No suttanāmikāti asuttanāmikā saṅgītikāle suttasamaññāya apaññātā. “Suddhikagāthā nāma vatthugāthā”ti tīsupi kira gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, vatthugāthāti ca pārāyanavaggassa nidānamāropentena āyasmatā ānandattherena saṅgītikāle vuttā chappaññāsa gāthāyo, nālakasuttassa nidānamāropentena teneva tadā vuttā vīsatimattā gāthāyo ca vuccanti. Suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.685) pana “parinibbute bhagavati saṅgītiṃ karontenāyasmatā mahākassapena tameva moneyyapaṭipadaṃ puṭṭho āyasmā ānando yena, yadā ca samādapito nālakatthero bhagavantaṃ pucchi, taṃ sabbaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetukāmo ‘ānandajāte’tiādikā (su. ni. 684) vīsati vatthugāthāyo vatvā vissajjesi, taṃ sabbampi ‘nālakasutta”nti vuccatī”ti āgatattā nālakasuttassa vatthugāthāyo nālakasuttaggahaṇeneva gahitāti pārāyanavaggassa vatthugāthāyo idha suddhikagāthāti gahetabbaṃ. Tattheva ca pārāyanavagge ajitamāṇavakādīnaṃ soḷasannaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ pucchāgāthā, bhagavato vissajjanagāthā ca pāḷiyaṃ suttanāmena avatvā ‘ajitamāṇavakapucchā, tissametteyyamāṇavakapucchā”tiādinā (su. ni. 1038) āgatattā, cuṇṇiyaganthe hi asammissattā ca “no suttanāmikā suddhikagāthā nāmā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

“‘That which is named “not included by the eight factors” is the Paṭisambhidā, and so on’—this, it is said, is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. Other teachers, however, say that the Paṭisambhidāmagga is included by the two factors of geyya and veyyākaraṇa. For it is stated in its commentary: ‘Among the nine factors of the Teacher’s Dispensation, it is included by the two factors of geyya and veyyākaraṇa, as is suitable.’ Here too, the fact of its inclusion by the geyya factor should be investigated by the method already stated. ‘Not named sutta’ means not having the name ‘sutta,’ not being known by the designation ‘sutta’ at the time of the council. ‘The Suddhikagāthā are the Vatthugāthā’—this, it is said, is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. And ‘Vatthugāthā’ refers to the fifty-six verses spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the council when establishing the introduction to the Pārāyanavagga, and the approximately twenty verses spoken by him at that time when establishing the introduction to the Nālaka Sutta. In the Suttanipāta commentary, however, it is said: ‘When the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Venerable Ānanda, having been asked by the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was conducting the council, about that very practice of sagacity, and wishing to make clear all about by whom and when the Elder Nālaka, having been instructed, questioned the Blessed One, answered by reciting the twenty Vatthugāthā beginning with “Ānandajāte.” All of that is called the “Nālaka Sutta.”’ Because it has come down thus, the Vatthugāthā of the Nālaka Sutta are included by the very taking up of ‘Nālaka Sutta’; therefore, the Vatthugāthā of the Pārāyanavagga should be taken here as the Suddhikagāthā. And in that very Pārāyanavagga, because the question verses of the sixteen brahmins beginning with the young brahmin Ajita, and the Blessed One’s answer verses, are not called by a sutta name in the Pāḷi but have come down as ‘The Question of the young brahmin Ajita,’ ‘The Question of the young brahmin Tissametteyya,’ and so on, and because they are not mixed with prose texts, it is fitting to say, ‘They are not named sutta; they are named Suddhikagāthā.’”

“Somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā”ti etena udānaṭṭhena udānanti anvatthasaññataṃ dasseti (udā. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) kimidaṃ udānaṃ nāma? Pītivegasamuṭṭhāpito udāhāro. Yathā hi yaṃ telādi minitabbavatthu mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ “avasesako”ti vuccati. Yañca [M 1.0129] jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati, taṃ “mahogho’ti vuccati, evameva yaṃ pītivegasamuṭṭhāpitaṃ vitakkavipphāraṃ antohadayaṃ sandhāretuṃ [V 1.0114] na sakkoti, so adhiko hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahi vacīdvārena nikkhanto paṭiggāhakanirapekkho udāhāraviseso “udāna”nti vuccati (udā. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) “uda mode kīḷāyañcā”ti hi akkharacintakā vadanti, idañca yebhuyyena vuttaṃ dhammasaṃvegavasena uditassāpi “sace bhāyatha dukkhassā”tiādiudānassa (udā. 44) udānapāḷiyaṃ āgatattā, tathā“gāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā”ti idampi yebhuyyeneva “atthi bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī, na āpo”tiādikassa (udā. 71) cuṇṇiyavākyavasena uditassāpi tattha āgatattā. Nanu ca udānaṃ nāma pītisomanassasamuṭṭāpito, dhammasaṃvegasamuṭṭhāpito vā dhammapaṭiggāhakanirapekkho gāthābandhavasena, cuṇṇiyavākyavasena ca pavatto udāhāro, tathā ceva sabbattha āgataṃ, idha kasmā “bhikkhave”ti āmantanaṃ vuttanti? Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saññāpanatthaṃ eva, na paṭiggāhakakaraṇatthaṃ. Nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttañhi bhagavā dhammaṃ desetvā nibbānaguṇānussaraṇena uppannapītisomanassena udānaṃ udānento “ayaṃ nibbānadhammo kathamapaccayo upalabbhatī”ti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cetoparivitakkamaññāya tesaṃ tamatthaṃ ñāpetukāmena “tadāyatana”nti vuttaṃ, na pana ekantato te paṭiggāhake katvāti veditabbanti.

By the phrase ‘Connected with verses consisting of knowledge and gladness,’ it is shown that ‘udāna’ is a designation that follows its meaning, signifying a joyful utterance. What is this thing called ‘udāna’? It is an utterance caused to arise by the force of joy. For just as a substance to be measured, such as oil, which cannot be held by a measure, flows out and is called ‘overflow,’ and just as water that cannot be held by a tank overflows and is called ‘a great flood,’ in the same way, a mental proliferation caused to arise by the force of joy that cannot be held within the heart, becoming excessive and not staying inside, goes out through the speech door, independent of a recipient—this special utterance is called ‘udāna.’ For the grammarians say, ‘The root ud is in the sense of rejoicing and playing.’ And this is said for the most part, because even an udāna uttered through the power of spiritual urgency, such as, ‘If you fear suffering…,’ has come down in the Udāna-pāḷi. Similarly, this phrase ‘connected with verses’ is also said for the most part, because even an udāna uttered by way of a prose sentence, such as, ‘There is, O bhikkhus, that base where there is neither earth nor water…,’ has come down there. Is it not so that an udāna is an utterance arisen from joy and gladness, or arisen from spiritual urgency, independent of a recipient of the Dhamma, proceeding by way of verse composition and by way of prose sentences? And it has come down thus everywhere. Why here is the address ‘O bhikkhus’ spoken? It is spoken only for the purpose of making those bhikkhus understand, not for the purpose of making them recipients. For the Blessed One, having taught the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna, while uttering an udāna with joy and gladness arisen from repeatedly recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna, knew the thought in the minds of those bhikkhus, ‘How is this Dhamma of Nibbāna obtained without a cause?’ and with the wish to make that meaning known to them, said, ‘that base.’ But it should be understood that it was not said having made them recipients in an absolute sense.

Tayidaṃ sabbaññubuddhabhāsitaṃ paccekabuddhabhāsitaṃ sāvakabhāsitanti tibbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha paccekabuddhabhāsitaṃ –

This udāna is of three kinds: spoken by the Omniscient Buddha, spoken by the Paccekabuddha, and spoken by a disciple. Among these, that spoken by the Paccekabuddha is as follows:

“Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

Aviheṭhayaṃ aññatarampi tesa”nti. ādinā (su. ni. 35) –

“Having laid down the rod for all beings, not harming even a single one of them,” and so on.

Khaggavisāṇasutte āgataṃ. Sāvakabhāsitampi –

It comes in the Khaggavisāṇasutta. That spoken by a disciple is also as follows:

“Sabbo [M 1.0130] rāgo pahīno me,

Sabbo doso samūhato;

Sabbo me vihato moho,

Sītibhūtosmi nibbuto”ti. ādinā (theragā. 79) –

“All my lust is abandoned, all hatred is eradicated; all my delusion is dispelled, I am cooled, extinguished,” and so on.

Theragāthāsu[V 1.0115],

in the Theragāthā,

“Kāyena saṃvutā āsiṃ, vācāya uda cetasā;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, sītibhūtāmhi nibbutā”ti. (therīgā. 15); –

“I was restrained in body, speech, and mind. Having completely uprooted craving, I am cooled, extinguished.”

Therīgāthāsu ca āgataṃ. Aññānipi sakkādīhi devehi bhāsitāni “aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ, kassape suppatiṭṭhita”ntiādīni (udā. 27). Soṇadaṇḍabrāhmaṇādīhi manussehi ca bhāsitāni “namo tassa bhagavato”tiādīni (dī. ni. 2.371; ma. ni. 1.290; 2.290, 357; saṃ. ni. 1187; 2.38; a. ni. 5.194) tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhāni udānāni santi eva, tāni sabbānipi idha na adhippetāni. Yaṃ pana sammāsambuddhena sāmaṃ āhaccabhāsitaṃ jinavacanabhūtaṃ, tadeva dhammasaṅgāhakehi “udāna”nti saṅgītaṃ, tadeva ca sandhāya bhagavatā pariyattidhammaṃ navadhā vibhajitvā uddisantena “udāna”nti vuttaṃ. Yā pana “anekajātisaṃsāra”ntiādikā (dha. pa. 153) gāthā bhagavatā bodhimūle udānavasena pavattitā, anekasatasahassānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ udānabhūtā ca, tā aparabhāge dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa bhagavatā desitattā dhammasaṅgāhakehi udānapāḷiyaṃ saṅgahaṃ anāropetvā dhammapade saṅgahitā, yañca “aññāsi vata bho koṇḍañño aññāsi vata bho koṇḍañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 17; paṭi. ma. 2.30) udānavacanaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuyā devamanussānaṃ pavedanasamatthanigghosavipphāraṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, tadapi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ sabbesaṃ eva bhikkhūnaṃ sammāpaṭipattipaccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ “ārādhayiṃsu vata maṃ bhikkhū ekaṃ samaya”ntiādivacanaṃ (ma. ni. 1.225) viya dhammacakkappavattanasuttantadesanāpariyosāne attanāpi adhigatadhammekadesassa yathādesitassa ariyamaggassa sabbapaṭhamaṃ sāvakesu therena adhigatattā attano parissamassa saphalabhāvapaccavekkhaṇahetutaṃ pītisomanassajanitaṃ [M 1.0131] udāhāramattaṃ, na pana “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”tiādivacanaṃ viya (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) pavattiyā, nivattiyā vā pakāsananti dhammasaṅgāhakehi udānapāḷiyaṃ na saṅgītanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Udānapāḷiyaṃ pana aṭṭhasu vaggesu dasa dasa katvā asītiyeva suttantā saṅgītā. Tathā hi tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ –

And it is found in the Therīgāthā. There are indeed other udānas included in the three councils, such as those spoken by deities like Sakka, beginning with, “Ah, the gift, the supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa,” and those spoken by humans like Soṇadaṇḍa the brahmin, beginning with, “Homage to that Blessed One”; however, all of those are not intended here. But that which was spoken directly by the Fully Enlightened One himself, being the word of the Victor, that very thing was compiled by the compilers of the Dhamma as “Udāna.” And with reference to that very thing, it was called “Udāna” by the Blessed One when, having divided the scriptural Dhamma into nine parts, he pointed it out.
