Furthermore, as for the verses beginning with “anekajātisaṃsāraṃ,” which were uttered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree by way of an udāna, and which are the udāna of many hundreds of thousands of Fully Enlightened Ones—because those verses were taught by the Blessed One in a later period to the treasurer of the Dhamma, they were compiled in the Dhammapada by the compilers of the Dhamma, without including them in the Udāna collection. And as for the udāna statement, “Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood! Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood!,” which was spoken by the Blessed One, making its resounding sound capable of informing the devas and humans in the ten-thousandfold world-system—that too, at the first awakening, like the statement beginning with “The monks have indeed pleased me at one time,” which was due to reflecting on the proper practice of all the monks, was merely an utterance generated by joy and gladness. It was uttered at the conclusion of the teaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, caused by reflecting on the fruitfulness of His own effort, because the elder was the very first among the disciples to attain the noble path, a part of the Dhamma which He himself had realized as it was taught. It is not, however, like the statement beginning with “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,” a declaration of either the process of becoming or the cessation from it. Therefore, it should be understood that it was not compiled in the Udāna collection by the compilers of the Dhamma. However, in the Udāna collection, exactly eighty suttas were compiled, having been arranged as ten in each of the eight chapters. For so it is stated in its commentary:

“Asītiyeva suttantā, vaggā aṭṭha samāsato”ti. (Udā. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā).

“Exactly eighty suttas, eight chapters in summary.”

Idha [V 1.0116] pana “dveasīti suttantā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ udānapāḷiyā na sameti, tasmā “asīti suttantā”ti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ. Apica na kevalaṃ idheva, atha kho aññāsupi (vi. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) vinayābhidhammaṭṭhakathāsu (dha. saṃ. nidānakathā) tathāyeva vuttattā “appakaṃ pana ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotī”ti pariyāyena anekaṃsena vuttaṃ siyā. Yathā vā tathā vā anumānena gaṇanameva hi tattha tattha ūnādhikasaṅkhyā, itarathā tāyeva na siyuntipi vadanti, pacchā pamādalekhavacanaṃ vā etaṃ.

Here, however, it is said, “eighty-two suttas,” which does not agree with the Udāna Pāḷi; therefore, the reading should be “eighty suttas.” Moreover, it is not only here, but because it is stated in the very same way in other commentaries on the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, it may have been stated indirectly and not definitively that “a small amount, whether less or more, is not counted.” Indeed, whether one way or another, the numbers with deficits or excesses stated in various places are merely a count by estimation; otherwise, those very numbers would not exist, so the teachers say. Or, this is a statement from a later time due to a scribal error.

Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatātiādinayappavattāti ettha ādisaddena “vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamarahatāti me sutaṃ. Ekadhammaṃ bhikkhave, pajahatha, ahaṃ vo pāṭibhogo anāgāmitāya. Katamaṃ ekadhammaṃ? Lobhaṃ bhikkhave, ekadhammaṃ pajahatha, ahaṃ vo pāṭibhogo anāgāmitāyā”ti (itivu. 1) evamādinā ekadukatikacatukkanipātavasena vuttaṃ dvādasuttarasatasuttasamūhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā hi itivuttakapāḷiyameva udānagāthāhi dvādasuttarasatasuttāni gaṇetvā saṅgītāni, tadaṭṭhakathāyampi (itivu. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) tathāyeva vuttaṃ. Tasmā “dvādasuttarasatasuttantā” icceva pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, yathāvuttanayena vā anekaṃsato vuttantipi vattuṃ sakkā, tathāpi īdise ṭhāne pamāṇaṃ dassentena yāthāvatova niyametvā dassetabbanti “dasuttarasatasuttantā”ti idaṃ pacchā pamādalekhamevāti gahetabbanti vadanti. Iti evaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ itivuttaṃ. Itivuttanti saṅgītaṃ itivuttakaṃ. Ruḷhināmaṃ vā etaṃ yathā “yevāpanakaṃ, natumhākavaggo”ti, vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamarahatāti me sutanti nidānavacanena saṅgītaṃ yathāvuttasuttasamūhaṃ.

In the phrase beginning with 'Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā,' the word 'etc.' includes the collection of one hundred and twelve suttas spoken by way of the Nipātas of Ones, Twos, Threes, and Fours, beginning with, “This was spoken by the Blessed One, spoken by the Arahant, so I have heard. Monks, abandon one thing, and I am your guarantor for non-returning. What one thing? Monks, abandon greed, that one thing, and I am your guarantor for non-returning.” For so, in the Itivuttaka Pāḷi itself, one hundred and twelve suttas are compiled, having been counted together with the udāna verses. It is stated in the very same way in its commentary as well. Therefore, the reading should be exactly “one hundred and twelve suttas.” Or, it can be said that it was stated non-definitively, according to the method already mentioned. Nevertheless, in such a place, one who is showing a measure should determine and show it precisely as it is. Therefore, they say that this, “one hundred and ten suttas,” should be taken as nothing but a later scribal error. Thus, “spoken by the Blessed One” is Itivuttaṃ. That which was compiled as “Thus it was spoken” is the Itivuttaka. Or, this is a conventional name, like “Yevāpanakaṃ” or “Natumhākavaggo.” The collection of suttas as mentioned, compiled with the introductory words, “This was spoken by the Blessed One, spoken by the Arahant, so I have heard,” is the Itivuttaka.

Jātaṃ [M 1.0132] bhūtaṃ purāvutthaṃ bhagavato pubbacaritaṃ kāyati katheti pakāseti etenāti jātakaṃ, taṃ pana imānīti dassetuṃ “apaṇṇakajātakādīnī”tiādimāha. Tattha “paññāsādhikāni pañcajātakasatānī”ti idaṃ appakaṃ pana ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti katvā anekaṃsena, vohārasukhatāmattena ca vuttaṃ. Ekaṃsato hi sattacattālīsādhikāniyeva yathāvuttagaṇanato tīhi ūnattā. Tathā hi ekanipāte paññāsasataṃ, dukanipāte sataṃ, tikanipāte paññāsa, tathā catukkanipāte, pañcakanipāte pañcavīsa, chakkanipāte vīsa, sattanipāte ekavīsa, aṭṭhanipāte dasa, navanipāte dvādasa, dasanipāte soḷasa, ekādasanipāte nava, dvādasanipāte dasa, tathā terasanipāte, pakiṇṇakanipāte terasa, vīsatinipāte cuddasa, tiṃsanipāte dasa, cattālīsanipāte pañca, paṇṇāsanipāte tīṇi, saṭṭhinipāte [V 1.0117] dve, tathā sattatinipāte, asītinipāte pañca, mahānipāte dasāti sattacattālīsādhikāneva pañca jātakasatāni saṅgītānīti.

That word of the Buddha is called 'Jātaka' because by it is told, related, and revealed what has happened, what has been, what was lived in the past—the past conduct of the Blessed One. To show which these are, the author said the words beginning with 'The Apaṇṇaka Jātaka and others.' Therein, the phrase 'five hundred and fifty Jātakas' was spoken not definitively and merely for ease of convention, because a small amount, whether less or more, does not amount to a count. Truly, it is definitively five hundred and forty-seven, being three less than the aforementioned count. For thus: in the Ekanipāta, there are one hundred and fifty; in the Dukanipāta, one hundred; in the Tikanipāta, fifty; similarly in the Catukkanipāta; in the Pañcakanipāta, twenty-five; in the Chakkanipāta, twenty; in the Sattakanipāta, twenty-one; in the Aṭṭhakanipāta, ten; in the Navakanipāta, twelve; in the Dasakanipāta, sixteen; in the Ekādasanipāta, nine; in the Dvādasakanipāta, ten; similarly in the Terasakanipāta; in the Pakiṇṇakanipāta, thirteen; in the Vīsatinipāta, fourteen; in the Tiṃsanipāte, ten; in the Cattālīsanipāte, five; in the Paṇṇāsanipāte, three; in the Saṭṭhinipāte, two; similarly in the Sattatinipāte; in the Asītinipāte, five; in the Mahānipāte, ten. Thus, five hundred and forty-seven Jātakas have been compiled.

Abbhuto dhammo sabhāvo vutto yatthāti abbhutadhammaṃ, taṃ panidanti āha “cattārome”tiādi. Ādisaddena cettha –

'Abbhutadhamma' is so called because in it is spoken a wonderful, unprecedented Dhamma or nature. To show what this is, the author said, 'These four,' and so on. And here, by the word 'and so on'...

“Cattārome bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutā dhammā ānande. Katame cattāro? Sace bhikkhave, bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamati, dassanenapi sā attamanā hoti. Tatra ce ānando, dhammaṃ bhāsati, bhāsitenapi sā attamanā hoti, atittāva bhikkhave bhikkhuparisā hoti, atha ānando tuṇhī bhavati. Sace bhikkhave, bhikkhunīparisā…pe… upāsakaparisā…pe… upāsikā – parisā…pe… tuṇhī bhavati. Ime kho bhikkhave…pe… ānande”ti (a. ni. 4.129) –

"Monks, there are these four astonishing and wonderful qualities in Ānanda. What four? If, monks, an assembly of monks approaches Ānanda to see him, they are pleased even by the sight of him. And if Ānanda teaches them the Dhamma, they are pleased also by his teaching. Yet, monks, the assembly of monks remains unsatisfied, and then Ānanda becomes silent. The same is true, monks, for an assembly of nuns… for an assembly of laymen… and for an assembly of laywomen, until he becomes silent. These, monks, are the four astonishing and wonderful qualities in Ānanda." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.129)

Evamādinayappavattaṃ tattha tattha bhāsitaṃ sabbampi acchariyabbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ suttantaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

It includes every Suttanta spoken in various places that proceeds in this manner and is connected with astonishing and wonderful Dhammas.

Cūḷavedallādīsu (ma. ni. 1.460) visākhena nāma upāsakena puṭṭhāya dhammadinnāya nāma bhikkhuniyā bhāsitaṃ suttaṃ cūḷavedallaṃ nāma. Mahākoṭṭhikattherena pucchitena āyasmatā sāriputtattherena bhāsitaṃ mahāvedallaṃ (ma. ni. 1.449) nāma. Sammādiṭṭhisuttampi [M 1.0133] (ma. ni. 1.89) bhikkhūhi puṭṭhena teneva bhāsitaṃ, etāni majjhimanikāyapariyāpannāni. Sakkapañhaṃ (dī. ni. 2.344) pana sakkena puṭṭho bhagavā abhāsi, taṃ dīghanikāyapariyāpannaṃ. Mahāpuṇṇamasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.85) pana tadahuposathe pannarase puṇṇamāya rattiyā aññatarena bhikkhunā puṭṭhena bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, taṃ majjhimanikāyapariyāpannaṃ. Evamādayo sabbepi tattha tatthāgatā vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitasuttantā “vedalla”nti veditabbaṃ. Vedanti ñāṇaṃ. Tuṭṭhinti yathābhāsitadhammadesanaṃ viditvā “sādhu ayye sādhāvuso”tiādinā abbhanumodanavasappavattaṃ pītisomanassaṃ. Laddhā laddhāti labhitvā labhitvā, punappunaṃ labhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti, etena vedasaddo ñāṇe, somanasse ca ekasesanayena, sāmaññaniddesena vā pavattati, vedamhi nissitaṃ tassa labhāpanavasenāti vedallanti ca dasseti.

Among the Cūḷavedalla and other suttas: the sutta named Cūḷavedalla was spoken by the nun named Dhammadinnā, who was asked by the layman named Visākha. The sutta named Mahāvedalla was spoken by the venerable Sāriputta, who was asked by the elder Mahākoṭṭhika. The Sammādiṭṭhisutta was also spoken by him, who was asked by the monks; these are included in the Majjhima Nikāya. The Sakkapañha, however, was spoken by the Blessed One, who was asked by Sakka; it is included in the Dīgha Nikāya. The Mahāpuṇṇamasutta was spoken by the Blessed One, who was asked by a certain monk on the Uposatha day, the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon; it is included in the Majjhima Nikāya. All such suttas found in various places, which were asked after gaining knowledge (veda) and satisfaction (tuṭṭhi) again and again, should be known as 'Vedalla.' 'Veda' is knowledge. 'Tuṭṭhi' is the joy and gladness that arises from the power of great rejoicing with words such as, 'Excellent, venerable lady!' 'Excellent, friend!' after understanding the Dhamma teaching as it was spoken. 'Laddhā laddhā' means having obtained, having obtained; that is to say, having obtained again and again. By this, the word 'veda' applies to both knowledge and gladness, either by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa) or by general reference. And it shows that it is 'Vedalla' because it is based on 'veda' (knowledge and joy) by means of causing it to be obtained.

Evaṃ [V 1.0118] aṅgavasena sakalampi buddhavacanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni dhammakkhandhavasena vibhajitukāmo “katha”ntiādimāha. Tattha dhammakkhandhavasenāti dhammarāsivasena. “Dvāsītī”ti ayaṃ gāthā vuttatthāva. Evaṃ paridīpitadhammakkhandhavasenāti gopakamoggallānena nāma brāhmaṇena puṭṭhena gopakamoggallānasutte (ma. ni. 3.79) attano guṇappakāsanatthaṃ vā theragāthāyaṃ (theragā. 1017 ādayo) āyasmatā ānandattherena samantato dīpitadhammakkhandhavasena iminā evaṃ tena aparidīpitāpi dhammakkhandhā santīti pakāseti, tasmā kathāvatthuppakaraṇa mādhuriyasuttādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 2.317) vimānavatthādīsu kesañci gāthānañca vasena caturāsītisahassatopi dhammakkhandhānaṃ adhikatā veditabbā.

Thus, having divided the entire word of the Buddha by way of its divisions (aṅga), now, wishing to divide it by way of the Dhammakkhandhas (aggregates of Dhamma), the author said the words beginning with 'How?'. Therein, 'by way of the Dhammakkhandhas' means by way of the aggregates of Dhamma. This verse 'Eighty-two...' has its meaning already explained. By the phrase 'by way of the Dhammakkhandhas thus explained'—that is, by way of the Dhammakkhandhas fully explained by the venerable Ānanda in the Gopakamoggallānasutta when asked by the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, or in the Theragāthā for the purpose of revealing his own qualities—by this he reveals that there are also Dhammakkhandhas not explained by him (Ānanda). Therefore, it should be known that by way of the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa, the Mādhuriyasutta, and certain verses in the Vimānavatthu and other texts, the number of Dhammakkhandhas is greater than eighty-four thousand.

Ettha ca subhasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 1.444), gopakamoggallānasuttañca parinibbute bhagavati ānandattherena bhāsitattā caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassesu antogadhaṃ hoti, na hotīti? Paṭisambhidāgaṇṭhipade tāva idaṃ vuttaṃ “sayaṃ vuttadhammakkhandhānampi bhikkhuto gahiteyeva saṅgahetvā evamāhāti daṭṭhabba”nti, bhagavatā pana dinnanaye ṭhatvā bhāsitattā “sayaṃ vuttampi cetaṃ suttadvayaṃ bhagavato gahiteyeva saṅgahetvā vutta”nti evampi vattuṃ yuttataraṃ viya dissati. Bhagavatā hi dinnanaye ṭhatvā sāvakā dhammaṃ desenti, teneva sāvakabhāsitampi kathāvatthādikaṃ buddhabhāsitaṃ nāma jātaṃ[M 1.0134], tatoyeva ca attanā bhāsitampi subhasuttādikaṃ saṅgītimāropentena āyasmatā ānandattherena “evaṃ me suta”nti vuttaṃ.

Here, a question arises: Are the Subhasutta and the Gopakamoggallānasutta, spoken by the elder Ānanda after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, included within the eighty-four thousand Dhammakkhandhas, or not? First, in the Paṭisambhidāgaṇṭhipada, this is said: 'It should be understood that he (Ānanda) spoke thus (of the eighty-four thousand) having included even the Dhammakkhandhas he himself spoke only within those he had received from the bhikkhus.' However, because they were spoken while standing in the method given by the Blessed One, it seems more fitting to say this as well: 'Even these two suttas, though spoken by himself, were spoken by the elder Ānanda having included them only within what was received from the Blessed One.' Indeed, this is fitting. For the disciples teach the Dhamma standing in the method given by the Blessed One. For that very reason, even what is spoken by disciples, such as the Kathāvatthu, has become known as 'spoken by the Buddha.' And for that very reason, the venerable Ānanda, while raising to the level of a formal recitation even the Subhasutta and other texts spoken by himself, said, 'Thus have I heard.'

Ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ satipaṭṭhānādi. Satipaṭṭhānasuttañhi “ekāyano ayaṃ bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106; saṃ. ni. 3.367-384) cattāro satipaṭṭhāne ārabhitvā tesaṃyeva vibhāgadassanavasena pavattattā “ekānusandhika”nti vuccati. Anekānusandhikaṃ parinibbānasuttādi (dī. ni. 2.131 ādayo) parinibbānasuttañhi nānāṭhānesu nānādhammadesanānaṃ vasena pavattattā “anekānusandhika”nti vuccati.

A discourse of a single connection is such as the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. For the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, beginning with 'This, bhikkhus, is the one-way path for the purification of beings,' and so on, undertakes the four foundations of mindfulness, and because it proceeds solely by way of showing their analysis, it is called 'of a single connection.' A discourse of multiple connections is such as the Parinibbāna Sutta. For the Parinibbāna Sutta proceeds by way of various teachings in various places, and thus it is called 'of multiple connections.'

“Kati chinde kati jahe, kati cuttari bhāvaye;

Kati saṅgātigo bhikkhu, ‘oghatiṇṇo’ti vuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.5); –

'How many should one cut off, how many should one abandon, and how many further should one cultivate? A bhikkhu gone beyond how many attachments is called 'one who has crossed the flood'?'

Evamādinā pañhāpucchanaṃ gāthābandhesu eko dhammakkhandho.

Thus, the asking of a question in verse compositions, beginning in this way, is one aggregate of the Dhamma.

“Pañca [V 1.0119] chinde pañca jahe, pañca cuttari bhāvaye;

Pañca saṅgātigo bhikkhu, ‘oghatiṇṇo’ti vuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.5); –

'Five should one cut off, five should one abandon, and five further should one cultivate; a bhikkhu who has gone beyond five attachments is called 'one who has crossed the flood.''

Evamādinā ca vissajjanaṃ eko dhammakkhandho.

And thus, the answering, beginning in this way, is one aggregate of the Dhamma.

Tikadukabhājanaṃ dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ nikkhepakaṇḍaaṭṭhakathākaṇḍavasena gahetabbaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ kusalattikamātikāpadassa (dha. sa. 1) vibhajanavasena nikkhepakaṇḍe vuttaṃ –

The analysis of triads and dyads in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī should be understood by way of the Nikkhepakaṇḍa and Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa. Therefore, what is said in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa by way of its analysis of the matrix term of the wholesome triad—

“Katame dhammā kusalā? Tīṇi kusalamūlāni…pe… ime dhammā kusalā. Katame dhammā akusalā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni…pe… ime dhammā akusalā. Katame dhammā abyākatā”? Kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipākā…pe… ime dhammā abyākatā”ti (dha. sa. 187),

'What states are wholesome? The three wholesome roots... these states are wholesome. What states are unwholesome? The three unwholesome roots... these states are unwholesome. What states are indeterminate? The results of wholesome and unwholesome states... these states are indeterminate.'

Ayameko dhammakkhandho. Esa nayo sesattikadukapadavibhajanesupi. Yadapi aṭṭhakathākaṇḍe vuttaṃ –

This is one aggregate of the Dhamma. This is the method for the analyses of the remaining triad and dyad terms as well. And what is said in the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa—

“Katame dhammā kusalā? Catūsu bhūmīsu kusalaṃ. Ime dhammā kusalā. Katame dhammā akusalā? Dvādasa akusalacittuppādā. Ime dhammā akusalā. Katame dhammā abyākatā? Catūsu [M 1.0135] bhūmīsu vipāko tīsu bhūmīsu kiriyābyākataṃ rūpañca nibbānañca. Ime dhammā abyākatā”ti (dha. sa. 1386),

'What are wholesome states? Wholesome states in the four planes. These states are wholesome. What are unwholesome states? The twelve unwholesome consciousness-arisings. These states are unwholesome. What are indeterminate states? Resultant states in the four planes, functional indeterminate states in the three planes, material form, and Nibbāna. These states are indeterminate.'

Ayaṃ kusalattikamātikāpadassa vibhajanavasena pavatto eko dhammakkhandho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Cittavārabhājanaṃ pana cittuppādakaṇḍa vasena (dha. sa. 1) gahetabbaṃ. Yañhi tattha vuttaṃ kusalacittavibhajanatthaṃ –

This is one aggregate of the Dhamma that proceeds by way of the analysis of the matrix term of the wholesome triad. This is the method for the remaining ones as well. But the analysis of the consciousness section should be understood by way of the Cittuppādakaṇḍa. For what is stated there for the purpose of analyzing wholesome consciousness—

“Katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1),

'What are wholesome states? At whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere arises, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, with a form as its object or... at that time there is contact... there is non-distraction.'

Ayameko [V 1.0120] dhammakkhandho. Evaṃ sesacittavāravibhajanesu. Eko dhammakkhandhoti (ekameko dhammakkhandho chaḷa aṭṭha.) ca ekeko dhammakkhandhoti attho. “Ekamekaṃ tikadukabhājanaṃ, ekamekaṃ cittavārabhājana”nti ca vacanato hi “ekeko”ti avuttepi ayamattho sāmatthiyato viññāyamānova hoti.

This is one aggregate of the Dhamma. It is similar in the analyses of the remaining consciousness sections. And 'one aggregate of the Dhamma' means 'each single aggregate of the Dhamma.' For, because of the statement 'each single analysis of triads and dyads, and each single analysis of the consciousness section,' this meaning is indeed understood by implication even when 'each single' is not explicitly stated.

Vatthu nāma sudinnakaṇḍādi. Mātikā nāma “yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”tiādinā (pārā. 44) tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ajjhācāre paññattaṃ uddesa sikkhāpadaṃ. Padabhājaniyanti tassa tassa sikkhāpadassa “yo panāti yo yādiso”tiādi (pārā. 45) nayappavattaṃ padavibhajanaṃ. Antarāpattīti “paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pāci. 355) evamādinā sikkhāpadantaresu paññattā āpatti. Āpattīti taṃtaṃsikkhāpadānurūpaṃ vutto tikacchedamutto āpattivāro. Anāpattīti “anāpatti ajānantassa asādiyantassa khittacittassa vedanāṭṭassa ādikammikassā”tiādi (pārā. 66) nayappavatto anāpattivāro. Tikacchedoti “dasāhātikkante atikkantasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, dasāhātikkante vematiko…pe… dasāhātikkante anatikkantasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti (pārā. 468) evamādinayappavatto tikapācittiya-tika-dukkaṭādibhedo tikaparicchedo. Tatthāti tesu vatthumātikādīsu.

The basis (vatthu) is such as the Sudinna section. The matrix (mātikā) is the recited training rule laid down for each and every transgression, beginning with 'Whatever bhikkhu, having entered upon the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus...' The word analysis (padabhājaniya) is the analysis of the words of each and every training rule that proceeds by the method beginning with '‘Yo pana’ means whoever, of whatever kind...' Intermediate offenses (antarāpatti) are the offenses laid down between the training rules, beginning with 'If one lifts up a firebrand, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' Offenses (āpatti) refers to the section on offenses, stated in accordance with each and every training rule, which is free from the threefold division. Non-offenses (anāpatti) refers to the section on non-offenses that proceeds by the method beginning with 'There is no offense for one who does not know, for one who does not consent, for one who is of distracted mind, for one who is afflicted by pain, for the first offender...' The threefold division (tikaccheda) is the threefold section, having divisions such as the triad-pācittiya and triad-dukkaṭa, that proceeds by the method beginning with 'When it has gone beyond ten days, if one perceives it as having gone beyond, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya; when it has gone beyond ten days, if one is in doubt... when it has gone beyond ten days, if one perceives it as not having gone beyond, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya.' Therein (tattha) means among those—the basis, matrix, and so on.

Evaṃ [M 1.0136] anekanayasamalaṅkataṃ saṅgītippakāraṃ dassetvā “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo…pe… imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti buddhavacanaṃ dhammavinayādibhedena vavatthapetvā saṅgāyantena mahākassapappamukhena vasīgaṇena anekacchariyapātubhāvapaṭimaṇḍitāya saṅgītiyā imassa dīghāgamassa dhammabhāvo, majjhimabuddhavacanādibhāvo ca vavatthāpitoti dassento “evameta”ntiādimāha. Sādhāraṇavacanena dassitepi hi “yadatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetuṃ idamārabhati, soyeva padhānavasena dassito”ti ācariyehi ayaṃ sambandho vutto. Aparo nayo – heṭṭhā vuttesu ekavidhādibhedabhinnesu pakāresu dhammavinayādibhāvo saṅgītikārake heva saṅgītikāle vavatthāpito, na pacchā kappanamattasiddhoti dassento “evameta”ntiādimāhātipi vattabbo. Na kevalaṃ yathāvuttappakārameva vavatthāpetvā saṅgītaṃ, atha kho aññampīti dasseti “na kevalañcā”tiādinā. Udānasaṅgaho nāma paṭhamapārājikādīsu āgatānaṃ vinītavatthuādīnaṃ saṅkhepato saṅgahadassanavasena dhammasaṅgāhakehi ṭhapitā –

Having thus shown the manner of the recitation, which is well adorned with many methods, and having established the Buddha's word—"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya... these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma"—by way of the distinction of Dhamma, Vinaya, and so on, the commentator, indicating that at the time of the recitation, which was adorned with the manifestation of many wonders, the state of this Dīgha Nikāya as Dhamma and its state as the Buddha's word, such as the Majjhima Nikāya, were established by the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa who were reciting, said the words beginning with "Thus, this...". Indeed, although it was shown by a common expression, this connection was stated by the teachers: "For the meaning of which this is undertaken to explain, that very meaning is shown by way of the principal method." Another method: it is also said that the commentator, indicating that among the types distinguished by the one-fold division, etc., stated below, the state of being Dhamma, Vinaya, and so on was established at the time of the recitation only by the reciters themselves, and was not accomplished later merely by conjecture, said the words beginning with "Thus, this...". He shows with the words beginning with "Not only..." that it was not recited having established only the aforesaid types, but rather, it was recited having established other types as well. What is called the Udāna Collection are the verses established by the compilers of the Dhamma by way of showing a concise collection of the Vinītavatthu (decided cases), etc., that appear in the first Pārājika, etc. –

“Makkaṭī [V 1.0121] vajjiputtā ca, gihī naggo ca titthiyā;

Dārikuppalavaṇṇā ca, byañjanehi pare duve”ti. ādikā (pārā. 66); –

The verses beginning with: "The she-monkey and the Vajjiputtas, the layman, the naked ascetic, the girl Uppalavaṇṇā, and the two after by their characteristics." –

Gāthāyo. Vuccamānassa hi vuttassa vā atthassa vippakiṇṇabhāvena pavattituṃ adatvā uddhaṃ dānaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ, saṅgahavacananti attho. Sīlakkhandhavaggamūlapariyāyavaggādivasena vaggasaṅgaho. Vaggoti hi dhammasaṅgāhakeheva katā suttasamudāyassa samaññā. Uttarimanussapeyyālanīlapeyyālādivasena peyyālasaṅgaho. Pātuṃ rakkhituṃ, vitthārituṃ vā alanti hi peyyālaṃ, saṅkhipitvā dassanavacanaṃ. Aṅguttaranikāyādīsu nipātasaṅgaho, gāthaṅgādivasena nipātanaṃ. Samudāyakaraṇañhi nipāto. Devatāsaṃyuttādivasena (saṃ. ni. 1.1) saṃyuttasaṅgaho. Vaggasamudāye eva dhammasaṅgāhakehi katā saṃyuttasamaññā. Mūlapaṇṇāsakādivasena paṇṇāsasaṅgaho, paññāsa paññāsa suttāni gaṇetvā saṅgahoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ādisaddena tassaṃ tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ dissamānaṃ saṅgītikārakavacanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Udānasaṅgaha…pe… paṇṇāsasaṅgahādīhi anekavidhaṃ tathā. Sattahi māsehīti kiriyāpavagge tatiyā “ekāheneva [M 1.0137] bārāṇasiṃ pāyāsi. Navahi māsehi vihāraṃ niṭṭhāpesī”tiādīsu viya. Kiriyāya āsuṃ pariniṭṭhāpanañhi kiriyāpavaggo.

These are verses. Indeed, without allowing the meaning of what is being said or has been said to proceed in a scattered manner, `udāna` means guarding upwards; it is a word of collection—this is the meaning. The collection by chapters (`vaggasaṅgaho`) is by way of the Sīlakkhandhavagga, Mūlapariyāyavagga, and so on. For 'vagga' is a designation for a collection of suttas made only by the compilers of the Dhamma. The collection by abbreviation (`peyyālasaṅgaho`) is by way of the Uttarimanussapeyyāla, Nīlapeyyāla, and so on. For `peyyāla` means that which is able to guard or to expand; it is a word that shows concisely. In the Aṅguttaranikāya and others, there is the collection by sections (`nipātasaṅgaho`); `nipātana` is by way of verse-sections and so on. For `nipāto` is the making of a collection. The collection by connection (`saṃyuttasaṅgaho`) is by way of the Devatāsaṃyutta and so on. The designation 'saṃyutta' was made by the compilers of the Dhamma only for a collection of chapters. The collection by fifties (`paṇṇāsasaṅgaho`) is by way of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka and so on; it is said that this is a collection made by counting fifty suttas at a time. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), he includes the words of the reciters seen in the various Pāḷi texts. Similarly, through the Udāna collection... the collection of fifties, etc., it is of many kinds. In "sattahi māsehi" (by seven months), the third case ending is in the sense of completion of an action (`kiriyāpavagge`), as in "He reached Bārāṇasī in just one day," and "He completed the monastery in nine months," and so on. For `kiriyāpavagga` is the swift completion of an action.

Tadā anekacchariyapātubhāvadassanena sādhūnaṃ pasādajananatthamāha “saṅgītipariyosāne cassā”tiādi. Assa buddhavacanassa saṅgītipariyosāne sañjātappamodā viya, sādhukāraṃ dadamānā viya ca saṅkampi…pe… pāturahesunti sambandho. Viyāti hi ubhayattha yojetabbaṃ. Pavattane, pavattanāya vā samatthaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ. Udakapariyantanti pathavīsandhārakaudakapariyosānaṃ katvā, saha tena udakena, taṃ vā udakaṃ āhaccāti vuttaṃ hoti, tena ekadesakampanaṃ nivāreti. Saṅkampīti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ gacchantī suṭṭhu kampi. Sampakampīti uddhamadho ca gacchantī sammā pakārena kampi. Sampavedhīti catūsu disāsu gacchantī suṭṭhu bhiyyo pavedhi. Evaṃ etena padattayena chappakāraṃ pathavīcalanaṃ dasseti. Atha vā puratthimato, pacchimato ca unnamanaonamanavasena saṅkampi. Uttarato, dakkhiṇato ca unnamanaonamanavasena sampakampi. Majjhimato, pariyantato ca unnamanaonamanavasena sampavedhi. Evampi chappakāraṃ pathavīcalanaṃ dasseti, yaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ –-

Then, for the purpose of generating faith in the virtuous by showing the manifestation of many wonders, the commentator said the words beginning with "At the conclusion of the recitation of this...". The connection is: at the conclusion of the recitation of this Buddha's word, the earth trembled... and so on... and wonders became manifest, as if with joy arisen and as if giving cries of "Sādhu!". Indeed, the word 'viya' (as if) should be applied in both places. `Udakapariyantaṃ` (water-bounded) means having made the earth-supporting water its limit, together with that water, or having struck that water; this is what is said. By this, he prevents a partial trembling. `Saṅkampi` means, going higher and higher, it trembled well. `Sampakampi` means, going up and down, it trembled in a proper manner. `Sampavedhi` means, going in the four directions, it trembled well and exceedingly. Thus, by this triad of words, he shows the six kinds of earth-quaking. Alternatively, `saṅkampi` means it trembled by way of rising and sinking from the east and west. `Sampakampi` means it trembled by way of rising and sinking from the north and south. `Sampavedhi` means it trembled by way of rising and sinking from the middle and the edge. In this way too, he shows the six kinds of earth-quaking, concerning which it is said in the commentaries: –

“Puratthimato unnamati pacchimato onamati, pacchimato unnamati puratthimato onamati, uttarato unnamati dakkhiṇato onamati, dakkhiṇato unnamati uttarato onamati[V 1.0122], majjhimato unnamati pariyantato onamati, pariyantato unnamati majjhimato onamatīti evaṃ chappakāraṃ…pe… akampitthā”ti (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 71).

"From the east it rises up, from the west it sinks down; from the west it rises up, from the east it sinks down; from the north it rises up, from the south it sinks down; from the south it rises up, from the north it sinks down; from the middle it rises up, from the edge it sinks down; from the edge it rises up, from the middle it sinks down—thus in six ways... it trembled."

Accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttāni acchariyāni, pupphavassacelukkhepādīni aññāyapi sā samaññāya pākaṭāti dassento āha “yā loke”tiādi. Yā paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti dhammasaṅgāhakehi mahākassapādīhi pañcahi satehi yena katā saṅgītā, tena pañca satāni etissāti “pañcasatā”ti ca thereheva katattā therā mahākassapādayo etissā, therehi vā katāti “therikā”ti ca loke pavuccati, ayaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāmāti sambandho.

`Acchariyāni` (wonders) are things fit for a snap of the fingers, such as showers of flowers, the tossing up of cloths, and so on. Indicating that this recitation is also famous in the world by another designation, the commentator said the words beginning with "That which in the world...". The connection is as follows: That First Great Recitation, which was recited by the five hundred compilers of the Dhamma headed by Mahākassapa, is called in the world both 'Pañcasatā' (of the Five Hundred)—because there were five hundred participants in it—and 'Therikā' (of the Elders)—because it was conducted only by the Elders, meaning the Elders such as Mahākassapa participated in it, or because it was conducted by the Elders. This is named the First Great Recitation.

Evaṃ [M 1.0138] paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti dassetvā yadatthaṃ sā idha dassitā, idāni taṃ nidānaṃ nigamanavasena dassento “imissā”tiādimāha. Ādinikāyassāti suttantapiṭakapariyāpannesu pañcasu nikāyesu ādibhūtassa dīghanikāyassa. Khuddakapariyāpanno hi vinayo paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “suttanta piṭake”ti. Tenāti tathāvuttattā, iminā yathāvuttapaṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ tathāvacanameva sandhāya mayā heṭṭhā evaṃ vuttanti pubbāparasambandhaṃ, yathāvuttavitthāravacanassa vā guṇaṃ dassetīti.

Having thus shown the First Great Council, and now, wishing to show by way of conclusion that introduction for the purpose of which that Council was shown here, he said the words beginning with 'imissā'. 'Ādinikāyassa' means: of the Dīgha Nikāya, which is the first among the five Nikāyas included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Indeed, the Vinaya, which is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya, was recited first. For thus it was said: 'in the Suttanta Piṭaka'. 'Tena' means: because it was spoken thus. By this, with reference to that very speech spoken in that manner in the aforementioned First Great Council, it was said thus by me below. Thus, he shows the connection between the preceding and the following, or he shows the quality of the aforementioned detailed statement.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya paramasukhumagambhīraduranubodhatthaparidīpanāya suvimalavipulapaññāveyyattiyajananāya ajjavamaddavasoraccasaddhāsatidhitibuddhikhanti vīriyādidhammasamaṅginā sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye asaṅgāsaṃhīravisāradañāṇacārinā anekappabhedasakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhinā mahāgaṇinā mahāveyyākaraṇena ñāṇābhivaṃsadhammasenāpatināmatherena mahādhammarājādhirājagarunā katāya sādhuvilāsiniyā nāma līnatthapakāsaniyā bāhiranidānavaṇṇanāya līnatthapakāsanā.

Thus, in the Sādhuvilāsinī, the sub-commentary which clarifies hidden meanings, composed by the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati—who is the teacher of the great king of kings of righteousness, a great grammarian, one with a large following, one who has plunged into the thickets of the numerous divisions of his own doctrine and other doctrines, one who fares with unattached, unhindered, and expert knowledge in the three Piṭakas together with their commentaries, and one endowed with qualities such as straightforwardness, gentleness, graciousness, faith, mindfulness, stability, wisdom, patience, and energy—the clarification of hidden meanings of the commentary on the external introduction of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya—which illuminates the meaning that is supreme, subtle, profound, and difficult to penetrate, and which generates the faculty of pure and extensive wisdom—is completed.

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Introductory Discourse is concluded.

1. Brahmajālasuttaṃ

1. The Brahmajāla Sutta

Paribbājakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse concerning Wanderers

1. Ettāvatā [V 1.0123][M 1.0139] ca paramasaṇhasukhumagambhīraduddasānekavidhanayasamalaṅkataṃ brahmajālassa sādhāraṇato bāhiranidānaṃ dassetvā idāni abbhantaranidānaṃ saṃvaṇṇento atthādhigamassa sunikkhittapadamūlakattā, sunikkhittapadabhāvassa ca “idameva”nti sabhāvavibhāvanena padavibhāgena sādhetabbattā paṭhamaṃ tāva padavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha eva”ntiādimāha. Padavibhāgena hi “idaṃ nāma etaṃ pada”nti vijānanena taṃtaṃpadānurūpaṃ liṅgavibhatti vacana kālapayogādikaṃ sammāpatiṭṭhāpanato yathāvuttassa padassa sunikkhittatā hoti, tāya ca atthassa samadhigamiyatā. Yathāha “sunikkhittassa bhikkhave – padabyañjanassa atthopi sunayohotī”tiādi. Apica sambandhato, padato, padavibhāgato, padatthato anuyogato, parihārato cāti chahākārehi atthavaṇṇanā kātabbā. Tattha sambandho nāma desanāsambandho, yaṃ lokiyā “ummugghāto”tipi vadanti, so pana pāḷiyā nidānapāḷivasena, nidānapāḷiyā ca saṅgītivasena veditabbo. Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiṃ dassentena hi nidānapāḷiyā sambandho dassito, tasmā padādivaseneva saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karonto “eva”ntiādimāha. Ettha ca “evanti nipātapadantiādinā padato, padavibhāgato ca saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karoti padānaṃ tabbisesānañca dassitattā. Padavibhāgoti hi padānaṃ visesoyeva adhippeto, na padaviggaho. Padāni ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgo. Atha vā padavibhāgo ca padaviggaho ca padavibhāgoti ekasesavasena padapadaviggahāpi padavibhāgasaddena vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Padaviggahato pana “bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho”tiādinā upari saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karissati, tathā padatthānuyogaparihārehipi. Evanti ettha luttaniddiṭṭhaiti-saddo ādiattho antarāsadda ca saddādīnampi saṅgahitattā, nayaggahaṇena vā te gahitā. Tenāha “metiādīni nāmapadānī”ti. Itarathā hi antarāsaddaṃ ca saddādīnampi nipātabhāvo vattabbo siyā. Metiādīnīti ettha pana ādi-saddena yāva [M 1.0140] paṭisaddo[V 1.0124], tāva tadavasiṭṭhāyeva saddā saṅgahitā. Paṭīti upasaggapadaṃ patisaddassa kāriyabhāvato.

1. And by this much, having shown the external introduction—which is common to the Brahmajāla Sutta and is adorned with many and various methods that are supreme, fine, subtle, profound, and difficult to see—now, the commentator, wishing to commentate on the internal introduction, said the words beginning with 'tattha evaṃ' in order to first show the analysis of words, because the attainment of the meaning has well-placed words as its root, and because the state of having well-placed words is to be accomplished by the analysis of words that clarifies their intrinsic nature. For by analysis of words, through knowing 'this particular word is that word', and because of correctly establishing the gender, case, number, tense, usage, and so on, in accordance with each respective word, there comes to be the well-placed nature of the aforesaid word, and through that, the meaning becomes fully attainable. As was said: 'Monks, of a well-placed word and syllable, the meaning too is easy to deduce,' and so on. Moreover, the commentary on the meaning should be done in six ways: by connection, by word, by analysis of the word, by the meaning of the word, by questioning, and by answering. Among these, 'connection' is the connection of the discourse, which worldly grammarians also call 'ummugghāta'. And that is to be understood by way of the introductory Pāḷi to the Pāḷi text, and by way of the Council to the introductory Pāḷi. Indeed, the connection with the introductory Pāḷi was shown by the commentator when showing the First Great Council. Therefore, wishing to commentate by way of the initial words and so on, he said the words beginning with 'evaṃ'. And here, with the words beginning 'evaṃ is a particle-word', he makes the commentary by way of the word and by way of the analysis of the word, because the words and their specifics are shown. Indeed, by 'analysis of the word' is intended only the specifics of the words, not the etymological analysis of the word. 'Words and analysis of the word' are 'analysis of the word'. Or, 'analysis of the word and etymological analysis of the word' are 'analysis of the word'; thus, by way of the 'ekasesa' (leaving one) compound, it should be understood that even the etymological analysis of the word is stated by the term 'analysis of the word'. But he will make the commentary later by way of etymological analysis with phrases beginning 'bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho' ('the community of monks'), and likewise by way of word-meaning, questioning, and answering. Here, in 'evaṃ', the 'iti' sound which is indicated as elided has the meaning of 'and so on' (ādi), because the words 'antarā', 'ca', and so on are also included; or, they are included by taking it as a methodological pointer. Therefore, he said, 'me and so on are noun-words'. Otherwise, the state of being a particle would have to be stated for the words 'antarā', 'ca', and so on as well. But here in 'me and so on', by the word 'ādi' (and so on), the remaining words up to the word 'paṭi' are included. 'Paṭi' is a prefix-word, because of the word 'paṭi' being a derivative.

Idāni atthuddhārakkamena padatthato saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karonto “atthato panā”tiādimāha. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne sotūnaṃ saṃvaṇṇanānayakosallatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāppakārā vattabbā. Kathaṃ?

Now, the commentator, wishing to make a commentary by way of the word-meaning according to the sequence of extracting the meaning, said the words beginning with 'atthato pana'. But in this place, the various types of commentary should be stated for the purpose of the listeners' skill in the method of commentary. How?

Ekanāḷikā kathā ca, caturassā tathāpi ca;

Nisinnavattikā ceva, tidhā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ vade.

The Ekanāḷikā discourse, and likewise the Caturassā; and the Nisinnavattikā discourse as well. One should speak of the commentary as threefold.

Tattha pāḷiṃ vatvā ekekapadassa atthakathanaṃ ekāya nāḷiyā minitasadisattā, ekekaṃ vā padaṃ nāḷaṃ mūlaṃ, ekamekaṃ padaṃ vā nāḷikā atthaniggamanamaggo etissāti katvā ekanāḷikā nāma. Paṭipakkhaṃ dassetvā, paṭipakkhassa ca upamaṃ dassetvā, sapakkhaṃ dassetvā, sapakkhassa ca upamaṃ dassetvā, kathanaṃ catūhi bhāgehi vuttattā, cattāro vā rassā sallakkhaṇūpāyā etissāti katvā caturassā nāma, visabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānaṃ gantvā puna sabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānagamanaṃ nisīdāpetvā patiṭṭhāpetvā āvattanayuttattā, niyamato vā nisinnassa āraddhassa vatto saṃvatto etissāti katvā nisinnavattikā nāma, yathāraddhassa atthassa visuṃ visuṃ pariyosānāpi niyuttāti vuttaṃ hoti, sodāharaṇā pana kathā aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāya taṭṭīkāyaṃ ekādasanipāte gopālakasuttavaṇṇanāto gahetabbā.

Therein, after stating the Pāḷi, the explanation of the meaning of each single word is called Ekanāḷikā because of its similarity to being measured out with a single measure; or, because for this discourse each single word is a stalk or root; or, for this discourse each single word is a channel, a path for the exit of the meaning. The explanation which proceeds by showing the opposing side, showing a simile for the opposing side, showing one's own side, and showing a simile for one's own side, is called Caturassā because it is spoken in four parts; or, because for this discourse there are four marks, which are means of recognition. Having reached a conclusion by way of dissimilar phenomena, and then again bringing it to a conclusion by way of similar phenomena—because it is connected with returning after having been made to settle and be established—it is called Nisinnavattikā; or, because for this discourse there is a firm and established progression of what has been undertaken. It is said that even when the meanings undertaken are concluded separately, they are connected again. But these discourses, together with examples, should be taken from the commentary on the Gopālaka Sutta in the Ekādasakanipāta in the Aṅguttara Commentary and its sub-commentary.

Bhedakathā tatvakathā, pariyāyakathāpi ca;

Iti atthakkame vidvā, tidhā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ vade.

The analytical discourse (Bhedakathā), the discourse on reality (Tatvakathā), and the discourse on synonyms (Pariyāyakathā) as well; thus in the sequence of meaning, a wise person should speak of the commentary as threefold.

Tattha pakatiādivicāraṇā bhedakathā yathā “bujjhatīti buddho”tiādi. Sarūpavicāraṇā tatvakathā yathā “buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako”tiādi (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 97; paṭi. ma. 1.161). Vevacanavicāraṇā pariyāyakathā yathā “buddho bhagavā sabbaññū lokanāyako”tiādi (netti. 38 vevacanāhāravibhaṅganissito pāḷi).

Therein, the examination of the nature, etc., is the analytical explanation, as in: 'He understands, therefore he is the Buddha,' and so on. The examination of the intrinsic nature is the explanation of reality, as in: 'The Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-arisen, without a teacher,' and so on. The examination of synonyms is the explanation by synonyms, as in: 'The Buddha, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, the Leader of the World,' and so on.

Payojanañca piṇḍattho, anusandhi ca codanā;

Parihāro ca sabbattha, pañcadhā vaṇṇanaṃ vade.

The purpose, the condensed meaning, the connection, the objection, and the resolution—a wise person should state the explanation to be fivefold in all instances.

Tattha [V 1.0125][M 1.0141] payojanaṃ nāma desanāphalaṃ, taṃ pana sutamayañāṇādi. Piṇḍattho nāma vippakiṇṇassa atthassa suvijānanatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā kathanaṃ. Anusandhi nāma pucchānusandhādi. Codanā nāma yathāvuttassa vacanassa virodhikathanaṃ. Parihāro nāma tassa avirodhikathanaṃ.

Therein, 'purpose' is the fruit of the teaching; and that is knowledge born of hearing, and so on. 'Condensed meaning' is the explanation that combines a scattered meaning for the purpose of knowing it well. 'Connection' is the connection to a question, and so on. 'Objection' is stating the contradiction of what has been said. 'Resolution' is stating its non-contradiction.

Ummugghāto padañceva, padattho padaviggaho;

Cālanā paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, chadhā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ vade. (vajira. ṭī. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītivaṇṇanā);

The introduction, the word, the meaning of the word, the analysis of the word, the challenge, and the presentation of the reply—a wise person should state the commentary to be sixfold.

Tattha ajjhattikādinidānaṃ ummugghāto. “Evamida”nti nānāvidhena padavisesatākathanaṃ padaṃ, saddatthādhippāyatthādi padattho. Anekadhā nibbacanaṃ padaviggaho. Cālanā nāma codanā. Paccupaṭṭhānaṃ parihāro.

Therein, the internal introduction, and so on, is 'introduction' (ummugghāto). The statement of a word's distinction in various ways, such as 'thus it is,' is 'word' (padaṃ). The literal meaning, intended meaning, and so on, is 'meaning of the word' (padattho). Manifold derivation is 'analysis of the word' (padaviggaho). 'Challenge' (cālanā) is objection (codanā). 'Presentation of the reply' (paccupaṭṭhānaṃ) is resolution (parihāro).

Samuṭṭhānaṃ padattho ca, bhāvānuvādavidhayo;

Virodho parihāro ca, nigamananti aṭṭhadhā.

The origin, the meaning of the word, the intention, the methods of initial and subsequent statement, the contradiction, the resolution, and the conclusion—thus it is eightfold.

Tattha samuṭṭhānanti ajjhattikādinidānaṃ. Padatthoti adhippetānadhippetādivasena anekadhā padassa attho. Bhāvoti adhippāyo. Anuvādavidhayoti paṭhamavacanaṃ vidhi, tadāvikaraṇavasena pacchā vacanaṃ anuvādo, visesanavisesyānaṃ vā vidhānuvāda samaññā. Virodhoti atthanicchayanatthaṃ codanā. Parihāroti tassā sodhanā. Nigamananti anusandhiyā anurūpaṃ appanā.

Therein, 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna) is the internal introduction, and so on. 'Meaning of the word' (padattho) is the meaning of a word in many ways, by way of the intended, unintended, and so on. 'Intention' (bhāva) is the speaker's intention. 'Methods of initial and subsequent statement' (anuvādavidhayo) are: the initial statement is the 'method' (vidhi), and by way of clarifying that, the subsequent statement is the 'restatement' (anuvādo); or it is the designation 'method-restatement' for qualifiers and the qualified. 'Contradiction' (virodho) is an objection for the purpose of determining the meaning. 'Resolution' (parihāro) is the clearing up of that objection. 'Conclusion' (nigamana) is the bringing to a conclusion in conformity with the connection.

Ādito tassa nidānaṃ, vattabbaṃ tappayojanaṃ;

Piṇḍattho ceva padattho, sambandho adhippāyako;

Codanā sodhanā ceti, aṭṭhadhā vaṇṇanaṃ vade.

At the beginning, its introduction and its purpose should be stated. The condensed meaning, the meaning of the words, the connection, the intention, the objection, and the clarification—thus the author of a commentary should state the explanation to be eightfold.

Tattha sambandho nāma pubbāparasambandho, yo “anusandhī”ti vuccati. Sesā vuttatthāva, evamādinā tattha tatthāgate saṃvaṇṇanāppakāre ñatvā sabbattha yathārahaṃ vicetabbāti.

Therein, 'connection' (sambandha) is the connection between what precedes and what follows, which is called 'sequential connection' (anusandhi). The remaining terms have meanings that have already been stated. Thus, having known the types of commentary that appear in various places by this method, they should be investigated appropriately everywhere.

Evamanekatthappabhedatā payogatova ñātabbāti tabbasena taṃ samatthetuṃ “tathā hesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā ayaṃ saddo imassatthassa vācakoti saṅketavavatthitāyeva saddā taṃ tadatthassa vācakā[V 1.0126], saṅketo ca nāma payogavasena siddhoti dassetumpi idaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evamīdisesu. Nanu ca –

Thus, the fact that it has a diversity of meanings is to be known only through usage. Therefore, to establish this by means of that usage, 'tathā hesā,' etc., was stated. Alternatively, this was stated also to show that: 'This word signifies this meaning'—thus, words signify their respective meanings only as established by convention, and convention is established by means of usage. This should be understood. It should be understood thus in such cases. But is it not so that—

“Yathāpi [M 1.0142] puppharāsimhā, kayirā mālāguṇe bahū;

Evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti. (dha. pa. 53);

As from a heap of flowers many garlands can be made, so by one born mortal, much good should be done.

Ettha evaṃ-saddena upamākārasseva vuttattā ākāratthoyeva evaṃ-saddo siyāti? Na, visesasabbhāvato. “Evaṃ byā kho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 234, 396) hi ākāramattavācakoyeva ākāratthoti adhippeto, na pana ākāravisesavācako. Ettha hi kiñcāpi puppharāsisadisato manussūpapatti sappurisūpanissaya saddhammasavana yonisomanasikārabhogasampattiādidānādipuññakiriyāhetusamudāyato sobhāsugandhatādiguṇayogena mālāguṇasadisiyo bahukā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena sattena kattabbāti atthassa jotitattā puppharāsimālāguṇāva upamā nāma upamīyati etāyāti katvā, tesaṃ upamākāro ca yathāsaddena aniyamato jotito, tasmā “evaṃ-saddo niyamato upamākāranigamanattho”ti vattuṃ yuttaṃ, tathāpi so upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamāva hoti nissayabhūtaṃ tamantarena nissitabhūtassa upamākārassa alabbhamānattāti adhippāyenāha “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti. Atha vā upamīyanaṃ sadisīkaraṇanti katvā puppharāsimālāguṇehi sadisabhāvasaṅkhāto upamākāroyeva upamā nāma. “Saddhammattaṃ siyopamā”ti hi vuttaṃ, tasmā ākāramattavācakova ākārattho evaṃ-saddo. Upamāsaṅkhātaākāravisesavācako pana upamātthoyevāti vuttaṃ “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti.

Here, since by the word 'evaṃ' only the mode of comparison is stated, would the word 'evaṃ' have only the meaning of 'mode'? No, because a specific distinction exists. For in passages like 'evaṃ byā kho,' the word 'evaṃ' which signifies only the bare mode is intended to have the meaning of 'mode,' but not that which signifies a specific mode. Here, because the meaning is illuminated that from the collection of causes for meritorious deeds—such as human birth, reliance on a good person, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and attainment of wealth—which is like a heap of flowers, many meritorious deeds, which are like garlands due to possessing qualities such as beauty and fragrance, should be performed by a mortal being who is subject to death, the heap of flowers and the garlands themselves are the simile, since one compares by means of them. And their mode of comparison is illuminated indefinitely by the word 'yathā'. Therefore, although it is fitting to say, 'The word “evaṃ” has the meaning of definitively concluding the mode of comparison,' nevertheless that mode of comparison, being specified, is in meaning the simile itself, because without that which is the basis, the dependent mode of comparison cannot be obtained. With this intention, the commentator said, 'it has come in the sense of a simile.' Alternatively, considering that 'comparing' is 'making similar,' the mode of comparison, designated as the state of similarity with the heap of flowers and garlands, is itself the simile. For it is said, 'Similarity of nature is a simile.' Therefore, the word 'evaṃ' that signifies only the bare mode has the meaning of 'mode.' But the word that signifies the specific mode designated as 'simile' has the meaning of 'simile.' Thus it was said, 'it has come in the sense of a simile.'

Tathā “evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā upadisanākāropi atthato upadesoyevāti āha “evaṃ…pe… upadese”ti. Evametanti ettha pana bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ tattha saṃvijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ. Tattha sampahaṃsanākāropi atthato sampahaṃsanamevāti vuttaṃ “sampahaṃsaneti. Evameva panāyanti ettha ca dosavibhāvanena gārayhavacanaṃ garahaṇaṃ, tadākāropi atthato garahaṇaṃ nāma, tasmā “garahaṇe”ti [M 1.0143] vuttaṃ. So cettha garahaṇākāro “vasalī”tiādikhuṃsanasaddasannidhānato evaṃ-saddena pakāsitoti viññāyati, yathā cettha evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jotakamattā hi nipātāti. Evamevāti ca adhunā bhāsitākāreneva. Ayaṃ [V 1.0127] vasalaguṇayogato vasalī kāḷakaṇṇī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā ṭhāne bhāsatīti sambandho. Evaṃ bhanteti sādhu bhante, suṭṭhu bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāre sanniyojitehi bhikkhūhi tattha attano ṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanameva vacanasampaṭiggaho, tadākāropi atthato vacanasampaṭiggahoyeva nāma, tenāha “vacanasampaṭiggahe”ti.

Likewise, regarding the accomplishment in deportment suitable for an ascetic, which is being instructed with phrases such as, 'Thus, in this manner, one should go forward,' the manner of instruction is, in meaning, instruction itself. Therefore, the Teacher said: 'evaṃ…pe… upadese' (Thus... in instruction). Furthermore, in the phrase 'Evam etaṃ', `sampahaṃsana` (gladdening) is the causing of elation through the various aspects of the qualities present therein, performed by those who know without distortion the meaning as spoken by the Blessed One. Therein, the manner of gladdening is also, in meaning, gladdening itself; thus it was said: 'sampahaṃsaneti' (in gladdening). And in the phrase 'Evameva panāyaṃ', censorious speech by way of pointing out a fault is `garahaṇa` (blame); that manner is also, in meaning, blame. Therefore, it was said: 'garahaṇe' (in blaming). And here, that manner of blaming is understood to be revealed by the word 'evaṃ' due to its proximity to abusive words such as 'vasalī' (outcast). It should be understood that just as it is here, so too are the manners of simile and so on revealed by the word 'evaṃ' due to the proximity of words such as 'puppharāsi' (heap of flowers) spoken by way of simile, etc. For particles are merely illuminative. And 'Evameva' means 'just in the manner of speaking praise now'. The connection is: 'This outcast (`vasalī`), this unlucky person (`kāḷakaṇṇī`), due to possessing the qualities of an outcast, speaks words of praise in any place whatsoever.' 'Evaṃ bhante' means 'Good, venerable sir; well said, venerable sir.' Here, moreover, the very acknowledgement by the bhikkhus—who have been well urged to properly listen to and apply their minds to the Dhamma—of their own established state therein is the acceptance of the word (`vacanasampaṭiggaho`). That manner is also, in meaning, the acceptance of the word itself. Therefore, he said: 'vacanasampaṭiggahe' (in the acceptance of the word).

Evaṃ byā khoti evaṃ viya kho. Evaṃ khoti hi imesaṃ padānamantare viyasaddassa byāpadesoti neruttikā “va-kārassa, ba-kāraṃ, ya-kārasaṃyogañca katvā dīghavasena padasiddhī”tipi vadanti. Ākāreti ākāramatte. Appābādhanti visabhāgavedanābhāvaṃ. Appātaṅkanti kicchajīvitakararogābhāvaṃ. Lahuṭṭhānanti niggelaññatāya lahutāyuttaṃ uṭṭhānaṃ. Balanti kāyabalaṃ. Phāsuvihāranti catūsu iriyāpathesu sukhavihāraṃ. Vitthāro dasama subhasuttaṭṭhakathāya meva (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.445) āvi bhavissati. Evañca vadehīti yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evampi samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehi. “Sādhu kira bhava”ntiādikaṃ idāni vattabbavacanaṃ, so ca vadanākāro idha evaṃ-saddena nidassīyatīti vuttaṃ “nidassane”ti. Kālāmāti kālāmagottasambandhe jane ālapati. “Ime…pe… vā”ti yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, taṃ kiṃ maññathāti attho. Samattāti paripūritā. Samādinnāti samādiyitā. Saṃvattanti vā no vā saṃvattanti ettha vacanadvaye kathaṃ vo tumhākaṃ mati hotīti yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ noti evameva amhākaṃ mati ettha hoti, amhākamettha mati hoti yevātipi attho. Ettha ca tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāve sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatiggahaṇavasena “saṃvattanti no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃ-saddena vibhāvitaṃ, so ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno atthato [M 1.0144] avadhāraṇamevāti vuttaṃ “avadhāraṇe”ti. Ākāratthamaññatra sabbattha vuttanayena codanā, sodhanā ca veditabbā.

'Evaṃ byā kho' is 'evaṃ viya kho'. For the grammarians say that between these words, 'evaṃ' and 'kho', the designation 'byā' occurs for the word 'viya'. They also say that the word is formed by changing the letter 'v' to 'b', adding a 'y'-conjunct, and by means of lengthening. 'Ākāre' means in the mere manner. 'Appābādhaṃ' means the absence of disagreeable feeling. 'Appātaṅkaṃ' means the absence of disease that makes life difficult. 'Lahuṭṭhānaṃ' means, due to the absence of illness, the ability to rise endowed with lightness. 'Balaṃ' means bodily strength. 'Phāsuvihāraṃ' means dwelling comfortably in the four postures. The detailed explanation will become clear in the commentary on the tenth Subha Sutta. 'Evañca vadehi' means: 'Just as I speak, so should you speak to the ascetic Ānanda.' The words to be spoken now are 'Sādhu kira bhava…' etc., and that manner of speaking is indicated here by the word 'evaṃ'. Thus, it was said: 'nidassane' (in indicating). 'Kālāmā' is an address to the people connected with the Kālāma clan. 'Ime…pe… vā' has the meaning: 'What do you think of what I have said?' 'Samattā' means fulfilled. 'Samādinnā' means well undertaken. Regarding the pair of words 'saṃvattanti vā no vā saṃvattanti', it should be construed as: 'What is your opinion on this?' 'Evaṃ no' means: 'Just so is our opinion on this,' and it also has the meaning: 'Our opinion on this is indeed so.' And here, for the purpose of generating a conclusion about the state of those aforementioned qualities being conducive to harm and suffering, by way of seeking their agreement, the question was asked: 'Do they conduce or not? What is your opinion on this?' Because it was answered, 'Evaṃ no ettha hoti' (Just so is our opinion on this), the conclusion in that manner is clarified by the word 'evaṃ'. And that manner of those qualities conducing to harm and suffering, being determined, is in meaning determination itself. Thus, it was said: 'avadhāraṇe' (in determination). Apart from the meaning of 'manner', the objection and refutation should be understood everywhere according to the method stated.

Ādisaddena cettha idamatthapucchāparimāṇādiatthānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evaṃgatāni, evaṃvidho, evamākāro”ti ca ādīsu idamatthe, gatavidhākārasaddā pana pakārapariyāyā. Gatavidhayuttākārasadde hi lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalābharaṇā odātavatthavasanā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārenti, seyyathāpi tvaṃ etarahi sācariyakoti? No hidaṃ bho gotamā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.286) pucchāyaṃ. “Evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ (a. ni. 1.48), evamāyupariyanto”ti [V 1.0128] (pārā. 12) ca ādīsu parimāṇe. Etthāpi “sunhātā suvilittā”tiādivacanaṃ pucchā, lahuparivattaṃ, āyūnaṃ pamāṇañca parimāṇaṃ, tadākāropi atthato pucchā ca parimāṇañca nāma, tasmā etesu pucchattho, parimāṇattho ca evaṃsaddo veditabboti. Idha pana so katamesu bhavati, sabbattha vā, aniyamato padese vāti codanāya “svāyamidhā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

And here, by the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of meanings such as 'this meaning', 'question', 'measure', etc., should be understood. For instance, in phrases such as 'evaṃgatāni' (of such a condition), 'evaṃvidho' (of such a sort), and 'evamākāro' (of such a form), it is in the sense of 'this meaning'; the words 'gata', 'vidha', and 'ākāra' are synonyms for 'pakāra' (mode). For worldly people use words such as 'gata', 'vidha', and 'ākāra' in the sense of 'pakāra'. For example, in the question, 'Do they, venerable Gotama, enjoy themselves with the five strands of sensual pleasure—being well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, adorned with jeweled earrings and ornaments, and dressed in white garments—just as you do now with your teacher? — No, this is not so, venerable Gotama,' it is in the sense of a question. Similarly, in phrases like 'so swift in change' (evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ) and 'so ending its lifespan' (evamāyupariyanto), it is in the sense of measure. Here too, the expression 'well-bathed, well-anointed,' etc., is a question, while 'swift in change' and the measure of the lifespan are measure, and that manner is in meaning both question and measure. Therefore, in these instances, the word 'evaṃ' should be understood as conveying both the sense of a question and of measure. Now, in response to the objection, 'In which cases does this occur? In all cases, or in particular instances without rule?', the passage beginning 'svāyamidhā...' was stated.

Nanu ekasmiṃyeva atthe siyā, kasmā tīsupīti ca, hotu tibbidhesu atthesu, kena kimatthaṃ dīpetīti ca anuyogaṃ pariharanto “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tatthāti tesu tīsu atthesu. Ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā, nandiyāvattatipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitaaṅkusadisālocanasaṅkhātā vā ādhārādibhedavasena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā, pāḷigatiyo vā nayā, tā ca paññattianupaññatti ādivasena, saṅkhepavitthārādivasena, saṃkilesabhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissakādivasena, kusalādivasena, khandhādivasena, saṅgahādivasena, samayavimuttādivasena, ṭhapanādivasena, kusalamūlādivasena, tikapaṭṭhānādivasena ca piṭakattayānurūpaṃ nānāppakārāti nānānayā. Tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ tathā. Āsayova ajjhāsayo, te ca sassatādibhedena, tattha ca apparajakkhatādivasena anekā, attajjhāsayādayo eva vā samuṭṭhānamuppattihetu etassāti tathā, upanetabbābhāvato atthabyañjane [M 1.0145] hi sampannaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ tathā. Apica saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkharapadabyañjanaākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca sampannaṃ samannāgataṃ tathā. Atha vā viññūnaṃ hadayaṅgamato, savane atittijananato, byañjanarasavasena paramagambhīrabhāvato, vicāraṇe atittijananato, attharasavasena ca sampannaṃ sādurasaṃ tathā.

Should it not be in just one meaning? Why then should it be in three? Let it be that there are three kinds of meanings; by which is what meaning shown? Avoiding such an inquiry, the commentator said, 'Therein,' etc. 'Therein' means: among those three meanings. The methods are of various kinds, designated as unity, diversity, non-activity, and 'such is the nature'; or designated as Nandiyāvatta, Tipukkhala, the lion's play, the hook, and observing the direction; differentiated by their bases and so on, they are diverse methods. Or, the ways of the Pāli texts are the methods. And these methods are of various kinds in accordance with the three Piṭakas: by way of primary designation and subsequent designation, the brief and the detailed, what is associated with defilements and what is worldly and a mixture of both, the wholesome, etc., by way of the aggregates, collections, temporal liberation, establishment, wholesome roots, and the threefold framework of the Paṭṭhāna; thus they are 'various methods.' By these, it is skillful, subtle, and minute. Thus. Inclination itself is underlying tendency. And these are many, distinguished by eternalism, etc., and therein, by way of the state of having little dust, etc. Alternatively, because its cause of origin is one's own underlying tendencies, etc., it is thus named. Because there is nothing to be brought in, it is complete and perfect in meaning and expression. Thus. Moreover, it is endowed with six terms of meaning—by way of showing in brief, showing in detail, explanation, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with six terms of expression—by way of letters, words, phrases, modes, etymology, and exposition. Thus it is complete and endowed. Alternatively, because it reaches the hearts of the wise, because it causes insatiability upon hearing, by the power of the flavor of the expression; because of its state of being extremely profound, because it causes insatiability upon investigation, by the power of the flavor of the meaning, it is complete and of delightful taste. Thus.

Pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ “paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato pāṭihāriya”nti vadanti. Bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi, ye haritabbā bodhimūleyeva savāsanasakalasaṃkilesānaṃ pahīnattā. Puthujjanānampi ca vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe satiyeva iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā puthujjanesu pavattavohārenapi na sakkā idha “pāṭihāriya”nti vattuṃ, sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatāva kilesā paṭipakkhā saṃsārapaṅkanimuggassa sattanikāyassa samuddharitukāmato, tasmā tesaṃ veneyyagatakilesasaṅkhātānaṃ paṭipakkhānaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyanti vuttaṃ assa, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ.

The teachers say that the etymological meaning of the word 'pāṭihāriya' is: 'it is a miracle (pāṭihāriya) because it removes opponents, because it dispels defilements such as lust.' However, the Blessed One has no opponents such as lust to be removed, since all defilements along with their latent tendencies were eradicated at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Even in ordinary beings, the psychic power of iddhividha arises only when the mind is free from corruptions, endowed with the eight qualities, and its opposing forces have been destroyed. Therefore, even by the common usage applicable to ordinary individuals, it is not possible to use the term 'pāṭihāriya' here. But if, for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, the defilements inherent in those to be trained are the opponents—because of his desire to uplift the multitude of beings sunk in the mire of saṃsāra—then it could be said that 'pāṭihāriya' is so-called because of the removal of those opponents, which are the defilements inherent in those to be trained. This being so, this is fitting.

Atha [V 1.0129] vā bhagavato sāsanassa paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ titthiyabhūtānaṃ paṭipakkhānaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyantipi yujjati. Kāmañcettha titthiyā haritabbā nāssu, tesaṃ pana santānagatadiṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthatākāraṇena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīsaṅkhātehi tīhipi pāṭihāriyehi te haritā apanītā nāma honti. Paṭīti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 985; cūḷani. 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpaklese katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, tadeva dīghavasena, sakatthavuttipaccayavasena vā pāṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upaklesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā tadaññesaṃ haraṇaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ vuttanayena. Iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo hi vigatūpaklesena, katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, hatesu ca attano upaklesesu parasattānaṃ upaklesaharaṇāni ca hontīti tadubhayampi nibbacanaṃ yujjati.

Alternatively, the opponents of the Blessed One's Dispensation are the sectarians (titthiyā); it is also fitting to call it 'pāṭihāriya' because of the removal of these sectarian opponents. Although the sectarians themselves might not be removed here, they are considered removed or dispelled by the three miracles—namely, psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction—by way of removing the views inherent in their mental continuum, and due to their inability to clarify their own views. Or, this word 'paṭi' conveys the meaning of 'afterward,' as in phrases like 'after he had entered, another brahmin arrived.' Therefore, 'paṭihāriya' is that which is to be practiced afterward, with a concentrated mind free from defilements, by one whose task is accomplished. The same word, by way of lengthening the vowel, or by way of a suffix indicating its own meaning, becomes 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, in the manner stated, after one's own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the paths, the removal of others' defilements is 'pāṭihāriya.' For psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction should be practiced again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from defilements and whose task is accomplished. And with the destruction of one's own defilements, the removal of the defilements of other beings also occurs; thus, both explanations are justified.

Apica [M 1.0146] yathāvuttehi nibbacanehi iddhiādesanānusāsanīsaṅkhāto samudāyo paṭihāriyaṃ nāma. Ekekaṃ pana tasmiṃ bhavaṃ “pāṭihāriya”nti vuccati visesatthajotakapaccayantarena saddaracanāvisesasambhavato, paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ, maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ, tasmiṃ vā nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Vicitrā hi taddhitavutti. Tassa pana iddhiādesanānusāsanībhedena, visayabhedena ca bahuvidhassa bhagavato desanāya labbhamānattā “vividhapāṭihāriyanti vuttaṃ. Bhagavā hi kadāci iddhivasenāpi desanaṃ karoti nimmitabuddhena saha pucchāvissajjanādīsu, kadāci ādesanāvasenāpi āmagandhabrāhmaṇassa dhammadesanādīsu (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.241), yebhuyyena pana anusāsaniyā. Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyañhi buddhānaṃ satataṃ dhammadesanā. Iti taṃtaṃdesanākārena anekavidhapāṭihāriyatā desanāya labbhati. Ayamattho upari ekādasamassa kevaṭṭasuttassa vaṇṇanāya (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.481) āvi bhavissati. Atha vā tassa vividhassāpi pāṭihāriyassa bhagavato desanāya saṃsūcanato “vividhapāṭihāriya”nti vuttaṃ, anekavidhapāṭihāriyadassananti attho.

Furthermore, the collection consisting of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, according to the explanations given, is called 'paṭihāriya.' However, each individual instance within that collection is called 'pāṭihāriya' due to the possibility of a special word-formation with an additional suffix indicating a specific meaning. Alternatively, 'pāṭihāriya' can refer to the fourth jhāna and the path, because they remove opposing forces; or what arises from them; or what is marked by them; or what comes from them. Indeed, the use of secondary derivatives (taddhita) is varied. Furthermore, because this manifold 'pāṭihāriya'—distinguished by psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, as well as by differences in subject matter—is obtained through the Blessed One's teaching, it is said to be 'manifold wonders.' For the Blessed One sometimes teaches by means of psychic power, as in dialogues and responses with a created Buddha; sometimes by means of mind-reading, as in the Dhamma teaching to the Brahmin Āmagandha; but mostly by means of instruction. Indeed, the wonder of instruction for the Buddhas is their constant teaching of the Dhamma. Thus, the teaching acquires the quality of manifold wonders through various modes of instruction. This meaning will become clear later in the commentary on the eleventh Kevaṭṭa Sutta. Alternatively, it is said to be 'manifold wonders' because the Blessed One's teaching indicates this manifold 'pāṭihāriya'; the meaning is the display of many kinds of wonders.

Dhammaniruttiyāva bhagavati dhammaṃ desente sabbesaṃ suṇantānaṃ nānābhāsitānaṃ taṃtaṃbhāsānurūpato desanā sotapathamāgacchatīti āha “sabba…pe… māgacchanta”nti. Sotameva sotapatho, savanaṃ vā sotaṃ, tassa patho tathā, sotadvāranti attho. Sabbākārenāti yathādesitākārena. Ko samattho viññātuṃ, asamatthoyeva, tasmāti pāṭhaseso. Panāti ekaṃsatthe[V 1.0130], tena saddhāsatidhitivīriyādibalasaṅkhātena sabbathāmena ekaṃseneva sotukāmatāsaṅkhātakusalacchandassa jananaṃ dasseti. Janetvāpīti ettha pi-saddo, api-saddo vā sambhāvanattho “buddhopi buddhabhāvaṃ bhāvetvā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha 1; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1; a. ni. aṭṭha 1.paṭhamaganthārambhakathā) viya, tena “sabbathāmena ekaṃseneva sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi nāma ekenākārena sutaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana aññathā”ti tathāsute dhamme sambhāvanaṃ karoti. Keci pana “edisesu garahattho”ti vadanti, tadayuttameva garahatthassa avijjamānattā, vijjamānatthasseva ca upasagganipātānaṃ jotakattā. “Nānānayanipuṇa”ntiādinā [M 1.0147] hi sabbappakārena sotumasakkuṇeyyabhāvena dhammassa idha sambhāvanameva karoti, tasmā “api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchatī”tiādīsuyeva (dha. pa. 187) garahatthasambhavesu garahattho veditabboti. Api-saddo ca īdisesu ṭhānesu nipātoyeva, na upasaggo. Tathā hi “api-saddo ca nipātapakkhiko kātabbo, yattha kiriyāvācakato pubbo na hotī”ti akkharacintakā vadanti. Mayāpīti ettha pana na kevalaṃ mayāva, atha kho aññehipi tathārūpehīti sampiṇḍanattho gahetabbo.

When the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma by means of the Dhamma-expression itself, the teaching reaches the path of hearing of all listeners of various languages in accordance with their respective languages. Thus, the Commentator said: 'All... reach.' The ear itself is the 'path of hearing' (sotapatha); or, 'hearing' (savana) is 'sota', and its 'path' (patho) is the cause; thus, the meaning is 'the ear-door'. 'In every way' means in the very manner it was taught. Who is able to understand? One is not able at all. Therefore, the remainder of the text should be understood thus. The particle 'pana' is in the sense of certainty. By it, it shows the arising of wholesome desire—designated as the wish to listen—with all one's strength, which is designated as the powers of faith, mindfulness, determination, energy, and so forth, and with absolute certainty. In the phrase 'janetvāpi', the particle 'pi', or 'api', has the meaning of praise, as in 'even the Buddha, having developed Buddhahood,' and so on. By this, it praises the Dhamma heard in such a way, thus: 'Even having generated the wish to listen with all one's strength and with absolute certainty, it is heard, as it were, in only one way; what then needs to be said of [hearing it] otherwise?' Some, however, say that in such instances it has the meaning of censure, but that is unsuitable, both because the meaning of censure is not present and because prefixes and particles only illuminate a meaning that is already present. For, by [implying] the inability to hear in every way, as in 'skilled in various methods,' etc., it here only praises the Dhamma. Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning of censure for the particle 'api' exists only in contexts where the meaning of censure is possible, such as in 'Even in divine pleasures, he finds no delight.' And the word 'api' in such places is only a particle, not a prefix. Indeed, grammarians say: 'The word 'api' is to be taken as belonging to the particle class where it does not come before a verb-denoting word.' In 'mayāpi', however, the collective meaning should be taken, thus: not only by me, but indeed also by others of such a nature.

Sāmaṃ bhavatīti sayambhū, anācariyako. Na mayaṃ idaṃ sacchikatanti ettha pana “na attano ñāṇeneva attanā sacchikata”nti pakaraṇato attho viññāyati. Sāmaññavacanassāpi hi sampayogavippayogasahacaraṇavirodhasaddantarasannidhānaliṅgaocityakāladesapakaraṇādivasena visesatthaggahaṇaṃ sambhavati. Evaṃ sabbattha. Parimocentoti “puna caparaṃ bhikkhave, idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī”ti (pārā. 195) vuttadosato parimocāpanahetu. Hetvatthe hi anta-saddo “asambudhaṃ buddhanisevita”ntiādīsu (vi. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā) viya. Imassa suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāppakāravicāraṇena attano ñāṇassa paccakkhataṃ sandhāya “idāni vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. Esā hi saṃvaṇṇanākārānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbadhamme sabbattha “ayamimassa attho, evamidha saṃvaṇṇayissāmī”ti puretarameva saṃvaṇṇanāppakāravicāraṇā.

'He becomes by himself' (sāmaṃ bhavati), therefore he is 'Self-become' (sayambhū); without a teacher. In 'We have not realized this' (na mayaṃ idaṃ sacchikataṃ), however, the meaning is understood from the context as: 'not realized by oneself through one's own knowledge alone.' For, even in the case of a general term, the grasping of a specific meaning is possible by way of association, dissociation, concomitance, opposition, proximity of another word, gender, suitability, time, place, context, and so forth. Thus it is in all cases. 'Parimocento' [means 'liberating'] because of the cause of wishing to liberate [the teaching] from the fault spoken of thus: 'Furthermore, monks, here some wicked monk, having learned the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, holds it in his own heart.' Indeed, the suffix '-anta' occurs in the sense of cause, as in 'because of not understanding (asambudhaṃ) [the teaching] frequented by the Buddhas (buddhanisevitaṃ).' With reference to the direct perception of his own knowledge, the commentator, by investigating the various ways of commenting on this sutta, said, 'Now it should be stated.' For this is the nature of commentators: namely, that concerning the Dhamma to be commented upon, there is in every case, beforehand, this investigation of the various ways of commenting, [thinking:] 'This is the meaning of this; thus will I comment on it here.'

Etadaggapadassattho vuttova. “Bahussutāna”ntiādīsu pana aññepi therā bahussutā, satimanto, gatimanto, dhitimanto, upaṭṭhākā ca atthi, ayaṃ panāyasmā buddhavacanaṃ gaṇhanto dasabalassa sāsane bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattiyaṃ ṭhatvā gaṇhi, tasmā bahussutānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Imassa ca therassa buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā dhāraṇasati aññehi therehi balavatarā ahosi, tasmā satimantānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Ayamevāyasmā ekapade ṭhatvā saṭṭhipadasahassāni [V 1.0131] gaṇhanto satthārā kathitaniyāmena sabbapadāni jānāti, tasmā gatimantānaṃ aggo nāma jāto[M 1.0148]. Tasseva cāyasmato buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhanavīriyaṃ, sajjhāyanavīriyañca aññehi asadisaṃ ahosi, tasmā dhitimantānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Tathāgataṃ upaṭṭhahanto cesa na aññesaṃ upaṭṭhākabhikkhūnaṃ upaṭṭhahanākārena upaṭṭhahati. Aññepi hi tathāgataṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu, na ca pana buddhānaṃ manaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhahituṃ sakkonti, ayaṃ pana thero upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya āraddhavīriyo hutvā tathāgatassa manaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhahi, tasmā upaṭṭhākānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Atthakusaloti bhāsitatthe, payojanatthe ca cheko. Dhammoti pāḷidhammo, nānāvidho vā hetu. Byañjananti akkharaṃ atthassa byañjanato. Padena hi byañjitopi attho akkharamūlakattā padassa “akkharena byañjito”ti vuccati. Atthassa viyañjanato vā vākyampi idha byañjanaṃ nāma. Vākyena hi attho paripuṇṇaṃ byañjīyati, yato “byañjanehi vivaratī”ti āyasmatā mahākaccāyanattherena vuttaṃ. Niruttīti nibbacanaṃ, pañcavidhā vā niruttinayā. Tesampi hi saddaracanāvisesena atthādhigamahetuto idha gahaṇaṃ yujjati. Pubbāparaṃ nāma pubbāparānusandhi, suttassa vā pubbabhāgena aparabhāgassa saṃsandanaṃ. Bhagavatā ca pañcavidhaetadaggaṭṭhānena dhammasenāpatinā ca pañcavidhakosallena pasaṭṭhabhāvānurūpanti sambandho. Dhāraṇabalanti dhāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ, dhāraṇe vā balaṃ, ubhayatthāpi dhāretuṃ sāmatthiyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Dassento hutvā, dassanahetūtipi attho. Tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikanti avadhāraṇaphalamāha. Na aññathā daṭṭhabbanti pana nivattetabbatthaṃ. Na aññathāti ca bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato na aññathā, na pana bhagavatā desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā, evañca katvā “sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātu”nti heṭṭhā vuttavacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti, itarathā bhagavatā desitākāreneva sotuṃ samatthattā tadetaṃ na vattabbaṃ siyā. Yathāvuttena pana atthena dhāraṇabaladassanañca na virujjhati sutākārāvirujjhanavasena dhāraṇassa adhippetattā, aññathā bhagavatā desitākāreneva dhārituṃ samatthanato heṭṭhā vuttavacanena virujjheyya.
