Nanu ca ānandattherassa “mametaṃ vacana”nti adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca tadāsaṅkāya abhāvato asappurisabhūmisamatikkamādivacanaṃ niratthakaṃ siyāti? Nayidamevaṃ “evaṃ me suta”nti vadantena ayampi attho anubhāvitoti atthasseva dassanato. Tena hi anubhāvetabbamatthaṃyeva tathā dasseti, na pana ānandattherassa adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca [V 1.0144] tadāsaṅkāya sambhavanti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Keci pana “devatānaṃ parivitakkāpekkhaṃ tathāvacanaṃ, tasmā edisī codanā anavakāsā”ti vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira samaye ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “bhagavā ca parinibbuto, ayañcāyasmā ānando desanākusalo, idāni dhammaṃ deseti, sakyakulappasuto tathāgatassa bhātā, cūḷapituputto ca, kiṃ nu kho so sayaṃ sacchikataṃ dhammaṃ deseti, udāhu bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ yathāsuta”nti, tesameva cetoparivitakkamaññāya tadabhipariharaṇatthaṃ asappurisabhūmisamatikkamanādiattho anubhāvitoti. Sāyeva yathāvuttā anariyavohārāvatthā asaddhammo, tadavatthānokkamanasaṅkhātā ca sāvakattapaṭijānanā saddhammo. Evaṃ sati pariyāyantarena purimatthameva dassetīti gahetabbaṃ. Apica kuhanalapanādivasena pavatto akusalarāsi asaddhammo, tabbirahitabhāvo ca saddhammo. “Kevala”ntiādināpi vuttassevatthassa pariyāyantarena dassanaṃ, yathāvuttāya anariyavohārāvatthāya parimoceti. Sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanena satthāraṃ apadisatīti attho. Apica satthukappādikiriyato attānaṃ parimoceti takkiriyāsaṅkāya [M 1.0164] sambhavato. “Satthu bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ mayāsuta”nti satthāraṃ apadisatīti atthantaramanubhāvanaṃ hoti. “Jinavacana”ntiādipi pariyāyantaradassanaṃ, atthantaramanubhāvanameva vā. Appetīti nidasseti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthesu yathārahaṃ satte netīti netti, dhammoyeva netti tathā. Vuttanayena cettha ubhayathā adhippāyo veditabbo.

Furthermore, wishing to make manifest the meaning that is to be made manifest by this pair of words which illuminates the meaning to be explained, the commentator said the passage beginning with, 'by this, evaṃ me sutaṃ'. In order to make it known that these words, although previously applied to separate meanings, are here taken as manifesting one single meaning, the word 'sakalenā' was stated. Although it is true that the word 'me' was not connected in the previous method in this place, it should nevertheless be understood that it was stated thus because of the association and inseparability of the words 'evaṃ' and 'suta' which are dependent on it. 'Proclaimed by the Tathāgata' means known in detail by the Tathāgata, or spoken by him. 'Not placing for oneself' means not establishing in oneself, thinking, 'This is mine.' And this is a genitive case in the sense of the locative. 'The plane of an unworthy person' means the domain of an unworthy person. And that, in meaning, is designated as the state of one who is ungrateful—the state of ignoble convention spoken of by the Blessed One, who illustrated the case of a great thief, thus: 'Here, a certain evil monk, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, places it for himself.' And thus he (the commentator) said, 'proclaimed by the Tathāgata... not placing for oneself.' And here, 'having been' (hutvā) is the remainder to be understood. Likewise, 'acknowledging discipleship' is a statement on the nature of entering the plane of a worthy person. Is it not so that, due to the absence of conceit in the Elder Ānanda—[thinking,] 'This is my utterance'—and due to the absence of suspicion about that on the part of the Elder Mahākassapa and others, the statement about transcending the plane of an unworthy person, etc., would be meaningless? It is not so. Because by (the Elder Ānanda) saying, 'Thus have I heard,' this meaning too was made manifest, this being simply a revelation of the meaning. For by that, it thus reveals only the meaning that is to be made manifest; but there is no possibility of conceit for the Elder Ānanda, nor of suspicion about that on the part of the Elder Mahākassapa and others. Thus, a conclusion should be reached here. Some, however, say: 'Such a statement was made with reference to the thoughts of the deities; therefore, such an objection is groundless.' It is said that at that time, a thought arose in the minds of certain deities, thus: 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, and this Venerable Ānanda is skilled in exposition. Now he teaches the Dhamma. He is renowned as from the Sakyan clan, the Tathāgata's brother, and the son of his paternal uncle. Does he teach a Dhamma realized by himself, or does he teach the Blessed One's utterance just as he heard it?' Having known this very thought in their minds, for the purpose of dispelling it, the meaning of transcending the plane of an unworthy person, etc., was made manifest. That very state of ignoble convention, as described, is the false Dhamma; and the acknowledgement of discipleship, which is designated as the non-entry into that state, is the true Dhamma. This being so, it should be understood that it shows only the former meaning by another method. Furthermore, the mass of unwholesome states that occurs by way of deceit, talkativeness, and so on, is the false Dhamma; and the state of being devoid of that is the true Dhamma. Also by the passage beginning with 'kevalaṃ,' there is a showing of the already stated meaning by another method; it liberates from the state of ignoble convention as described. By acknowledging discipleship, one refers to the Teacher—this is the meaning. Moreover, one frees oneself from the act of contriving Teachership, etc., because of the possibility of suspicion of such an act. By referring to the Teacher, [saying,] 'The utterance of the Teacher, the Blessed One himself, was heard by me,' it becomes the manifestation of another meaning. The passage beginning with 'The Victor's Word' is also a showing of another method, or it is simply the manifestation of another meaning. 'Appeti' means 'it indicates'. It is called 'netti' because it leads (neti) beings appropriately in matters concerning the visible world, the future life, and the ultimate goal; in that way, the Dhamma itself is the 'netti' (guide). And here, the intention should be understood in both ways according to the method stated.

Aparampi anubhāvetabbamatthamanubhāveti “apicā”tiādinā. Tattha uppāditabhāvatanti desanāvasena pavattitabhāvaṃ. Purimavacanaṃ vivarantoti bhagavatā desitavasena purimataraṃ saṃvijjamānaṃ bhagavatā vacanameva uttāniṃ karonto, idaṃ vacananti sambandho. Catūhi vesārajjañāṇehi visāradassa, visāradahetubhūtacatuvesārajjañāṇasampannassa vā. Dasañāṇabaladharassa. Sammāsambuddhabhāvasaṅkhāte uttamaṭṭhāne ṭhitassa, usabhassa idanti vā atthena āsabhasaṅkhāte akampanasabhāvabhūte ṭhāne ṭhitassa. “Evameva kho bhikkhave, yadā tathāgato loke uppajjati…pe… so dhammaṃ desetī”tiādinā (a. ni. 4.33) sīhopamasuttādīsu āgatena anekanayena sīhanādanadino. Sabbasattesu, sabbasattānaṃ vā uttamassa. Na cettha niddhāraṇalakkhaṇābhāvato niddhāraṇavasena samāso. Sabbattha hi sakkataganthesu, sāsanaganthesu ca evameva vuttaṃ. Dhammena sattānamissarassa. Dhammasseva issarassa taduppādanavasenātipi vadanti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tassevatthassa pariyāyantaradīpanaṃ. Dhammena lokassa padīpamiva bhūtassa, taduppādakabhāvena vā dhammasaṅkhātapadīpasampannassa. “Dhammakāyoti bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (dī. ni. 3.118) hi vuttaṃ. Dhammena lokapaṭisaraṇabhūtassa, dhammasaṅkhātena [V 1.0145] vā paṭisaraṇena sampannassa. “Yaṃnūnāhaṃ…pe… tameva dhammaṃ sakkatvā garuṃ katvā mānetvā pūjetvā upanissāya vihareyya”nti (a. ni. 4.21; saṃ. ni. 1.173) hi vuttaṃ. Saddhindriyādisaddhammasaṅkhātassa varacakkassa pavattino, saddhammānametassa vā āṇācakkavarassa pavattino sammāsambuddhassa tassa bhagavato idaṃ vacanaṃ sammukhāva mayā paṭiggahitanti yojetabbaṃ. Byañjaneti padasamudāyabhūte vākye. Kaṅkhā vā vimati vāti ettha daḷhataraṃ niviṭṭhā vicikicchā kaṅkhā. Nātisaṃsappanaṃ matibhedamattaṃ vimati. Sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayāti tathā akattabbabhāvakāraṇavacanaṃ. Attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimavacanaṃ [M 1.0165] vivarantoti pana assaddhiyavināsanassa, saddhāsampadamuppādanassa ca kāraṇavacanaṃ. “Teneta”ntiādinā yathāvuttamevatthaṃ udānavasena dasseti.

Furthermore, he makes manifest the meaning that is to be made manifest with 'apicā' and so on. Herein, 'uppāditabhāva' means the state of having been brought forth in the manner of a teaching. 'Purimavacanaṃ vivaranto' means making clear the earlier words of the Blessed One, which were already present as taught by the Blessed One; the connection is 'this statement'. Of one who is fearless through the four kinds of fearlessness-knowledge, or of one possessing the four kinds of fearlessness-knowledge which are the cause of fearlessness. Of one bearing the ten powers of knowledge. Of one established in the supreme state known as perfect Buddhahood, or standing firm in the unshakable state known as 'āsabha' (pre-eminent), from the meaning 'this is of the bull'. Of one roaring a lion's roar in many ways, as it is said in the Sīhopama Sutta and others: 'In the same way, monks, when the Tathāgata arises in the world... he teaches the Dhamma...' Of the supreme among all beings, or supreme over all beings. Here, it is not a determinative compound due to the absence of the characteristic of determination. For in all Sanskrit texts and scriptural texts, it is stated thus. Of the ruler of beings by means of the Dhamma. Some also say he is the lord of the Dhamma itself by virtue of bringing it forth. The remaining two terms are alternative expressions illuminating the same meaning. Of one who has become like a lamp for the world through the Dhamma, or endowed with the lamp known as Dhamma by virtue of being its originator. For it is said: 'Monks, "Dhamma-body" is a designation for the Tathāgata.' Of one who has become a refuge for the world through the Dhamma, or endowed with the refuge known as Dhamma. For it is said: 'What if I were to... honor, respect, esteem, and worship that very Dhamma, and dwell dependent on it?' This statement of that Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—who sets in motion the excellent wheel of the good Dhamma consisting of the spiritual faculties beginning with faith, or who sets in motion this excellent wheel of command of the good Dhammas—should be connected as 'received by me face to face'. 'Byañjane' (in the phrasing) refers to the collection of words forming a sentence. Here, in 'kaṅkhā vā vimati vā', 'kaṅkhā' means a firmly settled doubt, while 'vimati' means a mere difference of opinion, not very pervasive. 'This was received by me face to face' is a statement indicating the reason why it could not have been otherwise. Furthermore, the statement 'not acknowledging that he himself brought it forth, but clarifying the earlier statement' is a statement of the reason for dispelling disbelief and generating the accomplishment of faith. With 'teneta' and so on, he shows the meaning as previously stated by way of an inspired utterance.

“Evaṃ me suta”nti evaṃ vadanto gotamagottassa sammāsambuddhassa sāvako, gotamagottasambandho vā sāvako āyasmā ānando bhagavatā bhāsitabhāvassa, sammukhā paṭiggahitabhāvassa ca sūcanato, tathāsūcaneneva ca khalitadunniruttādigahaṇadosābhāvassa sijjhanato sāsane assaddhaṃ vināsayati, saddhaṃ vaḍḍhetīti attho. Ettha ca pañcamādayo tisso atthayojanā ākārādiatthesu aggahitavisesameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā dassitā, tato parā tisso ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vibhāvitā, pacchimā pana tisso yathākkamaṃ ākāratthaṃ, nidassanatthaṃ, avadhāraṇatthañca evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā yojitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Honti cettha –

'Thus have I heard'—by speaking thus, Venerable Ānanda, a disciple of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One of the Gotama clan, or a disciple connected to the Gotama clan, by indicating that it was spoken by the Blessed One and received face-to-face, and by such indication, through the accomplishment of the absence of faults such as slips of the tongue, incorrect grammar, and wrong grasping, dispels disbelief in the Dispensation and fosters faith—this is the meaning. Herein, the three applications of meaning, beginning with the fifth, are shown by taking the word 'evaṃ' without any specific distinction in meanings such as 'manner', etc. Then, the next three are explained by taking the word 'evaṃ' in the meaning of 'manner' itself. Lastly, the final three are to be understood as applying the word 'evaṃ' to denote, in order, the meaning of manner, the meaning of illustration, and the meaning of emphasis. It should be seen thus. And here there are:

“Dassanaṃ dīpanañcāpi, pakāsanaṃ vibhāvanaṃ;

Anubhāvanamiccattho, kiriyāyogena pañcadhā.

Showing, and also illuminating, revealing, making clear, and making manifest—thus the meaning is fivefold by connection with action.

Dassito paramparāya, siddho nekatthavuttiyā;

Evaṃ me sutamiccettha, padattaye nayaññunā”ti.

The meaning, established through having manifold applications and handed down by succession, is shown in these three words, 'evaṃ me sutaṃ', by one who knows the method.

Eka-saddo pana aññaseṭṭhāsahāyasaṅkhyādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27) aññatthe dissati, “cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.228; pārā. 11) seṭṭhe, “ekovūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.405; dī. ni. 2.215; ma. ni. 1.80; saṃ. ni. 3.63; vibha. 4.445) asahāye, “ekova kho bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) saṅkhyāyaṃ, idhāpi saṅkhyāyamevāti [V 1.0146] dassento āha “ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti (itivu. aṭṭha. 1; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paribbājakakathāvaṇṇanā) ekoyevesa samayo, na dve vā tayo vāti ūnādhikābhāvena gaṇanassa paricchedaniddeso ekanti ayaṃ saddoti attho, tena kassa paricchindananti anuyoge sati [M 1.0166] “samaya”nti vuttanti dassento āha “samayanti paricchinnaniddeso”ti. Evaṃ paricchedaparicchinnavasena vuttepi “ayaṃ nāma samayo”ti sarūpato aniyamitattā aniyamitavacanamevāti dasseti “ekaṃ…pe…. dīpana”nti iminā.

The word 'eka' (one), however, is seen in various meanings such as 'other', 'best', 'without a companion', and 'number'. For example, in phrases like 'The self and the world are eternal, this alone is true, anything else is false—thus some assert,' it appears in the sense of 'other'. In phrases like 'unification of mind', it denotes 'best'. In phrases like 'alone and secluded', it means 'without a companion'. In phrases like 'Monks, there is only one opportunity and occasion for living the spiritual life,' it refers to 'number'. Here too, it signifies 'number,' as shown by the statement: '"eka" is a designation of counting and delimitation.' This means 'this is only one occasion, not two or three'; thus, the word 'eka' is a designation that delimits a number by the absence of excess or deficiency. When the question arises, 'What is being delimited?', the answer is 'samaya' (occasion); to show this, he says, '"samaya" is the designation of what is delimited.' Even when expressed in terms of the delimiter and the delimited, since its form is not fixed as 'this particular occasion,' it is simply an indefinite expression, as indicated by the phrase 'ekaṃ…pe…. dīpana' (one… up to… illumination).

Idāni samayasaddassa anekatthavuttitaṃ atthuddhāravasena dassetvā idhādhippetamatthaṃ niyamento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tatthāti tasmiṃ “ekaṃ samaya”nti padadvaye, samabhiniviṭṭho samaya saddoti sambandho. Na pana dissatīti tesvekasmiṃyeva atthe idha pavattanato. Samavāyeti paccayasāmaggiyaṃ, kāraṇasamavāyeti attho. Khaṇeti okāse. Hetudiṭṭhīsūti hetumhi ceva laddhiyañca. Assāti samayasaddassa. Kālañca samayañca upādāyāti ettha kālo nāma upasaṅkamanassa yuttakālo. Samayo nāma tasseva paccayasāmaggī, atthato pana tadanurūpasarīrabalañceva tappaccayaparissayābhāvo ca. Upādānaṃ nāma ñāṇena tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttaṃ kālañca samayañca paññāya gahetvā upadhāretvāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace amhākaṃ sve gamanassa yuttakālo bhavissati, kāye balamattā ca pharissati, gamanapaccayā ca añño aphāsuvihāro na bhavissati, athetaṃ kālañca gamanakāraṇasamavāyasaṅkhātaṃ samayañca upadhāretvā appeva nāma svepi āgaccheyyāmāti. Khaṇoti okāso. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayapaṭilābhahetuttā. Khaṇo eva ca samayo. Yo “khaṇo”ti ca “samayo”ti ca vuccati, so ekovāti adhippāyo. Diyaḍḍho māso seso gimhānaṃ uṇhasamayo. Vassānassa paṭhamo māso pariḷāhasamayo. Mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Samāso vā esa, byāso vā. Pavuṭṭhaṃ vanaṃ pavanaṃ, tasmiṃ, kapilavatthusāmante mahāvanasaṅkhāte vanasaṇḍeti attho. Samayopi khoti ettha samayoti sikkhāpadapūraṇassa hetu. Bhaddālīti tassa bhikkhussa nāmaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tayā bhaddāli paṭivijjhitabbayuttakaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi, tampi te na paṭividdhaṃ na sallakkhitanti. Kiṃ taṃ kāraṇanti āha “bhagavāpi kho”tiādi.

Now, having shown that the word samaya has various meanings by way of extracting its meanings, while defining the meaning intended here, he says tatthā’tiādi. Therein, tatthā’ti means in that pair of words, ‘ekaṃ samayaṃ’; the connection should be made that the word samaya is well-included. However, the connection is not to be made with dissati ('it is seen'), because here it occurs in only one of those meanings. Samavāye’ti means in the assemblage of conditions; the meaning is in the combination of causes. Khaṇe’ti means in the sense of opportunity. Hetudiṭṭhīsū’ti means in cause and in view. Assā’ti means of this word samaya. In the phrase kālañca samayañca upādāya, kālo is the suitable time for approaching. Samayo is the assemblage of conditions for that very thing; by meaning, however, it is both the bodily strength appropriate to that and the absence of danger from that condition. Upādānaṃ is the grasping of them with knowledge; therefore, the meaning is: having grasped with wisdom and considered the aforementioned time and condition. This is what is said: ‘If tomorrow there will be a suitable time for our journey, and if there will be sufficient strength in the body, and if there will be no other discomfort from the condition of the journey, then, having considered that time and this samaya called the assemblage of conditions for the journey, perhaps we might come tomorrow as well.’ Khaṇo’ti means opportunity. Indeed, the arising of the Tathāgata and so on is the opportunity for the holy life of the path, because it is the cause for attaining the conditions for it. And khaṇo itself is samayo. The intention is that what is called khaṇo and samayo is one and the same. The remaining month and a half of the summer months is the hot season (uṇhasamayo). The first month of the rainy season is the season of scorching heat (pariḷāhasamayo). Mahāsamayo’ti means a great assembly. This is either a compound or an uncompounded phrase. A thriving forest is pavanaṃ; the meaning is in that forest grove called Mahāvana, near Kapilavatthu. Herein, in samayopi kho, samayo is the cause for the fulfillment of the training rule. Bhaddālī’ti is the name of that monk. This is what is said: ‘Bhaddāli, there is a certain reason fit to be penetrated by you, and that too has not been penetrated, not been marked by you.’ As to ‘What is that reason?’, he said bhagavāpi kho’tiādi.

“Uggahamāno”tiādīsu mānoti tassa paribbājakassa pakatināmaṃ, kiñci kiñci pana sippaṃ uggahetuṃ samatthatāya “uggahamāno”ti naṃ [M 1.0167] sañjānanti, tasmā “uggahamāno”ti vuccati. Samaṇamuṇḍikassa putto samaṇamuṇḍikāputto. So kira devadattassa upaṭṭhāko. Samayaṃ diṭṭhiṃ [V 1.0147] pakārena vadanti etthāti samayappavādako, tasmiṃ, diṭṭhippavādaketi attho. Tasmiṃ kira ṭhāne caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātippabhūtayo brāhmaṇā, nigaṇṭhācelakaparibbājakādayo ca pabbajitā sannipatitvā attano attano samayaṃ pakārena vadanti kathenti dīpenti, tasmā so ārāmo “samayappavādako”ti vuccati. Sveva tindukācīrasaṅkhātāya timbarūsakarukkhapantiyā parikkhittattā “tindukācīro”ti vuccati. Ekā sālā etthāti ekasālako. Yasmā panettha paṭhamaṃ ekā sālā ahosi, pacchā pana mahāpuññaṃ poṭṭhapādaparibbājakaṃ nissāya bahū sālā katā, tasmā tameva paṭhamaṃ kataṃ ekaṃ sālaṃ upādāya laddhapubbanāmavasena “ekasālako”ti vuccati. Mallikāya nāma pasenadirañño deviyā uyyānabhūto so pupphaphalasacchanno ārāmo, tena vuttaṃ “mallikāya ārāme”ti. Paṭivasatīti tasmiṃ phāsutāya vasati.

In Uggahamāno’tiādi, Māno is the given name of that wanderer. However, because of his ability to learn any small skill, people recognized him as Uggahamāno (the Learner); therefore, he is called Uggahamāno. The son of Samaṇamuṇḍika is Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta. It is said that he was an attendant of Devadatta. A place where they proclaim their doctrine (samayaṃ, i.e., their view, diṭṭhiṃ) in various ways is a samayappavādako; in that place, the meaning is, a place for proclaiming views. It is said that at that place, brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, and ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and wanderers, would gather and proclaim, relate, and explain their own doctrines in various ways; therefore, that park is called Samayappavādako. That very park, because it was enclosed by a row of Tinduka trees, also known as Timbarūsaka trees, is called Tindukācīro. A place where there is one hall is Ekasālako. Because at first there was one hall here, but later, on account of the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda of great merit, many halls were made, therefore, with reference to that one hall made first, it is called Ekasālako by way of the name previously acquired. That park, which was the pleasure garden of Queen Mallikā, King Pasenadi's consort, was covered with flowers and fruits; for that reason, it is called ‘Mallikā’s Park’. Paṭivasatī’ti means he dwells there in comfort.

Diṭṭhe dhammeti paccakkhe attabhāve. Atthoti vuḍḍhi. Kammakilesavasena samparetabbato sammā pāpuṇitabbato samparāyo, paraloko, tattha niyutto samparāyiko, paralokattho. Atthābhisamayāti yathāvuttaubhayatthasaṅkhātahitapaṭilābhā. Samparāyikopi hi attho kāraṇassa nipphannattā paṭiladdho nāma hotīti taṃ atthadvayamekato katvā “atthābhisamayā”ti vuttaṃ. Dhiyā paññāya taṃtadatthe rāti gaṇhāti, dhī vā paññā etassatthīti dhīro. Paṇḍā vuccati paññā. Sā hi sukhumesupi atthesu paḍati gacchati, dukkhādīnaṃ vā pīḷanādiākāraṃ jānātīti paṇḍā. Tāya ito gatoti paṇḍito. Atha vā itā sañjātā paṇḍā etassa, paḍati vā ñāṇagatiyā gacchatīti paṇḍito. Sammā mānābhisamayāti mānassa sammā pahānena. Sammāti cettha aggamaggañāṇena samucchedappahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Antanti avasānaṃ. Pīḷanaṃ taṃsamaṅgino hiṃsanaṃ avipphāritākaraṇaṃ. Tadeva attho tathā ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā. Samecca paccayehi katabhāvo saṅkhataṭṭho. Dukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahanaṃ santāpaṭṭho. Jarāya, maraṇena cāti dvidhā vipariṇāmetabbo vipariṇāmaṭṭho[M 1.0168]. Abhisametabbo paṭivijjhitabbo abhisamayaṭṭho, pīḷanādīniyeva. Tāni hi abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvamupanetvā “abhisamayaṭṭho”ti vuttāni. Abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa attho gocaro abhisamayaṭṭhoti tāniyeva tabbisaya-bhāvūpagamana-sāmaññato ekattena vuttāni. Ettha ca upasaggānaṃ jotakamattattā tassa tassa atthassa vācako samayasaddo evāti samayasaddassa atthuddhārepi saupasaggo abhisamayo vutto.

“In the present phenomenon” means in the present, manifest existence. “Benefit” means growth. The “future life” refers to the other world, as it is to be reached or rightly attained through the power of kamma and defilements. That which pertains to it is “of the future life,” the benefit in the other world. “Full understanding of the benefit” means the attainment of the benefit described as twofold, as stated before. For the benefit pertaining to the future life is also called “attained” because it is produced by its cause. Thus, having combined the pair of benefits into one, it is said “full understanding of the benefit.” By wisdom, one grasps those various benefits; or, this person has wisdom (dhī); therefore, they are called “wise” (dhīro). Wisdom (paññā) is called paṇḍā. For it goes to or penetrates even subtle meanings; or, it knows the characteristic of oppression, etc., of suffering, etc., hence it is called paṇḍā. One who has gone by means of that is a “wise one” (paṇḍito). Alternatively, for this person there is well-arisen wisdom (paṇḍā); or, one goes by way of knowledge; hence, “wise one” (paṇḍito). “Right full understanding of conceit” means by the right abandonment of conceit. And here, by “right” is meant the abandonment by eradication through the knowledge of the supreme path. “The end” means the conclusion. “Oppression” is the harming of one endowed with it, the causing of non-expansion. That very thing is the meaning; it is so by changing the letter ‘ttha’ to ‘ṭṭha’. The state of being formed by concordant conditions is the meaning of “conditioned.” By way of the suffering of suffering, etc., burning and torment is the meaning of “torment.” That which is to be transformed in two ways, namely by aging and by death, is the meaning of “transformation.” That which is to be fully understood or penetrated is the meaning of “full understanding”; this refers to oppression and so on. For these, having been brought to a state of oneness by their nature of being things to be fully understood, are called “the meaning of full understanding.” Or, the meaning or object of full understanding or penetration is “the meaning of full understanding”; therefore, those very things are spoken of as one due to the commonality of their becoming the domain of that penetration. And here, since prefixes are mere illuminators, the word ‘samaya’ itself is the conveyor of each respective meaning. Therefore, even in the exposition of the meaning of the word ‘samaya’, the form with a prefix, ‘abhisamayo’, is stated by the commentator.

Tesu pana atthesu ayaṃ vacanattho – sahakārīkāraṇavasena sannijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati maggabrahmacariyamettha tadādhārapuggalavasenāti samayo, khaṇo. Samenti ettha, etena vā saṃgacchanti dhammā, sattā vā sahajātādīhi, uppādādīhi cāti [V 1.0148] samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya hi atthato abhūtopi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ, karaṇaṃ viya ca parikappanāmattasiddhena rūpena voharīyati. Samaṃ, sammā vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavānaṃ sahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūho, na pana avayavavinimutto samūho nāma koci paramatthato atthi. Paccayantarasamāgame eti phalaṃ uppajjati, pavattati vā etasmāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudayo”ti. So hi paccayantarasamāgamaneneva attano phalaṃ uppādaṭṭhitisamaṅgībhāvaṃ karoti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandho hutvā eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggaṇabhāvato vā taṃsaññuttā sattā ayanti etena yathābhinivesaṃ pavattantīti samayo, diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhanti. Samiti saṅgati samodhānaṃ samayo, paṭilābho. Samassa nirodhassa yānaṃ pāpuṇanaṃ, sammā vā yānaṃ apagamo appavatti samayo, pahānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena sammā etabbo abhigantabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena taṃ taṃ sabhāvaṃ sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodho.

Furthermore, among these meanings, this is the etymology: because it comes together well and converges into a collection by the power of being a cooperating cause, it is ‘samayo’, meaning ‘convergence’ (samavāyo). The noble practice of the path comes to be here by way of the person who is its support; thus, ‘samayo’ means ‘opportunity’ (khaṇo). Here, or by this, dhammas or beings come together through co-nascence, etc., and through origination, etc.; thus, ‘samayo’ means ‘time’ (kālo). For although time is ultimately unreal, being merely the occurrence of dhammas, it is designated by a form established by mere conceptualization as if it were a basis or an instrument for the occurrence of dhammas. The even or right occurrence or establishment of parts is ‘samayo’, meaning ‘aggregate’ (samūho), as in ‘samudāyo’. For an aggregate is just the co-establishment of parts; there is no aggregate called ‘samūho’ that is separate from its parts in an ultimate sense. When there is a conjunction with other conditions, the fruit arises or proceeds from this; thus, ‘samayo’ means ‘cause’ (hetu), as in ‘samudayo’. For it is only through conjunction with other conditions that a cause produces its own fruit, bringing it to a state of arising and presence. A view, having become a bond due to its nature as a fetter, arises and proceeds in its own domain; or, due to being firmly grasped, beings connected with it proceed by means of it according to their adherence; thus, ‘samayo’ means ‘view’ (diṭṭhi). For beings are exceedingly bound by the fetter of views. Coming together (samiti), meeting (saṅgati), unification (samodhānaṃ) is ‘samayo’, meaning ‘attainment’ (paṭilābho). The going to the tranquil cessation; or, the right going away, non-occurrence, is ‘samayo’, meaning ‘abandonment’ (pahānaṃ). That which is to be rightly known or attained directly by knowledge is ‘abhisamayo’, meaning the undistorted nature of dhammas. That knowledge which, by way of direct confrontation, rightly goes to, reaches, and understands each respective nature is ‘abhisamayo’, meaning the understanding of the true nature of dhammas as it really is.

Nanu ca atthamattaṃ yathādhippetaṃ pati saddā abhinivisantīti na ekena saddena aneke atthā abhidhīyanti, atha kasmā idha samayasaddassa anekadhā attho vuttoti? Saccametaṃ saddavisese apekkhite saddavisese [M 1.0169] hi apekkhite na ekena saddena anekatthābhidhānaṃ sambhavati. Na hi yo kālādiattho samaya-saddo, soyeva samūhādiatthaṃ vadati. Ettha pana tesaṃ tesamatthānaṃ samayasaddavacanīyatāsāmaññamupādāya anekatthatā samaya-saddassa vuttāti. Evaṃ sabbattha atthuddhāre. Hoti cettha –

Is it not so that words settle upon only the intended meaning, and therefore many meanings are not expressed by one word? Then why is the meaning of the word ‘samaya’ stated here in many ways? This is true when a specific word is considered. For when a specific word is considered, it is not possible for one word to express many meanings. Indeed, the word ‘samaya’ that has the meaning of time, etc., does not itself express the meaning of aggregate, etc. Here, however, the polysemy of the word ‘samaya’ is stated by the commentator based on the commonality of those various meanings being expressible by the word ‘samaya’. Thus it should be understood in every exposition of meaning. And here there is this:

“Sāmaññavacanīyataṃ, upādāya anekadhā;

Atthaṃ vade na hi saddo, eko nekatthako siyā”ti.

“Based on general expressibility, a word may express a meaning in many ways; for a single word should not, in itself, be polysemous.”

Samavāyādiatthānaṃ idha asambhavato, kālasseva ca apadisitabbattā “idha panassa kālo attho”ti vuttaṃ. Desadesakādīnaṃ viya hi kālassa nidānabhāvena adhippetattā sopi idha apadisīyati. ‘Iminā kīdisaṃ kālaṃ dīpetīti āha “tenā”tiādi. Tenāti kālatthena samaya-saddena. Aḍḍhamāso pakkhavasena vutto, pubbaṇhādiko divasabhāgavasena, paṭhamayāmādiko pahāravasena. Ādi-saddena khaṇalayādayo saṅgahitā, aniyamitavasena ekaṃ kālaṃ dīpetīti attho.

Because the meanings of convergence, etc., are not possible here, and because only time is to be indicated, it is said, “But here, its meaning is time.” For just as the place, the speaker, etc., are indicated as the introduction, so too time is indicated here because it is intended as the introduction. To the question, “What kind of time does this indicate?” he said “tena,” etc. “Tena” means by the word ‘samaya’ in the sense of time. A half-month is stated by way of a fortnight; the forenoon, etc., by way of a division of the day; the first watch, etc., by way of a watch. By the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), moments, instants, etc., are included. The meaning is that it indicates a certain time in an unspecified way.

Kasmā [V 1.0149] panettha aniyamitavasena kālo niddiṭṭho, na utusaṃvaccharādinā niyamitavasenāti āha “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Kiñcāpi paññāya viditaṃ suvavatthāpitaṃ, tathāpīti sambandho. Vacasā dhāretuṃ vā sayaṃ uddisituṃ vā parena uddisāpetuṃ vā na sakkā nānappakārabhāvato bahu ca vattabbaṃ hoti yāva kālappabhedo, tāva vattabbattā. “Ekaṃ samaya”nti vutte pana na so kālappabhedo atthi, yo etthānantogadho siyāti dasseti “ekeneva padena tamatthaṃ samodhānetvā”ti iminā. Evaṃ lokiyasammatakālavasena samayatthaṃ dassetvā idāni sāsane pākaṭakālavasena samayatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ye vā ime”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apica utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamaṃ akatvā samayasaddassa vacane ayampi guṇo laddhoyevāti dassento “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhati tassā visesaparihāravisayattā. Tattha ye ime samayāti sambandho. Bhagavato mātukucchiokkamanakālo cettha gabbhokkantisamayo. Cattāri nimittāni passitvā saṃvejanakālo saṃvegasamayo. Chabbassāni sambodhisamadhigamāya cariyakālo [M 1.0170] dukkarakārikasamayo. Devasikaṃ jhānaphalasamāpattīhi vītināmanakālo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo, visesato pana sattasattāhāni jhānasamāpattivaḷañjanakālo. Pañcacattālīsavassāni taṃtaṃdhammadesanākālo desanāsamayo. Ādi-saddena yamakapāṭihāriyasamayādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Pakāsāti dasasahassilokadhātupakampanaobhāsapātubhāvādīhi pākaṭā. “Ekaṃ samaya”nti vutte tadaññepi samayā santīti atthāpattito tesu samayesu idha desanāsamayasaṅkhāto samayaviseso “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttoti dīpetīti adhippāyo.

Furthermore, why is time indicated here in an unspecified way, and not in a specified way by season, year, and so on? Regarding this, he said, 'Regarding that, although...' etc. The connection is: 'Although it is known and well-defined by wisdom, nevertheless...' It is not possible to bear it in mind through speech, or to indicate it oneself, or to have another indicate it, because of the manifold nature of time, and because much would have to be said; for as many distinctions of time as there are, that much would have to be said. Furthermore, when 'at one time' is said, there is no distinction of time that would not be included herein. This he shows with the phrase, 'having consolidated that meaning with a single phrase.' Having thus shown the meaning of 'samaya' by way of time conventionally accepted by the world, now, in order to show the meaning of 'samaya' by way of time that is manifest in the Dispensation, 'or whatever these times...' etc., was said. Moreover, showing that 'this quality is also obtained in the utterance of the word 'samaya' by not making a specification by way of season, year, etc.,' he said, 'or whatever these times...' etc. A general indication, indeed, is established in the particular, because its sphere is the avoidance of particulars. Therein, the connection is 'whatever these times are.' And here, the time of the Blessed One's descent into his mother's womb is the 'time of conception.' The time of experiencing spiritual urgency after seeing the four signs is the 'time of spiritual urgency.' The time of striving for six years to attain enlightenment is the 'time of austere practice.' The time of passing the days with the attainments of jhāna and fruition is the 'time of pleasant abiding in the here and now'; and especially, the time of enjoying the attainment of jhāna for seven weeks. The time of teaching the Dhamma in various ways for forty-five years is the 'time of teaching.' By the word 'etc.,' he includes the time of the Twin Miracle and so on. 'Manifest' means made manifest through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, the appearance of light, and so on. When 'at one time' is said, it is implied that other times also exist. He clarifies that among those times, here the particular time designated as the 'time of teaching' is what is said as 'at one time.' This is the intention.

Yathāvuttappabhedesuyeva samayesu ekadesaṃ pakārantarehi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “yo cāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hi ñāṇakiccasamayo, attahitapaṭipattisamayo ca abhisambodhisamayoyeva. Ariyatuṇhībhāvasamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo. Karuṇākiccaparahitapaṭipattidhammikathāsamayo desanāsamayo, tasmā tesu vuttappabhedesu samayesu ekadesova pakārantarena dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Sannipatitānaṃ vo bhikkhave dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ dhammī kathā vā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti (udā. 12) vuttasamaye sandhāya “sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesū”ti vuttaṃ. Tesupi samayesūti karuṇākiccaparahitapaṭipattidhammikathādesanāsamayesupi. Aññataraṃ samayaṃ sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttaṃ atthato abhedattā.

In order to show a certain aspect of the times with the aforementioned distinctions by consolidating them through other classifications, the phrase 'yo cāyaṃ...' etc., was stated. For therein, the time of the function of knowledge and the time of the practice for one's own welfare are indeed the time of full enlightenment. The time of the state of noble silence is the time of pleasant abiding in the here and now. The time of the function of compassion, the practice for the welfare of others, and Dhamma-talk is the time of teaching. Therefore, it should be understood that among those times with the aforementioned distinctions, only a certain aspect is shown by another classification. With reference to the times spoken of in the passage, 'O bhikkhus, for you who have assembled, two things are to be done: either Dhamma-talk or noble silence,' the phrase 'in the times of the two duties for those assembled' was stated. 'In those times as well' means: also in the times of the function of compassion, the practice for the welfare of others, Dhamma-talk, and teaching. With reference to a certain one of these times, 'at one time' was said, because in meaning there is no difference.

Aññattha viya bhummavacanena ca karaṇavacanena ca niddesamakatvā idha upayogavacanena niddesapayojanaṃ niddhāretukāmo parammukhena codanaṃ samuṭṭhapeti “kasmā panetthā”tiādinā. Etthāti [V 1.0150]“ekaṃ samaya”nti imasmiṃ pade, karaṇavacanena niddeso kato yathāti sambandho. Bhavanti etthāti bhummaṃ, okāso, tattha pavattaṃ vacanaṃ vibhatti bhummavacanaṃ. Karoti kiriyamabhinipphādebhi etenāti karaṇaṃ, kiriyānipphattikāraṇaṃ. Upayujjitabbo kiriyāyāti upayogo, kammaṃ, tattha vacanaṃ tathā. “Tatthā”tiādinā yathāvuttacodanaṃ pariharati. Tatthāti tesu abhidhammatadaññasuttapadavinayesu. Tathāti bhummavacanakaraṇavacanehi atthasambhavato cāti yojetabbaṃ, adhikaraṇabhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇatthānaṃ, hetukaraṇatthānañca [M 1.0171] sambhavatoti attho. Idhāti idhasmiṃ suttapade. Aññathāti upayogavacanena. Atthasambhavatoti accantasaṃyogatthassa sambhavato.

Wishing to determine the purpose of the indication by the accusative case here—without making the indication by the locative case and the instrumental case as elsewhere—the Teacher raises an objection indirectly, saying, 'But why here...' and so on. 'Here' (ettha) means in this phrase 'at one time'; the connection (of the objection) is: 'as the indication is made by the instrumental case (elsewhere).' `Bhumma` (location) is so called because 'things exist herein' (bhavanti ettha); it means 'place' (okāso). The word or case ending that occurs therein is `bhumma-vacana` (the locative case). `Karaṇa` (instrument) is so called because 'one accomplishes an action by means of this' (karoti etena); it means 'the cause for the accomplishment of an action.' `Upayoga` (application) is so called because 'it is to be connected with the action' (upayujjitabbo kiriyāya); it means 'object' (kammaṃ). The word occurring therein is likewise (the accusative case). With 'Therein...' (tatthā) and so on, he refutes the aforementioned objection. 'Therein' (tatthā) means: in those—the Abhidhamma, other suttas, verses, and the Vinaya. 'Thus' (tathā) should be construed as: because the meaning is possible through the locative and instrumental cases. The meaning is: because the meanings of location (adhikaraṇa) and the locative absolute (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa), and the meanings of cause (hetu) and instrument (karaṇa) are possible. 'Here' (idha) means: in this sutta phrase. 'Otherwise' (aññathā) means: by the accusative case. 'Because the meaning is possible' (atthasambhavato) means: because the meaning of continuous connection (accanta-saṃyoga) is possible.

“Tattha hī”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ. Itoti “ekaṃ samaya”nti suttapadato. Adhikaraṇatthoti ādhārattho. Bhavanaṃ bhāvo, kiriyā, kiriyāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇaṃ bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ, tadevattho tathā. Kena samayatthena idaṃ atthadvayaṃ sambhavatīti anuyoge sati tadatthadvayasambhavānurūpena samayatthena, taṃ daḷhaṃ karonto “adhikaraṇañhī”tiādimāha. Padatthatoyeva hi yathāvuttamatthadvayaṃ siddhaṃ, vibhatti pana jotakamattā. Tattha kālasaṅkhāto, kālasaddassa vā attho yassāti kālattho. Samūhasaṅkhāto, ‘samūhasaddassa vā attho yassāti samūhattho, ko so? Samayo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kālattho, samūhattho ca samayo tattha abhidhamme vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ ādhāroti, yasmiṃ kāle, dhammapuñje vā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva kāle, dhammapuñje vā phassādayopi hontīti ayañhi tattha attho. Nanu cāyaṃ upādāpaññattimatto kālo, vohāramatto ca samūho, so kathaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ siyā tattha vuttadhammānanti? Nāyaṃ doso. Yathā hi kālo sayaṃ paramatthato avijjamānopi sabhāvadhammaparicchinnattā ādhārabhāvena paññāto, sabhāvadhammaparicchinno ca taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato pubbe, parato ca abhāvato “pubbaṇhejāto, sāyanhe āgacchatī”tiādīsu, samūho ca avayavavinimutto visuṃ avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddhattā avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati “rukkhe sākhā, yavarāsiyaṃ pattasambhūto”tiādīsu, evamidhāpi sabhāvadhammaparicchinnattā, kappanāmattasiddhattā ca tadubhayaṃ tattha vuttadhammānaṃ adhikaraṇabhāvena paññāpīyatīti.

The phrase beginning with ‘Tattha hi’ is its explanation. ‘From this’ refers to the sutta phrase ‘ekaṃ samayaṃ’. ‘Adhikaraṇattho’ means the meaning of a basis. ‘Bhavanaṃ’ is ‘bhāvo’ (existence), an action; the marking of one action by another is ‘bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ’ (the marking of one state of being by another), and that very thing is the meaning. When the inquiry arises, ‘By what meaning of ‘samaya’ do these two meanings come to be?’, then, wishing to strengthen that statement with a meaning of ‘samaya’ suitable for the arising of those two meanings, he said the phrase beginning with ‘adhikaraṇañhi’. Indeed, the two meanings as stated are established from the meaning of the word itself; the case ending, however, is merely an illuminator. Therein, ‘kālattho’ is that which has the meaning designated as time, or the meaning of the word ‘time.’ ‘Samūhattho’ is that which has the meaning designated as a collection, or the meaning of the word ‘collection.’ What is that? It is ‘samaya.’ This is what is meant: ‘Samaya,’ which has the meaning of time and the meaning of collection, is the basis (adhikaraṇa), the support (ādhāra), for the phenomena of contact and so on mentioned there in the Abhidhamma. Indeed, this is the meaning there: at whatever time, or in whatever collection of phenomena, a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness has arisen, at that very time, or in that very collection of phenomena, contact and so on also exist. Now, is it not so that this time is merely a concept derived from grasping, and this collection is merely a convention? How then could they be a basis for the phenomena mentioned there? This is no fault. For just as time, though in itself not existing in an ultimate sense, is designated as a basis because it is delimited by intrinsic phenomena—and it is delimited by intrinsic phenomena because those phenomena occurring at that moment are absent before and after it, as in ‘born in the morning, arrives in the evening’ and so on—and just as a collection, though not existing separately apart from its components, is designated as a basis for its components because it is established by mere conceptual construction, as in ‘branches on a tree, leaves that have arisen in a heap of barley’ and so on; even so, here too, because both are delimited by intrinsic phenomena and established by mere conceptual construction, they are designated as a basis for the phenomena mentioned there.

“Khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassā”tiādi bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇatthasambhavadassanaṃ. Tattha khaṇo nāma aṭṭhakkhaṇavinimutto navamo buddhuppādakkhaṇo, yāni vā panetāni “cattārimāni bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi [M 1.0172] samannāgatānaṃ devamussānaṃ catucakkaṃ pavattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.31) ettha [V 1.0151] patirūpadesavāso sappurisūpanissayo attasammāpaṇīdhi pubbekatapuññatāti cattāri cakkāni vuttāni, tāni ekajjhaṃ katvā okāsaṭṭhena “khaṇo”ti veditabbāni. Tāni hi kusaluppattiyā okāsabhūtāni. Samavāyo nāma “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43, 44; saṃ. ni. 3.60; kathā. 465, 467) niddiṭṭhā cakkhuviññāṇādisādhāraṇaphalanipphādakattena saṇṭhitā cakkhurūpādipaccayasāmaggī. Cakkhurūpādīnañhi cakkhuviññāṇādi sādhāraṇaphalaṃ. Hetu nāma yonisomanasikārādijanakahetu. Yathāvuttassa khaṇasaṅkhātassa, samavāyasaṅkhātassa, hetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa sattāsaṅkhātena bhāvena tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ sattāsaṅkhāto bhāvo lakkhīyati viññāyatīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā “gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato”ti ettha dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evamidhāpi yathāvuttassa samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā, phassādīnaṃ bhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyatīti. Nanu cettha sattākiriyā avijjamānāva, kathaṃ tāya lakkhīyatīti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi “yasmiṃ samaye”ti ca vutte satīti ayamattho viññāyamāno evahoti aññakiriyāsambandhābhāve padatthassa sattāvirahābhāvato, tasmā atthato gamyamānāya tāya sattākiriyāya lakkhīyatīti. Ayañhi tattha attho – yasmiṃ yathāvutte khaṇe, paccayasamavāye, hetumhi vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, paccayasamavāye, hetumhi vā sati phassādayopi hontīti. Ayaṃ pana attho abhidhammeyeva (aṭṭhasā. kāmāvacarakusalapadabhājanīye) nidassanavasena vutto, yathārahamesa nayo aññesupi suttapadesūti. Tasmāti adhikaraṇatthassa, bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇatthassa ca sambhavato. Tadatthajotanatthanti tadubhayatthassa samayasaddatthabhāvena vijjamānasseva bhummavacanavasena dīpanatthaṃ. Vibhattiyo hi padīpo viya vatthuno vijjamānasseva atthassa jotakāti, ayamattho saddasatthesu pākaṭoyeva.

The phrase beginning with ‘khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa’ is to show the possibility of the meaning ‘the marking of one state of being by another.’ Therein, ‘khaṇa’ (moment) means the ninth moment, free from the eight inauspicious moments, which is the moment of a Buddha’s arising. Or else, the four wheels spoken of by the Blessed One in the passage, ‘Monks, there are these four wheels by which, being endowed with them, the fourfold wheel turns for gods and humans’—namely, dwelling in a suitable place, associating with true persons, right self-aspiration, and merit done in the past—these, taken together, are to be known as ‘khaṇa’ in the sense of ‘opportunity.’ Indeed, they are the opportunity for the arising of the wholesome. ‘Samavāya’ (concurrence) refers to the congruence of conditions such as the eye and forms, which, as indicated in the passage beginning, ‘Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises...’, is the aggregate of conditions, such as the eye and forms, established as producing a common result, such as eye-consciousness. For eye-consciousness and so on is indeed the common result of the eye, forms, and so on. ‘Hetu’ (cause) means the generative cause, such as wise attention. The meaning is that the existence, designated as ‘sattā,’ of those phenomena such as contact, is marked and understood by the existence, designated as ‘sattā,’ of the ‘samaya’ (occasion) which is designated as the aforesaid moment, concurrence, and cause. This is what is meant: just as in the example, ‘When the cows were being milked, he went; when they were milked, he returned,’ the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the being of contact and so on are marked by the action of being of the aforesaid ‘samaya.’ But is it not so that here the action of being is simply non-existent? How then is it marked by that? True. Nevertheless, when ‘yasmiṃ samaye’ is said, the meaning ‘being’ (sati) is indeed understood, because in the absence of a connection with another action, the meaning of the word is not devoid of existence. Therefore, it is marked by that action of being which is inferred from the meaning. Indeed, this is the meaning there: when, in the aforesaid moment, concurrence of conditions, or cause, a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness has arisen, then in that very moment, with that very concurrence of conditions, or with that very cause, contact and so on also exist. This meaning, however, is stated by way of illustration only in the Abhidhamma; it should be understood that this method applies to other sutta passages as is appropriate. ‘Therefore’ means: because of the possibility of the meaning of a basis and the meaning of ‘the marking of one state of being by another.’ ‘For the purpose of illuminating that meaning’ means: for the purpose of clarifying, by means of the locative case, that dual meaning which already exists as the meaning of the word ‘samaya.’ Indeed, case endings, like a lamp for an object, are illuminators of a meaning that already exists. This meaning is well-known in the grammatical sciences.

Hetuattho, karaṇattho ca sambhavatīti “annena vasati, vijjāya vasatī”tiādīsu viya hetuattho, “pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu [M 1.0173] viya karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Kathaṃ pana sambhavatīti āha “yo hi so”tiādi. Vinaye (pārā. 20) āgatasikkhāpadapaññattiyācanavatthuvasena theraṃ mariyādaṃ katvā “sāriputtādīhipi duviññeyyo”ti vuttaṃ. Tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtenāti ettha pana taṃtaṃvatthuvītikkamova sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hetu ceva karaṇañca. Tathā hi yadā bhagavā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā paṭhamameva tesaṃ tesaṃ tattha tattha sikkhāpadapaññattihetubhūtaṃ taṃ taṃ vītikkamaṃ apekkhamāno viharati[V 1.0152], tadā taṃ taṃ vītikkamaṃ apekkhitvā tadatthaṃ vasatīti siddho vatthuvītikkamassa sikkhāpadapaññattihetubhāvo “annenavasatī”tiādīsu annamapekkhitvā tadatthaṃ vasatītiādinā kāraṇena annādīnaṃ hetubhāvo viya. Sikkhāpadapaññattikāle pana teneva pubbasiddhena vītikkamena sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti, tasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sādhakatamattā karaṇabhāvopi vītikkamasseva siddho “asinā chindatī”tiādīsu asinā chindanakiriyaṃ sādhetītiādinā kāraṇena asiādīnaṃ karaṇabhāvo viya. Evaṃ santepi vītikkamaṃ apekkhamāno teneva saddhiṃ tannissitampi kālaṃ apekkhitvā viharatīti kālassāpi idha hetubhāvo vutto, sikkhāpadaṃ paññapento ca taṃ taṃ vītikkamakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetīti vītikkamanissayassa kālassāpi karaṇabhāvo vutto, tasmā iminā pariyāyena kālassāpi hetubhāvo, karaṇabhāvo ca labbhatīti vuttaṃ “tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtenā”ti, nippariyāyena pana vītikkamoyeva hetubhūto, karaṇabhūto ca. So hi vītikkamakkhaṇe hetu hutvā pacchā sikkhāpadapaññāpanakkhaṇe karaṇampi hotīti. Sikkhāpadāni paññāpayantoti vītikkamaṃ pucchitvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇavatthuṃ taṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā, vigarahitvā ca taṃ taṃ vatthuotiṇṇakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena karaṇabhūtena sikkhāpadāni paññapento. Sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamānoti tatiyapārājikādīsu (pārā. 162) viya sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hetubhūtaṃ taṃ taṃ vatthuvītikkamasamayaṃ apekkhamāno tena samayena hetubhūtena bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsīti attho.

The meaning of 'cause' and the meaning of 'instrument' are possible. For example, the meaning of 'cause' is possible as in 'he lives on account of food, he lives on account of knowledge,' and so on; and the meaning of 'instrument' is possible as in 'he cuts with an axe, he digs with a spade,' and so on. But how are they possible? He says, 'For indeed, that...' and so on. In the Vinaya, by way of the incident of requesting the establishment of a training rule, having set the Elder as the boundary, it is said, 'It is difficult to be understood even by Sāriputta and others.' Here, however, in the phrase 'at that time, which had become the cause, which had become the instrument,' it is the transgression of each particular incident itself that is both the cause and the instrument for the establishment of the training rule. For when the Blessed One, for the very first time in establishing a training rule, dwells considering each particular transgression that has become the cause for the establishment of that training rule in each case, then, by considering that transgression, he dwells for that purpose. Thus, the status of the incident’s transgression as the cause for establishing the training rule is established, just as in 'he lives on account of food' and so on, the status of food and so on as a cause is established by the reason that one lives for the purpose of food, having considered food. At the time of establishing the training rule, however, he establishes the training rule by means of that very transgression which was previously established. Therefore, because it is the most effective means for establishing the training rule, the status of the transgression itself as an instrument is also established, just as in 'he cuts with a sword' and so on, the status of the sword and so on as an instrument is established by the reason that one accomplishes the act of cutting with the sword. Even so, while considering the transgression, he dwells also considering the time dependent on it, along with it. Thus, here the status of time as a cause is also stated. And when establishing the training rule, he establishes the training rule by means of that very time, without passing beyond the time of that transgression. Thus, the status of time, which is the support for the transgression, as an instrument is also stated. Therefore, by this method, the status of time as both cause and instrument is obtained, as stated: 'at that time, which had become the cause, which had become the instrument.' In the direct sense, however, it is the transgression itself that has become the cause and has become the instrument. For that transgression, at the moment of transgression, having become the cause, later, at the moment of establishing the training rule, also becomes the instrument. 'Laying down training rules' means: having inquired about the transgression, having assembled the community of monks, having questioned again regarding the incident that had arisen and that person, and having reproved him, he lays down the training rules by means of that very time which has become the instrument, without passing beyond the time when that particular incident occurred. And 'considering the cause for establishing the training rule' means: just as in the case of the third pārājika and so on, the Blessed One dwelt here and there on account of that time which had become the cause, while considering that particular time of the incident’s transgression which had become the cause for establishing the training rule; this is the meaning.

“Sikkhāpadāni [M 1.0174] paññāpayanto, sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno”ti idaṃ yathākkamaṃ karaṇabhāvassa, hetubhāvassa ca samatthanavacanaṃ, tasmā tadanurūpaṃ “tenasamayena karaṇabhūtena hetubhūtenā”ti evaṃ vattabbepi paṭhamaṃ “hetubhūtenā”ti uppaṭipāṭivacanaṃ tattha hetubhāvassa sātisayamadhippetattā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Bhagavā hi verañjāyaṃ viharanto dhammasenāpatittherassa sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanahetubhūtaṃ parivitakkasamayaṃ apekkhamāno tena samayena hetubhūtena vihāsī”ti tīsupi kira gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. “Kiṃ panettha yutticintāya, ācariyassa idha kamavacanicchā natthīti evametaṃ gahetabbaṃ – aññāsupi hi aṭṭhakathāsu ayameva anukkamo vutto, na ca tāsu ‘tena samayena verañjāyaṃ viharatī’ti vinayapāḷipade hetuatthasseva sātisayaṃ adhippetabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vutto avisayattā, sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto hetubhūtena, karaṇabhūtena ca samayena vihāsi, sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno hetubhūtena samayena vihāsīti evamettha yathālābhaṃ sambandhabhāvato evaṃ vutto”tipi vadanti. Tasmāti [V 1.0153] yathāvuttassa duvidhassāpi atthassa sambhavato. Tadatthajotanatthanti vuttanayena karaṇavacanena tadubhayatthassa jotanatthaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ vinaye. Ettha ca sikkhāpadapaññattiyā eva vītikkamasamayassa sādhakatamattā tassa karaṇabhāve “sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto”ti ajjhāharitapadena sambandho, hetubhāve pana tadapekkhanamattattā “viharatī”ti padenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathāyeva hi vuttaṃ “tena samayena hetubhūtena, karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto, sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsī”ti. Karaṇañhi kiriyatthaṃ, na hetu viya kiriyākāraṇaṃ. Hetu pana kiriyākāraṇaṃ, na karaṇaṃ viya kiriyatthoti.

The statement 'While laying down the training rules, and considering the cause for laying down the training rules' is a statement that supports, respectively, the status as an instrument and the status as a cause. Therefore, although it should accordingly be said, 'at that time, which had become the instrument, which had become the cause,' the statement 'which had become the cause' is mentioned first, out of sequence, because the status as a cause is intended there with special emphasis; so it should be understood. Indeed, it is said in three difficult passages, it seems, that 'The Blessed One, while dwelling at Verañjā, considering the occasion of reflection that had become the cause for the Elder, the General of the Dhamma's, request for the laying down of the training rules, dwelt on account of that time which had become the cause.' 'What is the use of considering the logic here? It should be taken thus: the teacher here has no desire to speak in sequence. For in other commentaries as well, this very order is mentioned. And in those, in the Vinaya Pāḷi passage “at that time dwelling at Verañjā,” it is not stated in order to demonstrate that the meaning of cause is intended with special emphasis, because it is not the proper context. Rather, they say: “While laying down the training rules, he dwelt by means of the time that had become the cause and the instrument; and while considering the cause for laying down the training rules, he dwelt on account of the time that had become the cause.” Thus, here it is stated in this way due to the connection being made as is suitable.' So they also say. 'Therefore' means: because of the possibility of both kinds of meaning, as stated. 'For the purpose of illuminating that meaning' means: for the purpose of illuminating both those meanings by means of the instrumental word, in the manner stated. 'Therein' means: in that Vinaya. And here, because the time of transgression is the most effective means for the laying down of the training rule, when it has the status of an instrument, the connection is with the supplied phrase 'while laying down the training rules'; but when it has the status of a cause, because it is merely a matter of considering it, the connection is only with the word 'he dwells'; so it should be understood. For it was stated in just that way: 'The Blessed One, laying down the training rules by means of the time that had become the cause and the instrument, and considering the cause for laying down the training rules, dwelt here and there.' For an instrument is for the purpose of the action, not the reason for the action like a cause. A cause, however, is the reason for the action, not for the purpose of the action like an instrument.

“Idha panā”tiādinā upayogavacanassa accantasaṃyogatthasambhavadassanaṃ, accantameva dabbaguṇakiriyāhi saṃyogo accantasaṃyogo, nirantarameva tehi saṃyuttabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Soyevattho tathā. Evaṃjātiketi evaṃsabhāve. Kathaṃ sambhavatīti āha “yañhī”tiādi. Accantamevāti ārabbhato paṭṭhāya yāva desanāniṭṭhānaṃ, tāva ekaṃsameva, nirantaramevāti attho. Karuṇāvihārenāti parahitapaṭipattisaṅkhātena karuṇāvihārena. Tathā hi karuṇānidānattā [M 1.0175] desanāya idha parahitapaṭipatti “karuṇāvihāro”ti vuttā, na pana karuṇāsamāpattivihāro. Na hi desanākāle desetabbadhammavisayassa desanāñāṇassa sattavisayāya mahākaruṇāya sahuppatti sambhavati bhinnavisayattā, tasmā karuṇāya pavatto vihāroti katvā parahitapaṭipattivihāro idha “karuṇāvihāro”ti veditabbo. Tasmāti accantasaṃyogatthasambhavato. Tadatthajotanatthanti vuttanayena upayogavibhattiyā tadatthassa jotanatthaṃ upayoganiddeso kato yathā “māsaṃ sajjhāyati, divasaṃ bhuñjatī”ti. Tenāti yena kāraṇena abhidhamme, ito aññesu ca suttapadesu bhummavacanassa adhikaraṇattho, bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca, vinaye karaṇavacanassa hetuattho, karaṇattho ca idha upayogavacanassa accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati, tenāti attho. Etanti yathā vuttassatthassa saṅgahagāthāpadaṃ aññatrāti abhidhamme ito aññesu suttapadesu, vinaye ca. Samayoti samayasaddo. Saddeyeva hi vibhattiparā bhavatiatthe asambhavato. Soti sveva samayasaddo.

By the phrase beginning with 'Idha pana,' the possibility of the meaning of 'continuous connection' for the accusative case is shown. Continuous connection is connection with substances, qualities, and actions without interruption; it is said to be the state of being continuously conjoined with them. That is indeed the meaning in that case. As to 'evaṃjātike,' it means 'of such a nature.' Because it should be asked, 'How is it possible?,' he said the words beginning with 'yaṃ hi.' 'Accantameva' means: from the beginning of the undertaking to teach for as long as the teaching is not completed, for that long, certainly, continuously; this is the meaning. 'Karuṇāvihārena' means: by the dwelling in compassion, which is described as the practice for the welfare of others. Indeed, because the teaching has compassion as its cause, herein the practice for the welfare of others is called 'dwelling in compassion,' but not the dwelling in the attainment of compassion. For at the time of teaching, the simultaneous arising of the teaching-knowledge, which has the Dhamma-to-be-taught as its object, with great compassion, which has beings as its object, is not possible, because of having different objects. Therefore, having construed it as 'the dwelling that proceeds from compassion,' the dwelling in the practice for the welfare of others should be understood herein as 'dwelling in compassion.' 'Tasmā' means: because of the possibility of the meaning of continuous connection. 'Tadatthajotanatthaṃ' means: for the purpose of illuminating that meaning of the accusative case, the designation by the accusative case is made in the way that has been stated, just as in 'māsaṃ sajjhāyati' (he recites for a month) and 'divasaṃ bhuñjati' (he eats for a day). 'Tena' means: for the reason that in the Abhidhamma and in other Sutta passages apart from this one, the locative case has the meaning of location and the meaning of a sign of one state from another state, and in the Vinaya, the instrumental case has the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument, and herein the accusative case has the meaning of continuous connection; for that reason. This is the meaning. 'Etaṃ' is a summary verse for the meaning as stated. 'Aññatra' means: in the Abhidhamma, in other Sutta passages apart from this one, and in the Vinaya. 'Samayo' means: the word 'samaya.' For an inflection follows only a word; it is not possible in the meaning. 'So' means: that very word 'samaya.'

Evaṃ attano matiṃ dassetvā idāni porāṇācariyamatiṃ dassetuṃ “porāṇā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Porāṇāti ca purimā aṭṭhakathācariyā. “Tasmiṃ samaye”ti vā…pe… “ekaṃ samaya”nti vā esa bhedoti sambandho. Abhilāpamattabhedoti vacanamattena bhedo viseso, na pana atthena, tenāha “sabbattha bhummamevattho”ti, sabbesupi atthato ādhāro eva atthoti vuttaṃ hoti[V 1.0154]. Iminā ca vacanena suttavinayesu vibhattivipariṇāmo kato, bhummatthe vā upayogakaraṇavibhattiyo siddhāti dasseti. “Tasmā”tiādinā tesaṃ matidassane guṇamāha.

Having thus shown his own view, now, in order to show the view of the ancient teachers, the words beginning with 'Porāṇā pana' are stated. And 'porāṇā' means: the former commentary teachers. The connection should be made thus: this is the distinction, whether as 'tasmiṃ samaye'… or as 'ekaṃ samayaṃ.' 'Abhilāpamattabhedo' means: the distinction is by word only, a difference, but not in meaning. Therefore, he said, 'Everywhere, the meaning is only that of the locative.' It is said to mean that in all instances, in terms of meaning, the meaning is only that of a location. And by this statement, it is shown that in the Suttas and Vinaya, a change of inflection is made, or that in the meaning of the locative, the accusative and instrumental cases are established. By the words beginning with 'Tasmā,' in showing their view, the commentator states a virtue.

Bhāriyaṭṭhena garu. Tadevatthaṃ saṅketato samattheti “garuṃ hī”tiādinā saṅketavisayo hi saddo taṃvavatthitoyeva cesa atthabodhakoti. Garunti garukātabbaṃ janaṃ. “Loke”ti iminā na kevalaṃ sāsaneyeva, lokepi garukātabbaṭṭhena bhagavāti saṅketasiddhīti dasseti. Yadi garukātabbaṭṭhena bhagavā, atha ayameva sātisayaṃ bhagavā nāmāti dassento “ayañcā”tiādimāha. Tathā hi lokanātho aparimitanirupamappabhāvasīlādiguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya, sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya [M 1.0176] niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantupakāritāya ca aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānanti. Na kevalaṃ lokeyeva, atha kho sāsanepīti dasseti “porāṇehī”tiādinā, porāṇehīti ca aṭṭhakathācariyehīti attho. Seṭṭhavācakavacanampi seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato seṭṭhamevāti vuttaṃ “bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭha”nti. Vuccati attho, etenāti hi vacanaṃ, saddo. Atha vā vuccatīti vacanaṃ, attho, tasmā yo “bhagavā”ti vacanena vacanīyo attho, so seṭṭhoti attho. Bhagavāti vacanamuttamanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogattā, sātisayaṃ vā garukaraṇārahatāya gāravayutto, gāravārahoti attho. Yena kāraṇattayena so tathāgato garu bhāriyaṭṭhena, tena “bhagavā”ti vuccatīti sambandho. Garutākāraṇadassanañhetaṃ padattayaṃ. “Sippādisikkhāpakāpi garūyeva nāma honti, na ca gāravayuttā, ayaṃ pana tādiso na hoti, tasmā garūti katvā ‘gāravayutto’ti vutta”nti keci. Evaṃ sati tadetaṃ visesanapadamattaṃ, purimapadadvayameva kāraṇadassanaṃ siyā.

Because of the meaning of being weighty, he is 'garu' (venerable). He establishes that very meaning by convention with the words beginning with 'Garuṃ hi.' Indeed, a word has convention as its domain, and this word, being established by that convention, conveys meaning. 'Garuṃ' means: a person who should be revered. By this word 'loke,' he shows that not only in the Dispensation, but also in the world, the establishment by convention of 'Bhagavā' is due to the meaning of being one who should be revered. If the Blessed One is so called because of the meaning of being one who should be revered, then, showing that this very one is pre-eminently called Bhagavā, he says the words beginning with 'Ayañca.' Indeed, the Lord of the World, being endowed with special qualities such as limitless, incomparable, and immeasurable majesty and virtue; possessing unsurpassed perfection of effort which is preceded by the removal of all that is unbeneficial and is devoted to accomplishing complete welfare and happiness; and being of ultimate benefit to the populace with its gods and humans, is the supreme object of reverence for countless beings in countless world-systems. Not only in the world, but indeed also in the Dispensation, one who is venerable is called Bhagavā; the commentator shows this meaning with the words beginning with 'Porāṇehi.' And 'porāṇehi' means: by the commentary teachers. A word that expresses excellence is itself excellent because it accompanies excellent qualities; therefore, it is said, 'The word Bhagavā is excellent.' Indeed, because meaning is spoken by it, it is a 'word' (vacanaṃ), implying the sound. Alternatively, because it is spoken, it is a 'word' (vacanaṃ), implying the meaning. Therefore, the meaning which is to be expressed by the word 'Bhagavā' is excellent; this is the meaning. Here too, in the phrase 'The word Bhagavā is supreme,' this same method should be understood. 'Gāravayutto' means: endowed with the state of being venerable because of possessing qualities worthy of reverence. Or, because he is pre-eminently worthy of being revered, he is 'gāravayutto' (endowed with reverence); the meaning is 'worthy of reverence.' The connection should be made thus: by which triad of reasons that Tathāgata is 'garu' because of the meaning of being weighty, for that reason he is called 'Bhagavā.' This triad of phrases shows the reason for his venerability. Some say: 'Teachers of arts and so on are indeed called 'garu,' but they are not 'gāravayuttā' (endowed with reverence). This Blessed One, however, is not of such a nature. Therefore, having stated 'garu,' it is said 'gāravayutto.'' If this is so, then that phrase is merely a qualifying phrase; only the first two phrases would be showing the reason.

Apicāti atthantaravikappatthe nipāto, aparo nayoti attho. Tattha –

The word 'Apica' is a particle in the sense of considering another meaning; the meaning is 'another method.' Therein:

“Vaṇṇagamo vaṇṇavipariyāyo,

Dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā;

Dhātūnamatthātisayena yogo,

Taduccate pañcavidhā niruttī”ti. –

‘Insertion of a letter, inversion of a letter, and two others: alteration and loss of a letter; the connection of roots with a surpassing meaning—this is called the fivefold etymology.’

Vuttaṃ niruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā, “pisodarādīni yathopadiṭṭha”nti vuttasaddanayena vā pisodarādiākatigaṇapakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ [V 1.0155] gahetvā lokiya lokuttarasukhābhinibbattakaṃ sīlādipārappattaṃ bhāgyamassa atthīti “bhāgyavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuttanti āha “bhāgyavā”ti. Tathā anekabhedabhinnakilesasatasahassāni, saṅkhepato vā pañcamāre abhañjīti “bhaggavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuttanti dasseti “bhaggavā”ti iminā. Loke [M 1.0177] ca bhaga-saddo issariyadhammayasasirīkāmapayattesu chasu dhammesu pavattati, te ca bhagasaṅkhātā dhammā assa santīti bhagavāti atthaṃ dassetuṃ “yutto bhagehi cā”ti vuttaṃ. Kusalādīhi anekabhedehi sabbadhamme vibhaji vibhajitvā vivaritvā desesīti “vibhattavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuttanti āha “vibhattavā”ti. Dibbabrahmaariyavihāre, kāyacittaupadhiviveke, suññatānimittāppaṇihitavimokkhe, aññe ca lokiyalokuttare uttarimanussadhamme bhaji sevi bahulamakāsīti “bhattavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuttanti dasseti “bhattavā”ti iminā. Tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanamanena vantaṃ vamitanti “bhavesu vantagamano”ti vattabbe bhavasaddato bha-kāraṃ gamanasaddato ga-kāraṃ vantasaddato va-kāraṃ ādāya, tassa ca dīghaṃ katvā vaṇṇavipariyāyena “bhagavā”ti vuttanti dassetuṃ “vantagamano bhavesū”ti vuttaṃ. “Yato bhāgyavā, tato bhagavā”tiādinā paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Assa padassāti “bhagavā”ti padassa. Vitthāratthoti vitthārabhūto attho. “So cā”tiādinā ganthamahattaṃ pariharati. Vuttoyeva, na pana idha pana vattabbo visuddhimaggassa imissā aṭṭhakathāya ekadesabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

Having taken the stated characteristic of etymology, or by the method of the saying, 'pisodarādīni yathopadiṭṭhaṃ' (forms like pisodara are as instructed), or having taken the characteristic of inclusion in the form-group (ākati-gaṇa) beginning with 'pisodara'—because for Him there exists fortune (bhāgya), which brings forth worldly and supramundane happiness and has reached the pinnacle of virtue and so forth—when it should be said 'bhāgyavā' (the fortunate one), it is said 'bhagavā'. Thus, the commentator says, 'bhāgyavā'. Likewise, because He broke (abhañji) hundreds of thousands of defilements of numerous kinds, or in brief, the five Māras, when it should be said 'bhaggavā' (the breaker), it is said 'bhagavā'. This meaning is shown by the word 'bhaggavā'. And in the world, the word 'bhaga' is used for six things: sovereignty, Dhamma, fame, glory, desire, and effort. To show the meaning that because those things called 'bhaga' exist for Him, He is 'bhagavā', it is said, 'yutto bhagehi ca' (endowed with the bhagas). Because He analyzed (vibhaji) all phenomena into their numerous divisions, such as wholesome, etc., and having analyzed and explained them, He taught them, when it should be said 'vibhattavā' (the analyzer), it is said 'bhagavā' by way of etymology. Thus, he says, 'vibhattavā'. Because He resorted to (bhaji), associated with, and frequently cultivated the divine, Brahma, and noble abidings; the seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from the substrata of existence; the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and desirelessness; and other worldly and supramundane superior human qualities, when it should be said 'bhattavā' (one who resorts to), it is said 'bhagavā'. This meaning is shown by the word 'bhattavā'. Because in the three existences, the 'going' known as craving has been vomited out (vantaṃ) by Him, when it should be said 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one who has vomited out going in the existences), the word 'bhagavā' is formed by taking the letter 'bha' from 'bhava', the letter 'ga' from 'gamana', and the letter 'va' from 'vanta', lengthening the vowel of 'va', and reversing the letters. To show this meaning, it is said, 'vantagamano bhavesu'. By the phrase, 'Because he is bhāgyavā, therefore he is bhagavā,' and so on, each should be connected individually. 'Of this word' means of the word 'bhagavā'. 'The detailed meaning' means the expanded meaning. By 'so ca,' etc., he avoids making the text voluminous. It has already been stated, but it should not be stated again here. Why? Because the Visuddhimagga is a part of this commentary. This is the intention.

Apica bhage vani, vamīti vā bhagavā. So hi bhage sīlādiguṇe vani bhaji sevi, te vā bhagasaṅkhāte sīlādiguṇe vineyyasantānesu “kathaṃ nu kho uppajjeyyu”nti vani yāci patthayi, evaṃ bhage vanīti bhagavā, bhage vā siriṃ, issariyaṃ, yasañca vami kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya chaḍḍayi. Tathā hi bhagavā hatthagataṃ cakkavattisiriṃ, catudīpissariyaṃ, cakkavattisampattisannissayañca sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasaṃ anapekkho chaḍḍayi. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā ākārassa rassaṃ katvā, sineruyugandharādigatā bhājanalokasobhā. Tā bhagā vami tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahi, evaṃ bhage vamīti bhagavāti evamādīhi tattha tatthāgatanayehi cassa attho vattabbo, amhehi pana so ganthabhīrujanānuggahaṇatthaṃ, ganthagarutāpariharaṇatthañca ajjhupekkhitoti.

Furthermore, by another method, He is 'Bhagavā' because He resorted to (vani) the 'bhagas', or because He abandoned (vami) them. Indeed, that Blessed One resorted to, associated with, and served the 'bhagas', which are the qualities beginning with virtue. Or, concerning those qualities called 'bhaga', beginning with virtue, He desired, requested, and aspired, 'How might they arise in the mental continuities of those to be trained?' Thus, because He desired (vani) the 'bhagas', He is 'Bhagavā'. Or, He abandoned the 'bhagas'—glory, sovereignty, and fame—like a ball of spittle. Indeed, the Blessed One, being unconcerned, abandoned the glory of a universal monarch that had come into His hand, sovereignty over the four great continents, and the fame, resplendent with the seven treasures, which is the support for the fortune of a universal monarch. Alternatively, the constellations are called 'bhāni' (splendors). Because the splendors (sobhā) proceed in accordance with them (tehi), they are called 'bhagā', by shortening the vowel 'ā'. These are the splendors of the receptacle world, such as Sineru and Yugandhara. The Blessed One abandoned (vami) those 'bhagā' by abandoning the sensual passion connected with them. Thus, because He abandoned the 'bhagas', He is 'Bhagavā'. By these and other methods found in various places, the meaning of this word should be stated. However, that meaning has been disregarded by us for the sake of assisting students who are afraid of voluminous texts and for the sake of avoiding the text becoming burdensome.

Evametesaṃ avayavatthaṃ dassetvā idāni samudāyatthaṃ dassento purimapadattayassa samudāyatthena vuttāvasesena tesamatthānaṃ paṭiyogitāya tenāpi saha dassetuṃ “ettāvatā”tiādimāha. Ettāvatāti [V 1.0156][M 1.0178] etassa “evaṃ me suta”nti vacanena “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā” tivacanenāti imehi sambandho. Etthāti etasmiṃ nidānavacane. Yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ desentoti ettha anta-saddo hetuattho. Tathādesitattā hi paccakkhaṃ karoti nāma. Esa nayo aparatthāpi. “Yo kho ānanda, mayā dhammo ca…pe… satthā”ti vacanato dhammassa satthubhāvapariyāyo vijjatevāti katvā “dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karotī”ti vuttaṃ. Dhammakāyanti hi bhagavato sambandhībhūtaṃ dhammasaṅkhātaṃ kāyanti attho. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “dhammakāyoti bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Taṃ pana kimatthiyanti āha “tenā”tiādi. Tenāti ca tādisena paccakkhakaraṇenāti attho. Idaṃ adhunā vakkhamānasuttaṃ pāvacanaṃ pakaṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ buddhassa bhagavato vacanaṃ nāma. Tasmā tumhākaṃ atikkantasatthukaṃ atītasatthukabhāvo na hotīti attho. Bhāvappadhāno hi ayaṃ niddeso, bhāvalopo vā, itarathā pāvacanameva anatikkantasatthukaṃ, satthuadassanena pana ukkaṇṭhitassa janassa atikkantasatthukabhāvoti attho āpajjeyya, evañca sati “ayaṃ vo satthāti satthuadassanena ukkaṇṭhitaṃ janaṃ samassāsetī” tivacanena saha virodho bhaveyyāti vadanti. Idaṃ pāvacanaṃ satthukiccanipphādanena na atītasatthukanti pana attho. Satthūti kammatthe chaṭṭhī, samāsapadaṃ vā etaṃ satthuadassanenāti. Ukkaṇṭhanaṃ ukkaṇṭho, kicchajīvitā. “Kaṭha kicchajīvane”ti hi vadanti. Tamito pattoti ukkaṇṭhito, anabhiratiyā vā pīḷito vikkhittacitto hutvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā uddhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ katvā ito cito ca olokento āhiṇḍati, viharati cāti ukkaṇṭhito niruttinayena, taṃ ukkaṇṭhitaṃ. Saddasāmatthiyādhigatamatto cesa, vohārato pana anabhiratiyā pīḷitanti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Samassāsetīti assāsaṃ janeti.

Having thus shown the individual meaning of these words, now, wishing to show the collective meaning, the commentator, in order to show it together with the remaining meaning of the first three words—`evaṃ me sutaṃ`—by way of their collective meaning, due to the connection of those remaining meanings, said, '`ettāvatā`,' and so on. The connection of this word `ettāvatā` should be made with these words: with the phrase `evaṃ me sutaṃ` and with the phrase `ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā`. `Ettha` means 'in this introductory statement.' Here, in the phrase `yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ desento`, the suffix `-anta` has the meaning of cause. Indeed, because it was taught in such a way, it is said to make it directly perceptible. This method should be understood in subsequent instances as well. Because it was said, 'Ānanda, that Dhamma which was taught by me... is your teacher,' the Dhamma's state of being the Teacher certainly exists. Therefore, it was said, 'He makes the body of the Dhamma directly perceptible.' Indeed, the meaning of `dhammakāya` should be understood as the body, called Dhamma, which is related to the Blessed One. And so it was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, `dhammakāya` is a designation for the Tathāgata.' Furthermore, since it should be asked, 'For what purpose is that?' he said, '`tena`,' and so on. And `tena` means 'by such a direct perception.' Now, this discourse which is about to be spoken is called the `pāvacana`, the excellent, supreme word of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Therefore, the meaning is: for you, the state of having a teacher who has passed away does not exist. Indeed, this expression is one where the abstract noun (`bhāva`) is primary, or there is an elision of the word `bhāva`. Otherwise, if the meaning were taken differently, it would follow that only the `pāvacana` has a teacher who has not passed away, but for the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, the state of having a teacher who has passed away would exist. And if this were so, there would be a contradiction with the statement, 'He consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher by saying, "This is your teacher."' Thus say the teachers. Furthermore, the meaning is that this `pāvacana` does not have a teacher who has passed away because it accomplishes the Teacher's task. `Satthu` is the genitive case in the sense of the accusative, or this is a compound word meaning 'by not seeing the Teacher.' `Ukkaṇṭhanaṃ` (distress) is `ukkaṇṭho`, a difficult livelihood.
