For they say, 'The root `kaṭha` is in the sense of a difficult livelihood.' One is called `ukkaṇṭhito` because one has reached that state. Or, according to the etymological method, one is called `ukkaṇṭhito` because, being afflicted by discontent and having a distracted mind, one raises one's head, stretches one's neck upwards, and wanders about looking here and there. That is `ukkaṇṭhitaṃ`. And this meaning is obtained merely by the power of the word. In conventional usage, however, the intended meaning should be understood as 'afflicted by discontent.' This method should be understood everywhere. `Samassāseti` means 'he generates solace.'

Tasmiṃ samayeti imassa suttassa saṅgītisamaye. Kāmaṃ vijjamānepi bhagavati evaṃ vattumarahati, idha pana avijjamāneyeva tasmiṃ evaṃ vadati, tasmā sandhāyabhāsitavasena tadatthaṃ dassetīti āha “avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento”ti. Parinibbānanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuvasena khandhaparinibbānaṃ. Tenāti tathāsādhanena. Evaṃvidhassāti evaṃpakārassa, evaṃsabhāvassātipi [M 1.0179] attho. Nāma-saddo garahāyaṃ nipāto “atthi nāma ānanda theraṃ bhikkhuṃ vihesiyamānaṃ ajjhupekkhissathā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.166) viya, tena ediso api bhagavā parinibbuto, kā nāma kathā aññesanti garahatthaṃ joteti. Ariyadhammassāti ariyānaṃ dhammassa, ariyabhūtassa vā dhammassa. Dasavidhassa kāyabalassa, ñāṇabalassa ca vasena dasabaladharo. Vajirassa nāma maṇivisesassa saṅghāto samūho ekagghano, tena samāno kāyo yassāti tathā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā vajirasaṅghāto nāma na aññena maṇinā [V 1.0157] vā pāsāṇena vā bhejjo, api tu soyeva aññaṃ maṇiṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā bhindati. Teneva vuttaṃ “vajirassa natthi koci abhejjo maṇi vā pāsāṇo vā”ti, evaṃ bhagavāpi kenaci abhejjasarīro. Na hi bhagavato rūpakāye kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ sakkāti. Nāmasaddassa garahājotakattā pi-saddo sampiṇḍanajotako “na kevalaṃ bhagavāyeva, atha kho aññepī”ti. Ettha ca evaṃguṇasamannāgatattā aparinibbutasabhāvena bhavituṃ yuttopi esa parinibbuto evāti pakaraṇānurūpamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “eva”ntiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āsā patthanā kena janetabbā, na janetabbā evāti attho. “Ahaṃ ciraṃ jīviṃ, ciraṃ jīvāmi, ciraṃ jīvissāmi, sukhaṃ jīviṃ, sukhaṃ jīvāmi, sukhaṃ jīvissāmī”ti majjanavasena uppanno māno jīvitamado nāma, tena matto pamatto tathā. Saṃvejetīti saṃvegaṃ janeti, tatoyeva assa janassa saddhamme ussāhaṃ janeti. Saṃvejanañhi ussāhahetu “saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti vacanato.

`Tasmiṃ samaye` means: at the time of the communal recitation of this discourse. Although it would be appropriate to speak thus even if the Blessed One were present, here, however, he speaks thus only when He is not present. Therefore, to show that meaning by way of an implicit statement, he said, 'showing the state of being not present.' `Parinibbāna` means the final passing away of the aggregates by way of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. `Tena` means: by such an accomplishment. `Evaṃvidhassa` means: of such a kind; or the meaning is also 'of such a nature.' The word `nāma` is a particle used in the sense of reproach, as in such passages as: 'Is it possible, Ānanda, that you would look on indifferently while an elder monk is being harassed?' By this, it illuminates the meaning of reproach, thus: 'Even such a Blessed One has passed away into final Nibbāna; what, then, can be said of others?' `Ariyadhammassa` means: of the Dhamma of the noble ones, or of the Dhamma that has become noble. `Dasabaladharo` means the bearer of the ten powers by way of the ten kinds of bodily strength and the strength of knowledge. A `vajira` is a special kind of gem; `saṅghāta` is a mass, a collection, a solid block. He whose body is like that is so called. This is what is meant: just as a solid mass of vajira cannot be broken by another gem or stone, but rather it alone breaks another gem or stone. For that very reason it was said: 'For a vajira, there is no gem or stone that is unbreakable.' Similarly, the Blessed One has a body that cannot be broken by anyone. Indeed, no one is able to cause harm to the Blessed One's physical body. Because the word `nāma` illuminates reproach, the particle `pi` illuminates accumulation, meaning: 'Not only the Blessed One, but indeed others as well.' And here it should be understood that the words beginning with '`evaṃ`' were spoken to show the meaning in accordance with the context, thus: 'Although, being endowed with such qualities, it was fitting for him to be of a nature not to pass away into final Nibbāna, this one has indeed passed away into final Nibbāna.' `Āsā` is aspiration. By whom should it be generated? It should not be generated at all—this is the meaning. The conceit that arises by way of intoxication thus: 'I have lived long, I am living long, I will live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I will live happily,' is called intoxication with life. One is intoxicated and heedless because of that. `Saṃvejeti` means: it generates a sense of spiritual urgency. For that very reason, it generates effort in that person towards the good Dhamma. Indeed, a sense of spiritual urgency is the cause of effort, according to the saying: 'One who is spiritually stirred strives wisely.'

Desanāsampattiṃ niddisati vakkhamānassa sakalasuttassa “eva”nti nidassanato. Sāvakasampattinti suṇantapuggalasampattiṃ niddisati paṭisambhidāppattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena, pañcasu ca kosallesu āyasmatā dhammasenāpatinā pasaṃsitena mayā mahāsāvakena sutaṃ, tañca kho sayameva sutaṃ na anussutaṃ, na ca paramparābhatanti atthassa dīpanato. Kālasampattiṃ niddisati bhagavātisadasannidhāne payuttassa samayasaddassa buddhuppāda-paṭimaṇḍita-samaya-bhāva-dīpanato. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The excellence of the teaching is indicated, as the word 'evaṃ' points to the entirety of the Sutta to be spoken. The excellence of the disciple—that is, the excellence of the listening person—is indicated because it shows the meaning that: 'It was heard by me, a great disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges, who was placed by the Blessed One as foremost in five respects, and who was praised in five skills by the venerable General of the Dhamma; and that which was heard was heard by myself, not through hearsay, and not brought down through a succession of teachers.' The excellence of the time is indicated because the word 'samaya', used in proximity to the word 'Bhagavā', shows the nature of a time adorned by the arising of a Buddha. Indeed, the excellence of time is supreme through the arising of a Buddha. Therefore, this is said:

“Kappakasāyakaliyuge[M 1.0180], buddhuppādo aho mahacchariyaṃ;

Hutavahamajjhe jātaṃ, samuditamakarandamaravinda”nti. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.1; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1);

“In the degenerate Kali Yuga of the eon, the arising of a Buddha is, ah, a great wonder; like a smokeless lotus, well-arisen amidst a fire.”

Tassāyamattho – kappasaṅkhātakālasañcayassa lekhanavasena pavatte kaliyugasaṅkhāte sakarājasammate vassādisamūhe jāto buddhuppādakhaṇasaṅkhāto dinasamūho andhassa pabbatārohanamiva kadāci pavattanaṭṭhena, accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttaṭṭhena ca mahacchariyaṃ hoti. Kimiva jātanti ce? Hutavahasaṅkhātassa pāvakassa majjhe sammā uditamadhumantaṃ aravindasaṅkhātaṃ vārijamiva jātanti. Desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagāravādhivacanato.

This is its meaning: The collection of days reckoned as the moment of the Buddha’s appearance—which arises in the collection of years and so forth, designated as the royal era, known as the Kali Yuga, which unfolds by way of reckoning the accumulation of time called an eon—is a great wonder. This is because of its nature of occurring only sometimes, like a blind person climbing a mountain, and because its nature is fit for a snap of the fingers. If it is asked, 'What is it like?' It is like a water-born plant known as a lotus, well-arisen and smokeless in the midst of the fire called Hutavaha. He indicates the excellence of the Teacher because it is a term expressing great reverence for the one who is supreme among beings distinguished by virtue.

Evaṃ padachakkassa padānukkamena nānappakārato atthavaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni “antarā ca rājagaha”ntiādīnaṃ [V 1.0158] padānamatthavaṇṇanaṃ karonto “antarā cā”tiādimāha. Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandanti ettha samabhiniviṭṭho antarā-saddo dissati sāmaññavacanīyatthamapekkhitvā pakaraṇādisāmatthiyādigatatthamantarenāti attho. Evaṃ panassa nānatthabhāvo payogato avagamīyatīti dasseti “tadantara”ntiādinā. Tattha tadantaranti taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Mañca tañca mantenti, kimantaraṃ kiṃ kāraṇanti attho. Vijjantarikāyāti vijjuniccharaṇakkhaṇe. Dhovantī itthī addasāti sambandho. Antaratoti hadaye. Kopāti cittakālussiyakaraṇato cittapakopā rāgādayo. Antarā vosānanti ārambhanipphattīnaṃ vemajjhe pariyosānaṃ āpādi. Apicāti tathāpi, evaṃ pabhavasampannepīti attho. Dvinnaṃ mahānirayānanti lohakumbhīniraye sandhāyāha. Antarikāyāti antarena. Rājagahanagaraṃ kira āvijjhitvā mahāpetaloko. Tattha dvinnaṃ mahālohakumbhīnirayānaṃ antarena ayaṃ tapodā nadī āgacchati, tasmā sā kuthitā sandatīti. Svāyamidha vivare pavattati tadaññesamasambhavato. Ettha ca “tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya, (a. ni. 6.44; 10.75) etesaṃ antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā, (bu. vaṃ. 28.9) antarantarā kathaṃ opātetī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.426; pahā. va. 66; cūḷava. 376) viya kāraṇavemajjhesu vattamānā antarāsaddāyeva udāharitabbā siyuṃ, na pana cittakhaṇavivaresu vattamānā antarikaantarasaddā[M 1.0181]. Antarāsaddassa hi ayamatthuddhāroti. Ayaṃ panetthādhippāyo siyā – yesu atthesu antarikasaddo, antarasaddo ca pavattati, tesu antarāsaddopīti samānatthattā antarāsaddatthe vattamāno antarikasaddo, antarasaddo, ca udāhaṭoti. Atha vā antarāsaddoyeva “yassantarato”ti (udā. 20) ettha gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vutto –

Having thus explained the meaning of the six terms in various ways according to their sequence, now, wishing to explain the meaning of the terms beginning with 'antarā ca rājagahaṃ', he says 'antarā cā' and so on. Here, in 'antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ', the word 'antarā' is seen as firmly established; the meaning is that, considering its generally spoken sense, one should set aside meanings derived from the power of context and so on. Furthermore, he shows that its various meanings are to be understood from usage with 'tadantaraṃ' and so on. Therein, 'tadantaraṃ' means 'that cause'. As in 'They consult me and you', the meaning is 'What is the reason (antaraṃ)? What is the cause?' 'Vijjantarikāya' means 'at the moment of a lightning flash.' The connection is: 'A woman washing saw it.' 'Antarato' means 'in the heart.' 'Kopā' means defilements such as lust, which corrupt the mind, because they cause mental turbidity. 'Antarā vosānaṃ' means it brought about a conclusion in the middle of the beginning and the completion. 'Apicā' means 'nevertheless'; the meaning is 'even though endowed with such power.' 'Of two great hells'—he says this referring to the Lohakumbhī hells. 'Antarikāya' means 'in between.' It is said that the great realm of petas exists, having pierced through the city of Rājagaha. There, this river Tapodā comes between the two great Lohakumbhī hells; therefore, it flows boiling. Here, this same word 'antarā' occurs in the sense of 'interval' (vivara), because other meanings are impossible. And here, an objection might be raised: 'Only the word 'antarā' occurring in the sense of cause and middle, as in such examples as, "Who could know what is the cause (tadantaraṃ)?", "The eons in between (antarā kappā) them are innumerable", and "How does he drop a word in between (antarantarā)?", should be cited, but not the words 'antarika' and 'antara' occurring in the senses of mind, moment, and interval. For this is an exposition of the word 'antarā'.' To this, the intention might be as follows: in whichever meanings the words 'antarika' and 'antara' occur, in those the word 'antarā' also occurs. Thus, because they have the same meaning, 'antarika' and 'antara' occurring in the sense of 'antarā' are cited. Or else, the word 'antarā' itself, in 'yassantarato', is spoken shortened for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse—

“Yassantarato na santi kopā,

Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto;

Taṃ vigatabhayaṃ sukhiṃ asokaṃ,

Devā nānubhavanti dassanāyā”ti. (udā. 20); –

“He for whom there are no defilements within, who has overcome this state of becoming and non-becoming; that one, free from fear, happy, and sorrowless—the gods cannot attain to see.”

Hi ayaṃ udāne bhaddiyasutte gāthā. Soyeva ika-saddena sakatthapavattena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “antarikāyā”ti ca vutto, tasmā udāharaṇodāharitabbānamettha virodhābhāvo veditabboti. Kimatthaṃ atthavisesaniyamo katoti āha “tasmā”tiādi. Nanu cettha upayogavacanameva, atha kasmā sambandhīyattho vutto, sambandhīyatthe vā kasmā upayogavacanaṃ katanti anuyogasambhavato taṃ pariharituṃ “antarāsaddena panā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tena sambandhīyatthe sāmivacanappasaṅge [V 1.0159] saddantarayogena laddhamidaṃ upayogavacananti dasseti, na kevalaṃ sāsaneva, lokepi evamevidaṃ laddhanti dassento “īdisesu cā”tiādimāha. Visesayogatādassanamukhena hi ayamatthopi dassito. Ekenapi antarā-saddena yuttattā dve upayogavacanāni kātabbāni. Dvīhi pana yoge kā kathāti atthassa sijjhanato. Akkharaṃ cintenti liṅgavibhattiyādīhīti akkharacintakā, saddavidū. Akkhara-saddena cettha tammūlakāni padādīnipi gahetabbāni. Yadipi saddato ekameva yujjanti, atthato pana so dvikkhattuṃ yojetabbo ekassāpi padassa āvuttiyādinayena anekadhā sampajjanatoti dasseti “dutiyapadenapī”tiādinā. Ko pana doso ayojiteti āha “ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇātī”ti. Dutiyapadaṃ na pāpuṇātīti attho saddantarayogavasā saddeyeva sāmivacanappasaṅge upayogavibhattiyā icchitattā. Saddādhikāro hi vibhattipayogo.

Indeed, this is the verse in the Bhaddiyasutta of the Udāna. That very word is also stated as 'antarikāya' by expanding the word with the suffix 'ika', which functions in its own sense. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no contradiction here between the example and what is to be exemplified. To the question, 'For what purpose is the rule of a specific meaning made?', he says, 'therefore,' and so on. Is it not that here there is only the locative case? Then why is the relational meaning stated? Or, in the relational meaning, why is the locative case used? To avert such an objection, it is said, 'but with the word antarā,' and so on. By this, he shows that when there is an occasion for the genitive case in the relational meaning, this locative case is obtained through connection with another word. To show that this is obtained not only in the Teaching but also in the world in this very way, he says, 'and in such cases,' and so on. For this meaning is also shown by means of demonstrating the connection with a specific word. Even with one word 'antarā', two locative cases must be made due to its connection. But when there is a connection with two, what is there to say? For the meaning is established. Those who reflect on letters with regard to gender, case-endings, and so on, are grammarians, those who know words. And here, by the word 'letter', words and so on, which are based on them, should also be taken. By 'also with the second word,' and so on, he shows that although from the point of view of the word only one is connected, from the point of view of meaning it should be connected twice, because it occurs in many ways, by the method of repetition of a single word, and so on. To the question, 'But what is the fault if it is not connected?', he says, 'When it is not connected, it does not attain the locative case.' The meaning is that the second word does not attain it, because, due to the power of connection with another word, the locative case-ending is desired when there is an occasion for the genitive case in the word itself. For the application of case-endings is governed by the word.

Addhāna-saddo [M 1.0182] dīghapariyāyoti āha “dīghamagga”nti. Kittāvatā pana so dīgho nāma tadatthabhūtoti codanamapaneti “addhānagamanasamayassa hī”tiādinā. Addhānagamanasamayassa vibhaṅgeti gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadādīsu addhānagamanasamayasaddassa padabhājanīyabhūte vibhaṅge (pāci. 217). Aḍḍhayojanampi addhānamaggo, pageva taduttari. Aḍḍhameva yojanassa aḍḍhayojanaṃ, dvigāvutamattaṃ. Idha pana catugāvutappamāṇaṃ yojanameva, tasmā “addhānamaggapaṭipanno”ti vadatīti adhippāyo.

The word 'addhāna' is a synonym for 'dīgha' (long); thus, he says 'a long road'. But by what measure is that road, being the meaning of that word, called 'long'? He dispels this objection with 'for the time of journeying on a road,' and so on. 'In the analysis of the time of journeying on a road' means: in the Vibhaṅga (Pācittiya 217), which is the word-analysis of the term 'the time of journeying on a road' in the training rules on group meals and so on. Even half a yojana is a long road; what then is to be said of more than that. Half a yojana is just half of a yojana, the measure of two gāvutas. But here, a yojana is the measure of four gāvutas. Therefore, the intention is that he says, 'one who has entered upon a long road'.

Mahantasaddo uttamattho, bahvattho ca idhādhippetoti āha “mahatā”tiādi. Guṇamahattenāti appicchatādiguṇamahantabhāvena. Saṅkhyāmahattenāti gaṇanamahantabhāvena. Tadevatthaṃ samattheti “so hī”tiādinā. So bhikkhusaṅghoti idha āgato tadā parivārabhūto bhikkhusaṅgho. Mahāti uttamo. Vākyepi hi tamicchanti payogavasā. Appicchatāti nillobhatā saddo cettha sāvaseso, attho pana niravaseso. Na hi “appalobhatāti abhitthavitumarahatī”ti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Majjhimāgamaṭīkākāro pana ācariyadhammapālatthero evamāha “appasaddassa parittapariyāyaṃ manasi katvā ‘byañjanaṃ sāvasesaṃ viyā’ti (mahāni. aṭṭha. 85) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Appasaddo panettha ‘abhāvattho’ tipi sakkā viññātuṃ ‘appābādhatañcasañjānāmī’tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.225) viyā”ti. Saṅkhyāyapi mahāti gaṇanāyapi bahu ahosi, “bhikkhusaṅgho”ti padāvatthikantavacanavasena saṃvaṇṇetabbapadassa chedanamiva hotīti tadaparāmasitvā “tena bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti puna vākyāvatthikantavacanavasena saṃvaṇṇetabbapadena sadisīkaraṇaṃ. Esā hi saṃvaṇṇanakānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ vibhattiyānapekkhāvasena yathārahaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbapadatthaṃ [V 1.0160] saṃvaṇṇetvā puna tattha vijjamānavibhattivasena parivattetvā nikkhipananti. Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatattā saṅghoti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento āha “diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātena samaṇagaṇenā”ti. Ettha pana “yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324, 356; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; pari. 274) evaṃ vuttāya diṭṭhiyā. “Yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni [M 1.0183] viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni, tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.323; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.11; pari. 274) evaṃ vuttānañca sīlānaṃ sāmaññena saṅghāto saṅghaṭito sametoti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghāto, samaṇagaṇo, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghāṭasaṅkhātenā” tipi pāṭho. Tathā saṅkhātena katitenāti attho. Tathā hi diṭṭhisīlādīnaṃ niyatasabhāvattā sotāpannāpi aññamaññaṃ diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatā, pageva sakadāgāmiādayo, tathā ca vuttaṃ “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti, (saṃ. ni. 2.41; 5.198, 1004) “aṭṭhānametaṃ bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo sañciccapāṇaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti ca ādi. Ariyapuggalassa hi yattha katthaci dūre ṭhitāpi attano guṇasāmaggiyā saṃhatatāyeva, “tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati, (ma. ni. 1.492) tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.492) vacanato pana puthujjanānampi diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvo labbhatiyeva. Saddhiṃ-saddo ekatoti atthe nipāto. Pañca…pe… mattānīti pañca-saddena mattasaddaṃ saṅkhipitvā bāhiratthasamāso vutto. Etesanti bhikkhusatānaṃ. Puna pañca mattā pamāṇāti byāso, nikāralopo cettha napuṃsakaliṅgattā.

The word 'mahanta' has the meaning of 'supreme' and also the meaning of 'many', and it is intended here. Therefore, he said: 'mahatā,' and so on. By 'greatness of qualities' is meant the state of being great through qualities such as fewness of wishes. By 'greatness of number' is meant the state of being great in terms of count. That very meaning is supported by 'so hi,' and so on. By 'that community of bhikkhus' is meant the community of bhikkhus that had come there at that time and had become the retinue. 'Mahā' means 'supreme'. Indeed, also in a sentence, they desire that meaning by the force of usage. 'Fewness of wishes' (appicchatā) means 'greedlessness' (nillobhatā). Here the word [appa] is with a remainder, but the meaning is without remainder. For it is said in the commentaries: 'Indeed, having little greed is not worthy of praise.' However, the author of the sub-commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, says thus: 'Having kept in mind the synonym 'paritta' (little) for the word 'appa', it was said in the commentary: "the letter is as if with a remainder" (Mahāni. Aṭṭha. 85). Here, the word 'appa' can also be understood as having the meaning of 'absence', as in 'I perceive freedom from affliction,' and so on (MN 1.225).' Also in terms of number, 'great' means: they were many in number. Because stating `bhikkhusaṅgho` [in the nominative] by way of the word ending a constituent phrase is as if a cutting off of the word to be explained, without considering that, it is made similar to the word to be explained by stating `tena bhikkhusaṅghenā` [in the instrumental], again by way of the word ending a sentence. This is indeed the nature of the commentators: having explained the meaning of the word to be explained appropriately without regard for the inflection, they then present it by changing it according to the inflection existing there. Clarifying the meaning that it is a 'saṅgha' because of being united by commonality of view and virtue, he said: 'by the group of ascetics united by commonality of view and virtue.' Here, this is of the view thus stated: 'Whatever view is noble, leading out, which leads out the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering, with such a view one abides having attained commonality of view' (DN 3.324, 356; MN 1.492; 3.54; Ps 274). And of the virtues thus stated: 'Whatever virtues are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, and conducive to concentration, with such virtues one abides having attained commonality of virtue' (DN 3.323; MN 1.492; 3.54; AN 6.11; Ps 274). The union, being brought together and assembled by the commonality of these virtues, is a 'union by commonality of view and virtue,' a group of ascetics. It means 'united by commonality of view and virtue.' There is also the reading: `Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghāṭasaṅkhātena`. The meaning is: 'thus designated, called.' For so it is: because of the fixed nature of view, virtue, and so on, even stream-enterers are united with one another by commonality of view and virtue, how much more so once-returners and so on. And so it was said: 'Fixed, with enlightenment as his destination' (SN 2.41; 5.198, 1004), and 'This is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot be, that a person endowed with right view should intentionally deprive a living being of life. That possibility does not exist,' and so on. Indeed, for a noble person, even when staying far away anywhere at all, there is only unity through the harmony of their own qualities. However, from the statements 'one abides having attained commonality of view with such a view' (MN 1.492) and 'one abides having attained commonality of virtue with such virtues' (MN 1.492), a state of unity by commonality of view and virtue is indeed obtained even for worldlings. The word 'saddhiṃ' is a particle in the sense of 'ekato' (together). In 'Pañca...mattāni,' by abbreviating the word 'matta' with the word 'pañca,' an external compound is stated. 'Etesaṃ' means: of these hundreds of bhikkhus. Again, 'pañca mattā pamāṇā' is the full form; here, there is elision of the suffix `ni` due to the neuter gender.

Suppiyoti tassa nāmameva, na guṇādi. Na kevalaṃ bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ bhagavāyeva, atha kho suppiyopi paribbājako brahmadattena māṇavena saddhinti puggalaṃ sampiṇḍeti, tañca kho maggapaṭipannasabhāgatāya eva, na sīlācārādisabhāgatāyāti vuttaṃ “pi-kāro”tiādi. Sukhuccāraṇavasena pubbāparapadānaṃ sambandhamattakarabhāvaṃ sandhāya “padasandhikaro”ti vuttaṃ, na pana sarabyañjanādisandhibhāvaṃ, tenāha “byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasena vutto”ti, etena padapūraṇamattanti dasseti. Apica avadhāraṇatthopi kho-saddo yutto “assosi kho verañjo brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (pārā. 1) viya, tena addhānamaggapaṭipanno ahosiyeva, nāssa maggapaṭipattiyā koci antarāyo ahosīti ayamattho dīpito hoti. Sañjayassāti rājagahavāsino [V 1.0161] sañjayanāmassa paribbājakassa, yassa santike paṭhamaṃ upatissakolitāpi pabbajiṃsu channaparibbājakova[M 1.0184], na acelakaparibbājako. “Yadā, tadā”ti ca etena samakālameva addhānamaggapaṭipannataṃ dasseti. Atītakālattho pāḷiyaṃ hotisaddo yogavibhāgena, taṃkālāpekkhāya vā evaṃ vuttaṃ, tadā hotīti attho.

Suppiyo is just his name, not a name based on quality, etc. Not only the Blessed One with the community of bhikkhus, but also Suppiya the wanderer with the young man Brahmadatta—thus he groups together the persons. And that is only because of the shared nature of being on a journey, not because of a shared nature of virtue, conduct, etc. Thus it is said 'the particle pi,' etc. With reference to its nature of merely making a connection between the preceding and following words for the sake of easy pronunciation, it is called a 'word-joiner' (padasandhikaro), but not with reference to the nature of euphonic combination of vowels, consonants, etc. Therefore, he said: 'spoken for the sake of consonantal smoothness.' By this, he shows that it is a mere expletive. Moreover, the word 'kho' is also suitable in the sense of emphasis, as in 'the brahmin Verañja heard' (Pārā. 1), etc. By that, this meaning is revealed: he was indeed travelling on the long road, and for him there was no obstacle to his journey. 'Sañjayassa' means: of the wanderer named Sañjaya, a resident of Rājagaha, in whose presence Upatissa and Kolita also first went forth. He was a clothed wanderer, not a naked wanderer. And by 'yadā, tadā' (when, then), he shows that their travelling on the long road was at the very same time. In the Pāḷi, the word 'hoti' has a past tense meaning by separation of the grammatical rule, or it is said thus with reference to that time. The meaning is 'at that time, he was'.

Anteti samīpe. Vasatīti vattapaṭivattādikaraṇavasena sabbiriyāpathasādhāraṇavacanaṃ, avacaratīti vuttaṃ hoti, tenevāha “samīpacāro santikāvacaro sisso”ti. Coditā devadūtehīti daharakumāro jarājiṇṇasatto gilāno kammakāraṇā, kammakāraṇikā vā matasattoti imehi pañcahi devadūtehi coditā ovaditā saṃvegaṃ uppāditā samānāpi. Te hi devā viya dūtā, visuddhidevānaṃ vā dūtāti devadūtā. Hīnakāyūpagāti apāyakāyamupagatā. Narasaṅkhātā te māṇavāti sambandho. Sāmaññavasena cettha satto “māṇavo”ti vutto, itare pana visesavasena. Pakaraṇādhigato hesa atthuddhāroti. Katakammehīti katacorakammehi. Taruṇoti soḷasavassato paṭṭhāya pattavīsativasso, udānaṭṭhakathāyañhi “sattā jātadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva pañcadasavassakā, tāva ‘kumārakā, bālā’ti ca vuccanti. Tato paraṃ vīsativassāni ‘yuvāno’”ti (udā. aṭṭha. 44) vuttaṃ. Taruṇo, māṇavo, yuvāti ca atthato ekaṃ, lokiyā pana “dvādasavassato paṭṭhāya yāva jaramappatto, tāva taruṇo”tipi vadanti.

‘Anta’ means ‘nearby.’ ‘Vasati’ (he dwells) is a word common to all postures, in the sense of performing duties and counter-duties; the intended meaning is ‘he moves about.’ For that very reason, the commentator said: ‘A pupil is one who moves about nearby, who conducts himself in the vicinity.’ ‘Urged by the divine messengers’ means that even though they were urged, admonished, and stirred to a sense of urgency by these five divine messengers—a young boy, a being decrepit with old age, a sick person, one who inflicts punishment or one who undergoes it, and a dead being. For they are messengers like gods, or they are messengers of the pure gods; therefore, they are called ‘divine messengers.’ ‘Having gone to a low state’ means having gone to the plane of misery. The connection is to be made thus: ‘those youths designated as men.’ And here, a being is called a ‘youth’ in a general sense, while the others are so called in a specific sense. For this elucidation of meaning is understood from the context. ‘By those who have committed deeds’ means by those who have committed the act of theft. ‘Young’ means from sixteen years of age up to twenty years. For in the Udāna commentary, it is said: ‘From the day of birth up to fifteen years, beings are called “boys” and “children.” After that, those who are twenty years old are called “youths”’ (Udāna Commentary 44). ‘Taruṇa,’ ‘māṇava,’ and ‘yuvā’ are one in meaning. But worldly people also say, ‘From twelve years of age until one has not yet reached old age, so long is one called “young.”’

Tesu vā dvīsu janesūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Yo vā “ekaṃ samaya”nti pubbe adhigato kālo, tassa paṭiniddeso tatrāti yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā antarā rājagahañca nāḷandañca addhānamaggapaṭipanno, tasmiṃyeva samaye suppiyopi taṃ addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, brahmadatto ca vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti. Nipātamattanti ettha mattasaddena visesatthābhāvato padapūraṇattaṃ dasseti. Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyoti madhupiṇḍikadesanā nāma iti naṃ suttantaṃ dhārehi, rājaññāti pāyāsirājaññanāmakaṃ rājānamālapati. Pariyāyati parivattatīti pariyāyo, vāro. Pariyāyeti desetabbamatthaṃ paṭipādetīti pariyāyo, desanā. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ paṭiggahetvā pavattatīti pariyāyo, kāraṇaṃ. Anekasaddeneva anekavidhenāti attho viññāyati adhippāyamattenāti [M 1.0185] āha “anekavidhenā”ti. Kāraṇañcettha kāraṇapatirūpakameva, na ekaṃsakāraṇaṃ avaṇṇakāraṇassa abhūtattā, tasmā kāraṇenāti kāraṇapatirūpakenāti attho. Tathā hi vakkhati “akāraṇameva ‘kāraṇa’nti vatvā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1). Jātivasenidaṃ bahvatthe ekavacananti dasseti “bahūhī”tiādinā.

Or, ‘among those two people’ is the locative case in the sense of determination. Or, ‘there’ is a re-specification of the time previously understood as ‘at one time.’ For at the very time when the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda, at that same time Suppiya too was traveling along that road, speaking dispraise, while Brahmadatta spoke praise. In ‘a mere particle,’ the word ‘matta,’ due to the absence of a special meaning, shows that it is a mere expletive. ‘The Discourse on the Honey-ball’ means the teaching named ‘Honey-ball’; thus you should remember that Suttanta. By ‘O khattiya,’ he addresses the king named Pāyāsi, the khattiya. Because it turns around, it is a ‘pariyāya’; a turn. Because it accomplishes the meaning to be taught, it is a ‘pariyāya’; a teaching. Because it proceeds having received its own fruit, it is a ‘pariyāya’; a cause. The meaning ‘in many ways’ is understood by the word ‘many’ itself; it is not understood by mere intention. Therefore, he said ‘in many ways.’ And here the cause is only a semblance of a cause, not a definite cause, because the reason for the dispraise was unreal. Therefore, ‘by a cause’ means ‘by a semblance of a cause.’ For thus it will be said: ‘having said that what is not a cause is a “cause”’ (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary 1.1). This shows that this singular is used in a plural sense by way of class, as indicated by ‘with many,’ etc.

“Avaṇṇavirahitassa [V 1.0162] asamānavaṇṇasamannāgatassapī”ti vakkhamānakāraṇassa akāraṇabhāvahetudassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, dosavirahitassapi asadisaguṇasamannāgatassāpīti attho. Buddhassa bhagavato avaṇṇaṃ dosaṃ nindanti sambandho. “Yaṃ loke”tiādinā arasarūpanibbhogaakiriyavādaucchedavādajegucchīvenayikatapassīapagabbhabhāvānaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ dasseti. Tasmāti hi etaṃ “arasarūpo…pe… apagabbho”ti imehi padehi sambandhitabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – lokasammato abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalīkammasāmīcikammaāsanābhinimantanasaṅkhāto sāmaggīraso samaṇassa gotamassa natthi, tasmā so sāmaggīrasasaṅkhātena rasena asampannasabhāvo, tena sāmaggīrasasaṅkhātena paribhogena asamannāgato. Tassa akattabbatāvādo, ucchijjitabbatāvādo ca, taṃ sabbaṃ gūthaṃ viya maṇḍanajātiyo puriso jegucchī. Tassa vināsako sova tadakaraṇato vinetabbo. Tadakaraṇena vayovuḍḍhe tāpeti tadācāravirahitatāya vā kapaṇapuriso. Tadakaraṇena devalokagabbhato apagato, tadakaraṇato vā so hīnagabbho cāti evaṃ tadeva abhivādanādiakaraṇaṃ arasarūpatādīnaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Natthi…pe… viseso”ti etassa pana “sundarikāya nāma paribbājikāya maraṇānavabodho, saṃsārassa ādikoṭiyā apaññāyanapaṭiññā, ṭhapanīyapucchāya abyākatavatthubyākaraṇa”nti evamādīni kāraṇapatirūpakāni niddhāritabbāni, tathā “takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo…pe… sayampaṭibhāna”nti etassa “anācariyakena sāmaṃ paṭivedhena tattha tattha tathā tathā dhammadesanā, katthaci paresaṃ paṭipucchākathanaṃ, mahāmoggallānādīhi ārocitanayeneva byākaraṇa”nti evamādīni, “samaṇo…pe… na aggapuggalo”ti etesaṃ pana “sabbadhammānaṃ kameneva [M 1.0186] anavabodho, lokantassa ajānanaṃ, attanā icchitatapacārābhāvo”ti evamādīni. Jhānavimokkhādi heṭṭhā vuttanayena uttarimanussadhammo. Ariyaṃ visuddhaṃ, uttamaṃ vā ñāṇasaṅkhātaṃ dassanaṃ, alaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ ariyañāṇadassanaṃ ettha, etassāti vā alamariyañāṇadassano. Sveva viseso tathā. Ariyañāṇadassanameva vā visesaṃ vuttanayena alaṃ pariyattaṃ yassa, yasminti vā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, uttarimanussadhammova. Takkapariyāhatanti kappanāmattena samantato āharitaṃ, vitakkena vā parighaṭitaṃ. Vīmaṃsānucaritanti vīmaṃsanāya punappunaṃ parimajjitaṃ. Sayampaṭibhānanti sayameva attano vibhūtaṃ, tādisaṃ dhammanti sambandho. Akāraṇanti ayuttaṃ anupapattiṃ. Kāraṇapade cetaṃ visesanaṃ. Na hi arasarūpatādayo dosā bhagavati saṃvijjanti, dhammasaṅghesu ca durakkhātaduppaṭipannādayo akāraṇanti vā yuttikāraṇarahitaṃ attanā paṭiññāmattaṃ. Pakatikammapadañcetaṃ. Imasmiñca atthe kāraṇaṃ vatvāti ettha kāraṇaṃ ivāti iva-saddattho rūpakanayena yojetabbo patirūpakakāraṇassa [V 1.0163] adhippetattā. Tathā tathāti jātivuḍḍhānamanabhivādanādinā tena tena ākārena. Vaṇṇasaddassa guṇapasaṃsāsu pavattanato yathākkamaṃ “avaṇṇaṃ dosaṃ ninda”nti vuttaṃ.

“Even for one free from dispraise and endowed with incomparable praise” — this is stated to show that the reason to be mentioned is no reason, meaning, even for one free from faults and endowed with matchless qualities. The connection is as follows: [they speak] dispraise ('avaṇṇaṃ') of the Buddha, the Blessed One, meaning fault ('dosaṃ') and blame ('nindaṃ'). By the passage beginning with “Whatever in the world,” it shows a counterfeit reason for the states of being tasteless, without enjoyment, of the doctrine of inaction, of the doctrine of annihilation, of being repulsive, of being one who should be disciplined, of being an ascetic, and of being impudent. Indeed, this word ‘Therefore’ should be connected with these words: ‘tasteless… impudent.’ This is what is meant: The taste of harmony, known in the world as paying homage, rising to greet, making the añjali gesture, proper courtesy, and offering a seat, is absent in the ascetic Gotama. Therefore, he is of a nature not endowed with the taste called the taste of harmony; he is not endowed with that enjoyment called the taste of harmony. There is the view that this [harmony] should not be practiced, and the view that it should be cut off. A person of refined nature despises all that, just as one despises excrement. He is a destroyer of that, and for not doing it, he should be disciplined. By not doing it, he torments the elders; or, due to being devoid of such conduct, he is a wretched person. By not doing it, he has departed from the womb of the deva world; or, for not doing it, he is of inferior birth. Thus, that very non-performance of paying homage and so forth should be seen as a counterfeit reason for tastelessness and so on. Furthermore, for the phrase “There is no… distinction,” counterfeit reasons such as these should be determined: the non-comprehension of the death of the female wanderer named Sundarikā; the admission of not perceiving the beginning of saṃsāra; the explanation of an undeclared matter in a question to be set aside. Similarly, for the phrase “hammered out by reasoning… self-inspired,” [counterfeit reasons such as these should be determined]: preaching the Dhamma in various places and in various ways through his own penetration without a teacher; in some places, answering others after asking them back; explaining only in the way reported by Mahāmoggallāna and others. And for these words, “the ascetic… is not the foremost person,” [counterfeit reasons such as these should be determined]: the non-comprehension of all dhammas only in sequence; not knowing the end of the world; the absence of the ascetic practice desired by himself. Jhāna, liberation, and so on are a superhuman state, in the way explained previously. Vision ('dassanaṃ'), which is called knowledge ('ñāṇa'), is noble ('ariyaṃ'), pure ('visuddhaṃ'), or supreme ('uttamaṃ'). Noble knowledge and vision ('ariyañāṇadassanaṃ') is that which is capable of destroying defilements. Because this [superhuman state] possesses this, or because of it, it is called ‘alamariyañāṇadassano’ (one possessing sufficient noble knowledge and vision). That very thing is the distinction. Or, for whom or in whom noble knowledge and vision itself is the distinction, sufficient in the way explained, that is ‘alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso’ (one with the distinction of sufficient noble knowledge and vision), which is indeed a superhuman state. ‘Takkapariyāhataṃ’ (hammered out by reasoning) means brought forth from all around by mere conjecture, or hammered out by reasoning. ‘Vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ’ (followed by investigation) means repeatedly polished by investigation. ‘Sayampaṭibhānaṃ’ (self-inspired) means made manifest to oneself by oneself; the connection is to such a Dhamma. ‘Akāraṇaṃ’ (without reason) means improper, unfounded. And this is an adjective to the word ‘kāraṇa’. Indeed, faults such as tastelessness do not exist in the Blessed One, nor do things like being poorly explained or badly practiced exist in the Dhamma and Saṅgha. Or, ‘akāraṇaṃ’ means a mere assertion by oneself, devoid of valid reason. And this is a term for the direct object. And in this meaning, in the phrase ‘having stated a reason,’ the meaning of the word ‘iva’ (as if) in ‘as if a reason’ should be applied by way of a metaphor, because a counterfeit reason is intended. ‘Tathā tathā’ (in such and such a way) means in this and that manner, by not paying homage and so on to those senior by birth. Because the word ‘vaṇṇa’ occurs in the senses of ‘quality’ and ‘praise’, ‘avaṇṇaṃ’ is stated respectively as ‘dosaṃ’ (fault) and ‘nindaṃ’ (blame).

Durakkhātoti duṭṭhumākkhāto, tathā duppaṭivedito. Vaṭṭato niyyātīti niyyānaṃ, tadeva niyyāniko, tato vā niyyānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, tattha niyuttoti niyyāniko. Vaṭṭato vā niyyātīti niyyāniko ya-kārassa ka-kāraṃ, ī-kārassa ca rassaṃ katvā. “Anīya-saddo hi bahulā kattuabhidhāyako”ti saddavidū vadanti, na niyyāniko tathā. Saṃsāradukkhassa anupasamasaṃvattaniko vuttanayena. Paccanīkapaṭipadanti sammāpaṭipattiyā viruddhapaṭipadaṃ. Ananulomapaṭipadanti sappurisānaṃ ananulomapaṭipadaṃ. Adhammānulomapaṭipadanti lokuttaradhammassa ananulomapaṭipadaṃ. Kasmā panettha “avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti ca vattamānakālaniddeso kato, nanu saṅgītikālato so avaṇṇavaṇṇānaṃ bhāsanakālo atītoti? Saccametaṃ, “addhānamaggapaṭipanno hotī”ti ettha hoti-saddo viya atītakālatthattā pana bhāsati-saddassa evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā yasmiṃ kāle tehi avaṇṇo vaṇṇo ca bhāsīyati, tamapekkhitvā [M 1.0187] evaṃ vuttaṃ, evañca katvā “tatrā”ti padassa kālapaṭiniddesavikappanaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ avuttampi supapannaṃ hoti.

‘Durakkhāto’ (poorly explained) means badly explained, and similarly, badly understood. Because it leads out from the cycle of rebirths (vaṭṭa), it is an ‘exit’ (niyyānaṃ); that itself is ‘niyyānika’ (conducive to exit). Or, from that, ‘exit’ is release (nissaraṇaṃ); because one is engaged in that, it is ‘niyyānika’. Or, because it leads out from the cycle of rebirths, it is ‘niyyānika’, by changing the letter ‘ya’ to ‘ka’ and shortening the letter ‘ī’. Indeed, grammarians say, “The suffix ‘anīya’ mostly denotes an agent.” [The opponent argues:] It is not conducive to release in that way. In the manner explained, it is not conducive to the pacification of the suffering of saṃsāra. ‘Paccanīkapaṭipadaṃ’ (opposing practice) means a practice contrary to right practice. ‘Ananulomapaṭipadaṃ’ (non-conforming practice) means a practice not in accordance with noble persons. ‘Adhammānulomapaṭipadaṃ’ (practice conforming to non-Dhamma) means a practice not in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. Why here is an indication of the present tense made in “he speaks dispraise” and “he speaks praise”? Is it not that from the time of the Council, that time of speaking has passed? This is true. However, it should be understood that this was stated thus because the word ‘bhāsati’ has a past-tense meaning, just as the word ‘hoti’ has a past-tense meaning in the phrase ‘addhānamaggapaṭipanno hoti’ (he is one who has entered upon a long road). Or else, it was stated thus with reference to the time when dispraise and praise were being spoken by them. And this being so, the alternative specification of time for the word ‘tatra’ (there), even though not stated in the commentary, becomes well-established.

“Suppiyassa pana…pe… bhāsatī”ti pāḷiyā sambandhadassanaṃ “antevāsī panassā”tiādivacanaṃ. Aparāmasitabbaṃ ariyūpavādakammaṃ, tathā anakkamitabbaṃ. Svāyanti so ācariyo. Asidhāranti asinā tikhiṇabhāgaṃ. Kakacadanta pantiyanti khandhakakacassa dantasaṅkhātāya visamapantiyā. Hatthena vā pādena vā yena kenaci vā aṅgapaccaṅgena paharitvā kīḷamāno viya. Akkhikaṇṇakosasaṅkhātaṭṭhānavasena tīhi pakārehi bhinno mado yassāti pabhinnamado, taṃ. Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsamānoti avaṇṇaṃ bhāsanahetu. Hetuattho hi ayaṃ māna-saddo. Na ayo vuḍḍhi anayo. Soyeva byasanaṃ, atirekabyasananti attho, taṃ pāpuṇissati ekantamahāsāvajjattā ratanattayopavādassa. Tenevāha –

The words beginning with 'But his disciple' show the connection with the Pāḷi text 'Now, regarding Suppiya... he speaks.' The kamma of reviling the noble ones is not to be touched, and likewise not to be transgressed. That teacher. 'Asidhāraṃ' means the sharp part of a sword. 'Kakacadantapantiyaṃ' refers to the uneven row called the teeth of a coarse saw. As if a man playing, having struck with a hand or with a foot or with any major or minor limb whatsoever. 'Pabhinnamada' means an elephant whose musth is flowing in three ways, by way of the places called the sockets of the eyes and ears; to that one. 'Speaking dispraise' means because of speaking dispraise. For this sound 'māna' has the meaning of cause. Not welfare is misfortune. That itself is ruin, meaning excessive ruin; he will attain that because reviling the Triple Gem is an exceedingly great fault. Therefore, He said—

“Yo nindiyaṃ pasaṃsati,

Taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo;

Vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ,

Kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindatī”ti. (su. ni. 663; saṃ ni. 1.180-181; netti. 92);

He who praises what is blameworthy, or blames what is praiseworthy, gathers evil with his mouth; through that evil, he finds no happiness.

“Amhākaṃ [V 1.0164] ācariyo”tiādinā brahmadattassa saṃveguppattiṃ, attano ācariye ca kāruññappavattiṃ dassetvā kiñcāpi antevāsinā ācariyassa anukūlena bhavitabbaṃ, ayaṃ pana paṇḍitajātikattā na īdisesu ṭhānesu tamanuvattatīti idānissa kammassakatāñāṇappavattiṃ dassento “ācariye kho panā”tiādimāha. Halāhalanti taṅkhaṇaññeva māraṇakaṃ visaṃ. Hanatīti hi halo na-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā, halānampi viseso halo halāhalo majjhedīghavasena, etena ca aññe aṭṭhavidhe vise nivatteti. Vuttañca –

By the words beginning with 'Our teacher,' having shown the arising of spiritual urgency in Brahmadatta and the arising of compassion for his own teacher, and that although a disciple should be compliant with his teacher, this one, being of a wise nature, does not follow him in such matters; now, wishing to show the arising of the knowledge of ownership of kamma, he says, 'But as for the teacher,' and so on. 'Halāhalaṃ' means a poison that causes death in that very moment. Indeed, because it kills (hanati), it is called 'hala,' having changed the letter 'na' to the letter 'la'; and among killing poisons, a special killing poison is 'halāhala,' by way of the long vowel in the middle. And by this, it excludes the other eight kinds of poison. And it is said—

“Pume paṇḍe ca kākola, kāḷakūṭahalāhalā;

Sarotthikosuṅkike yo, brahmaputto padīpano;

Dārado vacchanābho ca, visabhedā ime navā”ti.

Kākola, Kāḷakūṭa, and Halāhala are in the masculine gender. And Sarotthika, Suṅkikeya, Brahmaputta, Padīpana, Dārada, and Vacchanābha; these nine are the varieties of poison.

Kharodakanti [M 1.0188] caṇḍasotodakaṃ. “Khārodaka”ntipi pāṭho, atiloṇatāya tittodakanti attho. Narakapapātanti corapapātaṃ. Māṇavakāti attānameva ovadituṃ ālapati “samayopi kho te bhaddāli appaṭividdhoahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) viya. “Kammassakā”ti kammameva attasantakabhāvaṃ vatvā tadeva vivarati “attano kammānurūpameva gatiṃ gacchantī”tiādinā. Yonisoti upāyena ñāyena. Ummujjitvāti ācariyo viya ayoniso ariyūpavāde animmujjanto yoniso ariyūpavādato ummujjitvā, uddhaṃ hutvāti attho. Maddamānoti maddanto bhindanto. Ekaṃsakāraṇameva idha kāraṇanti dassetukāmena “sammā”ti vuttaṃ. “Yathā ta”ntiādinā tassa samāraddhabhāvaṃ dasseti, nti ca nipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā añño paṇḍitasabhāvo jāti ācāravasena kulaputto anekapariyāyena tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitumārabhati, tathā ayampi āraddho, tañca kho api nāmāyamācariyo ettakenāpi ratanattayāvaṇṇabhāsato orameyyāti.

‘Kharodakaṃ’ means water with a fierce current. There is also the reading ‘khārodakaṃ,’ meaning bitter water due to excessive saltiness. ‘Narakapapātaṃ’ means a precipice for thieves. ‘Māṇavaka’ is an address to admonish oneself, as in instances like 'The time, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you' and so on. ‘Owners of their kamma’ means stating that kamma itself is one’s own possession, and this is elaborated by 'they go to a destination in accordance with their kamma,' and so on. ‘Yoniso’ means by means, by method. ‘Having emerged’ means: not sinking improperly into reviling the noble ones, as the teacher did, but emerging from reviling the noble ones properly; the meaning is having risen up. ‘Crushing’ means crushing, breaking. Here, ‘sammā’ (rightly) is stated with the wish to show that the cause is a definite cause. By ‘Yathā taṃ’ and so on, it shows his state of being well-endeavored, and ‘taṃ’ is merely a particle. This is what is said: just as another wise person, a clansman by birth and conduct, begins in various ways to speak of the virtues of the Triple Gem, so too has this one begun. And it is with the thought: 'Perhaps this teacher, even with this much, might desist from speaking dispraise of the Triple Gem.'

Sapparājavaṇṇanti ahirājavaṇṇaṃ. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasundaratāya, vaṇṇasarīrena vā. Vārijaṃ kamalaṃ na paharāmi na bhañjāmi, ārā dūratova upasiṅghāmīti attho. Athāti evaṃ santepi. Gandhatthenoti gandhacoro. Saññūḷhāti ganthitā bandhitā. Gahapatīti upāligahapatiṃ nāṭaputtassa ālapanaṃ. Ettha ca vaṇṇitabbo “ayamīdiso”ti pakāsetabboti vaṇṇo, saṇṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati asaṅkarato vavatthāpīyatīti vaṇṇo, jāti. Vaṇṇeti vikāramāpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti vaṇṇo, rūpāyatanaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati phalametena yathāsabhāvato vibhāvīyatīti vaṇṇo, kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati appamahantādivasena pamīyatīti vaṇṇo, pamāṇaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati pasaṃsīyatīti vaṇṇo[V 1.0165], guṇo. Vaṇṇanaṃ guṇasaṃkittanaṃ vaṇṇo, pasaṃsā. Evaṃ tattha tattha vaṇṇasaddassuppatti veditabbā. Ādisaddena jātarūpapuḷinakkharādayo saṅgaṇhāti. “Idha guṇopi pasaṃsāpī”ti vuttameva samattheti “ayaṃ kirā”tiādinā. Kirāti cettha anussavanatthe, padapūraṇamatte vā. Guṇūpasañhitanti guṇopasaññutaṃ. “Guṇūpasañhitaṃ pasaṃsa”nti pana vadanto pasaṃsāya eva guṇabhāsanaṃ siddhaṃ tassā tadavinābhāvato, tasmā idamatthadvayaṃ yujjatīti dasseti.

'Sapparājavaṇṇaṃ' means the appearance of a serpent king. 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means by the beauty of its appearance, or by its beautiful body. The meaning is: 'I do not strike, I do not break the water-born lotus; I only smell it from afar.' 'Atha' means even so. 'Gandhattheno' means a thief of fragrance. 'Saññūḷhā' means strung, bound. 'Gahapati' is Nāṭaputta's address to the householder Upāli. And here, 'vaṇṇa' is that which should be described or made clear as 'this is such and such'; it means appearance. 'Vaṇṇa' is that which is defined and distinguished without confusion; it means caste. 'Vaṇṇa' is that which, undergoing alteration, reveals a state that has gone to the heart; it means the visible object sense-base. 'Vaṇṇa' is that by which the result is clarified according to its true nature; it means cause. 'Vaṇṇa' is that by which something is measured by way of being small, large, etc.; it means measure. 'Vaṇṇa' is that which is praised; it means virtue. 'Vaṇṇanaṃ', the extolling of virtue, is 'vaṇṇa'; it means praise. Thus, the derivation of the word 'vaṇṇa' should be understood in these various contexts. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes gold, sand, letters, and so on. By the words beginning with 'ayaṃ kira', it supports what was said: 'Here, it is both virtue and praise.' Here, 'kira' is in the sense of hearsay, or it is merely a verse-filler. 'Guṇūpasañhitaṃ' means connected with virtue. But one who says 'praise connected with virtue' shows that by praise itself, the speaking of virtue is accomplished, because the former is not separate from the latter; therefore, this twofold meaning is suitable.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0189] bhāsatīti āha “tatthā”tiādi. Eko ca so puggalo cāti ekapuggalo. Kenaṭṭhena ekapuggalo? Asadisaṭṭhena, guṇavisiṭṭhaṭṭhena, asamasamaṭṭhena ca. So hi paṭhamābhinīhārakāle dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ paṭipāṭiyā āvajjanaṃ ādiṃ katvā bodhisambhārasambharaṇaguṇehi ceva buddhaguṇehi ca sesamahājanena asadiso. Ye cassa guṇā, tepi aññasattānaṃ guṇehi visiṭṭhā, purimakā ca sammāsambuddhā sabbasattehi asamā, tehi pana ayameveko rūpakāyanāmakāyehi samo. Loketi sattaloke. “Uppajjamāno uppajjatī”ti pana idaṃ ubhayampi vippakatavacanameva uppādakiriyāya vattamānakālikattā. Uppajjamāno bahujanahitāya uppajjati, na aññena kāraṇenāti evaṃ panettha attho veditabbo. Lakkhaṇe hesa māna-saddo, evarūpañcettha lakkhaṇaṃ na sakkā aññena saddalakkhaṇena paṭibāhituṃ. Apica uppajjamāno nāma, uppajjati nāma, uppanno nāmāti ayamettha bhedo veditabbo. Esa hi dīpaṅkarapādamūlato paṭṭhāya yāva anāgāmiphalaṃ, tāva uppajjamāno nāma, arahattamaggakkhaṇe uppajjati nāma, arahattaphalakkhaṇe uppanno nāma. Buddhānañhi sāvakānaṃ viya na paṭipāṭiyā iddhividhañāṇādīni uppajjanti, saheva pana arahattamaggena sakalopi sabbaññuguṇarāsi āgatova nāma hoti, tasmā nibbattasabbakiccattā arahattaphalakkhaṇe uppanno nāma, tadanibbattattā tadaññakkhaṇe yathārahaṃ “uppajjamāno uppajjati” cceva vuccati. Imasmimpi sutte arahattaphalakkhaṇaṃyeva sandhāya “uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Atītakālikassāpi vattamānapayogassa katthaci diṭṭhattā uppanno hotīti ayañhettha attho. Evaṃ sati “uppajjamāno”ti cettha māna-saddo sāmatthiyattho. Yāvatā sāmatthiyena mahābodhisattānaṃ carimabhave uppatti icchitabbā, tāvatā sāmatthiyena bodhisambhārabhūtena paripuṇṇena samannāgato hutvāti attho. Tathāsāmatthiyayogena hi uppajjamāno nāmāti. Sabbasattehi asamo, asamehi purimabuddheheva samo majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇa nikkhaṃ viya nibbisiṭṭho, “ekapuggalo”ti cetassa visesanaṃ. Ālayasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ samugghāteti samucchindatīti ālayasamugghāto. Vaṭṭaṃ upacchindatīti vaṭṭupacchedo.

To the question, 'For what reason does he speak?', he said the words beginning with 'tatthā'. He is one, and he is a person; therefore, he is the 'one person' (ekapuggala). For what reason is he the one person? By reason of being dissimilar, by reason of being distinguished by virtues, and by reason of being equal to the unequaled. For he, at the time of his first aspiration, beginning with his reflection on the ten perfections in sequence, is dissimilar to the rest of the great populace due to his qualities of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment and his Buddha-qualities. And whatever qualities he has, they are also distinguished from the qualities of other beings. The former Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas are unequal to all beings, but he alone is equal to them in terms of the physical body and the mental body. 'In the world' means in the world of beings. As for 'arising, he arises,' both these terms are indeed words indicating an incomplete action, because the act of arising is in the present tense. The meaning here should be understood thus: 'Arising, he arises for the welfare of many people, not for any other reason.' This suffix '-māna' is in the sense of a characteristic, and such a characteristic here cannot be prevented by another grammatical characteristic. Furthermore, the distinction here should be understood as: 'is arising' (uppajjamāno), 'arises' (uppajjati), and 'has arisen' (uppanno). For this one, starting from the feet of Dīpaṅkara up to the fruit of non-returning, is called 'is arising'; at the moment of the path of Arahantship, he is called 'arises'; and at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship, he is called 'has arisen'. For in the case of Buddhas, unlike their disciples, the knowledges of psychic powers and so on do not arise in sequence; rather, the entire collection of the qualities of omniscience is said to have arrived simultaneously with the path of Arahantship. Therefore, because all his duties have been accomplished, at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship, he is called 'has arisen'. Because that has not yet been accomplished, at other moments, he is appropriately called 'is arising, arises'. In this Sutta too, 'he arises' is said with reference to the moment of the fruit of Arahantship. Because the present tense is sometimes used for a past action, the meaning here is 'he has arisen'. This being so, here in 'uppajjamāno,' the suffix '-māna' has the meaning of capability. The meaning is: being endowed with as much capability—the complete capability which is the foundation for the requisites of enlightenment—as is desired for the arising of great Bodhisattas in their final existence. For by connection with such capability, he is called 'is arising'. He is unequal to all beings, equal only to the unequaled former Buddhas, without distinction, like a broken gold coin in the middle. 'One person' is a qualifier for this. He eradicates and cuts off craving, which is called 'ālaya' (attachment); therefore, he is the 'eradicator of attachment' (ālayasamugghāta). He cuts off the round of existence; therefore, he is the 'cutter of the round' (vaṭṭupaccheda).

Pahontenāti [V 1.0166] sakkontena. “Pañcanikāye”ti vatvāpi anekāvayavattā tesaṃ na ettakena sabbathā pariyādānanti “navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ caturāsīti [M 1.0190] dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti vuttaṃ. Atitthenāti anotaraṇaṭṭhānena. Na vattabbo aparimāṇavaṇṇattā buddhādīnaṃ, niravasesānañca tesaṃ idha pakāsanena pāḷisaṃvaṇṇanāya eva sampajjanato, cittasampahaṃsanakammaṭṭhānasampajjanavasena ca saphalattā. Thāmo veditabbo sabbathāmena pakāsitattā. Kiṃ pana so tathā ogāhetvā bhāsatīti āha. “Brahmadatto panā”tiādi. Anukkamena punappunaṃ vā savanaṃ anussavo, paramparasavanaṃ. Ādi-saddena ākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyo saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha “sundaramidaṃ kāraṇa”nti evaṃ sayameva kāraṇaparivitakkanaṃ ākāraparivitakko. Attano diṭṭhiyā nijjhāyitvā khamanaṃ ruccanaṃ diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, tehiyeva sambandhitenāti attho. Matta-saddo hettha visesanivattiattho, tena yathāvuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ nivatteti. Attano thāmenāti attano ñāṇabaleneva, na pana buddhādīnaṃ guṇānurūpanti adhippāyo. Asaṅkhyeyyāparimeyyappabhedā hi buddhādīnaṃ guṇā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'By one who is able' (pahontena) means by one who is capable (sakkontena). Even having said 'the five Nikāyas,' because they have many sections, they are not completely covered by this much; therefore, it was said, 'the nine-limbed teaching of the Teacher and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.' 'In a place without a ford' (atitthena) means in a place that is not a landing-place (anotaraṇaṭṭhānena). It should not be said, because the virtues of the Buddhas and others are immeasurable, and because by explaining them here without remainder, only the completion of the commentary on the Pāḷi is accomplished, and because it is fruitful by way of accomplishing the gladdening of the mind and the meditation subject. Strength should be understood, because it was explained with all strength. To the question, 'But for what reason does he speak, having entered into it thus?', he said the words beginning with 'Brahmadatto pana'. Hearing in sequence or again and again is 'tradition' (anussava), hearing from generation to generation. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), it includes reflection on reasons (ākāraparivitakka) and approval after scrutinizing a view (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti). Among them, reflecting on a reason by oneself thus, 'This reason is good,' is 'reflection on reasons'. It is said in the commentaries that scrutinizing with one's own view, and then enduring and approving, is 'approval after scrutinizing a view'. The meaning is 'connected with only those'. Here the word 'merely' (matta) has the meaning of negating a specific; by that, it negates the reason as stated. 'By his own strength' (attano thāmena) means by the power of his own knowledge, not, however, in accordance with the qualities of the Buddhas and others—this is the intention. For the qualities of the Buddhas and others have innumerable and immeasurable divisions. And this was said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.425; udā. aṭṭha. 53; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.1; apa. aṭṭha. 2.91; cariyā. aṭṭha. 9, 329);

“Even if one Buddha, speaking of nothing else, were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, the eon would be exhausted in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

Idhāpi vakkhati “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādi.

Here also he will say, 'But this is a trifle,' etc.

Iti-saddo nidassanattho vuttappakāraṃ nidasseti. Ha-kāro nipātamattanti āha “evaṃ te”ti. Aññamaññassā”ti idaṃ ruḷhipadaṃ “eko ekāyā”ti (pārā. 444, 452) padaṃ viyāti dassento “aññoaññassā”ti ruḷhipadeneva vivarati. “Ujumevā”ti sāvadhāraṇasamāsataṃ vatvā tena nivattetabbatthaṃ āha “īsakampi apariharitvā”ti, thokatarampi avirajjhitvāti attho. Kathanti āha “ācariyena hī”tiādi. Pubbe ekavāramiva avaṇṇavaṇṇabhāsane niddiṭṭhepi “ujuvipaccanīkavādā”ti (dī. ni. 1.1) vuttattā anekavārameva [V 1.0167] te evaṃ bhāsantīti veditabbanti dassetuṃ “puna itaro avaṇṇaṃ itaro vaṇṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tena hi visaddassa vividhatthataṃ samattheti. Sāraphalaketi sāradāruphalake[M 1.0191], uttamaphalake vā. Visarukkhaāṇinti visadārumayapaṭāṇiṃ. Iriyāpathānubandhanena anubandhā honti, na sammāpaṭipattianubandhanena.

The word 'iti' has the meaning of an example; it demonstrates the manner already stated. The commentator says that the letter 'ha' is merely a particle, as in 'evaṃ te'. This word 'aññamaññassa' is a conventional term. To show that it is like the word 'eko ekāya', the commentator explains it with the very conventional term 'aññoaññassa'. Having stated that 'ujumeva' is a compound with emphasis, he then states the meaning to be negated by it, saying 'without leaving out even a little,' which means 'without deviating even a little.' When asked how, he says: 'ācariyena hi,' etc. Although previously, the speaking of blame and praise was indicated as if happening only once, since it is said: 'those whose speech is directly opposed', to show that it should be known that they speak thus many times, it is stated: 'again, one blames while the other praises'. Indeed, by this, it establishes the varied meanings of the prefix 'vi'. 'Sāraphalake' means on a plank of heartwood, or on a superior plank. 'Visarukkhaāṇiṃ' means a peg made of poisonous wood. They are followers by way of adhering to the physical postures, not by way of adhering to the right practice.

Sīsānulokinoti sīsena anulokino, sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā maggānukkamena olokayamānāti attho. Tasmiṃ kāleti yamhi saṃvacchare, utumhi, māse, pakkhe vā bhagavā taṃ addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno, tasmiṃ kāle. Tena hi aniyamato saṃvaccharautumāsaḍḍhamāsāva niddisitā “taṃ divasa”nti divasassa visuṃ niddiṭṭhattā, muhuttādīnañca divasapariyāpannato. “Taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno”ti cettha ādhāravacanametaṃ. Teneva hi kiriyāvicchedadassanavasena “rājagahe piṇḍāya caratī”ti saha pubbakālakiriyāhi vattamānaniddeso kato, itarathā tasmiṃ kāle rājagahe piṇḍāya carati, taṃ addhānamaggañca paṭipannoti anadhippetattho āpajjeyya. Na hi asamānavisayā kiriyā ekādhārā sambhavanti, yā cettha adhippetā addhānapaṭipajjanakiriyā, sā ca aniyamitā na yuttāti. Rājagahaparivattakesūti rājagahaṃ parivattetvā ṭhitesu. “Aññatarasmi”nti iminā tesu bhagavato anibaddhavāsaṃ dasseti. Soti evaṃ rājagahe vasamāno so bhagavā. Piṇḍāya caraṇenapi hi tattha paṭibaddhabhāvavacanato sannivāsattameva dasseti. Yadi pana “piṇḍāya caramāno so bhagavā”ti paccāmaseyya, yathāvuttova anadhippetattho āpajjeyyāti. Taṃ divasanti yaṃ divasaṃ addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno, taṃ divasa. Taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipannoti ettha accantasaṃyogavacanametaṃ. Bhattabhuñjanato pacchā pacchābhattaṃ, tasmiṃ pacchābhattasamaye. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti yattha piṇḍapātatthāya caritvā bhuñjanti, tato apakkanto. Taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipannoti “nāḷandāyaṃ veneyyānaṃ vividhahitasukhanipphattiṃ ākaṅkhamāno imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā tividhasīlālaṅkataṃ nānāvidhakuhanalapanādimicchājīvaviddhaṃsanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhijālaviniveṭhanaṃ dasasahassilokadhātupakampanaṃ brahmajālasuttaṃ desessāmī”ti taṃ yathāvuttaṃ dīghamaggaṃ paṭipanno, idaṃ pana kāraṇaṃ pakaraṇatova pākaṭanti na vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā “kasmā pana bhagavā taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno”ti codanā visodhitā hoti.

“Sīsānulokino” means those who look along with the head; that is, lifting the head and looking along the sequence of the path. “At that time” refers to whatever year, season, month, or fortnight the Blessed One had set out on that long road, at that time. Indeed, by this, the year, season, month, and half-month are indicated as unspecified because “that day” is specified separately, and moments, etc., are included within the day. And here, this ['tasmiṃ kāle'] is a locative expression in relation to 'taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno'. For that very reason, by way of showing the interruption of an action, the indication in the present tense, “he walks for alms in Rājagaha,” is made together with prior actions. Otherwise, the unintended meaning, “at that time he walks for alms in Rājagaha and he has set out on that long road,” would arise. Indeed, actions with different domains cannot have a single locus. And here, the intended action of undertaking the journey, being unfixed, would not be suitable. “Rājagahaparivattakesu” means among those situated, having gone around Rājagaha. By this word “aññatarasmiṃ,” he shows the Blessed One’s non-fixed residence among them. “So” means that Blessed One, thus residing in Rājagaha. For even by his walking for alms, a connection to that place is stated, thus showing it to be his residence. But if one were to consider it as “that Blessed One walking for alms,” the aforementioned unintended meaning would arise. “Taṃ divasaṃ” means on the day that he set out on the long road, on that day. Here, this ['taṃ divasaṃ'] is an expression of continuous association in relation to 'taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno'. “Pacchābhattaṃ” is after the eating of the meal; at that time after the meal. “Piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto” means one who has departed from where, having walked for alms, one eats. “He had set out on that long road” means: thinking, “Desiring the accomplishment of the diverse welfare and happiness for the trainable ones in Nāḷandā, and on account of this occasion, I will teach the Brahmajāla Sutta—which is adorned with the threefold virtue, which destroys the various wrong livelihoods such as scheming and babbling, which disentangles the net of the sixty-two views, and which shakes the ten-thousandfold world-system,” he set out on that aforementioned long road. This reason, however, is evident from the context itself and so was not stated. By this much, the objection, “But why did the Blessed One set out on that long road?” is resolved.

Idāni itarampi codanaṃ visodhituṃ “suppiyopī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ kāle, taṃ divasaṃ anubandhoti ca vuttanayena sambandho. Pāto [M 1.0192] asitabboti pātarāso, so bhutto yenāti bhuttapātarāso. Iccevāti evameva manasi sannidhāya, na pana “bhagavantaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghañca piṭṭhito [V 1.0168] piṭṭhito anubandhissāmī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “bhagavato taṃ maggaṃ paṭipannabhāvaṃ ajānantovā”ti, tathā ajānanto eva hutvā anubandhoti attho. Na hi so bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhumeva icchati, tenāha “sace pana jāneyya, nānubandheyyā”ti. Ettāvatā “kasmā ca suppiyo anubandho”ti codanā visodhitā hoti. “So”tiādinā aparampi codanaṃ visodheti. Kadāci pana bhagavā aññataraveseneva gacchati aṅgulimāladamanapakkusātiabhiggamanādīsu, kadāci buddhasiriyā, idhāpi īdisāya buddhasiriyāti dassetuṃ “buddhasiriyā sobhamāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sirīti cettha sarīrasobhaggādisampatti, tadeva upamāvasena dasseti “rattakambalaparikkhittamivā”tiādinā. Gacchatīti jaṅgamo yathā “caṅkamo”ti. Cañcalamāno gacchanto giri, tādisassa kanakagirino sikharamivāti attho.

Now, to resolve the other objection, “Suppiyo, too…” was said. The connection, 'he followed at that time, on that day,' should be made in the manner already stated. 'Pātarāso' is so called because it is to be eaten in the morning; 'bhuttapātarāso' is one by whom that morning meal has been eaten. 'Icceva' means having resolved thus in mind, and not, “I will follow the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from behind.” Therefore it was said, “…not knowing that the Blessed One had set out on that road”; the meaning is that he followed while being thus ignorant. For he did not wish to see the Blessed One at all; therefore he says, “But if he had known, he would not have followed.” By this much, the objection, “And why did Suppiyo follow?” is resolved. With “So…,” etc., he resolves another objection. For sometimes the Blessed One goes in an unknown guise, as in the taming of Aṅgulimāla, the approach to Pukkusāti, and so on, and sometimes with the Buddha’s splendor. To show that here, too, he went with such a Buddha’s splendor, “…resplendent with the Buddha’s splendor,” etc., was said. Here, 'sirī' is the perfection of the body’s beauty and so on. He shows that very thing by way of a simile with “…as if wrapped in a red blanket,” etc. It is called 'jaṅgama' because it goes, just as there is 'caṅkama'. The meaning is: like the peak of such a golden mountain that is a mountain going while moving.

“Tasmiṃ kirā”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ adassitattā, porāṇaṭṭhakathāyañca anāgatattā anussavasiddhā ayaṃ kathāti dassetuṃ “kirā”ti vuttanti vadanti, tathā vā hotu aññathā vā, attanā adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, amutañca anussavamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassaravasena chabbaṇṇā. Samantāti samantato dasahi disāhi. Asītihatthappamāṇeti tesaṃ rasmīnaṃ pakatiyā pavattiṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā samantato, upari ca paccekaṃ asītihatthamatte padese pakatiyāva ghanībhūtā rasmiyo tiṭṭhantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, vinayaṭīkāyaṃ pana “tāyeva byāmappabhā nāma. Yato chabbaṇṇā rasmiyo taḷākato mātikā viya dasasu disāsu dhāvanti, sā yasmā byāmamattā viya khāyati, tasmā byāmappabhāti vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ, (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.16) saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ pana vakkhati “puratthimakāyato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmi uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti. Pacchimakāyato. Dakkhiṇahatthato. Vāmahatthato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmi uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti. Upari kesantato paṭṭhāya sabbakesāvaṭṭehi moragīvavaṇṇā rasmi uṭṭhahitvā gaganatale [M 1.0193] asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti. Heṭṭhā pādatalehi pavāḷavaṇṇā rasmi uṭṭhahitvā ghanapathaviyaṃ asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti. Evaṃ samantā asītihatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo vijjotamānā vipphandamānā vidhāvantī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.299) keci pana aññathāpi parikappanāmattena vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ tathā aññattha anāgatattā, ayuttattā ca. Tāsaṃ pana buddharasmīnaṃ tadā aniggūhitabhāvadassanatthaṃ “tasmiṃ kira samaye”ti vuttaṃ. Pakkusātiabhiggamanādīsu viya hi tadā tāsaṃ niggūhane kiñci kāraṇaṃ natthi. Ādhāvantīti abhimukhaṃ disaṃ dhāvanti. Vidhāvantīti vividhā hutvā vidisaṃ dhāvanti.

“‘Tasmiṃ kirā’ and so forth” is an explanation of that. Since it is not shown in the Pāḷi Canon and does not appear in the ancient commentaries, the teachers say that “kirā” is stated to show that this story is established by hearsay. Be it so or otherwise, it should be understood that what is unseen, unheard, and unencountered by oneself is merely hearsay. The six colors are by way of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant. “Samantā” means from all around, from the ten directions. “Asītihatthappamāṇaṃ” (eighty cubits in measure) is stated by way of the natural place of arising of those rays. Therefore, it should be understood that all around and also above, in each region of eighty cubits in measure, the rays, having become condensed, stand naturally. In the Vinaya-ṭīkā, however, it is said: “Those very rays are called ‘byāmappabhā’ (fathom-radiance). Because the six-colored rays run in the ten directions like small channels from a reservoir, and because it appears to be about a fathom in measure, it is called ‘byāmappabhā’.” In the commentary on the Saṅgīti Sutta, however, it will be stated: “From the eastern part of the body, a golden-colored ray arises and takes up a space of eighty cubits. From the western part of the body, from the right hand, from the left hand, a golden-colored ray arises and takes up a space of eighty cubits. Above, from the end of the hair, a peacock-neck-colored ray arises from all the hair whorls and takes up a space of eighty cubits in the sky. Below, from the soles of the feet, a coral-colored ray arises and takes up a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. Thus, the six-colored Buddha-rays, shining, vibrating, and darting, run through a space of eighty cubits all around.” Some teachers, however, also state it differently, merely by way of conjecture. That should not be accepted, as it does not appear elsewhere and is unsuitable. The phrase “tasmiṃ kira samaye” (at that time, it is said) is stated to show the state of those Buddha-rays not being concealed at that time. For indeed, just as in the cases of the going towards Pakkusāti and so on, there was no reason to conceal them at that time. “Ādhāvanti” means they run towards a cardinal direction. “Vidhāvanti” means, having become manifold, they run towards an intermediate direction.

Tasmiṃ [V 1.0169] vanantare dissamānākārena tāsaṃ rasmīnaṃ sobhā viññāyatīti āha “ratanāveḷā”tiādi. Ratanāveḷā nāma ratanamayavaṭaṃsakaṃ muddhaṃ avati rakkhatīti hi aveḷā, āveḷā vā, muddhamālā. Ukkā nāma yā sajotibhūtā, tāsaṃ sataṃ, nipatanaṃ nipāto, tassa nipāto, tena samākulaṃ tathā. Pisitabbattā piṭṭhaṃ, cīnadese jātaṃ piṭṭhaṃ cīnapiṭṭhaṃ, rattacuṇṇaṃ, yaṃ “sindūro”tipi vuccati, cīnapiṭṭhameva cuṇṇaṃ. Vāyuno vegena ito cito ca khittaṃ tanti tathā. Indassa dhanu lokasaṅketavasenāti indadhanu, sūriyarasmivasena gagane paññāyamānākāraviseso. Kuṭilaṃ aciraṭṭhāyittā virūpaṃ hutvā javati dhāvatīti vijju, sāyeva latā taṃsadisabhāvenāti tathā, vāyuvegato valāhakaghaṭṭaneneva jātarasmi. Tāyati avijahanavasena ākāsaṃ pāletīti tārā, gaṇasaddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Tassa pabhā tathā. Vipphuritaviccharitamivāti ābhāya vividhaṃ pharamānaṃ, vijjotayamānaṃ viya ca. Vanassa antaraṃ vivaraṃ vanantaraṃ, bhagavatā pattapattavanappadesanti vuttaṃ hoti.

In that forest-interior, the beauty of those rays was perceived by their visible appearance; hence it is said, “a jeweled diadem,” and so on. A ‘ratanāveḷā’ (jeweled diadem) is a jeweled head-ornament. Indeed, because it guards (avati) and protects (rakkhati) the head, it is called ‘aveḷā’, or ‘āveḷā’; a head-garland. ‘Ukkā’ (torch) refers to that which is blazing; a hundred of them. Their falling is a descent, the descent of those. By that, the place is agitated; thus it is so-called. Because it is to be ground, it is called ‘piṭṭhaṃ’ (powder); powder produced in the country of Cīna is ‘cīnapiṭṭhaṃ’, a red powder, which is also called ‘sindūra’ (vermilion); ‘cīnapiṭṭhaṃ’ is simply powder. Scattered here and there by the force of the wind; thus it is so-called. ‘Indadhanu’ (Indra’s bow) is so-called by worldly convention; it is a particular appearance seen in the sky by way of the sun’s rays. Because it is crooked and does not last long, it changes form and darts away; therefore, it is called ‘vijju’ (lightning). That very thing is a ‘latā’ (creeper) due to its similarity; thus it is so-called. It is a ray produced solely from the collision of clouds due to the force of the wind. Because it protects (tāyati/pāleti) the sky by not abandoning its course, it is called ‘tārā’ (star). The word ‘gaṇa’ (group) should be applied to each individually. The radiance of that group is thus. ‘Vipphuritaviccharitamiva’ means as if spreading in various ways with radiance, and as if illuminating. ‘Vanantaraṃ’ is the interior (antaraṃ) or opening (vivaraṃ) of the forest; it is said to mean the forest region that the Blessed One had reached.

Asītiyā anubyañjanehi tambanakhatādīhi anurañjitaṃ tathā. Kamalaṃ padumapuṇḍarīkāni, avasesaṃ nīlarattasetabhedaṃ saroruhaṃ uppalaṃ, iti pañcavidhā paṅkajajāti pariggahitā hoti. Vikasitaṃ phullitaṃ tadubhayaṃ yassa sarassa tathā. Sabbena pakārena parito samantato phullati vikasatīti sabbapāliphullaṃ a-kārassa ā-kāraṃ, ra-kārassa ca la-kāraṃ katvā yathā “pālibhaddo”ti, tārānaṃ marīci pabhā, tāya vikasitaṃ vijjotitaṃ [M 1.0194] tathā. Byāmappabhāya parikkhepo parimaṇḍalo, tena vilāsinī sobhinī tathā. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni aññamaññapaṭibaddhattā mālākāreneva ṭhitānīti vuttaṃ “dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇamālā”ti. Dvattiṃsacandādīnaṃ mālā kenaci ganthetvā paṭipāṭiyā ca ṭhapitāti na vattabbā “yadi siyā”ti parikappanāmattena hi “ganthetvā ṭhapitadvattiṃsacandamālāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parikappopamā hesā, lokepi ca dissati.

Adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, such as copper-colored nails and so on; thus it is so-called. The paduma and puṇḍarīka lotuses are ‘kamala’; the remaining lake-grown lotuses with varieties of blue, red, and white are ‘uppala’; thus, the fivefold species of mud-born lotuses is included. That lake for which both those kinds of lotuses are bloomed and fully opened is so-called. Because it blooms and unfolds in every way, all around, it is called ‘sabbapāliphullaṃ’, by changing the letter ‘a’ to ‘ā’ and the letter ‘ra’ to ‘la’, as in “pālibhaddo.” Illuminated by the radiance of the stars; thus it is so-called. The surrounding circle of fathom-span radiance; by that, it is resplendent and beautiful; thus it is so-called. The marks of a great man, being interconnected, stand only in the manner of a garland; therefore, it is called “the garland of thirty-two excellent marks.” It should not be said that a garland of thirty-two moons and so on is strung by someone and placed in sequence. For it is said, “a garland of thirty-two moons, strung and placed,” and so on, merely by way of conjecture, as in “if it were so.” This is a conceptualized simile (parikappopamā), and it is also seen in the world.

“Mayeva mukhasobhāsse, tyalaminduvikatthanā;

Yatombujepi sātthīti, parikappopamā aya”nti.

“O Moon, enough of your boasting: ‘His facial beauty is in me alone!’ For that beauty exists in the lotus as well. This is a conceptualized simile.”

Dvattiṃsacandamālāya siriṃ attano siriyā abhibhavantī ivāti sambandho. Esa nayo sesesupi.

The connection is thus: as if overpowering the splendor of the garland of thirty-two moons with his own splendor. This same method should be understood in the remaining cases as well.

Evaṃ bhagavato tadā sobhaṃ dassetvā idāni bhikkhusaṅghassāpi sobhaṃ dassento “tañca panā”tiādimāha[V 1.0170]. Catubbidhāya appicchatāya appicchā. Dvādasahi santosehi santuṭṭhā. Tividhena vivekena pavivittā. Rājarājamahāmattādīhi asaṃsaṭṭhā. Duppaṭipattikānaṃ codakā. Pāpe akusale garahino paresaṃ hitapaṭipattiyā vattāro. Paresañca vacanakkhamā. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ nāma paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Tesa”ntiādinā tadabhisambandhena bhagavato sobhaṃ dasseti. Rattapadumānaṃ saṇḍo samūho vanaṃ, tassa majjhe gatā tathā. “Rattaṃ padumaṃ, setaṃ puṇḍarīka”nti pattaniyamamantarena tathā vuttaṃ, pattaniyamena pana satapattaṃ padumaṃ, ūnakasatapattaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ. Pavāḷaṃ viddumo, tena katāya vedikāya parikkhitto viya. Migapakkhīnampīti pi-saddo, api-saddo vā sambhāvanāyaṃ, tenāha “pageva devamanussāna”nti. Mahātherāti mahāsāvake sandhāyāha. Surañjitabhāvena īsakaṃ kaṇhavaṇṇatāya meghavaṇṇaṃ. Ekaṃsaṃ karitvāti ekaṃsapārupanavasena vāmaṃse karitvā. Kattarassa jiṇṇassa ālambano daṇḍo kattaradaṇḍo, bāhullavasenāyaṃ samaññā. Suvammaṃ nāma sobhaṇuracchado, tena vammitā sannaddhāti suvammavammitā, idaṃ tesaṃ paṃsukūladhāraṇanidassanaṃ. Yesaṃ kucchigataṃ sabbampi tiṇapalāsādi gandhajātameva hoti, te gandhahatthino nāma, ye “hemavatā”tipi vuccanti, tesampi therānaṃ sīlādiguṇagandhatāya taṃsadisatā. Antojaṭābahijaṭāsaṅkhātāya [M 1.0195] taṇhājaṭāya vijaṭitabhāvato vijaṭitajaṭā. Taṇhābandhanāya chinnattā chinnabandhanā. “So”tiādi yathāvuttavacanassa guṇadassanaṃ. Anubuddhehīti buddhānamanubuddhehi. Tepi hi ekadesena bhagavatā paṭividdhapaṭibhāgeneva cattāri saccāni bujjhanti. Pattaparivāritanti pupphadalena parivāritaṃ. Kaṃ vuccati kamalādi, tasmiṃ sarati virājatīti kesaraṃ, kiñjakkho. Kaṇṇe karīyatīti kaṇṇikā. Kaṇṇālaṅkāro, taṃsadisaṇṭhānatāya kaṇṇikā, bījakoso. Channaṃ haṃsakulānaṃ seṭṭho dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā viya, hārito nāma mahābrahmā viya.

Thus, having shown the splendor of the Blessed One at that time, now, wishing to show the splendor of the community of monks also, he said the words beginning with 'tañca panā'. They are of few wishes due to the fourfold fewness of wishes. They are satisfied with the twelve kinds of contentment. They are secluded with the threefold seclusion. They are unassociated with kings, great ministers, and so on. They are reprovers of those with wrong practice. They are censurers of evil, unwholesome states, and speakers for the practice of others' welfare. And they are patient of the speech of others. What is called the knowledge and vision of liberation is the knowledge of reviewing. By the words beginning with 'tesaṃ', in connection with that simile, he shows the splendor of the Blessed One. A thicket or group of red lotuses is a 'vana' (forest); they have gone into the middle of it, thus. 'A red one is a paduma lotus, a white one is a puṇḍarīka lotus'—thus it is said without specifying the petals; but by specifying the petals, a hundred-petaled one is a paduma, and one with less than a hundred petals is a puṇḍarīka. Pavāḷa is coral (viddumo); as if surrounded by a railing made of that. In the phrase 'migapakkhīnampi', the particle 'pi' or 'api' is in the sense of praise; therefore, he said 'how much more so for devas and humans.' The word 'mahāthera' he said referring to the great disciples. Due to being well-dyed and slightly dark in color, it is the color of a cloud. The phrase 'ekaṃsaṃ karitvā' means having placed it on the left shoulder by way of wearing it over one shoulder. The supporting staff of an old man is a 'kattaradaṇḍa'; this designation is by way of common usage. 'Suvamma' is a beautiful chest-covering; armored, equipped with that, is 'suvammavammitā'; this is an illustration of their wearing of rag-robes.
