Those whose food, such as grass and leaves, that has gone into their belly becomes only a fragrant substance, are called 'gandhahatthī' (fragrant elephants), who are also called 'hemavatā'; for those elders too, because of the fragrance of their virtues such as morality, their similarity to them should be known. Because of having been disentangled from the tangle of craving—known as the internal tangle and the external tangle—they are 'vijaṭitajaṭā'. Because the bond of craving has been cut, they are 'chinnabandhanā'. The words beginning with 'so' are an illustration of the quality of the aforesaid statement. 'Anubuddhehi' means by those who have awakened in accordance with the Buddhas. For they too, in part, understand the four truths in the same measure as that penetrated by the Blessed One. 'Pattaparivāritaṃ' means surrounded by flower petals. 'Kaṃ' refers to a lotus, etc.; that which moves and shines in it is 'kesaraṃ', the stamen. 'Kaṇṇe karīyati' means that which is made on the 'ear' (protuberance) is 'kaṇṇikā'. It is an ornament for the 'ear' (protuberance); because of having a shape similar to that, it is 'kaṇṇikā', the seed-vessel. Like Dhataraṭṭha, the swan-king, the best of the six kinds of swans; like the great Brahmā named Hārita.

Evaṃ gacchantaṃ bhagavantaṃ, bhikkhū ca disvā attano parisaṃ olokesīti sambandho. Kājadaṇḍaketi kājasaṅkhāte bhārāvahadaṇḍake, kājasmiṃ vā bhāralaggitadaṇḍake. Khuddakaṃ pīṭhaṃ pīṭhakaṃ. Mūle, agge ca tidhā kato daṇḍo tidaṇḍo. Morahatthako morapiñchaṃ. Khuddakaṃ pasibbaṃ pasibbakaṃ. Kuṇḍikā kamaṇḍalu. Sā hi kaṃ udakaṃ udeti pasaveti, rakkhatīti vā kuṇḍikā niruttinayena. Gahitaṃ omakato lujjitaṃ, vividhaṃ lujjitañca pīṭhaka…pe… kuṇḍikādianekaparikkhārasaṅkhātaṃ bhāraṃ bharati vahatīti gahita…pe… bhārabharitā. Itīti nidassanattho. Evanti idamattho. Evaṃ idaṃ vacanamādi yassa vacanassa tathā, tadeva niratthakaṃ vacanaṃ yassāti evamādiniratthakavacanā. Mukhaṃ etassa atthīti mukharā, sabbepi mukhavantā eva, ayaṃ pana pharusābhilāpamukhavatī, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Nindāyañhi ayaṃ rapaccayo. Mukhena [V 1.0171] vā amanāpaṃ kammaṃ rāti gaṇhātīti mukharā. Vividhā kiṇṇā vācā yassāti vikiṇṇavācā. Tassāti suppiyassa paribbājakassa. Nti yathāvuttappakāraṃ parisaṃ.

Having seen the Blessed One and the monks thus going, he looked at his own assembly—thus the connection should be made. 'Kājadaṇḍake' means on a load-bearing pole called a 'kāja' (yoke-pole), or on a pole with a load attached to a 'kāja'. A small seat is a 'pīṭhaka'. A staff made with three parts at the base and at the tip is a 'tidaṇḍo'. 'Morahatthako' is a peacock feather bunch. A small bag is a 'pasibbaka'. 'Kuṇḍikā' is a water pot (kamaṇḍalu). Indeed, because it causes water (kaṃ udakaṃ) to arise (udeti) or produces it (pasaveti), or because it protects (rakkhati) it, it is called 'kuṇḍikā' by way of etymology. Because one carries or bears a load consisting of numerous accessories—such as a small seat, a three-part staff, a peacock feather bunch, an earthen bowl, a small bag, and a water pot—which are taken, lowly, and broken, and variously broken, one is called 'gahita... bhārabharitā'. The word 'iti' is for the purpose of illustration. The word 'evaṃ' has the meaning of 'idaṃ' (this). For which speech, 'this speech' is the beginning, it is called 'evamādi'. For whom there is meaningless speech which has just such a beginning, they are 'evamādiniratthakavacanā'. 'Mukharā' means 'one who has a mouth'; all indeed have mouths, but this one has a mouth that speaks harshly, therefore it is said thus. Indeed, this 'ra' suffix is in the sense of censure. Or, because one takes up disagreeable action with the mouth, one is 'mukharā'. One whose speech is various and mixed is 'vikiṇṇavācā'. 'Tassā' means of the wanderer Suppiya. 'Taṃ' refers to the assembly of the aforesaid kind.

Idānīti tassa tathārūpāya parisāya dassanakkhaṇe. Panāti arucisaṃsūcanattho, tathāpīti attho. Lābha…pe… hāniyā ceva hetubhūtāya. Kathaṃ hānīti āha “aññatitthiyānañhī”tiādi. Nissirīkatanti nisobhataṃ, ayamattho morajātakādīhipi dīpetabbo. “Upatissakolitānañcā”tiādinā pakkhahānitāya vitthāro. Āyasmato sāriputtassa, mahāmoggallānassa ca bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ sandhāya “tesu pana pakkantesū”ti vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ pabbajitakāleyeva aḍḍhateyyasataṃ paribbājakaparisā pabbaji, tato parampi [M 1.0196] tadanupabbajitā paribbājakaparisā aparimāṇāti dasseti “sāpi tesaṃ parisā bhinnā”ti iminā. Yāya kāyaci hi paribbājakaparisāya pabbajitāya tassa parisā bhinnāyeva nāma samānagaṇattāti tathā vuttaṃ. “Imehī”tiādinā lābhapakkhahāniṃ nigamanavasena dasseti. Usūyasaṅkhātassa visassa uggāro uggilanaṃ usūyavisuggāro, taṃ. Ettha ca “yasmā panesā”tiādināva “kasmā ca so ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti codanaṃ visodheti, “sace”tiādikaṃ pana sabbampi tapparivāravacanamevāti tehipi sā visodhitāyeva nāma. Bhagavato virodhānunayābhāvavīmaṃsanatthaṃ ete avaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. “Mārena anvāviṭṭhā evaṃ bhāsantī”ti ca keci vadanti, tadayuttameva aṭṭhakathāya ujuvipaccanīkattā. Pākaṭoyevāyamatthoti.

'Idāni' means at the moment of seeing his assembly of such a kind. The word 'pana' is for indicating displeasure; the meaning is 'even so'. Because of the loss of gain and honor, which is the cause. 'How is there a loss?'—he said the words beginning with 'aññatitthiyānañhi'. 'Nissirīkataṃ' means the state of being without splendor; this meaning should be illustrated by the Mora Jātaka and others. By the words beginning with 'Upatissakolitānañca', the details of the loss of faction are shown. Referring to the going forth of the Venerable Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna in the presence of the Blessed One, it is said 'tesu pana pakkantesu'. At the very time of their going forth, two hundred and fifty of the wanderers' assembly went forth; and after that, the wanderers' assemblies that went forth following them were immeasurable—this he shows with 'sāpi tesaṃ parisā bhinnā'. Indeed, when any wanderers' assembly went forth, his assembly was indeed split because of being of the same group; thus it is said. By the words beginning with 'imehi', he shows the loss of gain and faction by way of conclusion. The vomiting, the spewing forth, of the poison called envy is 'usūyavisuggāro'; that. And here, by the words beginning with 'yasmā panesā' alone, he purifies the charge, 'Why does he speak dispraise of the Triple Gem?'. But all the words beginning with 'sace' are merely the surrounding words for that; therefore, by them too, that charge is indeed purified. For the purpose of investigating the absence of opposition and approval towards the Blessed One, these two speak dispraise and praise. And some say, 'Possessed by Māra, they speak thus,' but that is indeed inappropriate because it is in direct opposition to the commentary. This meaning is quite clear.

2. Yasmā atthaṅgato sūriyo, tasmā akālo dāni gantunti sambandho.

2. Because the sun has set, it is therefore now not the time to go; thus the connection should be made.

Ambalaṭṭhikāti sāmīpikavohāro yathā “varuṇanagaraṃ, godāgāmo”ti āha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Taruṇapariyāyo laṭṭhikā-saddo rukkhavisaye yathā “mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā beluvalaṭṭhikāya mūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdī”tiādīsūti dasseti” “taruṇambarukkho”ti iminā. Keci pana “ambalaṭṭhikā nāma vuttanayena eko gāmo”ti vadanti, tesaṃ mate ambalaṭṭhikāyanti samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Chāyūdakasampannanti chāyāya ceva udakena ca sampannaṃ. Mañjusāti peḷā. Paṭibhānacittavicittanti itthipurisasaññogādinā paṭibhānacittena vicittaṃ, etena rañño agāraṃ, tadeva rājāgārakanti dasseti. Rājāgārakaṃ nāma vessavaṇamahārājassa devāyatananti eke.

As for 'Ambalaṭṭhikā', it is a designation of proximity, just as in 'Varuṇanagaraṃ, Godāgāmo'. To show this meaning, he said the words beginning with 'tassa kira'. The word 'laṭṭhikā' is a synonym for 'taruṇa' (young) in the context of trees, as in such passages as, 'having entered the great forest, he sat down at the foot of a young beluva tree for the day's abiding'. This meaning is shown by the phrase 'a young mango tree'. Some, however, say: 'Ambalaṭṭhikā is the name of a village, in the manner described.' In their view, 'ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ' is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. 'Endowed with shade and water' means endowed with both shade and water. 'Mañjusā' means a casket. 'Variegated by ingenious designs' means variegated by ingenious designs such as the union of male and female figures. By this, it is shown that it is the king's residence, and that very place is the 'royal residence'. Some say that the 'royal residence' is the name of the shrine of the great king Vessavaṇa.

Bahuparissayoti [V 1.0172] bahupaddavo. Kehīti vuttaṃ “core’hipī”tiādi. Handāti vacanavossaggatthe nipāto, tadānubhāvato nipparissayatthāya idāni upagantvā sve gamissāmīti adhippāyo. “Saddhiṃ antevāsinā brahmadattena māṇavenā” ticceva sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca kho pāḷiāruḷhavaseneva, na pana tadā suppiyassa parisāya abhāvatoti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “saddhiṃ attano parisāyā”ti idha vuttaṃ. Kasmā panettha brahmadattoyeva pāḷiyamāruḷho, na pana tadavasesā suppiyassa parisāti[M 1.0197]? Desanānadhīnabhāvena payojanābhāvato. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ aññampi edisaṃ payojanābhāvato saṅgītikārakehi na saṅgītanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana “pāḷiyaṃ vutta”nti ādhāraṃ vatvā ‘tadetaṃ na sīhaḷaṭṭhakathānayadassanaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ vuttabhāvadassanamevā’ti” vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Pāḷiāruḷhavaseneva pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti adhippetatthassa āpajjanato. Tasmā yathāvuttanayeneva attho gahetabboti. “Vuttanti vā amhehipi idha vattabbanti attho. Evañhi tadā aññāyapi parisāya vijjamānabhāvadassanatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ, pāḷiyamāruḷhavasena pana aññathāpi idha vattabbanti adhippāyo yutto”ti vadanti.

'Full of many dangers' means full of many troubles. Because the question 'By whom?' should be asked, it was said 'by thieves', etc. 'Handā' is a particle in the sense of releasing speech. The intention is: 'By his power, for the sake of being without danger, I will approach now and go tomorrow.' It is said thus in the Sinhala commentary: 'together with the disciple, the young man Brahmadatta'. And that was said only by the power of its inclusion in the Pāḷi, and not because Suppiya's assembly was absent at that time. To show this meaning, it is said here, 'together with his own assembly'. Why was only Brahmadatta included in the Pāḷi here, and not the rest of Suppiya's assembly? Because of their not being connected with the discourse and because of their being of no purpose. And just as this was not included in the canon by the compilers, so too it should be understood that other such things were not included by the compilers because they were of no purpose. Some, however, stating the basis as 'it is said in the Pāḷi', say: 'This is not a demonstration of the method of the Sinhala commentary; it is only a demonstration of the fact that it is said in the Pāḷi.' That is not correct. Because the intended meaning—that it is said in the Pāḷi only by the power of its being included in the Pāḷi—is arrived at. Therefore, the meaning should be taken only in the way already stated. Alternatively, 'vuttaṃ' means: 'it should be said by us also here'; this is the meaning. For, it was said thus at that time for the purpose of showing the existence of another assembly as well. 'But by the power of its inclusion in the Pāḷi, it should be stated otherwise here; this intention is suitable,' thus they say.

Idāni “tatrāpi suda”ntiādipāḷiyā sambandhaṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ vāsaṃ upagato panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parivāretvā nisinno hotīti sambandho. Kucchitaṃ kattabbanti kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ, kucchitakiriyā, ito cito ca cañcalananti attho, hatthassa kukkuccaṃ tathā. “Sā hī”tiādinā tathābhūtatāya kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Nivāteti vātavirahitaṭṭhāne. Yathāvuttadosābhāvena niccalā. Taṃ vibhūtinti tādisaṃ sobhaṃ. Vippalapantīti sativossaggavasena vividhā lapanti. Nillālitajivhāti ito cito ca nikkhantajivhā. Kākacchamānāti kākānaṃ saddasadisaṃ saddaṃ kurumānā. Gharugharupassāsinoti gharugharuiti saddaṃ janetvā passasantā. Issāvasenāti yathāvuttehi dvīhi kāraṇehi usūyanavasena. “Sabbaṃ vattabba”nti iminā “ādipeyyālanayoya”nti dasseti.

Now, to show the connection with the Pāḷi text beginning with 'tatrāpi sudaṃ', the words 'evaṃ vāsaṃ upagato pana', etc., were said. The connection should be made thus: he sits having been surrounded. Because it is a blameworthy thing to be done, it is 'kukataṃ'; its state is 'kukkuccaṃ', a blameworthy action, meaning agitation from here and there. Likewise, the 'kukkucca' of the hand is movement from here and there. By the words beginning with 'sā hi', he shows the reason for its being in such a state. 'Nivāte' means in a place free from wind. Because of the absence of the aforementioned faults, it is still. 'Taṃ vibhūtiṃ' means such splendor. 'Vippalapanti' means they speak variously by way of abandoning mindfulness. 'Nillālitajivhā' means having the tongue coming out from here and there. 'Kākacchamānā' means making a sound similar to the sound of crows. 'Gharugharupassāsino' means breathing while producing the sound 'gharugharu'. 'Issāvasena' means by way of envy due to the two aforementioned reasons. By this phrase 'sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ', it is shown that this is the method of abbreviation beginning with the first word.

3. Sammā pahonti taṃ taṃ kammanti sampahulā, bahavo, tenāha “bahukāna”nti. Sabbantimena paricchedena catuvaggasaṅgheneva vinayakammassa kattabbattā “vinayapariyāyenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tayo janāti cesa upalakkhaṇaniddeso dvinnampi sampahulattā. Tattha tattha tathāyevāgatattā “suttantapariyāyenā”tiādimāha. Taṃ taṃ pāḷiyā āgatavohāravasena hi ayaṃ bhedo. Tayo janā tayo eva nāma, tato paṭṭhāya uttari catupañcajanādikā sampahulāti attho. Tatoti cāyaṃ mariyādāvadhi. Maṇḍalamāḷoti anekatthapavattā samaññā, idha pana īdisāya evāti niyamento [V 1.0173] āha “katthacī”tiādi. Kaṇṇikā vuccati kūṭaṃ. Haṃsavaṭṭakacchannenāti haṃsamaṇḍalākārachannena. Tadeva channaṃ aññattha [M 1.0198] “supaṇṇavaṅkacchadana”nti vuttaṃ. Kūṭena yutto agāro, soyeva sālāti kūṭāgārasālā. Thambhapantiṃ parikkhipitvāti thambhamālaṃ parivāretvā, parimaṇḍalākārena thambhapantiṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upaṭṭhānasālā nāma payirupāsanasālā. Yattha upaṭṭhānamattaṃ karonti, na ekarattadirattādivasena nisīdanaṃ, idha pana tathā katā nisīdanasālāyevāti dasseti “idha panā”tiādinā. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “sannipatitāna” ntveva avatvā “sannisinnāna”ntipi vuttaṃ. Mānitabboti māḷo, mīyati pamīyatīti vā māḷo. Maṇḍalākārena paṭicchanno māḷoti maṇḍalamāḷo, anekakoṇavanto paṭissayaviseso. “Sannisinnāna”nti nisajjanavasena vuttaṃ, nisajjanavasena vā “sannisinnāna”nti saṃvaṇṇetabbapadamajjhāharitvā sambandho. Iminā nisīdanairiyāpathaṃ, kāyasāmaggīvasena ca samodhānaṃ sandhāya padadvayametaṃ vuttanti dasseti. Saṅkhiyā vuccati kathā sammā khiyanato kathanato. Kathādhammoti kathāsabhāvo, upaparikkhā vidhīti keci.

3. 'Because they are well able to perform this and that act' (Sammā pahonti taṃ taṃ kammaṃ), they are called 'sampahulā' (abundant), meaning 'many' (bahavo); hence, he said 'bahukānaṃ' (of many). Because a Vinaya act must be performed by the very last division, that is, only by a Saṅgha of a group of four, the words beginning with 'by the method of the Vinaya' were said. And this reference 'three persons' is an indication by way of a characteristic mark, because even two are 'sampahula'. Because it is found thus in various places, he said the words beginning with 'by the method of the Suttanta'. For this distinction is based on the terminology found in the respective Pāḷi texts. 'Three persons' are indeed just three; from that point onwards, four, five, and more persons are 'sampahula'—this is the meaning. And this 'tato' is an exclusive limit (mariyādāvadhi). 'Maṇḍalamāḷa' is a term that occurs with many meanings, but here, limiting it to this specific type, he said the words beginning with 'in some cases'. The pinnacle (kūṭaṃ) is called 'kaṇṇikā'. By 'haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena' is meant 'covered in the shape of a hamsa-circle'. That same covering is elsewhere called 'supaṇṇavaṅkacchadana' (a roof curved like a garuḍa's wing). A house joined with a pinnacle is a 'kūṭāgāra'; that same building is a hall (sālā), thus it is a 'kūṭāgārasālā'. By 'having enclosed a row of pillars' (Thambhapantiṃ parikkhipitvā) is meant 'having surrounded a garland of pillars', that is, 'having made a row of pillars in a circular shape'. An 'upaṭṭhānasālā' is a hall for attending upon (payirupāsanasālā). It is where they perform only attendance, not sitting for one night, two nights, and so on. But here, it is just a sitting-hall made in that way—this he shows with the words beginning with 'but here'. For that very reason, in the Pāḷi, instead of just saying 'sannipatitānaṃ' (of those who have assembled), 'sannisinnānaṃ' (of those who are seated) was also said. Because it is to be revered (mānitabbo), it is a 'māḷa'; or, because it is measured or estimated (mīyati pamīyati), it is a 'māḷa'. A 'māḷa' covered in a circular shape is a 'maṇḍalamāḷa', which is a special kind of residence with many corners. 'Sannisinnānaṃ' is said by way of sitting; or, the connection with 'sannisinnānaṃ' is to be made by way of sitting, having supplied the term to be explained. By this, he shows that these two terms are said in reference to the posture of sitting and the coming together by way of bodily unity. Discourse (kathā) is called 'saṅkhiyā' because of being well spoken (khiyanato) or told (kathanato). 'Kathādhammo' is the nature of discourse; some say it is the method of investigation.

“Acchariya”ntiādi tassa rūpadassananti āha “katamo pana so”tiādi. Soti kathādhammo. “Nīyatīti nayo, attho, saddasatthaṃ anugato nayo saddanayo”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.3) ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Nīyati attho etenāti vā nayo, upāyo, saddasatthe āgato nayo atthagahaṇūpāyo saddanayo. Tattha hi anabhiṇhavuttike acchariya-saddo icchito ruḷhivasena. Tenevāha “andhassa pabbatārohaṇaṃ viyā”tiādi. Tassa hi tadārohaṇaṃ na niccaṃ, kadāciyeva siyā, evamidampi. Accharāyoggaṃ acchariyaṃ niruttinayena yoggasaddassa lopato, taddhitavasena vā ṇiyapaccayassa vicitravuttito, so pana porāṇaṭṭhakathāyameva āgatattā “aṭṭhakathānayo”ti vutto. Pubbe abhūtanti abhūtapubbaṃ, etena na bhūtaṃ abhūtanti nibbacanaṃ, bhūta-saddassa ca atītatthaṃ dasseti. Yāvañcidanti sandhivasena niggahitāgamoti āha “yāva ca ida”nti, etassa ca “suppaṭividitā”ti etena sambandho. Yāva cayattakaṃ idaṃ ayaṃ nānādhimuttikatā suppaṭividitā, taṃ “ettakamevā”ti na sakkā amhehi paṭivijjhituṃ, akkhātuñcāti sapāṭhasesattho. Tenevāha “tena suppaṭividitatāya appameyyataṃ dassetī”ti.

The words beginning with 'Acchariyaṃ' are for showing its essential nature; therefore, the commentator said the words beginning with 'katamo pana so'. 'So' refers to the nature of the discourse. It was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla: 'Because it is known (nīyati), it is a "nayo" (method); the meaning is obtained. A method that accords with the science of words is a "saddanayo" (verbal method)'. Or, because meaning is known by this, it is a 'nayo', a means (upāyo); a method that has come down in the science of words, a means for grasping the meaning, is a 'saddanayo'. For there, the word 'acchariya' is intended in the sense of something that does not happen constantly, by way of convention. For that very reason, he said the words beginning with 'like a blind man's ascent of a mountain'. For that ascent of his is not constant; it would happen only sometimes—so too is this case. 'Acchariyaṃ' comes from 'accharāyoggaṃ' (fit for a finger-snap) by the elision of the word 'yogga', according to the method of etymology; or, it is 'acchariyaṃ' by way of a taddhita derivation, due to the varied application of the 'ṇiya' suffix. But since that method is found only in the ancient commentary, it is called the 'commentary method' (aṭṭhakathānayo). 'What has not been before' is 'abhūtapubbaṃ'. By this, he shows the derivation 'what has not been is abhūtaṃ', and the past sense of the word 'bhūta'. In 'yāvañcidaṃ', there is the insertion of a niggahīta by way of sandhi; therefore he said 'yāva ca idaṃ'. And the connection of this is with 'suppaṭividitā'. The meaning with the remainder of the text supplied is: 'To whatever extent this diversity of dispositions has been well penetrated, it is not possible for us to penetrate it or to declare, "It is just this much"'. For that very reason, he said: 'Thereby, he shows its immeasurability through its being well penetrated'.

“Bhagavatā”tiādīhi [M 1.0199] padehi samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttattā tenāti ettha ta-saddo sakatthapaṭiniddeso, tasmā yena abhisambuddhabhāvena bhagavā pakato samāno supākaṭo nāma hoti, tadabhisambuddhabhāvaṃ saddhiṃ āgamanapaṭipadāya tassa atthabhāvena dassento “yo so”tiādimāha[V 1.0174]. Na hettha so pubbe vutto atthi, yo attho tehi therehi ta-saddena parāmasitabbo bhaveyya. Tasmā yathāvuttaguṇasaṅkhātaṃ sakatthaṃyevesa padhānabhāvena parāmasatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti aggamaggañāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ, anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca aggamaggañāṇaṃ. Tadubhayañhi sammā aviparītaṃ sayameva bujjhati, sammā vā pasaṭṭhā sundaraṃ bujjhatīti sammāsambodhi. Sā pana buddhānaṃ sabbaguṇasampattiṃ deti abhiseko viya rañño sabbalokissariyabhāvaṃ, tasmā “anuttarā sammāsambodhī”ti vuccati. Abhisambuddhoti abbhaññāsi paṭivijjhi, tena tādisena bhagavatāti attho. Satipi ñāṇadassanānaṃ idha paññāvevacanabhāve tena tena visesena nesaṃ visayavisesappavattiṃ dassento “tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna”ntiādimāha. Ettha hi paṭhamamatthaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇavasena dasseti. Āsayānusayañāṇena jānatā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇehi passatāti attho.

Because it is stated in apposition with words beginning with 'Bhagavatā', the word 'ta' here in 'tena' is an indication of its own meaning. Therefore, wishing to show that state of having been fully awakened—by which the Blessed One, being manifest, becomes well-manifest—together with the practice that is the path of approach, as the meaning of that word 'ta', he said the words beginning with 'yo so'. For here there is no previously mentioned meaning that should be referred to by those elders with the word 'ta'. Therefore, it should be understood that this word 'ta' primarily refers to its own meaning, which is designated as the qualities as stated. 'Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment' is the unobstructed knowledge which has the supreme path-knowledge as its proximate cause, and the supreme path-knowledge which has the unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause. For he awakens to both of these rightly, without distortion, by himself; or, being praised, he awakens well and beautifully; therefore it is 'sammāsambodhi' (perfect self-enlightenment). Moreover, it bestows upon the Buddhas the fulfillment of all virtues, like an anointing bestows upon a king sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, it is called 'unsurpassed perfect enlightenment'. 'Abhisambuddho' means he specially knew, he penetrated; the meaning is 'by that Blessed One of such a kind'. Although 'knowledge' and 'vision' are here synonyms for wisdom, wishing to show the arising of their specific domains by means of those various distinctions, he said the words beginning with 'of those various beings'. For here, he shows the first meaning by way of the unique knowledges. The meaning is: knowing with the knowledge of dispositions and latent tendencies, and seeing with the knowledges of omniscience and non-obstruction.

Dutiyaṃ vijjattayavasena. Pubbenivāsādīhīti pubbenivāsāsavakkhayañāṇehi. Tatiyaṃ abhiññānāvaraṇañāṇavasena. Abhiññāpariyāpannepi “tīhi vijjāhī”ti tāsaṃ rāsibhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena samantacakkhunā passatāti attho. Catutthaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇamaṃsacakkhuvasena. Paññāyāti sabbaññutaññāṇena. Kuṭṭassa bhittiyā tiro paraṃ, anto vā, tadādīsu gatāni. Ativisuddhenāti ativiya visuddhena pañcavaṇṇasamannāgatena sunīlapāsādikaakkhilomasamalaṅkatena rattiñceva divā ca samantā yojanaṃ passantena maṃsacakkhunā. Pañcamaṃ paṭivedhadesanāñāṇavasena. “Attahitasādhikāyā”ti ekaṃsato vuttaṃ, pariyāyato panesā parahitasādhikāpi hoti. Tāya hi dhammasabhāvapaṭicchādakakilesasamugghātāya desanāñāṇādi sambhavati. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Vipassanāsahagato samādhi padaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0200] āsannakāraṇametissāti samādhipadaṭṭhānā, tāya. Desanāpaññāyāti desanākiccanipphādakena sabbaññutaññāṇena. Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ, pañcamārānaṃ vā, sāsanapaccatthikānaṃ vā aññatitthiyānaṃ. Tesaṃ hananaṃ pāṭihāriyehi abhibhavanaṃ appaṭibhānatākaraṇaṃ, ajjhupekkhanañca majjhimapaṇṇāsake pañcamavagge saṅgītaṃ caṅkīsuttañcettha (ma. ni. 2.422) nidassanaṃ, etena arayo hatā anenāti niruttinayena padasiddhimāha. Ato nāvacanassa tābyappadeso mahāvisayenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apica arayo hanatīti antasaddena padasiddhi, ikārassa ca akāro. Paccayādīnaṃ sampadānabhūtānaṃ, tesaṃ vā paṭiggahaṇaṃ, paṭiggahituṃ vā arahatīti arahanti dasseti “paccayādīnañca arahattā”ti iminā. Sammāti aviparītaṃ. Sāmañcāti sayameva, aparaneyyo hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ panettha “sabbadhammāna”nti ayaṃ viseso labbhatīti? Sāmaññajotanāya [V 1.0175] visese avaṭṭhānato, visesatthinā ca visesassa anupayojetabbato yajjevaṃ “dhammāna”nti visesovānupayojito siyā, kasmā sabbadhammānanti ayamattho anupayojīyatīti? Ekadesassa aggahaṇato. Padesaggahaṇe hi asati gahetabbassa nippadesatā viññāyati yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti, esa nayo īdisesu.

Secondly, by way of the threefold knowledge. ‘By remembering past lives, etc.’—this means by the knowledges of the recollection of past lives and the destruction of the taints. Thirdly, by way of the higher knowledge and the unobstructed knowledge. Though included in the higher knowledges, the phrase ‘by the three knowledges’ is stated to show their distinct grouping. The meaning is: seeing with the all-seeing eye, which is called the unobstructed knowledge. Fourthly, by way of the knowledge of omniscience and the physical eye. ‘By wisdom’—this means by the knowledge of omniscience. Things that have gone to the other side of a wall, or inside, and so forth. ‘Extremely pure’—this means with the physical eye, which is exceedingly pure, endowed with five colors, adorned with beautiful, dark blue, pleasing eyelashes, and which sees for a yojana all around, both by night and by day. Fifthly, by way of the knowledge of penetration and teaching. ‘Accomplishing one’s own welfare’—this is stated definitively, but figuratively, this wisdom also accomplishes the welfare of others. For by it, through the eradication of the defilements that conceal the true nature of phenomena, the knowledge of teaching, etc., arises. ‘By the wisdom of penetration’—this means by the wisdom of the noble path. Concentration accompanied by insight is its proximate cause; therefore, that wisdom is said to have concentration as its proximate cause. ‘By the wisdom of teaching’—this means by the knowledge of omniscience, which accomplishes the task of teaching. ‘Of enemies’—this means of the enemies that are the defilements, or of the five Māras, or of the opponents of the Dispensation who are adherents of other sects. Their killing, overcoming with miracles, rendering speechless, and looking on with equanimity—the Caṅkī Sutta, recited in the fifth chapter of the Middle Fifty (Majjhima Nikāya 2.422), is an example here. By this, he states the derivation of the word according to the etymological method: ‘enemies (arayo) were destroyed (hatā) by him (anena)’. It should be understood that after ‘a’, the instrumental ending ‘nā’ is indicated as ‘tā’ according to the Mahāvisaya Sutta. Furthermore, the derivation of the word is from ‘he destroys (hanati) enemies (arayo)’ with the suffix ‘anta’; and the ‘i’ becomes ‘a’. He shows that one is worthy (arahati) to receive or to accept requisites, etc., which are offerings, by the phrase ‘because of being worthy of requisites, etc.’ ‘Rightly’—this means without distortion. ‘By oneself’—this means by himself, not being led by another. How, then, is this specific term ‘of all phenomena’ obtained? It is obtained because a general indication stands for the specific, and because a specific term is not to be applied by one who desires a specific meaning. If it were so, the specific term ‘of phenomena’ would indeed be applied. Why, then, is the meaning ‘of all phenomena’ applied? Because a part is not taken. For when a part is not taken, it is understood that what is to be taken is without remainder, as in ‘an initiated one does not give’. This is the method in such cases.

Idāni ca catūhi padehi catuvesārajjavasena attanā adhippetataraṃ chaṭṭhamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “antarāyikadhamme vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tadeva nigamanaṃ karoti “eva”ntiādinā. Tattha antarāyakaradhammañāṇena jānatā, niyyānikadhammañāṇena passatā, āsavakkhayañāṇena arahatā, sabbaññutaññāṇena sammāsambuddhenaāti yathākkamaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Anatthacaraṇena kilesā eva arayoti kilesārayo, tesaṃ kilesārīnaṃ. Etthāha – yassa ñāṇassa vasena sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā bhagavā sammāsambuddho nāma jāto, kiṃ panidaṃ ñāṇaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ bujjhanavasena pavattamānaṃ sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, udāhu kamenāti. Kiñcettha – yadi tāva sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, evaṃ sati atītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhādibhedabhinnānaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ, asaṅkhatasammutidhammānañca ekajjhaṃ upaṭṭhāne dūrato cittapaṭaṃ pekkhantassa viya paṭibhāgenāvabodho na siyā, tathā ca sati “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti [M 1.0201] (a. ni. 3.137; dha. pa. 279; mahāni. 27; cūḷani. 8, 10; netti. 5) vipassantānaṃ anattākārena viya sabbe dhammā anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇavisayā hontīti āpajjati. Yepi “sabbañeyyadhammānaṃ ṭhitilakkhaṇavisayaṃ vikapparahitaṃ sabbakālaṃ buddhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tena te ‘sabbavidū’ti vuccanti. Evañca katvā –

Now, with four phrases, by way of the four confidences, to show the sixth meaning, which is more desired by himself, the words beginning with ‘or regarding obstructive phenomena’ were stated. For thus, he makes that very conclusion with the words beginning ‘thus’. Therein, it should be connected in order thus: by one who knows with the knowledge of obstructive phenomena, by one who sees with the knowledge of phenomena leading to release, by an Arahant with the knowledge of the destruction of taints, and by a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One with the knowledge of omniscience. Because they cause what is not beneficial, the defilements themselves are enemies; thus, they are ‘defilement-enemies’; of those enemies that are the defilements. Here someone says: By the power of which knowledge the Blessed One became known as a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, due to having rightly and by himself understood all phenomena—does this knowledge, proceeding by way of understanding all phenomena, arise just once in its entire sphere, or does it arise sequentially? And further on this point: if it arises just once in its entire sphere, then, with the simultaneous appearance of conditioned phenomena divided into past, future, present, internal, external, etc., and unconditioned and conventional phenomena, there would not be distinct comprehension, like one looking at a colorful cloth from afar. And if that were so, it would follow that all phenomena would become objects of the Blessed One's knowledge in an undetermined form, just as for those practicing insight meditation, phenomena appear in the aspect of 'not-self'. And those teachers who say: ‘The knowledge of the Buddhas operates at all times, free from conceptualization, having as its object the present characteristic of all knowable phenomena; for that reason, they are called “all-knowing.”’ And for this reason—

‘Gacchaṃ samāhito nāgo, ṭhito nāgo samāhito;

Seyyaṃ samāhito nāgo, nisinnopi samāhito’ti. (a. ni. 6.43); –

‘Composed while walking, he is a Nāga; composed while standing, he is a Nāga; composed while lying down, he is a Nāga; composed while sitting, he is also a Nāga.’

Idampi sabbadā ñāṇappavattidīpakaṃ aṅguttarāgame nāgopamasuttavacanaṃ suvuttaṃ nāma hotī”ti vadanti, tesampi vāde vuttadosā nātivatti. Ṭhitilakkhaṇārammaṇatāya ca atītānāgatadhammānaṃ tadabhāvato ekadesavisayameva bhagavato ñāṇaṃ siyā, tasmā sakiññeva sabbasmiṃ visaye ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti na yujjati. Atha kamena sabbasmimpi visaye ñāṇaṃ pavattati, evampi na yujjati. Na hi jātibhūmisabhāvādivasena, disādesakālādivasena ca anekabhedabhinne ñeyye kamena [V 1.0176] gayhamāne tassa anavasesapaṭivedho sambhavati apariyantabhāvato ñeyyassa. Ye pana “atthassa avisaṃvādanato ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā sesepi evanti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanena sabbaññū nāma bhagavā jāto, tañca ñāṇaṃ na anumānikaṃ nāma saṃsayābhāvato. Saṃsayānubaddhañhi ñāṇaṃ loke anumānika”nti vadanti, tesampi taṃ na yuttameva. Sabbassa hi appaccakkhabhāve atthāvisaṃvādanena ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā sesepi evanti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanasseva asambhavato tathā asakkuṇeyyattā ca. Yañhi sesaṃ, tadapaccakkhameva, atha tampi paccakkhaṃ, tassa sesabhāvo eva na siyā, apariyantabhāvato ñeyyassa tathāvavatthitumeva na sakkāti? Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Avisayavicāraṇabhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “buddhānaṃ bhikkhave, buddhavisayo acinteyyo na cintetabbo, yaṃ cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77) idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – yaṃ kiñci bhagavatā ñātuṃ icchitaṃ, sakalamekadeso vā, tattha tattha appaṭihatavuttitāya paccakkhato ñāṇaṃ pavattati niccasamādhānañca vikkhepābhāvato, ñātuṃ icchitassa ca sakalassa avisayabhāve tassa ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhavuttitā na siyā, ekanteneva [M 1.0202] sā icchitabbā, sabbe dhammā buddhassa bhagavato āvajjanapaṭibaddhā ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhā manasikārapaṭibaddhā cittuppādapaṭibaddhāti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato. Atītānāgatavisayampi bhagavato ñāṇaṃ anumānāgamatakkagahaṇavirahitattā paccakkhameva.

They say: 'This saying from the Nāgopama Sutta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which always illuminates the arising of knowledge, is also well-spoken.' Yet, even in their view, the aforementioned fault is not overcome. And because past and future phenomena lack the characteristic of the present moment as an object, the Blessed One's knowledge would have only a partial object. Therefore, it is not suitable that knowledge arises just once regarding the entire field of objects. If, then, knowledge arises sequentially regarding the entire field of objects, this too is not suitable. For, when the knowable—which is differentiated into countless divisions by way of birth, plane of existence, intrinsic nature, etc., and by way of direction, locality, time, etc.—is being cognized sequentially, a penetration of it without remainder is not possible, due to the boundless nature of the knowable. As for those who say: 'Because of the non-discrepancy of the meaning, having directly perceived a portion of the knowable, and having resolved, "The rest is also thus," the Blessed One became one called "All-Knowing" by this determination. And that knowledge is not what is called inferential, due to the absence of doubt. For in the world, knowledge connected with doubt is called inferential.'—their statement is also not suitable. For when the whole is not directly perceived, the very determination by resolving 'the rest is also thus' after directly perceiving a portion of the knowable through non-discrepancy of meaning is impossible, and because one is unable to do so. For whatever is the remainder, that is not directly perceived. And if that remainder were also directly perceived, its state of being a remainder would not exist. Because of the boundless nature of the knowable, is it not impossible to determine it in such a way? All this is without reason. Why? Because it is an investigation into what is not a proper domain. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, the domain of the Buddhas is unthinkable; it should not be thought about. One who thinks about it would partake of madness and vexation.' Herein, this is the conclusion: Whatever the Blessed One wished to know, whether the whole or a part, in every case knowledge arises directly with unobstructed functioning, due to his constant concentration and absence of distraction. And if the entirety of what is wished to be known were not its object, its functioning, which is dependent on his wish, would not exist. That functioning must be accepted definitively, because of the saying: 'All phenomena are connected to the attention of the Buddha, the Blessed One, connected to his wish, connected to his application of mind, connected to the arising of his thought.' Even regarding past and future objects, the Blessed One's knowledge is direct, being devoid of reliance on inference, tradition, or reasoning.

Nanu ca etasmimpi pakkhe yadā sakalaṃ ñātuṃ icchitaṃ, tadā sakiṃyeva sakalavisayatāya anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavatteyyāti vuttadosā nātivattiyevāti? Na, tassa visodhitattā. Visodhito hi so buddhavisayo acinteyyoti. Aññathā pacurajanañāṇasamānavuttitāya buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ ñāṇassa acinteyyatā na siyā, tasmā sakaladhammārammaṇampi taṃ ekadhammārammaṇaṃ viya suvavatthāpiteyeva te dhamme katvā pavattatīti idamettha acinteyyaṃ, “yāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ. Neyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ neyyaṃ. Neyyaṃ atikkamitvā ñāṇaṃ nappavattati, ñāṇaṃ atikkamitvā neyyapatho natthi. Aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino te dhammā, yathā dvinnaṃ samuggapaṭalānaṃ sammā phusitānaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ uparimaṃ nātivattati, uparimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ nātivattati. Aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino, evameva buddhassa bhagavato neyyañca ñāṇañca aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino…pe… te dhammā”ti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) evamekajjhaṃ, visuṃ, sakiṃ, kamena vā icchānurūpaṃ [V 1.0177] pavattassa tassa ñāṇassa vasena sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā bhagavā sammāsambuddho nāma jātoti.

Is it not so that in this position as well, when he wishes to know the whole, the Blessed One's knowledge would then arise at once with the whole as its object in an undetermined form, and thus the aforementioned fault would not be overcome? No, the fault is overcome because that has been cleared up. For that fault has been cleared up by the principle: 'The domain of a Buddha is unthinkable.' Otherwise, if the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas were to function in the same way as the knowledge of ordinary people, the inconceivability of their knowledge would not exist. Therefore, although that knowledge has all phenomena as its object, it arises having made those phenomena well-determined, as if it had a single phenomenon as its object. This is what is inconceivable here. 'As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge. As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not arise transcending the knowable; there is no path for the knowable transcending knowledge. Those phenomena, the knowable and knowledge, stand with each other as their limit. Just as with the two halves of a casket that are well-fitted together, the lower half does not transcend the upper, and the upper half does not transcend the lower; they stand with each other as their limit. Even so, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, the knowable and knowledge stand with each other as their limit.' Thus, by the power of that knowledge which arises in accordance with his wish—whether all together or separately, at once or sequentially—and because of having awakened to all phenomena rightly and by himself, the Blessed One is called the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – ṭhānāṭhānādīni chabbisayāni chahi ñāṇehi jānatā, yathākammūpage satte cutūpapātadibbacakkhuñāṇehi passatā, savāsanānamāsavānaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇena khīṇattā arahatā, jhānādidhamme saṃkilesavodānavasena sāmaṃyeva aviparītāvabodhato sammāsambuddhena, evaṃ dasabalañāṇavasena catūhākārehi thomitena. Apica tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāya jānatā, tiṇṇampi kammānaṃ ñāṇānuparivattito nisammakāritāya passatā, davādīnaṃ channamabhāvasādhikāya pahānasampadāya arahatā, chandādīnaṃ channamahānihetubhūtāya aparikkhayapaṭibhānasādhikāya sabbaññutāya sammāsambuddhena[M 1.0203], evaṃ aṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhammavasena (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305) catūhākārehi thomitenāti evamādinā tesaṃ tesaṃ ñāṇadassanapahānabodhanatthehi saṅgahitānaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbāti.

Herein, this is the method independent of the commentaries: He is praised in four aspects by way of the ten powers: as one who knows, by knowing the six objects beginning with the possible and impossible with the six knowledges; as one who sees, by seeing with the knowledge of the divine eye beings passing away and being reborn according to their kamma; as an Arahant, because of the destruction of the taints together with their latent tendencies by the knowledge of the destruction of the taints; as a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, because of unerringly understanding by himself the phenomena of jhāna and so on by way of their defilement and purification. Furthermore, he is praised in four aspects by way of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha: as one who knows, by possessing unhindered knowledge of the three times; as one who sees, by acting with careful consideration, as his three kinds of action are preceded by knowledge; as an Arahant, through the accomplishment of abandoning which brings about the absence of anything concealed, such as playful acts; as a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, through omniscience which accomplishes inexhaustible analytical knowledge and is the cause for the non-decline of the six qualities beginning with zeal. In this and other ways, the application should be made by way of the Buddha's qualities, which are comprised under the meanings of knowing, seeing, abandoning, and awakening.

Catuvesārajjaṃ sandhāya “catūhākārehī”ti vuttaṃ. “Thomitenā”ti etena imesaṃ “bhagavatā”ti padassa visesanataṃ dasseti. Yadipi hīnapaṇītabhedena duvidhāva adhimutti pāḷiyaṃ vuttā, pavattiākāravasena pana anekabhedabhinnāvāti āha “nānādhimuttikatā”ti. Sā pana adhimutti ajjhāsayadhātuyeva, tadapi tathā tathā dassanaṃ, khamanaṃ, rocanañcāti atthaṃ viññāpeti “nānajjhāsayatā”ti iminā. Tathā hi vakkhati “nānādhimuttikatā nānajjhāsayatā nānādiṭṭhikatā nānakkhantitā nānārucitā”ti. “Yāvañcida”nti etassa “suppaṭividitā”ti iminā sambandho. Tattha ca idanti padapūraṇamattaṃ, “nānādhimuttikatā”ti etena vā padena samānādhikaraṇaṃ, tassattho pana pākaṭoyevāti āha “yāva ca suṭṭhu paṭividitā”ti.

The phrase 'in four ways' refers to the four kinds of fearlessness. By the word 'thomitenā', he indicates that these words are qualifiers of the word 'Bhagavatā'. Although inclination (adhimutti) is spoken of in the Pāḷi as being of two kinds, distinguished as inferior and superior, by way of its mode of occurrence it is divided into many kinds; hence it is said 'diversity of inclinations' (nānādhimuttikatā). Furthermore, that inclination is the dispositional element itself, and the phrase 'diversity of dispositions' (nānajjhāsayatā) conveys the meaning of seeing, approving, and liking in various ways. For so it will be said: 'diversity of inclinations, diversity of dispositions, diversity of views, diversity of tolerances, diversity of tastes.' The phrase 'yāvañcidaṃ' is connected with 'suppaṭividitā' (thoroughly penetrated). Therein, the word 'idaṃ' is a mere expletive, or is in apposition with the word 'nānādhimuttikatā'; its meaning, however, is obvious, hence it is stated: 'insofar as it is thoroughly penetrated'.

“Yā ca aya”ntiādinā dhātusaṃyuttapāḷiṃ dassento tadeva saṃyuttaṃ manasi karitvā tesaṃ avaṇṇavaṇṇabhāsanena saddhiṃ ghaṭetvā therānamayaṃ saṅkhiyadhammo udapādīti dasseti. Ato assa bhagavato dhātusaṃyuttadesanānayena tāsaṃ suppaṭividitabhāvaṃ samatthanavasena dassetuṃ “ayaṃ hī”tiādimāhāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Suppaṭividitabhāvasamatthanañhi “ayaṃ hī”tiādivacanaṃ. Tattha yā ayaṃ nānādhimuttikatā…pe… rucitāti sambandho. Dhātusoti ajjhāsayadhātuyā. Saṃsandantīti sambandhenti vissāsenti. Samentīti sammā, saha vā bhavanti. “Hīnādhimuttikā”tiādi [V 1.0178] tathābhāvavibhāvanaṃ. Atītampi addhānanti atītasmiṃ kāle, accantasaṃyoge vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nānādhimuttikatā-padassa nānajjhāsayatāti atthavacanaṃ. Nānādiṭṭhi…pe… rucitāti tassa sarūpadassanaṃ. Sassatādiladdhivasena nānādiṭṭhikatā. Pāpācārakalyāṇācārādipakativasena nānakkhantitā. Pāpicchāappicchādivasena nānārucitā. Nāḷiyāti tumbena, āḷhakena vā. Tulāyāti mānena. Nānādhimuttikatāñāṇanti cettha sabbaññutaññāṇameva adhippetaṃ, na dasabalañāṇanti āha [M 1.0204] “sabbaññutaññāṇenā”ti. Evaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherena (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.3) vuttaṃ, abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, dasabalasuttaṭṭhakathāsu (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.149; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.21; vibha. aṭṭha. 831) ca evamāgataṃ.

By showing the Pāḷi of the Dhātusaṃyutta with 'yā ca ayaṃ', etc., and having paid attention to that very Saṃyutta, and having connected it with their speaking in dispraise and praise, he shows that this reasoned discourse of the elders arose. Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is that he said 'ayaṃ hi', etc., in order to show, by way of establishing it, the Blessed One's state of having thoroughly penetrated them through the method of the discourse on the Dhātusaṃyutta. For the words 'ayaṃ hi', etc., establish the state of being thoroughly penetrated. Therein, the connection is: 'Whatever this diversity of inclinations is... whatever this diversity of tastes is.' 'Dhātuso' means by way of the dispositional element. 'Saṃsandanti' (they converge) means they connect, they become intimate. 'Samenti' (they come together) means they exist rightly, or together. The words 'hīnādhimuttikā' (those of inferior inclination), etc., are an explanation of that state. 'Atītampi addhānaṃ' (even in past time) means in past time, or this is a word in the accusative case in the sense of continuous connection. 'Nānajjhāsayatā' (diversity of dispositions) is a word that explains the meaning of 'nānādhimuttikatā' (diversity of inclinations). The words 'nānādiṭṭhi... rucitā' (diversity of views... tastes) show its essential nature. Diversity of views is by way of holding to eternalism, etc. Diversity of tolerance is by way of the nature of evil conduct, good conduct, etc. Diversity of tastes is by way of evil desires, few desires, etc. 'Nāḷiyā' means by a gourd, or by an āḷhaka measure. 'Tulāyā' means by a balance. Here, by 'knowledge of diverse inclinations,' omniscient knowledge alone is intended, not the knowledge of the ten powers; hence it is said: 'by omniscient knowledge.' Thus it is stated by the elder Acariya Dhammapāla, and it is found thus in the Abhidhamma commentary and in the commentaries on the Dasabala Sutta.

Paravādī panāha “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedo”ti, taṃ tathā na daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇañhi sakakiccameva jānāti, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana tampi tato avasesampi jānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti, dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva, tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva, catutthaṃ dhātunānattakāraṇameva, pañcamaṃ sattānamajjhāsayādhimuttimeva, chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva, sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva, aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakkhandhasantatimeva, navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva, dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca jānāti, etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Apica paravādī evaṃ pucchitabbo “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma etaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ avitakkavicāramattaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ, kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ, lokiyaṃ lokuttara”nti. Jānanto paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇāni “savitakkasavicārānī”ti vakkhati, tato parāni dve “avitakkaavicārānī”ti vakkhati, āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ “siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkavicāramattaṃ, siyā avitakkaavicāra”nti vakkhati, tathā paṭipāṭiyā satta kāmāvacarāni, tato paraṃ dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ “lokuttara’nti vakkhati, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana savitakkasavicārameva, kāmāvacarameva, lokiyamevāti. Iti aññadeva dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇanti, tasmā pañcamabalañāṇasaṅkhātena nānādhimuttikatāñāṇena ca sabbaññutaññāṇena ca viditāti attho veditabbo. Ca-kāropi hi potthakesu dissati. Sāti yathāvuttā nānādhimuttikatā. “Dvepi nāmā”tiādinā yathāvuttasuttassatthaṃ [V 1.0179] saṅkhepena dassetvā “imesu cāpī”tiādinā tassa saṅkhiyadhammassa tadabhisambandhataṃ āvi karoti. Iti ha meti ettha evaṃsaddatthe iti-saddo, ha-kāro nipātamattaṃ, āgamo vā. Sandhivasena [M 1.0205] ikāralopo, akārādeso vāti dasseti “evaṃ ime”ti iminā.

But an opponent says: 'The knowledge of the ten powers is not separate; it is a division of omniscient knowledge itself.' This should not be understood so. For the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another. The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own function, whereas omniscient knowledge knows that and what remains beyond it. For among the knowledges of the ten powers: the first knows only cause and non-cause; the second, only the distinctions of kamma and the distinctions of their results; the third, only the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, only the cause for the diversity of elements; the fifth, only the dispositions and inclinations of beings; the sixth, only the sharp or dull state of the faculties; the seventh, only their defilements, etc., together with the jhānas, etc.; the eighth, only the continuity of aggregates formerly inhabited; the ninth, only the passing away and rebirth of beings; the tenth, only the delimitation of the truths. But omniscient knowledge knows what is to be known by these and what is beyond that; however, it does not perform all of their functions. For that knowledge, having become jhāna, cannot enter absorption; having become psychic power, it cannot perform transformations; having become the path, it cannot destroy the defilements. Furthermore, the opponent should be questioned thus: 'Is this knowledge of the ten powers with applied and sustained thought, with only sustained thought without applied thought, or without applied and sustained thought? Is it of the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, or the formless-sphere? Is it mundane or supramundane?' One who knows would reply in sequence that seven knowledges are 'with applied and sustained thought'; the two after that are 'without applied and sustained thought'; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints 'may be with applied and sustained thought, may be with only sustained thought without applied thought, or may be without applied and sustained thought.' Similarly, in sequence, seven are of the sense-sphere, the two after that are of the form-sphere, and the one at the end is 'supramundane'; but that omniscient knowledge is only with applied and sustained thought, only of the sense-sphere, and only mundane. Thus, the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another. Therefore, the meaning should be understood that this is known through the knowledge of diverse inclinations, which is reckoned as the fifth power-knowledge, and through omniscient knowledge. Indeed, the particle 'ca' is also seen in the manuscripts. 'Sā' refers to the aforementioned diversity of inclinations. Having shown the meaning of the aforementioned sutta in brief with 'dvepi nāmā', etc., with 'imesu cāpi', etc., he makes clear the connection of that reasoned discourse to it. Here in 'iti ha me', the word 'iti' is in the sense of 'evaṃ' (thus); the letter 'ha' is a mere particle, or it is an augment. He shows with the phrase 'evaṃ ime' that by way of sandhi there is elision of the letter 'i', or substitution of 'a' for 'i'.

4. “Viditvā”ti ettha pakatiyatthabhūtā vijānanakiriyā sāmaññena abhedavatīpi samānā taṃtaṃkaraṇayogyatāya anekappabhedāti dassetuṃ “bhagavā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vatthūnīti gharavatthūni. “Sabbaññutaññāṇena disvā aññāsī”ti ca vohāravacanamattametaṃ. Na hi tena dassanato aññaṃ jānanaṃ nāma natthi. Tadidaṃ ñāṇaṃ āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhaṃ manasikārapaṭibaddhaṃ cittuppādapaṭibaddhaṃ hutvā pavattati. Kiṃ nāma karonto bhagavā tena ñāṇena āvajjanādipaṭibaddhena aññāsīti sotūnamatthassa suviññāpanatthaṃ parammukhā viya codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti “kiṃ karonto aññāsī”ti iminā, pacchimayāmakiccaṃ karonto taṃ ñāṇaṃ āvajjanādipaṭibaddhaṃ hutvā tena tathā aññāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāmaññasmiṃ sati visesavacanaṃ sātthakaṃ siyāti anuyogenāha “kiccañcanāmeta”ntiādi. Arahattamaggena samugghātaṃ kataṃ tassa samuṭṭhāpakakilesasamugghāṭanena, yato “natthi abyāvaṭamano”ti aṭṭhārasasu buddhadhammesu vuccati. Niratthako cittasamudācāro natthīti hettha attho. Evampi vuttānuyogo tadavatthoyevāti codanamapaneti “taṃ pañcavidha”ntiādinā. Tattha purimakiccadvayaṃ divasabhāgavasena, itarattayaṃ rattibhāgavasena gahetabbaṃ tathāyeva vakkhamānattā.

4. In the phrase ‘Having known,’ the general act of knowing, which is the natural meaning, although being without distinction, has many distinctions due to its suitability for various functions. To show this, the commentary master said, ‘The Blessed One, indeed,’ and so on. ‘Objects’ means household objects. And the statement, ‘having seen with the knowledge of omniscience, he knew,’ is merely a conventional expression. Indeed, apart from seeing with that knowledge of omniscience, there is no other knowing. That knowledge operates, being connected with attention, connected with aspiration, connected with mental application, and connected with the arising of a great functional consciousness. To make the meaning easy for the listeners to understand, an objection is raised, as if from an unseen person, with the words, ‘What was the Blessed One doing when he knew with that knowledge connected with attention, and so on?’ It is meant to be said that while performing the duty of the last watch of the night, that knowledge, being connected with attention and so on, knew in that way through that omniscience. When there is a general statement, a specific statement would be meaningful. Thus, with a follow-up question, the commentary master says, ‘And what is that duty?’ and so on. Its eradication was accomplished by the path of Arahantship through the complete uprooting of the defilements that cause it to arise, because among the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, it is said, ‘There is no unengaged mind.’ Here, the meaning is that there is no useless mental activity. Even so, since the aforementioned follow-up question remains in the same state, he removes the objection with ‘That duty is fivefold,’ and so on. Therein, the first two duties should be understood as pertaining to the daytime, and the other three as pertaining to the nighttime, because it will be stated in that very way.

“Upaṭṭhākānuggahaṇatthaṃ, sarīraphāsukatthañcā”ti etena anekakappasamupacitapuññasambhārajanitaṃ bhagavato mukhavaraṃ duggandhādidosaṃ nāma natthi, tadubhayatthameva pana mukhadhovanādīni karotīti dasseti. Sabbopi hi buddhānaṃ kāyo bāhirabbhantarehi malehi anupakkiliṭṭho sudhotamaṇi viya hoti. Vivittāsaneti phalasamāpattīnamanurūpe vivekānubrūhanāsane. Vītināmetvāti phalasamāpattīhi vītināmanaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi na vivekaninnatāya, paresañca diṭṭhānugati āpajjanatthaṃ. Surattadupaṭṭaṃ antaravāsakaṃ vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasena nivāsetvā vijjulatāsadisaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā meghavaṇṇaṃ sugatacīvaraṃ pārupitvā selamayapattaṃ ādāyāti adhippāyo. Tathāyeva hi tattha tattha vutto. “Kadāci ekako”tiādi [M 1.0206] tesaṃ tesaṃ vineyyānaṃ vinayanānukūlaṃ bhagavato upasaṅkamanadassanaṃ. Gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vāti ettha vā-saddo vikappanattho, tena nagarampi vikappeti. Yathāruci vattamānehi anekehi pāṭihāriyehi pavisatīti sambandho.

By the phrase ‘For the purpose of helping the attendants and for bodily comfort,’ it is shown that the Blessed One's excellent mouth, produced by the accumulation of meritorious provisions over countless eons, has no such fault as bad odor; however, he performs actions like washing his face only for those two purposes. Indeed, the entire body of all Buddhas is unstained by external and internal impurities, like a well-cleansed gem. ‘In a secluded seat’ means in a place suitable for fruition attainments, which fosters seclusion. ‘Having passed the time’ refers to passing the time with fruition attainments. That too is not due to an inclination towards seclusion, but for the purpose of others following the example they have seen. The meaning is that, having put on a well-dyed, two-layered inner robe by way of changing his dwelling robe, having tied a body-band like a streak of lightning, having draped the Sugata’s robe, the color of a rain-cloud, he then takes a stone bowl. Indeed, it is explained in that very way in various places. ‘Sometimes alone,’ and so on, shows the Blessed One's approach, which is suitable for disciplining those various disciples to be trained. In ‘a village or a town,’ the word ‘or’ has the meaning of alternation; by it, he also specifies a city as an alternative. The connection is that he enters with many miracles that occur according to his wish.

“Seyyathida”ntiādinā [V 1.0180] pacchimapakkhaṃ vitthāreti. Seyyathidanti ca taṃ katamanti atthe nipāto, idaṃ vā sappāṭihīrapavisanaṃ katamantipi vaṭṭati. Mudugatavātāti mudubhūtā, mudubhāvena vā gatā vātā. Udakaphusitānīti udakabindūni. Muñcantāti osiñcantā. Reṇuṃ vūpasametvāti rajaṃ sannisīdāpetvā upari vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhanti caṇḍa-vātātapa-himapātādi-haraṇena vitānakiccanipphādakattā, tato tato himavantādīsu pupphūpagarukkhato upasaṃharitvāti atthassa viññāyamānattā tathā na vuttaṃ. Samabhāgakaraṇamattena onamanti, unnamanti ca, tatoyeva pādanikkhepasamaye samāva bhūmi hoti. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ sakkharakathalakaṇṭakasaṅkukalalādiapagamanassāpi sambhavato, tañca suppatiṭṭhitapādatālakkhaṇassa nissandaphalaṃ, na iddhinimmānaṃ. Padumapupphāni vāti ettha vā-saddo vikappanattho, tena “yadi yathāvuttanayena samā bhūmi hoti, evaṃ sati tāni na paṭiggaṇhanti, tathā pana asatiyeva paṭiggaṇhantī”ti bhagavato yathāruci pavattanaṃ dasseti. Sabbadāva bhagavato gamanaṃ paṭhamaṃ dakkhiṇapāduddharaṇasaṅkhātānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitanti āha “ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde”ti. Buddhānaṃ sabbadakkhiṇatāya tathā vuttanti ācariyadhammapālatthero,(dī. ni. ṭī. 1.4) ācariyasāriputtatthero (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.53) ca vadati, sabbesaṃ uttamatāya evaṃ vuttanti attho. Evaṃ sati uttamapurisānaṃ tathāpakatitāyāti āpajjati. Ṭhapitamatte nikkhamitvā dhāvantīti sambandho. Idañca yāvadeva vineyyajanavinayanatthaṃ satthu pāṭihāriyanti tesaṃ dassanaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Chabbaṇṇarasmiyo”ti vatvāpi “suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāni viyā”ti vacanaṃ bhagavato sarīre pītābhāya yebhuyyatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Rasa-saddo cettha udakapariyāyo, piñjara-saddo hemavaṇṇapariyāyo, suvaṇṇajaladhārā viya suvaṇṇavaṇṇānīti attho”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.buddhāciṇṇakathā.22) sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Pāsādakūṭāgārādīni tesu tesu gāmanigamādīsu saṃvijjamānāni alaṅkarontiyo hutvā.

With ‘Just as,’ and so on, he elaborates on the latter part. The word ‘seyyathidaṃ’ is a particle in the sense of ‘what is that miracle?’, or the meaning ‘what is this entering with miracles?’ is also suitable. ‘Gentle winds’ means winds that have become gentle, or winds that have come with gentleness. ‘Water droplets’ means drops of water. ‘Releasing’ means sprinkling. ‘Having settled the dust’ means having caused the dust to settle down well. They stand above, performing the function of a canopy by dispelling fierce winds, heat, falling dew, and so on. It is not stated that flowers are brought from flower-bearing trees in the Himalayas and so on, because that meaning is understood. Merely by making the ground level, they lower and they rise, and for that very reason, at the time of placing the foot, the ground becomes level. And this is merely an example, because the removal of pebbles, potsherds, thorns, rubbish, mud, and so on, is also possible. And that is the resultant fruit of the characteristic of having well-planted feet, not a creation of psychic power. In ‘or lotus flowers,’ the word ‘or’ has the meaning of alternation. By this, it shows that the Blessed One acts according to his wish: ‘If the ground becomes level in the aforementioned way, in that case they do not receive his feet; but if it is not so, they do receive them.’ The Blessed One's walking is always adorned with the minor characteristic known as first lifting the right foot; therefore, the commentary master said, ‘As soon as the right foot is placed.’ It is said thus because Buddhas are supreme over all (sabbadakkhiṇa), as the venerable teacher Dhammapāla and the venerable teacher Sāriputta state. The meaning is that it is said thus because of their supremacy over all. If this were so, the logical fault would arise that this is simply due to the nature of supreme persons. The connection is: ‘As soon as it is placed, they emerge and run forth.’ And this is said with reference to the place where they are seen by the disciples to be trained, as it is a miracle of the Teacher for the purpose of disciplining them. Even after saying ‘six-colored rays,’ the statement ‘like streams of golden liquid’ should be understood as referring to the predominance of the yellow hue in the Blessed One's body. As it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: ‘Here, the word “rasa” is a synonym for water, and the word “piñjara” is a synonym for golden-colored; the meaning is “golden-colored like streams of golden water.”’ These rays spread out, adorning the palaces, pinnacled buildings, and so on, that exist in those various villages and towns.

“Tathā”tiādinā [M 1.0207] sayameva dhammatāvasena tesaṃ saddakaraṇaṃ dasseti. Tadā kāyaṃ upagacchantīti kāyūpagāni, na yattha katthaci ṭhitāni. “Antaravīthi”nti iminā bhagavato piṇḍāya gamanānurūpavīthiṃ dasseti. Na hi bhagavā loluppacārapiṇḍacāriko viya yattha katthaci gacchati. Ye paṭhamaṃ gatā, ye vā tadanucchavikaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dātuṃ samatthā, te bhagavatopi pattaṃ gaṇhantīti veditabbaṃ. Paṭimānentīti patissamānasā pūjenti, bhagavantaṃ vā paṭimānāpenti paṭimānantaṃ karonti. Vohāramattañcetaṃ, bhagavato pana apaṭimānanā nāma natthi. Cittasantānānīti atīte, etarahi ca pavattacittasantānāni. Yathā keci arahatte patiṭṭhahanti, tathā dhammaṃ desetīti sambandho. Keci pabbajitvāti ca arahattasamāpannānaṃ pabbajjāsaṅkhepagatadassanatthaṃ[V 1.0181], na pana gihīnaṃ arahattasamāpannatāpaṭikkhepanatthaṃ. Ayañhi arahattappattānaṃ gihīnaṃ sabhāvo, yā tadaheva pabbajjā vā, kālaṃ kiriyāvāti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ āyasmatā nāgasenattherena “visamaṃ mahārāja, gihiliṅgaṃ, visame liṅge liṅgadubbalatāya arahattaṃ patto gihī tasmiṃyeva divase pabbajati vā parinibbāyati vā neso mahārāja, doso arahattassa, gihiliṅgasseveso doso yadidaṃ liṅgadubbalatā”ti (mi. pa. 5.2.2) sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Ettha ca sappāṭihīrappavesanasambandheneva mahājanānuggahaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, appāṭihīrappavesanena ca pana “te sunivatthā supārutā”tiādivacanaṃ yathārahaṃ sambandhitvā mahājanānuggahaṇaṃ atthato vibhāvetabbaṃ hoti. Tampi hi purebhattakiccamevāti. Upaṭṭhānasālā cettha maṇḍalamāḷo. Tattha gantvā maṇḍalamāḷeti idha pāṭho likhito. “Gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe”tipi (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.53) manorathapūraṇiyā dissati, taṭṭīkāyañca “catujjātiyagandhena paribhaṇḍe maṇḍalamāḷe”ti vuttaṃ. Gandhakuṭiṃ pavisatīti ca pavisanakiriyāsambandhatāya, tassamīpatāya ca vuttaṃ, tasmā pavisituṃ gacchatīti attho daṭṭhabbo, na pana anto tiṭṭhatīti. Evañhi “atha kho bhagavā”tiādivacanaṃ (dī. ni. 1.4) sūpapannaṃ hoti.

By the phrase beginning with 'Thus,' it shows that the making of sound by those instruments occurs automatically, by the power of their nature. At that time, because they approach the body, they are called kāyūpaga (body-approaching); they are not ornaments situated just anywhere. By this term 'antaravīthiṃ' (the street within), it indicates the street suitable for the Blessed One's alms-round. For indeed, the Blessed One does not go just anywhere like a monk who wanders for alms with greedy conduct. It should be understood that those who went first, or those who are capable of giving suitable alms-food, are the ones who take the Blessed One's bowl. Paṭimānenti means: they revere with a mind of esteem, or they cause the Blessed One to be revered, they perform an act of reverence. And this is merely a conventional expression, for indeed, there is no such thing as non-reverence for the Blessed One. Cittasantānāni means: the continuities of consciousness that have occurred in the past and at present. The connection should be made thus: He teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some become established in Arahantship. And the phrase 'Some, having gone forth' is stated for the purpose of showing, in brief, the going forth of laypeople who have attained Arahantship, but not for the purpose of rejecting the attainment of Arahantship by laypeople. For this is the nature of laypeople who have attained Arahantship: either going forth on that very day or dying. For thus it was said by the Venerable Nāgasenatthera: 'Incongruous, great king, is the lay state. In an incongruous state, due to the weakness of that state, a layperson who has attained Arahantship either goes forth on that very day or attains Parinibbāna. That, great king, is not a fault of Arahantship; it is a fault of the lay state itself, that is to say, the weakness of the state.' All of this should be stated. And here, the benefit to the great multitude is shown only in connection with the entrance accompanied by a miracle. However, in the case of the entrance without a miracle, the benefit to the great multitude should be made clear in its meaning by appropriately connecting the phrase beginning with 'they were well-dressed, well-robed.' For that too is indeed only the pre-meal duty. And here, the attendance hall is the circular pavilion. The reading 'having gone there, to the circular pavilion' is written here. The reading 'in the fragrant circular pavilion' is also seen in the Manorathapūraṇī, and in its sub-commentary it is said, 'in the circular pavilion adorned with the four kinds of perfumes.' And 'He enters the perfumed chamber' is said because of its connection with the act of entering and because of its proximity. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'he goes in order to enter,' and not 'he stands inside.' For only in this way is the phrase beginning with 'Then, the Blessed One' well-supported.

Atha khoti evaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisituṃ gamanakāle. Upaṭṭhāneti samīpapadese. “Pāde pakkhāletvā pādapīṭhe ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadatī”ti ettha pāde pakkhālentova pādapīṭhe tiṭṭhanto ovadatīti veditabbaṃ. Etadatthaṃyeva [M 1.0208] hi bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdi. Dullabhā sampattīti satipi manussattapaṭilābhe patirūpadesavāsaindriyāvekallasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo sampattisaṅkhātā guṇā dullabhāti attho. Potthakesu pana “dullabhā saddhāsampattī”ti pāṭho dissati, so ayuttova. Tatthāti tasmiṃ pādapīṭhe ṭhatvā ovadanakāle, tesu vā bhikkhūsu, rattiyā vasanaṃ ṭhānaṃ rattiṭṭhānaṃ, tathā divāṭhānaṃ. “Kecī”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ. Cātumahārājikabhavananti cātumahārājikadevaloke suññavimānāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Esa nayo tāvatiṃsabhavanādīsupi. Tato bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā pacchābhattaṃ tayo bhāge katvā paṭhamabhāge sace ākaṅkhati, dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti, sace nākaṅkhati, buddhāciṇṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, atha yathākālaparicchedaṃ tato vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyabhāge pacchimayāmassa tatiyakoṭṭhāse viya lokaṃ voloketi veneyyānaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ passituṃ, tenāha “sace ākaṅkhatī”tiādi. Sīhaseyyantiādīnamattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Yañhi apubbaṃ padaṃ anuttānaṃ, tadeva vaṇṇayissāma. Sammā assāsitabboti gāhāpanavasena upatthambhitabboti samassāsito. Tādiso kāyo yassāti tathā. Dhammassavanatthaṃ sannipatati. Tassā parisāya cittācāraṃ ñatvā katabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha [V 1.0182] “sampattaparisāyaanurūpena pāṭihāriyenā”ti. Yattha dhammaṃ saha bhāsanti, sā dhammasabhā nāma. Kālayuttanti “imissā velāya imassa evaṃ vattabba”nti taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ. Samayayuttanti tasseva vevacanaṃ, aṭṭhuppattianurūpaṃ vā samayayuttaṃ. Atha vā samayayuttanti hetudāharaṇehi yuttaṃ. Kālena sāpadesañhi bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti. Kālaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojeti, na yāva samandhakārā dhammaṃ desetīti adhippāyo. “Samayaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojesī”tipi katthaci pariyāyavacanapāṭho dissati, so pacchā pamādalikhito.

Atha kho refers to the time of going, thus, in order to enter the perfumed chamber. Upaṭṭhāne means in a nearby place. Here, in the text 'Having washed his feet and standing on the footstool, he advises the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,' it should be understood that he advises them while standing on the footstool, wanting to wash his feet. For it was for this very purpose that he sat down, awaiting the conclusion of the bhikkhus' meal-duty. Dullabhā sampatti (rare are attainments) means: even when there is the attainment of a human state, qualities reckoned as attainments—such as dwelling in a suitable country, non-deficiency of faculties, the attainment of faith, and so on—are rare. This is the meaning. However, in the books, the reading 'rare is the attainment of faith' is seen; that reading is quite unsuitable. Tatthā (there) means: at the time of advising while standing on that footstool, or among those bhikkhus. The place for dwelling at night is the night-residence; similarly, the day-residence. The phrase beginning with 'Some' is its explanation. 'The realm of the Cātumahārājika' is said in reference to the empty mansions in the devaloka of the Cātumahārājika. This same method should be understood also for the realms of the Tāvatiṃsa and so on. After that, the Blessed One, having entered the perfumed chamber and divided the post-meal time into three parts, in the first part, if he wishes, adopts the lion's posture on his right side; if he does not wish, he enters the attainment of fruition, which is the practice of Buddhas. Then, having arisen from that according to the allotted time, in the second part, like in the third portion of the last watch, he surveys the world in order to see the ripening of knowledge of those to be trained. Therefore, the commentator said the phrase beginning with 'if he wishes.' The meaning of the terms beginning with sīhaseyyaṃ has already been stated below. For we shall explain only that term which is new and not obvious. Samassāsito means: to be well comforted, that is, to be supported by way of causing one to grasp the teaching. Tathā (thus) refers to one who has such a body. The assembly gathers for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. Having known the mental conduct of that assembly, and in reference to the deed performed, the commentator said: 'with a miracle suitable for the assembled gathering.' The place where they speak the Dhamma together is called a Dhamma-hall. Kālayuttaṃ (suited to the time) means that which is suitable for each respective time, as in 'At this time, this should be said to this person in this way.' Samayayuttaṃ (suited to the occasion) is a synonym for that. Or, samayayuttaṃ is what is suitable for the occasion that has arisen. Alternatively, samayayuttaṃ means connected with reasons and examples. For the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma at the right time and with reference. Knowing the time, he dismisses the assembly; he does not teach the Dhamma until it is completely dark. This is the intended meaning. Somewhere, a synonymous reading is also seen: 'Knowing the occasion, he dismissed the assembly.' That was written later through negligence.

Gattānīti kāyoyeva anekāvayavattā vutto. “Utuṃ gaṇhāpetī”ti iminā utugaṇhāpanatthameva osiñcanaṃ, na pana malavikkhālanatthanti dasseti. Na hi bhagavato kāye rajojallaṃ upalimpatīti. Catujjātikena gandhena paribhāvitā kuṭī gandhakuṭī. Tassā pariveṇaṃ tathā. Phalasamāpattīhi muhuttaṃ paṭisallīno. Tato tatoti attano attano [M 1.0209] rattiṭṭhānadivāṭhānato, upagantvā, samīpe vā ṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ, bhajanaṃ sevananti attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ nisīdanaṭṭhāne, purimayāme vā, tesu vā bhikkhūsu.

The body itself, because of having many parts, is referred to in the plural as gattāni. By this phrase, ‘He causes it to absorb warmth,’ it is shown that the sprinkling of water is only for the purpose of absorbing warmth, and not for washing away impurities. Indeed, dust and grime do not adhere to the Blessed One’s body. A hut pervaded by fragrances of four kinds is a gandhakuṭī (fragrant hut). Its surrounding area is likewise. He was secluded for a moment in the attainment of fruition. ‘From there, from there’ means from their own respective night-dwellings and day-dwellings. Having approached, or, standing nearby (upaṭṭhānaṃ), the meaning is associating (bhajanaṃ), attending (sevanaṃ). ‘There’ means in that sitting place, or in the first watch, or among those monks.

Pañhākathanādivasena adhippāyaṃ sampādento “dasasahassilokadhātū”ti evaṃ avatvā tassā anekāvayavasaṅgahaṇatthaṃ “sakaladasasahassilokadhātū”ti vuttaṃ. Purebhattapacchābhattapurimayāmesu manussaparisābāhullato okāsaṃ alabhitvā idāni majjhimayāmeyeva okāsaṃ labhamānā, bhagavatā vā katokāsatāya okāsaṃ labhamānāti adhippāyo. Kīdisaṃ pana pucchantīti āha “yathābhisaṅkhataṃ antamaso caturakkharampī”ti. Yathābhisaṅkhatanti abhisaṅkhatānurūpaṃ, tadanatikkamma vā, etena yathā tathā attano paṭibhānānurūpaṃ pucchantīti dasseti.

Fulfilling the monks' intention by way of answering questions and so on, instead of saying 'ten-thousand world-system,' it was said as 'the entire ten-thousand world-system' for the purpose of encompassing its many components. The meaning is that, not having obtained an opportunity in the pre-meal time, post-meal time, and the first watch due to the multitude of the human assembly, they now obtained the opportunity only in the middle watch; or, they obtained the opportunity because one was made by the Blessed One. As to what kind of question they ask, he said: 'As it has been composed, down to a four-letter phrase.' 'As it has been composed' means in accordance with what was composed, or without transgressing it. By this, it is shown that they ask in whatever way, in accordance with their own ready wit.

Pacchābhattakālassa tīsu bhāgesu paṭhamabhāge sīhaseyyākappanaṃ ekantaṃ na hotīti āha “purebhattato paṭṭhāya nisajjāya pīḷitassa sarīrassā”ti. Teneva hi pubbe “sace ākaṅkhatī”ti tadā sīhaseyyākappanassa anibaddhatā vibhāvitā. Kilāsubhāvo kilamatho. Sarīrassa kilāsubhāvamocanatthaṃ caṅkamena vītināmeti sīhaseyyaṃ kappetīti sambandho. Buddhacakkhunāti āsayānusayaindriyaparopariyattañāṇasaṅkhātena pañcamachaṭṭhabalabhūtena buddhacakkhunā. Tena hi lokavolokanabāhullatāya taṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti vuccati, idañca pacchimayāme bhagavato bahulaṃ āciṇṇavasena vuttaṃ. Appekadā avasiṭṭhabalañāṇehi, sabbaññutaññāṇeneva ca bhagavā tamatthaṃ sādheti.

In the first of the three parts of the post-meal time, the act of lying down in the lion's posture is not absolute; therefore, the commentator said, 'of the body oppressed by sitting from the pre-meal time onwards.' Indeed, for that very reason, the non-fixed nature of adopting the lion's posture was previously made clear by the phrase 'if he wishes.' The state of fatigue (kilāsubhāvo) is weariness (kilamatho). The connection is to be made thus: to be freed from the body's state of fatigue, he passes the time by walking and adopts the lion's posture. 'With the Buddha-eye' means with the Buddha-eye which is designated as the knowledge of dispositions and latent tendencies and the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties, being the fifth and sixth powers. Indeed, because of the frequency of looking upon the world with that knowledge, it is called the 'Buddha-eye.' And this was said on account of the Blessed One's frequent practice in the last watch. Sometimes, the Blessed One accomplishes that purpose with the remaining power-knowledges, and with the knowledge of omniscience itself.

“Pacchimayāmakiccaṃ [V 1.0183] karonto aññāsī”ti pubbe vuttamatthaṃ samatthento “tasmiṃ pana divase”tiādimāha. Buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ yattha katthaci vasantānaṃ idaṃ pañcavidhaṃ kiccaṃ avijahitameva hoti sabbakālaṃ suppatiṭṭhitasatisampajaññattā, tasmā tadahepi tadavijahanabhāvadassanatthaṃ idha pañcavidhakiccapayojananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Caṅkamanti tattha caṅkamanānurūpaṭṭhānaṃ. Caṅkamamāno aññāsīti yojetabbaṃ. Pubbe vutte atthadvaye pacchimatthaññeva gahetvā “sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ārabbhā”ti vuttaṃ. Purimattho hi pakaraṇādhigatattā suviññeyyoti.

Wishing to establish the meaning previously stated as 'While performing the duty of the last watch, he knew,' the commentator said, 'On that day,' and so on. For the Blessed Buddhas, wherever they may be dwelling, this fivefold duty is never abandoned, because of their well-established mindfulness and clear comprehension at all times. Therefore, it should be understood that on that day also, the engagement with the fivefold duties here was for the purpose of showing the state of their non-abandonment. By `caṅkamaṃ` is meant a place suitable for walking there. It should be connected as 'While walking, he knew.' Of the two meanings stated previously, taking only the latter meaning, it was said, 'with reference to the knowledge of omniscience.' For the former meaning, because it is understood from the context, is easily knowable.

“Atha [M 1.0210] kho bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ imaṃ saṅkhiyadhammaṃ viditvā yena maṇḍalamāḷo, tenupasaṅkamī”ti ayaṃ sāvasesapāṭho, tasmā etaṃ viditvā, evaṃ cintetvā ca upasaṅkamīti attho veditabboti dassetuṃ “ñatvā ca panassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha assa etadahosīti assa bhagavato etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ, eso vā cetaso parivitakko ahosi, liṅgavipallāsoyaṃ “etadagga”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 1.188 ādayo) viya. Sabbaññutaññāṇakiccaṃ na sabbathā pākaṭaṃ. Nirantaranti anupubbārocanavasena nibbivaraṃ, yathābhāsitassa vā ārocanavasena nibbisesaṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ. Taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvāti taṃ yathārocitaṃ vacanaṃ imassa suttassa uppattikāraṇaṃ katvā, imassa vā suttassa desanāya uppannaṃ kāraṇaṃ katvātipi attho. Attha-saddo cettha kāraṇe, tena imassa suttassa aṭṭhuppattikaṃ nikkhepaṃ dasseti. Dvāsaṭṭhiyā ṭhānesūti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigataṭṭhānesu. Appaṭivattiyanti samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ anivattiyaṃ. Sīhanādaṃ nadantoti seṭṭhanādasaṅkhātaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadanto. Yaṃ pana lokiyā vadanti –

‘Then the Blessed One, having understood the nature of this talk of those monks, approached the assembly hall.’ This is a text with a remainder. Therefore, to show that the meaning should be known as, ‘having known this and having thought thus, he approached,’ the commentator said, ‘And having known,’ and so on. Therein, ‘to him this occurred’ means: to that Blessed One this reflection occurred, or this reflection of the mind occurred. This is a change of gender, as in ‘the foremost of these,’ and so on. The function of the knowledge of omniscience is not apparent in all respects. ‘Uninterrupted’ means without a gap, by way of sequential explanation; or, without distinction, by way of explanation according to what was taught. And this is a neuter abstract noun. ‘Having made that the occasion of arising’ means: having made that statement, which was spoken of, the cause for the arising of this sutta; or, another meaning is: having made it the cause that arose for the teaching of this sutta. And here, the word ‘attha’ is in the sense of ‘cause.’ By that, he shows the exposition of this sutta which has an occasion of arising. ‘In sixty-two instances’ means in the sixty-two grounds of views. ‘That which cannot be turned back’ means that which cannot be turned back in the world by any ascetic or brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, by a brahmā, or by anyone. ‘Uttering a lion’s roar’ means uttering a fearless roar, designated as a supreme roar. As for what the worldly grammarians say:

“Uttarasmiṃ pade byagghapuṅgavosabhakuñjarā;

Sīhasaddūlanāgādyā, pume seṭṭhatthagocarā”ti.
