‘When they are in the latter part of a compound word and in the masculine gender, the words byaggha (tiger), puṅgava (bull), usabha (bull), kuñjara (elephant); sīha (lion), saddūla (tiger), nāga (serpent/elephant), and others, have the meaning of “most excellent”.’

Taṃ yebhuyyavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadanto. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena (a. ni. 6.64; 10.21) dīpetabbo. Yathā vā kesaro migarājā sahanato, hananato, ca “sīho”ti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgatopi lokadhammānaṃ sahanato, parappavādānaṃ hananato ca “sīho”ti vuccati. Tasmā sīhassa tathāgatassa nādaṃ nadantotipi attho daṭṭhabbo. Yathā hi sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso “ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena nānāvidhadesanāvilāsasampannaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati[V 1.0184]. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sīhoti kho bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Yaṃ kho bhikkhave, tathāgato parisāya dhammaṃ deseti, idamassa hoti sīhanādasmi”nti (a. ni. 10.21). “Ime [M 1.0211] diṭṭhiṭṭhānā”tiādikā hi idha vakkhamānadesanāyeva sīhanādo. Tesaṃ “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”tiādinā vakkhamānanayena paccayākārassa samodhānampi veditabbaṃ. Sineruṃ…pe… viya cāti upamādvayena brahmajāladesanāya anaññasādhāraṇattā sudukkarataṃ dasseti. Suvaṇṇakūṭenāti suvaṇṇamayapaharaṇopakaraṇavisesena. Ratananikūṭena viya agāraṃ arahattanikūṭena brahmajālasuttantaṃ niṭṭhapento, nikūṭenāti ca niṭṭhānagatena accuggatakūṭenāti attho. Idañca arahattaphalapariyosānattā sabbaguṇānaṃ tadeva sabbesaṃ uttaritaranti vuttaṃ. Purimo pana me-saddo desanāpekkhoti parinibbutassāpi me sā desanā aparabhāge pañcavassasahassānīti attho yutto. Savanauggahaṇadhāraṇavācanādivasena paricayaṃ karonte, tathā ca paṭipanne nibbānaṃ sampāpikā bhavissatīti adhippāyo.

This should be understood as being said by way of prevalence. Or, uttering a proclamation similar to a lion's roar. This meaning should be clarified by the Sīhanādasutta. Alternatively, just as the lion, the king of beasts, is called a 'sīha' because of enduring and destroying, so too is the Tathāgata called a 'sīha' because of enduring worldly conditions and destroying the doctrines of others. Therefore, the meaning should also be understood as 'uttering the proclamation of the Tathāgata, the Lion.' For just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, is confident everywhere, with bristling of the hairs ceased, and utters a lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the Tathāgata's powers, is confident in the eight assemblies, with bristling of the hairs ceased, and utters a lion's roar endowed with the grace of manifold teachings, by the method beginning with 'these are the grounds for views.' In reference to which it was said: 'Monks, "lion" is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. When, monks, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to an assembly, this is his lion's roar.' Indeed, here the teaching about to be spoken, beginning with 'These are the grounds for views,' is itself the Lion's Roar. The combination of the causal structure by the method about to be spoken, beginning with 'Because of their feeling, craving arises,' should also be understood. And by the pair of similes 'like Sineru… etc.', it shows the extreme difficulty of the Brahmajāla teaching, because of its being not in common with others. As for `suvaṇṇakūṭena`: it means by a special striking implement made of gold. Just as one might complete a house with a jeweled peak, so he completes the Brahmajālasuttanta with the peak of Arahantship. And `nikūṭena` means a peak that has reached completion, a very high peak. And this was said because, since all virtues culminate in the fruit of Arahantship, that very fruit is the most excellent of all. Moreover, the preceding word 'me' refers to the teaching; therefore, the meaning is fitting: 'Even though I have attained Parinibbāna, that teaching of mine will last for five thousand years in a later period.' The intention is that for those who cultivate familiarity by way of listening, learning, retaining, reciting, etc., and for those who practice accordingly, it will be a conveyor to Nibbāna.

Yadaggena yenāti karaṇaniddeso, tadaggena tenā tipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etanti “yena tenā”ti etaṃ padadvayaṃ. Tatthāti hi tasmiṃ maṇḍalamāḷeti attho. Yenāti vā bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tenāti pana upayogatthe. Tasmā tatthāti taṃ maṇḍalamāḷantipi vadanti. Upasaṅkamīti ca upasaṅkamantoti attho paccuppannakālassa adhippetattā, tadupasaṅkamanassa pana atītabhāvassa sūcanato “upasaṅkamī”ti takkālāpekkhanavasena atītapayogo vutto. Evañhi “upasaṅkamitvā”ti vacanaṃ sūpapannaṃ hoti. Itarathā dvinnampi vacanānaṃ atītakālikattā tathāvattabbameva na siyā. Upasaṅkamanassa ca gamanaṃ, upagamanañcāti dvidhā attho, idha pana gamanameva. Sampattukāmatāya hi yaṃ kiñci ṭhānaṃ gacchanto taṃ taṃ padesātikkamanavasena “taṃ ṭhānaṃ upasaṅkami upasaṅkamanto”ti vattabbataṃ labhati, tenāha “tattha gato”ti, tena upagamanatthaṃ nivatteti. Yañhi ṭhānaṃ pattumicchanto gacchati, taṃ pattatāyeva “upagamana”nti vuccati. Yamettha na saṃvaṇṇitaṃ “upasaṅkamitvā”ti padaṃ, taṃ upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā gatoti upagato. Anupasaggopi hi saddo saupasaggo viya atthantaraṃ vadati saupasaggopi anupasaggo viyāti. Ato “upasaṅkamitvā”ti padassa evaṃ upagato tato āsannataraṃ bhikkhūnaṃ samīpasaṅkhātaṃ pañhaṃ vā kathetuṃ, dhammaṃ vā desetuṃ sakkuṇeyyaṭṭhānaṃ upagantvāti attho veditabbo. Apica yenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Yena kāraṇena bhagavatā so [M 1.0212] maṇḍalamāḷo upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti attho. Kāraṇaṃ pana “ime bhikkhū”tiādinā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva.

The instrumental word `yena` is a designation for `yadaggena` (by which direction); `tena` should also be understood as `tadaggena` (by that direction). `Etanti` refers to this pair of words, `yena tenā`. Indeed, `tatthā` means 'in that assembly hall.' Alternatively, `yena` is an instrumental word in the locative sense. `Tena`, however, is in the accusative sense. Therefore, they also say that `tatthā` means 'to that assembly hall.' And `upasaṅkami` (approached) has the meaning of `upasaṅkamanto` (approaching), because the present tense is intended. However, because it indicates the past nature of that approach, the past tense usage `upasaṅkami` is stated with reference to that time. For in this way, the word `upasaṅkamitvā` (having approached) is well-established. Otherwise, since both words would be in the past tense, it would not be possible to speak thus. And the meaning of `upasaṅkamana` is twofold, 'going' and 'arriving'; here, however, it is only 'going'. For one who is going to any place with the desire to arrive, by way of passing through various regions, obtains the state of being called 'he approaches, is approaching that place'. Therefore, he said `tatthagato` (gone there); by this, he excludes the meaning of 'arriving'. Indeed, when one goes wishing to reach a certain place, it is only upon having reached it that it is called 'arrival'. The word `upasaṅkamitvā` which was not commented on here, is what indicates the conclusion of the approach. Alternatively, `gato` (gone) means `upagato` (arrived). For it should be known that a word without a prefix can express a different meaning like one with a prefix, and a word with a prefix can express a different meaning like one without a prefix. Therefore, the meaning of the word `upasaṅkamitvā` should be understood thus: having arrived, and then having gone to a place nearer, known as the proximity of the monks, a place suitable for answering a question or for teaching the Dhamma. Furthermore, `yena` is an instrumental word in the sense of cause. The meaning is: for which reason that assembly hall was to be approached by the Blessed One, for that reason he approached. The reason, however, has indeed been stated in the commentary, beginning with 'these monks...'

Paññatte [V 1.0185] āsane nisīdīti ettha kenidaṃ paññattanti anuyoge sati bhikkhūhīti dassetuṃ “buddhakāle kirā”tiādimāha. Tattha buddhakāleti dharamānassa bhagavato kāle. Visesanti yathāladdhato uttari jhānamaggaphalaṃ. Athāti saṃsayatthe nipāto, yadi passatīti attho. Vitakkayamānaṃ naṃ bhikkhunti sambandho, tathā tato passanahetu dassetvā, ovaditvāti ca. Anamataggeti anādimati. Ākāsaṃ uppatitvāti ākāse uggantvā. Īdisesu hi bhummattho eva yujjatīti udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhāroti taṅkhaṇeyeva bhagavato anucchavikāsanassa dullabhattā garukammaṃ. Phalakanti nisīdanatthāya kataṃ phalaṃ. Kaṭṭhakanti nisīdanayogyaṃ phalakato aññaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ. Saṅkaḍḍhitvāti saṃharitvā. Tatthāti purāṇapaṇṇesu, kevalaṃ tesu eva nisīditumananucchavikattā tathā vuttaṃ, tatthāti vā tesu pīṭhādīsu. Evaṃ sati saṅkaḍḍhitvā paññapentīti atthavasā vibhattiṃ vipariṇāmetvā sambandho. Papphoṭetvāti yathāṭhitaṃ rajojallādi-saṃkiṇṇamananurūpanti tabbisodhanatthaṃ sañcāletvā. “Amhākaṃ īdisā kathā aññatarissā desanāya kāraṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttā, avassaṃ bhagavā āgamissatī”ti ñatvā yathānisīdanaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “idhāgato samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā tāvakālikaṃ gaṇhitvā paribhuñjatū”ti raññā ṭhapitaṃ, tena ca āgatakāle paribhuttaṃ āsanaṃ rañño nisīdanāsananti veditabbaṃ. Na hi tathā aṭṭhapitaṃ bhikkhūhi paribhuñjituṃ, bhagavato ca paññapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā tādisaṃ rañño nisīdanāsanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ kathitanti dassetuṃ “taṃ sandhāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Adhimuttiñāṇanti ca sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatārammaṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, balañāṇañca, vuttovāyamattho.

Regarding the phrase 'he sat on a prepared seat,' when the inquiry arises, 'By whom was this prepared?', to show the meaning 'it was prepared by the monks,' the Commentator said the words beginning with 'It is said that in the Buddha's time...' Therein, 'in the Buddha's time' means in the time of the Blessed One who was then living. 'Special' means the state of jhāna, path, and fruition which is superior to that which has been attained. 'Atha' is a particle in the sense of doubt; the meaning is 'if he sees.' The connection should be made thus: 'that monk who was reflecting'; and similarly: 'having shown because of that seeing, and having advised.' 'Anamatagga' means having an unknown beginning. 'Having flown up to the sky' means having ascended into the sky. Indeed, in such cases, only the locative sense is suitable; thus it is said in the Udāna Commentary. 'A burden' means a heavy task, because of the difficulty of obtaining a suitable seat for the Blessed One at that very moment. 'A plank' means a board made for the purpose of sitting. 'A piece of wood' means a block of wood, other than a plank, suitable for sitting. 'Having dragged' means having brought together. 'There' means on the old leaves; it was said thus because it was unsuitable to sit merely on them alone. Or, 'there' means on those stools, etc. This being the case, the connection should be made as 'having dragged, they prepare,' by changing the grammatical case according to the sense. 'Having shaken it out' means having moved it for the purpose of cleaning it, because as it was, being strewn with coarse dust, fine dust, etc., it was unsuitable. It was said thus with reference to the seating arrangement, having known: 'It is suitable for such a talk of ours to become the cause for some other discourse; surely the Blessed One will come.' And here, it should be understood that 'the king's sitting-seat' is a seat established by the king with the thought, 'Let a recluse or a brahmin who has come here take it for a time and use it,' and which is used by him when he comes. For it is not proper for monks to use a seat not so established, nor to prepare it for the Blessed One. Therefore, to show that such a sitting-seat of the king was spoken of in the Pāḷi, the words beginning with 'with reference to that' were said. And 'knowledge of disposition' is the omniscience and the knowledge of the powers which has as its object the various dispositions of beings. This meaning has already been stated.

“Nisajjā”ti idaṃ nisīdanapariyosānadīpananti dasseti “eva”ntiādinā. “Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ime saṅkhiyadhammaṃ viditvā”ti vuttattā jānantoyeva pucchīti ayamattho siddhoti āha “jānantoyevā”ti. Asati kathāvatthumhi tadanurūpā uparūpari vattabbā visesakathā na samūpabrūhatīti kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nu-iti pucchanatthe. Asa-saddo pavattanattheti vuttaṃ “katamāya nu…pe… bhavathā”ti. Etthāti etasmiṃ ṭhāne [M 1.0213] sandhivasena ukārassa okārādesova, na paṭhamāya pāḷiyā atthato visesoti dasseti “tassāpi purimoyeva attho”ti iminā. Purimoyevatthoti ca “katamāya nu bhavathā”ti evaṃ vutto attho.

He shows by the words beginning with 'evaṃ' that this word 'nisajjā' indicates the conclusion of the sitting. Because it was said, 'having known these enumerable qualities of those monks,' this meaning is established: 'he asked while knowing.' Therefore, the Commentator said, 'while knowing indeed.' When there is no topic of conversation, a special talk suitable to it, to be spoken in succession, does not develop. Therefore, the questioning should be understood as being for the purpose of initiating a conversation. 'Nu' is in the sense of questioning. The word 'asa' is in the sense of being; this is said in 'katamāya nu…pe… bhavathā' (By which...do you exist?). Here, in this instance, by means of sandhi, there is only the substitution of 'o' for the letter 'u'. He shows by this phrase, 'its meaning is the same as the former,' that there is no difference in meaning from the first Pāḷi text. And 'the meaning is the same as the former' is the meaning stated as 'katamāya nu bhavathā' (By which do you exist?).

“Kā ca panā”ti ettha ca-saddo byatireke “yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato”tiādīsu viya. Byatireko ca nāma pubbe vuttatthāpekkhako visesātirekattho, so ca taṃ pubbe yathāpucchitāya kathāya vakkhamānaṃ vippakatabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ byatirekatthaṃ joteti. Pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāro[V 1.0186]. Tādiso pana attho saddasatthatova suviññeyyoti katvā tadaññesameva atthaṃ dassetuṃ “antarākathāti kammaṭṭhāna…pe… kathā”tiādimāha. Kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādayo samaṇakaraṇīyabhūtāti antarāsaddena apekkhite karaṇīyavisese sambandhāpādānabhāvena vattabbe tesameva vattabbarūpattā “kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādīna”nti vuttaṃ. Yāya hi kathāya te bhikkhū sannisinnā, sā eva antarākathā vippakatā visesena puna pucchīyati, na tadaññe kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādayoti. Antarāsaddassa aññatthamāha “aññā, ekā”ti ca. Pariyāyavacanañhetaṃ padadvayaṃ. Yasmā aññatthe ayaṃ antarāsaddo “bhūmantaraṃ, samayantara”ntiādīsu viya. Tasmā “kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādīna”nti nissakkatthe sāmivacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vemajjhe vā antarāsaddo, sā pana tesaṃ vemajjhabhūtattā aññāyeva, tehi ca asammissattā visuṃ ekāyevāti adhippāyaṃ dassetuṃ “aññā, ekā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Pakārena karaṇaṃ pakato, tato vigatā, vigataṃ vā pakataṃ yassāti vippakatā, apariniṭṭhitā. Sikhanti pariyosānaṃ. Ayaṃ pana tadabhisambandhavasena uttari kathetukamyatāpucchā, taṃ sandhāyāha “nāha”ntiādi. Kathābhaṅgatthanti kathāya bhañjanatthaṃ. Atthato āpannattā sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāreti. Aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā kathā tiracchānakathā. Tiracchānabhūtāti ca tirokaraṇabhūtā, vibandhanabhūtāti attho. Ādi-saddena cettha coramahāmattasenābhayakathādikaṃ anekavihitaṃ niratthakakathaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ayaṃ kathā evāti antogadhāvadhāraṇataṃ[M 1.0214], aññatthāpohanaṃ vā sandhāya cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Athāti tassā avippakatakāleyeva. “Taṃ no”tiādinā atthato āpannamāha. Esa nayo īdisesu. Nanu ca tehi bhikkhūhi sā kathā “iti ha me”tiādinā yathādhippāyaṃ niṭṭhāpitāyevāti? Na niṭṭhāpitā bhagavato upasaṅkamanena upacchinnattā. Yadi hi bhagavā tasmiṃ khaṇe na upasaṅkameyya, bhiyyopi tappaṭibaddhāyeva tathā pavatteyyuṃ, bhagavato upasaṅkamanena pana na pavattesuṃ, tenevāha “ayaṃ no…pe… anuppatto”ti.

In the phrase, “Kā ca panā,” the particle “ca” is in the sense of distinction, similar to its use in phrases like, “yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato.” Distinction (byatireka) refers to a meaning that is special or additional with respect to what has been said before. And that particle “ca” illuminates this meaning of distinction—designated as the state of being unfinished—which is to be spoken of in relation to the talk that was previously asked about. The particle “pana” is a verbal embellishment. Furthermore, thinking, “Such a meaning is easily understood from grammar itself,” the commentator, in order to show the meaning of only the other words, said, “antarākathāti kammaṭṭhāna…pe… kathā,” and so on. Because attending to the meditation subject, recitation, questioning, and so on are duties to be done by a recluse, and because, when the specific duties referred to by the word “antarā” are to be spoken of in the sense of connection (genitive) and ablation (ablative), it is precisely these things that are of a nature to be spoken of, it is said, “of attending to the meditation subject, recitation, questioning, and so on.” For that very unfinished talk for which those monks were assembled is the “intermediate talk” that is now specifically being asked about again, not those other things such as attending to the meditation subject, recitation, and questioning. He states another meaning of the word “antarā” with “aññā, ekā” (“another,” “one”). This pair of words are synonyms. Because this word “antarā” occurs in the sense of “other,” as in “another plane of existence” (bhūmantaraṃ), “another doctrine” (samayantaraṃ), and so on. Therefore, in the phrase “of attending to the meditation subject, recitation, questioning, and so on,” the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the ablative. Alternatively, the word “antarā” means “in the middle.” And because that talk occurs in the middle of those things, it is indeed “other” (aññā); and because it is not mixed with them, it is separate and indeed “one” (ekā). To show this meaning, it is said, “aññā, ekā.” “Pakata” is making in detail (pakārena karaṇaṃ); “vippakatā” is that which is devoid of that. Or, it is “vippakatā” because for it the detailed making (pakataṃ) is gone (vigataṃ); thus, “unfinished” is obtained. “Sikhā” means conclusion. This question, however, is a question prompted by the desire to speak further in connection with that previous talk. Referring to that, the teacher said, “Not I,” and so on. “Kathābhaṅgatthaṃ” means for the purpose of breaking off the talk. Because it is implied by the meaning, he makes the invitation of an omniscient one. Because it is not conducive to release and is obstructive to the paths to heaven and liberation, such talk is called “animal talk” (tiracchānakathā). And “obstructive” (tiracchānabhūtā) means being a hindrance, being a fetter. And here, by the word “ādi” (etc.), he includes various kinds of pointless talk, such as talk about thieves, chief ministers, armies, and dangers. This was said with reference to either the implicit emphasis in “this talk alone,” or the exclusion of other meanings. “Atha” means: at the very time when that talk was not unfinished. With “Taṃ no,” etc., he states what is implied by the meaning. This is the method in such cases. But was not that talk indeed concluded by those monks according to their intention, with “iti ha me,” etc.? It was not concluded, because it was cut short by the Blessed One's arrival. For if the Blessed One had not approached at that moment, they would have continued that talk connected with that topic even further. But because of the Blessed One's arrival, they did not continue. For that very reason, he said, “This of ours…pe… has arrived.”

Idāni nidānassa, nidānavaṇṇanāya vā pariniṭṭhitabhāvaṃ dassento tassa bhagavato vacanassānukūlabhāvampi samatthetuṃ “ettāvatā”tiādimāha. Ettāvatāti hi ettakena “evaṃ me suta”ntiādivacanakkamena yaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitanti vā ettakena “tattha evanti nipātapada”ntiādivacanakkamena atthavaṇṇanā samattāti vā dvidhā attho daṭṭhabbo. “Kamala…pe… salilāyā”tiādinā pana tassa nidānassa bhagavato vacanassānukūlabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tattha kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādhurasasalilāyāti kamalasaṅkhātehi padumapuṇḍarīkasetuppalarattuppalehi [V 1.0187] ceva kuvalayasaṅkhātena nīluppalena ca ujjalavimalasādhurasasalilavatiyā. Nimmalasilātalaracanavilāsasobhitaratanasopānanti nimmalena silātalena racanāya vilāsena līlāya sobhitaratanasopānavantaṃ, nimmalasilātalena vā racanavilāsena, susaṅkhatakiriyāsobhena ca sobhitaratanasopānaṃ, vilāsasobhitasaddehi vā ativiya sobhitabhāvo vutto. Vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāganti vividhena pakiṇṇāya muttāya talasadisānaṃ vālukānaṃ cuṇṇehi paṇḍaravaṇṇabhūmibhāgavantaṃ. Suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassāti suṭṭhu vibhattāhi bhittīhi vicitrassa, vedikāhi parikkhittassa ca. Uccatarena nakkhattapathaṃ ākāsaṃ phusitukāmatāya viya, vijambhitasaddena cetassa sambandho. Vijambhitasamussayassāti vikkīḷanasamūhavantassa. Dantamayasaṇhamuduphalakakañcanalatāvinaddhamaṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhanti dantamaye ativiya siniddhaphalake kañcanamayāhi latāhi vinaddhānaṃ maṇīnaṃ gaṇappabhāsamudāyena samujjalasobhāsampannaṃ. Suvaṇṇavalayanupurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitakathitahasita- madhurassaragehajanavicaritassāti suvaṇṇamayaniyurapādakaṭakādīnaṃ [M 1.0215] aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanena janitasaddehi sammissitakathitasarahasitasarasaṅkhātena madhurassarena sampannānaṃ gehanivāsīnaṃ naranārīnaṃ vicaritaṭṭhānabhūtassa. Uḷārissariyavibhavasobhitassāti uḷāratāsampannajanaissariyasampannajanavibhavasampannajanehi, tannivāsīnaṃ vā naranārīnaṃ uttamādhipaccabhogehi sobhitassa. Suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāpavāḷādijutivissaravijjotitasuppatiṭṭhitavisāla dvārabāhanti suvaṇṇarajatanānāmaṇimuttāpavāḷādīnaṃ jutīhi pabhassaravijjotitasuppatiṭṭhitavitthatadvārabāhaṃ.

Now, wishing to show the state of completion of the introduction, or of the commentary on the introduction, and also to establish its conformity with the word of that Blessed One, the compiler said the words beginning with “ettāvatā.” Indeed, the meaning of “ettāvatā” should be understood in two ways: either, “by this much,” that is, by the sequence of words beginning with “evaṃ me sutaṃ,” the introduction was spoken; or, “by this much,” that is, by the sequence of words beginning with “tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ,” the explanation of the meaning is completed. Furthermore, with the words beginning “kamala…pe… salilāyā,” he shows the conformity of that introduction with the word of the Blessed One. Therein, “kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādhurasasalilāyā” means: possessing water that is bright, stainless, and of sweet taste, with lotuses known as paduma, puṇḍarīka, white lotuses, and red lotuses, and with the blue water lily known as kuvalaya. “Nimmalasilātalaracanavilāsasobhitaratanasopānaṃ” means: possessing a jeweled staircase made splendid by a flawless stone floor, by its arrangement, and by its playful elegance; or, a jeweled staircase made beautiful by a flawless stone floor, by its elegant arrangement, and by the beauty of its fine workmanship; or, by the words “vilāsa” and “sobhita,” a state of extreme splendor is expressed. “Vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāgaṃ” means: possessing a ground-portion of white color from the powder of sand resembling the surface of variously scattered pearls. “Suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassa” means: of that which is enclosed by well-divided walls and variegated railings. “Uccatarena nakkhattapathaṃ ākāsaṃ phusitukāmatāya viya,” means: as if with a desire to touch the sky, the path of the constellations, by its great height; and the connection of this phrase is with the word “vijambhita.” “Vijambhitasamussayassa” means: of that which possesses an assemblage of playful elegance. “Dantamayasaṇhamuduphalakakañcanalatāvinaddhamaṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhaṃ” means: endowed with a radiant splendor from the collective glow of a multitude of gems interwoven with golden vines on an exceedingly smooth ivory plank. “Suvaṇṇavalayanupurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitakathitahasita- madhurassaragehajanavicaritassa” means: of that which has become a place frequented by the men and women dwelling in the house, who are endowed with sweet voices, characterized by the sounds of speech and laughter well-mingled with the sounds produced by the striking of golden bracelets, anklets, and so on, against one another. “Uḷārissariyavibhavasobhitassāti” means: of that which is adorned by people endowed with nobility, people endowed with sovereignty, and people endowed with wealth; or, adorned by the supreme dominion and enjoyments of the men and women dwelling there. “Suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāpavāḷādijutivissaravijjotitasuppatiṭṭhitavisāla dvārabāhaṃ” means: possessing wide door-posts, well-established and brilliantly illuminated by the spreading radiance of gold, silver, various gems, pearls, coral, and so on.

Tividhasīlādidassanavasena buddhassa guṇānubhāvaṃ sammā sūcetīti buddhaguṇānubhāvasaṃsūcakaṃ, tassa. Kālo ca deso ca desako ca vatthu ca parisā ca, tāsaṃ apadesena nidassanena paṭimaṇḍitaṃ tathā.

Because it properly indicates the majestic power of the Buddha’s virtues by way of showing the threefold virtue and so on, it is called ‘that which indicates the majestic power of the Buddha’s virtues.’ Of that Sutta. The time, the place, the speaker, the subject matter, and the assembly; it is adorned by reference to them, by their indication, thus.

Kimatthaṃ panettha dhammavinayasaṅgahe kariyamāne nidānavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu bhagavatā bhāsitavacanasseva saṅgaho kātabboti? Vuccate – desanāya ṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakavatthuparisāpadesehi upanibandhitvā ṭhapitā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā hoti, asammosadhammā, saddheyyā ca desakālavatthuhetunimittehi upanibandho viya vohāravinicchayo, teneva cāyasmatā mahākassapena “brahmajālaṃ āvuso ānanda kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 439) desādipucchāsu katāsu tāsaṃ vissajjanaṃ [V 1.0188] karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena āyasmatā ānandattherena nidānaṃ bhāsitanti tadevidhāpi vuttaṃ “kāladesadesakavatthuparisāpadesapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nidāna”nti.

For what reason was the introductory passage spoken here when the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya was being made? Should not a compilation be made only of the words spoken by the Blessed One? It is said: For the purpose of accomplishing for the teaching the state of being long-standing, free from confusion, and trustworthy. For a teaching that is established, having been bound together with references to time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly, becomes long-lasting, its principles are not forgotten, and it is trustworthy; just as a legal decision is bound by the causal signs of place, time, and subject matter. And for that very reason, when questions about the place and so on were asked by the venerable Mahākassapa with the words beginning, “Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken?”, the introduction was spoken by the venerable Elder Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma, as he was giving the answers to them. That same introduction is spoken of here also as “the introduction adorned with reference to time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly.”

Apica satthusampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubba-racanā-numānāgama-takkābhāvato sammāsambuddhattasiddhi. Sammāsambuddhabhāvena hissa puretaraṃ racanāya, “evampi nāma bhaveyyā”ti anumānassa, āgamantaraṃ nissāya parivitakkassa ca abhāvo sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya ekappamāṇattā ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasāsanasāvakānurodhabhāvato khīṇāsavattasiddhi. Khīṇāsavatāya hi ācariyamuṭṭhiādīnamabhāvo, visuddhā ca parānuggahappavatti. Iti desakasaṃkilesabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhisīlasampattidūsakānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ abhāvasaṃsūcakehi[M 1.0216], ñāṇappahānasampadābhibyañjanakehi ca sambuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi. Tatoyeva ca antarāyikaniyyānikesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo, attahitaparahitapaṭipatti ca nidānavacanena pakāsitā hoti sampattaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato, “jānatā passatā”tiādivacanato ca, tena vuttaṃ “satthusampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Furthermore, the introductory passage is for the purpose of proclaiming the Teacher's accomplishment. Indeed, for the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the accomplishment of perfect self-enlightenment is due to the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, and reasoning. Indeed, due to his state as a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, for him there is an absence of prior composition, of inference such as “It might be thus,” and of pondering based on another tradition. This is because of the functioning of his unimpeded knowledge everywhere among all knowable things, and because of his having a single standard of knowledge. Likewise, the accomplishment of the destruction of the taints is due to the absence of a teacher's closed fist, of stinginess regarding the Dhamma, of needing an instructor, and of compliance with disciples. Indeed, because of the destruction of the taints, there is the absence of the teacher's closed fist and so on, and his practice of benefiting others is pure. Thus, the accomplishment of the first two kinds of confidence is due to the states of a Buddha and his purity, which indicate the absence of ignorance and craving—things that are defilements for a teacher and corrupt the accomplishment of view and virtue—and which manifest the perfection of knowledge and relinquishment. And from that very reason, due to the established absence of delusion regarding obstructive and liberating things, the accomplishment of the latter two kinds of confidence occurs. Thus, the Blessed One is endowed with the four kinds of confidence. And the practice for one's own welfare and the welfare of others is revealed by the introductory passage, because of the illumination of the Dhamma-teaching through spontaneous wisdom arising in accordance with the disposition of the assembled audience, and because of the words such as “knowing, seeing.” Therefore it was said, “The introductory passage is for the purpose of proclaiming the Teacher's accomplishment.”

Apica sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa hi bhagavato natthi niratthikā pavatti, attahitatthā vā, tasmā paresaṃyeva hitāya pavattasabbakiriyassa sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ yathāpavattaṃ vuccamānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsanaṃ, na kabbaracanā. Tayidaṃ satthu caritaṃ kāladesadesakavatthuparisāpadesehi saddhiṃ tattha tattha nidānavacanehi yathāsambhavaṃ pakāsīyati. Atha vā satthuno pamāṇabhāvappakāsanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvappakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ, tañcassa pamāṇabhāvadassanaṃ “bhagavā”ti iminā tathāgatassa guṇavisiṭṭhasabbasattuttamabhāvadīpanena ceva “jānatā passatā”tiādinā āsayānusayañāṇādipayogadīpanena ca vibhāvitaṃ hoti, idamettha nidānavacanapayojanassa mukhamattanidassanaṃ. Ko hi samattho buddhānubuddhena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena bhāsitassa nidānassa payojanāni niravasesato vibhāvitunti. Honti cettha –

Furthermore, the introductory discourse is for the purpose of proclaiming the perfection of the Dispensation. Indeed, for the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by knowledge and compassion, there is no occurrence that is without purpose, nor for his own welfare. Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, which occur solely for the welfare of others, when spoken of as they occurred, constitute the Dispensation in the sense of instructing beings according to their capacity with benefits related to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—it is not a poetic composition. This conduct of the Teacher is made clear, as is suitable, in the respective suttas by the introductory words, along with indications of the time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly. Alternatively, the introductory discourse is for the purpose of showing the authoritativeness of the Dispensation by showing the authoritativeness of the Teacher. And this demonstration of its authoritativeness is made clear both by this term 'Bhagavā,' which shows the Tathāgata's state of being the highest of all beings through his distinct qualities, and by such phrases as 'knowing, seeing,' which show the application of his knowledge of dispositions, latent tendencies, and so forth. This here is but a glimpse of the purpose of the introductory discourse. For who is able to explain without remainder the purposes of the introduction spoken by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who understood in accordance with the Buddha? And in this regard, there are these summary verses:

“Desanāciraṭṭhitatthaṃ, asammosāya bhāsitaṃ;

Saddhāya cāpi nidānaṃ, vedehena yasassinā.

For the long endurance of the teaching, for non-bewilderment, and also for the purpose of faith, the introduction was spoken by the illustrious son of the Videhan queen.

Satthusampattiyā [V 1.0189] ceva, sāsanasampadāya ca;

Tassa pamāṇabhāvassa, dassanatthampi bhāsita”nti.

And for the perfection of the Teacher, and for the perfection of the Dispensation, and also for the purpose of showing its authoritativeness, it was spoken.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya paramasukhumagambhīraduranubodhatthaparidīpanāya suvimalavipulapaññāveyyattiyajananāya ajjavamaddavasoraccasaddhāsatidhitibuddhikhantivīriyādidhammasamaṅginā sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye asaṅgāsaṃhīravisāradañāṇacārinā anekappabhedasakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhinā mahāgaṇinā mahāveyyākaraṇena ñāṇābhivaṃsadhammasenāpatināmatherena [M 1.0217] mahādhammarājādhirājagarunā katāya sādhuvilāsiniyā nāma līnatthapakāsaniyā abbhantaranidānavaṇṇanāya līnatthapakāsanā.

Thus ends the Illumination of the Hidden Meaning of the Explanation of the Internal Introduction, in the Līnatthapakāsanī named Sādhuvilāsinī—a sub-commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, which illuminates the supreme, subtle, profound, and hard-to-penetrate meaning and generates skill in very pure and vast wisdom—composed by the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, the teacher of the great king of kings who upholds the Dhamma, a great leader of the community, a great grammarian, who is endowed with such qualities as straightforwardness, gentleness, affability, faith, mindfulness, firmness, wisdom, patience, and energy; whose knowledge moves without attachment, without hesitation, and with confidence in the Three Piṭakas with their commentaries; and who has penetrated with knowledge the thickets of his own school and other schools, which have numerous divisions.

Nidānavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the introduction is concluded.

5. Evaṃ abbhantaranidānasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni yathānikkhittassa suttassa saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karonto anupubbāvirodhinī saṃvaṇṇanā kamānatikkamanena byākuladosappahāyinī, viññūnañca cittārādhinī, āgatabhāro ca avassaṃ āvahitabboti saṃvaṇṇakassa sampattabhārāvahanena paṇḍitācārasamatikkamābhāvavibhāvinī, tasmā tadāvikaraṇasādhakaṃ saṃvaṇṇanokāsavicāraṇaṃ kātumāha “idānī”tiādi. Nikkhittassāti desitassa, “desanā nikkhepo”ti hi etaṃ atthato bhinnampi sarūpato ekameva, desanāpi hi desetabbassa sīlādiatthassa veneyyasantānesu nikkhipanato “nikkhepo”ti vuccati. Nanu suttameva saṃvaṇṇīyatīti āha “sā panesā”tiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā saṃvaṇṇanā “ayaṃ desanā evaṃsamuṭṭhānā”ti suttassa sammadeva nidānaparijjhānena tabbaṇṇanāya suviññeyyattā pākaṭā hoti, tasmā tadeva sādhāraṇato paṭhamaṃ vicārayissāmāti. Yā hi sā kathā suttatthasaṃvaṇṇanāpākaṭakārinī, sā sabbāpi saṃvaṇṇakena vattabbā. Tadatthavijānanupāyattā ca sā pariyāyena saṃvaṇṇanāyevāti. Idha pana tasmiṃ vicārite yassā aṭṭhuppattiyā idaṃ suttaṃ nikkhittaṃ, tassā vibhāgavasena “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.5), “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.7), “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.28) ca vuttānaṃ suttapadesānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā vuccamānā taṃtaṃanusandhidassanasukhatāya suviññeyyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha yathā anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttantāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādisāsanapaṭṭhānanayena soḷasavidhabhāvaṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ attajjhāsayādi-sutta-nikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvanti āha “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti. Nanu saṃsaggabhedopi [V 1.0190] sambhavati, atha kasmā “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti vuttanti? Saṃsaggabhedassa sabbattha alabbhamānattā. Attajjhāsayassa, hi aṭṭhuppattiyā ca parajjhāsayapucchāvasikehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati. “Attajjhāsayo [M 1.0218] ca parajjhāsayo ca, attajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, attajjhāsayo ca parajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca aṭṭhuppattiko ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko cā”ti ajjhāsayapucchānusandhisabbhāvato. Attajjhāsayaṭṭhuppattīnaṃ pana aññamaññaṃ saṃsaggo natthi, tasmā niravasesaṃ patthāranayena saṃsaggabhedassa alabbhanato evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

5. Having thus made the explanation of the internal introduction, the author now wishes to explain the sutta as it was laid down. A commentary should be sequentially consistent; by not transgressing the order, it dispels the fault of confusion and delights the minds of the wise. And the burden that has arrived must certainly be borne; thus, by the commentator's bearing of this burden, it makes clear the non-transgression of the conduct of the wise. Therefore, to accomplish the clarification of that matter, he says 'idāni,' etc., in order to undertake the investigation of the opportunity for the commentary. 'Laid down' means 'taught.' For 'teaching' and 'laying down,' though different in meaning, are one in form. Indeed, a teaching is also called a 'laying down' because it places the meaning to be taught, such as virtue, in the mental continuums of those to be trained. In response to the objection, 'Is it not the sutta itself that is being explained?' he says, 'sā panesā,' etc. This is what is meant: The commentary that is spoken after investigating the laying down of the sutta—'This teaching arose in this way'—becomes clear through correctly discerning the origin of the sutta, making its explanation easy to understand. Therefore, the meaning is, 'We will first investigate that very thing in a general way.' For whatever discourse makes the explanation of the sutta's meaning clear, all of that must be stated by the commentator. And because it is a means for knowing that meaning, it is, figuratively, the commentary itself. Here, however, when that is investigated, the explanation of the sutta passages spoken by way of classifying the occasion for which this sutta was laid down—such as 'mamaṃ vā bhikkhave,' etc., 'appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ,' etc., and 'atthi bhikkhave,' etc.—when it is being given, should be understood as easy to understand because of the ease of seeing the respective connections. Therein, just as the suttas, though having many hundreds and thousands of divisions, do not go beyond the sixteen-fold state by way of the stages of the teaching, such as the part pertaining to defilements, so too, they do not go beyond the four-fold state by way of the laying down of suttas, such as based on one's own inclination. Therefore, he said, 'There are four ways of laying down a sutta.' To the objection, 'Is it not that a division by combination is also possible? Then why was "four ways of laying down a sutta" said?' The answer is: Because a division by combination is not found everywhere. Indeed, for one's own inclination and for an occasion that has arisen, a division by combination with those based on another's inclination and a question is possible. The combinations are: one's own inclination and another's inclination; one's own inclination and a question-based one; one's own inclination, another's inclination, and a question-based one; an occasion-based one and another's inclination; an occasion-based one and a question-based one; and an occasion-based one, another's inclination, and a question-based one. This is possible due to the existence of a connection between inclination and question. However, there is no mutual combination of one's own inclination and an occasion that has arisen. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said thus because a division by combination is not found without remainder when set out in detail.

Atha vā aṭṭhuppattiyā attajjhāsayenapi siyā saṃsaggabhedo, tadantogadhattā pana saṃsaggavasena vuttānaṃ sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepeyeva sandhāya “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana atthavikappe yathārahaṃ ekakadukatikacatukavasena sāsanapaṭṭhānanayena suttanikkhepā vattabbāti nayamattaṃ dassetīti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – nikkhipanaṃ kathanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Nikkhipīyatīti vā nikkhepo, suttameva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi kāraṇavasenāti attajjhāsayo, attano ajjhāsayo vā etassa yathāvuttanayenāti attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayepi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vaso pucchāvaso, so etassa atthi yathāvuttanayenāti pucchāvasiko. Araṇīyato avagantabbato attho vuccati suttadesanāya vatthu, tassa uppatti atthuppatti, sā eva aṭṭhuppatti ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā, sā etassa atthi vuttanayenāti aṭṭhuppattiko. Apica nikkhipīyati suttametenāti nikkhepo, attajjhāsayādisuttadesanākāraṇameva. Etasmiṃ pana atthavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo. Paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo. Pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitabbo attho. Tassā pucchāya vasena pavattaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasikaṃ. Tadeva nikkhepasaddāpekkhāya pulliṅgavasena vuttaṃ “pucchāvasiko”ti. Vuttanayena aṭṭhuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppattikoti evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, the division of association could be together with the exposition due to an occasion arising and the exposition due to one's own inclination. However, because the remaining expositions spoken of by way of association are included within those, it is said, “four expositions of the suttas,” with reference only to the root expositions. In this alternative meaning, however, it should be known that the Commentator shows merely the method, stating that the expositions of the suttas should be spoken of according to what is appropriate by way of single, double, triple, and quadruple, following the method of establishing the Dispensation. Therein, this is the word-meaning: `nikkhipanaṃ`, 'placing down,' is `kathanaṃ`, 'stating'; this is `nikkhepo`, 'exposition.' The exposition of a sutta (`suttassa nikkhepo`) is `suttanikkhepo`; the meaning is 'the teaching of a sutta' (`suttadesanā`). Alternatively, it is expounded (`nikkhipīyati`), therefore it is an exposition (`nikkhepo`); the sutta itself is the exposition, `suttanikkhepo`. One's own inclination (`attano ajjhāsayo`) is `attajjhāsayo`; that exists for this (exposition) as a cause, therefore it is `attajjhāsayo`; alternatively, one's own inclination exists for this in the aforesaid manner, therefore it is `attajjhāsayo`. This same method applies also to `parajjhāsaya`. Dependence on a question (`pucchāya vaso`) is `pucchāvaso`; that exists for this in the aforesaid manner, therefore it is `pucchāvasiko`. The basis for the teaching of a sutta is called the meaning (`attho`) because it is to be practiced (`araṇīyato`) and understood (`avagantabbato`); the arising (`uppatti`) of that (basis) is `atthuppatti`; that itself, by changing the `ttha`-character to a `ṭṭha`-character, becomes `aṭṭhuppatti`; that exists for this in the aforesaid manner, therefore it is `aṭṭhuppattiko`. Moreover, the sutta is expounded by means of this, therefore it is an exposition (`nikkhepo`); it is just the cause for the teaching of a sutta, such as one's own inclination, etc. However, in this alternative meaning: one's own inclination is `attajjhāsayo`. The inclination of others is `parajjhāsayo`. It is asked (`pucchīyati`), therefore it is a question (`pucchā`); the meaning is 'what is to be asked.' The speech to the receivers of the Dhamma, which proceeds by way of that question, is `pucchāvasikaṃ`. That very word, with reference to the word `nikkhepa`, is stated in the masculine gender as `pucchāvasiko`. In the aforesaid manner, `aṭṭhuppatti` itself is `aṭṭhuppattiko`. Thus the meaning should be understood.

Ettha ca paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇaṃ nirapekkhitvā attano ajjhāsayeneva dhammatantiṭhapanatthaṃ pavattitadesanattā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ nikkhepabhāvo yutto. Teneva vakkhati “attano ajjhāsayeneva [M 1.0219] kathetī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.5). Parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ desanānimittabhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattattā kathaṃ aṭṭhuppattike anavarodho siyā, pucchāvasikaṭṭhuppattikānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattitadesanattā kathaṃ parajjhāsaye [V 1.0191] anavarodho siyāti na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinimuttasseva suttadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattivasena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi dhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 1.29) āmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ “aṭṭhuppattī”ti vuccati. Paresaṃ pucchaṃ vinā ajjhāsayameva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo. Pucchāvasena desito pucchāvasikoti pākaṭovāyamattho.

And here, because the teaching is given for the sake of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma by one's own inclination alone, without regard for the cause such as the ripening of others' faculties, it is proper for `attajjhāsaya` to be a separate exposition. For that very reason, it will be said, 'He speaks by his own inclination alone.' However, this objection should not be raised: 'Since `parajjhāsaya` and `pucchāvasika` proceed upon the arising of others' inclinations and questions, which are the occasion for the teaching, how are they not included in `aṭṭhuppattika`? Or, since `pucchāvasika` and `aṭṭhuppattika` are teachings given in accordance with others' inclinations, how are they not included in `parajjhāsaya`?' For, since the arising of a cause for teaching a sutta that is free from others' urging, questioning, and so forth, is taken as being by way of `aṭṭhuppatti`, the taking of `parajjhāsaya` and `pucchāvasika` is separate. Thus, for the Dhammadāyāda Sutta and others, the occasion for the teaching, such as the arising of material gain, is called `aṭṭhuppatti`. A teaching given having made only the inclination of others the occasion, without their question, is `parajjhāsayo`. A teaching given by way of a question is `pucchāvasiko`. Thus this meaning is indeed clear.

Anajjhiṭṭhoti pucchādinā anajjhesito ayācito, attano ajjhāsayeneva katheti dhammatantiṭhapanatthanti adhippāyo. Hāroti āvaḷi yathā “muttāhāro”ti, sveva hārako, sammappadhānasuttantānaṃ hārako tathā. Anupubbena hi saṃyuttake niddiṭṭhānaṃ sammappadhānapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ suttantānaṃ āvaḷi “sammappadhānasuttantahārako”ti vuccati, tathā iddhipādahārakādi. Iddhipādaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgasuttantahārakoti pubbapadesu parapadalopo, dvandagabbhasamāso vā eso, peyyālaniddeso vā. Tesanti yathāvuttasuttānaṃ.

`Anajjhiṭṭho` means not prompted or requested by a question and so on; the intention is that he speaks by his own inclination alone for the sake of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma. `Hāro` means a series, as in `muttāhāro` (a pearl necklace); that itself is `hārako`. Likewise, it is the `hārako` (series) of the Sammappadhāna Suttantas. For the series of suttantas connected with the Right Exertions, which are pointed out in sequence in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, is called `sammappadhānasuttantahārako`; likewise, `iddhipādahāraka`, etc. In `Iddhipādaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgasuttantahārako`, there is elision of the latter word in the preceding terms; or this is a compound with a hidden dvanda; or it is an abbreviated reference. `Tesaṃ` means 'of the aforesaid suttas'.

Paripakkāti pariṇatā. Vimuttiparipācanīyāti arahattaphalaṃ paripācentā saddhindriyādayo dhammā. Khayeti khayanatthaṃ, khayakāraṇabhūtāya vā dhammadesanāya. Ajjhāsayanti adhimuttiṃ. Khantinti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiṃ. Mananti cittaṃ. Abhinīhāranti paṇidhānaṃ. Bujjhanabhāvanti bujjhanasabhāvaṃ, bujjhanākāraṃ vā. Avekkhitvāti paccavekkhitvā, apekkhitvā vā.

`Paripakkā` means ripened. `Vimuttiparipācanīyā` means the dhammas, such as the faith faculty and so on, that bring the fruit of Arahantship to maturity. `Khaye` means for the purpose of destruction, or for the teaching of the Dhamma which is the cause of destruction. `Ajjhāsayaṃ` means resolve. `Khantiṃ` means the tolerance for contemplation by insight. `Manaṃ` means mind. `Abhinīhāraṃ` means aspiration. `Bujjhanabhāvaṃ` means the nature of awakening, or the mode of awakening. `Avekkhitvā` means having reflected, or having regarded.

Cattāro vaṇṇāti cattāri kulāni, cattāro vā rūpādipamāṇā sattā. Mahārājānoti cattāro mahārājāno devā. Vuccanti kiṃ, pañcupādānakkhandhā kinti attho.

`Cattāro vaṇṇā` means the four families, or the four kinds of beings whose measure is form and so on. `Mahārājāno` means the four Great King devas. The meaning is: What are called? What are the five aggregates of clinging?

Kasmāti āha “aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ hī”tiādi. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇeti nimitte bhummaṃ, vaṇṇasaddena cettha “acchariyaṃ āvuso”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.4) bhikkhusaṅghena vuttopi vaṇṇo saṅgahito. Tampi hi aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā “atthi bhikkhave aññe [M 1.0220] dhammā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.28) upari desanaṃ ārabhissati. Tadeva vivarati “ācariyo”tiādinā. “Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”nti imissā desanāya brahmadattena vuttaṃ vaṇṇaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā desitattā āha “antevāsī vaṇṇa”nti. Idāni pāḷiyā sambandhaṃ dassetuṃ “itī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Desanākusaloti “imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā ayaṃ desanā sambhavatī”ti desanāya kusalo, etena pakaraṇānuguṇaṃ bhagavato thomanamakāsi. Esā hi saṃvaṇṇanakānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ tattha tattha pakaraṇādhigataguṇena bhagavato thomanā. Vā-saddo cettha upamānasamuccayasaṃsayavacanavossaggapadapūraṇasadisavikappādīsu [V 1.0192] bahūsvatthesu dissati. Tathā hesa “paṇḍitovāpi tena so”tiādīsu upamāne dissati, sadisabhāveti attho. “Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muniṃ pavedayantī”tiādīsu (su. ni.213) samuccaye. “Ke vā ime kassa vā”tiādīsu (pārā. 296) saṃsaye. “Ayaṃ vā (ayañca) (dī. ni. 1.181) imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.181) vacanavossagge. “Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.154) padapūraṇe. “Madhuṃ vā maññati bālo, yāva pāpaṃ na paccatī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 69) sadise. “Ye hi keci bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.170; saṃ. ni. 5.1092) vikappe. Idhāpi vikappeyeva. Mama vā dhammassa vā saṅghassa vāti vividhā visuṃ vikappanassa jotakattāti āha “vā-saddo vikappanattho”ti. Para-saddo pana attheva aññattho “ahañceva kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.64; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; mahāva. 7, 8) atthi adhikattho “indriyaparopariyatta”ntiādīsu (vibha. 814; a. ni. 10.21; ma. ni. 1.148; paṭi. ma. 1.68; 1.111) atthi pacchābhāgattho “parato āgamissatī”tiādīsu. Atthi paccanīkattho “uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.168; saṃ. ni. 5.822; a. ni. 8.70; udā. 51) idhāpi paccanīkatthoti dasseti “paṭiviruddhā sattā”ti iminā. Sāsanassa paccanīkabhūtā paccatthikā sattāti attho. Ta-saddo pareti vuttamatthaṃ avaṇṇabhāsanakiriyāvisiṭṭhaṃ parāmasatīti vuttaṃ “ye avaṇṇaṃ vadanti, tesū”ti.

Why? The Commentator says, “Because in the occasion of arising,” and so on. In `vaṇṇāvaṇṇe`, the locative case is used in the sense of a sign. And here, by the word `vaṇṇa`, the praise spoken by the community of monks, beginning with “Wonderful, friend,” is also included. For, having made that an occasion of arising, the Blessed One will begin the teaching further on with, “There are, monks, other states,” and so on. He explains that very point with 'the teacher,' and so on. Because this teaching, “Monks, if others were to speak praise of me,” was taught by making the praise spoken by Brahmadatta the occasion of its arising, the Commentator says, “the disciple’s praise.” Now, to show the connection with the Pāḷi, “thus,” and so on, was said. 'Skilled in teaching' means: he is skilled in teaching in that “this teaching arises from this occasion of arising.” By this, he offered praise to the Blessed One that was in accordance with the treatise. For this is the nature of commentators: namely, to praise the Blessed One here and there with a quality obtained from the treatise. And here the particle `vā` is seen in many senses, such as: comparison, conjunction, doubt, relinquishment of speech, expletive, similarity, and alternative. For so it is seen in the sense of comparison in phrases such as “he is like a wise person,” the meaning being a state of similarity. In the sense of conjunction, in phrases such as “the wise make known that sage also.” In the sense of doubt, in phrases such as “Who are these, or whose?” In the sense of relinquishment of speech, in phrases such as “As for this one, among these ascetics and brahmins, he is the most foolish, the most deluded.” In the sense of an expletive, in phrases such as “This boy did not know moderation.” In the sense of similarity, in phrases such as “A fool considers evil to be like honey, so long as the evil has not ripened.” In the sense of alternative, in phrases such as “Whatever ascetics or brahmins.” Here too, it is precisely in the sense of alternative. Because it illuminates the distinct and various alternatives—“of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Sangha”—the Commentator says, “the particle `vā` has the sense of alternative.” The word `para`, however, does exist with the meaning 'other', as in “If I alone were to teach the Dhamma, and others were not to understand my teaching.” It has the sense of 'superiority' in “mastery over the faculties,” and so on. It has the sense of 'subsequent' in “it will come later,” and so on. It has the sense of 'opposition' in “having refuted an arisen opposing doctrine with what is in accordance with the Dhamma,” and so on. Here too, that it has the sense of opposition is shown by the Commentator with the phrase “opposing beings.” The meaning is: beings who have become opposed to the Dispensation are adversaries. The word `ta` refers to the meaning stated by `pare`, a meaning qualified by the action of speaking dispraise. This is why it was said, “among those who speak dispraise.”

Nanu [M 1.0221] tesaṃ āghāto natthi guṇamahattattā, atha kasmā evaṃ vuttanti codanālesaṃ dassetvā tadapaneti “kiñcāpī”tiādinā. Kiñcāpi natthi, atha kho tathāpīti attho. Īdisesupīti ettha pi-saddo sambhāvanattho, tena ratanattayanimittampi akusalacittaṃ na uppādetabbaṃ, pageva vaṭṭāmisalokāmisanimittanti sambhāveti. Pariyattidhammoyeva saddhammanayanaṭṭhena nettīti dhammanetti. Āhanatīti ābhuso ghaṭṭeti, hiṃsati vā, vibādhati, upatāpeti cāti attho. Katthaci “etthā”ti pāṭho dissati, so pacchālikhito porāṇapāṭhānugatāya ṭīkāya virodhattā, atthayuttiyā ca abhāvato. Yadipi domanassādayo ca āhananti, kopeyeva panāyaṃ niruḷhoti dasseti “kopassetaṃ adhivacana”nti iminā. Avayavatthañhi dassetvā tattha pariyāyena atthaṃ dassento evamāha. Adhivacananti ca adhikicca pavattaṃ vacanaṃ, pasiddhaṃ vā vacanaṃ, nāmanti attho. Evamitaresupi. Ettha ca sabhāvadhammato aññassa kattuabhāvajotanatthaṃ “āhanatī”ti [V 1.0193] kattutthe āghātasaddaṃ dasseti. Āhanati etena, āhananamattaṃ vā āghātoti karaṇabhāvatthāpi sambhavantiyeva. “Appatītā”ti etassattho “atuṭṭhā asomanassikā”ti vutto, idaṃ pana pākaṭapariyāyena apaccayasaddassa nibbacanadassanaṃ, tammukhena pana na pacceti tenāti appaccayoti kātabbaṃ. Abhirādhayatīti sādhayati. Etthāti etesu tīsu padesu. Dvīhīti āghātaanabhiraddhipadehi. Ekenāti apaccayapadena. Ettakesu gahitesu taṃsampayuttā aggahitā siyuṃ, na ca sakkā tepi aggahituṃ ekuppādādisabhāvattāti codanaṃ visodhetuṃ “tesa”ntiādi vuttaṃ, tesanti yathāvuttānaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhavedanākkhandhekadesānaṃ. Sesānanti saññāviññāṇāvasiṭṭhasaṅkhārakkhandhekadesānaṃ. Karaṇanti uppādanaṃ. Āghātādīnañhi pavattiyā paccayasamavāyanaṃ idha “karaṇa”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana atthato uppādanameva. Tadanuppādanañhi sandhāya pāḷiyaṃ “na karaṇīyā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭikkhittameva yathārahaṃ ekuppādanirodhārammaṇavatthubhāvato.

Is it not that for them there is no resentment, due to the greatness of their virtues? Then why is it said thus? — showing a trace of an objection and then dispelling it with 'kiñcāpi' and so on. Even if there is none, the meaning is 'yet still.' Here, in īdisesupi, the particle pi has the meaning of esteem, implying that an unwholesome thought should not be produced even with the Triple Gem as the cause; how much more so with the allure of the round of rebirth and the allure of the world as the cause. The Dhamma of the scriptures itself, because of the meaning of leading to the good Dhamma, is netti, hence dhammanetti. Āhanati means it strikes intensely, or it harms, it oppresses, and it torments. In some places, the reading etthā is seen; that was written later, because it conflicts with the subcommentary that follows the ancient reading and because it lacks logical consistency. Although displeasure and the like also strike, this term āghāta is established in the sense of anger itself, as is shown by 'this is a designation for anger.' For, after showing the meaning of the component parts, he thus shows the meaning by way of a synonym. And adhivacana means a word that has arisen with reference to something, or a well-known word; the meaning is 'a name.' So too in other cases. And here, to show the absence of an agent other than the intrinsic phenomenon, he shows the word āghāta in the agentive sense with āhanati. 'One strikes with this,' or 'the mere striking' is āghāta; thus, the instrumental and abstract noun senses are also possible. The meaning of appatītā is stated as 'displeased, unhappy.' This, however, is the showing of the analysis of the word apaccaya by way of a manifest synonym; but by means of that, the analysis 'one is not pleased by that, hence apaccayo' should be made. Abhirādhayati means 'accomplishes.' Ettha means 'in these three terms.' 'By two' means by the terms āghāta and anabhiraddhi. 'By one' means by the term apaccaya. To clarify the objection that 'when this many are taken, their associated factors might not be taken, and yet it is not possible not to take them, because they have the nature of co-arising, etc.,' tesaṃ and so on are stated. Tesaṃ refers to portions of the aggregate of formations and the aggregate of feelings as previously stated. Sesānaṃ refers to the perception and consciousness aggregates, and to the remaining portions of the formation aggregate. Karaṇa means 'production.' For here, the assemblage of conditions for the occurrence of resentment and the like is called karaṇa, but in essence, it is production itself. For, referring to the non-production of that, it is stated in the Pāḷi as na karaṇīyā. It is entirely rejected, as appropriate, due to having the nature of co-arising, co-cessation, common object, and common basis.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ manopadose. “Tesu avaṇṇabhāsakesū”ti iminā ādhāratthe bhummaṃ dasseti. Nimittatthe, bhāvalakkhaṇe vā etaṃ bhummanti āha “tasmiṃ vā avaṇṇe”ti. Na hi aguṇo, nindā vā kopadomanassānaṃ ādhāro sambhavati tabbhāsakāyattattā tesaṃ. Assathāti [M 1.0222] sattamiyā rūpaṃ ce-saddayogena parikappanavisayattāti dasseti “bhaveyyāthā”ti iminā. “Bhaveyyātha ce, yadi bhaveyyāthā’ti ca vadanto ‘yathākkamaṃ pubbāparayogino ete saddā’ti ñāpetī”ti vadanti. “Kupitā kopena anattamanā domanassenā”ti iminā “evaṃ paṭhamena nayenā”tiādinā vuttavacanaṃ atthantarābhāvadassanena samattheti. “Tumhāka”nti iminā samānattho “tumha”nti eko saddo “amhāka”nti iminā samānattho “amha”nti saddo viya yathā “tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti (jā. 1.93) āha “tumhākaṃyevā”ti. Atthavasā liṅgavipariyāyoti katvā “tāya ca anattamanatāyā”ti vuttaṃ. “Antarāyo”ti vutte samaṇadhammavisesānanti atthassa pakaraṇato viññāyamānattā, viññāyamānatthassa ca saddassa payoge kāmacārattā “paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ antarāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “antarāyo”ti idaṃ manopadosassa akaraṇīyatāya kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā tumhākameva tena kopādinā paṭhamajjhānādīnamantarāyo bhaveyya, tasmā te kopādipariyāyena vuttā āghātādayo na karaṇīyāti adhippāyo, tena “nāhaṃ sabbaññū”ti issarabhāvena tumhe tato nivāremi, atha kho imināva kāraṇenāti dasseti. Taṃ pana kāraṇavacanaṃ yasmā ādīnavavibhāvanaṃ hoti, tasmā “ādīnavaṃ dassento”ti heṭṭhā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Therein’ refers to that mental defilement. By ‘in those who speak dispraise,’ he shows the locative case in the sense of a basis. Or, this is the locative case in the sense of a sign, or in the characteristic of a state, thus he says, ‘or in that dispraise.’ For neither a fault nor blame can be the basis of anger and displeasure, since these are dependent on those who speak them. ‘Assatha’ is a form of the optative mood, and by its connection with the particle ‘ce,’ it indicates the realm of supposition, as shown by ‘bhaveyyāthā’ (you would be). And by saying ‘bhaveyyātha ce’ or ‘yadi bhaveyyāthā,’ they explain that ‘these words are used in sequence, connecting the preceding and the following.’ By ‘angry with anger, displeased with displeasure,’ he supports the words stated by ‘thus by the first method’ and so on by showing the absence of a different meaning. The single word ‘tumha’ has the same meaning as ‘tumhākaṃ,’ just as the word ‘amha’ has the same meaning as ‘amhākaṃ,’ as in ‘therefore, our young ones do not die’; thus, he says ‘tumhākaṃyeva’ (indeed, of yours). By the force of meaning, a change of gender is made, hence ‘by that displeasure’ is said. When ‘obstacle’ is mentioned, since the meaning ‘to the special qualities of the ascetic's duty’ is understood from the context, and since the use of a word whose meaning is understood is optional, it is said, ‘an obstacle to the first jhāna, etc.’ And here, ‘obstacle’ is a term indicating the reason for not cultivating mental defilement. Because for you alone, due to that anger and so on, there would be an obstacle to the first jhāna and so on, therefore, those states of resentment and so on, described by way of anger and so on, should not be cultivated—this is the intention. Thus, he shows: ‘It is not that I, with the authority of an omniscient one, prevent you from that; rather, it is for this very reason.’ That term indicating a reason, because it reveals the danger, should be understood as what was stated below as ‘showing the danger.’

So [V 1.0194] pana manopadoso na kevalaṃ kālantarabhāvinoyeva hitasukhassa antarāyakaro, atha kho taṅkhaṇapavattanārahassapi hitasukhassa antarāyakaroti manopadose ādīnavaṃ daḷhataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ “api nū”tiādimāhātipi sambandho vattabbo. Paresanti ye attato aññe, tesanti attho, na pana “pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādīsu viya paṭiviruddhasattānanti āha “yesaṃ kesañcī”ti. Tadevatthaṃ samattheti “kupito hī”tiādinā. Pāḷiyaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitavacanajānanampi tadatthajānaneneva siddhanti āha “subhāsitadubbhāsitassa attha”nti.

This mental defilement, however, is not only an obstacle to well-being and happiness that would arise in the future, but it is also an obstacle to well-being and happiness that is worthy of occurring at that very moment. Thus, to show the danger in mental defilement more strongly, he states 'api nū' and so on; this is also the connection that should be stated. 'Paresaṃ' means 'those who are other than oneself.' It does not mean 'antagonistic beings' as in 'lest others speak ill' and so on; thus he says 'whomever it may be.' He supports that very meaning with 'for one who is angry' and so on. In the Pāḷi, knowing the speech as well-spoken or ill-spoken is also accomplished only by knowing its meaning; hence, he says 'the meaning of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken'.

Andhaṃtamanti andhabhāvakaraṃ tamaṃ, ativiya vā tamaṃ. Yaṃ naraṃ sahate abhibhavati, tassa andhatamanti sambandho. Yanti vā bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ, yasmiṃ kāle sahate, tadā andhatamaṃ hotīti attho[M 1.0223], kāraṇaniddeso vā, yena kāraṇena sahate, tena andhatamanti. Evaṃ sati yaṃtaṃ-saddānaṃ niccasambandhattā “yadā”ti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Kiriyāparāmasanaṃ vā etaṃ, “kodho sahate”ti yadetaṃ kodhassa abhibhavanaṃ vuttaṃ, etaṃ andhatamanti. Tato ca kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passatīti yojetabbaṃ. Atthaṃ dhammanti pāḷiatthaṃ, pāḷidhammañca. Cittappakopanoti cittassa pakatibhāvavijahanena padūsako. Antaratoti abbhantarato, cittato vā kodhavasena bhayaṃ jātaṃ. Nti tathāsabhāvaṃ kodhaṃ, kodhassa vā anatthajananādippakāraṃ.

‘Andhaṃtamaṃ’ means delusion that causes the state of blindness, or alternatively, exceedingly great darkness. The connection is to be made thus: for the person whom it overcomes and oppresses, for that person there is blinding darkness. Alternatively, ‘yaṃ’ is a nominative word in the locative sense; the meaning is: at which time it oppresses, at that time there is blinding darkness. Or, it is an indication of cause: for which reason it oppresses, for that reason it is blinding darkness. This being the case, because of the constant connection of the words ‘yaṃ’ and ‘taṃ’, the word ‘yadā’ should be supplied. Or, this is a reference to the action: that which is said to be the overcoming by anger in the phrase ‘anger overcomes,’ that overcoming is blinding darkness. And from that, it should be connected thus: ‘an angry person does not know the meaning; an angry person does not see the Dhamma.’ ‘Meaning’ and ‘Dhamma’ refer to the meaning of the Pāli and the Dhamma of the Pāli. ‘Cittappakopano’ means that which corrupts the mind by the abandoning of its natural state. ‘Antarato’ means from within, or from the mind; fear arises by the power of anger. ‘Taṃ’ refers to anger of such a nature, or to the various ways of anger, such as generating harm, and so on.

Sabbatthāpīti sabbesupi paṭhamadutiyatatiyanayesu. “Avaṇṇe paṭipajjitabbākāra”nti adhikāro. Avaṇṇabhāsakānamavisayattā “tatrā”ti padassa tasmiṃ avaṇṇeti atthova dassito. Abhūtanti kattubhūtaṃ vacanaṃ, yaṃ vacanaṃ abhūtaṃ hotīti attho. Abhūtatoti pana abhūtatākiriyāva bhāvappadhānattā, bhāvalopattā cāti dasseti “abhūtabhāvenevā”ti iminā. “Itipeta”ntiādi nibbeṭhanākāranidassananti dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatrāti tasmiṃ vacane. Yojanāti adhippāyapayojanā. Tuṇhīti abhāsanatthe nipāto, bhāvanapuṃsako cesa. “Itipetaṃ abhūta”nti vatvā “yaṃ tumhehī”tiādinā tadatthaṃ vivarati. Imināpīti pi-saddena anekavidhaṃ kāraṇaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Kāraṇasarūpamāha “sabbaññuyevā”tiādinā. Eva-saddo tīsupi padesu yojetabbo, sabbaññubhāvato na asabbaññū, svākkhātattā na durakkhāto, suppaṭipannattā na duppaṭipannoti imināpi kāraṇena nibbeṭhetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. “Kasmā pana sabbaññū”tiādipaṭicodanāyapi taṃkāraṇadassanena nibbeṭhetabbamevāti āha “tatra idañcidañca kāraṇa”nti. Tatrāti tesu sabbaññutādīsu. Idañca idañca kāraṇanti anekavidhena kāraṇānukāraṇaṃ dassetvā “na sabbaññū”tiādivacanaṃ nibbeṭhetabbanti attho. Tatridaṃ kāraṇaṃ [V 1.0195] – sabbaññū eva amhākaṃ satthā aviparītadhammadesanattā. Svākkhāto eva dhammo ekantaniyyānikattā. Suppaṭipanno eva saṅgho saṃkilesarahitattāti. Kāraṇānukāraṇadassanampettha asabbaññutādivacana-nibbeṭhanameva tathādassanassa tesampi kāraṇabhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāraṇakāraṇampi hi “kāraṇa”ntveva vuccati, patiṭṭhānapatiṭṭhānampi “patiṭṭhāna”ntveva yathā “tiṇehi bhattaṃ [M 1.0224] siniddhaṃ, pāsāde dhammamajjhāyatī”ti. Dutiyaṃ padanti “ataccha”nti padaṃ. Paṭhamassa padassāti “abhūta”nti padassa. Catutthanti “na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjatī”ti padaṃ. Tatiyassāti “natthi cetaṃ amhesū”ti padassa. Vividhamekattheyeva pavattaṃ vacanaṃ vivacanaṃ, tadeva vevacanaṃ, vacananti vā attho saddena vacanīyattā “bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttama”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1 ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1; a. ni. 1.rūpādivaggavaṇṇanā; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1) viya. Nānāsabhāvato vigataṃ vacanaṃ yassāti vevacanaṃ vuttanayena, pariyāyavacananti attho.

‘Sabbatthāpi’ means in all the first, second, and third methods. The governing topic is ‘the manner of conduct in a case of dispraise.’ Because it is not the domain of those who speak dispraise, the meaning of the word ‘tatra’ is shown only as ‘in that dispraise.’ ‘Abhūtaṃ’ is a statement that has become the agent; the meaning is ‘that statement which is untrue.’ As for ‘abhūtato,’ it indicates the very action of being untrue, due to the predominance of the abstract state and the elision of the abstract suffix; this is shown by the phrase ‘abhūtabhāveneva.’ To show that the phrase beginning with ‘itipetaṃ’ is an illustration of the manner of refutation, the compiler of the commentary stated the phrase beginning with ‘kathaṃ.’ ‘Tatra’ means ‘in that statement.’ ‘Yojanā’ means the connection to the intention and purpose. ‘Tuṇhī’ is a particle in the sense of not speaking, and it is a neuter noun of state. Having said, ‘Thus this is untrue,’ he explains its meaning with the phrase beginning ‘yaṃ tumhehi.’ In ‘imināpi,’ with the word ‘pi,’ he combines many kinds of reasons. The compiler of the commentary states the nature of the reason with the phrase beginning ‘sabbaññuyeva.’ The word ‘eva’ should be connected with all three terms: because of the state of being omniscient, he is not non-omniscient; because of the state of being well-proclaimed, it is not ill-proclaimed; because of the state of being of good practice, they are not of bad practice. The meaning intended is that it should be refuted by this reason as well. And even for the counter-question beginning ‘But why is he omniscient?’, it should be refuted by showing that reason. Therefore, the compiler of the commentary said, ‘Therein, this and this is the reason.’ ‘Tatra’ means ‘among those things such as omniscience, etc.’ ‘This and this is the reason’ means: having shown the reason and the reason for the reason in many ways, the statement beginning ‘he is not omniscient’ should be refuted. Therein, this is the reason: our Teacher is indeed omniscient because of teaching the Dhamma without error. The Dhamma is indeed well-proclaimed because it is absolutely emancipating. The Saṅgha is indeed of good practice because it is free from defilements. Herein, the showing of the reason and the reason for the reason is itself the refutation of the statement ‘not omniscient,’ etc., because such showing is also a reason for those qualities. This should be understood. Indeed, even the cause of a cause is called simply ‘a cause,’ and the foundation of a foundation is called simply ‘a foundation,’ as in ‘Because of the grass, the rice is smooth,’ and ‘He recites the Dhamma in the palace.’ The second term is the word ‘atacchaṃ’; it is a synonym of the first term, the word ‘abhūtaṃ.’ The fourth term is the phrase ‘na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjati’; it is a synonym of the third, the phrase ‘natthi cetaṃ amhesu.’ A word that occurs variously with a single meaning is a ‘vivacanaṃ’; that itself is a ‘vevacanaṃ.’ Or, ‘vacanaṃ’ can mean ‘meaning,’ because it is what is to be expressed by a word, as in ‘The meaning of “Bhagavā” is excellent...’ A ‘vevacanaṃ,’ according to the method stated, is that which has a meaning devoid of diverse natures; the meaning is a synonym.

Etthāha – kasmā panettha pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu ekekapadavaseneva adhippeto attho siddho, evaṃ siddhe sati kimete tena pariyāyavacanena. Tadetañhi ganthagāravādianekadosakaraṃ, yadi ca taṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, tadeva vuttaṃ assa, na tadaññanti? Vuccate – desanākāle, hi āyatiñca kassaci kathañci tadatthapaṭivedhanatthaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Desanāpaṭiggāhakesu hi yo tesaṃ pariyāyavacanānaṃ yaṃ pubbe saṅketaṃ karoti “idamimassatthassa vacana”nti, tassa teneva tadatthapaṭivedho hoti. Apica tasmiṃ khaṇe vikkhittacittānaṃ aññavihitānaṃ vipariyāyānaṃ aññena pariyāyena tadatthāvabodhanatthampi pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Yañhi ye na suṇanti, tapparihāyanavasena tesaṃ sabbathā paripuṇṇassa yathāvuttassa atthassa anavabodho siyā, pariyāyavacane pana vutte tabbasena paripuṇṇamatthāvabodho hoti. Atha vā mandabuddhīnaṃ punappunaṃ tadatthalakkhaṇena asammohanatthaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Mandabuddhīnañhi ekeneva padena ekatthassa sallakkhaṇena sammoho hoti, anekena pariyāyena pana ekatthassa sallakkhaṇena tathāsammoho na hoti anekappavattinimittena ekattheyeva pavattasaddena yathādhippetassa atthassa nicchitattā.

Herein, an objector says: ‘Why is a synonymous expression stated here? Is not the intended meaning established by each single word? This being established, what is the purpose of this synonymous expression? Indeed, this causes many faults, such as making the text heavy. And if it should be stated, then that very same thing would be stated again, not something else.’ The reply is given: A synonymous expression is stated for the purpose of someone's penetration of the meaning in some way, both at the time of the teaching and in the future. Indeed, among the recipients of the teaching, whoever has previously made a convention for one of those synonymous expressions, thinking ‘this is the word for this meaning,’ for that person, the penetration of the meaning occurs through that very word. Moreover, a synonymous expression is also stated for the purpose of making the meaning understood through another synonymous expression for those who at that moment have distracted minds, are otherwise engaged, or are perverse. Indeed, whatever word they do not hear due to a lapse, for them there might be a non-understanding of the complete meaning as stated. But when a synonymous expression is stated, by means of that, there is a complete understanding of the meaning. Or else, a synonymous expression is stated for the purpose of not confusing those of dull intellect by repeatedly marking the characteristic of that meaning. Indeed, for those of dull intellect, confusion arises from marking a single meaning with just a single word. But from marking a single meaning with many synonymous expressions, such confusion does not arise, because the intended meaning is ascertained by words occurring with a single meaning but with many grounds for their occurrence.

Aparo nayo – “anekepi atthā samānabyañjanā hontī”ti yā atthantaraparikappanā siyā, tassā parivajjanatthampi pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Anekesampi hi atthānaṃ ekapadavacanīyatāvasena samānabyañjanattā yathāvuttassa padassa “ayamattho nu kho adhippeto, udāhu ayamatthovā”ti pavattaṃ sotūnamatthantaraparikappanaṃ vevacanaṃ aññamaññaṃ bhedakavasena parivajjeti. Vuttañca –

Another method: It should be understood that a synonymous expression is spoken also for the purpose of avoiding whatever consideration of a different meaning might arise from the statement, 'many meanings may have the same expression.' For, because many meanings have the same expression by way of being expressed by a single word, a synonym, by way of distinguishing one from another, avoids the listeners' consideration of a different meaning, which occurs thus: 'Is this the intended meaning of the spoken word, or is it that meaning?' And it is said:

“Nekatthavuttiyā [V 1.0196][M 1.0225] saddo, na visesatthañāpako;

Pariyāyena yutto tu, pariyāyo ca bhedako”ti.

A word with multiple meanings is not an indicator of a specific meaning; but when joined with a synonym, it is, and the synonym is the distinguisher.

Aparo nayo – anaññassāpi pariyāyavacanassa vacane anekāhi tāhi tāhi nāmapaññattīhi tesaṃ tesaṃ atthānaṃ paññāpanatthampi pariyāyavacanaṃ vattabbaṃ hoti. Tathā hi pariyāyavacane vutte “imassatthassa idamidampi nāma”nti sotūnaṃ anekadhā nāmapaññattivijānanaṃ. Tato ca taṃtaṃpaññattikosallaṃ hoti seyyathāpi nighaṇṭusatthe paricayataṃ. Apica dhammakathikānaṃ tantiatthupanibandhanaparāvabodhanānaṃ sukhasiddhiyāpi pariyāyavacanaṃ. Tabbacanena hi dhammadesakānaṃ tantiatthassa attano citte upanibandhanena ṭhapanena paresaṃ sotūnamavabodhanaṃ sukhasiddhaṃ hoti. Atha vā sammāsambuddhassa attano dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattiyā vibhāvanatthaṃ, veneyyānañca tattha bījavāpanatthaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ bhagavā niddisati. Tadasampattikassa hi tathāvacanaṃ na sambhavati. Tena ca pariyāyavacanena yathāsutena tassaṃ dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattiyaṃ tapparicaraṇena, tadaññasucaritasamupabrūhanena ca puññasaṅkhātassa bījassa vapanaṃ sambhavati. Ko hi īdisāya sampattiyā viññāyamānāya tadetaṃ nābhipattheyyāti, kiṃ vā bahunā. Yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā sammāsambuddho yathā sabbasmiṃ atthe appaṭihatañāṇacāro, tathā sabbasmiṃ saddavohāreti ekampi atthaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi bodheti, natthi tattha dandhāyitattaṃ vitthāritattaṃ, nāpi dhammadesanāya hāni, āveṇiko cāyaṃ buddhadhammo. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa hi suppaṭividitabhāvena paṭisambhidāñāṇehi viya tenapi ñāṇena atthe, dhamme, niruttiyā ca appaṭihatavuttitāya buddhalīḷāya ekampi atthaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi bodheti, na pana tasmiṃ saddavohāre, tathābodhane vā mandabhāvo sammābodhanassa sādhanattā, na ca tena atthassa vitthārabhāvo ekassevatthassa desetabbassa subbijānanakāraṇattā, nāpi tabbacanena dhammadesanāhāni tassa desanāsampattibhāvato. Tasmā sātthakaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ, na cāpi taṃ ganthagāravādianekadosakaranti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ panetaṃ vuttaṃ “yadi ca taṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, tadeva vuttaṃ assa, na tadañña”nti, tampi na yuttaṃ payojanantarasambhavato. Tadeva hi avatvā tadaññassa vacanena desanākkhaṇe samāhitacittānampi sammadeva paṭiggaṇhantānaṃ taṃtaṃpadantogadhapavattinimittamārabbha [M 1.0226] tadatthādhigamo hoti, itarathā tasmiṃyeva pade punappunaṃ vutte tesaṃ tadatthānadhigatatā siyāti. Honti cettha –

Another method: Even when it is not a different synonymous expression, in the speaking of it, a synonymous expression should be spoken for the purpose of making those various meanings known through those various name-concepts. Indeed, when a synonymous expression is spoken, there arises for the listeners a manifold understanding of name-concepts, thus: 'This and that are also names for this meaning.' And from that, skill in those various concepts arises, just as skill arises from familiarity with a glossary. Furthermore, a synonymous expression is also for the easy accomplishment of the thorough comprehension of Dhamma-preachers who connect the text and its meaning. Indeed, by that expression, the understanding of other listeners is easily accomplished through the Dhamma-teacher's establishing and connecting the meaning of the text in his own mind. Alternatively, the Blessed One points out a synonymous expression for the purpose of revealing his own attainment of the analytical knowledges of Dhamma and language, and for planting the seed thereof in those to be trained. Indeed, for one who does not possess that attainment, such speech is not possible. And by that synonymous expression as heard, when there is that attainment in the analytical knowledges of Dhamma and language, the planting of the seed called merit becomes possible through practicing with it and through the thorough cultivation of other good practices. Indeed, who, when such an attainment is understood, would not aspire to that? Or what is the use of saying much? Because of having well penetrated the Dhamma-element, just as the Perfectly Enlightened One's sphere of knowledge is unobstructed in every meaning, so too is it unobstructed in every verbal expression. Therefore, he makes known even a single meaning through many synonymous expressions. In this, there is no slowness or prolixity, nor is there any deficiency in the Dhamma teaching. And this is a unique quality of a Buddha. Indeed, due to the state of having well penetrated omniscient knowledge, just as with the analytical knowledges, so also with that omniscient knowledge, because of his unobstructed functioning in meaning, Dhamma, and language, he makes known even a single meaning with many synonymous expressions with the grace of a Buddha. However, there is no dullness in that verbal expression or in so teaching, because it accomplishes perfect understanding. And through it, there is no prolixity of meaning, because it is the cause for easily knowing the single meaning that is to be taught. Nor by that expression is there any deficiency in the Dhamma teaching, because it is a state of perfection in teaching. Therefore, a synonymous expression is meaningful and should be seen as not causing the many faults of textual heaviness and so on.
