As for the statement that was made, 'If it should be said, that very thing should be said, not another,' that too is not correct, because of the possibility of another purpose. Indeed, by not saying that very thing but by speaking another instead, at the moment of teaching, even for those with concentrated minds who are receiving it perfectly well, understanding of the meaning occurs by focusing on the underlying sign occurring within those various words. Otherwise, if that same word were spoken again and again, they would be in a state of not having understood its meaning. And here there are these summary verses:

“Yena kenaci atthassa, bodhāya aññasaddato;

Vikkhittakamanānampi, pariyāyakathā katā.

The discourse of synonyms was made for understanding, through another word, the meaning expressed by any word whatsoever, even for those with distracted minds.

Mandānañca [V 1.0197] amūḷhatthaṃ, atthantaranisedhayā;

Taṃtaṃnāmaniruḷhatthaṃ, pariyāyakathā katā.

The discourse of synonyms was made for the non-bewilderment of the dull-witted, for prohibiting a different meaning, and for being established in those various names.

Desakānaṃ sukaratthaṃ, tantiatthāvabodhane;

Dhammaniruttibodhatthaṃ, pariyāyakathā katā.

The discourse of synonyms was made for the ease of teachers in understanding the meaning of the text, and for the purpose of understanding Dhamma and language.

Veneyyānaṃ tattha bījavāpanatthañca attano;

Dhammadhātuyā līḷāya, pariyāyakathā katā.

The discourse of synonyms was made for planting the seed therein for those to be trained, and for his own graceful display with the Dhamma-element.

Tadeva tu avatvāna, tadaññehi pabodhanaṃ;

Sammāpaṭiggaṇhantānaṃ, atthādhigamāya kata”nti.

Furthermore, not having said that very thing, awakening was brought about through other words; it was done for the attainment of meaning for those who receive it correctly.

Idaṃ pana nibbeṭhanaṃ īdiseyeva, na sabbattha kātabbanti dassento “idañcā”tiādimāha. Tattha avaṇṇeyevāti kāraṇapatirūpaṃ vatvā, avatvā vā dosapatiṭṭhāpanavasena nindāya eva. Na sabbatthāti na kevalaṃ akkosanakhuṃsanavambhanādīsu sabbattha nibbeṭhanaṃ kātabbanti attho. Tadevatthaṃ “yadi hī”tiādinā pākaṭaṃ karoti. “Sāsaṅkanīyo hotī”ti vuttaṃ tathānibbeṭhetabbatāya kāraṇameva “tasmā”ti paṭiniddisati. “Oṭṭhosī”tiādi “na sabbatthā”ti etassa vivaraṇaṃ. Jātināmagottakammasippaābādha liṅga kilesa āpatti akkosanasaṅkhātehi dasahi akkosavatthūhi. Adhivāsanameva khanti, na diṭṭhinijjhānakkhamanādayoti adhivāsanakhanti.

However, showing that this explanation is to be made only in such a case, and not in all cases, he said, 'And this...' and so on. Therein, 'only in the case of dispraise' means: it is only for blame by way of establishing a fault, whether having stated a semblance of a reason or not. 'Not in all cases' means that an explanation is not to be made in all cases, such as in mere abuse, denigration, contempt, and so on. He makes that very meaning clear with 'If indeed...' and so on. The statement 'he becomes suspect' is the very reason why it must be explained in that way, which he refers back to with 'therefore.' 'You are a camel,' etc., is an explanation for 'not in all cases.' That is, with the ten grounds for abuse, namely: birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, disease, physical appearance, defilement, offense, and reviling. Endurance alone is patience, not the acceptance that comes from scrutinizing views and so on; therefore, it is the patience of endurance.

6. Evaṃ avaṇṇabhūmiyā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni vaṇṇabhūmiyāpi saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kātumāha “eva”ntiādi. Tattha avaṇṇabhūmiyanti avaṇṇappakāsanaṭṭhāne. Tādilakkhaṇanti ettha “pañcahākārehi tādī iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī, cattāvīti tādī, tiṇṇāvīti tādī, muttāvīti tādī, taṃniddesā tādī”ti (mahāni. 38) niddesanayena pañcasu atthesu idha paṭhamenatthena tādī. Tatrāyaṃ niddeso –

6. Having thus given an explanation of the unpraiseworthy state, he now speaks the words beginning with 'evaṃ' in order to give an explanation of the praiseworthy state as well. Therein, 'in the unpraiseworthy state' means in the place of revealing dispraise. Here, in the phrase 'the characteristic of such a one (tādī),' among the five meanings according to the method of the Niddesa—'Such a one (tādī) is so-called in five ways: such a one in the desirable and undesirable; such a one because he has abandoned (cattāvī); such a one because he has crossed over (tiṇṇāvī); such a one because he is liberated (muttāvī); such a one by that explanation (taṃniddesā)' (Mahāni. 38)—here 'tādī' is taken in the first meaning. Therein, this is the explanation:

Kathaṃ arahā iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī, arahā lābhepi tādī, alābhepi tādī, yasepi, ayasepi, pasaṃsāyapi, nindāyapi, sukhepi[M 1.0227], dukkhepi tādī, ekañce bāhaṃ gandhena limpeyyuṃ, ekañce bāhaṃ vāsiyā taccheyyuṃ, amusmiṃ natthi rāgo, amusmiṃ natthi paṭigho[V 1.0198], anunayapaṭighavippahīno ugghāṭinigghāṭivītivatto, anurodhavirodhasamatikkanto, evaṃ arahā iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādīti (mahāni. 38).

How is the Arahant steadfast in the desirable and undesirable? The Arahant is steadfast in gain and also in loss; steadfast in honor and also in dishonor; in praise and also in blame; in pleasure and also in pain. If they were to anoint one arm with perfume and carve the other with an adze, in the former there is no lust, in the latter there is no aversion. He has abandoned affection and aversion, has gone beyond the bolt and bar, has transcended conformity and opposition. Thus is the Arahant steadfast in the desirable and undesirable (Mahāni. 38).

Vacanattho pana tamiva dissatīti tādī, iṭṭhamiva aniṭṭhampi passatīti attho. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ tādilakkhaṇaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samapekkhanasabhāvo. Atha vā tamiva dissate tādī, so eva sabhāvo, tadeva lakkhaṇaṃ tādilakkhaṇanti. Vaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ tādilakkhaṇaṃ dassetunti sambandho. Para-saddo aññattheti āha “ye kecī”tiādi. Ānandanti bhusaṃ pamodanti taṃsamaṅgino sattā etenāti ānandasaddassa karaṇatthataṃ dasseti. Sobhanamano sumano, cittaṃ, sobhanaṃ vā mano yassāti sumano, taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo. Nanu ca cittavācakabhāve sati cetasikasukhassa bhāvatthatā yuttā, puggalavācakabhāve pana cittameva bhāvattho siyā, na cetasikasukhaṃ, sumanasaddassa dabbanimittaṃ pati pavattattā yathā “daṇḍittaṃ sikhitta”ntiādīti? Saccametaṃ dabbe apekkhite, idha pana tadanapekkhitvā tena dabbena yuttaṃ mūlanimittabhūtaṃ cetasikasukhameva apekkhitvā sumanasaddo pavatto, tasmā etthāpi cetasikasukhameva bhāvattho sambhavati, tenāha “cetasikasukhassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Etena hi vacanena tadaññacetasikānampi cittapaṭibaddhattā, cittakiriyattā ca yathāsambhavaṃ somanassabhāvo āpajjatīti codanaṃ nāpajjateva ruḷhisaddattā tassa yathā “paṅkaja”nti pariharati. Ubbilayatīti ubbilaṃ, bhindati purimāvatthāya visesaṃ āpajjatīti attho. Tadeva ubbilāvitaṃ paccayantarāgamādivasena. Uddhaṃ palavatīti vā ubbilāvitaṃ akārānaṃ ikāraṃ, ākārañca katvā, cittameva “cetaso”ti vuttattā. Taddhite pana siddhe taṃ abyatirittaṃ tasmiṃ pade vacanīyassa sāmaññabhāvato, tassa vā saddassa nāmapadattā, tasmā kassāti sambandhīvisesānuyoge “cetaso”ti vuttanti dassetuṃ “kassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Esa nayo īdisesu. Yāya uppannāya kāyacittaṃ vātapūritabhastā viya uddhumāyanākārappattaṃ hoti tassā gehasitāya odagyapītiyā etaṃ adhivacananti sarūpaṃ dasseti “uddhaccāvahāyā”tiādinā. Uddhaccāvahāyāti uddhatabhāvāvahāya. Uppilāpeti [M 1.0228] cittaṃ uppilāvitaṃ karotīti ubbilāpanā, sā eva pīti, tassā. Khandhavasena dhammavisesattaṃ āha “idhāpī”tiādinā. Avaṇṇabhūmimapekkhāya api-saddo “ayampi pārājiko”tiādīsu (pārā. 1.89, 91, 167, 171, 195, 197) viya, idha ca kiñcāpi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ubbilāvitameva natthi, atha kho āyatiṃ kulaputtānaṃ edisesupi ṭhānesu akusaluppattiṃ paṭisedhento dhammanettiṃ ṭhapetīti. Dvīhi padehi saṅkhārakkhandho, ekena vedanākkhandho vuttoti etthāpi “tesaṃ vasena sesānaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ karaṇaṃ paṭikkhittamevā”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena sakkā viññātunti [V 1.0199] na vuttaṃ. “Pi-saddo sambhāvanattho”tiādinā vuttanayena cettha attho yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbo.

The etymological meaning is: because it is seen just like that (tamiva dissati), it is called 'tādī'; the meaning is that one sees the undesirable just as the desirable. Its characteristic is the 'characteristic of such a one' (tādilakkhaṇa), which is the nature of regarding the desirable and undesirable with equanimity. Or, 'tādī' means it is seen just like that; that very nature, that very characteristic, is the 'characteristic of such a one.' The connection is: 'in order to show the characteristic of such a one in the praiseworthy state.' The word 'para' (other) is in the sense of 'añña' (another); thus he said 'whatever,' etc. He shows the instrumental sense of the word 'ānanda' thus: 'Beings endowed with it greatly rejoice (ānandanti) by means of this.' 'Sumano' means a beautiful mind (sobhana-mano), i.e., the mind; or, one whose mind is beautiful is a 'sumano,' i.e., a person endowed with that. Surely, an objection: when it denotes the mind, it is proper for the abstract meaning to be mental happiness; but when it denotes a person, the abstract meaning would be the mind itself, not mental happiness, because the word 'sumana' proceeds in relation to a substance-sign, as in 'the state of having a stick' (daṇḍittaṃ), 'the state of having a topknot' (sikhittaṃ), etc.? This is true when a substance is intended. But here, without intending that substance, the word 'sumana' proceeds by intending only the mental happiness which is connected with that substance and is the root-sign. Therefore, here too, mental happiness itself can be the abstract meaning. For that reason, he said, 'This is a designation for mental happiness.' He refutes the objection that 'By this statement, for other mental factors too, since they are connected to the mind and are activities of the mind, the state of gladness would arise as is possible,' because ('sumana') is a conventional term (ruḷhisadda), just like 'paṅkaja' (lotus). Because it floats up (ubbilayati), it is 'ubbilaṃ'; the meaning is that it breaks from a previous state and reaches a special state. That very thing, by way of the arrival of other conditions, etc., is 'ubbilāvitaṃ.' Or, because it floats upward (uddhaṃ palavati), it is 'ubbilāvitaṃ,' having made the letter 'a' into 'i' and 'ā'; for the mind itself is called 'cetaso.' But when the derivative is formed, that term is non-specific, because of the general nature of what is to be expressed in that term, or because that word is a noun. Therefore, when there is a specific inquiry about the possessor ('of what?'), 'cetaso' is said. To show this, 'kassā' etc. was said. This is the method in such cases. He shows its nature by means of the words beginning with 'uddhaccāvahāya,' saying: 'This is a designation for that household-based uplifting joy (odagyapīti) by which, when it has arisen, the body and mind become as if inflated like a wind-filled bellows.' 'Uddhaccāvahāya' means 'bringing about a state of agitation.' Because it makes the mind float up (uppilāpeti), makes it elated, it is 'ubbilāpanā'; that itself is joy (pīti), of that. He states its distinctness as a phenomenon by way of the aggregates with the words beginning 'idhāpi' (here too). The word 'api,' with reference to the unpraiseworthy state, is used as in 'this too is a pārājika offense,' etc. (Pārā. 1.89, etc.). And here, although for those monks there is no elation at all, nevertheless, the Buddha, wishing to prevent the arising of the unwholesome for clansmen in the future in such situations, establishes the guideline of the Dhamma. 'By two terms the formations aggregate is stated, and by one the feeling aggregate is stated.' Here too, it is not stated because it can be understood by the method stated in the commentary: 'By means of them, the function of the remaining associated states is indeed rejected.' And here the meaning should be understood as is possible, according to the method stated in 'The word 'pi' has the sense of praise,' etc.

Tumhaṃyevassa tena antarāyoti etthāpi “antarāyo”ti idaṃ “ubbilāvitattassa akaraṇīyatākāraṇavacana”tiādinā heṭṭhā avaṇṇapakkhe amhehi vuttanayānusārena attho daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca “ānandino ubbilāvitā”ti dīpitaṃ pītimeva gahetvā “tena ubbilāvitattenā”ti vacanaṃ somanassarahitāya pītiyā abhāvato tabbacaneneva “sumanā”ti dīpitaṃ somanassampi siddhamevāti katvā vuttaṃ. Atha vā somanassassa antarāyakaratā pākaṭā, na tathā pītiyāti evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā panetanti yathāvuttaṃ atthaṃ avibhāgato manasi katvā codeti. Ācariyo “sacca”nti tamatthaṃ paṭijānitvā “taṃ panā”tiādinā vibhajjabyākaraṇavasena pariharati.

As for 'for you, indeed, by that, there would be an obstacle,' here too, the meaning of 'obstacle' should be understood according to the method stated by us below in the unpraiseworthy section, such as 'the statement of the reason why the state of elation should not be engaged in.' And here, having taken only the joy indicated by 'delighted and elated,' the statement 'by that state of elation' is made having considered that, due to the absence of joy devoid of gladness, the gladness indicated by 'sumanā' is indeed established by that very statement. Alternatively, it should be understood that the statement is made thus because the obstructing nature of gladness is evident, but not so with joy. 'But why is this so?'—having brought to mind the meaning as stated without differentiation, one objects. The teacher acknowledges that meaning as true and then refutes it through an explanation by way of analysis, starting with 'but that...'

Tattha etanti ānandādīnamakaraṇīyatāvacanaṃ, nanu bhagavatā vaṇṇitanti sambandho. Buddhoti kittayantassāti “buddho”ti vacanaṃ guṇānussaraṇavasena kathentassa sādhujanassa. Kasiṇenāti kasiṇatāya sakalabhāvena. Jambudīpassāti cetassa avayavabhāvena sambandhīvacanaṃ. Apare pana “jambudīpassāti karaṇavacanatthe sāmivacana”ti vadanti, tesaṃ matena kasiṇajambudīpasaddānaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvo daṭṭhabbo, karaṇavacanañca nissakkatthe. Pageva ekadesato panāti api-saddo sambhāvane. Ādi-saddena cettha –

Herein, the connection is as follows: 'This' refers to the statement that delight and so on should not be done; 'was it not praised by the Blessed One?' 'Of one who proclaims "Buddha"' (buddhoti kittayantassa) means of a good person who speaks the word 'Buddha' by way of recollecting his virtues. 'Completely' (kasiṇena) means by the state of being whole, by the state of being complete. 'Of Jambudīpa' (jambudīpassa) is a word connected to this by way of being a part of it. Others, however, say, "'Of Jambudīpa' is the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental case." According to their view, the words 'complete' and 'Jambudīpa' should be understood as having the same referent, and the instrumental case is in the sense of the ablative. Furthermore, regarding 'what need is there to speak of from a part,' the word 'also' (api) is in the sense of affirmation. And here, by the word 'etc.' (ādi)...

“Mā soci udāyi, ānando avītarāgo kālaṃ kareyya, tena cittappasādena sattakkhattuṃ devarajjaṃ kāreyya, sattakkhattuṃ [M 1.0229] imasmiṃyeva jambudīpe mahārajjaṃ kāreyya, apica udāyi ānando diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyissatī”tiādisuttaṃ (a. ni. 3.81) –

The following sutta is included: 'Do not sorrow, Udāyī. If Ānanda were to die with passion unabandoned, by that confidence of mind he would exercise the sovereignty of devas seven times, and he would exercise great sovereignty in this very Jambudīpa seven times. But indeed, Udāyī, Ānanda will attain final Nibbāna in this very life' (AN 3.81).

Saṅgahitaṃ. Nti suttantare vuttaṃ pītisomanassaṃ. Nekkhammassitanti kāmato nikkhamane kusaladhamme nissitaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Gehassitanti gehavāsīnaṃ samudāciṇṇato gehasaṅkhāte kāmaguṇe nissitaṃ. Kasmā tadevidhādhippetanti āha “idañhī”tiādi. “Āyasmato channassa uppannasadisa”nti vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ, samatthetuṃ vā “tenevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi bhagavati, dhamme ca pavattagehassitapematāya. Parinibbānakāleti parinibbānāsannakāle bhagavatā paññattena tajjitoti vā sambandho. Parinibbānakāleti [V 1.0200] vā bhagavato parinibbutakāle saṅghena tajjito nibbattetīti vā sambandho. Brahmadaṇḍenāti “bhikkhūhi itthannāmo neva vattabbo, na ovaditabbo, nānusāsitabbo”ti (cūḷava. 445) katena brahmadaṇḍena. Tajjitoti saṃvejito. Tasmāti yasmā gehassitapītisomanassaṃ jhānādīnaṃ antarāyakaraṃ, tasmā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā sakkapañhasutte “somanassaṃpāhaṃ devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi asevitabbampī”ti (dī. ni. 2.359).

Included. That refers to the joy and gladness spoken of in another sutta. 'Based on renunciation' (nekkhammassitaṃ) means based on the wholesome states that are a departure from sensual pleasure. 'Here' (idha) means in this sutta. 'Based on the household' (gehassitaṃ) means based on the sensual pleasures designated as 'household' due to the practice of householders. Because the objection, 'Therefore, is only that intended here?' is possible, he said, 'For this...' (idañhi), and so on. To make clear or to establish the meaning stated as 'similar to what arose for the Venerable Channa,' the words 'Therefore...' (teneva), and so on, were stated. Due to his household-based affection that had arisen towards the Blessed One and the Dhamma, he was unable to bring about a special attainment. The connection is: 'At the time of Parinibbāna' (parinibbānakāle) means at the time near the Parinibbāna, being admonished by what was laid down by the Blessed One. Alternatively, the connection is: 'At the time of Parinibbāna' means at the time after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, being admonished by the Saṅgha, he brought about a special attainment. 'By the brahmā-punishment' (brahmadaṇḍena) means by the brahmā-punishment imposed thus: 'A monk of such-and-such a name should not be spoken to, advised, or instructed by the monks' (Cv.XI.1.9). 'Admonished' (tajjito) means stirred with a sense of urgency. 'Therefore' (tasmā) means: because household-based joy and gladness are an obstacle to jhāna and so on, therefore. Indeed, this was stated by the Blessed One in the Sakkapañha Sutta: 'Sovereign of the devas, I speak of gladness in two ways: as that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated' (DN 21).

“Ayañhī”tiādinā tadevatthaṃ kāraṇato samattheti. Rāgasahitattā hi sā antarāyakarāti. Ettha pana “idañhi rāgasañhitaṃ pītisomanassa”nti vattabbaṃ siyā, tathāpi pītiggahaṇena somanassampi gahitameva hoti somanassarahitāya pītiyā abhāvatoti heṭṭhā vuttanayena pītiyeva gahitā. Apica sevitabbāsevitabbavibhāgassa sutte vacanato somanassassa pākaṭo antarāyakarabhāvo, na tathā pītiyāti sāyeva rāgasahitatthena visesetvā vuttā. Avaṇṇabhūmiyā saddhiṃ sambandhitvā pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “lobho cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kodhasadisovāti avaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ vuttakodhasadiso eva. “Luddho”tiādigāthānaṃ “kuddho”tiādigāthāsu vuttanayena attho daṭṭhabbo.

By the words 'For this...' (ayañhi), and so on, he establishes that very meaning by way of reason. For indeed, because it is accompanied by lust, that joy is an obstacle. Here, however, it should be said, 'For this is joy and gladness connected with lust.' Nevertheless, by the taking of 'joy,' 'gladness' is also taken, because there is no joy devoid of gladness. Thus, by the method stated previously, only 'joy' is taken. Moreover, because the division of what is to be cultivated and not to be cultivated was taught in the sutta, the fact that gladness is an obstacle is clear; similarly, the fact that joy is an obstacle is not clear. Therefore, only that joy is mentioned specifically as being accompanied by lust. To make it clear by connecting it with the ground of dispraise, the words 'and greed...' (lobho ca), and so on, were said. 'Just like anger' (kodhasadiso va) means it is just like the anger mentioned in the ground of dispraise. The meaning of the verses beginning with 'The greedy one...' (luddho) should be understood in the way stated in the verses beginning with 'The angry one...' (kuddho).

“Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, dhammassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, saṅghassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, tatra ce tumhe assatha ānandino sumanā ubbilāvitā[M 1.0230], api nu tumhe paresaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ ājāneyyāthāti? No hetaṃ bhante”ti ayaṃ tatiyavāro nāma avaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ vuttanayavasena tatiyavāraṭṭhāne nīharitabbattā, so desanākāle tena vārena bodhetabbapuggalābhāvato desanāya anāgatopi tadatthasambhavato atthato āgatoyeva. Yathā taṃ vitthāravasena kathāvatthuppakaraṇanti dassetuṃ “tatiyavāro panā”tiādi vuttaṃ, etena saṃvaṇṇanākāle tathābujjhanakasattānaṃ vasena so vāro ānetvā saṃvaṇṇetabboti dasseti. “Yatheva hī”tiādinā tadevatthasambhavaṃ vibhāveti. Kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti yathevāti sambandho.

'Monks, if others should speak praise of me, or speak praise of the Dhamma, or speak praise of the Saṅgha, and if, on that occasion, you were to be delighted, glad, and elated, would you then be able to know what is well-spoken and ill-spoken by others?' 'Certainly not, venerable sir.' This is called the third section, because it is to be brought out in the place of the third section in the manner stated in the ground of dispraise. Although that section did not come in the discourse—because at the time of the discourse there was no person to be awakened by that section—it has indeed come by way of meaning, due to the possibility of that meaning. To show that this is like the Kathāvatthu treatise, which is presented in detail, the phrase 'The third section, however...' (tatiyavāro pana), and so on, was stated. By this, he shows that at the time of commenting, that section should be brought in and commented upon for the sake of beings who would understand in that way. By the words 'Just as...' (yatheva hi), and so on, he clarifies that very possibility of meaning. The connection is: just as an angry person does not know the meaning.

Paṭipajjitabbākāradassanavāreti yathāvuttaṃ tatiyavāraṃ upādāya vattabbe catutthavāre. “Tumhākaṃ satthā”ti vacanato pabhuti yāva “imināpi kāraṇena taccha”nti vacanaṃ, tāva yojanā. “So hi bhagavā”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ. Tattha itipīti imināpi kāraṇena. Vitthāro visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 123 ādayo) “anāpatti upasampannassa bhūtaṃ ārocetī”ti [V 1.0201] (pāci. 77) vuttepi sabhāgānameva ārocanaṃ yuttanti āha “sabhāgānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃyeva paṭijānitabba”nti. Teyeva hi tassa atthakāmā, saddheyyavacanattañca maññanti, tato ca “sāsanassa amoghatā dīpitā hotī”ti vuttatthasamatthanaṃ siyā. “Evañhī”tiādi kāraṇavacanaṃ. Pāpicchatā ceva parivajjitā, kattubhūtā vā sā, hotīti sambandho. Amoghatāti niyyānikabhāvena atucchatā. Vuttanayenāti “tatra tumhehīti tasmiṃ vaṇṇe tumhehī”tiādinā ceva “dutiyaṃ padaṃ paṭhamassa padassa, catutthañca tatiyassa vevacana”ntiādinā ca vuttanayena.

In the section showing the mode of practice to be undertaken, which is the fourth section to be spoken of by taking up the third section as stated. The application is from the statement 'Your teacher...' (tumhākaṃ satthā) up to the statement '...for this reason also it is true' (imināpi kāraṇena tacchaṃ). The words 'For that Blessed One...' (so hi bhagavā), and so on, are its explanation. Therein, 'for this reason also' (iti pi) means 'by this reason also.' The detailed explanation is in the Visuddhimagga. Even though it is said, 'There is no offense for an ordained person who declares a true superhuman state' (Pāc. 8), it is proper to declare it only to those of a similar disposition. Therefore, he said, 'It should be acknowledged only to monks of a similar disposition.' For only they desire his welfare and consider his words to be trustworthy. And because of that, the non-futility of the teaching is shown; thus it would be a confirmation of the meaning stated. The words 'For thus...' (evañhi), and so on, are a statement of reason. Evil desire is thereby avoided; or, that evil desire is the agent of the verb 'is' (hoti). This is the connection. 'Non-futility' (amoghatā) means non-emptiness by way of being a means of escape. 'In the manner stated' (vuttanayena) means in the manner stated by 'Therein, by you...' (tatra tumhehi), and so on, and by 'The second term is a synonym of the first term, and the fourth of the third,' and so on.

Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Minor Morality

7. Ko anusandhīti pucchā “nanu ettakeneva yathāvuttehi avaṇṇavaṇṇehi sambandhā desanāmatthakaṃ pattā”ti anuyogasambhavato katā. Vaṇṇena ca avaṇṇena cāti tadubhayapadena. Atthaniddeso viya hi saddaniddesopīti akkharacintakā. Atha vā tathābhāsanassa kāraṇattā, koṭṭhāsattā ca “padehī”ti vuttaṃ. Avaṇṇena ca vaṇṇena cāti pana aguṇaguṇavasena, nindāpasaṃsāvasena ca sarūpadassanaṃ. “Nivatto amūlakatāya [M 1.0231] vissajjetabbatābhāvato”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Taṃ vitthāretvā desanāya bodhetabbapuggalābhāvato ettakāva sā yuttarūpāti bhagavato ajjhāsayeneva adesanābhāvena nivatto, yathā taṃ vaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ tatiyavārotipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā bodhetabbapuggalasambhavena vissajjetabbatāya adhigatabhāvato anuvattatiyeva. Itipetaṃ bhūtanti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho taduparipi anuvattakattā, tena vakkhati “idha panā”tiādi. Ettāvatā ayaṃ vaṇṇānusandhīti dassetvā duvidhesu pana tesu vaṇṇesu brahmadattassa vaṇṇānusandhīti dassento “so panā”tiādimāha. Upari suññatāpakāsane anusandhiṃ dassessati “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.28).

7. The question, 'What is the connection?' is asked because of the possibility of the inquiry, 'Has not the discourse, connected with the aforementioned dispraise and praise, reached its conclusion with just this much?' 'With praise and with dispraise' refers to both these terms. Indeed, like the explanation of meaning, there is also the explanation of the term, thus say the grammarians. Alternatively, because it is the cause for such speaking and because it is a section, it is said 'by the terms.' But 'by dispraise and by praise' is a demonstration of its nature by way of demerit and merit, and by way of blame and praise. 'It has ceased because of being groundless and because there is no need for it to be answered,' thus it was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla. Elaborating on that, because there is no person to be made to understand by the teaching, that teaching of just this much is suitable. Thus, by the Blessed One's own intention, through not teaching, it has ceased; this should be seen as being like the third instance in that section on praise. Similarly, because of the possibility of a person to be made to understand and because it is understood as something that should be answered, it does indeed continue. In the phrase 'Thus this is true,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning' because it continues even after that. Therefore, the commentator will say, 'But here...' and so on. Having shown that with this much, 'this is the connection of praise,' then, wishing to show that among those two kinds of praise, this is the connection of praise for Brahmadatta, he said, 'But that one...' and so on. Later, in the exposition on emptiness, he will show the connection with 'There are, monks...' and so on.

Evaṃ pucchāvissajjanāmukhena samudāyatthataṃ vatvā idāni avayavatthataṃ dasseti “tatthā”tiādinā. Appameva parito samantato khaṇḍitattā parittaṃ nāmāti āha “appamattakanti parittassa nāma”nti. Mattā vuccati pamāṇaṃ mīyate parimīyateti katvā. Samāsantakakārena appamattakaṃ yathā “bahuputtako”ti, evaṃ oramattakepi. Eteneva “appā mattā appamattā, sā etassāti appamattaka”ntiādinā kapaccayassa sātthakatampi dasseti atthato abhinnattā. Mattakasaddassa anatthakabhāvato sīlameva sīlamattakaṃ. Anatthakabhāvoti ca sakatthatā [V 1.0202] purimapadattheyeva pavattanato. Na hi saddā kevalaṃ anatthakā bhavantīti akkharacintakā. Nanu ca bhagavato pāramitānubhāvena niratthakamekakkharampi mukhavaraṃ nārohati, sakalañca pariyattisāsanaṃ pade pade catusaccappakāsananti vuttaṃ, kathaṃ tassa anatthakatā sambhavatīti? Saccaṃ, tampi padantarābhihitassa atthassa visesanavasena tadabhihitaṃ atthaṃ vadati eva, so pana attho vināpi tena padantareneva sakkā viññātunti anatthakamicceva vuttanti. Nanu avocumha “anatthakabhāvo…pe… pavattanato”ti. Apica vineyyajjhāsayānurūpavasena bhagavato desanā pavattati, vineyyā ca anādimatisaṃsāre lokiyesuyeva saddesu paribhāvitacittā, loke ca asatipi atthantarāvabodhe vācāsiliṭṭhatādivasena saddapayogo dissati “labbhati palabbhati, khañjati nikhañjati, āgacchati paccāgacchatī”tiādinā. Tathāparicitānañca tathāvidheneva saddapayogena atthāvagamo [M 1.0232] sukho hotīti anatthakasaddapayogo vuttoti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Hoti cettha –

Having thus spoken of the collective meaning by way of question and answer, he now shows the meaning of the parts with 'therein,' and so on. Because it is just small, being demarcated all around, it is called 'paritta' (trifling); thus he said, 'appamattakaṃ is a name for paritta.' 'Mattā' is called 'pamāṇa' (measure), because it is measured or gauged. With the final 'ka' of the compound, it becomes 'appamattakaṃ', just as in 'bahuputtako'; it is the same in 'oramattakepi'. By this very reasoning, he also shows the meaningfulness of the suffix 'ka' with 'A small measure is appamattā; that [sīla] has it, therefore it is appamattakaṃ,' and so on, because in meaning there is no difference. Because the word 'mattaka' is without separate meaning, 'sīla' itself is 'sīlamattakaṃ'. And 'being without separate meaning' means it functions only in the context of the meaning of the preceding word. For, according to the grammarians, 'Words are not merely without meaning.' Is it not said that, by the power of the Blessed One's perfections, not even a single meaningless letter proceeds from his noble mouth, and that the entire scriptural teaching in every single word proclaims the Four Truths? How then is it possible for that [word] to be without meaning? True, but that [word] too, by way of specifying the meaning expressed by the other word, does indeed state the meaning expressed by it. However, that meaning can be understood even without that other word; therefore it is called 'as if without meaning.' Did we not say, 'being without separate meaning... functions only in the context of the meaning of the preceding word'? Moreover, the Blessed One's teaching proceeds in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained. And those to be trained, in beginningless saṃsāra, have minds accustomed only to worldly words. And in the world, even when there is no understanding of a different meaning, the use of words is seen by way of polished speech and so on, as in 'labbhati palabbhati' (is gotten, is obtained), 'khañjati nikhañjati' (is dug, is dug up), 'āgacchati paccāgacchati' (comes, comes back), and so on. And for those accustomed to such, the understanding of meaning is easy through that very kind of word usage. Thus, the use of a word 'as if without meaning' is spoken of. This is so in all cases. And here there is this:

“Padantaravacanīya-ssatthassa visesanāya;

Bodhanāya vineyyānaṃ, tathānatthapadaṃ vade”ti.

For specifying the meaning to be expressed by another word; for making understood by those to be trained, thus one should speak a word without [separate] meaning.

Atha vā sīlamattakanti ettha matta-saddo visesanivattiattho “avitakkavicāramattā dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā) manomattā dhātu manodhātū”ti (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 499) ca ādīsu viya. “Appamattakaṃ oramattaka”nti padadvayena sāmaññato vuttoyeva hi attho “sīlamattaka”nti padena visesato vutto, tena ca sīlaṃ eva sīlamattaṃ, tadeva sīlamattakanti nibbacanaṃ kātabbanti dassetuṃ “sīlameva sīlamattaka”nti vuttaṃ.

Alternatively, here in 'sīlamattakaṃ', the word 'matta' has the meaning of negating a specification, as in 'dhammas that are merely without thought and investigation' and 'the element that is merely mind is the mind-element,' and so on. For the meaning that was spoken of generally by the two words 'appamattakaṃ' and 'oramattakaṃ' is indeed spoken of specifically by the word 'sīlamattakaṃ'. And therefore, to show that the derivation should be made as 'sīla itself is sīlamattaṃ, and that very thing is sīlamattakaṃ,' it was said, 'sīla itself is sīlamattakaṃ'.

Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – oramattakanti ettha oranti apārabhāgo “orato bhogaṃ (mahāva. 66) oraṃ pāra”ntiādīsu viya. Atha vā heṭṭhāattho orasaddo oraṃ āgamanāya ye paccayā, te orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānītiādīsu viya. Sīlañhi samādhipaññāyo apekkhitvā apārabhāge, heṭṭhābhāge ca hoti, ubhayatthāpi “ore pavattaṃ mattaṃ yassā”tiādinā viggaho. Sīlamattakanti etthāpi mattasaddo amahatthavācako “bhesajjamattā”tiādīsu viya. Atha vā sīlepi tadekadesasseva saṅgahaṇatthaṃ amahatthavācako ettha mattasaddo vutto. Tathā hi indriyasaṃvarapaccayasannissitasīlāni idha desanaṃ anāruḷhāni. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā tāni pātimokkhasaṃvaraājīvapārisuddhisīlāni viya na sabbaputhujjanesu [V 1.0203] pākaṭānīti. Mattanti cettha visesanivattiatthe napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ. Pamāṇappakatthesu pana “matta”nti vā “mattā”ti vā napuṃsakitthiliṅgaṃ.

But this is the method independent of the commentary. Here in 'oramattakaṃ', 'oraṃ' is the near side, as in 'a portion from the near side,' 'the near shore and the far shore,' and so on. Alternatively, the word 'ora' has the meaning of 'lower,' as in 'the conditions which are for coming to the lower [realms], they are the fetters pertaining to the lower part,' and so on. For sīla, with respect to concentration and wisdom, is on the near side and on the lower side. In both meanings, the analysis is 'that which has its measure occurring on the near/lower side,' and so on. Also here in 'sīlamattakaṃ', the word 'matta' is expressive of a small amount, as in 'a measure of medicine,' and so on. Alternatively, the word 'matta', expressive of a small amount, is used here for the purpose of including only one part of sīla. For so it is that the virtues of sense-restraint and those dependent on the requisites are not included in the teaching here. If asked why, it is because they, unlike the virtues of Pātimokkha-restraint and purity of livelihood, are not manifest in all ordinary people. And here, 'mattaṃ' in the sense of negating a specification is neuter. But in the meanings of 'measure' and 'small amount', it is neuter ('mattaṃ') or feminine ('mattā').

“Idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādinā saha yojanāya piṇḍatthaṃ dasseti. Yena sīlena vadeyya, etaṃ sīlamattakaṃ nāmāti sambandho. “Vaṇṇaṃ vadāmīti ussāhaṃ katvāpī”ti idaṃ “vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno”ti etassa vivaraṇaṃ. Etena hi “ekapuggalo bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 1.170) viya mānasaddassa sāmatthiyatthataṃ dasseti. “Ussāhaṃ kurumāno”ti [M 1.0233] avatvā “katvā”ti ca vacanaṃ tvādipaccayantapadānamiva mānantapaccayantapadānampi parakiriyāpekkhamevāti dassanatthaṃ. “Tattha siyā”tiādinā sandhāyabhāsitamatthaṃ ajānitvā nītatthameva gahetvā suttantaravirodhitaṃ maññamānassa kassaci īdisī codanā siyāti dasseti. Tatthāti tasmiṃ “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādivacane (dī. ni. 1.7). Kammaṭṭhānabhāvane yuñjati sīlenāti yogī, tassa.

By 'This was said,' etc., it shows the collective meaning together with the construing. The connection should be made thus: By which virtue one might speak, that is called mere virtue. This phrase, 'Even having made an effort, thinking, “I will speak praise,”' is an explanation of 'speaking praise.' For by this, as in texts such as, 'One person, monks, arising in the world, arises,' it shows that the suffix '-māna' has the meaning of capability. And not saying 'making an effort' but saying 'having made' is for the purpose of showing that, like words ending in suffixes such as '-tvā', words ending in the suffixes '-māna' and '-anta' also require a subsequent action. By 'There, it might be,' etc., it shows that for someone who, not knowing the intended meaning, takes only the direct meaning and thinks it contradicts another sutta, such a criticism might arise. 'There' means in that statement, 'But this is a trifle,' etc. One who applies themself to the development of a meditation subject by habit is a yogī; for that yogī [this is said].

Alaṅkaraṇaṃ vibhūsanaṃ alaṅkāro, pasādhanakiriyā. Alaṃ karoti etenevāti vā alaṅkāro, kuṇḍalādipasādhanaṃ. Maṇḍīyate maṇḍanaṃ, ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ. Maṇḍīyati etenāti vā maṇḍanaṃ, mukhacuṇṇādiūnapūraṇopakaraṇaṃ. Idha pana sadisavohārena, taddhitavasena vā sīlameva tathā vuttaṃ. Maṇḍaneti maṇḍanahetu, maṇḍanakiriyānimittaṃ gatoti attho. Atha vā maṇḍati sīlenāti maṇḍano, maṇḍanajātiko puriso. Bahumhi cetaṃ jātyāpekkhāya ekavacanaṃ. Ubbāhanatthepi hi ekavacanamicchanti keci, tadayuttameva saddasatthe anāgatattā, atthayuttiyā ca abhāvato. Kathañhi ekavacananiddiṭṭhato ubbāhanakaraṇaṃ yuttaṃ siyā ekasmiṃ yevatthe ubbāhitabbassa aññassatthassa abhāvato. Tasmā vipallāsavasena bahvatthe idaṃ ekavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, maṇḍanasīlesūti attho. Ācariyadhammapālattherenapi hi ayamevidha vinicchayo (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) vutto. Aggatanti uttamabhāvaṃ.

Adornment (alaṅkaraṇa) is embellishment (vibhūsana), an ornament (alaṅkāro), the act of beautifying. Alternatively, because one adorns (alaṃ karoti) with it (etena), it is an ornament (alaṅkāro); it is an embellishment such as an earring. Adornment (maṇḍana) is being adorned (maṇḍīyate), the filling of a deficient place. Alternatively, because one is adorned (maṇḍīyati) with it (etena), it is an adornment (maṇḍana); it is an implement for filling a deficiency, such as face powder. Here, however, virtue itself is called thus, either by similar usage or by the power of a derivative suffix. 'In adornment' (maṇḍane) means: because it is a cause of adornment, it has gone to the purpose of the act of adorning—this is the meaning. Alternatively, one who adorns by habit (sīlena) is an adorner (maṇḍano), a person of an adorning nature. And this is a singular form used in a plural sense with reference to the class. Indeed, some desire the singular form even in the sense of exaggeration, but that is inappropriate because it is not found in the grammatical texts and because there is no justification in meaning. For how could the act of exaggeration be appropriate from the indication of the singular, since in just one meaning there is no other meaning to be exaggerated? Therefore, this singular form should be seen as being in the plural sense by way of inversion of number; the meaning is 'in virtues that are adornments.' Indeed, this very same determination was stated here by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. 'Supremacy' (aggataṃ) means the state of being supreme.

Assaṃ bhavissāmīti ākaṅkheyyāti sambandho. Assāti bhaveyya. Paripūrakārīti cettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena sakalampi sīlathomanasuttaṃ dasseti.

The connection should be made thus: 'One should desire, “I shall be.”' 'Assa' means 'he should be.' Here in 'paripūrakārīti' (one who fulfills), the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning' or, alternatively, the meaning of 'manner.' By this, it indicates the entire sutta on the praise of virtue.

Kikīva aṇḍanti etthāpi tadatthena iti-saddena –

Here also in 'like a kiki bird its egg,' by the word 'iti' with that same meaning—

“Kikīva [V 1.0204] aṇḍaṃ camarīva vāladhiṃ,

Piyaṃva puttaṃ nayanaṃva ekakaṃ;

Tatheva sīlaṃ anurakkhamānā,

Supesalā hotha sadā sagāravā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.19); –

'As the kiki bird its egg, as the yak its tail, as a beloved only child, as one's single eye; just so, while guarding virtue, be very amiable and always respectful.'

Gāthaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Pupphagandho”ti vatvā tadekadesena dassetuṃ “na candana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Candanaṃ tagaraṃ mallikāti hi taṃsahacaraṇato tesaṃ [M 1.0234] gandhova vutto. Pupphagandhoti ca pupphañca tadavaseso gandho cāti attho. Tagaramallikāhi vā avasiṭṭho “pupphagandho”ti vutto. Satañca gandhoti ettha sīlameva sadisavohārena vā taddhitavasena vā gandho. Sīlanibandhano vā thutighoso vuttanayena “gandho”ti adhippeto. Sīlañhi kittiyā nimittaṃ. Yathāha “sīlavato kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.150; 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 785; udā. 76). Sappuriso pavāyati pakārehi gandhati tassa gandhūpagarukkhapaṭibhāgattā.

It includes the verse. Having said 'the fragrance of flowers,' in order to indicate it by one of its components, 'not sandalwood,' etc., was said. For regarding sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine, only their fragrance is mentioned due to their association with it. And 'fragrance of flowers' means both the flower and the fragrance remaining from it. Alternatively, the fragrance remaining from tagara and jasmine is called 'fragrance of flowers.' Here in 'and the fragrance of the virtuous,' virtue itself is called 'fragrance' either by similar usage or by the power of a derivative suffix. Alternatively, the sound of praise connected with virtue is intended as 'fragrance' by the method already stated. Indeed, virtue is a cause of renown. As it is said: 'For one who is virtuous, a good sound of fame goes forth.' A good person wafts forth, is fragrant in various ways, because of being like a tree endowed with fragrance.

Vassikīti sumanapupphaṃ, “vassika”ntipi pāṭho, tadatthova. Gandhā eva gandhajātā, gandhappakārā vā. Yvāyanti yadidaṃ, uttamo gandho vātīti sambandho.

'Vassikī' is the sumana flower (jasmine); 'vassikaṃ' is also a reading, with the very same meaning. Fragrances themselves are gandhajātā (types of fragrance), or alternatively, kinds of fragrance. The connection is: yvāyanti means yadidaṃ (that which is this), its supreme fragrance (uttamo gandho) wafts (vāti).

Sammadaññā vimuttānanti sammā aññāya jānitvā, aggamaggena vā vimuttānaṃ. Maggaṃ na vindatīti kāraṇaṃ na labhati, na jānāti vā.

'Sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ' means: of those liberated having known rightly, or alternatively, of those liberated by the supreme path having known rightly. 'Maggaṃ na vindati' (does not find the path) means: does not find the cause, or alternatively, does not know.

“Sīle patiṭṭhāyā”ti gāthāya paṭisandhipaññāya sapañño ātāpī vīriyavā pārihārikapaññāya nipako narasaṅkhāto bhikkhu sīle patiṭṭhāya cittaṃ tappadhānena vuttaṃ samādhiṃ bhāvayaṃ bhāvayanto bhāvanāhetu tathā paññaṃ vipassanañca imaṃ antojaṭābahijaṭāsaṅkhātaṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭaye vijaṭeyya vijaṭituṃ samattheyyāti saṅkhepattho.

Regarding the verse 'Established in virtue...': A person (nara) who is wise (sapañño) with rebirth-linking wisdom, ardent (ātāpī), energetic (vīriyavā), and skilled (nipako) with protective wisdom—such a bhikkhu, established in virtue (sīle patiṭṭhāya), developing the mind (cittaṃ)—that is, the concentration spoken of with that as its chief—and likewise developing wisdom (paññaṃ)—that is, insight (vipassanā)—should disentangle (vijaṭaye) this tangle (jaṭaṃ) known as the internal tangle and the external tangle. He should be able to disentangle it. This is the concise meaning.

Pathaviṃ nissāyāti pathaviṃ rasaggahaṇavasena nissāya, sīlasmiṃ pana paripūraṇavasena nissāya patiṭṭhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Depending on the earth' means depending on the earth by way of taking up its nutritive essence; but in the case of virtue, the establishment should be seen as depending on it by way of fulfillment.

Appakamahantatāya pārāpārādi viya upanidhāpaññattibhāvato aññamaññaṃ upanidhāya āhāti vissajjetuṃ “upari guṇe upanidhāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Sīlañhīti ettha hi-saddo kāraṇattho, tenidaṃ [V 1.0205] kāraṇaṃ dasseti “yasmā sīlaṃ kiñcāpi patiṭṭhābhāvena samādhissa bahūpakāraṃ, pabhāvādiguṇavisese panassa upanidhāya kalampi bhāgaṃ na upeti, tathā samādhi ca paññāyā”ti. Tenevāha “tasmā”tiādi. Na pāpuṇātīti guṇasamabhāvena na sampāpuṇāti, na sametīti vuttaṃ hoti. Uparimanti samādhipaññaṃ. Upanidhāyāti upatthambhaṃ katvā. Tañhi tādisāya paññattiyā upatthambhanaṃ hoti. Heṭṭhimanti sīlasamādhidvayaṃ.

In order to explain that, because of being a designation by comparison due to smallness and greatness—like the near and far shores—he spoke by comparing them with one another, it was said, 'by comparing the higher qualities.' Here in sīlañhi, the word hi has the meaning of reason. By that, it shows this reason: 'Because virtue, although it is of great help to concentration by being its foundation, yet when compared with concentration's special qualities of power and so on, it does not come up to even a fraction. Likewise, concentration when compared with wisdom.' For that very reason, the compiler of the commentary said, 'Therefore,' etc. 'Does not reach' means: does not attain by way of equality in qualities, does not equal—this is what is meant to be said. 'The higher' means concentration and wisdom. 'Upanidhāya' (by comparing) means having made a support. Indeed, that virtue is a support for such a designation by comparison. 'The lower' means the pair of virtue and concentration.

“Katha”ntiādi [M 1.0235] vitthāravacanaṃ. Kaṇḍambamūlikapāṭihāriyakathanañcettha yathākathañcipi sīlassa samādhimapāpuṇatāsiddhiyevidhādhippetāti pākaṭatarapāṭihāriyabhāvena, nidassananayena cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Abhi…pe… titthiyamaddana”nti idaṃ pana tassa yamakapāṭihāriyassa supākaṭabhāvadassanatthaṃ, aññehi bodhimūle ñātisamāgamādīsu ca katapāṭihāriyehi visesadassanatthañca vuttaṃ. Sambodhito hi aṭṭhamepi divase devatānaṃ “buddho vā no vā”ti uppannakaṅkhāvidhamanatthaṃ ākāse ratanacaṅkamaṃ māpetvā caṅkamanto pāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi, tato dutiyasaṃvacchare kulanagaragato kapilavatthupure nigrodhārāme ñātīnaṃ samāgamepi tesaṃ mānamadappahānatthaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi. Tattha abhisambodhitoti abhisambujjhanakālato. Sāvatthinagaradvāreti sāvatthinagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre. Kaṇḍambarukkhamūleti kaṇḍena nāma pasenadirañño uyyānapālena ropitattā kaṇḍambanāmakassa rukkhassa mūle. Yamakapāṭihāriyakaraṇatthāya bhagavato citte uppanne “tadanucchavikaṃ ṭhānaṃ icchitabba”nti ratanamaṇḍapādi sakkena devaraññā āṇattena vissakammunā katanti vadanti keci. Bhagavatā nimmitanti apare. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana anekāsu “sakkena devānamindena āṇāpitena vissakammadevaputtena maṇḍapo kato, caṅkamo pana bhagavatā nimmito”ti vuttaṃ. Dibbasetacchatte devatāhi dhāriyamāneti attho viññāyati aññesamasambhavato. “Dvādasayojanāya parisāyā”ti idaṃ catūsu disāsu paccekaṃ dvādasayojanaṃ manussaparisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadā kira dasasahassilokadhātuto cakkavāḷagabbhaṃ paripūretvā devabrahmānopi sannipatiṃsu. Yo koci evarūpaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ kātuṃ samattho ce, so āgacchatūti codanāsadisattā vuttaṃ “attādānaparidīpana”nti. Attādānañhi anuyogo paṭipakkhassa attassa ādānaṃ gahaṇanti katvā. Titthiyamaddananti “pāṭihāriyaṃ karissāmā”ti kuhāyanavasena pubbe uṭṭhitānaṃ titthiyānaṃ maddanaṃ, tañca tathā kātuṃ asamatthatāsampādanameva. Tadetaṃ padadvayaṃ “yamakapāṭihāriya”nti etena sambandhitabbaṃ. Rājagahaseṭṭhino candanaghaṭikuppattito paṭṭhāya sabbameva cettha vattabbaṃ.

The words 'Kathaṃ', etc., are a detailed explanation. And here, it should be understood that the telling of the miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree is due to it being a very evident miracle and by way of illustration, for what is intended here is precisely the accomplishment of the state where virtue, in any way whatsoever, does not attain concentration. But this phrase, 'Abhi…pe… the crushing of the sectarians,' is stated to show the very evident nature of that Twin Miracle, and to show its distinction from other miracles performed at the foot of the Bodhi tree, at the gathering of relatives, and so on. For on the eighth day after His full awakening, to dispel the doubt that had arisen among the devas, 'Is he a Buddha or not?', He created a jeweled walkway in the sky and, while walking on it, performed a miracle. Then, in the second year, having gone to His ancestral city, in the Nigrodhārāma in Kapilavatthu, at the gathering of His relatives, He performed the Twin Miracle to abandon their pride and intoxication. Therein, 'from His full awakening' means from the time of His full awakening. 'At the gate of the city of Sāvatthī' means at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī. 'At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree' means at the foot of the tree named Kaṇḍamba because it was planted by Kaṇḍa, the gardener of King Pasenadi. Some say that when the thought to perform the Twin Miracle arose in the Blessed One's mind, 'A suitable place should be desired,' a jeweled pavilion and so on were made by Vissakamma, who was commanded by Sakka, king of the devas. Others say they were created by the Blessed One. But in many commentaries it is said: 'The pavilion was made by the devaputta Vissakamma, who was instructed by Sakka, lord of the devas, but the walkway was created by the Blessed One.' The meaning 'while the divine white canopy was being held by the devas' is understood from the impossibility of it for others. This phrase, 'by the assembly of twelve yojanas,' is said with reference to the human assembly extending twelve yojanas in each of the four directions. At that time, it is said, devas and brahmās also assembled, filling the sphere of the universe from the ten-thousand world-systems. Because it is like a challenge, 'If anyone is able to perform such a miracle, let them come!', it is called 'the illumination of taking up the challenge'. For `attādāna` is a challenge, in the sense of taking up or grasping the opponent's position. 'The crushing of the sectarians' means the crushing of the sectarians who had previously arisen by way of deception, saying, 'We will perform a miracle'; and that crushing is precisely the bringing about of their inability to do so in that way. This pair of terms should be connected with 'the Twin Miracle'. And here, everything should be told, beginning from the arising of the sandalwood bowl of the merchant of Rājagaha.

Uparimakāyatotiādi [V 1.0206][M 1.0236] paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.116) āgatanayadassanaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “itiādinayappavatta”nti, “sabbaṃ vitthāretabba”nti ca. Tatthāyaṃ pāḷiseso –

The words 'From the upper body', etc., show the method that comes in the Paṭisambhidāmagga; therefore it is said, 'proceeding according to this and other methods,' and 'everything should be elaborated.' Therein, this is the remainder of the Pāli:

“Heṭṭhimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, uparimakāyato udakadhārā pavattati. Puratthimakāyato aggi, pacchimakāyato udakaṃ. Pacchimakāyato aggi, puratthimakāyato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇaakkhito aggi, vāmaakkhito udakaṃ. Vāmaakkhito aggi, dakkhiṇaakkhito udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato aggi, vāmakaṇṇasotato udakaṃ. Vāmakaṇṇasotato aggi, dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇanāsikāsotato aggi, vāmanāsikāsotato udakaṃ. Vāmanāsikāsotato aggi, dakkhiṇanāsikāsotato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato aggi, vāmaaṃsakūṭato udakaṃ. Vāmaaṃsakūṭato aggi, dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇahatthato aggi, vāmahatthato udakaṃ. Vāmahatthato aggi, dakkhiṇahatthato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇapassato aggi, vāmapassato udakaṃ. Vāmapassato aggi, dakkhiṇapassato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇapādato aggi, vāmapādato udakaṃ. Vāmapādato aggi, dakkhiṇapādato udakaṃ. Aṅgulaṅgulehi aggi, aṅgulantarikāhi udakaṃ. Aṅgulantarikāhi aggi, aṅgulaṅgulehi udakaṃ. Ekekalomato aggi, ekekalomato udakaṃ. Lomakūpato lomakūpato aggikkhandho pavattati, lomakūpato lomakūpato udakadhārā pavattatī”ti.

From the lower body, a mass of fire proceeds; from the upper body, a stream of water proceeds. From the front of the body, fire proceeds; from the back of the body, a stream of water proceeds. From the back of the body, a mass of fire proceeds; from the front of the body, a stream of water proceeds. From the right eye, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left eye, a stream of water proceeds. From the left eye, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right eye, a stream of water proceeds. From the right ear-hole, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left ear-hole, a stream of water proceeds. From the left ear-hole, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right ear-hole, a stream of water proceeds. From the right nostril, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left nostril, a stream of water proceeds. From the left nostril, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right nostril, a stream of water proceeds. From the right shoulder-tip, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left shoulder-tip, a stream of water proceeds. From the left shoulder-tip, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right shoulder-tip, a stream of water proceeds. From the right hand, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left hand, a stream of water proceeds. From the left hand, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right hand, a stream of water proceeds. From the right side, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left side, a stream of water proceeds. From the left side, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right side, a stream of water proceeds. From the right foot, a mass of fire proceeds; from the left foot, a stream of water proceeds. From the left foot, a mass of fire proceeds; from the right foot, a stream of water proceeds. From the fingers and toes, a mass of fire proceeds; from between the fingers and toes, a stream of water proceeds. From between the fingers and toes, a mass of fire proceeds; from the fingers and toes, a stream of water proceeds. From each single body-hair, a mass of fire proceeds; from each single body-hair, a stream of water proceeds. From each hair-pore, a mass of fire proceeds; from each hair-pore, a stream of water proceeds.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ekekalomakūpato” icceva (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.116) āgataṃ.

But in the commentary, it comes only as 'from each single hair-pore'.

Channaṃ vaṇṇānanti etthāpi nīlānaṃ pītakānaṃ lohitakānaṃ odātānaṃ mañjiṭṭhānaṃ pabhassarānanti ayaṃ sabbopi pāḷiseso peyyālanayena, ādi-saddena ca dassito. Ettha ca channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ ubbāhanabhūtānaṃ yamakā yamakā vaṇṇā pavattantīti pāṭhasesena sambandho, tena vakkhati “dutiyā dutiyā rasmiyo”tiādi. Tattha hi tāsaṃ yamakaṃ [M 1.0237] yamakaṃ pavattanākārena saha āvajjanaparikammādhiṭṭhānānaṃ visuṃ pavatti dassitā. Keci pana “channaṃ vaṇṇāna”nti etassa “aggikkhandho udakadhārā”ti purimehi padehi sambandhaṃ vadanti, tadayuttameva aggikkhandhaudakadhārānaṃ atthāya tejokasiṇavāyokasiṇānaṃ samāpajjanassa vakkhamānattā. Channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ chabbaṇṇā pavattantīti kattuvasena vā sambandho yathā “ekassa cepi bhikkhuno na paṭibhāseyya taṃ bhikkhuniṃ apasādetu”nti (pāci. 558). Kattukammesu hi bahulā sāmivacanaṃ ākhyātapayogepi icchanti neruttikā.

In this passage `channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ` also—of the blue, of the yellow, of the red, of the white, of the crimson, and of the radiant—this entire remaining portion of the Pāḷi is shown by way of elision (`peyyāla`) and by the word `ādi`. And here, the connection should be made with the remaining text thus: 'pairs of colors of the six colors, which have become the source, arise.' Therefore, it will be said, 'the second, the second rays,' and so on. For therein is shown the separate arising of adverting, preliminary work, and determination, together with the manner of the arising of their pairs. Some, however, say that this `channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ` has a connection with the preceding words `aggikkhandho udakadhārā`. That is indeed inappropriate, because the attainment of the fire-kasiṇa and the air-kasiṇa for the sake of the mass of fire and the stream of water will be spoken of. Alternatively, the connection is in the sense of the agent, thus: 'the six colors of the six colors arise,' just as in 'if it does not occur to even one monk (`ekassa cepi bhikkhuno`) to admonish that nun...' For many grammarians desire the genitive case even in connection with a finite verb for the sense of the agent and the object.

Evaṃ [V 1.0207] pāḷinayena yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ aṭṭhakathānayena vivaranto paccāsattinayena “channaṃ vaṇṇāna”nti padameva paṭhamaṃ vivarituṃ “tassā”tiādimāha. Tattha tassāti bhagavato. “Suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmiyo”ti idaṃ tāsaṃ pītābhānaṃ yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ, chabbaṇṇāhi rasmīhi alaṅkaraṇakālo viyāti attho. Tāpi hi cakkavāḷagabbhato uggantvā brahmalokamāhacca paṭinivattitvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭimeva gaṇhiṃsu. Ekacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ vaṅkagopānasikaṃ viya bodhigharaṃ ahosi ekālokaṃ. Dutiyā dutiyā rasmiyoti purimapurimato pacchā pacchā nikkhantā rasmiyo. Kasmā sadisākāravasena “viyā”ti vacanaṃ vuttanti āha “dvinnañcā”tiādi. Dvinnañca cittānaṃ ekakkhaṇe pavatti nāma natthi, yehi tā evaṃ siyuṃ, tathāpi iminā kāraṇadvayena evameva khāyantīti adhippāyo. Bhavaṅgaparivāsassāti bhavaṅgavasena parivasanassa, bhavaṅgasaṅkhātassa parivasanassa vā, bhavaṅgapatanassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Āciṇṇavasitāyāti āvajjanasamāpajjanādīhi pañcahākārehi samāciṇṇaparicayatāya. Nanu ca ekassāpi cittassa pavattiyā dve kisso rasmiyopi sambhaveyyunti anuyogamapaneti “tassā tassā pana rasmiyā”tiādinā. Cittavāranānattā āvajjanaparikammacittāni, kasiṇanānattā adhiṭṭhānacittavārānipi visuṃ visuṃyeva pavattanti. Āvajjanāvasāne tikkhattuṃ pavattajavanāni parikammanāmeneva idha vuttāni.

Having thus shown the Twin Miracle according to the method of the Pāḷi, now, wishing to explain it according to the method of the commentary, in order to first explain the very phrase `channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ` by the method of proximity, he said `tassa`, etc. Therein, `tassa` means 'of the Blessed One'. This statement, 'rays of a golden color,' was said because of the predominance of those that were of a yellow luster. The meaning is: like a time of adornment with the six-colored rays. For those rays, having ascended from within the world-sphere, having struck the Brahma-world and turned back, took hold of the very rim of the world-sphere's opening. The interior of a single world-sphere became a single light, like a Bodhi-house with a curved gable-end. `Dutiyā dutiyā rasmiyo` means rays that issued forth later and later from the very preceding ones. Because the question arises, 'Why was the word `viya` (like) spoken in the sense of a similar appearance?', he said `dvinnañca`, etc. And there is no such thing as the arising of two minds in a single moment, by which those rays would be thus. Nevertheless, by these two reasons, they appear just so—this is the intention. `Bhavaṅgaparivāsassa` means: of the dwelling by way of `bhavaṅga`, or of the dwelling called `bhavaṅga`; it is said to mean 'of the falling into `bhavaṅga`'. `Āciṇṇavasitāya` means: due to the familiarity well-practiced by the five modes: adverting, attaining, etc. He removes the objection, 'Surely, by the arising of even a single mind, two or three rays could also be possible, could they not?' with `tassā tassā pana rasmiyā`, etc. Due to the diversity of mind-courses, the adverting and preliminary-work minds arise quite separately; due to the diversity of kasiṇas, the courses of determination-minds also arise quite separately. At the end of adverting, the impulsions that arise three times are here called by the name 'preliminary work' only.

Kathanti āha “nīlarasmiatthāya hī”tiādi. “Mañjiṭṭharasmiatthāya lohitakasiṇaṃ, pabhassararasmiatthāya pītakasiṇa”nti idaṃ lohitapītarasmīnaṃ kāraṇeyeva vutte siddhanti na vuttaṃ. Tāsameva hi mañjiṭṭhapabhassararasmiyo [M 1.0238] visesapabhedabhūtāti. “Aggikkhandhatthāyā”tiādinā “uparimakāyato”tiādīnaṃ vivaraṇaṃ. Aggikkhandhaudakakkhandhāpi aññamaññaasammissā yāva brahmalokā uggantvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ patiṃsu, taṃ divasaṃ pana satthā yo yo yasmiṃ yasmiṃ dhamme ca pāṭihāriye ca pasanno, tassa tassa ajjhāsayavasena taṃ taṃ dhammañca kathesi, pāṭihāriyañca dassesi, evaṃ dhamme bhāsiyamāne, pāṭihāriye ca kariyamāne mahājano dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Tasmiñca samāgame attano manaṃ gahetvā pañhaṃ pucchituṃ samatthaṃ adisvā nimmitaṃ buddhaṃ māpesi, tena pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ satthā vissajjesi. Satthārā pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ so vissajjesi, satthu caṅkamanakāle nimmito ṭhānādīsu aññataraṃ kappesi, tassa caṅkamanakāle satthā ṭhānādīsu aññataraṃ kappesīti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “satthā caṅkamatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Sabbaṃ vitthāretabba”nti etena “satthā tiṭṭhati, nimmito caṅkamati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappetī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.116) catūsu iriyāpathesu ekekamūlakā satthupakkhe cattāro[V 1.0208], nimmitapakkhe cattāroti sabbe aṭṭha vārā vitthāretvā vattabbāti dasseti. Yasmā sīlaṃ samādhissa patiṭṭhāmattameva hutvā nivattati, samādhiyeva tattha patiṭṭhāya yathāvuttaṃ sabbaṃ pāṭihāriyakiccaṃ pavatteti, tasmā tadetaṃ samādhikiccamevāti vuttaṃ “ettha ekampī”tiādi.

Because the question 'How?' should be asked, he said `nīlarasmi-atthāya hi`, etc. This—'for the sake of the crimson ray, the red kasiṇa; for the sake of the radiant ray, the yellow kasiṇa'—was not stated because it is established when the cause of the red and yellow rays alone is stated. For the crimson and radiant rays are themselves particular divisions of those very rays. By `aggikkhandhatthāya`, etc., is the explanation of `uparimakāyato`, etc. The masses of fire and water, unmixed with each other, having ascended as far as the Brahma-world, fell upon the rim of the world-sphere's opening. Furthermore, on that day, the Teacher taught that very Dhamma and showed that very miracle according to the disposition of whoever was pleased with whatever Dhamma and miracle. Thus, while the Dhamma was being spoken and the miracle was being performed, the great populace had a breakthrough to the Dhamma. And in that assembly, not seeing anyone capable of asking a question by grasping His (the Teacher's) mind, he created a created Buddha. The Teacher answered the question asked by that one. That one answered the question asked by the Teacher. To show this meaning—that when the Teacher was walking, the created one adopted one of the postures, standing, etc., and when that one was walking, the Teacher adopted one of the postures, standing, etc.—`satthā caṅkamati`, etc., was said. By this, `sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ` (all should be elaborated), he shows that all eight occasions—four on the Teacher's side and four on the created one's side, each based on one of the four postures, as in 'the Teacher stands, the created one walks or sits or lies down,' etc.—should be elaborated and stated. Because virtue, having become merely a foundation for concentration, ceases, and it is concentration alone that, being established thereon, brings about the entire function of the miracle as described, therefore, that is solely the function of concentration. Thus, `ettha ekampi`, etc., was said.

“Yaṃ panā”tiādinā samādhissa paññamapāpuṇatā vibhāvitā, yaṃ pana paṭivijjhi, idaṃ paṭivijjhanaṃ paññākiccanti attho. Taṃ anukkamato dasseti “bhagavā”tiādinā. “Kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyānī”ti idaṃ dīpaṅkarapādamūle katapaṭhamābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya vuttaṃ, tato pubbepi yattakena tasmiṃ bhave icchanto sāvakabodhiṃ pattuṃ sakkuṇeyya, tattakaṃ puññasambhāraṃ samupacinīti veditabbaṃ. Tatoyeva hi “manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassana”ntiādinā (bu. vaṃ. 59) vuttesu aṭṭhadhammesu hetusampannatā ahosi. Keci pana manopaṇidhānavacīpaṇidhānavasena anekadhā asaṅkhyeyyaparicchedaṃ katvā pubbasambhāraṃ vadanti, tadayuttameva saṅgahāruḷhāsu aṭṭhakathāsu tathā avuttattā. Tāsu hi yathāvuttanayena paṭhamābhinīhārato pubbe hetusampannatāyeva dassitā. Ekūnatiṃsavassakāle nikkhamma pabbajitvāti sambandho. Cakkaratanārahapuññavantatāya [M 1.0239] bodhisatto cakkavattisirisampannoti tassa nivāsabhavanaṃ “cakkavattisirinivāsabhūta”nti vuttaṃ. Bhavanāti rammasurammasubhasaṅkhātā niketanā. Padhānayoganti dukkaracariyāya uttamavīriyānuyogaṃ.

By the phrase beginning, “And what…,” the state of concentration not reaching wisdom is shown clearly. Whatsoever was penetrated, this penetration is the function of wisdom—this is the meaning. The Compiler of the Commentary shows that function of wisdom in sequence with the phrase beginning, “The Blessed One….” The statement, “Four incalculables and one hundred thousand more aeons,” is spoken starting from the first aspiration made at the feet of Dīpaṅkara. It should be understood that even before that, he had accumulated as much of a store of merit as would have enabled him, had he so wished in that existence, to attain the enlightenment of a disciple. For that very reason, among the eight factors stated in the passage beginning, “human existence, the attainment of the proper gender, the cause, the sight of the Teacher,” he was endowed with the cause. Some, however, speak of the previous store of merit, having made the division of incalculables in many ways by means of mental and verbal aspiration; but that is indeed inappropriate, because it is not stated thus in the commentaries that have been accepted in the recitals. For in them, by the method already stated, only the endowment with the cause before the first aspiration is shown. The connection is: “having gone forth from home at the age of twenty-nine.” Because of possessing merit worthy of the Wheel-Treasure, the Bodhisatta was endowed with the splendor of a Universal Monarch; therefore his dwelling-place was called “one that has become the residence of the splendor of a Universal Monarch.” Bhavana means the residences called Ramma, Suramma, and Subha. Padhānayoga means the application of supreme effort for the practice of austerities.

Uruvelāyaṃ kira senānigame kuṭumbikassa dhītā sujātā nāma dārikā vayappattā nerañjarāya tīre nigrodhamūle patthanamakāsi “sacāhaṃ samajātikaṃ kulagharaṃ gantvā paṭhamagabbhe puttaṃ labhissāmi, khīrapāyāsena balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti, (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.284; jā. aṭṭha. 1.avidūre nidānakathā) tassā sā patthanā samijjhi. Sā satta dhenuyo laṭṭhivane khādāpetvā tāsampi dhītaro gāviyo laddhā tatheva khādāpetvā puna tāsampi dhītaro tathevāti sattaputtinattipanattiparamparāgatāhi dhenūhi khīraṃ gahetvā khīrapāyāsaṃ pacitumārabhi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahābrahmā tiyojanikaṃ setacchattaṃ upari dhāresi, sakko devarājā aggiṃ ujjālesi, sakalaloke vijjamānarasaṃ devatā pakkhipiṃsu, pāyāsaṃ dakkhiṇāvaṭṭaṃ hutvā pacati, taṃ sā suvaṇṇapātiyā satasahassagghanikāya saheva bodhisattassa datvā pakkāmi. Atha bodhisatto taṃ gahetvā nerañjarāya tīre suppatiṭṭhite nāma titthe ekatālaṭṭhippamāṇe ekūnapaññāsapiṇḍe karonto paribhuñji, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “visākhāpuṇṇamāyaṃ uruvelagāme sujātāya dvinnaṃ pakkhittadibbojaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā”ti. Tattha sujātāyāti āyasmato yasattherassa mātubhūtāya pacchā saraṇagamanaṭṭhāne etadaggappattāya sujātāya nāma seṭṭhibhariyāya. Aṅgamaṅgānusārino [V 1.0209] rasassa sāro upatthambhabalakaro bhūtanissito eko viseso ojā nāma, sā divi bhavā pakkhittā etthāti pakkhittadibbojo, taṃ. Pātabbo ca so asitabbo cāti pāyāso, rasaṃ katvā pivituṃ, ālopaṃ katvā ca bhuñjituṃ yutto bhojanaviseso, madhunā sitto pāyāso madhupāyāso, taṃ.

At Uruvelā, it is said, in the army market town, a young girl named Sujātā, the daughter of a householder, having reached marriageable age, made an aspiration at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā river: “If I, having gone to a family of equal birth, should obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I will make a votive offering with milk-rice.” Her aspiration was fulfilled. She had seven cows fed in a licorice forest, and having obtained their female calves, had them fed in the same way, and again their female calves in the same way. Thus, from cows descended through a lineage of seven generations of daughters and granddaughters, she took the milk and began to cook milk-rice. At that moment, Mahābrahmā held a white parasol of three yojanas above, Sakka, king of the devas, kindled the fire, and the devas placed therein the nutritive essences existing in the entire world. The milk-rice cooked, swirling to the right. She, having given it to the Bodhisatta together with the golden bowl worth one hundred thousand, departed. Then the Bodhisatta took it and, on the bank of the Nerañjarā river at the ford named Suppatiṭṭhita, made forty-nine morsels the size of a palmyra fruit stone and partook of it. In reference to that it was said: “On the full-moon day of Visākhā, in the village of Uruvelā, having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice with divine nutritive essence placed in it by Sujātā.” Therein, “by Sujātā” means by the wife of the merchant named Sujātā, who became the mother of the venerable elder Yasa, and who later, in the matter of taking refuge, attained the foremost place. A certain special quality called ojā (nutritive essence) is the essence of flavor that pervades the major and minor limbs, is a supporter and strength-giver, and is based on the primary elements. That nutritive essence, being of the heavens, was placed herein, thus it is called pakkhittadibboja (that which has divine nutritive essence placed in it). It is both drinkable and edible, thus it is pāyāsa: a special kind of food suitable to be drunk as a liquid and to be eaten as morsels. The pāyāsa sprinkled with honey is madhupāyāsa. That.

Tato nerañjarāya tīre mahāsālavane nānāsamāpattīhi divāvihārassa katattā “sāyanhasamaye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vitthāro tattha tattha gahetabbo. Dakkhiṇuttarenāti divāvihārato bodhiyā pavisanamaggaṃ sandhāyāha, ujukaṃ dakkhiṇuttaragatena devatāhi alaṅkatena maggenāti attho[M 1.0240]. Evampi vadanti “dakkhiṇuttarenāti dakkhiṇapacchimuttarena ādiavasānagahaṇena majjhimassāpi gahitattā, tathā luttapayogassa ca dassanato. Evañhi sati ‘dakkhiṇapacchimuttaradisābhāgena bodhimaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā tiṭṭhatī’ti (jā. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā) jātakanidāne vuttavacanena sametī”ti. Dakkhiṇadisato gantabbo uttaradisābhāgo dakkhiṇuttaro, tena pavisitvāti apare. Keci pana “uttarasaddo cettha maggavācako. Yadi hi disāvācako bhaveyya, ‘dakkhiṇuttarāyā’ti vadeyyā”ti, taṃ na “uttarena nadī sīdā, gambhīrā duratikkamā”tiādinā disāvācakassāpi enayogassa dassanato, uttarasaddassa ca maggavācakassa anāgatattā. Apica disābhāgaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Disābhāgopi hi disā evāti. Atha antarāmagge sotthiyena nāma tiṇahārakabrāhmaṇena dinnā aṭṭha kusatiṇamuṭṭhiyo gahetvā asitañcanagirisaṅkāsaṃ sabbabodhisattānamassāsajananaṭṭhāne samāviruḷhaṃ bodhiyā maṇḍanabhūtaṃ bodhimaṇḍamupagantvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇadisābhāge aṭṭhāsi, so pana padeso paduminipatte udakabindu viya pakampittha, tato pacchimadisābhāgaṃ, uttaradisābhāgañca gantvā tiṭṭhantepi mahāpurise tatheva te akampiṃsu, tato “nāyaṃ sabbopi padeso mama guṇaṃ sandhāretuṃ samattho”ti puratthimadisābhāgamagamāsi, tattha pallaṅkappamāṇaṃ niccalamahosi, tasseva ca nippariyāyena bodhimaṇḍasamaññā, mahāpuriso “idaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanaṭṭhāna”nti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā pubbuttaradisābhāge ṭhito tattha akampanappadese tāni tiṇāni agge gahetvā sañcālesi, tāvadeva cuddasahattho pallaṅko ahosi, tānipi tiṇāni vicittākārena tūlikāya lekhā gahitāni viya ahesuṃ. So tattha tisandhipallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā caturaṅgikaṃ vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi, tamatthaṃ saṅkhipitvā dassento “bodhimaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā”tiādimāha.

Then, because he had spent the day in various meditative attainments on the bank of the Nerañjarā River in the great sāla grove, it is said, 'in the evening time,' etc. The details should be understood from the relevant contexts. 'By way of the south-north' refers to the path leading from the day-dwelling to the Bodhi tree, meaning the straight path, adorned by deities, that goes from south to north. Some also say: '“South-north” means south-west-north, as the middle is also included by taking the beginning and end, and because an elided usage is seen. For this being so, it aligns with the statement in the Jātaka Nidāna: “Having entered the Bodhi platform through the south-west-north direction, he stood.”' Others say: 'The northern part to be gone to from the southern direction is the south-north; having entered by that...' Some, however, say: 'Here the word “uttara” denotes a path. For if it were a word denoting a direction, one would say “dakkhiṇuttarāya”.' That is not so, because the instrumental ending is seen even for a word denoting a direction, as in 'To the north, the river Sīdā, deep and hard to cross,' etc., and because the word “uttara” denoting a path is not found. Moreover, this was spoken with reference to a directional portion, for a directional portion is indeed a direction. Then, on the way, a grass-carrier brahmin named Sotthiya offered eight handfuls of kusa grass. Taking them, the Great Being approached the Bodhi platform—which resembled a mountain of black collyrium, was a place that brings solace to all Bodhisattas, and was an adornment for the Bodhi—and circumambulated it three times. He stood in the southern quarter, but that spot trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Then, when the Great Being went to the western and northern quarters and stood, those places also shook in the same way. Then, thinking, 'This entire place is not capable of sustaining my virtue,' he went to the eastern quarter. There, a space the size of a seat became unmoving. And that very spot is, in the primary sense, called the Bodhi platform. The Great Being, having made the resolution, 'This is the place for the destruction of defilements,' stood in the north-eastern quarter. There, in that unshakeable spot, taking that grass by the tips, he scattered it. Instantly, a fourteen-cubit seat appeared. That grass, too, appeared in a variegated pattern, as if lines had been drawn with a brush. There, having folded his legs into the three-jointed cross-legged posture, making the meditation on loving-kindness endowed with four factors his forerunner, he resolved upon the fourfold energy and sat down. The commentator, summarizing and showing that meaning, said, 'Having entered the Bodhi platform,' etc.

Tattha bodhi vuccati arahattamaggañāṇaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇañca, sā maṇḍati thāmagatatāya pasīdati [V 1.0210] etthāti bodhimaṇḍo, nippariyāyena yathāvuttappadeso, pariyāyena pana idha dumarājā. Tathā hi ācariyānandattherena vuttaṃ “bodhimaṇḍasaddopaṭhamābhisambuddhaṭṭhāne eva daṭṭhabbo, na yattha katthaci bodhirukkhassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne”ti, taṃ.

There, 'bodhi' is said to be the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience. It is the Bodhimaṇḍa because herein that bodhi becomes clear (maṇḍati), that is, serene (pasīdati), having reached its full strength. In the primary sense, it is the aforesaid place; but in the secondary sense, here it means the king of trees. For so it was stated by the teacher, the Elder Ānanda: 'The term “bodhimaṇḍa” should be understood as referring only to the place of the first full awakening, not to just any place where a Bodhi tree is established.'

Māravijayasabbaññutaññāṇapaṭilābhādīhi [M 1.0241] bhagavantaṃ assāsetīti assattho. Āpubbañhi sāsasaddaṃ anusiṭṭhitosanesu icchanti, yaṃ tu loke “caladalo, kuñjarāsano” tipi vadanti. Accuggatabhāvena, ajeyyabhūmisīsagatabhāvena, sakalasabbaññuguṇapaṭilābhaṭṭhānaviruḷhabhāvena ca dumānaṃ rājāti dumarājā, assattho ca so dumarājā cāti assatthadumarājā taṃ. Dvinnaṃ ūrujāṇusandhīnaṃ, ūrumūlakaṭisandhissa ca vasena tayo sandhayo, saṇṭhānavasena vā tayo koṇā yassāti tisandhi, sveva pallaṅko ūrubaddhāsanaṃ parisamantato aṅkanaṃ āsananti atthena ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ, dvibhāvañca katvā, tīhi vā sandhīhi lakkhito pallaṅko tisandhipallaṅko, taṃ. Ābhujitvāti ābandhitvā, ubho pāde samañchite katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vitthāro sāmaññaphalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.216) āgamissati. Attā, mitto, majjhatto, verīti catūsupi samappavattanavasena caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ. “Caturaṅgasamannāgata”nti idaṃ pana “vīriyādhiṭṭhāna”nti etenāpi yojetabbaṃ. Tampi hi –

Because it comforts the Blessed One through the conquest of Māra, the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience, and so on, it is called 'Assattha.' For they desire the word 'sāsa' with the prefix 'ā' in the senses of instruction and delighting; it is this which in the world they also call 'trembling-leaved' and 'elephant-seated.' Because of its extremely lofty nature, because it stands at the head of unconquerable ground, and because it grew in the place for the attainment of all the qualities of an omniscient one, it is the king of trees (dumarājā). That Assattha is also the king of trees, hence 'Assattha-dumarājā.' Due to the two joints of the thighs and knees, and the joint at the base of the thigh and hip, there are three joints (tisandhi). Or, because it has three corners in terms of its shape, it is 'three-jointed.' That very cross-legged posture (pallaṅka) is a seat bound by the thighs; in the sense of 'a seat marked all around,' the 'ra' is changed to 'la' and doubled to form 'pallaṅka.' Or, a cross-legged posture marked by three joints is a 'tisandhipallaṅka.' 'Having folded' means 'having bound,' that is to say, 'having made both legs drawn in.' The details will come in the commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. The meditation on loving-kindness is endowed with four factors by being equally applied to all four: oneself, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy. This phrase 'endowed with four factors' should also be connected with 'the resolve on energy.' For that too—

Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatu, upasussatu sarīre maṃsalohitaṃ, yaṃ taṃ purisathāmena purisavīriyena purisaparakkamena pattabbaṃ, na taṃ apāpuṇitvā vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 1.266; a. ni. 3.51; a. ni. 8.13; mahāni. 17, 196) –

“Willingly, let skin, sinews, and bones remain; let flesh and blood dry up in my body; but there will be no stopping of energy until I have attained that which is to be attained by a man's strength, a man's energy, and a man's striving.”

Vuttanayena caturaṅgasamannāgatameva.

is endowed with the four factors in the manner described.

Cuddasa hatthā vitthatappamāṇabhāvena yassāti cuddasahattho. Parisamantato aṅkīyate lakkhīyate paricchedavasenāti pallaṅko ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ, tassa ca dvittaṃ katvā. Apica “idaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanaṭṭhāna”nti aṭṭhakathāsu vacanato pallaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ karoti etthāti pallaṅko niggahitāgamavasena, aluttasamāsavasena vā, cuddasahattho ca so pallaṅko ca, sveva uttamaṭṭhena patthanīyaṭṭhena ca varoti cuddasahatthapallaṅkavaro, tattha gato pavatto nisinno tathā. Cuddasahatthatā cettha vitthāravasena gahetabbā. Tāniyeva [M 1.0242] hi tiṇāni aparimitapuññānubhāvato cuddasahatthavitthatapallaṅkabhāvena pavattāni, na ca tāni aṭṭhamuṭṭhippamāṇāni cuddasahatthaaccuggatāni sambhavanti[V 1.0211]. Tatoyeva ca idha “tiṇasantharaṃ santharitvā”ti vuttaṃ, dhammapadaṭṭhakathādīsu ca “tiṇāni santharitvā…pe… puratthimābhimukho nisīditvā”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.sāriputtheravaṇṇanā; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā). Aññattha ca “tiṇāsane cuddasahatthasammate”ti. Keci pana “accuggatabhāveneva cuddasahattho”ti yathā tathā parikappanāvasena vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ yathāvuttena kāraṇena, sādhakena ca viruddhattā. Kāmañca manorathapūraṇiyā caturaṅguttaravaṇṇanāya “tikkhattuṃ bodhiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha cuddasahatthubbedhe ṭhāne tiṇasantharaṃ santharitvā caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nisinnakālato”ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.33) pāṭho dissati, tathāpi tattha ubbedhasaddo vitthāravācakoti veditabbo, yathā “tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho, uddhamāhu sahassadhā”ti (jā. 1.3.40) mahāpanādajātake. Tathā hi tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedhoti vitthārato soḷasakaṇḍapātavitthāro ahosī”ti (jātaka aṭṭha. 2-302 piṭṭhe). Aññathā hi ākāseyeva ukkhipitvā tiṇasantharaṇaṃ kataṃ, na acalapadeseti attho āpajjeyya santharaṇakiriyādhārabhāvato tassa, so cattho anadhippeto aññattha anāgatattāti.

Because it has a measure of fourteen cubits in width, it is called 'fourteen-cubited.' It is called 'pallaṅka' because it is marked and delineated all around by way of demarcation, by changing the letter 'ra' to 'la' and doubling it. Furthermore, according to the commentaries, since it is said, 'This is the place for the destruction of defilements,' 'pallaṅka' means 'that which accomplishes the destruction of defilements here,' either by way of the arrival of a nasal sound or as an unelided compound. And that fourteen-cubit pallaṅka is 'vara' (excellent) in the supreme sense and in the sense of being wished for, hence 'the excellent fourteen-cubit pallaṅka.' Having gone there, having arisen there, he was seated thus. Here, the state of being fourteen cubits should be understood in terms of width. Indeed, those very grasses, by the power of immeasurable merit, arose as a pallaṅka fourteen cubits in width; and those grasses, being of the measure of eight handfuls, did not become fourteen cubits high. For this reason, it is said here, 'having spread a grass mat,' and in the Dhammapada commentary and elsewhere, 'having spread the grasses... facing east, he sat down.'
