And elsewhere, 'on a grass seat considered to be fourteen cubits.' Some, however, say, 'It is fourteen cubits only by way of height,' speaking by way of whatever conjecture. That should not be accepted for the reason stated and because it contradicts the evidence. Although in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Caturaṅguttara, the passage appears: 'Having circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times, ascending the Bodhi platform, spreading a grass mat on a spot fourteen ubbedha in measure, and resolving upon the fourfold exertion, from the time he sat down,' nevertheless, it should be known that there the word 'ubbedha' denotes width, just as in the Mahāpanāda Jātaka: 'Sixteen ubbedha across, a thousand high, they say.' For so it is said in its commentary: '"Sixteen ubbedha across" means it was sixteen arrow-falls in width.' For otherwise, the meaning would result that the spreading of grass was done by lifting it up into the sky itself, and not on a firm place—because that firm place is the support for the act of spreading; and that meaning is not intended, as it does not occur elsewhere.

Rajatakkhandhaṃ piṭṭhito katvā viyāti sambandho. Atthanti pacchimapabbataṃ. Mārabalanti māraṃ, mārabalañca, mārassa vā sāmatthiyaṃ. Pubbenivāsanti pubbe nivutthakkhandhaṃ. Dibbacakkhunti dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ. “Kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4) jarāmaraṇamukhena paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāretvā. Ānāpānacatutthajjhānanti etthāpi “sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇa”nti vibhattivipariṇāmaṃ katvā yojetabbaṃ. Tampi hi buddhānamāciṇṇamevāti vadanti. Pādakaṃ katvāti kāraṇaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṃ vā katvā. “Vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvāti chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena āsavakkhayañāṇasaṅkhātamahāvajirañāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpanavasena vipassanaṃ bhāvetvā. Sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamāya anupadadhammavipassanāvasena anekākāravokāre saṅkhāre sammasato chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena pavattaṃ vipassanāñāṇampi hi “mahāvajirañāṇa”nti [M 1.0243] vuccati, catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyāya devasikaṃ vaḷañjanakasamāpattīnaṃ purecarānucarañāṇampi. Idha pana maggañāṇameva, visesato ca aggamaggañāṇaṃ, tasmā tasseva vipassanāgabbhabhāvo veditabboti. Sabbabuddhaguṇeti sabbaññutādiniravasesabuddhaguṇe. Tassā pādakaṃ katvā samādhi nivattoti vuttaṃ “idamassa paññākicca”nti. Assāti bhagavato.

The connection should be made as: 'as if having placed the mass of silver behind his back.' 'Atthaṃ' means the western mountain. 'Mārabalaṃ' means Māra, Māra's army, or Māra's power. 'Pubbenivāsaṃ' means the aggregates previously dwelt in. 'Dibbacakkhuṃ' means the knowledge of the divine eye. Beginning with 'This world has indeed fallen into hardship,' it means having directed knowledge to the conditional relations, with aging and death as the entry point. Here too, in the phrase 'the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing,' it should be connected by changing the case ending to mean 'practiced by all Buddhas.' For they say that this too is indeed practiced by the Buddhas. 'Having made it a foundation' means having made it a cause or a basis. 'Having developed insight' means having cultivated insight by way of causing the grasping of the womb of the great diamond knowledge—called the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—which has thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis as its entry point. Indeed, for the attainment of omniscient knowledge, for one contemplating conditioned formations, which are mixed with manifold aspects, by way of insight into phenomena group by group, the insight knowledge that proceeds by way of thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis is also called 'great diamond knowledge,' as is the preceding and succeeding knowledge of the daily attainments for use, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand koṭis. Here, however, it is only path knowledge that is called 'great diamond knowledge,' and especially the supreme path knowledge. Therefore, its nature as the womb of insight should be known. 'All the qualities of the Buddhas' refers to omniscience and the other unreserved qualities of the Buddhas. Having made that insight the foundation, concentration turned away; for this reason it is said, 'This is the task of his wisdom.' 'Assa' refers to 'of the Blessed One.'

“Tattha yathā hatthe”tiādinā upamāya pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ. Hattheti hatthapasate, karapuṭe vā. Pātiyanti [V 1.0212] sarāvake. Ghaṭeti udakaharaṇaghaṭe. Dvattiṃsadoṇagaṇhanappamāṇaṃ kuṇḍaṃ kolambo. Tato mahatarā cāṭi. Tatopi mahatī mahākumbhī. Soṇḍī kusobbho. Nadībhāgo kandaro. Cakkavāḷapādesu samuddo cakkavāḷamahāsamuddo. Sinerupādake mahāsamuddeti sīdantarasamuddaṃ sandhāyāha. “Pātiya”ntiādināpi tadevatthaṃ pakārantarena vibhāveti. Parittaṃ hoti yathāti sambandho. Yassā pāḷiyā atthavibhāvanatthāya yā saṃvaṇṇanā vuttā, tadeva tassā guṇabhāvena dassetuṃ “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha.

There, by the simile beginning with 'just as in the hand,' a clarification is made. 'In the hand' means in the outstretched hand, or in the cupped hands. 'In a bowl' means in a small cup. 'In a pot' means in a water-carrying pot. A basin of a measure that holds thirty-two doṇas is a 'kolamba.' Larger than that is a 'cāṭi.' Even larger than that is a 'mahākumbhī.' A pool is a 'kusobbha.' A river-gorge is a 'kandara.' The ocean at the foot of the Cakkavāḷa is the 'great Cakkavāḷa ocean.' The phrase 'in the great ocean at the foot of Sineru' is said referring to the Sīdantara ocean. Also by the phrase beginning 'in a bowl,' it clarifies that very meaning in another way. The connection should be made as 'just as it becomes small.' The phrase beginning 'therefore he said' was spoken in order to present that very Pāḷi text—for the clarification of whose meaning the commentary was spoken—as a quality of that commentary. Thus it should be understood everywhere by the wise.

“Duve puthujjanā”tiādi puthujjanesu labbhamānavibhāgadassanatthameva vuttaṃ, na pana mūlapariyāyasaṃvaṇṇanādīsu (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2) viya puthujjanavisesaniddhāraṇatthaṃ niravasesaputhujjanasseva idha adhippetattā. Sabbopi hi puthujjano bhagavato upariguṇe vibhāvetuṃ na sakkoti, tiṭṭhatu tāva puthujjano, ariyasāvakapaccekabuddhānampi avisayā eva buddhaguṇā. Tathā hi vakkhati “sotāpanno”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7). Gottasambandhatāya ādiccassa sūriyadevaputtassa bandhūti ādiccabandhu, tena vuttaṃ niddese –

“Two ordinary people,” etc., is said merely for the purpose of showing the distinction that is found among ordinary persons, and not, as in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta and other texts, for the purpose of determining a specific type of ordinary person, because here the ordinary person without remainder is intended. Indeed, no ordinary person is able to make manifest the higher qualities of the Blessed One; let alone an ordinary person, the qualities of the Buddha are beyond the range even of noble disciples and Paccekabuddhas. For thus it will be said: “A stream-enterer,” etc. By connection of clan, he is a kinsman of Ādicca, the son of the sun-god, thus he is Ādiccabandhu. Therefore, it is said in the Niddesa—

“Ādicco vuccati sūriyo. Sūriyo gotamo gottena, bhagavāpi gotamo gottena, bhagavā sūriyassa gottañātako gottabandhu, tasmā buddho ādiccabandhū”ti (mahāni. 150; cūḷani. 99).

“The sun is called Ādicca. The sun is Gotama by clan; the Blessed One is also Gotama by clan. The Blessed One is a kinsman of the sun by clan, a relative by clan; therefore, the Buddha is Ādiccabandhu.”

Saddavidū pana “buddhassādiccabandhunā”ti pāṭhamicchanti. Ādiccassa bandhunā gottena samāno gottasaṅkhāto bandhu yassa, buddho ca so ādiccabandhu cāti katvā. Yasmā pana khandhakathādikosallenāpi upakkilesānupakkilesānaṃ jānanahetubhūtaṃ bāhusaccaṃ hoti, yathāha –

However, grammarians prefer the reading “buddhassādiccabandhunā.” This is construed as: He for whom there is a kinsman, designated as a clan, which is the same by clan as that of the kinsman Ādicca; thus he is both the Buddha and Ādiccabandhu. Furthermore, because great learning, which is a cause for knowing the defilements and minor defilements, also comes through skill in the discourse on the aggregates and so on, as it is said—

“Kittāvatā [M 1.0244] nu kho bhante bahussuto hotīti? Yato kho bhikkhu khandhakusalo hoti. Dhātu…pe… āyatana…pe… paṭiccasamuppādakusalo hoti, ettāvatā kho bhikkhu bahussuto hotī”ti.

“Venerable sir, to what extent is one truly of great learning? When a monk is skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, and skilled in dependent origination, to that extent, a monk is of great learning.”

Tasmā “yassa khandhadhātuāyatanādīsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena cettha yāva paṭiccasamuppādā saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Atthassa paripucchanaṃ paripucchā. Aṭṭhakathāvasena atthassa sotadvārapaṭibaddhatākaraṇaṃ savanaṃ. Byañjanatthānaṃ sunikkhepasunayanena dhammassa pariharaṇaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sutadhātaparicitānaṃ vitakkanaṃ manasānupekkhanaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ.

Therefore, it was said, “For whom in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, etc.” And here, by the word “ādi” (etc.), he includes up to dependent origination. Therein, making it arise in speech is learning by heart (uggaha). Repeatedly questioning the meaning is inquiry (paripucchā). By way of the commentary, making the meaning connect with the ear-door is listening (savana). Bearing the Dhamma in mind through the good placement and guidance of the letter and the meaning is retention (dhāraṇa). Thus, thinking about and mentally examining the teachings that have been heard, retained, and practiced is reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).

Evaṃ [V 1.0213] pabhedaṃ dassetvā vacanatthampi dasseti “duvidho”tiādinā. Puthūnanti anekavidhānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ. Puthujjanantogadhattāti bahūnaṃ janānaṃ abbhantare samavarodhabhāvato puthujjanoti sambandho. Puthucāyaṃ janoti puthu eva visuṃyeva ayaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gato. Itīti tasmā puthujjanoti sambandho. Evaṃ gāthābandhena saṅkhepato dassitamatthaṃ “so hī”tiādinā vivarati. “Nānappakārāna”nti iminā puthu-saddo idha bahvatthoti dasseti.

Having thus shown the classification, he also shows the etymological meaning with “of two kinds,” etc. “Puthūnaṃ” means “of many kinds” of defilements, etc. “Because of being included among ordinary persons” (puthujjanantogadhatta): the connection should be made that one is a puthujjana because of being included within many “janas” (beings). “And this is a separate person” (puthu c'āyaṃ jano): this person is counted as separate, indeed distinct (from the noble ones). Thus, the connection should be made: therefore, one is a puthujjana. He clarifies the meaning thus shown briefly in verse form with “for he,” etc. By this “of various kinds,” he shows that the word “puthu” here has the meaning of “many.”

Ādi-saddena saṅgahitamatthaṃ, tadatthassa ca sādhakaṃ ambasecanagarusinānanayena niddesapāḷiyā dassento “yathāhā”tiādimāha. Avihatā sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo, puthu bahukā tā etesanti puthuavihatasakkāyadiṭṭhikā, etena avihatattā puthu sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo janenti, puthūhi vā sakkāyadiṭṭhīhi janitāti atthaṃ dasseti. Avihatatthameva vā janasaddo vadati, tasmā puthu sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo janenti na vihananti, janā vā avihatā puthu sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo etesanti atthaṃ dassetītipi vaṭṭati, visesanaparanipātanañcettha daṭṭhabbaṃ yathā “agyāhito”ti. “Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā”ti etena puthu bahavo janā satthāro etesanti nibbacanaṃ dassitaṃ. Puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti ettha pana kammakilesehi janetabbā, jāyanti vā sattā etthāti janā, gatiyo, puthu sabbā eva janā gatiyo etesanti vacanattho. “Puthu nānābhisaṅkhāre [M 1.0245] abhisaṅkharontī”ti etena ca jāyanti etehi sattāti janā, puññābhisaṅkhārādayo, puthu nānāvidhā janā saṅkhārā etesaṃ vijjanti, puthu vā nānābhisaṅkhāre janenti abhisaṅkharontīti atthamāha. Tato paraṃ pana “puthu nānāoghehi vuyhantī”tiādiatthattayaṃ janenti etehi sattāti janā, kāmoghādayo, rāgasantāpādayo, rāgapariḷāhādayo ca, sabbepi vā kilesapariḷāhā. Puthu nānappakārā te etesaṃ vijjanti, tehi vā janenti vuyhanti, santāpenti, pariḍahanti cāti nibbacanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. “Rattā giddhā”tiādi pariyāyavacanaṃ.

Wishing to show, by means of the Niddesa Pāḷi and by the method of Ambasecanagarusināna, the meaning summarized by the word 'ādi' and the canonical text that establishes that meaning, he said, 'as it is said,' etc. 'Unabandoned identity views': for them there are many of these, hence they are puthuavihatasakkāyadiṭṭhikā (those with many unabandoned identity views). By this he shows the meaning that, because they are unabandoned, they generate many identity views, or that they are generated by many identity views. Alternatively, the word jana expresses the meaning of 'unabandoned'. Therefore, they generate (janenti) many identity views and do not abandon (na vihananti) them. Or, it shows the meaning that for them there are many unabandoned (janā = avihatā) identity views; this meaning is also suitable. And here, the post-positioning of the adjective should be seen, as in agyāhito. By 'looking up to the faces of many teachers' (puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā), the derivation is shown: for them there are many people (janā) as teachers. As for 'not risen from all the many destinies' (puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitā), here janā means destinies (gatiyo), because they are to be produced by kamma and defilements, or because beings are born (jāyanti) in them. The etymological meaning is: for them there are all the many destinies (janā). And by 'they form the many various formations' (puthu nānābhisaṅkhāre abhisaṅkharontī), janā means meritorious formations, etc., because beings are born from them. The meaning is: for them there exist many various kinds of formations (janā), or they generate and form many various formations. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent threefold meaning beginning with 'they are swept away by the many various floods' (puthu nānāoghehi vuyhantī), janā refers to the floods of sensuality, etc., the torments of lust, etc., and the burnings of lust, etc., or all the burnings of the defilements, because by these, beings are produced. The derivation is stated to show that for them there exist many various kinds of these things, or that by them beings are produced, swept away, tormented, and burned. 'Infatuated, greedy' (rattā giddhā), etc., are synonyms.

Api ca rattāti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmakarena chandarāgena rattā. Giddhāti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhigijjhanena giddhā. Gathitāti ganthitā viya dummocanīyabhāvena tattha paṭibaddhā. Mucchitāti kilesāvisanavasena visaññībhūtā viya anaññakiccamohaṃ samāpannā. Ajjhosannāti anaññāsādhāraṇe viya katvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā ṭhitā. Laggāti gāvo kaṇṭake viya āsattā, mahāpalipe vā patanena nāsikaggapalipannapuriso viya uddharitumasakkuṇeyyabhāvena nimuggā. Laggitāti makkaṭālepena viya makkaṭo pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena āsaṅgitā, palibuddhāti sambaddhā, upaddutā vāti ayamattho [V 1.0214] aṅguttaraṭīkāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.51) vutto. Etena jāyatīti jano, “rāgo gedho”ti evamādiko, puthu nānāvidho jano rāgādiko etesaṃ, puthūsu vā pañcasu kāmaguṇesu janā rattā giddhā…pe… palibuddhāti atthaṃ dasseti.

Furthermore, 'rattā' means impassioned by sensual passion, which causes the mind to alter, like a cloth by a dye. 'Giddhā' means greedy by its nature of desiring, by craving. 'Gathitā' means bound as if tied in a knot, attached there by its state of being difficult to untie. 'Mucchitā' means stupefied by the power of the poison of defilements, as if having become unconscious, having fallen into a delusion devoid of any other task. 'Ajjhosannā' means having made it as if not shared with another, having swallowed it, having brought it to completion, they abide. 'Laggā' means stuck like cattle on a thorn; or, by falling into a great swamp, they are submerged by the state of being unable to be pulled out, like a man sunk up to the tip of his nose. 'Laggitā' means stuck by the power of the five faculties, like a monkey by birdlime. 'Palibuddhā' means bound, or troubled—this meaning is stated in the Aṅguttara-ṭīkā. By this, it shows the meaning that 'jana' is so called because it is born (jāyati), referring to lust, greed, and so forth; that for them, 'jana'—lust and so on—is diverse and varied; or that in the five diverse strands of sensual pleasure, people are impassioned, greedy... up to obstructed.

“Āvutā”tiādipi pariyāyavacanameva. Apica “āvutāti āvaritā. Nivutāti nivāritā. Ophutāti paliguṇṭhitā, pariyonaddhā vā. Pihitāti pidahitā. Paṭicchannāti chāditā. Paṭikujjitāti heṭṭhāmukhajātā”ti tattheva (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.51) vuttaṃ. Ettha ca janenti etehīti janā, nīvaraṇā, puthu nānāvidhā janā nīvaraṇā etesaṃ, puthūhi vā nīvaraṇehi janā āvutā…pe… paṭikujjitāti nibbacanaṃ dasseti. Puthūsu nīcadhammasamācāresu jāyati, puthūnaṃ vā abbhantare jano antogadho, puthu vā bahuko janoti atthaṃ dasseti “puthūna”ntiādinā, etena ca tatiyapādaṃ vivarati, samattheti vā. “Puthuvā”tiādinā pana catutthapādaṃ. Puthu visaṃsaṭṭho eva jano puthujjanoti ayañhettha vacanattho.

'Āvutā' and so forth are merely synonymous terms. Furthermore, 'āvutā' means obstructed; 'nivutā' means hindered; 'ophutā' means enveloped, or enmeshed; 'pihitā' means closed; 'paṭicchannā' means concealed; 'paṭikujjitā' means having become face-down—as stated in that very text. And here, 'janā' means they are generated by these, that is, the hindrances. Or, for them, 'janā'—the hindrances—are diverse and varied. Or, it shows the etymology that people are obstructed... up to inverted, by the many hindrances. It is generated among the many who have base conduct; or 'jana' is included within the many; or 'puthu' means many people—this meaning is shown by 'puthūnaṃ' and so on. And by this, the third line is explained, or established. By 'puthuvā' and so on, however, the fourth line is explained. A 'puthujjana' is a person who is indeed unassociated with the noble ones; this is the meaning of the word here.

Yehi [M 1.0246] guṇavisesehi nimittabhūtehi bhagavati “tathāgato”ti ayaṃ samaññā pavattā, taṃ dassanatthaṃ “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekopi hi saddo anekapavattinimittamadhikicca anekadhā atthappakāsako, bhagavato ca sabbepi nāmasaddā anekaguṇanemittikāyeva. Yathāha –

To show those distinctive qualities, which have become the cause, by which the designation 'Tathāgata' for the Blessed One has arisen, it is said: 'The Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons,' and so on. For even a single word, based on many causes for its usage, is an indicator of meaning in many ways; and all the Blessed One's names indeed have many qualities as their cause. As it is said:

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti. (dha. sa. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 57; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.76; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.413);

Countless are the names of the Great Sage, according to his virtues; from a quality a name may be derived, even a thousand names.

Kāni pana tānīti anuyoge sati paṭhamaṃ tassarūpaṃ saṅkhepato uddisitvā “katha”ntiādinā niddisati. Tathā āgatoti ettha ākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo. Sāmaññajotanāya visesāvaṭṭhānato, visesatthinā ca sāmaññasaddassāpi visesattheyeva anupayujjitabbato paṭipadāgamanattho āgata saddo daṭṭhabbo, na ñāṇagamanattho tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.170; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.43; itivu. aṭṭha. 38; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.37; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 2; mahāni. aṭṭha. 14) viya[V 1.0215], nāpi kāyagamanādi attho “āgato kho mahāsamaṇo, māgadhānaṃ giribbaja”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 53) viya. Tattha yassa ākārassa niyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo, tadākāraṃ karuṇāpadhānattā tassa mahākaruṇāmukhena purimabuddhānaṃ āgamanapaṭipadāya udāharaṇavasena sāmaññato dassento “yathā sabbaloke”tiādimāha. Yaṃtaṃ-saddānaṃ ekantasambandhabhāvato cettha tathā-saddassatthadassane yathā-saddena attho vibhāvito. Tadeva vitthāreti “yathā vipassī bhagavā”tiādinā, vipassīādīnañcettha channaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ mahāpadānasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 2.4) sampahulaniddesena (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.sambahulaparicchedavaṇṇanā) supākaṭattā, āsannattā ca tesaṃ vasena taṃ paṭipadaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āgato yathā, tathā āgatoti sabbatra sambandho. “Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādināpi tadeva paṭiniddisati. Tattha yena abhinīhārenāti manussattaliṅgasampattihetusatthāradassanapabbajjāguṇasampattiadhikārachandānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena mahāpaṇidhānena[M 1.0247]. Sabbesañhi buddhānaṃ paṭhamapaṇidhānaṃ imināva nīhārena samijjhati. Abhinīhāroti cettha mūlapaṇidhānassetaṃ adhivacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But what are these? When there is such an inquiry, first their form is briefly stated, and then it is explained with 'how' and so on. Here, in 'tathā āgato', the word 'tathā' has the meaning of establishing a comparison by way of fixing the manner. Because a generality is indicated by establishing a specific, and because even a general word, when a specific meaning is intended, should be applied only in that specific sense, the word 'āgata' should be understood as meaning 'having come by way of practice,' not as 'having come by way of knowledge,' as in phrases like 'one who has come with such characteristics', nor does it have the meaning of physical arrival, as in 'the Great Ascetic has arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans'. There, the word 'tathā' has the meaning of establishing a comparison by way of fixing a certain manner. Showing that manner generally—because compassion is predominant—through great compassion as the means, by way of an example of the practice of arrival of previous Buddhas, he said, 'as in the whole world,' and so on. And here, because of the invariable connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ', in showing the meaning of the word 'tathā', the meaning is clarified by the word 'yathā'. This is elaborated with 'as the Blessed One Vipassī,' and so on. And here, it should be understood that he shows that practice by means of those six Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, beginning with Vipassī, because they are very well-known through the extensive description in the Mahāpadāna Sutta and elsewhere, and because they are recent. The connection should be made everywhere thus: 'As he has come, so he has come.' With 'What is meant?' and so on, he further explains the same. There, 'by which aspiration' means by the great aspiration endowed with eight factors, by way of: being human, possessing the male gender, possessing the supporting conditions, seeing a Teacher, going forth, possessing the special qualities, the undertaking, and the aspiration. For the first aspiration of all Buddhas succeeds only by this method. And here, it should be understood that this word 'abhinīhāra' is a designation for the root aspiration.

Evaṃ mahābhinīhāravasena “tathāgato”ti padassa atthaṃ dassetvā idāni pāramīpūraṇavasenapi dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. “Ettha ca suttantikānaṃ mahābodhiyānapaṭipadāya kosallajananatthaṃ pāramīsu ayaṃ vitthārakathā”tiādinā ācariyadhammapālattherena (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) yā pāramīsu vinicchayakathā vuttā, kiñcāpi sā amhehi idha vuccamānā ganthavitthārakarā viya bhavissati, yasmā panāyaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā etissaṃ pacchā pamādalekhavisodhanavasena, tadavasesatthapariyādānavasena ca pavattā, tasmā sāpi pāramīkathā idha vattabbāyevāti tato ceva cariyāpiṭakaṭṭhakathāto ca āharitvā yathārahaṃ gāthābandhehi samalaṅkaritvā atthamadhippāyañca visodhayamānā bhavissati. Kathaṃ?

Having thus shown the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata' by way of the great aspiration, now, in order to show it also by way of the fulfillment of the perfections, he stated what begins with 'Or else.' And here, 'For the purpose of generating skill in those who are masters of the Suttantas regarding the practice for attaining Great Enlightenment, this is the detailed discourse on the perfections,' and so on—this is the decisive discourse on the perfections that was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. Although that decisive discourse, if stated by us here, might seem to expand the text, yet since this sub-commentary proceeds after that one by way of correcting scribal errors due to negligence and by way of taking up the remaining meanings, therefore that discourse on the perfections must indeed be stated here. Thus, having brought it from that very source and from the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, and having adorned it well with verses as is appropriate, it will proceed, clarifying the meaning and the intention. How?

Kā panetā pāramiyo, kenaṭṭhena katīvidhā;

Ko ca tāsaṃ kamo kāni, lakkhaṇādīni sabbathā.

What, then, are these perfections? In what sense are they 'pāramī'? How many kinds are there? And what is their order? In every way, what are their characteristics and so forth?

Ko paccayo, saṃkileso, vodānaṃ paṭipakkhako;

Paṭipattivibhāgo ca, saṅgaho sampadā tathā.

What is the cause? What is the defilement? What is the purification? What is the opposing factor? What is the practice? And what is the division? And what is the summary? Furthermore, what is the accomplishment?

Kittakena [V 1.0216] sampādanaṃ, ānisaṃso ca kiṃ phalaṃ;

Pañhametaṃ vissajjitvā, bhavissati vinicchayo.

In how long is their accomplishment? And what is their benefit? What is their fruit? Having answered this question, there will be a decisive determination.

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ –

Therein, this is the answer:

Kā panetā pāramiyoti –

Regarding 'What, then, are these perfections?':

Taṇhāmānādimaññatra, upāyakusalena yā;

Ñāṇena pariggahitā, pāramī sā vibhāvitā.

That which, apart from craving, conceit, and so forth, is comprehended by the wisdom of one skilled in means—that is explained as a perfection.

Taṇhāmānādinā hi anupahatā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā dānādayo guṇasaṅkhātā etā kiriyā “pāramī”ti vibhāvitā.

For indeed, these actions, such as giving, which are reckoned as virtues, when unafflicted by craving, conceit, and so forth, and comprehended by the skill in means based on compassion, are explained as 'perfections'.

Kenaṭṭhena pāramiyoti –

Regarding 'In what sense are they perfections?':

Paramo uttamaṭṭhena, tassāyaṃ pāramī tathā;

Kammaṃ bhāvoti dānādi, taddhitato tidhā matā.

He is 'parama' (supreme) in the highest sense; 'pāramī' is that which is his. Likewise, it is his action or his state. Thus, by way of a taddhita derivative, it is understood in three ways.

Pūreti [M 1.0248] mavati pare, paraṃ majjati mayati;

Munāti minoti tathā, minātīti vā paramo.

Because he fulfills; because he binds others to himself; because he is exceedingly purified; because he goes to the supreme; because he comprehends; likewise, because he places [virtues in himself]; or because he destroys [defilements]—therefore, he is called 'parama' (supreme).

Pāre majjati sodheti, mavati mayatīti vā;

Māyeti taṃ vā munāti, minoti mināti tathā.

He is purified on the further shore and purifies others; or he binds, or he goes; or he causes them to go to it, or he comprehends it; he places them there, and likewise, he destroys [their defilements].

Pāramīti mahāsatto, vuttānusārato pana;

Taddhitatthattayeneva, pāramīti ayaṃ matā.

The great being is called 'pāramī'. Furthermore, following what has been said, this term 'pāramī' is known only through the three meanings of the taddhita derivative.

Dānasīlādiguṇavisesayogena hi sattuttamatāya mahābodhisatto paramo, tassa ayaṃ, bhāvo, kammanti vā pāramī, dānādikiriyā. Atha vā parati pūretīti paramo niruttinayena, dānādiguṇānaṃ pūrako, pālako ca bodhisatto, paramassa ayaṃ, bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī. Apica [V 1.0217] pare satte mavati attani bandhati guṇavisesayogena, paraṃ vā atirekaṃ majjati saṃkilesamalato, paraṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ visesena mayati gacchati, paraṃ vā lokaṃ pamāṇabhūtena ñāṇavisesena idhalokamiva munāti paricchindati, paraṃ vā ativiya sīlādiguṇagaṇaṃ attano santāne minoti pakkhipati, paraṃ vā attabhūtato dhammakāyato aññaṃ, paṭipakkhaṃ vā tadanatthakaraṃ kilesacoragaṇaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti paramo, mahāsatto, “paramassa aya”ntiādinā vuttanayena pāramī. Pāre vā nibbāne majjati sujjhati, satte ca sodheti, tattha vā satte mavati bandhati yojeti, taṃ vā mayati gacchati, satte ca māyeti gameti, taṃ vā yāthāvato munāti paricchindati, tattha vā satte minoti pakkhipati, tattha vā sattānaṃ kilesāriṃ mināti hiṃsatīti pāramī, mahāsatto, “tassa aya”ntiādinā dānādikiriyāva pāramīti. Iminā nayena pāramīnaṃ vacanattho veditabbo.

Indeed, because of being supreme among beings through his connection with the special virtues such as giving and morality, the Mahābodhisatta is 'parama' (supreme). 'Pāramī' is that which is his property, or his state, or his action, such as the act of giving. Alternatively, by way of etymology, he is 'parama' because he fulfills (pūreti); the Bodhisatta is the fulfiller and protector of virtues like giving. 'Pāramī' is the property, state, or action of the 'parama'. Furthermore, he is 'parama' because he binds (mavati) other beings to himself through his special virtues; or because he is exceedingly purified (majjati) from the stain of defilements; or because he especially goes (mayati) to the supreme Nibbāna; or because he comprehends (munāti) the next world as if it were this world with his special knowledge that is a standard of measure; or because he exceedingly places (minoti) the collection of virtues such as morality in his own continuum; or because he harms (mināti) the host of thieves, the defilements, which are other than and inimical to his own Dhammakāya. Thus he is 'parama', the great being. By the method stated, 'This is the property of the parama,' and so on, it is 'pāramī'. Or, it is 'pāramī' because he is purified (majjati) in the further shore, Nibbāna, and he purifies beings; or because he binds (mavati) and yokes beings there; or because he goes (mayati) to it, and causes beings to go (māyeti) to it; or because he comprehends (munāti) it as it really is; or because he places (minoti) beings there; or because he harms (mināti) the enemy of beings, the defilements, there. Thus the great being is 'pāramī'. By the method, 'This is his property,' and so on, the very action of giving and so forth is 'pāramī'. In this way, the etymological meaning of the perfections should be understood.

Katividhāti saṅkhepato dasavidhā, tā pana buddhavaṃsapāḷiyaṃ (bu. vaṃ. 1.76) sarūpato āgatāyeva. Yathāha “vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”ntiādi (bu. vaṃ. 2.116). Yathā cāha –

Regarding 'How many kinds?': In brief, they are tenfold. Indeed, they have come down in their own form in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi. As it is said: "Searching, at that time I saw, first, the perfection of giving," and so on. And as he also said:

“Kati nu kho bhante buddhakārakā dhammāti? Dasa kho sāriputta buddhakārakā dhammā, katame dasa? Dānaṃ kho sāriputta buddhakārako dhammo, sīlaṃ nekkhammaṃ paññā vīriyaṃ khanti saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0249] mettā upekkhā buddhakārako dhammo, ime kho sāriputta dasa buddhakārakā dhammāti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

"Venerable sir, how many qualities are there that make a Buddha?" "Sāriputta, there are ten qualities that make a Buddha. What are the ten? Sāriputta, giving is a quality that makes a Buddha; morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity are qualities that make a Buddha. These, Sāriputta, are the ten qualities that make a Buddha." This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:

‘Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññāvīriyena pañcamaṃ;

Khantisaccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhāti te dasā’ti”. (bu. vaṃ. 1.76);

"Giving and morality, renunciation, wisdom with energy as the fifth; patience, truth, resolution, loving-kindness and equanimity—these are the ten."

Keci pana “chabbidhā”ti vadanti, taṃ etāsaṃ saṅgahavasena vuttaṃ. So pana saṅgaho parato āvi bhavissati.

Some, however, say they are sixfold. That is stated by way of grouping them. That grouping, however, will become clear later.

Ko ca tāsaṃ kamoti ettha kamo nāma desanākkamo, so ca paṭhamasamādānahetuko, samādānaṃ pavicayahetukaṃ, iti yathā ādimhi paṭhamābhinīhārakāle pavicitā, samādinnā ca, tathā [V 1.0218] desitā. Yathāha “vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”ntiādi (bu. vaṃ. 2.116) tenetaṃ vuccati –

Regarding 'And what is their order?': Here, 'order' means the order of teaching, and that is caused by the initial undertaking. The undertaking is caused by investigation. Thus, in the way they were investigated and undertaken at the beginning, at the time of the first aspiration, in that way they were taught. As it is said: “Searching, at that time I saw, first, the perfection of giving,” and so on. Therefore, this is said:

“Paṭhamaṃ samādānatā-vasenāyaṃ kamo ruto;

Atha vā aññamaññassa, bahūpakāratopi cā”ti.

This order is taught, firstly, by way of the undertaking; or alternatively, also because of their great helpfulness to one another.

Tattha hi dānaṃ sīlassa bahūpakāraṃ, sukarañcāti taṃ ādimhi vuttaṃ. Dānaṃ pana sīlapariggahitaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsanti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlaṃ nekkhammapariggahitaṃ…pe… nekkhammaṃ paññāpariggahitaṃ…pe… paññā vīriyapariggahitā…pe… vīriyaṃ khantipariggahitaṃ…pe… khanti saccapariggahitā…pe… saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānapariggahitaṃ…pe… adhiṭṭhānaṃ mettāpariggahitaṃ…pe… mettā upekkhāpariggahitā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsāti mettānantaraṃ upekkhā vuttā. Upekkhā pana karuṇāpariggahitā, karuṇā ca upekkhāpariggahitāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ pana mahākāruṇikā bodhisattā sattesu upekkhakā hontīti? Upekkhitabbayuttakesu kañci kālaṃ upekkhakā honti, na pana sabbattha, sabbadā cāti keci. Apare pana na ca sattesu upekkhakā, sattakatesu pana vippakāresu upekkhakā hontīti, idamevettha yuttaṃ.

Herein, generosity is of great assistance to virtue and is easy to do—thus it was stated first. Furthermore, generosity when encompassed by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit—thus virtue was stated after generosity. Virtue when encompassed by renunciation... [etc.]... renunciation when encompassed by wisdom... [etc.]... wisdom when encompassed by energy... [etc.]... energy when encompassed by patience... [etc.]... patience when encompassed by truth... [etc.]... truth when encompassed by determination... [etc.]... determination when encompassed by loving-kindness... [etc.]... loving-kindness when encompassed by equanimity is of great fruit and great benefit—thus equanimity was stated after loving-kindness. Furthermore, equanimity should be understood as encompassed by compassion, and compassion as encompassed by equanimity. But how are Bodhisattas of great compassion equanimous towards beings? Some say: They are equanimous at certain times towards those who should be regarded with equanimity, but not everywhere and not always. Others, however, say: They are not equanimous towards beings, but are equanimous towards the misdeeds done by beings. This latter view is fitting here.

Aparo nayo –

Another approach:

Sabbasādhāraṇatādi-kāraṇehipi īritaṃ;

Dānaṃ ādimhi sesā tu, purimepi apekkhakā.

Generosity was taught at the beginning for reasons such as its being common to all; but the remaining perfections are dependent on the preceding ones.

Pacurajanesupi [M 1.0250] hi pavattiyā sabbasattasādhāraṇattā, appaphalattā, sukarattā ca dānaṃ ādimhi vuttaṃ. Sīlena dāyakapaṭiggāhakasuddhito parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato, kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato, bhogasampattihetuṃ vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānassānantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Nekkhammena sīlasampattisiddhito, kāyavacīsucaritaṃ vatvā manosucaritavacanato, visuddhasīlassa sukheneva jhānasamijjhanato, kammāparādhappahānena payogasuddhiṃ vatvā kilesāparādhappahānena āsayasuddhivacanato, vītikkamappahāne ṭhitassa pariyuṭṭhānappahānavacanato ca sīlassānantaraṃ nekkhammaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññāya nekkhammassa siddhiparisuddhito, jhānābhāve paññābhāvavacanato. Samādhipadaṭṭhānā hi paññā, paññāpaccupaṭṭhāno [V 1.0219] ca samādhi. Samathanimittaṃ vatvā upekkhānimittavacanato, parahitajjhānena parahitakaraṇūpāyakosallavacanato ca nekkhammassānantaraṃ paññā vuttā. Vīriyārambhena paññākiccasiddhito, sattasuññatādhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā sattahitāya ārambhassa acchariyatāvacanato, upekkhānimittaṃ vatvā paggahanimittavacanato, nisammakāritaṃ vatvā uṭṭhānavacanato ca. Nisammakārino hi uṭṭhānaṃ phalavisesamāvahatīti paññāyānantaraṃ vīriyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Indeed, generosity was stated first because it is practiced even among lowly people, is common to all beings, has little fruit, and is easy to do. After generosity, virtue was stated because, through virtue, there is purity of the giver and receiver; and because, having spoken of benefiting others, he then spoke of refraining from harming others; because, having spoken of the principle of action, he then spoke of the principle of non-transgression; and because, having spoken of the cause for the accomplishment of wealth, he then spoke of the cause for the accomplishment of good existence. After virtue, renunciation was stated because the accomplishment of virtue is perfected by renunciation; because, having spoken of good bodily and verbal conduct, he then spoke of good mental conduct; because for one of pure virtue, the attainment of jhāna is accomplished with ease; because, having spoken of the purity of endeavor through abandoning offenses of action, he then spoke of the purity of intention through abandoning offenses of defilement; and because for one established in the abandoning of transgression, he then spoke of the abandoning of obsession. After renunciation, wisdom was stated because the perfection and purity of renunciation is due to wisdom; and because, having spoken of the development of jhāna, he then spoke of the development of wisdom. For indeed, wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause, and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation. Because, having spoken of the sign of tranquility, he then spoke of the sign of equanimity; and because, through the jhāna for the welfare of others, he then spoke of skill in the means for acting for the welfare of others. After wisdom, energy was stated because the task of wisdom is accomplished by the undertaking of energy; because, having spoken of the patient acceptance of contemplating the doctrine of the emptiness of beings, he then spoke of the wondrous nature of the effort for the welfare of beings; because, having spoken of the sign of equanimity, he then spoke of the sign of exertion; and because, having spoken of acting with careful consideration, he then spoke of exertion. For indeed, the exertion of one who acts with careful consideration brings a special fruit.

Vīriyena titikkhāsiddhito. Vīriyavā hi āraddhavīriyattā sattasaṅkhārehi upanītaṃ dukkhaṃ abhibhuyya viharati. Vīriyassa titikkhālaṅkārabhāvato. Vīriyavato hi titikkhā sobhati. Paggahanimittaṃ vatvā samathanimittavacanato, accārambhena uddhaccadosappahānavacanato. Dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā hi uddhaccadoso pahīyati. Vīriyavato sātaccakaraṇavacanato. Khantibahulo hi anuddhato sātaccakārī hoti. Appamādavato parahitakiriyārambhe paccupakārataṇhābhāvavacanato. Yāthāvato dhammanijjhāne hi sati taṇhā na hoti. Parahitārambhe paramepi parakatadukkhasahanatāvacanato ca vīriyassānantaraṃ khanti vuttā. Saccena khantiyā cirādhiṭṭhānato, apakārino apakārakhantiṃ vatvā tadupakārakaraṇe avisaṃvādavacanato, khantiyā apavādavācāvikampanena bhūtavāditāya avijahanavacanato, sattasuññatādhamma-nijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā tadupabrūhitañāṇasaccassa vacanato ca khantiyānantaraṃ saccaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānena saccasiddhito. Acalādhiṭṭhānassa hi virati sijjhati. Avisaṃvāditaṃ vatvā [M 1.0251] tattha acalabhāvavacanato. Saccasandho hi dānādīsu paṭiññānurūpaṃ niccalo pavattati. Ñāṇasaccaṃ vatvā sambhāresu pavattiniṭṭhāpanavacanato. Yathābhūtañāṇavā hi bodhisambhāresu adhiṭṭhāti, te ca niṭṭhāpeti. Paṭipakkhehi akampiyabhāvato ca saccassānantaraṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Mettāya parahitakaraṇasamādānādhiṭṭhānasiddhito, adhiṭṭhānaṃ vatvā hitūpasaṃhāravacanato. Bodhisambhāre hi adhitiṭṭhamāno mettāvihārī hoti. Acalādhiṭṭhānassa samādānāvikopanena samādānasambhavato ca adhiṭṭhānassānantaraṃ mettā vuttā. Upekkhāya mettāvisuddhito, sattesu hitūpasaṃhāraṃ vatvā tadaparādhesu udāsīnatāvacanato, mettābhāvanaṃ vatvā tannissandabhāvanāvacanato, “hitakāmasattepi upekkhako”ti acchariyaguṇatāvacanato ca mettāyānantaraṃ upekkhā vuttāti evametāsaṃ kamo veditabbo.

Because forbearance is accomplished by energy. For indeed, one with energy, having undertaken energy, dwells having overcome the suffering brought about by the conditioned phenomena of beings. Because forbearance is the ornament of energy. For indeed, forbearance is resplendent for one with energy. Because, having spoken of the sign of exertion, he then spoke of the sign of tranquility; and because he spoke of abandoning the fault of restlessness through excessive striving. For the fault of restlessness is abandoned by patient acceptance of contemplating the Dhamma. Because he spoke of constant application for one with energy. For indeed, one who is rich in patience is unagitated and acts with perseverance. Because he spoke of the absence of craving for reciprocation for one who is heedful when undertaking actions for the welfare of others. For indeed, when there is contemplation of the Dhamma as it really is, craving does not arise. And because he spoke of the ability to endure suffering caused by others, even in the supreme undertaking for the welfare of others, forbearance was stated after energy. Because through truth, the resolve of forbearance is long-lasting; because, having spoken of forbearance towards an offender, he then spoke of not speaking falsely when doing a good turn to that person; because he spoke of not abandoning truthfulness through being unshaken by words of blame due to forbearance; and because, having spoken of patient acceptance of contemplating the doctrine of the emptiness of beings, he then spoke of the truth of knowledge augmented by it, truth was stated after forbearance. Because truth is accomplished by determination. For indeed, for one of unshakable determination, the truth of abstinence is accomplished. Because, having spoken of non-deception, he then spoke of the state of being unshakable therein. For indeed, one who is true to their word proceeds unshakably in giving, etc., in accordance with their promise. Because, having spoken of the truth of knowledge, he then spoke of bringing to completion the practice of the accumulations; and because of being unshakable by opposing factors, determination was stated after truth. For indeed, one with knowledge of things as they really are resolves upon the accumulations for enlightenment and brings them to completion. Because the determination of undertaking to act for the welfare of others is accomplished by loving-kindness; because, having spoken of determination, he then spoke of bringing about welfare. For indeed, one who is firmly resolved on the accumulations for enlightenment dwells with loving-kindness. And because for one of unshakable determination, the undertaking is possible through its non-corruption, loving-kindness was stated after determination. Because loving-kindness is purified by equanimity; because, having spoken of bringing about the welfare of beings, he then spoke of being impartial towards their offenses; because, having spoken of the development of loving-kindness, he then spoke of the development of its result; and because he spoke of the wondrous quality, 'one is equanimous even towards a being for whom one wishes well,' equanimity was stated after loving-kindness. Thus, the sequence of these perfections should be understood.

Kāni lakkhaṇādīni sabbathāti ettha pana avisesena –

Furthermore, to the question, 'What are their characteristics and so forth in all respects?', the general answer is:

Paresamanuggahaṇaṃ[V 1.0220], lakkhaṇanti pavuccati;

Upakāro akampo ca, raso hitesitāpi ca.

Assisting others is said to be the characteristic. Helpfulness and being unshakable are its function, as is desiring their welfare.

Buddhattaṃ paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, dayā ñāṇaṃ pavuccati;

Padaṭṭhānanti tāsantu, paccekaṃ tāni bhedato.

Buddhahood is their manifestation. Compassion and wisdom are called their proximate cause. However, these—their characteristics and so forth—should be known individually and in detail for each perfection.

Sabbāpi hi pāramiyo parānuggahalakkhaṇā, paresaṃ upakārakaraṇarasā, avikampanarasā vā, hitesitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, buddhattapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, mahākaruṇāpadaṭṭhānā, karuṇūpāyakosallapadaṭṭhānā vā.

Indeed, all the perfections have the characteristic of assisting others; their function is to benefit others, or their function is to be unshaken; their manifestation is the seeking of welfare, or their resultant manifestation is Buddhahood; their proximate cause is great compassion, or their proximate cause is skill in the means of performing them.

Visesena pana yasmā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā attupakaraṇapariccāgacetanā dānapāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ kāyavacīsucaritaṃ atthato akattabbavirati, kattabbakaraṇacetanādayo ca sīlapāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamo kāmabhavehi nikkhamanacittuppādo nekkhammapāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito dhammānaṃ sāmaññavisesalakkhaṇāvabodho paññāpāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito kāyacittehi parahitārambho vīriyapāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito sattasaṅkhārāparādhasahanasaṅkhāto adosappadhāno tadākārappavatto cittuppādo khantipāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ viraticetanādibhedaṃ avisaṃvādanaṃ saccapāramī[M 1.0252]. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānasaṅkhāto tadākārappavatto cittuppādo adhiṭṭhānapāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito lokassa hitasukhūpasaṃhāro atthato abyāpādo mettāpāramī. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsanasaṅkhātā iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu sattasaṅkhāresu samappavatti upekkhāpāramī.

Furthermore, specifically, because it is embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the volition for relinquishing one's own requisites is the perfection of giving. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, good bodily and verbal conduct—which in essence is abstinence from what should not be done, and the volitions for doing what should be done, etc.—is the perfection of virtue. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the arising of a mind that departs from sensual pleasures and states of becoming, preceded by seeing the danger therein, is the perfection of renunciation. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the understanding of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena is the perfection of wisdom. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the undertaking for the welfare of others with body and mind is the perfection of energy. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the arising of a mind that proceeds in that manner of forbearance, is predominated by non-aversion, and is designated as the endurance of the offenses of beings and formations, is the perfection of patience. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, non-deception, which has distinctions such as the volition of abstinence, etc., is the perfection of truthfulness. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the arising of a mind that proceeds in that manner, designated as the unshaken undertaking of a resolution, is the perfection of determination. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, the bringing of welfare and happiness to the world, which in essence is non-ill will, is the perfection of loving-kindness. Embraced by skill in the means of performing it, even-mindedness towards agreeable and disagreeable beings and formations, designated as the destruction of attraction and aversion, is the perfection of equanimity.

Tasmā pariccāgalakkhaṇaṃ dānaṃ, deyyadhamme lobhaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, anāsattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bhavavibhavasampattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, pariccajitabbavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlanalakkhaṇaṃ sīlaṃ, samādhānalakkhaṇaṃ, patiṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, anavajjarasaṃ vā, soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, hirottappapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Kāmato, bhavato ca nikkhamanalakkhaṇaṃ nekkhammaṃ, tadādīnavavibhāvanarasaṃ, tatoyeva vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanarasā padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesako viya, samādhipadaṭṭhānā[V 1.0221], catusaccapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ussāhalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyaṃ, upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā.

Therefore, giving has the characteristic of relinquishing; its function is to destroy greed for the objects to be given; its manifestation is non-attachment, or its resultant manifestation is the attainment of existence and prosperity; its proximate cause is the object to be relinquished. Virtue has the characteristic of composing, or of concentrating, or of establishing, so it is said; its function is to destroy immorality, or its function is blamelessness; its manifestation is purity; its proximate cause is moral shame and moral dread. Renunciation has the characteristic of departure from sensual pleasures and from existence; its function is to make clear the danger in them; its manifestation is the state of turning away from them; its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency. Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer; its function is to illuminate its object, like a lamp; its manifestation is non-delusion, like a good guide in a forest; its proximate cause is concentration, or its proximate cause is the Four Truths. Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support; its manifestation is not sinking down; its proximate cause is the grounds for arousing energy, or its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency.

Khamanalakkhaṇā khanti, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasahanarasā, adhivāsanapaccupaṭṭhānā, avirodhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, yathābhūtadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Avisaṃvādanalakkhaṇaṃ saccaṃ, yāthāvavibhāvanarasaṃ, sādhutāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, soraccapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Bodhisambhāresu adhiṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tesaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavanarasaṃ, tattha acalatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bodhisambhārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā mettā, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayanarasā vā, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā upekkhā, samabhāvadassanarasā, paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇapadaṭṭhānā. Ettha ca karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitatā dānādīnaṃ pariccāgādilakkhaṇassa visesanabhāvena vattabbā, yato tāni pāramīsaṅkhyaṃ labhanti. Na hi sammāsambodhiyādipatthanamaññatra akaruṇūpāyakosallapariggahitāni vaṭṭagāmīni dānādīni pāramīsaṅkhyaṃ labhantīti.

Patience has the characteristic of forbearance; its function is to endure the agreeable and disagreeable; its manifestation is tolerance, or its manifestation is non-opposition; its proximate cause is seeing things as they really are. Truthfulness has the characteristic of not speaking deceptively; its function is to make clear what is true; its manifestation is pleasantness; its proximate cause is gentleness. Determination has the characteristic of being established in the requisites for enlightenment; its function is to overcome their opposites; its manifestation is steadfastness therein; its proximate cause is the requisites for enlightenment. Loving-kindness has the characteristic of proceeding in the manner of welfare; its function is to bring welfare, or its function is to remove resentment; its manifestation is a gentle state; its proximate cause is seeing the agreeable aspect of beings. Equanimity has the characteristic of proceeding in a neutral manner; its function is to see with equanimity; its manifestation is the calming of aversion and affection; its proximate cause is the reviewing of ownership of kamma. And here, the fact of being embraced by skill in the means of performing them should be stated as a qualifier of the characteristic of relinquishment, etc., of giving, etc., since it is for this reason that they obtain the designation of 'perfections'. For, without the aspiration for Perfect Self-Enlightenment, etc., acts of giving, etc., that are not embraced by skill in the means of performing them and that lead to the round of existence do not obtain the designation of 'perfections'.

Ko [M 1.0253] paccayoti –

As to the question, 'What is the condition?'—

Abhinīhāro ca tāsaṃ, dayā ñāṇañca paccayo;

Ussāhummaṅgavatthānaṃ, hitācārādayo tathā.

Aspiration, compassion, and wisdom are the condition for them; likewise, exertion, wisdom, determination, conduct for the welfare of others, and so forth.

Abhinīhāro tāva pāramīnaṃ sabbāsampi paccayo. Yo hi ayaṃ “manussattaṃ liṅgasampattī”tiādi (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) aṭṭhadhammasamodhānasampādito “tiṇṇo tāreyyaṃ mutto moceyyaṃ, buddho bodheyyaṃ suddho sodheyyaṃ, danto dameyyaṃ, santo sameyyaṃ, assattho assāseyyaṃ, parinibbuto parinibbāpeyya”ntiādinā pavatto abhinīhāro, so avisesena sabbapāramīnaṃ paccayo. Tappavattiyā hi uddhaṃ pāramīnaṃ pavicayupaṭṭhānasamādānādhiṭṭhānanipphattiyo mahāpurisānaṃ sambhavanti, abhinīhāro ca nāmesa atthato bhesamaṭṭhaṅgānaṃ samodhānena tathāpavatto cittuppādo, “aho vatāhaṃ anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjheyyaṃ, sabbasattānaṃ hitasukhaṃ nipphādeyya”ntiādipatthanāsaṅkhāto acinteyyaṃ buddhabhūmiṃ, aparimāṇaṃ lokahitañca ārabbha pavattiyā sabbabuddhakārakadhammamūlabhūto paramabhaddako paramakalyāṇo aparimeyyappabhāvo puññavisesoti daṭṭhabbo.

First, aspiration is a condition for all the perfections. For this aspiration—which is accomplished by the combination of eight factors beginning with 'human existence, attainment of the proper gender,' etc., and which proceeds in the manner of 'Having crossed, may I help others cross; having been freed, may I free others; having been awakened, may I awaken others; having been purified, may I purify others; having been tamed, may I tame others; having been calmed, may I calm others; having been comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final Nibbāna, may I lead others to final Nibbāna'—is, without distinction, a condition for all perfections. For, subsequent to its arising, the accomplishments of the perfections—through investigation, manifestation, undertaking, and resolution—occur for the great beings. And this so-called aspiration should be understood as follows: in essence, it is a wholesome arising of mind that proceeds in such a way through the combination of those eight factors; it is designated as the wish, 'Oh, may I awaken to the unsurpassed Perfect Self-Enlightenment! Oh, may I bring about the welfare and happiness of all beings!'; and because it proceeds with the inconceivable state of a Buddha and the immeasurable welfare of the world as its object, it is a special kind of merit that is the root of all qualities that make a Buddha, is supremely excellent, supremely fine, and of immeasurable power.

Tassa [V 1.0222] ca uppattiyā saheva mahāpuriso mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiṃ otiṇṇo nāma hoti, niyatabhāvasamadhigamanato, tato ca anivattanasabhāvato “bodhisatto”ti samaññaṃ labhati, sabbabhāgena sammāsambodhiyaṃ sammāsattamānasatā, bodhisambhāre sikkhāsamatthatā cassa santiṭṭhati. Yathāvuttābhinīhārasamijjhanena hi mahāpurisā sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamanapubbaliṅgena sayambhuñāṇena sammadeva sabbapāramiyo vicinitvā samādāya anukkamena paripūrenti, yathā taṃ katamahābhinīhāro sumedhapaṇḍito. Yathāha –

And with its very arising, the great being is said to have entered upon the practice of the Great Bodhi-vehicle; because of attaining the state of certainty, and because of his irreversible nature from that practice, he obtains the designation 'Bodhisatta'. In every way, because his mind is rightly attached to Perfect Self-Enlightenment, his ability to train in the requisites for enlightenment is well established for him. For, by the success of the aspiration as described, great beings, by means of self-born knowledge which is a prior sign of attaining the knowledge of omniscience, rightly discern all the perfections, undertake them well, and fulfill them in sequence, just as did the wise Sumedha who had made the great aspiration. As he said:

“Handa buddhakare dhamme, vicināmi ito cito;

Uddhaṃ adho dasa disā, yāvatā dhammadhātuyā;

Vicinanto tadā dakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.115, 116); –

“Come now, I shall investigate the Buddha-making qualities, searching here and there; upwards, downwards, in the ten directions, as far as the Dhamma-element extends. Investigating then, I saw first the perfection of giving.”

Vitthāro. Lakkhaṇādito panesa sammadeva sammāsambodhipaṇidhānalakkhaṇo, “aho vatāhaṃ anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjheyyaṃ, sabbasattānaṃ [M 1.0254] hitasukhaṃ nipphādeyya”ntiādipatthanāraso, bodhisambhārahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, mahākaruṇāpadaṭṭhāno, upanissayasampattipadaṭṭhāno vā.

This is the detailed explanation. Now, from the perspective of its characteristics and so on, this aspiration is rightly characterized by the aspiration for Perfect Self-Enlightenment; its function is the wish, 'Oh, would that I might awaken to unsurpassed Perfect Self-Enlightenment and accomplish the welfare and happiness of all beings!' and so forth; its manifestation is its being a cause for the requisites of enlightenment; its proximate cause is great compassion, or the accomplishment of supporting conditions.

Tassa pana abhinīhārassa cattāro paccayā, cattāro hetū, cattāri ca balāni veditabbāni. Tattha katame cattāro paccayā mahābhinīhārāya? Idha mahāpuriso passati tathāgataṃ mahatā buddhānubhāvena acchariyabbhutaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ karontaṃ, tassa taṃ nissāya taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā mahābodhiyaṃ cittaṃ santiṭṭhati “mahānubhāvā vatāyaṃ dhammadhātu, yassā suppaṭividdhattā bhagavā evaṃ acchariyabbhutadhammo, acinteyyānubhāvo cā”ti, so tameva mahānubhāvadassanaṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti, ayaṃ paṭhamo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

Furthermore, for that aspiration, four supporting conditions, four generative causes, and four strengths should be known. Among these, what are the four supporting conditions for the great aspiration? Here, a great being sees a Tathāgata performing a wonderful and astonishing miracle by means of great Buddha-power. Relying on that, making it his object, his mind becomes well established in great enlightenment, thinking: 'Truly, this Dhamma-element is of great power, due to the good penetration of which the Blessed One is of such a wonderful and astonishing nature and of inconceivable power.' Relying on that very vision of great power, making it a supporting condition, and inclining his mind towards enlightenment, he establishes his mind therein. This is the first supporting condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, apica kho suṇāti “ediso ca ediso ca bhagavā”ti, so taṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti, ayaṃ dutiyo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

He does not, indeed, see the Tathāgata's great power as described, but he hears: 'The Blessed One is of such a nature and such a nature.' Relying on that, making it a supporting condition, and inclining his mind towards enlightenment, he establishes his mind therein. This is the second supporting condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, nāpi taṃ parato suṇāti, apica kho tathāgatassa dhammaṃ desentassa “dasabalasamannāgato bhikkhave, tathāgato”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.21) buddhānubhāvapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [V 1.0223] dhammaṃ suṇāti, so taṃ nissāya…pe… ayaṃ tatiyo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

He does not, indeed, see the Tathāgata's great power as described, nor does he hear of it from another. But he hears the Dhamma connected with the Buddha's power from the Tathāgata as he is teaching the Dhamma, such as, 'Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers,' and so forth. Relying on that… this is the third supporting condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, nāpi taṃ parato suṇāti, nāpi tathāgatassa dhammaṃ suṇāti, apica kho uḷārajjhāsayo kalyāṇādhimuttiko “ahametaṃ buddhavaṃsaṃ buddhatantiṃ buddhapaveṇiṃ buddadhammataṃ paripālessāmī”ti yāvadeva dhammaññeva sakkaronto garuṃ karonto mānento pūjento dhammaṃ apacayamāno taṃ nissāya…pe… ṭhapeti, ayaṃ catuttho paccayo mahābhinīhārāyāti.

He does not, indeed, see the Tathāgata's great power as described, nor does he hear of it from another, nor does he hear the Dhamma from the Tathāgata. But, having a noble disposition and a virtuous inclination, he thinks: 'I will maintain this Buddha-lineage, this Buddha-succession, this Buddha-tradition, and this nature of a Buddha.' By greatly honoring, respecting, esteeming, venerating, and paying homage to the Dhamma itself, relying on that… he establishes his mind. This is the fourth supporting condition for the great aspiration.

Katame [M 1.0255] cattāro hetū mahābhinīhārāya? Idha mahāpuriso pakatiyā upanissayasampanno hoti purimakesu buddhesu katādhikāro, ayaṃ paṭhamo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso pakatiyāpi karuṇājjhāsayo hoti karuṇādhimutto sattānaṃ dukkhaṃ apanetukāmo, apica attano kāyañca jīvitañca pariccaji, ayaṃ dutiyo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso sakalatopi vaṭṭadukkhato sattahitāya dukkaracariyato sucirampi kālaṃ ghaṭento vāyamanto anibbinno hoti anutrāsī, yāva icchitatthanipphatti, ayaṃ tatiyo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso kalyāṇamittasannissito hoti, yo ahitato naṃ nivāreti, hite patiṭṭhāpeti, ayaṃ catuttho hetu mahābhinīhārāya.

What are the four generative causes for the great aspiration? Here, a great being is by nature endowed with supporting conditions, having performed eminent merit in the presence of past Buddhas. This is the first generative cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, a great being is by nature of a compassionate disposition, intent on compassion, desiring to remove the suffering of beings; indeed, he gives up his own body and life. This is the second generative cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, striving and making effort through difficult practices for a very long time for the welfare of beings and to lift them from the entire suffering of the round of existence, he is not disheartened and is fearless until the desired goal is accomplished. This is the third generative cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, a great being relies on a good friend, who restrains him from what is unbeneficial and establishes him in what is beneficial. This is the fourth generative cause for the great aspiration.

Tatrāyaṃ mahāpurisassa upanissayasampadā – ekantenevassa yathā ajjhāsayo sambodhininno hoti sambodhipoṇo sambodhipabbhāro, tathā sattānaṃ hitacariyāya, yato anena purimabuddhānaṃ santike sambodhiyā paṇidhānaṃ kataṃ hoti manasā, vācāya ca “ahampi ediso sammāsambuddho hutvā sammadeva sattānaṃ hitasukhaṃ nipphādeyya”nti. Evaṃ sampannūpanissayassa panassa imāni upanissayasampattiyā liṅgāni sambhavanti, yehi samannāgatassa sāvakabodhisattehi, paccekabodhisattehi ca mahāviseso mahantaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati indriyato, paṭipattito, kosallato ca. Idha hi upanissayasampanno mahāpuriso yathā visadindriyo hoti visadañāṇo, na tathā itare. Parahitāya paṭipanno hoti, no attahitāya. Tathā hi so yathā bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ paṭipajji, na tathā itare, tattha ca kosallaṃ āvahati ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena, ṭhānāṭhānakusalatāya ca.

In this regard, this is the great being's accomplishment of supporting conditions: just as his disposition is entirely inclined toward enlightenment, leaning toward enlightenment, and tending toward enlightenment, so too is he dedicated to the practice of the welfare of beings. This is because he has made the aspiration for enlightenment in the presence of past Buddhas with mind and with speech, saying: 'May I too, having become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha like this, rightly bring about the welfare and happiness of beings!' Now, for one endowed with such accomplished supporting conditions, these signs of the accomplishment of supporting conditions arise, by which a great difference and a vast distinction from disciple-bodhisattas and paccekabodhisattas is apparent with respect to faculties, practice, and skill. For here, just as the great being endowed with supporting conditions has clear faculties and clear knowledge, others do not. He is one who practices for the welfare of others, not for his own welfare. For, just as he practices for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans, others do not. And in this, he demonstrates skill by means of intelligence that arises on the spot and by skill in what is cause and not cause.

Tathā [V 1.0224] mahāpuriso pakatiyā dānajjhāsayo hoti dānābhirato, sati deyyadhamme detiyeva, na dānato saṅkocaṃ āpajjati, satataṃ samitaṃ saṃvibhāgasīlo hoti, pamuditova deti ādarajāto, na udāsīnacitto, mahantampi dānaṃ datvā neva [M 1.0256] dānena santuṭṭho hoti, pageva appaṃ. Paresañca ussāhaṃ janento dāne vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, dānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ karoti, aññe ca paresaṃ dente disvā attamano hoti, bhayaṭṭhānesu ca paresaṃ abhayaṃ detīti evamādīni dānajjhāsayassa mahāpurisassa dānapāramiyā liṅgāni.

Furthermore, a great person is by nature inclined to giving and delights in giving. When there is a thing to be given, he gives indeed. He does not become stingy with regard to giving, but is constantly and perpetually of a sharing disposition. He gives with joy and with respect, not with an indifferent mind. Even after giving a great gift, he is not satisfied with that gift, how much more so a small one. And generating enthusiasm in others, he speaks in praise of giving and gives a Dhamma talk connected with giving. And seeing others giving to others, he is pleased at heart. And in situations of fear, he gives fearlessness to others. These and so forth are the signs of the perfection of giving of a great person who is inclined to giving.

Tathā pāṇātipātādīhi pāpadhammehi hirīyati ottappati, sattānaṃ aviheṭhanajātiko hoti, sorato sukhasīlo asaṭho amāyāvī ujujātiko subbaco sovacassakaraṇīyehi dhammehi samannāgato mudujātiko athaddho anatimānī, parasantakaṃ nādiyati antamaso tiṇasalākamupādāya, attano hatthe nikkhittaṃ iṇaṃ vā gahetvā paraṃ na visaṃvādeti, parasmiṃ vā attano santake byāmūḷhe, vissarite vā taṃ saññāpetvā paṭipādeti yathā taṃ na parahatthagataṃ hoti, aloluppo hoti, parapariggahitesu pāpakaṃ cittampi na uppādeti, itthibyasanādīni dūrato parivajjeti, saccavādī saccasandho bhinnānaṃ sandhātā sahitānaṃ anuppadātā piyavādī mihitapubbaṅgamo pubbabhāsī atthavādī dhammavādī anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto aviparītadassano kammassakatāñāṇena, saccānulomikañāṇena ca, kataññū katavedī vuḍḍhāpacāyī suvisuddhājīvo dhammakāmo, paresampi dhamme samādapetā sabbena sabbaṃ akiccato satte nivāretā kiccesu patiṭṭhapetā attanā ca tattha kicce yogaṃ āpajjitā, katvā vā pana sayaṃ akattabbaṃ sīghaññeva tato paṭivirato hotīti evamādīni sīlajjhāsayassa mahāpurisassa sīlapāramiyā liṅgāni.

Furthermore, he is ashamed and has moral dread regarding evil states beginning with the destruction of life. He is of a nature not to harm beings; he delights in wholesome bodily and verbal conduct, is of a pleasant disposition, is not deceitful, not fraudulent, easy to instruct, and endowed with qualities that make one easy to instruct. He is of a gentle nature, not stubborn, and has no excessive conceit. He does not take what belongs to others, not even so much as a blade of grass. Having taken a loan placed in his own hand, he does not deceive the other person. Or if another is confused or forgetful regarding their own property, he makes them understand and arranges it so that it does not fall into the hands of another. He is not covetous; he does not give rise to even an evil thought regarding possessions acquired by others. He avoids from afar misfortunes arising from women and so forth. He is a speaker of truth, is true to his word, a reconciler of the divided, and one who gives further support to those who are in harmony. He speaks endearing words, greets with a smile, is accustomed to speaking first, speaks what is beneficial, and speaks in accordance with the Dhamma. He is not covetous, has a mind without ill will, and has non-perverted vision through the knowledge of kamma as one's own property and through the knowledge conforming to the truths. He is grateful, knows how to repay kindness, is respectful to elders, has a very pure livelihood, and desires the Dhamma. He also establishes others in wholesome states. He restrains beings completely from what should not be done and establishes them in what should be done, and he himself engages in that duty. Or, having done what should not be done, he himself quickly refrains from it. These and so forth are the signs of the perfection of virtue of a great person who is inclined to virtue.

Tathā mandakileso hoti mandanīvaraṇo pavivekajjhāsayo avikkhepabahulo, na tassa pāpakā vitakkā cittamanvāssavanti, vivekagatassa cassa appakasireneva cittaṃ samādhiyati, amittapakkhepi tuvaṭaṃ mettacittatā santiṭṭhati, pageva itarasmiṃ, satimā ca hoti cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi susaritā anussaritā, medhāvī ca hoti dhammojapaññāya samannāgato, nipako ca hoti tāsu tāsu itikattabbatāsu, āraddhavīriyo ca hoti sattānaṃ hitakiriyāsu, khantibalasamannāgato ca hoti sabbasaho, acalādhiṭṭhāno ca hoti daḷhasamādāno, ajjhupekkhako ca hoti upekkhāṭhānīyesu dhammesūti evamādīni mahāpurisassa nekkhammajjhāsayādīnaṃ vasena nekkhammapāramiyādīnaṃ liṅgāni veditabbāni.

Furthermore, he has few defilements and few hindrances. His inclination is toward seclusion, and he has much non-distraction. Evil thoughts do not pursue and oppress his mind. And for him who has gone to seclusion, his mind becomes concentrated without difficulty. Even toward the hostile faction, a mind of loving-kindness is quickly established; what need is there to speak of the other side. And he is mindful; he is able to remember well and recollect again and again what was done long ago and what was said long ago. And he is wise, endowed with wisdom born of the Dhamma. And he is skilled in those various matters of what should be done. And he has aroused energy for the performance of welfare for beings. And he is endowed with the strength of patience, able to endure all things. And he has an unshakable determination and a firm undertaking. And he is very equanimous towards states that are a basis for equanimity. These and so forth, by way of the great person's inclination to renunciation and so on, should be known as the signs of the perfections of renunciation and so on.

Evametehi [V 1.0225][M 1.0257] bodhisambhāraliṅgehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa yaṃ vuttaṃ “mahābhinīhārāya kalyāṇamittasannissayo hetū”ti, tatridaṃ saṅkhepato kalyāṇamittalakkhaṇaṃ – idha kalyāṇamitto saddhāsampanno hoti sīlasampanno sutasampanno cāgavīriyasatisamādhipaññāsampanno. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ kammaṃ, kammaphalañca, tena sammāsambodhiyā hetubhūtaṃ sattesu hitesitaṃ na pariccajati. Sīlasampattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo codako pāpagarahiko vattā vacanakkhamo. Sutasampattiyā sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ gambhīraṃ dhammakathaṃ kattā hoti. Cāgasampattiyā appiccho hoti samāhito santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho. Vīriyasampattiyā āraddhavīriyo hoti sattānaṃ hitapaṭipattiyā. Satisampattiyā upaṭṭhitassatī hoti anavajjesu dhammesu. Samādhisampattiyā avikkhitto hoti samāhitacitto. Paññāsampattiyā aviparītaṃ pajānāti. So satiyā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamāno paññāya sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā samādhinā tattha ekaggacitto hutvā vīriyena ahitā satte nisedhetvā hite niyojeti. Tenāha –

Thus, for a great person endowed with these signs of the requisites for enlightenment, regarding what was said, 'Reliance on a good friend is a cause for the great aspiration,' this, in brief, is the characteristic of a good friend: Here, a good friend is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therein, through the accomplishment of faith, he has faith in the Tathāgata's enlightenment, in kamma, and in the result of kamma; therefore, he does not abandon the search for the welfare of beings, which is the cause for perfect full enlightenment. Through the accomplishment of virtue, he is dear to beings, pleasing, respected, esteemed, an admonisher, a censurer of evil, a speaker who instructs, and patient with words. Through the accomplishment of learning, he is a speaker of profound Dhamma. Through the accomplishment of generosity, he is of few wants, composed, content, secluded, and unentangled. Through the accomplishment of energy, he has aroused energy for the practice of the welfare of beings. Through the accomplishment of mindfulness, he has established mindfulness regarding blameless states. Through the accomplishment of concentration, he is undistracted, with a concentrated mind. Through the accomplishment of wisdom, he understands without distortion. That good friend, with mindfulness, thoroughly investigating the courses of wholesome states, and with wisdom, having known as it really is the welfare and non-welfare of beings, and with concentration, having become one-pointed in mind therein, with energy, having restrained beings from what is not for their welfare, urges them towards what is for their welfare. Therefore, it is said:

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37; netti. 113);

He is dear, respected, and esteemed; a speaker who instructs and is patient with words; a speaker of profound speech, and does not urge one in an unsuitable matter.

Evaṃ guṇasamannāgataṃva kalyāṇamittaṃ upanissāya mahāpuriso attano upanissayasampattiṃ sammadeva pariyodapeti. Suvisuddhāsayapayogova hutvā catūhi balehi samannāgato nacireneva aṭṭhaṅge samodhānetvā mahābhinīhāraṃ karonto bodhisattabhāve patiṭṭhahati anivattidhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo.

Relying on a good friend who is thus endowed with virtues, a great person rightly purifies his own accomplishment of supporting conditions. Having a very pure inclination and application, being endowed with the four powers, before long, having combined the eight factors and making the great aspiration, he becomes established in the state of a Bodhisatta—of an irreversible nature, certain, with full enlightenment as his final destination.

Tassimāni cattāri balāni ajjhattikabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ attasannissayā dhammagāravena abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso attādhipatilajjāsannissayo, abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Bāhirabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ parasannissayā abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso lokādhipatiottappanasannissayo, abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo [M 1.0258] pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Upanissayabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ upanissayasampattiyā abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso tikkhindriyo, visadadhātuko, satisannissayo, abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Payogabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyā [V 1.0226] tajjā payogasampadā sakkaccakāritā sātaccakāritā, yāya mahāpuriso visuddhapayogo, nirantarakārī, abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Evamayaṃ catūhi paccayehi, catūhi hetūhi, catūhi ca balehi sampannasamudāgamo aṭṭhaṅgasamodhānasampādito abhinīhāro pāramīnaṃ paccayo hoti mūlakāraṇabhāvato.

For that great being, there are these four strengths. Internal strength should be known thus: that which is the disposition exclusively inclined towards perfect self-enlightenment, having self-reliance and reverence for the Dhamma. By this, the great being, relying on the shame that has oneself as sovereign and endowed with the aspiration, having fulfilled the perfections, attains perfect self-enlightenment. External strength should be known thus: that which is the disposition exclusively inclined towards perfect self-enlightenment, having reliance on others. By this, the great being, relying on the moral dread that has the world as sovereign and endowed with the aspiration, having fulfilled the perfections, attains perfect self-enlightenment. The strength of supporting condition should be known thus: that which is the disposition exclusively inclined towards perfect self-enlightenment through the accomplishment of a powerful supporting condition. By this, the great being, having keen faculties, pure elements, relying on mindfulness, and endowed with the aspiration, having fulfilled the perfections, attains perfect self-enlightenment. The strength of exertion should be known thus: that which, for perfect self-enlightenment, is the accomplishment of suitable exertion, the state of acting respectfully, and the state of acting constantly. By this, the great being, having purified exertion, acting without interruption, and endowed with the aspiration, having fulfilled the perfections, attains perfect self-enlightenment. Thus, this aspiration—which has come to the fullness of accomplishment through four conditions, four causes, and four strengths, and is brought to completion by the combination of eight factors—is a condition for the perfections due to being a root cause.

Yassa ca pavattiyā mahāpurise cattāro acchariyā abbhutā dhammā patiṭṭhahanti, sabbaṃ sattanikāyaṃ attano orasaputtaṃ viya piyacittena pariggaṇhāti, na cassa cittaṃ puna saṃkilesavasena saṃkilissati, sattānaṃ hitasukhāvaho cassa ajjhāsayo, payogo ca hoti, attano ca buddhakārakadhammā uparūpari vaḍḍhanti, paripaccanti ca, yato mahāpuriso uḷāratarena puññābhisandena kusalābhisandena pavaḍḍhiyā [pavattiyā (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathā)] paccayena sukhassāhārena samannāgato sattānaṃ dakkhiṇeyyo uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānaṃ, asadisaṃ puññakkhettañca hoti. Evamanekaguṇo anekānisaṃso mahābhinīhāro pāramīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbo.

And due to the occurrence of which aspiration, four amazing and wonderful qualities are established in the great being: he embraces the entire community of beings with a loving mind, as if they were his own breast-born son; his mind is not defiled again through the power of defilements; his disposition and exertion are for the welfare and happiness of beings; and his own Buddha-making qualities grow and mature successively. From when this occurs, the great being, endowed with a more sublime stream of merit and a stream of the wholesome as a condition for growth, becomes worthy of offerings from beings, a supreme basis for reverence, and an incomparable field of merit. Thus, it should be understood that the great aspiration, possessing many virtues and many benefits, is a condition for the perfections.

Yathā ca mahābhinīhāro, evaṃ mahākaruṇā, upāyakosallañca. Tattha upāyakosallaṃ nāma dānādīnaṃ bodhisambhārabhāvassa nimittabhūtā paññā, yāhi mahākaruṇūpāyakosallatāhi mahāpurisānaṃ attasukhanirapekkhatā, nirantaraṃ parasukhakaraṇapasutatā, sudukkarehi mahābodhisattacaritehi visādābhāvo, pasādasaṃvuddhidassanasavanānussaraṇāvatthāsupi sattānaṃ hitasukhapaṭilābhahetubhāvo ca sampajjati. Tathā hi tassa paññāya buddhabhāvasiddhi, karuṇāya buddhakammasiddhi. Paññāya sayaṃ tarati, karuṇāya pare tāreti. Paññāya paradukkhaṃ parijānāti, karuṇāya paradukkhapaṭikāraṃ ārabhati. Paññāya dukkhaṃ nibbindati, karuṇāya dukkhaṃ sampaṭicchati. Paññāya nibbānābhimukho hoti, karuṇāya [M 1.0259] taṃ na pāpuṇāti. Tathā karuṇāya saṃsārābhimukho hoti, paññāya tatra nābhiramati. Paññāya sabbattha virajjati, karuṇānugatattā na ca na sabbesamanuggahāya pavatto, karuṇāya sabbepi anukampati, paññānugatattā na ca na sabbattha virattacitto. Paññāya ahaṃkāramamaṃkārābhāvo, karuṇāya ālasiyadīnatābhāvo.

Just as the great aspiration is a condition, so too are great compassion and skill in means.
