Therein, skill in means is the wisdom that is the cause for giving and so forth to become requisites for enlightenment. By this state of great compassion and skill in means, the following are accomplished for great beings: indifference to their own happiness, constant dedication to bringing about the happiness of others, absence of despair in the extremely difficult practices of great bodhisattvas, and their being a cause for beings to attain welfare and happiness even in situations of seeing, hearing, and recollecting which increase faith. For indeed, through his wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished; through compassion, the work of a Buddha is accomplished. By wisdom, he himself crosses over; by compassion, he helps others cross over. By wisdom, he fully understands the suffering of others; by compassion, he undertakes the remedy for the suffering of others. By wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with suffering; by compassion, he accepts suffering. By wisdom, he is faced towards Nibbāna; by compassion, he does not attain it. Likewise, by compassion, he is faced towards saṃsāra; by wisdom, he does not delight in it. By wisdom, he is dispassionate towards everything; and because it is accompanied by compassion, it is not that he is not engaged in helping all beings. By compassion, he has compassion for all; and because it is accompanied by wisdom, it is not that his mind is not detached from everything. By wisdom, there is the absence of 'I-making' and 'mine-making'; by compassion, there is the absence of laziness and dejection.

Tathā paññākaruṇāhi yathākkamaṃ attanāthaparanāthatā, dhīravīrabhāvo, anattantapāparantapatā, attahitaparahitanipphatti, nibbhayābhīsanakabhāvo, dhammādhipatilokādhipatitā, kataññupubbakāribhāvo, mohataṇhāvigamo, vijjācaraṇasiddhi, balavesārajjanipphattīti sabbassāpi [V 1.0227] pāramitāphalassa visesena upāyabhāvato paññā karuṇā pāramīnaṃ paccayo. Idaṃ pana dvayaṃ pāramīnaṃ viya paṇidhānassāpi paccayo.

Likewise, by wisdom and compassion, respectively, there is the state of being a refuge for oneself and a refuge for others; the state of being wise and heroic; the state of not tormenting oneself and not tormenting others; the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others; the state of being fearless and not causing fear in others; the state of having the Dhamma as sovereign and the world as sovereign; the state of being grateful and being a benefactor; the removal of delusion and craving; the accomplishment of knowledge and conduct; and the accomplishment of the powers and states of fearlessness. Therefore, because they are especially the means for the entire fruit of the perfections, wisdom and compassion are a condition for the perfections. Moreover, this pair is a condition for the aspiration, just as it is for the perfections.

Tathā ussāhaummaṅgaavatthānahitacariyā ca pāramīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbo. Yā ca buddhabhāvassa uppattiṭṭhānatāya “buddhabhūmiyo”ti vuccanti. Tattha ussāho nāma bodhisambhārānaṃ abbhussāhanavīriyaṃ. Ummaṅgo nāma bodhisambhāresu upāyakosallabhūtā paññā. Avatthānaṃ nāma adhiṭṭhānaṃ, acalādhiṭṭhānatā. Hitacariyā nāma mettābhāvanā, karuṇābhāvanā ca. Yathāha –

Likewise, exertion, ingenuity, resolution, and beneficial conduct should also be understood as conditions for the perfections. And these are called 'Buddha-grounds' because they are the place of arising for the state of Buddhahood. Therein, exertion is the energy of striving for the requisites of enlightenment. Ingenuity is the wisdom that is skill in means regarding the requisites of enlightenment. Resolution is determination, the state of unshakable determination. Beneficial conduct is the cultivation of loving-kindness and the cultivation of compassion. As it is said:

“Kati pana bhante, buddhabhūmiyoti? Catasso kho sāriputta, buddhabhūmiyo. Katamā catasso? Ussāho ca hoti vīriyaṃ, ummaṅgo ca hoti paññābhāvanā, avatthānañca hoti adhiṭṭhānaṃ, hitacariyā ca hoti mettābhāvanā. Imā kho sāriputta, catasso buddhabhūmiyo”ti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34).

“Venerable sir, how many are the Buddha-grounds?” “Sāriputta, there are four Buddha-grounds. What four? There is exertion, which is energy; there is ingenuity, which is the cultivation of wisdom; there is resolution, which is determination; and there is beneficial conduct, which is the cultivation of loving-kindness. These, Sāriputta, are the four Buddha-grounds.”

Tathā nekkhammapavivekaalobhādosāmohanissaraṇappabhedā ca cha ajjhāsayā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Likewise, there are the six dispositions distinguished as renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-aversion, non-delusion, and escape. For this was said:

“Nekkhammajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā kāmesu, gharāvāse ca dosadassāvino, pavivekajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā saṅgaṇikāya dosadassāvino. Alobha…pe… lobhe…pe… adosa…pe… dose…pe… amoha…pe… mohe…pe… nissaraṇa…pe… sabbabhavesu dosadassāvino”ti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34; visuddhi. 1.49).

“Bodhisattvas have an inclination for renunciation and see the danger in sensual pleasures and the household life. Bodhisattvas have an inclination for seclusion and see the danger in company. Bodhisattvas have an inclination for non-greed and see the danger in greed. Bodhisattvas have an inclination for non-aversion and see the danger in aversion. Bodhisattvas have an inclination for non-delusion and see the danger in delusion. Bodhisattvas have an inclination for escape and see the danger in all states of existence.”

Tasmā [M 1.0260] ete ca cha ajjhāsayāpi pāramīnaṃ paccayāti veditabbā. Na hi lobhādīsu ādīnavadassanena, alobhādīnaṃ adhikabhāvena ca vinā dānādipāramiyo sambhavanti. Alobhādīnañhi adhikabhāvena pariccāgādininnacittatā, alobhajjhāsayāditā cāti, yathā cete, evaṃ dānajjhāsayatādayopi. Yathāha –

Therefore, these six inclinations should also be known as conditions for the perfections. For the perfections such as giving do not arise without seeing the danger in greed and so on, and without the predominance of non-greed and so on. Indeed, by the predominance of non-greed and so on, there is the state of having a mind inclined towards relinquishment and so forth, and the state of having the inclination of non-greed and so on. And just as these are conditions for the perfections, so too are the states of having an inclination for giving and so on. As it is said:

“Kati pana bhante bodhāya carantānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ajjhāsayāti? Dasa kho sāriputta, bodhāya carantānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ajjhāsayā. Katame dasa? Dānajjhāsayā sāriputta, bodhisattā macchere dosadassāvino. Sīla…pe… asaṃvare…pe… nekkhamma…pe… kāmesu…pe… yathābhūtañāṇa…pe… vicikicchāya.…Pe… vīriya [V 1.0228] …pe… kosajje…pe… khanti…pe… akkhantiyaṃ…pe… sacca…pe… visaṃvādane…pe… adhiṭṭhāna…pe… anadhiṭṭhāne…pe… mettā…pe… byāpāde…pe… upekkhā…pe… sukhadukkhesu ādīnavadassāvino”ti.

“Venerable sir, how many inclinations are there for Bodhisattvas practicing for enlightenment? Sāriputta, there are ten inclinations for Bodhisattvas practicing for enlightenment. What are the ten? Sāriputta, Bodhisattvas have an inclination for giving; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in stinginess. They have an inclination for virtue; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in non-restraint. They have an inclination for renunciation; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in sensual pleasures. They have an inclination for knowledge of things as they are; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in doubt. They have an inclination for energy; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in laziness. They have an inclination for patience; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in impatience. They have an inclination for truth; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in deceptive speech. They have an inclination for resolution; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in lack of resolution. They have an inclination for loving-kindness; they are accustomed to seeing the fault in ill will. They have an inclination for equanimity; they are accustomed to seeing the danger in pleasure and pain.”

Etesu hi maccheraasaṃvarakāmavicikicchākosajjaakkhantivisaṃvādanaanadhiṭṭhāna- byāpādasukhadukkhasaṅkhātesu ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā dānādininnacittatāsaṅkhātā dānajjhāsayatādayo dānādipāramīnaṃ nibbattiyā paccayo. Tathā apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇampi dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayo hoti.

Indeed, in these faults termed stinginess, non-restraint, sensual pleasure, doubt, laziness, impatience, deceptive speech, lack of resolution, ill will, and pleasure and pain, the states of having an inclination for giving and so on—which are preceded by seeing the danger and are called the state of having a mind inclined towards giving and so on—are a condition for the arising of the perfections such as giving. Furthermore, reflecting in due order on the danger in non-relinquishment and the benefit in relinquishment and so on is also a condition for the perfections such as giving.

Tatrāyaṃ paccavekkhaṇāvidhi – khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇagomahiṃ sadāsīdāsaputtadārādipariggahabyāsattacittānaṃ sattānaṃ khettādīnaṃ vatthukāmabhāvena bahupatthanīyabhāvato, rājacorādisādhāraṇabhāvato, vivādādhiṭṭhānato, sapattakaraṇato, nissārato, paṭilābhaparipālanesu paraviheṭhanahetubhāvato, vināsanimittañcasokādianekavihitabyasanāvahato tadāsattinidānañca maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitacittānaṃ apāyūpapattihetubhāvatoti evaṃ vividhavipulānatthāvahāni pariggahitavatthūni nāma, tesaṃ pariccāgoyeveko sotthibhāvoti pariccāge appamādo karaṇīyo.

Herein, this is the method of reflection: For beings whose minds are engrossed in possessions such as fields, land, gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, male and female slaves, children, and wives, these so-called possessions bring manifold and extensive harm. This is because these things, such as fields, being objects of sensual pleasure, are much desired; because they are common to kings, thieves, and so on; because they are a basis for disputes; because they create rivals; because they are without essence; because in their acquisition and protection they are a cause for harming others; because they are a cause of destruction and bring various misfortunes such as sorrow; and for those whose minds are beset by the stain of stinginess, attachment to them is a cause for arising in a woeful state. Their relinquishment alone is the one state of well-being; therefore, diligence should be practiced in relinquishment.

Apica “yācako yācamāno attano guyhassa ācikkhanato mayhaṃ vissāsiko”ti ca “pahāya gamanīyaṃ attano santakaṃ gahetvā paralokaṃ yāhītiupadisanato mayhaṃ upadesako”ti ca “āditte viya [M 1.0261] agāre maraṇagginā āditte loke tato mayhaṃ santakassa apaharaṇato apavāhakasahāyo”ti ca “apavāhitassa cassa ajjhāpananikkhepaṭṭhānabhūto”ti ca “dānasaṅkhāte kalyāṇakammasmiṃ sahāyabhāvato, sabbasampattīnaṃ aggabhūtāya paramadullabhāya buddhabhūmiyā sampattihetubhāvato ca paramo kalyāṇamitto”ti ca paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, it should be reflected: ‘The beggar, by asking, tells of his own secret need; therefore, he is my confidant.’ And: ‘By advising, “Having abandoned what must be left behind, go to the next world taking your own property,” he is my advisor.’ And: ‘When the world is ablaze with the fire of death like a house on fire, by helping to carry my property away from it, he is a companion who helps remove it.’ And: ‘He is a safe place for depositing that which has been carried away.’ And: ‘Because he is a companion in the wholesome action called giving, and because he is a cause for the attainment of the state of a Buddha—which is the highest of all attainments and supremely difficult to obtain—he is the supreme good friend.’ Thus it should be reflected.

Tathā “uḷāre kammani anenāhaṃ sambhāvito, tasmā sā sambhāvanā avitathā kātabbā”ti ca “ekantabheditāya jīvitassa āyācitenāpi mayā dātabbaṃ, pageva yācitenā”ti ca “uḷārajjhāsayehi gavesitvāpi dātabbo, [dātabbato (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā)] sayamevāgato mama puññenā”ti ca “yācakassa dānāpadesena mayhamevāyamanuggaho”ti ca “ahaṃ viya ayaṃ sabbopi loko mayā anuggahetabbo”ti ca “asati yācake kathaṃ mayhaṃ dānapāramī pūreyyā”ti ca “yācakānamevatthāya mayā sabbopi pariggahetabbo”ti ca “ayācitvāpi maṃ mama santakaṃ yācakā kadā sayameva gaṇheyyu”nti ca [V 1.0229] “kathamahaṃ yācakānaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo”ti ca “kathaṃ vā te mayhaṃ piyā cassu manāpā”ti ca “kathaṃ vāhaṃ dadamāno datvāpi ca attamano assaṃ pamudito pītisomanassajāto”ti ca “kathaṃ vā me yācakā bhaveyyuṃ, uḷāro ca dānajjhāsayo”ti ca “kathaṃ vāhamayācito eva yācakānaṃ hadayamaññāya dadeyya”nti “sati dhane, yācake ca apariccāgo mahatī mayhaṃ vañcanā”ti ca “kathamahaṃ attano aṅgāni, jīvitañcāpi pariccajeyya”nti ca cāganinnatā upaṭṭhapetabbā.

Likewise, it should be reflected: ‘By this noble deed I am honored; therefore, that honor must be made true.’ And: ‘Since life is certain to break up, I should give even unasked, what to speak of when asked?’ And: ‘A recipient should be given to even after searching with noble intentions; if one has come by himself, it is through my merit.’ And: ‘By the beggar’s indication of a gift, this is a favor to me alone.’ And: ‘Just like myself, this entire world should be favored by me.’ And: ‘If there were no beggar, how could my perfection of giving be fulfilled?’ And: ‘For the sake of beggars alone I should acquire all possessions.’ And: ‘When might beggars, even unasked, take my possessions of their own accord?’ And: ‘How might I become dear and pleasing to beggars?’ And: ‘Or how might they become dear and pleasing to me?’ And: ‘Or how might I, while giving and after having given, be glad of heart, joyful, and filled with rapture and happiness?’ And: ‘Or how might there be beggars for me, and a noble inclination for giving?’ And: ‘Or how might I, even unasked, know the heart of beggars and give?’ And: ‘When there is wealth and a beggar, not to relinquish is a great deception of myself.’ And: ‘How might I relinquish my own limbs and even my life?’ Thus, an inclination towards relinquishment should be established.

Apica “attho nāmāyaṃ nirapekkhaṃ dāyakamanugacchati yathā taṃ nirapekkhaṃ khepakaṃ kiṭako”ti atthe nirapekkhatāya cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Yācamāno pana yadi piyapuggalo hoti “piyo maṃ yācatī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Atha udāsīnapuggalo hoti “ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena mitto hotī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Dadanto hi yācakānaṃ piyo hotīti. Atha pana verīpuggalo yācati, “paccatthiko maṃ yācati, ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena verīpi piyo mitto hotī”ti visesato somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Evaṃ [M 1.0262] piyapuggale viya majjhattaverīpuggalesupi mettāpubbaṅgamaṃ karuṇaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva dātabbaṃ.

Moreover: ‘This so-called benefit follows the giver who is without attachment, just as an insect follows where it is thrown without attachment.’ Thus, a mind without attachment to the benefit should be produced. Furthermore, if the one who asks is a dear person, joy should be produced, thinking: ‘A dear one is asking of me.’ If it is a neutral person, joy should be produced, thinking: ‘Surely, by this relinquishment, this person asking of me will become a friend.’ For a giver becomes dear to those who ask. And if an enemy asks, special joy should be produced, thinking: ‘An adversary is asking of me. Surely, by this relinquishment, even this enemy will become a dear friend.’ Thus, just as towards a dear person, so also towards neutral and hostile persons, one should give only after having established compassion preceded by loving-kindness.

Sace panassa cirakālaṃ paribhāvitattā lobhassa deyyadhammavisayā lobhadhammā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “nanu tayā sappurisa sambodhāya abhinīhāraṃ karontena sabbasattānamupakārāya ayaṃ kāyo nissaṭṭho, tappariccāgamayañca puññaṃ, tattha nāma te bāhirepi vatthusmiṃ abhisaṅgappavatti hatthisinānasadisī hoti, tasmā tayā na katthaci abhisaṅgo uppādetabbo. Seyyathāpi nāma mahato bhesajjarukkhassa tiṭṭhato mūlaṃ mūlatthikā haranti, papaṭikaṃ, tacaṃ, khandhaṃ, viṭapaṃ, sākhaṃ, palāsaṃ, pupphaṃ, phalaṃ phalatthikā haranti, na tassa rukkhassa ‘mayhaṃ santakaṃ ete harantī’ti vitakkasamudācāro hoti, evameva sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpajjantena mayā mahādukkhe akataññuke niccāsucimhi kāye paresaṃ upakārāya viniyujjamāne aṇumattopi micchāvitakko na uppādetabbo. Ko vā ettha viseso ajjhattikabāhiresu mahābhūtesu ekantabhedanavikiraṇaviddhaṃsanadhammesu. Kevalaṃ pana sammohavijambhitametaṃ, yadidaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti abhiniveso, tasmā bāhiresu mahābhūtesu viya ajjhattikesupi karacaraṇanayanādīsu, maṃsādīsu ca anapekkhena hutvā ‘taṃ tadatthikā harantū’ti nissaṭṭhacittena bhavitabba”nti. Evaṃ paṭisañcikkhato cassa sambodhāya pahitattassa kāyajīvitesu nirapekkhassa appakasireneva kāyavacīmanokammāni [V 1.0230] suvisuddhāni honti, so visuddhakāyavacīmanokammanto visuddhājīvo ñāyapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito āyāpāyupāyakosallasamannāgamena bhiyyoso mattāya deyyadhammapariccāgena, abhayadānasaddhammadānehi ca sabbasatte anuggaṇhituṃ samattho hoti, ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇānayo.

If, however, on account of greed having been cultivated for a long time, states of greed concerning objects to be given should arise in him, then he who has professed to be a bodhisatta should reflect thus: 'Good man, when you made the aspiration for enlightenment, was not this body relinquished by you for the benefit of all beings? And is there not also the merit consisting of that relinquishment? That being so, is not the occurrence of clinging in you even toward an external object similar to bathing an elephant? Therefore, you must not generate clinging toward anything whatsoever. Just as, for a great, standing medicinal tree, those who need the root take the root, those who need the outer bark, the inner bark, the trunk, the branches, the twigs, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruit take the fruit, yet for that tree, there is no occurrence of a thought, “They are taking my property,” so too, when I am striving for the welfare of the entire world, and this body—fraught with great suffering, ungrateful, and ever impure—is being employed for the benefit of others, not even the slightest wrong thought should be generated. Or what difference is there between the internal and external great elements, which are by nature subject to certain breaking, scattering, and destruction? This is merely the display of delusion—this adherence that, “This is mine, this I am, this is my self.” Therefore, just as with the external great elements, so also with the internal ones like hands, feet, eyes, and flesh, one should be unconcerned, thinking with a mind of relinquishment, “Let those who need them take them.”’ For one who reflects thus, whose mind is directed towards enlightenment and who is unconcerned about body and life, his bodily, verbal, and mental actions become exceedingly pure with little difficulty. He, with purified bodily, verbal, and mental actions and pure livelihood, and endowed with skill in the means for progress and decline, becomes capable of helping all beings to a greater degree through the relinquishment of things to be given, and through the gift of fearlessness and the gift of the good Dhamma. This, in the first place, is the method of reviewing the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyaṃ pana evaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – “idañhi sīlaṃ nāma gaṅgodakādīhi visodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa dosamalassa vikkhālanajalaṃ, haricandanādīhi vinetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa rāgādipariḷāhassa vinayanaṃ, muttāhāramakuṭakuṇḍalādīhi pacurajanālaṅkārehi asādhāraṇo sādhūnamalaṅkāraviseso, sabbadisāvāyanako atikittimo [sabbadisāvāyanato akittimo (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7)] sabbakālānurūpo [M 1.0263] ca surabhigandho, khattiyamahāsālādīhi, devatāhi ca vandanīyādibhāvāvahanato paramo vasīkaraṇamanto, cātumahārājikādidevalokārohaṇasopānapanti, jhānābhiññānaṃ adhigamūpāyo, nibbānamahānagarassa sampāpakamaggo, sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhīnaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūmi, yaṃ yaṃ vā panicchitaṃ patthitaṃ, tassa tassa samijjhanūpāyabhāvato cintāmaṇikapparukkhādike ca atiseti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “ijjhati bhikkhave, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā”ti (dī. ni. 3.337; saṃ. ni. 4.352; a. ni. 8.35). Aparampi vuttaṃ “ākaṅkheyya ce bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cāti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.65). Tathā “avippaṭisāratthāni kho ānanda kusalāni sīlānī”ti, (a. ni. 10.1; 11.1) “pañcime gahapatayo, ānisaṃsā sīlavato sīlasampadāyā”tiādisuttānañca (dī. ni. 2.150; a. ni. 5.213; udā. 76; mahāva. 385) vasena sīlaguṇā paccavekkhitabbā. Tathā aggikkhandhopamasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 7.72) vasena sīlavirahe ādīnavā.

Furthermore, the perfection of virtue should be reflected upon thus: 'This virtue is indeed the cleansing water that washes away the stain of aversion, which cannot be cleansed by the waters of the Ganges and other rivers. It is the allaying agent that calms the burning fever of lust and other passions, which cannot be allayed by sandalwood and other remedies. It is the supreme and unique adornment of the virtuous, unmatched by the multitude of ornaments like pearl necklaces, crowns, and earrings worn by ordinary people. It is a fragrant scent that pervades all directions, exceedingly famous, and suitable for all times. It is the highest enchanting spell, as it makes one worthy of reverence by khattiya nobles, wealthy householders, and deities. It is the staircase leading to the realms of the Four Great Kings and other divine worlds. It is the means to attaining meditative absorptions and higher knowledges. It is the road that leads to the great city of Nibbāna. It is the foundation for the enlightenment of disciples, solitary Buddhas, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas. Whatever one wishes for or aspires to, virtue serves as the means to its fulfillment, surpassing even the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-fulfilling tree. As the Blessed One has said: “Monks, the heart’s aspiration of a virtuous one succeeds because of purity.” Further, it is said: “If a monk wishes to be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by his fellow practitioners, he should be a perfect fulfiller of the precepts of virtue.” Likewise, “Wholesome moral precepts, Ānanda, have non-remorse as their benefit,” and by way of suttas such as, “Householders, there are these five benefits for a virtuous person accomplished in virtue,” the qualities of virtue should be reviewed. Similarly, by way of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta and others, the dangers in the absence of virtue should be reviewed.'

Apica pītisomanassanimittato, attānuvādaparānuvādadaṇḍaduggatibhayābhāvato, viññūhi pāsaṃsabhāvato, avippaṭisārahetuto, paramasotthiṭṭhānato, kulasāpateyyādhipateyyajīvitarūpaṭṭhānabandhumittasampattīnaṃ atisayanato ca sīlaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Sīlavato hi attano sīlasampadāhetu mahantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati “kataṃ vata mayā kusalaṃ, kataṃ kalyāṇaṃ, kataṃ bhīruttāṇa”nti.

Moreover, virtue should be reviewed as a cause for rapture and gladness; as the absence of the fears of self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, and a bad destination; as being praised by the wise; as a cause for non-remorse; as the ground of supreme well-being; and as surpassing the accomplishments of family, wealth, sovereignty, life, beauty, position, relatives, and friends. For to a virtuous person, on account of their own accomplishment in virtue, great rapture and gladness arise, thinking: 'Indeed, what is wholesome has been done by me, what is good has been done, what is a protection from fear has been done!'

Tathā [V 1.0231] sīlavato attā na upavadati, na ca pare viññū, daṇḍaduggatibhayānañca sambhavoyeva natthi, “sīlavā purisapuggalo kalyāṇadhammo”ti viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso ca hoti. Tathā sīlavato yvāyaṃ “kataṃ vata mayā pāpaṃ, kataṃ luddaṃ, kataṃ kibbisa”nti dussīlassa vippaṭisāro uppajjati, so na hoti. Sīlañca nāmetaṃ appamādādhiṭṭhānato, bhogabyasanādiparihāramukhena mahato atthassa sādhanato, maṅgalabhāvato, paramaṃ sotthiṭṭhānaṃ. Nihīnajaccopi sīlavā khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ pūjanīyo hotīti kulasampattiṃ atiseti sīlasampadā, “taṃ kiṃ maññasi [M 1.0264] mahārāja, idha te assa dāso kammakaro”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.183) vakkhamānasāmaññasuttavacanañcettha sādhakaṃ, corādīhi asādhāraṇato, paralokānugamanato, mahapphalabhāvato, samathādiguṇādhiṭṭhānato ca bāhiradhanaṃ sāpateyyaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Paramassa cittissariyassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato khattiyādīnamissariyaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Sīlanimittañhi taṃtaṃsattanikāyesu sattānamissariyaṃ, vassasatādidīghappamāṇato ca jīvitato ekāhampi sīlavato jīvitassa visiṭṭhatāvacanato, satipi jīvite sikkhānikkhipanassa maraṇatāvacanato ca sīlaṃ jīvitato visiṭṭhataraṃ. Verīnampi manuññabhāvāvahanato, jarārogavipattīhi anabhibhavanīyato ca rūpasampattiṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Pāsādahammiyādiṭṭhānappabhede rājayuvarājasenāpatiādiṭhānavisese ca sukhavisesādhiṭṭhānabhāvato atiseti sīlaṃ. Sabhāvasiniddhe santikāvacarepi bandhujane, mittajane ca ekantahitasampādanato, paralokānugamanato ca atiseti sīlaṃ. “Na taṃ mātā pitā kayirā”tiādi (dha. pa. 43) vacanañcettha sādhakaṃ. Tathā hatthiassarathapattibalakāyehi, mantāgadasotthānapayogehi ca durārakkhānamanāthānaṃ attādhīnato, anaparādhīnato, mahāvisayato ca ārakkhabhāvena sīlameva visiṭṭhataraṃ. Tenevāha “dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”ntiādi (theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102). Evamanekaguṇasamannāgataṃ sīlanti paccavekkhantassa aparipuṇṇā ceva sīlasampadā pāripūriṃ gacchati, aparisuddhā ca pārisuddhiṃ.

Furthermore, for the virtuous, one's self does not reproach, nor do other wise ones; and there is no arising of the fear of punishment and of a bad destination. There is also the praise of the wise: "A virtuous person is of good character." Furthermore, for the virtuous, that remorse which arises for the unvirtuous—"Alas, I have done evil, I have done a harsh deed, I have done a cruel deed"—does not occur. And this, which is called virtue, is the supreme basis for well-being, because it is the foundation of heedfulness, because it accomplishes a great benefit by way of preventing the destruction of wealth and so on, and because it is of the nature of a blessing. Even one of low birth, if virtuous, becomes worthy of veneration by khattiyas of great wealth and so on; thus, the accomplishment of virtue surpasses the accomplishment of lineage. And the words from the Sāmaññaphala Sutta to be spoken, "What do you think, great king? Here there might be your slave, a worker..." (Dī. Ni. 1.183), are proof in this matter. Because it is not shared with thieves and so on, because it follows one to the next world, because it has a great fruit, and because it is the foundation for qualities such as tranquility, virtue surpasses external wealth and property. Because it is the foundation for supreme mastery of the mind, virtue surpasses the sovereignty of khattiyas and others. For, on account of virtue, there is sovereignty over beings in their respective classes of beings. And because it is stated that the life of a virtuous person, even for a single day, is more distinguished than a life of a hundred years or more, and because the laying down of the training, even while one is alive, is stated to be death, virtue is more excellent than life. Because it brings about a state of being agreeable even to enemies, and because it is not to be overcome by the misfortunes of old age and disease, virtue surpasses the accomplishment of beauty. Because it is the foundation for special happiness, virtue surpasses the various kinds of places such as palaces and mansions, and the special positions such as king, crown prince, and general. Because it accomplishes certain welfare and follows one to the next world, virtue surpasses even relatives and friends who are naturally affectionate and live nearby. And the saying, "What neither mother nor father can do..." (Dha. Pa. 43), is proof here. Furthermore, as a protection for those who are difficult to protect and without a protector, virtue alone is more excellent than the forces of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and the application of mantras, medicines, and means for well-being, because it is dependent on oneself, not dependent on others, and of great scope. Therefore, He said: "The Dhamma indeed protects one who practices the Dhamma" (Theragā. 303; Jā. 1.10.102). Thus, for one reflecting, "Virtue is endowed with many qualities," the accomplishment of virtue, if incomplete, goes to completion, and if impure, goes to purity.

Sace panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena sīlapaṭipakkhadhammā dosādayo antarantarā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena evaṃ paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “nanu tayā bodhāya paṇidhānaṃ kataṃ, sīlavekallena ca na sakkā na ca sukarā lokiyāpi sampattiyo pāpuṇituṃ, pageva lokuttarā”ti. Sabbasampattīnamaggabhūtāya sammāsambodhiyā adhiṭṭhānabhūtena sīlena paramukkaṃsagatena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā “kikīva aṇḍa”ntiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; visuddhi. 1.19) vuttanayena sammadeva sīlaṃ rakkhantena suṭṭhu tayā pesalena bhavitabbaṃ.

But if, for this person, through long familiarity, qualities opposed to virtue, such as aversion, should arise from time to time, it should be reflected upon thus by that one who has professed to be a bodhisatta: "Have you not made an aspiration for enlightenment? And with a deficiency in virtue, it is neither possible nor easy to attain even worldly accomplishments, how much more so supramundane ones?" One must have virtue that has reached the highest excellence, which is the foundation for perfect self-enlightenment, the foremost of all accomplishments. Therefore, guarding virtue perfectly in the way that was stated, "like a kiki bird her egg," and so on (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.7; Visuddhi. 1.19), you must be thoroughly devoted to virtue.

Apica [V 1.0232][M 1.0265] tayā dhammadesanāya yānattaye sattānamavatāraṇaparipācanāni kātabbāni, sīlavekallassa ca vacanaṃ na paccetabbaṃ hoti, asappāyāhāravicārassa viya vejjassa tikicchanaṃ, tasmā “kathāhaṃ saddheyyo hutvā sattānamavatāraṇaparipācanāni kareyya”nti sabhāvaparisuddhasīlena bhavitabbaṃ. Kiñca jhānādiguṇavisesayogena me sattānamupakārakaraṇasamatthatā, paññāpāramīādiparipūraṇañca jhānādayo guṇā ca sīlapārisuddhiṃ vinā na sambhavantīti sammadeva sīlaṃ sodhetabbaṃ.

Moreover, by you, the causing of beings to enter and mature in the three vehicles must be done through the teaching of the Dhamma. And the word of one deficient in virtue is not to be trusted, just as the treatment of a physician who administers unsuitable food is not to be trusted. Therefore, thinking, "How can I, having become trustworthy, cause beings to enter and mature?" one must have virtue that is pure by its very nature. Furthermore, my ability to be of service to beings through the attainment of special qualities such as the jhānas, and the fulfillment of the perfections such as the perfection of wisdom, and qualities such as the jhānas, do not come to be without purity of virtue. Therefore, virtue must be perfectly purified.

Tathā “sambādho gharāvāso rajopatho”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.111; ma. ni. 1.291, 371; 2.10; 3.13, 218; saṃ. ni. 2.154; 5.1002; a. ni. 10.99; netti. 94) gharāvāse, “aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.234; 2.42; pāci. 417; cūḷani. 147) “mātāpi puttena vivadatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.168) ca kāmesu, “seyyathāpi puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojeyyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.426) kāmacchandādīsu ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā, vuttavipariyāyena “abbhokāso pabbajjā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.191, 398; ma. ni. 1.291, 371; 2.10; 3.13, 218; saṃ. ni. 1.291; saṃ. ni. 5.1002; a. ni. 10.99; netti. 98) pabbajjādīsu ānisaṃsāpaṭisaṅkhāvasena nekkhammapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇā kātabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana dukkhakkhandhaāsivisopamasuttādi (ma. ni. 1.163, 175; saṃ. ni. 4.238) vasena veditabbo.

Furthermore, reflection on the perfection of renunciation should be done. This reflection is preceded by seeing the danger: in household life, as in 'Household life is confining, a path of dust,' and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.111; etc.); in sensual pleasures, as in 'Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.234; etc.), and 'Even a mother quarrels with her son,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.168); and in sensual desire and so on, as in 'Just as a person, having taken on a debt, might engage in business,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.426). Conversely, this reflection proceeds by way of considering the benefits in the going forth and so on, as in 'The going forth is the open air,' and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.191; etc.). This is the summary here. But the detail should be understood by way of the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta, the Āsīvisopama Sutta, and others (Ma. Ni. 1.163, 175; Saṃ. Ni. 4.238).

Tathā “paññāya vinā dānādayo dhammā na visujjhanti, yathāsakaṃ byāpārasamatthā ca na hontī”ti paññāya guṇā manasi kātabbā. Yatheva hi jīvitena vinā sarīrayantaṃ na sobhati, na ca attano kiriyāsu paṭipattisamatthaṃ hoti. Yathā ca cakkhādīni indriyāni viññāṇena vinā yathāsakaṃ visayesu kiccaṃ kātuṃ nappahonti, evaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni paññāya vinā sakakiccapaṭipattiyamasamatthānīti pariccāgādipaṭipattiyaṃ paññā padhānakāraṇaṃ. Ummīlitapaññācakkhukā hi mahāsattā bodhisattā attano aṅgapaccaṅgānipi datvā anattukkaṃsakā, aparavambhakā ca honti, bhesajjarukkhā viya vikapparahitā kālattayepi somanassajātā. Paññāvasena hi upāyakosallayogato pariccāgo parahitapavattiyā dānapāramibhāvaṃ upeti. Attatthañhi dānaṃ muddhasadisaṃ [vuddhisadisaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7)] hoti.

Furthermore, 'without wisdom, virtues such as generosity are not purified, nor are they capable of their respective functions.' Therefore, the qualities of wisdom should be kept in mind. For just as a body-mechanism without life does not shine, nor is it capable of performing its own functions, and just as the faculties such as the eye, without consciousness, are unable to perform their function in their respective objects, so too the faculties such as faith, without wisdom, are incapable in the practice that is their own function. Therefore, in the practice of relinquishment and so on, wisdom is the principal cause. For indeed, the great beings, the bodhisattas, with the eye of wisdom opened, having given even their own major and minor limbs, are without self-exaltation and without disparagement of others; like medicinal trees, being free from conceptualization, they are joyful in all three periods of time. For by the power of wisdom, through association with skill in means, relinquishment, because it occurs for the welfare of others, attains the state of the perfection of generosity. For giving for one's own benefit is like the capital.

Tathā [V 1.0233][M 1.0266] paññāya abhāvena taṇhādisaṃkilesāviyogato sīlassa visuddhiyeva na sambhavati, kuto sabbaññuguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvo. Paññavā eva ca gharāvāse kāmaguṇesu saṃsāre ca ādīnavaṃ, pabbajjāya jhānasamāpattiyaṃ nibbāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ suṭṭhu sallakkhento pabbajitvā jhānasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā nibbānaninno, pare ca tattha patiṭṭhapeti.

Furthermore, due to the absence of wisdom, because of non-disjunction from defilements such as craving, the purification of virtue itself does not come to be; whence the state of being the foundation for the qualities of omniscience? And only the wise one, having clearly discerned the danger in household life, in sensual pleasures, and in saṃsāra, and the benefit in the going forth, in meditative attainments, and in Nibbāna, having gone forth and produced the meditative attainments, becomes inclined towards Nibbāna, and also establishes others therein.

Vīriyañca paññārahitaṃ yathicchitamatthaṃ na sādheti durārambhabhāvato. Anārambhoyeva hi durārambhato seyyo, paññāsahitena pana vīriyena na kiñci duradhigamaṃ upāyapaṭipattito. Tathā paññavā eva parāpakārādīnamadhivāsakajātiyo hoti, na duppañño. Paññāvirahitassa ca parehi upanītā apakārā khantiyā paṭipakkhameva anubrūhenti. Paññavato pana te khantisampattiyā anubrūhanavasena assā thirabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Paññavā eva tīṇipi saccāni tesaṃ kāraṇāni paṭipakkhe ca yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā paresaṃ avisaṃvādako hoti. Tathā paññābalena attānamupatthambhetvā dhitisampadāya sabbapāramīsu acalasamādānādhiṭṭhāno hoti. Paññavā eva ca piyamajjhattaverivibhāgamakatvā sabbattha hitūpasaṃhārakusalo hoti. Tathā paññāvasena lābhālābhādilokadhammasannipāte nibbikāratāya majjhatto hoti. Evaṃ sabbāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ paññāva pārisuddhihetūti paññāguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

And energy devoid of wisdom does not accomplish the desired aim, because it is a wrong undertaking. For non-undertaking is indeed better than a wrong undertaking. But with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is difficult to attain, due to the practice of the right means. Likewise, only a wise person is of a nature to endure harms from others and so on, not an unwise person. For one lacking wisdom, the harms inflicted by others increase only the opposite of patience. But for the wise, those harms conduce to the stability of that patience by way of developing the accomplishment of patience. Only the wise one, having known as they truly are the three truths, their causes, and their opposing factors, is one who does not deceive others. Likewise, having supported oneself with the strength of wisdom, one becomes of unwavering undertaking and resolve in all perfections for the sake of the accomplishment of steadfastness. And only the wise one, not making a distinction between the dear, the neutral, and the hostile, is skilled in bringing about welfare everywhere. Likewise, by the power of wisdom, one is equanimous through being unperturbed amidst the confluence of worldly conditions such as gain and loss. Thus, 'Wisdom alone is the cause of purity for all the perfections.' In this way, the qualities of wisdom should be contemplated.

Apica paññāya vinā na dassanasampatti, antarena ca diṭṭhisampadaṃ na sīlasampadā, sīladiṭṭhisampadārahitassa ca na samādhisampadā, asamāhitena ca na sakkā attahitamattampi sādhetuṃ, pageva ukkaṃsagataṃ parahitanti. “Nanu tayā parahitāya paṭipannena sakkaccaṃ paññāpārisuddhiyā āyogo karaṇīyo”ti bodhisattena attā ovaditabbo. Paññānubhāvena hi mahāsatto caturadhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhito catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto satte niyyānamagge avatāreti, indriyāni ca nesaṃ paripāceti. Tathā paññābalena khandhāyatanādīsu pavicayabahulo pavattinivattiyo yāthāvato parijānanto dānādayo guṇavisese nibbedhabhāgiyabhāvaṃ nayanto bodhisattasikkhāya paripūrakārī hotīti evamādinā anekākāravokāre paññāguṇe vavatthapetvā paññāpāramī anubrūhetabbā.

Furthermore, without wisdom there is no accomplishment in vision; and without the accomplishment in view, there is no accomplishment in virtue; and for one devoid of the accomplishment in virtue and view, there is no accomplishment in concentration. And one who is unconcentrated is not able to achieve even his own welfare, how much more so the supreme welfare of others. The Bodhisatta should admonish himself thus: 'Should you, who are practicing for the welfare of others, not diligently make an effort for the complete purity of wisdom?' For by the power of wisdom, the Great Being, established in the four determinations, while favoring the world with the four bases of beneficence, leads beings onto the path of deliverance, and brings their faculties to maturity. Likewise, by the strength of wisdom, being one who investigates much into the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, thoroughly understanding occurrence and cessation as they really are, and leading special qualities such as giving to a state conducive to penetration, one becomes a fulfiller of the Bodhisatta's training. Thus, having determined the qualities of wisdom which are endowed with manifold aspects in these and other ways, the perfection of wisdom should be developed.

Tathā [M 1.0267] dissamānapārānipi lokiyāni kammāni nihīnavīriyena pāpuṇitumasakkuṇeyyāni, agaṇitakhedena pana āraddhavīriyena duradhigamaṃ nāma natthi. Nihīnavīriyo hi “saṃsāramahoghato sabbasatte santāressāmī”ti ārabhitumeva na sakkuṇoti. Majjhimo pana ārabhitvāna [V 1.0234] antarāvosānamāpajjati. Ukkaṭṭhavīriyo pana attasukhanirapekkho ārabhitvā pāramadhigacchatīti vīriyasampatti paccavekkhitabbā.

Likewise, even worldly tasks with a visible further shore cannot be reached by one with deficient energy, but for one with aroused energy who disregards weariness, there is nothing at all that is difficult to attain. For one with deficient energy cannot even begin with the thought: 'I will ferry all beings across the great flood of saṃsāra.' One with medium energy, however, having begun, comes to a stop midway. But one with supreme energy, being indifferent to his own happiness, having begun, reaches the further shore. Thus the accomplishment in energy should be reflected upon.

Apica “yassa attano eva saṃsārapaṅkato samuddharaṇatthamārambho, tassāpi vīriyassa sithilabhāvena manorathānaṃ matthakappatti na sakkā sambhāvetuṃ, pageva sadevakassa lokassa samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhārenā”ti ca “rāgādīnaṃ dosagaṇānaṃ mattamahānāgānamiva dunnivāraṇabhāvato, tannidānānañca kammasamādānānaṃ ukkhittāsikavadhakasadisabhāvato, tannimittānañca duggatīnaṃ sabbadā vivaṭamukhabhāvato, tattha niyojakānañca pāpamittānaṃ sadā sannihitabhāvato, tadovādakāritāya ca vasalassa puthujjanabhāvassa sati sambhave yuttaṃ sayameva saṃsāradukkhato nissaritu”nti ca “micchāvitakkā vīriyānubhāvena dūrī bhavantī”ti ca “yadi pana sambodhiṃ attādhīnena vīriyena sakkā samadhigantuṃ, kimettha dukkara”nti ca evamādinā nayena vīriyaguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Furthermore, one should reflect: 'Even for one whose effort is to raise only himself from the mud of saṃsāra, if his energy slackens, the fulfillment of his aspirations cannot be brought about—how much more so for one who has made the aspiration to raise the world with its devas!' And: 'Because the host of faults such as lust are as difficult to restrain as intoxicated great elephants; and because the undertakings of kamma rooted in them are like executioners with upraised swords; and because the bad destinations caused by them always have their mouths wide open; and because evil friends who incite one to them are always near; and because, while there is the possibility of being a base worldling who acts on their advice, it is proper to escape from the suffering of saṃsāra by oneself.' And: 'Wrong thoughts are driven far away by the power of energy.' And: 'If, however, perfect enlightenment can be attained by energy that is dependent on oneself, what herein is difficult?' In these and other ways, the qualities of energy should be reflected upon.

Tathā “khanti nāmāyaṃ niravasesaguṇapaṭipakkhassa kodhassa vidhamanato guṇasampādane sādhūnaṃ appaṭihatamāyudhaṃ, parābhibhavane samatthānamalaṅkāro, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ balasampadā, kodhaggivinayanā udakadhārā, kalyāṇakittisaddassa sañjātideso, pāpapuggalānaṃ vacīvisavūpasamakaro mantāgado, saṃvare ṭhitānaṃ paramā dhīrapakati, gambhīrāsayatāya sāgaro, dosamahāsāgarassa velā, apāyadvārassa pidhānakavāṭaṃ devabrahmalokānaṃ ārohaṇasopānaṃ, sabbaguṇānamadhivāsabhūmi, uttamā kāyavacīmanovisuddhī”ti manasi kātabbaṃ. Apica “ete sattā khantisampattiyā abhāvato idhaloke tapanti, paraloke ca tapanīyadhammānuyogato”ti ca “yadipi parāpakāranimittaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa pana dukkhassa khettabhūto attabhāvo, bījabhūtañca kammaṃ mayāva abhisaṅkhata”nti ca “tassa ca dukkhassa āṇaṇyakaraṇameta”nti ca “apakārake asati kathaṃ mayhaṃ khantisampadā sambhavatī”ti ca “yadipāyaṃ etarahi apakārako[M 1.0268], ayaṃ nāma pubbe anena mayhaṃ upakāro kato”ti ca “apakāro eva vā khantinimittatāya upakāro”ti ca “sabbepime sattā mayhaṃ puttasadisā, puttakatāparādhesu ca ko kujjhissatī”ti ca “yena kodhabhūtāvesena ayaṃ mayhaṃ aparajjhati, svāyaṃ kodhabhūtāveso mayā vinetabbo”ti ca “yena apakārena idaṃ mayhaṃ dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa ahampi nimitta”nti ca “yehi dhammehi apakāro kato, yattha ca kato, sabbepi te tasmiṃyeva khaṇe niruddhā, kassidāni kena kopo kātabbo”ti ca “anattatāya sabbadhammānaṃ ko kassa aparajjhatī”ti ca paccavekkhantena khantisampadā brūhetabbā.

Furthermore, it should be borne in mind by the wise: 'This so-called patience, by dispelling anger—the opponent of all virtues without remainder—is the unopposed weapon of the good in the accomplishment of virtues; an ornament for those capable of overcoming others; the endowment of strength for ascetics and brahmins; a stream of water for subduing the fire of anger; the birthplace of a good reputation; a magical antidote that pacifies the verbal poison of evil people; the supreme nature of the wise for those established in restraint; an ocean due to its profound basis; the shore for the great ocean of hatred; a closing door-leaf for the gate to the planes of misery; a staircase for ascending to the worlds of devas and brahmās; the dwelling place for all virtues; and the supreme purity of body, speech, and mind.' Moreover, 'These beings, due to the absence of the accomplishment of patience, are tormented in this world, and in the next world due to their application to tormenting states'; and, 'Although suffering arises on account of harm from others, nevertheless, the personal existence which is the field for that suffering, and the kamma which is the seed, were produced by me alone'; and, 'This is the making of freedom from debt for that suffering'; and, 'If there were no wrongdoer, how could my accomplishment of patience arise?'; and, 'Although this person is a wrongdoer now, in the past, such-and-such a benefit was done to me by this one'; and, 'Or, the harm itself, by being a condition for patience, is a benefit'; and, 'All these beings are like my children; and what parent would get angry at offenses committed by their children?'; and, 'By whatever possession by the demon of anger this one offends against me, that very possession by the demon of anger should be subdued by me'; and, 'For the harm by which this suffering has arisen in me, I too am a condition'; and, 'The states by which the harm was done, and where it was done—all of them ceased in that very moment. Now, towards whom and by whom should anger be made?'; and, 'Due to the non-self nature of all phenomena, who wrongs whom?'—by one reflecting thus, the accomplishment of patience should be cultivated.

Yadi [V 1.0235] panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena parāpakāranimittako kodho cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya, tena iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “khanti nāmesā parāpakārassa paṭipakkhapaṭipattīnaṃ paccupakārakāraṇa”nti ca “apakāro ca mayhaṃ dukkhuppādanena dukkhupanisāya saddhāya, sabbaloke anabhiratisaññāya ca paccayo”ti ca “indriyapakatiresā, yadidaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo, tattha aniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo mayhaṃ na siyāti taṃ kutettha labbhā”ti ca “kodhavasiko satto kodhena ummatto vikkhittacitto, tattha kiṃ paccapakārenā”ti ca “sabbepime sattā sammāsambuddhena orasaputtā viya paripālitā, tasmā na tattha mayā cittakopo kātabbo”ti ca “aparādhake ca sati guṇe guṇavati mayā kopo na kātabbo”ti ca “asati guṇe kassacipi guṇassābhāvato visesena karuṇāyitabbo”ti ca “kopena mayhaṃ guṇayasā nihīyantī”ti ca “kujjhanena mayhaṃ dubbaṇṇadukkhaseyyādayo sapattakantā āgacchantī”ti ca “kodho ca nāmāyaṃ sabbadukkhāhitakārako sabbasukhahitavināsako balavā paccatthiko”ti ca “sati ca khantiyā na koci paccatthiko”ti ca “aparādhakena aparādhanimittaṃ yaṃ dukkhaṃ āyatiṃ laddhabbaṃ, sati ca khantiyā mayhaṃ tadabhāvo”ti ca “cintentena, kujjhantena ca mayā paccatthikoyeva anuvattito”ti ca “kodhe ca mayā khantiyā abhibhūte tassa dāsabhūto paccatthiko sammadeva abhibhūto”ti ca “kodhanimittaṃ khantiguṇapariccāgo mayhaṃ na yutto”ti ca “sati ca kodhe guṇavirodhapaccanīkadhamme kathaṃ me sīlādidhammā pāripūriṃ gaccheyyuṃ, asati ca tesu kathāhaṃ sattānaṃ upakārabahulo [M 1.0269] paṭiññānurūpaṃ uttamaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti ca “khantiyā ca sati bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato samāhitassa sabbe saṅkhārā aniccato dukkhato sabbe dhammā anattato nibbānaṃ asaṅkhatāmatasantapaṇītatādibhāvato nijjhānaṃ khamanti, ‘buddhadhammā ca acinteyyāparimeyyappabhavā’ti”, tato ca “anulomikakhantiyaṃ ṭhito ‘kevalā ime attattaniyabhāvarahitā dhammamattā yathāsakaṃ paccayehi uppajjanti vinassanti, na kutoci āgacchanti, na kuhiñci gacchanti, na ca katthaci patiṭṭhitā, na cettha koci kassaci byāpāro’ti ahaṃkāramamaṃkārānadhiṭṭhānatā nijjhānaṃ khamati, yena bodhisatto bodhiyā niyato anāvattidhammo hotī”ti evamādinā khantipāramiyā paccavekkhaṇā veditabbā.

Furthermore, if, through long familiarity, anger caused by the harm of others should take possession of his mind and persist, he should reflect thus: 'This patience is the cause of rendering a benefit in return, which is among the practices that counteract the harm of others'; and, 'The harm done to me, by producing suffering, is a condition for faith that has suffering as its support, and for the perception of non-delight in the whole world'; and, 'This is the nature of the faculties, namely, the encounter with agreeable and disagreeable objects; therein, that the encounter with disagreeable objects should not happen to me—where could that be obtained?'; and, 'A being under the sway of anger is maddened by anger, his mind is distracted; what is the use of retaliating against him?'; and, 'All these beings were cared for by the Perfectly Enlightened One like his own breast-born sons; therefore, corruption of mind should not be done by me towards them'; and, 'And if a wrongdoer has virtues, anger should not be directed by me towards that virtuous one'; and, 'If he has no virtues, because of the absence of any virtue whatsoever, he is especially to be regarded with compassion'; and, 'Through anger, my virtues and fame decline'; and, 'By my getting angry, ugliness, painful sleep, and other such things dear to my enemies come to me'; and, 'And this so-called anger is the cause of all suffering and non-benefit, the destroyer of all happiness and welfare, a powerful enemy'; and, 'And when patience is present, there is no enemy at all'; and, 'Whatever suffering is to be received in the future on account of the wrongdoing, for me, when patience is present, that suffering is absent'; and, 'By thinking and by getting angry, I have only followed the enemy'; and, 'And when anger is overcome by my patience, the enemy, who has become its slave, is truly overcome'; and, 'It is not proper for me to abandon the virtue of patience on account of anger'; and, 'And when anger is present—a state contrary and hostile to virtue—how can my qualities such as virtue reach fulfillment? And without them, how can I, being of great benefit to beings, attain the supreme fulfillment in accordance with my vow?'; and, 'And when patience is present, due to the absence of external distraction, for one who is concentrated, it is fit to contemplate all formations as impermanent and as suffering, all phenomena as non-self, and Nibbāna by way of its nature as unconditioned, deathless, peaceful, sublime, etc., and that the qualities of the Buddha are of inconceivable and immeasurable origin'; and from that, established in conformable patience, 'These are merely phenomena, devoid of the state of self and what belongs to self, arising and ceasing according to their respective conditions. They do not come from anywhere, nor go anywhere, nor are they established anywhere, and herein there is no activity of any one for any other'—the contemplation of the non-establishment of 'I-making' and 'mine-making' is fit, by which the Bodhisatta becomes fixed for enlightenment, one of a non-regressing nature.' In these and other ways, the reflections on the perfection of patience are to be understood.

Tathā “saccena vinā sīlādīnamasambhavato, paṭiññānurūpapaṭipattiyā abhāvato, saccadhammātikkame ca sabbapāpadhammānaṃ samosaraṇabhāvato, asaccasandhassa appaccayikabhāvato, āyatiñca anādeyyavacanatāvahanato, sampannasaccassa sabbaguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvato, saccādhiṭṭhānena sabbasambodhisambhārānaṃ pārisuddhipāripūrisamanvāyato, sabhāvadhammāvisaṃvādanena sabbabodhisambhārakiccakaraṇato[V 1.0236], bodhisattapaṭipattiyā ca parinipphattito”tiādinā saccapāramiyā sampattiyo paccavekkhitabbā.

Furthermore, the accomplishments of the perfection of truth should be reflected upon in these and other ways: because without truth, virtues such as morality are impossible; because of the absence of practice in accordance with one’s promise; because when the principle of truth is transgressed, it becomes a convergence point for all evil qualities; because a person of inconsistent truth is untrustworthy; because in the future it leads to one's words not being accepted; because one accomplished in truth is the foundation of all virtues; because through the determination of truth, all the requisites of perfect enlightenment properly attain thorough purity and thorough fulfillment; because by not misrepresenting the true nature of things, the tasks of all the requisites for enlightenment are accomplished; and because the Bodhisatta's practice is brought to thorough perfection.

Tathā “dānādīsu daḷhasamādānaṃ, tappaṭipakkhasannipāte ca nesaṃ acalādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tattha ca dhīravīrabhāvaṃ vinā na dānādisambhārā sambodhinimittā sambhavantī”tiādinā adhiṭṭhānaguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Furthermore, the qualities of resolution should be reflected upon in this and other ways: ‘Without firm undertaking in giving and so on, their unwavering determination when opposing factors converge, and the state of being steadfast and heroic therein, the requisites such as giving, which are causes for enlightenment, do not arise.’

Tathā “attahitamatte avatiṭṭhantenāpi sattesu hitacittataṃ vinā na sakkā idhalokaparalokasampattiyo pāpuṇituṃ, pageva sabbasatte nibbānasampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetukāmenā”ti ca “pacchā sabbasattānaṃ lokuttarasampattimākaṅkhantena idāni lokiyasampattimākaṅkhā yuttarūpā”ti ca “idāni āsayamattena paresaṃ hitasukhūpasaṃhāraṃ kātumasakkonto kadā payogena taṃ sādhayissāmī”ti ca “idāni mayā hitasukhūpasaṃhārena saṃvaddhitā pacchā dhammasaṃvibhāgasahāyā mayhaṃ bhavissantī”ti ca “etehi vinā na mayhaṃ bodhisambhārā sambhavanti, tasmā sabbabuddhaguṇavibhūtinipphattikāraṇattā mayhaṃ ete paramaṃ puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ kusalāyatanaṃ uttamaṃ [M 1.0270] gāravaṭṭhāna”nti ca “savisesaṃ sabbesupi sattesu hitajjhāsayatā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā, kiñca karuṇādhiṭṭhānatopi sabbasattesu mettā anubrūhetabbā. Vimariyādīkatena hi cetasā sattesu hitasukhūpasaṃhāraniratassa tesaṃ ahitadukkhāpanayanakāmatā balavatī uppajjati daḷhamūlā, karuṇā ca sabbesaṃ buddhakārakadhammānaṃ ādi caraṇaṃ patiṭṭhā mūlaṃ mukhaṃ pamukha”nti evamādinā mettāguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Furthermore, the qualities of loving-kindness should be reflected upon in these and other ways: ‘Even by one who is established only in their own welfare, without a mind wishing for the welfare of beings, it is not possible to attain the accomplishments of this world and the next—how much more so for one who wishes to establish all beings in the accomplishment of Nibbāna.’ And, ‘For one who later aspires to the supramundane accomplishment of all beings, to now aspire for worldly accomplishment is of a fitting nature.’ And, ‘If I am now unable to bring about the welfare and happiness of others with mere intention, when will I accomplish it through effort?’ And, ‘Those nurtured by me now through bringing about their welfare and happiness will later become my companions in sharing the Dhamma.’ And, ‘Without these, my requisites for enlightenment do not arise. Therefore, because they are the cause for accomplishing the splendor of all the Buddha's virtues, for me they are the supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed basis of the wholesome, the highest object of reverence.’ And, ‘Especially, an inclination for the welfare of all beings should be established. Furthermore, from the basis of compassion, loving-kindness towards all beings should be repeatedly cultivated. Indeed, for one who delights in bringing about the welfare and happiness of beings with a mind made boundless, the wish to dispel their harm and suffering arises strong and with firm roots. And compassion is the beginning, the conduct, the foundation, the root, the face, and the foremost of all the qualities that make a Buddha.’ In this and other ways, the qualities of loving-kindness should be reflected upon.

Tathā “upekkhāya abhāve sattehi katā vippakārā cittassa vikāraṃ uppādeyyuṃ, sati ca cittavikāre dānādisambhārānaṃ sambhavo eva natthī”ti ca “mettāsinehena sinehite citte upekkhāya vinā sambhārānaṃ pārisuddhi na hotī”ti ca “anupekkhako saṅkhāresu puññasambhāraṃ, tabbipākañca sattahitatthaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ na sakkotī”ti ca upekkhāya abhāve deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ vibhāgamakatvā pariccajituṃ na sakkotī”ti ca “upekkhārahitena jīvitaparikkhārānaṃ, jīvitassa vā antarāyaṃ amanasikaritvā sīlavisodhanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā”ti ca tathā “upekkhāvasena aratiratisahasseva nekkhammabalasiddhito, upapattito ikkhanavaseneva sabbasambhārakiccanipphattito, accāraddhavīriyassa anupekkhane padhānakiccākaraṇato, upekkhato eva titikkhānijjhānasambhavato, upekkhāvasena sattasaṅkhārānaṃ avisaṃvādanato, lokadhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhanena samādinnadhammesu acalādhiṭṭhānasiddhito, parāpakārādīsu [V 1.0237] anābhogavaseneva mettāvihāranipphattitoti sabbasambodhisambhārānaṃ samādānādhiṭṭhānapāripūrinipphattiyo upekkhānubhāvena sampajjantī”ti evamādinā nayena upekkhāpāramī paccavekkhitabbā. Evaṃ apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇā dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the perfection of equanimity should be reflected upon with reasoning such as this: ‘In the absence of equanimity, wrongdoings done by beings might cause a disturbance of the mind; and when there is a disturbance of the mind, the arising of the requisites such as giving is simply not possible.’ And, ‘In a mind made affectionate with the affection of loving-kindness, without equanimity the thorough purity of the requisites does not occur.’ And, ‘One who is not equanimous regarding formations is not able to dedicate the requisite of merit and its result for the welfare of beings.’ And, ‘In the absence of equanimity, one is not able to relinquish without making distinctions among things to be given and recipients.’ And, ‘One devoid of equanimity is not able to purify morality by disregarding danger to the requisites of life or to life itself.’ Furthermore, ‘The accomplishments of the thorough fulfillment of the undertaking and determination of all the requisites for perfect enlightenment are fulfilled through the power of equanimity because: only for one who endures discontent and content by means of equanimity is the power of renunciation accomplished; all the tasks of the requisites are accomplished merely by the power of seeing things as they arise; for one with excessive effort, in the absence of equanimity, the primary task is not done; the arising of forbearance and contemplation is possible only for one who is equanimous; by means of equanimity, there is no misrepresentation of the formations of beings; through looking upon the worldly conditions with equanimity, unwavering determination in the principles one has undertaken is accomplished; and the abiding in loving-kindness is accomplished merely by the power of not paying attention to the wrongdoings of others.’ In this and other ways, the perfection of equanimity should be reflected upon. Thus, it should be understood that the sequential reflection on the dangers and benefits in non-relinquishment, relinquishment, and so on, is a condition for the perfections of giving and so on.

Tathā saparikkhārā pañcadasa caraṇadhammā pañca ca abhiññāyo. Tattha caraṇadhammā nāma sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, cattāri jhānāni ca. Tesu sīlādīnaṃ catunnaṃ terasapi dhutaṅgadhammā, appicchatādayo ca parikkhārā. Saddhammesu saddhāya buddhadhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatupasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanā, siniddhapuggalasevanā, sampasādanīyadhammapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatā ca parikkhārā. Hirottappānaṃ akusalādīnavapaccavekkhaṇā, apāyādīnavapaccavekkhaṇā[M 1.0271], kusaladhammūpatthambhabhāvapaccavekkhaṇā, hirottapparahitapuggalaparivajjanā, hirottappasampannapuggalasevanā, tadadhimuttatā ca. Bāhusaccassa pubbayogo, paripucchakabhāvo, saddhammābhiyogo, anavajjavijjāṭṭhānādiparicayo, paripakkindriyatā, kilesadūrībhāvo, appassutapuggalaparivajjanā bahussutapuggalasevanā, tadadhimuttatā ca. Vīriyassa apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇā, gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇā, dhammamahattapaccavekkhaṇā, thinamiddhavinodanā, kusītapuggalaparivajjanā, āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanā, sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatā ca. Satiyā satisampajaññaṃ, muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanā, tadadhimuttatā ca. Paññāya paripucchakabhāvo, vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā, duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā, paññavantapuggalasevanā, gambhīrañāṇacariyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇā, dhammamahattapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatā ca. Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ sīlādicatukkaṃ, aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu pubbabhāgabhāvanā, āvajjanādivasībhāvakaraṇañca parikkhārā.

Furthermore, the fifteen qualities of conduct with their requisites and the five supernormal knowledges are conditions for the perfections of giving and so on. Herein, the qualities of conduct are named: restraint in virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, application to wakefulness, the seven qualities of a good person, and the four jhānas. Among these, for the four beginning with virtue, the thirteen ascetic practices and qualities such as fewness of wishes are the requisites. Among the good qualities, for faith, the requisites are: recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, and peace; avoidance of coarse persons; association with refined persons; reflection on inspiring qualities; and inclination towards that. For moral shame and moral dread, the requisites are: reflection on the danger of unwholesome deeds, reflection on the danger of the woeful states, reflection on the supporting nature of wholesome qualities, avoidance of those lacking moral shame and moral dread, association with those possessing moral shame and moral dread, and inclination towards that. For great learning, the requisites are: prior effort, being inquisitive, earnest application to the true Dhamma, familiarity with faultless fields of knowledge, maturity of faculties, being far from defilements, avoidance of the unlearned, association with the learned, and inclination towards that. For energy, the requisites are: reflection on the fear of the woeful states, reflection on the path of passage, reflection on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling of sloth and torpor, avoidance of the lazy, association with the energetic, reflection on the right strivings, and inclination towards that. For mindfulness, the requisites are: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoidance of those with confused mindfulness, association with those of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that. For wisdom, the requisites are: being inquisitive, clarifying the subject-matter, establishing balanced faculties, avoidance of the unwise, association with the wise, reflection on discourses that are the domain of profound knowledge, reflection on the greatness of the Dhamma, and inclination towards that. For the four jhānas, the requisites are the tetrad beginning with virtue, preliminary development on the thirty-eight objects, and the accomplishment of mastery beginning with adverting.

Tattha sīlādīhi payogasuddhiyā sattānaṃ abhayadāne, āsayasuddhiyā āmisadāne, ubhayasuddhiyā dhammadāne samatthohotītiādinā caraṇādīnaṃ dānādisambhārapaccayatā yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Ativitthārabhayena pana mayaṃ na vitthārayimha. Tathā sampatticakkādayopi dānādīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbā.

Herein, through purity of effort by means of virtue and so forth, one becomes capable of giving fearlessness to beings; through purity of intention, one becomes capable of giving material gifts; through purity of both, one becomes capable of giving the gift of the Dhamma. In this way and so on, the status of conduct and so on as a condition for the requisites of giving and so on should be determined appropriately. However, due to fear of excessive extension, we have not elaborated. Similarly, it should be understood that the wheel of accomplishment and so on are also conditions for giving and so on.

Ko saṃkilesoti ettha –

What is defilement? Herein:

Taṇhādīhi [V 1.0238] parāmaṭṭha-bhāvo tāsaṃ kilissanaṃ;

Sāmaññato visesena, yathārahaṃ vikappatā.

The state of being wrongly grasped by craving and so on is their defilement, generally. Specifically, it is the discrimination that occurs as is appropriate.

Avisesena hi taṇhādīhi parāmaṭṭhabhāvo pāramīnaṃ saṃkileso. Visesena pana deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakavikappā dānapāramiyā saṃkileso. Sattakālavikappā sīlapāramiyā. Kāmabhavatadupasamesu abhiratianabhirativikappā nekkhammapāramiyā. “Ahaṃ mamā”ti vikappā paññāpāramiyā. Līnuddhaccavikappā vīriyapāramiyā. Attaparavikappā khantipāramiyā. Adiṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhādivikappā saccapāramiyā. Bodhisambhāratabbipakkhesu dosaguṇavikappā adhiṭṭhānapāramiyā. Hitāhitavikappā mettāpāramiyā. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhavikappā upekkhāpāramiyā saṃkilesoti veditabbo.

Indeed, without distinction, the state of being wrongly grasped by craving and so on is the defilement of the perfections. Specifically, however, discriminations concerning the gift and the recipient are the defilement of the perfection of giving. Discriminations concerning beings and time are the defilement of the perfection of virtue. Discriminations of delight and non-delight in sensual existence, existence, and their pacification are the defilement of the perfection of renunciation. Discriminations such as 'I' and 'mine' are the defilement of the perfection of wisdom. Discriminations of sluggishness and restlessness are the defilement of the perfection of energy. Discriminations of self and other are the defilement of the perfection of patience. Discriminations of the seen, etc., in regard to the unseen, etc., are the defilement of the perfection of truthfulness. Discriminations of fault and virtue in regard to the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites are the defilement of the perfection of determination. Discriminations of the beneficial and the unbeneficial are the defilement of the perfection of loving-kindness. Discriminations of the desirable and the undesirable are to be understood as the defilement of the perfection of equanimity.

Kiṃ [M 1.0272] vodānanti –

What is purification?

Taṇhādīhi aghātatā, rahitatā vikappānaṃ;

Vodānanti vijāniyā, sabbāsameva tāsampi.

Unafflictedness by craving and so on, and the state of being devoid of discriminations—this a wise person should know as the purification of all of them indeed.

Anupaghātā hi taṇhā māna diṭṭhi kodhu panāha makkha palāsa issāmacchariya māyā sāṭheyya thambha sārambha mada pamādādīhi kilesehi deyyapaṭiggāhakavikappādirahitā ca dānādipāramiyo parisuddhā pabhassarā bhavantīti.

For the perfections such as giving, being unafflicted by the defilements—craving, conceit, views, anger, hostility, contempt, rivalry, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, intoxication, heedlessness, and so on—and being devoid of discriminations concerning the gift, the recipient, and so on, become thoroughly pure and radiant.

Ko paṭipakkhoti –

What is the opponent?

Akusalā kilesā ca, paṭipakkhā abhedato;

Bhedato pana pubbepi, vuttā macchariyādayo.

Unwholesome states and defilements, without distinction, are the opponents. Furthermore, with distinction, avarice and so on, which were mentioned before, are the opponents.

Avisesena hi sabbepi akusalā dhammā, sabbepi kilesā ca etāsaṃ paṭipakkhā. Visesena pana pubbe vuttā macchariyādayoti veditabbā. Apica deyyapaṭiggāhakadānaphalesu alobhādosāmohaguṇayogato lobhadosamohapaṭipakkhaṃ dānaṃ, kāyādidosattayavaṅkāpagamato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ sīlaṃ, kāmasukhaparūpaghātaattakilamathaparivajjanato dosattayapaṭipakkhaṃ nekkhammaṃ, lobhādīnaṃ andhīkaraṇato, ñāṇassa ca anandhīkaraṇato lobhādipaṭipakkhā paññā, alīnānuddhatañāyārambhavasena [V 1.0239] lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ vīriyaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasuññatānaṃ khamanato lobhādipaṭipakkhā khanti, satipi paresaṃ upakāre, apakāre ca yathābhūtappavattiyā lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ saccaṃ, lokadhamme abhibhuyya yathāsamādinnesu sambhāresu acalanato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, nīvaraṇavivekato lobhādipaṭipakkhā mettā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsanato, samappavattito ca lobhādipaṭipakkhā upekkhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Indeed, without distinction, all unwholesome states and all defilements are opponents of these perfections. Furthermore, with distinction, avarice and so on, which were mentioned before, should be understood as the opponents. Moreover, another method will be stated: Due to its connection with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion in regard to the gift, the recipient, and the fruit of giving, giving is the opponent of greed, hatred, and delusion. Due to the removal of the crookedness of the triad of faults beginning with the body, virtue is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to the avoidance of sensual pleasure, harming others, and self-mortification, renunciation is the opponent of the triad of faults. Because greed and so on are blinding, and because knowledge is not blinding, wisdom is the opponent of greed and so on. By the power of undertaking things rightly, being neither sluggish nor agitated, energy is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to enduring the absence of the desirable and the undesirable, patience is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to proceeding according to reality even when there is help or harm from others, truthfulness is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to, having overcome the worldly conditions, not wavering in the requisites one has undertaken, determination is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to seclusion from the hindrances, loving-kindness is the opponent of greed and so on. Due to destroying attraction and repulsion towards the desirable and undesirable, and due to proceeding evenly, equanimity is to be seen as the opponent of greed and so on.

Kā paṭipattīti –

What is the practice?

Dānākārādayo eva, uppāditā anekadhā;

Paṭipattīti viññeyyā, pāramīpūraṇakkame.

The modes of giving and so on, produced in many ways in the course of fulfilling the perfections, should be known as the practice.

Dānapāramiyā hi tāva sukhūpakaraṇasarīrajīvitapariccāgena, bhayāpanayanena, dhammopadesena ca bahudhā sattānaṃ anuggahakaraṇaṃ paṭipatti. Tattha [M 1.0273] āmisadānaṃ abhayadānaṃ dhammadānanti dātabbavatthuvasena tividhaṃ dānaṃ. Tesu bodhisattassa dātabbavatthu ajjhattikaṃ, bāhiranti duvidhaṃ. Tattha bāhiraṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ mālā gandhaṃ vilepanaṃ seyyā āvasathaṃ padīpeyyanti dasavidhaṃ. Annādīnaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyādivibhāgena anekavidhañca. Tathā rūpārammaṇaṃ yāva dhammārammaṇanti ārammaṇato chabbidhaṃ. Rūpārammaṇādīnañca nīlādivibhāgena anekavidhaṃ. Tathā maṇikanakarajatamuttāpavāḷādikhettavatthuārāmādi dāsīdāsagomahiṃsādinānāvidhavatthūpakaraṇavasena anekavidhaṃ.

Indeed, with regard to the perfection of giving, first of all, the practice is the benefiting of beings in many ways: through the relinquishing of the body, which is an instrument for happiness, and of life; through the removal of fear; and through the teaching of the Dhamma. Herein, giving is threefold according to the objects to be given: material giving, the giving of fearlessness, and the giving of the Dhamma. Among these, for a Bodhisatta, objects to be given are twofold: internal and external. Therein, external objects are of ten kinds: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps. And food and so on are of many kinds by way of divisions such as hard and soft foods. Similarly, from forms as objects up to mental phenomena as objects, giving is sixfold according to the sense-objects. And forms and other sense-objects are of many kinds by way of divisions such as blue and so on. Likewise, giving is of many kinds by way of various objects and accessories such as jewels, gold, silver, pearls, coral, fields, land, gardens, female and male slaves, cattle, buffaloes, and so on.

Tattha mahāpuriso bāhiraṃ vatthuṃ dento “yo yena atthiko, taṃ tasseva deti. Dento ca tassa atthiko”ti sayameva jānanto ayācitopi deti, pageva yācito. Muttacāgo deti, no amuttacāgo. Pariyattaṃ deti, no apariyattaṃ. Sati deyyadhamme paccupakārasannissito na deti, asati deyyadhamme, pariyatte ca saṃvibhāgārahaṃ vibhajati. Na ca deti parūpaghātāvahaṃ satthavisamajjādikaṃ, nāpi kīḷanakaṃ, yaṃ anatthupasaṃhitaṃ, pamādāvahañca, na ca gilānassa yācakassa pānabhojanādiasappāyaṃ, pamāṇarahitaṃ vā deti, pamāṇayuttaṃ pana sappāyameva deti.

Therein, the great being, when giving an external object, knowing by himself that one gives to a person the very thing they need and that this person is in need, gives even unasked—how much more so when asked. He gives with complete relinquishment, not without complete relinquishment. He gives what is sufficient, not what is insufficient. When a gift is available, he does not give relying on a return favor; when no gift is available and there is no sufficiency, he still divides what is suitable for sharing. And he does not give what brings harm to others, such as weapons, poison, and intoxicants; nor does he give playthings that are connected with non-benefit and are conducive to heedlessness. And to a sick beggar, he does not give unsuitable food, drink, and so on, nor does he give without measure; rather, he gives only what is suitable and in proper measure.

Tathā yācito gahaṭṭhānaṃ gahaṭṭhānucchavikaṃ deti, pabbajitānaṃ pabbajitānucchavikaṃ deti. Mātāpitaro ñātisālohitā mittāmaccā puttadāradāsakammakarāti etesu kassaci pīḷaṃ ajanento deti, na ca uḷāraṃ deyyadhammaṃ paṭijānitvā lūkhaṃ deti, na ca lābhasakkārasilokasannissito [V 1.0240] deti, na ca paccupakārasannissito deti, na ca phalapāṭikaṅkhī deti aññatra sammāsambodhiyā, na ca yācito, deyyadhammaṃ vā jigucchanto deti, na ca asaññatānaṃ yācakānaṃ akkosakaparibhāsakānampi apaviddhā dānaṃ deti, aññadatthu pasannacitto anukampanto sakkaccameva deti, na ca kotūhalamaṅgaliko hutvā deti, kammaphalameva pana saddahanto deti, nāpi yācake payirupāsanādīhi saṃkilametvā deti, aparikilamento eva pana deti, na ca paresaṃ vañcanādhippāyo, bhedādhippāyo vā dānaṃ deti, asaṃkiliṭṭhacittova deti, nāpi pharusavāco bhākuṭikamukho dānaṃ deti, piyavādī ca pana pubbabhāsī mihitasitavacano hutvā deti, yasmiṃ ce deyyadhamme uḷāramanuññatāya vā ciraparicayena [M 1.0274] vā gedhasabhāvatāya vā lobhadhammo adhimatto hoti, jānanto bodhisatto taṃ khippameva paṭivinodayitvā yācake pariyesetvāpi deti, yañca deyyavatthu parittaṃ, yācakopi paccupaṭṭhito, taṃ acintetvā api attānaṃ dhāvitvā dento yācakaṃ sammāneti yathā taṃ akittipaṇḍito, na ca mahāpuriso attano puttadāradāsakammakaraporise yācito te asaññāpite domanassappatte yācakānaṃ deti, sammadeva pana saññāpite somanassappatte deti, dento ca yakkharakkhasapisācādīnaṃ vā manussānaṃ vā kurūrakammantānaṃ jānanto na deti, tathā rajjampi tādisānaṃ na deti, ye lokassa ahitāya dukkhāya anatthāya paṭipajjanti, ye pana dhammikā dhammena lokaṃ pālenti, tesaṃ rajjadānaṃ deti. Evaṃ tāva bāhiradāne paṭipatti veditabbā.

Likewise, when asked, he gives to householders what is suitable for householders, and to renunciants what is suitable for renunciants. He gives without causing affliction to anyone among his parents, relatives and kinsmen, friends and ministers, children and wife, or slaves and workers. He does not, having promised a superior gift, then give an inferior one. He does not give relying on gain, honor, or fame. He does not give relying on a return favor. He does not give desiring any fruit other than perfect enlightenment. When asked, he does not give while being disgusted with the gift to be given. He does not give contemptuously even to unrestrained beggars who are abusive or insulting; on the contrary, with a serene mind and with compassion, he gives respectfully. He does not give being one who believes in omens and auspicious signs; rather, he gives while having faith only in the fruit of kamma. Nor does he give after wearying beggars with attendance and so on; rather, he gives without wearying them. He does not give with an intention to deceive or to cause division in others; he gives only with an undefiled mind. Nor does he give with harsh speech and a frowning face; rather, he gives being one who speaks kindly, who speaks first, and whose speech is accompanied by a smile. And if, with regard to a certain gift, excessive greed should arise due to its excellence and pleasantness, or through long familiarity, or due to a greedy nature, the Bodhisatta, knowing this, quickly dispels it and, even seeking out beggars, gives that gift. And if the object to be given is small and a beggar is present, without giving it thought, even rushing forward as he gives, he honors the beggar, just as Akitti the wise did. And the great being, when asked for his own children, wife, slaves, or workers, does not give them to beggars if they have not been made to understand and are distressed; rather, he gives them only when they have been properly made to understand and are joyful. And when giving, knowing them to be yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, and so on, or humans who perform cruel deeds, he does not give to them. Similarly, he does not give the kingdom to such beings—to those who practice for the harm, for the suffering, for the non-benefit of the world. Rather, to those who are righteous and who protect the world righteously, he gives the gift of the kingdom. Thus, first of all, the practice in external giving should be understood.

Ajjhattikadānampi dvīhākārehi veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yathā nāma koci puriso ghāsacchādanahetu attānaṃ parassa nissajjati, vidheyyabhāvaṃ upagacchati dāsabyaṃ, evameva mahāpuriso sambodhihetu nirāmisacitto sattānaṃ anuttaraṃ hitasukhaṃ icchanto attano dānapāramiṃ paripūretukāmo attānaṃ parassa nissajjati, vidheyyabhāvaṃ upagacchati yathākāmakaraṇīyataṃ, karacaraṇanayanādiaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ tena tena atthikānaṃ akampito alīno anuppadeti, na tattha sajjati, na saṅkocaṃ āpajjati yathā taṃ bāhiravatthusmiṃ. Tathā hi mahāpuriso dvīhākārehi bāhiravatthuṃ pariccajati yathāsukhaṃ paribhogāya vā yācakānaṃ, tesaṃ manorathaṃ pūrento attano vasībhāvāya vā. Tattha sabbena sabbaṃ muttacāgo evamāha “nissaṅgabhāvenāhaṃ sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti, evaṃ ajjhattikavatthusmimpi veditabbaṃ.

Internal giving, too, should be understood in two ways. How? Just as some person, for the sake of food and clothing, surrenders himself to another, enters a state of being directed, of servitude, even so the great being, for the sake of enlightenment, with a mind free from materialism, desiring the unsurpassed welfare and happiness of beings, and wishing to fulfill his own perfection of giving, surrenders himself to another, enters a state of being directed, of being subject to another's will. To those in need of them, he gives his hands, feet, eyes, and other major and minor limbs, unwavering and unhesitant. He does not cling to them, nor does he shrink back, just as with an external object. For indeed, the great being relinquishes an external object in two ways: for the enjoyment of beggars as they please, fulfilling their heart's desire, or for his own mastery. Therein, being one of complete relinquishment in every way, he speaks thus: 'Through this non-attachment, I will attain enlightenment.' In this same way, it should be understood with regard to internal objects as well.

Tattha yaṃ ajjhattikavatthu diyyamānaṃ yācakassa ekanteneva hitāya saṃvattati, taṃ deti, na itaraṃ. Na ca mahāpuriso mārassa, mārakāyikānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vihiṃsādhippāyānaṃ attano attabhāvaṃ[V 1.0241], aṅgapaccaṅgāni vā jānamāno deti “mā tesaṃ anattho ahosī”ti. Yathā ca mārakāyikānaṃ, evaṃ tehi anvāviṭṭhānampi na deti, nāpi ummattakānaṃ, itaresaṃ pana yāciyamāno samanantarameva deti tādisāya yācanāya dullabhabhāvato, tādisassa ca dānassa dukkarabhāvato.

In this regard, whatever internal object, when being given, leads solely to the benefit of the requester, that he gives, not another.
