And the great being, knowing, does not give his own body or his limbs to Māra, or to deities belonging to Māra's host, or to those who intend harm, thinking, 'May there be no harm for them.' And just as he does not give to those of Māra's host, so too he does not give to those possessed by them, nor to the insane. But to others, when requested, he gives immediately, because of the rarity of such a request and because of the difficulty of such a gift.

Abhayadānaṃ [M 1.0275] pana rājato corato aggito udakato verīpuggalato sīhabyagghādivāḷamigato nāgayakkharakkhasapisācādito sattānaṃ bhaye paccupaṭṭhite tato parittāṇabhāvena dātabbaṃ.

The gift of fearlessness, however, should be given as a means of protection when a fearsome danger has arisen for beings from kings, from thieves, from fire, from water, from hostile individuals, from wild beasts such as lions and tigers, or from nāgas, yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, and so forth.

Dhammadānaṃ pana asaṃkiliṭṭhacittassa aviparītadhammadesanā. Opāyiko hi tassa upadeso diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthavasena, yena sāsane anotiṇṇānaṃ avatāraṇaṃ otiṇṇānaṃ paripācanaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ nayo – saṅkhepato tāva dānakathā sīlakathā saggakathā kāmānaṃ ādīnavo saṃkileso okāro ca nekkhamme ānisaṃso. Vitthārato pana sāvakabodhiyaṃ adhimuttacittānaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ, sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu kammakaraṇavasena samathānuyogo, rūpamukhādīsu vipassanābhinivesesu yathārahaṃ abhinivesanamukhena vipassanānuyogo, tathā visuddhipaṭipadāya sammattagahaṇaṃ, tisso vijjā, cha abhiññā, catasso paṭisambhidā, sāvakabodhīti etesaṃ guṇasaṃkittanavasena yathārahaṃ tattha tattha patiṭṭhāpanā, pariyodapanā ca. Tathā paccekabodhiyaṃ, sammāsambodhiyañca adhimuttacittānaṃ yathārahaṃ dānādipāramīnaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇādisaṃkittanamukhena tīsupi avatthābhedesu tesaṃ buddhānaṃ mahānubhāvatāvibhāvanena yānadvaye patiṭṭhāpanā, pariyodapanā ca. Evaṃ mahāpuriso sattānaṃ dhammadānaṃ deti.

The gift of Dhamma, however, is the non-distorted teaching of the Dhamma by one with an undefiled mind. Indeed, the instruction is suitable, by way of the benefit in the present life, the benefit in future lives, and the ultimate benefit, through which, for those not yet entered into the Dispensation, their entering is accomplished, and for those already entered, their maturation is accomplished. Herein, this is the method: in brief, first there is the talk on giving, the talk on virtue, the talk on heaven, the danger, defilement, and lowliness of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation. In detail, however, for those with minds inclined towards the enlightenment of a disciple, there is the going for refuge, restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, the application of wakefulness, the seven qualities of a good person, the application of serenity by way of undertaking the practice on the thirty-eight objects, and the application of insight, as appropriate, by means of mental application to the objects of insight meditation, which begin with form and so forth. Likewise, there is the proper grasp of the path of purification, the three true knowledges, the six direct knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and the disciple’s enlightenment—by way of proclaiming the qualities of these, the establishing and purifying of beings in them wherever appropriate. Similarly, for those with minds inclined to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and to perfect self-enlightenment, there is, as appropriate, by means of proclaiming the intrinsic nature, individual essence, characteristics, and so forth of the perfections beginning with giving, and by revealing the great power of those Buddhas, the establishing and purifying of beings in the three divisions of states and in the two vehicles. In this way, the great being gives the gift of Dhamma to beings.

Tathā mahāpuriso āmisadānaṃ dento “imināhaṃ dānena sattānaṃ āyuvaṇṇasukhabalapaṭibhānādisampattiñca ramaṇīyaṃ aggaphalasampattiñca nipphādeyya”nti annaṃ deti, tathā sattānaṃ kāmakilesapipāsavūpasamāya pānaṃ deti, tathā suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya, hirottappālaṅkārassa ca nipphattiyā vatthāni deti, tathā iddhividhassa ceva nibbānasukhassa ca nipphattiyā yānaṃ deti, tathā sīlagandhanipphattiyā gandhaṃ deti, tathā buddhaguṇasobhānipphattiyā mālāvilepanaṃ deti, tathā bodhimaṇḍāsananipphattiyā āsanaṃ deti, tathāgataseyyanipphattiyā seyyaṃ deti, saraṇabhāvanipphattiyā āvasathaṃ deti, pañcacakkhupaṭilābhāya padīpeyyaṃ deti.

Furthermore, the great being, when giving a material gift, gives food, thinking: 'By this gift, may I bring about for beings the accomplishment of longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, wisdom, and so forth, as well as the delightful accomplishment of the supreme fruit.' Similarly, to appease the thirst which is the defilement of sensual craving for beings, he gives drink. Likewise, for the attainment of a golden complexion and for the accomplishment of the adornment of moral shame and moral dread, he gives clothing. Similarly, for the accomplishment of the various psychic powers and the bliss of Nibbāna, he gives a vehicle. Similarly, for the accomplishment of the fragrance of virtue, he gives scents. Similarly, for the accomplishment of the splendor of the Buddha's qualities, he gives garlands and unguents. Similarly, for the accomplishment of the seat at the Bodhimaṇḍa, he gives a seat. For the accomplishment of the Tathāgata's resting place, he gives a bed. For the accomplishment of the state of being a refuge, he gives a dwelling. For the acquisition of the five eyes, he gives a lamp.

Byāmappabhānipphattiyā [V 1.0242] rūpadānaṃ deti, brahmassaranipphattiyā saddadānaṃ deti, sabbalokassa piyabhāvāya rasadānaṃ deti, buddhasukhumālabhāvāya phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ [M 1.0276] deti, ajarāmaraṇabhāvāya bhesajjadānaṃ deti, kilesadāsabyavimocanatthaṃ dāsānaṃ bhujissatādānaṃ deti, saddhammābhiratiyā anavajjakhiḍḍāratihetudānaṃ deti, sabbepi satte ariyāya jātiyā attano puttabhāvūpanayanāya puttadānaṃ deti, sakalassāpi lokassa patibhāvūpagamanāya dāradānaṃ deti, subhalakkhaṇasampattiyā suvaṇṇamaṇimuttāpavāḷādidānaṃ, anubyañjanasampattiyā nānāvidhavibhūsanadānaṃ, saddhammakosādhigamāya vittakosadānaṃ, dhammarājabhāvāya rajjadānaṃ, dānādisampattiyā ārāmuyyānādivanadānaṃ, cakkaṅkitehi pādehi bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamanāya caraṇadānaṃ, caturoghanittharaṇe sattānaṃ saddhammahatthadānatthaṃ hatthadānaṃ, saddhindriyādipaṭilābhāya kaṇṇanāsādidānaṃ, samantacakkhupaṭilābhāya cakkhudānaṃ, “dassanasavanānussaraṇapāricariyādīsu sabbakālaṃ sabbasattānaṃ hitasukhāvaho sabbalokena ca upajīvitabbo me kāyo bhaveyyā”ti maṃsalohitādidānaṃ. “Sabbalokuttamo bhaveyya”nti uttamaṅgadānaṃ deti.

For the accomplishment of the fathom-wide radiance, he gives the gift of form. For the accomplishment of a Brahma-like voice, he gives the gift of sound. For the sake of becoming dear to the entire world, he gives the gift of taste. For the sake of the subtle nature of Buddhahood, he gives the gift of tangibles. For the sake of the state of non-aging and non-dying, he gives the gift of medicine. For the sake of liberation from the servitude of defilements, he gives the gift of freedom to slaves. For delight in the good Dhamma, he gives the gift that is the cause of blameless sport and delight. To lead all beings to the state of being his own children by way of the noble birth, he gives the gift of a son. To attain the state of being a lord to the entire world, he gives the gift of a wife. For the attainment of the auspicious major marks, he gives the gift of gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth. For the attainment of the minor characteristics, he gives the gift of various ornaments. To acquire the treasury of the good Dhamma, he gives the gift of a treasury of wealth. For the state of a Dhamma King, he gives the gift of a kingdom. For the accomplishment of giving and other virtues, he gives the gift of forests such as parks and gardens. To approach the Bodhimaṇḍa with feet marked with wheels, he gives the gift of feet. To give beings the hand of the good Dhamma for crossing the four floods, he gives the gift of hands. To acquire the spiritual faculty of faith and so forth, he gives the gift of ears, nose, and so forth. To acquire the all-round eye, he gives the gift of eyes. Thinking, 'May my body be beneficial and conducive to happiness for all beings at all times in seeing, hearing, recollecting, attending to needs, and so forth, and may it be lived upon by the whole world,' he gives the gift of flesh, blood, and so forth. Making the aspiration, 'May I be the most supreme in all the world,' he gives the gift of the supreme limb, the head.

Evaṃ dadanto ca na anesanāya deti, na paropaghātena, na bhayena, na lajjāya, na dakkhiṇeyyarosanena, na paṇīte sati lūkhaṃ, na attukkaṃsanena, na paravambhanena, na phalābhikaṅkhāya, na yācakajigucchāya, na acittīkārena, atha kho sakkaccaṃ deti, sahatthena deti, kālena deti, cittiṃ katvā deti, avibhāgena deti, tīsu kālesu somanassiko deti, tato eva ca datvā na pacchānutāpī hoti, na paṭiggāhakavasena mānāvamānaṃ karoti, paṭiggāhakānaṃ piyasamudācāro hoti vadaññū yācayogo saparivāradāyako. Annadānañhi dento “taṃ saparivāraṃ katvā dassāmī”ti vatthādīhi saddhiṃ deti, tathā vatthadānaṃ dento “taṃ saparivāraṃ katvā dassāmī”ti annādīhi saddhiṃ deti. Pānadānādīsupi eseva nayo, tathā rūpadānaṃ dento itarārammaṇānipi tassa parivāraṃ katvā deti, evaṃ sesesupi.

Furthermore, giving in this way, one does not give through improper seeking, nor by oppressing others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor by seeking out a worthy recipient; when a superior item is available, one does not give an inferior one; one does not give for self-exaltation, nor for disparaging others, nor with a desire for a result, nor out of disgust for the petitioner, nor disrespectfully. But rather, one gives respectfully, gives with one's own hand, gives at a suitable time, gives having shown respect, gives without discrimination, and gives with a joyful mind in the three periods. And precisely for that reason, having given, one does not later feel remorse. One does not show pride or disdain based on the recipients. One is of pleasant speech towards recipients, is understanding of what is said, is amenable to requests, and is a giver of things with their accompaniments. For when giving food, one thinks, 'I will give it along with its accompaniments,' and so provides it together with clothing and so forth. Similarly, when giving clothing, one thinks, 'I will give it along with its accompaniments,' and so provides it together with food and so forth. The same principle applies to giving drink and other things. Likewise, when giving the gift of form, one also gives other sense-objects as its retinue. The same applies to all other types of giving.

Tattha rūpadānaṃ nāma nīlapītalohitodātādivaṇṇādīsu pupphavatthadhātūsu aññataraṃ labhitvā rūpavasena ābhujitvā “rūpadānaṃ dassāmi, rūpadānaṃ mayha”nti cintetvā tādise dakkhiṇeyye dānaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti, etaṃ rūpadānaṃ nāma.

Herein, what is called the gift of form is this: having obtained any one among flowers, cloths, or minerals of colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white, and having adverted to it by way of form, thinking, 'I will give a gift of form; a gift of form there will be for me,' one establishes the gift in such a worthy recipient. This is called the gift of form.

Saddadānaṃ [M 1.0277] pana bherīsaddādivasena veditabbaṃ. Tattha saddaṃ kandamūlāni viya uppāṭetvā, nīluppalahatthakaṃ viya ca hatthe ṭhapetvā dātuṃ na sakkoti, savatthukaṃ pana katvā dadanto saddadānaṃ deti nāma, tasmā yadā “saddadānaṃ dassāmī”ti bherīmudiṅgādīsu aññatarena tūriyena tiṇṇaṃ [V 1.0243] ratanānaṃ upahāraṃ karoti, kāreti ca, “saddadānaṃ dassāmi, saddadānaṃ me”ti bherīādīni ṭhapāpeti, dhammakathikānaṃ pana saddabhesajjaṃ, telaphāṇitādīni ca deti, dhammassavanaṃ ghoseti, sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇati, dhammakathaṃ katheti, upanisinnakathaṃ, anumodanakathañca karoti, kāreti ca, tadā saddadānaṃ nāma hoti.

The gift of sound, however, should be understood by way of the sound of great drums and so forth. Therein, one is not able to give sound by uprooting it like tubers and roots, or by placing it in the hand like a bunch of blue lotuses. But rather, when giving by providing it with a physical basis, it is called giving the gift of sound. Therefore, when, thinking, 'I will give the gift of sound,' one makes an offering to the Three Jewels with a musical instrument such as a great drum, or causes it to be made; or when, reflecting, 'I will give the gift of sound; a gift of sound there will be for me,' one has great drums and so on set up; or when one gives voice-medicine, and oil, molasses, and so forth to Dhamma-preachers; announces the hearing of the Dhamma; recites with a clear voice; gives a Dhamma talk; gives a talk to one sitting nearby and a talk of appreciation—and causes others to do so—then it is called the gift of sound.

Tathā mūlagandhādīsu aññataraṃ rajanīyaṃ gandhavatthuṃ, pisitameva vā gandhaṃ yaṃ kiñci labhitvā gandhavasena ābhujitvā “gandhadānaṃ dassāmi, gandhadānaṃ mayha”nti buddharatanādīnaṃ pūjaṃ karoti, kāreti ca, gandhapūjanatthāya agarucandanādike gandhavatthuke pariccajati, idaṃ gandhadānaṃ.

Likewise, having obtained any delightful fragrant substance among root-scents and so forth, or any powdered fragrance whatsoever, and having adverted to it by way of scent, thinking, 'I will give a gift of fragrance; a gift of fragrance there will be for me,' one performs worship to the Buddha Jewel and so forth, or causes it to be performed. For the purpose of worship with fragrance, one relinquishes fragrant substances like agarwood, sandalwood, and so forth. This is the gift of fragrance.

Tathā mūlarasādīsu yaṃ kiñci rajanīyaṃ rasavatthuṃ labhitvā rasavasena ābhujitvā “rasadānaṃ dassāmi, rasadānaṃ mayha”nti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ deti, rasavatthumeva vā aññaṃ gavādikaṃ pariccajati, idaṃ rasadānaṃ.

Likewise, having obtained any delightful taste-object among root-tastes and so forth, and having adverted to it by way of taste, thinking, 'I will give a gift of taste; a gift of taste there will be for me,' one gives it to worthy recipients; or one relinquishes the taste-object itself, or other things such as cows and so on. This is the gift of taste.

Tathā phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ mañcapīṭhādivasena, attharaṇapāvuraṇādivasena ca veditabbaṃ. Yadā hi mañcapīṭhabhisibibbohanādikaṃ, nivāsanapārupanādikaṃ vā sukhasamphassaṃ rajanīyaṃ anavajjaṃ phoṭṭhabbavatthuṃ labhitvā phoṭṭhabbavasena ābhujitvā “phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ dassāmi, phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ mayha”nti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ deti. Yathāvuttaṃ phoṭṭhabbavatthuṃ labhitvā pariccajati, etaṃ phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ.

Similarly, the gift of tangibles should be understood by way of beds, chairs, and so forth, and by way of floor-coverings, robes, and so forth. For when one obtains any delightful, blameless tangible object that is pleasant to touch, such as beds, chairs, cushions, pillows, and so forth, or lower garments, upper robes, and so forth, and having adverted to it by way of the tangible, thinking, 'I will give a gift of tangibles; a gift of tangibles there will be for me,' one gives it to worthy recipients. Having obtained and relinquished the aforementioned tangible object—this is the gift of tangibles.

Dhammadānaṃ pana dhammārammaṇassa adhippetattā ojāpānajīvitavasena veditabbaṃ. Ojādīsu hi aññataraṃ rajanīyaṃ dhammavatthuṃ labhitvā dhammārammaṇavasena ābhujitvā “dhammadānaṃ dassāmi, dhammadānaṃ mayha”nti sappinavanītādi ojadānaṃ deti, ambapānādiaṭṭhavidhaṃ pānadānaṃ deti, jīvitadānanti ābhujitvā salākabhattapakkhikabhattādīni deti. Aphāsukabhāvena abhibhūtānaṃ byādhikānaṃ vejjaṃ paṭṭhapeti, jālaṃ phālāpeti, kumīnaṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, sakuṇapañjaraṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, bandhanena baddhānaṃ sattānaṃ bandhanamokkhaṃ kāreti, māghātabheriṃ carāpeti, aññānipi sattānaṃ jīvitaparittāṇatthaṃ evarūpāni kammāni karoti, kārāpeti ca, idaṃ dhammadānaṃ nāma.

The gift of Dhamma, however, since a mental-object is intended, should be understood by way of nutriment, drink, and life. For having obtained any delightful Dhamma-object among nutriment and so forth, and having adverted to it by way of a mental-object, thinking, 'I will give the gift of Dhamma; the gift of Dhamma there will be for me,' one gives the gift of nutriment such as ghee, fresh butter, and so forth. One gives the gift of the eight kinds of drink, such as mango juice and so forth. Adverting, 'A gift of life there will be for me,' one gives meals such as ticket-food, fortnightly food, and so forth. For the sick who are overcome by discomfort, one provides a physician; one has nets torn, destroys fish-traps, and destroys bird-cages; one causes the release from bonds for beings bound by bonds. One causes the drum of non-killing to be circulated, and one performs or causes to be performed other such deeds for the sake of protecting the lives of beings. This is called the gift of Dhamma.

Sabbampetaṃ [M 1.0278] yathāvuttadānasampadaṃ sakalalokahitasukhāya pariṇāmeti attano ca akuppāya vimuttiyā aparikkhayassa chandassa aparikkhayassa vīriyassa aparikkhayassa samādhissa aparikkhayassa paṭibhānassa aparikkhayassa jhānassa aparikkhayāya sammāsambodhiyā pariṇāmeti[V 1.0244], imañca dānapāramiṃ paṭipajjantena mahāsattena jīvite aniccasaññā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā. Tathā bhogesu, bahusādhāraṇatā ca nesaṃ manasi kātabbā, sattesu ca mahākaruṇā satataṃ samitaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetabbā. Evañhi bhogehi gahetabbasāraṃ gaṇhanto ādittato viya agārato sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ, attānañca bahi nīharanto na kiñci seseti, na katthaci vibhāgaṃ karoti, aññadatthu nirapekkho nissajjati eva. Ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo.

All this aforesaid perfection of giving, the Bodhisatta directs to the welfare and happiness of the entire world, and to one’s own unshakeable liberation, for the non-exhaustion of aspiration, for the non-exhaustion of energy, for the non-exhaustion of concentration, for the non-exhaustion of ready-wit, for the non-exhaustion of jhāna, and for non-exhaustible perfect enlightenment. Moreover, while practicing this perfection of giving, the great being should establish the perception of impermanence regarding life. Likewise, regarding wealth, its nature of being common to many should be kept in mind, and great compassion towards beings should be constantly and unremittingly established. For in this way, while taking the essence that should be taken from wealth, like one who, removing all possessions and oneself out from a burning house, leaves nothing behind, one leaves nothing behind. One makes no distinction anywhere, but rather, being without attachment, one simply relinquishes. This, for now, is the course of practice for the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyā pana ayaṃ paṭipattikkamo – yasmā sabbaññusīlālaṅkārehi satte alaṅkaritukāmena mahāpurisena ādito attano eva tāva sīlaṃ visodhetabbaṃ. Tattha catūhākārehi sīlaṃ visujjhati ajjhāsayavisuddhito, samādānato, avītikkamanato, sati vītikkame puna pākaṭīkaraṇato ca. Visuddhāsayatāya hi ekacco attādhipati hutvā pāpajigucchanasabhāvo ajjhattaṃ hiridhammaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā suparisuddhasamācāro hoti, tathā parato samādāne sati ekacco lokādhipati hutvā pāpato uttasanto ottappadhammaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā suparisuddhasamācāro hoti, iti ubhayathāpi ete avītikkamanato sīle patiṭṭhahanti. Atha ca pana kadāci satisammosena sīlassa khaṇḍādibhāvo siyā, tāyayeva yathāvuttāya hirottappasampattiyā khippameva naṃ vuṭṭhānādinā paṭipākatikaṃ karontīti.

Furthermore, this is the course of practice for the perfection of virtue: because the Great Being, wishing to adorn beings with the ornaments of the virtue of the Omniscient One, must first of all purify his own virtue. Therein, virtue is purified in four ways: by purity of intention, by undertaking, by non-transgression, and, should a transgression occur, by making it manifest again. For, by purity of intention, a certain person, having themself as sovereign and possessing a nature that is disgusted by evil, establishes internally the state of shame and thus becomes one of perfectly pure conduct. Similarly, when there is undertaking from another, a certain person, having the world as sovereign and fearing evil, establishes the state of moral dread and thus becomes one of perfectly pure conduct. Thus, in both ways, they are established in virtue through non-transgression. And yet, should virtue become broken or flawed at some time due to a lapse of mindfulness, through that very accomplishment of shame and moral dread as described, they quickly restore it to its natural state by means of rising up from unwholesomeness and so forth.

Tayidaṃ sīlaṃ vārittaṃ cārittanti duvidhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ bodhisattassa vārittasīle paṭipattikkamo – tena sabbasattesu tathā dayāpannacittena bhavitabbaṃ, yathā supinantenapi na āghāto uppajjeyya, parūpakaraṇaviratatāya parasantako alagaddo viya na parāmasitabbo. Sace pabbajito hoti, abrahmacariyatopi ārācārī hoti sattavidhamethunasaṃyogavirato, pageva paradāragamanato. Gahaṭṭho samāno paresaṃ dāresu sadā pāpakaṃ cittampi na uppādeti. Kathento saccaṃ hitaṃ piyaṃ parimitameva ca kālena dhammiṃ kathaṃ bhāsitā hoti. Sabbattha anabhijjhālu[M 1.0279], abyāpannacitto, aviparītadassano kammassakatāñāṇena ca samannāgato. Samaggatesu sammāpaṭipannesu niviṭṭhasaddho hoti niviṭṭhapemoti.

That virtue is twofold: the virtue of avoidance and the virtue of performance. Therein, this is the Bodhisatta's course of practice in the virtue of avoidance: he should have a mind that has attained such compassion for all beings that not even ill will would arise, even in a dream. Through abstention from delighting in others' requisites, what belongs to others should not be handled, like a viper. If he is a renunciant, he practices far from unchastity, abstaining from the seven kinds of sexual union—how much more so from going to another's wife. Being a householder, he never generates even an evil thought towards the wives of others. When speaking, he is one who utters, at the proper time, a talk connected with the Dhamma that is true, beneficial, pleasant, and only what is measured. Everywhere, he is non-covetous, with a mind free of ill will, of non-perverted view, and endowed with the knowledge of kamma as one's own property. Towards those who are harmonious and practicing rightly, he is one of settled faith and settled affection.

Iti caturāpāyavaṭṭadukkhānaṃ pathabhūtehi akusalakammapathehi, akusaladhammehi ca oramitvā saggamokkhānaṃ pathabhūtesu kusalakammapathesu, kusaladhammesu ca patiṭṭhitassa mahāpurisassa parisuddhāsayapayogato yathābhipatthitā sattānaṃ hitasukhūpasañhitā manorathā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ abhinipphajjanti, pāramiyo paripūrenti. Evaṃbhūto hi ayaṃ. Tattha hiṃsānivattiyā sabbasattānaṃ [V 1.0245] abhayadānaṃ deti, appakasireneva mettābhāvanaṃ sampādeti, ekādasa mettānisaṃse adhigacchati, appābādho hoti appātaṅko, dīghāyuko sukhabahulo, lakkhaṇavisese pāpuṇāti, dosavāsanañca samucchindati. Tathā adinnādānanivattiyā corādīhi asādhāraṇe bhoge adhigacchati, parehi anāsaṅkanīyo, piyo, manāpo, vissāsanīyo, bhavasampattīsu alaggacitto pariccāgasīlo, lobhavāsanañca samucchindati. Abrahmacariyanivattiyā alobho hoti santakāyacitto, sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo aparisaṅkanīyo, kalyāṇo cassa kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, alaggacitto hoti mātugāmesu aluddhāsayo, nekkhammabahulo, lakkhaṇavisese adhigacchati, lobhavāsanañca samucchindati.

Thus, for the Great Being who has abstained from the unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome states that are the ground for the suffering of the round of the four woeful states, and is established in the wholesome courses of action and wholesome states that are the ground for heaven and liberation, through the application of a pure intention, the heart's desires of beings connected with their welfare and happiness are, as wished for, very swiftly accomplished, and the perfections are fulfilled. For such is this Great Being. Therein, by refraining from harming, he gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, accomplishes the development of loving-kindness without difficulty, attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, is free from illness and free from affliction, is long-lived and abounding in happiness, attains the special characteristics, and eradicates the latent tendency of hatred. Likewise, by refraining from taking what is not given, he attains wealth not shared with thieves and others, is beyond suspicion by others, is beloved, pleasing, and trustworthy, has a mind unattached to the accomplishments of existence, is of a generous nature, and eradicates the latent tendency of greed. By refraining from unchastity, he is without greed and has a tranquil body and mind, is beloved and pleasing to beings and beyond suspicion; a good sound of fame rises up for him, his mind is unattached to womenfolk, his disposition is ungreedy, he abounds in renunciation, attains the special characteristics, and eradicates the latent tendency of greed.

Musāvādanivattiyā sattānaṃ pamāṇabhūto hoti paccayiko theto ādeyyavacano devatānaṃ piyo manāpo surabhigandhamukho asaddhammārakkhitakāyavacīsamācāro, lakkhaṇavisese adhigacchati, kilesavāsanañca samucchindati. Pesuññanivattiyā parūpakkamehi abhejjakāyo hoti abhejjaparivāro, saddhamme ca abhejjanakasaddho, daḷhamitto bhavantaraparicitānampi sattānaṃ ekantapiyo, asaṃkilesabahulo. Pharusavācānivattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo sukhasīlo madhuravacano sambhāvanīyo, aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato cassa saro nibbattati. Samphappalāpanivattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo, garubhāvanīyo ca, ādeyyavacano parimitālāpo, mahesakkho ca hoti [M 1.0280] mahānubhāvo, ṭhānuppattikena paṭibhānena pañhābyākaraṇakusalo, buddhabhūmiyañca ekāya eva vācāya anekabhāsānaṃ sattānaṃ anekesaṃ pañhānaṃ byākaraṇasamattho hoti.

By refraining from false speech, he becomes a standard for beings, reliable, steadfast, and one whose word is to be accepted; he is dear and pleasing to the devas, has a fragrant-smelling mouth, and his bodily and verbal conduct is guarded from bad states. He attains the special characteristics and eradicates the latent tendency of the defilements. By refraining from divisive speech, his body is unbreakable by the undertakings of others, his retinue is unbreakable, his faith in the true Dhamma is unbreakable, he is a firm friend, exclusively dear even to beings familiar from other existences, and he abounds in non-defilement. By refraining from harsh speech, he is dear and pleasing to beings, of pleasant character, sweet-spoken, and worthy of esteem; and a voice endowed with eight factors arises for him. By refraining from frivolous chatter, he is dear and pleasing to beings, respected and esteemed, one whose word is to be accepted, and of measured speech; he is of great power and great might, skilled in answering questions with intelligence that arises on the spot; and in the state of a Buddha, with but a single utterance, he is capable of answering the many questions of beings of many languages.

Anabhijjhālutāya akicchalābhī hoti, uḷāresu ca bhogesu ruciṃ paṭilabhati, khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ sammato hoti, paccatthikehi anabhibhavanīyo, indriyavekallaṃ na pāpuṇāti, appaṭipuggalo ca hoti. Abyāpādena piyadassano hoti sattānaṃ sambhāvanīyo, parahitābhinanditāya ca satte appakasireneva pasādeti, alūkhasabhāvo ca hoti mettāvihārī, mahesakkho ca hoti mahānubhāvo. Micchādassanābhāvena kalyāṇe sahāye paṭilabhati, sīsacchedaṃ pāpuṇantopi pāpakammaṃ na karoti, kammassakatādassanato akotūhalamaṅgaliko ca hoti, saddhamme cassa saddhā patiṭṭhitā hoti mūlajātā, saddahati ca tathāgatānaṃ bodhiṃ, samayantaresu nābhiramati ukkāraṭṭhāne rājahaṃso viya, lakkhaṇattayavijānane kusalo hoti, ante ca anāvaraṇañāṇalābhī, yāva ca bodhiṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho hoti, uḷāruḷārasampattiyo pāpuṇāti.

By non-covetousness, one becomes a gainer without difficulty and acquires a taste for excellent wealth. One is esteemed by great khattiyas and wealthy householders, etc., cannot be overpowered by enemies, does not suffer from deficiency of faculties, and is without a rival. By non-ill-will, one becomes pleasing to behold and esteemed by beings, and with delight in others' welfare, one easily pleases them. One is of a gentle nature, dwelling in loving-kindness, and becomes greatly powerful and mighty. By absence of wrong view, one gains virtuous friends. Even when facing the severing of one's head, one does not commit evil. Due to seeing that kamma is one's own property, one is not given to superstitious rites and omens. Faith in the true Dhamma becomes established and rooted in one, and one believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas. One does not delight in other doctrines, like a royal swan on a refuse heap. One becomes skilled in discerning the three characteristics, and in the end gains unobstructed knowledge. And until one attains enlightenment, one is the most excellent of the excellent in every group of beings and attains the most excellent of excellent accomplishments.

“Iti [V 1.0246] hidaṃ sīlaṃ nāma sabbasampattīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ pabhavabhūmi, sabbabuddhakārakadhammānaṃ ādi caraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ mukhaṃ pamukha”nti bahumānaṃ uppādetvā kāyavacīsaṃyame, indriyadamane, ājīvapārisuddhiyaṃ, paccayaparibhoge ca satisampajaññabalena appamatto hoti, lābhasakkārasilokaṃ ukkhittāsikapaccatthikaṃ viya sallakkhetvā “kikīva aṇḍa”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.7; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena sakkaccaṃ sīlaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva vārittasīle paṭipattikkamo.

“Thus, this virtue is indeed the foundation of all accomplishments, the ground for the arising of all the qualities of the Buddhas, the initial practice, the cause, the entrance, and the foremost of all the qualities that make one a Buddha.” Having given rise to great respect, one is heedful in bodily and verbal restraint, in controlling the senses, in purity of livelihood, and in the consumption of requisites, with the strength of mindfulness and clear comprehension. One should carefully fulfill virtue, regarding gain, honor, and renown as if they were an enemy with an upraised sword, in the manner described by the phrase beginning ‘like a hen pheasant protects her egg’. This, indeed, is the course of practice in the virtue of restraint.

Cārittasīle pana paṭipatti evaṃ veditabbā – idha bodhisatto kalyāṇamittānaṃ garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ kālena kālaṃ kattā hoti, tathā tesaṃ kālena kālaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ kattā hoti, gilānānaṃ kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ, vācāya pucchanañca kattā hoti, subhāsitapadāni sutvā sādhukāraṃ kattā [M 1.0281] hoti, guṇavantānaṃ guṇe vaṇṇetā, paresaṃ apakāre khantā, upakāre anussaritā, puññāni anumoditā, attano puññāni sammāsambodhiyā pariṇāmetā, sabbakālaṃ appamādavihārī kusalesu dhammesu, sati accaye accayato disvā tādisānaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ āvi kattā, uttariñca sammāpaṭipattiṃ sammadeva paripūretā.

As for the practice in the virtue of conduct, it should be understood thus: Here, the Bodhisatta performs from time to time bowing, rising to greet, joining palms in reverence, and courteous duties to spiritual friends and those worthy of reverence. He also attends to them at suitable intervals, provides bodily service for the sick, and inquires after their well-being with his words. Upon hearing well-spoken words, he expresses approval. He praises the virtues of the virtuous, is patient with the harm done by others, and remembers benefits. He rejoices in the merits of others and dedicates his own merits to perfect self-awakening. At all times, he dwells heedfully in wholesome states. If a transgression occurs, seeing it as a transgression, he discloses it as it actually is to such fellow Dhamma-farers. Furthermore, he perfectly fulfills the higher right practice.

Tathā attano anurūpāsu atthūpasaṃhitāsu sattānaṃ itikattabbatāpurekkhāro analaso sahāyabhāvaṃ upagacchati. Uppannesu ca sattānaṃ byādhiādidukkhesu yathārahaṃ patikāravidhāyako, ñātibhogādibyasanapatitesu sokapanodano, ullumpanasabhāvāvaṭṭhito hutvā niggahārahānaṃ dhammeneva niggaṇhanako yāvadeva akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpanāya, paggahārahānaṃ dhammeneva paggaṇhanako. Yāni purimakānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ uḷāratamāni paramadukkarāni acinteyyānubhāvāni sattānaṃ ekantahitasukhāvahāni caritāni, yehi nesaṃ bodhisambhārā sammadeva paripākaṃ agamiṃsu, tāni sutvā anubbiggo anutrāso “tepi mahāpurisā manussā eva, anukkamena pana sikkhāpāripūriyā bhāvitattā tādisāya uḷāratamāya ānubhāvasampattiyā bodhisambhāresu ukkaṃsapāramippattā ahesuṃ, tasmā mayāpi sīlādisikkhāsu sammadeva tathā paṭipajjitabbaṃ, yāya paṭipattiyā ahampi anukkamena sikkhaṃ paripūretvā ekantato padaṃ anupāpuṇissāmī”ti saddhāpurecārikaṃ vīriyaṃ avissajjanto sammadeva sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti.

Likewise, he diligently enters into friendship with others, giving precedence to what should be done for them in ways that are suitable and conducive to their welfare. When suffering such as illness arises for beings, he provides fitting remedies. For those afflicted by the loss of relatives, wealth, and so on, he dispels their sorrow. Established in a disposition to uplift them, he restrains with the Dhamma those deserving of restraint—solely to raise them from the unwholesome and establish them in the wholesome—and he encourages with the Dhamma those deserving of encouragement. Hearing of the magnificent, supremely difficult, and inconceivably powerful deeds of past great bodhisattas, which brought exclusive welfare and happiness to beings—deeds by which their requisites for enlightenment reached perfect maturity—he is neither agitated nor afraid, reflecting: 'Those great beings were also human beings, but through the gradual perfection of the training and the development of their minds, they attained such a supreme accomplishment of power and reached the highest perfection in the requisites for enlightenment. Therefore, I too must practice rightly in the trainings of virtue and so on, so that through such practice I too may gradually perfect the training and will certainly attain the ultimate state.' Not abandoning energy led by faith, he becomes one who rightly brings the virtues to fulfillment.

Tathā paṭicchannakalyāṇo hoti vivaṭāparādho, appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho dukkhasaho [V 1.0247] aviparītadassanajātiko anuddhato anunnaḷo acapalo amukharo avikiṇṇavāco saṃvutindriyo santamānaso kuhanādimicchājīvavirahito ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu, āraddhavīriyo pahitatto kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkho, appamattakampi kāye, jīvite vā apekkhaṃ nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti, pageva adhimattaṃ. Sabbepi dussīlyahetubhūte kodhupanāhādike kilesupakkilese pajahati vinodeti, appamattakena visesādhigamena aparituṭṭho hoti, na saṅkocaṃ āpajjati, uparūparivisesādhigamāya vāyamati.

Likewise, he is one who conceals his good deeds and reveals his faults. He has few wishes, is content, secluded, unentangled, and endures hardship. His nature is to have non-perverted view; he is not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not sharp-tongued, and not of scattered speech. His senses are restrained and his mind is peaceful. Free from wrong livelihood such as scheming, he is accomplished in conduct and resort. Seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains by undertaking the training rules. With energy aroused and mind resolute, he is unconcerned about body and life; he does not tolerate even a slight concern for his body or life but abandons it and dispels it—how much more so an excessive one! He abandons and dispels all defilements and secondary defilements that are the cause of immorality. He is not content with a slight attainment of distinction; he does not shrink back but strives for higher and higher attainment of distinction.

Yena [M 1.0282] yathāladdhā sampatti hānabhāgiyā vā ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na hoti, tathā mahāpuriso andhānaṃ pariṇāyako hoti, maggaṃ ācikkhati, badhirānaṃ hatthamuddāya saññaṃ deti, atthamanuggāheti, tathā mūgānaṃ. Pīṭhasappikānaṃ pīṭhaṃ deti, vāheti vā. Assaddhānaṃ saddhāpaṭilābhāya vāyamati, kusītānaṃ ussāhajananāya, muṭṭhassatīnaṃ satisamāyogāya. Vibbhantattānaṃ samādhisampadāya, duppaññānaṃ paññādhigamāya vāyamati. Kāmacchandapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ kāmacchandapaṭivinodanāya vāyamati. Byāpādathinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccavicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitānaṃ vicikicchāvinodanāya vāyamati. Kāmavitakkādipakatānaṃ kāmavitakkādimicchāvitakkavinodanāya vāyamati. Pubbakārīnaṃ sattānaṃ kataññutaṃ nissāya pubbabhāsī piyavādī saṅgāhako sadisena, adhikena vā paccupakāre sammānetā hoti.

He strives with that energy by which whatever wealth has been gained is neither of a declining part nor of a static part. Furthermore, the great being becomes a guide for the blind, pointing out the path. To the deaf, he gives signs with hand gestures and helps them to grasp the meaning; likewise for the mute. To cripples, he gives a stool or carries them. He strives for the attainment of faith in the faithless, for arousing energy in the lazy, and for the proper connection with mindfulness in the forgetful. For those with distracted minds, he strives for the accomplishment of concentration; for the unwise, for the attainment of wisdom. He strives to dispel sensual desire in those beset by it. For those beset by ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, he strives to dispel doubt. For those afflicted by sensual thoughts and the like, he strives to dispel sensual thoughts and other wrong thoughts. Relying on gratitude towards beings who have previously done him a good turn, he is one who speaks first, speaks kindly, is a benefactor, and is a proper guide in returning favors, whether equal or greater.

Āpadāsu sahāyakiccaṃ anutiṭṭhati, tesaṃ tesañca sattānaṃ pakatiṃ, sabhāvañca parijānitvā yehi yathā saṃvasitabbaṃ hoti, tehi tathā saṃvasati. Yesu ca yathā paṭipajjitabbaṃ hoti, tesu tathā paṭipajjati. Tañca kho akusalato vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpanavasena, na aññathā. Paracittānurakkhaṇā hi bodhisattānaṃ yāvadeva kusalābhivaḍḍhiyā. Tathā hitajjhāsayenāpi paro na sāhasitabbo, na bhaṇḍitabbo, na maṅkubhāvamāpādetabbo, na parassa kukkuccaṃ uppādetabbaṃ, na niggahaṭṭhāne codetabbo, na nīcataraṃ paṭipannassa attā uccatare ṭhapetabbo, na ca paresu sabbena sabbaṃ asevinā bhavitabbaṃ, na atisevinā, na akālasevinā bhavitabbaṃ.

In times of calamity, he attends to the duty of a friend. And having understood the nature and disposition of those various beings, he associates with them in whatever way one should associate. And he acts toward them in whatever way one should act. This, however, is done for the sake of raising them from the unwholesome and establishing them in the wholesome, not otherwise. For the bodhisattvas' protection of others' minds is solely for the growth of the wholesome. Likewise, even with a helpful intention, another person should not be treated rashly, should not be quarreled with, should not be made dejected, remorse should not be aroused in another, one should not be reproved on an occasion for censure, and one should not place oneself in a higher position than one who is of inferior conduct. And with others, one should not be completely unassociating, one should not be excessively associating, and one should not be associating at the wrong time.

Yutte pana satte desakālānurūpaṃ sevati, na ca paresaṃ purato piyepi garahati, appiye vā pasaṃsati, na adhiṭṭhāya vissāsī hoti, na dhammikaṃ upanimantanaṃ paṭikkhipati, na paññattiṃ upagacchati, nādhikaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti, saddhāsampanne saddhānisaṃsakathāya sampahaṃseti, sīlasutacāgapaññāsampanne [V 1.0248] paññānisaṃsakathāya sampahaṃseti. Sace pana bodhisatto abhiññābalappatto hoti, pamādāpanne satte abhiññābalena yathārahaṃ nirayādike dassento saṃvejetvā assaddhādike saddhādīsu patiṭṭhāpeti, sāsane otāreti, saddhādiguṇasampanne paripāceti. Evamassa mahāpurisassa cārittabhūto aparimāṇo puññābhisando kusalābhisando uparūpari abhivaḍḍhatīti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the great being associates with suitable beings in a way appropriate to time and place. He does not disparage a dear one in front of others, nor praise a disliked one. He is not one who becomes familiar through his own resolve. He does not reject a righteous invitation. He does not follow worldly convention. He does not accept more than is proper. He gladdens those endowed with faith with talk on the benefits of faith. He gladdens those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom with talk on the benefits of wisdom. If, however, the bodhisatta has attained the power of the higher knowledges, he stirs a sense of urgency in heedless beings by showing them, through that power, the hells and other such states as is appropriate, and he establishes the faithless and others in faith and the like, brings them into the Dispensation, and brings to maturity those endowed with the qualities of faith and so on. Thus it should be understood that for this great being, the immeasurable flow of merit and flow of the wholesome that constitutes his conduct grows ever higher.

Apica [M 1.0283] yā sā “kiṃ sīlaṃ, kenaṭṭhena sīla”ntiādinā pucchaṃ katvā “pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa, vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā sīla”ntiādinā nayena nānappakārato sīlassa vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.6) vuttā, sā sabbāpi idha āharitvā vattabbā. Kevalañhi tattha sāvakabodhisattavasena sīlakathā āgatā, idha mahābodhisattavasena karuṇūpāyakosallapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā vattabbāti ayameva viseso. Yato idaṃ sīlaṃ mahāpuriso yathā na attano duggatiyaṃ parikilesavimuttiyā, sugatiyampi na rajjasampattiyā, na cakkavattī, na deva, na sakka, na māra, na brahmasampattiyā pariṇāmeti, tathā na attano tevijjatāya, na chaḷabhiññatāya, na catupaṭisambhidādhigamāya, na sāvakabodhiyā, na paccekabodhiyā pariṇāmeti, atha kho sabbaññubhāvena sabbasattānaṃ anuttarasīlālaṅkārasampādanatthameva pariṇāmetīti ayaṃ sīlapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo.

Furthermore, that detailed discourse on virtue in its various aspects given in the Visuddhimagga—which proceeds by asking such questions as, 'What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue?' and answering, 'Virtue consists of volition and other mental states in one who abstains from killing living beings, etc., or in one who fulfills the observances and duties'—all that should be brought in and stated here. The only difference is that there the discourse on virtue is given in terms of disciple-bodhisattas, while here it must be stated in terms of great bodhisattas, giving precedence to compassion and skill in means. For the great being does not direct this virtue towards his own release from defilements in a bad destination; nor, in a good destination, does he direct it towards the attainment of kingship, nor towards the state of a wheel-turning monarch, a deva, Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. Likewise, he does not direct it towards his own attainment of the threefold true knowledge, the six higher knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the enlightenment of a disciple, or the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha. Rather, through the state of omniscience, he directs it for the sole purpose of endowing all beings with the adornment of unsurpassed virtue. This is the course of practice for the perfection of virtue.

Tathā yasmā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā kāmehi ca bhavehi ca nikkhamanavasena pavattā kusalacittuppatti nekkhammapāramī, tasmā sakalasaṃkilesanivāsanaṭṭhānatāya, puttadārādīhi mahāsambādhatāya, kasivāṇijjādinānāvikammantādhiṭṭhānabyākulatāya ca gharāvāsassa nekkhammasukhādīnaṃ anokāsataṃ, kāmānañca “satthadhārālaggamadhubindu viya ca kadalī viya ca avaleyhamānaparittassādavipulānatthānubandhā”ti ca vijjulatobhāsena gahetabbaṃ naccaṃ viya parittakālūpalabbhā, ummattakālaṅkāro viya viparītasaññāya anubhavitabbā, karīsāvacchādanamukhaṃ viya paṭikārabhūtā, udake temitaṅguliyā nisārudakapānaṃ viya atittikarā, chātajjhattabhojanaṃ viya sābādhā, balisāmisaṃ viya byāsanupanipātakāraṇā (byasanasannipātakāraṇā – dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7), aggisantāpo viya kālattayepi dukkhuppattihetubhūtā, makkaṭālepo viya bandhananimittā, ghātakāvacchādanakimālayo viya anatthacchādanā, sapattagāmavāso viya bhayaṭṭhānabhūtā, paccatthikaposako viya kilesamārādīnaṃ āmisabhūtā, chaṇasampattiyo viya vipariṇāmadukkhā, koṭaraggi [V 1.0249] viya antodāhakā, purāṇakūpāvalambabīraṇamadhupiṇḍaṃ viya anekādīnavā, loṇūdakapānaṃ viya pipāsāhetubhūtā, surāmerayaṃ viya nīcajanasevitā[M 1.0284], appassādatāya aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā”tiādinā ca nayena ādīnavaṃ sallakkhetvā tabbipariyāyena nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ passantena nekkhammapavivekaupasamasukhādīsu ninnapoṇapabbhāracittena nekkhammapāramiyaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, since the perfection of renunciation is the arising of a wholesome thought that is embraced by the wisdom of skill in the means of compassion, is preceded by seeing the danger, and proceeds by way of renouncing sensual pleasures and states of existence, therefore, having discerned the danger and, in contrast, seeing the benefit in renunciation, one should practice the perfection of renunciation with a mind inclined, sloping, and tending towards the happiness of renunciation, seclusion, peace, and so on. The danger is to be discerned in the household life—in that it is a dwelling place for all defilements, is greatly confining due to wife, children, and so on, and is distracting as the basis for various activities such as agriculture and commerce, thus offering no opportunity for the happiness of renunciation and so on—and in sensual pleasures by the method beginning with: ‘they have little taste and are followed by great harm, like a drop of honey on a razor’s edge and like a banana tree; they are available for only a short time, like a dance to be seen by a flash of lightning; they are to be experienced with perverted perception, like the adornments of a madman; they are repulsive, like a face covered with excrement; they are unsatisfying, like drinking tasteless water with a wet finger; they are accompanied by affliction, like eating when famished; they are a cause for falling into disaster, like bait on a hook; they are a cause for the arising of suffering in all three periods of time, like the heat of a fire; they are a cause of bondage, like monkey-lime; they conceal what is harmful, like worms that cover a deadly fault; they are a place of fear, like living in an enemy village; they are bait for the defilements, Māra, and so on, like one who nourishes an enemy; they are subject to the suffering of change, like the prosperity of a festival; they burn within, like a fire in a hollow tree; they have many dangers, like a honeycomb in a hollow tree hanging down into an old well; they are a cause of thirst, like drinking salt water; they are frequented by base people, like liquor and spirits; and because of their slight gratification, they are comparable to a chain of bones.’

Yasmā pana nekkhammaṃ pabbajjāmūlakaṃ, tasmā pabbajjā tāva anuṭṭhātabbā. Pabbajjamanutiṭṭhantena mahāsattena asati buddhuppāde kammavādīnaṃ kiriyavādīnaṃ tāpasaparibbājakānaṃ pabbajjā anuṭṭhātabbā. Uppannesu pana sammāsambuddhesu tesaṃ sāsane eva pabbajitabbaṃ. Pabbajitvā ca yathāvutte sīle patiṭṭhitena tassā eva sīlapāramiyā vodāpanatthaṃ dhutaguṇā samādātabbā. Samādinnadhutadhammā hi mahāpurisā sammadeva te pariharantā appicchāsantuṭṭhasallekhapavivekaasaṃsaggavīriyārambhasubharatādiguṇasalilavikkhālitakilesamalatāya anavajjasīlavataguṇaparisuddhasamācārā porāṇe ariyavaṃsattaye patiṭṭhitā catutthaṃ bhāvanārāmatāsaṅkhātaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ gantuṃ cattārīsāya ārammaṇesu yathārahaṃ upacārappanābhedaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharanti. Evañhissa sammadeva nekkhammapāramī pāripūritā hoti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne terasahi dhutadhammehi saddhiṃ dasa kasiṇāni dasāsubhāni dasānussatiyo cattāro brahmavihārā cattāro āruppā ekā saññā ekaṃ vavatthānanti cattārīsa samādhibhāvanākammaṭṭhānāni, bhāvanāvidhānañca vitthārato vattabbāni, taṃ panetaṃ sabbaṃ yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.22, 47) sabbākārato vitthāretvā vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha sāvakabodhisattassa vasena vuttaṃ, idha mahābodhisattassa vasena karuṇūpāyakosallapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā vattabbanti ayameva viseso. Evamettha nekkhammapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo veditabbo.

Furthermore, since renunciation is rooted in going forth, going forth should first be undertaken. When a Bodhisatta undertakes going forth in the absence of a Buddha’s arising, he should undertake the going forth of ascetics and wanderers who are proponents of kamma and of action. But when Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones have arisen, one should go forth only in their Dispensation. And having gone forth and established oneself in the precepts as described, the great being should undertake the ascetic practices in order to purify that very perfection of virtue. For when great beings who have undertaken the ascetic practices properly maintain them, with their defilements and stains washed away by the water of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-association, energetic striving, and being easy to support, they become irreproachable in their virtuous observances and purified in their conduct. Established in the three ancient noble lineages, they attain and abide in the jhānas—distinguished into access and absorption—as is appropriate among the forty meditation subjects, in order to proceed to the fourth noble lineage, called delight in development. Thus his perfection of renunciation is rightly fulfilled. Furthermore, in this place, along with the thirteen ascetic practices, the forty meditation subjects for developing concentration—namely, the ten kasiṇas, the ten kinds of foulness, the ten recollections, the four divine abidings, the four formless attainments, the one perception, and the one analysis—and the methods of development should be explained in detail. However, since all this has been explained in full in every way in the Visuddhimagga by the teacher Buddhaghosa, it should be understood by a wise person who so desires according to the method stated there. The only difference is this: there it is stated from the perspective of a disciple, whereas here it should be stated from the perspective of a great Bodhisatta, making it preceded by skill in the means of compassion. Thus, the course of practice for the perfection of renunciation should be understood here according to this stated method.

Tathā paññāpāramiṃ sampādetukāmena yasmā paññā āloko viya andhakārena mohena saha na vattati, tasmā mohakāraṇāni tāva bodhisattena parivajjetabbāni. Tatthimāni mohakāraṇāni-arati tandī vijambhitā ālasiyaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmatā niddāsīlatā anicchayasīlatā ñāṇasmiṃ akutūhalatā micchādhimāno aparipucchakatā kāyassa nasammāparihāro asamāhitacittatā duppaññānaṃ [M 1.0285] puggalānaṃ sevanā paññavantānaṃ apayirupāsanā attaparibhavo micchāvikappo viparītābhiniveso kāyadaḷhībahulatā asaṃvegasīlatā pañca nīvaraṇāni, saṅkhepato yevāpanadhamme āsevato anuppannā paññā nuppajjati, uppannā parihāyati[V 1.0250], iti imāni mohakāraṇāni, tāni parivajjantena bāhusacce, jhānādīsu ca yogo karaṇīyo.

Furthermore, by a Bodhisatta who desires to fulfill the perfection of wisdom—since wisdom, like light, does not coexist with the darkness of delusion—the causes of delusion must first be abandoned. Herein, these are the causes of delusion: discontent, lethargy, stretching, idleness, delight in company, being in the habit of sleeping, indecisiveness, lack of curiosity about knowledge, wrong pride, not making inquiries, improper care of the body, associating with unwise persons, not attending upon the wise, self-contempt, wrong thinking, perverse adherence, excessive nourishment of the body, lack of spiritual urgency, and the five hindrances. In short, for one who cultivates any of these unwholesome states, unarisen wisdom does not arise, and arisen wisdom declines. Therefore, one who avoids these causes of delusion should apply himself to great learning and to the jhānas and other such states.

Tatthāyaṃ bāhusaccassa visayavibhāgo – pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo cattāri saccāni bāvīsatindriyāni dvādasapadiko paṭiccasamuppādo, tathā satipaṭṭhānādayo kusalādidhammappabhedā ca, yāni ca loke anavajjāni vijjāṭṭhānāni, yo ca sattānaṃ hitasukhavidhānanayo byākaraṇaviseso. Iti evaṃ pakāraṃ sakalameva sutavisayaṃ upāyakosallapubbaṅgamāya paññāya, satiyā, vīriyena ca sādhukaṃ uggahaṇasavanadhāraṇaparicayaparipucchāhi ogāhetvā tattha ca paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanena sutamayā paññā nibbattetabbā, tathā sattānaṃ itikattabbatāsu ṭhānuppattikā paṭibhānabhūtā, āyāpāyaupāyakosallabhūtā ca paññā hitesitaṃ nissāya tattha tattha yathārahaṃ pavattetabbā, tathā khandhādīnaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ ākāraparitakkanamukhena ceva nijjhānaṃ khamāpentena ca cintāmayā paññā nibbattetabbā.

Herein, this is the classification of the scope of extensive learning: the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the twelve-factored dependent origination; furthermore, the foundations of mindfulness and so on, and other divisions of wholesome states; and whatever blameless fields of knowledge there are in the world, and that special grammar which is the method for securing the welfare and happiness of beings. Thus, this entire scope of learning should be thoroughly penetrated by means of wisdom preceded by skill in means, mindfulness, and energy, through careful study, listening, retention, practice, and inquiry. And therein, by establishing others in it, the wisdom born of learning should be generated. Likewise, based on the search for their welfare, wisdom that arises on the spot, wisdom that is ready wit, and wisdom that is skill in the means for the progress and decline of beings should be applied appropriately in each and every case. Furthermore, wisdom born of reflection should be generated by way of reflecting on the characteristics of phenomena in their intrinsic nature, such as the aggregates, and by making oneself patient in scrutinizing them.

Khandhādīnaṃyeva pana salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇapariggahaṇavasena lokiyapariññaṃ nibbattentena pubbabhāgabhāvanāpaññā sampādetabbā. Evañhi “nāmarūpamattamidaṃ, yathārahaṃ paccayehi uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, na ettha koci kattā vā kāretā vā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā”ti ajjhattikadhamme, bāhirakadhamme ca nibbisesaṃ parijānanto tattha āsaṅgaṃ pajahanto, pare ca tattha taṃ pajahāpento kevalaṃ karuṇāvaseneva yāva na buddhaguṇā hatthatalaṃ āgacchanti, tāva yānattaye satte avatāraṇaparipācanehi patiṭṭhāpento, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiyo, abhiññāyo ca lokiyavasībhāvaṃ pāpento paññāya matthakaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Furthermore, by generating mundane full understanding through comprehending the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates and so on, the wisdom of development in the preliminary stage should be accomplished. For thus: 'This is merely name-and-form, which arises and ceases appropriately due to conditions; herein there is no agent or instigator. It is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been; it is suffering in the sense of being constantly oppressed by arising and passing away; it is not-self in the sense of not being subject to one's will.' Fully understanding internal and external phenomena without distinction, abandoning attachment to them and also causing others to abandon that attachment, purely by the power of compassion, for as long as the qualities of a Buddha do not yet come into the palm of his hand, one establishes beings in the three vehicles by causing them to enter and to mature. Reaching mundane mastery of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, as well as the direct knowledges, one reaches the summit of wisdom.

Tattha yācimā iddhividhañāṇaṃ dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ yathākammūpagañāṇaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇanti saparibhaṇḍā pañcalokiyābhiññāsaṅkhātā bhāvanāpaññā, yā ca [M 1.0286] khandhāyatanadhātuindriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedesu catubhūmakesu dhammesu uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā sīlavisuddhi cittavisuddhīti mūlabhūtāsu imāsu dvīsu visuddhīsu patiṭṭhāya diṭṭhivisuddhi kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti sarīrabhūtā imā pañca visuddhiyo sampādentena bhāvetabbā lokiyalokuttarabhedā [V 1.0251] bhāvanāpaññā, tāsaṃ sampādanavidhānaṃ yasmā “tattha ‘ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī’tiādikaṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ kātukāmena ādikammikena yoginā”tiādinā, (visuddhi. 2.365) “khandhāti pañcha khandhā rūpakkhandho vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.431) ca visayavisayivibhāgena (visayavibhāgena – cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathā) saddhiṃ visuddhimagge sabbākārato vitthāretvā vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha sāvakabodhisattassa vasena paññā āgatā, idha mahābodhisattassa vasena karuṇūpāyakosallapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā vattabbā. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ apāpetvā paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiyaṃyeva vipassanā ṭhapetabbāti ayameva visesoti. Evamettha paññāpāramiyā paṭipattikkamo veditabbo.

Herein, there is the wisdom of development called the five mundane direct knowledges, together with their accessories—namely, the knowledge of various psychic powers, the knowledge of the divine ear element, the knowledge of penetrating minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of beings' rebirth according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future. And there is that wisdom of development, divided into mundane and supramundane, which is to be cultivated by one who, having practiced with knowledge by means of learning and inquiry regarding the states belonging to the four planes—which are divided into aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so on—and having been established in these two fundamental purifications, namely, purification of virtue and purification of mind, accomplishes these five purifications which form the body: purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision. Since the method for accomplishing these has been stated and elaborated in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga by the teacher Buddhaghosa Thera, together with the division of object and subject, with passages beginning, 'Herein, a beginner yogi who wishes to perform the various psychic transformations such as, "Having been one, he becomes many..."' and '"Aggregates" means the five aggregates: the form aggregate, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate...', therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein. However, therein, wisdom is presented from the perspective of a disciple bodhisatta; here, it is to be stated from the perspective of a Great Bodhisatta, having made it be preceded by compassion and skill in means. This itself is the distinction: that insight is to be established in the purification by knowledge and vision of the way itself, without having reached the purification by knowledge and vision. Thus, the course of practice for the perfection of wisdom should be understood herein.

Tathā yasmā sammāsambodhiyā katābhinīhārena mahāsattena pāramīparipūraṇatthaṃ sabbakālaṃ yuttappayuttena bhavitabbaṃ ābaddhaparikaraṇena, tasmā kālena kālaṃ “ko nu kho ajja mayā puññasambhāro, ñāṇasambhāro vā upacito, kiṃ vā mayā parahitaṃ kata”nti divase divase paccavekkhantena sattahitatthaṃ ussāho karaṇīyo, sabbesampi sattānaṃ upakārāya attano pariggahabhūtaṃ vatthuṃ, kāyaṃ, jīvitañca nirapekkhanacittena ossajjitabbaṃ, yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ karoti kāyena, vācāya vā, taṃ sabbaṃ sambodhiyaṃ ninnacitteneva kātabbaṃ, bodhiyā pariṇāmetabbaṃ, uḷārehi, ittarehi ca kāmehi vinivattacitteneva bhavitabbaṃ, sabbāsu ca itikattabbatāsu upāyakosallaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, since a Great Being who has made the aspiration for perfect self-enlightenment must, for the sake of fulfilling the perfections, always be diligently engaged and constantly committed, therefore, from time to time, reflecting day by day, 'What accumulation of merit or accumulation of wisdom have I amassed today? Or what welfare for others have I performed?', effort should be made for the welfare of beings. For the benefit of all beings, one's own possessions, body, and life should be relinquished with a mind free from attachment. Whatever action one performs by body or speech, all of it should be done with a mind inclined towards enlightenment; it should be dedicated to enlightenment. One must be with a mind turned away from both lofty and trifling sensual pleasures. And in all that should be done, one should practice having established skill in means.

Tasmiṃ tasmiñca sattahite āraddhavīriyena bhavitabbaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhādisabbasahena avisaṃvādinā. Sabbepi sattā anodhiso mettāya, karuṇāya ca pharitabbā. Yā kāci sattānaṃ dukkhuppatti, sabbā sā attani pāṭikaṅkhitabbā. Sabbesañca sattānaṃ puññaṃ abbhanumoditabbaṃ, buddhānaṃ mahantatā mahānubhāvatā [M 1.0287] abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbā, yañca kiñci kammaṃ karoti kāyena, vācāya vā, taṃ sabbaṃ bodhicittapubbaṅgamaṃ kātabbaṃ. Iminā hi upāyena dānādīsu yuttappayuttassa thāmavato daḷhaparakkamassa mahāsattassa bodhisattassa aparimeyyo puññasambhāro, ñāṇasambhāro ca divase divase upacīyati.

In every matter concerning the welfare of beings, one must be of aroused energy, enduring all things such as the desirable and undesirable, and be unfailing. All beings should be pervaded without distinction with loving-kindness and compassion. Whatever suffering arises for beings, all of it should be desired for oneself. The merit of all beings should be greatly rejoiced in. The greatness and great power of the Buddhas should be frequently contemplated. Whatever action one performs, whether by body or speech, all of it should be done with the thought of enlightenment as its forerunner. Indeed, by this method, for the great being, the Bodhisatta, who is strenuously engaged in giving and so forth, strong, and of firm effort, an immeasurable accumulation of merit and knowledge grows day by day.

Apica sattānaṃ paribhogatthaṃ, paripālanatthañca attano sarīraṃ, jīvitañca pariccajitvā khuppipāsasītuṇhavātātapādidukkhapatikāro pariyesitabbo ca uppādetabbo ca, yañca yathāvuttadukkhapatikārajaṃ sukhaṃ attanā paṭilabhati, tathā ramaṇīyesu ārāmuyyānapāsādataḷākādīsu[V 1.0252], araññāyatanesu ca kāyacittasantāpābhāvena abhinibbutattā attanā sukhaṃ paṭilabhati, yañca suṇāti “buddhānubuddhapaccekabuddhā, mahābodhisattā ca nekkhammapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitā”ti ca “diṭṭhadhammikasukhavihārabhūtaṃ īdisaṃ nāma jhānasamāpattisukhamanubhavantī”ti ca, taṃ sabbaṃ sattesu anodhiso upasaṃharati. Ayaṃ tāva nayo asamāhitabhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitassa.

Furthermore, for the use and protection of beings, having relinquished one's own body and life, a remedy for suffering from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, sun, and so forth should be sought and produced. And whatever happiness one obtains for oneself, born from remedying the aforesaid suffering; and likewise, whatever happiness one obtains for oneself in delightful parks, gardens, palaces, ponds, and so forth, and in forest abodes, due to being calmed by the absence of bodily and mental distress; and whatever one hears, such as, 'Buddhas, Anubuddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great Bodhisattas are established in the practice of renunciation,' and, 'They experience such bliss of jhāna-attainment, which constitutes a pleasant abiding in the present life'—all of that one applies to beings without distinction. This, for now, is the method for one established in the unconcentrated stage.

Samāhitabhūmiyaṃ pana patiṭṭhito attanā yathānubhūtaṃ visesādhigamanibbattaṃ pītiṃ, passaddhiṃ, sukhaṃ, samādhiṃ, yathābhūtañāṇañca sattesu adhimuccanto upasaṃharati pariṇāmeti, tathā mahati saṃsāradukkhe, tassa ca nimittabhūte kilesābhisaṅkhāradukkhe nimuggaṃ sattanikāyaṃ disvā tatrāpi khādanachedanabhedanasedanapisanahiṃsanaaggisantāpādijanitā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā nirantaraṃ cirakālaṃ vedayante narake, aññamaññaṃ kujjhanasantāsanavisodhanahiṃsanaparādhīnatādīhi mahādukkhaṃ anubhavante tiracchānagate, jotimālākulasarīre khuppipāsavātātapādīhi ḍayhamāne, visussamāne ca vantakheḷādiāhāre, uddhabāhu viravante nijjhāmataṇhikādike mahādukkhaṃ vedayamāne pete ca pariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ mahantaṃ anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇante hatthacchedādikaraṇayogena dubbaṇṇaduddasikadaliddādibhāvena khuppipāsādiābādhayogena balavantehi abhibhavanīyato, paresaṃ vahanato, parādhīnato ca narake, pete, tiracchānagate ca atisayante apāyadukkhanibbisesaṃ dukkhamanubhavante manusse ca tathā visayaparibhogavikkhittacittatāya rāgādipariḷāhena ḍayhamāne vātavegasamuṭṭhitajālāsamiddhasukkhakaṭṭhasannipāte aggikkhandhe viya anupasantapariḷāhavuttike anupasantanihataparādhīne [M 1.0288] (anihataparādhīne dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) kāmāvacaradeve ca mahatā vāyāmena vidūramākāsaṃ vigāhitasakuntā viya, balavatā dūre pāṇinā khittasarā viya ca “satipi cirappavattiyaṃ anaccantikatāya pātapariyosānā anatikkantajātijarāmaraṇā evā”ti rūpāvacarārūpāvacaradeve ca passantena mahantaṃ saṃvegaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā mettāya, karuṇāya ca anodhiso sattā pharitabbā. Evaṃ kāyena, vācāya, manasā ca bodhisambhāre nirantaraṃ upacinantena yathā pāramiyo paripūrenti, evaṃ sakkaccakārinā sātaccakārinā anolīnavuttinā ussāho pavattetabbo, vīriyapāramī paripūretabbā.

Furthermore, one established in the concentrated stage, being resolved upon beings, applies and directs towards them the joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, and knowledge of things as they are, which is personally experienced and produced by the attainment of distinction. Likewise, the Bodhisatta sees the host of beings submerged in the great suffering of saṃsāra and in the suffering of defilements and formations which are its cause. He sees beings in hell continuously and for a long time experiencing intense, harsh, and bitter pains produced by being eaten, cut, split, boiled, ground, harmed, and scorched by fire. He sees those in the animal realm experiencing great suffering from mutual anger, intimidation, oppression, harm, and dependence on others. He sees petas with bodies afflicted by garlands of flame, being burned by hunger, thirst, wind, and heat, withering away, having vomit and phlegm as food, wailing with arms upraised, and those like the Nijjhāmataṇhika petas experiencing great suffering. He sees humans who are like beings in hell, petas, and animals in the extreme, experiencing suffering indistinguishable from that of the lower realms, attaining great misfortune and ruin rooted in the search for sustenance, through connection with acts such as having hands cut off, through the state of being ugly, unsightly, and poor, through connection with afflictions such as hunger and thirst, from being oppressed by the powerful, from carrying the burdens of others, and from being dependent on others. Likewise, he sees the sense-sphere devas who, due to minds scattered by the enjoyment of sense-objects, are burned by the torment of lust and so forth, whose state is one of unpacified torment like a great mass of fire in a heap of dry wood fanned by the force of the wind, who are dependent on others through an unsuppressed fall. And he sees the form-sphere and formless-sphere devas who, like birds that have plunged into the distant sky with great effort, or like arrows shot far by a strong man's hand, although their existence is long, because it is not eternal and ends in a fall, have not gone beyond birth, aging, and death. Seeing all this, he should arouse great spiritual urgency and pervade all beings without distinction with loving-kindness and compassion. Thus, while continuously accumulating the requisites for enlightenment with body, speech, and mind, acting respectfully, constantly, and with unshrinking conduct, effort should be exerted in such a way that the perfections are fulfilled. The perfection of energy should be fulfilled.

Apica “acinteyyāparimeyyavipuloḷāravimalanirupamanirupakkilesaguṇagaṇanicayanidānabhūtassa buddhabhāvassa ussakkitvā sampahaṃsanayoggaṃ vīriyaṃ nāma acinteyyānubhāvameva, yaṃ na pacurajanā sotumpi sakkuṇanti, pageva paṭipajjituṃ. Tathā hi tividhā abhinīhāracittuppatti, catasso buddhabhūmiyo, (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34) cattāri saṅgahavatthūni[V 1.0253], (dī. ni. 3.210; a. ni. 4.32) karuṇekarasatā, buddhadhammesu sacchikaraṇena visesappaccayo, nijjhānakkhanti, sabbadhammesu nirupalepo, sabbasattesu piyaputtasaññā, saṃsāradukkhehi aparikhedo, sabbadeyyadhammapariccāgo, tena ca niratimānatā, adhisīlādiadhiṭṭhānaṃ, tattha ca acañcalatā, kusalakiriyāsu pītipāmojjatā, vivekaninnacittatā, jhānānuyogo, anavajjadhammesu atittiyatā, yathāsutassa dhammassa paresaṃ hitajjhāsayena desanāya ārambhadaḷhatā, dhīravīrabhāvo, parāpavādaparāpakāresu vikārābhāvo, saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, samāpattīsu vasībhāvo, abhiññāsu balappatti, lakkhaṇattayāvabodho, satipaṭṭhānādīsu abhiyogena lokuttaramaggasambhārasambharaṇaṃ, navalokuttarāvakkantī”ti evamādikā sabbāpi bodhisambhārapaṭipatti vīriyānubhāveneva samijjhatīti abhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi anossajjantena sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ vīriyaṃ yathā uparūpari visesāvahaṃ hoti, evaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Sampajjamāne ca yathāvutte vīriye, khantisaccādhiṭṭhānādayo ca dānasīlādayo ca sabbepi bodhisambhārā tadadhīnavuttitāya sampannā eva hontītikhantiādīsupi imināva nayena paṭipatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, I will state another method. For the state of Buddhahood—which is the cause for the accumulation of a host of virtues that are inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, excellent, stainless, incomparable, and free from defilements—the energy, so-called, which is worthy of being greatly gladdened through striving, is indeed of inconceivable power. It is an energy that inferior people are not even able to hear of, what need is there to speak of practicing it? Thus, I will elaborate on that statement: The three kinds of arising of the mind that aspires towards great enlightenment, the four Buddha-grounds, the four bases of sympathy, the state of having the single function of compassion, the special condition through the direct realization of the Buddha-qualities, patience in contemplation with wisdom, non-adherence to all worldly phenomena, the perception of all beings as a beloved son, non-weariness of the sufferings of saṃsāra, the relinquishment of all things fit to be given, and through that, the absence of excessive pride, the determination for higher virtue and so forth, and steadfastness therein, the state of having joy and gladness in wholesome actions, the state of having a mind inclined to seclusion, the application to attain absorption, insatiability in blameless wholesome qualities, firmness of effort in teaching the Dhamma as heard to others with the intention of their welfare, the state of having steadfast energy, the absence of alteration in the face of others' blame and harm, the determination for truth, mastery over the attainments, the attainment of power in the higher knowledges, the thorough understanding of the three characteristics, the accomplishment of the requisites for the supramundane path through extreme application to the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, and the entry into the nine supramundane states. Thus, all such practices for accumulating the requisites of enlightenment succeed solely through the power of energy. Therefore, from the aspiration for Buddhahood up to great enlightenment, energy should be accomplished respectfully and continuously, without abandoning it, in such a way that it brings about higher and higher distinction. And when the aforementioned energy is being accomplished, patience, truth, determination, and so forth, and generosity, virtue, and so forth—all the requisites of enlightenment—are indeed accomplished because their existence is dependent on it. Thus, the practice in regard to patience and the rest should also be understood by this very method.

Iti [M 1.0289] sattānaṃ sukhūpakaraṇapariccāgena bahudhānuggahakaraṇaṃ dānena paṭipatti, sīlena tesaṃ jīvitasāpateyyadārarakkhābhedapiyahitavacanāvihiṃsādikaraṇāni, nekkhammena tesaṃ āmisapaṭiggahaṇadhammadānādinā anekavidhā hitacariyā, paññāya tesaṃ hitakaraṇūpāyakosallaṃ, vīriyena tattha ussāhārambhaasaṃhīrakaraṇāni, khantiyā tadaparādhasahanaṃ, saccena nesaṃ avañcanatadupakārakiriyāsamādānāvisaṃvādanādi, adhiṭṭhānena tadupakaraṇe anatthasampātepi acalanaṃ, mettāya nesaṃ hitasukhānucintanaṃ, upekkhāya nesaṃ upakārāpakāresu vikārānāpattīti evaṃ aparimāṇe satte ārabbha anukampitasabbasattassa bodhisattassa puthujjanehi asādhāraṇo aparimāṇo puññañāṇasambhārupacayo ettha paṭipattīti veditabbaṃ. Yo cetāsaṃ paccayo vutto, tattha ca sakkaccaṃ sampādanaṃ.

Thus, the practice by means of giving is the act of supporting beings in many ways by relinquishing subtle instruments of pleasure. By means of virtue, there are the acts of protecting their life, protecting the wealth that benefits its owner, protecting their wives, speaking words that are undivided, endearing, and beneficial, not harming, and so forth. By means of renunciation, there is the conduct for their welfare in many ways, such as accepting material things like alms-food, giving the gift of the Dhamma, and so forth. By means of wisdom, there is skill in the means of acting for their welfare. By means of energy, there are the acts of great exertion, initiative, and not shrinking back in that regard. By means of patience, there is the endurance of their offenses. By means of truth, there is not deceiving them, undertaking beneficial actions for them, speaking without error, and so forth. By means of determination, there is unshakeability in benefiting them even when encountering a lack of benefit. By means of loving-kindness, there is repeated contemplation of their welfare and happiness. By means of equanimity, there is the non-occurrence of alteration regarding their helpful and harmful actions. Thus, taking limitless beings as the object, the immeasurable accumulation of the requisites of merit and knowledge of the bodhisatta who has compassion for all beings—an accumulation not shared with ordinary people—should be understood as the practice here. And the respectful accomplishment in regard to that condition which was stated for these perfections should be known as the practice.

Ko vibhāgoti –

What is the analysis?

Sāmaññabhedato etā, dasavidhā vibhāgato;

Tidhā hutvāna paccekaṃ, samatiṃsavidhā samaṃ.

By way of general distinction, these are of ten kinds; when analyzed, each one, having become threefold, they become equally thirtyfold.

Dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyoti hi samatiṃsa pāramiyo. Tattha “katābhinīhārassa [V 1.0254] bodhisattassa parahitakaraṇābhininnāsayapayogassa kaṇhadhammavokiṇṇā sukkā dhammā pāramiyo, tehi avokiṇṇā sukkā dhammā upapāramiyo, akaṇhā asukkā dhammā paramatthapāramiyo”ti keci. “Samudāgamanakālesu pūriyamānā pāramiyo, bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ puṇṇā upapāramiyo, buddhabhūmiyaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇā paramatthapāramiyo. Bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ vā parahitakaraṇato pāramiyo, attahitakaraṇato upapāramiyo, buddhabhūmiyaṃ balavesārajjasamadhigamena ubhayahitaparipūraṇato paramatthapāramiyoti evaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānesu paṇidhānārambhapariniṭṭhānesu tesaṃ vibhāgo”ti apare. “Dosupasamakaruṇāpakatikānaṃ bhavasukhavimuttisukhaparamasukhappattānaṃ puññūpacayabhedato tabbibhāgo”ti aññe.

There are thirty perfections: ten perfections, ten higher perfections, and ten ultimate perfections. Among these, some say: 'For a bodhisatta who has made the aspiration, and whose intention and effort are inclined towards acting for the welfare of others, the bright qualities mixed with dark qualities are the perfections; the bright wholesome qualities unmixed with those are the higher perfections; the qualities that are neither dark nor bright are the ultimate perfections.' Others say: 'Those being fulfilled at the times of accumulation are the perfections; those fulfilled in the bodhisatta-ground are the higher perfections; those completely fulfilled in all aspects in the Buddha-ground are the ultimate perfections. Or, in the bodhisatta-ground, those fulfilled due to acting for the welfare of others are the perfections; those fulfilled due to acting for one's own welfare are the higher perfections; in the Buddha-ground, due to the fulfillment of the welfare of both through the attainment of the powers and fearlessness, they are the ultimate perfections. Thus is their analysis in the beginning, middle, and end, which are the aspiration, the undertaking, and the consummation.' Still others say: 'Their analysis is by way of the division of the accumulation of merit of those whose nature is compassion that pacifies faults, and who have attained the happiness of existence, the happiness of liberation, and the supreme happiness.'

“Lajjāsatimānāpassayānaṃ lokuttaradhammādhipatīnaṃ sīlasamādhipaññāgarukānaṃ tāritataritatārayitūnaṃ anubuddhapaccekabuddhasammāsambuddhānaṃ pāramīupapāramīparamatthapāramīhi bodhittayappattito yathāvuttavibhāgo”ti keci. “Cittapaṇidhito yāva vacīpaṇidhi, tāva pavattā sambhārā pāramiyo[M 1.0290], vacīpaṇidhito yāva kāyapaṇidhi, tāva pavattā upapāramiyo, kāyapaṇidhito pabhuti paramatthapāramiyo”ti apare. Aññe pana “parapuññānumodanavasena pavattā sambhārā pāramiyo, paresaṃ kārāpanavasena pavattā upapāramiyo, sayaṃ karaṇavasena pavattā paramatthapāramiyo”ti vadanti. Tathā “bhavasukhāvaho puññañāṇasambhāro pāramī, attano nibbānasukhāvaho upapāramī, paresaṃ tadubhayasukhāvaho paramatthapāramī”ti eke.

Some say: 'The aforementioned analysis is due to the attainment of the three kinds of enlightenment by the Anubuddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Sammāsambuddhas—who rely on moral shame, mindfulness, and self-respect; for whom the supramundane qualities are dominant; who hold virtue, concentration, and wisdom in high esteem; and who have been guided across, have crossed, and cause others to cross—by means of the perfections, higher perfections, and ultimate perfections.' Others say: 'The requisites that have occurred from the mental aspiration up to the verbal aspiration are the perfections; those that have occurred from the verbal aspiration up to the physical aspiration are the higher perfections; from the physical aspiration onwards are the ultimate perfections.' But still others say: 'The requisites that have occurred by way of rejoicing in the merit of others are the perfections; the requisites that have occurred by way of causing others to make merit are the higher perfections; the requisites that have occurred by way of doing it oneself are the ultimate perfections.' Similarly, some say: 'The accumulation of the requisites of merit and knowledge that brings the happiness of existence is the perfection; that which brings the happiness of one's own Nibbāna is the higher perfection; that which brings both those kinds of happiness for others is the ultimate perfection.'

Puttadāradhanādiupakaraṇapariccāgo pana dānapāramī, attano aṅgapariccāgo dānaupapāramī, attano jīvitapariccāgo dānaparamatthapāramī.
