Gavampati usabho samehi pādehi vasūnaṃ ratanānaṃ dhāraṇato vasundarasaṅkhātaṃ [V 1.0270] bhūmiṃ phusī yathā, tathā manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā muhuttajāto so gotamo samehi pādehi vasundharaṃ phusīti attho. Vikkamīti agamāsi. Satta padānīti sattapadavaḷañjanaṭṭhānāni. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, sattapadavārehīti vā karaṇattho uttarapadalopavasena daṭṭhabbo. Marūti devā yathāmariyādaṃ maraṇasabhāvato. Samāti vilokanasamatāya samā sadisiyo. Mahāpuriso hi yathā ekaṃ disaṃ vilokesi, evaṃ sesadisāpi, na katthaci vilokane vinibandho tassa ahosi, samāti vā viloketuṃ yuttāti attho. Na hi tadā bodhisattassa virūpabībhacchavisamarūpāni viloketumayuttāni disāsu upaṭṭhahanti[M 1.0307], vissaṭṭhamañjūviññeyyādivasena aṭṭhaṅgupetaṃ giraṃ abbhudīrayi pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito sīho yathā abhinadīti attho.

‘Porāṇā’ means the commentary teachers. Just as Gavampati, the chief of beings, with even feet touched the earth called Vasundharā because it bears treasures, so too, having been released from the hands of humans, that Gotama, born just a moment ago, touched the earth with even feet; this is the meaning. ‘Vikkami’ means he went. ‘Satta padāni’ means the places of the seven footsteps. And this is an accusative case in the sense of continuous connection, or the instrumental sense ‘by seven steps’ should be understood by way of elision of the subsequent word. ‘Marū’ means devas, because they have the nature of dying according to the limit of their lifespan. ‘Samā’ means equal, similar, due to the equality of looking. Indeed, just as the Great Being looked in one direction, so too did he look in the other directions; nowhere in his looking was there an obstacle for him. Or, ‘samā’ means suitable for looking; this is the meaning. Indeed, at that time, for the Bodhisatta, unsuitable things to look at—deformed, disgusting, and uneven forms—did not appear in the directions. He uttered a voice endowed with eight qualities, by way of being clear, pleasant, intelligible, and so on; just as a lion standing on a mountain peak roars, he spoke fearlessly; this is the meaning.

Evaṃ kāyagamanatthena gatasaddena tathāgatasaddaṃ niddisitvā idāni ñāṇagamanatthena niddisituṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha “yathā vipassī bhagavā”tiādīsupi “nekkhammena kāmacchandaṃ pahāyā”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Nekkhammenāti alobhapadhānena kusalacittuppādena. Kusalā hi dhammā idha nekkhammaṃ tesaṃ sabbesampi kāmacchandapaṭipakkhattā, na pabbajjādayo eva. “Paṭhamajjhānenā”tipi vadanti keci, tadayuttameva paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya eva idha icchitattā. Pahāyāti pajahitvā. Gatoti uttarivisesaṃ ñāṇagamanena paṭipanno. Pahāyāti vā pahānahetu, pahāne vā sati. Hetulakkhaṇatthesu hi ayaṃ tvā-saddo “sakko hutvā nibbattī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.355) viya. Kāmacchandādippahānahetukañca “gato”ti ettha vuttaṃ avabodhasaṅkhātaṃ, paṭipattisaṅkhātaṃ vā gamanaṃ kāmacchandādippahānena ca taṃ lakkhīyati, esa nayo “padāletvā”tiādīsupi. Abyāpādenāti mettāya. Ālokasaññāyāti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikārena upaṭṭhitālokasañjānanena. Avikkhepenāti samādhinā. Dhammavavatthānenāti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvanicchayena, sappaccayanāmarūpavavatthānenātipi vadanti.

Thus, having explained the word Tathāgata with the word ‘gata’ in the sense of bodily movement, now, to explain it in the sense of movement by knowledge, he said ‘atha vā’, etc. Therein, in phrases like ‘as the Blessed One Vipassī’, it should be connected with ‘having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation’, etc. ‘By renunciation’ (nekkhammena) means by the arising of wholesome consciousness in which non-greed is predominant. Indeed, wholesome states here are ‘renunciation’ because all of them are the opposite of sensual desire, not just ordination and so on. Some also say ‘by the first jhāna’, but that is inappropriate, as here only the preliminary practice for the first jhāna is intended. ‘Having abandoned’ (pahāya) means having given up. ‘Gone’ (gato) means he has attained a higher distinction by the movement of knowledge. Or, ‘pahāya’ can mean ‘because of abandoning’, or ‘when there is abandoning’. For this ‘tvā’ suffix is used in the sense of cause and characteristic, as in ‘he was born because he was Sakka’ and so on. And in ‘gato’, the ‘going’ spoken of—called understanding or called practice—has the abandoning of sensual desire and so on as its cause, and that going is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire and so on. This is the method in ‘having split open’ (padāletvā), etc., as well. ‘By non-ill will’ (abyāpādena) means by loving-kindness. ‘By the perception of light’ (ālokasaññāya) means by knowing the arisen light through attention, having made it manifest. ‘By non-distraction’ (avikkhepena) means by concentration. ‘By the determination of phenomena’ (dhammavavatthānenā) means by the correct determination of wholesome and other states. The teachers also say it means ‘by the determination of name-and-form together with its conditions’.

Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā vuttāya paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya bhagavato ñāṇagamanavisiṭṭhaṃ tathāgatabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni saha upāyena aṭṭhahi samāpattīhi, aṭṭhārasahi ca mahāvipassanāhi taṃ dassetuṃ “ñāṇenā”tiādimāha. Nāmarūpapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇānañhi vinibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti, tasmā avijjāpadālanaṃ vipassanāya upāyo. Tathā jhānasamāpattīsu abhiratinimittena pāmojjena, tattha anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādīnaṃ samadhigamoti samāpattiyā arativinodanaṃ upāyo. Samāpattivipassanānukkamena [V 1.0271] pana upari vakkhamānanayena niddisitabbepi nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhā kāmacchandādivasena dassitanīvaraṇesupi saṅgahadassanatthaṃ uppaṭipāṭiniddeso daṭṭhabbo.

Thus, having shown the Blessed One's state of being a Tathāgata—distinguished by the movement of knowledge—by means of the preliminary practice for the first jhāna, which was spoken of as ‘having abandoned covetousness in the world’, etc., through the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire, now, to show that state together with its means—by the eight attainments and by the eighteen great insights—he said ‘by knowledge’, etc. For, by the removal of delusion, which is an obstacle to the comprehension of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt, the perceptions of impermanence and so on are accomplished for one established in the full understanding of the known. Therefore, the splitting of ignorance is the means for insight. Likewise, in the jhāna-attainments, through the joy which is a sign of delight, non-delight in them is dispelled, and there is the full attainment of jhāna and so on. Therefore, the dispelling of discontent is the means for attainment. However, although it should be explained in the sequence of attainment and insight according to the method to be spoken of later, the explanation in reverse order should be understood for the sake of showing the inclusion of ignorance, which has the nature of a hindrance, even in the hindrances shown below by way of sensual desire and so on.

Samāpattivihārapavesananibandhanena [M 1.0308] nīvaraṇāni kavāṭasadisānīti āha “nīvaraṇakavāṭaṃ ugghāṭetvā”ti. “Rattiṃ anuvitakketvā anuvicāretvā divā kammante payojetī”ti majjhimāgamavare mūlapaṇṇāsake vammikasutte (ma. ni. 1.249) vuttaṭṭhāne viya vitakkavicārā vūpasamā [dhūmāyanā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7)] adhippetāti sandhāya “vitakkavicāradhūmaṃ vūpasametvā”ti vuttaṃ, vitakkavicārasaṅkhātaṃ dhūmaṃ vūpasametvāti attho. “Vitakkavicāra”micceva adhunā pāṭho, so na porāṇo ācariyadhammapālattherena, ācariyasāriputtattherena ca yathāvuttapāṭhasseva uddhatattā. Virājetvāti jigucchitvā, samatikkamitvā vā. Tadubhayattho hesa “pītiyā ca virāgā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.7; ma. ni. 3.155; pārā. 11; vibha. 625) viya. Kāmaṃ paṭhamajjhānūpacāre eva dukkhaṃ, catutthajjhānūpacāre eva ca sukhaṃ pahīyati, atisayappahānaṃ pana sandhāyāha “catutthajjhānena sukhadukkhaṃ pahāyā”ti.

The hindrances are like doors because they obstruct entry into the dwelling of attainments; therefore, the commentator says, 'having opened the door of the hindrances.' With reference to the fact that the calming of initial and sustained thought is intended—as in the passage from the Vammika Sutta in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa of the Majjhima Nikāya: 'Having repeatedly thought and repeatedly pondered at night, one engages in work during the day'—it was said, 'having calmed the smoke of initial and sustained thought,' meaning 'having calmed the smoke called initial and sustained thought.' Now, the reading is just 'initial and sustained thought,' but that is not the ancient reading, for the aforementioned reading was cited by the teachers, the Venerable Dhammapāla and the Venerable Sāriputta. 'Having become dispassionate' means having become disgusted with, or having transcended. For this word has both meanings, as in 'and from the fading away of rapture,' and so on. Although it is true that pain is abandoned right in the access concentration of the first jhāna, and pleasure right in the access concentration of the fourth jhāna, the commentator said, 'by the fourth jhāna, having abandoned pleasure and pain,' with reference to the surpassing abandonment.

Rūpasaññāti saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānāni ceva tadārammaṇāni ca vuttāni. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi “rūpa”nti vuccati uttarapadalopena “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 248) tassa ārammaṇampi kasiṇarūpaṃ purimapadalopena “bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 223 ādayo) tasmā idha rūpe rūpajjhāne taṃsahagatā saññā rūpasaññāti evaṃ saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānāni vuttāni, rūpaṃ saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ, rūpasaññāsamannāgatanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Paṭighasaññāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ, rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānañca paṭighātena paṭihananena visayivisayasamodhānena samuppannā dvipañcaviññāṇasahagatā saññā. Nānattasaññāti aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasa akusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā, dve akusalavipākasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti etāsaṃ catucattālīsasaññānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Etā hi yasmā rūpasaddādibhede nānatte nānāsabhāve gocare pavattanti, yasmā ca nānattā nānāsabhāvā aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā “nānattasaññā”ti vuccanti.

By 'perception of form,' with perception as the principal term, both the form-sphere jhānas and their objects are stated. For the form-sphere jhāna is also called 'form' by elision of the final member of the compound, as in 'one with form sees forms,' and its object, the kasiṇa-form, is also called 'form' by elision of the first member, as in 'one sees external forms, beautiful and ugly.' Therefore, here, the perception associated with the form-jhāna is the 'perception of form.' Thus, with perception as the principal term, the form-sphere jhānas are stated. That jhāna is called 'that which has form-perception,' meaning it is endowed with the perception of form. Thus, this should be understood as a designation for its object, which is differentiated as the earth-kasiṇa, and so on. 'Perception of resistance' is the perception, associated with the two sets of five consciousnesses, that has arisen through the impact and striking of the bases beginning with the eye and the objects beginning with form, that is, through the conjunction of subject and object. 'Perception of diversity' is a designation for these forty-four perceptions: eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven sense-sphere wholesome-resultant perceptions, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven sense-sphere functional perceptions. For because these perceptions occur in a diverse field of objects, differentiated as form, sound, and so on, and of various natures, and because, being diverse and of various natures, they are dissimilar to one another, they are therefore called 'perceptions of diversity'.

Aniccassa[V 1.0272], aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya vipassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññanti saṅkhatadhamme “niccā [M 1.0309] sassatā”ti pavattamicchāsaññaṃ, saññāsīsena cettha diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbindanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Virāgānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya, “te saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ samudayavasena na uppajjantī”ti evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti, no samudetī”ti. Muñcitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattāti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Paṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ. Ādānanti niccādivasena gahaṇaṃ. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Avatthāvisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññanti thirabhāvaggahaṇasaññaṃ. Nimittanti samūhādighanavasena sakiccaparicchedatāya saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahataṃ. Paṇidhinti rāgādipaṇidhiṃ. Sā panatthato taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu ninnatā.

Contemplation of the impermanent, or as 'impermanent,' is the contemplation of impermanence; this is a name for the insight that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena of the three planes. 'Perception of permanence' is the wrong perception that occurs regarding conditioned phenomena as 'permanent, lasting.' Here, by way of the principal term 'perception,' the inclusion of consciousness associated with wrong view should also be understood. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. By 'contemplation of disenchantment' is meant the contemplation that proceeds in the mode of being disenchanted with formations. 'Delight' means craving accompanied by rapture. By 'contemplation of dispassion' is meant the contemplation that proceeds in the mode of becoming dispassionate towards formations. By 'contemplation of cessation' is meant the contemplation of the cessation of formations; or, the contemplation that 'these formations are just ceasing; they do not arise in the future by way of origination.' For that very reason, it was said, 'Through the contemplation of cessation, one brings about cessation; one does not bring about origination.' For this desire to be liberated has become powerful. The contemplation that proceeds in the mode of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment. For this is the firm establishment of reflective understanding. 'Grasping' is the grasping by way of permanence, and so on. The perception of compactness is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, mass, function, and object. 'Striving' (āyūhana) is accumulation (abhisaṅkharaṇa). 'Alteration' is the attainment of a different state. 'Perception of stability' is the perception of grasping a stable state. 'The sign' is the individuality of formations, due to the delimitation of their own function by way of the compactness of the mass, and so on. 'Aspiration' is aspiration based on lust, and so on. In essence, it is the inclination towards formations by way of craving.

Abhinivesanti attānudiṭṭhiṃ. Aniccādivasena sabbadhammatīraṇaṃ adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivisenti asāre sāraggahaṇavipallāsaṃ. Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppannoti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso nāma. Keci pana “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna’ntiādinā pavattasaṃsayāpatti sammohābhiniveso”ti vadanti. Saṅkhāresu leṇatāṇabhāvaggahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasamuditā”ti (dī. ni. 2.64; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; mahāva. 7, 8) vacanato ālayo vuccati taṇhā, sāyeva cakkhādīsu, rūpādīsu ca abhinivesavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti keci. “Evaṃvidhā saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantī’ti pavattañāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ, nibbānaṃ, tattha ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavattiyā vivaṭṭānupassanā, gotrabhu. Saṃyogābhinivesanti saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu abhinivisanaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe, pahānekaṭṭhe ca. Oḷāriketi uparimaggavajjhe kilese apekkhitvā vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanapahātabbā ca dutiyamaggavajjhehipi oḷārikāti tesampi tabbacanīyatā siyā. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte. Tabbhāvavuttiko hi ettha sahagatasaddo. Idaṃ pana heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe apekkhitvā vuttaṃ[M 1.0310]. Sabbakileseti avasiṭṭhasabbakilese. Na hi paṭhamādimaggehi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyanti. Sabbasaddo cettha sappadesavisayo “sabbe tasanti daṇḍassā”tiādīsu viya (dha. pa. 129).

Clinging is the view of self. The investigation of all phenomena by means of impermanence and so on is the insight into phenomena as higher wisdom. The clinging of grasping at an essence is the perversion of grasping at an essence in what is non-essential. The clinging that the world arose by means of a creator and so on is called the clinging of delusion. Some, however, say that the clinging of delusion is the falling into doubt that arises from thinking, 'Did I exist in the past?' and so on. The grasping of formations as a refuge and shelter is the clinging of attachment. From the statement, 'They delight in attachment, are engrossed in attachment,' craving is called attachment. Some say that this very craving, due to its occurrence by way of clinging to the eye, etc., and to forms, etc., is the clinging of attachment. The knowledge that arises from the thought, 'Such formations are to be relinquished,' is the contemplation of reviewing. Because it is free from the round of rebirth, Nibbāna is the unrolling. Because of its occurrence through contemplation which is designated as making that Nibbāna its object, the change-of-lineage consciousness is the contemplation of the unrolling. The clinging of bondage is the clinging to formations by way of fettering. 'Having a single basis' means having a single basis in co-nascence with view, and in abandonment. 'Coarse' is said with reference to the defilements to be eliminated by the higher paths; otherwise, those defilements to be abandoned by vision are coarser than those to be eliminated by the second path, and thus that term would be applicable to them as well. 'Associated with the subtle' means subtle. For here the word 'associated' (sahagata) expresses that very state. This, however, is said with reference to the defilements to be eliminated by the lower paths. 'All defilements' means all remaining defilements. For defilements abandoned by the first path and so on are not abandoned again. And here the word 'all' has a limited scope, as in, 'All tremble at punishment'.

Kakkhaḷattaṃ [V 1.0273] kaṭhinabhāvo. Paggharaṇaṃ dravabhāvo. Lokiyavāyunā bhastassa viya yena taṃtaṃkalāpassa uddhumāyanaṃ, thambhabhāvo vā, taṃ vitthambhanaṃ. Vijjamānepi kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi phuṭṭhabhāve taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ yo paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhova, aññathā bhūtānaṃ paricchedabhāvo na siyā byāpitabhāvāpattito. Yasmiṃ kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, tehi tattha asamphuṭṭhabhāvo asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ, tenāha bhagavā ākāsadhātuniddese “asamphuṭṭho catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti (dha. sa. 637).

Harshness is the state of being hard. Flowing is the state of being liquid. That wind by which there is the swelling of this or that material group—like a bellows filled with worldly wind—or rigidity, is distension. Even though there exists contact of the primary elements of one material group with those of another, the boundary of matter which is the separateness of the various primary elements is space. Therefore, whatever delimitation of which elements there is, that delimitation is untouched by them; otherwise, there would be no delimitation of the primary elements, due to their becoming pervasive. In whatever material group there is a delimitation of the primary elements, the state of being untouched by them there is the characteristic of being untouched. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the exposition of the space element: 'untouched by the four great elements'.

Virodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti ruppanaṃ. Cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ cetanāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa”nti. Tathā hi suttantabhājaniye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā (vibha. 12) cetanāva vibhattā. Abhisaṅkhāralakkhaṇā ca cetanā. Yathāha “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro, kusalā cetanā”tiādi (vibha. 226) sampayuttadhammānaṃ ārammaṇe ṭhapanaṃ abhiniropanaṃ. Ārammaṇānamanubandhanaṃ anumajjanaṃ. Savipphārikatā pharaṇaṃ. Adhimuccanaṃ saddahanaṃ adhimokkho. Assaddhiyeti assaddhiyahetu. Nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Esa nayo kosajjādīsupi. Kāyacittapariḷāhūpasamo vūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ. Līnuddhaccarahite adhicitte vattamāne paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatāya ajjhupekkhanaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ pakkhapātupacchedato.

When there is a conjunction of opposing conditions, dissimilar arising is affliction. Because of the prominence of volition among the phenomena of the formations aggregate, this was said by way of volition: 'The characteristic of formations is forming.' For indeed, in the Suttanta analysis, in the analysis of the formations aggregate, only volition is analyzed by the Blessed One with the phrase, 'volition born of eye-contact,' and so on. And volition has the characteristic of forming, as it is said: 'Therein, what is the meritorious formation? Wholesome volition,' etc. The placing of associated phenomena on an object is directing. The pursuing of objects is stroking. Pervasiveness is suffusing. Resolving, believing, is conviction. 'Assaddhiye' means 'on account of faithlessness.' And this is a locative case in the sense of cause. This same method should be understood for laziness and other states as well. The calming of bodily and mental distress is the characteristic of tranquility. When the higher mind, free from sloth and restlessness, is present, looking on with equanimity through non-involvement in encouragement, restraint, and gladdening is reviewing, because it cuts off partiality.

Musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato pariggāhakasabhāvā sammāvācā siniddhabhāvato sampayuttadhamme, sammāvācāpaccayasubhāsitaṃ sotārañca puggalaṃ pariggaṇhātīti sā pariggahalakkhaṇā. Kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hotīti sammākammantasaṅkhātā virati samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇāti daṭṭhabbā, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0311] kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā jīvitindriyavuttiyā, ājīvasseva vā suddhi vodānaṃ.

Right speech has the characteristic of embracing. This is because it is the opposite of things like false speech, which have the function of deceiving and so on, are coarse, and are non-embracing; and because of its smooth nature, right speech, which has an embracing nature, embraces associated states, the person whose speech is well-spoken conditioned by right speech, and the listener. Bodily action originates something to be done, and is itself an origination, an effort. Thus, the abstinence called right action should be understood as having the characteristic of origination. Alternatively, origination is the uplifting of associated states, like the lifting of a burden by bodily action. The purification of a living being, or of associated states, by the functioning of the life faculty, or the purification of livelihood itself, is cleansing.

“Saṅkhārā”ti idha cetanā adhippetā, na pana “saṅkhārā saṅkhārakkhandho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 583, 985; vibha. 1, 20, 52) viya samapaññāsacetasikāti vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇa”nti. Avijjāpaccayā hi puññābhisaṅkhārādikāva cetanā. Ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvo namanaṃ. Āyatanaṃ pavattanaṃ. Saḷāyatanavasena hi cittacetasikānaṃ pavatti. Taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇati ettha vaṭṭassa janakahetubhāvo taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇaṃ, maggassa pana [V 1.0274] vakkhamānassa nibbānasampāpakattanti ayametesaṃ viseso. Ārammaṇassa gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Puna uppattiyā āyūhanalakkhaṇaṃ. Sattajīvato suññatālakkhaṇaṃ. Padahanaṃ ussāhanaṃ. Ijjhanaṃ sampatti. Vaṭṭato nissaraṇaṃ niyyānaṃ. Aviparītabhāvo tathalakkhaṇaṃ. Aññamaññānativattanaṃ ekaraso, anūnādhikabhāvova. Yuganaddhā nāma samathavipassanā aññamaññopakāratāya yugaḷavasena bandhitabbato. “Saddhāpaññā paggahāvikkhepā”tipi vadanti. Cittavisuddhi nāma samādhi. Diṭṭhivisuddhi nāma paññā. Khayoti kilesakkhayo maggo, tasmiṃ pavattassa sammādiṭṭhisaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa samucchedanalakkhaṇaṃ. Kilesānamanuppādapariyosānatāya anuppādo, phalaṃ. Kilesavūpasamo passaddhi. Chandassāti kattukāmatāchandassa. Patiṭṭhābhāvo mūlalakkhaṇaṃ. Ārammaṇapaṭipādakatāya sampayutta-dhammānamuppattihetutā samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇaṃ. Visayādisannipātena gahetabbākāro samodhānaṃ. Yā “saṅgatī”ti vuccati “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādīsu. Samaṃ, sammā vā odahanti sampiṇḍitā bhavanti sampayuttadhammā anenātipi samodhānaṃ, phasso, tabbhāvo samodhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Samosaranti sannipatanti etthāti samosaraṇaṃ, vedanā. Tāya hi vinā appavattamānā sampayuttadhammā vedanānubhavananimittaṃ samosaṭā viya hontīti evaṃ vuttaṃ, tabbhāvo samosaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Pāsādādīsu gopānasīnaṃ kūṭaṃ viya sampayuttadhammānaṃ pāmokkhabhāvo pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ. Satiyā sabbatthakattā sampayuttānaṃ adhipatibhāvo ādhipateyyalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato sampayuttadhammato, tesaṃ vā sampayuttadhammānaṃ uttari padhānaṃ tatuttari, tabbhāvo tatuttariyalakkhaṇaṃ. Paññuttarā hi kusalā dhammā. Vimuttīti phalaṃ kilesehi vimuccitthāti katvā. Taṃ [M 1.0312] pana sīlādiguṇasārassa paramukkaṃsabhāvena sāraṃ. Tato uttari dhammassābhāvato pariyosānaṃ. Ayañca lakkhaṇavibhāgo chadhātupañcajhānaṅgādivasena taṃtaṃsuttapadānusārena porāṇaṭṭhakathāyamāgatanayena vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi pubbe vuttopi koci dhammo pariyāyantarappakāsanatthaṃ puna dassito. Tato eva ca “chandamūlakā dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā phassasamodhānā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti “paññuttarā kusalā dhammā”ti, “vimuttisāramidaṃ brahmacariya”nti, “nibbānogadhañhi āvuso brahmacariyaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti [saṃ. ni. 3.512 (atthato samānaṃ)] ca suttapadānaṃ vasena chandassa mūlalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti atthaṃ dasseti “eva”ntiādinā. Taṃ pana gamanaṃ idha ñāṇagamanamevāti vuttaṃ “ñāṇagatiyā”ti. Satipi gatasaddassa avabodhanatthabhāve ñāṇagamanattheneveso siddhoti na vutto. Ā-saddassa cettha gatasaddānuvattimattameva. Tenāha “patto anuppatto”ti.

Here, by 'formations' (saṅkhārā), intention (cetanā) is intended, not, as in passages such as 'formations as the aggregate of formations,' the fifty associated mental factors. Therefore, it was said, 'The characteristic of formations is intention.' For, conditioned by ignorance, it is precisely intentions such as meritorious formations and so on that arise. The state of facing an object is bending (namana). A base (āyatana) is an occurrence (pavattana); for the occurrence of mind and mental factors is by way of the six sense bases. Here, in the phrase 'the characteristic of craving as cause,' the state of being the generative cause of the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is the cause-characteristic of craving; whereas for the path, which will be spoken of, its function of leading to Nibbāna is its cause-characteristic—this is the distinction between them. [For clinging,] the characteristic is grasping an object. [For becoming,] the characteristic is striving for renewed existence. [For the elements,] the characteristic is emptiness of a being or life-principle. Striving (padahana) is exertion (ussāhana). Accomplishment (ijjhana) is success (sampatti). Escape (nissaraṇa) from the cycle of rebirth is liberation (niyyāna). The state of being non-inverted is the characteristic of thusness (tathalakkhaṇa). Mutual non-transgression is one function (ekarasa), which is the state of being neither deficient nor excessive. Tranquility and insight are called 'yoked together' (yuganaddhā) because they are to be bound as a pair due to their mutual assistance. The teachers also say that 'faith and wisdom' and 'exertion and non-distraction' are 'yoked together.' Concentration (samādhi) is called purity of mind (cittavisuddhi). Wisdom (paññā) is called purity of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi). By 'destruction' (khaya) is meant the path, which is the destruction of defilements; the characteristic of the knowledge, designated as right view, that occurs therein is that of eradication. 'Non-arising' (anuppādo) is the fruit (phala), due to the finality of the non-arising of defilements. The pacification of defilements is tranquility (passaddhi). 'Of desire' (chandassa) means of the desire that is the wish to act. The state of being a foundation is the characteristic of a root. The state of being a cause for the arising of associated states by way of providing an object is the characteristic of origination. The mode to be grasped through the coming together of the object and so on is cohesion (samodhāna). This is what is called 'conjunction' (saṅgati) in passages such as 'the conjunction of the three is contact.' Also, because associated states are placed together or combined equally or rightly by this, contact (phassa) is also called cohesion (samodhāna); the state of being so is the characteristic of cohesion. 'They assemble or congregate here' (samosaranti... ettha); thus it is an assembly (samosaraṇa), which is feeling (vedanā). For without it, non-occurring associated states are as if assembled for the purpose of experiencing feeling; thus it is said. The state of being so is the characteristic of assembly. Like the peak of the rafters in a palace, the state of being foremost among associated states is the characteristic of prominence. Due to mindfulness's quality of being universally applicable, its state of dominance over associated states is the characteristic of sovereignty. Being chief beyond those associated states, or chief among those associated states, is 'superiority' (tatuttari); the state of being so is the characteristic of superiority. For wholesome states have wisdom as their highest element. 'Liberation' (vimutti) is the fruit (phala), because of the etymology 'one was freed (vimuccittha) from defilements.' That [fruit], however, is the 'essence' (sāra) by being the state of supreme excellence of the essence which is the virtues such as morality. Because there is no state higher than that, [Nibbāna] is the 'culmination' (pariyosāna). And it should be understood that this analysis of characteristics is stated according to the method found in the ancient commentaries, in accordance with the words of the respective suttas, by way of topics such as the six elements and the five jhāna factors. Thus, indeed, a certain teaching, even though stated before, is shown again for the purpose of clarifying another aspect. And for that very reason, based on the words of the suttas—'States are rooted in desire, originate from attention, have contact as their cohesion, and feeling as their assembly'; 'Wholesome states have wisdom as their highest element'; 'This holy life has liberation as its essence'; and 'For, friend, the holy life is plunged into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its culmination'—it was said, 'The characteristic of desire is the root,' and so on. By 'thus' (evaṃ) and so on, he shows the meaning: 'He has arrived at the true, unfailing characteristic of these various states.' But that 'going' is here only the 'going of knowledge'; therefore it was said, 'by the course of knowledge' (ñāṇagatiyā). Although the word 'gata' (gone) has the meaning of 'understanding,' since it is established here only with the meaning of 'the movement of knowledge,' that meaning of understanding is not stated. And here, the prefix 'ā-' merely follows the word 'gata.' Therefore, he said, 'reached, attained' (patto, anuppatto).

Aviparītasabhāvattā “tathadhammā nāma cattāri ariyasaccānī”ti vuttaṃ. Aviparītasabhāvato [V 1.0275] tathāni. Amusāsabhāvato avitathāni. Aññākārarahitato anaññathāni. Saccasaṃyuttādīsu āgataṃ paripuṇṇasaccacatukkakathaṃ sandhāya “iti vitthāro”ti āha. “Tasmā”ti vatvā tadaparāmasitabbameva dasseti “tathānaṃ abhisambuddhattā”ti iminā. Esa nayo īdisesu.

Because of their non-inverted nature, it is said, 'The four noble truths are called true phenomena (tathadhammā).' Because of their non-inverted nature, they are 'thus' (tathāni). Because of their non-deceiving nature, they are 'unfailing' (avitathāni). Because they are devoid of any other mode, they are 'not otherwise' (anaññathāni). With reference to the complete discourse on the fourfold truths found in the Connected Discourses on the Truths and so on, the Teacher says, 'Thus in detail.' Having said 'Therefore,' he shows the very thing to be referred to by that word with the phrase 'because of having fully awakened to these realities.' This is the method in such cases.

Evaṃ saccavasena catutthakāraṇaṃ dassetvā idāni paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena aviparītasabhāvattā tathabhūtānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānaṃ vasenāpi dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayā sambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatasabhāvo, anupavattaṭṭhoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho pubbapade uttarapadalopavasena. Samāhāradvandepi hi pulliṅgamicchanti neruttikā. Na cettha jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotīti jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho. Itthameva jātito samudāgacchatīti jāti paccayasamudāgataṭṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo [M 1.0313] hoti, tadanurūpaṃ pātubhūtasabhāvoti. Paccayapakkhe pana avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭhoti ettha na avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo na hoti, na ca avijjaṃ vinā saṅkhārā uppajjanti. Yā yā avijjā yesaṃ yesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ yathā yathā paccayo hoti, ayaṃ avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho paccayasabhāvoti attho. Tathānaṃ dhammānanti paccayākāradhammānaṃ. “Sugato”tiādīsu (pārā. 1) viya gamusaddassa buddhiyatthataṃ sandhāya “abhisambuddhattā”ti vuttaṃ, na ñāṇagamanatthaṃ. Gatibuddhiyatthā hi saddā aññamaññapariyāyā. Tasmā “abhisambuddhattho hettha gatasaddo”ti adhikāro, gamyamānattā vā na payutto.

Having thus shown the fourth reason by way of truth, now, to demonstrate also by way of the factors of dependent origination—which are real because of their non-inverted nature as conditions and conditioned phenomena—the commentator says, “Moreover,” and so on. Therein, “the meaning of being arisen and come about from birth as a condition” is that, having arisen from birth as a condition, it is the nature of arising successively in accordance with its own accompanying condition; the meaning is the state of recurring. Alternatively, “the meaning of arisen” and “the meaning of come about” form “the meaning of arisen and come about” by elision of the latter part (aṭṭha) in the first member of the compound. For grammarians desire the masculine gender even in a collective dvanda compound. And here, it is not that aging-and-death does not arise from birth, nor does it arise from any other cause without birth; therefore, this is the meaning of “arisen from birth as a condition.” In this very way, it comes about repeatedly from birth; therefore, this is the meaning of “come about from birth as a condition.” This is what is said: whatever birth is a condition in whatever way, a nature corresponding to it manifests. On the side of the condition, however, regarding “the meaning of ignorance as a condition for formations,” it is not that ignorance is not a condition for formations, nor do formations arise without ignorance. Whatever ignorance is a condition for whatever formations in whatever way, this is the meaning: ignorance has the meaning of a condition for formations, its nature as a condition. “Of such phenomena” means of the phenomena of the conditional process. As in “Sugato” and so on, with reference to the meaning “understanding” of the root gam, it is said “because of having fully awakened,” not in the sense of “going by knowledge.” For words with the meaning of “going” and “understanding” are synonyms for one another. Therefore, the governing rule is, “Here the word gata has the meaning of fully awakened.” Or, because it is understood, it is not employed.

Yaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ bhagavā jānāti passatīti sambandho. Sadevake…pe… pajāyāti ādhāro “atthī”ti padeti puna aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsaūti taṃnivāsasattāpekkhāya, āpāthagamanāpekkhāya vā vuttaṃ. Tena bhagavatā vibhajjamānaṃ taṃ rūpāyatanaṃ tathameva hotīti yojetabbaṃ. Tathāvitathabhāve kāraṇamāha “evaṃ jānatā passatā”ti. Sabbākārato ñātattā passitattāti hi hetvantogadhametaṃ padadvayaṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhādivasenāti ettha ādi-saddena majjhattaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā atītānāgatapaccuppannaparittaajjhattabahiddhātadubhayādibhedampi. Labbhamānakapadavasenāti “rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ mutaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ manasā viññāta”nti (dha. sa. 966) vacanato diṭṭhapadañca viññātapadañca rūpārammaṇe labbhati. Rūpārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ majjhattaṃ parittaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ [V 1.0276] paccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā diṭṭhaṃ viññātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ rūpadhātu vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītakanti evamādīhi anekehi nāmehi. “Iṭṭhāniṭṭhādivasenā”tiādinā hi anekanāmabhāvaṃ sarūpato nidasseti. Terasahi vārehīti dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ rūpakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 615) āgate terasa niddesavāre sandhāyāha. Ekekasmiṃ vāre cettha catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vavatthāpananayānaṃ vasena “dvipaññāsāya nayehī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathamevāti yathāvuttena jānanena appaṭivattiyadesanatāya, yathāvuttena ca passanena aviparītadassitāya saccameva. Tamatthaṃ caturaṅguttare kāḷakārāmasuttena (a. ni. 4.24) sādhento “vuttañceta”ntiādimāha. Ca-saddo cettha daḷhīkaraṇajotako, tena [M 1.0314] yathāvuttassatthassa daḷhīkaraṇaṃ joteti, sampiṇḍanattho vā aṭṭhānapayutto, na kevalaṃ mayā eva, atha kho bhagavatāpīti. Anuvicaritanti paricaritaṃ. Jānāmi abbhaññāsinti paccuppannātītakālesu ñāṇappavattidassanena anāgatepi ñāṇappavatti dassitāyeva nayato dassitattā. Vidita-saddo pana anāmaṭṭhakālaviseso kālattayasādhāraṇattā “diṭṭhaṃ suttaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.187; ma. ni. 1.7; saṃ. ni. 2.208; a. ni. 4.23; paṭi. ma. 1.121) viya, pākaṭaṃ katvā ñātanti attho, iminā cetaṃ dasseti “aññe jānantiyeva, mayā pana pākaṭaṃ katvā vidita”nti. Bhagavatā hi imehi padehi sabbaññubhūmi nāma kathitā. Na upaṭṭhāsīti taṃ chadvārikamārammaṇaṃ taṇhāya vā diṭṭhiyā vā tathāgato attattaniyavasena na upaṭṭhāsi na upagacchati, iminā pana padena khīṇāsavabhūmi kathitā. Yathā rūpārammaṇādayo dhammā yaṃsabhāvā, yaṃpakārā ca, tathā te dhamme taṃsabhāve taṃpakāre gamati passati jānātīti tathāgatoti imamatthaṃ sandhāya “tathadassīatthe”ti vuttaṃ. Anekatthā hi dhātusaddā. Keci pana niruttinayena, pisodarādigaṇapakkhepena (pārā. aṭṭha. 1; visuddhi. 1.142) vā dassī-saddalopaṃ, āgata-saddassa cāgamaṃ katvā “tathāgato”ti padasiddhimettha vaṇṇenti, tadayuttameva vijjamānapadaṃ chaḍḍetvā avijjamānapadassa gahaṇato. Vuttañca buddhavaṃsaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Whatever form-object there is, the Blessed One knows it and sees it—this is the connection. 'With its devas... up to its beings' is the basis for the word 'there is'; and 'in the immeasurable world-elements' is also said with reference to the beings dwelling therein, or with reference to their coming within range. When analyzed by that Blessed One, that form-base is indeed just so—thus it should be connected. Regarding the reason for its being true and not false, he says: 'by knowing thus, by seeing thus.' For these two words are included within the cause, due to knowing and seeing in all aspects. In the phrase 'by way of what is agreeable, disagreeable, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes the neutral. Similarly, it also includes distinctions such as past, future, present, limited, internal, external, both, and so on. By way of obtainable terms: from the statement, 'The form-base is seen, the sound-base is heard, the smell-base, the taste-base, and the tangible-base are sensed, all form is cognized by the mind' (Dhs. 966), the terms 'seen' and 'cognized' are obtainable in relation to the form-object. The form-object has many such names: agreeable, disagreeable, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, cognized, form, form-base, form-element, color-and-appearance, visible, resistant, blue, yellow, and so on. By the phrase 'by way of what is agreeable, disagreeable, etc.,' he indicates, in accordance with its nature, the state of having many names. 'By thirteen modes'—this he says referring to the thirteen expositions that come in the Form Section of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (Dhs. 615). And in each of these modes, by way of the fourfold methods of determination, it is said: 'by fifty-two methods.' 'Just so' means it is truly so, because of the aforementioned knowing with its irrefutable teaching, and because of the aforementioned seeing with its undistorted vision. To establish that meaning with the Kāḷakārāma Sutta from the Fours section of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 4.24), he says, 'And this was said,' etc. Here, the particle 'ca' indicates reinforcement, thereby highlighting the strengthening of the aforementioned meaning; or it has a summative meaning, used in an unusual position, signifying: 'not only by me, but also by the Blessed One.' 'Investigated' (anuvicaritaṃ) means 'thoroughly examined' (paricaritaṃ). 'I know, I have fully known'—by showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past, the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also shown by implication. The word 'vidita' (known), however, has no specified time, being common to the three times, like 'seen, heard, sensed,' etc. (DN 3.187, etc.). The meaning is 'known by making it manifest.' And by this, he shows the following: 'Others merely know, but I have known it by making it manifest.' For by these words, the Blessed One has described what is called the ground of omniscience. 'He did not attend to it' (na upaṭṭhāsi) means that the Tathāgata did not attend to or approach that six-doored object through craving or views, by way of 'self' and 'what belongs to self.' By this phrase, the ground of one whose taints are destroyed is described. Just as phenomena such as the form-object are of a certain nature and of a certain kind, so he goes to, sees, and knows those phenomena in that very nature and in that very kind; therefore he is the Tathāgata—referring to this meaning, it was said 'in the sense of one who sees thus.' For verbal roots have many meanings. Some, however, explain the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' here by way of etymology or by inclusion in the 'pisodara' group of words, positing the elision of the word 'dassī' and the augment of the word 'āgata.' But that is inappropriate, because it is to discard an existing word and grasp a non-existing one. And it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa commentary:

“Tathākārena yo dhamme, jānāti anupassati;

Tathadassīti sambuddho, tasmā vutto tathāgato”ti. (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍavaṇṇanā);

The Fully Awakened One who knows and sees phenomena in such a manner, and is one who sees thus, is therefore called the Tathāgata.

Ettha “anupassatī”ti āgatasaddatthaṃ vatvā tadidaṃ ñāṇapassanamevāti dassetuṃ “jānātī”ti, saddādhigatamatthaṃ pana vibhāvetuṃ “tathadassī”ti ca vuttaṃ.

Here, having stated the meaning of the word 'anupassati' as it occurs, 'jānāti' is said in order to show that this seeing is precisely seeing with knowledge. Furthermore, to clarify the meaning understood through that word, 'tathadassī' is also stated.

Yaṃ [V 1.0277] rattinti yassa rattiyaṃ, accantasaṃyoge vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ rattekadesabhūtassa abhisambujjhanakkhaṇassa accantasaṃyogattā, sakalāpi vā esā ratti abhisambodhāya padahanakālattā pariyāyena accantasaṃyogabhūtāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pathavīpukkhalaniruttarabhūmisīsagatattā na parājito aññehi etthāti aparājito, sveva pallaṅkoti aparājitapallaṅko, tasmiṃ. Tiṇṇaṃmārānanti kilesābhisaṅkhāradevaputtamārānaṃ, idañca nippariyāyato vuttaṃ, pariyāyato pana heṭṭhā vuttanayena pañcannampi mārānaṃ [M 1.0315] maddanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Matthakanti sāmatthiyasaṅkhātaṃ sīsaṃ. Etthantareti ubhinnaṃ rattīnamantare. “Paṭhamabodhiyāpī”tiādinā pañcacattālīsavassaparimāṇakālameva antogadhabhedena niyametvā viseseti. Tāsu pana vīsativassaparicchinnā paṭhamabodhīti vinayagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ, tañca tadaṭṭhakathāyameva “bhagavato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsativassantare nibaddhupaṭṭhāko nāma natthī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.16) kathitattā paṭhamabodhi nāma vīsativassānīti gahetvā vuttaṃ. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana “pañcacattālīsāya vassesu ādito pannarasa vassāni paṭhamabodhī”ti vuttaṃ, evañca sati majjhe pannarasa vassāni majjhimabodhi, ante pannarasa vassāni pacchimabodhīti tiṇṇaṃ bodhīnaṃ samappamāṇatā siyā, tampi yuttaṃ. Pannarasatikena hi pañcacattālīsavassāni paripūrenti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana pannarasavassappamāṇāya paṭhamabodhiyā vīsativassesuyeva antogadhattā “paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsativassantare”ti vuttanti evampi sakkā viññātuṃ. “Yaṃ sutta”ntiādinā sambandho.

The phrase 'yaṃ rattiṃ' means 'yassa rattiyaṃ' (on which night); or, this is a usage in the accusative case in the sense of absolute connection, because of the absolute connection of the moment of awakening, which is a part of the night. Alternatively, this entire night should be understood as having an absolute connection by way of implication, because it was the time of striving for awakening. Because of having reached the beautiful, unsurpassed summit of the earth, he was not defeated by others here—thus he is called 'aparājito' (unconquered). That very seat is the 'aparājitapallaṅko' (unconquered seat); on that. 'Of the three Māras' means of the Māras of defilements, formations, and the son of a deva. And this is stated in the direct sense. In the indirect sense, however, it should be understood as the crushing of all five Māras according to the method stated below. 'Matthakaṃ' means the head, designated as capability. 'Etthantare' means in the interval between the two nights. With the text beginning 'Paṭhamabodhiyāpi,' it specifies the period of forty-five years, having determined it by way of internal division. Among those, 'the first awakening is defined by a period of twenty years'—so it is said in the Vinaya Gaṇṭhipada. And that was stated based on what is said in that very commentary: 'For the Blessed One, during the first twenty years in the first awakening, there was no regular attendant,' thus taking 'first awakening' to mean twenty years. By the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, however, it was said: 'Of the forty-five years, from the beginning, fifteen years are the first awakening.' And this being so, the middle fifteen years would be the middle awakening, and the last fifteen years the final awakening; thus there would be an equal measure for the three awakenings. That too is reasonable, for the forty-five years are completed by three sets of fifteen. In the commentary, however, since the first awakening of fifteen years' duration is included within the twenty years, it is said, 'within twenty years in the first awakening'; it can also be understood in this way. The connection should be made with the text beginning 'Yaṃ suttaṃ'.

Niddosatāya anupavajjaṃ anupavadanīyaṃ. Pakkhipitabbābhāvena anūnaṃ. Apanetabbābhāvena anadhikaṃ. Atthabyañjanādisampattiyā sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ. Nimmadanahetu nimmadanaṃ. Vālaggamattampīti vāladhilomassa koṭippamāṇampi. Avakkhalitanti virādhitaṃ musā bhaṇitaṃ. Ekamuddikāyāti ekarājalañchanena. Ekanāḷiyāti ekāḷhakena, ekatumbena vā. Ekatulāyāti ekamānena. “Tathamevā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ no aññathāti byatirekato dasseti, tena yadatthaṃ bhāsitaṃ, ekantena tadatthanipphādanato yathā bhāsitaṃ bhagavatā, tathāyevāti aviparītadesanataṃ dasseti. “Gadattho”ti etena tathaṃ gadati bhāsatīti tathāgato da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ, niruttinayena ca ākārāgamaṃ katvā, dhātusaddānugatena vā ākārenāti nibbacanaṃ dasseti.

Because of being faultless, it is blameless and not to be censured. Because of the absence of anything to be added, it is not deficient. Because of the absence of anything to be removed, it is not excessive. Due to the accomplishment in meaning, phrasing, and so on, it is complete in all aspects. Because it is a cause for subduing conceit, it is 'nimmadanaṃ' (that which subdues). 'Vālaggamattampi' means even the measure of the tip of a tail-hair. 'Avakkhalitaṃ' means failed, spoken falsely. 'Ekamuddikāya' means with a single royal seal. 'Ekanāḷiyā' means with a single āḷhaka, or with a single tumba. 'Ekatulāya' means with a single measure. With 'tathameva,' it shows by way of exclusion the very meaning stated as 'no aññathā' (not otherwise). By that, it shows the undistorted nature of the teaching thus: because it exclusively accomplishes that meaning which was spoken, it is just as it was spoken by the Blessed One. By this, 'gadattho,' it shows the derivation: 'Because he speaks (gadati) the truth (tathaṃ), he is Tathāgata'—having changed the letter 'd' to 't', and having caused the arrival of 'ā' by the etymological method, or by the 'ā' that follows the root-word.

Evaṃ “sugato”tiādīsu (pārā. 1) viya dhātusaddanipphattiparikappena niruttiṃ dassetvā bāhiratthasamāsenapi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āgadananti sabbahitanipphādanato bhusaṃ kathanaṃ vacanaṃ, tabbhāvamatto vā ā-saddo.

Thus, as in the cases of 'sugato' and so on, having shown the etymology by way of a conception of the derivation from the root-word, 'apica' and so on was stated in order to show it also by way of a compound of external meaning. 'Āgadanaṃ' means strong speaking or speech, because it accomplishes all benefit; or, the prefix 'ā' is merely indicative of that state.

Tathā [V 1.0278][M 1.0316] gatamassāti tathāgato. Yathā vācāya gataṃ pavatti, tathā kāyassa, yathā vā kāyassa gataṃ pavatti, tathā vācāya assa, tasmā tathāgatoti attho. Tadeva nibbacanaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavato”tiādimāha. Tattha hi “gato pavatto, gatā pavattā”ti ca etena kāyavacīkiriyānaṃ aññamaññānulomanavacanicchāya kāyassa, vācāya ca pavatti idha gata-saddena kathitāti dasseti, “evaṃbhūtassā”tiādinā bāhiratthasamāsaṃ, “yathā tathā”ti etena yaṃtaṃ-saddānaṃ abyabhicāritasambandhatāya “tathā”ti vutte “yathā”ti ayamattho upaṭṭhitoyeva hotīti tathāsaddatthaṃ, “vādī kārī”ti etena pavattisarūpaṃ, “bhagavato hī”ti etena yathāvādītathākāritādikāraṇanti. “Evaṃbhūtassā”ti yathāvādītathākāritādinā pakārena pavattassa, imaṃ pakāraṃ vā pattassa. Itīti vuttappakāraṃ niddisati. Yasmā panettha gata-saddo vācāya pavattimpi dasseti, tasmā kāmaṃ tathāvāditāya tathāgatoti ayampi attho siddho hoti, so pana pubbe pakārantarena dassitoti pārisesanayena tathākāritāatthameva dassetuṃ “evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttañca –

His going is thus, therefore he is Tathāgata. Just as is the proceeding of his speech, so is that of his body; or, just as is the proceeding of his body, so is that of his speech; therefore, this is the meaning of 'Tathāgata.' To show that very derivation, he said, 'bhagavato,' and so on. For there, by 'gato pavatto' (gone, proceeded) and 'gatā pavattā' (gone, proceeded), it is shown that, with the wish to speak in mutual conformity with the actions of body and speech, the proceeding of the body and of speech is here spoken of by the word 'gata.' With 'evaṃbhūtassa' and so on, it shows the compound of external meaning. With 'yathā tathā,' it shows the meaning of the word 'tathā': because of the invariable connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ,' when 'tathā' is said, this meaning 'yathā' is already present. With 'vādī kārī' (speaker, doer), it shows the nature of the proceeding. With 'bhagavato hi,' it shows the reason, which is 'acting thus as one speaks thus,' and so on. 'Evaṃbhūtassa' means of one who proceeds in the manner of acting thus as one speaks thus, and so on, or of one who has attained this manner. 'Iti' indicates the manner that has been stated. Because the word 'gata' here also indicates the proceeding of speech, this meaning is also certainly established: 'Tathāgata' because of speaking thus. But since that meaning was previously shown in a different manner, in order to show only the meaning of 'acting thus' by the method of elimination, it was said, 'Thus, because of acting thus, he is a Tathāgata.' And it is said:

“Yathā vācā gatā yassa,

Tathā kāyo gato yato;

Yathā kāyo tathā vācā,

Tato satthā tathāgato”ti.

As his speech has gone, so has his body gone; as is his body, so is his speech. For that reason, the Teacher is the Tathāgata.

Bhavaggaṃ pariyantaṃ katvāti sambandho. Yaṃ paneke vadanti “tiriyaṃ viya upari, adho ca santi aparimāṇā lokadhātuyo”ti, tesaṃ taṃ paṭisedhetuṃ evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vimuttiyāti phalena. Vimuttiñāṇadassanenāti paccavekkhaṇāñāṇasaṅkhātena dassanena. Tuloti sadiso. Pamāṇanti minanakāraṇaṃ. Pare abhibhavati guṇena ajjhottharati adhiko bhavatīti abhibhū. Parehi na abhibhūto ajjhotthaṭoti anabhibhūto. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Dassanavasena daso, sabbaṃ passatīti attho. Pare attano vasaṃ vattetīti vasavattī.

The connection should be made thus: 'having made the summit of existence the limit.' As for what some say, 'As if sideways, and above, and below, there are immeasurable world-systems,' it should be understood that this was stated to refute them. 'By liberation' means by the fruit. 'By the knowledge and vision of liberation' means by the vision designated as reviewing knowledge. Because He overcomes others by virtue, overwhelms them, and becomes superior, He is the Overcomer (Abhibhū). Because He is not overcome or overwhelmed by others, He is the Unovercome (Anabhibhū). Aññadatthu is a particle in the sense of certainty. By way of seeing, He is Dasa; the meaning is 'He sees all.' Because He makes others subject to His will, He is the Wielder of Power (Vasavattī).

“Abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato”ti ayaṃ na saddato labbhati, saddato pana evanti dassetuṃ “tatreva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha agadoti dibbāgado agaṃ rogaṃ dāti avakhaṇḍati, natthi vā gado rogo etenāti katvā[M 1.0317], tassadisaṭṭhena idha desanāvilāsassa, puññussayassa ca agadatā labbhatīti āha “agado viyā”ti. Yāya dhammadhātuyā desanāvijambhanappattā, sā desanāvilāso. Dhammadhātaūti ca sabbaññutaññāṇameva. Tena hi dhammānamākārabhedaṃ ñatvā tadanurūpaṃ [V 1.0279] desanaṃ niyāmeti. Desanāvilāsoyeva desanāvilāsamayo yathā “dānamayaṃ sīlamaya”nti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60; netti. 34) adhunā pana potthakesu bahūsupi maya-saddo na dissati. Puññussayoti ussanaṃ, atirekaṃ vā ñāṇādisambhārabhūtaṃ puññaṃ. “Tenā”tiādi opammasampādanaṃ. Tenāti ca tadubhayena desanāvilāsena ceva puññussayena ca so bhagavā abhibhavatīti sambandho. “Itī”tiādinā bāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. Sabbalokābhibhavanena tatho, na aññathāti vuttaṃ hoti.

This etymological meaning, 'Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming,' is not obtained from the word itself; however, to show that it is obtained from the word thus, 'therein,' etc., was stated. Therein, agado (remedy) means a divine remedy. It is called agada because 'it cuts off (dāti) illness (agaṃ),' or because 'by means of it, there is no (natthi) illness (gado).' By similarity to that, the state of being a remedy is here obtained for the grace of the teaching and for the abundance of merit; thus he said, 'like a remedy.' That Dhamma-element by which the teaching attains splendor is the grace of the teaching. And 'Dhamma-element' is precisely the knowledge of omniscience. For by that, having known the various modes of phenomena, He directs the teaching accordingly. The grace of the teaching itself is 'made of the grace of the teaching,' just as in 'made of giving, made of virtue.' However, nowadays, in many books, the word '-maya' is not seen. Puññussayo (abundance of merit) means abundant or excellent merit which is the foundation for knowledge and so on. 'By that,' etc., is for the completion of the simile. And 'by that' means the connection is that the Blessed One overcomes by means of both of these: by the grace of the teaching and by the abundance of merit. By 'thus,' etc., he shows an external compound meaning. It means that He is 'thus' (tatho) by overcoming all the world, and not otherwise.

Tathāya gatoti purimasaccattayaṃ sandhāyāha, tathaṃ gatoti pana pacchimasaccaṃ. Catusaccānukkamena cettha gata-saddassa atthacatukkaṃ vuttaṃ. Vācakasaddasannidhāne upasagganipātānaṃ tadatthajotanabhāvena pavattanato gata-saddoyeva anupasaggo avagatatthaṃ, atītatthañca vadatīti dasseti “avagato atīto”ti iminā.

He said 'gone in accordance with truth' (tathāya gato) with reference to the first three truths; however, he said 'gone to the truth' (tathaṃ gato) with reference to the final truth. And here, the fourfold meaning of the word 'gata' has been stated in the sequence of the four truths. Because prefixes and particles, in the presence of a meaningful word, function by illuminating its meaning, the commentator shows by means of 'understood, past' that the word 'gata' itself, without a prefix, expresses the meaning of 'understood' and 'past'.

“Tatthā”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ. Lokanti dukkhasaccabhūtaṃ lokaṃ. Tathāya tīraṇapariññāyāti yojetabbaṃ. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadanti ariyamaggaṃ, na pana abhisambujjhanamattaṃ. Tattha kattabbakiccampi katamevāti dassetuṃ “lokasmā tathāgato visaṃyutto”tiādinā saccacatukkepi dutiyapakkhaṃ vuttaṃ, abhisambujjhanahetuṃ vā etehi dasseti. Tatoyeva hi tāni abhisambuddhoti. “Yaṃ bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa samārakassa sabrahmakassa sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, sabbaṃ taṃ tathāgatena abhisambuddhaṃ, tasmā tathāgatoti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23) aṅguttarāgame catukkanipāte āgataṃ pāḷimimaṃ peyyālamukhena dasseti, tañca atthasambandhatāya eva, na imassatthassa sādhakatāya. Sā hi peyyālaniddiṭṭhā pāḷi tathadassitā atthassa sādhikāti. “Tassapi evaṃ attho veditabbo”ti iminā sādhyasādhakasaṃsandanaṃ karoti. “Idampi cā”tiādinā tathāgatapadassa mahāvisayataṃ[M 1.0318], aṭṭhavidhassāpi yathāvuttakāraṇassa nidassanamattañca dasseti. Tattha idanti atibyāsarūpena vuttaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāraṇaṃ, pi-saddo, api-saddo vā sambhāvane “itthampi mukhamattameva, pageva aññathā”ti. Tathāgatabhāvadīpaneti tathāgatanāmadīpane. Guṇena hi bhagavā tathāgato nāma, nāmena ca bhagavati tathāgata-saddoti. “Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino”tiādi (udā. aṭṭha. 306; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.277) hi vuttaṃ. Appamādapadaṃ viya sakalakusaladhammapaṭipattiyā sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ tathāgatapadaṃ saṅgāhakanti dassetuṃ “sabbākārenā”tiādimāha[V 1.0280]. Vaṇṇeyyāti parikappavacanametaṃ “vaṇṇeyya vā, na vā vaṇṇeyyā”ti. Vuttañca –

'Therein,' etc., is its explanation. 'The world' means the world which has become the truth of suffering. It should be connected thus: 'in accordance with truth' by the full understanding of judgment. 'The path leading to the cessation of the world' means the noble path, and not merely awakening. To show that therein the task to be done has indeed been done, the second aspect regarding the four truths has been stated by 'the Tathāgata is detached from the world,' etc.; or by these words he shows the cause of awakening. For it is precisely for that reason that He has fully awakened to them. 'Whatever, monks, in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans—whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and traversed by the mind—all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.' This Pāḷi text, which appears in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Book of Fours, is shown by way of an abbreviation. And that is shown only for the sake of the connection of meaning, not for the sake of proving this meaning. For that Pāḷi text, indicated by the abbreviation, is a proof for the meaning shown as 'thus-seeing' (tathadassitā). By this, 'its meaning should be understood thus,' he makes a correlation between what is to be proven and the proof. By 'And this too,' etc., he shows the vast scope of the term 'Tathāgata' and that the eightfold reason as stated is merely an indication. Therein, 'this' means the eightfold reason stated in a very extensive form. The particle 'pi,' or 'api,' is in the sense of esteem: 'Even this is merely an introduction; what to speak of otherwise?' 'In the elucidation of the state of a Tathāgata' means in the elucidation of the name 'Tathāgata.' For the Blessed One is named Tathāgata by virtue of His qualities, and the word 'Tathāgata' applies to the Blessed One by name. For it has been said: 'Countless are the names of the great sage, corresponding to his qualities.' To show that just as the term 'heedfulness' is a summary of the practice of all wholesome states, so the term 'Tathāgata' is a summary of all the Buddha's qualities, the teacher said 'in every way,' etc. The word 'vaṇṇeyya' (one might praise) is a word of supposition: 'one might praise, or one might not praise.' And it has been said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; udā. aṭṭha. 52; apa. aṭṭha. 2.7.20; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. koṇḍaññabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā; cariyā. pakiṇṇakakathā); –

Even if a Buddha, speaking of nothing else, were to speak the praise of a Buddha for an entire eon, in that long interval the eon would be exhausted, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Samatthane vā etaṃ “so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.23) viyātipi vadanti keci.

Alternatively, some say that this word is in the sense of capacity, as in such passages as, 'He might untangle this tangle.'

Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva sammāsambodhi, etthantare mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiyā hānaṭṭhānasaṃkilesanivattīnaṃ abhāvato yathāpaṇidhānaṃ tathāgato abhinīhārānurūpaṃ paṭipannoti tathāgato. Atha vā mahiddhikatāya, paṭisambhidānaṃ ukkaṃsādhigamena anāvaraṇañāṇatāya ca katthacipi paṭighātābhāvato yathāruci, tathā kāyavacīcittānaṃ gatāni gamanāni pavattiyo etassāti tathāgato. Apica yasmā loke vidhayuttagatapakārasaddā samānatthā dissanti, tasmā yathā vidhā vipassiādayo bhagavanto nikhilasabbaññuguṇasamaṅgitāya, ayampi bhagavā tathā vidhoti tathāgato, yathā yuttā ca te bhagavanto vuttanayena, ayampi bhagavā tathā yuttoti tathāgato. Aparo nayo-yasmā saccaṃ tacchaṃ tathanti ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā tathena ñāṇena āgatoti tathāgatoti.

Now, herein is a method independent of the commentaries: From the aspiration onwards up to perfect self-awakening, within this interval, through the practice for the vehicle of great awakening, due to the absence of decline, stagnation, defilement, and turning back, as was the aspiration, so (`tathā`) he has gone (`gato`), having practiced in accordance with that aspiration; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Or alternatively, due to his great psychic power, the supreme attainment of the analytical knowledges, his unobstructed knowledge, and the absence of resistance in regard to any object whatsoever, for this Blessed One, just as his inclination is, so (`tathā`) are the goings (`gatāni`) of his body, speech, and mind; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, because in the world the words `vidha`, `yutta`, `gata`, and `pakāra` are seen to have similar meanings, therefore, just as the Blessed Ones, such as Vipassī, were of such a kind (`tathāvidhā`) due to being endowed with all the qualities of an omniscient one, this Blessed One is also of such a kind (`tathāvidho`); therefore, he is the Tathāgata. And just as those Blessed Ones were thus endowed (`tathāyuttā`) in the aforementioned manner, this Blessed One is also thus endowed (`tathāyutto`); therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Another method: because 'true' (`saccaṃ`), 'real' (`tacchaṃ`), and 'thus' (`tathaṃ`) are designations for knowledge, therefore, he has come (`āgato`) with that true (`tathena`) knowledge; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.

“Pahāya [M 1.0319] kāmādimale yathā gatā,

Samādhiñāṇehi vipassiādayo;

Mahesino sakyamunī jutindharo,

Tathā gato tena tathāgato mato.

Just as the great seers, such as Vipassī, having abandoned the stains of defilements such as sensual craving by means of concentration and knowledge, have gone; so too, this Sakyamuni, the bearer of the light of wisdom, has gone. Therefore, he is known as the Tathāgata.

Tathañca dhātāyatanādilakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabhāvasāmaññavibhāgabhedato;

Sayambhuñāṇena [V 1.0281] jino samāgato,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo.

And because the Victor, with self-originated knowledge, has well come to the true characteristic of the elements, sense bases, and so on, by way of the distinction in the analysis of their specific and general characteristics; therefore, the Bull of the Sakyans is called the Tathāgata.

Tathāni saccāni samantacakkhunā,

Tathā idappaccayatā ca sabbaso;

Anaññaneyyena yato vibhāvitā,

Yāthāvato tena jino tathāgato.

Because the true Noble Truths and the true principle of specific conditionality have, in all ways, been made manifest by him with the all-seeing eye of wisdom, not to be led by another; therefore, the Victor is the Tathāgata, in accordance with reality.

Anekabhedāsupi lokadhātūsu,

Jinassa rūpāyatanādigocare;

Vicittabhede tathameva dassanaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantalocano.

Even in the world-systems of many kinds, the Victor's seeing in the sphere of the form-base and so on, which are of variegated kinds, is indeed true. Therefore, the one with the all-seeing eye is the Tathāgata.

Yato ca dhammaṃ tathameva bhāsati,

Karoti vācāyanulomamattano;

Guṇehi lokaṃ abhibhuyyirīyati,

Tathāgato tenapi lokanāyako.

And because he speaks the Dhamma that is indeed true, and acts in conformity with his speech; having overcome the world with his virtues, he comports himself. For that reason also, the leader of the world is the Tathāgata.

Yathābhinīhāramato yathāruci,

Pavattavācātanucittabhāvato;

Yathāvidhā yena purā mahesino,

Tathāvidho tena jino tathāgato.

Furthermore, due to the state of having speech, body, and mind that have proceeded in accordance with his aspiration and in accordance with his inclination; and because, just as the great seers of the past were of a certain kind, this Victor is also of such a kind; therefore, the Victor is the Tathāgata.

Yathā ca yuttā sugatā purātanā,

Tathāva yutto tathañāṇato ca so;

Samāgato tena samantalocano,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 38 thokaṃ visadisaṃ); –

Furthermore, just as the Sugatas of old were endowed, so too is he endowed; therefore, the one with the all-seeing eye is called the Tathāgata. Alternatively, by means of true knowledge, he has well come; therefore, the Bull of the Sakyans is called the Tathāgata.

Saṅgahagāthā.

Summary Verses.

“Katamañca [V 1.0282][M 1.0320] taṃ bhikkhave”ti ayaṃ kassa pucchāti āha “yenā”tiādi. Evaṃ sāmaññato yathāvuttassa sīlamattakassa pucchābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni pucchāvisesabhāvañāpanatthaṃ mahāniddese (mahāni. 150) āgatā sabbāva pucchā atthuddhāravasena dasseti “tattha pucchā nāmā”tiādinā. Tattha tatthāti “taṃ katamanti pucchatī”ti ettha yadetaṃ sāmaññato pucchāvacanaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ.

Regarding 'And what is that, O bhikkhus?', whose question is this? He said, 'by which,' and so on. Thus, having shown in a general way the nature of the question regarding mere virtue as stated above, now, in order to make known the nature of the specific question, the teacher shows all the questions that come in the Mahāniddesa by way of extracting their meaning, with the words 'Therein, a question is named...' and so on. Therein, the word 'therein' refers to this: in the phrase 'He asks, "What is that?"', in that general expression of a question which was stated.

Pakatiyāti attano dhammatāya, sayamevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇanti yo koci ñātumicchito sabhāvo. Aññātanti dassanādivisesayuttena, itarena vā yena kenacipi ñāṇena aññātaṃ. Avatthāvisesāni hi ñāṇadassanatulanatīraṇāni. Adiṭṭhanti dassanabhūtena ñāṇena paccakkhamiva adiṭṭhaṃ. Atulitanti “ettakameta”nti tulanabhūtena atulitaṃ. Atīritanti “evamevida”nti tīraṇabhūtena akatañāṇakiriyāsamāpanaṃ. Avibhūtanti ñāṇassa apākaṭabhūtaṃ. Avibhāvitanti ñāṇena apākaṭakataṃ. Tassāti yathāvuttalakkhaṇassa. Adiṭṭhaṃ jotīyati pakāsīyati etāyāti adiṭṭhajotanā. Saṃsandanatthāyāti sākacchāvasena vinicchayakaraṇatthāya. Saṃsandanañhi sākacchāvasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ. Diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandīyati etāyāti diṭṭhasaṃsandanā. “Saṃsayapakkhando”tiādīsu daḷhataraṃniviṭṭhā vicikicchā saṃsayo. Nātisaṃsappanamatibhedamattaṃ vimati. Tatopi appataraṃ “evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā dvidhā viya pavattaṃ dveḷhakaṃ. Dvidhā elati kampati cittametenāti hi dveḷhakaṃ hapaccayaṃ, sakatthavuttikapaccayañca katvā, tena jāto, taṃ vā jātaṃ yassāti dveḷhakajāto. Vimati chijjati etāyāti vimaticchedanā. Anattalakkhaṇasuttādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.59) āgataṃ khandhapañcakapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ pucchaṃ sandhāyāha “sabbaṃ vattabba”nti. Anumatiyā pucchā anumatipucchā. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave”tiādipucchāya hi “kā tumhākaṃ anumatī”ti anumati pucchitā hoti. Kathetukamyatāti kathetukāmatāya. “Aññāṇatā āpajjatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 295) viya hi ettha ya-kāralopo, karaṇatthe vā paccattavacanaṃ, kathetukamyatāya vā pucchā kathetukamyatāpucchātipi vaṭṭati. Atthato pana sabbāpi tathā pavattavacanaṃ, taduppādako vā cittuppādoti veditabbaṃ.

`Pakatiyā` means: by its own nature; that is to say, spontaneously. `Lakkhaṇaṃ` means: any specific nature that one wishes to know. `Aññātaṃ` means: not known by a knowledge endowed with a distinction such as seeing, or by any other kind of knowledge whatsoever. For knowing, seeing, weighing, and judging are distinctions of state. `Adiṭṭhaṃ` means: not seen as if directly perceived by the knowledge that is seeing. `Atulitaṃ` means: not weighed by the knowledge that is weighing, as in 'it is this much.' `Atīritaṃ` means: the non-completion of the act of knowing by the knowledge that is judging, as in 'it is just so.' `Avibhūtaṃ` means: not become manifest to knowledge. `Avibhāvitaṃ` means: not made manifest by knowledge. `Tassa` means: of the characteristic as described. Because the unseen is illuminated, made clear by this question, it is `adiṭṭhajotanā` (illumination of the unseen). `Saṃsandanatthāya` means: for the purpose of making a decision by way of discussion. For collation is making a decision by way of discussion. Because the seen is collated by this question, it is `diṭṭhasaṃsandanā` (collation of the seen). In phrases such as 'plunging into doubt,' `saṃsayo` is doubt that is more firmly settled. `Vimati` is a mere division of opinion that is not very pervasive. Even less than that, that which proceeds in a twofold way, as in 'Is it so? Or is it not so?', is `dveḷhakaṃ`. For the mind wavers and trembles in two ways because of this; hence, it is `dveḷhakaṃ`, formed with the suffix `-ha` and a suffix expressing its own meaning. One who is born from that, or one for whom that is born, is `dveḷhakajāto`. Because indecision is cut off by this question, it is `vimaticchedanā` (cutting off of indecision). Referring to the question connected with the five aggregates that comes in the Anattalakkhaṇasutta and so on, he says, 'all should be said.' A question by way of consent is an `anumatipucchā`. For by the question 'What do you think of this, O bhikkhus?' and so on, consent is asked for, as in 'What is your consent?'. `Kathetukamyatā` means: by the desire to speak. For here, as in phrases like `aññāṇatā āpajjatī`, the elision of the letter `ya` should be seen. Or, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Or, a question due to the desire to speak is a `kathetukamyatāpucchā`; this is also valid. In terms of meaning, however, every question should be understood as an utterance that proceeds in such a way, or as the thought-moment that produces it.

Yadatthaṃ [M 1.0321] panāyaṃ niddesanayo āharito, tassa pucchāvisesabhāvassa ñāpanatthaṃ “imāsū”tiādimāha. Cittābhogo samannāhāro. Bhusaṃ, samantato ca saṃsappanā kaṅkhā āsappanā, parisappanā ca. Sabbā kaṅkhā chinnā sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānena aggamaggena samucchindanato. Paresaṃ anumatiyā, kathetukamyatāya ca dhammadesanāsambhavato, tathā eva tattha tattha [V 1.0283] diṭṭhattā ca vuttaṃ “avasesā pana dve pucchā buddhānaṃ atthī”ti. Yā panetā “sattādhiṭṭhānā pucchā dhammādhiṭṭhānā pucchā ekādhiṭṭhānā pucchā anekādhiṭṭhānā pucchā”tiādinā aparāpi anekadhā pucchāyo niddese āgatā, tā sabbāpi niddhāretvā idha avicayanaṃ “alaṃ ettāvatāva, atthikehi pana iminā nayena niddhāretvā vicetabbā”ti nayadānassa sijjhanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, as for the purpose for which this method of the Niddesa was brought forth, the commentator said, “in these,” etc., in order to make known the nature of that special question. Attention of the mind is application (samannāhāra). Doubt (kaṅkhā), which is a wavering (saṃsappanā), is also called āsappanā and parisappanā, meaning wavering intensely and from all around. All doubts are cut off by the supreme path, which has omniscience as its proximate cause, because of having completely severed them. It was said, “Furthermore, there are two remaining questions for the Buddhas,” because the teaching of the Dhamma arises from the consent of others and the desire to speak, and because it is seen thus in various places. As for those other various questions that have come in the Niddesa, such as “the question with beings as its foundation,” “the question with phenomena as its foundation,” “the question with a single foundation,” “the question with multiple foundations,” and so on—all of them, having been determined, are not investigated here. This should be understood as due to the successful presentation of the method, implying: “This much is sufficient; however, those who are interested should determine and investigate them by this method.”

8. Pucchā ca nāmesā vissajjanāya satiyeva yuttarūpāti codanāya “idānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atipātanaṃ atipāto. Ati-saddo cettha atirekattho. Sīghabhāvo eva ca atirekatā, tasmā saraseneva patanasabhāvassa antarā eva atirekaṃ pātanaṃ, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātananti attho, abhibhavanattho vā, atikkamma satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātananti vuttaṃ hoti, vohāravacanametaṃ “atipāto”ti. Atthato pana pakaraṇādivasenādhigatattā pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Vohāratoti paññattito. Sattoti khandhasantāno. Tattha hi sattapaññatti. Vuttañca –

8. Because of the possibility of the challenge that “this so-called question is appropriate only when there is an answer,” “now,” etc., was stated. Excessive felling (atipātana) is atipāta. Here, the word ati has the meaning of “excess.” And swiftness is indeed the excess; therefore, the meaning is an excessive felling in the very midst of its natural tendency to fall, not allowing it to fall slowly but causing it to fall swiftly. Or, it has the meaning of “overpowering”; it is meant that it is a felling by transgressing and overpowering with weapons and so on. This word “atipāta” is a conventional expression. In terms of ultimate meaning, however, because it is understood by way of the context and so on, it is meant to be the killing of a living being (pāṇavadha) or the slaughter of a living being (pāṇaghāta)—this is the intention. “By convention” means by designation. “A being” means the continuum of the aggregates. For therein lies the designation “a being.” And it is said:

“Yathā hi aṅgasambhārā, hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu, hoti sattoti sammutī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.171);

“Just as from a collection of parts, the word ‘chariot’ comes to be; so too, when the aggregates are present, there is the convention ‘a being.’”

Jīvitindriyanti rūpārūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Rūpajīvitindriye hi vikopite itarampi taṃsambandhatāya vinassati. Kasmā panettha “pāṇassa atipāto”ti, “pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto”ti ca ekavacananiddeso kato, nanu niravasesānaṃ pāṇānaṃ atipātato virati idha adhippetā. Tathā hi vakkhati “sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti sabbe pāṇabhūte”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) bahuvacananiddesanti? Saccametaṃ, pāṇabhāvasāmaññena panettha ekavacananiddeso kato, tattha pana sabbasaddasannidhānena [M 1.0322] puthuttaṃ suviññāyamānamevāti sāmaññaniddesamakatvā bhedavacanicchāvasena bahuvacananiddeso kato. Kiñca bhiyyo – sāmaññato saṃvarasamādānaṃ, tabbisesato saṃvarabhedoti imassa visesassa ñāpanatthampi ayaṃ vacanabhedo katoti veditabbo. “Pāṇassa atipāto”tiādi hi saṃvarabhedadassanaṃ. “Sabbe pāṇabhūte”tiādi pana saṃvarasamādānadassananti. Saddavidū pana “īdisesu ṭhānesu jātidabbāpekkhavasena vacanabhedamattaṃ, atthato samāna”nti vadanti.

The life faculty (jīvitindriya) means the material and immaterial life faculty. For when the material life faculty is disrupted, the other also perishes due to its connection with it. Why is the singular expression used here, “the destruction of a living being” (pāṇassa atipāto), and “here, ‘a living being’ (pāṇa) is, by convention, a being (satta)”? Is not abstinence from the destruction of all living beings without remainder intended here? For indeed, the commentator will state the plural expression in the passage beginning, “compassionate for the welfare of all living beings and creatures” (sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī). This is true. Here, the singular expression is used with reference to the generality of the state of being a living being. There, however, since the plurality is clearly understood by the proximity of the word “all” (sabba), the plural expression is used out of a desire to speak of the distinction, without making a general statement. And what is more? The undertaking of restraint (saṃvara-samādāna) is general, while the distinction of restraint (saṃvarabheda) is particular. It should be understood that this difference in number was made in order to make this distinction known. For “the destruction of a living being,” etc., shows a distinction of restraint, whereas “all living beings and creatures,” etc., shows the undertaking of restraint. Those who know grammar, however, say: “In such instances, it is merely a difference in number based on consideration of class and substance; in meaning, they are the same.”

Tasmiṃ pana pāṇeti yathāvutte dubbidhepi pāṇe. Pāṇasaññinoti pāṇasaññāsamaṅgino puggalassa[V 1.0284]. Yāya pana cetanāya pavattamānassa jīvitindriyassa nissayabhūtesu mahābhūtesu upakkamakaraṇahetu taṃmahābhūtapaccayā uppajjanakamahābhūtā nuppajjissanti, sā tādisapayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pāṇātipātoti āha “jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā”ti, jīvitindriyupacchedakassa kāyavacīpayogassa tannissayesu mahābhūtesu samuṭṭhāpikāti attho. Laddhupakkamāni hi bhūtāni purimabhūtāni viya na visadāni, tasmā samānajātiyānaṃ bhūtānaṃ kāraṇāni na hontīti tesuyeva upakkame kate tato parānaṃ asati antarāye uppajjamānānaṃ bhūtānaṃ, tannissitassa ca jīvitindriyassa upacchedo hoti. “Kāyavacīdvārāna”nti etena vitaṇḍavādimataṃ manodvāre pavattāya vadhakacetanāya pāṇātipātabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati.

Now, “regarding that living being” (tasmiṃ pana pāṇe) means regarding a living being of both kinds as described. “Of one who perceives a living being” (pāṇasaññino) means of a person endowed with the perception of a living being. Furthermore, that volition (cetanā) which gives rise to such an application—whereby, because of an effort being made in the great elements that are the support for the ongoing life faculty, the great elements that would be produced conditioned by those great elements will not arise—is pāṇātipāta. Thus, he says, “that which originates the effort that cuts off the life faculty.” The meaning is: that which originates, in the great elements that are its support, the bodily or verbal application that cuts off the life faculty. For elements that have been subjected to an effort are not pure like the previous elements; therefore, they do not become causes for elements of the same kind. Thus, when an effort is made upon those very elements, there is a cutting off of the subsequent elements that would be arising if there were no obstacle, and of the life faculty dependent on them. By “through the doors of body and speech,” he rejects the view of the Vitaṇḍavādins that a killing volition occurring at the mind-door constitutes pāṇātipāta.

Payogavatthumahantatādīhi mahāsāvajjatā tehi paccayehi uppajjamānāya cetanāya balavabhāvato veditabbā.
