Ekassāpi hi payogassa sahasā nipphādanavasena, kiccasādhikāya bahukkhattuṃ pavattajavanehi laddhāsevanāya ca sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya vasena payogassa mahantabhāvo. Satipi kadāci khuddake ceva mahante ca pāṇe payogassa samabhāve mahantaṃ hanantassa cetanā tibbatarā uppajjatīti vatthussa mahantabhāvo. Iti ubhayampetaṃ cetanāya balavabhāveneva hoti. Satipi ca payogavatthūnaṃ amahantabhāve hantabbassa guṇamahattenapi tattha pavattaupakāracetanā viya khettavisesanipphattiyā apakāracetanāpi balavatī, tibbatarā ca uppajjatīti tassā mahāsāvajjatā daṭṭhabbā[M 1.0323]. Tenāha “guṇavantesū”tiādi. “Kilesāna”ntiādinā pana satipi payogavatthuguṇānaṃ amahantabhāve kilesupakkamānaṃ mudutibbatāya cetanāya dubbalabalavabhāvavasena appasāvajjamahāsāvajjabhāvo veditabboti dasseti.

Great blameworthiness should be understood as due to the strength of the volition arising from such conditions as the greatness of the application and the object. For the greatness of the application is due to the sudden accomplishment of even a single application, and due to the concluding volition which accomplishes the task and has gained habitual practice from impulsions that have occurred many times. The greatness of the object is that, even though the application may sometimes be the same towards a small being and a great being, the volition of one who kills a great being arises more intensely. Thus, both of these occur only through the strength of the volition. And even when the application and the object are not great, due to the great virtue of the one to be killed, the volition to do harm also arises strong and more intense—like a volition to do benefit that occurs with regard to the production of a special field of merit—and thus its great blameworthiness should be seen. Therefore, he said, “In those endowed with virtue,” etc. Furthermore, by the phrase beginning “of the defilements,” he shows that even when the application, object, and virtues are not great, the state of being of little blame or great blame should be understood according to the weakness or strength of the volition, which is due to the mildness or intensity of the defilements' assault.

Sambharīyanti saharīyanti etehīti sambhārā, aṅgāni. Tesu pāṇasaññitā, vadhakacittañca pubbabhāgiyānipi honti. Upakkamo pana vadhakacetanāsamuṭṭhāpito sahajātova. Pañcasambhāravatī pana pāṇātipātacetanāti sā pañcasambhāravinimuttā daṭṭhabbā. Esa nayo adinnādānādīsupi.

Because they are brought together and assembled by these factors, they are called 'sambhārā' (requisites); they are the factors. Among them, the perception of a living being and the thought of killing are also preliminary. However, the effort, instigated by the volition to kill, is indeed co-nascent. Further, the volition of taking life possesses five requisites; therefore, that volition should be understood as distinct from the five requisites. This same method should be understood in the case of taking what is not given, and so on.

Etthāha – khaṇe khaṇe nirujjhanasabhāvesu saṅkhāresu ko hanti, ko vā haññati, yadi cittacetasikasantāno, evaṃ so anupatāpanachedanabhedanādivasena na vikopanasamattho, nāpi vikopanīyo, atha rūpasantāno, evampi so acetanatāya kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamoti na tattha chedanādinā pāṇātipāto labbhati yathā matasarīre. Payogopi pāṇātipātassa paharaṇappakārādiatītesu [V 1.0285] vā saṅkhāresu bhaveyya, anāgatesu vā paccuppannesu vā. Tattha na tāva atītānāgatesu sambhavati tesaṃ abhāvato. Paccuppannesu ca saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikattā saraseneva nirujjhanasabhāvatāya vināsābhimukhesu nippayojano eva payogo siyā. Vināsassa ca kāraṇarahitattā na paharaṇappakārādipayogahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, nirīhakatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ kassa so payogo, khaṇikattā vadhādhippāyasamakālabhijjanakassa kiriyāpariyosānakālānavaṭṭhānato kassa vā pāṇātipātakammabaddhoti?

Herein, a certain questioner says: Among formations that have the nature of ceasing moment by moment, what kills, and what is killed? If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, this being so, that continuum is not capable of being destroyed by way of afflicting, cutting, breaking, and so on, nor can it be destroyed. If, then, it is the continuum of material form, even so, that continuum, due to being insentient, is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth; therefore, the taking of life is not obtained therein by cutting and so on, just as it is not obtained in a dead body. Moreover, the effort of taking life, such as the manner of striking, could occur in past formations, or in future ones, or in present ones. Therein, firstly, it is not possible in past and future formations because of their non-existence. And in present formations, because of the momentariness of formations, since they have the nature of ceasing by their own intrinsic nature and are facing destruction, the effort would indeed be useless. And since destruction is without a cause, death is not caused by the effort of the manner of striking and so on. And due to the inactivity of formations, whose is that effort? And because of the momentariness of that which breaks up at the same time as the intention to kill, and because it does not last until the time of the completion of the action, to whom is the kamma of taking life bound?

Vuccate – vadhakacetanāsahito saṅkhārānaṃ puñjo sattasaṅkhāto hanti, tena pavattitavadhappayoganimittāpagatusmāviññāṇajīvitindriyo matavohārappavattinibandhano yathāvuttavadhappayogākaraṇe uppajjanāraho rūpārūpadhammasamūho haññati, kevalo vā cittacetasikasantāno, vadhappayogāvisayabhāvepi tassa pañcavokārabhave rūpasantānādhīnavuttitāya rūpasantāne parena payojitajīvitindriyupacchedakapayogavasena tannibbattivibandhakavisadisarūpuppattiyā vihate vicchedo hotīti na pāṇātipātassa asambhavo, nāpi ahetuko pāṇātipāto, na ca payogo nippayojano paccuppannesu saṅkhāresu katapayogavasena tadanantaraṃ uppajjanārahassa saṅkhārakalāpassa tathāanuppattito, khaṇikānaṃ [M 1.0324] saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikamaraṇassa idha maraṇabhāvena anadhippetattā santatimaraṇassa ca yathāvuttanayena sahetukabhāvato na ahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, na ca katturahito pāṇātipātappayogo nirīhakesupi saṅkhāresu sannihitatāmattena upakārakesu attano attano anurūpaphaluppādananiyatesu kāraṇesu kattuvohārasiddhito yathā “padīpo pakāseti, nisākaro candimā”ti, na ca kevalassa vadhādhippāyasahabhuno cittacetasikakalāpassa pāṇātipāto icchito santānavasena avaṭṭhitasseva paṭijānanato, santānavasena pavattamānānañca padīpādīnaṃ attakiriyāsiddhi dissatīti attheva pāṇātipātena kammabaddhoti. Ayañca vicāro adinnādānādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ vibhāvetabbo.

The reply is spoken: The heap of formations accompanied by the volition to kill, designated as a 'being', kills. By that being, what is killed is the collection of material and immaterial phenomena which is fit to arise when the aforesaid effort of killing is not performed, and which, on account of the effort of killing set in motion, has its heat, consciousness, and life faculty departed, and is the basis for the arising of the convention 'dead'. Or, the mere continuum of mind and mental factors is killed. Even when it is not an object for the effort of killing, in the five-constituent existence, due to its existence being dependent on the material continuum, when the material continuum is destroyed—by means of an effort applied by another that cuts off the life faculty through the arising of dissimilar matter that obstructs its production—a cutting off of the mind-continuum occurs. Thus, the impossibility of taking life does not exist, nor is taking life without a cause, and the effort is not purposeless. This is because, by means of the effort made in regard to present formations, the aggregate of formations fit to arise immediately after that does not arise in such a way; and because the momentary death of momentary formations is not intended here as 'death', and because the death of the continuum has a cause in the way stated, death is not without a cause. And the effort of taking life is not without an agent, because the convention of an 'agent' is established for causes which, though inactive formations, are helpful by their mere presence and are fixed in producing their own respective appropriate results, just as 'the lamp illuminates,' and 'the moon, the night-maker, illuminates.' And the taking of life is not intended for the mere aggregate of mind and mental factors that is co-nascent with the intention to kill, because it is acknowledged only as established by way of a continuum. And the accomplishment of its function is seen for lamps and so on that proceed by way of a continuum. Therefore, there is indeed a binding by kamma through the taking of life. And this investigation should be explained in the case of taking what is not given, and so on, as may be appropriate.

Sāhatthikoti sayaṃ mārentassa kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā paharaṇaṃ. Āṇattikoti aññaṃ āṇāpentassa “evaṃ vijjhitvā vā paharitvā vā mārehī”ti āṇāpanaṃ. Nissaggiyoti dūre ṭhitaṃ māretukāmassa kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā usuyantapāsāṇādīnaṃ nissajjanaṃ. Thāvaroti asañcārimena upakaraṇena māretukāmassa opātāpassenaupanikkhipanaṃ, bhesajjasaṃvidhānañca. Vijjāmayoti māraṇatthaṃ mantaparijappanaṃ āthabbaṇikādīnaṃ viya. Āthabbaṇikā hi āthabbaṇaṃ payojenti nagare vā ruddhe saṅgāme vā paccupaṭṭhite paṭisenāya paccatthikesu paccāmittesu ītiṃ uppādenti upaddavaṃ uppādenti rogaṃ uppādenti pajjarakaṃ uppādenti [V 1.0286] sūcikaṃ uppādenti visūcikaṃ karonti pakkhandiyaṃ karonti. Vijjādharā ca vijjaṃ parivattetvā nagare vā ruddhe…pe… pakkhandiyaṃ karonti. Iddhimayoti kammavipākajiddhimayo dāṭhākoṭanādīni viya. Piturañño kira sīhaḷanarindassa dāṭhākoṭanena cūḷasumanakuṭumbiyassa maraṇaṃ hoti. “Imasmiṃ panatthe”tiādinā ganthagāravaṃ pariharitvā tassa anūnabhāvampi karoti “atthikehī”tiādinā. Idha avuttopi hi esa attho atidisanena vutto viya anūno paripuṇṇoti.

'Sāhatthika' (by one's own hand) is the striking by one who is killing by oneself, either with the body or with something connected to the body. 'Āṇattika' (by command) is the commanding of one who is ordering another, saying, 'Kill by piercing or by striking thus.' 'Nissaggiya' (by projection) is the releasing of arrows, machines, stones, and so on, by one who desires to kill someone standing at a distance, either with the body or with something connected to the body. 'Thāvara' (by a permanent fixture) is, for one who desires to kill with an immovable instrument, the setting of a pitfall or a trap, and the preparing of poison. 'Vijjāmaya' (by means of spells) is the muttering of mantras for the purpose of killing, like that of the practitioners of the Atharva Veda and so on. For the practitioners of the Atharva Veda employ the Atharva spells when a city is besieged or a battle is imminent; they produce calamity, disaster, disease, fever, and sharp pain for the opposing army, the adversaries, the enemies; they cause cholera and dysentery. And the bearers of knowledge, having recited their spell when a city is besieged... and so on... cause dysentery. 'Iddhimaya' (by means of psychic power) is psychic power born of kamma-result, like the striking of the tooth-relic and so on. It is said that by the striking of the tooth-relic of the Father King, the ruler of the Sinhalese, the death of the householder Cūḷasumana occurred. By the phrase beginning 'But in this meaning...', having set aside the gravity of the text, he also makes it complete by the phrase beginning 'by those who desire it...'. For even though this meaning is not stated here, it is, as it were, stated by extension, and is thus not deficient, but complete.

Dussīlassa bhāvo dussīlyaṃ, yathāvuttā cetanā. “Pahāyā”ti ettha tvā-saddo pubbakāleti āha “pahīnakālato paṭṭhāyā”ti, hetuatthataṃ vā sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi pahānahetukā idhādhippetā samucchedanikā viratīti dasseti. Kammakkhayañāṇena hi pāṇātipātadussīlyassa [M 1.0325] pahīnattā bhagavā accantameva tato paṭiviratoti vuccati samucchedavasena pahānaviratīnamadhippetattā. Kiñcāpi “pahāya paṭivirato”ti padehi vuttānaṃ pahānaviramaṇānaṃ purimapacchimakālatā natthi, maggadhammānaṃ pana sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ, paccayabhūtānaṃ sammāvācādīnañca paccayuppannabhūtānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannabhāve apekkhite sahajātānampi paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena gahaṇaṃ purimapacchimabhāvena viya hoti. Paccayo hi purimataraṃ paccayasattiyā ṭhito, tato paraṃ paccayuppannaṃ paccayasattiṃ paṭicca pavattati, tasmā gahaṇappavattiākāravasena sahajātādipaccayabhūtesu sammādiṭṭhiādīsu pahāyakadhammesu pahānakiriyāya purimakālavohāro, tappaccayuppannāsu ca viratīsu viramaṇakiriyāya aparakālavohāro sambhavati. Tasmā “sammādiṭṭhiādīhi pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya sammāvācādīhi pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”ti pāḷiyaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo.

The state of an immoral person is immorality; this is the volition as stated. Here, in the word ‘pahāya’ (having abandoned), the particle ‘tvā’ indicates a prior time; thus, the Teacher said, ‘from the time of having abandoned.’ Or, it was stated thus with reference to its causal meaning. By this, it is shown that the abstention intended here is the one that eradicates, which is caused by abandonment. Indeed, because the immorality of taking life has been abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of kamma, the Blessed One is said to be completely abstaining from it, for abandonment and abstention are intended by way of eradication. Although there is no earlier or later time for the abandoning and abstaining stated in the words ‘having abandoned, he abstains,’ nevertheless, when the relationship of condition and conditioned is considered with regard to the path factors—such as right view, etc., which are conditions, and right speech, etc., which are conditioned—the apprehension even of co-arisen factors as condition and conditioned becomes as if it were an earlier-later relationship. For a condition stands earlier by its conditioning power, and thereafter the conditioned proceeds dependent on the power of the condition. Therefore, by way of the mode of apprehension and occurrence, a conventional designation of an earlier time is possible for the act of abandoning in the abandoning factors like right view, etc., which are co-arisen condition-factors; and a conventional designation of a later time is possible for the act of abstaining in the abstentions that are conditioned by them. Thus, in the Pāli, the meaning should be understood as: ‘Having abandoned the taking of life by means of right view, etc., he abstains from the taking of life by means of right speech, etc.’

Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – pahānaṃ samucchedavasena viratipaṭippassaddhivasena yojetabbā, tasmā maggena pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya phalena pāṇātipātā paṭiviratoti attho. Apica pāṇo atipātīyati etenāti pāṇātipāto, pāṇaghātahetubhūto dhammasamūho. Ko paneso? Ahirikānottappadosamohavihiṃsādayo kilesā. Te hi bhagavā ariyamaggena pahāya samugghāṭetvā pāṇātipātadussīlyato accantameva paṭivirato kilesesu pahīnesu tannimittakammassa anuppajjanato, tasmā maggena pāṇātipātaṃ yathāvuttakilesaṃ pahāya teneva pāṇātipātā dussīlyacetanā paṭiviratoti attho. Esa nayo “adinnādānaṃ pahāyā”tiādīsupi.

Here, however, is a method independent of the commentary: abandonment should be connected with eradication, and abstention with tranquilization. Therefore, the meaning is: having abandoned the taking of life by the path, he abstains from the taking of life by the fruit. Furthermore, a living being is struck down by this, thus it is called ‘pāṇātipāta’; it is the group of states that is the cause for killing a living being. What is this group? It is the defilements such as shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, aversion, delusion, cruelty, and so on. Indeed, the Blessed One, having abandoned and eradicated these by the noble path, is completely abstaining from the immorality of taking life. This is because when the defilements are abandoned, the kamma caused by them does not arise. Therefore, the meaning is: having abandoned the aforementioned defilements—which are called ‘pāṇātipāta’—by the path, by that very path he abstains from the immoral volition of taking life. This method should be understood also in the cases of ‘having abandoned taking what is not given,’ and so on.

Orato [V 1.0287] viratoti pariyāyavacanametaṃ, pati-visaddānaṃ vā paccekaṃ yojetabbato tathā vuttaṃ. Oratoti hi avarato abhimukhaṃ rato, tena ujukaṃ viramaṇavasena sātisayataṃ dasseti. Paṭiratassa cetaṃ atthavacanaṃ. Viratoti visesena rato, tena saha vāsanāya viramaṇabhāvaṃ, ubhayena pana samucchedaviratibhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Eva-saddo pana tassā viratiyā kālādivasena apariyantataṃ dassetuṃ vutto. So ubhayattha yojetabbo. Yathā hi aññe samādinnaviratikāpi anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lābhajīvitādihetu samādānaṃ bhinnanti, na evaṃ bhagavā, sabbaso [M 1.0326] pahīnapāṇātipātattā panesa accantavirato evāti. “Natthi tassā”tiādinā eva-saddena dassitaṃ yathāvuttamatthaṃ nivattetabbatthavasena samattheti. Tattha vītikkamissāmīti uppajjanakā dhammāti saha pāṭhasesena sambandho. Te pana anavajjadhammehi vokiṇṇā antarantarā uppajjanakā dubbalā sāvajjā dhammā, yasmā ca “kāyavacīpayogaṃ upalabhitvā imassa kilesā uppannā”ti viññunā sakkā ñātuṃ, tasmā te imināva pariyāyena “cakkhusotaviññeyyā”ti vuttā, na pana cakkhusotaviññāṇārammaṇattā. Ato sasambhārakathāya cakkhusotehi, tannissitaviññāṇehi vā kāyikavācasikapayogamupalabhitvā manoviññāṇena viññeyyāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Kāyikāti kāyena katā pāṇātipātādinipphādakā balavanto akusalā. “Kāḷakā” tipi ṭīkāyaṃ uddhatapāṭho, kaṇhapakkhikā balavanto akusalāti attho. “Imināvā”tiādinā nayadānaṃ karoti, tañca kho “adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato”tiādipadesu.

The words ‘orato’ and ‘virato’ are synonyms. Or, it is stated thus because the prefixes ‘pati-’ and ‘vi-’ are to be applied individually. For ‘orato’ means ‘turned away from’ (avarato) and ‘delighting towards’ (abhimukhaṃ rato); by this, it shows excellence by way of straightforward abstention. And this word explains the meaning of ‘paṭivirato.’ ‘Virato’ means ‘especially delighting’ (visesena rato); by this, it shows the state of abstention together with the latent tendencies. By both, however, it clarifies the state of abstention by eradication. The word ‘eva’ (indeed) is used to show that this abstention is unlimited in terms of time, etc. It should be applied to both words. For just as others, even when they have undertaken abstention, break their undertaking due to an unsteady mind for the sake of gain, life, etc., the Blessed One does not do so. Because he has entirely abandoned the taking of life, he is indeed completely abstinent. By the phrase ‘Natthi tassa’ (‘There is not for him’), etc., he establishes the aforementioned meaning shown by the word ‘eva’ by way of negating what is to be negated. There, the connection is with the remainder of the text: ‘states that arise with the thought, “I will transgress.”’ These, however, are weak, faulty states, interspersed with blameless states, that arise intermittently. And because a wise person can know, ‘Having perceived bodily and verbal application, defilements have arisen in this person,’ they are therefore called ‘knowable by eye and ear’ by this very method, and not because they are objects of eye- and ear-consciousness. Therefore, in the discussion with constituents, the meaning should be understood as: states knowable by mind-consciousness after perceiving bodily or verbal application by means of the eye and ear, or by the consciousnesses dependent on them. ‘Bodily’ (kāyikā) refers to strong unwholesome states created by the body that bring about the taking of life, etc. ‘Kāḷakā’ (dark ones) is also a reading cited in the subcommentary, meaning strong unwholesome states belonging to the dark side. By the phrase ‘imināva’ (‘by this very’), etc., he gives a method, and he does so in passages such as ‘having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given.’

Pāpe sametīti samaṇo, gotamasamaññā, tena gottenasambandho gotamoti atthaṃ sandhāya “samaṇoti bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gottavasena laddhavohāroti sambandho. Brahmadattena bhāsitavaṇṇānusandhiyā imissā desanāya pavattanato, tena ca bhikkhusaṅghavaṇṇassāpi bhāsitattā bhikkhusaṅghavaṇṇopi vuttanayena desitabbo, so na desito. Kiṃ so pāṇātipātā paṭiviratabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghassa na vijjatīti anuyogamapanento “na kevalañcā”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sati kasmā na desitoti punānuyogaṃ pariharati “desanā panā”tiādinā. Evanti evameva.

He pacifies evil deeds, thus he is a ‘samaṇa.’ This is a designation of Gotama. Therefore, with reference to the meaning that ‘Gotama’ is one connected with that clan, it is said, ‘The samaṇa, the Blessed One,’ etc. The connection is that it is a conventional designation obtained by way of lineage. Because this discourse proceeds in connection with the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, and because the praise of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was also spoken by him, the praise of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus should also be taught in the manner stated; but it was not taught. Dispelling the question, ‘What, does the state of abstaining from the taking of life not exist for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?’ the Teacher says, ‘Not only…,’ etc. He refutes the further question, ‘This being so, why was it not taught?’ with the words, ‘But the teaching…,’ etc. ‘Evaṃ’ means ‘just so.’

Etthāyamadhippāyo –“atthi bhikkhave, aññe ca dhammā”tiādinā anaññasādhāraṇe buddhaguṇe ārabbha upari desanaṃ vaḍḍhetukāmo bhagavā ādito paṭṭhāya “tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyyā”tiādinā buddhaguṇavaseneva desanaṃ ārabhi, na bhikkhusaṅghaguṇavasenāpi. Esā hi bhagavato desanāya pakati, yadidaṃ ekaraseneva desanaṃ dassetuṃ labbhamānassāpi kassaci [V 1.0288] aggahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi rūpakaṇḍe dukādīsu, tanniddesesu ca hadayavatthu na gahitaṃ. Itaravatthūhi asamānagatikattā desanābhedo hotīti. Yathā hi cakkhuviññāṇādīni [M 1.0327] ekantato cakkhādinissayāni, na evaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ ekantena hadayavatthunissayaṃ āruppe tadabhāvato, nissayanissitavasena ca vatthudukādidesanā pavattā “atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthu, atthi rūpaṃ na cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā. Yampi manoviññāṇaṃ ekantato hadayavatthunissayaṃ, tassa vasena “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā dukādīsu vuccamānesupi na tadanurūpā ārammaṇadukādayo sambhavanti. Na hi “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ, atthi rūpaṃ na manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇa”nti sakkā vattuṃ tadanārammaṇarūpassābhāvatoti vatthārammaṇadukā bhinnagatikā siyuṃ, tasmā na ekarasā desanā bhaveyyāti na vuttaṃ, tathā nikkhepakaṇḍe cittuppādavibhāgena visuṃ avuccamānattā avitakkaavicārapadavissajjane “vicāro cā”ti vattuṃ na sakkāti āvitakkavicāramattapadavissajane labbhamānopi vitakko na uddhato. Aññathā hi “vitakko cā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, evamevidhāpi bhikkhusaṅghaguṇo na desitoti. Kāmaṃ saddato evaṃ na desito, atthato pana brahmadattena bhāsitavaṇṇassa anusandhidassanavasena imissā desanāya āraddhattā dīpetuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “atthaṃ panā”tiādi.

Herein is the commentator's intention: The Blessed One, wishing to expand the discourse further by focusing on the unique qualities of the Buddha, as stated in 'Monks, there are other phenomena...' and so forth, began the discourse from the outset by way of the Buddha's qualities alone, as stated in 'One speaking in praise of the Tathāgata might say...' and so forth, and not by way of the qualities of the Sangha of bhikkhus. For this is the nature of the Blessed One's discourse: the non-inclusion of a certain thing even when it is possible to present the teaching with a single essence. Thus, in the section on form, in the dyads and so forth, and in their expositions, the heart-base is not taken up. Because it has a course dissimilar to the other bases, there would be a division in the discourse. For just as eye-consciousness and so forth are exclusively dependent on the eye-base and so forth, mind-consciousness is not exclusively dependent on the heart-base, due to its absence in the formless realm. And the teaching on the base-dyads and so on proceeds by way of the support and the supported, as in 'There is form that is a base for eye-consciousness; there is form that is not a base for eye-consciousness,' and so forth. And for that mind-consciousness which is exclusively dependent on the heart-base, even when the dyads and so forth are stated by way of it, as in 'There is form that is a base for mind-consciousness,' and so forth, the corresponding object-dyads and so forth do not arise. For it cannot be said, 'There is form that is an object for mind-consciousness; there is form that is not an object for mind-consciousness,' since there is no form that is not its object. Thus, the base-dyads and object-dyads would have different courses, and therefore the discourse would not have a single essence; hence, the heart-base was not mentioned. Similarly, in the section on classification, because it is not stated separately in the analysis of the arising of consciousness, in the explanation of the term 'without directed thought and without evaluation,' it is not possible to say 'and evaluation.' Thus, in the explanation of the term 'without directed thought, with evaluation only,' directed thought is not extracted, although it is obtainable. For otherwise, it would have to be said 'and directed thought.' In the same way, here also, the quality of the Sangha of bhikkhus was not taught. Although it was not taught thus in words, it is fitting to explain it in terms of meaning, because this discourse was begun by way of showing the connection to the praise spoken by Brahmadatta. Therefore, the commentator said, 'But as for the meaning...' and so forth.

Tatthāyaṃ dīpanā – “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakasaṅgho nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho”ti vitthāretabbaṃ. Nanu dhammassāpi vaṇṇo brahmadattena bhāsitoti? Saccaṃ bhāsito, so pana sammāsambuddhapabhavattā, ariyasaṅghādhārattā ca dhammassa dhammānubhāvasiddhattā ca tesaṃ, tadubhayavaṇṇadīpaneneva dīpitoti visuṃ na uddhato. Saddhammānubhāveneva hi bhagavā, bhikkhusaṅgho ca pāṇātipātādippahānasamattho hoti. Atthāpattivasena paraviheṭhanassa parivajjitabhāvadīpanatthaṃ daṇḍasatthānaṃ nikkhepavacanti āha “parūpaghātatthāyā”tiādi. Avattanatoti apavattanato, asañcaraṇato vā. Nikkhitto daṇḍo yenāti nikkhittadaṇḍo. Tathā nikkhittasattho. Majjhimassa purisassa catuhatthappamāṇo cettha daṇḍo. Tadavaseso muggarakhaggādayo satthaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “ettha cā”tiādi. Viheṭhanabhāvatoti vihiṃ sanabhāvato, etena sasati hiṃsati anenāti satthanti atthaṃ dasseti. “Parūpaghātatthāyā”tiādinā āpannamatthaṃ [M 1.0328] vivarituṃ “yaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kataro jiṇṇo, tassa, tenavā ālambito daṇḍo kattaradaṇḍo. Dantasodhanaṃ kātuṃ yoggaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ, na pana dantasodhanakaṭṭhaṃ. “Dantakaṭṭhavāsiṃ vā”tipi pāṭho, dantakaṭṭhacchedanakavāsinti attho. Khuddakaṃ nakhacchedanādikiccanipphādakaṃ [V 1.0289] satthaṃ pipphalikaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhikkhusaṅghādhīnavacanaṃ. “Bhikkhusaṅghavasenapi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttatā tassāpi ekadesena dīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here is the explanation: 'Having abandoned the taking of life, abstaining from the taking of life, the Sangha of disciples of the recluse Gotama has laid down the rod and laid down the weapon'—this should be elaborated. Was not the praise of the Dhamma also spoken by Brahmadatta? Indeed, it was spoken. But since the Dhamma originates from the Perfectly Enlightened One and is the support for the Noble Sangha, and since they (the Buddha and Sangha) are accomplished through the power of the Dhamma, that praise of the Dhamma is illuminated by explaining the praise of both of them, and thus it is not extracted separately. For it is only through the power of the true Dhamma that the Blessed One and the Sangha of bhikkhus become capable of abandoning the taking of life and so forth. To show, by way of implication, the avoidance of harming others, the statement about laying down rods and weapons is made. Therefore, the teacher said, 'For the purpose of harming others,' and so forth. 'Not being current' (avattanato) means not recurring (apavattanato) or not circulating (asañcaraṇato). 'One by whom the rod is laid down' is nikkhittadaṇḍo. Similarly, 'one by whom the weapon is laid down' is nikkhittasattho. Here, a daṇḍa (rod) is one of four cubits in length for a man of average height. The rest, such as clubs, swords, and so on, are sattha (weapons). Therefore, it was said, 'And here...' and so forth. 'Because of its nature to harm' (viheṭhanabhāvato) means because of its nature to injure (vihiṃsanabhāvato). By this, he shows the meaning: 'that by which one injures or harms is a sattha (weapon).' To explain the meaning implied by 'For the purpose of harming others,' and so forth, the passage beginning 'But whatever...' was stated. An old person (jiṇṇa); the staff (daṇḍa) held by him is a kattaradaṇḍa (an old person's staff). A piece of wood suitable for cleaning the teeth is a dantakaṭṭha (tooth-stick), but a splintered piece of wood for cleaning teeth is not a dantakaṭṭha. There is also the reading dantakaṭṭhavāsiṃ vā, which means 'an adze for cutting tooth-sticks.' A small weapon that accomplishes tasks such as cutting nails is a pipphalika. This statement, however, pertains to the Sangha of bhikkhus. Since it was said, 'It is fitting to explain it also by way of the Sangha of bhikkhus,' it was stated to explain a part of that statement as well.

Lajjā-saddo hiriatthoti āha “pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāyā”ti. Dhammagarutāya hi buddhānaṃ, dhammassa ca attādhīnattā attādhipatibhūtā lajjāva vuttā, na lokādhipatibhūtaṃ ottappaṃ. Apica “lajjī”ti ettha vuttalajjāya ottappampi vuttameva, tasmā lajjāti hiriottappānamadhivacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi pāpajigucchanaṃ pāputtāsanarahitaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ nāma atthīti. “Dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpanno”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu dayā-saddo “dayāpanno”tiādīsu karuṇāyapi vattatīti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana dayāsaddo anurakkhaṇatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya, karuṇāya ca pavattatīti idha mettāya pavattamāno vutto karuṇāya, vakkhamānattā. Midati sinehatīti mettā, sā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, mettaṃ cittaṃ etassāti mettacitto, mettāya sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ etassāti vā, tassa bhāvo mettacittatā mettā eva mūlabhūtena tannimittena puggalasmiṃ buddhiyā, saddassa ca pavattanato.

The word lajjā has the meaning of hiri (shame); thus, he said, 'It has the characteristic of disgust for evil.' Indeed, for the Buddhas, due to their reverence for the Dhamma and because the Dhamma is self-dependent, it is lajjā (shame), which has the self as its dominant influence, that is spoken of, not ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), which has the world as its dominant influence. Moreover, in the word lajjī (one who has shame), ottappa is also included by the lajjā that is mentioned. Therefore, lajjā should be understood as a term for both hiri and ottappa. For there is no disgust for evil that is devoid of dread of evil, nor is there a fear of evil that could be called shamelessness. Why is it said, 'He has attained compassion (dayā), that is, the state of having a mind of loving-kindness (mettacittatā)'? Is it not the case that the word dayā also occurs in the sense of karuṇā (compassion) in phrases like dayāpanno (compassionate)? This is true. However, this word dayā, when it proceeds having incorporated the meaning of 'protecting,' occurs in the sense of both mettā (loving-kindness) and karuṇā (compassion). Here, it is said to occur in the sense of mettā because karuṇā will be spoken of later. Mettā is so called because one loves (midati) or is affectionate (sinehati). A mind (citta) that has this (mettā) is metta. A person who has this metta mind is mettacitto; or, a person whose mind is associated with mettā. The state of that person is mettacittatā. This is because both the cognition (buddhi) and the term (sadda) arise in a person from mettā itself as the fundamental cause.

“Pāṇabhūteti pāṇajāte”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sati pāṇo bhūto yesanti pāṇabhūtāti nibbacanaṃ kattabbaṃ. Atha vā jīvitindriyasamaṅgitāya pāṇasaṅkhāte taṃtaṃkammānurūpaṃ pavattanato bhūtanāmake satteti attho. Anukampakoti karuṇāyanako. Yasmā pana mettā karuṇāya visesapaccayo hoti, tasmā purimapadatthabhūtā mettā eva paccayabhāvena “tāya eva dayāpannatāyā”ti vuttā. Iminā hi padena karuṇāya gahitāya yehi dhammehi pāṇātipātā paṭivirati sampajjati, tehi lajjāmettākaruṇāhi samaṅgibhāvo yathākkamaṃ padattayena dassito. Paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāpi hi hitānukampanamevāti avassaṃ ayamattho sampaṭicchitabboti. Imāya pāḷiyā, saṃvaṇṇanāya ca tassā viratiyā sattavasena apariyantataṃ dasseti.

It is said, 'A living being (pāṇabhūta)' means 'one born with life (pāṇajāte).' This being so, the etymological explanation should be made that 'living beings' (pāṇabhūtā) are 'those for whom life has come into being' (pāṇo bhūto yesaṃ). Or alternatively, the meaning is that because a being, designated as possessing life (pāṇa) through being endowed with the life faculty, proceeds in accordance with its respective kamma, it is named a 'being' (bhūta). 'Compassionate (anukampako)' refers to one inclined toward compassion. Furthermore, since loving-kindness is a special condition for compassion, loving-kindness, which is the meaning of the preceding term, is itself referred to as 'by that very compassionateness' in its capacity as a condition. For by this phrase, when compassion is taken, the state of being endowed with shame, loving-kindness, and compassion—by which qualities abstention from killing living beings is accomplished—is shown sequentially by the triad of terms. For the desire to remove the suffering of others is indeed compassion for their welfare; therefore, this meaning must certainly be accepted. By this Pāḷi text and its commentary, the unlimited nature of that abstinence is shown in terms of beings.

Viharatīti [M 1.0329] ettha vi-saddo vicchindanatthe, hara-saddo nayanatthe, nayanañca nāmetaṃ idha pavattanaṃ, yāpanaṃ, pālanaṃ vāti āha “iriyati yapeti yāpeti pāletī”ti. Yapeti yāpetīti cettha pariyāyavacanaṃ. Tasmā yathāvuttappakāro hutvā ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā harati pavatteti, attabhāvaṃ vā yāpeti pāletīti attho veditabbo. Iti vā hīti ettha hi-saddo vacanasiliṭṭhatāmatte kassacipi tena jotitatthassa abhāvato. Tenāha “evaṃ vā bhikkhave”ti. Visuṃ kappanameva attho vikappatthoti so anekabhinnesuyeva atthesu [V 1.0290] labbhati, anekabhedā ca atthā uparivakkhamānā evāti vuttaṃ “upari adinnā…pe… apekkhitvā”ti. “Eva”ntiādi ganthagāravapariharaṇaṃ, nayadānaṃ vā.

In 'He dwells' (viharati), the prefix 'vi-' is in the sense of cutting off, and the root 'hara' is in the sense of carrying. And this 'carrying' here means proceeding, sustaining, or protecting; thus, it is said, 'he moves, sustains, maintains, or protects.' Herein, 'sustains' (yapeti) and 'maintains' (yāpeti) are synonyms. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: having become as described, he cuts off the suffering that has arisen in one posture with another posture and carries on or proceeds; or, he sustains or protects his personal existence. In 'Or indeed' (iti vā hi), the word 'hi' is merely for stylistic smoothness, because there is no meaning whatsoever illuminated by it. Therefore, it is said, 'or thus, monks.' The meaning of 'alternative' (vikappa) is precisely 'separate arrangement'; therefore, that word is found only in meanings that are distinct in many ways, and since the meanings with many distinctions are precisely those that will be explained later on, it was said, 'later on... not given... etc... having considered.' The words 'Thus,' and so on, are for avoiding textual heaviness, or for giving a method.

Idāni sampiṇḍanatthaṃ dassento “ayaṃ panetthā”tiādimāha. Tattha na hanatīti na hiṃsati. Na ghātetīti na vadhati. Tatthāti pāṇātipāte. Samanuññoti santuṭṭho. Aho vata reti bhonto ekaṃsato acchariyāti attho. Ācārasīlamattakanti sādhujanācāramattakaṃ, matta-saddo cettha visesanivattiattho, tena indriyasaṃvarādiguṇehipi lokiyaputhujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ na sakkotīti dasseti. Tathā hi indriyasaṃvarapaccayaparibhogasīlāni idha na vibhattāni. Eva-saddo padapūraṇamattaṃ, matta-saddena vā yathāvuttatthassāvadhāraṇaṃ karoti, eva-saddena ācārasīlameva vattuṃ sakkotīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Evamīdisesu. “Iti vā hi bhikkhave puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyyā”ti vacanasāmatthiyeneva taduttari guṇaṃ vattuṃ na sakkhissati. “Taṃ vo upari vakkhāmī”ti ca atthassāpajjanato tathāpannamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “upari asādhāraṇabhāva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Na kevalañcā”tiādinā puggalavivecanena pana “puthujjano”ti idaṃ nidassanamattanti dassitaṃ. “Ito para”ntiādinā ganthagāravaṃ pariharati. Pubbe vuttaṃ padaṃ pubbapadaṃ,na pubbapadaṃ tathā, na pubbaṃ vā apubbaṃ, tameva padaṃ tathā.

Now, to show the summarized meaning, he says, 'And here, this...' and so on. Therein, 'does not kill' means does not harm. 'Does not slay' means does not destroy. 'Therein' refers to the killing of living beings. 'Approves' means is satisfied. The meaning of 'Aho vata re' is: 'Sirs, it is absolutely marvelous!' 'Merely conduct and virtue' means merely the conduct of good people. And here the word 'merely' has the meaning of excluding specifics; by this it shows that a worldly ordinary person is not able to praise the Tathāgata even with respect to qualities such as restraint of the senses. For indeed, the virtues of sense restraint and proper use of requisites are not analyzed here. The word 'eva' is a mere expletive. Or, with the word 'matta', it serves for emphasis of the aforesaid meaning; with the word 'eva', it makes the conclusion that one is able to speak only of conduct and virtue. Thus it should be understood in similar cases. By the very power of the statement, 'Thus, indeed, monks, an ordinary person, praising the Tathāgata, might speak,' he will not be able to speak of a quality higher than that. And because the meaning, 'That I will explain to you later,' arises, in order to show the meaning that has thus arisen, it was said, 'the uncommon nature hereafter,' and so on. Furthermore, by the passage beginning 'Not only that,' through the analysis of persons, it is shown that this word 'ordinary person' is a mere illustration. By the words 'From here onward,' he avoids textual prolixity. A word spoken before is a preceding word; not a preceding word as such; or, not before is not-before; that very word is so.

Saddantarayogena dhātūnamatthavisesavācakattā “ādāna”nti etassa gahaṇanti attho daṭṭhabbo, tenāha “haraṇa”ntiādi. Parassāti attasantakato parabhūtassa santakassa, yo vā attato añño, so [M 1.0330] puggalo paro nāma, tassa idaṃ parantipi yujjati, “parasaṃharaṇa”ntipi pāṭho, saṃ-saddo cettha dhanattho,parasantakaharaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Theno vuccati coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ, corakammaṃ. Corikāti corassa kiriyā. Tadatthaṃ vivarati “tatthā”tiādinā. Tatthāti “ādinnādāna”nti pade. Parapariggahitameva ettha adinnaṃ, na pana dantapoṇasikkhāpade viya appaṭiggahitakaṃ attasantakanti adhippāyo. “Yattha paro”tiādi ubhayattha sambandho āvuttiyādinayena. Tasmā “taṃ parapariggahitaṃ nāma, tasmiṃ parapariggahite”ti ca yojetabbaṃ. Yathākāmaṃ karotīti yathākāmakārī, tassa bhāvo yathākāmakaritā, taṃ. Tathārucikaraṇaṃ āpajjantoti attho. Sasantakattā adaṇḍāraho dhanadaṇḍarājadaṇḍavasena. Anupavajjo ca codanāsāraṇādivasena. Taṃ parapariggahitaṃ ādiyati etenāti tadādāyako, sveva upakkamo, taṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā. Theyyā eva cetanā theyyacetanā. Khuddakatāappagghatādivasena hīne. Mahantatāmahagghatādivasena paṇīte. Kasmā? Vatthuhīnatāyāti gamyamānattā na vuttaṃ, hīne, hīnaguṇānaṃ santake ca cetanā dubbalā, paṇīte, paṇītaguṇānaṃ santake [V 1.0291] ca balavatīti heṭṭhā vuttanayena tehi kāraṇehi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā veditabbā. Ācariyā pana hīnapaṇītato khuddakamahante visuṃ gahetvā “idhāpi khuddake parasantake appasāvajjaṃ, mahante mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Vatthuguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānamupakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjaṃ, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjanti ayampi nayo yojetabbo”ti vadanti.

Due to the connection with another word (i.e., adinna), and because roots express specific meanings, for this term 'ādāna', the meaning should be understood as 'taking'. Therefore, he said 'haraṇa', etc. ‘Parassa’ means: of a possession that has become other than one's own possession. Or, whichever person is other than oneself, that person is called 'another' (paro). His possession is 'another's' (paraṃ); this meaning is also suitable. There is also the reading 'parasaṃharaṇa'. And here, the word 'saṃ' has the meaning of wealth; it comes to be said: 'the taking of another's possession'. A thief (coro) is called 'theno'; his state is 'theyyaṃ', the act of a thief (corakammaṃ). ‘Corikā’ is the action of a thief. He explains that meaning with 'katthā', etc. ‘Katthā’ means: in the phrase 'adinnādāna'. Here, only that which is possessed by another is 'not given' (adinnaṃ). But one's own possession that has not been formally offered, as in the training rule on tooth-cleaners, is not 'not given'; this is the intention. The connection of 'Yattha paro', etc., in both places (i.e., with adaṇḍāraho and anupavajjo) is by the method of recurrence, etc. Therefore, it should be construed thus: 'That is called "possessed by another", and "in that which is possessed by another".' One who acts as he wishes (yathākāmaṃ karoti) is a yathākāmakārī; his state is yathākāmakaritā; that state. The meaning is: engaging in action according to his liking. Because it is his own possession, he is not liable to punishment by way of monetary penalty or royal penalty. And he is blameless by way of accusation, reminding of the fault, etc. That which is possessed by another is taken by this (endeavor), thus it is a tadādāyaka (that which causes the taking). That very thing is the endeavor (upakkamo). The volition that gives rise to that (endeavor) is tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā (that which gives rise to the endeavor that causes the taking). The intention of theft itself is theyyacetanā. In the case of the inferior, by way of smallness, low value, etc. In the case of the superior, by way of largeness, high value, etc. Why? It is not stated because 'due to the inferiority of the object' is understood. In the case of an inferior possession and a possession of those with inferior qualities, the volition is weak; in the case of a superior possession and a possession of those with superior qualities, it is strong. Therefore, by the method previously stated, due to those reasons, the state of being of little blame and of great blame should be understood. The teachers, however, taking 'small' and 'large' separately from 'inferior' and 'superior', say: 'Here too, in the case of a small possession of another, there is little blame; in the case of a large one, there is great blame. Why? Due to the magnitude of the effort. But when the qualities of the object are equal, due to the mildness of the defilements and the endeavor, there is little blame; due to their intensity, there is great blame. This method should also be applied.'

Sāhatthikādayoti ettha parasantakassa sahatthā gahaṇaṃ sāhatthiko. Aññe āṇāpetvā gahaṇaṃ āṇattiko. Antosuṅkaghāte ṭhitena bahisuṅkaghātaṃ pātetvā gahaṇaṃ nissaggiyo. “Asukaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā avaharā”ti atthasādhakāvahāranipphādakena, āṇāpanena vā, yadā kadāci parasantakavināsakena sappitelakumbhiādīsu dukūlasāṭakacammakhaṇḍādipakkhipanādinā vā gahaṇaṃ thāvaro. Mantaparijappanena gahaṇaṃ vijjāmayo. Vinā mantena, kāyavacīpayogehi tādisaiddhiyogena parasantakassa ākaḍḍhanaṃ iddhimayo. Kāyavacīpayogesu [M 1.0331] hi santesuyeva iddhimayo avaharaṇapayogo hoti, no asantesu. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “anāpatti bhikkhave, iddhimassa iddhivisaye”ti (pārā. 159), te ca kho payogā yathānurūpaṃ pavattāti sambandho. Tesaṃ pana payogānaṃ sabbesaṃ sabbattha avahāresu asambhavato “yathānurūpa”nti vuttaṃ.

Here, regarding 'sāhatthika, etc.': the taking of another's possession with one's own hand is sāhatthiko (taking by one's own hand). Having commanded others, the taking is āṇattiko (taking by command). Standing inside a customs house and causing goods to fall outside the customs house, the taking is nissaggiyo (taking by disposal). The taking is thāvaro (established taking) when it is done by a command such as, 'Steal such-and-such goods whenever you are able,' which accomplishes the result of the offense and accomplishes the theft; or when it is done at some time by destroying another's possession, such as by placing a piece of fine cloth, a piece of leather, etc., into pots of ghee, oil, etc. Taking by muttering a spell is vijjāmayo (taking by knowledge). Without a spell, the drawing of another's possession by bodily and verbal effort together with such a use of psychic power is iddhimayo (taking by psychic power). For the effort of taking by psychic power occurs only when there are bodily and verbal efforts, not when they are absent. Thus indeed it was said: 'There is no offense, monks, for one with psychic power in the sphere of psychic power'. And those efforts proceed according to circumstances; this is how the connection should be made. But since all of those efforts are not possible in all cases of theft, 'according to circumstances' was said.

Sandhicchedādīni katvā adissamānena vā, kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vañcanena vā, avaharaṇaṃ theyyāvahāro. Pasayha balasā abhibhuyya santajjetvā, bhayaṃ dassetvā vā avaharaṇaṃ pasayhāvahāro. Parabhaṇḍaṃ paṭicchādetvā avaharaṇaṃ paṭicchannāvahāro. Bhaṇḍokāsaparikappavasena parikappetvā avaharaṇaṃ parikappāvahāro. Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā avaharaṇaṃ kusāvahāro. Iti-saddena cettha ādiatthena, nidassananayena vā avasesā cattāro pañcakāpi gahitāti veditabbaṃ. Pañcannañhi pañcakānaṃ samodhānabhūtā pañcavīsati avahārā sabbepi adinnādānameva, aviññattiyā vā ariyāya viññattiyā vā dinnamevāti attho. “Dinnādāyī”ti idaṃ payogato parisuddhabhāvadassanaṃ. “Dinnapāṭikaṅkhī”ti idaṃ pana āsayatoti āha “cittenā”tiādi.

Having done things like breaking through joints of walls, or by being unseen, or by deception with false measures, false coins, etc., the taking is theyyāvahāro (theft by stealth). Taking by force, having overpowered, or having intimidated, or having shown a fearsome danger is pasayhāvahāro (theft by force). Having concealed another's goods, the taking is paṭicchannāvahāro (theft by concealment). Having contrived by way of contriving a place for the goods, the taking is parikappāvahāro (theft by contrivance). Having moved a boundary marker, the taking is kusāvahāro (theft by means of a marker). And here, it should be understood that by the word 'iti', with the meaning of 'etc.', or by way of example, the remaining four pentads are also included. Indeed, the twenty-five types of taking, which are the combination of the five pentads, are all simply 'taking what is not given'. The meaning is that what is received either without an intimation or by a noble intimation is 'given'. This phrase 'dinnādāyī' (one who takes what is given) is a demonstration of purity with respect to effort. But this phrase 'dinnapāṭikaṅkhī' (one who expects what is given) is a demonstration of purity with respect to intention. Therefore, the compiler of the commentary said 'cittena', etc.

Athenenāti ettha -saddo na-saddassa kāriyo, a-saddo vā eko nipāto na-saddatthoti dassetuṃ “na thenenā”ti vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ dissamānavākyāvatthikavibhattiyantapaṭirūpakatākaraṇena saddhiṃ samāsadassanametaṃ. Pakaraṇādhigate pana atthe viveciyamāne idha athenatoyeva sucibhūtatā adhigamīyati adinnādānādhikārattāti āha “athenattāyeva sucibhūtenā”ti tena hetālaṅkāravacanametanti [V 1.0292] dasseti. Āhito ahaṃmāno etthāti attā, attabhāvo. Bhagavato pana so ruḷhiyā yathā taṃ nicchandarāgesu sattavohāro. Adati vā saṃsāradukkhanti attā, tenāha “attabhāvenā”ti. Padattayepi itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacananti ñāpetuṃ “athenaṃ…pe… katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Athenena attanā athenattā hutvā sucibhūtena attanā sucibhūtattā hutvā viharatītipi attho.

Here in 'athenena', the sound 'a' is a derivative of the sound 'na'. Or, to show that the sound 'a' is a particle with the meaning of the sound 'na', it is said 'na thenena'. This is a demonstration of a compound, together with making it resemble a word ending in a case-inflection that delimits the apparent sentence in the Pāli. But when the meaning understood from the context is analyzed, here the state of being pure is understood precisely from not being a thief, because this is the section on taking what is not given. Therefore, he said 'athenattāyeva sucibhūtena'. By this, he shows that this is a statement adorned with a reason. The conceit 'I am' is placed (āhito) in this (ettha), thus it is 'attā', individual existence (attabhāvo). For the Blessed One, however, that term for individual existence is by convention (ruḷhiyā), just as the designation 'being' (sattavohāro) is used for those free from desire and passion. Or, it eats (adati) the suffering of saṃsāra, thus it is 'attā'. Therefore, he said 'attabhāvena'. To show that in the triad of words as well, the instrumental case is used in the sense of 'characteristic of such a state' (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa), it was said by the commentator 'athenaṃ...pe...katvā'. The meaning should also be understood thus: He dwells, being non-thieving in himself due to his non-thieving nature, and pure in himself due to his pure nature.

Sesanti [M 1.0332] “pahāya paṭivirato”ti evamādikaṃ. Tañhi pubbe vuttanayaṃ. Kiñcāpi nayidha sikkhāpadavohārena virati vuttā, ito aññesu pana suttapadesesu, vinayābhidhammesu ca pavattavohārena viratiyo, cetanā ca adhisīlasikkhānamadhiṭṭhānabhāvato, tesamaññatarakoṭṭhāsabhāvato ca “sikkhāpada”ntveva vattabbāti āha “paṭhamasikkhāpade”ti. Kāmañcettha “lajjī dayāpanno”ti na vuttaṃ, adhikāravasena, pana atthato ca vuttamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi lajjādayo pāṇātipātappahānassa visesapaccayo, evaṃ adinnādānappahānassāpīti. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Atha vā sucibhūtenāti hirottappādisamannāgamanaṃ, ahirikādīnañca pahānaṃ vuttamevāti “lajjī dayāpanno”ti na vuttaṃ.

The rest is the passage beginning with 'having abandoned, he abstains.' For that has been explained by the previous method. Although here abstinence is not spoken of by the term 'training precept,' nevertheless, in other sutta passages apart from this one, and in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, by the established terminology, both abstinences and volition, because of being the foundation for the training in higher virtue and because of being a component of one or the other of those, are to be called simply 'training precepts.' Therefore, he said, 'in the first training precept.' And although 'conscientious, compassionate' is not stated here, it should be understood that it is stated by way of the context and by way of the meaning. For just as conscientiousness and so on are a special condition for the abandoning of killing living beings, so too are they for the abandoning of taking what is not given. This is the method for the subsequent precepts as well. Alternatively, by 'being purified,' the possession of conscience and moral shame, and the abandoning of shamelessness and so on, are indeed stated. Therefore, 'conscientious, compassionate' was not stated.

Brahma-saddo idha seṭṭhavācako, abrahmānaṃ nihīnānaṃ, abrahmaṃ vā nihīnaṃ cariyaṃ vutti abrahmacariyaṃ, methunadhammo. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāranti methunaviratiṃ. Na ācaratīti anācārī, [ārācārī (dī. ni. 1.8)] tadācāravirahitoti attho, tenāha “abrahmacariyato dūracārī”ti. Dūro methunasaṅkhāto ācāro, so virahena yassatthīti dūracārī, methunadhammato vā dūro hutvā tabbiratiṃ ācaratīti dūracārītipi vaṭṭati. Mithunānaṃ rāgapariyuṭṭhānena sadisānaṃ ubhinnaṃ ayaṃ methunoti atthaṃ dasseti “rāgapariyuṭṭhānavasenā”tiādinā. Asataṃ dhammo ācāroti asaddhammo, tasmā. Abhedavohārena gāmasaddeneva gāmavāsino gahitāti vuttaṃ “gāmavāsīna”nti, gāme vasataṃ dhammotipi yujjati. “Dūracārī”ti cettha vacanato, pāḷiyaṃ vā “methunā” tveva avatvā “gāmadhammā”tipi vuttattā

Here, the word 'brahma' denotes 'excellent.' 'Abrahmacariya' is the conduct or practice of the non-excellent, the inferior; or, it is non-excellent, inferior conduct—that is, the practice of sexual intercourse. To practice the excellent (brahmaṃ) conduct is to practice abstinence from sexual intercourse. One who does not practice it is 'anācārī,' meaning devoid of that conduct. Hence, it is said, 'one who fares far from unchastity.' The conduct called sexual intercourse is far; one for whom this is so through its absence is a 'dūracārī.' Alternatively, being far from the practice of sexual intercourse, one practices abstinence from it; thus, 'dūracārī' is also suitable. The teacher shows the meaning of 'methuno'—that it is the practice of two people who are similar due to the arising of lust—with the text beginning 'by way of the arising of lust.' The 'dhamma' or conduct of the non-virtuous is 'asaddhammo' (unrighteous conduct); therefore... By an undifferentiated expression, through the word 'gāma' (village) itself, the village-dwellers are taken; thus it is said 'of village-dwellers.' The 'dhamma' of those dwelling in a village is also a suitable etymology. And here, because it is said 'one who fares far,' and because in the Pāḷi, instead of saying just 'methunā,' it is also said 'gāmadhammā'...

“Idha brāhmaṇa, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā sammā brahmacārī paṭijānamāno na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaparimaddananhāpanasambāhanaṃ sādiyati, so taṃ assādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjati, idampi kho brāhmaṇa brahmacariyassa khaṇḍampi chiddampi [V 1.0293] sabalampi kammāsampi, ayaṃ vuccati brāhmaṇa aparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati saṃyutto methunena saṃyogena, na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi [M 1.0333] paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Here, brahmin, some ascetic or brahmin, while professing to live the holy life rightly, does not indeed engage in sexual intercourse with a woman, but he delights in a woman anointing, massaging, bathing, or rubbing him. He savors that, desires that, and attains satisfaction from it. This, brahmin, is a broken, flawed, spotted, and blemished holy life. This one is said to practice an impure holy life, yoked with the yoke of sexual intercourse. He is not freed from birth, aging, death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs—he is not freed from suffering, I say.”

Puna caparaṃ…pe… napi mātugāmassa ucchādanaparimandananhāpanasambāhanaṃ sādiyati, apica kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ sañjagghati saṃkīḷati saṃkelāyati…pe… napi mātugāmena saddhiṃ sañjagghati saṃkīḷati saṃkelāyati, apica kho mātugāmassa cakkhunā cakkhuṃ upanijjhāyati pekkhati…pe… napi mātugāmassa cakkhunā cakkhuṃ upanijjhāyati pekkhati, apica kho mātugāmassa saddaṃ suṇāti tirokuṭṭaṃ vā tiropākāraṃ vā hasantiyā vā bhaṇantiyā vā gāyantiyā vā rodantiyā vā…pe… napi mātugāmassa saddaṃ suṇāti tirokuṭṭaṃ vā tiropākāraṃ vā hasantiyā vā bhaṇantiyā vā gāyantiyā vā rodantiyā vā, apica kho yānissa tāni pubbe mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitalapitakīḷitāni, tāni anussarati…pe… napi yānissa tāni pubbe mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitalapitakīḷitāni, tāni anussarati, apica kho passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgibhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ…pe… napi passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgibhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ, apica kho aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati “imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti. So taṃ assādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjati. Idampi kho brāhmaṇa brahmacariyassa khaṇḍampi chiddampi sabalampi kammāsampi. Ayaṃ vuccati brāhmaṇa, aparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati saṃyutto methunena saṃyogena, na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 7.50) –

“Furthermore... nor does he delight in a woman anointing, massaging, bathing, or rubbing him. Yet he jokes, plays, and amuses himself with a woman... nor does he joke, play, or amuse himself with a woman. Yet he gazes intently and stares into a woman’s eyes... nor does he gaze intently or stare into a woman’s eyes. Yet he listens to the sound of a woman laughing, speaking, singing, or crying from behind a wall or a fence... nor does he listen to the sound of a woman laughing, speaking, singing, or crying from behind a wall or a fence. Yet he recollects the laughing, talking, and playing he formerly did with a woman... nor does he recollect the laughing, talking, and playing he formerly did with a woman. Yet he sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed with, possessed of, and being served by the five strands of sensual pleasure... nor does he see a householder or a householder’s son endowed with, possessed of, and being served by the five strands of sensual pleasure. Yet he practices the holy life aspiring to some group of gods, thinking, ‘By this virtue, or by this observance, or by this austerity, or by this holy life, I will become a god or some other god!’ He savors that, desires that, and attains satisfaction from it. This too, brahmin, is a broken, flawed, spotted, and blemished holy life. This one, brahmin, is said to practice an impure holy life, yoked with the yoke of sexual intercourse, not freed from birth, aging, death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs—not freed from suffering, I say.”

Aṅguttarāgame sattakanipāte jāṇusoṇisutte āgatā sattavidhamethunasaṃyogāpi paṭivirati dassitāti daṭṭhabbā. Idhāpi asaddhammasevanādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā maggenamaggapaṭipattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā abrahmacariyaṃ[M 1.0334]. Pañcasikkhāpadakkame micchācāre pana agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā yathāvuttā kāmesu micchācāroti yojetabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be seen that in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, in the Book of Sevens, in the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta, abstinence even from the seven kinds of yokes of sexual intercourse that are mentioned has been shown. Here too, the volition, occurring at the body-door with the intention of indulging in unrighteous practice, which brings about the connection of path with path, is unchastity. However, in the sequence of the five training precepts, regarding misconduct in sensual pleasures, the volition to transgress in a forbidden place, as has been stated, should be connected with 'misconduct in sensual pleasures'.

Tattha [V 1.0294] agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purisānaṃ tāva māturakkhitādayo dasa, dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dasannaṃ dhanakkītādīnaṃ, sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānañca vasena dvādasannaṃ aññe purisā. Ye paneke vadanti “cattāro kāmesu micchācārā akālo, adeso, anaṅgo, adhammo cā”ti, te vippaṭipattimattaṃ pati parikappetvā vadanti. Na hi sāgamanīyaṭṭhāne pavattā vippaṭipatti micchācāro nāma sambhavati. Sā panesā duvidhāpi vippaṭipatti guṇavirahite appasāvajjā, guṇasampanne mahāsāvajjā. Guṇarahitepi ca abhibhavitvā vippaṭipatti mahāsāvajjā, ubhinnaṃ samānacchandabhāve appasāvajjā, samānacchandabhāvepi kilesānaṃ, upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjā, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjāti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, what is called an improper partner is, for men, firstly, twenty types of women: the ten beginning with one protected by her mother, and the ten beginning with one purchased with wealth. For women, however—specifically for twelve types, namely the ten beginning with one purchased with wealth, and also those who have a guardian and those subject to punishment—other men are an improper partner. As for those who say, 'There are four kinds of sexual misconduct: improper time, improper place, improper organ, and improper conduct,' they speak having conceived this based merely on wrongful conduct. Indeed, wrongful conduct that occurs with a proper partner cannot be called sexual misconduct. Now, this wrongful conduct, of two kinds, is of little fault in one devoid of virtue, and of great fault in one endowed with virtue. And even in one devoid of virtue, wrongful conduct by overpowering is of great fault. When there is mutual consent of both, it is of little fault. Even with mutual consent, due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, it is of little fault; due to their intensity, it is of great fault. Thus it should be known.

Tassa pana abrahmacariyassa dve sambhārā sevetukāmatācittaṃ, maggenamaggapaṭipattīti. Micchācārassa pana cattāro sambhārā agamanīyavatthu, tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ, sevanāpayogo, maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsananti evaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu “cattāro sambhārā”ti (dha. sa. akusalakammapathakathā; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.89; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.109-111) vuttattā abhibhavitvā vītikkamane maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsane satipi purimuppannasevanābhisandhipayogābhāvato abhibhuyyamānassa micchācāro na hotīti vadanti keci. Sevanacitte sati payogābhāvo na pamāṇaṃ itthiyā sevanapayogassa yebhuyyena abhāvato, purisasseva yebhuyyena sevanapayogo hotīti itthiyā puretaraṃ sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā nisinnāya [nipannāya (dha. sa. anuṭī. kammakathāvaṇṇanā)] micchācāro na siyāti āpajjati. Tasmā purisassa vasena ukkaṃsato “cattāro sambhārā”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā hi itthiyā purisakiccakaraṇakāle purisassāpi sevanāpayogābhāvato micchācāro na siyāti vadanti eke.

Now, for that unchastity, there are two components: the mind with the desire to engage, and the penetration of one path by another. But for sexual misconduct, there are four components: an improper object, the thought to engage with it, the effort of engaging, and consenting to the penetration of one path by another. Since it is stated thus in the commentaries, 'There are four components,' some say that in a transgression by overpowering, even when there is consent to the penetration of one path by another, sexual misconduct does not occur for the one being overpowered, due to the absence of a previously arisen intention and effort to engage. When the thought to engage is present, the absence of effort is not the standard, because for a woman, there is generally no effort of engaging; it is generally the man who makes the effort of engaging. Thus, it would undesirably follow that for a woman who, having first established the thought to engage, is sitting, sexual misconduct would not occur. Therefore, 'four components' is stated primarily from the man's perspective. For otherwise, some say, when a woman performs the man's act, sexual misconduct would not occur for the man either, due to his lack of effort in engaging.

Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – attano ruciyā pavattitassa sevanāpayogeneva sevanacittatāsiddhito agamanīyavatthu, sevanāpayogo, maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsananti tayo, balakkārena pavattitassa purimuppannasevanābhisandhipayogābhāvato agamanīyavatthu, tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ[M 1.0335], maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsananti tayo, anavasesaggahaṇena pana vuttanayena cattāroti, tampi keciyeva vadanti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbanti abhidhammānuṭīkāyaṃ (dha. sa. anuṭī. akusalakammapathakathāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Eko payogo sāhatthikova.

Herein, this is the conclusion: For misconduct that proceeds by one's own inclination, because the state of having the thought to engage is established by the very effort of engaging, there are three components: an improper object, the effort of engaging, and consenting to the penetration of one path by another. For misconduct that proceeds by force, due to the absence of a previously arisen intention and effort to engage, there are three components: an improper object, the thought to engage with it, and consenting to the penetration of one path by another. However, by taking them all without remainder in the manner stated, there are four. That too, only some say. 'It should be accepted after investigation'—thus it is said in the Abhidhammānuṭīkā. One effort is that done by one's own hand.

9. Musāti [V 1.0295] tatiyanto, dutiyanto vā nipāto micchāpariyāyo, kiriyāpadhānoti āha “visaṃvādanapurekkhārassā”tiādi. Pure karaṇaṃ purekkhāro, visaṃvādanassa purekkhāro yassāti tathā, tassa kammapathappattameva dassetuṃ “atthabhañjanako”ti vuttaṃ, parassa hitavināsakoti attho. Musāvādo pana sasantakassa adātukāmatāya, hasādhippāyena ca bhavati. Vacasā katā vāyāmappadhānā kiriyā vacīpayogo. Tathā kāyena katā kāyapayogo. Visaṃvādanādhippāyo pubbabhāgakkhaṇe, taṅkhaṇe ca. Vuttañhi “pubbevassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇissa’nti, bhaṇantassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇāmī’ti” (pārā. 200; pāci. 4) etadeva hi dvayaṃ aṅgabhūtaṃ. Itaraṃ “bhaṇitassa hoti ‘musā mayā bhaṇita’nti” (pārā. 200; pāci. 4) vuttaṃ pana hotu vā, mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Assāti visaṃvādakassa. “Cetanā”ti etena sambandho. Visaṃ vādeti etenāti visaṃvādanaṃ, tadeva kāyavacīpayogo, taṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti tathā, iminā musāsaṅkhātena kāyavacīpayogena, musāsaṅkhātaṃ vā kāyavacīpayogaṃ vadati viññāpeti, samuṭṭhāpeti vā etenāti musāvādoti atthamāha. “Vādo”ti vutte visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti lakkhaṇattayaṃ vibhāvitameva hoti.

9. The word `musā` is an indeclinable ending in the third or, alternatively, the second case, a synonym for `micchā` (falsely), and has action as its primary meaning. Therefore, the Teacher said, 'for one who has deception as a forerunner,' etc. `Purekkhāro` is 'placing before'; one for whom there is the placing before of deception is so called. To show that this very act has reached the course of action, it is said, 'a destroyer of welfare,' the meaning of which is 'a destroyer of another's benefit.' False speech, however, also arises from the unwillingness to give what is one's own and from the intention to jest. An action done by speech, with effort as its principal factor, is verbal effort. Similarly, an action done by body is bodily effort. The intention to deceive is present in the preliminary moment and in that very moment of speaking. For it was said, 'Beforehand, it occurs to him, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, it occurs to him, "I am speaking falsely."' Indeed, these two are the constituent factors. The other statement, 'Having spoken, it occurs to him, "I have spoken falsely,"' whether it is present or not, is not a cause. `Assa` refers to the deceiver. It should be connected with the word `cetanā` (volition). `Visaṃvādanaṃ` is that by which one deceives; that itself is bodily and verbal effort. The volition that originates it is so called. By this, the author explains the meaning of `musāvādo`: it is the volition by which one speaks, makes known, or originates the bodily and verbal effort designated as 'falsehood'. When `vādo` (speech) is said, the three characteristics—the mind that wishes to deceive, the effort born of that, and the other's understanding of that meaning—are indeed made clear.

“Atathaṃ vatthu”nti lakkhaṇaṃ pana avibhāvitameva musā-saddassa payogasaṅkhātakiriyāvācakattā. Tasmā idha naye lakkhaṇassa abyāpitatāya, musā-saddassa ca visaṃvāditabbatthavācakatāsambhavato paripuṇṇaṃ katvā musāvādalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “aparo nayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Lakkhaṇatoti sabhāvato. Tathāti tena tathākārena. Kāyavacīviññattiyo samuṭṭhāpetīti viññattisamuṭṭhāpikā. Imasmiṃ pana naye musā vatthu vadīyati vuccati etenāti musāvādoti nibbacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “So yamattha”ntiādinā kammapathappattassa vatthuvasena appasāvajjamahāsāvajjabhāvamāha. Yassa atthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjo[M 1.0336], mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjoti adinnādāne viya guṇavasenāpi yojetabbaṃ. Kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvasenāpi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā labbhatiyeva.

However, the characteristic 'an untrue thing' is not made clear, because the word `musā` denotes an action designated as effort. Therefore, in this method, because of the non-pervasiveness of the characteristic, and because of the possibility that the word `musā` denotes the thing to be misrepresented, in order to present the characteristic of false speech completely, 'another method,' etc., was stated. `Lakkhaṇato` means 'by nature.' `Tathā` means 'in that true manner.' It originates bodily and verbal intimations, thus it is an originator of intimations. But in this method, the derivation should be seen as: `musāvādo` is so called because an untrue thing is spoken or said by means of it. By the words 'Whatever welfare...' etc., he states the state of being of little or great fault, according to the object, for one who has reached the course of action. It is of little fault due to the few virtues of the one whose welfare he destroys, and of great fault due to their great virtues. As in the case of taking what is not given, it should also be connected by way of virtue. The state of being of little or great fault is certainly obtained also by way of the mildness and intensity of the defilements.

“Apicā”tiādinā musāvādasāmaññassāpi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjabhāvaṃ dasseti. Attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāyāti, hi hasādhippāyenāti ca musāvādasāmaññato vuttaṃ. Ubhayatthāpi ca visaṃvādanapurekkhāreneva musāvādo, na pana vacanamattena. Tattha pana cetanā balavatī na hotīti appasāvajjatā vuttā. Nadī maññeti nadī viya. Appatāya ūnassa atthassa pūraṇavasena pavattā kathā pūraṇakathā, bahutarabhāvena vuttakathāti vuttaṃ hoti.

By 'Moreover,' etc., he shows the state of being a minor or major offense even for the generality of false speech. For, 'due to the desire not to give what is one's own' and 'with the intention of joking' are said with respect to the generality of false speech. And in both cases, false speech occurs only with deception as the forerunner, and not by mere utterance. There, however, because the volition is not strong, the state of being a minor offense is stated. 'Nadī maññe' means 'like a river'. Speech that occurs by way of filling a deficient meaning, due to its insufficiency, is 'filling speech'; this means it is speech spoken for the most part.

Tenākārena [V 1.0296] jāto tajjo, tassa visaṃvādanassa anurūpoti attho. Vāyāmoti vāyāmasīsena payogamāha. Vīriyappadhānā hi kāyikavācasikakiriyā idha adhippetā, na vāyāmamattaṃ. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena payoge katepi aparena tasmiṃ atthe aviññāte visaṃvādanassa asijjhanato parassa tadatthavijānanampi ekasambhārabhāvena vuttaṃ. Keci pana “abhūtavacanaṃ, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, parassa tadatthavijānana”nti tayo sambhāre vadanti. Kāyikova sāhatthikoti koci maññeyyāti taṃ nivāraṇatthaṃ “so kāyena vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānātīti taṅkhaṇe vā dandhatāya vicāretvā pacchā vā jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ayanti visaṃvādako. Kiriyasamuṭṭhāpikacetanākkhaṇeyevāti kāyikavācasikakiriyasamuṭṭhāpikāya cetanāya pavattakkhaṇe eva. Musāvādakammunā bajjhatīti visaṃvādanacetanāsaṅkhātena musāvādakammunā sambandhīyati, allīyatīti vā attho. Sacepi dandhatāya vicāretvā pacchā cirenāpi paro tadatthaṃ jānāti, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya nibbattattā taṅkhaṇeyeva bajjhatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Born of that manner, it is 'tajja'; the meaning is 'appropriate to that deception.' By 'effort' (`vāyāmo`), he speaks of the application (`payoga`) with effort as its head. Indeed, bodily and verbal actions with energy as predominant are intended here, not mere effort. Even when an application is made with the intention to deceive, if the other does not understand that meaning, because the deception is not accomplished, the other's understanding of that meaning is also stated as a single constituent factor. Some, however, state three constituent factors: 'untrue speech, the mind to deceive, and the other’s understanding of that meaning.' Lest someone think, 'Only the bodily act is personal (`sāhatthika`),' to prevent that, 'he by body or...' etc., is stated. 'And if by that action the other knows that meaning' is said with reference to knowing either at that moment, or afterwards, having deliberated due to dullness. 'This' (`ayaṃ`) means the deceiver. 'At the very moment of the volition that originates the action' means at the very moment of the arising of the volition that originates the bodily or verbal action. 'Is bound by the kamma of false speech' means is connected with, or clings to, the kamma of false speech, which is designated as the volition to deceive; this is the meaning. Even if the other understands that meaning later, after a long time, having deliberated due to dullness, it is said that one is bound at that very moment because it has been produced by the concluding volition.

“Eko payogo sāhatthikovā”ti idaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāsu āgatanayena vuttanti idha saṅgahaṭṭhakathāya saṅgahakārassa attano matibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “yathā…pe… tathā”ti etena sāhatthiko viya āṇattikādayopi gahetabbā, aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthi parassa visaṃvādanabhāvena tassadisattāti dasseti[M 1.0337], “idamassa…pe… āṇāpentopī”ti āṇattikassa gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ, “paṇṇaṃ…pe… nissajjantopī”ti nissaggiyassa, “ayamattho…pe… ṭhapentopī”ti thāvarassa. Yasmā visaṃvādetīti sabbattha sambandho. Paṇṇaṃ likhitvāti tālādīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ akkharena likhitvā, paṇṇanti vā bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “tirokuṭṭādīsū”ti [kuḍḍādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8)] paṇṇe akkharaṃ lekhaniyā likhitvāti attho. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbāti attanomatiyā sabbadubbalattā anattukkaṃsanena vuttaṃ. Kiñhettha vicāretabbakāraṇaṃ atthi sayameva vicāritattā.

This statement, 'One application is personal (`sāhatthika`),' is stated according to the method that has come down in the ancient commentaries. Therefore, here in the Saṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā, to show his own difference of opinion, the compiler states, 'But since...' etc. There, by 'just as... so...', it is shown that, like the personal (`sāhatthika`), the commanded (`āṇattika`), etc., should also be taken; there is no reason for not taking them, because of their similarity in being a means of deceiving another. By 'this is his... commanding...', the reason for taking the commanded is shown; by 'a leaf... discarding...', for the relinquishing (`nissaggiya`); by 'this meaning... placing...', for the stationary (`thāvara`). 'Because he deceives' is the connection in all cases. 'Having written on a leaf' means having written with letters on a leaf of a palm tree, etc., or 'on a leaf' (`paṇṇaṃ`) is a usage in the accusative case with the meaning of the locative. Therefore, it is stated, 'on a wall, etc.,' meaning having written letters on a leaf with a stylus. 'It should be taken after investigation' is stated without self-exaltation, because one's own opinion is the weakest of all. What reason is there here to be investigated, since it has been investigated by himself?

Saccanti vacīsaccaṃ, saccena saccanti purimena vacīsaccena pacchimaṃ vacīsaccaṃ. Paccayavasena dhātupadantalopaṃ sandhāya “sandahatī”ti vuttaṃ. Saddavidū pana –

'Truth' (`saccaṃ`) means verbal truth. 'Truth with truth' (`saccena saccaṃ`) means the latter verbal truth with the former verbal truth. With reference to the elision of the end of a root-word due to a suffix, 'connects' (`sandahati`) is stated. But the experts in grammar—

“Vipubbo dhā karotyatthe, abhipubbo tu bhāsane;

Nyāsaṃpubbo yathāyogaṃ, nyāsāropanasandhisū”ti. –

'The root `dhā` preceded by `vi` is in the sense of 'doing'; but preceded by `abhi`, it is in the sense of 'speaking'; preceded by `ni`, `ā`, and `saṃ`, as appropriate, it is in the senses of depositing, placing upon, and joining.'

Dhā-saddameva [V 1.0297] ghaṭanatthe paṭhanti. Tasmā pariyāyavasena “sandahatī”ti vuttantipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadadhippāyaṃ dasseti “na antarantarā”tiādinā. “Yo hī”tiādi tabbivaraṇaṃ. Antaritattāti antarā paricchinnattā. Na tādisoti na evaṃvadanasabhāvo. Jīvitahetupi, pageva aññahetūti api-saddo sambhāvanattho.

They recite the word `dhā` itself in the sense of joining. Therefore, it should also be understood that 'connects' (`sandahati`) is stated by way of a synonym. He shows its meaning by 'not in between,' etc. 'For he who...' etc., is its explanation. 'Because of being interrupted' (`antaritattā`) means because of being cut off in between. 'Not of such a kind' (`na tādiso`) means not having a nature of speaking in such a way. 'Even for the sake of life, how much more so for other reasons'—here the word 'even' (`api`) has the sense of emphasis.

“Saccato thetato”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.19) viya theta-saddo thirapariyāyo, thirabhāvo ca saccavāditādhikārattā kathāvasena veditabboti āha “thirakathoti attho”ti. Thitassa bhāvoti hi theto, thirabhāvo, tena yuttattā puggalo idha theto nāma. Haliddīti suvaṇṇavaṇṇakandanipphattako gacchaviseso. Thuso nāma dhaññattaco, dhaññapalāso ca. Kumbhaṇḍanti mahāphalo sūpasampādako latāviseso. Indakhīlo nāma gambhīranemo esikāthambho. Yathā haliddirāgādayo anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya na ṭhitā, evaṃ na ṭhitā kathā etassāti naṭhitakatho [nathirakatho (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8)] yathā pāsāṇalekhādayo avaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya ṭhitā, evaṃ ṭhitā kathā etassāti ṭhitakathoti [M 1.0338] [thirakatho (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8)] haliddirāgādayo yathā kathāya upamāyo honti, evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Kathāya hi etā upamāyoti.

As in 'from truth, from firmness' (`saccato thetato`), etc., the word `theta` is a synonym for `thira` (firm). And the state of being firm, because it is in the context of truthfulness, should be understood by way of speech; therefore, he says, 'the meaning is "firm speech"' (`thirakathoti attho`). For `theto` is the state of being established (`ṭhitassa bhāvo`), that is, firmness (`thirabhāvo`); because of being endowed with that, a person here is called `theto`. `Haliddī` is a particular kind of plant produced from a tuber with a golden color. `Thuso` is the husk of grain and also the straw of grain. `Kumbhaṇḍa` is a particular kind of creeper with large fruit that serves for curry. `Indakhīla` is a city-gate post with a deep foundation. Just as the dye of turmeric and so on are not stable due to their unstable nature, so this person has speech that is not stable; thus he is `naṭhitakatha` (one of unstable speech). Just as writing on stone and so on are stable due to their stable nature, so this person has speech that is stable; thus he is `ṭhitakatha` (one of stable speech). Just as the turmeric dye and so on are similes for speech, so it should be connected. For these are indeed similes for speech.

Pattisaṅkhātā saddhā ayati pavattati etthāti paccayikoti āha “pattiyāyitabbako”ti. Pattiyā ayitabbā pavattetabbāti pattiyāyitabbā ya-kārāgamena, vācā. Sā etassāti pattiyāyitabbako, tenāha “saddhāyitabbako”ti. Tadevatthaṃ byatirekena, anvayena ca dassetuṃ “ekacco hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vattabbataṃ āpajjati visaṃvādanato. Itarapakkhe ca avisaṃvādanatoti adhippāyo. “Loka”nti etena “lokassā”ti ettha kammatthe chaṭṭhīti dasseti.

Faith, reckoned as reliance (patti), arises in this person, hence he is called 'paccayika'. He said: 'pattiyāyitabbako' (one in whom reliance should be placed). 'Pattiyā ayitabbā pavattetabbā' means that by which reliance should be made to arise; thus, with the addition of the letter 'ya', it becomes 'pattiyāyitabbā', referring to speech. That speech belongs to this person, hence he is 'pattiyāyitabbako'. Therefore, he said: 'saddhāyitabbako' (one in whom faith should be placed). To show that very meaning by way of contrast and conformity, the passage beginning 'ekacco hī' was spoken. Because of deception, it comes to be spoken of. And in the other case, because of non-deception, it comes to be spoken of—this is the intention. By this word 'Lokaṃ', he shows that in 'lokassa', the sixth case ending is in the sense of the object.

Satipi paccekaṃ pāṭhakkame aññāsu abhidhammaṭṭhakathā dīsu (dha. sa. aṭṭha. akusalakammapathakathā; ma. ni. 1.89) saṃvaṇṇanākkamena tiṇṇampi padānaṃ ekatthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ kātuṃ “yāya vācāyā”tiādimāha, yāya vācāya karotīti sambandho. Parassāti yaṃ bhindituṃ taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa. Ca-saddo aṭṭhānapayutto, so dvandagabbhabhāvaṃ jotetuṃ kammadvaye payujjitabbo. Suññabhāvanti piyavirahitatāya rittabhāvaṃ. Sāti yathāvuttā saddasabhāvā vācā, etena piyañca suññañca piyasuññaṃ, taṃ karoti etāyāti pisuṇā niruttinayenāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti, pisatīti vā pisuṇā, samagge satte avayavabhūte vaggabhinne karotīti attho.

Although there is a separate order of the text in other Abhidhamma commentaries and so on, in order to give a single explanation for all three terms according to the order of exposition, he said the passage beginning 'yāya vācāya'.
