The connection is: 'by which speech one does'. As for 'for another' (parassa), it refers to the person whose affection he speaks that speech to destroy. The particle 'ca' is used in the wrong place; it should be applied to the pair of objects to illuminate its inclusion in a dvanda compound. 'The state of being empty' (suññabhāvaṃ) means the state of being void due to being devoid of affection. As for 'that' (sā), it is speech whose nature is a word, as stated. By this, he shows the word-meaning: 'dear' (piya) and 'empty' (suñña) become 'piyasuññaṃ' (a dvanda compound); 'one does that by this speech' (taṃ karoti etāya), therefore, by the method of etymology, it is 'pisuṇā'. Or, because it 'crushes' (pisati), it is 'pisuṇā'; the meaning is that it takes united beings and makes them fragmented and divided into groups.

Pharusanti [V 1.0298] sinehābhāvena lūkhaṃ. Sayampi pharusāti domanassasamuṭṭhitattā sabhāvena sayampi kakkasā. Pharusasabhāvato neva kaṇṇasukhā. Atthavipannatāya na hadayaṅgamā. Ettha pana paṭhamanaye pharusaṃ karotīti vacanatthena vā phalūpacārena vā vācāya pharusasaddappavatti veditabbā. Dutiyanaye mammacchedavasena pavattiyā ekantaniṭṭhuratāya ruḷhisaddavasena sabhāvena, kāraṇūpacārena vā vācāya pharusasaddappavatti daṭṭhabbā.

'Harsh' (pharusaṃ) means rough due to a lack of affection. 'It is harsh even by itself' (sayampi pharusā) means that because it arises from displeasure, it is by its very nature harsh. Because of its harsh nature, it is not pleasing to the ear. Because its benefit is ruined, it does not go to the heart. Here, however, in the first method, the application of the word 'pharusa' to speech should be understood either by its word-meaning as 'it makes harsh' or by the metaphor of the result. In the second method, the application of the word 'pharusa' to speech should be seen as occurring by way of cutting the vitals, due to its utterly cruel nature, by way of its being a conventional term, by its nature, or by the metaphor of the cause.

Yenāti palāpasaṅkhātena niratthakavacanena. Samphanti “sa”nti vuttaṃ sukhaṃ, hitañca phalati paharati vināsetīti atthena “sampha”nti laddhanāmaṃ attano, paresañca anupakārakaṃ yaṃ kiñci atthaṃ, tenāha “niratthaka”nti, iminā samphaṃ palapati etenāti samphappalāpoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti.

'By which' (yena) means by meaningless speech (niratthakavacanena) reckoned as chatter (palāpasaṅkhātena). As for 'samphaṃ', it gets its name from the meaning that it destroys (phalati paharati vināseti) happiness (sukhaṃ) and welfare (hitaṃ), which are called 'saṃ', and is whatever matter is unhelpful to oneself and others. Therefore, he said it is 'meaningless' (niratthakaṃ). By this, he shows the word-meaning of 'samphappalāpo' as: 'by this (speech) one utters samphaṃ'.

“Tesa”ntiādinā [M 1.0339] cetanāya phalavohārena pisuṇādisaddappavatti vuttā. “Sā evā”tiādinā pana cetanāya pavattiparikappanāya hetuṃ vibhāveti. Tattha “pahāyā”tiādivacanasannidhānato tassāyeva ca pahātabbatā yuttito adhippetāti attho.

By the passage beginning 'Tesaṃ', the application of words such as 'pisuṇā' to volition, by way of designation by its result, was stated. Furthermore, by the passage beginning 'Sā eva', he clarifies the cause for the conceptualization of the occurrence of that volition. Therein, due to the proximity of the words beginning 'pahāya', the meaning intended, by way of logic, is that that very volition is what should be abandoned.

Tatthāti tāsu pisuṇavācādīsu. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittassāti lobhena, dosena vā vibādhitacittassa, upatāpitacittassa vā, dūsitacittassāti vuttaṃ hoti, “cetanā”ti etena sambandho. Yena saha paresaṃ bhedāya vadati, tassa attano piyakamyatāyāti attho. Cetanā pisuṇavācā nāma pisuṇaṃ vadanti etāyāti katvā. Samāsavisaye hi mukhyavasena attho gahetabbo, byāsavisaye upacāravasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yassa yato bhedaṃ karoti, tesu abhinnesu appasāvajjaṃ, bhinnesu mahāsāvajjaṃ. Tathā kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvisesesupi yojetabbaṃ.

'Tattha' means among those, such as divisive speech. 'Of one with a defiled mind' (saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa) means of one whose mind is afflicted, tormented, or corrupted by greed or hatred; this is what is said. It is to be connected with the word 'volition' (cetanā). The meaning is: when one speaks for the division of others from someone, it is for the sake of one's own desire to be dear to that person. Volition is called 'divisive speech' because of the word-meaning: 'by this (volition) they speak divisively'. It should be seen that in the context of a compound, the primary meaning should be taken, whereas in the context of an analytical phrase, the figurative meaning should be taken. When one causes division between two people, if they remain undivided, the fault is slight; if they become divided, the fault is great. Similarly, this should be applied to the distinctions in the softness and intensity of the defilements.

Yassa pesuññaṃ upasaṃharati, so bhijjatu vā, mā vā, tassa tadatthaviññāpanameva pamāṇanti āha “tassa tadatthavijānana”nti. Bhedapurekkhāratāpiyakamyatānamekekapakkhipanena cattāro. Kammapathappatti pana bhinne eva. Imesanti aniyamatāya parammukhāpavattānampi attano buddhiyaṃ parivattamāne sandhāya vuttanti dassetuṃ “yesa”ntiādimāha. Itoti idha padese, vuttānaṃ yesaṃ santike sutanti yojetabbaṃ.

To whomever one presents slander, whether they become divided or not, the mere making known of that meaning to him is the measure. Thus, he said: 'that person's understanding of that meaning'. By including each of the factors—having division as the foremost aim and desiring to be dear—there are four constituents. However, the completion of the course of action occurs only when division actually takes place. To show that this word 'imesaṃ' is said with reference to what revolves in one's own mind even concerning those who are absent, due to its non-specific nature, he said the passage beginning 'yesaṃ'. As for 'ito', it means 'in this place', and it should be connected thus: 'from whom, among those mentioned, it was heard'.

“Dvinna”nti nidassanavacanaṃ bahūnampi sandhānato. “Mittāna”ntiādi “sandhāna”nti ettha kammaṃ, tena pāḷiyaṃ “bhinnāna”nti etassa kammabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sandhānakaraṇañca nāma tesamanurūpakaraṇamevāti [V 1.0299] vuttaṃ “anukattā”ti. Anuppadātāti anubalappadātā, anuvattanavasena vā padātā. Kassa pana anubalappadānaṃ, anuvattanañcāti? “Sahitāna”nti vuttattā sandhānassāti viññāyatīti āha “sandhānānuppadātā”ti. Yasmā pana anubalavasena, anuvattanavasena ca sandhānassa padānaṃ ādānaṃ, rakkhaṇaṃ vā daḷhīkaraṇaṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “daḷhīkammaṃ kattā”ti. Āramanti etthāti ārāmo. Ramitabbaṭṭhānaṃ samaggoti hi tadadhiṭṭhānānaṃ vasena tabbisesanatā vuttā. “Samagge”tipi paṭhanti, tadayuttaṃ “yatthā”tiādivacanena viruddhattā. Yasmā pana ākārena vināpi ayamattho labbhati, tasmā “ayamevettha attho”ti vuttaṃ samaggesūti samaggabhūtesu janakāyesu, tenāha “te pahāyā”tiādi. Tappakatiyatthopi kattuatthovāti dasseti [M 1.0340] “nandatī”ti iminā. Tappakatiyatthena hi “disvāpi sutvāpī”ti vacanaṃ supapannaṃ hoti. Samagge karoti etāyāti samaggakaraṇī. Sāyeva vācā, taṃ bhāsitāti atthamāha “yā vācā”tiādinā. Tāya vācāya samaggakaraṇaṃ nāma. “Sukhā saṅghassa sāmaggī, samaggānaṃ tapo sukho”tiādinā (dha. pa. 194) samaggānisaṃsadassanamevāti vuttaṃ “sāmaggiguṇaparidīpikamevā”ti. Itaranti tabbiparītaṃ bhedanikaṃ vācaṃ.

The word 'dvinnaṃ' (of two) is an illustrative term, because of the reconciliation of many as well. In the passage beginning with 'mittānaṃ' (of friends), etc., the word 'sandhānaṃ' (reconciliation) here is the object; thereby, it shows that 'bhinnānaṃ' (of the divided) in the Pāḷi text is the object. And the act of reconciliation is simply acting in accordance with them; therefore, it is said 'anukattā' (one who acts in accordance). 'Anuppadātā' means a giver of support, or a giver in the sense of compliance. But for whom is there giving of support and compliance? Since it is said 'sahitānaṃ' (of the united), it is understood to be for reconciliation; therefore, the teacher said 'sandhānānuppadātā' (a giver of support to reconciliation). Moreover, because by way of giving support and by way of compliance, the giving to, taking up of, or protecting reconciliation becomes a strengthening, it is said 'daḷhīkammaṃ kattā' (a performer of strengthening). 'They delight herein' (āramanti ettha), therefore it is an 'ārāma' (a place of delight). Indeed, the place to be delighted in, 'samaggo' (harmonious), is stated as its qualifier by way of the abodes of those who are harmonious. Some also recite 'samagge', but that is incorrect because it contradicts the statement beginning with 'yattha'. Moreover, because this meaning is obtained even without the specific form, it is said 'this is the meaning here'. 'Samaggesu' means among groups of people who have become harmonious; for that reason, he said 'te pahāya' (having abandoned them), etc. That the meaning of its nature is also the meaning of the agent is shown by 'nandati' (rejoices). Indeed, by the meaning of its nature, the statement 'disvāpi sutvāpi' (having seen or heard) is well-established. 'By this, one makes (people) harmonious' (samagge karoti etāya), therefore it is 'samaggakaraṇī' (that which makes harmonious). It is that very speech; one speaks that speech. The teacher stated the meaning with the passage beginning 'yā vācā' (which speech). The making of harmony by that speech is meant. 'Happy is harmony in the Saṅgha, happy is the austerity of the harmonious' (Dhp. 194), etc., is simply showing the benefits of harmony; therefore, it was said 'sāmaggiguṇaparidīpikam eva' (that which illuminates the virtue of harmony). 'Itaraṃ' (the other) means the opposite, divisive speech.

Mammānīti duṭṭhārūni, tassadisatāya pana idha akkosavatthūni “mammānī”ti vuccanti. Yathā hi duṭṭhārūsu yena kenaci vatthunā ghaṭitesu cittaṃ adhimattaṃ dukkhappattaṃ hoti, tathā tesu dasasujātiādīsu akkosavatthūsu pharusavācāya phusitamattesūti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “mammāni viya mammāni, yesu pharusavācāya chupitamattesu duṭṭhārūsu viya ghaṭṭitesu cittaṃ adhimattaṃ dukkhappattaṃ hoti, kāni pana tāni? Jātiādīni akkosavatthūnī”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.9) “yassa sarīrappadesassa satthādipaṭihanena bhusaṃ rujjanaṃ, so mammaṃ nāma. Idha pana yassa cittassa pharusavācāvasena domanassasaṅkhātaṃ bhusaṃ rujjanaṃ, taṃ mammaṃ viyāti mamma”nti apare. Tāni mammāni chijjanti bhijjanti yenāti mammacchedako, sveva kāyavacīpayogo, tāni samuṭṭhāpetīti tathā. Ekantapharusacetanā pharusā vācā pharusaṃ vadanti etāyāti katvā. “Pharusacetanā” icceva avatvā “ekantapharusacetanā”ti vacanaṃ duṭṭhacittatāya eva pharusacetanā adhippetā, na pana savanapharusatāmattenāti ñāpanatthaṃ. Tassāti ekantapharusacetanāya eva. Āvibhāvatthanti pharusavācābhāvassa pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ. Tassāti vā ekantapharusacetanāya eva, pharusavācābhāvassāti attho. Tathevāti mātuvuttākāreneva, uṭṭhāsi anubandhitunti attho. Saccakiriyanti yaṃ “caṇḍā taṃ mahiṃsī anubandhatū”ti vacanaṃ mukhena kathesi, taṃ mātucitte natthi, tasmā “taṃ mā hotu, yaṃ pana uppalapattampi mayhaṃ upari na patatū”ti [V 1.0300] kāraṇaṃ cittena cintesi, tadeva mātucitte atthi, tasmā “tameva hotū”ti saccakaraṇaṃ, kattabbasaccaṃ vā. Tatthevāti uṭṭhānaṭṭhāneyeva. Baddhā viyāti yottādinā paribandhi viya. Evaṃ mammacchedakoti ettha savanapharusatāmattena mammacchedakatā veditabbā.

'Mammāni' means malignant sores; however, due to their similarity, here the objects of abuse are called 'mammāni'. For just as when malignant sores are struck by some object, the mind experiences extreme suffering, so too when those ten objects of abuse, such as birth, etc., are merely touched by harsh speech. Indeed, it is said: 'Vital spots (mammāni) are like malignant sores; when these are merely touched by harsh speech, the mind experiences extreme suffering, just as when malignant sores are struck. What are they? The objects of abuse, such as birth, etc.' 'That part of the body where there is severe pain from being struck by a weapon, etc., is called a "mamma". But here, others say: that mind which, by means of harsh speech, has severe pain called displeasure, is like a "mamma", hence it is a "mamma".' That by which those 'mammāni' are cut and broken is a 'mammacchedaka'; that is the very bodily and verbal exertion. The volition that produces that exertion is so-called. Exclusively harsh volition is harsh speech; it is so called because 'they speak harshly (pharusaṃ vadanti) by means of this (etāya)'. Not merely saying 'harsh volition', the statement 'exclusively harsh volition' is for the purpose of making it known that a harsh volition due to a corrupted mind is intended, and not one that is merely harsh to the ear. 'Tassa' means: of the exclusively harsh volition. 'Āvibhāvattham' means: for the purpose of making manifest the state of being harsh speech. Or, 'tassa' means: of the exclusively harsh volition; the meaning is 'of the state of being harsh speech'. 'Tatheva' means: in the very manner spoken by the mother; the meaning is 'she arose to pursue'. The 'saccakiriyaṃ' (truth-act) is this: The words she spoke with her mouth, 'May the fierce buffalo pursue you,' were not in the mother's mind. Therefore, 'Let that not be.' But the fact that she thought with her mind, 'May not even a lotus petal fall upon me,' that is in the mother's mind. Therefore, 'Let that very thing be' is the making of a truth-act, or the truth that should be performed. 'Tattheva' means: in the very place of arising. 'Baddhā viya' means: as if bound all around with a rope, etc. Thus, here in 'mammacchedako', the state of being a 'mammacchedaka' should be understood by mere harshness to the ear.

Payogoti [M 1.0341] vacīpayogo. Cittasaṇhatāyāti ekantapharusacetanāya abhāvamāha. Tatoyeva hi pharusavācā na hoti kammapathappattā, kammabhāvaṃ pana na sakkā vāretunti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Mātāpitaro hī”tiādināpi tadevatthaṃ samattheti. Evaṃ byatirekavasena cetanāpharusatāya pharusavācābhāvaṃ sādhetvā idāni tameva anvayavasena sādhetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apharusā vācā na hoti pharusā vācā hotiyevāti attho sāti pharusavācā. Yanti puggalaṃ.

'Payogo' means verbal exertion. By 'cittasaṇhatāya' (gentleness of mind), he speaks of the absence of an exclusively harsh volition. Indeed, for that very reason, harsh speech does not reach the level of a course of action (kammapatha), but it should be understood that its nature as kamma cannot be prevented. The passage beginning 'Mātāpitaro hi' also establishes that same meaning. Thus, having established the absence of harsh speech by way of exclusion due to the non-harshness of volition, now, to establish that very thing by way of inclusion, the passage beginning 'yathā' was stated. The meaning is: it is not non-harsh speech; it is indeed harsh speech. 'Sā' refers to harsh speech. 'Yaṃ' refers to the person.

Etthāpi kammapathabhāvaṃ appattā appasāvajjā, itarā mahāsāvajjā. Tathā kilesānaṃ mudutibbatābhedepi yojetabbaṃ. Keci pana “yaṃ uddissa pharusavācā payujjati, tassa sammukhāyeva sīsaṃ etī”ti vadanti, eke pana “parammukhāpi pharusavācā hotiyevā”ti. Tatthāyamadhippāyo yutto siyā, sammukhā payoge agāravādīnaṃ balavabhāvato siyā cetanā balavatī, parassa ca tadatthavijānanaṃ, na tathā parammukhā. Yathā pana akkosite mate āḷahane katā khamanā upavādantarāyaṃ nivatteti, evaṃ parammukhā payuttāpi pharusavācā hotiyevāti sakkā ñātunti, tasmā ubhayatthāpi pharusavācā sambhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi parassa tadatthavijānanamaññatra tayova tassā sambhārā aṭṭhakathāsu vuttāti. Kupitacittanti akkosanādhippāyeneva vuttaṃ, na pana maraṇādhippāyena. Maraṇādhippāyena hi sati cittakope atthasiddhiyā, tadabhāve ca yathārahaṃ pāṇātipātabyāpādāva honti.

Herein also, harsh speech that has not attained the state of a course of action is of little fault; the other is of great fault. Similarly, this should be applied also to the distinction of mildness and intensity of the defilements. Some, however, say: 'When harsh speech is uttered directed at someone, it reaches its culmination only in their presence.' But others say: 'Harsh speech indeed occurs even in absence.' Therein, this interpretation would be suitable: when uttered in presence, because of the strength of disrespect and so on, the volition would be strong, and the other person would understand its meaning; it would not be so in absence. Just as, when one who was reviled has died, the asking for forgiveness done at the cremation ground removes the danger of censure, so too it can be known that harsh speech uttered in absence indeed occurs. Therefore, it should be understood that harsh speech occurs in both cases. For indeed, apart from the other person's understanding of its meaning, its three requisites alone are stated in the commentaries. 'With an angry mind' is said only with the intention to revile, but not with the intention to kill. For, with the intention to kill, when there is anger of mind, through the accomplishment of the purpose it is killing, and in the absence thereof it is ill will, as is appropriate.

Elaṃ vuccati doso ilati cittaṃ, puggalo vā kampati etenāti katvā. Etthāti –

A fault (dosa) is called 'elaṃ' because by it (etena) the mind (cittaṃ) shakes (ilati) or a person (puggalo) trembles (kampati). As to 'ettha':

“Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattatī ratho;

Anīghaṃ passa āyantaṃ, chinnasotaṃ abandhana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 4.347; udā. 65; peṭako. 25); –

The chariot with no fault and a white covering, with a single axle, rolls on; behold him coming, free from affliction, with the stream cut off, without bonds.

Imissā udānagāthāya. Sīlañhettha niddosatāya “nela”nti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha citto gahapati āyasmatā kāmabhūtherena puṭṭho saṃyuttāgamavare saḷāyatanavagge “nelaṅga”nti kho bhante sīlānametaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.347) vācā nāma saddasabhāvā taṃtadatthanibandhanāti [V 1.0301] sādurasasadisattā madhurameva byañjanaṃ, attho ca tabbhāvatoti atthameva sandhāya byañjanamadhuratāya[M 1.0342], atthamadhuratāyā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Visesanaparanipātopi hi loke dissati “agyāhito”tiādīsu. Apica avayavāpekkhane sati “madhuraṃ byañjanaṃ yassā”tiādinā vattabbo. Sukhāti sukhakaraṇī, sukhahetūti vuttaṃ hoti. Kaṇṇasūlanti kaṇṇasaṅkuṃ. Kaṇṇasaddena cettha sotaviññāṇapaṭibaddhatadanuvattakā viññāṇavīthiyo gahitā. Vohārakathā hesā suttantadesanā, tassā vaṇṇanā ca, tathā ceva vuttaṃ “sakalasarīre kopaṃ, pema”nti ca. Na hi hadayavatthunissito kopo, pemo ca sakalasarīre vattati. Esa nayo īdisesu. Sukhena cittaṃ pavisati yathāvuttakāraṇadvayenāti attho, aluttasamāso cesa yathā “amataṅgato”ti. Pureti guṇapāripure, tenāha “guṇaparipuṇṇatāyā”ti. Pure saṃvaḍḍhā porī, tādisā nārī viyāti vācāpi porīti atthamāha “pure”tiādinā. Sukumārāti sutaruṇā. Upameyyapakkhe pana apharusatāya mudukabhāvo eva sukumāratā. Purassāti ettha pura-saddo tannivāsīvācako sahacaraṇavasena “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya, tenevāha “nagaravāsīna”nti. Esāti taṃsambandhīniddesā vācā. Evarūpī kathāti atthattayena pakāsitā kathā. Kantāti kāmitā tuṭṭhā yathā “pakkanto”ti, māna-saddassa vā antabyappadeso, kāmiyamānāti attho. Yathā “anāpatti asamanubhāsantassā”ti (pārā. 416, 430, 441) manaṃ appeti vaḍḍhetīti manāpā, tena vuttaṃ “cittavuḍḍhikarā”ti. Tathākārinīti attho. Ato bahuno janassāti idha sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ, na tu purimasmiṃ viya kattari.

In this Udāna verse. Herein, virtue (sīla), because of its faultlessness, is called 'nela'. Therefore, the householder Citta, when asked by the Venerable Kāmabhū Thera in the excellent Saṃyutta Āgama, in the Saḷāyatana Vagga, said: 'Bhante, "nelaṅga" is a designation for virtues.' Speech, by nature, is sound, and it is bound to its respective meaning. Because it is like a pleasant taste, the phrasing is sweet, and because of that quality, the meaning is also sweet. With reference only to this meaning, it was said 'due to sweetness of phrasing' and 'due to sweetness of meaning'. Indeed, in the world, the post-positioning of an adjective is also seen, as in 'agyāhito', etc. Moreover, when considering the components, it is stated as 'that (speech) which has sweet phrasing', etc. 'Sukhā' means it is productive of happiness, a cause of happiness. 'Kaṇṇasūla' means a thorn in the ear. And here, by the word 'ear' (kaṇṇa), the cognitive series that are connected with and follow upon ear-consciousness are taken. For this Suttanta teaching is conventional speech, as is its commentary. And just so it was said: 'anger in the whole body' and 'love'. For anger and love, which are based on the heart-base, do not occur in the entire body. This is the method in such cases. The meaning is: 'it enters the mind easily due to the two reasons mentioned.' And this is an unelided compound (aluttasamāsa), like 'amataṅgato'. 'Pure' is in the sense of 'fulfillment of virtues'; therefore he said 'due to being full of virtues'. She who is raised in a town (pure) is a townswoman (porī); like such a woman, speech is also 'porī'. He states this meaning with 'pure', etc. 'Sukumārā' means very tender. But on the side of the thing compared, tenderness (sukumāratā) is simply the state of being soft due to non-harshness. Here, in 'purassa', the word 'pura' denotes a resident of that town by way of association, as in 'the village has come', etc. Therefore he said 'of the city-dwellers' (nagaravāsīnaṃ). 'Esā' is the speech indicated in connection with that resident. 'Such speech' is speech explained by way of three meanings. 'Kantā' means desired, pleasing, as in 'pakkanto'. Or it is the designation of the final part of the word 'māna'; the meaning is 'being desired'. As in 'no offense for one who is not admonishing'. It pleases or increases the mind, therefore it is 'manāpā'. For that reason it was said 'it increases the mind' (cittavuḍḍhikarā). The meaning is 'acting in such a way'. Therefore, here in 'bahuno janassa', it is the genitive case in the sense of relation, and not in the sense of agent as in the previous instance.

Kāmaṃ tehi vattumicchito attho sambhavati, so pana aphalattā bhāsitatthapariyāyena atthoyeva nāma na hotīti āha “anatthaviññāpikā”ti. Apica payojanatthābhāvato anatthā, vācā, taṃ viññāpikātipi vaṭṭati. Akusalacetanā samphappalāpo samphaṃ palapanti etāyāti katvā. Āsevanaṃ bhāvanaṃ bahulīkaraṇaṃ. Yaṃ janaṃ gāhāpayituṃ pavattito, tena aggahite appasāvajjo, gahite mahāsāvajjo. Kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvasenāpi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā yojetabbā. Bhāratanāmakānaṃ dvebhātukarājūnaṃ yuddhakathā, dasagiriyakkhena sītāya nāma deviyā āharaṇakathā, rāmaraññā paccāharaṇakathā[M 1.0343], yathā taṃ adhunā bāhirakehi paricayitā sakkaṭabhāsāya gaṇṭhitā rāmapurāṇabhāratapurāṇādikathāti, evamādikā niratthakakathā samphappalāpoti vuttaṃ “bhārata…pe… purekkhāratā”ti.

Granted, the meaning they intended to speak may exist, but since it is fruitless, it is not truly a meaning in the sense of a spoken meaning; therefore he said it is 'that which makes known what is not the meaning.' Moreover, this meaning is also suitable: because of the absence of a purposeful meaning, it is meaningless speech, which makes that known. The unwholesome volition is frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa) because 'they prattle frivolously (samphaṃ palapanti) with it.' Cultivating is developing, making much of. When it is undertaken to make a person grasp it, if it is not grasped by that person, it is of little fault; if grasped, it is of great fault. The state of having little or great fault should also be applied according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements. The story of the war between the two brother-kings named Bhārata, the story of the ten-headed yakkha abducting the queen named Sītā, the story of King Rāma bringing her back—just as now the stories of the ancient Rāma, the ancient Bhārata, etc., composed in the Sanskrit language and practiced by outsiders—such and similar useless talk is frivolous chatter. Therefore it was said: 'the Bhārata... and so on... being prominent.'

“Kālavādī”tiādi samphappalāpā paṭiviratassa paṭipattisandassanaṃ yathā “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.8, 194) pāṇātipātappahānassa paṭipattidassanaṃ. “Pāṇātipātaṃ [V 1.0302] pahāya viharatī”ti hi vutte kathaṃ pāṇātipātappahānaṃ hotīti apekkhāsambhavato “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Sā pana virati kathanti āha “nihitadaṇḍo nihita sattho”ti. Tañca daṇḍasatthanidhānaṃ kathanti vuttaṃ “lajjī”tiādi. Evaṃ uttaruttaraṃ purimassa purimassa upāyasandassanaṃ. Tathā adinnādānādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “kālavādītiādi samphappalāpā paṭiviratassa paṭipattisandassana”nti. Atthasaṃhitāpi hi vācā ayuttakālapayogena atthāvahā na siyāti anatthaviññāpanabhāvaṃ anulometi, tasmā samphappalāpaṃ pajahantena akālavāditā parivajjetabbāti dassetuṃ “kālavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Kāle vadantenāpi ubhayattha asādhanato abhūtaṃ parivajjetabbanti āha “bhūtavādī”ti. Bhūtañca vadantena yaṃ idhalokaparalokahitasampādanakaṃ, tadeva vattabbanti vuttaṃ “atthavādī”ti. Atthaṃ vadantenāpi na lokiyadhammanissitameva vattabbaṃ, atha kho lokuttaradhammanissitampīti āha “dhammavādī”ti. Yathā ca attho lokuttaradhammanissito hoti, tathā dassanatthaṃ “vinayavādī”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Speaking at the right time’ and so on is a demonstration of the practice of one who abstains from frivolous chatter, just as ‘abstaining from the destruction of life’ and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.8, 194) is a demonstration of the practice of abandoning the destruction of life. For when it is said, ‘He dwells having abandoned the destruction of life,’ since the expectation of the question, ‘How does the abandoning of the destruction of life come to be?’ is possible, it is said, ‘He is one who abstains from the destruction of life.’ Furthermore, as to the question, ‘What is that abstinence?’ the Teacher says, ‘He has laid down the rod, he has laid down the weapon.’ And as to the question, ‘What is that laying down of rod and weapon?’ it is said, ‘He is conscientious,’ and so on. Thus, each succeeding statement is a demonstration of the means for each preceding one. Similarly, it should be applied to taking what is not given and the rest as is appropriate. Therefore, it was said, ‘“Speaking at the right time” and so on is a demonstration of the practice of one who abstains from frivolous chatter.’ For even speech connected with benefit, if used at an unsuitable time, would not be beneficial; it conforms to the nature of communicating what is without benefit. Therefore, to show that one who is abandoning frivolous chatter should avoid speaking at an unsuitable time, it is said, ‘He speaks at the right time.’ Even when speaking at the right time, one should avoid what is not true, since it does not accomplish benefit for both parties; thus, it is said, ‘He speaks what is factual.’ And when speaking what is factual, only that which accomplishes welfare in this world and the next should be spoken; thus, it was said, ‘He speaks what is beneficial.’ Even when speaking what is beneficial, one should not speak only what is based on worldly Dhamma, but rather also what is based on supramundane Dhamma; thus, he said, ‘He speaks the Dhamma.’ And to show in what way the meaning is based on the supramundane Dhamma, it was said, ‘He speaks the Vinaya.’

Pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satiñāṇakhantivīriyasaṃvaroti hi pañcannaṃ saṃvaravinayānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇappahānanti pañcannaṃ pahānavinayānañca vasena vuccamāno attho nibbānādhigamahetubhāvato lokuttaradhammasannissito hoti. Evaṃ guṇavisesayutto ca attho vuccamāno desanākosalle sati sobhati, kiccakaro ca hoti, nāññathāti dassetuṃ “nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni tameva desanākosallaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kālenā”tiādimāha. Ajjhāsayaṭṭhuppattīnaṃ, pucchāya ca vasena otiṇṇe desanāvisaye ekaṃsādibyākaraṇavibhāgaṃ sallakkhetvā ṭhapanāhetudāharaṇasaṃsandanāni taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ [M 1.0344] vibhāventiyā parimitaparicchinnarūpāya gambhīrudānapahūtatthavitthārasaṅgāhikāya desanāya pare yathājjhāsayaṃ paramatthasiddhiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpento “desanākusalo”ti vuccatīti evametthāpi atthayojanā veditabbā.

Indeed, the meaning spoken of by way of the five discipline-restraints—restraint of the Pātimokkha, and restraint of mindfulness, knowledge, patience, and energy—and of the five discipline-abandonments—abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by cutting off, abandonment by tranquillization, and abandonment by escape—becomes based on the supramundane Dhamma, because of its being a cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. And thus the meaning, being endowed with special qualities, when spoken with skill in teaching, shines and is effective; it is not otherwise. To show this, it was said, ‘He has spoken words that are a treasure-trove.’ Now, to make clear that very skill in teaching, the Teacher said, ‘At the right time,’ and so on. One who, when the domain of the teaching has been entered by way of the dispositions, the circumstances of the teaching's origin, and questions, having marked the analysis of the explanations, such as the categorical one, and clarifying the establishment, reason, example, and connection in accordance with each respective time, by means of a teaching that has a measured and defined nature, that is profound in utterance, abundant in meaning, and comprehensive in scope, establishes others, according to their disposition, in the accomplishment of the ultimate goal, is called ‘one skilled in teaching.’ Thus, the application of the meaning should be understood here also in this way.

Vattabbayuttakālanti vattabbavacanassa anurūpakālaṃ, tattha vā payujjitabbakālaṃ. Sabhāvavaseneva bhūtatāti āha “sabhāvamevā”ti. Atthaṃ vadatīti atthavādī. Atthavadanañca tannissitavācākathanamevāti adhippāyena vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthasannissitameva katvā”ti. Dhammavādī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘The time suitable for speaking’ means the time appropriate for the speech to be spoken, or the time when it should be employed. Truthfulness exists simply by way of its intrinsic nature; therefore, he said, ‘simply its nature.’ Because one speaks what is beneficial, one is a ‘speaker of what is beneficial.’ And the speaking of what is beneficial is simply the speaking of speech based on that benefit; with this intention it was said, ‘having made it based solely on the benefit pertaining to the present life and the future life.’ In the case of ‘speaker of Dhamma’ and so on, this same method should be understood.

Nidheti sannidhānaṃ karoti etthāti nidhānaṃ. Ṭhapanokāso. “Ṭhānavatī”ti vutte tasmiṃ ṭhāne [V 1.0303] ṭhapetuṃ yuttātipi attho sambhavatīti āha “hadaye”tiādi. Nidhānavatīpi vācā kālayuttāva atthāvahā, tasmā “kālenā”ti idaṃ “nidhānavatiṃ” vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti etassāpekkhavacananti dasseti “evarūpi”ntiādinā. Icchitatthanibbattanatthaṃ apadisitabbo, apadisīyati vā icchitattho anenāti apadeso, upamā, hetudāharaṇādikāraṇaṃ vā, tena saha vattatīti sāpadesā, vācā, tenāha “saupamaṃ sakāraṇanti attho”ti. Paricchedaṃ dassetvāti yāvatā pariyosānaṃ sambhavati, tāvatā mariyādaṃ dassetvā, tena vuttaṃ “yathā…pe… bhāsatī”ti. Sikhamappattā hi kathā atthāvahā nāma na hoti. Atthasaṃhitanti ettha attha-saddo bhāsitatthapariyāyoti vuttaṃ “anekehipī”tiādi. Bhāsitattho ca nāma saddānusārena adhigato sabbopi pakatyatthapaccayatthabhāvatthādiko, tatoyeva bhagavato vacanaṃ ekagāthāpadampi saṅkhepavitthārādiekattādinandiyāvattādinayehi anekehipi niddhāraṇakkhamatāya pariyādātumasakkuṇeyyaṃ atthamāvahatīti. Evaṃ atthasāmaññato saṃvaṇṇetvā icchitatthavisesatopi saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “yaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Atthavādinā vattumicchitatthoyeva hi idha gahito. Nanu sabbesampi vacanaṃ attanā icchitatthasahitaṃyeva, kimettha vattabbaṃ atthīti antolīnacodanaṃ parisodheti “na añña”ntiādinā. Aññamatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhipitvā ananusandhivasena pacchā aññamatthaṃ na bhāsati. Yathānikkhittānusandhivaseneva pariyosāpetvā kathetīti adhippāyo.

One stores, one makes a repository in it, thus it is a ‘repository’ (nidhāna), a place for keeping. When ‘possessing a place’ (ṭhānavatī) is said, since the meaning ‘suitable to be kept in that place’ is also possible, he says, ‘in the heart,’ etc. Even speech that is a treasure-trove is beneficial only when timely. Therefore, ‘at the right time’ is a phrase dependent on ‘speaks words that are a treasure-trove’; this he shows with ‘of such a kind,’ etc. A reason (apadeso) is so called because a reason should be pointed out for producing the desired meaning, or because the desired meaning is pointed out by it—it may be a simile, a cause such as a reason or an example, etc. Speech that occurs together with that is ‘with reason’ (sāpadesā). Therefore, he said, ‘The meaning is “with simile, with reason.”’ ‘Having shown the limit’ means having shown the boundary as far as the conclusion is possible; therefore, it was said, ‘just as… he speaks.’ For speech that has not reached its culmination is not called beneficial. Here in ‘connected with meaning’ (atthasaṃhitaṃ), the word ‘meaning’ (attha) is a synonym for ‘the meaning of what is spoken’ (bhāsitattha); thus it was said, ‘by many,’ etc. And ‘the meaning of what is spoken’ is all that is understood according to the words—the root meaning, the suffix meaning, the abstract meaning, and so on. For that very reason, even a single verse or phrase of the Blessed One, due to its capacity to be determined in many ways through methods such as the concise and the detailed, the singular, and the ‘nandiyāvatta,’ brings forth a meaning that cannot be exhausted. Thus, having explained it in terms of its general meaning, in order to explain it also in terms of its specific intended meaning, he said, ‘or whatever,’ etc. For here, it is only the meaning intended to be spoken by the speaker of what is beneficial that is taken. He clarifies the latent objection—‘Surely, is not all speech accompanied by the meaning intended by oneself? What is there to be said here?’—with ‘not another,’ etc. The intention is that he does not, after first setting down one meaning, later speak another meaning in a disconnected way; he speaks, bringing it to a conclusion only in accordance with the connection as it was laid down.

10. Evaṃ [M 1.0345] paṭipāṭiyā sattamūlasikkhāpadāni vibhajitvā satipi abhijjhādippahānassa saṃvarasīlasaṅgahe upariguṇasaṅgahato, lokiyaputhujjanāvisayato ca uttaridesanāya saṅgahituṃ taṃ pariharitvā pacurajanapākaṭaṃ ācārasīlameva vibhajanto bhagavā “bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā”tiādimāhāti pāḷiyaṃ sambandho vattabbo. Tattha vijāyanti viruhanti etehīti bījāni. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhanasamatthānaṃ sāraphalādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhavanti, ahuvunti cāti bhūtā, jāyanti vaḍḍhanti jātā, vaḍḍhitā cāti attho. Vaḍḍhamānakānaṃ vaḍḍhitvā, ṭhitānañca rukkhagacchādīnaṃ yathākkamamadhivacanaṃ. Viruḷhamūlā hi nīlabhāvaṃ āpajjantā taruṇarukkhagacchā jāyanti vaḍḍhantīti vuccanti. Vaḍḍhitvā ṭhitā mahantā rukkhagacchā jātā vaḍḍhitāti. Gāmoti samūho, so ca suddhaṭṭhakadhammarāsi, bījānaṃ, bhūtānañca tathāladdhasamaññānaṃ aṭṭhadhammānaṃ gāmo, teyeva vā gāmoti tathā. Avayavavinimuttassa hi samudāyassa abhāvato duvidhenāpi atthena teyeva tiṇarukkhalatādayo gayhanti.

10. Thus, having analyzed the seven root training rules in sequence, although the abandonment of covetousness and so on is included in the virtue of restraint, the Blessed One—in order to include it in a higher teaching by way of collecting higher qualities and as being beyond the sphere of worldly ordinary people—set that aside and, explaining only the virtue of conduct which is well-known to the common people, said, beginning with ‘the destruction of seed-life and plant-life.’ Thus, the connection in the Pāli text is stated. Therein, ‘seeds’ (bījāni) are so called because by them things are born and sprout. This is a designation for things capable of sprouting—such as essential fruits and the like—because of their being a special cause for the production of a similar fruit when there is a conjunction of other conditions. ‘Grown things’ (bhūtā) are what exist or have existed; the meaning is that they are born and grow, or have been born and have grown. It is a designation, in sequence, for trees, shrubs, and so on that are growing, and for those that have grown and are established. Indeed, young trees and shrubs that have rooted and are becoming green are said to ‘be born and grow.’ Large trees and shrubs that have grown and are established are called ‘born and grown.’ ‘Group’ (gāmo) means a collection, and that is a mass of pure octad-phenomena; it is a group of the eight phenomena that have received the designation of ‘seeds’ and ‘grown things,’ or they themselves are the group. Indeed, since there is no aggregate separate from its parts, by both meanings, those very grasses, trees, creepers, and so on are taken.

Apica bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā haritabhāvamāpannā rukkhagacchādayo devatā pariggayhanti, tasmā [V 1.0304] bhūtānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānatāya gāmoti bhūtagāmotipi vadanti, te sarūpato dassetuṃ “mūlabīja”ntiādimāha. Mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ. Sesesupi ayaṃ nayo. Phaḷubījanti pabbabījaṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhanasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bīja-saddo tadatthasiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā “bījabīja”nti vuttaṃ yathā “rūpaṃrūpaṃ, dukkhadukkha”nti ca. Nīlatiṇarukkhādikassāti allatiṇassa ceva allarukkhādikassa ca. Ādi-saddena osadhigacchalatādayo veditabbā. Samārambho idha vikopanaṃ, tañca chedanādiyevāti vuttaṃ “chedanabhedanapacanādibhāvenā”ti. Nanu ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca paripphandanābhāvato, chinne viruhanato, visadisajātikabhāvato, catuyoniapariyāpannato ca veditabbā. Vuḍḍhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇādīnampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvatābhāve kāraṇaṃ. Visayaggahaṇañca nesaṃ parikappanāmattaṃ supanaṃ viya ciñcādīnaṃ, tathā kaṭukambilāsādinā dohaḷādayo. Tattha kasmā bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā [M 1.0346] paṭivirati icchitāti? Samaṇasāruppato, tannissitasattānukampanato ca. Tenevāha āḷavakānaṃ rukkhacchedanādivatthūsu “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisā manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi (pārā. 89).

Moreover, deities take possession of trees, shrubs, and so forth that are established on the earth and have become green; therefore, because they are a dwelling place for spirits, the teachers also say it is a ‘community of spirits’ (bhūtagāma). To show them in their essential nature, the author said ‘root-seed’ and so forth. The root itself is the seed, hence ‘root-seed.’ This method applies to the rest as well. ‘Segment-seed’ (phaḷubīja) means ‘joint-seed’ (pabbabīja). The word ‘seed’ (bīja) is established in the sense of an essential fruit capable of sprouting, due to its being a special cause for the production of a similar fruit when there is a conjunction of other conditions. For the accomplishment of that meaning, it also occurs in some cases for roots and so forth. Therefore, to distinguish it from roots and the like, it is specified with the one word ‘seed’ and called ‘seed-seed’ (bījabīja), just as in ‘form-form’ (rūparūpa) and ‘suffering-suffering’ (dukkhadukkha). ‘Of green grass, trees, etc.’ means of fresh grass and fresh trees and so forth. By the word ‘etc.,’ medicinal plants, shrubs, creepers, and so forth should be understood. Here, ‘destruction’ (samārambha) means injury, and that is just cutting and so forth; therefore it was said: ‘by way of cutting, breaking, cooking, etc.’ But are not trees and so forth not living beings because they lack consciousness? And their lack of consciousness should be understood from the absence of movement, from their sprouting when cut, from their being of a dissimilar species, and from their not being included in the four kinds of birth. However, growth is also found in coral, rock, salt, and so forth, so that is not a reason for their being alive. And their grasping of objects is mere supposition, like the sleeping of the tamarind tree, and similarly, cravings and so forth due to bitter, sour, etc. In that case, why is abstinence from the destruction of seed-life and plant-life desired? Because it is fitting for a contemplative, and out of compassion for the beings dependent on them. Therefore, concerning the Āḷavakas’ cutting of trees and so forth, the Blessed One said: ‘Indeed, foolish men, humans have the perception of life in trees...’

Ekaṃ bhattaṃ ekabhattaṃ, tamassa atthi ekasmiṃ divase ekavārameva bhuñjanatoti ekabhattiko. Tayidaṃ ekabhattaṃ kadā bhuñjitabbanti sandhāya vuttaṃ “pātarāsabhatta”ntiādi, dvīsu bhattesu pātarāsabhattaṃ sandhāyāhāti adhippāyo. Pāto asitabbanti pātarāsaṃ. Sāyaṃ asitabbanti sāyamāsaṃ, tadeva bhattaṃ tathā. Eka-saddo cettha majjhanhikakālaparicchedabhāvena payutto, na tadantogadhavārabhāvenāti dasseti “tasmā”tiādinā.

One meal is 'ekabhatta.' One who eats only once a day has this, hence 'one-meal eater' (ekabhattiko). Concerning when this one meal should be eaten, it is stated 'the morning meal' and so forth. The intention is that he speaks with reference to the morning meal among the two meals. What is eaten in the morning is 'pātarāsa' (morning meal). What is eaten in the evening is 'sāyamāsa' (evening meal); that meal is likewise. And here, the word 'one' (eka) is used in the sense of defining the midday period, not in the sense of the number of times included therein, as he shows with 'therefore' and so forth.

Rattiyā bhojanaṃ uttarapadalopato rattisaddena vuttaṃ, taddhitavasena vā tathāyevādhippāyasambhavato, tenāha “rattiyā”tiādi. Aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikā ayaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Tattha dutiyapadena rattibhojanassa paṭikkhittattā aparanhova idha vikāloti pārisesanayena tatiyapadassa atthaṃ dīpetuṃ “atikkante majjhanhike”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhāvasādhano cettha bhojana-saddo ajjhoharaṇatthavācakoti dīpeti “yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojana”nti iminā. Kassa pana tadajjhoharaṇanti? Yāmakālikādīnamanuññātattā, vikālabhojanasaddassa ca yāvakālikajjhoharaṇeyeva niruḷhattā “yāvakālikassā”ti viññāyati. Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathāvaseso ācariyānaṃ nayo – bhuñjitabbaṭṭhena bhojanaṃ, yāgubhattādi sabbaṃ yāvakālikavatthu[V 1.0305]. Yathā ca “rattūparato”ti ettha rattibhojanaṃ rattisaddena vuccati, evamettha bhojanajjhoharaṇaṃ bhojanasaddena. Vikāle bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ, tato vikālabhojanā. Vikāle yāvakālikavatthussa ajjhoharaṇāti atthoti. Īdisā guṇavibhūti na buddhakāleyevāti āha “anomānadītīre”tiādi. Ayaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ anusandhikkamo – ekasmiṃ divase ekavārameva bhuñjanato “ekabhattiko”ti vutte rattibhojanopi siyāti [M 1.0347] tannivāraṇatthaṃ “rattūparato”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sati sāyanhabhojīpi ekabhattiko siyāti tadāsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ “virato vikālabhojanā”ti vuttanti.

Eating at night is expressed by the word 'night' due to the elision of the latter word, or it is so expressed by way of a taddhita derivative, as the intended meaning is possible in that way. Therefore, the teacher said, 'at night,' and so forth. From the rising of dawn until midday is the time for meals, customarily practiced by the noble ones such as the Buddhas; any other time is an improper time. Therein, since eating at night is rejected by the second term, it is said, 'when midday has passed,' and so on, in order to clarify by the method of elimination that here the 'improper time' (vikāla) is the afternoon, which is the meaning of the third term. And here, the word 'eating' (bhojana), being a noun of action, conveys the meaning of consumption, as the teacher shows with 'eating until sunset.' But the consumption of what is that? Since yāmakālika items and so forth are permitted, and since the term 'eating at an improper time' (vikālabhojana) is established only in the consumption of a yāvakālika item, it is understood as 'of a yāvakālika item.' This, however, is a supplementary explanation from the commentary, the method of the teachers: 'food' (bhojana) in the sense of what is to be eaten; everything, such as gruel and rice, is a yāvakālika substance. And just as in 'refraining from [eating at] night,' eating at night is expressed by the word 'night,' so here the consumption of food is expressed by the word 'eating.' Eating at an improper time is vikālabhojana; hence, 'from eating at an improper time.' The meaning is the consumption of a yāvakālika substance at an improper time. Such a splendor of virtue was not only in the Buddha's time; hence, he said, 'on the banks of the Anomā River,' and so forth. This, however, is the sequence of connection in the Pāli: When it is said 'one-session-eater' (ekabhattiko) because one eats only once a day, one who eats at night could also be so considered. To prevent that, it is stated, 'refraining from [eating at] night.' This being so, an evening eater could also be a 'one-session-eater.' To dispel that doubt, it is stated, 'refraining from eating at an improper time.'

Saṅkhepato “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183; netti. 30, 50, 116, 124) nayappavattaṃ bhagavato sāsanaṃ sachandarāgappavattito naccādīnaṃ dassanaṃ nānulometīti āha “sāsanassa ananulomattā”ti. Visucati sāsanaṃ vijjhati ananulomikabhāvenāti visūkaṃ, paṭiviruddhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatra upamaṃ dasseti “paṭāṇībhūta”nti iminā, paṭāṇīsaṅkhātaṃ kīlaṃ viya bhūtanti attho. “Visūka”nti etassa paṭāṇībhūtanti atthamāhātipi vadanti. Attanā payojiyamānaṃ, parehi payojāpiyamānañca naccaṃ naccabhāvasāmaññato pāḷiyaṃ ekeneva naccasaddena sāmaññaniddesanayena gahitaṃ, ekasesanayena vā. Tathā gītavāditasaddehi gāyanagāyāpanavādanavādāpanānīti āha “naccananaccāpanādivasenā”ti. Suddhahetutājotanavasena hi dvādhippāyikā ete saddā. Naccañca gītañca vāditañca visūkadassanañca naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ, samāhāravasenettha ekattaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yathāpāṭhaṃ vākyāvatthikantavacanena saha samuccayasamāsadassanatthaṃ “naccā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha īdisesu. (Dassanavisaye mayūranaccādipaṭikkhipanena naccāpanavisayepi paṭikkhipanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ) “naccādīni hī”tiādinā yathāvuttatthasamatthanaṃ. Dassanena cettha savanampi saṅgahitaṃ virūpekasesanayena, yathāsakaṃ vā visayassa ālocanasabhāvatāya pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ savanakiriyāyapi dassanasaṅkhepasambhavato “dassanā” icceva vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kiñci dhammaṃ paṭijānāti aññatra atinipātamattā”ti.

Because it proceeds with desire and passion, the seeing of dancing and so on is not in conformity with the Blessed One's teaching, which proceeds in brief according to the method of 'the non-doing of all evil,' etc. Therefore, the teacher said, 'because of its non-conformity with the teaching.' It is called visūka because it pierces the teaching through its non-conformity; this means it is said to be 'contrary.' Therein, he shows a simile with this: 'having become a stake.' The meaning is: 'become like a stake called a paṭāṇī.' Some teachers also say that he states the meaning of visūka as 'having become a stake.' Dancing performed by oneself and causing others to dance are included in the Pāli by the single word 'dancing' (nacca) due to the generality of the state of dancing, by the method of general indication, or by the method of ekasesa. Similarly, by the words 'singing' (gīta) and 'music' (vādita), singing oneself, causing others to sing, playing music oneself, and causing others to play are included. Therefore, the teacher said, 'by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so on.' Indeed, these words have a dual meaning by way of indicating both the simple agent and the causative agent. 'Dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows' (naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ) is a compound of dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows that are like stakes to the teaching. Herein, it is in the singular due to being an aggregative copulative compound. In the commentary, however, in order to show the cumulative compound together with the word ending the clause, according to the text, it is said by the teacher, 'naccā ca,' and so on. Thus it should be understood by the wise in all such cases. (In the sphere of seeing, by the rejection of the dancing of peacocks and so on, the rejection in the sphere of causing to dance should also be seen.) By the text beginning 'naccādīni hi,' the meaning as stated is established. And here, by 'seeing' (dassana), hearing is also included by the method of virūpekasesa. Or, because the five consciousnesses have the nature of apprehending their respective objects, and since the action of hearing can be included under 'seeing,' it was said by the Blessed One only as 'seeing.' For that very reason, it is said in the commentary: 'By the five consciousnesses, one does not know any phenomenon apart from the mere falling upon the object.'

“Visūkabhūtā dassanā cā”ti etena avisūkabhūtassa pana gītassa savanaṃ kadāci vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭhaṭṭhakathāya “dhammūpasaṃhitampi cettha gītaṃ na vaṭṭati, gītūpasaṃhito pana dhammo vaṭṭatī”ti (khu. pā. aṭṭha. pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) katthaci pana na-kāravipariyāyena pāṭho dissati. Ubhayatthāpi ca [V 1.0306] gīto ce dhammānulomatthapaṭisaṃyuttopi na vaṭṭati, dhammo ce gītasaddapaṭisaṃyuttopi vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo veditabbo. “Na bhikkhave, gītassarena [M 1.0348] dhammo gāyitabbo, yo gāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 149) hi desanāya eva paṭikkhepo, na savanāya. Imassa ca sikkhāpadassa visuṃ paññāpanato viññāyati “gītassarena desitopi dhammo na gīto”ti. Yañca sakkapañhasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbasaddaṃ niddharantena “yaṃ pana atthanissitaṃ dhammanissitaṃ kumbhadāsigītampi suṇantassa pasādo vā uppajjati, nibbidā vā saṇṭhāti, evarūpo saddo sevitabbo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.365) vuttaṃ, taṃ asamādānasikkhāpadassa sevitabbatāmattapariyāyena vuttaṃ. Samādānasikkhāpadassa hi evarūpaṃ suṇantassa sikkhāpadasaṃvaraṃ bhijjati gītasaddabhāvatoti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi vinayaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ “gītanti naṭādīnaṃ vā gītaṃ hotu, ariyānaṃ parinibbānakāle ratanattayaguṇūpasaṃhitaṃ sādhukīḷanagītaṃ vā, asaṃyatabhikkhūnaṃ dhammabhāṇakagītaṃ vā, antamaso dantagītampi, yaṃ “gāyissāmā”ti pubbabhāge okūjitaṃ karonti, sabbametaṃ gītaṃ nāmā”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 835; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 34.25).

By this phrase, 'and the seeing of spectacles,' it is shown that listening to singing which is not like a thorn to the Sāsana is sometimes permissible. For thus it is stated in the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha: 'Here, even a song connected with the Dhamma is not permissible; but the Dhamma connected with singing is permissible.' In some places, however, a reading with the negation reversed is seen. And in both cases, the meaning should be understood thus: if it is singing, even if connected with a meaning that conforms to the Dhamma, it is not permissible; but if it is the Dhamma, even if connected with the sound of singing, it is permissible. Indeed, the prohibition 'Bhikkhus, the Dhamma should not be chanted with a musical intonation; whoever should chant it, there is an offense of wrongdoing' is only for the preaching, not for the listening. And from the separate promulgation of this training rule, it is understood that 'even the Dhamma taught with a musical intonation is not singing.' And what is stated in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta, when distinguishing the words 'to be associated with' and 'not to be associated with'—'But if, on hearing a sound, even the singing of a potter's female servant, which is based on meaning and based on the Dhamma, either serenity arises or dispassion is established, such a sound should be associated with'—that is stated by way of mere permissibility of association for one who has not undertaken the training rule. For one who has undertaken the training rule, it should be understood that if one listens to such a thing, the restraint of the training rule is broken because of its nature as the sound of singing. For thus it is stated in the Vinaya commentaries: ''Singing' means: whether it be the singing of actors and so forth; or the auspicious, playful singing connected with the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the noble ones' final Nibbāna; or the Dhamma-reciting singing of unrestrained bhikkhus; or even, at the least, tooth-singing; or that which they hum in the preliminary stage with the thought, 'We will sing'—all this is called 'singing'.

Kiñcāpi mālā-saddo loke baddhapupphavācako, sāsane pana ruḷhiyā abaddhapupphesupi vaṭṭati, tasmā yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ baddhamabaddhaṃ vā, taṃ sabbaṃ “mālā” tveva daṭṭhabbanti āha “yaṃ kiñci puppha”nti. “Yaṃ kiñci gandha”nti cettha vāsacuṇṇadhūpādikaṃ vilepanato aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci gandhajātaṃ. Vuttatthaṃ viya hi vuccamānatthamantarenāpi saddo atthavisesavācako. Chavirāgakaraṇanti vilepanena chaviyā rañjanatthaṃ pisitvā paṭiyattaṃ yaṃ kiñci gandhacuṇṇaṃ. Piḷandhanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ maṇḍanaṃ. Gandhavasena, chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanaṃ vibhūsanaṃ. Tadevatthaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānena dīpeti “tattha piḷandhanto”tiādinā. Tathā ceva majjhimaṭṭhakathāyampi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.147) vuttaṃ, paramatthajotikāyaṃ pana khuddakapāṭhaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “mālādīsu dhāraṇādīni yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojetabbānī”ti (khu. pā. aṭṭha. pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ettakameva vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi yojentena yathāvuttanayeneva yojetabbāni. Kiṃ panetaṃ kāraṇanti āha “yāyā”tiādi. Yāya dussīlyacetanāya karoti, sā idha kāraṇaṃ. “Tato paṭivirato”ti hi ubhayattha sambandhitabbaṃ, eteneva “mālā…pe… vibhūsanānaṃ ṭhānaṃ, mālā…pe… vibhūsanāneva vā ṭhāna”nti samāsampi dasseti. Tadākārappavatto [M 1.0349] cetanādidhammoyeva hi dhāraṇādikiriyā. Tattha ca cetanāsampayuttadhammānaṃ kāraṇaṃ sahajātādopakārakato, padhānato ca. “Cetayitvā kammaṃ karoti kāyena vācāya manasā”ti (a. ni. 6.63) hi [V 1.0307] vuttaṃ. Dhāraṇādibhūtā eva ca cetanā ṭhānanti. Ṭhāna-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo dvandapadato suyyamānattā.

Although in the world the word 'mālā' denotes strung flowers, in the Sāsana, by convention, it also applies to unstrung flowers. Therefore, because any flower whatsoever, whether strung or unstrung, should be regarded simply as 'mālā', he says 'whatever flower'. Here, 'whatever fragrance' refers to any kind of fragrant substance other than unguent, such as perfumes, powders, and incense. For a word can denote a specific meaning in its own right, apart from the meaning that has been stated or is about to be stated. 'Coloring the complexion' means any scented powder prepared by grinding for the purpose of coloring the skin with an unguent. Wearing is 'dhāraṇa'. Adornment is 'maṇḍana', the filling of deficient places. Beautification is 'vibhūsana', the enjoyment by way of fragrance and by way of coloring the complexion. The teacher illustrates that very meaning by reference to a person with the words 'there, one who adorns,' and so on. And it is stated in the same way in the Majjhima Aṭṭhakathā. In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, however, only this much is stated: 'In the case of garlands, etc., the terms wearing, etc., should be applied sequentially.' There too, when applying them, one should do so in the manner already stated. But what is the reason for this? He says 'by which,' and so on. The immoral intention by which one acts is the cause here. For 'is abstinent from that' must be connected in both instances. By this very phrase, he also shows the compound construction: 'the ground for garlands...beautification,' or 'garlands...beautification themselves are the ground.' For the act of wearing, etc., is indeed the mental states, beginning with intention, that occur in that manner. And there, intention is the cause of the associated mental states because it assists them as a co-nascent condition and because it is predominant. For it is said: 'Having intended, one performs an action by body, speech, or mind.' And it should be understood that the intention which has become the act of wearing, etc., is the 'ground'. The word 'ṭhāna' (ground) should be applied to each member, as it is heard after the dvandva compound.

Uccāti uccasaddena akārantena samānatthaṃ ākārantaṃ ekaṃ saddantaraṃ accuggatavācakanti āha “pamāṇātikkanta”nti. Seti etthāti sayanaṃ, mañcādi. Samaṇasārupparahitattā, gahaṭṭhehi ca seṭṭhasammatattā akappiyapaccattharaṇaṃ “mahāsayana”nti idhādhippetanti dassetuṃ “akappiyattharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Nisīdanaṃ panettha sayaneneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā pana ādhāre paṭikkhitte tadādhārakiriyāpi paṭikkhittāva hoti, tasmā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā” icceva vuttaṃ. Atthato pana tadupabhogabhūtanisajjānipajjanehi virati dassitāti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā”ti esa niddeso ekasesanayena yathā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) etasmimpi vikappe āsanapubbakattā sayanakiriyāya sayanaggahaṇeneva āsanampi gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Kiriyāvācakaāsanasayanasaddalopato uttarapadalopaniddesotipi vinayaṭīkāyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 2.106) vuttaṃ.

'Uccā' is another word, ending in 'ā', which has the same meaning as the word 'ucca' ending in 'a', signifying something exceedingly elevated. Therefore, he says, 'exceeding the measure'. 'One lies on it' (seti ettha), thus it is a 'bed' (sayana), such as a couch. To show that here 'great bed' (mahāsayana) is intended to mean an improper covering, because it is unsuitable for ascetics and considered superior by householders, it is said 'improper covering'. It should be understood that sitting is included here by the word 'bed'. And since, when the basis is prohibited, the action dependent on that basis is also prohibited, it is therefore stated simply as 'high beds and great beds'. In terms of meaning, however, it should be understood that what is shown is the abstention from sitting and lying down, which constitute the use of them. Alternatively, this directive 'high beds and great beds' is made by the Blessed One using the method of retention of one (ekasesa), as in 'conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense-bases arise'. In this alternative too, it should be understood that since the act of lying down is preceded by sitting, sitting is also included by the taking up of 'bed'. It is also stated in the Vinaya-ṭīkā that this is an explanation involving the elision of the final term of a compound, due to the elision of the action-denoting words 'āsana' and 'sayana'.

Jātameva rūpamassa na vippakāranti jātarūpaṃ, satthuvaṇṇaṃ. Rañjīyati setavaṇṇatāya, rañjanti vā ettha sattāti rajataṃ yathā “nesaṃ padakkanta”nti. “Cattāro vīhayo guñjā, dve guñjā māsako bhave”ti vuttalakkhaṇena vīsatimāsako nīlakahāpaṇo vā dudradāmakādiko vā taṃtaṃdesavohārānurūpaṃ kato kahāpaṇo. Lohādīhi kato lohamāsakādiko. Ye vohāraṃ gacchantīti pariyādānavacanaṃ. Vohāranti ca kayavikkayavasena sabbohāraṃ. Aññehi gāhāpane, upanikkhittasādiyane ca paṭiggahaṇattho labbhatīti āha “na uggaṇhāpeti na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatī”ti. Atha vā tividhaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyena vācāya manasā. Tattha kāyena paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahaṇaṃ. Vācāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahāpanaṃ. Manasā paṭiggahaṇaṃ sādiyanaṃ. Tividhampetaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā gahetvā paṭiggahaṇāti vuttanti āha [M 1.0350] “neva naṃ uggaṇhātī”tiādi. Esa nayo āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇātiādīsupi.

‘Its nature is just as it is produced and does not alter’ is gold (jātarūpa), the color of the Teacher. ‘It is delighted in because of its white color,’ or ‘beings delight in it,’ is silver (rajata), as in the phrase ‘nesaṃ padakkantaṃ.’ ‘Four vīhi grains are a guñjā; two guñjās are a māsaka’—by this stated characteristic, twenty māsakas are a nīlakahāpaṇa, or a dudradāmaka, etc., or a kahāpaṇa made according to the usage of each respective region. Made from copper and other metals, it is a copper māsaka, etc. The phrase ‘which are in currency’ is a term of complete inclusion. And they are in currency by way of buying and selling. The meaning of ‘acceptance’ is obtained in causing others to take and in consenting to what is deposited; therefore, the Teacher said, ‘he does not cause to take, nor does he consent to what is deposited.’ Alternatively, acceptance is threefold: by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, acceptance by body is ‘taking’ (uggahaṇa). Acceptance by speech is ‘causing to take’ (uggahāpana). Acceptance by mind is ‘consenting’ (sādiyana). This threefold acceptance, having been taken by way of a general description or by the method of ekasesa, is called ‘acceptance.’ Therefore, the Teacher said, ‘he does not take it,’ and so on. This is the method to be understood in cases like ‘the acceptance of raw grain,’ etc., as well.

Nīvārādiupadhaññassa sāliyādimūladhaññantogadhattā “sattavidhassāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Saṭṭhidinaparipāko sukadhaññaviseso sāli nāma salīyate sīlāghateti katvā. Dabbaguṇapakāse pana –

Because the secondary grains such as wild rice (nīvāra) are included within the primary grains such as cultivated rice (sāli), the Teacher said, ‘of all seven kinds.’ A special kind of awned grain that ripens in sixty days is called sāli because it is praised (salīyate, sīlāghate). However, in the Dabbaguṇapakāsa:

“Atha [V 1.0308] dhaññaṃ tidhā sāli-saṭṭhikavīhibhedato;

Sālayo hemantā tatra, saṭṭhikā gimhajā api;

Vīhayo tvāsaḷhākhyātā, vassakālasamubbha vā”ti. –

‘Furthermore, grain is of three kinds, distinguished as sāli, saṭṭhika, and vīhi. Among these, sāli are grown in the winter season; saṭṭhika are also grown in the summer season; and vīhi are said to be grown in the rainy season, starting from the month of Āsaḷha.’

Vuttaṃ. Vahati, brūheti vā sattānaṃ jīvitanti vīhi, sassaṃ. Yuvitabbo missitabboti yavo. So hi atilūkhatāya aññena missetvā paribhuñjīyati. Gudhati parivedhati palibuddhatīti godhūmo, yaṃ “milakkhabhojana”ntipi vadanti. Sobhanattā kamanīyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti kaṅgu, atisukhumadhaññaviseso. Varīyati atilūkhatāya nivārīyati, khuddāpaṭivinayanato vā bhajīyatīti varako. Koraṃ rudhiraṃ dūsatīti kudrūsako, vaṇṇasaṅkamanena yo “govaḍḍhano”tipi vuccati. Tāni sattapi sappabhedā nidhāne posane sādhuttena “dhaññānī”ti vuccanti. “Na kevalañcā”tiādinā sampaṭicchanaṃ, parāmasanañca idha paṭiggahaṇasaddena vuttanti dasseti. Evamīdisesu. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā idaṃ pañcavidhampi bhesajjaṃ odissa anuññātaṃ nāma. Tassa pana “kāle paṭiggahita”nti vuttattā paṭiggahaṇaṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “aññatra odissa anuññātā”ti. Maṃsa-saddena macchānampi maṃsaṃ gahitaṃ evāti dassetuṃ “āmakamaṃsamacchāna”nti vuttaṃ, tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ anuññātaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, aparisaṅkitanti vā payogassa dassanato virūpekasesanayo dassito anenāti veditabbaṃ.

It is said: ‘Because it carries (vahati) or increases (brūheti) the life of beings,’ it is vīhi; this refers to a crop. ‘Because it should be mixed (yuvitabbo missitabbo),’ it is yava (barley). Indeed, due to its extreme coarseness, it is consumed mixed with something else. ‘Because it wraps around, afflicts, or binds (gudhati, parivedhati, palibuddhati),’ it is godhūma (wheat), which they also call ‘the food of barbarians.’ ‘Because of its beauty, it attains a state of being desirable (kamanīyabhāvaṃ),’ it is kaṅgu (millet); this refers to a very fine type of grain. ‘Because it is avoided or rejected (varīyati, nivārīyati) due to its extreme coarseness, or alternatively, because it dispels hunger (khuddāpaṭivinayanato), it is partaken of (bhajīyati),’ it is varaka. ‘Because it spoils the sinews/blood (koraṃ rudhiraṃ dūsati),’ by a transposition of letters it is kudrūsaka, which is also called govaḍḍhana. These seven types of grain with their varieties are called ‘dhaññāni’ because of their excellence in nourishing (posane). By the text beginning with ‘Not only…,’ it shows that here, both receiving (sampaṭicchana) and handling (parāmasana) are expressed by the word ‘acceptance’ (paṭiggahaṇa). Thus it should be understood in such cases. ‘I allow, bhikkhus, these five medicinal fats: bear fat, fish fat, crocodile fat, pig fat, and donkey fat.’ Because this was said, these five kinds of medicine are what is called ‘specifically permitted.’ However, since it is said of it, ‘received at the proper time,’ acceptance is allowable. Therefore, the Teacher said, ‘except for what is specifically permitted.’ To show that by the word ‘flesh,’ the flesh of fish is also included, it is said, ‘of raw flesh and fish.’ Alternatively, it should be understood that by this phrase the method of virūpekasesa is shown, because of seeing the usage that fish-flesh purified in three aspects—unseen, unheard, and unsuspected—is permitted.

Kāmaṃ lokiyā –

Granted, worldly authorities say:

“Aṭṭhavassā bhave gorī, dasavassā tu kaññakā;

Sampatte dvādasavasse, kumārītibhidhīyate”ti. –

‘An eight-year-old female is a gorī; a ten-year-old female, however, is a kaññakā; upon reaching twelve years of age, she is known as a kumārī.’

Vadanti[M 1.0351]. Idha pana purisantaragatāgatavasena itthikumārikābhedoti āha “itthīti purisantaragatā”tiādi. Dāsidāsavasenevāti dāsidāsavohāravaseneva. Evaṃ vutteti tādisena kappiyavacanena vutte. Vinayaṭṭhakathāsu āgatavinicchayaṃ sandhāya “vinayavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. So kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanādīsu (pārā. aṭṭha. 364) gahetabbo.

They say. Here, however, the distinction between a woman (itthi) and a girl (kumārikā) is by way of whether she has gone to another man or not. Therefore, the Teacher said, ‘A woman is one who has gone to another man,’ and so on. ‘By way of female and male slaves’ means solely by way of the designation ‘female slave, male slave.’ ‘When it is said thus’ means when it is said with such an allowable expression. Referring to the decision that has come down in the Vinaya commentaries, it is said, ‘according to the Vinaya.’ That decision should be taken from the explanations of the Kuṭikāra training rule and so on.

Bījaṃ khipanti ettha, khittaṃ vā bījaṃ tāyatīti khettaṃ, kedāroti āha “yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhatī”ti. Aparaṇṇassa pubbe pavattamannaṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ na-kārassa ṇa-kāraṃ katvā, sāliādi[V 1.0309]. Vasanti patiṭṭhahanti aparaṇṇāni etthāti vatthūti atthaṃ dasseti “vatthu nāmā”tiādinā. Pubbaṇṇassa aparaṃ pavattamannaṃ aparaṇṇaṃ vuttanayena. Evaṃ aṭṭhakathānayānurūpaṃ atthaṃ dassetvā idāni “khettaṃ nāma yattha pubbaṇṇaṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā jāyatī”ti (pārā. 104) vuttavinayapāḷinayānurūpampi atthaṃ dassento “yattha vā”tiādimāha. Tadatthāyāti khettatthāya. Akatabhūmibhāgoti aparisaṅkhato taduddesiko bhūmibhāgo. “Khettavatthu sīsenā”tiādinā nidassanamattametanti dasseti. Ādi-saddena pokkharaṇīkūpādayo saṅgahitā.

‘They cast seeds in this place (ettha),’ or ‘it protects (tāyati) the cast seed’; therefore, it is a field (khetta). This refers to a paddy field (kedāra). Therefore, he said, ‘wherein an early crop grows.’ The grain that occurs before the later crop is pubbaṇṇa; by changing the letter ‘na’ to ‘ṇa,’ it becomes pubbaṇṇa. This refers to rice (sāli), etc. ‘Later crops (aparaṇṇāni) dwell or are established (vasanti patiṭṭhahanti) in this place (ettha)’; therefore, it is a site (vatthu). The Teacher shows this meaning with the text beginning ‘vatthu nāma...’ The grain that occurs after the early crop is aparaṇṇa, in the manner stated. Having thus shown the meaning in accordance with the method of the Aṭṭhakathā, now, wishing to show the meaning also in accordance with the method of the Vinaya Pāḷi which states, ‘A field is where an early crop or a later crop is produced,’ he said the text beginning ‘or where...’ ‘For that purpose’ means for the sake of the field. ‘An unprepared portion of land’ is an uncultivated portion of land designated for that purpose. By the phrase beginning with ‘under the heading of field and site,’ it shows that this is a mere indication. By the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), ponds, wells, and so on are included.

Dūtassa idaṃ, dūtena vā kātumarahatīti dūteyyaṃ. Paṇṇanti lekhasāsanaṃ. Sāsananti mukhasāsanaṃ. Gharā gharanti aññasmā gharā aññaṃ gharaṃ. Khuddakagamananti dūteyyagamanato appataragamanaṃ, anaddhānagamanaṃ rassagamananti attho. Tadubhayesaṃ anuyuñjanaṃ anuyogoti āha “tadubhayakaraṇa”nti. Tasmāti tadubhayakaraṇasseva anuyogabhāvato.

‘This belongs to a messenger,’ or ‘what is fit to be done by a messenger’; therefore, it is dūteyya (a messenger’s duty). Paṇṇaṃ is a written message. Sāsanaṃ is a verbal message. ‘From house to house’ means from one house to another house. ‘A minor journey’ is a smaller journey than a messenger’s journey; the meaning should be understood as a journey that is not a long distance, a short journey. The undertaking (anuyuñjana) of both of these is anuyoga (application); therefore, he said, ‘the doing of both.’ ‘Therefore’ is because anuyoga is the very nature of doing both of these.

Kayanaṃ kayo, paramparā gahetvā attano dhanassa dānaṃ. Kī-saddañhi dabbavinimaye paṭhanti vikkayanaṃ vikkayo, paṭhamameva attano dhanassa paresaṃ dānanti vadanti. Sāratthadīpaniyādīsu pana “kaya”nti parabhaṇḍassa gahaṇaṃ. Vikkayanti attano bhaṇḍassa dāna”nti (sārattha. ṭī. 2.594) vuttaṃ. Tadeva “kayitañca hoti parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ karontena, vikkītañca attano bhaṇḍaṃ parahatthagataṃ karontenā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 515) vinayaṭṭhakathāvacanena sameti. Vañcanaṃ māyākaraṇaṃ, paṭibhānakaraṇavasena upāyakusalatāya parasantakaggahaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tulā nāma yāya tulīyati pamīyati, tāya [M 1.0352] kūṭaṃ “tulākūṭa”nti vuccati. Taṃ pana karonto tulāya rūpaaṅgagahaṇākārapaṭicchannasaṇṭhānavasena karotīti catubbidhatā vuttā. Attanā gahetabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ pacchābhāge, paresaṃ dātabbaṃ pubbabhāge katvā minentīti āha “gaṇhanto pacchābhāge”tiādi. Akkamati nippīḷati, pubbabhāge akkamatīti sambandho. Mūle rajjunti tulāya mūle yojitaṃ rajjuṃ. Tathā agge. Tanti ayacuṇṇaṃ.

Selling (kayanaṃ) is selling (kayo): having taken from a succession, it is the giving of one's own wealth. Indeed, scholars recite the word 'kī' in the context of the exchange of goods. Buying (vikkayanaṃ) is buying (vikkayo): it is the very first giving of one's own wealth to others—thus say the teachers. In the Sāratthadīpanī and other texts, however, it is said: 'kaya' is the taking of another's goods; 'vikkayo' is the giving of one's own goods. That very statement accords with the words of the Vinaya commentary: 'It is "bought" (kayita) when one makes another's goods come into one's own hand, and it is "sold" (vikkīta) when one makes one's own goods come into another's hand.' Deception (vañcana) is the act of illusion (māyākaraṇa); this means it is the taking of another's property through skill in stratagems, by means of creating a convincing impression. A scale (tulā) is that by which one weighs or measures; fraud with it is called a 'false scale' (tulākūṭa). One who does this does so by means of the appearance of its form, the appearance of its parts, the appearance of its handling, and its concealed configuration; thus, its fourfold nature is stated. He said, 'taking in the back part,' etc., because they weigh by placing the goods to be taken by oneself in the back part and the goods to be given to others in the front part. 'Akkamati' means to press down, to oppress; the connection is made thus: 'one presses down in the front part.' 'Mūle rajjuṃ' means the rope attached to the base of the scale. Likewise at the top. 'Tanti' is iron powder.

Kanati dibbatīti kaṃso, suvaṇṇarajatādimayā bhojanapānapattā. Idha pana sovaṇṇamaye pānapatteti āha “suvaṇṇapātī”ti. Tāya vañcananti nikativasena vañcanaṃ. “Patirūpakaṃ dassetvā parasantakagahaṇañhi nikati, paṭibhānakaraṇavasena pana upāyakusalatāya vañcana”nti nikativañcanaṃ bhedato kaṇhajātakaṭṭhakathādīsu (jā. aṭṭha. 4.10.19; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.10; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.149; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.1165; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.198 atthato samānaṃ) vuttaṃ[V 1.0310], idha pana tadubhayampi “vañcana”micceva. “Katha”ntiādinā hi patirūpakaṃ dassetvā parasantakagahaṇameva vibhāveti. Samagghataranti tāsaṃ pātīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ samakaṃ agghavisesaṃ. Pāsāṇeti bhūtābhūtabhāvasañjānanake pāsāṇe. Ghaṃsaneneva suvaṇṇabhāvasaññāpanaṃ siddhanti “ghaṃsitvā”tveva vuttaṃ.

'Because it shines (kanati, dippati), it is called kaṃsa,' which refers to eating and drinking vessels made of gold, silver, and so on. Here, however, it refers to a drinking vessel made of gold; thus he said 'golden bowl' (suvaṇṇapātī). 'Deception by that' means deception by way of trickery. 'Indeed, showing a counterfeit and taking another's property is trickery (nikati); but taking another's property by means of creating a convincing impression, due to skill in stratagems, is deception (vañcana)'—thus the distinction between trickery and deception is stated in the Kaṇhajātaka commentary and other texts. Here in this commentary, however, both are called simply 'deception' (vañcana). For by the words 'How?' and so on, he indeed explains the taking of another's property by showing a counterfeit. 'Samagghataraṃ' means the equal, special value among those bowls. 'Pāsāṇe' means on a touchstone that makes known the state of being real or unreal. Since making known the state of being gold is accomplished by rubbing alone, it is stated simply as 'having rubbed' (ghaṃsitvā).

Hadayanti nāḷiādiminanabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ, tasmiṃ bhedo chiddakaraṇaṃ hadayabhedo. Tilādīnaṃ nāḷiādīhi minanakāle ussāpitā sikhāyeva sikhā, tassā bhedo hāpanaṃ sikhābhedo.

'Hadaya' (heart) means the interior of measuring vessels such as a nāḷi; a breach (bhedo) in that, the making of a hole (chiddakaraṇa), is 'breaching the heart' (hadayabhedo). When measuring sesame seeds and so on with a nāḷi, etc., the raised-up peak is itself the 'sikhā' (crest); a breach (bhedo) of that, which is a reduction (hāpana), is 'breaching the crest' (sikhābhedo).

Rajjuyā bhedo visamakaraṇaṃ rajjubhedo. Tānīti sappitelādīni. Antobhājaneti paṭhamaṃ nikkhittabhājane. Ussāpetvāti uggamāpetvā, uddhaṃ rāsiṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Chindantoti apanento.

A breach (bhedo) of the rope (rajjuyā), which is making it uneven (visamakaraṇa), is 'breaching the rope' (rajjubhedo). 'Those' (tāni) refers to ghee, oil, and so on. 'Within the vessel' (antobhājane) means in the vessel placed first. 'Having raised up' (ussāpetvā) means having caused to rise up; that is to say, having made a pile upwards. 'Cutting off' (chindanto) means removing.

Kattabbakammato uddhaṃ koṭanaṃ paṭihananaṃ ukkoṭanaṃ. Abhūtakārīnaṃ lañjaggahaṇaṃ, na pana puna kammāya ukkoṭanamattanti āha “assāmike…pe… ggahaṇa”nti. Upāyehīti kāraṇapatirūpakehi. Tatrāti tasmiṃ vañcane. “Vatthu”nti avatvā “ekaṃ vatthu”nti vadanto aññānipi atthi bahūnīti dasseti. Aññānipi hi sasavatthuādīni tattha tattha vuttāni. Miganti mahantaṃ migaṃ. Tena hīti migaggahaṇe uyyojanaṃ, yena vā kāraṇena “migaṃ me dehī”ti āha, tena kāraṇenāti attho. Hi-saddo [M 1.0353] nipātamattaṃ. Yogavasenāti vijjājappanādipayogavasena. Māyāvasenāti mantajappanaṃ vinā abhūtassāpi bhūtākārasaññāpanāya cakkhumohanamāyāya vasena. Yāya hi amaṇiādayopi maṇiādiākārena dissanti. Pāmaṅgo nāma kulācārayutto ābharaṇaviseso, yaṃ loke “yaññopavitta”nti vadanti. Vakkalittherāpadānepi vuttaṃ –

Striking (koṭanaṃ) or beating (paṭihananaṃ) beyond the duty to be done is 'ukkoṭana'. It is the taking of bribes from those who act falsely. But it is not merely extortion for a new case; thus he said, 'taking... without an owner... etc.' 'By means of devices' (upāyehi) means by counterfeit reasons. 'Therein' (tatrā) means in that deception. By saying 'one story' (ekaṃ vatthu) instead of 'a story' (vatthu), he indicates that there are many others. For indeed, other stories, such as the story of the hare and so on, are mentioned in various places. 'A deer' (migaṃ) means a large deer. 'Tena hi' is an incitement to seize the deer; or, the meaning is: 'for that reason' by which he said, 'Give me the deer.' The word 'hi' is merely a particle. 'By the power of application' (yogavasena) means by the power of the application of knowledge, incantations, and so on. 'By the power of illusion' (māyāvasena) means by the power of eye-deceiving illusion that makes known the unreal as having a real appearance, without the chanting of mantras. For by this, even non-gems and so on appear in the form of gems. A 'pāmaṅga' is a special ornament connected with family tradition, which in the world is called a 'yaññopavitta' (sacrificial thread). Even in the Apadāna of Elder Vakkali, it is said:

“Passathetaṃ māṇavakaṃ, pītamaṭṭhanivāsanaṃ;

Hemayaññopavittaṅgaṃ, jananettamanohara”nti. (apa. 2.54.40);

"Behold that young man, wearing a polished yellow garment, his body adorned with a golden sacrificial thread, captivating the eyes and minds of the people."

Tadaṭṭhakathāyampi “pītamaṭṭhanivāsananti siliṭṭhasuvaṇṇavaṇṇavatthe nivatthanti attho. Hemayaññopavittaṅganti suvaṇṇapāmaṅgalaggitagattanti attho”ti (apa. aṭṭha. 2.54.40) savanaṃ saṭhanaṃ sāvi, anujukatā, tenāha “kuṭilayogo”ti, jimhatāyogoti attho. “Etesaṃyevā”tiādinā [V 1.0311] tulyādhikaraṇataṃ dasseti. “Tasmā”tiādi laddhaguṇadassanaṃ. Ye pana catunnampi padānaṃ bhinnādhikaraṇataṃ vadanti, tesaṃ vādamāha “kecī”tiādinā. Tattha “kecī”ti sārasamāsakārakā ācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca, tesaṃ taṃ na yuttaṃ vañcanena saṅgahitasseva puna gahitattāti dasseti “taṃ panā”tiādinā.

In its commentary too, it is said: 'Pītamaṭṭhanivāsanaṃ means wearing a smooth, gold-colored garment. Hemayaññopavittaṅgaṃ means having a body to which a golden pāmaṅga is attached.' Savanaṃ, saṭhanaṃ is sāvi; it is crookedness (anujukatā). Therefore, the teacher said 'crooked application' (kuṭilayogo); the meaning is 'application of crookedness' (jimhatāyogo). By the text beginning with 'Of these very ones,' he shows their appositional relationship. The words beginning with 'Therefore' show an acquired quality. But as for those who say the four terms have a different grammatical basis, he states their view with the words beginning 'some.' Therein, 'some' refers to the teachers who authored the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttaravihāra (Northern Monastery). He shows that their view is not correct because what was already included under 'deception' is taken up again, with the words beginning 'But that...'

Māraṇanti muṭṭhipahārakasātāḷanādīhi hiṃsanaṃ viheṭhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na tu pāṇātipātaṃ. Viheṭhanatthepi hi vadha-saddo dissati “attānaṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā rodeyyā”tiādīsu (pāci. 880) māraṇa-saddopi idha viheṭhaneyeva vattatīti daṭṭhabbo. Keci pana “pubbe pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā’tiādīsu sayaṃkāro, idha paraṃkāro”ti vadanti, taṃ na sakkā tathā vattuṃ “kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā, cha payogā”ti ca vuttattā. Yathā hi appaṭiggāhabhāvasāmaññepi sati pabbajitehi appaṭiggahitabbavatthuvisesabhāvasandassanatthaṃ itthikumāridāsidāsādayo vibhāgena vuttā. Yathā ca parasantakassa haraṇabhāvato adinnādānabhāvasāmaññepi sati tulākūṭādayo adinnādānavisesabhāvasandassanatthaṃ vibhāgena vuttā, na evaṃ pāṇātipātapariyāyassa vadhassa puna gahaṇe payojanaṃ atthi tathāvibhajitabbassābhāvato, tasmā yathāvuttoyevattho sundarataroti.

The word 'māraṇa' is said with reference to harming or harassing by means of blows with the fist, striking with a whip, and so on, but not with reference to the destruction of life. Indeed, the word 'vadha' is also found in the sense of harassing in such phrases as, "having struck himself again and again, he would weep." Thus, it should be understood that the word 'māraṇa' here also occurs only in the sense of harassing. Some, however, say, "Previously, in 'having abandoned the destruction of life,' and so on, it is an act done by oneself; here, it is causing another to act." Such a statement cannot be made, because it is said, "volition that originates bodily and verbal application" and "six applications." For just as, although there is the general state of being unreceivable, women, young girls, female slaves, male slaves, and so on are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the specific nature of things that should not be received by renunciants; and just as, although there is the general state of taking what is not given due to the act of stealing another's property, false scales and so on are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the specific nature of taking what is not given; in the same way, there is no purpose in taking up 'vadha', a synonym for 'pāṇātipāta', again, because there is no meaning to be analyzed in that way. Therefore, the meaning as stated is indeed far better.
