Viparāmosoti [M 1.0354] visesena samantato bhusaṃ mosāpanaṃ muyhanakaraṇaṃ, thenanaṃ vā. Theyyaṃ corikā mosoti hi pariyāyo. So kāraṇavasena duvidhoti āha “himaviparāmoso”tiādi. Musantīti corenti, mosenti vā muyhanaṃ karonti, mosetvā tesaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yanti ca tassā kiriyāya parāmasanaṃ. Maggappaṭipannaṃ jananti parapakkhepi adhikāro. Ālopanaṃ vilumpanaṃ ālopo. Sahasā karaṇaṃ sahasākāro. Sahasā pavattitā sāhasikā, sāva kiriyā tathā.

'Viparāmosa' is, in a special sense, from all around, severely causing deception, causing confusion, or theft. Indeed, 'theyyaṃ' (theft), 'corikā' (robbery), and 'moso' (deception) are synonyms. That is of two kinds by way of cause; therefore, it is said, "himaviparāmosa," and so on. 'Musanti' means they steal, or they deceive, they cause confusion. It is said: having deceived, they take their property. And 'yaṃ' is a word that refers to that action. The phrase 'maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ' is also applicable in the other case. 'Ālopanaṃ' is plundering (vilumpanaṃ); 'ālopo'. 'Sahasākaraṇaṃ' is acting with force; 'sahasākāro'. That which proceeds with force is 'sāhasikā'; that very action is so called.

Ettāvatāti “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādinā “sahasākārā paṭivirato”ti pariyosānena etapparimāṇena pāṭhena. Antarabhedaṃ aggahetvā pāḷiyaṃ yathārutamāgatavaseneva chabbīsatisikkhāpadasaṅgahametaṃ sīlaṃ yebhuyyena sikkhāpadānamavibhattattā cūḷasīlaṃ nāmāti attho. Desanāvasena hi idha cūḷamajjhimādibhāvo veditabbo, na dhammavasena. Tathā hi idhasaṅkhittena uddiṭṭhānaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ avibhattānaṃ vibhajanavasena majjhimasīladesanā pavattā, tenevāha “majjhimasīlaṃ vitthārento”ti.Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

'Ettāvatā' means: by this much of the text, beginning with "pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya" and ending with "sahasākārā paṭivirato". Without taking the internal divisions, and just as it has come down in the Pāli text according to what has been handed down, this morality—a collection of twenty-six training rules—is called the Cūḷasīla (Minor Morality) because the training rules are for the most part undivided; this is the meaning. Indeed, here the state of being Cūḷa (Minor), Majjhima (Middle), and so on should be understood by way of the teaching, not by way of the Dhamma itself. For this reason, the teaching of the Majjhimasīla (Middle Morality) proceeds by way of analyzing the training rules that have been pointed out concisely and are undivided here. For that very reason, he said, "expounding the Majjhimasīla." The commentary on the Cūḷasīla is finished.

Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Middle Morality

11. “Yathā [V 1.0312] vā paneke bhonto”tiādidesanāya sambandhamāha “idānī”tiādinā. Tatthāyamaṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – yathāti opammatthe nipāto. Vāti vikappanatthe, tena imamatthaṃ vikappeti “ussāhaṃ katvā mama vaṇṇaṃ vadamānopi puthujjano pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādinā parānuddesikanayena vā sabbathāpi ācārasīlamattameva vadeyya, na taduttariṃ. “Yathāpaneke bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇabhāvaṃ paṭijānamānā, parehi ca tathā sambhāviyamānā tadanurūpapaṭipattiṃ ajānanato, asamatthanato ca na abhisambhuṇanti, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana samaṇo gotamo sabbathāpi samaṇasāruppapaṭipattiṃ pūresiyevā”ti evaṃ aññuddesikanayena vā sabbathāpi ācārasīlamattameva vadeyya, na taduttarinti. Panāti [M 1.0355] vacanālaṅkāre vikappanattheneva upanyāsādiatthassa sijjhanato. Eketi aññe. “Ekacce”tipi vadanti. Bhontoti sādhūnaṃ piyasamudāhāro. Sādhavo hi pare “bhonto”ti vā “devānaṃ piyā”ti vā “āyasmanto”ti vā samālapanti. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti yaṃ kiñci pabbajjaṃ upagatatāya samaṇā. Jātimattena ca brāhmaṇāti.

11. He states the connection of the teaching beginning "Yathā vā paneke bhonto..." with the words "idāni..." and so on. Therein, this is the method independent of the commentary: 'Yathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison. 'Vā' is in the sense of an alternative; by that, it presents this meaning as an alternative: "Making an effort, a worldling, while speaking my praise, should... abandon the destruction of life and refrain from the destruction of life," and so on; or, by the method of referring to another, in every way, they should speak only of conduct and morality, not beyond that. "Just as some venerable ones, claiming to be ascetics and brahmins, and being esteemed by others as such, yet, due to not knowing the proper practice and being unable, do not accomplish it; this is not so with him. This ascetic Gotama, however, in every way, fulfills the conduct befitting an ascetic"; or, by this method of referring to another, in every way, they should speak only of conduct and morality, not beyond that. 'Pana' is a particle for embellishment of speech, because the meaning of introduction, etc., is accomplished by 'vā' which has the sense of an alternative. 'Eke' means others; they also say 'ekacce'. 'Bhonto' is an endearing address of the virtuous. Indeed, the virtuous address others as 'bhonto' (venerable ones), 'devānaṃ piyā' (dear to the gods), or 'āyasmanto' (venerable ones). 'Samaṇabrāhmaṇā' means 'samaṇas' by having undertaken some form of going forth, and 'brāhmaṇas' merely by birth.

Saddhā nāma idha catubbidhesu ṭhānesūti āha “kammañcā”tiādi. Kammakammaphalasambandheneva idhalokaparalokasaddahanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “ettha kammaṃ vipaccati, kammaphalañca anubhavitabba”nti. Tadatthaṃ byatirekato ñāpeti “ayaṃ me”tiādinā. Paṭikarissatīti paccupakāraṃ karissati. Tadeva samatthetuṃ “evaṃdinnāni hī”tiādimāha. Desanāsīsamattaṃ padhānaṃ katvā nidassanato. Tena catubbidhampi paccayaṃ nidassetīti vuttaṃ “atthato panā”tiādi.

Faith, here, occurs in four instances; therefore, he said, "kammañca..." and so on. Belief in this world and the next should be understood as connected with kamma and the fruit of kamma, thus: "Here, kamma ripens, and the fruit of kamma is to be experienced." He makes that meaning known by way of exclusion with "ayaṃ me..." and so on. 'Paṭikarissati' means 'it will make a return benefit'. To establish that very point, he said, "evaṃdinnāni hi..." and so on. This is because it is shown having made the essence of the teaching the main point. By that, it shows the four kinds of requisites; therefore, it was said, "atthato pana..." and so on.

“Seyyathida”nti ayaṃ saddo “so katamo”ti atthe eko nipāto, nipātasamudāyo vā, tena ca bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhapade saddakkamena appadhānabhūtopi bījagāmabhūtagāmo vibhajjitabbaṭṭhāne padhānabhūto viya paṭiniddisīyati. Añño hi saddakkamo añño atthakkamoti āha “katamo so bījagāmabhūtagāmo”ti. Tasmiñhi vibhatte tabbisayasamārambhopi vibhattova hoti. Imamatthañhi dassetuṃ “yassa samārambhaṃ anuyuttā viharantī”ti vuttaṃ. Teneva ca pāḷiyaṃ “mūlabīja”ntiādinā so niddiṭṭhoti. Mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassātipi mūlabījanti idha dvidhā attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ato na codetabbametaṃ “kasmā panettha bījagāmabhūtagāmaṃ pucchitvā bījagāmo eva vibhatto”ti. Tattha hi paṭhamena atthena bījagāmo niddiṭṭho, dutiyena bhūtagāmo, duvidhopesa sāmaññaniddesena [V 1.0313] vā mūlabījañca mūlabījañca mūlabījanti ekasesanayena vā niddiṭṭhoti veditabbo, teneva vakkhati “sabbañheta”ntiādiṃ. Atīva visati bhesajjapayogesūti ativisaṃ, ativisā vā, yā “mahosadha”ntipi vuccati kacchakoti kāḷakacchako, yaṃ “pilakkho”tipi vadanti. Kapitthanoti ambilaṅkuraphalo setarukkho. So hi kampati calatīti kapithano thanapaccayena, kapīti vā makkaṭo, tassa [M 1.0356] thanasadisaṃ phalaṃ yassāti kapitthano. “Kapitthanoti pippalirukkho”ti (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.108) hi visuddhimaggaṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Phaḷubījaṃ nāma pabbabījaṃ. Ajjakanti setapaṇṇāsaṃ. Phaṇijjakanti samīraṇaṃ. Hiriveranti vāraṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhanasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bījasaddoti dasseti “viruhanasamatthamevā”ti iminā. Itarañhi abījasaṅkhyaṃ gataṃ, tañca kho rukkhato viyojitameva. Aviyojitaṃ pana tathā vā hotu, aññathā vā “bhūtagāmo”tveva vuccati yathāvuttena dutiyaṭṭhena. Vinayā (pāci. 91) nurūpato tesaṃ visesaṃ dasseti “tatthā”tiādinā. Yamettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

The word `Seyyathidaṃ` is a single particle, or a collection of particles, in the sense of 'Which is that?'. And by it, in the term `bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambha` (destruction of the group of seeds and the group of plants), although the group of seeds and the group of plants is secondary in the sequence of words, it is pointed out in detail as if it were primary in the place where it is to be analyzed. For the sequence of words is one thing, and the sequence of meaning is another; therefore, it is said, 'Which is that group of seeds and group of plants?'. For when that is analyzed, the destruction concerning it also becomes analyzed. To show this meaning, it was said, 'in the destruction of which they dwell engaged'. And for that very reason, it is indicated in the Pāḷi by 'root-seed', etc. The root itself is the seed, [hence] `mūlabīja` (root-seed); or, that which has a root as its seed is also `mūlabīja`. Here, the meaning is twofold. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Therefore, this should not be questioned: 'Why here, having asked about the group of seeds and the group of plants, is only the group of seeds analyzed?'. For there, by the first meaning, the group of seeds is indicated; by the second, the group of plants. This twofold meaning should be understood as indicated either by a general indication, or by the method of eliding one of two similar terms (`ekasesanaya`), as in: `mūlabījañca mūlabījañca` becomes `mūlabījaṃ`. For that very reason, it will be said, 'all of this', etc. Because it is exceedingly used (`visati`) in medicinal applications, it is `ativisaṃ` or `ativisā`, which is also called `mahosadha` (great medicine). `Kacchaka` is the black `kacchaka` plant, which they also call `pilakkha`. `Kapitthana` is the white tree with sour shoots and fruits. Because it trembles (`kampati`), it shakes (`calati`), it is called `kapithana` with the suffix `thana`; or, `kapi` means monkey, and that which has fruit similar to its (`tassa`) breast (`thana`) is `kapitthano`. Indeed, in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā it is said: '`Kapitthana` is the `pippali` tree'. `Phaḷubīja` is joint-seed (`pabbabīja`). `Ajjaka` is the white `paṇṇāsa`. `Phaṇijjaka` is `samīraṇa`. `Hirivera` is `vāra`. Because it is a specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when other conditions are present, the word 'seed' is established in the sense of a fruit with a core that is capable of sprouting; this is shown by the phrase 'only that which is capable of sprouting'. For anything else is counted as a non-seed. And that fruit with a core is only when it is separated from the tree. But that which is not separated, whether it be capable of sprouting or otherwise, is called only 'group of plants' (`bhūtagāma`) according to the second meaning as stated before. In accordance with the Vinaya, he shows the distinction between them with 'Therein', etc. Whatever is to be said here has already been said below.

12. Sannidhānaṃ sannidhi, tāya karīyateti sannidhikāro, annapānādi. Evaṃ kāra-saddassa kammatthataṃ sandhāya “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti vuttaṃ. Ayamaparo nayo – yathā “ācayaṃ gāmino”ti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “ācayagāmino”ti (dha. sa. 10) niddeso kato, evamidhāpi “sannidhikāraṃ paribhoga”nti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti vuttaṃ, sannidhiṃ katvā paribhoganti attho. Vinayavasenāti vinayāgatācāravasena. Vinayāgatācāro hi uttaralopena “vinayo”ti vutto, kāyavācānaṃ vā vinayanaṃ vinayo. Suttantanayapaṭipattiyā visuṃ gahitattā vinayācāroyeva idha labbhati. Sammā kilese likhatīti sallekhoti ca vinayācārassa visuṃ gahitattā suttantanayapaṭipatti eva. Paṭiggahitanti kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā paṭiggahitaṃ. Aparajjūti aparasmiṃ divase. Datvāti parivattanavasena datvā. Ṭhapāpetvāti ca attano santakakaraṇena ṭhapāpetvā. Tesampi santakaṃ vissāsaggāhādivasena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Suttantanayavasena sallekho eva na hoti.

12. Storing (`sannidhānaṃ`) is `sannidhi`. Because food, drink, etc., are prepared (`karīyate`) by means of that (`tāya`), it is called `sannidhikāra` (making a store). Thus, with reference to the word `kāra` having the meaning of an object, it is said `sannidhikāraparibhoga` (consumption of what is stored). This is another method: just as when `ācayaṃ gāmino` should be said, the indication `ācayagāmino` is made by dropping the nasal, so too here, when `sannidhikāraṃ paribhogaṃ` should be said, `sannidhikāraparibhogaṃ` is said by dropping the nasal; the meaning is 'consuming after having stored'. `Vinayavasena` means by way of the conduct that comes in the Vinaya. For the conduct that comes in the Vinaya (`vinayāgatācāra`) is called `vinaya` by eliding the latter part. Or, `vinaya` is the disciplining of body and speech. Since the practice according to the Suttanta method is taken separately, only the Vinaya conduct is obtained here. It scrapes away (`likhati`) defilements (`kilese`) rightly (`sammā`), therefore it is `sallekha` (effacement). And since the Vinaya conduct is taken separately, only the practice according to the Suttanta method is meant. `Paṭiggahitaṃ` means received by the body or by what is connected to the body. `Aparajju` means on another day. `Datvā` means having given by way of exchange. And `ṭhapāpetvā` means having had it put aside by making it one's own property. It is allowable to consume their property also by way of taking with confidence, etc. According to the Suttanta method, this does not constitute effacement.

Yāni ca tesaṃ anulomānīti ettha sānulomadhaññarasaṃ, madhukapuppharasaṃ, pakkaḍākarasañca ṭhapetvā avasesā sabbepi phalapupphapattarasā anulomapānānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, yathāparicchedakālaṃ anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitanti attho.

Here, in the phrase 'And those which are allowable for them', it should be understood that, excepting the juice of grain with husks, the juice of madhuka flowers, and the juice of cooked leaves, all remaining juices of fruits, flowers, and leaves are allowable drinks. The meaning is that they may be kept for the designated period without being formally determined (`anadhiṭṭhita`) and without being formally shared (`avikappita`).

Sannidhīyateti [M 1.0357] sannidhi, vatthameva. Pariyāyati kappīyatīti pariyāyo, kappiyavācānusārena [V 1.0314] paṭipatti, tassa kathāti pariyāyakathā. Tabbiparīto nippariyāyo, kappiyampi anupaggamma santuṭṭhivasena paṭipatti, pariyāya-saddo vā kāraṇe, tasmā kappiyakāraṇavasena vuttā kathā pariyāyakathā. Tadapi avatvā santuṭṭhivasena vuttā nippariyāyo. “Sace”tiādi aññassa dānākāradassanaṃ. Pāḷiyā uddisanaṃ uddeso. Atthassa pucchā paripucchanaṃ. “Adātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti iminā adāne sallekhakopanaṃ dasseti. Appahonteti kātuṃ appahonake sati. Paccāsāyāti cīvarapaṭilābhāsāya. Anuññātakāleti anatthate kathine eko pacchimakattikamāso, atthate kathine pacchimakattikamāsena saha hemantikā cattāro māsā, piṭṭhisamaye yo koci eko māsoti evaṃ tatiyakathinasikkhāpadādīsu anuññātasamaye. Suttanti cīvarasibbanasuttaṃ. Vinayakammaṃ katvāti mūlacīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā paccāsācīvarameva mūlacīvaraṃ katvā ṭhapetabbaṃ, taṃ puna māsaparihāraṃ labhati, etena upāyena yāva icchati, tāva aññamaññaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ labbhatīti vuttanayena, vikappanāvasena vā vinayakammaṃ katvā. Kasmā na vaṭṭatīti āha “sannidhi ca hoti sallekhañca kopetī”ti.

Because it is stored, it is called 'sannidhi'; it refers only to the robe-cloth. Because it is considered, because it is allowable, it is 'pariyāya'; it is the practice in accordance with allowable speech, and the discussion of that is 'pariyāyakathā.' The opposite of that is 'nippariyāya,' the practice by way of contentment without resorting to what is allowable. Alternatively, the term 'pariyāya' is used in the sense of a reason; therefore, a discussion stated by way of a reason for what is allowable is 'pariyāyakathā.' Even without saying that, what is stated by way of contentment is 'nippariyāya.' 'Sace,' etc., is a statement showing the manner of giving to another. Reciting the Pāḷi is 'uddeso.' Questioning the meaning is 'paripucchanaṃ.' By the phrase 'It is not proper not to give,' it shows the corrupting of effacement in not giving. 'Appahonte' means: when one is unable to do so. 'Paccāsāya' means: for the hope of obtaining a robe. The permitted time means: when the Kathina is not spread, the one last month of Kattika; when the Kathina is spread, along with the last month of Kattika, the four winter months; during the post-robe-season, any one month—thus, during the permitted time in the third Kathina training rule and so on. 'Suttaṃ' means: the thread for sewing a robe. 'Having performed a Vinaya act' means: having determined the original robe as an accessory cloth, the expected robe itself should be made the original robe and set aside. That robe again obtains a month's keeping period. By this method, for as long as one wishes, it is allowable to set aside robes, making them the original robe one after another. Thus, having performed a Vinaya act either in the aforesaid manner or by way of shared ownership. To the question, 'Why is it not allowable?', he said: 'Because it is storing and it corrupts effacement.'

Upari maṇḍapasadisaṃ padaracchannaṃ, sabbapaliguṇṭhimaṃ vā chādetvā kataṃ vayhaṃ. Ubhosu passesu suvaṇṇarajatādimayā gopānasiyo datvā garuḷapakkhakanayena katā sandamānitā. Phalakādinā kataṃ pīṭhakayānaṃ sivikā. Antolikāsaṅkhātā paṭapoṭalikā pāṭaṅkī. “Ekabhikkhussa hī”tiādi tadatthassa samatthanaṃ. Araññatthāyāti araññagamanatthāya. Dhotapādakatthāyāti dhovitapādānamanurakkhaṇatthāya. Saṃhanitabbā bandhitabbāti saṅghāṭā, upāhanāyeva saṅghāṭā tathā, yugaḷabhūtā upāhanāti attho. Aññassa dātabbāti ettha vuttanayena dānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

A 'vayha' is a carriage covered with planks above like a pavilion, or a carriage made by covering it so it is completely enclosed. A 'sandamānikā' is a carriage made in the manner of a Garuḷa's wings, having attached rafters made of gold, silver, and so on, to both sides. A 'sivikā' is a seat-vehicle made with planks and the like. A 'pāṭaṅkī' is a cloth litter also known as an 'antolikā'. The phrase 'For one monk,' etc., is a statement that establishes that meaning. 'Araññatthāya' means: for the purpose of going to the forest. 'Dhotapādakatthāya' means: for the purpose of protecting washed feet. Because they are to be fastened, to be bound, they are called 'saṅghāṭā'; sandals themselves are thus 'saṅghāṭā'. The meaning is: sandals that have become a pair. Regarding 'It should be given to another,' here the giving should be understood in the manner stated for robes.

Mañcoti nidassanamattaṃ. Sabbepi hi pīṭhabhisādayo nisīdanasayanayoggā gahetabbā tesupi tathāpaṭipajjitabbato.

The bed is mentioned merely as an example. Indeed, all seats, couches, and the like that are suitable for sitting or lying down should be included, because one should act in the same way regarding them too.

Ābādhapaccayā eva attanā paribhuñjitabbā gandhā vaṭṭantīti dasseti “kaṇḍukacchuchavidosādiābādhe satī”ti iminā. “Lakkhaṇe hi sati hetutthopi katthaci sambhavatī”ti heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Tattha kaṇḍūti [M 1.0358] khajju. Kacchūti vitacchikā. Chavidosoti kilāsādi. Āharāpetvāti ñātipavāritato bhikkhācāravattena vā na yena kenaci vā ākārena harāpetvā. Bhesajjapaccayehi gilānassa viññattipi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave[V 1.0315], gandhaṃ gahetvā kavāṭe pañcaṅgulikaṃ dātuṃ, pupphaṃ gahetvā vihāre ekamantaṃ nikkhipitu”nti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato “dvāre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gharadhūpanaṃ vihāravāsanā, cetiyagharavāsanā vā. Ādi-saddena cetiyapaṭimāpūjādīni saṅgaṇhāti.

By this phrase, 'when there is an illness such as scabies, an itchy rash, skin disease, etc.,' it shows that fragrances are allowable to be used by oneself only on account of illness. 'Indeed, when there is a characteristic, the meaning of cause is also possible in some cases' has already been stated below. Herein, 'kaṇḍū' is scabies. 'Kacchū' is an itchy rash. 'Chavidoso' is a skin disease such as ringworm and the like. 'Having had it brought' means: having it brought from relatives or from those who have invited one, by means of the alms-round practice, or by any means whatsoever. For a sick person, even a request for medicinal requisites is allowable. Because it is said, 'I allow, monks, taking fragrance to apply a five-finger mark on the door-leaf, or taking a flower to place aside in the monastery,' the phrase 'at the door,' etc., was stated by the commentator. 'Gharadhūpanaṃ' is the perfuming of the monastery, or the perfuming of the shrine-house. By the word 'etc.,' he includes the worship of cetiyas, images, and so on.

Kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisaṃ, yaṃ kiñci upabhogārahaṃ vatthu, tasmā yathāvuttānampi pasaṅgaṃ nivāretuṃ “vuttāvasesaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti āha, pārisesanayato gahitattā vuttāvasesaṃ daṭṭhabbanti adhippāyo. Kiṃ panetanti vuttaṃ “seyyathida”ntiādi. Tathārūpe kāleti gāmaṃ pavisituṃ dukkarādikāle. Vallūroti sukkhamaṃsaṃ. Bhājana-saddo sappitelaguḷasaddehi yojetabbo tadavinābhāvittā. Kālassevāti pageva. Udakakaddameti udake ca kaddame ca. Nimitte cetaṃ bhummaṃ, bhāvalakkhaṇe vā. Acchathāti nisīdatha. Bhuñjantassevāti bhuñjato eva bhikkhuno, sampadānavacanaṃ, anādaratthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. Kiriyantarāvacchedanayogena hettha anādaratā. Gīvāyāmakanti bhāvanapuṃsakavacanaṃ, gīvaṃ āyametvā āyataṃ katvāti attho, yathā vā bhutte atibhuttatāya gīvā āyamitabbā hoti, tathātipi vaṭṭati. Catumāsampīti vassānassa cattāro māsepi. Kuṭumbaṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, tadassatthīti kuṭumbiko, muṇḍo ca so kuṭumbiko cāti muṇḍakuṭumbiko, tassa jīvikaṃ tathā, taṃ katvā jīvatīti attho. Nayadassanamattañcetaṃ āmisapadena dassitānaṃ sannidhivatthūnanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because it is to be handled by defilements, it is 'āmisa,' meaning any object fit for consumption. Therefore, to prevent the application of this term even to the things already mentioned, he said, 'the remainder of what has been said should be understood.' The meaning is that because it is taken by the method of elimination, the remainder of what has been said should be understood as 'āmisa.' But what is this? It is stated in the passage beginning 'That is to say.' 'At such a time' means: at a time when it is difficult, etc., to enter a village. 'Vallūro' means: dried meat. The word 'bhājana' (vessel) should be connected with the words for ghee, oil, and molasses, because they are inseparable from it. 'Kālasseva' means: early in the morning. 'Udakakaddame' means: on account of water and mud. This is a locative of cause or a locative absolute. 'Acchatha' means: sit down. 'Bhuñjantasseva' refers to the monk who is eating; this is a dative case, or a genitive case in the sense of disregard. Here, disregard arises from the connection with interrupting another action. 'Gīvāyāmakaṃ' is a neuter noun denoting an action; the meaning is 'having stretched the neck, making it long.' Alternatively, it is also suitable that it means: in such a way that when one has eaten, the neck has to be stretched due to overeating. 'Catumāsampi' means: even the four months of the rainy season. Wealth is called 'kuṭumba'; one who has it is a 'kuṭumbika.' He is shaven ('muṇḍo') and he is a 'kuṭumbika,' thus he is a 'muṇḍakuṭumbiko.' His livelihood is like that; the meaning is that he lives by doing that. And this should be seen as merely showing the method regarding the stored items indicated by the word 'āmisa.'

Tabbirahitaṃ samaṇapaṭipattiṃ dassento “bhikkhuno panā”tiādimāha. Tattha “guḷapiṇḍo tālapakkappamāṇa”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Catubhāgamattanti kuṭumbamattanti vuttaṃ. “Ekā taṇḍulanāḷī”ti vuttattā pana tassā catubhāgo ekapatthoti vadanti. Vuttañca –

Showing the ascetic's practice devoid of that, he said, 'But for a monk,' etc. Therein, it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: 'a lump of molasses the size of a ripe palm fruit.' 'A quarter part' is said to mean 'the measure of one kuṭumba.' However, since it is said, 'one nāḷī of rice,' the teachers say that a quarter of that is one pattha. And it is said:

“Kuḍuvo pasato eko, pattho te caturo siyuṃ;

Āḷhako caturo patthā, doṇaṃ vā caturāḷhaka”nti.

“A kuḍuva is one pasata; four of those would be a pattha; four patthas are an āḷhaka; and four āḷhakas are a doṇa.”

Kasmāti [M 1.0359] vuttaṃ “te hī”tiādi. Āharāpetvāpi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, pageva yathāladdhaṃ. “Aphāsukakāle”tiādinā suddhacittena ṭhapitassa paribhogo sallekhaṃ na kopetīti dasseti. Sammutikuṭikādayo catasso, avāsāgārabhūtena vā uposathāgārādinā saha pañcakuṭiyo sandhāya “kappiyakuṭiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sannidhi nāma natthi tattha antovutthaantopakkassa anuññātattā. “Tathāgatassā”tiādinā adhikārānurūpaṃ atthaṃ payojeti. Pilotikakhaṇḍanti jiṇṇacoḷakhaṇḍaṃ.

The words beginning with 'te hi' are spoken because it should be asked, 'Why?' It is proper to store even after having something brought; what need is there to speak of storing what is received as it is? By the words beginning with 'aphāsukakāle', it is shown that the partaking of what was stored with a pure mind does not corrupt the practice of effacement. The words beginning with 'kappiyakuṭiyaṃ' are spoken in reference to the four huts beginning with the conventional hut, or to the five huts together with the Uposatha hall and the like, which is not a dwelling place. There is no such thing as storing there, because storing inside and cooking inside has been permitted. By the text beginning with 'tathāgatassa', it applies the meaning in accordance with the section. 'Pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ' means a piece of old, worn-out cloth.

13. “Gīvaṃ [V 1.0316] pasāretvā”ti etena sayameva āpāthagamane doso natthīti dasseti. Ettakampīti vinicchayavicāraṇā vatthukittanampi. Payojanamattamevāti padatthayojanamattameva. Yassa pana padassa vitthārakathaṃ vinā na sakkā attho viññātuṃ, tattha vitthārakathāpi padatthasaṅgahameva gacchati.

13. By this phrase, 'gīvaṃ pasāretvā' (having stretched out the neck), it is shown that there is no fault when something comes into the range of vision by itself. 'Ettakampi' means the investigation of the decision and also the statement of the subject matter. 'Payojanamattameva' means only the application of the meaning of the word. However, for a word whose meaning cannot be known without a detailed explanation, in that case, the detailed explanation also is included in the collection of the word's meaning.

Kutūhalavasena pekkhitabbato pekkhaṃ, naṭasatthavidhinā payogo. Naṭasamūhena pana janasamūhe kattabbavasena “naṭasammajja”nti vuttaṃ. Janānaṃ sammadde samūhe katanti hi sammajjaṃ. Sārasamāse pana “pekkhāmaha”ntipi vadanti, “sammajjadassanussava”nti tesaṃ mate attho. Bhāratanāmakānaṃ dvebhātukarājūnaṃ, rāmarañño ca yujjhanādikaṃ tappasutehi ācikkhitabbato akkhānaṃ. Gantumpi na vaṭṭati, pageva taṃ sotuṃ. Pāṇinā tāḷitabbaṃ saraṃ pāṇissaranti āha “kaṃsatāḷa”nti, lohamayo tūriyajātiviseso kaṃso, lohamayapatto vā, tassa tāḷanasaddanti attho. Pāṇīnaṃ tāḷanasaranti atthaṃ sandhāya pāṇitāḷantipi vadanti. Ghanasaṅkhātānaṃ tūriyavisesānaṃ tāḷanaṃ ghanatāḷaṃ nāma, daṇḍamayasammatāḷaṃ silātalākatāḷaṃ vā. Mantenāti bhūtāvisanamantena. Eketi sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca, yathā cettha, evamito paresupi “eke”ti āgataṭṭhānesu. Te kira dīghanikāyassatthavisesavādino. Caturassaambaṇakatāḷaṃ nāma rukkhasāradaṇḍādīsu yena kenaci caturassaambaṇaṃ katvā catūsu passesu dhammena onaddhitvā vāditabhaṇḍassa tāḷanaṃ. Tañhi ekādasadoṇappamāṇamānavisesasaṇṭhānattā “ambaṇaka”nti vuccati, bimbisakantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tathā kumbhasaṇṭhānatāya kumbho, ghaṭoyeva vā, tassa dhunananti khuddakabhāṇakā. Abbhokkiraṇaṃ raṅgabalikaraṇaṃ. Te hi naccaṭṭhāne devatānaṃ balikaraṇaṃ nāma katvā kīḷanti, yaṃ “nandī”tipi vuccati[M 1.0360]. Itthipurisasaṃyogādikilesajanakaṃ paṭibhānacittaṃ sobhanakaraṇato sobhanakaraṃ nāma. “Sobhanagharaka”nti sārasamāse vuttaṃ. Caṇḍāya alanti caṇḍālaṃ, ayoguḷakīḷā. Caṇḍālā nāma hīnajātikā sunakhamaṃsabhojino, tesaṃ idanti caṇḍālaṃ. Sāṇe udakena temetvā aññamaññaṃ ākoṭanakīḷā sāṇadhovanakīḷā. Vaṃsena kataṃ kīḷanaṃ vaṃsanti āha “veḷuṃ ussāpetvā kīḷana”nti.

It is called 'pekkhaṃ' because it is to be watched out of curiosity; the application is according to the method of the actors' text. However, it is called 'naṭasammajja' because it is to be performed by a troupe of actors in a gathering of people. Indeed, it is called 'sammajjaṃ' because it is done in a crowd, a gathering of people. In the Sārasamāsa, however, they also say 'pekkhāmaha' (we shall look); in their view, the meaning should be understood as 'a festival for seeing the gathering'. It is called 'akkhānaṃ' because the fighting and so on of the two royal brothers named Bhārata and of King Rāma is to be narrated by those proficient in it. It is not proper even to go, what need is there to speak of listening to it? He said 'kaṃsatāḷa' because a sound to be struck by the hand is a 'pāṇissara'. 'Kaṃso' is a special kind of musical instrument made of bronze, or a bronze bowl; the meaning is the sound of striking it. Referring to the meaning 'the sound of clapping the hands', they also say 'pāṇitāḷa'. The striking of special musical instruments called solid is named 'ghanatāḷaṃ'; or it is the striking of a cymbal made of wood, or the striking of a stone slab. 'Mantena' means with a spell that causes spirit possession. 'Eke' refers to the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttara Vihāra; just as here, so too it should be understood in subsequent places where 'eke' appears. It is said that those teachers are proponents of a special meaning of the Dīghanikāya. The striking of a four-cornered 'ambaṇa' drum is the striking of a musical instrument made by fashioning a four-cornered 'ambaṇa' from any kind of hardwood, stick, or the like, and covering it with leather on the four sides. Indeed, because it has the shape of a special measuring vessel with a capacity of eleven 'doṇa', it is called 'ambaṇaka'; 'bimbisaka' is also its name. Likewise, because it has the shape of a pot, it is 'kumbho'; or a pot itself is 'kumbho'. The reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya say it means the shaking of it. 'Abbhokkiraṇaṃ' is making an offering on the stage. For they play after having made an offering to the deities in the dancing area, which is also called 'nandī'. The ingenious art which generates defilements such as the union of men and women is called 'sobhanakaraṃ' because it makes things beautiful. In the Sārasamāsa, it is called 'sobhanagharaka'. Because it is sufficient for fierceness ('caṇḍāya alaṃ'), it is 'caṇḍālaṃ', which refers to the game of iron balls. 'Caṇḍālā' are those of low birth who eat dog meat; because this belongs to them, it is 'caṇḍālaṃ'. The game of striking one another after wetting hemp cloths with water is the 'sāṇadhovanakīḷā'. Wishing to show the etymology 'a game played with bamboo is `vaṃsa`', he said, 'playing by raising a bamboo pole' ('veḷuṃ ussāpetvā kīḷana').

Nikhaṇitvāti bhūmiyaṃ nikhātaṃ katvā. Nakkhattakāleti nakkhattayogachaṇakāle. Tamatthaṃ aṅguttarāgame dasakanipātapāḷiyā (a. ni. 10.106) sādhento “vuttampiceta”ntiādimāha. Tatthāti tasmiṃ aṭṭhidhovane. Indajālenāti aṭṭhidhovanamantaṃ parijappetvā yathā pare aṭṭhīniyeva passanti, na maṃsādīni, evaṃ maṃsādīnamantaradhāpanamāyāya. Indassa [V 1.0317] jālamiva hi paṭicchādituṃ samatthanato “indajāla”nti māyā vuccati indacāpādayo viya. Aṭṭhidhovananti aṭṭhidhovanakīḷā.

‘Nikhaṇitvā’ means having buried it in the ground. ‘Nakkhattakāle’ means at the time of a festival connected with a constellation. Wishing to establish that meaning with the Pāḷi of the Dasaka Nipāta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, he said the words beginning with ‘vuttampi cetaṃ’. ‘Tattha’ means in that bone-washing. ‘Indajālena’ means by means of an illusion that makes the flesh and so on disappear, after having recited the bone-washing spell in such a way that others see only the bones, not the flesh and so on. Indeed, because it is able to cover like Indra's net, the illusion is called ‘indajāla’, like the word ‘indacāpa’ (Indra's bow) and so on. ‘Aṭṭhidhovanaṃ’ is the game of bone-washing.

Hatthiādīhi saddhiṃ yujjhitunti hatthiādīsu abhiruhitvā aññehi saddhiṃ yujjhanaṃ, hatthiādīhi ca saddhiṃ sayameva yujjhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, hatthiādīhi saddhiṃ aññehi yujjhituṃ, sayaṃ vā yujjhitunti hi attho. Teti hatthiādayo. Aññamaññaṃ mathenti vilothentīti mallā, bāhuyuddhakārakā, tesaṃ yuddhaṃ. Sampahāroti saṅgāmo. Balassa senāya aggaṃ gaṇanakoṭṭhāsaṃ karonti etthāti balaggaṃ, “ettakā hatthī, ettakā assā”tiādinā balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ. Senaṃ viyūhanti ettha vibhajitvā ṭhapenti, senāya vā ettha byūhanaṃ vinyāsoti senābyūho, “ito hatthī hontu, ito assā hontū”tiādinā yuddhatthaṃ caturaṅgabalāya senāya desavisesesu vicāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ pana bhedato sakaṭabyūhādivasena. Ādi-saddena cakkapadumabyūhānaṃ daṇḍabhogamaṇḍalāsaṃhatabyūhānañca gahaṇaṃ, “tayo hatthī pacchimaṃ hatthānīkaṃ, tayo assā pacchimaṃ assānīkaṃ, tayo rathā pacchimaṃ rathānīkaṃ, cattāro purisā sarahatthā pattī pacchimaṃ pattānīka”nti (pāci. 324 uyyodhikasikkhāpade) kaṇḍaviddhasikkhāpadassa padabhājanaṃ sandhāya “tayo…pe…ādinā nayena vuttassā”ti āha. Tañca kho “dvādasapuriso hatthī, tipuriso asso, catupuriso [M 1.0361] ratho, cattāro purisā sarahatthā pattī”ti (pāci. 314 uyyuttasenāsikkhāpade) vuttalakkhaṇato hatthiādigaṇanenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, etena ca “cha hatthiniyo, eko ca hatthī idameka”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 245) cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttamanīkaṃ paṭikkhipati.

The phrase ‘to engage in battle with elephants, etc.’ refers to mounting elephants and so on and fighting with others, or fighting by oneself with elephants and so on. Indeed, the meaning is to fight with others using elephants and so on, or to fight by oneself. ‘Those’ (te) are elephants, etc. ‘Wrestlers’ (mallā) are those who crush and roll with each other, those who engage in combat with their arms; their fight is wrestling. ‘A clash’ (sampahāro) is a battle. A ‘military review’ (balaggaṃ) is so called because here (ettha) they make a primary (aggaṃ) count of the divisions (koṭṭhāsaṃ) of the army (balassa senāya); it is a place for counting the troops (balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ), saying, ‘So many elephants, so many horses,’ and so on. An ‘army-formation’ (senābyūho) is so called because here (ettha) they arrange (viyūhanti) the army (senaṃ) by dividing and placing it; or, it is so called because here (ettha) there is the deployment (byūhanaṃ) or arrangement (vinyāso) of the army (senāya). It is a place for deploying (vicāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ) the fourfold army in various positions for battle, saying, ‘Let the elephants be here, let the horses be here,’ and so on. That, again, is divided by way of the cart-formation and so on. By the word ‘and so on’ (ādi-saddena), the wheel-formation, lotus-formation, staff-formation, snake-formation, circle-formation, and compact-formation are included. Referring to the word-analysis section of the training rule on going to see a battle (Uyyodhika Sikkhāpada), he says, “‘A minimum of three elephants is an elephant division; a minimum of three horses is a horse division; a minimum of three chariots is a chariot division; a minimum of four men with arrows in hand, who are infantry, is an infantry division’—in the manner stated, ‘three… etc.’” And this should be understood as being by the counting of elephants, etc., according to the characteristics stated in the training rule concerning a deployed army (Uyyuttasenā Sikkhāpada): ‘An elephant unit consists of twelve men, a horse unit of three men, a chariot unit of four men, and four men with arrows in hand are the infantry.’ And by this, he rejects the division (anīkaṃ) mentioned in the commentary on the Cammakkhandhaka: ‘Six female elephants and one young elephant are one division.’”

14. Kāraṇaṃ nāma phalassa ṭhānanti vuttaṃ “pamādo…pe… ṭhāna”nti. Padānīti sārīādīnaṃ patiṭṭhānāni. Aṭṭhāpadanti saññāya dīghatā. “Aṭṭhapada”ntipi paṭhanti. Dasapadaṃ nāma dvīhi pantīti vīsatiyā padehi kīḷanajūtaṃ. Aṭṭhapadadasapadesūti aṭṭhapadadasapadaphalakesu. Ākāseyeva kīḷananti “ayaṃ sārī asukapadaṃ mayā nītā, ayaṃ asukapada”nti kevalaṃ mukheneva vadantānaṃ ākāseyeva jūtassa kīḷanaṃ. Nānāpathamaṇḍalanti anekavihitasārīmaggaparivaṭṭaṃ. Pariharitabbanti sāriyo pariharituṃ yuttakaṃ. Ito cito ca saranti parivattantīti sāriyo, yena kenaci katāni akkhabījāni. Tatthāti tāsu sārīsu, tasmiṃ vā apanayanupanayane. Jūtakhaliketi jūtamaṇḍale. “Jūtaphalake”tipi adhunā pāṭho. Pāsakaṃ vuccati chasu passesu ekekaṃ yāva chakkaṃ dassetvā katakīḷanakaṃ, taṃ vaḍḍhetvā yathāladdhaṃ [V 1.0318] ekakādivasena sāriyo apanento, upanento ca kīḷanti, pasati aṭṭhapadādīsu bādhati, phusati cāti hi pāsako, catubbīsatividho akkho. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

14. It is said that ‘cause’ (kāraṇaṃ) is the basis of the result, as in ‘heedlessness… is the basis’ (pamādo…pe… ṭhānaṃ). ‘Squares’ (padāni) are the positions for the game pieces (sārī), etc. ‘Eight-square’ (aṭṭhāpadaṃ) is ‘length’ by designation. They also recite it as ‘aṭṭhapada.’ ‘Ten-square’ (dasapadaṃ) is a game of dice played with twenty squares in two rows. ‘In eight-square and ten-square’ (aṭṭhapadadasapadesu) means on eight-square and ten-square boards. ‘Playing only in the air’ (ākāseyeva kīḷanaṃ) is the playing of a game of dice only in the air by those who merely say with their mouths, ‘This piece was moved by me to such-and-such a square, this one to such-and-such a square.’ ‘Various circular paths’ (nānāpathamaṇḍalaṃ) refers to the turning of the many various paths of the game pieces. ‘To be moved’ (pariharitabbaṃ) means suitable for moving the game pieces. ‘Pieces’ (sāriyo) are so called because they move (saranti) and turn (parivattanti) here and there; they are dice-seeds (akkhabījāni) made of anything whatsoever. ‘Therein’ (tattha) means among those pieces, or in that act of removing and placing. ‘In a gaming pit’ (jūtakhalike) means on a gaming circle. The current reading is also ‘on a gaming board’ (jūtaphalake). A game played with a die that shows from one to six on its six sides is called Pāsaka. They play by increasing that and, according to what is obtained, by way of one, etc., removing and placing the pieces. Indeed, a ‘pāsaka’ is so called because in eight-square games and so on, it ensnares (pasati), obstructs (bādhati), and touches (phusati); the game of dice (akkho) is of twenty-four kinds. Regarding which it is said:

“Aṭṭhakaṃ mālikaṃ vuttaṃ, sāvaṭṭañca chakaṃ mataṃ;

Catukkaṃ bahulaṃ ñeyyaṃ, dvi bindusantibhadrakaṃ;

Catuvīsati āyā ca, munindena pakāsitā”ti.

“The garland-game is said to be eightfold, and the turning-game is considered sixfold. The abundant-game should be known as fourfold, and the auspicious-row-of-dots game as twofold. And thus the twenty-four types were proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.”

Tena kīḷanamidha pāsakakīḷanaṃ. Ghaṭanaṃ paharaṇaṃ, tena kīḷā ghaṭikāti āha “dīghadaṇḍakenā”tiādi. Ghaṭena kumbhena kīḷā ghaṭikāti eke. Mañjiṭṭhikāya vāti mañjiṭṭhisaṅkhātassa yojanavallirukkhassa sāraṃ gahetvā pakkakasāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sitthodakena vāti [piṭṭhodakena vā (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] ca pakkamadhusitthodakaṃ. Salākahatthanti tālahīrādīnaṃ kalāpassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bahūsu salākāsu visesarahitaṃ ekaṃ salākaṃ gahetvā tāsu pakkhipitvā puna taññeva uddharantā salākahatthena kīḷantīti keci. Guḷakīḷāti guḷaphalakīḷā, yena kenaci vā kataguḷakīḷā. Paṇṇena vaṃsākārena katā nāḷikā paṇṇanāḷikā, tenevāha “taṃdhamantā”ti. Khuddake ka-paccayoti [M 1.0362] dasseti “khuddakanaṅgala”nti iminā. Hatthapādānaṃ mokkhena mocanena cayati parivattati etāyāti mokkhacikā, tenāha “ākāse vā”tiādi. Paribbhamanattāyeva taṃ cakkaṃ nāmāti dassetuṃ “paribbhamanacakka”nti vuttaṃ.

Here, the game with these twenty-four kinds is called the Pāsaka-game. ‘Ghaṭanaṃ’ means striking (paharaṇaṃ); the game played with that is ‘ghaṭikā,’ hence he says, ‘with a long stick,’ etc. Some say that ‘ghaṭikā’ is a game played with a pot (ghaṭa) or jar (kumbha). ‘Or with mañjiṭṭhikā’ refers to the cooked astringent liquid taken from the heartwood of the yojanavalli tree, known as mañjiṭṭhi. ‘Or with beeswax-water’ (sitthodakena vā) means cooked honey-beeswax water. ‘A handful of slips’ (salākahatthaṃ) is a designation for a bundle of palm-fibres, etc. Some say that they play ‘a handful of slips’ by taking one unmarked slip from among many slips, putting it among them, and then drawing out that same one again. ‘Playing with balls’ (guḷakīḷā) means playing with guḷa fruits, or a game played with balls made of anything whatsoever. A tube (nāḷikā) made from a leaf in the shape of a bamboo flute is a ‘leaf-tube’ (paṇṇanāḷikā); that is why he said, ‘blowing it.’ By the phrase ‘a small plough’ (khuddakanaṅgalaṃ), he shows that the suffix ‘ka’ is used in the sense of ‘small.’ ‘Acrobatics’ (mokkhacikā) is so called because by this game (etāya), through the release (mokkhena) or freeing (mocanena) of the hands and feet, one tumbles (cayati) or turns (parivattati); that is why he said, ‘in the air, or…’ etc. To show that it is called a ‘wheel’ (cakkaṃ) precisely because of its revolving (paribbhamanattā), it was called a ‘revolving wheel’ (paribbhamanacakkaṃ).

Paṇṇena katā nāḷi paṇṇanāḷi, iminā pattāḷhakapadadvayassa yathākkamaṃ pariyāyaṃ dasseti. Tena katā pana kīḷā pattāḷhakāti vuttaṃ “tāyā”tiādi. Khuddako ratho rathako ka-saddassa khuddakatthavacanato. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Ākāse vā yaṃ ñāpeti, tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ vā yathā vā tathā vā akkharaṃ likhitvā “evamida”nti jānanena kīḷā akkharikā, pucchantassa mukhāgataṃ akkharaṃ gahetvā naṭṭhamuttilābhādijānanakīḷātipi vadanti. Vajja-saddo aparādhatthoti āha “yathāvajjaṃ nāmā”tiādi. Vāditānurūpaṃ naccanaṃ, gāyanaṃ vā yathāvajjantipi vadanti. “Evaṃ kate jayo bhavissati, evaṃ kate parājayo”ti jayaparājayaṃ purakkhatvā payogakaraṇavasena parihārapathādīnampi jūtappamādaṭṭhānabhāvo veditabbo, paṅgacīrādīhi ca vaṃsādīhi kattabbā kiccasiddhi, asiddhi cāti jayaparājayāvaho payogo vutto, yathāvajjanti ca kāṇādīhi sadisākāradassanehi jayaparājayavasena jūtakīḷikabhāvena vuttaṃ. Sabbepi [V 1.0319] hete jotenti pakāsenti etehi tappayogikā jayaparājayavasena, javanti ca gacchanti jayaparājayaṃ etehīti vā atthena jūtasaddavacanīyataṃ nātivattanti.

A tube made of leaves is called a ‘leaf-tube’ (paṇṇanāḷi). By this, it shows the synonym, in respective order, for the compound term pattāḷhaka. Furthermore, the game played with that leaf-cup is called pattāḷhakā; therefore, it is said, "by that," etc. A small chariot (ratho) is a rathako; this is because the suffix 'ka' has the meaning of 'small'. This method should be understood for the remaining terms as well. The game of writing a letter either in the air or on the back of another person, or in whatever manner, and making them know, "This is such and such a letter," is called akkharikā. The teachers also say that akkharikā is the game of taking a letter that comes from the mouth of one who asks and thereby discerning things such as the finding of a lost pearl. The word 'vajja' has the meaning of 'offense'; therefore, he said, "yathāvajjaṃ nāma," etc. The teachers also say that dancing or singing in accordance with musical instruments is called yathāvajjaṃ. "If one does thus, there will be victory; if one does thus, there will be defeat"—having thus placed victory and defeat foremost, by means of making an effort, the state of being a basis for gambling and negligence should be understood even for things such as avoiding the path of the dice. Thus, the effort that brings victory and defeat is spoken of, namely, the accomplishment or non-accomplishment of the task to be done with things such as leaf-pipes and flutes. And the term 'yathāvajjaṃ' is spoken of as being a form of gambling by way of victory and defeat through showing features similar to the one-eyed, etc. Indeed, all these games illuminate, that is, they make clear, these gambles by means of those efforts. Or alternatively, by this meaning: those engaged in such efforts proceed, that is, they go towards victory and defeat by means of these games through victory and defeat; they do not go beyond what is meant by the word 'jūta' (gambling).

15. Pamāṇātikkantāsananti “aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ kāretabbaṃ sugataṅgulenā”ti vuttappamāṇato atikkantāsanaṃ. Kammavasena payojanato “anuyuttā viharantīti padaṃ apekkhitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni sīhabyagghādivāḷarūpāni. Vuttañhi bhikkhunivibhaṅge “pallaṅko nāma āharimehi vāḷehi kato”ti (pāci. 984) “akappiyarūpākulo akappiyamañco pallaṅko”ti sārasamāse vuttaṃ. Dīghalomako mahākojavoti caturaṅgulādhikalomo kāḷavaṇṇo mahākojavo. Kuvuccati pathavī, tassaṃ javati sobhanavitthaṭavasenāti kojavo. “Caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomānī”ti vacanato caturaṅgulato heṭṭhā [M 1.0363] vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Uddalomī ekantalomīti visesadassanametaṃ, tasmā yadi tāsu na pavisati, vaṭṭatīti gahetabbaṃ. Vānavicittanti bhitticchadādiākārena vānena sibbanena vicitraṃ. Uṇṇāmayattharaṇanti migalomapakatamattharaṇaṃ. Setattharaṇoti dhavalattharaṇo. Sītatthikehi sevitabbattā setattharaṇo, “bahumudulomako”tipi vadanti. Ghanapupphakoti sabbathā pupphākārasampanno. “Uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti uṇṇāmayo lohitattharaṇo”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 258) sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Āmalakapattākārāhi pupphapantīhi yebhuyyato katattā āmalakapattotipi vuccati.

15. 'A seat exceeding the prescribed measurement' (pamāṇātikkantāsanaṃ) is a seat that exceeds the measurement stated thus: "Its legs should be made eight Sugata finger-widths long." It is said "in consideration of the phrase 'they dwell devoted to'" because of its connection by way of the action. 'Figures of beasts of prey' (vāḷarūpāni) means artificial figures of beasts of prey such as lions, tigers, etc. Indeed, it is said in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga: "A couch (pallaṅko) is one made with artificial figures of beasts of prey." In the Sārasamāsa it is said: "A pallaṅka is an unacceptable couch filled with unacceptable figures of beasts of prey." 'A long-fleeced great rug' (dīghalomako mahākojavo) is a great rug of black color with fleece longer than four finger-widths. The earth is called 'ku'. Because it spreads upon it in a beautiful and extensive manner, it is called 'kojavo'. Because it is said in the commentary, "Its fleece, it seems, is longer than four finger-widths," some teachers say that it is permissible if it is less than four finger-widths. This statement 'uddalomī ekantalomī' is for showing a specific case. Therefore, it should be understood that if a rug does not fall into these categories, it is permissible. 'Variegated by weaving' (vānavicittaṃ) means a spread made variegated by weaving, that is, by sewing, with patterns of walls, roofs, etc. 'A woolen spread' (uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ) is a spread made of animal fleece. 'A white spread' (setattharaṇo) is a white spread. Because it is to be used by those who desire coolness, it is called setattharaṇo. They also call it 'one with much soft fleece' (bahumudulomako). 'Thickly flowered' (ghanapupphako) means completely endowed with the appearance of flowers. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: "'A woolen spread' is a red spread made of wool." Because it is mostly made with rows of flowers in the shape of āmalaka leaves, it is also called 'āmalaka-leaf patterned' (āmalakapattopi).

Tiṇṇaṃ tūlānanti rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakītūlasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ. Uditaṃ dvīsu lomaṃ dasā yassāti uddalomī i-kārassa akāraṃ, ta-kārassa lopaṃ, dvibhāvañca katvā. Ekasmiṃ ante lomaṃ dasā yassāti ekantalomī. Ubhayattha kecīti sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca. Tesaṃ vāde pana uditamekato uggataṃ lomamayaṃ pupphaṃ yassāti uddalomī vuttanayena. Ubhato antato ekaṃ sadisaṃ lomamayaṃ pupphaṃ yassāti ekantalomīti vacanattho. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “uddalomīti ekato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. ‘Uddhalomī’tipi pāṭho. Ekantalomīti ubhato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 254) vuttaṃ, nāmamattamesa viseso. Atthato pana aggahitāvaseso aṭṭhakathādvayepi natthīti daṭṭhabbo.

'Of the three kinds of cotton' means of the three kinds of cotton designated as tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and grass-cotton. A spread which has fleece or a fringe rising on two sides is called uddalomī; the word is formed by changing the vowel 'i' to 'a', eliding the consonant 't', and doubling the consonant. A spread which has fleece or a fringe on one end is called ekantalomī. 'Some, in both cases' refers to the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttaravihāra. However, in their view, a spread which has a woolen flower rising up from one side is called uddalomī, according to the method already stated. A spread which has a similar woolen flower at both ends is called ekantalomī. This is the word-meaning. However, in the Vinaya Commentary it is said: "Uddalomī is a woolen spread with fleece rising from one side. There is also the reading 'uddhalomī'. Ekantalomī is a woolen spread with fleece rising from both sides." This is merely a difference in name. As for the meaning, however, it should be understood that there is nothing left unstated in either of the two commentaries.

Koseyyañca kaṭṭissañca kaṭṭissāni virūpekasesavasena. Tehi pakatamattharaṇaṃ kaṭṭissaṃ. Etadevatthaṃ dassetuṃ “koseyyakaṭṭissamayapaccattharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ, koseyyasuttānamantarantaraṃ suvaṇṇamayasuttāni pavesetvā vītamattharaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Suvaṇṇasuttaṃ kira “kaṭṭissaṃ, kassaṭa”nti [V 1.0320] ca vadanti. Teneva “koseyyakassaṭamaya”nti ācariyadhammapālattherena (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.15) vuttaṃ. Kaṭṭissaṃ nāma vākavisesotipi vadanti. Ratanaparisibbitanti ratanehi saṃsibbitaṃ, suvaṇṇalittanti keci. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ. Vinayeti vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ, vinayapariyāyaṃ vā sandhāya vuttaṃ. Idha hi suttantikapariyāye “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ. Vinayapariyāyaṃ pana patvā garuke [M 1.0364] ṭhātabbattā suddhakoseyyameva vaṭṭati, netarānīti vinicchayo veditabbo, suttantikapariyāye pana ratanaparisibbanarahitāpi tūlikā na vaṭṭati, itarāni vaṭṭanti, sacepi tāni ratanaparisibbitāni, bhūmattharaṇavasena yathānurūpaṃ mañcapīṭhādīsu ca upanetuṃ vaṭṭantīti. Suttantadesanāya gahaṭṭhānampi vasena vuttattā tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “ṭhapetvā…pe… na vaṭṭantīti vutta”nti apare. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyanti katthaci pāṭho, porāṇadīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyanti attho. Naccayogganti naccituṃ pahonakaṃ. Karonti ettha naccanti kuttakaṃ, taṃ pana uddalomīekantalomīvisesameva. Vuttañca –

Silk thread and gold thread. By way of dissimilar singular remainder, `kaṭṭissāni` means silk and gold threads. A spread made from them is called `kaṭṭissa`. To show just this meaning, it was said, 'a spread made of silk and gold thread.' This is what is meant: a spread woven by inserting threads made of gold in between the silk threads. It is said that teachers call gold thread `kaṭṭissa` and `kassaṭa`. For that very reason, it was stated as `koseyyakassaṭamaya` by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. Teachers also say that `kaṭṭissa` is a special kind of bark fiber. `Ratanaparisibbita` means sewn with jewels; some say it means gilded with gold. `Suddhakoseyya` means devoid of being sewn with jewels. The word `vinaye` was stated in reference to either the Vinaya Commentary or the Vinaya discourse. Indeed, here in the Suttanta discourse, it is said: 'Excluding a cotton-stuffed mattress, all spreads such as `goṇaka` and so on, even if sewn with jewels, are allowable.' However, with respect to the Vinaya discourse, because one must stand on serious ground, only a pure silk spread is allowable; the others are not. This is the ruling that should be known. However, in the Suttanta discourse, a cotton-stuffed mattress, even if devoid of being sewn with jewels, is not allowable. The other spreads are allowable. And if those spreads are sewn with jewels, it is allowable to use them appropriately as floor coverings and on beds, chairs, and so on. Other teachers say: 'Because the Suttanta teaching was also spoken for the sake of householders, for the purpose of including them, it was said, "Excluding... (etc.)... are not allowable."' In some places, there is the reading `dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ`; the meaning is 'in the ancient Dīghanikāya Commentary'. `Naccayogga` means suitable for dancing. Because they perform dancing on it, that spread is called `kuttaka`. However, that `kuttaka` is just a special type of `uddalomī` and `ekantalomī`. And it has been said:

“Dvidasekadasānyudda-lomīekantalomino;

Tadeva soḷasitthīnaṃ, naccayoggañhi kuttaka”nti.

Spreads with fringes on two sides and one side are called `uddalomī` and `ekantalomī` respectively. When that very same spread is suitable for sixteen female dancers to dance upon, it is called `kuttaka`.

Hatthino piṭṭhiyaṃ attharaṃ hatthattharaṃ. Evaṃ sesapadesupi. Ajinacammehīti ajinamigacammehi, tāni kira cammāni sukhumatarāni, tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī”ti, uparūpari ṭhapetvā sibbanavasena hi santatibhūtā “paveṇī”ti vuccati. Kadalīmigoti mañjārākāramigo, tassa dhammena kataṃ pavarapaccattharaṇaṃ tathā. “Taṃ kirā”tiādi tadākāradassanaṃ, tasmā suddhameva kadalīmigacammaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Uttaraṃ uparibhāgaṃ chādetīti uttaracchado, vitānaṃ. Tampi lohitameva idhādhippetanti āha “rattavitānenā”ti. “Yaṃ vattati, taṃ sauttaraccheda”nti ettha seso, saṃsibbitabhāvena saddhiṃ vattatīti attho. Rattavitānesu ca kāsāvaṃ vaṭṭati, kusumbhādirattameva na vaṭṭati, tañca kho sabbarattameva. Yaṃ pana nānāvaṇṇaṃ vānacittaṃ vā lepacittaṃ vā, taṃ vaṭṭati. Paccattharaṇasseva padhānattā tappaṭibaddhaṃ setavitānampi na vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Ubhatoti ubhayattha mañcassa sīsabhāge, pādabhāge cāti attho. Etthāpi sauttaracchade viya vinicchayo. Padumavaṇṇaṃ vāti nātirattaṃ sandhāyāha. Vicitraṃ vāti pana sabbathā kappiyattā vuttaṃ, na pana ubhato upadhānesu akappiyattā. Na hi lohitaka-saddo citte vaṭṭati. Paṭalikaggahaṇeneva cittakassāpi attharaṇassa saṅgahetabbappasaṅgato. Sace pamāṇayuttanti vuttamevatthaṃ byatirekato samatthetuṃ [V 1.0321] āha “mahāupadhānaṃ pana paṭikkhitta”nti. Mahāupadhānanti ca pamāṇātikkantaṃ upadhānaṃ. Sīsappamāṇameva hi tassa pamāṇaṃ. Vuttañca “anujānāmi bhikkhave, sīsappamāṇaṃ [M 1.0365] bibbohanaṃ kātu”nti (cūḷava. 297) sīsappamāṇañca nāma yassa vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ miniyamānaṃ vidatthi ceva caturaṅgulañca hoti. Bibbohanassa majjhaṭṭhānaṃ tiriyato muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, dīghato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ vā dviratanaṃ vā. Taṃ pana akappiyattāyeva paṭikkhittaṃ, na tu uccāsayanamahāsayanapariyāpannattā. Dvepīti sīsūpadhānaṃ, pādūpadhānañca. Paccattharaṇaṃ datvāti paccattharaṇaṃ katvā attharitvāti attho, idañca gilānameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ “agilānassāpi sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti dvayameva vaṭṭati. Gilānassa bibbohanāni santharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ katvā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭatī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) vuttanayenevāti vinaye bhagavatā vuttanayeneva. Kathaṃ pana vuttanti āha “vuttañheta”ntiādi. Yathā aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ hoti, evaṃ āsandiyā pādacchindanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pallaṅkassa pana āharimāni vāḷarūpāni āharitvā puna appaṭibaddhatākāraṇampi bhedanameva. Vijaṭetvāti jaṭaṃ nibbedhetvā. Bibbohanaṃ kātunti tāni vijaṭitatūlāni anto pakkhipitvā bibbohanaṃ kātuṃ.

A spread laid on an elephant's back is `hatthatthara`. This should be understood in the same way for the remaining terms as well. `Ajinacammehi` means with the hides of the black antelope. It is said that those hides are very fine; therefore, they make them into two or three layers and sew them. For that reason, it is called `ajinappaveṇī`. Indeed, because it is made continuous by way of placing them one on top of another and sewing, it is called `paveṇī`. `Kadalīmiga` is a deer with the appearance of a cat; the excellent spread made from its hide is likewise. The phrase beginning with `taṃ kira` shows the manner of its making. Therefore, teachers say that only the pure hide of the `kadalīmiga` is allowable. Because it covers the upper part, it is an `uttaracchada` (upper cover); this means a canopy. And here, that canopy is intended to be only red; therefore, he said `rattavitānena`. Here, the elided text should be understood as: 'That which exists together with an upper cover is `sauttaracchada`.' The meaning is that it exists together with the state of being well-sewn. And among red canopies, brownish-red is allowable; only red dyed with safflower and so on is not allowable, and that, indeed, is entirely red. However, whatever is of various colors, or variegated by stitching, or variegated by painting, that is allowable. Because the bedspread itself is primary, it is said that even a white canopy connected to it is not allowable. `Ubhato` means on both sides: at the head-part and at the foot-part of the couch. Here too, the ruling should be understood as in the case of the spread with an upper cover. He said `padumavaṇṇaṃ vā` in reference to a pillow that is not excessively red. However, `vicitraṃ vā` was said because it is allowable in every way; it was not, however, said regarding pillows on both sides, as it is unallowable for them. Indeed, the word `lohitaka` (red) does not apply to what is variegated. Because by the very inclusion of `paṭalikā`, there would be the unwanted consequence of including even a variegated spread. Regarding `sace pamāṇayuttaṃ` (if it is of proper size), to support this very point by way of contrast, he said, 'but a large pillow is rejected.' And `mahāupadhāna` is a pillow that exceeds the proper measure. Indeed, its proper measure is just the size of a head. And it was said by the Blessed One: 'I allow, monks, to make a bolster the size of a head.' And 'the size of a head' means that of which, when the distance between two of its three corners is measured across its breadth, is one span and four finger-breadths. The middle part of the bolster is a 'fist-cubit' in width, while in length it is one and a half cubits or two cubits. That large pillow was rejected simply because it is unallowable, but not because it is included under 'high and great beds'. `Dvepi` means the head-pillow and the foot-pillow. `Paccattharaṇaṃ datvā` means having made a bedspread and spread it over. And this statement was made in reference only to a sick monk. Therefore, in the explanation of the Senāsanakkhandhaka, he said: 'For one who is not sick, only the pair—a head-pillow and a foot-pillow—is allowable. For one who is sick, it is allowable to spread out bolsters, place a bedspread on top, and lie down.' `Vuttanayeneva` means 'in the very way stated by the Blessed One in the Vinaya.' Since the question 'But how was it stated?' should be asked, he said the passage beginning with `vuttañhetaṃ`. The cutting of the legs of a long-legged chair should be understood in such a way that, when cut, it has legs of eight finger-breadths. However, in the case of a couch, removing the removable animal figures and then making them unattached again is also considered 'breaking'. `Vijaṭetvā` means having disentangled the matted material. `Bibbohanaṃ kātuṃ` means to make a bolster by putting that disentangled cotton inside.

16. “Mātukucchito nikkhantadārakāna”nti etena aṇḍajajalābujānameva gahaṇaṃ, mātukucchito nikkhantattāti ca kāraṇaṃ dasseti, tenevāyamattho sijjhati “anekadivasāni antosayanahetu esa gandho”ti. Ucchādenti ubbaṭṭenti. Saṇṭhānasampādanatthanti susaṇṭhānatāsampādanatthaṃ. Parimaddantīti samantato maddanti.

16. By this phrase, 'of children who have come forth from the mother's womb,' the taking is of only the egg-born and the womb-born. And it shows the reason thus: 'because of having come forth from the mother's womb.' Therefore, this meaning is accomplished: 'For many days, because of the cause of having to lie inside, this body-odor exists.' They anoint; they rub. 'For the purpose of accomplishing the form' means for the purpose of accomplishing a well-formed state. 'They massage' means they knead from all around.

Tesaṃyeva dārakānanti puññavantānameva dārakānaṃ. Tesameva hi pakaraṇānurūpatāya gahaṇaṃ. Mahāmallānanti mahataṃ bāhuyuddhakārakānaṃ. Ādāso nāma maṇḍanakapakatikānaṃ manussānaṃ attano mukhachāyāpassanatthaṃ kaṃsalohādīhi kato bhaṇḍaviseso. Tādisaṃ sandhāya “yaṃ kiñci…pe… na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Alaṅkārañjanameva na bhesajjañjanaṃ. Maṇḍanānuyogassa hi adhippetattā tamidhānadhippetaṃ. Loke mālā-saddo baddhamālāyameva “mālā mālyaṃ pupphadāme”ti vacanato. Sāsane pana suddhapupphesupi niruḷhoti āha “abaddhamālā vā”ti. Kāḷapīḷakādīnanti kāḷavaṇṇapīḷakādīnaṃ. Mattikakakkanti osadhehi abhisaṅkhataṃ yogamattikācuṇṇaṃ. Dentīti vilepenti. Caliteti vikārāpajjanavasena calanaṃ patte[M 1.0366], kupiteti attho. Tenāti sāsapakakkena. Doseti kāḷapīḷakādīnaṃ hetubhūte lohitadose. Khāditeti apanayanavasena khādite. Sannisinneti tādise duṭṭhalohite parikkhīṇe. Mukhacuṇṇakenāti mukhavilepanena[V 1.0322]. Cuṇṇentīti vilimpenti. Taṃ sabbanti mattikākakkasāsapatilahaliddikakkadānasaṅkhātaṃ mukhacuṇṇaṃ, mukhavilepanañca na vaṭṭati. Atthānukkamasambhavato hi ayaṃ padadvayassa vaṇṇanā. Mukhacuṇṇasaṅkhātaṃ mukhavilepananti vā padadvayassa tulyādhikaraṇavasena atthavibhāvanā.

'Of those very children' means of only the children who are meritorious. Indeed, the taking is of them, due to the suitability to the context. 'Of great wrestlers' means of great performers of arm-combat. A mirror, it is said, is a special item made from bronze, iron, etc., for people who have the nature of adorning themselves, for the purpose of seeing their own facial reflection. Referring to such a thing, it was said: 'Whatever... is not allowable.' It is only ornamental eye-ointment, not medicinal eye-ointment. Indeed, because devotion to adornment is intended, that medicinal eye-ointment is not intended here. In the world, the word 'mālā' occurs only for a bound garland, according to the saying: 'mālā, mālyaṃ in the sense of a flower-garland.' But in the Dispensation, it is also established for plain flowers; therefore, he said, 'or an unbound garland.' 'Of black boils, etc.' means of black-colored boils and the like. 'Clay paste' means a suitable clay powder prepared with medicines. 'They give' means they smear. 'When it is agitated' means when it has reached a state of movement by way of arriving at an alteration; the meaning is 'when it is corrupted.' 'By that' means by mustard paste. 'The corruption' means the corruption of the blood which is the cause of black boils and the like. 'When eaten away' means when eaten away by way of removal. 'When settled' means when such bad blood is exhausted. 'By facial powder' means by facial ointment. 'They powder' means they anoint. All that—designated as the giving of clay paste, mustard paste, sesame paste, turmeric paste, and facial powder, and facial ointment—is not allowable. Indeed, because of the possible sequence of meaning, this is the explanation of the pair of words. Or, 'facial ointment designated as facial powder'; this is the clarification of the meaning of the pair of words by way of having the same referent.

Hatthabandhanti hatthe bandhitabbamābharaṇaṃ, taṃ pana saṅkhakapālādayoti āha “hatthe”tiādi. Saṅkho eva kapālaṃ tathā. “Apare”tiādinā yathākkamaṃ “sikhābandha”ntiādi padānamatthaṃ saṃvaṇṇeti. Tattha sikhanti cūḷaṃ. Cīrakaṃ nāma yena cūḷāya thirakaraṇatthaṃ, sobhanatthañca vijjhati. Muttāya, muttā eva vā latā muttālatā, muttāvaḷi. Daṇḍo nāma catuhatthoti vuttaṃ “catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ vā”ti. Alaṅkatadaṇḍakanti pana tato omakaṃ rathayaṭṭhiādikaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhesajjanāḷikanti bhesajjatumbaṃ. Pattādiolambanaṃ vāmaṃseyeva aciṇṇanti vuttaṃ “vāmapasse olaggita”nti. Kaṇṇikā nāma kūṭaṃ, tāya ca ratanena ca parikkhitto koso yassa tathā. Pañcavaṇṇasuttasibbitanti nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhavasena pañcavaṇṇehi suttehi sibbitaṃ tividhampi chattaṃ. Ratanamattāyāmaṃ caturaṅgulavitthatanti tesaṃ paricayaniyāmena vā nalāṭe bandhituṃ pahonakappamāṇena vā vuttaṃ. “Kesantaparicchedaṃ dassetvā”ti etena tadanajjhottharaṇavasena bandhanākāraṃ dasseti. Meghamukheti abbhantare. “Maṇi”nti idaṃ siromaṇiṃ sandhāya vuttanti āha “cūḷāmaṇi”nti, cūḷāyaṃ maṇinti attho. Camarassa ayaṃ cāmaro, sveva vālo, tena katā bījanī cāmaravālabījanī. Aññāsaṃ pana makasabījanīvākamayabījanīusīramayabījanīmorapiñchamayabījanīnaṃ, vidhūpanatālavaṇṭānañca kappiyattā tassāyeva gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'A hand-band' means an ornament to be fastened on the hand. But that is a conch-bowl, etc.; therefore, he said 'on the hand,' etc. The conch itself is the bowl, thus. By the text 'others,' etc., he explains in sequence the meaning of the words 'a top-knot band,' etc. Therein, 'a crest' means the top-knot. A 'cīraka', it is said, is that by which one pierces the top-knot for the purpose of making it firm and for making it beautiful. Of a pearl; or, a pearl itself is a creeper, hence 'muttālatā' (pearl-creeper), a string of pearls. A staff, it is said, is four cubits; thus it was said, 'or a four-cubit staff.' But he said 'an ornamented staff' referring to something lesser than that, such as a chariot-goad. 'A medicine-tube' means a medicine-container. The slinging of a bowl, etc., is practiced only on the left shoulder; therefore it was said, 'slung on the left side.' 'Kaṇṇikā' means a peak; that which has a sheath surrounded by that peak and by a jewel is so-called. 'Sewn with five-colored thread' means an umbrella of three kinds, sewn with threads of five colors: blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. 'A jewel-measure in length, four finger-breadths in width' was said either by way of their customary rule or by way of a suitable measure for tying on the forehead. By this phrase, 'having shown the limit of the hair,' he shows the manner of tying by way of not covering that. 'In the mouth of a cloud' means inside a cloud. This word 'a jewel' was said referring to a head-jewel; therefore he said 'a crest-jewel,' the meaning being 'a jewel on the top-knot.' This belongs to the camara (yak), hence 'cāmaro'. That very thing is the tail-hair ('vālo'). A fan made with that is a 'cāmaravālabījanī' (a fan of yak tail-hair). But because other fans—mosquito-fans, fans made of bark-fibre, fans made of usīra-grass, and fans made of peacock feathers, and also palm-leaf fans for fanning—are allowable, it should be understood that the taking here is of that very yak-tail fan.

17. Duggatito, saṃsārato ca niyyāti etenāti niyyānaṃ, saggamaggo, mokkhamaggo ca. Taṃ niyyānamarahati, tasmiṃ vā niyyāne niyuttā, taṃ vā niyyānaṃ phalabhūtaṃ etissāti niyyānikā, vacīduccaritakilesato niyyātīti vā niyyānikā ī-kārassa rassattaṃ, ya-kārassa ca ka-kāraṃ [M 1.0367] katvā. Anīya-saddo hi bahulā katvatthābhidhāyako. Cetanāya saddhiṃ samphappalāpavirati idha adhippetā. Tappaṭipakkhato aniyyānikā, samphappalāpo, tassā bhāvo aniyyānikattaṃ, tasmā aniyyānikattā. Tiracchānabhūtāti tirokaraṇabhūtā vibandhanabhūtā. Sopi nāmāti ettha nāma-saddo garahāyaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānabhāveti aniccatāpaṭisaṃyuttattā catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāve. Kāmassādavasenāti kāmasaṅkhātaassādavasena. Saha atthenāti sātthakaṃ, hitapaṭisaṃyuttanti attho. Upāhanāti yānakathāsambandhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Suṭṭhu nivesitabboti suniviṭṭho. Tathā dunniviṭṭho. Gāma-saddena gāmavāsī janopi gahitoti āha “asukagāmavāsino”tiādi.

17. One goes forth from a woeful state and from saṃsāra by means of this; therefore, it is 'niyyāna' (a going forth); the path to heaven and the path to liberation are obtained. That talk is worthy of that going forth; or, it is devoted to that going forth; or, that going forth exists as its fruit; therefore, it is 'niyyānikā'. Or, because it goes forth from the defilement of verbal misconduct, that talk is 'niyyānikā', after shortening the ī-kāra and making ka-kāra for the ya-kāra. Indeed, the suffix '-anīya' mostly expresses the meaning of the agent. Here, abstinence from frivolous talk together with volition is intended. The opposite of that is 'aniyyānikā'; frivolous talk is obtained. The state of that is 'aniyyānikattaṃ'. Therefore, because of its non-leading-forth nature. 'Having become animal-like' means having become obstructive, having become a hindrance. Here in 'sopi nāma,' the word 'nāma' occurs in the sense of censure. 'In the state of a meditation subject' means in the state of the meditation subject of the Four Truths, because of its connection with impermanence. 'By the power of the taste of sensual pleasure' means by the power of the taste designated as sensual pleasure. 'With meaning' means 'sātthakaṃ'; the meaning is 'connected with benefit.' 'Footwear' was said referring to its connection with talk on vehicles. 'It should be well entered,' hence 'suniviṭṭho' (well-entered). Likewise, 'dunniviṭṭho' (badly-entered). By the word 'gāma', the people dwelling in the village are also taken; therefore, he said 'the dwellers of such-and-such a village,' etc.

Sūrakathāti [V 1.0323] ettha sūra-saddo vīravācakoti dasseti “sūro ahosī”ti iminā. Visikhā nāma maggasanniveso, idha pana visikhāgahaṇena tannivāsinopi gahitā “sabbo gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya, tenevāha “saddhā pasannā”tiādi.

'Heroic talk'—here, the word 'hero' expresses the meaning of 'brave,' as he shows with 'he was a hero.' 'Visikhā', it is said, is a street-junction. But here, by the taking of 'visikhā', its inhabitants are also taken, just as in 'the whole village has come,' etc. Therefore, he said 'faithful, confident,' etc.

Kumbhassa ṭhānaṃ nāma udakaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “udakaṭṭhānakathā”ti. Udakatitthakathātipi vuccati tattheva samavarodhato. Apica kumbhassa karaṇaṭṭhānaṃ kumbhaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadapadesena pana kumbhadāsiyo vuttāti dasseti “kumbhadāsikathā vā”ti iminā. Pubbe petā kālaṅkatāti pubbapetā. “Peto pareto kālaṅkato”ti hi pariyāyavacanaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttanayamatidisituṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“The place of the pot” (kumbhassa ṭhānaṃ) is a place for water (udakaṭṭhānaṃ); hence, it is called “talk about a place for water.” It is also called “talk about a water-ford” because of descending well into that very place. Moreover, the place for making a pot is a “pot-place” (kumbhaṭṭhānaṃ). By that designation, however, female potters' slaves are spoken of; this is shown by the phrase “or talk about female potters' slaves.” `Pubbapetā` means those who were formerly departed and deceased. Indeed, “departed” (peto), “gone beyond” (pareto), and “deceased” (kālaṅkato) are synonymous terms. To apply by extension the method previously stated, “there,” etc., is said.

Purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttāti idhāgatāhi purimāhi, pacchimāhi ca kathāhi vimuttā. Nānāsabhāvāti atta-saddassa sabhāvapariyāyabhāvamāha. Asukena nāmāti pajāpatinā brahmunā, issarena vā. Uppattiṭhitisambhārādivasena lokaṃ akkhāyati etāyāti lokakkhāyikā, sā pana lokāyatasamaññe vitaṇḍasatthe nissitā sallāpakathāti dasseti “lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā”ti iminā. Lokā bālajanā āyatanti ettha ussahanti vādassādenāti lokāyataṃ, loko vā hitaṃ na yatati na īhati tenāti lokāyataṃ. Tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakiriyāya cittampi na uppādenti[M 1.0368]. Aññamaññaviruddhaṃ, saggamokkhaviruddhaṃ vā kathaṃ tanonti etthāti vitaṇḍo, viruddhena vā vādadaṇḍena tāḷenti ettha vādinoti vitaṇḍo, sabbattha niruttinayena padasiddhi.

`Purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttā` means: freed from the former and latter talks that have come here. `Nānāsabhāvā` states that `sabhāva` is a synonym for the word `atta`. `Asukena nāma` means: by Pajāpati, by Brahmā, or by Issara. By this talk, the world is declared in terms of its origin, duration, constituents, etc.; therefore, it is `lokakkhāyikā`. Furthermore, that talk, being based on the sophistical treatise known as Lokāyata, is frivolous talk (`sallāpakathā`); this is shown by “talk that is Lokāyata sophistry and frivolous.” Worldly, foolish people strive (`āyatanti`) here, delighting in debate; therefore, it is `lokāyata`. Alternatively, by means of it, the world does not strive (`na yatati`) for what is beneficial; therefore, it is `lokāyata`. Indeed, relying on that book, beings do not even give rise to a thought of meritorious action. They elaborate (`tanonti`) here on talk that is mutually contradictory or contradictory to heaven and liberation; therefore, it is `vitaṇḍa`. Alternatively, they strike (`tāḷenti`) debaters here with the rod of contradictory debate; therefore, it is `vitaṇḍa`. In all cases, the derivation of the word should be understood by the method of etymology.

Sāgaradevena khatoti ettha sāgararañño puttehi khatotipi vadanti. Vijjati pavedanahetubhūtā muddhā yassāti samuddo dha-kārassa da-kāraṃ katvā, saha-saddo cettha vijjamānatthavācako “salomakosapakkhako”tiādīsu viya. Bhavoti vuddhi bhavati vaḍḍhatīti katvā. Vibhavoti hāni tabbirahato. Dvandato pubbe suyyamāno itisaddo paccekaṃ yojetabboti āha “iti bhavo iti abhavo”ti. Yaṃ vā taṃ vāti yaṃ kiñci, atha taṃ aniyamanti attho. Abhūtañhi aniyamatthaṃ saha vikappena yaṃtaṃ-saddehi dīpenti ācariyā. Apica bhavoti sassato. Abhavoti ucchedo. Bhavoti vā kāmasukhaṃ. Abhavoti attakilamatho.

Regarding “dug by the ocean-god,” here they also say “dug by the sons of King Sāgara.” That which has a head (`muddhā`) that is a cause for announcement is `samudda`, having changed the letter `dha` to `da`. And here the word `sa` indicates existence, as in `salomako` (having hair) and `sapakkhako` (having wings). `Bhava` is growth, because “it becomes, it grows.” `Vibhava` is decline, because it is devoid of that. The word `iti`, when heard before a dvandva compound, should be connected to each member separately; thus, he says, “thus `bhava`, thus `abhava`.” `Yaṃ vā taṃ vā` means: whatever is untrue and indefinite. Indeed, the teachers explain the untrue and indefinite meaning with the words `yaṃ` and `taṃ` together with the alternative (`vā`). Moreover, `bhava` is eternalism. `Abhava` is annihilationism. Alternatively, `bhava` is sensual pleasure. `Abhava` is self-mortification.

Iti imāya chabbidhāya itibhavābhavakathāya saddhiṃ bāttiṃsa tiracchānakathā nāma honti. Atha [V 1.0324] vā pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato anāgatāpi araññapabbatanadīdīpakathā iti-saddena saṅgahetvā battiṃsa tiracchānakathāti vuccanti. Pāḷiyañhi “iti vā”ti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho, vā-saddo vikappanattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “evaṃpakāraṃ, ito aññaṃ vā tādisaṃ niratthakakathaṃ anuyuttā viharantī”ti, ādiattho vā iti-saddo iti vā iti evarūpā “naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.10, 164; ma. ni. 1.293, 411; 2.11, 418; 3.14, 102; a. ni. 10.99) viya, iti evamādiṃ aññampi tādisaṃ kathamanuyuttā viharantīti attho.

Together with this sixfold “talk of ‘thus existence, thus non-existence’,” there are thirty-two kinds of animal-talk. Alternatively, although talk of forests, mountains, rivers, and islands does not appear in its own form in the Pāḷi, by including them with the word `iti`, they are called the thirty-two kinds of animal-talk. Indeed, in the Pāḷi, in the phrase `iti vā`, the word `iti` has the meaning of “kind,” and the word `vā` has the meaning of “alternative.” This is what is meant: “They dwell engaged in such a kind of meaningless talk, or other such talk different from this.” Alternatively, the word `iti` has the meaning of “and so forth” (`ādi`), as in such phrases as “He abstains from watching dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows, and so forth...” The meaning is: “They dwell engaged in other such talk of this kind and so forth.”

18. Viruddhassa gahaṇaṃ viggaho, so yesanti viggāhikā, tesaṃ tathā, viruddhaṃ vā gaṇhāti etāyāti viggāhikā, sāyeva kathā tathā. Sārambhakathāti upārambhakathā. Sahitanti pubbāparāviruddhaṃ. Tatoyeva siliṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ pana atthakāraṇayuttatāyāti dassetuṃ “atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttanti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Nti vacanaṃ. Parivattitvā ṭhitaṃ sapattagato asamattho yodho viya na kiñci jānāsi, kintu sayameva parājesīti adhippāyo. Vādo dosoti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Tathā cara [M 1.0369] vicarāti. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ācariyakule. Nibbedhehīti mayā ropitaṃ vādaṃ vissajjehi.

18. Grasping the contradictory is `viggaha` (conflict); those for whom this exists are `viggāhikā` (disputatious); their talk is likewise. Alternatively, by this talk one grasps the contradictory; therefore, it is `viggāhikā`; that very talk is likewise. `Sārambhakathā` (contentious talk) is `upārambhakathā` (reproachful talk). `Sahitaṃ` (connected) means not contradictory between its former and latter parts. For that very reason, it is `siliṭṭhaṃ` (smooth). Furthermore, to show that it is smooth because of its connection with meaning and reason, it is said, “The meaning is ‘connected with meaning, connected with reason’.” That speech, having turned back, stands like an incompetent warrior who has fallen into the hands of the enemy; you know nothing, but only defeat yourself—this is the intention. The expression `vādo doso` is a set of synonyms. Likewise is the expression `cara vicara`. `Tattha tattha` means: in this and that school of teachers. `Nibbedhehi` means: refute the view established by me.

19. Dūtassa kammaṃ dūteyyaṃ, tassa kathā tathā, tassaṃ. Idha, amutrāti upayogatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tenāha “asukaṃ nāma ṭhāna”nti. Vitthārato vinicchayo vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 436-437) vuttoti saṅkhepato idha dassetuṃ “saṅkhepato panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gihisāsananti yathāvuttaviparītaṃ sāsanaṃ. Aññesanti gihīnaññeva.

19. The work of an envoy is `dūteyyaṃ` (envoy's work); his talk is likewise. In that talk, `idha` (here) and `amutra` (there) are locative expressions used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, he says, “to such and such a place.” The detailed analysis has been stated in the Vinaya Commentary; therefore, to show it concisely here, “But in brief...” and so forth is said. `Gihisāsanaṃ` (a householder's message) is a message contrary to what has been said. `Aññesaṃ` (of others) means: only of householders.

20. Tividhenāti sāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitapaccayapaṭisevanabhedato tividhena. Vimhāpayantīti “ayamacchariyapuriso”ti attani paresaṃ vimhayaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ acchariyaṃ uppādenti. Vipubbañhi mhi-saddaṃ sampahaṃsane vadanti saddavidū. Sampahaṃsanākāro ca acchariyaṃ. Lapantīti attānaṃ vā dāyakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā yathā so kiñci dadāti, evaṃ ukkācetvā ukkhipanavasena dīpetvā kathenti. Nimittaṃ sīlametesanti nemittikāti taddhitavasena tassīlattho yathā “paṃsukūliko”ti (mahāni. 52) apica nimittena vadanti, nimittaṃ vā karontīti nemittikā. Nimittanti ca paresaṃ paccayadānasaññuppādakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ vuccati. Nippeso nippisanaṃ cuṇṇaṃ viya karaṇaṃ. Nippisantīti vā nippesā, nippesāyeva nippesikā, nippisanaṃ vā nippeso, taṃ karontītipi nippesikā. Nippeso ca nāma [V 1.0325] bhaṭapuriso viya lābhasakkāratthaṃ akkosanakhuṃsanuppaṇḍanaparapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā. Lābhena lābhanti ito lābhena amutra lābhaṃ. Nijigīsanti magganti pariyesantīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Kuhakādayo saddā kuhānādīni nimittaṃ katvā taṃsamaṅgipuggalesu pavattāti āha “kuhanā…pe… adhivacana”nti. Aṭṭhakathañcāti taṃtaṃpāḷisaṃvaṇṇanābhūtaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathañca.

20. ‘Threefold’ means: threefold by the distinctions of murmuring in the vicinity of the requisites, relying on postures, and partaking of the requisites. ‘They cause astonishment’ means: they produce wonder, elation, and astonishment in others regarding themselves, causing them to think, “This is an astonishing person.” For, indeed, experts in language say the sound ‘mhi’ with the prefix ‘vi’ is in the sense of elation. And the state of elation is astonishment. ‘They talk’ means: having exalted themselves or the donor, they speak, making the donor free from stinginess and revealing their wish by way of praise, so that he gives something. They are ‘nemittikā’ because making a sign (nimitta) is their habit (sīla), formed by way of a taddhita suffix in the sense of ‘it is their habit,’ just as in ‘paṃsukūliko.’ Moreover, they are ‘nemittikā’ because they speak by means of a sign, or they make a sign. And a ‘sign’ is said to be a bodily or verbal action that produces in others the perception of giving requisites. ‘Nippeso’ is the act of making something as if into fine powder. Or, they are ‘nippesā’ because they grind down; ‘nippesā’ itself is ‘nippesikā.’ Or, ‘nippisanaṃ’ (grinding down) is ‘nippeso’; they are also ‘nippesikā’ because they do that. And ‘nippeso’ is, for the sake of gain and honour, like a hired man, the state of abusing, belittling, deriding, and backbiting. ‘They seek gain with gain’ means: with the gain from here, they seek, search for, and look for gain elsewhere. ‘Nijigīsanti,’ ‘magganti,’ and ‘pariyesanti’ are synonyms.
