The words ‘kuhaka,’ etc., are current for individuals endowed with ‘kuhanā,’ etc., having made them a sign; therefore, he said, “‘Kuhanā’... and so on... is a designation.” And ‘the commentary’ means the ancient commentary which is an explanation of the respective Pāḷi texts.

Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Middle Morality is concluded.

Mahāsīlavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Great Morality

21. Aṅgāni [M 1.0370] ārabbha pavattattā aṅgasahacaritaṃ satthaṃ “aṅga”nti vuttaṃ uttarapadalopena vā. Nimittanti etthāpi eseva nayo, tenāha “hatthapādādīsū”tiādi. Keci pana “aṅganti aṅgavikāraṃ paresaṃ aṅgavikāradassanenāpi lābhālābhādivijānana”nti vadanti. Nimittasatthanti nimittena sañjānanappakāradīpakaṃ satthaṃ, taṃ vatthunā vibhāvetuṃ “paṇḍurājā”tiādimāha. Paṇḍurājāti ca “dakkhiṇārāmādhipati” icceva vuttaṃ. Sīhaḷadīpe dakkhiṇārāmanāmakassa saṅghārāmassa kārakoti vadanti. “Dakkhiṇamadhurādhipatī”ti ca katthaci likhitaṃ, dakkhiṇamadhuranagarassa adhipatīti attho. Muttāyoti muttikā. Muṭṭhiyāti hatthamuddāya. Gharagolikāyāti sarabunā. So “muttā”ti saññānimittenāha, saṅkhyānimittena pana “tisso”ti.

21. Because it proceeds in relation to the limbs (aṅga), the science (sattha) associated with the limbs is called ‘aṅga.’ Or, it is so called by the elision of the latter word. The same method applies here in ‘nimittaṃ’ (sign) as well; therefore, he said, “in the hands, feet, etc.” and so on. Some, however, say: “‘Aṅga’ is the deformity of a limb; it is the discerning of gain, loss, and so on, by seeing the deformity of another's limbs.” ‘The science of signs’ is the science that illuminates the various ways of knowing by means of a sign. To make this clear with a story, he said, “King Paṇḍu,” and so on. And “King Paṇḍu” is just said to be “the lord of Dakkhiṇārāma.” The teachers say he was the builder of the monastic complex named Dakkhiṇārāma on the island of Sīhaḷa. And in some places, it is written, “the lord of Dakkhiṇamadhurā”; the meaning is the lord of the city of Dakkhiṇamadhurā. ‘Muttāyo’ means pearls. ‘Muṭṭhiyā’ means by a fist-gesture. ‘Gharagolikāyā’ means by a house-lizard. He said, “Pearls” (muttā), by the sign of perception (saññānimitta). But by the numerical sign (saṅkhyānimitta), he said, “Three” (tisso).

“Mahantāna”nti etena appakaṃ nimittameva, mahantaṃ pana uppādoti nimittuppādānaṃ visesaṃ dasseti. Uppatitanti uppatanaṃ. Subhāsubhaphalaṃ pakāsento uppajjati gacchatīti uppādo, uppātopi, subhāsubhasūcikā bhūtavikati. So hi dhūmo viya aggissa kammaphalassa pakāsanamattameva karoti, na tu tamuppādetīti. Idanti idaṃ nāma phalaṃ. Evanti iminā nāma ākārena. Ādisantīti niddisanti. Pubbaṇhasamayeti kālavasena. Idaṃ nāmāti vatthuvasena vadati. Yo vasabhaṃ, kuñjaraṃ, pāsādaṃ, pabbataṃ vā āruḷhamattānaṃ supine passati, tassa “idaṃ nāma phala”ntiādinā hi vatthukittanaṃ hoti. Supinakanti supinasatthaṃ. Aṅgasampattivipattidassanamattena pubbe “aṅga”nti vuttaṃ, idha pana mahānubhāvatādinipphādakalakkhaṇavisesadassanena “lakkhaṇa”nti ayametesaṃ viseso, tenāha “iminā [V 1.0326] lakkhaṇenā”tiādi. Lakkhaṇanti hi aṅgapaccaṅgesu dissamānākāravisesaṃ sattisirivacchagadāpāsādādikamadhippetaṃ taṃ taṃ phalaṃ lakkhīyati anenāti katvā, satthaṃ pana tappakāsanato lakkhaṇaṃ. Āhateti purāṇe. Anāhateti nave. Ahateti pana pāṭhe vuttavipariyāyena attho. Ito paṭṭhāyāti devarakkhasamanussādibhedena yathāphalaṃ parikappitena vividhavatthabhāge ito vā etto vā sañchinne idaṃ nāma bhogādiphalaṃ hoti. Evarūpena dārunāti palāsasiriphalādidārunā, tathā dabbiyā. Yadi dabbihomādīnipi aggihomāneva[M 1.0371], atha kasmā visuṃ vuttānīti āha “evarūpāyā”tiādi. Dabbihomādīni homopakaraṇādivisesehi phalavisesadassanavasena vuttāni, aggihomaṃ pana vuttāvasesasādhanavasena vuttanti adhippāyo. Tenāha “dabbihomādīnī”tiādi.

By this word ‘mahantānaṃ,’ he shows the distinction between a sign and a portent: a small one is merely a sign, but a great one is a portent (uppādo). ‘Uppatitaṃ’ means arising. It is an ‘uppādo’ because it arises and occurs while indicating a good or bad result. It is also an ‘uppāto,’ a distortion of the elements that indicates good or bad fortune. For it merely indicates the result of kamma, just as smoke indicates fire, but it does not produce that result; thus it should be understood. ‘Idaṃ’ means this particular result. ‘Evaṃ’ means in this particular manner. ‘Ādisanti’ means they point out. He says ‘pubbaṇhasamaye’ (in the morning) by way of time. He says ‘idaṃ nāma’ (this particular thing) by way of the object. For, the announcing of the object occurs thus: “For one who in a dream sees himself mounted on a bull, an elephant, a palace, or a mountain, this particular result will be.” ‘Supinakaṃ’ is the science of dreams. Previously, it was called ‘aṅga’ merely by seeing the perfection or imperfection of the limbs. Here, however, it is called ‘lakkhaṇa’ by seeing the special characteristic that accomplishes great power and so on. This is the distinction between them. Therefore, he said, “by this characteristic,” and so on. For it is a ‘lakkhaṇa’ (mark) because by this—that is, by the special feature appearing on the major and minor limbs, which is intended as a spear, a sirivaccha, a mace, a palace, and so on—that particular result is marked. The science, however, is called ‘lakkhaṇa’ because it explains that. ‘Āhaṭe’ means on an old garment. ‘Anāhaṭe’ means on a new one. In the reading ‘ahaṭe,’ however, the meaning should be understood as the reverse of what has been said. ‘Ito paṭṭhāya’ means: when a portion of a garment, imagined according to the result for different beings such as devas, yakkhas, humans, and so on, is gnawed from here or from there, this particular result of wealth, etc., occurs. ‘Evarūpena dārunā’ means: with wood such as that of the Palāsa or Sirīsa tree. Likewise for ‘dabbiyā’ (with a ladle). If ladle-oblations and so on are also just fire-oblations, then why are they mentioned separately? Because this objection can be raised, the teacher said, “‘evarūpāya,’” and so on. The intention is that ladle-oblations and so on were spoken of to show a special result due to the specific oblation-implements, etc., whereas the fire-oblation was spoken of to complete what remained unsaid. Therefore, he said, “ladle-oblations and so on,” and so on.

Kuṇḍakoti taṇḍulakhaṇḍaṃ, tilassa idanti telaṃ, samāsataddhitapadāni pasiddhesu sāmaññabhūtānīti visesakaraṇatthaṃ “tilatelādika”nti vuttaṃ. Pakkhipananti pakkhipanatthaṃ. “Pakkhipanavijja”ntipi pāṭho, pakkhipanahetubhūtaṃ vijjanti attho. Dakkhiṇakkhakajaṇṇulohitādīhīti dakkhiṇakkhakalohitadakkhiṇajaṇṇulohitādīhi. “Pubbe”tiādinā aṅgaaṅgavijjānaṃ visesadassanena punaruttabhāvamapaneti. Aṅgulaṭṭhiṃ disvāti aṅgulibhūtaṃ, aṅguliyā vā jātaṃ aṭṭhiṃ passitvā, aṅgulicchavimattaṃ apassitvā tadaṭṭhivipassanavaseneva byākarontīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Aṅgalaṭṭhinti sarīra”nti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.21) pana ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ viruhanabhāvena laṭṭhisadisattā sarīrameva aṅgalaṭṭhīti viññāyati. Kulaputtoti jātikulaputto, ācārakulaputto ca. Disvāpīti ettha api-saddo adisvāpīti sampiṇḍanattho. Abbhino satthaṃ abbheyyaṃ. Māsurakkhena kato gantho māsurakkho. Rājūhi paribhūttaṃ satthaṃ rājasatthaṃ. Sabbānipetāni khattavijjāpakaraṇāni. Siva-saddo santiatthoti āha “santikaraṇavijjā”ti, upasaggūpasamanavijjāti attho. Sivā-saddameva rassaṃ katvā evamahāti sandhāya “siṅgālarutavijjā”ti vadanti, siṅgālānaṃ rute subhāsubhasañjānanavijjāti attho. “Bhūtavejjamantoti bhūtavasīkaraṇamanto. Bhūrighareti antopathaviyaṃ kataghare, mattikāmayaghare vā. “Bhūrivijjā sassabuddhikaraṇavijjā”ti sārasamāse. Sappāvhāyanavijjāti sappāgamanavijjā. Visavantameva vāti visavamānameva vā. Bhāvaniddesassa hi māna-saddassa antabyappadeso. Yāya karonti, sā visavijjāti yojanā. “Visatantrameva vā”tipi pāṭho. Evaṃ sati sarūpadassanaṃ hoti, visavicāraṇaganthoyevāti attho. Tantranti hi ganthassa parasamaññā. Sapakkhakaapakkhakadvipadacatuppadānanti piṅgalamakkhikādisapakkhakagharagolikādiapakkhakadevamanussacaṅgorādidvipada- kaṇṭasasajambukādicatuppadānaṃ[V 1.0327]. Rutaṃ vassitaṃ. Gataṃ gamanaṃ, etena “sakuṇavijjā”ti idha migasaddassa [M 1.0372] lopaṃ, nidassanamattaṃ vā dasseti. Sakuṇañāṇanti sakuṇavasena subhāsubhaphalassa jānanaṃ. Nanu sakuṇavijjāya eva vāyasavijjāpaviṭṭhāti āha “taṃ visuññeva sattha”nti. Taṃtaṃpakāsakasatthānurūpavasena hi idha tassa tassa vacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Kuṇḍaka is broken rice. 'This is of sesame (tilassa idaṃ),' therefore it is called tela (oil). Compound and derivative words, when they are well-known, become general; therefore, for the purpose of specification, 'sesame oil, etc.' (tilatelādikaṃ) is said. Pakkhipanaṃ is for the purpose of putting into the fire. There is also the reading pakkhipanavijjaṃ; the meaning is the art which is the cause for putting into the fire. By dakkhiṇakkhakajaṇṇulohitādīhi is meant by the blood of the right collarbone, the blood of the right knee, and so on. By the text beginning with 'pubbe', he removes the state of redundancy by showing the distinction between the treatises on limbs and the science of limbs. Having seen the aṅgulaṭṭhi means: having seen a bone that has become a finger, or a bone that has arisen in a finger, without looking at the mere skin of the finger, they prophesy solely by the power of special observation of that bone. However, 'aṅgalaṭṭhi means body'—this was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla. This being so, because of the similarity to a creeper due to the way the major and minor limbs grow, the body itself is understood as aṅgalaṭṭhi. Kulaputta means one from a good family by birth and one from a good family by conduct. Here in disvāpi, the particle api has the collective sense of 'and not having seen'. The treatise of the teacher Abbhi is abbheyyaṃ. The book composed by Māsurakkha is māsurakkho. The treatise used by kings is rājasatthaṃ. All these are treatises on the science of the warrior class (khattavijjā). The word siva has the meaning of 'peace'; showing this, he said santikaraṇavijjā, the meaning of which is the science of pacifying dangers. Having shortened the word sivā, he said this. Referring to this word, they say siṅgālarutavijjā. The meaning is: the science of knowing the auspicious and inauspicious in the cries of jackals. Bhūtavejjamanto is a mantra for bringing spirits under one's control. Bhūrighare means in a house made inside the earth, or in a house made of clay. In the Sārasamāsa it is said: 'Bhūrivijjā is the science of making the crops prosper.' Sappāvhāyanavijjā is the science of making snakes come. Or visavantaṃ means just visavamānaṃ (causing poison to flow). Indeed, the suffix -māna, which indicates a state of being, is a designation for the suffix -anta. The construction is thus: the science by which they cause the flowing of poison is visavijjā. There is also the reading visatantrameva vā. This being the reading, it is a statement of its own nature; the meaning is: it is simply a treatise investigating poison. For tantra is another name for a treatise. Sapakkhakaapakkhakadvipadacatuppadānaṃ means: of winged creatures such as tawny-eyed flies, etc.; of wingless creatures such as house lizards, spiders, etc.; of bipeds such as gods, humans, partridges, etc.; and of quadrupeds such as chameleons, hares, jackals, etc. Rutaṃ is crying. Gataṃ is going. By this, here in sakuṇavijjā, he shows either the elision of the word miga or that it is merely an example. Sakuṇañāṇaṃ is the knowing of auspicious and inauspicious results by means of birds. 'Is not the science of crows included in the science of birds?' Due to this question, he said: 'That is a separate treatise.' For here, it should be understood by the wise that the wording for each is in accordance with the respective treatise that explains it.

Paripakkagatabhāvo attabhāvassa, jīvitakālassa ca vasena gahetabboti dasseti “idānī”tiādinā. Ādiṭṭhañānanti ādisitabbassa ñāṇaṃ. Sararakkhaṇanti sarato attānaṃ, attato vā sarassa rakkhaṇaṃ. “Sabbasaṅgāhika”nti iminā miga-saddassa sabbasakuṇacatuppadesu pavattiṃ dasseti, ekasesaniddeso vā esa catuppadesveva miga-saddassa niruḷhattā. Sabbesampi sakuṇacatuppadānaṃ rutajānanasatthassa migacakkasamaññā, yathā taṃ subhāsubhajānanappakāre sabbato bhadraṃ cakkādisamaññāti āha “sabba…pe… vutta”nti.

He shows by the text beginning with 'idāni' that the state of having reached maturity is to be understood by way of one's individual existence and one's lifespan. Ādiṭṭhañāṇaṃ is the knowledge of what is to be pointed out. Sararakkhaṇaṃ is the protection of oneself from an arrow, or of an arrow from oneself. By this word 'sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ', he shows the application of the word 'miga' to all birds and quadrupeds. Or, this is an indication by ekasesa (ellipsis), because the word 'miga' is established only for quadrupeds. The designation 'migacakka' is for the treatise that knows the cries of all birds and quadrupeds. Just as, in the method of knowing the auspicious and inauspicious, that which is the most excellent of all has the designation 'cakka', etc., therefore he said 'all... etc. ... is said'.

22. “Sāmino”tiādi pasaṭṭhāpasaṭṭhakāraṇavacanaṃ. Lakkhaṇanti tesaṃ lakkhaṇappakāsakasatthaṃ. Pārisesanayena avasesaṃ āvudhaṃ. “Yamhi kule”tiādinā imasmiṃ ṭhāne tathājānanahetu eva sesaṃ lakkhaṇanti dasseti. Ayaṃ visesoti “lakkhaṇa”nti heṭṭhā vuttā lakkhaṇato viseso. Tadatthāvikaraṇatthaṃ “idañcettha vatthū”ti vuttaṃ aggiṃ dhamamānanti aggiṃ mukhavātena jālentaṃ. Makkhesīti vināseti. Piḷandhanakaṇṇikāyāti kaṇṇālaṅkārassa. Gehakaṇṇikāyāti gehakūṭassa, etena ekasesanayaṃ, sāmaññaniddesaṃ vā upetaṃ. Kacchapalakkhaṇanti kummalakkhaṇaṃ. Sabbacatuppadānanti miga-saddassa catuppadavācakattamāha.

22. The words beginning with 'sāmino' are a statement of the cause of what is praiseworthy and not praiseworthy. Lakkhaṇaṃ is the treatise that explains their characteristics. By the method of remainder, the remaining is the weapon (āvudhaṃ). By the words beginning with 'yamhi kule', he shows that in this context, the cause for knowing thus is itself the remaining characteristic. 'Ayaṃ viseso' means: this is a distinction from the 'lakkhaṇa' mentioned below. To make that meaning clear, 'idañcettha vatthu' was said. 'Aggiṃ dhamamānaṃ' means making the fire blaze with the wind from the mouth. 'Makkhesi' means he destroys. 'Piḷandhanakaṇṇikāya' means of an ear-ornament. 'Gehakaṇṇikāya' means of the peak of a house; by this, he shows that it comprises either the method of ekasesa or a general designation. 'Kacchapalakkhaṇaṃ' means the characteristics of a tortoise. By 'sabbacatuppadānaṃ', he states that the word 'miga' is a term for quadrupeds.

23. Asukadivaseti dutiyātatiyāditithivasena vuttaṃ. Asukanakkhattenāti assayujabharaṇīkattikārohaṇīādinakkhattayogavasena. Vippavutthānanti vippavasitānaṃ sadesato nikkhantānaṃ. Upasaṅkamanaṃ upayānaṃ. Apayānaṃ paṭikkamanaṃ. Dutiyapadepīti “bāhirānaṃ raññaṃ…pe… bhavissatī”ti vutte dutiyavākyepi. “Abbhantarānaṃ raññaṃ jayo”tiādīhi dvīhi vākyehi vuttā jayaparājayā pākaṭāyeva.

23. The statement 'asukadivase' (on a certain day) was said by way of the lunar days, such as the second, third, etc. The statement 'asukanakkhattena' (under a certain constellation) was said by way of conjunction with the lunar mansions such as Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Rohaṇī, etc. 'Vippavutthānaṃ' (of those who have departed) means of those who dwell away, who have departed from their own country. Approaching is 'upayānaṃ'. Retreating is 'apayānaṃ'. Even in the second phrase: When it is said, 'For the external kings... etc. ... there will be,' even in that second sentence, the victories and defeats stated by the two sentences beginning with, 'Victory for the internal kings,' are indeed evident.

24. Rāhūti rāhu nāma asurissaro asurarājā. Tathā hi mahāsamayasutte asuranikāye vuttaṃ –

24. 'Rāhu' is the one named Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, the king of the asuras. For so it is said in the Mahāsamayasutta, in the host of asuras:

“Satañca [V 1.0328][M 1.0373] baliputtānaṃ, sabbe verocanāmakā;

Sannayhitvā balisenaṃ, rāhubhaddamupāgamu”nti. (dī. ni. 2.339);

'And the hundred sons of Bali, all named Verocana, having arrayed Bali's army, approached the good Rāhu.'

Tassa candimasūriyānaṃ gahaṇaṃ saṃyuttanikāye candimasuttasūriyasuttehi dīpetabbaṃ. Iti-saddo cettha ādiattho “candaggāhādayo”ti vuttattā, tena sūriyaggāhanakkhattaggāhā saṅgayhanti. Tasmā candimasūriyānamiva nakkhattānampi rāhunā gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tato eva hi “api cā”tiādinā nakkhattagāhe dutiyanayo vutto. Aṅgārakādigāhasamāyogopīti aggahitaggahaṇena aṅgārakasasiputtasūragarusukkaravisutaketusaṅkhātānaṃ gāhānaṃ samāyogo api nakkhattagāhoyeva saha payogena gahaṇato. Sahapayogopi hi vedasamayena gahaṇanti vuccati. Ukkānaṃ patananti ukkobhāsānaṃ patanaṃ. Vātasaṅghātesu hi vegena aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭentesu dīpikobhāso viya obhāso uppajjitvā ākāsato patati, tatrāyaṃ ukkāpātavohāro. Jotisatthepi vuttaṃ –

His seizing of the moon and sun should be explained by the Candimasutta and Sūriyasutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Here, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'etc.' because it is said, 'candaggāhādayo' (the seizing of the moon, etc.); by this, the seizing of the sun and the seizing of the constellations are included. Therefore, just as with the moon and sun, the seizing of the constellations by Rāhu should also be understood. For that very reason, by 'api ca' (and moreover), etc., the second method regarding the seizing of the constellations is stated. As for the 'conjunction with planets such as Aṅgāraka': by including what was not previously included, the conjunction with the planets known as Aṅgāraka, Sasiputta, Sūragaru, Sukkara, Visuta, and Ketu is also indeed a seizing of the constellations, because it is considered a seizing on account of the conjunction. Indeed, a conjunction is also called a 'seizing' according to Vedic tradition. 'The falling of ukkās' means the falling of fiery lights. For, when masses of wind forcefully collide with one another, a light like the light of a torch arises and falls from the sky; therein, this is the term 'the fall of a meteor'. It is also stated in the Jotisattha:

“Mahāsikhā ca sukkhaggā-rattānilasikhojjalā;

Porisī ca pamāṇena, ukkā nānāvidhā matā”ti.

Having a great flame-base and small tips, blazing with a reddish-blue flame, and about a person's height in measure—the meteor is known to be of various kinds.

Disākālusiyanti disāsu khobhanaṃ, taṃ sarūpato dasseti “aggisikhadhūmasikhādīhi ākulabhāvo viyā”ti iminā, aggisikhadhūmasikhādīnaṃ bahudhā pātubhāvo eva disādāho nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tadeva “dhūmaketū”ti lokiyā vadanti. Vuttañca jotisatthe –

'Disākālusiya' means a disturbance in the directions. Its nature is shown by this: 'like a state of agitation due to flames of fire, plumes of smoke, and so on.' Thus, it is meant that the manifold manifestation of flames of fire, plumes of smoke, and so on is itself called 'disādāha' (burning of the directions). This very thing is what worldly people call 'dhūmaketu' (smoke-banner). And it is said in the Jotisattha:

“Ketu viya sikhāvatī, joti uppātarūpinī”ti.

Like a banner, possessing a crest, a light having a form that falls from the sky is called 'joti'.

Sukkhavalāhakagajjananti vuṭṭhimantarena vāyuvegacalitassa valāhakassa nadanaṃ. Yaṃ lokiyā “nighāto”ti vadanti. Vuttañca jotisatthe –

'Sukkhavalāhakagajjana' (the rumbling of a dry cloud) is the roaring of a cloud shaken by the force of wind, without rain. This is what worldly people call 'nighāta' (thunderclap). And it is said in the Jotisattha:

“Yadāntalikkhe balavā, māruto mārutāhato;

Patatyadho sa nīghāto, jāyate vāyusambhavo”ti.

When in the sky a mighty wind, struck by another wind, falls downwards, then that 'nīghāta' arises, being born of wind.

Udayananti lagganamāyūhanaṃ.

'Udayana' (rising) means arising, or the rising of the sun.

“Yadodeti tadā laganaṃ, rāsīnamanvayaṃ kamā”ti –

When [the sun] rises, that is the ascendant; [there is] the succession of the zodiacal signs in order.

Hi [V 1.0329][M 1.0374] vuttaṃ. Atthaṅgamanampi tato sattamarāsippamāṇavasena veditabbaṃ. Abbhā dhūmo rajo rāhūti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi avisuddhatā. Tabbinimuttatā vodānaṃ. Vuttañca “cattārome bhikkhave, candimasūriyānaṃ upakkilesā, yehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhā candimasūriyā na tapanti na bhāsanti na virocanti. Katame cattāro? Abbhā bhikkhave, candimasūriyānaṃ upakkilesā, yena…pe… dhūmo…pe… rajo…pe… rāhu bhikkhave…pe… ime kho…pe… na virocantī”ti (a. ni. 4.50).

For it is said. The setting should also be understood by way of the measure of the seventh zodiacal sign from that. Impurity is due to these four causes: clouds, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. Freedom from them is purity. And it is said: 'Monks, there are these four defilements of the moon and sun, by which defilements the defiled moon and sun do not shine, do not blaze, do not radiate. What four? Clouds, monks, are a defilement of the moon and sun... smoke... dust... Rāhu, monks... These, indeed... they do not radiate.' (A. Ni. 4.50).

25. Devassāti meghassa. Dhārānuppavecchanaṃ vassanaṃ. Avaggāhoti dhārāya avaggahaṇaṃ duggahaṇaṃ, tenāha “vassavibandho”ti. Hatthamuddāti hatthena adhippetaviññāpanaṃ, taṃ pana aṅgulisaṅkocanena gaṇanāyevāti ācariyadhammapālattherena (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.21) vuttaṃ. Ācariyasāriputtattherena pana “hatthamuddā nāma aṅgulipabbesu saññaṃ ṭhapetvā gaṇanā”ti dassitā. Gaṇanā vuccati acchiddakagaṇanā parisesañāyena, sā pana pādasikamilakkhakādayo viya “ekaṃ dve”tiādinā navantavidhinā nirantaragaṇanāti veditabbā. Samūhanaṃ saṅkalanaṃ visuṃ uppādanaṃ apanayanaṃ paṭuppādanaṃ [saṭuppādanaṃ (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] “saduppādana”ntipi paṭhanti, sammā uppādananti attho. Ādi-saddena vokalanabhāgahārādike saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha vokalanaṃ visuṃ samūhakaraṇaṃ, vomissananti attho. Bhāgakaraṇaṃ bhāgo. Bhuñjanaṃ vibhajanaṃ hāro. Sāti yathāvuttā piṇḍagaṇanā disvāti ettha diṭṭhamattena gaṇetvāti attho gahetabbo.

25. 'Of the deva' means of the cloud. The uninterrupted downpour of streams is raining. 'Avaggāha' means a bad downpour, a poor taking of the stream; hence it says 'vassavibandha' (rain-obstruction). 'Hatthamuddā' (hand-signs) is making a desired quantity known with the hand. But according to the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, that is simply counting by contracting the fingers. The teacher, the Elder Sāriputta, however, has shown that 'hatthamuddā' is counting by placing a mark on the finger joints. 'Gaṇanā' (counting) is called 'acchiddakagaṇanā' (unbroken counting) by the method of elimination. It should be known as continuous counting by the method ending in nine, such as 'one,' 'two,' etc., like that of barbarians, hill-tribesmen, and so on. 'Samūhana' is 'saṅkalana' (addition). 'Visuṃ uppādana' is 'apanayana' (subtraction). 'Paṭuppādana'—some also read 'saduppādana'—means correct subtraction. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes 'vokalana' (analysis), 'bhāgahāra' (division), and so on. Therein, 'vokalana' is making separate groups, meaning analysis or mixing. 'Bhāgakaraṇa' is 'bhāga' (making a share). 'Bhuñjana' or 'vibhajana' is 'hāra' (division). 'Sā' refers to the aforementioned 'piṇḍagaṇanā' (counting in heaps). Here, in the word 'disvā' (having seen), the meaning 'having counted merely by seeing' should be taken.

Paṭibhānakavīti ettha aṅguttarāgame (a. ni. 4.231) vuttānanti seso, kavīnaṃ kabyakaraṇanti sambandho, etena kavīhi kataṃ, kavīnaṃ vā idaṃ kāveyyanti atthaṃ dasseti. “Attano cintāvasenā”tiādi tesaṃ sabhāvadassanaṃ. Tathā hi vatthuṃ, anusandhiñca sayameva cirena cintetvā karaṇavasena cintākavi veditabbo. Kiñci sutvā sutena asutaṃ anusandhetvā karaṇavasena sutakavi, kiñci atthaṃ upadhāretvā tassa saṅkhipanavitthāraṇādivasena atthakavi, yaṃ kiñci parena kataṃ kabbaṃ vā nāṭakaṃ vā disvā taṃsadisameva aññaṃ attano ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena karaṇavasena paṭibhānakavīti. Nti tamatthaṃ. Tappaṭibhāganti [M 1.0375] tena diṭṭhena sadisaṃ. “Kattabba”nti ettha visesanaṃ, “karissāmī”ti ettha vā bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ. Ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānavasenāti kāraṇānurūpaṃ pavattanakañāṇavasena. Jīvikatthāyāti pakaraṇādhigatavaseneva vuttaṃ. Kavīnaṃ idanti kabyaṃ, yaṃ “gīta”nti vuccati.

Here, regarding 'paṭibhānakavi' (spontaneous poet), the remainder of the text, 'of those spoken of in the Aṅguttara Nikāya' (A. Ni. 4.231), should be understood. The connection is 'the making of poetry by poets.' By this, it shows the meaning: 'kāveyya' (poetry) is what is made by poets, or it is 'this of the poets.' 'By the power of one's own thought,' and so on, is the statement showing their nature. Thus, one who, having reflected for a long time on a subject and its connections by oneself, composes by the power of that act, should be known as a 'cintākavi' (thought-poet). One who, having heard something, connects what was not heard by means of what was heard and composes by the power of that act, is a 'sutakavi' (heard-poet). One who, having grasped a certain meaning, composes by the power of contracting, expanding, etc., that meaning, is an 'atthakavi' (meaning-poet). One who, having seen any poetry or drama made by another, creates another work just like it by means of one's own spontaneous intelligence arising from the situation, is a 'paṭibhānakavi' (spontaneous-poet). 'Nti' refers to that meaning. 'Tappaṭibhāga' means similar to that which was seen. In the word 'kattabba', it is an adjective, or in the word 'karissāmi', it is a neuter noun of state. 'By the power of spontaneous intelligence arising from the situation' means by the power of knowledge that proceeds in accordance with the cause. 'For the sake of livelihood' is said only by the power of understanding the context. 'This of the poets' is 'kabya' (poetry), which is called 'gīta' (song).

26. Pariggahabhāvena dārikāya gaṇhanaṃ āvāhanaṃ. Tathā dānaṃ vivāhanaṃ. Idha pana tathākaraṇassa [V 1.0330] uttarapadalopena niddeso, hetugabbhavasena vā, tenāha “imassa dārakassā”tiādi. Itīti evaṃhontesu, evaṃbhāvato vā. Uṭṭhānanti khettādito uppannamāyaṃ. Iṇanti dhanavaḍḍhanatthaṃ parassa dinnaṃ pariyudañcanaṃ. Pubbe paricchinnakāle asampattepi uddharitamiṇaṃ uṭṭhānaṃ, yathāparicchinnakāle pana sampatte iṇanti keci, tadayuttameva iṇagahaṇeneva sijjhanato. Paresaṃ dinnaṃ iṇaṃ vā dhananti sambandho. Thāvaranti ciraṭṭhitikaṃ. Desantare diguṇatiguṇādigahaṇavasena bhaṇḍappayojanaṃ payogo. Tattha vā aññattha vā yathākālaparicchedaṃ vaḍḍhigahaṇavasena payojanaṃ uddhāro. “Bhaṇḍamūlarahitānaṃ vāṇijaṃ katvā ettakena udayena saha mūlaṃ dethā’ti dhanadānaṃ payogo, tāvakālikadānaṃ uddhāro”tipi vadanti. Ajja payojitaṃ diguṇaṃ catuguṇaṃ hotīti yadi ajja payojitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, evaṃ aparajja diguṇaṃ, ajja catuguṇaṃ hotīti attho. Subhassa, subhena vā gamanaṃ pavattanaṃ subhago, tassa karaṇaṃ subhagakaraṇaṃ, taṃ pana piyamanāpassa, sassirīkassa vā karaṇamevāti āha “piyamanāpakaraṇa”ntiādi. Sassirīkakaraṇanti sarīrasobhaggakaraṇaṃ. Vilīnassāti patiṭṭhahitvāpi paripakkamapāpuṇitvā vilopassa. Tathā paripakkabhāvena aṭṭhitassa. Pariyāyavacanametaṃ padacatukkaṃ. Bhesajjadānanti gabbhasaṇṭhāpanabhesajjassa dānaṃ. Tīhi kāraṇehīti ettha vātena, pāṇakehi vā gabbhe vinassante na purimakammunā okāso kato, tappaccayā eva kammaṃ vipaccati, sayameva pana kammunā okāse kate na ekantena vātā, pāṇakā vā apekkhitabbāti kammassa visuṃ kāraṇabhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vi. aṭṭha. 2.185) pana vātena pāṇakehi vā gabbho vinassanto kammaṃ vinā na vinassatīti adhippāyena tamaññātra dvīhi kāraṇehīti vuttaṃ. Nibbāpanīyanti upasamakaraṃ. Paṭikammanti yathā te na khādanti, tathā paṭikaraṇaṃ.

26. The taking of a girl by way of possession is ‘āvāhana’ (bringing home). Likewise, giving is ‘vivāhana’ (marrying off). Here, however, the explanation of such an action is made by the elision of the subsequent word, or by way of including the cause; hence it is said, ‘for this boy,’ etc. ‘Iti’ means ‘when it is thus,’ or ‘because it is thus.’ ‘Uṭṭhāna’ refers to the income that arises from a field, etc. ‘Iṇa’ means a loan given to another for the purpose of increasing wealth, an acquisition. Some say that a loan drawn out even before the previously determined time has been reached is ‘uṭṭhāna,’ but when the determined time is reached, it is ‘iṇa.’ That is indeed incorrect, because it is accomplished by the term ‘iṇa’ itself. The connection is: a loan or wealth given to others. ‘Thāvara’ means long-lasting. ‘Payoga’ is the employment of goods in another country by way of taking double, triple, etc. There or elsewhere, ‘uddhāra’ is the employment of goods by way of taking interest according to the determined period of time. Teachers also say: “Giving wealth to those who are without capital goods, having done business, saying, ‘Give back the principal together with this much profit,’ is ‘payoga.’ Giving for a temporary period is ‘uddhāra.’” The meaning of ‘Employed today, it becomes double, quadruple’ is: if goods are employed today, thus tomorrow it becomes double, and today it becomes quadruple. ‘Subhaga’ is the going or proceeding of the auspicious, or auspiciously; its doing is ‘subhagakaraṇa’ (making auspicious). That, however, is indeed the doing of what is dear and agreeable, or of what is prosperous; hence it is said, ‘piyamanāpakaraṇa’ (making dear and agreeable), etc. ‘Sassirīkakaraṇa’ means making the body beautiful. ‘Vilīnassa’ refers to that which, even after being established, perishes without reaching maturity. Similarly, it refers to that which is not established in a state of maturity. This group of four words is a synonym. ‘Bhesajjadāna’ means giving medicine for stabilizing a pregnancy. Here, in ‘by three causes’: when the fetus is being destroyed by wind or by living creatures, an opportunity is not made by previous kamma; kamma ripens only because of that condition. On the other hand, when an opportunity is made by kamma itself, wind or living creatures are not necessarily to be regarded. Thus, it should be understood that the status of kamma as a separate cause is stated. In the Vinaya commentary, however, with the intention that a fetus being destroyed by wind or by living creatures does not get destroyed without kamma, it was said: ‘that is apart from two causes.’ ‘Nibbāpanīya’ means that which causes pacification. ‘Paṭikamma’ means a remedy so that they do not consume it.

Bandhakaraṇanti [M 1.0376] yathā jiṃ cāletuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ anāloḷitakaraṇaṃ. Parivattanatthanti āvudhādinā saha ukkhittahatthānaṃ aññattha parivattanatthaṃ, attanā gopitaṭṭhāne akhipetvā parattha khipanatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Khipatīti ca aññattha khipatīti attho. Vinicchayaṭṭhāneti aḍḍavinicchayaṭṭhāne. Icchitatthassa devatāya kaṇṇe kathanavasena jappanaṃ kaṇṇajappananti ca vadanti. Devataṃ otāretvāti ettha mantajappanena devatāya otāraṇaṃ. Jīvikatthāyāti yathā pāricariyaṃ katvā jīvitavutti hoti, tathā jīvitavuttikaraṇatthāya. Ādiccapāricariyāti karamālāhi pūjaṃ katvā sakaladivasaṃ ādiccābhimukhāvaṭṭhānena ādiccassa paricaraṇaṃ. “Tathevā”ti iminā “jīvikatthāyā”ti padamākaḍḍhati. Sirivhāyananti ī-kārato a-kāralopena sandhiniddeso, tenāha “siriyā avhāyana”nti. “Sirenā”ti pana ṭhānavasena avhāyanākāraṃ [V 1.0331] dasseti. Ye tu a-kārato a-kārassa lopaṃ katvā “siravhāyana”nti paṭhanti, tesaṃ pāṭhe ayamattho “mantaṃ jappetvā sirasā icchitassa atthassa avhāyana”nti.

‘Bandhakaraṇa’ is making it so that one is not able to move the tongue; thus, it is the act of making it unstirred. ‘Parivattanattha’ refers to the purpose of turning elsewhere those with hands raised together with weapons, etc.; it means for the purpose of throwing it elsewhere, without throwing it in a place guarded by oneself. And ‘khipati’ means ‘throws elsewhere.’ ‘Vinicchayaṭṭhāne’ means in a place of judgment, a place of partial judgment. Commentators also say that ‘kaṇṇajappana’ (ear-muttering) is muttering in a deity's ear by way of speaking about a desired matter. Here, in ‘devataṃ otāretvā’ (having brought down a deity), it is the bringing down of a deity by the muttering of a mantra. ‘Jīvikatthāya’ means for the purpose of making a livelihood, just as a livelihood is made by performing service. ‘Ādiccapāricariyā’ is attending on the sun by making offerings with radiant garlands and standing facing the sun for the entire day. By this ‘tathevā’ (just so), it draws in the word ‘jīvikatthāya’ (for the sake of livelihood). ‘Sirivhāyana’ is an explanation of the sandhi by the elision of the ‘a’-vowel after the ‘ī’-vowel; therefore, it says ‘siriyā avhāyana’ (invoking of prosperity). But by ‘sirenā’ (with the head), it shows the manner of invoking by way of position. But those teachers who, having elided the ‘a’-vowel after the ‘a’-vowel, read ‘siravhāyana,’ in their reading this is the meaning: ‘invoking the desired purpose with the head, having muttered a mantra.’

27. Devaṭṭhānanti devāyatanaṃ. Upahāranti pūjaṃ. Samiddhikāleti āyācitassa atthassa siddhakāle. Santipaṭissavakammanti devatāyācanāya yā santi paṭikattabbā, tassā paṭissavakaraṇaṃ. Santīti cettha mantajappanena pūjākaraṇaṃ, tāya santiyā āyācanappayogoti attho. Tasminti yaṃ “sace me idaṃ nāma samijjhissatī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ paṭissavaphalabhūte yathābhipatthitakammasmiṃ. Tassāti yo “paṇidhī”ti ca vutto, tassa paṭissavassa. Yathāpaṭissavañhi upahāre kate paṇidhiāyācanā katā niyyātitā hotīti. Gahitamantassāti uggahitamantassa. Payogakaraṇanti upacārakammakaraṇaṃ. Itīti kāraṇatthe nipāto, tena vassavossa-saddānaṃ purisapaṇḍakesu pavattiṃ kāraṇabhāvena dasseti, paṇḍakato visesena asati bhavatīti vasso. Purisaliṅgato virahena avaasati hīḷito hutvā bhavatīti vosso. Viseso rāgassavo yassāti vasso. Vigato rāgassavo yassāti vossoti niruttinayena padasiddhītipi vadanti. Vassakaraṇaṃ tadanurūpabhesajjena. Vossakaraṇaṃ pana uddhatabījatādināpi, teneva jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vossavarāti uddhatabījā orodhapālakā”ti vuttaṃ[M 1.0377]. Acchandikabhāvamattanti itthiyā akāmabhāvamattaṃ. Liṅganti purisanimittaṃ.

27. ‘Devaṭṭhāna’ means a shrine of a deva. ‘Upahāra’ means an offering. ‘Samiddhikāle’ means at the time of the fulfillment of a requested purpose. ‘Santipaṭissavakamma’ is the act of making a promise concerning the propitiatory offering that is to be performed for a request to a deity. And here, ‘santi’ is the making of an offering by muttering a mantra; the meaning is the undertaking of a request by means of that propitiatory offering. ‘Tasmiṃ’ refers to that action which was wished for, which has become the fruit of the promise, about which the words were spoken, ‘If this thing will be successful for me.’ ‘Tassa’ refers to that promise, which is also called ‘paṇidhi’ (aspiration). For when the offering is made in accordance with the promise, the aspiration and request is made and fulfilled. ‘Gahitamantassa’ means of one who has learned a mantra. ‘Payogakaraṇa’ is the performance of a preliminary rite. ‘Iti’ is a particle in the sense of cause; by it, it shows the occurrence of the words ‘vassa’ and ‘vossa’ in relation to men and eunuchs by way of cause. Because a man exists with a special quality compared to a eunuch, he is a ‘vassa.’ Because a eunuch exists, being despised, due to the absence of the male organ, he is a ‘vossa.’ Teachers also say that the derivation of the words is by the method of etymology thus: ‘vassa’ is he whose flow of passion is special. ‘Vossa’ is he whose flow of passion is gone. Making a ‘vassa’ (a man) is done with medicine appropriate for that. But making a ‘vossa’ (a eunuch) is done by removal of the testicles, etc. For that very reason, in the Jātaka commentary it is said: “‘Vossavarā’ means those with removed testicles, the guardians of the harem.” ‘Acchandikabhāvamatta’ means merely the state of a woman’s lack of desire. ‘Liṅga’ means the male organ.

Vatthubalikammakaraṇanti gharavatthusmiṃ balikammassa karaṇaṃ, taṃ pana upaddavapaṭibāhanatthaṃ, vaḍḍhanatthañca karonti, mantajappanena attano, aññesañca mukhasuddhikaraṇaṃ. Tesanti aññesaṃ. Yoganti bhesajjapayogaṃ. Vamananti pacchindanaṃ. Uddhaṃvirecananti vamanabhedameva “uddhaṃ dosānaṃ nīharaṇa”nti vuttattā. Virecananti pakativirecanameva. Adhovirecananti suddhavatthikasāvavatthiādivatthikiriyā “adho dosānaṃ nīharaṇa”nti vuttattā. Atho vamanaṃ uggiraṇameva, uddhaṃvirecanaṃ dosanīharaṇaṃ. Tathā virecanaṃ virekova, adhovirecanaṃ dosanīharaṇanti ayametesaṃ viseso pākaṭo hoti. Dosānanti ca pittādidosānanti attho. Semhanīharaṇādi sirovirecanaṃ. Kaṇṇabandhanatthanti chinnakaṇṇānaṃ saṅghaṭanatthaṃ. Vaṇaharaṇatthanti arupanayanatthaṃ. Akkhitappanatelanti akkhīsu usumassa nīharaṇatelaṃ. Yena akkhimhi añjite uṇhaṃ usumaṃ nikkhamati. Yaṃ nāsikāya gaṇhīyati, taṃ natthu. Paṭalānīti akkhipaṭalāni. Nīharaṇasamatthanti apanayanasamatthaṃ. Khārañjananti khārakamañjanaṃ. Sītameva saccaṃ niruttinayena, tassa kāraṇaṃ añjanaṃ saccañjananti āha “sītalabhesajjañjana”nti. Salākavejjakammanti akkhirogavejjakammaṃ. Salākasadisattā salākasaṅkhātassa akkhirogassa vejjakammanti [V 1.0332] hi sālākiyaṃ. Idaṃ pana vuttāvasesassa akkhirogapaṭikammassa saṅgahaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ “tappanādayopi hi sālākiyānevā”ti. Paṭividdhassa salākassa nikkhamanatthaṃ vejjakammaṃ salākavejjakammanti keci, taṃ pana sallakattiyapadeneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

`Vatthubalikammakaraṇa` means the making of a bali offering on a house site. This, moreover, is done for the purpose of warding off danger and for the purpose of prosperity. By the muttering of mantras, it is the purification of the mouth for oneself and for others. `Tesaṃ` means 'of others'. `Yogaṃ` means the application of medicine. `Vamanaṃ` means inducing vomiting. `Uddhaṃvirecanaṃ` is just a type of vomiting, because it is said, “the removal of humors upwards.” `Virecanaṃ` is just natural purgation. `Adhovirecanaṃ` is the procedure of cleansing the rectum and bladder, such as a cleansing enema or an astringent enema, because it is said, “the removal of humors downwards.” Furthermore, `vamanaṃ` is simply retching; `uddhaṃvirecanaṃ` is the removal of humors. Similarly, `virecanaṃ` is just purgation; `adhovirecanaṃ` is the removal of humors—this is the clear distinction between them. And `dosānaṃ` means 'of humors such as bile, etc.' The removal of phlegm, etc., is `sirovirecanaṃ` (head-purgation). `Kaṇṇabandhanatthaṃ` means for the purpose of joining severed ears. `Vaṇaharaṇatthaṃ` means for the purpose of healing a wound. `Akkhitappanatelaṃ` is oil for removing heat from the eyes. By this, when applied to the eye, warmth and vapor exit. That which is taken in through the nose is `natthu` (nasal medication). `Paṭalāni` means films on the eye. `Nīharaṇasamatthanti` means capable of removing. `Khārañjanaṃ` is a harsh eye-ointment. By way of etymology, `sīta` (cool) itself is `sacca` (true); an eye-ointment that is the cause of that is `saccañjana` (true eye-ointment). Therefore, the Teacher said, “cooling medicinal eye-ointment” (`sītalabhesajjañjana`). `Salākavejjakammaṃ` is the medical practice for eye diseases. Indeed, because of its resemblance to a probe, the medical practice for the eye disease called `salāka` is `sālākiyaṃ`. This, however, is stated for the purpose of including the remaining treatments for eye diseases, as it is said, “for soothing and other treatments are also `sālākiyāni`.” Some say that `salākavejjakammaṃ` is the medical practice for the purpose of extracting a pierced splinter, but that should be understood as being included by the term `sallakattiya` itself.

Sallassa paṭividdhassa kattanaṃ ubbāhanaṃ sallakattaṃ, tadatthāya vejjakammaṃ sallakattavejjakammaṃ. Kumāraṃ bharatīti kumārabhato, tassa bhāvo komārabhaccaṃ, kumāro eva vā komāro, bhatanaṃ bhaccaṃ, tassa bhaccaṃ tathā, tadabhinipphādakaṃ vejjakammanti attho. Mūlāni padhānāni rogūpasamane samatthāni bhesajjāni mūlabhesajjāni, mūlānaṃ vā byādhīnaṃ bhesajjāni tathā. Mūlānubandhavasena hi duvidho byādhi. Tatra mūlabyādhimhi tikicchite yebhuyyena itaraṃ vūpasamati, tenāha “kāyatikicchataṃ dassetī”tiādi[M 1.0378]. Tattha kāyatikicchatanti mūlabhāvato sarīrabhūtehi bhesajjehi, sarīrabhūtānaṃ vā rogānaṃ tikicchakabhāvaṃ. Khārādīnīti khārodakādīni. Tadanurūpe vaṇeti vūpasamitassa mūlabyādhino anucchavike arumhi. Tesanti mūlabhesajjānaṃ. Apanayanaṃ apaharaṇaṃ, tehi atikicchananti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca komārabhaccasallakattasālākiyādivisesabhūtānaṃ tantīnaṃ pubbe vuttattā pārisesavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā tadavasesāya tantiyā idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, sabbāni cetāni ājīvahetukāniyeva idhādhippetāni “micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.21) vuttattā. Yaṃ pana tattha tattha pāḷiyaṃ “iti vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha itī-ti pakāratthe nipāto, vā-ti vikappanatthe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – iminā pakārena, ito aññena vāti. Tena yāni ito bāhirakapabbajitā sippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānādīni jīvikopāyabhūtāni ājīvikapakatā upajīvanti, tesaṃ pariggaho katoti veditabbaṃ.

The cutting and extracting of a pierced dart is `sallakattaṃ`; the medical practice for that purpose is `sallakattavejjakammaṃ`. Because 'he nurtures a boy' (`kumāraṃ bharati`), he is a `kumārabhaṭa`; the state of that is `komārabhaccaṃ` (pediatrics). Alternatively, `kumāra` itself is `komāra`; nurturing is `bhaccaṃ`; his nurturing is thus. The meaning is the medical practice that accomplishes that. `Mūlāni` means principal; medicines capable of pacifying disease are `mūlabhesajjāni` (root medicines). Alternatively, medicines for root (`mūlānaṃ`) diseases are likewise. For disease is twofold by way of the root and its consequence. Therein, when the root disease is treated, the other mostly subsides; therefore, he said, “he shows the treatment of the body (`kāyatikicchataṃ`),” etc. Therein, `kāyatikicchataṃ` means by medicines that are fundamental to the body, due to its being the root; or, the state of being a healer of diseases that are of the body. `Khārādīni` means alkaline liquids, etc. 'On a wound suitable for that' means on a sore suitable for the subsided root disease. `Tesaṃ` means 'of the root medicines'. `Apanayanaṃ` is `apaharaṇaṃ` (removal); 'non-treatment by them' (`tehi atikicchanam`) is what is said. And this, because the special textual traditions such as pediatrics, surgery, ophthalmology, etc., were stated before, is stated by way of elimination; therefore, the inclusion here should be understood as for the remaining textual tradition. And all these are intended here only as being for the sake of livelihood, because it is said, “they make a living by wrong livelihood.” But where it is said in the Pāḷi here and there 'iti vā', therein 'iti' is a particle in the sense of manner, and 'vā' is in the sense of an alternative. This is what is meant: in this manner, or in another manner than this. By that, it should be understood that an inclusion is made of whatever arts, sciences, fields of knowledge, etc., which are means of livelihood, that wanderers outside of this dispensation make into a livelihood and live by.

Mahāsīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Morality is concluded.

Pubbantakappikasassatavādavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Eternalist Doctrines of Those Who Speculate on the Past

28. Idāni suññatāpakāsanavārassatthaṃ vaṇṇento anusandhiṃ pakāsetuṃ “eva”ntiādimāha. Tattha vuttavaṇṇassāti sahatthe chaṭṭhivacanaṃ, sāmiatthe vā anusandhi-saddassa bhāvakammavasena kiriyādesanāsu pavattanato. Bhikkhusaṅghena vuttavaṇṇassāti “yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā”tiādinā [V 1.0333] vuttavaṇṇassa. Tatra pāḷiyaṃ ayaṃ sambandho – na bhikkhave, ettakā eva buddhaguṇā ye tumhākaṃ pākaṭā, apākaṭā pana “atthi bhikkhave, aññe dhammā”ti vitthāro. “Ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃ gahitā”tiādinā sassatādidiṭṭhiṭṭhānānaṃ yathāgahitākārassa suññabhāvappakāsanato, “tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasatī”ti sīlādīnañca aparāmasanīyabhāvadīpanena niccasārādivirahappakāsanato, yāsu vedanāsu avītarāgatāya bāhirānaṃ etāni diṭṭhivibandhakāni sambhavanti, tāsaṃ paccayabhūtānañca sammohādīnaṃ vedakakārakasabhāvābhāvadassanamukhena sabbadhammānaṃ attattaniyatāvirahadīpanato, anupādāparinibbānadīpanato ca ayaṃ desanā [M 1.0379] suññatāvibhāvanappadhānāti āha “suññatāpakāsanaṃ ārabhī”ti.

28. Now, explaining the meaning of the section on the declaration of emptiness, in order to show the connection, he said 'evaṃ', etc. Therein, in `vuttavaṇṇassa`, the genitive case is used in the sense of 'with' (`sahatthe`), or in the sense of possession (`sāmiatthe`), because the word `anusandhi` functions in the designation of actions either as a verbal noun (`bhāva`) or as an object (`kamma`). `Vuttavaṇṇassa` by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus refers to the praise spoken, beginning with 'yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā...' Therein, in the Pāḷi, this is the connection: 'Bhikkhus, the qualities of the Buddha that are manifest to you are not just this many. But there are other qualities not manifest,' the detailed explanation is 'There are, bhikkhus, other dhammas...' And because of showing the state of being empty of the wrongly grasped manner of the grounds for views such as eternalism, etc., by the passage beginning 'These grounds for views are thus grasped...'; and by the Pāḷi 'And that understanding one does not misapprehend,' by showing the state of not being fit for misapprehension of virtue, etc., and because of showing the absence of permanent essence, etc.; and because in those feelings where passion is not abandoned, these fetters of views arise for outsiders, and of contact, etc., which are the conditions for those feelings, by means of showing the absence of the nature of an experiencer and an agent, and because of showing the absence of self and what belongs to a self in all phenomena; and because of showing parinibbāna without clinging, this discourse has the clarification of emptiness as its principal theme. Therefore, the Teacher said, 'He began the declaration of emptiness'.

Pariyattīti vinayādibhedabhinnā manasā vavatthāpitā tanti. Desanāti tassā tantiyā manasā vavatthāpitāya vibhāvanā, yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpabhūtā vā paññāpanā, anulomādivasena vā kathananti pariyattidesanānaṃ viseso pubbeyeva vavatthāpitoti imamatthaṃ sandhāya “desanāya, pariyattiya”nti ca vuttaṃ. Evamādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena saccasabhāvasamādhipaññāpakatipuññāpattiñeyyādayo saṅgayhanti. Tathā hi ayaṃ dhamma-saddo “catunnaṃ bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ ananubodhā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.1) sacce pavattati, “kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. tikamātikā 1) sabhāve, “evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.13, 94, 145; 3.142; ma. ni. 3.167; saṃ. ni. 5.378) samādhimhi, “saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, sa ve pecca na socati”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 190) paññāyaṃ, “jātidhammānaṃ bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.131; 3.373; paṭi. ma. 1.33) pakatiyaṃ, “dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahātī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 184; theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102; 15.385) puññe, “cattāro pārājikā dhammā”tiādīsu (pārā. 233) āpattiyaṃ, “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”tiādīsu (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) ñeyye pavattati. Dhammā hontīti sattajīvato suññā dhammamattā hontīti attho. Kimatthiyaṃ guṇe pavattananti āha “tasmā”tiādi.

Learning (pariyatti) is the text (tanti) that is differentiated by the divisions of the Vinaya, etc., and established by mind. Teaching (desanā) is the clarification of that text established by mind; or a designation that is a declaration of Dhamma in accordance with Dhamma; or a discourse by way of conformity, etc. The distinction between learning and teaching has already been established. With this meaning in mind, it is said, 'in teaching' and 'in learning.' In 'and so on' (evamādīsu), the word 'etc.' (ādi) includes truth, intrinsic nature, concentration, wisdom, natural disposition, merit, offense, knowable objects, and so on. For this word 'Dhamma' occurs in the sense of truth, as in 'Monks, due to not thoroughly understanding four Dhammas...'; in the sense of intrinsic nature, as in 'wholesome Dhammas, unwholesome Dhammas...'; in the sense of concentration, as in 'Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature (evaṃdhammā)'; in the sense of wisdom, as in 'Truth, Dhamma, resolve, generosity—he truly does not grieve after passing away'; in the sense of natural disposition, as in 'Monks, for beings subject to birth, such a wish arises...'; in the sense of merit, as in 'Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness'; in the sense of offense, as in 'the four pārājika offenses (dhammā)'; and in the sense of knowable object, as in 'All Dhammas in every way come into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.' 'They are Dhammas' (dhammā honti) means they are mere phenomena, void of a being or life-principle. As to why it occurs in the sense of 'quality,' he said, 'Therefore,' etc.

Makasatuṇḍasūciyāti sūcimukhamakkhikāya tuṇḍasaṅkhātāya sūciyā. Alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho viyāti sambandho. Aññatra tathāgatāti ṭhapetvā tathāgataṃ. “Duddasā”ti padeneva tesaṃ dhammānaṃ dukkhogāhatā [V 1.0334] pakāsitāti “alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā” icceva vuttaṃ. Labhitabbāti labbhanīyā, sā eva labbhaneyyā, labhīyate vā labbhanaṃ, tamarahatīti labbhaneyyā, na labbhaneyyā alabbhaneyyā, patiṭṭhahanti etthāti patiṭṭhā, patiṭṭhahanaṃ vā patiṭṭhā, alabbhaneyyā patiṭṭhā etthāti alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace koci attano pamāṇaṃ ajānanto ñāṇena [M 1.0380] te dhamme ogāhituṃ ussāhaṃ kareyya, tassa taṃ ñāṇaṃ appatiṭṭhameva makasatuṇḍasūci viya mahāsamuddeti. Ogāhitumasakkuṇeyyatāya “ettakā ete īdisā vā”ti te passituṃ na sakkāti vuttaṃ “gambhīrattā eva duddasā”ti. Ye pana daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tesaṃ ogāhitvā anu anu bujjhane kathā eva natthīti āha “duddasattā eva duranubodhāti. Sabbakilesapariḷāhapaṭippassaddhisaṅkhātaaggaphalamatthake samuppannatā, purecarānucaravasena nibbutasabbakilesapariḷāhasamāpattisamokiṇṇattā ca nibbutasabbapariḷāhā. Tabbhāvato santāti attho. Santārammaṇāni maggaphalanibbānāni anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ, saṅkhārānañca abhāvato.

'By a needle like a mosquito's proboscis' means: by the needle that is the proboscis of a mosquito with a needle-like mouth. The connection should be made thus: 'like one with an unobtainable foundation'. 'Except for the Tathāgata' means setting aside the Tathāgata. By the very word 'hard to see,' the difficulty of plunging into those dhammas is shown; hence, it was said, 'having an unobtainable foundation.' 'To be attained' (labhitabbā) means 'attainable' (labbhanīyā); that itself is 'attainable' (labbhaneyyā). Or, 'attainment' (labbhanaṃ) is what is obtained (labhīyate); that which is worthy of it is 'attainable' (labbhaneyyā). What is not attainable is 'unattainable' (alabbhaneyyā). 'Foundation' (patiṭṭhā) is where one stands (patiṭṭhahanti ettha), or the act of standing (patiṭṭhahanaṃ). Where there is an unattainable foundation (alabbhaneyyā patiṭṭhā ettha), that is 'having an unobtainable foundation' (alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā). This is what is meant: If someone, not knowing their own measure, were to strive with knowledge to plunge into those dhammas, that knowledge of theirs would find no footing, just like a mosquito's needle-like proboscis in the great ocean. Because of the inability to plunge into them, it is not possible to see them and say, 'They are of such a number or of such a kind'; thus it was said, 'Because of being deep, they are hard to see.' As for those that simply cannot be seen, there is no question of plunging into and gradually comprehending them; thus he said, 'Because of being hard to see, they are difficult to comprehend.' Because they arise at the summit, which is the supreme fruit known as the pacification of the torment of all defilements, and because they are suffused with attainments where the torment of all defilements is quenched, by way of preceding and succeeding, they are 'quenched of all torment.' Because of that state, they are 'peaceful'—this is the meaning. The path, fruition, and Nibbāna are peaceful objects because of the absence of defilements and formations, which are of an unpeaceful nature.

Atha vā kasiṇugghāṭimākāsatabbisayaviññāṇānaṃ anantabhāvo viya susamūhatavikkhepatāya niccasamāhitassa manasikārassa vasena tadārammaṇadhammānaṃ santabhāvo veditabbo. Avirajjhitvā nimittapaṭivedho viya issāsānaṃ avirajjhitvā dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodho sāduraso mahārasova hotīti āha “atittikaraṇaṭṭhenā”ti, atappanakaraṇasabhāvenāti attho. Sohiccaṃ titti tappananti hi pariyāyo. Atittikaraṇaṭṭhenāti patthetvā sādurasakaraṇaṭṭhenātipi atthaṃ vadanti. Paṭivedhappattānaṃ tesu ca buddhānameva sabbākārena visayabhāvūpagamanato na takkabuddhiyā gocarāti āha “uttamañāṇavisayattā”tiādi. Nipuṇāti ñeyyesu tikkhappavattiyā chekā. Yasmā pana so chekabhāvo ārammaṇe appaṭihatavuttitāya, sukhumañeyyaggahaṇasamatthatāya ca supākaṭo hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā”ti. Paṇḍitehiyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ samatthetuṃ “bālānaṃ avisayattā”ti āha.

Alternatively, like the infinitude of the space revealed by removing the kasiṇa-object and of the consciousness that takes it as object, the peaceful state of the dhammas that have that peaceful state as their object is to be known by means of constantly concentrated attention, due to the thorough removal of distraction. Just as an archer's penetration of the target is without failure, so too the realization of the true nature of these dhammas, being without failure, is of a pleasing taste, like a great flavor; thus he said, 'because of the meaning of not causing satisfaction,' which means, because of the nature of causing non-satiation. For 'contentment' (sohiccaṃ), 'satisfaction' (titti), and 'gratification' (tappanaṃ) are synonyms. Regarding 'because of the meaning of not causing satisfaction,' some also state the meaning as 'because of the meaning of producing a delightful flavor through longing.' And because, for those who have attained penetration and for the Buddhas alone, these dhammas in every way become their object, they are not the domain of conjectural wisdom; thus he said, 'because it is the domain of supreme knowledge,' etc. 'Subtle' (nipuṇā) means they are skilled due to their sharp functioning regarding knowable things. And since that skillfulness is very evident due to their unobstructed activity regarding the object and their ability to grasp subtle knowables, it is therefore said, 'because of their gentle and subtle nature.' To support the emphasis in 'only by the wise,' he said, 'because it is not the domain of fools.'

Ayaṃ aṭṭhakathānayato aparo nayo – vinayapaṇṇattiādigambhīraneyyavibhāvanato gambhīrā. Kadāciyeva asaṅkhyeyye mahākappe atikkamitvāpi dullabhadassanatāya duddasā. Dassanañcettha paññācakkhuvaseneva veditabbaṃ. Dhammanvayasaṅkhātassa anubodhassa kassacideva sambhavato duranubodhā. Santasabhāvato, veneyyānañca sabbaguṇasampadānaṃ pariyosānattā santā. Attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītatāya paṇītā. Samadhigatasaccalakkhaṇatāya atakkehi puggalehi, atakkena [M 1.0381] vā ñāṇena avacaritabbato atakkāvacarā. Nipuṇaṃ, nipuṇe vā atthe saccapaccayākārādivasena [V 1.0335] vibhāvanato nipuṇā. Loke aggapaṇḍitena sammāsambuddhena veditabbato pakāsitabbato paṇḍitavedanīyā.

This is another method, different from that of the commentary: They are profound (gambhīrā) because they make clear profound knowable matters, such as the Vinaya regulations. They are hard to see (duddasā) because sight of them is difficult to obtain, even after countless great aeons have passed. And here, 'sight' should be understood only by way of the wisdom-eye. They are difficult to comprehend (duranubodhā) because the corresponding comprehension, known as conformity with the Dhamma, is possible only for a certain person. They are peaceful (santā) because of their peaceful nature, and because they are the culmination of all accomplishments of virtue for those to be trained. They are excellent (paṇītā) because they are led to a state of preeminence by their own causes. They are beyond the sphere of conjecture (atakkāvacarā) because, having the characteristic of truth well realized, they are to be comprehended by persons who do not use conjecture, or by non-conjectural knowledge. They are subtle (nipuṇā) because they make clear a subtle meaning, or subtle meanings, by way of truth, dependent origination, and so on. They are to be known by the wise (paṇḍitavedanīyā) because they are to be known and proclaimed by the supreme sage in the world, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhato hi bhagavā “sabbavidūhamasmi, (ma. ni. 1.178; 2.342; dha. pa. 353; mahāva. 11) dasabalasamannāgato bhikkhave, tathāgato”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.21; 2.22) attano sabbaññutādiguṇe pakāsesi, tenevāha “sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetī”ti. Sayaṃ-saddena, niddhāritāvadhāraṇena vā nivattetabbamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “anaññaneyyo hutvā”ti vuttaṃ, aññehi abodhito hutvāti attho. Abhiññāti ya-kāralopo “aññāṇatā āpajjatī”tiādīsu (pari. 296) viyāti dasseti “abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇenā”ti iminā. Apica “sayaṃ abhiññā”ti padassa anaññaneyyo hutvāti atthavacanaṃ, “sacchikatvā”ti padassa pana sayameva…pe… katvāti. Sayaṃ-saddā hi sacchikatvāti etthāpi sambajjhitabbo. Abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇenāti ca tassa hetuvacanaṃ, karaṇavacanaṃ vā.

Indeed, because of the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the Blessed One declared His qualities such as omniscience with statements such as, 'I am the All-Knowing One; the Tathāgata, O monks, is endowed with the ten powers.' Therefore, He said, 'He declares after having directly known and realized it for Himself.' To show the meaning to be excluded by the word 'sayaṃ' (for Himself)—or by the resolute emphasis—it is said, 'having become one not led by another,' the meaning of which is 'having become one not taught by others.' That in 'abhiññā' there is an elision of the letter 'ya', as in such phrases as 'aññāṇatā āpajjatī' (one falls into ignorance), is shown by this phrase: 'with superior knowledge' (abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena). Furthermore, for the phrase 'sayaṃ abhiññā', 'anaññaneyyo hutvā' (having become one not led by another) is the explanatory phrase; but for the word 'sacchikatvā', the explanatory phrase is '...having made...' Indeed, the word 'sayaṃ' should also be connected here with 'sacchikatvā'. And 'with superior knowledge' is the word stating the reason for that, or it is a word in the instrumental case.

Tattha kiñcāpi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ phalanibbānāni viya sacchikātabbasabhāvaṃ na hoti, āsavakkhayañāṇe pana adhigate adhigatameva hoti, tasmā tassa paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sacchikiriyāti āha “abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ katvā”ti. Hetuatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, aggamaggañāṇasaṅkhātassa abhivisiṭṭhañāṇassādhigamahetūti attho. Abhivisiṭṭhañāṇanti vā paccavekkhaṇāñāṇe adhippete karaṇatthe karaṇavacanampi yujjateva. Pavedanañcettha aññāvisayānaṃ saccādīnaṃ desanākiccasādhanato, “ekomhi sammāsambuddho”tiādinā (mahāva. 11; kathā. 405) paṭijānanato ca veditabbaṃ. Guṇadhammehīti guṇasaṅkhātehi dhammehi. Yathābhūtameva yathābhuccaṃ sakatthe ṇyapaccayavasena.

Therein, although the Omniscient Knowledge is not of a nature to be realized like the fruits and Nibbāna, yet when the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers is attained, it is indeed attained. Therefore, the direct realization of it is called the act of realization. Thus, he said, 'having made it manifest with superior knowledge.' And this is a word in the instrumental case in the sense of cause; the meaning is: on account of the attainment of the superior knowledge called the knowledge of the supreme path. Alternatively, if by 'superior knowledge' reviewing knowledge is intended, a word in the instrumental case in the sense of instrument is also indeed appropriate. And the declaration here should be understood from its accomplishment of the task of teaching the truths and so on, which have other objects, and from the assertion, 'I am the one, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' and so forth. 'By the qualities' (guṇadhammehi) means by the dhammas designated as qualities. 'Yathābhūtameva' (exactly as it is) becomes 'yathābhuccaṃ' by the power of the 'ṇya' suffix in the sense of its own meaning.

Vadamānāti ettha sattiattho mānasaddo yathā “ekapuggalo bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjatī”ti, (a. ni. 1.170; kathā. 405) tasmā vattuṃ ussāhaṃ karontoti attho. Evaṃbhūtā hi vattukāmā nāma honti, tenāha “tathāgatassā”tiādi[M 1.0382]. Sāvasesaṃ vadantāpi viparītavadantā viya sammā vadantīti na vattabbāti yathā sammā vadanti, tathā dassetuṃ “ahāpetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena hi anavasesavadanameva sammā vadananti dasseti. “Vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyu”nti iminā ca “vadeyyu”nti etassa samatthanatthabhāvamāha yathā “so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 1.1.9) ye evaṃ bhagavatā thomitā, te dhammā katameti yojanā. “Atthi bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā”tiādipāḷiyā [V 1.0336] “sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti vuttavacanassa virodhibhāvaṃ codento “yadi eva”ntiādimāha. Tattha yadi evanti evaṃ “sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti vuttavacanaṃ yadi siyāti attho. Bahuvacananiddesoti “atthi bhikkhave”tiādīni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthi-saddopi hi idha bahuvacanoyeva “atthi khīrā, atthi gāvo”tiādīsu viya nipātabhāvasseva icchitattā. Yadipi tadidaṃ ñāṇaṃ ekameva sabhāvato, tathāpi sampayogato, ārammaṇato ca puthuvacanappayogamarahatīti vissajjeti “puthucitta…pe… rammaṇato”ti iminā. Puthucittasamāyogatoti puthūhi cittehi sampayogato. Puthūni ārammaṇāni etassāti puthuārammaṇaṃ, tabbhāvato sabbārammaṇattāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Here in 'vadamānā', the suffix '-māna' has the meaning of capability (satti), as in 'Monks, a certain person, arising (uppajjamāno), arises in the world...'; therefore, the meaning is 'making an effort to speak'. Indeed, such ones are called 'those who wish to speak'; hence, he said 'of the Tathāgata,' and so on. Since even those who speak with omissions should not be said to speak rightly, like those who speak perversely, to show how they do speak rightly, 'ahāpetvā' (without omitting) and so on was said. By this, he shows that only speaking without omission is right speech. And by 'vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyuṃ' (they would be able to speak), he states that 'vadeyyuṃ' (they would speak) has the meaning of capability, as in 'he would unravel this tangle' (so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa). The construction is: 'What are those dhammas that were thus praised by the Blessed One?' Challenging the contradiction between the Pāli text beginning 'Monks, there are other dhammas...' and the statement 'the Omniscient Knowledge', the questioner says 'yadi evaṃ' (if so), and so on. Therein, 'yadi evaṃ' means: 'if the statement 'the Omniscient Knowledge' were so'. 'The plural designation' was said with reference to 'Monks, there are...' and so on. For indeed, the word 'atthi' here is also plural, as in 'atthi khīrā, atthi gāvo' (there is milk, there are cows), because it is intended simply as a particle. He resolves the issue with 'puthucitta…pe…rammaṇato' (because of association with many minds... and because of many objects), saying: 'Although that knowledge is indeed one by nature, nevertheless, by way of association and by way of object, it is worthy of the use of the plural.' 'Puthucittasamāyogato' means because of association with many minds. 'It has many objects' (puthūni ārammaṇāni etassa), therefore it is 'puthuārammaṇaṃ' (having many objects); because of that state, it is said to have all objects (sabbārammaṇattā).

Apica puthu ārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇametassāti puthuārammaṇārammaṇanti etasmiṃ atthe “oṭṭhamukho, kāmāvacara”ntiādīsu viya ekassa ārammaṇasaddassa lopaṃ katvā “puthuārammaṇato”ti vuttaṃ, tenassa puthuñāṇakiccasādhakattaṃ dasseti. Tathā hetaṃ ñāṇaṃ tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ, chasu asādhāraṇañāṇesu sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, sattāriyapuggalavibhāvanakañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ, navasattāvāsaparijānanañāṇaṃ, dasabalañāṇanti evamādīnaṃ anekasatasahassabhedānaṃ ñāṇānaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ kiccaṃ sādheti, tesaṃ ārammaṇabhūtānaṃ anekesampi dhammānaṃ tadārammaṇabhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Tañhī”tiādi yathākkamaṃ tabbivaraṇaṃ. “Yathāhā”tiādinā paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷiṃ sādhakabhāvena dasseti. Tatthāti atītadhamme. Ekavāravasena puthuārammaṇabhāvaṃ nivattetvā anekavāravasena kamappavattiyā taṃ dassetuṃ “punappunaṃ uppattivasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Kamenāpi hi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ visayesu pavattati, na tathā sakiṃyeva[M 1.0383]. Yathā bāhirakā vadanti “sakiṃyeva sabbaññū sabbaṃ jānāti, na kamenā”ti.

Furthermore, in the sense of 'its object is a manifold object' (puthu ārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassa), it is 'puthuārammaṇārammaṇaṃ'. In this sense, as in 'oṭṭhamukho', 'kāmāvacara', and so on, after eliding one word 'ārammaṇa', it is stated as 'puthuārammaṇato' (because of having a manifold object). By this, he shows its nature of accomplishing the tasks of many knowledges. Indeed, this knowledge appropriately accomplishes the tasks of countless hundreds of thousands of varied knowledges, such as: the unimpeded knowledge in the three periods of time; the knowledge that defines the four kinds of birth; the knowledge that defines the five destinations; the remaining uncommon knowledges among the six uncommon knowledges; the knowledge that clarifies the seven types of noble individuals; the unshaken knowledge in the eight assemblies; the knowledge that fully understands the nine abodes of beings; and the ten powers. This should be understood to be because the many dhammas that are the objects of those knowledges are also the object of this omniscient knowledge. 'Tañhī' and so on is the explanation of that in due order. With 'Yathāhā' and so on, he shows the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāli as proof. 'Tattha' (therein) refers to past dhammas. Having excluded the state of having a manifold object on a single occasion, to show its gradual progression over many occasions, it is said 'by way of repeated arising'. For Omniscient Knowledge proceeds regarding its objects sequentially, not just all at once, as the outsiders say: 'The Omniscient One knows everything all at once, not sequentially.'

Yadi evaṃ acinteyyāparimeyyappabhedassa ñeyyassa paricchedavatā ekena ñāṇena niravasesato kathaṃ paṭivedhoti, ko vā evamāha “paricchedavantaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti. Aparicchedañhi taṃ ñāṇaṃ ñeyyamiva. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇa”nti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5 adhippāyatthameva gahitaṃ viya dissati) evampi jātibhūmisabhāvādivasena, disādesakālādivasena ca anekabhedabhinne ñeyye kamena gayhamāne anavasesapaṭivedho na sambhavatiyevāti? Nayidamevaṃ. Yañhi kiñci bhagavatā ñātumicchitaṃ sakalamekadeso vā, tattha appaṭihatacāritāya paccakkhato ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Vikkhepābhāvato ca bhagavā sabbakālaṃ samāhitoti [V 1.0337] ñātumicchitassa paccakkhabhāvo na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Vuttañhi “ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇa”ntiādi, (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) nanu cettha dūrato cittapaṭaṃ passantānaṃ viya, “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti vipassantānaṃ viya ca anekadhammāvabodhakāle anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti gahetabbanti? Gahetabbaṃ acinteyyānubhāvatāya buddhañāṇassa. Tenevāha “buddhavisayo acinteyyo”ti, (a. ni. 4.77) idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – sabbākārena sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthassa ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhavuttino anāvaraṇañāṇassa paṭilābhena bhagavā santānena sabbadhammapaṭivedhasamattho ahosi sabbaneyyāvaraṇassa pahānato, tasmā sabbaññū, na sakiṃyeva sabbadhammāvabodhato yathāsantānena sabbassa indhanassa dahanasamatthatāya pāvako “sabbabhū”ti vuccatīti.

If so, how can the knowable, which has inconceivable and immeasurable distinctions, be penetrated without remainder by a single, limited knowledge? Or who says, 'The knowledge of omniscience is limited'? For that knowledge is limitless, like the knowable. It has been said: 'As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge.' Even so, with the knowable being divided into many distinctions by way of birth, plane, nature, and so on, and by way of direction, region, time, and so on, when it is grasped sequentially, penetration without remainder is surely not possible—this is the objection. This should not be so understood. For whatever the Blessed One wishes to know, whether in whole or in part, knowledge arises in him directly because its course is unimpeded. And because of the absence of distraction, the Blessed One is always concentrated; therefore, the direct appearance of what he wishes to know cannot be prevented. For it has been said: 'The knowledge of the Blessed Buddha is connected to his aspiration,' and so on. Now, is it not to be understood here that, just as for those who see a painted cloth from afar, or for those who practice insight meditation on 'all phenomena are not-self,' the Blessed One's knowledge proceeds with an undetermined form when comprehending many phenomena? This is not to be understood thus, because of the inconceivable power of the Buddha’s knowledge. For that very reason, he said, 'The domain of a Buddha is inconceivable.' Here is the conclusion: Through the attainment of unobstructed knowledge—which is capable of comprehending all phenomena in all their aspects and which proceeds in connection with his aspiration—the Blessed One, through his continuity, became capable of penetrating all phenomena, because of having abandoned all obstructions to the knowable. Therefore, he is omniscient; not from comprehending all phenomena at once, just as fire is called 'all-consuming' because it is capable, through its continuity, of burning all fuel.

Kāmañcāyamattho pubbe vitthāritoyeva, pakārantarena pana sotujanānuggahakāmatāya, imissā ca porāṇasaṃvaṇṇanāvisodhanavasena pavattattā puna vibhāvitoti na cettha punaruttidoso pariyesitabbo, evamīdisesu. Ettha ca kiñcāpi bhagavato dasabalādiñāṇānipi anaññasādhāraṇāni, sabbadesavisayattā pana tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ na tehi buddhaguṇā ahāpetvā gahitā nāma honti. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa pana nippadesavisayattā [M 1.0384] tasmiṃ gahite sabbepi buddhaguṇā gahitā eva nāma honti, tasmā pāḷiatthānusārena tadeva ñāṇaṃ gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyampi hi “yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyu”nti tameva pakāsitaṃ tamantarena aññassa nippadesavisayassa abhāvato, nippadesavisayeneva ca yathābhuccaṃ sammā vadanasambhavatoti.

Although this matter has indeed been explained in detail before, it is made clear again here by another method, out of a desire to benefit the student-listeners, and because this proceeds by way of clarifying the ancient commentary. Therefore, the fault of repetition should not be sought here, nor in similar instances. And here, although the Blessed One's knowledges such as the ten powers are unique to him, because those knowledges have a partial domain, the Buddha's qualities are not grasped by them without omission. However, since the knowledge of omniscience has an all-encompassing domain, when that is grasped, all the Buddha’s qualities are indeed grasped. Therefore, it should be understood that in accordance with the meaning of the Pāli, that very knowledge is grasped. For in the Pāli too, when it says, 'Speaking of which qualities, they would rightly speak the true praise of the Tathāgata,' that very knowledge is revealed. This is because, apart from it, there is no other knowledge with an all-encompassing domain, and only through a knowledge with an all-encompassing domain is it possible to speak truly and rightly.

Aññevāti ettha eva-saddo sanniṭṭhāpanatthoti dassetuṃ “aññevāti idaṃ panettha vavatthāpanavacana”nti vuttaṃ, vavatthāpanavacananti ca sanniṭṭhāpanavacananti attho, sanniṭṭhāpanañca avadhāraṇameva. Kathanti āha “aññevā”tiādi. “Na pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādayo”ti iminā avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ dasseti. Ayañca eva-saddo aniyatadesatāya ca-saddo viya yattha vutto, tato aññatthāpi vacanicchāvasena upatiṭṭhatīti āha “gambhīrāvā”tiādi. Iti-saddena ca ādiatthena duddasāva na sudasā, duranubodhāva na suranubodhā, santāva na darathā, paṇītāva na hīnā, atakkāvacarāva na takkāvacarā, nipuṇāva na lūkhā, paṇḍitavedanīyāva na bālavedanīyāti nivattitaṃ dasseti. Sabbapadehīti yāva “paṇḍitavedanīyā”ti idaṃ padaṃ, tāva sabbapadehi.

Here, in the word `aññeva`, to show that the particle `eva` has the meaning of ascertainment, it is said: 'Here, `aññeva` is a term of determination.' A 'term of determination' means a term of ascertainment, and ascertainment is simply emphasis. How so? He says, `aññeva`, and so on. By this emphasis, 'not abstention from killing living beings, etc.,' he shows what is excluded. And this particle `eva`, like the particle `ca`, because of its unfixed position, appears not only where it is stated but also elsewhere according to the speaker's intention. Thus he says, `gambhīrāva` ('profound indeed'), and so on. And by the word `iti`, in the sense of 'and so on,' he shows what is excluded: 'difficult to see indeed, not easy to see; difficult to understand indeed, not easy to understand; peaceful indeed, not agitated; sublime indeed, not base; beyond the sphere of logic indeed, not within the sphere of logic; subtle indeed, not coarse; to be known by the wise indeed, not to be known by fools.' By 'with all the words' it is meant that the particle `eva` should be connected with all the words up to and including `paṇḍitavedanīyā`.

Evaṃ [V 1.0338] nivattetabbataṃ yuttiyā daḷhīkaronto “sāvakapāramiñāṇa”ntiādimāha. Tattha sāvakapāramiñāṇanti sāvakānaṃ dānādipāramipāripūriyā nipphannaṃ vijjattayachaḷabhiññācatupaṭisambhidābhedaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tathā paccekabuddhānaṃ paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ. Tatoti sāvakapāramiñāṇato. Tatthāti sāvakapāramiñāṇe. Tatopīti anantaraniddiṭṭhato paccekabodhiñāṇatopi. Api-saddena, pi-saddena vā ko pana vādo sāvakapāramiñāṇatoti sambhāveti. Tatthāpīti paccekabodhiñāṇepi. Ito panāti sabbaññutaññāṇato pana, tasmā ettha sabbaññutaññāṇe vavatthānaṃ labbhatīti adhippāyo. Gambhīresu visesā, gambhīrānaṃ vā visesena gambhīrā. Ayañca gambhīro ayañca gambhīro ime imesaṃ visesena gambhīrāti vā gambhīratarā. Tarasaddenevettha byavacchedanaṃ siddhaṃ.

Thus, strengthening by reasoning the principle of what is to be excluded, he says, 'the disciple's perfection-knowledge,' and so on. Therein, 'the disciple's perfection-knowledge' is the knowledge—differentiated as the three true knowledges, the six supernormal abilities, and the four analytical knowledges—that is produced by the disciples' fulfillment of the perfections beginning with giving; similarly, it is the Paccekabuddhas' enlightenment-knowledge. `Tato` means 'than the disciple's perfection-knowledge.' `Tattha` means 'in the disciple's perfection-knowledge.' `Tatopi` means 'also than the Paccekabuddha's enlightenment-knowledge.' By the particle `api`, or `pi`, he extols it thus: 'What then to say of it being more profound than the disciple's perfection-knowledge?' `Tatthāpi` means 'also in the Paccekabuddha's enlightenment-knowledge.' `Ito pana` means 'but than the knowledge of omniscience.' Therefore, the intention is that a determination is obtained herein, regarding the knowledge of omniscience. `Gambhīratarā` (more profound) means: distinctions among profound things; or, profound by way of distinction among profound things. Or: 'This is profound, and that is profound; these are profound by way of distinction from those,' therefore they are `gambhīratarā`. Here, the distinction is established by the suffix `-tara` itself.

Etthāyaṃ yojanā – kiñcāpi sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ sekkhañāṇaṃ puthujjanañāṇañca upādāya gambhīraṃ, paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ pana upādāya na tathā gambhīranti “gambhīramevā”ti na sakkā byavacchijjituṃ, tathā paccekabodhiñāṇampi [M 1.0385] yathāvuttaṃ ñāṇamupādāya gambhīraṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana upādāya na evaṃ gambhīranti “gambhīramevā”ti na sakkā byavacchijjituṃ, tasmā tattha vavatthānaṃ na labbhati. Sabbaññutaññāṇadhammā pana sāvakapāramiñāṇādīnamiva kiñci upādāya gambhīrābhāvābhāvato “gambhīrā evā”ti vavatthānaṃ labbhatīti. Yathā cettha vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ duddasaṃ. “Paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ pana tato duddasataranti tattha vavatthānaṃ natthī”tiādinā vavatthānasambhavo netabbo, tenevāha “tathā duddasāva…pe… veditabba”nti.

Here is the application: Although the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is profound in relation to the lower and lower knowledge of trainees and the knowledge of ordinary people, it is not so profound in relation to the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. Therefore, it cannot be determined as 'profound only.' Similarly, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha is profound in relation to the aforementioned knowledge, but it is not so profound in relation to omniscient knowledge. Hence, it cannot be determined as 'profound only.' Therefore, in that case, a determination is not obtained. However, for the qualities of omniscient knowledge, unlike those of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and so on, because of the absence of a state of not being profound in relation to anything, the determination that 'they are profound only' is obtained. And just as a determination is shown here, so too is the knowledge of a disciple's perfection difficult to see. By the reasoning 'But the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha is more difficult to see than that; in that case there is no determination,' and so on, the possibility of determination should be understood. For that very reason, he said, 'Likewise, they are difficult to see...and should be understood.'

Pucchāvissajjanantipi pāṭho, tassā pucchāya vissajjananti attho. Etanti yathāvuttaṃ vissajjanavacanaṃ. Evanti iminā diṭṭhīnaṃ vibhajanākārena. Etthāyamadhippāyo – bhavatu tāva niravasesabuddhaguṇavibhāvanupāyabhāvato sabbaññutaññāṇameva ekampi puthunissayārammaṇañāṇakiccasiddhiyā “atthi bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.18) bahuvacanena uddiṭṭhaṃ, tassa pana vissajjanaṃ saccapaccayākārādivisayavisesavasena anaññasādhāraṇena vibhajananayena anārabhitvā sanissayānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ vibhajananayena kasmā āraddhanti? Tattha yathā saccapaccayākārādīnaṃ vibhajanaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasseva visayo, evaṃ niravasesadiṭṭhigatavibhajanampīti dassetuṃ “buddhānañhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ, tattha ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hotīti desetabbassa atthassa anekavidhatāya, dubbiññeyyatāya ca nānānayehi pavattamānaṃ desanāgajjitaṃ mahantaṃ vipulaṃ, bahuppabhedañca hoti[V 1.0339]. Ñāṇaṃ anupavisatīti tato eva ca desanāñāṇaṃ desetabbadhamme vibhāgaso kurumānaṃ anupavisati, te anupavisitvā ṭhitaṃ viya hotīti attho.

The reading is also 'questions and answers,' meaning the answer to that question. 'This' (etaṃ) refers to the aforementioned word 'answer.' 'Thus' (evaṃ) indicates this manner of classifying views. Here, the intention is this: Let it be that omniscient knowledge itself, even though single, is designated by the plural form ('There are, bhikkhus, other dhammas,' etc.) because it is a means of manifesting all the Buddha's qualities without remainder, and because it accomplishes the function of knowledge with diverse supports and objects. But why is its answer not begun by analyzing with the exclusive method concerning the specific domains of truths, conditional modes, etc., but by analyzing views together with their supports? Here, just as the analysis of truths, conditional modes, etc., is exclusive and the domain of omniscient knowledge only, so too is the analysis of all views without remainder. To show this, 'For the Buddhas,' etc., is begun. In that context, 'bases' (ṭhānāni) means reasons. The 'great roar' (gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti) means that because the meaning to be taught is manifold and difficult to comprehend, the roar of the teaching, proceeding in various ways, is great, vast, and of many kinds. The 'knowledge enters' (ñāṇaṃ anupavisati) means that from that very reason, the knowledge of teaching, making distinctions in the dhammas to be taught, enters into them. The meaning is that it is as if it remains having entered into them.

Buddhañāṇassa mahantabhāvo paññāyatīti evaṃvidhassa nāma dhammassa desakaṃ, paṭivedhakañcāti buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇassa, paṭivedhañāṇassa ca uḷārabhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Desanā gambhīrā hotīti sabhāvena gambhīrānaṃ tesaṃ catubbidhānampi desanā desetabbavasena gambhīrāva hoti, sā pana buddhānaṃ desanā sabbattha, sabbadā ca yānattayamukhenevāti vuttaṃ “tilakkhaṇāhatā suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttā”ti, tīhi lakkhaṇehi āhatā, attattaniyato suññabhāvapaṭisaññuttā cāti attho.
