Ettha ca kiñcāpi [M 1.0386] “sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattī”ti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5; netti. 15) vacanato sabbāpi bhagavato desanā ñāṇarahitā nāma natthi, samasamaparakkamanavasena sīhasamānavuttitāya ca sabbattha samānussāhappavatti, desetabbadhammavasena pana desanā visesato ñāṇena anupaviṭṭhā, gambhīratarā ca hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The greatness of the Buddha's knowledge is evident: thus, the exalted nature of the Buddhas' teaching-knowledge and penetrative-knowledge, as the expounder and penetrator of such a Dhamma, becomes manifest. The teaching is profound: among those four kinds of profundity which are profound by nature, the teaching is invariably profound in terms of what is to be taught. Moreover, that teaching of the Buddhas is always and everywhere only through the entrance of the three vehicles, as it is said: 'Struck by the three characteristics, connected with emptiness.' This means it is struck by the three characteristics and connected with the state of being void of self and what belongs to a self. Here, although it is stated, 'All verbal actions of the Blessed One, the Buddha, are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge,' none of the Blessed One's teachings are devoid of knowledge; and although due to the equal exertion and lion-like conduct, there is a consistent application of effort everywhere, it should be understood that the teaching, in terms of the Dhamma to be taught, is especially entered by knowledge and becomes more profound.

Kathaṃ pana vinayapaṇṇattiṃ patvā desanā tilakkhaṇāhatā, suññatāpaṭisaññuttā ca hoti, nanu tattha vinayapaṇṇattimattamevāti? Na tattha vinayapaṇṇattimattameva. Tatthāpi hi sannisinnaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ pavattamānā desanā saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatādivibhāvinī sabbadhammānaṃ attattaniyatā, suññabhāvappakāsinī ca hoti, tenevāha “anekapariyāyena dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā”tiādi. Vinayapaññattinti vinayassa paññāpanaṃ. Ñña-kārassa pana ṇṇa-kāre kate vinayapaṇṇattintipi pāṭho. Bhūmantaranti dhammānaṃ avatthāvisesañca ṭhānavisesañca. Bhavanti dhammā etthāti bhūmīti hi avatthāviseso, ṭhānañca vuccati. Tattha avatthāviseso satiādidhammānaṃ satipaṭṭhānindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgādibhedo “vaccho, dammo, balībaddo”ti ādayo viya. Ṭhānaviseso kāmāvacarādibhedo. Paccayākāra-saddassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Samayantaranti diṭṭhivisesaṃ, nānāvihitā diṭṭhiyoti attho, aññasamayaṃ vā, bāhirakasamayanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vinayapaññattiṃ patvā mahantaṃ gajjitaṃ hotītiādinā sambandho. Tasmāti yasmā gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ…pe… paṭisaṃyuttā, tasmā. Chejjagāminīti atekicchagāminī.

But how, when it comes to a disciplinary regulation, is the teaching struck by the three characteristics and connected with emptiness? Is it not merely a disciplinary regulation there? No, it is not merely a disciplinary regulation there. For there too, the teaching that proceeds in accordance with the disposition of the assembled company reveals the impermanence and so forth of conditioned formations, and manifests that all phenomena are void of self and what belongs to a self. Hence it is said, 'Having given a Dhamma talk in many ways,' etc. 'Vinayapaññatti' means the laying down of the Vinaya. However, when the syllable 'ñña' is changed to 'ṇṇa,' the reading is also 'vinayapaṇṇatti.' 'Bhūmantara' refers to the particular states and locations of phenomena. For because 'phenomena exist here' (bhavanti dhammā ettha), it is called 'bhūmi'; this refers to a particular state and a location. There, the particular state is the distinction of phenomena such as mindfulness, etc., divided into foundations of mindfulness, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors, like 'calf, bullock to be tamed, draught ox,' etc. The particular location is the distinction into the sense-sphere realm, etc. The meaning of the word 'paccayākāra' has already been stated above. 'Samayantara' means a specific view—that is, various kinds of views—or another doctrine, meaning an external doctrine. The connection is with 'having come to a disciplinary regulation, a great roar occurs,' etc. Therefore: because the roar is great... connected with emptiness, therefore. 'Chejjagāminī' means incurable.

Evaṃ otiṇṇe vatthusminti yathāvuttanayena lahukagarukādivasena tadanurūpe vatthumhi otarante. Yaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ nāma atthi, tatthāti sambandho. Thāmoti ñāṇasāmatthiyaṃ. Balanti akampanasaṅkhāto vīrabhāvo. Thāmo balanti vā sāmatthiyavacanameva paccavekkhaṇādesanāñāṇavasena [V 1.0340] yojetabbaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇāñāṇapubbaṅgamañhi desanāñāṇaṃ. Esāti sikkhāpadapaññāpanameva vuccamānapadamapekkhitvā pulliṅgena niddisati, eso sikkhāpadapaññāpanasaṅkhāto visayo aññesaṃ avisayoti attho. Itīti tathāvisayāvisayabhāvassa hetubhāvena paṭiniddesavacanaṃ[M 1.0387], nidassanattho vā iti-saddo, tena “idaṃ lahukaṃ, idaṃ garuka”ntiādinayaṃ niddisati. Evamaparatthāpi yathāsambhavaṃ.

When the matter is thus entered upon (`Evaṃ otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ`): when one enters into the subject matter that is appropriate to that, by way of what is light, grave, and so on, in accordance with the method stated. The connection is with `tattha` ('therein'), which refers to that which is called the laying down of a training rule. 'Strength' (`thāmo`) means the capability of knowledge. 'Power' (`balaṃ`) means the state of being courageous, which is called unshakability. Alternatively, 'strength' and 'power' are simply words for capability and should be connected by way of reviewing-knowledge and teaching-knowledge. For teaching-knowledge is indeed preceded by reviewing-knowledge. 'This' (`eso`): this refers to the laying down of a training rule itself; anticipating the word about to be stated, it indicates it in the masculine gender. The meaning is: this subject, designated as the laying down of a training rule, is not a subject for others. 'Thus' (`iti`): this is a word that points back, being the reason for the state of being a subject or non-subject in that way. Alternatively, the word `iti` has the meaning of an example; by it, the method such as, 'This is light, this is grave,' is indicated. Similarly in other places, as is appropriate.

Yadipi kāyānupassanādivasena satipaṭṭhānādayo suttantapiṭake (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107) vibhattā, tathāpi suttantabhājanīyādivasena abhidhammeyeva te visesato vibhattāti āha “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā…pe… abhidhammapiṭakaṃ vibhajitvā”ti. Tattha satta phassāti sattaviññāṇadhātusampayogavasena vuttaṃ. Tathā “satta vedanā”tiādipi. Lokuttarā dhammā nāmāti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena vuttāvasesaṃ abhidhamme āgataṃ dhammānaṃ vibhajitabbākāraṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānāni etthāti catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānanti bāhiratthasamāso. “Abhidhammapiṭaka”nti etassa hi idaṃ visesanaṃ. Ettha ca paccayanayaṃ aggahetvā dhammavaseneva samantapaṭṭhānassa catuvīsatividhatā vuttā. Yathāha –

Although the foundations of mindfulness and so on are analyzed in the Suttanta Piṭaka by way of the contemplation of the body, etc., nevertheless, they are analyzed in a special way only in the Abhidhamma by way of the Suttanta analysis method and so on. Thus, the Teacher said: 'These four foundations of mindfulness... having analyzed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.' Therein, 'seven contacts' is stated by way of association with the seven consciousness-elements. Similarly, 'seven feelings,' and so on. In the phrase `Lokuttarā dhammā nāma`, the word `iti` has the meaning of 'and so on' (`ādi`), or alternatively, the meaning of 'manner' (`pakāra`). By it, he includes the manner of analyzing the remaining dhammas that are found in the Abhidhamma, which were not mentioned. The phrase `catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhāna` is an external compound meaning 'that in which there are twenty-four comprehensive relations'. Indeed, this is a qualifier for 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka'. And here, without taking up the method of conditions, the twenty-fourfold nature of the Comprehensive Relations is stated solely by way of the dhammas. As it is said:

“Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā…pe…

Cha paccanīyamhi…pe… anulomapaccanīyamhi…pe…

Paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti. [paṭṭhā. 1.1.41(ka), 44(kha), 48(ga), 52(gha)];

The desirable Triplet Paṭṭhāna and the supreme Couplet, the Couplet-Triplet and the Triplet-Couplet, the Triplet-Triplet and the Couplet-Couplet—these six methods in the Concurrence are very profound... six in the Opposition... in the Concurrence-Opposition... in the Opposition-Concurrence, the methods are very profound.

Evaṃ dhammavasena catuvīsatibhedesu tikapaṭṭhānādīsu ekekaṃ paccayanayena anulomādivasena catubbidhaṃ hotīti channavutisamantapaṭṭhānāni. Tattha pana dhammānulome tikapaṭṭhāne kusalattike paṭiccavāre paccayānulome hetumūlake hetupaccayavasena ekūnapaññāsa pucchānayā satta vissajjananayātiādinā dassiyamānā anantabhedā nayāti āha “anantanaya”nti.

Thus, by way of the dhammas, among the twenty-four divisions such as the Triplet Paṭṭhāna, each one becomes fourfold by the method of conditions, by way of Concurrence and so on; thus there are ninety-six Comprehensive Relations. Furthermore, therein, in the Concurrence of Dhammas, in the Triplet Paṭṭhāna, in the Wholesome Triplet, in the Chapter on Dependence, in the Concurrence of Conditions, in the Root-group, by way of the root-condition, there are forty-nine methods of questioning and seven methods of answering. By this and other ways, the methods being shown are of infinite divisions. Therefore, the commentator said it is 'of infinite methods'.

Navahākārehīti uppādādīhi navahi paccayākārehi. Taṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “uppādo hutvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha uppajjati etasmā phalanti uppādo, phaluppattiyā kāraṇabhāvo. Sati [V 1.0341] ca avijjāya saṅkhārā uppajjanti, nāsati. Tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo hutvā paccayo hoti, tathā pavattati dharati etasmiṃ phalanti pavattaṃ. Nimīyati phalametasminti nimittaṃ. [M 1.0388] (Nidadāti phalaṃ attano paccayuppannaṃ etenāti nidānaṃ.) (Etthantare aṭṭhakathāya na sameti) āyūhati phalaṃ attano paccayuppannuppattiyā ghaṭeti etenāti āyūhanaṃ. Saṃyujjati phalaṃ attano paccayuppannena etasminti saṃyogo. Yattha sayaṃ uppajjati, taṃ palibuddhati phalametenāti palibodho. Paccayantarasamavāye sati phalamudayati etenāti samudayo. Hinoti kāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchatīti hetu. Avijjāya hi sati saṅkhārā pavattanti, dharanti ca, te avijjāya sati attano phalaṃ (nidadanti) (paṭi. ma. 1.45; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.28 passitabbaṃ) bhavādīsu khipanti, āyūhanti attano phaluppattiyā ghaṭenti, attano phalena saṃyujjanti, yasmiṃ santāne sayaṃ uppannā taṃ palibuddhanti, paccayantarasamavāye udayanti uppajjanti, hinoti ca saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchati, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ pavattaṃ hutvā…pe… paccayo hutvā paccayo hoti. Evaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvūpagamanavisesā uppādādayo veditabbā. Saṅkhārādīnaṃ viññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

'By nine modes' means by the nine modes of conditioning, such as arising. To show this in its own nature, 'by being an arising,' etc., was said. Therein, 'arising' (`uppādo`) is so called because from this the fruit arises; it is the state of being a cause for the arising of the fruit. When ignorance exists, formations arise; when it does not, they do not. Therefore, ignorance, by being an arising for the formations, is a condition. Similarly, 'continuance' (`pavattaṃ`) is so called because in this the fruit continues and is maintained. 'Sign' (`nimittaṃ`) is so called because in this the fruit is marked. 'Source' (`nidānaṃ`) is so called because by this it gives its fruit, the conditioned resultant. (Here, it does not agree with the commentary). 'Accumulation' (`āyūhanaṃ`) is so called because by this it strives for, endeavors for, the arising of its fruit, the conditioned resultant. 'Bond' (`saṃyogo`) is so called because in this the fruit is conjoined with its conditioned resultant. 'Obstruction' (`palibodho`) is so called because by this the fruit obstructs that wherein it itself arises. 'Origin' (`samudayo`) is so called because by this, when there is a conjunction of other conditions, the fruit arises. 'Cause' (`hetu`) is so called because it goes to the state of being a cause. For when ignorance exists, formations continue and are maintained; when ignorance exists, they give their fruit (see Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.45; Dīghanikāya-ṭīkā 1.28), cast it into states of being and so on, strive for and endeavor for the arising of their own fruit, are conjoined with their own fruit, obstruct that continuum in which they themselves have arisen, arise when there is a conjunction of other conditions, and go to the state of being a cause for formations. Therefore, ignorance, by being a continuance for the formations... and so on... by being a condition, is a condition. In this way, the particular ways in which ignorance approaches the state of being a cause for formations—arising and so on—should be understood. This same method applies to formations in relation to consciousness, and so on.

Tamatthaṃ paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷiyā sādhentena “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tiṭṭhati etenāti ṭhiti, paccayo, uppādo eva ṭhiti uppādaṭṭhiti. Evaṃ sesesupi. Yasmā pana “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vuttattā āsavāva avijjāya paccayo, tasmā vuttaṃ “ubhopete dhammā “paccayasamuppannā”ti, avijjā ca saṅkhārā ca ubhopete dhammā paccayato eva samuppannā, na vinā paccayenāti attho. Paccayapariggahe paññāti saṅkhārānaṃ, avijjāya ca uppādādike paccayākāre paricchinditvā gahaṇavasena pavattā paññā. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti paccayuppannadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvato dhammaṭṭhitisaṅkhāte paṭiccasamuppāde ñāṇaṃ. “Dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādā”ti vacanato hi dvādasa paccayā eva paṭiccasamuppādo. Ayañca nayo na paccuppanne eva, atha kho atītānāgatesupi, na ca avijjāya eva saṅkhāresu, atha kho saṅkhārādīnaṃ viññāṇādīsupi labbhatīti paripuṇṇaṃ katvā paccayākārassa vibhattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “atītampi addhāna”ntiādi pāḷimāhari. Paṭṭhāne (paṭṭhā. 1.1) pana dassitā hetādipaccayāevettha uppādādipaccayākārehi gahitāti tepi yathāsambhavaṃ nīharitvā yojetabbā. Ativitthārabhayena pana na yojayimha, atthikehi ca visuddhimaggādito (visuddhi. 2.594) gahetabbā.

To establish that meaning, the commentator, by means of the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, said, 'As he said,' and so on. Therein, the meaning of the words should be understood in the following way: 'It stands (tiṭṭhati) by this (etena)'; therefore, it is 'standing' (ṭhiti), which is a condition. Arising itself is the cause of standing; hence, 'arising-standing' (uppādaṭṭhiti). Thus it is also in the remaining cases. Furthermore, because it was said, 'From the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance,' the taints themselves are the condition for ignorance. Therefore, it was said, 'Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen.' The meaning is that both ignorance and formations are arisen solely from a condition, not without a condition. 'Wisdom in the comprehension of conditions' is the wisdom that arises by way of grasping after having demarcated the conditioning modes, such as arising, of formations and of ignorance. 'Knowledge of the stability of phenomena' is the knowledge in dependent origination—called 'the stability of phenomena' because it is the state of being a condition for conditionally arisen phenomena. For, according to the saying, 'The twelve dependent originations,' the twelve conditions themselves are dependent origination. And this method applies not only in the present but also in the past and future; and it is obtained not only for formations in relation to ignorance but also for consciousness and so on in relation to formations and so on. Thus, to show in full the analyzed state of the conditional mode, the commentator cited the Pāḷi text beginning 'The past period,' and so on. Moreover, the conditions such as root-condition, etc., shown in the Paṭṭhāna, are included here by the conditioning modes such as arising. Therefore, they too should be extracted and applied as is appropriate. However, for fear of excessive elaboration, we have not applied them. Those who are interested should take them from the Visuddhimagga, and so on.

Tassa [M 1.0389] tassa dhammassāti saṅkhārādipaccayuppannadhammassa. Tathā tathā paccayabhāvenāti uppādādihetādipaccayasattiyā[V 1.0342]. Kammakilesavipākavasena tīṇi vaṭṭāni yassāti tivaṭṭaṃ. Atītapaccuppannānāgatavasena tayo addhā kālā etassāti tiyaddhaṃ. Hetuphalaphalahetuhetuphalavasena tayo sandhayo etassāti tisandhi. Saṅkhippanti ettha avijjādayo, viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepā, hetu, vipāko ca. Atha vā hetu vipākoti saṅkhippantīti saṅkhepā. Avijjādayo, viññāṇādayo ca koṭṭhāsapariyāyo vā saṅkhepasaddo. Atītahetusaṅkhepādivasena cattāro saṅkhepā yassāti catusaṅkhepaṃ. Sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ saṅkhepe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā, atītahetuādīnaṃ pakārā. Te saṅkhepe pañca pañca katvā vīsati ākārā etassāti vīsatākāraṃ.

'Of each respective phenomenon' means: of the conditionally arisen phenomenon, such as formations, and so on. 'In each respective way by being a condition' means: by the power of the conditions, such as arising, etc., and root-condition, etc. Because it has three cycles by way of the cycle of kamma, the cycle of defilements, and the cycle of results, it is 'the threefold cycle.' Because it has three periods by way of the past, present, and future, it is 'the threefold time.' Because it has three links by way of cause-and-result, result-and-cause, and cause-and-result, it is 'the threefold link.' 'Summaries' (saṅkhepā) are so called because herein ignorance, etc., and consciousness, etc., are summarized; this refers to cause and result. Alternatively, because they—that is, ignorance, etc., and consciousness, etc.—are summarized as 'cause' and 'result,' they are 'summaries.' Or, the word 'saṅkhepa' is a synonym for 'koṭṭhāsa' (section). Because it has four sections by way of the section of past cause, etc., it is 'the fourfold section.' Though not stated in their own form, in each respective section they are shown by the taking up of ignorance, formations, etc.; therefore, they are called 'modes' (ākārā), which are the divisions of past cause, etc. Because it has twenty modes, by taking those sections as five each, it is 'that with twenty modes.'

Khattiyādibhedena anekabhedabhinnāpi sassatavādino jātisatasahassānussaraṇādikassa abhinivesahetuno vasena cattārova honti, na tato uddhaṃ, adho vāti sassatavādīnaṃ parimāṇaparicchedassa anaññavisayataṃ dassetuṃ “cattāro janā”tiādimāha. Esa nayo itaresupi. Tattha cattāro janāti cattāro janasamūhāti attho gahetabbo tesu ekekassāpi anekappabhedato. Teti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavādino. Idaṃ nissāyāti idappaccayatāya sammā aggahaṇaṃ. Tatthāpi ca hetuphalabhāvena sambandhānaṃ dhammānaṃ santatighanassa abheditattā paramatthato vijjamānampi bhedanibandhanaṃ nānattanayaṃ anupadhāretvā gahitaṃ ekattaggahaṇaṃ nissāya. Idaṃ gaṇhantīti idaṃ sassataggahaṇaṃ abhinivissa voharanti, iminā nayena ekaccasassatavādādayopi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā vattabbā. Bhinditvāti “ātappamanvāyā”tiādinā vibhajitvā, “tayidaṃ bhikkhave tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.36) vā vidhamitvā. Nijjaṭanti anonaddhaṃ. Nigumbanti anāvuṭaṃ. Apica veḷuādīnaṃ heṭṭhupariyasaṃsibbanaṭṭhena jaṭā. Kusādīnaṃ ovaraṇaṭṭhena gumbo. Tassadisatāya diṭṭhigatānaṃ byākulā pākaṭatā “jaṭā, gumbo”ti ca vuccati, diṭṭhijaṭāvijaṭanena, diṭṭhigumbavivaraṇena ca nijjaṭaṃ nigumbaṃ katvāti attho.

Although the eternalists are divided into many kinds, such as khattiyas, etc., by the power of the cause for adherence, such as the recollection of a hundred thousand births, they are only four. To show that the determination of the limit of the eternalists—that there are none above or below that number—is not the domain of anyone else but the Buddha, the commentator said, 'four persons,' and so on. This method also applies to the others. Therein, for the phrase 'four persons,' the meaning 'four groups of persons' should be taken, because each one of them has many different kinds of views. 'They' refers to the proponents of the sixty-two views. 'Depending on this' means: not grasping correctly due to this-conditionality. And in that case, it is due to depending on the grasping of oneness—which is grasped without considering the method of diversity founded on division that exists in an ultimate sense—because of the undividedness of the dense continuity of phenomena connected by way of cause and effect. 'They grasp this' means: they speak, adhering to this grasping of eternalism. By this method, the partial-eternalists, and so on, should also be explained by applying it as is appropriate. 'Having broken' means: having analyzed it with the words 'by undertaking ardour,' and so on, or having dispelled it with the words 'This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,' and so on. 'Untangled' (nijjaṭaṃ) means without a web. 'Uncovered' (nigumbaṃ) means without obstruction. Moreover, due to the meaning of being interwoven below and above, bamboo, etc., are called a 'tangle' (jaṭā). Due to the meaning of covering, kusa grass, etc., is called a 'thicket' (gumbo). Due to similarity with that, the confused and manifest state of the holdings of views is called a 'tangle' and a 'thicket.' The meaning is: having made it untangled and uncovered by disentangling the tangle of views and by opening up the thicket of views.

“Tasmā”tiādinā [M 1.0390] buddhaguṇe ārabbha desanāya samuṭṭhitattā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ uddisitvā desanākusalo bhagavā samayantaraṃ viggahaṇavasena sabbaññutaññāṇameva vissajjetīti dasseti.

With the words 'Therefore,' and so on, the commentator shows that because the discourse arose in connection with the qualities of the Buddha, the Blessed One, skilled in discourse, having indicated omniscient knowledge, answers by way of a specific analysis of another doctrine, using that very omniscient knowledge.

29. Atthi pariyāyo santi-saddo, so ca saṃvijjantipariyāyo, saṃvijjamānatā ca ñāṇena upalabbhamānatāti āha “santī”tiādi. Saṃvijjamānaparidīpanena pana “santī”ti iminā padena tesaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vijjamānatāya avicchinnataṃ, tato ca nesaṃ micchāgāhato sithilakaraṇavivecanehi [V 1.0343] attano desanāya kiccakāritaṃ, avitathatañca dīpeti dhammarājā. Atthīti ca santipadena samānattho puthuvacanavisayo eko nipāto “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; 3.154; saṃ. ni. 4.127) viya. Ālapanavacananti buddhālapanavacanaṃ. Bhagavāyeva hi “bhikkhave, bhikkhavo”ti ca ālapati, na sāvakā. Sāvakā pana “āvuso, āyasmā”tiādisambandhaneneva. “Eke”ti vutte ekacceti attho eva saṅkhyāvācakassa eka-saddassa niyatekavacanattā, na samitabahitapāpatāya samaṇabrāhmaṇāti āha “pabbajjūpagatabhāvenā”tiādi. Tathā vā hontu, aññathā vā, sammutimatteneva idhādhippetāti dasseti “lokenā”tiādinā. Sassatādivasena pubbantaṃ kappentīti pubbantakappikā. Yasmā pana tesaṃ pubbantaṃ purimasiddhehi taṇhādiṭṭhikappehi kappetvā āsevanabalavatāya, vicitravuttitāya ca vikappetvā aparabhāgasiddhehi abhinivesabhūtehi taṇhādiṭṭhigāhehi gaṇhanti abhinivisanti parāmasanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pubbantaṃ kappetvā vikappetvā gaṇhantī”ti. Purimabhāgapacchimabhāgasiddhānaṃ vā taṇhāupādānānaṃ vasena yathākkamaṃ kappanagahaṇāni veditabbāni. Taṇhāpaccayā hi upādānaṃ sambhavati. Pahutapasaṃsānindātisayasaṃsagganiccayogādivisayesu idha niccayogavasena vijjamānattho sambhavatīti vuttaṃ “pubbanta kappo vā”tiādi vuttañca –

29. The word 'santi' is a synonym for 'atthi', and that in turn is a synonym for 'saṃvijjanti'. The state of being present is the state of being obtainable by knowledge; therefore, the Teacher said, "santi," etc. Furthermore, by this word "santi," which clarifies the state of being present, the King of Dhamma reveals the uninterruptedness of those with wrong views due to their existence. Moreover, through the loosening and dispelling of their wrong grasp, He reveals the efficacy of His own teaching and its infallibility. And 'atthi' is a single particle that has the same meaning as the word 'santi' and has the sphere of the plural, as in "atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā" ("There are hairs in this body"), etc. "The word of address" means the Buddha's word of address. Indeed, only the Blessed One addresses others as "bhikkhave" and "bhikkhavo," not the disciples. The disciples, however, address others only with relational terms such as "āvuso," "āyasmā," etc. When "eke" is said, the meaning should be understood only as "ekacce" (some), because the numeral-denoting word 'eka' is restricted to the singular. They are not called samaṇas and brāhmaṇas because of having pacified and expelled evil; therefore, the Teacher said, "due to the state of having gone forth," etc. Whether they are so or otherwise, they are intended here by mere convention; this meaning he shows by "lokena," etc. They speculate on the past by way of eternalism, etc., thus they are 'pubbantakappikā' (speculators on the past). Furthermore, because they, having speculated on the past with speculations of craving and views established in a former part, and having variously speculated due to the strength of habituation and the diversity of conduct, grasp, adhere to, and misapprehend with grasps of craving and views that have become adherences established in a later part, it was therefore said, "having speculated on the past and variously speculated, they grasp." Alternatively, the speculating and grasping should be understood sequentially by way of craving and clinging established in the former and latter parts respectively. For clinging arises with craving as its condition. Among the spheres of abundance, praise, blame, excess, association, constant application, etc., here the meaning of 'being present' is possible by way of constant application. Therefore, it was said, "or the speculation on the past," etc. And it has been said:

“Pahute ca pasaṃsāyaṃ, nindāyañcātisayane;

Niccayoge ca saṃsagge, hontime mantuādayo”ti.

These suffixes, mantu and so forth, occur in the sense of abundance and praise, in blame and excess, and in constant application and association.

Koṭṭhāsesūti [M 1.0391] ettha koṭṭhāsādīsūti attho veditabbo ādi-saddalopena, nidassananayena ca vuttattā. Padapūraṇasamīpaummaggādīsupi hi anta-saddo dissati. Tathā hi “iṅgha tāva suttante vā gāthāyo vā abhidhammaṃ vā pariyāpuṇassu (pāci. 442), suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā”tiādīsu (pāci. 1221) ca padapūraṇe anta-saddo vattati, “gāmantasenāsana”ntiādīsu (visuddhi. 1.31) samīpe, “kāmasukhallikānuyogo eko anto, atthīti kho kaccāna ayameko anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.258; saṃ. ni. 2.110) ca ummaggeti.

Here, in "koṭṭhāsesu," the meaning should be understood as "in parts, etc.," because it is stated with the elision of the word 'ādi' and by way of example. Indeed, the word 'anta' is also seen in the sense of an expletive, proximity, a wrong path, etc. For instance, in "Come now, first learn the Suttas, or the verses, or the Abhidhamma," and "having made an opportunity in the Sutta," the word 'anta' is used as an expletive. In "gāmantasenāsana" ("a dwelling near a village"), etc., it is used in the sense of proximity. And in "The practice of indulgence in sensual pleasure is one 'anta' (extreme)," and "Indeed, Kaccāna, 'it exists' is one 'anta' (extreme)," etc., it is used in the sense of a wrong path.

Antapūroti mahāantaantaguṇehi pūro. “Sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.304) majjhimanikāye mahāhatthipadopamasuttantapāḷi. Tattha sāti tejodhātu. Haritantanti haritatiṇarukkhamariyādaṃ[V 1.0344]. Panthantanti maggamariyādaṃ. Āgamma anāhārā nibbāyatīti seso. “Antamidaṃ bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolya”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.80; itivu. 91) piṇḍiyālopasuttantapāḷi. Tattha piṇḍaṃ ulati gavesatīti piṇḍolo, piṇḍācāriko, tassa bhāvo piṇḍolyaṃ, piṇḍacaraṇena jīvikatāti attho. Esevāti sabbapaccayasaṅkhayabhūto nibbānadhammo eva, tenāha “sabba…pe… vuccatī”ti. Etena sabbapaccayasaṅkhayanato asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ saṅkhatabhūtassa vaṭṭadukkhassa parabhāgaṃ pariyosānabhūtaṃ, tasmā ettha parabhāgova attho yuttoti dasseti. Sakkāyoti sakkāyagāho.

'Antapūro' means filled with the large and small intestines. The Pāḷi "Sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā" is from the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya. Therein, 'sā' refers to the fire element. 'Haritantaṃ' means the boundary of green grass and trees. 'Panthantaṃ' means the boundary of the path. The remainder should be understood as: "having reached it, without fuel, it is extinguished." The Pāḷi "Antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ" ("This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods, that is, the alms-round") is from the Piṇḍiyālopasutta. Therein, one who seeks (`ulati gavesati`) alms (`piṇḍaṃ`) is a 'piṇḍola', an alms-goer; his state is 'piṇḍolyaṃ', meaning livelihood by going for alms. 'Eseva' means only the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the exhaustion of all conditions; therefore he said, "all... is called." By this, he shows that because the unconditioned Nibbāna, due to the exhaustion of all conditions, is the other shore and the end of the conditioned suffering of the round, the meaning 'the other shore' is therefore suitable here. 'Sakkāya' means the grasp of personality-belief.

Kappoti leso. Kappakatenāti tiṇṇaṃ dubbaṇṇakaraṇānaṃ aññataradubbaṇṇakatena. Ādi-saddena cettha kappa-saddo mahākappasamantabhāvakilesakāmavitakkakālapaññattisadisabhāvādīsupi vattatīti dasseti. Tathā hesa “cattārimāni bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.156) mahākappe vattati, “kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāve, “saṅkappo kāmo rāgo kāmo saṅkapparāgo kāmo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 1; cūḷani. 8) kilesakāme, “takko vitakko saṅkappo”tiādīsu vitakke, “yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kāle[M 1.0392], “iccāyasmā kappo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 1018) paññattiyaṃ, “satthukappena vata kira bho sāvakena saddhiṃ mantayamānā na jānimhā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.260) sadisabhāveti.

'Kappo' means a semblance. 'Kappakatena' means by making one of the three kinds of disfigurement. He shows that by the word 'ādi', the word 'kappa' is also used here in the senses of a great aeon, entirety, defilement-lust, thought, time, designation, similarity, etc. Thus, it is used in the sense of a great aeon in "These four, monks, are the incalculables of an aeon," etc.; in the sense of entirety in "having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana," etc.; in the sense of defilement-lust in "Intention is lust, passion is lust, intentional passion is lust," etc.; in the sense of thought in "reasoning, thought, intention," etc.; in the sense of time in "where I dwell constantly," etc.; in the sense of designation in "thus the Venerable Kappa," etc.; and in the sense of similarity in "Indeed, sir, while conversing with a disciple similar to the Teacher, we did not know," etc.

Taṇhādiṭṭhīsu pavattiṃ mahāniddesapāḷiyā (mahāni. 28) sādhento “vuttampi ceta”ntiādimāha. Tattha uddānatoti saṅkhepato. “Tasmā”tiādi yathāvuttāya atthavaṇṇanāya guṇavacanaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhivasenāti upanissayasahajātabhūtāya abhinandanasaṅkhātāya taṇhāya ceva sassatādiākārena abhinivisantassa micchāgāhassa ca vasena. Pubbe nivutthadhammavisayāya kappanāya idha adhippetattā atītakālavācakoyeva pubba-saddo, na pana “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”tiādīsu viya padhānādivācako, rūpādikhandhavinimuttassa kappanavatthuno abhāvā anta-saddo ca koṭṭhāsavācako, na pana abbhantarādivācakoti dassetuṃ “atītaṃ khandhakoṭṭhāsa”nti vuttaṃ. Kappetvāti ca tasmiṃ pubbante taṇhāyanābhinivesanānaṃ samatthanaṃ pariniṭṭhāpanamāha. Ṭhitāti tassā laddhiyā avijahanaṃ, pubbantameva anugatā diṭṭhi tesamatthīti yojanā. Atthitā, anugatatā ca nāma punappunaṃ pavattiyāti dasseti “punappunaṃ uppajjanavasenā”ti iminā. “Te eva”ntiādinā “pubbantaṃ ārabbhā”tiādipāḷiyā atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇeti. Tattha ārabbhāti ālambitvā. Visayo hi tassā diṭṭhiyā pubbanto. Visayabhāvato hesa tassā āgamanaṭṭhānaṃ[V 1.0345], ārammaṇapaccayo cāti vuttaṃ “āgamma paṭiccā”ti. Tadetaṃ aññesaṃ patiṭṭhāpanadassananti āha “aññampi janaṃ diṭṭhigatitaṃ karontā”ti.

To establish the occurrence of craving and views by means of the Mahāniddesa-pāḷi, the commentator said, 'vuttampi cetaṃ,' and so on. Therein, `uddānato` means concisely. `Tasmā,` and so on, is a statement commending the previously stated explanation. `Taṇhādiṭṭhivasena` means by the power of craving—which is a condition of decisive support and conascence, characterized by delight—and by the power of wrong adherence that clings in the manner of eternalism and so on. Because here the speculation is intended to be about phenomena experienced in the past, the word `pubba` refers only to past time, and not to 'primary' or other meanings as in phrases like 'manopubbaṅgamā dhammā'. And because there is no object of speculation separate from the aggregates like form, etc., the word `anta` refers to a portion, not to 'inner' or other meanings. To show this, it is said, 'the past portion of the aggregates.' And `kappetvā` refers to the establishing and completion of craving and adherence in that past-end. `Ṭhitā` means not abandoning that doctrine; the construction is that they have a view that follows only the past-end. 'Existence' and 'following' indeed mean repeated occurrence, as he shows by the phrase 'by the power of repeated arising.' By 'te eva,' and so on, he elaborates on the meaning of the Pāḷi passage 'pubbantaṃ ārabbha,' and so on. Therein, `ārabbha` means 'having taken as object.' Indeed, the past-end is the domain of that view. Because it is its domain, it is the place of its origin and its object-condition—hence, it is said, 'having approached, having been dependent on.' This shows the establishing of others in their views, as stated: 'they also make other people have a fixed view.'

Adhivacanapathānīti [adhivacanapaadāni (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] ruḷhimattena paññattipathāni. Dāsādīsu hi sirivaḍḍhakādisaddā viya vacanamattameva adhikāraṃ katvā pavattiyā tathā paṇṇattiyeva adhivacanaṃ, sā ca vohārassa pathoti. Atha vā adhi-saddo uparibhāge, vuccatīti vacanaṃ. Adhi uparibhāge vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Upādāniyabhūtānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ [upādābhūtarūpādīnaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.29)] upari paññāpiyamānā upādāpaññatti, tasmā paññattidīpakapathānīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Paññattimattañhetaṃ vuccati, yadidaṃ “attā, loko”ti ca, na rūpavedanādayo viya [M 1.0393] paramatthoti. Adhimutti-saddo cettha adhivacana-saddena samānattho “niruttipatho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 107 dukamātikā) viya uttisaddassa vacanapariyāyattā. “Bhūtaṃ attha”ntiādinā pana bhūtasabhāvato atirekaṃ. Tamatidhāvitvā vā muccantīti adhimuttiyo, tāsaṃ pathāni taddīpakattāti atthaṃ dasseti, adhikaṃ vā sassatādikaṃ muccantīti adhimuttiyo. Adhikañhi sassatādiṃ, pakatiādiṃ, dabbādiṃ, jīvādiṃ, kāyādiñca abhūtaṃ atthaṃ sabhāvadhammesu ajjhāropetvā diṭṭhiyo pavattanti.

`Adhivacanapathāni` means paths of designation that are merely conventional. For just as words such as 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' are applied to slaves and others by taking mere speech as the basis for their usage, so too designation itself is `adhivacana`, and it serves as a path for conventional usage. Alternatively, the prefix `adhi-` means 'above,' and `vacana` means 'speech.' Thus, `adhivacana` means 'speech concerning what is above.' It refers to the derivative designation that is designated 'above' the forms and other phenomena that are the basis for clinging. Therefore, it should be understood as 'paths that illuminate designation.' This is called mere designation, such as 'self' or 'world,' and not an ultimate reality like form and feeling. Here, the term `adhimutti` (conviction) is synonymous with the term `adhivacana` (designation), as seen in phrases like 'the path of expression' (`niruttipatho`), because the word `utti` is a synonym for `vacana` (speech). However, by 'bhūtaṃ atthaṃ' (true meaning), etc., he shows the meaning that `adhimuttiyo` (convictions) are so called because they are inclined towards what is in excess of the true nature, or having overrun that true nature; their paths are so called because they illuminate that. Alternatively, `adhimuttiyo` are so called because they are inclined towards what is excessive, such as eternalism, etc. For views arise by superimposing unreal meanings—such as excessive eternalism, etc., primordial nature, etc., substance, etc., a life-principle, etc., or the body, etc.—upon phenomena that have their own intrinsic nature.

30. Abhivadantīti “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti abhinivisitvā vadanti. “Ayameva dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo”tiādinā abhibhavitvāpi vadanti. Abhivadanakiriyāya ajjāpi avicchedabhāvadassanatthaṃ vattamānavacanaṃ katanti ayamettha pāḷivaṇṇanā. Kathetukamyatāya hetubhūtāya pucchitvāti sambandho. Micchā passatīti diṭṭhi, diṭṭhi eva diṭṭhigataṃ “muttagataṃ, (a. ni. 9.11) saṅkhāragata”ntiādīsu (mahāni. 41) viya gata-saddassa tabbhāvavuttito, gantabbābhāvato vā diṭṭhiyā gatamattanti diṭṭhigataṃ. Diṭṭhiyā gahaṇamattameva, natthaññaṃ avagantabbanti attho, diṭṭhipakāro vā diṭṭhigataṃ. Lokiyā hi vidhayuttagatapakārasadde samānatthe icchanti. Ekasmiṃyeva khandhe “attā”ti ca “loko”ti ca gahaṇavisesaṃ upādāya paññāpanaṃ hotīti āha “rūpādīsu aññataraṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gahetvā”ti. Amaraṃ niccaṃ dhuvanti sassatavevacanāni, maraṇābhāvena vā amaraṃ. Uppādābhāvena sabbadāpi atthitāya niccaṃ. Thiraṭṭhena vikārābhāvena dhuvaṃ. “Yathāhā”tiādinā mahāniddesa paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷīhi yathāvuttamatthaṃ vibhāveti. Tattha “rūpaṃ gahetvā”ti pāṭhasesena sambandho. Ayaṃ panattho – “rūpaṃ attato samanupassati. Vedanaṃ, saññaṃ, saṅkhāre, viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti imissā pañcavidhāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā vasena vutto, “rūpavantaṃ attāna”ntiādikāya pana pañcadasavidhāyapi [V 1.0346] tadavasesāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā vasena cattāro khandhe “attā”ti gahetvā tadañño “loko”ti paññapentīti ayampi attho labbhateva. Tathā ekaṃ khandhaṃ “attā”ti gahetvā añño attano upabhogabhūto “loko”ti ca. Sasantatipatite khandhe “attā”ti gahetvā tadañño parasantatipatito “loko”ti ca paññapetīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Etthāha [M 1.0394] – “sassato vādo etesa”nti kasmā heṭṭhā vuttaṃ, nanu tesaṃ attā ca loko ca sassatoti adhippeto, na vādoti? Saccametaṃ, sassatasahacaritatāya pana vādopi sassatoti vutto yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti, sassato iti vādo etesanti vā tattha iti-saddalopo daṭṭhabbo. Sassataṃ vadanti “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti abhinivissa voharantīti sassatavādā tipi yujjati.

30. As for `Abhivadanti`: they speak, having wrongly adhered to the view, 'This alone is true; anything else is vain.' They also speak by overpowering others, saying such things as, 'This alone is the Dhamma; this is not the Dhamma.' The explanation of the Pāḷi herein is this: the present tense is used to show that this act of assertive speech has continued unbroken even to this day. The connection should be made by asking a question prompted by the desire to speak. Because it sees wrongly, it is called a 'view' (diṭṭhi). A view itself is 'that which has gone to a view' (diṭṭhigata), just as in such phrases as `muttagataṃ` and `saṅkhāragataṃ`, because the word `gata` expresses that very state. Or, because there is nothing further to be reached, it is merely that which is reached by a view; hence, it is `diṭṭhigata`. The meaning is that it is merely the grasping of a view, and there is nothing else to be understood. Alternatively, `diṭṭhigata` is a type of view. For worldly scholars desire the words `vidha`, `yutta`, `gata`, and `pakāra` to have similar meanings. Because the designation of 'self' and 'world' arises with regard to a single aggregate based on a particular mode of grasping, the Teacher said, '...having taken one of the aggregates, such as form, as self and as the world.' The terms `amaraṃ` (deathless), `niccaṃ` (permanent), and `dhuvaṃ` (stable) are synonyms for 'eternal' (`sassata`). Alternatively, it is `amaraṃ` due to the absence of death. It is `niccaṃ` due to the absence of arising and its existence at all times. It is `dhuvaṃ` due to the absence of change, in the sense of being firm. By the phrase 'As it is said...' and so on, he clarifies the aforesaid meaning with the Pāḷi of the Mahāniddesa and the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Therein, the connection should be made with the remaining part of the text, '...having taken form...' This, however, is the meaning: it is stated by way of this fivefold personality view: 'One regards form as self. One regards feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as self.' Furthermore, by way of the remaining fifteenfold personality view, such as 'self as possessing form,' this meaning is also obtained: having taken the four aggregates as 'self,' they designate what is other than that as 'world.' Similarly, the meaning should be understood in this way: having taken one aggregate as 'self,' another that is for one's own enjoyment is designated as 'world'; and having taken the aggregates that fall within one's own continuity as 'self,' what is other than that, which falls within the continuity of others, is designated as 'world.' Here, one might say: Why was it stated below, 'Theirs is an eternalist doctrine'? Is it not intended that for them, the self and the world are eternal, not the doctrine? That is true. However, because of its association with eternalism, the doctrine is also called 'eternal' by way of figurative speech, just as in the expression, 'The spears are advancing.' Or, the analysis is: 'For them, there is the doctrine "it is eternal",' and in this case, the elision of the word `iti` should be understood. This verbal analysis is also suitable: they are eternalists because they declare what is eternal and transact, wrongly adhering to the view, 'This alone is true; anything else is vain.'

31. Ātāpanabhāvenāti vibādhanassa bhāvena, vibādhanaṭṭhena vā. Pahānañcettha vibādhanaṃ. Padahanavasenāti samādahanavasena. Samādahanaṃ pana kosajjapakkhe patitumadatvā cittassa ussāhanaṃ. Yathā samādhi visesabhāgiyataṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ vīriyassa bahulīkaraṇaṃ anuyogo. Iti padattayena vīriyameva vuttanti āha “evaṃ tippabhedaṃ vīriya”nti. Yathākkamañhiha tīhi padehi upacārappanācittaparidamanavīriyāni dasseti. Na pamajjati etenāti appamādo, satiyā avippavāso. So pana satipaṭṭhānā cattāro khandhā eva. Sammā upāyena manasi karoti kammaṭṭhānametenāti sammāmanasikāro, so pana ñāṇameva, na ārammaṇavīthijavanapaṭipādakā, tenāha “atthato ñāṇa”nti. Pathamanasikāroti kāraṇamanasikāro. Tadevatthaṃ samattheti “yasmiñhī”tiādinā. Tattha yasmiṃ manasikāreti kammaṭṭhānamanasikaraṇūpāyabhūte ñāṇasaṅkhāte manasikāre. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne”ti iminā saddantarasampayogādinā viya pakaraṇavasenāpi saddo visesavisayoti dīpeti. Vīriyañcāti yathāvuttehi tīhi padehi vuttaṃ tippabhedaṃ vīriyañca. Etthāti “ātappa…pe… manasikāramanvāyā”ti imasmiṃ pāṭhe, sīlavisuddhiyā saddhiṃ catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ adhigamanapaṭipadā idha vattabbā, sā pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.401) vitthārato vuttāti āha “saṅkhepattho”ti. Tathājātikanti tathāsabhāvaṃ, etena cuddasavidhehi cittaparidamanehi rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa paguṇatāpādanena damitataṃ dasseti. Cetaso samādhi cetosamādhi, so pana aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatarūpāvacaracatutthajjhānasseva samādhi. Yathā-saddo “yenā”ti atthe nipātoti āha “yena samādhinā”ti.

31. As for `ātāpanabhāvena`: it means by the state of tormenting, or in the sense of tormenting. Herein, this 'tormenting' means abandonment. As for `padahanavasena`: it means by way of application. Application, furthermore, is the exertion of the mind, not allowing it to fall into the side of laziness. `Anuyoga` (devotion) is the frequent practice of energy so that concentration may attain a state of partaking in distinction. Thus, by these three terms, energy itself is spoken of; therefore, he said, 'Thus, energy is threefold.' For herein, by the three terms, he shows, in sequence, the energies of access, absorption, and mind-taming. Because one is not heedless by means of this, it is `appamāda` (heedfulness); it is non-separation from mindfulness. That, however, is simply the four aggregates which are the foundations of mindfulness. Because one attends to the meditation subject with a proper method by means of this, it is `sammāmanasikāra` (right attention). That, however, is knowledge itself, not the types of attention that produce the object, the cognitive process, or the impulsion. For that reason, he said, 'in meaning, it is knowledge.' `Pathamamanasikāra` (initial attention) means causal attention. He establishes that very meaning with the phrase beginning 'For in which...' Therein, 'in which attention' refers to the attention, reckoned as knowledge, that is the means for attending to the meditation subject. By the phrase 'in this place,' he indicates that, just as through connection with other words, so too by the force of the context, the word has a specific scope. 'And energy' refers to the threefold energy spoken of by the three aforesaid terms. As for `ettha`: in this passage, 'ardor... following upon attention,' the path for the attainment of the four form-sphere jhānas, together with the purification of virtue, should be stated here. But since that has been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga, the commentator said, 'the meaning in brief.' `Tathājātikaṃ` (of such a kind) means of such a nature. By this, he shows the state of being tamed through the production of proficiency in the fourth form-sphere jhāna by means of the fourteen kinds of mind-taming. Concentration of the mind is `cetosamādhi`. That, however, is the concentration of the fourth form-sphere jhāna which is endowed with eight factors. The word `yathā` is a particle that occurs in the sense of `yena` (by which); therefore, the commentator said, 'by which concentration.'

Vijambhanabhūtehi [M 1.0395] lokiyābhiññāsaṅkhātehi jhānānubhāvehi sampannoti jhānānubhāvasampanno. So [V 1.0347] diṭṭhigatiko evaṃ vadatīti vattamānavacanaṃ, tathāvadanassa avicchedabhāvena sabbakālikatādassanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Aniyamite hi kālavisese vippakatakālavacananti. Vanati yācati puttanti vañjhā jha-paccayaṃ, na-kārassa ca niggahitaṃ katvā, vadhati puttaṃ, phalaṃ vā hanatītipi vañjhā sapaccayaghya-kārassa jha-kāraṃ, niggahitāgamañca katvā. Sā viya kassaci phalassa ajanenāti vañjho, tenāha “vañjhapasū”tiādi. Evaṃ padatthavatā iminā kīdisaṃ sāmatthiyatthaṃ dassetīti antolīnacodanaṃ pariharituṃ “etenā”tiādimāha. Jhānalābhissa visesena jhānadhammā āpāthamāgacchanti, tammukhena pana sesadhammāpīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya “jhānādīna”nti vuttaṃ. Rūpādijanakabhāvanti rūpādīnaṃ janakasāmatthiyaṃ. Paṭikkhipatīti “nayime kiñci janentī”ti paṭikkhipati. Kasmāti ce? Sati hi janakabhāve rūpādidhammānaṃ viya, sukhādidhammānaṃ viya ca paccayāyattavuttitāya uppādavantatā viññāyati, uppāde ca sati avassaṃbhāvī nirodhoti anavakāsāva niccatā siyā, tasmā taṃ paṭikkhipatīti.

He is endowed with the powers of jhāna, which are of a splendid, unfolding nature and are known as worldly higher knowledges; therefore, he is called Jhānānubhāvasampanna. That this person with a wrong view speaks thus is a statement in the present tense; this should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that it pertains to all time, due to the uninterrupted nature of such speech. For, when a specific time is not determined, the present tense verb indicates an action not yet completed. A barren woman (`vañjhā`) is so called because 'she begs (`vanati`) for a son (`puttaṃ`)', formed by applying the `jha` suffix and changing the letter `na` to a nasal (`niggahita`). Alternatively, she is called `vañjhā` because 'she kills (`vadhati`) a son, or destroys (`hanati`) fruit (`phalaṃ`)', formed by changing the `dhya` (together with its `ṇya` suffix) to `jha` and inserting a nasal. Like her, because of not producing any fruit, it is called `vañjha`; therefore, the commentator said 'a barren birth' (`vañjhapasū`), etc. Thus, in order to refute the implicit objection, 'What sort of meaning of capability does he show by this word which has a literal meaning?', the commentator said 'by this' (`etena`), etc. For one who has attained jhāna, the jhāna-factors especially come into range; moreover, through them, the remaining associated states also come into range. With reference to this meaning, the commentator said 'of jhāna, etc.' (`jhānādīnaṃ`). The state of being a generator of form, etc., means the capability to generate form, etc. He rejects this, saying, 'These do not generate anything.' If it is asked why, it is because if there were a generative power, then like form-dharmas or feeling-dharmas, their nature of having an arising would be known due to their dependence on conditions. And if there is arising, cessation is inevitable. Therefore, permanence would have no place. That is why he rejects it.

Ṭhitoti niccalaṃ patiṭṭhito, kūṭaṭṭha-saddoyeva vā loke accantaṃ nicce niruḷho daṭṭhabbo. Tiṭṭhatīti ṭhāyī, esikā ca sā ṭhāyī cāti esikaṭṭhāyī, visesanaparanipāto cesa, tasmā gambhīranemo niccalaṭṭhitiko indakhīlo viyāti attho, tenāha “yathā”tiādi. “Kūṭaṭṭho”ti iminā cettha aniccatābhāvamāha. “Esikaṭṭhāyī ṭhito”ti iminā pana yathā esikā vātappahārādīhi na calati, evaṃ na kenaci vikāramāpajjatīti vikārābhāvaṃ, vikāropi atthato vināsoyevāti vuttaṃ “ubhayenāpi lokassa vināsābhāvaṃ dassetī”ti.

'Standing' (`ṭhito`) means unmovingly established. Alternatively, the word `kūṭaṭṭha` itself should be seen as well-known in the world in the sense of 'absolutely permanent'. Because it stands (`tiṭṭhati`), it is steadfast (`ṭhāyī`); it is a post (`esikā`) and it is steadfast (`ṭhāyī`), thus it is `esikaṭṭhāyī`. And this is a case of the adjective being placed after the noun (`visesanaparanipāto`); therefore, the meaning is 'like an `indakhīla` (city-gate post) that is deeply embedded and unmovingly established'. For this reason, the teacher said 'just as' (`yathā`), etc. Herein, by this word `kūṭaṭṭho`, he speaks of the absence of impermanence. Furthermore, by this phrase `esikaṭṭhāyī ṭhito`, he speaks of the absence of alteration, meaning: just as a post does not move due to the striking of the wind and so on, so too it does not undergo alteration due to any cause. Alteration, in essence, is just destruction. Therefore, it was said, 'by both, he shows the absence of the world's destruction'.

Evamaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ dassetvā idāni kecivādaṃ dassetuṃ “keci panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Muñjatoti [muñje (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] muñjatiṇato. Īsikāti kaḷīro. Yadidaṃ attasaṅkhātaṃ dhammajātaṃ jāyatīti vuccati, taṃ sattirūpavasena pubbe vijjamānameva byattirūpavasena nikkhamati, abhibyattiṃ gacchatīti attho. “Vijjamānamevā”ti hi etena kāraṇe phalassa atthibhāvadassanena byattirūpavasena [M 1.0396] abhibyattivādaṃ dasseti. Sāligabbhe saṃvijjamānaṃ sālisīsaṃ viya hi sattirūpaṃ, tadabhinikkhantaṃ viya byattirūpanti. Kathaṃ pana sattirūpavasena vijjamānoyeva pubbe anabhibyatto byattirūpavasena abhibyattiṃ gacchatīti? Yathā andhakārena paṭicchanno ghaṭo ālokena abhibyattiṃ gacchati, evamayampīti.

Having thus shown the view of the commentary, now, in order to show the view of some, 'But some...' (`keci pana`), etc., was said. `Muñjato` means from muñja grass. `Īsikā` means a shoot. Whatever collection of phenomena, designated as 'self', is said to 'arise', that very same thing, already existing previously in the form of potentiality, emerges in the form of manifestation; it reaches full manifestation. This is the meaning. Indeed, by this phrase 'already existing' (`vijjamānameva`), by showing the existence of the effect in the cause, he shows the doctrine of manifestation (`abhibyattivāda`) by way of the manifest form. For the potential form is like an ear of rice existing within the rice husk (`sāligabbha`), and the manifest form is like that which has emerged from it. But how does that which already exists by way of potential form, being previously unmanifest, reach manifestation by way of manifest form? Just as a pot covered by darkness reaches manifestation by light, so too does this.

Idamettha vicāretabbaṃ – kiṃ karonto āloko ghaṭaṃ pakāsetīti vuccati, yadi ghaṭavisayaṃ [V 1.0348] buddhiṃ karonto pakāseti, anuppannāya eva buddhiyā uppattidīpanato abhibyattivādo hāyati. Atha ghaṭavisayāya buddhiyā āvaraṇabhūtaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamanto pakāseti, evampi abhibyattivādo hāyateva. Sati hi ghaṭavisayāya buddhiyā kathaṃ andhakāro tassā āvaraṇaṃ hotīti. Yathā ca ghaṭassa abhibyatti na yujjati, evaṃ diṭṭhigatikaparikappitassa attanopi abhibyatti na yujjatiyeva. Tatthāpi hi yadi indriyavisayādisannipātena anuppannā eva buddhi uppannā, uppattivacaneneva abhibyattivādo hāyati abhibyattimattamatikkamma anuppannāya eva buddhiyā uppattidīpanato. Tathā sassatavādopi teneva kāraṇena. Atha buddhippavattiyā āvaraṇabhūtassa andhakāraṭṭhāniyassa mohassa vidhamanena buddhi uppannā. Evampi sati atthavisayāya buddhiyā kathaṃ moho tassā āvaraṇaṃ hotīti, hāyateva abhibyattivādo, kiñca bhiyyo – bhedasabbhāvatopi abhibyattivādo hāyati. Na hi abhibyañjanakānaṃ candimasūriyamaṇipadīpādīnaṃ bhedena abhibyañjitabbānaṃ ghaṭādīnaṃ bhedo hoti, hoti ca visayabhedena buddhibhedo yathāvisayaṃ buddhiyā sambhavatoti bhiyyopi abhibyatti na yujjatiyeva, na cettha vijjamānatābhibyattivasena vuttikappanā yuttā vijjamānatābhibyattikiriyāsaṅkhātāya vuttiyā vuttimato ca anaññathānujānanato. Anaññāyeva hi tathā vuttisaṅkhātā kiriyā tabbantavatthuto, yathā phassādīhi phusanādibhāvo, tasmā vuttimato anaññāya eva vijjamānatābhibyattisaṅkhātāya vuttiyā parikappito kesañci abhibyattivādo na yutto evāti. Ye pana “īsikaṭṭhāyī ṭhito”ti paṭhitvā yathāvuttamatthamicchanti, te tadidaṃ kāraṇabhāvena gahetvā “te ca sattā sandhāvanti saṃsaranti cavanti upapajjantī”ti padehi atthasambandhampi karonti, na aṭṭhakathāyamiva asambandhanti dassento “yasmā cā”tiādimāha. Te ca sattā sandhāvantīti ettha ye [M 1.0397] idha manussabhāvena avaṭṭhitā, teyeva devabhāvādiupagamanena ito aññattha gacchantīti attho. Aññathā katassa kammassa vināso, akatassa ca abbhāgamo āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo.

Herein, this should be considered: By doing what is it said that light illuminates a pot? If it illuminates by producing a cognition having the pot as its object, the doctrine of manifestation is refuted, because it shows the arising of a cognition that had not yet arisen. Or, if it illuminates by dispelling the darkness that has become an obstruction to the cognition having the pot as its object, even so, the doctrine of manifestation is certainly refuted. For, when a cognition having the pot as its object exists, how can darkness be an obstruction to it? And just as the manifestation of the pot is not tenable, so too the manifestation of the self as conceived by one holding speculative views is certainly not tenable. For there too, if a cognition that had not yet arisen has arisen through the conjunction of sense faculties, objects, and so on, the doctrine of manifestation is refuted by the very statement of 'arising', because it shows the arising of a cognition that had not yet arisen, transcending mere manifestation. Likewise, the doctrine of eternalism is also refuted for that very reason. Or, if cognition has arisen through the dispelling of delusion—which is in the place of darkness and has become an obstruction to the occurrence of cognition—even so, when a cognition having the self as its object exists, how can delusion be an obstruction to it? Thus, the doctrine of manifestation is certainly refuted. Furthermore, the doctrine of manifestation is also refuted because of the existence of difference. For a difference in the things to be manifested, such as pots, does not arise from a difference in the manifesting agents, such as the moon, sun, gems, and lamps. But a difference of cognitions does arise from a difference of objects, because of the arising of cognition in accordance with its object. Therefore, manifestation is even more untenable. And here, the conception of a function by way of manifesting what is existent is not proper, because of the admission that the function—called the action of manifesting existence—is not other than that which possesses the function. For the action called 'function' is indeed not other than the thing possessing it, just as the state of touching, etc., is not other than contact, etc. Therefore, the doctrine of manifestation conceived by some, through a function called the manifestation of what is existent which is not other than that which possesses the function, is certainly not proper. But those teachers who, having recited 'standing like a reed stalk,' desire the meaning as stated, take this as a reason and also make a connection of meaning with the words 'and those beings run on, transmigrate, pass away, and are reborn,' not unconnected as in the commentary. Showing this, the Teacher said, 'And because...' and so on. Here, in 'and those beings run on,' the meaning is: those beings who are established here in a human state, they themselves go elsewhere from here by approaching a divine state, and so on. Otherwise, the destruction of kamma that has been done and the arrival of kamma that has not been done would result—this is the intention.

Aparāparanti aparasmā bhavā aparaṃ bhavaṃ, aparamaparaṃ vā, punappunanti attho. “Cavantī”ti padamulliṅgetvā “evaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gacchantī”ti atthaṃ vivarati, attano tathāgahitassa niccasabhāvattā na cutūpapattiyo. Sabbabyāpitāya nāpi sandhāvanasaṃsaraṇāni, dhammānaṃyeva pana pavattivisesena evaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti evaṃ voharīyantīti adhippāyo. Etena “avaṭṭhitasabhāvassa attano, dhammino ca dhammamattaṃ uppajjati ceva vinassati cā”ti imaṃ vipariṇāmavādaṃ dasseti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ imissaṃ sassatavādavicāraṇāyameva “evaṃgatikā”ti [V 1.0349] padatthavibhāvane vakkhāma. Idāni aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ asambandhamattaṃ dassetuṃ “aṭṭhakathāyaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sandhāvantītiādinā vacanena attano vādaṃ bhindati vināseti sandhāvanādivacanasiddhāya aniccatāya pubbe attanā paṭiññātassa sassatavādassa viruddhabhāvatoti attho. “Diṭṭhigatikassā”tiādi tadatthasamatthanaṃ. Na nibaddhanti na thiraṃ. “Sandhāvantī”tiādivacanaṃ, sassatavādañca sandhāya “sundarampi asundarampi hotiyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbadā saranti pavattantīti sassatiyo ra-kārassa sa-kāraṃ, dvibhāvañca katvā, pathavīsinerucandimasūriyā, sassatīhi samaṃ sadisaṃ tathā, bhāvanapuṃsakavacanañcetaṃ. “Attā ca loko cā”ti hi kattuadhikāro. Sassatisamanti vā liṅgabyattayena kattuniddeso. Sassatisamo attā ca loko ca atthi evāti attho, iti-saddo cettha padapūraṇamattaṃ. Eva-saddassa hi e-kāre pare iti-sadde i-kārassa va-kāramicchanti saddavidū. Sassatisamanti sassataṃ thāvaraṃ niccakālantipi attho, sassatisama-saddassa sassatapadena samānatthataṃ sandhāya ṭīkāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.31) vutto.

'Aparāparaṃ' means from another existence to another existence, or to one after another, or again and again; this is the meaning. Skipping over the word 'cavanti' (they pass away), he explains the meaning as 'they come to be reckoned thus'. Because of the eternal nature of the self so grasped, there are no passings away and rebirths. Due to its all-pervasiveness, there are no runnings on or transmigrations either. But the intention is that it is only by a particular occurrence of dhammas that they come to be reckoned thus and are spoken of thus. By this, he shows this doctrine of transformation: 'Of the self, which has a stable nature, and of the possessor of dhammas, only the dhammas themselves arise and cease.' Whatever should be said on this matter, we will state in this very investigation of the doctrine of eternalism, in the analysis of the meaning of the word 'evaṃgatikā'. Now, to show the mere lack of connection stated in the commentary, 'But in the commentary...' and so on was said. By the words 'they run on,' etc., he breaks and destroys his own doctrine, because of the contradiction between the impermanence established by the words 'running on,' etc., and the doctrine of eternalism previously professed by himself; this is the meaning. 'Of one with speculative views...' and so on is in support of that meaning. 'They are not bound' means they are not stable. In reference to both the words 'they run on,' etc., and the doctrine of eternalism, it was said, 'Whether beautiful or ugly, it certainly exists.' Because they always proceed (saranti) and occur, they are 'sassatiyo' (eternal ones), by changing the letter 'r' to 's' and doubling it. The earth, Sineru, the moon, and the sun are obtained. 'Samaṃ' means similar to the eternal things (sassatīhi). And this word is a neuter term expressing a state. For 'the self and the world' is the governing agent. Or, 'sassatisamaṃ' is a designation of the agent by a change of gender. The meaning is: 'The self and the world, which are like the eternal, certainly exist.' And here the word 'iti' is a mere expletive. For, when the 'e' of the word 'eva' is followed by the 'i' of the word 'iti', experts in grammar wish for the 'i' to become 'v'. 'Sassatisamaṃ' also has the meaning 'eternal, stable, at all times'. This was stated in the subcommentary in reference to the term 'sassatisama' having the same meaning as the word 'sassata'.

Hetuṃ dassentoti yesaṃ “sassato”ti attānañca lokañca paññapeti, tesaṃ hetuṃ dassento ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko āhāti sambandho. Na hi attano diṭṭhiyā paccakkhakatamatthaṃ attanoyeva sādheti, attano pana paccakkhakatena atthena attano appaccakkhabhūtampi atthaṃ sādheti, attanā ca yathānicchitaṃ atthaṃ parepi viññāpeti, na anicchitaṃ[M 1.0398], idaṃ pana hetudassanaṃ etesu anekesu jātisatasahassesu ekovāyaṃ me attā ca loko ca anussaraṇasambhavato. Yo hi yamatthaṃ anubhavati, so eva taṃ anussarati, na añño. Na hi aññena anubhūtamatthaṃ añño anussarituṃ sakkoti yathā taṃ buddharakkhitena anubhūtaṃ dhammarakkhito. Yathā cetāsu, evaṃ ito purimatarāsupi jātīsu, tasmā “sassato me attā ca loko ca, yathā ca me, evaṃ aññesampi sattānaṃ sassato attā ca loko cā”ti sassatavasena diṭṭhigahaṇaṃ pakkhandanto diṭṭhigatiko parepi tattha patiṭṭhapeti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “anekavihitāni adhimuttipathāni abhivadanti, so evamāhā”ti vacanato parānugāhāpanavasena idha hetudassanaṃ adhippetanti viññāyati. Etanti attano ca lokassa ca sassatabhāvaṃ. “Na kevala”ntiādi atthato āpannadassanaṃ. Ṭhāna-saddo kāraṇe, tañca kho idha pubbenivāsānussatiyevāti āha “ida”ntiādi. Kāraṇañca nāmetaṃ tividhaṃ sampāpakaṃ nibbattakaṃ ñāpakanti. Tattha ariyamaggo nibbānassa sampāpakakāraṇaṃ, bījaṃ aṅkurassa nibbattakakāraṇaṃ, paccayuppannatādayo aniccatādīnaṃ ñāpakakāraṇaṃ, idhāpi ñāpakakāraṇameva adhippetaṃ. Ñāpako hi attho ñāpetabbatthavisayassa ñāṇassa hetubhāvato kāraṇaṃ. Tadāyattavuttitāya [V 1.0350] taṃ ñāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti ṭhānaṃ, vasati taṃ ñāṇamettha tiṭṭhatīti “vatthū”ti ca vuccati. Tathā hi bhagavatā vatthu-saddena uddisitvāpi ṭhāna-saddena niddiṭṭhanti.

Regarding `Hetuṃ dassento` (showing the reason): The connection should be made thus: 'This person holding a wrong view speaks, showing the reason for those who declare the self and the world to be "eternal".' Indeed, he does not accomplish the meaning made evident by his own view for himself alone; rather, by means of a meaning made evident by himself, he also establishes a meaning not directly perceived by himself. And he makes others understand the meaning as he has decided, not what is undecided. But this is the showing of the reason: in these many hundreds of thousands of births, 'this one self of mine and the world is eternal,' due to the possibility of recollection. For whoever experiences a certain matter, that very one recollects it, not another. Indeed, another cannot recollect a matter experienced by someone else, just as Dhammarakkhita cannot recollect what was experienced by Buddharakkhita. As in these, so also in births even earlier than this one. Therefore, rushing into the grasp of a view by way of eternity—'My self and the world are eternal, and just as for me, so too for other beings the self and the world are eternal'—the person holding a wrong view establishes others in that as well. In the Pāḷi text, however, from the statement, 'They declare various kinds of adherence; thus he speaks,' it is understood that the showing of the reason here is intended for the sake of inducing others to follow. `Etaṃ` refers to the eternal nature of the self and the world. The passage beginning with `Na kevalaṃ` shows what is arrived at by way of meaning. The word `ṭhāna` is used in the sense of 'reason', and here that reason is precisely the recollection of past lives; thus the teacher stated the passage beginning with `idaṃ`. And this 'reason' is threefold: attaining, generative, and indicative. Among these, the noble path is the attaining reason for Nibbāna; a seed is the generative reason for a sprout; and the state of being conditionally arisen, etc., are the indicative reasons for impermanence, etc. Here, only the indicative reason is intended. For an indicative matter is a reason because it is the cause of the knowledge whose object is the matter to be indicated. Because that knowledge's occurrence is dependent on it, it 'stands' (`tiṭṭhati`) there (`ettha`), thus it is called a `ṭhāna` (standing place). Because that knowledge 'dwells' (`vasati`) and 'stands' (`tiṭṭhati`) there, it is also called a `vatthu` (basis). Thus, indeed, the Blessed One, having designated it with the word `vatthu`, also indicated it with the word `ṭhāna`.

32-33. Dutiyatatiyavārānaṃ paṭhamavārato viseso natthi ṭhapetvā kālabhedanti āha “upari vāradvayepi eseva nayo”ti. Tadetaṃ kālabhedaṃ yathāpāḷiṃ dassetuṃ “kevalañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Itarena dutiyatatiyavārā yāva dasasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappā, yāva cattālīsasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappā ca anussaraṇavasena vuttāti adhippāyo. Yadevaṃ kasmā sassatavādo catudhā vibhatto, nanu tidhā kālabhedamakatvā adhiccasamuppattikavādo viya duvidheneva vibhajitabbo siyāti codanaṃ sodhetuṃ “mandapañño hī”tiādimāha. Mandapaññādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇalābhīnaṃ vasena tidhā kālabhedaṃ katvā takkanena saha catudhā vibhattoti adhippāyo. Nanu ca anussavādivasena takkikānaṃ viya mandapaññādīnampi visesalābhīnaṃ hīnādivasena anekabhedasambhavato [M 1.0399] bahudhā bhedo siyā, atha kasmā sabbepi visesalābhino tayo eva rāsī katvā vuttāti? Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena dassetukāmattā. Tīsu hi rāsīsu ye hīnamajjhimapaññā, te vuttaparicchedato ūnakameva anussaranti. Ye pana ukkaṭṭhapaññā, te vuttaparicchedaṃ atikkamitvā nānussarantīti tattha tattha ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena dassetukāmato anekajātisatasahassadasacattārīsasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭānussaraṇavasena tayo eva rāsī katvā vuttāti. Na tato uddhanti yathāvuttakālattayato, cattārīsasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappato vā uddhaṃ nānussarati, kasmā? Dubbalapaññattā. Tesañhi nāmarūpaparicchedavirahato dubbalā paññā hotīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ.

32-33. There is no difference between the second and third sections and the first, except for the difference in time; thus, the teacher said: 'The same method applies to the two sections above.' To show this difference in time in accordance with the Pāḷi, the passage beginning with 'kevalañhī' was stated. The meaning is that the second and third sections are spoken of by way of recollection extending up to ten eons of contraction and expansion, and up to forty eons of contraction and expansion. If this is so, why is the eternalist doctrine divided into four parts? Should it not, like the doctrine of fortuitous origination, be divided into just two, without making a threefold distinction of time? To resolve this objection, the teacher stated the passage beginning with 'For one of dull wisdom...'. The meaning is that a threefold distinction of time is made based on the three types of persons—the one of dull wisdom, etc.—who have attained the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and thus, together with the one based on reasoning, the doctrine is divided fourfold. But surely, just as the reasoners have their basis in hearsay, etc., might not those of dull wisdom, etc., who possess special attainments, also have many divisions based on inferior, etc., types? Why then are all those with special attainments grouped into just three classes? It is because of the desire to show the highest limit. For among these three classes, those with inferior and mediocre wisdom recollect less than the stated limit, while those with superior wisdom do not recollect beyond the stated limit. Therefore, to show the highest limit in each case, they are grouped into just three classes, based on recollection up to many hundreds of thousands of births, ten eons of contraction and expansion, and forty eons of contraction and expansion. 'Not beyond that' means they do not recollect beyond the three stated periods, or beyond forty eons of contraction and expansion. Why? Because their wisdom is weak. As stated in the commentaries, their wisdom is weak due to the lack of discernment of name-and-form.

34. Tappakatiyattopi kattutthoyevāti āha “takkayatī”ti. Tappakatiyattattā eva hi dutiyanayopi upapanno hoti. Tattha takkayatīti ūhayati, sassatādiākārena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropayatīti attho. Takkoti ākoṭanalakkhaṇo, vinicchayalakkhaṇo vā diṭṭhiṭṭhānabhūto vitakko. Tena tena pariyāyena takkanaṃ sandhāya “takketvā vitakketvā”ti vuttaṃ vīmaṃsāya samannāgatoti atthavacanamattaṃ. Nibbacanaṃ pana takkipade viya dvidhā vattabbaṃ. Vīmaṃsā nāma vicāraṇā, sā ca duvidhā paññā ceva paññāpatirūpikā ca. Idha pana paññāpatirūpikāva, sā catthato lobhasahagatacittuppādo, micchābhinivesasaṅkhāto vā ayonisomanasikāro. Pubbabhāge vā micchādassanabhūtaṃ diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ, tadetamatthattayaṃ dassetuṃ “tulanā ruccanā khamanā”ti vuttaṃ. “Tulayitvā”tiādīsupi yathākkamaṃ “lobhasahagatacittuppādenā”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Samantato, punappunaṃ vā āhananaṃ pariyāhataṃ, taṃ [V 1.0351] pana vitakkassa ārammaṇaṃ ūhanameva, bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ padanti dasseti “tena tena pariyāyena takketvā”ti iminā. Pariyāyenāti ca kāraṇenāti attho. Vuttappakārāyāti tidhā vuttappabhedāya. Anuvicaritanti anupavattitaṃ, vīmaṃsānugatena vā vicārena anumajjitaṃ. Tadanugatadhammakiccampi hi padhānadhamme āropetvā tathā vuccati. Paṭibhāti dissatīti paṭibhānaṃ, yathāsamāhitākāravisesavibhāvako diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādo, tato jātanti paṭibhānaṃ, tathā paññāyanaṃ, sayaṃ attano paṭibhānaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ[M 1.0400], tenevāha “attano paṭibhānamattasañjāta”nti. Matta-saddena cettha visesādhigamādayo nivatteti. Anāmaṭṭhakālavacane vattamānavaseneva atthaniddeso upapannoti āha “evaṃ vadatī”ti.

34. Although it is also related to that nature, it is only the agent-meaning; therefore, the Teacher said, 'takkayati'. Indeed, it is precisely because of its connection to that nature that the second method is also established. Therein, 'takkayati' means: one ponders; one directs the mind towards this or that object in the manner of eternalism and so on. This is the meaning. 'Takka' is initial thought that is the basis for wrong view, characterized by striking or by deciding. With reference to reasoning by this or that method, it was said, 'having reasoned, having reflected'. The phrase 'endowed with investigation' is merely a statement of the meaning. The derivation, however, should be stated in two ways, as in the word 'takki' (reasoner). 'Vīmaṃsā' is the name for investigation. And that is twofold: wisdom and that which resembles wisdom. Here, however, only that which resembles wisdom should be taken. And that, in terms of its essential meaning, is a consciousness-moment accompanied by greed, or it is unwise attention called wrong adherence. Or, in the preliminary stage, it is the agitation of views which is wrong seeing. To show this threefold meaning, it was said, 'weighing, approving, accepting'. In the phrases beginning with 'having weighed', it should be connected in sequence with the phrases beginning with 'by a consciousness-moment accompanied by greed'. 'Struck all around' means striking from all sides or repeatedly. That, however, is simply the pondering on the object of initial thought. And he shows that this word is a neuter noun of state with the phrase, 'having reasoned by this or that method'. And 'pariyāyena' means 'by reason'. 'Of the kind stated' means of the threefold kind stated. 'Investigated' means followed along, or scrutinized by reflection that follows investigation. For even the function of a phenomenon that follows it is so called by ascribing it to the principal phenomenon. 'It appears, it is seen', thus it is 'paṭibhāna' (appearance); it is the consciousness-moment associated with wrong view that clarifies the specific mode of what has been well-established; 'born from that', thus it is 'paṭibhāna'; in that way, it is a making manifest. 'One's own appearance' is 'sayaṃpaṭibhāna' (self-appearance). Therefore, he said, 'arisen from merely one's own appearance'. And here, by the word 'merely', he excludes special attainments and so on. Since in a statement about unconsidered time, the explanation of the meaning is established by the force of the present tense, the Teacher said, 'thus he speaks'.

Pāḷiyaṃ “takkī hoti vīmaṃsī”ti sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesena vā vuttaṃ takkībhedaṃ vibhajanto “tattha catubbidho”tiādimāha. Parehi puna savanaṃ anussuti, sā yassāyaṃ anussutiko. Purimaṃ anubhūtapubbaṃ jātiṃ saratīti jātissaro. Labbhateti lābho, yaṃ kiñci attanā paṭiladdhaṃ rūpādi, sukhādi ca, na pana jhānādiviseso, tenevāha pāḷiyaṃ “so takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānuvicaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ evamāhā”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyampi vuttaṃ “attano paṭibhānamattasañjāta”nti. Ācariyadhammapālattheropi vadati “matta-saddena visesādhigamādayo nivattetī”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.34) so etassāti lābhī. Suddhena purimehi asammissena, suddhaṃ vā takkanaṃ suddhatakko, so yassāyaṃ suddhatakkiko. Tena hīti uyyojanatthe nipāto, tena tathā vessantararaññova bhagavati samāneti diṭṭhiggāhaṃ uyyojeti. Lābhitāyāti rūpādisukhādilābhībhāvato. “Anāgatepi evaṃ bhavissatī”ti idaṃ lābhītakkino evampi sambhavatīti sambhavadassanavasena idhādhippetaṃ takkanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Anāgataṃsatakkaneneva hi sassataggāhī bhavati. “Atītepi evaṃ ahosī”ti idaṃ pana anāgataṃsatakkanassa upanissayanidassanamattaṃ. So hi “yathā me idāni attā sukhī hoti, evaṃ atītepīti paṭhamaṃ atītaṃsānutakkanaṃ upanissāya anāgatepi evaṃ bhavissatī”ti takkayanto diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. “Evaṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti iminā aniccesu bhāvesu añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedetīti doso āpajjati, tathā ca sati katassa vināso akatassa ca ajjhāgamo siyā. Niccesu pana bhāvesu añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedetīti doso nāpajjati. Evañca sati katassa avināso, akatassa ca anajjhāgamo siyāti takkikassa yuttigavesanākāraṃ dasseti.

In the Pāḷi, 'he is a reasoner, an investigator' was stated by way of a general indication, or by way of ellipsis. The Commentator, dividing the types of reasoners, said, 'Therein, he is fourfold', and so on. 'Anussuti' is hearing again from others. He who has this is an 'anussutiko'. 'He remembers a former birth, previously experienced', thus he is a 'jātissara'. 'Lābha' (gain) is so called because 'it is obtained'. It is whatever form, etc., and happiness, etc., has been obtained by oneself, but not a special attainment like jhāna. For that very reason, in the Pāḷi, the Blessed One said, 'Regarding that which is struck by reasoning, investigated by inquiry, and self-inspired, he speaks thus'. And in the Commentary it is said, 'arisen from merely one's own inspiration'. The Teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, also says, 'By the word "merely", he excludes special attainments and so on'. He who has this gain is a 'lābhī'. 'Suddhatakka' (pure reasoning) is reasoning that is pure, unmixed with previous ones, or it is pure reasoning. He who has this is a 'suddhatakkiko'. The phrase 'tena hi' is a particle in the sense of urging. By this, he urges on the grasping of a view, just as when the Blessed One was King Vessantara... 'Because of being a gainer' means because of the state of being a gainer of form, happiness, and so on. The statement, 'In the future, too, it will be thus', was said with reference to the reasoning intended here, in the sense of showing a possibility, as in 'this is also possible for a reasoner who is a gainer'. For it is precisely by reasoning about the future portion that one becomes a grasper of eternalism. The statement, 'In the past, too, it was thus', however, is merely an illustration of the supporting condition for reasoning about the future portion. For that person, first relying on the sequential reasoning about the past portion—'Just as my self is happy now, so it was in the past'—reasons, 'In the future, too, it will be thus', and so grasps a view. With the phrase, 'When this exists, that comes to be,' he shows the reasoner's manner of seeking a rationale: In the case of impermanent states, the fault arises that one person acts and another experiences, and so there would be the destruction of what was done and the arrival of what was not done. In the case of permanent states, however, the fault that one person acts and another experiences does not arise, and so there would be the non-destruction of what was done and the non-arrival of what was not done.

Takkamattenevāti suddhatakkaneneva. Matta-saddena hi āgamādīnaṃ, anussavādīnañca abhāvaṃ [V 1.0352] dasseti. “Nanu ca visesalābhinopi sassatavādino [M 1.0401] visesādhigamahetu anekesu jātisatasahassesu, dasasu saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu, cattālīsāya ca saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu yathānubhūtaṃ attano santānaṃ, tappaṭibaddhañca dhammajātaṃ “attā, loko”ti ca anussaritvā tato purimatarāsupi jātīsu tathābhūtassa atthitānuvitakkanamukhena anāgatepi evaṃ bhavissatīti attano bhavissamānānutakkanaṃ, sabbesampi sattānaṃ tathābhāvānutakkanañca katvā sassatābhinivesino jātā, evañca sati sabbopi sassatavādī anussutikajātissaralābhītakkikā viya attano upaladdhavatthunimittena takkanena pavattavādattā takkīpakkheyeva tiṭṭheyya, tathā ca sati visesabhedarahitattā ekovāyaṃ sassatavādo vavatthito bhaveyya, avassañca vuttappakāraṃ takkanamicchitabbaṃ, aññathā visesalābhī sassatavādī ekaccasassatikapakkhaṃ, adhiccasamuppannikapakkhaṃ vā bhajeyyāti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Visesalābhīnañhi khandhasantānassa dīghadīghataraṃ dīghatamakālānussaraṇaṃ sassataggāhassa asādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ. Tathā hi “anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Imināmahaṃ etaṃ jānāmī”ti anussaraṇameva padhānakāraṇabhāvena dassitaṃ. Yaṃ pana tassa “imināmahaṃ etaṃ jānāmī”ti pavattaṃ takkanaṃ, na taṃ idha padhānaṃ anussaraṇaṃ paṭicca tassa apadhānabhāvato, padhānakāraṇena ca asādhāraṇena niddeso sāsane, lokepi ca niruḷho yathā “cakkhuviññāṇaṃ yavaṅkuro”tiādi.

"By mere reasoning" (takkamatteneva) means by pure reasoning alone. For the word "mere" (matta) indicates the absence of the attainment of special states, etc., and of hearsay, etc. "But surely, do not even eternalists who have attained special knowledge, by reason of their special attainment, recollect their own continuity of aggregates as experienced in many hundreds of thousands of births, through ten world-cycles of contraction and expansion, and forty world-cycles of contraction and expansion, along with the collection of phenomena connected to it, thinking 'the self is eternal, and the world is eternal'? And then, by means of reasoning sequentially from the existence of such a state in even earlier lives, they reason sequentially about their own future, thinking 'it will be so in the future,' and reason sequentially that it is so for all beings, and thus become attached to eternalism. This being so, would not every eternalist—like the reasoners who rely on hearsay, memory of past births, and other attainments—stand only in the faction of reasoners, since their view proceeds from reasoning based on a ground obtained by themselves? And if so, due to the absence of special distinctions, this eternalist view would be established as just one. And must not reasoning of the kind described be necessarily accepted? Otherwise, might not the eternalist who possesses special attainment resort to the faction of the partial-eternalists or the faction of the fortuitous-originators?" No, it should not be seen in this way. For those with special attainment, the recollection of the continuity of aggregates over a very long, a longer, and a very longest time is the uncommon cause for grasping at eternalism. Thus, recollection itself was shown as the primary cause: "I recollect my manifold past lives... By this means, I know this."
