As for the reasoning that proceeds from "By this means, I know this," that is not the primary cause here, for it is non-primary because it is dependent on recollection. And designation by a primary and uncommon cause is well-known in the Dispensation and also in the world, as in "eye-consciousness" and "barley sprout," etc.

Evaṃ panāyaṃ desanā padhānakāraṇavibhāvinī, tasmā satipi anussavādivasena, takkikānaṃ hīnādivasena ca mandapaññādīnaṃ visesalābhīnaṃ bahudhā bhede aññatarabhedasaṅgahavasena bhagavatā cattāriṭṭhānāni vibhajitvā vavatthitā sassatavādānaṃ catubbidhatā. Na hi, idha sāvasesaṃ dhammaṃ deseti dhammarājāti. Yadevaṃ anussutikādīsupi anussavādīnaṃ padhānabhāvo āpajjatīti? Na tesaṃ aññāya sacchikiriyāya abhāvena takkapadhānattā, “padhānakāraṇena ca asādhāraṇena niddeso sāsane, lokepi ca niruḷho”ti vuttovāyamatthoti. Atha vā visesādhigamanimittarahitassa takkanassa sassataggāhe visuṃ kāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ visesādhigamo visuṃ sassataggāhakāraṇabhāvena vattabbo, so ca mandamajjhimatikkhapaññāvasena tividhoti tidhā vibhajitvā, sabbatakkino [M 1.0402] ca takkībhāvasāmaññato ekajjhaṃ gahetvā catudhā eva vavatthāpito sassatavādo bhagavatāti.

Thus, this teaching makes clear the primary cause. Therefore, although there are many divisions—by way of hearsay and the like; by way of the inferior and other views of reasoners; and of those with dull wisdom and so on who have special attainments—the fourfold nature of the eternalists was established by the Blessed One by analyzing the four grounds, by way of grouping a certain division. For, in this matter, the King of Dhamma does not teach a doctrine with anything remaining. "If so, does the primacy of hearsay and the like also follow in the case of those who rely on hearsay and the like?" No, because for them, reasoning is primary due to their lack of realization through direct knowledge. And this meaning has already been stated: "Designation by a primary and uncommon cause is well-known in the Dispensation and also in the world." Or alternatively, in order to show that reasoning devoid of the sign of special attainment is a separate cause for grasping at eternalism, special attainment is stated as a separate cause for grasping at eternalism. And that person is threefold by way of dull, middling, and sharp wisdom. Thus, having divided it into three, and taking all reasoners together under the general characteristic of being a reasoner, the eternalist view was established as fourfold by the Blessed One.

35. “Aññatarenā”ti etassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “ekenā”ti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhānapayuttassa pana vā-saddassa aniyamatthataṃ sandhāyāha “dvīhi vā tīhi vā”ti, tena catūsu vatthūsu yathārahamekaccaṃ ekaccassa paññāpane sahakārīkāraṇanti dasseti. “Bahiddhā”ti bāhyatthavācako [V 1.0353] kattuniddiṭṭho nipātoti dassetuṃ “bahī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etthāha – kiṃ panetāni vatthūni attano abhinivesassa hetu, udāhu paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanassāti. Kiñcettha, yadi tāva attano abhinivesassa hetu, atha kasmā anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva gahitāni, na saññāvipallāsādayo. Tathā hi viparītasaññāayonisomanasikāraasappurisūpanissayaasaddhammassavanādīnipi diṭṭhiyā pavattanaṭṭhena diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni. Atha pana paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanassa hetu, anussaraṇahetubhūto adhigamo viya, takkanapariyeṭṭhibhūtā yutti viya ca āgamopi vatthubhāvena vattabbo, ubhayathāpi ca yathāvuttassa avasesakāraṇassa sambhavato “natthi ito bahiddhā”ti vacanaṃ na yujjatevāti? No na yujjati, kasmā? Abhinivesapakkhe tāva ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko asappurisūpanissayaasaddhammassavanehi ayoniso ummujjitvā vipallāsasañño rūpādidhammānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanasabhāvassa anavabodhato dhammayuttiṃ atidhāvanto ekattanayaṃ micchā gahetvā yathāvuttānussaraṇatakkanehi khandhesu “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti (dī. ni. 31) abhinivesaṃ upanesi, iti āsannakāraṇattā, padhānakāraṇattā ca taggahaṇeneva ca itaresampi gahitattā anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva idha gahitāni. Patiṭṭhāpanapakkhe pana āgamopi yuttiyameva ṭhito visesena nirāgamānaṃ bāhirakānaṃ takkaggāhibhāvato, tasmā anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva sassataggāhassa vatthubhāvena gahitāni.

35. "By one of them" (aññatarena)—to explain the meaning of this, it is said "by one" (ekena). However, with reference to the indeterminate meaning of the particle 'vā' when used in an inappropriate place, he says "by two or by three," thereby showing that among the four grounds, one cause is, as appropriate, a cooperative cause for postulating another. "Bahiddhā" (outside)—to show that this is a particle expressive of an external meaning and indicating the agent, "bahī" (outside), etc., is said. Here one might ask: Are these grounds the cause of one's own adherence, or for establishing it for others? In this regard, if they are the cause of one's own adherence, then why are only recollection and reasoning taken, and not perceptual distortions and the like? For indeed, distorted perception, unwise attention, association with unworthy people, and listening to the false Dhamma are also grounds for views, in that they cause views to arise. But if they are a cause for establishing it for others, then just as there is the attainment that is the cause for recollection, and the logic that is the search for reasoning, scriptural tradition, too, should be stated as a ground. And since in both cases the possibility of the remaining causes exists, is the statement 'there is nothing outside of this' not appropriate?" No, it is appropriate. Why? On the side of adherence, this person given to views, having applied his mind unwisely through association with unworthy people and listening to the false Dhamma, with distorted perception, fails to understand the nature of phenomena like form, etc., as disintegrating from moment to moment. Overstepping the logic of the Dhamma and wrongly grasping the method of oneness, through the aforementioned recollection and reasoning, he brought about the adherence upon the aggregates that 'the self and the world are eternal.' Thus, because these are the proximate and primary causes, and because the others are also included by taking these, only recollection and reasoning are taken here. On the side of establishing it for others, scriptural tradition also stands on reasoning itself, especially because outsiders without scriptural tradition are prone to grasp by reasoning. Therefore, only recollection and reasoning are taken as the ground for grasping at eternalism.

Kiñca bhiyyo – duvidhaṃ paramatthadhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ, sāmaññalakkhaṇañca. Tattha sabhāvalakkhaṇāvabodho paccakkhañāṇaṃ, sāmaññalakkhaṇāvabodho anumānañāṇaṃ. Āgamo ca sutamayāya paññāya sādhanato [M 1.0403] anumānañāṇameva āvahati, sutānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ ākāraparivitakkanena nijjhānakkhantiyaṃ ṭhito cintāmayapaññaṃ nibbattetvā anukkamena bhāvanāya paccakkhañāṇaṃ adhigacchatīti evaṃ āgamopi takkanavisayaṃ nātikkamati, tasmā cesa takkaggahaṇena gahitovāti veditabbo. So aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anussutitakkaggahaṇena vibhāvito, evaṃ anussaraṇatakkanehi asaṅgahitassa avasiṭṭhassa kāraṇassa asambhavato yuttamevidaṃ “natthi ito bahiddhā”ti vacananti veditabbaṃ. “Anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.29), “sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.30) ca vacanato pana patiṭṭhāpanavatthūniyeva idha desitāni taṃdesanāya eva abhinivesassāpi sijjhanato. Anekabhedesu hi desitesu yasmiṃ desite tadaññepi desitā siddhā honti, tameva desetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhinivesapatiṭṭhāpanesu ca abhinivese desitepi patiṭṭhāpanaṃ na sijjhati abhinivesassa patiṭṭhāpane aniyamato. Abhinivesinopi hi keci patiṭṭhāpenti[V 1.0354], keci na patiṭṭhāpenti. Patiṭṭhāpane pana desite abhinivesopi sijjhati patiṭṭhāpanassa abhinivese niyamato. Yo hi yattha pare patiṭṭhāpeti, sopi tamabhinivisatīti.

Furthermore, the characteristics of ultimate realities are twofold: the intrinsic characteristic and the general characteristic. Herein, the realization of the intrinsic characteristic is direct knowledge, while the realization of the general characteristic is inferential knowledge. Moreover, the transmitted teaching (Āgama), being an instrument for wisdom based on hearing, brings forth only inferential knowledge. However, by reflecting on the aspects of the teachings that have been heard, one who is established in reflective acceptance generates wisdom based on reflection and, gradually through cultivation, attains direct knowledge. Thus, even the transmitted teaching does not transcend the sphere of reasoning; therefore, it should be understood that it is included by the term 'reasoning.' It is explained in the commentary by the term 'reasoning based on tradition.' Thus, since there is no possibility of any remaining cause not included by recollection and reasoning, it should be understood that this statement, 'There is nothing outside of this,' is indeed appropriate. However, from the statements, 'They assert positions consisting of various kinds of convictions' and 'They propound the self and the world as eternal,' it is only the grounds for establishing false views that are taught here, since by that very teaching, adherence is also accomplished. For when many distinctions are taught, if one is taught, the others are also established as having been taught; thus, it should be seen that only that one is taught. And between adherence and establishing false views, even when adherence is taught, establishing is not accomplished, because adherence is not invariable with respect to establishing. For some who adhere establish others in their views, while some do not. But when establishing false views is taught, adherence is also accomplished, because establishing invariably implies adherence. For whoever establishes others in some view, they themselves also adhere to that.

36. Tayidanti ettha ta-saddena “sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti etassa parāmasananti āha “taṃ idaṃ catubbidhampi diṭṭhigata”nti. Tatoti tasmā pakārato jānanattā. Paramavajjatāya anekavihitānaṃ anatthānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato diṭṭhiyo eva ṭhānā diṭṭhiṭṭhānā. Yathāha “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ bhikkhave, vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti tadevatthaṃ sandhāya “diṭṭhiyova diṭṭhiṭṭhānā”ti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhīnaṃ kāraṇampi diṭṭhiṭṭhānameva diṭṭhīnaṃ uppādāya samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena. “Yathāhā”tiādi paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā (paṭi. ma. 1.124) sādhanaṃ. Tattha khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇaṭṭhena. Vuttañhi “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādi, (saṃ. ni. 3.81) avijjāpi upanissayādibhāvena. Yathāha “assutavā bhikkhave, puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.2; paṭi. ma. 1.131) phassopi phusitvā gahaṇūpāyaṭṭhena. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “tadapi phassapaccayā [M 1.0404] (dī. ni. 1.118) phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.144) saññāpi ākāramattaggahaṇaṭṭhena. Vuttañhetaṃ “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”ti (su. ni. 880; mahā. ni. 109) pathaviṃ pathavito saññatvā”ti (ma. ni. 1.2) ca ādi. Vitakkopi ākāraparivitakkanaṭṭhena. Tena vuttaṃ “takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū”ti, (su. ni. 892; mahāni. 121) “takkī hoti vīmaṃsī”ti (dī. ni. 1.34) ca ādi. Ayoniso manasikāropi akusalānaṃ sādhāraṇakāraṇaṭṭhena. Tenāha “tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoto channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati. Atthi me attā’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhiuppajjatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.19) pāpamittopi diṭṭhānugati āpajjanaṭṭhena. Vuttampi ca “bāhiraṃ bhikkhave, aṅganti karitvā nāññaṃ ekaṅgampi samanupasssāmi, yaṃ evaṃ mahato anatthāya saṃvattati, yathayidaṃ bhikkhave, pāpamittatā”tiādi (a. ni. 1.110) paratoghosopi durakkhātadhammassavanaṭṭhena. Tathā ceva vuttaṃ “dveme bhikkhave, paccayā micchādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya. Katame dve? Parato ca ghoso, ayoniso ca manasikāro”tiādi (a. ni. 2.126) parehi sutā, desitā vā desanā paratoghoso.

36. Here, in the phrase 'tayidaṃ,' by the word 'ta' (that), there is a reference to 'they propound the self and the world as eternal'; therefore, the Teacher said, 'that this is the fourfold view.' 'Tato' means because of knowing in that way. Due to being supremely blameworthy and being the cause of various kinds of harm, views themselves are the grounds, hence 'diṭṭhiṭṭhānā' (grounds of views). As it is said, 'Monks, I declare wrong view to be the supreme fault.' Referring to this very meaning, it was said, 'Views themselves are the grounds of views.' The cause of views is also a 'ground of views' in the sense of being a basis for the arising of views. The phrase 'As it is said,' etc., is a proof from the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali. Therein, the aggregates are also a ground of views in the sense of being an object. For it has been said, 'He regards form as self,' and so on. Ignorance is also a ground of views by way of being a supporting condition, etc. As it is said, 'Monks, an uninstructed worldling, who does not see the noble ones, is not skilled in the noble Dhamma,' and so on. Contact is also a ground of views in the sense of being a means for grasping through touching. For thus it is said, 'That too is conditioned by contact,' and 'they experience it, having touched again and again.' Perception is also a ground of views in the sense of grasping mere aspects. For this has been said, 'For the classifications of proliferation have perception as their source,' and 'having perceived earth as earth,' and so on. Thought is also a ground of views in the sense of pondering on aspects. Therefore it is said, 'Having fashioned reasoning in views, they speak of a dual teaching: true and false,' and 'he is a reasoner, an investigator,' and so on. Unwise attention is also a ground of views in the sense of being a common cause for unwholesome states. Hence He said, 'For one who thus attends unwisely, one of six views arises. For him, the view, “I have a self,” arises as true and established,' and so on. An evil friend is also a ground of views in the sense of causing one to fall into following a wrong view. And it has been said, 'Monks, having considered the external factors, I do not see a single other factor that leads to such great harm as this, monks: bad friendship,' and so on. The voice of another is also a ground of views in the sense of hearing a badly-expounded Dhamma. And thus it is said, 'Monks, there are these two conditions for the arising of wrong view. What two? The voice of another and unwise attention,' and so on. 'The voice of another' is a teaching heard from others, or a teaching taught by others.

“Khandhā hetū”tiādipāḷi tadatthavibhāvinī. Tattha janakaṭṭhena hetu, upatthambhakaṭṭhena paccayo. Upādāyāti upādiyitvā, paṭiccāti attho. “Uppādāyā”tipi pāṭho, uppajjanāyāti [V 1.0355] attho. Samuṭṭhāti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ, khandhādayo eva. Idha pana samuṭṭhānabhāvoyeva samuṭṭhāna-saddena vutto bhāvalopattā, bhāvappadhānattā ca. Ādinnā sakasantāne. Pavattitā saparasantānesu. Para-saddo abhiṇhatthoti vuttaṃ “punappuna”nti. Pariniṭṭhāpitāti “idameva dassanaṃ saccaṃ, aññaṃ pana moghaṃ tucchaṃ musā”ti abhinivesassa pariyosānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpitāti attho. Ārammaṇavasenāti aṭṭhasu diṭṭhiṭṭhānesu khandhe sandhāyāha. Pavattanavasenāti avijjāphassasaññāvitakkāyonisomanasikāre. Āsevanavasenāti pāpamittaparatoghose. Yadipi sarūpatthavasena vevacanaṃ, saṅketatthavasena pana evaṃ vattabboti dassetuṃ “evaṃvidhaparalokā”ti vuttaṃ. Yena kenaci hi visesaneneva vevacanaṃ sātthakaṃ siyā. Paraloko [M 1.0405] ca kammavasena abhimukho sampareti gacchati pavattati etthāti abhisamparāyoti vuccati. “Iti kho ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni anupubbena aggāya parentī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 10.2) viya hi curādigaṇavasena para-saddaṃ gatiyamicchanti saddavidū, ayamettha aṭṭhakathāto aparo nayo.

The Pāli text beginning, "The aggregates are the cause," clarifies its meaning. Therein, 'hetu' (cause) is in the sense of being generative, and 'paccaya' (condition) is in the sense of supporting. 'Upādāya' has the meaning of 'having taken up' (upādiyitvā) and 'having depended on' (paṭicca). There is also the reading 'uppādāya,' meaning 'for arising.' 'It arises by means of this,' thus it is 'samuṭṭhāna' (source), which refers to the aggregates and so forth. Here, however, by the word 'samuṭṭhāna,' only the state of being a source is stated, due to the elision of the word 'bhāva' (state) and because the state is predominant. 'Ādinnā' means taken up in one’s own continuity. 'Pavattitā' means caused to occur in one's own and others' continuities. The word 'para' has the meaning of 'repeatedly,' therefore it is stated as 'punappuna' (again and again). 'Pariniṭṭhāpitā' means brought to the conclusion, the peak, of the adherence that "This view alone is true; any other is vain, empty, and false." "By way of object" (ārammaṇavasena) is said in reference to the aggregates among the eight grounds for views. "By way of occurrence" (pavattana­vasena) refers to ignorance, contact, perception, thought, and unwise attention. "By way of cultivation" (āsevanavasena) refers to bad friends and the speech of others. Although it is a synonym by way of its intrinsic meaning, the phrase "of such a kind is the other world" is stated to show that it should be spoken of thus by way of convention. For indeed, a synonym becomes meaningful only by some or other distinguishing feature. And the 'other world' (paraloko) is called 'abhisamparāya' (future life) because a being proceeds, goes, and occurs there, facing towards it, by the power of kamma. Indeed, just as in passages like, "Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtues gradually lead (parenti) to the highest" (AN 10.2), those skilled in grammar desire the word 'para' in the sense of 'going' by way of the curādi group of roots. Herein, this is a method different from that of the Commentary.

Evaṃgatikāti evaṃgamanā evaṃniṭṭhā, evamanuyuñjanena bhijjananassanapariyosānāti attho. Gati-saddo cettha “yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavantī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.258; 2.33, 35; 3.199, 200; ma. ni. 2.384, 397) viya niṭṭhānattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime diṭṭhisaṅkhātā diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃ paramatthato asantaṃ attānaṃ, sassatabhāvañca tasmiṃ ajjhāropetvā gahitā, parāmaṭṭhā ca samānā bālalapanāyeva hutvā yāva paṇḍitā na samanuyuñjanti, tāva gacchanti, pātubhavanti ca, paṇḍitehi samanuyuñjiyamānā pana anavaṭṭhitavatthukā avimaddakkhamā sūriyuggamane ussāvabindū viya, khajjopanakā viya ca bhijjanti, vinassanti cāti.

'Evaṃgatikā' means having such an outcome, having such a conclusion; that is, culminating in being shattered and destroyed through such inquiry. And here, the word 'gati' has the meaning of 'conclusion' (niṭṭhā), like the word 'gati' in passages such as, "For a Great Man endowed with which [marks], there are only two possible destinies (gatiyo)" (DN 14, etc.). This is what is meant: These grounds for views, which are called views, having been taken up and misapprehended by superimposing upon that ultimate reality a self and a state of eternity which in the ultimate sense do not exist, become just like the babbling of fools; and they proceed and appear for as long as the wise do not inquire into them. But when inquired into by the wise, being without a stable basis and unable to withstand scrutiny, they are shattered and destroyed like dewdrops at sunrise and like fireflies.

Tatthāyaṃ anuyuñjane saṅkhepakathā – yadi hi parehi kappito attā loko vā sassato siyā, tassa nibbikāratāya purimarūpāvijahanato kassaci visesādhānassa kātumasakkuṇeyyatāya ahitato nivattanatthaṃ, hite ca paṭipajjanatthaṃ upadeso eva sassatavādino nippayojano siyā, kathaṃ vā tena so upadeso pavattīyati vikārābhāvato. Evañca sati parikappitassa attano ajaṭākāsassa viya dānādikiriyā, hiṃsādikiriyā ca na sambhavati, tathā sukhassa, dukkhassa ca anubhavananibandho eva sassatavādino na yujjati kammabaddhābhāvato. Jātiādīnañca asambhavato vimokkho na bhaveyya, atha pana dhammamattaṃ tassa uppajjati ceva vinassati ca, yassa vasenāyaṃ kiriyādivohāroti vadeyya, evampi [V 1.0356] purimarūpāvijahanena avaṭṭhitassa attano dhammamattanti na sakkā sambhāvetuṃ, te vā panassa dhammā avatthābhūtā, tasmā tassa uppannā aññe vā siyuṃ anaññe vā, yadi aññe, na tāhi avatthāhi tassa uppannāhipi koci viseso atthi, yāhi karoti paṭisaṃvedeti cavati uppajjati cāti icchitaṃ, evañca dhammakappanāpi [M 1.0406] niratthakā siyā, tasmā tadavattho eva yathāvuttadoso, athānaññe, uppādavināsavantīhi avatthāhi anaññassa attano tāsaṃ viya uppādavināsasabbhāvato kuto bhaveyya niccatāvakāso, tāsampi vā attano viya niccatāpavatti, tasmā bandhavimokkhānaṃ asambhavo evāti na yujjatiyeva sassatavādo, na cettha koci vādī dhammānaṃ sassatabhāve parisuddaṃ yuttiṃ vattuṃ samattho bhaveyya, yuttirahitañca vacanaṃ na paṇḍitānaṃ cittaṃ ārādheti, tenāvocumha “yāva paṇḍitā na samanuyuñjanti, tāva gacchanti, pātubhavanti cā”ti.

Therein, this is the concise statement on inquiry: For if the self or the world conceived by others were eternal, then due to its immutable nature, its non-abandonment of its former state, and the inability to create any special distinction, the instruction of the eternalist for the purpose of turning away from the unbeneficial and undertaking the beneficial would be useless. Or how could that instruction be put forth by him, due to the absence of change? And this being so, for a conceived self, actions such as giving and harming would not be possible, just as for the untangled sky; likewise, for the eternalist, the connection with experiencing pleasure and pain would not be tenable, due to the absence of a connection with kamma. And due to the impossibility of birth and so forth, there would be no liberation. Now, if one were to say that for it a mere phenomenon arises and ceases, by the power of which this discourse on action and so on occurs, even so, it is not possible to conceive of a 'mere phenomenon' for a stable self that does not abandon its former nature. Or, those phenomena of his are states. Therefore, those that have arisen for it might be other than it or not other. If they are other, then by those states that have arisen for it, there is no special quality for it, by which it acts, feels, passes away, and is reborn—so it is wished. And thus, the positing of phenomena would be meaningless. Therefore, the aforementioned fault exists in that very state. Now, if they are not other, then for a self that is not other than the states which possess arising and ceasing, since there would be the existence of arising and ceasing just like those states, whence could there be an opportunity for permanence? Or for those states too, how could there be a permanent occurrence, like that of the self? Therefore, there is only the impossibility of bondage and liberation. Thus, the doctrine of eternalism is simply not tenable. And no proponent here would be able to state a pure reason for the eternal nature of phenomena. And a statement devoid of reason does not please the minds of the wise. Therefore we have said: "For as long as the wise do not inquire into them, they proceed and appear."

Sakāraṇaṃ sagatikanti ettha saha-saddo vijjamānattho “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu viya, na pana samavāyattho ca-saddena “tayidaṃ bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānātī”ti vuttassa diṭṭhigatassa samuccinitattā, “tañca tathāgato pajānātī”ti iminā ca kāraṇagatīnameva pajānanabhāvena vuttattā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tayidaṃ bhikkhave, kāraṇavantaṃ gativantaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ tathāgato pajānāti, na kevalañca tadeva, atha kho tassa kāraṇagatisaṅkhātaṃ tañca sabbanti. “Tato…pe… pajānātī”ti vuttavākyassa atthaṃ vuttanayena saṃvaṇṇeti “tato cā”tiādinā. Sabbaññutaññāṇassevidha vibhajananti pakaraṇānurūpamatthaṃ āha “sabbaññutaññāṇañcā”ti, tasmiṃ vā vutte tadadhiṭṭhānato āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ, tadavinābhāvato vā sabbampi dasabalādiñāṇaṃ gahitamevātipi tadeva vuttaṃ.

Herein, in "sakāraṇaṃ sagatikaṃ," the word 'saha' has the meaning of 'existing,' as in "salomako sapakkhako," etc., and not the meaning of 'combination.' This is because the wrong view mentioned in "tayidaṃ bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānāti" is aggregated by the 'ca' particle, and because by "tañca tathāgato pajānāti" it is stated that only the causes and destinations are known. This is what is meant: "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata knows this wrong view as having a cause and having a destination. And not only that, but indeed also all of that which is designated as its cause and destination." With "tato cā," etc., he explains the meaning of the sentence "Tato…pe… pajānāti" in the manner stated. On the grounds that "Herein is the analysis of the knowledge of omniscience," the Teacher stated the meaning appropriate to the context with "sabbaññutaññāṇañca." Or, when that is stated, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is included because it is its foundation; or, because of its inseparability, all the knowledges, such as the ten powers, are indeed included. Therefore, that very thing was stated.

Evaṃvidhanti “sīlañcā”tiādinā evaṃvuttappakāraṃ. Pajānantopīti ettha pi-saddena, api-saddena vā “tañcā”ti vutta ca-saddassa sambhāvanatthabhāvaṃ dasseti, tena tato diṭṭigatato uttaritaraṃ sārabhūtaṃ sīlādiguṇavisesampi tathāgato nābhinivisati, ko pana vādo vaṭṭāmiseti sambhāveti. “Aha”nti diṭṭimānavasena parāmasanākāradassanaṃ. Pajānāmīti ettha iti-saddena pakāratthena, nidassanatthena vā. “Mama”nti taṇhāvasena parāmasanākāraṃ dasseti. Taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparāmāsavasenāti taṇhādiṭṭhimānasaṅkhātaparāmāsavasena. Dhammasabhāvamatikkamitvā “ahaṃ mama”nti parato abhūtato āmasanaṃ parāmāso, taṇhādayo eva. Na hi taṃ atthi, yaṃ khandhesu “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā gahetabbaṃ siyā, aparāmasato [M 1.0407] aparāmasantassa assa tathāgatassa nibbuti viditāti sambandho. “Aparāmasato”ti cedaṃ nibbutipavedanāya (nibbutivedanassa dī. ni. ṭī. 1.36) hetugabbhavisesanaṃ[V 1.0357]. “Viditā”ti padamapekkhitvā kattari sāmivacanaṃ. Aparāmasato parāmāsarahitapaṭipattihetu assa tathāgatassa kattubhūtassa nibbuti asaṅkhatadhātu viditā, adhigatāti vā attho. “Aparāmasato”ti hedaṃ hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ.

"Evaṃvidhaṃ" refers to the type thus stated, beginning with "sīlañca." In "Pajānantopi," by the word 'pi' (or 'api'), he shows that the word 'ca' in "tañca" has the meaning of esteem. By that, he esteems thus: "The Tathāgata does not adhere even to the special qualities such as virtue, which are more excellent and essential than that wrong view; what then to say of worldly bait?" "Ahaṃ" shows the mode of misapprehension by way of view and conceit. In "pajānāmi," the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'manner' or 'example.' "Mama" shows the mode of misapprehension by way of craving. "Taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparāmāsavasena" means by way of the misapprehension designated as craving, view, and conceit. Transcending the true nature of things, touching upon "I" and "mine" externally and falsely is misapprehension; it is just craving and so on. For there is nothing in the aggregates that could be grasped as "I" or "mine." The connection is: "For that Tathāgata who does not misapprehend, due to not misapprehending, Nibbāna is known." And this "Aparāmasato" is a qualifier containing the cause for the declaration of Nibbāna. With reference to the word "Viditā," it is a genitive in the sense of the agent. The meaning is: due to the practice free from misapprehension ("Aparāmasato"), for that Tathāgata who is the agent, Nibbāna, the unconditioned element, is known, or attained. And this "Aparāmasato" is an ablative expression in the sense of cause.

“Aparāmāsapaccayā”ti paccattaññeva pavedanāya kāraṇadassanaṃ. Assāti kattāraṃ vatvāpi paccattaññevāti visesadassanatthaṃ puna kattuvacananti āha “sayameva attanāyevā”ti. Sayaṃ, attanāti vā bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ. Nipātapadañhetaṃ. “Aparāmasato”ti vacanato parāmāsānameva nibbuti idha desitā, taṃdesanāya eva tadaññesampi nibbutiyā sijjhanatoti dasseti “tesaṃ parāmāsakilesāna”nti iminā, parāmāsasaṅkhātānaṃ kilesānanti attho. Apica kāmaṃ “aparāmasato”ti vacanato parāmāsānameva nibbuti idha desitāti viññāyati, taṃdesanāya pana tadavasesānampi kilesānaṃ nibbuti desitā nāma bhavati pahānekaṭṭhatādibhāvato, tasmā tesampi nibbuti niddhāretvā dassetabbāti vuttaṃ “tesaṃ parāmāsakilesāna”nti, taṇhādiṭṭhimānasaṅkhātānaṃ parāmāsānaṃ, tadaññesañca kilesānanti attho. Gobalībaddanayo hesa. Nibbutīti ca nibbāyanabhūtā asaṅkhatadhātu, tañca bhagavā bodhimūleyeva patto, tasmā sā paccattaññeva viditāti.

"Aparāmāsapaccayā" shows the cause for the declaration being personal. Although the agent is stated with "assa," the agent is stated again with "paccattaññeva" for the purpose of showing a distinction; therefore the Teacher said "sayameva attanāyevā." Or, "sayaṃ" and "attanā" are adverbs; for this is a particle-word. Because it is said "aparāmasato," the Nibbāna of only the misapprehensions is taught here. To show that by that very teaching the Nibbāna of other defilements is also accomplished, he states "tesaṃ parāmāsakilesānaṃ," meaning "of the defilements designated as misapprehensions." Moreover, although it is indeed understood from the statement "aparāmasato" that only the Nibbāna of misapprehensions is taught here, by that teaching the Nibbāna of the remaining defilements also comes to be taught, because of their being a single object of abandonment, etc. Therefore, their Nibbāna should also be specified and shown; thus it was said "tesaṃ parāmāsakilesānaṃ," meaning of the misapprehensions designated as craving, view, and conceit, and also of other defilements. For this is the gobalībaddanaya. And "nibbuti" is the unconditioned element which is the state of being extinguished. The Blessed One attained that at the very foot of the Bodhi tree; therefore, it is known personally.

Yathāpaṭipannenāti yena paṭipannena. Tappaṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ “tāsaṃyeva…pe… ādimāhā”ti anusandhidassanaṃ. Kasmā pana vedanānaññeva kammaṭṭhānamācikkhatīti āha “yāsū”tiādi, iminā desanāvilāsaṃ dasseti. Desanāvilāsappatto hi bhagavā desanākusalo khandhāyatanādivasena anekavidhāsu catusaccadesanāsu sambhavantīsupi diṭṭhigatikā vedanāsu micchāpaṭipattiyā diṭṭhigahanaṃ pakkhandāti dassanatthaṃ tathāpakkhandanamūlabhūtā vedanāyeva pariññābhūmibhāvena uddharatīti. Idhāti imasmiṃ vāde. Evaṃ etthātipi. Kammaṭṭhānanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Ettha hi [M 1.0408] vedanāgahaṇena gahitā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ. Vedanānaṃ samudayaggahaṇena gahito avijjāsamudayo samudayasaccaṃ, atthaṅgamanissaraṇapariyāyehi nirodhasaccaṃ, “yathābhūtaṃ viditvā”ti etena maggasaccanti evaṃ cattāri saccāni veditabbāni. “Yathābhūtaṃ viditvā”ti idaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇatthapadanti tadatthaṃ vibhajja dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Visesato hi “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo”tiādilakkhaṇānaṃ vasena samudayādīsu attho yathārahaṃ vibhajja dassetabbo. Avisesato pana vedanāya samudayādīni vipassanāpaññāya ārammaṇapaṭivedhavasena, maggapaññāya asammohapaṭivedhavasena jānitvā [V 1.0358] paṭivijjhitvāti attho. Paccayasamudayaṭṭhenāti “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.404; saṃ. ni. 2.21; udā. 1) vuttalakkhaṇena avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ uppādena ceva maggena asamugghāṭena ca. Yāva hi maggena na samugghāṭīyati, tāva paccayoti vuccati. Nibbattilakkhaṇanti uppādalakkhaṇaṃ, jātinti attho. Pañcannaṃ lakkhaṇānanti ettha ca catunnampi paccayānaṃ uppādalakkhaṇameva aggahetvā paccayalakkhaṇampi gahetabbaṃ samudayaṃ paṭicca tesaṃ yathārahaṃ upakārakattā. Tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ “maggena asamugghāṭena cā”ti. Paccayanirodhaṭṭhenāti “imasmiṃ niruddhe idaṃ niruddhaṃ hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.406; udā. 3; saṃ. ni. 2.41) vuttalakkhaṇena avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ nirodhena ceva maggena samugghāṭena ca. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇanti nirodhalakkhaṇaṃ, bhaṅganti attho. Vayanti nirodhaṃ. Yanti yasmā paccayabhāvasaṅkhātahetuto. Vedanaṃ paṭiccāti purimuppannaṃ ārammaṇādipaccayabhūtaṃ vedanaṃ labhitvā. Sukhaṃ somanassanti sukhañceva somanassañca. Ayanti purimavedanāya yathārahaṃ pacchimuppannānaṃ sukhasomanassānaṃ paccayabhāvo. Assādo nāma assāditabboti katvā.

‘Yathāpaṭipannena’ means by which practice. To show that practice, the statement ‘tāsaṃyeva…pe… ādimāhā’ is a showing of the connection. But why does he teach only feelings as the meditation subject? The teacher says ‘yāsū’ and so on; by this, he shows the elegance of the teaching. For the Blessed One, having attained the elegance of teaching and being skilled in teaching—although there are many kinds of teachings of the Four Noble Truths by way of aggregates, sense bases, and so on—in order to show that those with wrong views rush into a thicket of views through wrong practice in regard to feelings, he singles out only feelings, which are the root of such rushing in, as the ground for full understanding. ‘Idha’ means in this doctrine. Likewise for ‘ettha’. ‘Kammaṭṭhāna’ means the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths. For here, by the taking up of feeling, the five aggregates subject to clinging are the truth of suffering. By the taking up of the origin of feelings, the arising of ignorance is the truth of origin. By the modes of cessation and escape, the truth of cessation is stated. By ‘yathābhūtaṃ viditvā’ (having known as it truly is), the truth of the path is stated. Thus the four truths should be known. The phrase ‘yathābhūtaṃ viditvā’ is a term with the meaning of analytical explanation; therefore, to show that meaning by analyzing it, ‘tatthā’ and so on was stated. Specifically, the meaning in origin and so on should be shown, having been analyzed appropriately, by way of the characteristics such as ‘from the origin of ignorance is the origin of feeling.’ Generally, however, the meaning is: having known the origin, etc., of feeling through insight-wisdom by way of penetrating the object, and having penetrated it through path-wisdom by way of penetrating without delusion. ‘By the meaning of the arising of conditions’ means by the characteristic stated as ‘when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises,’ and by the arising of conditions such as ignorance, and by their not being uprooted by the path. For as long as a condition is not uprooted by the path, so long is it called a ‘condition.’ ‘Nibbattilakkhaṇa’ (the characteristic of production) means the characteristic of arising; the meaning is birth. And here in the phrase ‘of the five characteristics,’ not taking only the characteristic of arising of the four conditions, the characteristic of being a condition should also be taken, because they are appropriately helpful in dependence on the origin. And for that very reason it was explained as: ‘and by their not being uprooted by the path.’ ‘By the meaning of the cessation of conditions’ means by the characteristic stated as ‘when this ceases, that ceases; from the cessation of this, that ceases,’ and by the cessation of conditions such as ignorance, and by their being uprooted by the path. ‘Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa’ (the characteristic of change) means the characteristic of cessation; the meaning is dissolution. ‘Vayaṃ’ means cessation. ‘Yaṃ’ means because of the cause designated as the state of being a condition. ‘Vedanaṃ paṭicca’ (dependent on feeling) means having obtained a previously arisen feeling that has become a condition such as an object. ‘Sukhaṃ somanassaṃ’ (pleasure and joy) means both pleasure and joy. ‘Ayaṃ’ means the state of being a condition, as appropriate, for subsequently arisen pleasure and joy in relation to the previous feeling. It is called ‘assādo’ (gratification) because it is to be gratified in.

Aparo nayo – yanti sukhaṃ, somanassañca. Ayanti ca napuṃsakaliṅgena niddiṭṭhaṃ sukhasomanassameva assādapadamapekkhitvā pulliṅgena niddisīyati, imasmiṃ pana vikappe sukhasomanassānaṃ uppādoyeva tehi uppādavantehi niddiṭṭho, sattiyā, sattimato ca abhinnattā. Na hi sukhasomanassamantarena tesaṃ uppādo labbhati. Iti purimavedanaṃ paṭicca sukhasomanassuppādopi purimavedanāya assādo nāma assādīyateti katvā[M 1.0409]. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – purimamuppannaṃ vedanaṃ ārabbha somanassuppattiyaṃ yo purimavedanāya paccayabhāvasaṅkhāto assādetabbākāro, somanassassa vā uppādasaṅkhāto tadassādanākāro, ayaṃ purimavedanāya assādoti. Kathaṃ pana vedanaṃ ārabbha sukhaṃ uppajjati, nanu phoṭṭhabbārammaṇanti? Cetasikasukhasseva ārabbha pavattiyamadhippetattā nāyaṃ doso. Ārabbha pavattiyañhi visesanameva somanassaggahaṇaṃ somanassaṃ sukhanti yathā “rukkho sīsapā”ti aññapaccayavasena uppattiyaṃ pana kāyikasukhampi assādoyeva, yathālābhakathā vā esāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Another method: ‘Yaṃ’ means pleasure and joy. And ‘ayaṃ’ is indicated in the masculine gender with reference to the word ‘assāda’, which refers to ‘sukhasomanassaṃ’ (pleasure and joy), itself indicated in the neuter gender. Furthermore, in this alternative, the very arising of pleasure and joy is indicated by them, which possess arising, because of the non-difference between the potentiality and the possessor of potentiality. For their arising is not obtained without pleasure and joy. Thus, because the arising of pleasure and joy dependent on a previous feeling is also gratified in, it is called the gratification of the previous feeling. And this is the concise meaning here: when there is the arising of joy with a previously arisen feeling as its object, whatever mode of being gratified in, designated as the state of being a condition, belongs to the previous feeling, or whatever mode of its gratification, designated as the arising of joy, exists—this is the gratification of the previous feeling. But how does pleasure arise having a feeling as its object? Is it not the case that it has a tangible object? This fault does not arise, because what is intended is its occurrence having only mental pleasure as its object. For in an occurrence having it as an object, the use of the word ‘somanassa’ is just a qualifier, as in ‘somanassaṃ sukhaṃ’ (joy which is pleasure), just like ‘rukkho sīsapā’ (a tree which is a sīsapā). Furthermore, when there is an arising by way of another condition, bodily pleasure is also just gratification. Or, this should be seen as a statement according to what is obtained.

“Yā vedanā aniccā”tiādinā sattimatā satti nidassitā. Tatrāyamattho – yā vedanā hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā, jarāya, maraṇena cāti dvidhā vipariṇāmetabbaṭṭhena vipariṇāmadhammā. Tassā evaṃbhūtāya ayaṃ aniccadukkhavipariṇāmabhāvo [V 1.0359] vedanāya sabbāyapiādīnavoti. Ādīnaṃ paramakāruññaṃ vāti pavattati etasmāti hi ādīnavo. Apicaādīnaṃ ativiya kapaṇaṃ pavattanaṭṭhena kapaṇamanusso ādīnavo, ayampi evaṃsabhāvoti tathā vuccati. Sattimatā hi satti abhinnā tadavinābhāvato.

By ‘yā vedanā aniccā’ (whatever feeling is impermanent) and so on, the potentiality is shown by the possessor of potentiality. Herein, this is the meaning: whatever feeling, by the meaning of non-existence after having been, is impermanent; by the meaning of being oppressed by arising and passing away, is suffering; and by the meaning of being subject to change in two ways—that is, by aging and by death—it has the nature of change. For all such feeling, this state of being impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is the drawback. For from this, a pitiable state (ādīnaṃ) or extreme compassion proceeds (vāti); therefore it is called ‘ādīnavo’ (drawback). Moreover, because it causes a pitiable (ādīnaṃ), very wretched state, a wretched person is called ‘ādīnavo’. This fault, too, has such a nature, and therefore is so called. For the potentiality is inseparable from the possessor of potentiality, because of their inseparability.

Ettha ca “aniccā”ti iminā saṅkhāradukkhatāvasena upekkhāvedanāya, sabbāsu vā vedanāsuādīnavamāha, “dukkhā”ti iminā dukkhadukkhatāvasenadukkhavedanāya, “vipariṇāmadhammā”ti iminā vipariṇāmadukkhatāvasena sukhavedanāya. Avisesena vā tīṇipi padāni tissannampi vedanānaṃ vasena yojetabbāni. Chandarāgavinayoti chandasaṅkhātarāgavinayanaṃ vināso. “Atthavasā liṅgavibhattivipariṇāmo”ti vacanato yaṃ chandarāgappahānanti yojetabbaṃ. Pariyāyavacanamevidaṃ padadvayaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ viditvāti maggassa vuttattā magganibbānavasena vā yathākkamaṃ yojanāpi vaṭṭati. Vedanāyāti nissakkavacanaṃ. Nissaraṇanti nekkhammaṃ. Yāva hi vedanāpaṭibaddhaṃ chandarāgaṃ nappajahati, tāvāyaṃ puriso vedanāya allīnoyeva hoti. Yadā pana taṃ chandarāgaṃ pajahati, tadāyaṃ puriso vedanāya nissaṭo visaṃyutto hoti, tasmā chandarāgappahānaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tabbacanena [M 1.0410] pana vedanāsahajātanissayārammaṇabhūtā rūpārūpadhammā gahitā eva hontītipi pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi nissaraṇavacanaṃ siddhameva. Vedanāsīsena hi desanā āgatā, tattha pana kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Lakkhaṇahāravasenāpi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Vuttañhi āyasmatā mahākaccānattherena –

Here, by ‘impermanent,’ he states the drawback in the feeling of equanimity by way of the suffering inherent in formations, or alternatively, the drawback in all feelings. By ‘suffering,’ he states the drawback in painful feeling by way of the suffering of pain. By ‘subject to change,’ he states the drawback in pleasant feeling by way of the suffering of alteration. Alternatively, all three terms can be applied without distinction to all three types of feelings. ‘The removal of desire and lust’ means the destruction, the removal of the lust known as desire. In accordance with the grammatical rule, ‘There is a transformation of gender and case-ending according to the meaning,’ this should be connected with ‘the abandoning of desire and lust.’ These two terms are merely synonyms. Since the path has been stated in the phrase ‘having known it as it really is,’ a sequential application by way of the path and Nibbāna is also suitable. The word ‘from feeling’ (vedanāya) is a term of departure. ‘Escape’ (nissaraṇa) means renunciation. For as long as a person does not abandon the desire and lust connected with feeling, that person remains attached to feeling. But when they abandon that desire and lust, that person becomes freed and detached from feeling. Therefore, the abandoning of desire and lust is called the escape from feeling. Moreover, by this statement, the material and immaterial phenomena that are co-nascent with feeling, serve as its support, or are its object, are indeed included. Thus, the statement of ‘escape’ from the five aggregates of clinging is established. For the teaching has been delivered with feeling as its heading, and the reason for this has already been stated below. This meaning should also be clarified by way of the Lakkhaṇahāra method. For it was said by the Venerable Mahākaccāna:

“Vuttamhi ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā keci;

Vuttā bhavanti sabbo, so hāro lakkhaṇo nāmā”ti. (netti. 485);

“When one phenomenon has been stated, whatever phenomena have a single characteristic, they are thereby stated. That entire method is called the ‘characteristic’ method.”

Kāmupādānamūlakattā sesupādānānaṃ pahīne ca kāmupādāne upādānasesābhāvato “vigatachandarāgatāya anupādāno”ti vuttaṃ, etena “anupādāvimutto”ti etassatthaṃ saṅkhepena dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – vigatachandarāgatāya anupādāno, anupādānattā ca anupādāvimuttoti. Tamatthaṃ vitthāretuṃ, samatthetuṃ vā “yasmi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmiṃ upādāneti sesupādānamūlabhūte kāmupādāne. Tassāti kāmupādānassa. Anupādiyitvāti chandarāgavasena anādiyitvā, etena “anupādāvimutto”ti padassa ya-kāralopena samāsabhāvaṃ, byāsabhāvaṃ vā dasseti.

Because sensual clinging is the root of the other kinds of clinging, and because when sensual clinging is abandoned there is no remainder of clinging, it is said, ‘due to being without desire and lust, one is without clinging.’ By this, he briefly shows the meaning of ‘liberated without clinging.’ This is what is meant: due to being without desire and lust, one is without clinging; and due to being without clinging, one is liberated without clinging. To elaborate or to establish that meaning, the passage beginning with ‘in which’ was stated. There, ‘in which clinging’ refers to sensual clinging, which is the root of the other kinds of clinging. ‘Of that’ refers to sensual clinging. ‘Without grasping’ means not taking up by way of desire and lust. By this, he shows that the word ‘liberated without clinging’ (anupādāvimutto) is either a compound, through the elision of the letter ‘ya,’ or an analytical phrase.

37. “Ime [V 1.0360] kho”tiādi yathāpuṭṭhassa dhammassa vissajjitabhāvena nigamanavacanaṃ, “pajānātī”ti vuttapajānanameva ca ima-saddena niddiṭṭhanti dassetuṃ “ye te”tiādimāha. Ye te sabbaññutaññāṇadhamme…pe… apucchiṃ, yehi sabbaññutaññāṇadhammehi…pe… vadeyyuṃ, tañca…pe… pajānātīti evaṃ niddiṭṭhā ime sabbaññutaññāṇadhammā gambhīrā…pe… paṇḍitavedanīyā cāti veditabbāti yojanā. “Eva”ntiādi piṇḍatthadassanaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi “anupādāvimutto bhikkhave, tathāgato”ti iminā aggamaggaphaluppattiṃ dasseti, “vedanānaṃ, samudayañcā”tiādinā ca catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathāpi yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā imaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ sakāraṇaṃ sagatikaṃ pabhedato vibhajituṃ samattho hoti, tassā padaṭṭhānena ceva saddhiṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya uppattibhūmiyā ca tadeva pākaṭataraṃ kattukāmo dhammarājā evaṃ dassetīti vuttaṃ “tadeva niyyātita”nti, nigamitaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho[M 1.0411]. Antarāti pucchitavissajjitadhammadassanavacanānamantarā diṭṭhiyo vibhattā tassa pajānanākāradassanavasenāti attho.

37. ‘These indeed,’ etc., is a concluding statement, being the answer concerning the quality about which he was questioned. To show that the very understanding mentioned in ‘he understands’ is indicated by this word ‘these,’ he said, ‘Those which,’ etc. The connection is to be understood thus: ‘Those qualities of omniscient knowledge... about which I asked, by which qualities of omniscient knowledge... they would speak, and that... he understands’—these qualities of omniscient knowledge thus indicated are profound... to be experienced by the wise. ‘Thus,’ etc., shows the condensed meaning. Although ‘the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is liberated through non-clinging’ indicates the attainment of the highest path and its fruit, and ‘the arising of feelings,’ etc., refers to the meditation subject of the four noble truths, nevertheless, because of his thorough penetration of that element of phenomena, he is capable of analyzing this viewpoint with its cause and its future course, classifying it in detail. The King of Dhamma, wishing to make that very thing clearer—together with its proximate cause, the preliminary practice, and the ground of its arising—teaches in this way. Therefore, it is said, ‘that very thing is finalized,’ meaning it is concluded, it is finished. ‘In between’ means that the views are distinguished in the interval between the statements showing the questioned and answered Dhamma, by way of showing the mode of his understanding.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the First Recitation Section.

Ekaccasassatavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Doctrine of Partial Eternalism

38. “Ekaccasassatikā”ti taddhitapadaṃ samāsapadena vibhāvetuṃ “ekaccasassatavādā”ti vuttaṃ. Sattesu, saṅkhāresu ca ekaccaṃ sassatametassāti ekaccasassato, vādo, so etesanti ekaccasassatikā taddhitavasena, samāsavasena pana ekaccasassato vādo etesanti ekaccasassatavādā. Esa nayo ekaccaasassatikapadepi. Nanu ca “ekaccasassatikā”ti vutte tadaññesaṃ ekaccaasassatikabhāvasanniṭṭhānaṃ siddhamevāti? Saccaṃ atthato, saddato pana asiddhameva tasmā saddato pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ tathā vuttaṃ. Na hi idha sāvasesaṃ katvā dhammaṃ deseti dhammassāmī. “Issaro nicco, aññe sattā aniccā”ti evaṃpavattavādā sattekaccasassatikā seyyathāpi issaravādā. Tathā “nicco brahmā, aññe aniccā”ti evaṃpavattavādāpi. “Paramāṇavo niccā, dviaṇukādayo aniccā”ti (visisikadassane sattamaparicchede paṭhamakaṇḍe passitabbaṃ) evaṃpavattavādā saṅkhārekaccasassatikā seyyathāpi kāṇādā. Tathā “cakkhādayo aniccā, viññāṇaṃ nicca”nti (nyāyadassane, visesikadassane ca passitabbaṃ) evaṃpavattavādāpi[V 1.0361]. Idhāti “ekaccasassatikā”ti imasmiṃ pade, imissā vā desanāya. Gahitāti vuttā, desitabbabhāvena vā desanāñāṇena samādinnā tathā ceva desitattā. Tathā hi idha purimakā tayo vādā sattavasena, catuttho saṅkhāravasena desito. “Saṅkhārekaccasassatikā”ti idaṃ pana tehi sassatabhāvena gayhamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ yāthāvasabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ, na pana ekaccasassatikamatadassanavasena. Tassa hi sassatābhimataṃ asaṅkhatamevāti laddhi. Tenevāha pāḷiyaṃ “cittanti vā…pe… ṭhassatī”ti. Na hi yassa sabhāvassa paccayehi abhisaṅkhatabhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, tasseva niccadhuvādibhāvo anummattakena sakkā paṭijānituṃ, etena ca “uppādavayadhuvatāyuttā sabhāvā siyā niccā, siyā aniccā, siyā [M 1.0412] na vattabbā”tiādinā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.38) pavattasattabhaṅgavādassa ayuttatā vibhāvitā hoti.

38. To explain the derivative word 'ekaccasassatikā' by means of a compound word, it is said 'ekaccasassatavādā'. Among beings and conditioned phenomena, something is eternal; therefore, this doctrine is 'ekaccasassato' (partially eternal). This doctrine is theirs; therefore, by way of derivation, they are 'ekaccasassatikā'. By way of compounding, however, a partially eternal doctrine is theirs; therefore, they are 'ekaccasassatavādā'. This method should also be known in the case of the term 'ekaccaasassatikā'. Now, when 'ekaccasassatikā' is said, is not the conclusion of the state of being partially non-eternal for others already established? In terms of meaning, this is true, but in terms of wording, it is not established. Therefore, to show it by making it more evident in terms of wording, it was said thus. For here, the Master of the Dhamma does not teach the Dhamma leaving a remainder. Those whose doctrine proceeds thus: 'The Lord is eternal, other beings are non-eternal,' are partial-eternalists regarding beings (sattekaccasassatikā), just like the proponents of a Creator-God. Similarly, those whose doctrine proceeds thus: 'Brahmā is eternal, others are non-eternal,' are also of this kind. Those whose doctrine proceeds thus: 'Atoms are eternal, dyads, etc., are non-eternal,' are partial-eternalists regarding conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārekaccasassatikā), just like the followers of Kaṇāda. Similarly, those whose doctrine proceeds thus: 'The eye, etc., are non-eternal, consciousness is eternal,' are also of this kind. 'Here' means in this term 'ekaccasassatikā', or in this discourse. 'Grasped' means spoken of, or undertaken by the knowledge of teaching as fit to be taught, because it was taught in just that way. For here, the first three doctrines were taught by way of beings, the fourth by way of conditioned phenomena. However, this phrase 'saṅkhārekaccasassatikā' was said by way of showing the real nature of the phenomena that are grasped by them as being eternal, and not by way of showing the view of the partial-eternalists. For their doctrine is that what is considered eternal is only the unconditioned. Therefore, in the Pāḷi text, He said: 'Mind, or... will remain.' For it is not possible for a sane person to acknowledge the state of being permanent, stable, etc., of that very nature whose state of being conditioned by causes one acknowledges. And by this, the unsuitability of the sevenfold-assertion doctrine, which proceeds as 'Natures endowed with arising, passing away, and stability might be eternal, might be non-eternal, might be indescribable,' etc., is explained.

Tatrāyaṃ ayuttatāvibhāvanā – yadi hi “yena sabhāvena yo dhammo atthīti vuccati, teneva sabhāvena so dhammo natthī”ti vucceyya, siyā anekantavādo. Atha aññena, na siyā anekantavādo. Na cettha desantarādisambandhabhāvo yutto vattuṃ tassa sabbalokasiddhattā, vivādābhāvato ca. Ye pana vadanti “yathā suvaṇṇaghaṭena makuṭe kate ghaṭabhāvo nassati, makuṭabhāvo uppajjati, suvaṇṇabhāvo tiṭṭhatiyeva, evaṃ sabbasabhāvānaṃ koci dhammo nassati, koci dhammo uppajjati, sabhāvo eva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Te vattabbā “kiṃ taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ, yaṃ ghaṭe, makuṭe ca avaṭṭhitaṃ, yadi rūpādi, so saddo viya anicco. Atha rūpādisamūho sammutimattaṃ, na tassa atthitā vā natthitā vā niccatā vā labbhatī”ti, tasmā anekantavādo na siyā. Dhammānañca dhammino aññathānaññathā ca pavattiyaṃ doso vuttoyeva sassatavādavicāraṇāyaṃ. Tasmā so tattha vuttanayena veditabbo. Apica na niccāniccanavattabbarūpo attā, loko ca paramatthato vijjamānatāparijānanato yathā niccādīnaṃ aññataraṃ rūpaṃ, yathā vā dīpādayo. Na hi rūpādīnaṃ udayabbayasabhāvānaṃ niccāniccanavattabbasabhāvatā sakkā viññātuṃ, jīvassa ca niccādīsu aññataraṃ rūpaṃ siyāti, evaṃ sattabhaṅgo viya sesabhaṅgānampi asambhavoyevāti sattabhaṅgavādassa ayuttatā veditabbā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.38).

Therein, this is the explanation of its unsuitability: For if it were said, 'By the very same nature by which a phenomenon is said to exist, by that same nature that phenomenon is said not to exist,' there would be a doctrine of indeterminacy. But if it were by a different nature, there would not be a doctrine of indeterminacy. And here it is not suitable to speak of a connection with a different place, etc., because of its being established throughout the world and because of the absence of dispute. But as for those who say: 'Just as when a crown is made from a golden pot, the pot-state perishes, the crown-state arises, but the gold-state remains; even so, of all natures, some phenomenon perishes, some phenomenon arises, but the intrinsic nature alone remains,' they should be told: 'What is that gold which is established in the pot and in the crown? If it is form, etc., it is non-eternal like sound. If it is a collection of form, etc., that is a mere convention, its existence, non-existence, or permanence cannot be obtained.' Therefore, there would not be a doctrine of indeterminacy. And the fault in the occurrence of phenomena and that which possesses phenomena as both other and not other has already been stated in the investigation of the doctrine of eternalism. Therefore, that fault should be understood there in the manner stated. Furthermore, the self and the world are not of a nature that can be described as permanent, non-permanent, or indescribable, because their existence is acknowledged in an ultimate sense, just as form is one among permanent, etc., or just as lamps, etc., are. For it is not possible to know a nature that can be described as permanent, non-permanent, or indescribable for form, etc., which have the nature of arising and passing away; and the nature of the life-principle would be one among permanent, etc. Thus, just as the sevenfold assertion is impossible, so too are the remaining assertions impossible. Therefore, the unsuitability of the sevenfold-assertion doctrine should be known.

Nanu ca “ekacce dhammā sassatā, ekacce asassatā”ti etasmiṃ vāde cakkhādīnaṃ asassatabhāvasanniṭṭhānaṃ yathāsabhāvāvabodho eva, atha evaṃvādīnaṃ kathaṃ micchādassanaṃ siyāti, ko vā evamāha “cakkhādīnaṃ asassatabhāvasanniṭṭhānaṃ micchādassana”nti? Asassatesuyeva pana [V 1.0362] kesañci dhammānaṃ sassatabhāvasanniṭṭhānaṃ idha micchādassananti gahetabbaṃ, tena pana ekavāde pavattamānena cakkhādīnaṃ asassatabhāvāvabodho vidūsito saṃsaṭṭhabhāvato visasaṃsaṭṭho viya sappipiṇḍo, tato ca tassa sakiccakaraṇāsamatthatāya sammādassanapakkhe ṭhapetabbataṃ nārahatīti. Asassatabhāvena nicchitāpi vā cakkhuādayo [M 1.0413] samāropitajīvasabhāvā eva diṭṭhigatikehi gayhantīti tadavabodhassa micchādassanabhāvo na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Tenevāha pāḷiyaṃ “cakkhuṃ itipi…pe… kāyo itipi ayaṃ attā”tiādi. Evañca katvā asaṅkhatāya, saṅkhatāya ca dhātuyā vasena yathākkamaṃ “ekacce dhammā sassatā, ekacce asassatā”ti evaṃpavatto vibhajjavādopi ekaccasassatavādoyeva bhaveyyāti evampakārā codanā anavakāsā hoti aviparītadhammasabhāvapaṭipattibhāvato. Aviparītadhammasabhāvapaṭipattiyeva hesa vuttanayena asaṃsaṭṭhattā, anāropitajīvasabhāvattā ca.

Is it not so that in this doctrine, 'Some things are eternal, some are not eternal,' the determination of the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth is indeed the understanding of their true nature? Then how could it be a wrong view for those who hold such a doctrine? Or who says thus, 'The determination of the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth is a wrong view'? However, it should be understood that here, the determination of the eternal nature of some phenomena, even among the impermanent ones, is wrong view. But by that which proceeds as a single doctrine, the understanding of the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth is corrupted, due to being mixed, like a ball of ghee mixed with poison. And therefore, due to its inability to perform its own function, it is not worthy of being placed in the category of right view. Or, although the eye and so forth are determined to be impermanent, they are grasped by those with speculative views as having a superimposed nature of a living soul, so the state of that understanding being a wrong view cannot be prevented. For this reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: 'The eye is the self... the body is the self,' and so on. And for this reason, by means of the unconditioned and conditioned elements respectively, the view that proceeds thus, 'Some things are eternal, some are not eternal,' even such an analytical doctrine would become only a partial-eternalist doctrine. Thus, an objection of this kind is baseless, because of the practice according to the undeviating true nature of things. For this is indeed the practice according to the undeviating true nature of things because, in the way stated, it is unmixed and has no superimposed nature of a living soul.

Etthāha – purimasmimpisassatavāde asassatānaṃ dhammānaṃ “sassatā”ti gahaṇaṃ visesato micchādassanaṃ bhavati. Sassatānaṃ pana “sassatā”ti gāho na micchādassanaṃ yathāsabhāvaggāhabhāvato. Evañca sati imassa vādassa vādantaratā na vattabbā, idha viya purimepi ekaccesveva dhammesu sassataggāhasambhavatoti, vattabbāyeva asassatesveva “kecideva dhammā sassatā, keci asassatā”ti parikappanāvasena gahetabbadhammesu vibhāgappavattiyā imassa vādassa dassitattā. Nanu ca ekadesassa samudāyantogadhattā ayaṃ sappadesasassataggāho purimasmiṃ nippadesasassataggāhe samodhānaṃ gaccheyyātī? Tathāpi na sakkā vattuṃ vādī tabbisayavisesavasena vādadvayassa pavattattā. Aññe eva hi diṭṭhigatikā “sabbe dhammā sassatā”ti abhiniviṭṭhā, aññe “ekacceva sassatā, ekacce asassatā”ti. Saṅkhārānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ, ekadesapariggaho ca vādadvayassa paribyattoyeva. Kiñca bhiyyo – anekavidhasamussaye, ekavidhasamussaye ca khandhapabandhena abhinivesabhāvato tathā na sakkā vattuṃ. Catubbidhopi hi sassatavādī jātivisesavasena nānāvidharūpakāyasannissaye eva arūpadhammapuñje sassatābhinivesī jāto abhiññāṇena, anussavādīhi ca rūpakāyabhedagahaṇato. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “tato cuto amutra udapādi”nti, (dī. ni. 1.244; ma. ni. 1.148; pārā. 12) “cavanti upapajjantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.255; ma. ni. 1.148; pārā. 12) ca ādi. Visesalābhī pana ekaccasassatiko anupadhāritabhedasamussaye dhammapabandhe sassatākāragahaṇena abhinivesaṃ janesi ekabhavapariyāpannakhandhasantānavisayattā tadabhinivesassa. Tathā hi tīsupi vādesu “taṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati[M 1.0414], tato paraṃ nānussaratī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Takkīnaṃ pana ubhinnampi [V 1.0363] sassatekaccasassatavādīnaṃ sassatābhinivesaviseso rūpārūpadhammavisayatāya supākaṭoyevāti.

Here one says: In the previous eternalist doctrine as well, the grasping of impermanent things as 'eternal' is especially a wrong view. But the grasping of eternal things as 'eternal' is not a wrong view, because of grasping according to their true nature. This being so, it should not be said that this doctrine is a different doctrine, because, as in this case, in the previous one too, the grasping of eternity is possible only with regard to some things. It must indeed be said that it is a different doctrine, because this doctrine is shown by the occurrence of a division among the things to be grasped, by way of the speculation 'some things are eternal, some are not eternal' precisely among the impermanent things. Is it not so that since a part is included in the whole, this grasping of eternity with parts would merge into the previous grasping of eternity without parts? Even so, it cannot be said, because the two doctrines proceed by way of the distinction of their respective objects. For some with speculative views are intent on 'all things are eternal,' and others on 'some are eternal, some are not eternal.' The taking up of formations without remainder and the grasping of a part are indeed a clear distinction of the two doctrines. Furthermore, because of the adherence to the continuity of aggregates in a manifold collection and in a single-type collection, it cannot be said so. For the fourfold eternalist, by way of distinctions in birth, has become one who adheres to eternalism regarding the aggregate of formless things that is dependent on various kinds of form-bodies, by means of direct knowledge and by tradition, etc., grasping the destruction of the form-body. And so it is said: 'Having passed away from there, he arose there,' and 'they pass away and are reborn,' and so on. But the partial-eternalist who has attained a special state generates adherence by grasping the aspect of eternity in a continuity of things which is a collection whose distinctions are not ascertained, because that adherence has as its object the continuity of aggregates pertaining to a single existence. For indeed, in all three doctrines, only this much is said: 'He recollects that past life, but not beyond that.' But for the reasoners, the distinction in the adherence to eternalism of both the eternalists and the partial-eternalists is very clear due to its domain being material and immaterial things.

39. Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyīvivaṭṭavivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīsaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇampi asaṅkhyeyyakappānamatikkamena puna saṃvaṭṭanato, addhā-saddassa ca kālapariyāyattā evaṃ vuttanti āha “dīghassā”tiādi. Atikkamma ayanaṃ pavattanaṃ accayo. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ, upasaggavasena ca atthavisesavācakattā saṃ-saddena yutto vaṭṭa-saddo vināsavācīti vuttaṃ “vinassatī”ti, vatu-saddo vā gatiyameva. Saṅkhayatthajotakena pana saṃ-saddena yuttattā tadatthasambandhanena vināsattho labbhatīti dasseti “vinassatī”ti iminā. Saṅkhayavasena vattatīti hi saddato attho, ta-kārassa cettha ṭa-kārādeso. Vipattikaramahāmeghasamuppattitto hi paṭṭhāya yāva aṇusahagatopi saṅkhāro na hoti, tāva loko saṃvaṭṭatīti vuccati. Pāḷiyaṃ lokoti pathavīādibhājanaloko adhippeto tadavasesassa bāhullato, tadeva sandhāya “yebhuyyenā”ti vuttanti dasseti “ye”tiādinā. Uparibrahmalokesūti ābhassarabhūmito uparibhūmīsu. Agginā kappavuṭṭhānañhi idhādhippetaṃ, tenevāha pāḷiyaṃ “ābhassarasaṃvattanikā hontī”ti. Kasmā tadeva vuttanti ce? Tasseva bahulaṃ pavattanato. Ayañhi vāraniyamo –

39. Because of the dissolving again after the passing of the three incalculable aeons called 'remaining in dissolution,' 'evolving,' and 'remaining in evolution,' and because the word 'addhā' is a synonym for time, it is said thus; he says 'dīghassa,' etc. 'Accayo' means passing beyond, going, proceeding. Because roots have many meanings, and because prefixes are expressive of special meanings, the word 'vaṭṭa' joined with the word 'saṃ' is expressive of destruction; therefore it is said 'vinassati' (it perishes). Or, the word 'vatu' is only in the sense of 'going.' But because it is joined with the word 'saṃ' which indicates the meaning of 'ending,' by connection with that meaning, the meaning of 'destruction' is obtained; this he shows by 'vinassati.' For the meaning from the word is 'it proceeds by way of ending,' and here there is a substitution of 'ṭa' for 'ta'. For from the arising of the great, destructive cloud, for as long as not even a formation accompanied by an atom exists, so long is the world said to be dissolving. In the Pāḷi, by 'world' is intended the receptacle-world, such as the earth. Because of the abundance of what remains from that, referring to that very thing, it is said 'for the most part'; this he shows by 'ye,' etc. 'In the upper brahma-worlds' means in the planes above the Ābhassara plane. For here the destruction of the aeon by fire is intended, and for that reason he says in the Pāḷi, 'they are reborn in the Ābhassara realm.' If it is asked, 'Why is just that mentioned?' Because of its frequent occurrence. For this is the rule of the cycles:

“Sattasattagginā vārā, aṭṭhame aṭṭhame dakā;

Catusaṭṭhi yadā puṇṇā, eko vāyuvaro siyā”ti. (abhidhammatthavibhāvanīṭīkāya pañcamaparicchedavaṇṇanāyampi);

Seven are the occurrences by fire, and on each eighth time by water; when sixty-four are complete, there will be one cycle of wind.

Āruppesu vāti ettha vikappanatthena vā-saddena saṃvaṭṭamānalokadhātūhi aññalokadhātūsu vāti vikappeti. Na hi sabbe apāyasattā tadā rūpārūpabhavesu uppajjantīti sakkā viññātuṃ apāyesu dīghatarāyukānaṃ manussalokūpapattiyā asambhavato, manussalokūpapattiñca vinā tadā tesaṃ tatrūpapattiyā anupapattito. Niyatamicchādiṭṭhikopi hi saṃvaṭṭhamāne kappe nirayato na muccati, piṭṭhicakkavāḷeyeva nibbattatīti aṭṭhakathāsu (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.311) vuttaṃ. Satipi sabbasattānaṃ puññāpuññābhisaṅkhāramanasā nibbattabhāve bāhirapaccayehi vinā manasāva nibbattattā [M 1.0415] rūpāvacarasattā eva “manomayā”ti vuccanti, na pana bāhirapaccayapaṭiyattā tadaññeti dassetuṃ “manena nibbattattā manomayā”ti āha. Yadevaṃ kāmāvacarasattānampi opapātikānaṃ manomayabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, adhicittabhūtena atisayamanasā nibbattasattesuyeva manomayavohāratoti dassentena jhāna-saddena visesetvā [V 1.0364] “jhānamanenā”ti vuttaṃ. Evampi arūpāvacarasattānaṃ manomayabhāvo āpajjatīti? Na tattha bāhirapaccayehi nibbattetabbatāsaṅkāya abhāvena manasā eva nibbattāti avadhāraṇāsambhavato. Niruḷhovāyaṃ loke manomayavohāro rūpāvacarasattesu. Tathā hi annamayo pānamayo manomayo ānandamayo viññāṇamayoti pañcadhā attānaṃ vedavādino parikappenti. Ucchedavādepi vakkhati “dibbo rūpī manomayo”ti, (dī. ni. 1.87) te pana jhānānubhāvato pītibhakkhā sayaṃpabhā antalikkhacarāti āha “pīti tesa”ntiādi, tesaṃ attanova pabhā atthīti attho. Sobhanā vā ṭhāyī sabhā etesanti subhaṭṭhāyinotipi yujjati. Ukkaṃsenāti ābhassare sandhāya vuttaṃ. Parittābhāppamāṇābhā pana dve, cattāro ca kappe tiṭṭhanti. Aṭṭha kappeti catunnamasaṅkhyeyyakappānaṃ samudāyabhūte aṭṭha mahākappe.

Here, regarding the text āruppesu vā, by the word vā, which has the meaning of an alternative, it specifies an alternative thus: 'from the world-systems that are in the process of destruction, or in other world-systems'. For it cannot be known that all beings in the woeful states are reborn in the realms of form and formlessness at that time, due to the impossibility of arising in the human world for those with very long lifespans in the woeful states, and because, without arising in the human world, their rebirth there at that time cannot occur. Indeed, even one with fixed wrong view is not freed from hell when the aeon is being destroyed; he is reborn only in an outer world-system, as it is said in the commentaries. Although for all beings there is the state of being produced by the mind of meritorious and demeritorious formations, only beings of the form realm are called 'mind-made' because they are produced by mind alone, without external conditions. To show that others, being connected with external conditions, are not so called, he said, 'Because they are produced by the mind, they are mind-made'. If so, would the state of being mind-made not also apply to spontaneously born beings of the sense-sphere? It does not, because the designation 'mind-made' is used only for beings produced by a superior mind that is a higher consciousness. Showing this, having specified with the word 'jhāna', it is said 'by the jhāna-mind'. Even so, would the state of being mind-made not apply to beings of the formless realm? It does not, because there, due to the absence of any doubt about their being producible by external conditions, an exclusive emphasis such as 'they are produced by mind alone' is not possible. Moreover, this designation 'mind-made' is well-established in the world for beings of the form realm. For those who hold the Vedic doctrine conceive of the self in five ways: as made of food, made of drink, made of mind, made of bliss, and made of consciousness. Also in the doctrine of annihilationism, it will be said, 'divine, having form, mind-made'. Furthermore, he said 'joy is theirs' and so on, because those beings, through the power of jhāna, have joy as their food, are self-luminous, and travel through the sky; the meaning is that they have their own radiance. Alternatively, the etymology 'they have a beautiful, stable assembly' (sobhana ṭhāyī sabhā etesanti) is also suitable for subhaṭṭhāyino. The phrase 'at the utmost' is stated referring to the Ābhassara realm. The Parittābhā and Appamāṇābhā deities, however, last for two and four aeons respectively. 'Eight aeons' means eight great aeons, which are an aggregate of four incalculable aeons.

40. Vināsavācīyeva vaṭṭa-saddo paṭisedhajotakena upasaggena yuttattā saṇṭhāhanatthañāpakoti āha “saṇṭhātī”ti, anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ nibbattati, vaḍḍhatīti vā attho. Sampattimahāmeghasamuppattito hi paṭṭhāya pathavīsandhārakudakataṃsandhārakavāyuādīnaṃ samuppattivasena yāva candimasūriyānaṃ pātubhāvo, tāva loko vivaṭṭatīti vuccati. Pakatiyāti sabhāvena, tassa “suñña”nti iminā sambandho. Tathāsuññatāya kāraṇamāha “nibbattasattānaṃ natthitāyā”ti. Purimataraṃ aññesaṃ sattānamanuppannattāti bhāvo, tena yathā ekaccāni vimānāni tattha nibbattasattānaṃ chaḍḍitattā suññāni, na evamidanti dasseti.

40. The word vaṭṭa, which signifies destruction, when joined with a prefix indicating negation, indicates the meaning of establishing; hence he says saṇṭhāti (it becomes established). Alternatively, because roots have many meanings, the meaning is 'it arises' or 'it grows'. For from the arising of the great world-forming cloud onwards, for as long as the appearance of the moon and sun endures, the world is said to evolve by way of the arising of the earth-supporting water, the water-supporting wind, and so on. Pakatiyā means 'by nature', and its connection is with the word suññaṃ (empty). He states the reason for such emptiness thus: 'because of the non-existence of arisen beings'. The meaning is that this is because other beings had not yet arisen previously. By this, he shows that this is not like certain mansions that are empty because they have been abandoned by the beings who arose there.

Aparo nayo – sakakammassa paṭhamaṃ karaṇaṃ pakati, tāya nibbattasattānanti sambandho, tena yathā etassa attano kammabalena paṭhamaṃ nibbatti, na evaṃ aññesaṃ tassa purimataraṃ, samānakāle vā nibbatti atthi, tathā [M 1.0416] nibbattasattānaṃ natthitāya suññamidanti dasseti. Brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāno idha brahmakāyikā, tesaṃ nivāsatāya bhūmipi “brahmakāyikā”ti vuttā, brahmakāyikabhūmīti pana pāṭhebrahmakāyikānaṃ sambandhinī bhūmīti attho. Kattā sayaṃ kārako. Kāretā paresaṃ āṇāpako. Visuddhimagge pubbenivāsañāṇakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.408) vuttanayena, etena nibbattakkamaṃ kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānabhāve ca kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Kammaṃ upanissayabhāvena paccayo etissāti kammapaccayā. Atha vā tattha nibbattasattānaṃ vipaccanakakammassa sahakārīkārakabhāvato kammassa paccayāti kammapaccayā. Utu samuṭṭhānametissāti utusamuṭṭhānā. “Kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā”tipi samāsavasena pāṭho kammasahāyo paccayo, vuttanayena vā kammassa sahāyabhūto paccayoti kammapaccayo, so eva utu tathā, sova samuṭṭhānametissāti kammapaccayautusamuānā. Ratanabhūmīti ukkaṃsagatapuññakammānubhāvato [V 1.0365] ratanabhūtā bhūmi, na kevalaṃ bhūmiyeva, atha kho tapparivārāpīti āha “pakatī”tiādi. Pakatinibbattaṭṭhāneti purimakappesu purimakānaṃ nibbattaṭṭhāne. Etthāti “brahmavimāna”nti vuttāya brahmakāyikabhūmiyā. Sāmaññavisesavasena cetaṃ ādhāradvayaṃ. Kathaṃ paṇītāya dutiyajjhānabhūmiyā ṭhitānaṃ hīnāya paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyā upapatti hotīti āha “atha sattāna”ntiādi, nikantivasena paṭhamajjhānaṃ bhāvetvāti vuttaṃ hoti, pakatiyā sabhāvena nikanti taṇhā uppajjatīti sambandho. Vasitaṭṭhāneti vutthapubbaṭṭhāne. Tato otarantīti upapattivasena dutiyajjhānabhūmito paṭhamajjhānabhūmiṃ apasakkanti, gacchantīti attho. Appāyuketi yaṃ uḷārapuññakammaṃ kataṃ, tassa upajjanārahavipākapabandhato appaparimāṇāyuke. Tassa devalokassāti tasmiṃ devaloke, nissayavasena vā sambandhaniddeso. Āyuppamāṇenevāti paramāyuppamāṇeneva. Parittanti appakaṃ. Antarāva cavantīti rājakoṭṭhāgāre pakkhittataṇḍulanāḷi viya puññakkhayā hutvā sakakammappamāṇena tassa devalokassa paramāyuantarā eva cavanti.

Another method will be stated. The first performance of one's own kamma is called 'pakati' (nature). The connection with 'beings born from it' (nibbhattasattānaṃ) should be made thus: by that term, just as for this being there is a first birth through the power of their own kamma, so too for other beings there is no birth earlier than that or at the same time. Thus, due to the non-existence of beings born at that time, it shows that this mansion is empty. The Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities here are called Brahmakāyikā. Because it is their dwelling place, the plane is also called 'Brahmakāyikā'. Furthermore, in the reading 'brahmakāyikabhūmi', the meaning is 'the plane belonging to the Brahmakāyikā beings'. The 'kattā' (doer) is one who acts oneself. The 'kāretā' (instigator) is one who commands others. By the method stated in the Visuddhimagga's discourse on the knowledge of past lives, with this, it shows the sequence of arising and the reason for its being 'conditioned by kamma and originated from temperature'. Kamma is a condition for this plane by way of decisive support; therefore, it is called 'kammapaccayā'. Alternatively, because it acts as a cooperative cause for the ripening kamma of the beings born there, it is a condition for kamma; therefore, it is called 'kammapaccayā'. Temperature is the origin for this plane; therefore, it is called 'utusamuṭṭhānā'. There is also the reading as a compound, 'Kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā'. 'Kammapaccayo' means a condition that has kamma as its companion, or, by the method stated, a condition that has become a companion to kamma. That itself is temperature. That very thing is the origin for this plane; therefore, it is called 'kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā'. 'Ratanabhūmi' means a plane that has become a jewel due to the power of superior meritorious kamma. Not just the plane alone, but indeed its surroundings also arise; therefore, the Teacher said 'pakati', etc. 'Pakatinibbattaṭṭhāne' means in the place of arising of former beings in former aeons. 'Ettha' means in the Brahmakāyika plane which is called the 'Brahmā mansion'. And this pair of locatives is by way of general and specific. Because the question should be asked, 'How is there rebirth in the inferior first jhāna plane for those established in the superior second jhāna plane?', the Teacher said 'atha sattānaṃ', etc. This is the intended meaning: 'having developed the first jhāna through the power of craving for it'. The connection should be made thus: 'By nature, inherently, the craving of desire arises'. 'Vasitaṭṭhāne' means in the place previously dwelt in. 'Tato otaranti' means by the power of rebirth, they retreat from the second jhāna plane to the first jhāna plane; they go. 'Appāyuke' means 'of limited lifespan' because of the resultant continuity worthy of arising from whatever superior meritorious kamma was done. 'Tassa devalokassa' means 'in that deva world', or it is a genitive connection by way of dependence. 'Āyuppamāṇenevāti' means precisely by the measure of the maximum lifespan. 'Parittanti' means 'little'. 'Antarāva cavanti' means like a measure of rice placed in the king's granary, their merit having been exhausted, they pass away according to the measure of their own kamma, right in the middle of the maximum lifespan of that deva world.

Kiṃ panetaṃ paramāyu nāma, kathaṃ vā taṃ paricchinnappamāṇanti? Vuccate – yo tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhavavisese vipākappabandhassa ṭhitikālaniyamo [M 1.0417] purimasiddhabhavapatthanūpanissayavasena sarīrāvayavavaṇṇasaṇṭhānappamāṇādivisesā viya taṃtaṃgatinikāyādīsu yebhuyyena niyataparicchedo hoti, gabbhaseyyakakāmāvacaradevarūpāvacarasattānaṃ sukkasoṇitādiutubhojanādiutuādipaccayuppannapaccayūpatthambhito ca, so āyuhetukattā kāraṇūpacārena āyu, ukkaṃsaparicchedavasena paramāyūti ca vuccati. Yathāsakaṃ khaṇamattāvaṭṭhāyīnampi hi attanā sahajātānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ṭhapanākāravuttitāya pavattakāni rūpārūpajīvitindriyāni na kevalaṃ nesaṃ khaṇaṭṭhitiyā eva kāraṇabhāvena anupālakāni, atha kho yāva bhaṅgupacchedā [bhavaṅgupacchedā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.40)] anupabandhassa avicchedahetubhāvenāpi. Tasmā cesa āyuhetukoyeva, taṃ pana devānaṃ, nerayikānañca yebhuyyena niyataparicchedaṃ, uttarakurukānaṃ pana ekantaniyataparicchedameva. Avasiṭṭhamanussapetatiracchānagatānaṃ pana ciraṭṭhitisaṃvattanikakammabahule kāle taṃkammasahitasantānajanitasukkasoṇitapaccayānaṃ, tammūlakānañca candimasūriyasamavisamaparivattanādijanitautuāhārādisamavisamapaccayānaṃ vasena cirācirakālatāya aniyataparicchedaṃ, tassa ca yathā purimasiddhabhavapatthanāvasena taṃtaṃgatinikāyādīsu vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivisesaniyamo siddho, dassanānussavādīhi tathāyeva ādito gahaṇasiddhiyā, evaṃ tāsu tāsu upapattīsu nibbattasattānaṃ [V 1.0366] yebhuyyena samappamāṇaṃ ṭhitikālaṃ dassanānussavehi labhitvā taṃ paramataṃ ajjhosāya pavattitabhavapatthanāvasena ādito paricchedaniyamo veditabbo.

Now, what is this called 'maximum lifespan'? Or for what reason is its measure determined? It is said: That life-span which, for those various beings in their various specific existences, is the fixed duration of the resultant continuity, is, by way of dependence on the aspiration for a previously accomplished existence, generally a fixed measure in those various destinies, groups, etc., just like the distinctions of bodily limbs, color, shape, size, and so on. And for womb-born beings, sensual-sphere devas, and fine-material-sphere beings, it is supported by presently-arisen conditions such as the semen and blood of the parents, temperature, nutriment, etc. That life-span, because it is a cause, is called 'āyu' (life-span) by a metaphorical usage of the cause for the effect, and by way of its supreme limit, it is called 'paramāyu' (maximum lifespan). Indeed, the material and immaterial life faculties, which cause the persistence of the material and immaterial phenomena co-arisen with them—even though they last for only a moment according to their own nature—are protectors not merely by being the cause for their momentary existence, but rather, they are also protectors by being the cause for the non-interruption of the continuity until its final break-up. Therefore, this life-span is indeed causal. Furthermore, that life-span for devas and hell-beings is generally of a fixed measure, but for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, it is of an absolutely fixed measure. However, for the remaining humans, petas, and animals, in a time when kamma conducive to long life is abundant, the life-span is of an unfixed measure, being of long or short duration, by the power of the conditions of semen and blood generated by a continuum accompanied by that kamma, and of the harmonious and disharmonious conditions of temperature, nutriment, etc., generated by the harmonious and disharmonious revolutions of the sun and moon, etc., which are rooted in that kamma. And for that unfixed measure, just as the fixity of distinctions such as color, shape, etc., in those various destinies, groups, etc., is accomplished by the power of the aspiration for a previously accomplished existence, and is accomplished from the beginning through being grasped by means of seeing, hearing tradition, etc., so too, the fixity of the measure should be understood as established from the beginning by the power of the aspiration for existence that was set in motion by learning, through seeing and hearing tradition, of the generally similar duration of existence for beings born in those various rebirths, and by clinging to that duration as the maximum.

Yasmā pana kammaṃ tāsu tāsu upapattīsu yathā taṃtaṃupapattinissitavaṇṇādinibbattane samatthaṃ, evaṃ niyatāyuparicchedāsu upapattīsu paricchedātikkamena vipākanibbattane samatthaṃ na hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “āyuppamāṇeneva cavantī”ti.
