Yasmā pana upatthambhakapaccayasahāyehi anupālakapaccayehi upādinnakakkhandhānaṃ pavattetabbākāro atthato paramāyukassa hoti yathāvuttaparicchedānatikkamanato, tasmā satipi kammāvasese ṭhānaṃ na sambhavati, tena vuttaṃ “attano puññabalena ṭhātuṃ na sakkontī”ti. “Āyukkhayā vā puññakkhayā vā ābhassarakāyā cavitvā”ti vacanato panettha kāmāvacaradevānaṃ viya [M 1.0418] brahmakāyikānampi yebhuyyeneva niyatāyuparicchedabhāvo veditabbo. Tathā hi devalokato devaputtā āyukkhayena puññakkhayena āhārakkhayena kopenāti catūhi kāraṇehi cavantīti aṭṭhakathāsu (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.appamādavagge) vuttaṃ. Kappaṃ vā upaḍḍhakappaṃ vāti ettha asaṅkhyeyyakappo adhippeto, so ca tathārūpo kāloyeva, vā-saddo pana kappassa tatiyabhāgaṃ vā tato ūnamadhikaṃ vāti vikappanattho.

Furthermore, because kamma, just as it is capable in those respective rebirths of producing form, etc., dependent on those respective rebirths, is likewise not capable in rebirths with a fixed lifespan of producing results by exceeding that limit; therefore, it was said by the commentator, 'they pass away only by the measure of their lifespan.' Furthermore, because for one with a maximum lifespan, the manner in which the appropriated aggregates are to be maintained by supporting and sustaining conditions as companions is, in essence, one of not exceeding the aforementioned limit, therefore, even if a remainder of kamma exists, remaining is not possible. For that reason, it was said by the Teacher, 'they are unable to remain by the power of their own merit.' From the statement, 'having passed away from the Ābhassarakāya realm due to the exhaustion of lifespan or the exhaustion of merit,' it should be understood that, like the sense-sphere devas, the state of having a fixed lifespan exists for the Brahmā-group beings for the most part. For thus it is said in the commentaries that devaputtas pass away from the deva world for four reasons: due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of merit, the exhaustion of nutriment, or anger. Here, in 'an eon or half an eon,' an incalculable eon is intended, and that is just such a period of time. The word 'vā', however, has the meaning of an alternative: a third part of an eon, or less or more than that.

41. Anabhiratīti ekakavihārena anabhiramaṇasaṅkhātā aññehi samāgamicchāyeva. Tattha “ekakassa dīgharattaṃ nivasitattā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vacanatoti vuttaṃ “aparassāpī”tiādi. Evamanvayamatthaṃ dassetvā nanu ukkaṇṭhitāpi siyāti codanāsodhanavasena byatirekaṃ dasseti “yā panā”tiādinā. Piyavatthuvirahena, piyavatthualābhena vā cittavigghāto ukkaṇṭhitā, sā panatthato domanassacittuppādova, tenāha “paṭighasampayuttā”ti. Sā brahmaloke natthi jhānānubhāvapahīnattā. Taṇhādiṭṭhisaṅkhātā cittassa purimāvatthāya ubbijjanā phandanā eva idha paritassanā. Sā hi dīgharattaṃ jhānaratiyā ṭhitassa yathāvuttānabhiratinimittaṃ uppannā “ahaṃ mama”nti gahaṇassa ca kāraṇabhūtā. Tena vakkhati “taṇhātassa nāpi diṭṭhitassanāpi vaṭṭatī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.41) nanu vuttaṃ atthuddhāre imaṃyeva pāḷiṃ nīharitvā “aho vata aññepi sattā itthattaṃ āgaccheyyunti ayaṃ taṇhātassanā nāmā”ti? Saccaṃ, taṃ pana diṭṭhitassanāya visuṃ udāharaṇaṃ dassentena taṇhātassanameva tato niddhāretvā vuttaṃ, na pana ettha diṭṭhitassanāya alabbhamānattāti na doso. Idāni samānasaddavacanīyānaṃ atthānamuddharaṇaṃ katvā idhādhippetaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “sā panesā”tiādimāha. Paṭighasaṅkhāto cittutrāso eva tāsatassanā. Evamaññatthāpi yathārahaṃ. “Jātiṃ paṭiccā”tiādi vibhaṅgapāḷi, (vibha. 921) tatrāyamatthakathā [V 1.0367] – jātiṃ paṭicca bhayanti jātipaccayā uppannabhayaṃ. Bhayānakanti ākāraniddeso. Chambhitattanti bhayavasena gattakampo, visesato hadayamaṃsacalanaṃ. Lomahaṃsoti lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ, bhittiyaṃ nāgadantānamiva uddhaggabhāvo, iminā padadvayena kiccato bhayaṃ dassetvā puna cetaso utrāsoti sabhāvato dassitanti. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “bhayānakanti bheravārammaṇanimittaṃ balavabhayaṃ, tena sarīrassa thaddhabhāvo chambhitatta”nti [M 1.0419] (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.41) vuttaṃ, aneneva bhayanti ettha khuddakabhayaṃ dassitaṃ, iti ettha payoge ayaṃ tassanāti evaṃ sabbattha attho. Paritassitavipphanditamevāti ettha “diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitamevā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.105-117) aṭṭhakathāyamatthaṃ vakkhati. Tena viññāyati labbhamānampi taṇhātassanamantarena diṭṭhitassanāyeva nihaṭāti. “Tepī”tiādi sīhopamasuttantapāḷi (a. ni. 4.33) tattha tepīti dīghāyukā devāpi. Bhayanti bhaṅgānupassanāpariciṇṇante sabbasaṅkhārato bhāyanavasena uppannaṃ bhayañāṇaṃ. Saṃveganti sahottappañāṇaṃ, ottappameva vā. Santāsanti ādīnavanibbidānupassanāhi saṅkhārehi santāsanañāṇaṃ. Upapattivasenāti paṭisandhivaseneva.

41. 'Discontent' (anabhirati) is simply the wish for association with others, which is known as not delighting in dwelling alone. Because of the statement in the Pāḷi, 'due to dwelling alone for a long time,' it was therefore said by the Teacher, 'for another as well,' etc. Having thus shown the concordant meaning, he shows the distinction by way of question and answer, 'Might there not also be weariness (ukkaṇṭhitā)?', with 'But what is...' etc. Weariness is mental affliction due to the absence of a beloved object or the non-attainment of a beloved object. And that, in essence, is just a thought-moment of displeasure. Therefore, the Teacher said, 'associated with aversion.' That does not exist in the Brahma-world because it has been abandoned by the power of jhāna. Here, anxiety (paritassanā) is just the agitation and trembling of the mind in its preliminary state, known as craving and view. For it arises in one who has abided for a long time in the delight of jhāna due to the aforementioned cause of discontent, and it becomes the cause for the grasping 'I' and 'mine'. Therefore, the Teacher will say, 'craving-anxiety and view-anxiety are appropriate.' Was it not said in the explanation of the meaning, having extracted this very Pāḷi passage, '"Oh, that other beings might also come to this state!"—this is called craving-anxiety'? True. But that was said by one showing a separate example for view-anxiety, having extracted only craving-anxiety from that; but not because view-anxiety is unobtainable here. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, having made an extraction of the meanings of words with similar sounds, in order to clarify the intended meaning here, the compiler said, 'But this...' etc. Mental terror known as aversion is itself terror-anxiety (tāsatassanā). Thus it should be understood appropriately elsewhere as well. 'Dependent on birth,' etc., is the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi. Therein, this is the commentary: 'Fear dependent on birth' is fear that has arisen because of birth as a condition. 'Terrifying' is a designation of its mode. 'Horror' is trembling of the body due to fear, specifically the quivering of the heart-flesh. 'Hair-raising' is the bristling of the hairs, like the upward-pointing state of elephant-tusks on a wall. Having shown fear by its function with these two terms, it is then shown by its intrinsic nature as 'mental terror.' But in the subcommentary it is said: ''Terrifying' is strong fear due to a frightful object as a cause; due to that, stiffness of the body is 'horror'.' By this very word 'fear', lesser fear is shown. Thus, in this usage, 'this is anxiety'—in this way the meaning should be understood everywhere. Here, in 'just agitation and trembling,' the meaning will be stated in the commentary as: 'just agitation, just shaking, just trembling due to anxiety which is known as view and as craving.' By this it is known that even though craving-anxiety is obtainable, view-anxiety alone is extracted, excluding it. 'They too,' etc., is the Sīhopama Suttanta-pāḷi. Therein, 'they too' means even the long-lived devas. 'Fear' is the knowledge of fear that has arisen by way of fearing all formations at the culmination of having practiced the contemplation of dissolution. 'Urgency' is knowledge together with moral dread, or just moral dread itself. 'Alarm' is the knowledge of being alarmed by formations through the contemplations of danger and disenchantment. 'By way of rebirth' means precisely by way of rebirth-linking.

Sahabyatanti sahāyabhāvamiccheva saddato attho sahabya-saddassa sahāyatthe pavattanato. So hi saha byāyati pavattati, dosaṃ vā paṭicchādetīti sahabyoti vuccati, tassa bhāvo sahabyatā. Sahāyabhāvo pana sahabhāvoyeva nāmāti adhippāyato atthaṃ dassetuṃ “sahabhāva”nti vuttaṃ. Sasādhanasamavāyattho vā saha-saddo adhikiccapade adhisaddo viya, tasmā saha ekato vattamānassa bhāvo sahabyaṃ yathā “dāsabya”nti tadeva sahabyatā, sakatthavuttivasena imamevatthaṃ sandhāyāha “sahabhāva”nti. Apica saha vāti pavattatīti sahavo, tassa bhāvo sahabyaṃ yathā “vīrassa bhāvo vīriya”nti, tadeva sahabyatāti evaṃ vimānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vi. va. aṭṭha. 172) vuttaṃ, tasmā tadatthaṃ dassetuṃ evaṃ vuttantipi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

As for 'sahabyatā', the meaning should be understood literally as 'the state of being a companion', because the word 'sahabya' occurs in the sense of 'companion'. Indeed, he 'proceeds together' (saha byāyati) or 'conceals a fault' (dosaṃ paṭicchādeti), thus he is called a 'sahabya'; his state is 'sahabyatā'. However, the state of being a companion is indeed just 'co-existence' (sahabhāva). To show the meaning according to this intention, it is said 'co-existence'. Alternatively, the word 'saha' has the meaning of association together with its means, like the prefix 'adhi' in the word 'adhikicca'. Therefore, the state of one who exists together is 'sahabyaṃ', just as in 'dāsabyaṃ'. That very state is 'sahabyatā'. Intending this very meaning, by way of the suffix '-tā' being used in the sense of its own meaning, the Commentator said 'co-existence'. Furthermore: 'He proceeds together' (saha vāti), thus he is a 'sahavo'; his state is 'sahabyaṃ', just as 'the state of a hero (vīra) is heroism (vīriya)'. That very state is 'sahabyatā'. Thus it is said in the Vimanavatthu Commentary. Therefore, it should also be understood that it was said thus to show that meaning.

42. Ime satte abhibhavitvāti seso. Abhibhavanā cettha pāpasabhāvena jeṭṭhabhāvena “te satte abhibhavitvā ṭhito”ti attano maññanāyevāti vuttaṃ “jeṭṭhakohamasmī”ti. Aññadatthūti dassane antarāyābhāvavacanena, dasoti ettha dassaneyyavisesapariggahābhāvena ca anāvaraṇadassāvitaṃ paṭijānātīti āha “sabbaṃ passāmīti attho”ti. Dassaneyyavisesassa hi padesabhūtassa aggahaṇe sati gahetabbassa nippadesatā viññāyati yathā “dikkhito na [M 1.0420] dadātī”ti, deyyadhammavisesassa cettha padesabhūtassa aggahaṇato pabbajito sabbampi na dadātīti gahetabbassa deyyadhammassa nippadesatā viññāyati. Evamīdisesu. Vase vattemīti vasavattī. [V 1.0368] Ahaṃ-saddayogato hi sabbattha amhayogena vacanattho. Sattabhājanabhūtassa lokassa nimmātā cāti sambandho. “Pathavī”tiādi cettha bhājanalokavasena adhippāyakathanaṃ. Sajitāti racitā, vibhajitā vā, tenāha “tvaṃ khattiyo nāmā”tiādi. Ciṇṇavasitāyāti samāciṇṇapañcavidhavasibhāvato. Tatthāti bhūtabhabyesu. Antovatthimhīti antogabbhāsaye. Paṭhamacittakkhaṇeti paṭisandhicittakkhaṇe. Dutiyatoti paṭhamabhavaṅgacittakkhaṇato. Paṭhamairiyāpatheti yena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhāti, tasmiṃ iriyāpathe. Iti atītavasena, bhūta-saddassa vattamānavasena ca bhabya-saddassa attho dassito. Ṭīkāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.42) pana bhabya-saddattho anāgatavasenāpi vutto. Ahesunti hi bhūtā. Bhavanti, bhavissanti cāti bhabyā tabbānīyā viya ṇyapaccayassa kattaripi pavattanato.

42. 'Having overcome these beings'—this is the remainder of the text. And here, the overcoming, through a wicked nature and through the state of being the eldest, is just his own conceiving, 'I stand having overcome those beings'; therefore it is said, 'I am the eldest.' By the word 'aññadatthu', which is a statement of the absence of obstacles in seeing, and here in 'daso', by the absence of grasping a particular object to be seen, he professes the state of seeing without obstruction. Therefore, the Commentator said, 'The meaning is, "I see all."' Indeed, when a particular object to be seen, which is a part, is not grasped, the state of what is to be grasped as being without remainder is known. For example, 'a renunciate does not give'. Here, because a particular gift-object, which is a part, is not grasped, it is known that the renunciate does not give anything at all; thus the state of the gift-object to be grasped as being without remainder is known. Thus it is in such cases. 'I make them act according to my will' (vase vattemi), therefore I am a master (vasavattī). Indeed, due to the connection with the word 'ahaṃ', the etymological analysis should be made everywhere with the first-person pronoun. The connection should be made thus: 'and the creator of the world which is the receptacle for beings'. 'Earth', etc., here is a statement explaining the intention by way of the receptacle-world. 'Sajitā' means created, or divided; therefore he said, 'You are a Khattiya by name,' etc. 'Ciṇṇavasitāya' means because of the state of having well-practiced the fivefold mastery. 'Tattha' means among beings that have been (bhūta) and beings that will be (bhabya). 'Antovattimhi' means inside the womb. 'Paṭhamacittakkhaṇe' means at the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness. 'Dutiyato' means from the first moment of life-continuum consciousness. 'Paṭhamairiyāpathe' means in that posture by which one takes rebirth-linking. Thus, the meaning of the word 'bhūta' is shown by way of the past, and of the word 'bhabya' by way of the present. In the Subcommentary, however, the meaning of the word 'bhabya' is also stated by way of the future. Indeed, 'they were' (ahesuṃ), therefore they are called 'bhūtā'. 'They are and they will be' (bhavanti, bhavissanti ca), therefore they are called 'bhabyā', because of the occurrence of the '-ṇya' suffix also in the agent sense, like the suffixes '-tabba' and '-anīya'.

“Issaro kattā nimmātā”ti vatvāpi puna “mayā ime sattā nimmitā”ti vacanaṃ kimatthiyanti āha “idāni kāraṇavasenā”tiādi [kāraṇato (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] kāraṇavasena sādhetukāmatāya paṭiññākaraṇatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Nanu cesa brahmā anavaṭṭhitadassanattā puthujjanassa purimatarajātiparicitampi kammassakatāñāṇaṃ vissajjetvā vikubbaniddhivasena cittuppādamattapaṭibaddhena sattanimmānena vipallaṭṭho “mayā ime sattā nimmitā”tiādinā issarakuttadassanaṃ pakkhandamāno abhinivisanavasena patiṭṭhito, na pana patiṭṭhāpanavasena. Atha kasmā kāraṇavasena sādhetukāmo paṭiññaṃ karotīti vuttanti? Na cevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesampi hi “evaṃ hotī”tiādinā pacchā uppajjantānampi tathāabhinivesassa vakkhamānattā paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanakkameneva tassa so abhiniveso jāto, na tu abhinivisanamattena, tasmā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “taṃ kissa hetū”tiādi. Pāḷiyaṃ manaso paṇidhīti manaso patthanā, tathā cittuppattimattamevāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Even after having said, 'The Lord is the maker, the creator,' what is the purpose of again saying, 'These beings were created by me'? The Commentator answers with the words beginning, 'Now, by way of cause...' The meaning is that it was said for the purpose of making an affirmation, due to the desire to establish it by way of a cause. Is it not that this Brahmā, being a worldling with an unstable view, having abandoned the knowledge of action as one's own property though it was familiar from previous lives, and having become perverted by the creation of beings connected merely with the arising of a thought through the power of transformation, rushes into the view of a creator-god with statements like, 'These beings were created by me,' and is established by way of adherence, and not by way of being established by others? Then why is it said that he makes an affirmation, desiring to establish it by way of a cause? This should not be understood thus. Because it will be stated, with the words beginning 'For them, too, it is thus...', that for those Brahmās arising later, too, there is a similar adherence, that adherence of his arose only through the process of being established by others, not merely by his own adherence. Therefore, it should be understood by the wise that it was said thus. For that very reason, he said the words beginning, 'What is the reason for that?'. In the Pāḷi, 'manaso paṇidhi' is the aspiration of the mind; the meaning is that it is merely the arising of a thought in that way.

Itthabhāvanti idappakārabhāvaṃ. Yasmā pana so pakāro brahmattabhāvoyevidhādhippeto, tasmā “brahmabhāva”nti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pakāro itthaṃ, tassa [M 1.0421] bhāvo itthattanti hi nibbacanaṃ. Kevalanti kammassakatāñāṇena asammissaṃ suddhaṃ. Maññanāmattenevāti diṭṭhimaññanāmatteneva, na adhimānavasena. Vaṅkachiddena vaṅkaāṇī viya onamitvā vaṅkaladdhikena vaṅkaladdhikā onamitvā tasseva brahmuno pādamūlaṃ gacchanti, taṃpakkhakā bhavantīti attho. Nanu ca devānaṃ upapattisamanantaraṃ “imāya nāma gatiyā cavitvā iminā nāma kammunā idhūpapannā”ti paccavekkhaṇā hoti, atha kasmā tesaṃ evaṃ maññanā siyāti? Purimajātīsu kammassakatāñāṇe sammadeva niviṭṭhajjhāsayānameva tathāpaccavekkhaṇāya pavattito. Tādisānameva hi tathāpaccavekkhaṇā [V 1.0369] sambhavati, sā ca kho yebhuyyavasena, ime pana purimāsupi jātīsu issarakuttadiṭṭhivasena nibaddhābhinivesā evameva maññamānā ahesunti. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ “iminā maya”ntiādi.

'Itthabhāvaṃ' means the state of being of this kind. But since that kind is here intended as the state of being a Brahmā, it is therefore called 'brahmabhāvaṃ'. Indeed, the etymology is: 'This kind is "itthaṃ"; its state is "itthattaṃ"'. 'Kevalaṃ' means unmixed with the knowledge of action as one's own property, pure. 'Maññanāmatteneva' means merely by the conceiving that is wrong view, not by way of excessive conceit. Just as a crooked pin is bent by a crooked hole, so those with a crooked view, being bent by a crooked view, go to the feet of that very Brahmā and become his partisans—this is the meaning. Is it not that for devas, immediately after rebirth, there is the reflection, 'Having passed away from such-and-such a destination, by such-and-such an action, I have been reborn here'? Then why would such a conceiving arise for them? It is because in previous lives, such reflection occurs only for those whose dispositions were well-established in the knowledge of action as one's own property. Indeed, such reflection is possible only for such beings, and that, indeed, occurs for the most part. But these beings, having a firm adherence to the view of a creator-god even in previous lives, were conceiving in just this way. Indeed, thus it is said in the Pāḷi, with the words beginning 'By this we...'.

43. Īsati abhibhavatīti īso, mahanto īso maheso, suppatiṭṭhitamahesatāya parehi “maheso” iti akkhāyatīti mahesakkho, mahesakkhānaṃ atisayena mahesakkhoti mahesakkhataroti vacanattho. So pana mahesakkhatarabhāvo ādhipateyyaparivārasampattiyā kāraṇabhūtāya viññāyatīti vuttaṃ “issariyaparivāravasena mahāyasataro”ti.

43. “He lords over” (īsati), “he overcomes” (abhibhavati), therefore he is “Īsa” (lord). A great oppressive power (mahanto īso) is “Mahesa.” Because he is called “Mahesa” (one of great power) by others due to his well-established great power, he is “Mahesakkha.” Than the Mahesakkhas, he is exceedingly a Mahesakkha, therefore he is “Mahesakkhatara”—thus the word analysis should be made. Furthermore, that state of being Mahesakkhatara is known by means of the accomplishment of sovereignty and retinue, which is the cause. Therefore, it is said: “more greatly renowned by reason of sovereignty and retinue.”

44. Kiṃ panetaṃ kāraṇanti anuyogenāha “so tato”tiādi, tena “itthattaṃ āgacchatī”ti vuttaṃ idhāgamanameva kāraṇanti dasseti. Idheva āgacchatīti imasmiṃ manussaloke eva paṭisandhivasena āgacchati. Etanti “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ bhikkhave, vijjatī”ti vacanaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ yaṃ aññataro sattoti ettha yanti nipātamattaṃ, kāraṇatthe vā esa nipāto, hetumhi vā paccattaniddeso, yena ṭhānenāti attho, kiriyāparāmasanaṃ vā etaṃ. “Itthattaṃ āgacchatī”ti ettha yadetaṃ itthattassa āgamanasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tadetaṃ vijjatīti attho. Esa na so pabbajati, cetosamādhiṃ phusati, pubbenivāsaṃ anussatīti etesupi padesu. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ aññataro satto”ti hi imāni padāni “pabbajatī”tiādīhipi padehi paccekaṃ yojetabbāni. Na gacchatīti agāraṃ, gehaṃ, agārassa hitaṃ āgāriyaṃ, kasigorakkhādikammaṃ, tamettha natthīti anāgāriyaṃ, pabbajjā, tenāha “agārasmā”tiādi. Pa-saddena visiṭṭho vaja-saddo upasaṅkamaneti vuttaṃ “upagacchatī”ti. Paranti [M 1.0422] pacchā, atisayaṃ vā, aññaṃ pubbenivāsantipi attho. “Na saratī”ti vutteyeva ayamattho āpajjatīti dasseti “saritu”ntiādinā. Apassantoti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena apassanahetu, passituṃ asakkonto hutvātipi vaṭṭati. Māna-saddo viya hi anta-saddo idha sāmatthiyattho. Sadābhāvatoti sabbadā vijjamānattā. Jarāvasenāpīti ettha pi-saddena maraṇavasenāpīti sampiṇḍeti.

44. With the inquiry, “But what is this reason?,” the Commentator says, “so tato,” and so on. Thereby he shows that the coming here, which was stated as “he comes to this state,” is the very reason. “He comes right here” means he comes to this very human world by way of rebirth-linking. “This” (etaṃ) refers to the statement, “Indeed, monks, this is a possibility that exists.” In the Pāḷi, in “that a certain being” (yaṃ aññataro satto), “yaṃ” is a mere particle; or it is a particle in the sense of a reason; or it is a nominative designation in the sense of a cause, the meaning being “for which reason”; or it is a reference to the action. In “he comes to this state,” the meaning is: that which is the condition called the coming to this state, that exists. This is the method also in these passages: “he goes forth,” “he attains concentration of mind,” and “he recollects a former existence.” For these words, “Indeed, monks, this is a possibility that exists, that a certain being,” should be connected individually with the words “goes forth,” and so on. “It is not gone to” (na gacchati), therefore it is `agāraṃ` (a house), a home. Beneficial to the house is `āgāriyaṃ`, the work of ploughing, cattle-herding, etc. That is not present here, therefore it is `anāgāriyaṃ` (homelessness), the going forth. Therefore, the Commentator said, “from the household,” and so on. The word `vaja` qualified by the prefix `pa-` is in the sense of “approaching,” thus it is said `upagacchati` (he approaches). `Paraṃ` means “after,” or “exceedingly,” or the meaning is also “another former existence.” He shows by “sarituṃ,” etc., that this meaning is obtained only when “na sarati” is said. `Apassanto` (not seeing) is because of not seeing with the knowledge of recollecting former existences; it is also suitable as “being unable to see.” For here the suffix `-anta`, like the word `māna`, is in the sense of capability. `Sadābhāvato` (from its constant existence) means “because of existing at all times.” In `jarāvasenāpi` (also by reason of old age), by the particle `pi`, he includes “also by reason of death.”

45. Khiḍḍāpadosinoti kattuvasena padasiddhi, khiḍḍāpadosikāti pana sakatthavuttivasena, saddamanapekkhitvā pana atthameva dassetuṃ “khiḍḍāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Khiḍḍāpadosakā”ti vā vattabbe i-kārāgamavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Padussanaṃ vā padoso, khiḍḍāya padoso khiḍḍāpadoso, so etesanti khiḍḍāpadosikā. “Padūsikātipi pāḷiṃ likhantī”ti aññanikāyikānaṃ pamādalekhataṃ dasseti[V 1.0370]. Mahāvihāravāsīnikāyikānañhi vācanāmaggavasena ayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā pavattā. Apica tena potthakāruḷhakāle pamādalekhaṃ dasseti. Tampi hi padatthasodhanāya aṭṭhakathāya sodhitaniyāmeneva gahetabbaṃ, tenāha “sā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthī”ti. Velaṃ atikkantaṃ ativelaṃ, taṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ, tenāha “aticira”nti, āhārūpabhogakālaṃ atikkamitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ratidhamma-saddo hassakhiḍḍā-saddehi paccekaṃ yojetabbo “hassakhiḍḍāsu ratidhammo ramaṇasabhāvo”ti. Hasanaṃ hasso, keḷihasso. Kheḍanaṃ kīḷanaṃ khiḍḍā, kāyikavācasikakīḷā. Anuyogavasena taṃsamāpannāti dassento āha “hassaratidhammañcevā”tiādi. Kīḷā yesaṃ te keḷino, tesaṃ hasso tathā. Kīḷāhassapayogena uppajjanakasukhañcettha keḷihassasukhaṃ. Tadavasiṭṭhakīḷāpayogena uppajjanakaṃ kāyikavācasikakīḷāsukhaṃ.

45. The word-formation of `Khiḍḍāpadosino` is in the agent sense. But the word-formation of `khiḍḍāpadosikā` is by means of the `ṇika` suffix which occurs in its own meaning. However, disregarding the word and just to show the meaning, “khiḍḍāya,” etc., was said. Or, when `Khiḍḍāpadosakā` should have been said, it was said thus (`khiḍḍāpadosikā`) by means of the insertion of the letter `i`. Or, corruption is `padoso`; corruption by play is `khiḍḍāpadoso`; that exists for them, therefore they are `khiḍḍāpadosikā`. The phrase “they also write `Padūsikā` in the Pāḷi” shows the careless writing of those from other schools. For this commentary proceeds by way of the recitation-lineage of the residents of the Mahāvihāra school. Moreover, by that he shows a careless transcription at the time of inscribing it on palm-leaf. For that too should be taken only in the way it has been corrected in the commentary for the purification of the word's meaning. Therefore, he said, “That is not in the commentary.” Having passed the time (`velaṃ atikkantaṃ`) is `ativelaṃ`. And this is a neuter abstract noun or an adverb, therefore the Commentator said `aticiraṃ` (for a very long time); it means “having passed the time for consuming food.” The word `ratidhamma` (nature of delight) should be connected individually with the words `hassa` (laughter) and `khiḍḍā` (play) thus: “In laughter and play, `ratidhamma` is the nature of delighting.” Laughter (`hasanaṃ`) is `hasso`; the laughter of those who are playful (`keḷino`) is `keḷihasso`. Playing (`kheḍanaṃ`, `kīḷanaṃ`) is `khiḍḍā`; it is bodily and verbal play. Showing that they are engaged in it through application, he says, “and the nature of delighting in laughter,” and so on. Those for whom there is play (`kīḷā`) are `keḷino`; their laughter is likewise. And here, the happiness that arises from the application of playful laughter is `keḷihassasukhaṃ`. The happiness that arises from the application of the remaining play is `kāyikavācasikakīḷāsukhaṃ` (the happiness of bodily and verbal play).

“Te kirā”tiādi vitthāradassanaṃ. Kira-saddo hettha vitthārajotakoyeva, na tu anussavanāruciyādijotako tathāyeva pāḷiyaṃ, aṭṭhakathāsu ca vuttattā. Sirivibhavenāti sarīrasobhaggādisiriyā, parivārādisampattiyā ca. Nakkhattanti chaṇaṃ. Yebhuyyena hi nakkhattayogena katattā tathāyogo vā hotu, mā vā, nakkhattamicceva vuccati. Āhāranti ettha ko devānamāhāro, kā ca tesamāhāravelāti? Sabbesampi kāmāvacaradevānaṃ sudhāhāro. Dvādasapāpadhammavigghātena [M 1.0423] hi sukhassa dhāraṇato devānaṃ bhojanaṃ “sudhā”ti vuccati. Sā pana setā saṅkhūpamā atulyadassanā suci sugandhā piyarūpā. Yaṃ sandhāya sudhābhojanajātake vuttaṃ –

The passage beginning “Te kira” is a detailed explanation. Here the word `kira` only illuminates the detail, and not hearsay, displeasure, and so on, because it is said so in the Pāḷi and in the commentaries. “With the splendor of glory” (`sirivibhavena`) means: by the glory of bodily beauty, etc., and by the accomplishment of retinue, etc. `Nakkhattaṃ` means a festival. For it is generally done in connection with a constellation; whether there is such a connection or not, it is still called a `nakkhattaṃ`. Regarding `āhāraṃ` (food), here the questions are: what is the food of the devas, and what is their mealtime? For all devas of the sense-sphere, the food is ambrosia. For because it sustains happiness by dispelling the twelve evil states, the food of the devas is called `sudhā` (ambrosia). Furthermore, it is white, like a conch, of incomparable appearance, pure, fragrant, and of pleasing form. In reference to which it was said in the Sudhābhojana Jātaka:

“Saṅkhūpamaṃ seta’matulyadassanaṃ,

Suciṃ sugandhaṃ piyarūpa’mabbhutaṃ;

Adiṭṭhapubbaṃ mama jātu cakkhubhi,

Kā devatā pāṇisu kiṃ sudho’dahī”ti. (jā. 2.21.227);

“Like a conch, white, of incomparable appearance, pure, fragrant, of pleasing form, and wondrous, never before seen at all by my eyes—what deva, and for what reason, has placed this ambrosia in my hands?”

“Bhuttā ca sā dvādasahanti pāpake,

Khuddaṃ pipāsaṃ aratiṃ daraklamaṃ;

Kodhūpanāhañca vivādapesuṇaṃ,

Sītuṇha tandiñca rasuttamaṃ ida”nti ca. (jā. 2.21.229);

“And that, having been consumed, dispels the twelve evil things: hunger, thirst, discontent, anxiety, fatigue, anger, malice, disputes, slander, cold, heat, and torpor. This is the best of tastes.”

Sā ca heṭṭhimehi heṭṭhimehi uparimānaṃ uparimānaṃ paṇītatamā hoti, taṃ yathāsakaṃ parimitadivasavasena [V 1.0371] divase divase bhuñjanti. Keci pana vadanti “biḷārapadappamāṇaṃ sudhāhāraṃ te bhuñjanti, so jivhāya ṭhapitamatto yāva kesagganakhaggā kāyaṃ pharati, yathāsakaṃ gaṇitadivasavasena satta divase yāpanasamattho hotī”ti. Kecivāde panettha biḷārapada-saddo suvaṇṇasaṅkhātassa saṅkhyāvisesassa vācako. Pamāṇato pana udumbaraphalappamāṇaṃ, yaṃ pāṇitalaṃ kabaḷaggahantipi vuccati. Vuttañhi madhukose –

And for the devas of the higher and higher realms, it is more excellent than for those of the lower and lower realms; and they consume it day by day according to their allotted number of days. But some say, ‘They consume a portion of divine ambrosia the size of a cat’s footprint, which, as soon as it is placed on the tongue, pervades the body up to the tips of the hair and nails, and is able to sustain them for seven days, counted according to their own realm.’ Here, in this view of some, the term `biḷārapada` is a designator for the specific number called `suvaṇṇa`. In terms of measure, however, it is the size of an udumbara fruit; that which is the palm of the hand is also called `kabaḷaggaha`. For it is stated in the Madhukosa—

“Pāṇirakkho picu cāpi, suvaṇṇakamudumbaraṃ;

Biḷārapadakaṃ pāṇi-talaṃ taṃ kabaḷaggaha”nti.

“`Pāṇi` and `akkho`, and also `picu`, `suvaṇṇakaṃ`, `udumbaraṃ`; `biḷārapadakaṃ`, `pāṇitalaṃ`—that is `kabaḷaggaha`.”

“Nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpī”ti idaṃ parikappanāvasena vuttaṃ, na pana evaṃ niyamavasena tathā khādanapivanānamaniyamabhāvato. Kammajatejassa balavabhāvo uḷārapuññanibbattattā, uḷāragarusiniddhasudhāhārajīraṇato ca. Karajakāyassa mandabhāvo pana sukhumālabhāvato. Teneva hi bhagavā indasālaguhāyaṃ pakatipathaviyaṃ patiātuṃ asakkontaṃ sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ “oḷārikaṃ kāyaṃ adhiṭṭhehī”ti avoca. Manussānaṃ pana kammajatejassa mandabhāvo, karajakāyassa balavabhāvo ca vuttaviparītena veditabbo. Karajakāyoti ettha ko vuccati sarīraṃ, tattha pavatto. Rajo [M 1.0424] karajo, kiṃ taṃ? Sukkasoṇitaṃ. Tañhi “rāgo rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccatī”ti (mahāni. 209; cūḷani. 74) evaṃ vuttarāgarajaphalattā sarīravācakena ka-saddena visesetvā kāraṇavohārena “karajo”ti vuccati. Tena sukkasoṇitasaṅkhātena karajena sambhūto kāyo karajakāyoti ācariyā. Tathā hi kāyo mātāpettikasambhavoti vutto. Mahāassapūrasuttantaṭīkāyaṃ pana “karīyati gabbhāsaye khipīyatīti karo, sambhavo, karato jātoti karajo, mātāpettikasambhavoti attho. Mātuādīnaṃ saṇṭhāpanavasena karato hatthato jātoti karajoti apare. Ubhayathāpi karajakāyanti catusantatirūpamāhā”ti vuttaṃ. Karoti putte nibbattetīti karo, sukkasoṇitaṃ, tena jāto karajotipi vadanti. Tathā asambhūtopi ca devādīnaṃ kāyo tabbohārena “karajakāyo”ti vuccati yathā “pūtikāyo, jarasiṅgālo”ti. Tesanti manussānaṃ. Acchayāgu nāma pasannā akasaṭā yāgu. Vatthunti karajakāyaṃ. Ekaṃ āhāravelanti ekadivasamattaṃ, kesañci matena pana sattāhaṃ.

The statement, “Even while continuously eating and drinking,” is said by way of conjecture, not as a fixed rule, because of the unfixed nature of such eating and drinking. The kamma-born heat element is strong due to being produced by lofty merit and due to the digestion of the lofty, heavy, and subtle divine ambrosia. The `karajakāya`, however, is weak due to its subtle and delicate nature. For that very reason, in the Indasāla cave, the Blessed One told Sakka, the king of devas, who was unable to stand on the natural earth, “Resolve upon a gross body.” For humans, however, the weakness of the kamma-born heat element and the strength of the `karajakāya` should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said. Herein, regarding `karajakāya`: `ka` is said to be the body; the `raja` that occurs therein is `karaja`. What is that? Semen and blood. For that is called `raja` which is passion, but not `reṇu`. Because it is the result of that `raja` which is passion, as stated, it is specified by the word `ka`, which denotes the body, and is called `karaja` by a causal designation. Therefore, the teachers say that the body produced by that `karaja`, which is called semen and blood, is the `karajakāya`. Indeed, the body is said to be of maternal and paternal origin. In the subcommentary to the Mahāassapūra Sutta, however, it is said: “It is made and deposited in the womb, thus it is `kara`; it is the origin. Born from `kara`, it is `karaja`; the meaning is ‘of maternal and paternal origin.’ Others say it is `karaja` because it is born from the hand by way of the establishing action of the mother and others. In both ways, `karajakāya` refers to the form of the four continuities.” They also say: “It makes, produces offspring, thus it is `kara`—this is semen and blood; born from that is `karaja`.” Similarly, even the body of devas and others, though not produced in this way, is called `karajakāya` by that designation, just as one might say “a foul body” or “an old jackal.” `Tesaṃ` refers to humans. `Acchayāgu` means clear, unstrained gruel. `Vatthu` refers to the `karajakāya`. `Ekaṃ āhāravelaṃ` means for a single day, but according to the opinion of some, for seven days.

Evaṃ anvayato byatirekato ca dassetvā upamāvasenapi tamāvikaronto “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattapāsāṇeti accuṇhapāsāṇe. Rattasetapadumato avasiṭṭhaṃ uppalaṃ. Akathāyanti [V 1.0372] mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Avisesenāti “devāna”nti avisesena, devānaṃ kammajatejo balavā hoti, karajaṃ mandanti vā kammajatejakarajakāyānaṃ balavamandatāsaṅkhāta kāraṇasāmaññena. Tadetañhi kāraṇaṃ sabbesampi devānaṃ samānameva, tasmā sabbepi devā gahetabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kabaḷīkārabhūtaṃ sudhāhāraṃ upanissāya jīvantīti kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvino. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. “Khiḍḍāpadussanamatteneva hete khiḍḍāpadosikāti vuttā”ti ayaṃ pāṭho “teyeva cavantīti veditabbā”ti etassānantare paṭhitabbo tadanusandhikattā. Ayañhetthānusandhi – yadi sabbepi evaṃ karontā kāmāvacaradevā caveyyuṃ, atha kasmā “khiḍḍāpadosikā”ti nāmavisesena bhagavatā vuttāti? Vicāraṇāya evamāhāti, etena imamatthaṃ dasseti “sabbepi devā evaṃ cavantāpi khiḍḍāya padussanasabhāvamattaṃ pati nāmavisesena [M 1.0425] tathā vuttā”ti. Yadeke vadeyyuṃ “kecivādapatiṭṭhāpakoyaṃ pāṭho”ti, tadayuttameva iti-saddantarikattā, ante ca tassa avijjamānattā. Atthikehi pana tassa kecivādasamavarodhanaṃ ante itisaddo yojetabboti.

Having thus shown by way of positive and negative concomitance, and making the meaning clear by way of a simile, he said, “Just as…” and so on. `Tattapāsāṇe` means on a very hot stone. From the red and white lotuses, what remains is the `uppala`. `Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ` means in the Great Commentary. `Avisesena` means “of the devas” without specification, or by the generality of the cause called the strength and weakness of the kamma-born heat and the `karajakāya`, as in “for devas, the kamma-born heat is strong, the `karaja` is weak.” For this reason is the same for all devas; therefore, it is meant that all devas should be included. They are `kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvino` because they live depending on the divine ambrosia which serves as physical nutriment. `Keci` refers to the Abhayagirivāsins. The passage, “For it is only by being corrupted by play that they are called `khiḍḍāpadosikā`,” should be recited immediately after “it should be understood that they alone pass away,” because it has a connection with it. Herein, this is the connection: If all sense-sphere devas who act thus were to pass away, then why were they spoken of by the Blessed One with the specific name `Khiḍḍāpadosikā`? Upon investigation, he says thus. By this, he shows this meaning: “Although all devas pass away in this way, they were called thus by a specific name on account of the mere nature of being corrupted by play.” If some were to say, “This passage establishes the view of the `keci`,” that is indeed incorrect, because it is separated by the word `iti`, and because that word is not present at the end. However, by those who desire its inclusion in the `keci` view, the word `iti` should be supplied at the end.

47-48. Manopadosinoti kattuvasena padasiddhi, manopadosikāti ca sakatthavuttivasena, atthamattaṃ pana dassetuṃ “manenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Manopadosakā”ti vā vattabbe i-kārāgamavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Manenāti issāpakatattā paduṭṭhena manasā. Aparo nayo – usūyanavasena manasā padoso manopadoso, vināsabhūto so etesamatthīti manopadosikāti. “Te aññamaññamhi paduṭṭhacittā kilantakāyā kilantacittā te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti vacanato “ete cātumahārājikā”ti āha. Manena padussanamatteneva hete manopadosikāti vuttā. “Tesu kirā”tiādi vitthāro. Rathena vīthiṃ paṭipajjatīti upalakkhaṇamattaṃ aññehi aññatthāpi paṭipajjanasambhavato. Etanti attano sampattiṃ. Uddhumāto viyāti pītiyā karaṇabhūtāya unnato viya. Bhijjamāno viyāti tāya bhijjanto viya, pītiyā vā kattubhūtāya bhañjito viya. Kuddhā nāma suvijānanā honti, tasmā kuddhabhāvamassa ñatvāti attho.

47-48. Herein, the formation of the word `manopadosino` is by the agent, and `manopadosikā` is by the power of the suffix used in its own sense. However, merely to convey the meaning, the passage beginning `manenā` was stated. Alternatively, when `manopadosakā` should have been said, it is stated thus (`manopadosikā`) with the addition of the letter `i`. `Manenā` means with a mind corrupted from being afflicted by envy. Another interpretation: corruption by the mind through envy is `manopadoso`, and since this destructive state exists in them, they are called `manopadosikā`. In accordance with the canonical statement, 'These deities, with minds corrupted towards each other, with bodies and minds exhausted, fall from that existence,' he said, 'These are the Cātumahārājika devas.' They are called `manopadosikā` merely because of the mind's corruption. The detailed explanation begins with `Tesu kira`. 'He travels the street by chariot' is merely an illustration, as it is possible to travel elsewhere by other means. `Etaṃ` refers to one's own prosperity. `Uddhumāto viya` means as if swollen by rapture, which is the instrument. `Bhijjamāno viya` means as if shattered by it, or as if broken by rapture, which is the agent. Angry people are easily recognized; therefore, the meaning is 'having known his state of anger'.

Akuddho rakkhatīti kuddhassa so kodho itarasmiṃ akujjhante anupādāno ceva ekavāramattaṃ uppattiyā anāsevano ca hutvā cāvetuṃ na sakkoti, udakantaṃ patvā aggi viya nibbāyati, tasmā akuddho itaraṃ cavanato rakkhati. Ubhosu pana kuddhesu bhiyyo bhiyyo aññamaññamhi parivaḍḍhanavasena tikhiṇasamudācāro nissayadahanaraso kodho uppajjamāno hadayavatthuṃ nidahanto accantasukhumālakarajakāyaṃ vināseti, tato sakalopi attabhāvo antaradhāyati[V 1.0373], tamatthaṃ dassetumāha “ubhosu panā”tiādi. Tathā cāha pāḷiyaṃ “te aññamaññamhi paduṭṭhacittā kilantakāyā kilantacittā te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti. Ekassa kodho itarassa paccayo hoti, tassapi kodho itarassa paccayo hotīti ettha kodhassa bhiyyo bhiyyo parivaḍḍhanāya eva paccayabhāvo veditabbo, na cavanāya nissayadahanarasena attanoyeva kodhena hadayavatthuṃ nidahantena accantasukhumālassa [M 1.0426] karajakāyassa cavanato. Kandantānaṃyeva orodhānanti anādaratthe sāmivacanaṃ. Ayamettha dhammatāti ayaṃ tesaṃ karajakāyamandatāya, tathāuppajjanakassa ca kodhassa balavatāya ṭhānaso cavanabhāvo etesu devesu rūpārūpadhammānaṃ dhammaniyāmo sabhāvoti attho.

‘The non-angry one protects’ means that the anger of an angry one, when directed towards one who is not angry, being without fuel and uncultivated in its single arising, is unable to cause him to fall away; it is extinguished like a fire reaching the water's edge. Thus, the non-angry one protects the other from falling away. When both are angry, however, anger—which is sharp in its arising and has the nature of burning its support—arises through ever-increasing mutual escalation, and burning up the heart-base, it destroys the extremely subtle `karajakāya`. From that, the entire individual existence disappears. To show this meaning, the Teacher said, ‘When both, however...’ and so on. And so it is said in the Pāḷi: ‘Those devas, with minds corrupted towards one another, with weary bodies and weary minds, fall from that body.’ Herein, in the passage ‘One's anger is a condition for the other's, and that one's anger is also a condition for the other's,’ the state of being a condition should be understood only for the ever-increasing growth of anger, not for the falling away. This is because the falling away is due to the destruction of the extremely subtle `karajakāya` when its heart-base is burned up by one's own anger, which has the nature of burning its support. `Kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ` is a genitive case used in the sense of disregard. `Ayamettha dhammatā` means: this state of falling away instantly for these devas is due to the weakness of their `karajakāya` and the strength of the anger that arises in such a way; this is the fixed, natural law of material and immaterial phenomena in these devas. This is the meaning.

49-52. Cakkhādīnaṃ bhedaṃ passatīti virodhipaccayasannipāte vikārāpattidassanato, ante ca adassanūpagamanato vināsaṃ passati oḷārikattā rūpadhammabhedassa. Paccayaṃ datvāti anantarapaccayādivasena paccayasattiṃ datvā, paccayo hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā na passatīti sambandho, balavatarampi samānaṃ iminā kāraṇena na passatīti adhippāyo. Balavataranti ca cittassa lahutarabhedaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tathā hi ekasmiṃ rūpe dharanteyeva soḷasa cittāni bhijjanti. Cittassa bhedaṃ na passatīti ettha khaṇe khaṇe bhijjantampi cittaṃ parassa anantarapaccayabhāveneva bhijjati, tasmā purimacittassa abhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā viya pacchimacittassa uppattito bhāvapakkho balavataro pākaṭova hoti, na abhāvapakkhoti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “cittaṃ panā”tiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayañcattho alābhacakkanidassanena dīpetabbo. Yasmā pana takkīvādī nānattanayassa duravadhānatāya, ekattanayassa ca micchāgahitattā “yadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sabbadāpi evarūpena pavattati, ayaṃ me attā nicco”tiādinā abhinivesaṃ janesi, tasmā tamatthaṃ “so taṃ apassanto”tiādinā saha upamāya vibhāveti.

49-52. 'He sees the breaking up of the eye and so forth' means that he sees destruction because he perceives the occurrence of alteration when opposing conditions converge, and because it reaches the point of non-seeing at the end; this is owing to the grossness of the breaking up of material phenomena. 'Having given the condition' means having given the conditional power by way of the proximity condition, etc., or having become a condition. Therefore, the connection should be made with 'he does not see.' The intention is that even though it is stronger, he does not see it for this reason. And 'stronger' is said with reference to the much quicker breaking up of consciousness. For indeed, while one material form is still present, sixteen consciousnesses break up. Here, in 'He does not see the breaking up of consciousness,' although consciousness breaks up moment by moment, it breaks up only by being the proximity condition for the next. Therefore, because of the arising of the subsequent consciousness, as if concealing the non-existence of the preceding consciousness, the side of existence is stronger and more manifest, not the side of non-existence. To show this reason, it should be understood that the passage beginning 'But consciousness...' was said. And this meaning should be illustrated by the example of the circle of a firebrand. Moreover, because a logician, due to the difficulty of attending to the method of diversity and due to wrongly grasping the method of unity, generates the adherence that 'This very consciousness always continues in such a form; this is my permanent self,' etc., therefore, he clarifies that meaning with the phrase 'he, not seeing that,' etc., together with a simile.

Antānantavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Doctrine of the Finite and the Infinite

53. Antānantasahacarito vādo antānanto yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti, antānantasannissayo vā yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti, so etesanti antānantikāti atthaṃ dassetuṃ “antānantavādā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttanayena antānantasahacarito, tannissayo vā, antānantesu vā pavatto vādo etesanti antānantavādā. Idāni “antavā ayaṃ loko”tiādinā vakkhamānapāṭhānurūpaṃ atthaṃ vibhajanto “antaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Amati gacchati [V 1.0374] bhāvo osānametthāti hi anto, mariyādā[M 1.0427], tappaṭisedhanena ananto. Anto ca ananto ca antānanto ca nevantanānanto ca antānanto tveva vutto sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesenavā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) viya. Catutthapadañhettha tatiyapadena samānatthanti antānantapadeneva yathāvuttanayadvayena catudhā attho viññāyati. Kassa panāyaṃ antānantoti? Lokīyati saṃsāranissaraṇatthikehi diṭṭhigatikehi avapassīyati, lokiyanti vā ettha tehi puññāpuññāni, tabbipāko cāti “loko”ti saṅkhyaṃ gatassa attano. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ “antānantaṃ lokassa paññapentī”ti. Ko paneso attāti? Jhānavisayabhūtaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ. Ayañhi diṭṭhigatiko paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ, apariyantaṃ vā vaḍḍhanavasena, tadanussavādivasena ca tattha lokasaññī viharati, tathā ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vakkhati “taṃ ‘loko’ti gahetvā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.54-60) keci pana vadanti “jhānaṃ, taṃsampayuttadhammā ca idha attā, lokoti ca gahitā”ti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya na sameti.

53. A doctrine that is co-occurrent with the finite and the infinite is called 'Antānanta,' for example, 'spears are moving'; or a doctrine that is based on the finite and the infinite, for example, 'beds are shouting'. That doctrine exists for these ascetics and brahmins, therefore they are called Antānantikā. To show this meaning, it was said by the commentator, 'Antānantavādā'. In the manner stated: for these, there exists a doctrine that is co-occurrent with the finite and infinite, or is based on them, or occurs in relation to the finite and infinite; therefore, they are called Antānantavādā. Now, analyzing the meaning in accordance with the text that is about to be spoken, beginning with 'this world is finite,' he said 'antaṃ vā,' etc. Indeed, 'anta' is so called because herein, in this boundary, being comes to a conclusion; it is a boundary. By its negation, it is 'ananta'. 'Finite,' 'infinite,' 'finite-and-infinite,' and 'neither-finite-nor-infinite' are all spoken of simply as 'antānanta' by way of general designation, or by way of elliptical compound, as in such cases as 'conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases...'. For herein, the fourth term has the same meaning as the third term. Therefore, by the term 'antānanta' alone, through the two aforementioned methods, the meaning is understood in four ways. But of what is this 'finite and infinite'? It is of the self, which has come to be designated as 'world'. This is because it is looked down upon by those with wrong views who desire escape from saṃsāra; or, because herein meritorious and demeritorious actions and their results are looked down upon by them. Therefore, in the Pāḷi, the Blessed One said: 'They declare the world to be finite and infinite.' But what is this self? It is the kasiṇa-sign which has become the object of jhāna. For this person with wrong views, perceiving the counterpart sign as the world, dwells with it as either limited to the world-sphere or as unlimited, by way of expansion and by way of hearsay about it, and so on. And so, in the commentary it will be said: 'taking that as "the world".' Some, however, say: 'Herein, jhāna and the states associated with it are taken as "self" and as "world".' That does not agree with the commentary.

Etthāha – yuttaṃ tāva purimānaṃ tiṇṇampi vādīnaṃ antānantikattaṃ antañca anantañca antānantañca ārabbha pavattavādattā, pacchimassa pana takkikassa tadubhayapaṭisedhanavasena pavattavādattā kathaṃ antānantikattanti? Tadubhayapaṭisedhanavasena pavattavādattā eva. Antānantapaṭisedhanavādopi hi so antānantavisayoyeva tamārabbha pavattattā. Etadatthameva hi sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “antaṃ vā antantaṃ vā antānantaṃ vā nevantānānantaṃ vā ārabbha pavattavādā”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā yathā tatiyavāde desapabhedavasena ekasseva lokassa antavatā, anantavatā ca sambhavati, evamettha takkīvādepi kālapabhedavasena ekasseva tadubhayasambhavato aññamaññapaṭisedhena tadubhayaññeva vuccati, dvinnampi ca paṭisedhānaṃ pariyudāsatā. Kathaṃ? Antavantapaṭisedhena hi anantavā vuccati, anantavantapaṭisedhena ca antavā. Dvipaṭisedho hi pakatiyatthañāpako. Iti paṭisedhanavasena antānantasaṅkhātassa ubhayassa vuttattā yuttoyeva tabbisayassa pacchimassāpi antānantikabhāvoti. Yadevaṃ so antānantikavādabhāvato tatiyavādasamavarodheyeva siyāti? Na, kālapabhedassa adhippetattā. Desapabhedavasena hi antānantiko tatiyavādī viya pacchimopi [M 1.0428] takkiko kālapabhedavasena antānantiko hoti. Kathaṃ? Yasmā ayaṃ lokasaññito attā ananto kadā ci sakkhidiṭṭhoti adhigatavisesehi mahesīhi anusuyyati, tasmā nevantavā. Yasmā panāyaṃ antavā kadāci, sakkhidiṭṭhoti tehiyeva anusuyyati, tasmā nānantavāti. Ayaṃ takkiko avaḍḍhitabhāvapubbakattā paṭibhāganimittānaṃ vaḍḍhitabhāvassa ubhayathā labbhamānassa parikappitassa attano appaccakkhakāritāya [V 1.0375] anussavādimatte ṭhatvā vaḍḍhitakālavasena “nevantavā”ti paṭikkhipati, avaḍḍhitakālavasena pana “nānantavā”ti, na pana antatānantatānaṃ accantamabhāvena yathā taṃ “nevasaññānāsaññā”ti. Yathā cānussutikatakkino, evaṃ jātissaratakkiādīnampi vasena yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, someone objects: Let it be granted, for now, that it is fitting for the first three proponents of views to be called Antānantikā, because their doctrines arise in connection with the finite, the infinite, and the finite-and-infinite. But for the last one, the sophist, since his doctrine arises by way of negating both of these, how is it fitting for him to be called an Antānantika? [Reply:] It is precisely because his doctrine arises by way of negating both. For even one who advocates the negation of the finite and infinite still has the finite and infinite as his subject, since his view arises in connection with them. Indeed, it was with reference to this very meaning that it was said in the commentary: 'They are proponents of views that arise in connection with the finite, or the infinite, or the finite-and-infinite, or neither-finite-nor-infinite.' Alternatively, just as in the third view it is possible for one and the same world to be both finite and infinite by way of spatial distinction, so too here in the sophist's view, because it is possible for both states to apply to one and the same thing by way of temporal distinction, both are spoken of through mutual negation. And for both negations, there is the state of being a 'negation by implication' (pariyudāsa). How so? For by negating the finite, the infinite is stated; and by negating the infinite, the finite is stated. Indeed, a double negation makes known the natural meaning. Thus, because both aspects, designated as 'finite and infinite,' are stated by way of negation, it is indeed fitting for the last one too, whose subject is this, to be an Antānantika. [Objection:] If so, then because he is a proponent of a finite-and-infinite view, he would surely be included in the third view. [Reply:] No, because a temporal distinction is intended. For just as the third proponent of a view is an Antānantika by way of spatial distinction, so too the last one, the sophist, is an Antānantika by way of temporal distinction. How so? Because it is heard from the great seers who have attained special distinction that 'this self, designated as the world, was directly seen by me at some time as infinite,' therefore, it is not finite. And because it is heard from those very same ones that 'this was directly seen by me at some time as finite,' therefore, it is not infinite. This sophist, because he has not directly realized for himself the conceived self—which is obtainable in two ways, as a developed state and as having the prior state of being undeveloped, with regard to the counterpart signs—stands merely on hearsay and so on. By way of the time of development, he rejects, saying, 'It is not finite'; and by way of the time of non-development, 'It is not infinite.' He does not, however, reject them through the absolute non-existence of finitude and infinitude, as in the case of 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'. And just as this is to be applied by way of the sophist who relies on hearsay, so too it should be applied, as may be appropriate, by way of the sophists who remember past lives, and so on.

Keci pana yadi panāyaṃ attā antavā, evaṃ sati dūradese upapajjanānussaraṇādikiccanibbatti na siyā. Atha anantavā, evañca idha ṭhitasseva devalokanirayādīsu sukhadukkhānubhavanaṃ siyā. Sace pana antavā ceva anantavā ca, evampi tadubhayadosasamāyogo siyā. Tasmā “antavā, anantavā”ti ca abyākaraṇīyo attāti evaṃ takkanavasena catutthavādappavattiṃ vaṇṇenti. Yadi panesa vuttanayena antānantiko bhaveyya, atha kasmā “ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu ‘antavā ayaṃ loko parivaṭumo’ti, tesaṃ musā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.57) tassa purimavādattayapaṭikkhepo vuttoti? Purimavādattayassa tena yathādhippetappakāravilakkhaṇabhāvato. Teneva hi kāraṇena tathā paṭikkhepo vutto, na pana tassa antānantikattābhāvena, na ca pariyantarahitadiṭṭhivācāhi paṭikkhepena, avassañcetaṃ evameva ñātabbaṃ. Aññathā hesa amarāvikkhepapakkhaññeva bhajeyya catutthavādo. Na hi antatāanantatātadubhayavinimutto attano pakāro atthi, takkīvādī ca yuttimaggakoyeva. Kālabhedavasena ca ekasmimpi loke tadubhayaṃ no na yujjatīti. Bhavatu tāva pacchimavādīdvayassa antānantikabhāvo yutto antānantānaṃ vasena ubhayavisayattā tesaṃ vādassa. Kathaṃ pana purimavādīdvayassa paccekaṃ antānantikabhāvo yutto siyā [M 1.0429] ekekavisayattā tesaṃ vādassāti? Vuccate – samudāye pavattamāna-saddassa avayavepi upacāravuttito. Samuditesu hi antānantavādīsu pavattamāno antānanti ka-saddo tattha niruḷhatāya tadavayavesupi paccekaṃ antānantikavādīsu pavattati yathā “arūpajjhānesu paccekaṃ aṭṭhavimokkhapariyāyo”, yathā ca “loke sattāsayo”ti. Atha vā abhinivesato purimakāle pavattavitakkavasena ayaṃ tattha vohāro kato. Tesañhi diṭṭhigatikānaṃ tathārūpacetosamādhisamadhigamato pubbakāle “antavā nu kho ayaṃ loko, udāhu anantavā”ti ubhayākārāvalambino vitakkassa vasena niruḷho antānantikabhāvo pacchā visesalābhena tesu antānantavādesu ekasseva vādassa saṅgahe uppannepi purimasiddharuḷhiyā vohārīyati yathā “sabbe sattā maraṇadhammā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.133) arahati sattapariyāyo, yathā ca bhavantaragatepi maṇḍūkādivohāroti.

Some teachers, however, explain the occurrence of the fourth doctrine by way of reasoning thus: If this self were finite, this being so, the accomplishment of the task of recollecting rebirth in a distant place, etc., would not be. If it were infinite, this also being so, the experiencing of pleasure and pain that occurs in the deva world, hell, etc., of one who is established right here would be. Furthermore, if it were both finite and infinite, even this being so, the conjunction with the fault of both of those would be. Therefore, the self should not be declared as 'finite' and as 'infinite'. An objection is raised: If this person were to hold the view of finite and infinite by the method already stated, for what reason is the refutation of the three former doctrines stated in the text beginning with, 'Those ascetics and brahmins who thus said, "This world is finite and spherical," their speech is false,' and so on? The answer is: Because the three former doctrines have a characteristic different from the intended manner of that fourth doctrine. For that very reason, the refutation is stated in that manner, but not because of his not being one who holds the view of finite and infinite, and not by refuting with views and words that are devoid of a limit. And this, without fail, should be known just so. Otherwise, this fourth doctrine would fall into the camp of the eel-wrigglers. Truly, there is no mode of the self that is liberated from the state of being finite, the state of being infinite, and both of those, and a reasoner is one who seeks what is suitable. And by way of the distinction of time, even in one world, both of those are not unsuitable. Let it be so for now; the state of being one who holds the view of finite and infinite is suitable for the two proponents of the later views, because their doctrine has both the finite and the infinite as its object by way of the finite and the infinite. But an objection is raised: How then could the state of being one who holds the view of finite and infinite be suitable for each of the two proponents of the former views individually, since their doctrine has a single object? The answer is stated: Because a term that occurs in a collection is also used figuratively for its parts. To elaborate, the term 'antānantika', which occurs among those who hold the views of finite and infinite collectively, because of being established there, also occurs for the individual proponents of the finite and infinite views, who are parts of that, just as the term 'the eight liberations' occurs for each of the formless absorptions individually, and just as 'the dispositions of beings' in the world. Alternatively, this designation is used there out of adherence, by way of the reasoning that occurred in a former time. To elaborate, for those who hold wrong views, from properly attaining such a mental concentration, in a former time, by way of the reasoning that depends on both aspects, 'Is this world finite, or is it infinite?', the established state of being one who holds the view of finite and infinite, even when, later, having obtained a special attainment, the taking up of only one doctrine among those finite and infinite doctrines has arisen, is designated by the convention established in the past, just as in 'all beings are subject to death,' etc., the term 'being' is applicable, and just as the designation 'frog', etc., is applicable even when it has gone to another existence.

54-60. Paṭibhāganimittavaḍḍhanāya [V 1.0376] heṭṭhā, upari, tiriyañca cakkavāḷapariyantagatāgatavasena antānantabhāvoti dassetuṃ “paṭibhāganimitta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Nti paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvāti etthāpi “cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā”ti adhikāravasena yojetabbaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “takkayatīti takkī”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34) saddato, “catubbidho takkī”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34) atthato ca sassatavāde vuttanayena. Diṭṭhapubbānusārenāti dassanabhūtena viññāṇena upaladdhapubbassa antavantādino anussaraṇena, evañca katvā anussutitakkīsuddhatakkīnampi idha saṅgaho siddho hoti. Atha vā diṭṭhaggahaṇeneva “naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.10, 194) viya sutādīnampi gahitabhāvo veditabbo. “Antavā”tiādinā icchitassa attano sabbadābhāvaparāmasanavaseneva imesaṃ vādānaṃ pavattanato sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi vakkhati “satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.97, 98).

In order to show that for the development of the counterpart sign—below, above, and across—the state of being finite and infinite arises by way of reaching or not reaching the Cakkavāḷa-limit, the words beginning with 'the counterpart sign' were stated. 'That' refers to the counterpart sign. Also in the phrase 'not developing it upwards and downwards, but developing it across', the phrase 'having made the Cakkavāḷa the limit' should be connected by way of the context. 'By the stated method' means: by the method stated in the section on eternalism, both in terms of the word, beginning with 'one who reasons is a reasoner', and in terms of the meaning, beginning with 'the reasoner is fourfold'. 'By following what was previously seen' means: by repeatedly recollecting the finite, etc., which was previously apprehended by consciousness that has become seeing; and having done so, the inclusion of the reasoner by hearsay and the pure reasoner is established here. Alternatively, by the very taking of 'seeing', as in 'seeing dancing, singing, music, and shows', etc., it should be known that what is heard, etc., is also included. By 'finite', etc., because these doctrines arise precisely by way of generally considering the ever-existing state of the desired self, their inclusion in the eternalist view should be understood. For so the commentator will say, 'There are seven annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views.'

Amarāvikkhepavādavaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Eel-Wriggling Doctrine

61. Na [M 1.0430] maratīti “evamevā”ti sanniṭṭhānābhāvena na upacchijjati, anekantikāyeva hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pariyantarahitāti osānavigatā, aniṭṭhaṅgatāti attho. Vividhoti “evampi me no”tiādinā nānappakāro. Khepoti sakavādena paravādānaṃ khipanaṃ. Ko paneso amarāvikkhepoti? Tathāpavatto diṭṭhippadhāno tādisāya vācāya samuṭṭhāpako cittuppādoyeva. Amarāya diṭṭhiyā, vācāya ca vikkhipanti, vividhamapanentīti vā amarāvikkhepino, teyeva “amarāvikkhepikā”tipi yujjati. “Macchajāti” cceva avatvā “ekā”ti vadanto macchajātiviseso esoti dasseti. Ito cito ca sandhāvati ekasmiṃ sabhāve anavaṭṭhānato. Yathā gāhaṃ na upagacchati, tathā sandhāvanato, etena amarāya vikkhepo tathā, so viyāti amarāvikkhepoti atthamāha “sā ummujjananimujjanādivasenā”tiādinā vikkhepapadatthena upamitattā. Ayameva hi attho ācariyasāriputtattherenāpi sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 1.tatiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vutto. Amarā viya vikkhepo amarāvikkhepoti keci. Atha vā amarā viya vikkhipantīti amarāvikkhepino, teyeva amarāvikkhepikā.

61. 'Na marati' (it does not die) means: because of the absence of a conclusion 'it is just so', it is not cut off; it is just inconclusive. This is what is meant. 'Pariyantarahitā' (devoid of a limit) means: devoid of an end, not having reached a conclusion. This is the meaning. 'Vividho' (various) means: of many kinds, beginning with 'even this is not for me'. 'Khepo' (throwing) means: the casting down of others' doctrines with one's own doctrine. What, then, is this Amarāvikkhepa? It is just the mind-moment which is the originator of such speech, which is predominated by view, and which occurs in that way. They prevaricate with a view and speech that is endless, or, they cast away in various ways; therefore, they are called Amarāvikkhepino. They themselves are also called Amarāvikkhepikā; this meaning is also suitable. By not saying 'a species of fish' but saying 'one', he shows that this is a special kind of fish species. It runs from here to there because of not being established in one nature. Because of running in such a way that it does not come to be grasped, by this he states the meaning: the prevarication of the amarā fish is like that; therefore, it is called Amarāvikkhepa, because it is compared by the meaning of the word 'vikkhepa' with 'by way of emerging and submerging', etc. Truly, this very meaning was also stated by the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta, in the Sāratthadīpanī. Some say: 'A prevarication like an amarā fish is Amarāvikkhepa'. Alternatively: they prevaricate like an amarā fish; therefore, they are called Amarāvikkhepino. They themselves are also called Amarāvikkhepikā.

62. Vikkhepavādino uttarimanussadhamme, abyākatadhamme ca (akusaladhammepi dī. ni. ṭī. 1.62) sabhāvabhedavasena paṭivijjhituṃ ñāṇaṃ natthīti kusalākusalapadānaṃ kusalākusalakammapathavaseneva [V 1.0377] attho vutto. Vighāto vihesā kāyikadukkhaṃ “vippaṭisāruppattiyā”ti domanassassa hetubhāvena vacanato, tenāha “dukkhaṃ bhaveyyā”ti. Musāvādeti nimitte bhummavacanaṃ, nissakkatthe vā. Musāvādahetu, musāvādato vā ottappena ceva hiriyā cāti attho. Kīdisaṃ amarāvikkhepamāpajjatīti āha “apariyantavikkhepa”nti, tena amarāsadisavikkhepasaṅkhātaṃ dutiyanayaṃ nivatteti. Yathāvutte hi nayadvaye paṭhamanayavasenāyamattho dassito, dutiyanayavasena pana amarāsadisavikkhepaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kusalanti puṭṭho”tiādivacanaṃ vakkhati.

62. For one who advocates equivocation, there is no knowledge to penetrate the superhuman states and the indeterminate states by way of the distinction of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, the meaning of the terms 'wholesome' and 'unwholesome' is stated only by way of the wholesome and unwholesome courses of action. `Vighāta` is vexation. Bodily suffering would arise. Why? Because of the statement, 'due to the arising of remorse,' as the cause of displeasure; therefore, he said, 'suffering would arise.' The term `musāvāde` is a locative in the sense of a cause, or in the sense of the ablative. The meaning is: 'because of false speech' or 'from false speech,' through both fear of wrongdoing and shame of wrongdoing. Because it should be asked, 'What kind of eel-wriggling does one fall into?', he said, 'endless equivocation.' By this, he refutes the second method, which is known as 'equivocation similar to the amara fish.' Indeed, in the two methods stated, this meaning is shown by way of the first method. However, to show the equivocation similar to the amara fish by way of the second method, he will state the words beginning with, 'When asked, "Is this wholesome?"'.

“Evantipi me no”ti yaṃ tayā puṭṭhaṃ, taṃ evantipi me laddhi no hotīti attho. Evaṃ sabbattha yathārahaṃ. Aniyamitavikkhepoti sassatādīsu ekasmimpi [M 1.0431] pakāre aṭṭhatvā vikkhepakaraṇaṃ, paravādinā yasmiṃ kismiñci pakāre pucchite tassa paṭikkhepavikkhepoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā apariyantavikkhepadassanaṃyeva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ kataṃ “evantipi me noti aniyamitavikkhepo”tiādinā, “idaṃ kusalanti vā akusalanti vā puṭṭho”tiādinā ca. “Evantipi me no”tiādinā hi aniyametvā, niyametvā ca sassatekaccasassatucchedatakkīvādānaṃ paṭisedhanena taṃ taṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipateva apariyantavikkhepavādattā. “Amarāvikkhepino”ti dassetvā attanā pana anavaṭṭhitavādattā na kismiñci pakkhe avatiṭṭhatīti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “sayaṃ pana idaṃ…pe… na byākarotī”ti āha. Idāni kusalādīnaṃ abyākaraṇena tadeva anavaṭṭhānaṃ vibhāveti “idaṃ kusalanti puṭṭho”tiādinā. Tenevāha “ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhatī”ti. Kiṃ no noti te laddhīti neva na hotīti tava laddhi hoti kinti attho. No notipi me noti neva na hotītipi me laddhi no hoti.

'Even thus it is not for me' means: regarding that which you asked, 'even thus it is not my view.' Thus should the meaning be understood as appropriate in all instances. 'Unrestricted equivocation' is the act of equivocating without standing on any single type of view among eternalism and so on; it is said to be the rejection and equivocation regarding a view when an opponent asks about any particular type of it. Alternatively, in the commentary, only the showing of endless equivocation is done, by the passage beginning with 'Even thus it is not for me is unrestricted equivocation,' and by the passage beginning with 'When asked, "Is this wholesome or unwholesome?"'. Indeed, by the passage beginning with 'Even thus it is not for me,' by rejecting the doctrines of eternalism, partial eternalism, annihilationism, and sophistry, both without defining and by defining, he simply rejects those various doctrines because of holding the doctrine of endless equivocation. Having shown them as 'Eel-wrigglers,' to show this meaning—that he himself, because of holding an unstable doctrine, does not stand on any side—he said, 'But he himself... does not declare this.' Now, by not answering regarding wholesome states and so on, he clarifies that very instability with the passage beginning with, 'When asked, "Is this wholesome?"'. For that very reason, he said, 'He does not stand on any single side.' 'Is "not not" your view?' means, 'Is your view "it is not not"?'. '"Not not" is not my view, and "it is not not" is also not my view.'

63. Attano paṇḍitabhāvavisayānaññeva rāgādīnaṃ vasena yojanaṃ kātuṃ “ajānantopī”tiādimāha. Sahasāti anupadhāretvā vegena. “Bhadramukhāti paṇḍitānaṃ samudāciṇṇamālapanaṃ, sundaramukhāti attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ byākaraṇe, nimitte cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Chandarāgapadānaṃ samānatthabhāvepi vikappanajotakena vā-saddena yogyattā gobalībaddādinayena bhinnatthatāva yuttāti āha “chando dubbalarāgo, rāgo balavarāgo”ti. Dosapaṭighesupi eseva nayo. Ettakampi nāmāti ettha api-saddo sampiṇḍane vattati, nāma-saddo garahāyaṃ. Na kevalaṃ ito uttaritarameva, atha kho ettakampi na jānāmi nāma, pageva taduttarijānaneti attho. Parehi katasakkārasamānavisayānaṃ pana rāgādīnaṃ vasena ayaṃ yojanā – kusalākusalaṃ yathābhūtaṃ [V 1.0378] apajānantopi yesamahaṃ samavāyena kusalameva “kusala”nti, akusalameva “akusala”nti ca byākareyyaṃ, tesu tathā byākaraṇahetu “aho vata re paṇḍito”ti sakkārasammānaṃ karontesu mama chando vā rāgo vā assāti. Dosapaṭighesupi vuttavipariyāyena yojetabbaṃ. “Taṃ mamassa upādānaṃ, so mamassa vighāto”ti idaṃ abhidhammanayena (dha. sa. 1219 ādayo) yathālābhavacanaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbanti āha “chandarāgadvaya”ntiādi. Taṇhādiṭṭhiyo [M 1.0432] eva hi “upādāna”nti abhidhamme vuttā (dha. sa. 1219 ādayo) idāni suttantanayena avisesayojanaṃ dasseti “ubhayampi vā”tiādinā. Suttante hi dosopi “upādāna”nti vutto “kodhupādānavinibandhā vighātaṃ āpajjantī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.63) “ubhayampī”ti ca atthato vuttaṃ, na saddato catunnampi saddānamatthadvayavācakattā. Daḷhaggahaṇanti amuñcanaggahaṇaṃ. Paṭighopi hi ārammaṇaṃ na muñcati upanāhādivasena pavattanato, lobhasseva upādānabhāvena pākaṭattā dosassāpi upādānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ. Vihananaṃ vihiṃsanaṃ vibādhanaṃ. Rāgopi hi pariḷāhavasena sāraddhavuttitāya nissayaṃ vihanati. “Rāgo hī”tiādinā rāgadosānaṃ upādānabhāve visesadassanamukhena tadatthasamatthanaṃ. Vināsetukāmatāya ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhātīti sambandho. Itīti tasmā gahaṇavihananato.

63. To make the connection by way of lust and so on, which are solely the domain of one's own state of being a wise person, he said the words beginning with, 'even without knowing.' `Sahasā` means hastily, without reflection. `Bhadramukha` is a customary address of the wise; the meaning is 'O one with a beautiful face.' `Tattha` means 'in that declaration,' and this is a locative in the sense of a cause. Although the terms `chanda` (desire) and `rāga` (lust) have a similar meaning, because they are connected with the word `vā` which indicates an alternative, it is fitting that they have distinct meanings, according to the principle of 'go-balībadda,' etc. Therefore, he said, '`chanda` is weak lust, `rāga` is strong lust.' This same principle should be understood for aversion (`dosa`) and resistance (`paṭigha`) as well. In `ettakampi nāma`, the particle `api` is used for aggregation, and the particle `nāma` is used in the sense of censure. The meaning is: 'It is not just that I do not know what is beyond this; rather, I do not even know this much, indeed! What is to be said of knowing what is beyond that?' But this is the connection by way of lust and so on, which are the objects of honor and respect made by others: 'Even without truly knowing the wholesome and unwholesome, if I were to declare to them, according to my own view, that the wholesome is "wholesome" and the unwholesome is "unwholesome," then when they, on account of that declaration, show me honor and respect, thinking, "Oh, what a wise person!", desire or lust would arise in me.' For aversion and resistance, the connection should be made in the opposite way of what was said. The statement, 'That would be my clinging, that would be my vexation,' should be connected according to the Abhidhamma method, in accordance with the word as obtained and as is possible. Therefore, he said the words beginning with, 'the pair of desire and lust.' Indeed, only craving (`taṇhā`) and views (`diṭṭhi`) are called 'clinging' (`upādāna`) in the Abhidhamma. Now, he shows the non-specific connection according to the Suttanta method with the words beginning with, 'or both.' Indeed, in the Suttas, even aversion (`dosa`) is called 'clinging,' as in 'those bound by the clinging of anger fall into distress,' etc. And 'both' is stated in terms of meaning, not in terms of the word, because all four words convey two meanings. `Daḷhaggahaṇa` means a grasping that does not let go. Indeed, resentment (`paṭigha`) also does not let go of its object, because it proceeds by way of bearing a grudge, etc. Because only greed is prominent as being of the nature of clinging, this was said to show that aversion also has the nature of clinging. `Vihanana` is vexing, harming, oppressing. Indeed, lust also, by way of its burning fever and agitated state, vexes its support. With the words beginning with 'For lust,' he shows the establishment of that meaning—the nature of clinging of lust and aversion—by means of showing their distinction. The connection should be made thus: 'it grasps the object with the desire to destroy it.' `Iti` means: therefore, because of grasping and vexing.

64. Paḍati sabhāvadhamme jānāti, yathāsabhāvaṃ vā gacchatīti paṇḍā, sā yesaṃ te paṇḍitāti atthaṃ dasseti “paṇḍiccenā”tiādinā. Paṇḍitassa bhāvo paṇḍiccaṃ, paññā. Yena hi dhammena pavattinimittabhūtena yutto “paṇḍito”ti vuccati, soyeva dhammo paṇḍiccaṃ. Tena sutacintāmayapaññā vuttā tāsameva visayabhāvato. Samāpattilābhino hi bhāvanāmayapaññā. “Nipuṇā”ti iminā pana kammanibbattaṃ paṭisandhipaññāsaṅkhātaṃ sābhāvikañāṇaṃ vuttanti āha “saṇhasukhumabuddhino”ti. Atthantaranti atthanānattaṃ, atthameva vā. “Viññātaparappavādā”ti etena kata-saddassa kiriyāsāmaññavācakattā “katavijjo”tiādīsu viya kata-saddo ñāṇānuyuttataṃ vadatīti dasseti. “Katavādaparicayā”ti etena pana “katasippo”tiādīsu viya samudāciṇṇavādataṃ. Ubhinnamantarā pana samuccayadvayena sāmaññaniddesaṃ, ekasesaṃ vāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vālavedhīnaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo viya rūpametesanti vālavedhirūpāti āha “vālavedhidhanuggahasadisā”ti. Satadhā bhinnassa vālaggassa aṃsukoṭivedhakadhanuggahasadisāti attho. Tādisoyeva hi “vālavedhī”ti adhippeto. Maññe-saddo upamājotakoti vuttaṃ “bhindantā viyā”ti. Paññāgatenāti paññāpabhedena, paññāya eva vā. Samanuyuñjanā laddhiyā pucchā. Samanugāhanā taṃkāraṇassāti dasseti “kiṃ kusala”ntiādinā. Samanubhāsanāpi [V 1.0379] ovādavasena samanuyuñjanāyevāti āha [M 1.0433] “samanuyuñjeyyu”nti. “Na sampāyeyya”nti ettha da-kārassa ya-kārādesataṃ, eyya-saddassa ca sāmatthiyatthataṃ dassetuṃ “na sampādeyya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

64. That wisdom which knows inherent phenomena, or alternatively, proceeds to their true nature, is therefore called 'paṇḍā'; those who possess it are 'paṇḍitā'. The commentator shows this meaning with 'paṇḍiccena', and so on. The state of being wise is 'paṇḍiccaṃ', which is wisdom. Indeed, the very quality that serves as the sign of its occurrence, by which one is called 'wise', is itself 'paṇḍiccaṃ'. Through this, wisdom born of learning and reflection is spoken of, as this is their domain. For one who has attained meditative absorption, it is wisdom born of mental development. By 'nipuṇā' (subtle), however, is meant the natural knowledge produced by kamma, which is called rebirth-linking wisdom; thus, he said, 'those with subtle and refined intellect.' 'Atthantara' means either diversity of meaning or simply meaning itself. By 'viññātaparappavādā' (knowing the doctrines of others), it is shown that because the word 'kata' (done) denotes a general action, as in 'katavijjo' (one who has mastered knowledge), the word 'kata' indicates being endowed with knowledge. By 'katavādaparicayā' (familiarity with doctrines), however, it indicates the state of having a thoroughly practiced doctrine, as in 'katasippo' (one skilled in craft). It should be understood that between these two, a general description is indicated by a pair of conjunctions, or an elliptical compound. 'Vālavedhirūpā' (having the nature of hair-splitters) means their nature is like that of hair-splitting archers; thus, it is said, 'they are like hair-splitting archers.' The meaning is that they are like archers who can pierce the tip of a hair split into a hundred parts. Indeed, such a one is intended by 'vālavedhī' (hair-splitter). The word 'maññe' highlights a simile; thus, it is said, 'bhindantā viyā' (as if splitting). 'Paññāgatena' means either 'by the varieties of wisdom' or 'by wisdom itself.' 'Samanuyuñjanā' (questioning) is an inquiry about a doctrine. 'Samanugāhanā' is the investigation of its cause, as shown by 'kiṃ kusala' (what is skillful?), and so on. 'Samanubhāsanā' (exhortation) is also questioning in the manner of an admonition; thus, it is said, 'they would question.' In 'na sampāyeyya' (he would not succeed), 'na sampādeyya' (he would not accomplish), and so on, was said in order to show the substitution of the letter 'ya' for 'da' and that the 'eyya' suffix conveys the sense of ability.

65-66. Mandā atikkhā paññā yassāti mandapañño, tenāha “apaññassevetaṃ nāma”nti. “Mohamūho”ti vattabbe ha-kāralopena “momūho”ti vuttaṃ, tañca atisayatthadīpakaṃ pariyāyadvayassa atirekatthabhāvatoti yathā “padaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ “atisammūḷho”ti. Siddhe hi sati punārambho niyamāya vā hoti, atthantaraviññāpanāya vā. Yathā pubbe kammunā āgato, tathā idhāpīti tathāgato, satto. Ettha ca kāmaṃ purimānampi tiṇṇaṃ kusalādidhammasabhāvānavabodhato attheva mandabhāvo, tesaṃ pana attano kusalādidhammānavabodhassa avabodhanato viseso atthīti. Pacchimoyeva tadabhāvato mandamomūhabhāvena vutto. Nanu ca pacchimassāpi attano dhammānavabodhassa avabodho atthiyeva “atthi paro loko’ti iti ce me assa, ‘atthi paro loko’ti iti te naṃ byākareyyaṃ, evantipi me no”tiādivacanatoti? Kiñcāpi atthi, na pana tassa purimānaṃ viya apariññātadhammabyākaraṇanimittamusāvādādibhāyanajigucchanākāro atthi, atha kho mahāmūḷhoyevāti tathāvesa vutto. Atha vā “evantipi me no”tiādinā pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇatthaṃ “atthi paro loko”ti iti ce maṃ pucchasīti pucchāṭhapanameva tena dassīyati, na attano dhammānavabodhāvabodhoti ayameva visesena “mando momūho”ti vutto. Teneva hi tathāvādīnaṃ sañcayaṃ belaṭṭhaputtaṃ ārabbha “ayañca imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”ti (dī. ni. 1.181) vuttaṃ. Tattha “atthi paro loko”ti sassatadassanavasena, sammādiṭṭhivasena vā pucchā. Yadi hi diṭṭhigatiko sassatadassanavasena puccheyya, yadi ca sammādiṭṭhiko sammādassanavasenāti dvidhāpi attho vaṭṭati. “Natthi paro loko”ti natthikadassanavasena, sammādiṭṭhivasena vā, “atthi ca natthi ca paro loko”ti ucchedadassanavasena, sammādiṭṭhivasena vā, “nevatthi na natthi paro loko”ti vuttapakārattayapaṭikkhepe sati pakārantarassa asambhavato atthitānatthitāhi na vattabbākāro paro lokoti vikkhepaññeva purakkhārena[M 1.0434], sammādiṭṭhivasena vā pucchā. Sesacatukkattayepi vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Puññasaṅkhārattiko viya hi kāyasaṅkhārattikena purimacatukkasaṅgahito eva attho sesacatukkattayena sattaparāmāsapuññādisaphalatācodanānayena (attaparāmāsapuññādiphalatācodanānayena dī. ni. ṭī. 1.65, 66) saṅgahito. Ettha hi tatiyacatukkena [V 1.0380] puññādikammasaphalatāya, sesacatukkattayena ca sattaparāmāsatāya codanānayo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

65-66. One whose wisdom is 'mandā atikkhā' (dull and not sharp) is a 'mandapañño' (one with dull wisdom); hence, he said, 'this is indeed a name for one without wisdom.' When 'mohamūho' should be said, 'momūho' is said with the elision of the letter 'ha'. And that indicates an extreme meaning, because of the intensified meaning of the pair of synonyms; therefore, it is glossed as 'atisammūḷho' (utterly confused). Indeed, when something is established, a further undertaking is either for the sake of a rule or for making known a different meaning. Just as one has come in the past through kamma, so too one has come here; thus, 'tathāgato' (one who has thus come) refers to a being. And here, for the first three, there is indeed a state of dullness due to not understanding the nature of wholesome states, etc. However, for them there is a distinction because they understand their own non-understanding of wholesome states, etc. Only the last one, due to the absence of that, is spoken of as being dull and utterly deluded.
