But surely for the last one too there is an understanding of his own non-understanding of the Dhamma, because of the statement, 'If it were to occur to me, "there is another world," I would declare, "there is another world," but even that is not so for me,' and so on? Although it exists, for him there is not, as there is for the first ones, the characteristic of fear and disgust towards false speech, etc., caused by declaring a Dhamma that is not fully understood. Rather, he is just greatly deluded; thus he is spoken of in that way. Alternatively, by 'evantipi me no,' and so on, for the purpose of evading the question, 'If you ask me, "Is there another world?"', only the setting aside of the question is shown by him, not the understanding of his own non-understanding of the Dhamma. Therefore, this very one is specifically called 'mando momūho' (dull and utterly deluded). Indeed, for that very reason, concerning Sañcaya Belaṭṭhaputta among those with such a doctrine, it was said, 'And this one among these ascetics and brahmins is the most foolish, the most deluded.' Therein, the question 'Is there another world?' is a question either from the perspective of the eternalist view or from the perspective of right view. Indeed, if one holding a wrong view were to ask from the perspective of the eternalist view, and if one with right view were to ask from the perspective of right view, the meaning is suitable in both ways. The question 'There is no other world' is from the perspective of the nihilist view or right view. The question 'There both is and is not another world' is from the perspective of the annihilationist view or right view. As for 'Neither is there nor is there not another world,' since the three aforementioned types are rejected and another type is impossible, the other world has the characteristic of not being speakable in terms of existence or non-existence; thus, the question is put forward with evasion itself, or it is from the perspective of right view. The meaning of the remaining three tetrads should be understood according to the method stated. Indeed, the meaning included in the first tetrad is also included by the remaining three tetrads through the method of censuring the wrong grasp of 'a being' and the fruitfulness of merit, etc. Herein, it should be understood that the method of censure is spoken of by means of the third tetrad regarding the fruitfulness of meritorious actions, etc., and by means of the remaining three tetrads regarding the wrong grasp of 'a being'.

Amarāvikkhepiko pana sassatādīnaṃ attano aruccanatāya sabbattha “evantipi me no”tiādinā vikkhepaññeva karoti. Tattha “evantipi me no”tiādi tattha tattha pucchitākārapaṭisedhanavasena vikkhepākāradassanaṃ. Kasmā pana vikkhepavādino paṭikkhepova sabbattha vutto. Nanu vikkhepapakkhassa “evameva”nti anujānanampi vikkhepapakkhe avaṭṭhānato yuttarūpaṃ siyāti? Na, tatthāpi tassa sammūḷhattā, paṭikkhepavaseneva ca vikkhepavādassa pavattanato. Tathā hi sañcayo belaṭṭhaputto raññā ajātasattunā sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ puṭṭho paralokatthitādīnaṃ paṭisedhanamukheneva vikkhepaṃ byākāsi.

The eel-wriggler (Amarāvikkhepika), however, due to his disapproval of eternalism and other such views, resorts only to equivocation in all cases by saying, 'It is not so for me,' and so on. Herein, the statement 'It is not so for me,' and so on, shows the manner of equivocation by way of rejecting the form of the question in each and every case. But why is only rejection mentioned in all cases with regard to the equivocationist? Should not the affirmation 'It is just so' also be appropriate for the side of equivocation, since it would stand on the side of equivocation? No, because even in that case, it is due to his confusion and because the doctrine of equivocation proceeds only by way of rejection. For so it is that Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, when asked by King Ajātasattu about the visible fruit of recluseship, responded with equivocation by means of rejecting the existence of the next world and so on.

Etthāha – nanu cāyaṃ sabbopi amarāvikkhepiko kusalādayo dhamme, paralokatthitādīni ca yathābhūtaṃ anavabujjhamāno tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho pucchāya vikkhepanamattaṃ āpajjati, atha tassa kathaṃ diṭṭhigatikabhāvo siyā. Na hi avattukāmassa viya pucchitatthamajānantassa vikkhepakaraṇamattena diṭṭhigatikatā yuttāti? Vuccate – na heva kho pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇamattena tassa diṭṭhigatikatā, atha kho micchābhinivesavasena. Sassatābhinivesavasena hi micchābhiniviṭṭhoyeva puggalo mandabuddhitāya kusalādidhamme, paralokatthitādīni ca yāthāvato appaṭibujjhamāno attanā aviññātassa atthassa paraṃ viññāpetumasakkuṇeyyatāya musāvādabhayena ca vikkhepamāpajjatīti. Tathā hi vakkhati “yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.97, 98) atha vā puññapāpānaṃ, tabbipākānañca anavabodhena, asaddahanena ca tabbisayāya pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇameva sundaranti khantiṃ ruciṃ uppādetvā abhinivisantassa uppannā visuṃyevesā ekā diṭṭhi sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā ca vuttaṃ [M 1.0435] “pariyantarahitā diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhi ceva vācā” cāti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.61). Yaṃ panetaṃ vuttaṃ “imepi cattāro pubbe pavattadhammānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā”ti, tadetassa amarāvikkhepavādassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgahavaseneva vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ panassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgahoti? Ucchedavasena anabhinivesanato. Natthi hi koci dhammānaṃ yathābhūtavedī vivādabahulattā lokassa. “Evameva”nti pana saddantarena dhammanijjhānanā anādikālikā loke, tasmā sassatalesassa ettha labbhanato sassatadiṭṭhiyā etassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, it is said: 'Is it not the case that this eel-wriggler, not understanding wholesome states and so on, nor the existence of the next world and so on, as they really are, when questioned on various points, resorts merely to evasion of the question? Then how could he be one who holds a wrong view? For it is not fitting to call one a holder of a wrong view merely for the act of evasion, like one who is unwilling to speak or one who does not know the meaning of what is asked.' To this, it is replied: It is not merely by the act of evading the question that he is one who holds a wrong view, but rather by way of wrong adherence. For it is a person who is indeed wrongly adherent by way of adherence to eternalism who, due to dullness of wisdom, not penetratingly knowing wholesome states and so on, nor the existence of the next world and so on, as they are, resorts to evasion due to his inability to make others understand a matter he himself has not understood, and out of fear of false speech. For so it will be said: 'Of these, seven are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views.' Alternatively, due to not understanding and not having faith in merit and demerit and their results, for one who adheres to a view after generating the inclination and preference that 'it is better simply to evade' in response to a question on that topic, this is a distinct, single view that has arisen, like the Sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi. And so it is said: 'The view and the speech of one who holds a wrong view are without limit.' As for what was said: 'These four, due to grasping a view in accordance with phenomena that occurred in the past, are included among the Pubbantakappikas,' that is said by way of including this Amarāvikkhepavāda in the eternalist view. But how is it included in the eternalist view? Because of not adhering to it by way of annihilationism. For there is no one who knows phenomena as they really are, due to the world being full of disputes. Furthermore, the reflection on phenomena with another expression, 'it is just so,' is beginningless in the world; therefore, since a trace of eternalism is found herein, its inclusion under the eternalist view should be understood.

Adhiccasamuppannavādavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Doctrine of Fortuitous Origination

67. Adhicca [V 1.0381] yadicchakaṃ yaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ kassaci buddhipubbaṃ vinā samuppannoti attalokasaññitānaṃ khandhānaṃ adhiccuppattiākārārammaṇadassanaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ tadākārasannissayeneva pavattito, tadākārasahacaritato ca yathā “mañcā ghosanti, kuntā pacarantī”ti, adhiccasamuppannadassanaṃ vā antapadalopena adhiccasamuppannaṃ yathā “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti, imamatthaṃ sandhāya “adhiccasamuppanno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Akāraṇasamuppannanti kāraṇamantarena yadicchakaṃ samuppannaṃ.

67. The view which has as its object the mode of fortuitous origination of the aggregates perceived as self and world—a view that holds 'It has arisen without reference to any cause whatsoever, without the prior intelligence of anyone'—is called `adhiccasamuppannaṃ`. This is because it proceeds only in dependence on that mode and occurs together with that mode, just as one says 'the beds are shouting' or 'the spears are advancing.' Alternatively, `adhiccasamuppannadassanaṃ` (the view of fortuitous origination) becomes `adhiccasamuppannaṃ` by elision of the final word, just as `rūpabhavo` (form-existence) becomes `rūpaṃ` (form). It is with reference to this meaning that 'adhiccasamuppanno,' etc., is stated. `Akāraṇasamuppannaṃ` means that which has arisen by chance, without a cause.

68-73. Asaññasattāti ettha etaṃ asaññāvacananti attho. Desanāsīsanti desanāya jeṭṭhakaṃ padhānabhāvena gahitattā, tena saññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā bhagavatā ayaṃ desanā katā, na pana tattha aññesaṃ arūpadhammānampi atthitāyāti dasseti, tenevāha “acittuppādā”tiādi. Bhagavā hi yathā lokuttaradhammaṃ desento samādhiṃ, paññaṃ vā dhuraṃ katvā deseti, evaṃ lokiyadhammaṃ desento cittaṃ, saññaṃ vā. Tattha “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti (dha. sa. 277), pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi (dī. ni. 3.355) pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi, (dī. ni. 3.355; vibha. 804) paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”ti, tathā “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, (dha. sa. 1) kiṃ citto tvaṃ bhikkhu (pārā. 146, 180) manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, (dha. pa. 1; netti. 90; peṭako. 83, 84) santi bhikkhave, sattā [M 1.0436] nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, (dī. ni. 3.332, 341, 357; a. ni. 7.44; a. ni. 9.24; cūḷani. 83) nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti (dī. ni. 3.358) ca evamādīni suttāni etassatthassa sādhakāni. Titthaṃ vuccati micchāladdhi tattheva bāhullena paribbhamanato taranti bālā etthāti katvā, tadeva anappakānamanatthānaṃ titthiyānañca sañjātidesaṭṭhena, nivāsaṭṭhena vā āyatananti titthāyatanaṃ, tasmiṃ, aññatitthiyasamayeti attho. Titthiyā hi upapattivisese vimuttisaññino, saññāvirāgāvirāgesu ādīnavānisaṃsadassāvino ca hutvā asaññasamāpattiṃ nibbattetvā akkhaṇabhūmiyaṃ upapajjanti, na sāsanikā, tena vuttaṃ “ekacco titthāyatane pabbajitvā”ti. Vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvāti catutthe bhūtakasiṇe paṭhamādīni tīṇi jhānāni nibbattetvā tatiyajjhāne ciṇṇavasī hutvā tato vuṭṭhāya catutthajjhānādhigamāya parikammaṃ katvā, tenevāha “catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā”ti.

68-73. Herein, regarding 'asaññasattā', the meaning is this word 'asaññā'. 'Desanāsīsa' means the chief of the teaching, because it is taken as primary. By that, it is shown that the Blessed One delivered this teaching by making perception primary, and not, however, because of the existence there of other formless mental states. For that very reason, he said, 'without the arising of consciousness,' etc. Indeed, just as the Blessed One, when teaching the supramundane Dhamma, teaches by making either concentration or wisdom primary, so too, when teaching the mundane Dhamma, he teaches by making either consciousness or perception primary. In this regard, suttas such as: 'At the time when one develops the supramundane jhāna' (Dhs. 277), 'the five-factored right concentration' (DN 3.355), 'the five-knowledge right concentration' (DN 3.355; Vibh. 804), and 'having seen with wisdom, for him the taints are destroyed'; and also 'At the time when wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises' (Dhs. 1), 'What is your consciousness, monk?' (Pārā. 146, 180), 'Mental phenomena are preceded by mind' (Dhp. 1; Netti. 90; Peṭako. 83, 84), 'There are, monks, beings diverse in body and diverse in perception' (DN 3.332, 341, 357; AN 7.44; AN 9.24; Cūḷanī. 83), and 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (DN 3.358) are proofs for this meaning. 'Tittha' is called wrong view because fools wander extensively in it, and because they 'cross over' in it. That very 'tittha' is an 'āyatana' (domain) in the sense of being a place of origin or a dwelling place for countless unbeneficial things and for sectarians; therefore, it is called 'titthāyatana'. In that, the meaning is 'in the doctrine of other sectarians'. Indeed, sectarians, being those who perceive liberation in a particular kind of rebirth, and being those who see the danger and advantage in dispassion and non-dispassion towards perception, produce the attainment of non-perception and are reborn in an inopportune plane; followers of the Dispensation are not. Therefore, it was said, 'a certain one, having gone forth in a sectarian domain...'. 'Having done the preliminary work on the air kasiṇa' means: having produced the first three jhānas in the fourth elemental kasiṇa, having become one with practiced mastery in the third jhāna, having arisen from that, and having done the preliminary work for the attainment of the fourth jhāna. For that very reason, he said, 'having produced the fourth jhāna'.

Kasmā [V 1.0382] panettha vāyokasiṇeyeva parikammaṃ vuttanti? Vuccate – yatheva hi rūpapaṭibhāgabhūtesu kasiṇavisesesu rūpavibhāvanena rūpavirāgabhāvanāsaṅkhāto arūpasamāpattiviseso sacchikarīyati, evaṃ aparibyattaviggahatāya arūpapaṭibhāgabhūte kasiṇavisese arūpavibhāvanena arūpavirāgabhāvanāsaṅkhāto rūpasamāpattiviseso adhigamīyati, tasmā ettha “saññā rogo saññā gaṇḍo”tiādinā, (ma. ni. 3.24) “dhi cittaṃ, dhibbate taṃ citta”ntiādinā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.68-73) ca nayena arūpapavattiyā ādīnavadassanena, tadabhāve ca santapaṇītabhāvasanniṭṭhānena rūpasamāpattiyā abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ, rūpavirāgabhāvanā pana saddhiṃ upacārena arūpasamāpattiyo visesena paṭhamāruppajjhānaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “paricchinnākāsakasiṇepī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tassāpi hi arūpapaṭibhāgatā labbhatīti? Vattabbamevetaṃ kesañci, avacanaṃ pana pubbācariyehi aggahitabhāvena. Yathā hi rūpavirāgabhāvanā virajjanīyadhammabhāvamatte parinibbindā (virajjanīyadhamma bhāvamattena parinipphannā dī. ni. ṭī. 1.6-73) virajjanīyadhammapaṭibhāgabhūte ca visayavisese pātubhavati, evaṃ arūpavirāgabhāvanāpīti vuccamāne na koci virodho. Titthiyeheva pana tassā samāpattiyā paṭipajjitabbatāya, tesañca visayapadesanimittasseva tassa jhānassa paṭipattito taṃ kāraṇaṃ passantehi [M 1.0437] pubbācariyehi catuttheyeva bhūtakasiṇe arūpavirāgabhāvanāparikammaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo – vaṇṇakasiṇesu viya purimabhūtakasiṇattayepi vaṇṇapaṭicchāyāva paṇṇattiārammaṇaṃ jhānassa lokavohārānurodheneva pavattito, evañca katvā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.96) pathavīkasiṇassa ādāsacandamaṇḍalūpamāvacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti. Catutthe pana bhūtakasiṇe bhūtapaṭicchāyā eva jhānassa gocarabhāvaṃ gacchatīti tasseva arūpapaṭibhāgatā yuttā, tasmā vāyokasiṇeyeva parikammaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Why is the preliminary work mentioned here only for the air kasiṇa? It is said: Indeed, just as in the special kasiṇas that are counterparts to form, by making form manifest, the special formless attainment called 'the development of dispassion towards form' is realized; so too, in the special kasiṇa that is a counterpart to the formless due to its indistinct body, by making the formless manifest, the special form attainment called 'the development of dispassion towards the formless' is attained. Therefore, herein, by the method of such sayings as 'Perception is a disease, perception is a boil,' etc., and 'Fie on consciousness! That consciousness is to be loathed,' etc., and by seeing the danger in the occurrence of the formless, and by determining the state of peace and excellence in its absence, there is the formation of the form attainment. Furthermore, the development of dispassion towards form, together with access concentration, are the formless attainments, specifically the first formless jhāna. If so, should it not be said, 'also in the limited-space kasiṇa'? For its state of being a counterpart to the formless is also obtained. This should indeed be said according to some, but its non-mention is due to its not being accepted by the ancient teachers. For just as the development of dispassion towards form, being disenchanted with the mere state of being a thing from which one should be dispassionate, arises in a special object that is a counterpart to a thing from which one should be dispassionate; so too, when it is said 'also the development of dispassion towards the formless', there is no contradiction. However, it should be understood thus: because that attainment is to be practiced only by sectarians, and because of the practice of that jhāna which is solely the sign for the region of their objective realm, the ancient teachers, seeing that reason, stated that the preliminary work for the development of dispassion towards the formless is in the fourth elemental kasiṇa only. And what is more: just as in the color kasiṇas, so also in the triad of the preceding elemental kasiṇas, only the color-reflection is the conceptual object of the jhāna, because it proceeds only in accordance with worldly convention. And for this reason, the statement in the Visuddhimagga comparing the earth kasiṇa to a mirror-disk and the moon-disk is supported. However, in the fourth elemental kasiṇa, it is the reflection of the element itself that becomes the domain of the jhāna. Therefore, for that very kasiṇa, the state of being a counterpart to the formless is suitable. Therefore, it should be known that the preliminary work is mentioned only for the air kasiṇa.

Kathaṃ passatīti āha “citte satī”tiādi. Santoti nibbuto, diṭṭhadhammanibbānametanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kālaṃ katvāti maraṇaṃ katvā, yo vā manussaloke jīvanakālo upatthambhakapaccayehi karīyati, taṃ karitvātipi attho. Asaññasattesu nibbattatīti asaññasattasaṅkhāte sattanikāye rūpapaṭisandhivaseneva upapajjati, aññesu vā cakkavāḷesu tassā bhūmiyā atthitāya anekavidhabhāvaṃ sandhāya puthuvacananiddesotipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idhevāti pañcavokārabhaveyeva. Tatthāti asaññībhave. Yadi rūpakkhandhamattameva asaññībhave pātubhavati, kathaṃ arūpasannissayena vinā tattha rūpaṃ pavattati, nanu siyā arūpasannissitāyeva rūpakkhandhassa uppatti idheva pañcavokārabhave tathā uppattiyā adassanatoti[V 1.0383]? Nāyamanuyogo aññatthāpi appaviṭṭho, kathaṃ pana rūpasannissayena vinā arūpadhātuyā arūpaṃ pavattatīti. Idampi hi tena samānajātiyameva. Kasmā? Idheva adassanato, kathañca kabaḷīkārāhārena vinā rūpadhātuyā rūpaṃ pavattatīti. Idampi ca taṃsabhāvameva, kiṃ kāraṇā? Idha adassanatoyeva. Iti aññatthāpi tathā pavattidassanato, kimetena aññanidassanena idheva anuyogena. Apica yathā yassa cittasantānassa nibbattikāraṇaṃ rūpe avigatataṇhaṃ, tassa saha rūpena sambhavato rūpaṃ nissāya pavatti rūpasāpekkhatāya kāraṇassa. Yassa pana nibbattikāraṇaṃ rūpe vigatataṇhaṃ, tassa vinā rūpena pavatti rūpanirapekkhatāya kāraṇassa, evaṃ yassa rūpappabandhassa nibbattikāraṇaṃ arūpe vigatataṇhaṃ, tassa vinā arūpena pavatti arūpanirapekkhatāya kāraṇassa, evaṃ bhāvanābalābhāvato pañcavokārabhave rūpārūpasambhavo viya, bhāvanābalena catuvokārabhave arūpasseva [M 1.0438] sambhavo viya ca. Asaññībhavepi bhāvanābalena rūpasseva sambhavo daṭṭhabboti.

Because the question 'How does one see?' should be asked, the Commentator says the words beginning with 'citte sati' ('with the mind present'). The word 'santo' means 'extinguished'; this is said to be Nibbāna in the present life. The phrase 'kālaṃ katvā' means 'having died'; or, it also has the meaning of 'having completed that lifespan in the human world which is maintained by supporting conditions.' 'One is reborn among the non-percipient beings' means one is reborn in the group of beings called non-percipient beings solely by the power of material rebirth-linking. Or, the plural designation should also be understood as being made with reference to the manifold nature due to the existence of that plane in other world-systems. 'Idheva' ('here') means only in the five-constituent existence. 'Tattha' ('there') means in the non-percipient existence. If only the material aggregate manifests in the non-percipient existence, how does materiality persist there without dependence on the immaterial? Should not the arising of the material aggregate be dependent on the immaterial, since such an arising is not seen here in the five-constituent existence? This objection is not inapplicable elsewhere. For how do mental phenomena persist in the immaterial realm without dependence on the material? For this is of the same nature as that. Why? Because it is not seen here. And how does materiality persist in the material realm without physical nutriment? This too is of the same nature. For what reason? Solely because it is not seen here. Thus, since such persistence is seen elsewhere, what is the use of this objection, which is another example, only here? Furthermore, just as for a mind-continuum whose cause of arising is unabandoned craving for materiality, its process is dependent on materiality—because it arises together with materiality—due to the cause's dependence on materiality. But for a mind-continuum whose cause of arising is craving-free regarding materiality, its process occurs without materiality, due to the cause's independence from materiality. Similarly, for a material continuum whose cause of arising is craving-free regarding the immaterial, its process occurs without the immaterial, due to the cause's independence from the immaterial. Thus, just as in the five-constituent existence there is the arising of the material and the immaterial due to the absence of the power of meditation, and just as in the four-constituent existence there is the arising of only the immaterial by the power of meditation, so too in the non-percipient existence, the arising of only materiality by the power of meditation should be understood.

Kathaṃ pana tattha kevalo rūpappabandho paccuppannapaccayarahito cirakālaṃ pavattatīti paccetabbaṃ, kittakaṃ vā kālaṃ pavattatīti codanaṃ manasi katvā “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Tena na kevalaṃ idha ceva aññattha ca vutto āgamoyeva etadatthañāpane, atha kho ayaṃ panettha yuttīti dasseti. Jiyāvegukkhittoti dhanujiyāya vegena khipito. Jhānavego nāma jhānānubhāvo phaladāne samatthatā. Tattakameva kālanti ukkaṃsato pañca mahākappasatāni. Tiṭṭhantīti yathānibbattairiyāpathameva cittakammarūpakasadisā hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Jhānavegeti asaññasamāpattiparikkhitte catutthajjhānakammavege, pañcamajjhānakammavege vā. Antaradhāyatīti paccayanirodhena nirujjhati na pavattati. Idhāti kāmāvacarabhaveti attho aññattha tesamanuppattito. Paṭisandhisaññāti paṭisandhicittuppādoyeva saññāsīsena vutto. Kathaṃ pana anekakappasatamatikkamena ciraniruddhato viññāṇato idha viññāṇamuppajjati. Na hi niruddhe cakkhupasāde cakkhuviññāṇamuppajjamānaṃ diṭṭhanti? Nayidamekantato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Niruddhampi hi cittaṃ samānajātikassa antarā anuppajjanato samanantarapaccayamattaṃ hotiyeva, na bījaṃ. Bījaṃ pana kammameva, tasmā kammato bījabhūtato ārammaṇādīhi paccayehi asaññībhavato cutānaṃ kāmadhātuyā upapattiviññāṇaṃ hotiyeva, tenāha “idha paṭisandhisaññā uppajjatī”ti. Ettha ca yathā nāma utuniyāmena pupphaggahaṇe niyatakālānaṃ rukkhānaṃ vidāraṇasaṅkhāte vekhe dinne vekhabalena aniyamatā hoti pupphaggahaṇassa, evameva pañcavokārabhave avippayogena vattamānesu rūpārūpadhammesu rūpārūpavirāgabhāvanāsaṅkhāte vekhe dinne tassa samāpattivekhabalassa anurūpato [V 1.0384] arūpabhave, asaññabhave ca yathākkamaṃ rūparahitā, arūparahitā ca khandhānaṃ pavatti hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, how is it to be believed that the mere continuum of materiality persists there for a long time, devoid of present conditions? Or, for how long does it persist? Keeping this objection in mind, the Commentator says the words beginning with 'yathā nāma' ('just as'). By this, he shows that it is not merely the scriptural tradition stated both here and elsewhere that makes this meaning known, but rather that this here is the reasoning. 'Jiyāvegukkhitto' ('shot by the force of a bowstring') means hurled by the force of a bowstring. The 'force of jhāna' is the power of jhāna, its capability in giving the fruit of rebirth-linking. 'Tattakameva kālaṃ' ('for just that long') means, at most, five hundred great aeons. 'Tiṭṭhanti' ('they remain') means they remain in the very same posture in which they arose, having become like a variegated form produced by kamma, or like a painted picture. 'Jhānavege' ('in the force of jhāna') means in the karmic force of the fourth jhāna, which is encompassed by the attainment of non-perception, or in the karmic force of the fifth jhāna. 'Antaradhāyati' ('it disappears') means it ceases due to the cessation of its causal kamma; it does not persist. 'Idha' ('here') means in the sense-sphere existence; this is because of their non-arising elsewhere. 'Paṭisandhisaññā' ('rebirth-linking perception') is the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness itself, spoken of with perception as the heading. But how does consciousness arise here from a consciousness that has long ceased, after the passing of many hundreds of aeons? For it is not seen that eye-consciousness arises when the eye-sensitivity has ceased. This should not be regarded as absolute. For even though a mind has ceased, it is still just a proximity condition, since no other of its same class arises in the interval; it is not the seed. But kamma itself is the seed. Therefore, for those who have passed away from the non-percipient existence, rebirth-linking consciousness certainly arises in the sense-sphere from kamma which has become the seed, with conditions such as object, etc. Therefore he said, 'here rebirth perception arises.' And in this context, just as for trees that have a fixed time for flowering according to the seasonal order, when a splitting incision is made, there is irregularity in their flowering due to the force of that incision; so too, for the material and immaterial phenomena that proceed inseparably in the five-constituent existence, when the incision called 'the development of dispassion for the material and immaterial' is made, then, in conformity with the force of that attainment-incision, the process of the aggregates occurs respectively devoid of materiality in the immaterial existence, and devoid of the immaterial in the non-percipient existence. This should be understood.

Kasmā panettha puna saññuppādā ca pana “te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti saññuppādo tesaṃ cavanassa kāraṇabhāvena vutto, “saññuppādā”ti vacanaṃ vā kimatthadassananti codanāya “yasmā panā”tiādimāha. Idha paṭisandhisaññuppādena tesaṃ cavanassa paññāyanato ñāpakahetubhāvena vutto, “saññuppādā”ti vacanaṃ vā tesaṃ cavanassa [M 1.0439] paññāyanabhāvadassananti adhippāyo. “Saññuppādā”ti hi etassa saññuppādena hetubhūtena cavanti, saññuppādā vā uppādasaññā te devāti sambandho. Santabhāvāyāti nibbānāya. Nanu cettha jātisatasahassadasasaṃvaṭṭādīnamatthake, tadabbhantare vā pavattāya asaññūpapattiyā vasena lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādopi lābhīsassatavādo viya anekabhedo sambhavatīti? Saccameva, anantarattā pana āsannāya asaññūpapattiyā vasena lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādo nayadassanavasena ekova dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgahato adhiccasamuppannikavādassa sassatavāde āgato sabbopi desanānayo yathāsambhavaṃ adhiccasamuppannikavādepi gahetabboti imassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ bhagavatā lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādo avibhajitvā dassito, avassañcassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho icchitabbo saṃkilesapakkhe sattānamajjhāsayassa sassatucchedavaseneva duvidhattā, tesu ca ucchedappasaṅgābhāvato. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āsaya-saddassa atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ “sassatucchedadiṭṭhi cā”ti, tathā ca vakkhati “yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.97, 98).

Why, in this context, is 'from the arising of perception' stated as the cause for the passing away of those deities from that corporeal existence? Or, what meaning is shown by the expression 'from the arising of perception'? In response to this objection, the commentator says, 'Because...' and so on. Here, it is stated as an indicating cause because their passing away is known through the arising of rebirth-linking perception. Or, the intention is that the expression 'from the arising of perception' shows the fact that their passing away is known. For, regarding this 'from the arising of perception,' the connection should be made thus: 'they pass away because of the arising of perception which is the cause'; or, 'those deities are ones for whom perception has arisen.' 'For the state of peace' means for Nibbāna. Now, is it not possible that, at the end of or within one hundred thousand births, ten world-cycles, and so on, by means of a non-percipient becoming that has occurred, the doctrine of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna, like the eternalist doctrine held by one who has attained jhāna, could have many divisions? This is indeed true. However, it should be understood that because of the immediacy and proximity of the non-percipient becoming, the doctrine of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna is shown as only one, by way of demonstrating the method. Alternatively, since the doctrine of fortuitous origination is included under the eternalist view, every method of teaching that comes under the eternalist doctrine should, as far as possible, also be applied to the doctrine of fortuitous origination. To show this distinction, the Blessed One taught the doctrine of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna without dividing it. And its inclusion under the eternalist view must certainly be accepted, because in the faction of defilement, the disposition of beings is twofold only by way of eternalism and annihilationism, and among these two, there is no occasion for annihilationism. Thus, in the commentary, by way of extracting the meaning of the word 'disposition,' it is said, 'and the eternalist and annihilationist views.' And so, he will say, 'Among which views, there are only seven annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.97, 98).

Nanu ca adhiccasamuppannikavādassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho na yutto “ahañhi pubbe nāhosi”ntiādivasena pavattanato apubbasattapātubhāvagāhakattā. Sassatadiṭṭhi pana attano, lokassa ca sadābhāvagāhinī “atthitveva sassatisama”nti pavattanatoti? No na yutto anāgatakoṭiadassanena sassataggāhasamavarodhattā. Yadipi hi ayaṃ vādo “somhi etarahi ahutvā santatāya pariṇato”ti (dī. ni. 1.68) attano, lokassa ca atītakoṭiparāmasanavasena pavatto, tathāpi vattamānakālato paṭṭhāya na tesaṃ katthaci anāgate pariyantaṃ passati, visesena ca paccuppannānāgatakālesu apariyantadassanapabhāvito sassatavādo, yathāha “sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.31 atthato samānaṃ) yadevaṃ siyā imassa ca vādassa, sassatavādādīnañca pubbantakappikesu saṅgaho na yuttoyeva anāgatakālaparāmasanavasena [V 1.0385] pavattattāti? Yutto eva samudāgamassa atītakoṭṭhāsikattā. Tathā hi nesaṃ samudāgamo [M 1.0440] atītaṃsapubbenivāsañāṇehi, tappatirūpakānussavādipabhāvitehi ca takkanehi saṅgahitoti, tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Atha vā sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacārena dhammassāminā niravasesato agatiṃ, gatiñca yathābhūtaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā paveditā etā diṭṭhiyo, tasmā yāvatikā diṭṭhiyo bhagavatā desitā, yathā ca desitā, tāvatikā tathā ceva sanniṭṭhānato sampaṭicchitabbā, na cettha yuttivicāraṇā kātabbā buddhavisayattā. Acinteyyo hi buddhānaṃ buddhavisayo, tathā ca vakkhati “tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabba”nti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.78-82).

But is it not inappropriate to include the doctrine of fortuitous origination under the eternalist view, since it proceeds by way of 'I did not exist before,' and so forth, and because it grasps the manifest arising of a being that was not before? The eternalist view, however, grasps the perpetual existence of oneself and the world, proceeding by way of 'it exists indeed, like unto the eternal.' No, it is not inappropriate, because by not seeing the future end, it is well included in the grasp of eternalism. For although this doctrine proceeds by way of considering the past end of oneself and the world, stating, 'That I, not having been before, have now been transformed into a state of being' (Dī. Ni. 1.68), nevertheless, from the present time onward, they do not see any end in the future. And especially in the present and future times, the eternalist view is developed by not seeing an end, as he said, 'it will remain just so, like unto the eternal' (Dī. Ni. 1.31, similar in meaning). If this is so, then is it not indeed inappropriate to include this doctrine, along with the eternalist doctrines and others, among the speculators on the past, since they proceed by way of considering the future time? It is indeed appropriate, because their origin has a past portion. For their origin is included by the knowledges of past lives, which have a past component, and by reasonings developed through hearsay and the like, which are counterparts to such knowledge. And it has been explained in just this way. Alternatively, these views were proclaimed by the Master of the Dhamma, who has an unobstructed range of knowledge everywhere, having himself, without omission, directly known and realized the wrong course and the right course as they truly are. Therefore, however many views were taught by the Blessed One, and in whatever way they were taught, they should be accepted with that same number and in that same way by firm decision. And no logical scrutiny should be made here, for this is the domain of a Buddha. The domain of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable, and thus it will be said, 'In this matter, a reason should not be sought with certainty' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.78-82).

Dutiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second recitation section is concluded.

Aparantakappikavādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Doctrines of Speculation on the Future

74. “Aparanteñāṇaṃ (dha. sa. 1067), aparantānudiṭṭhino”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.74) viya aparanta –saddānaṃ yathākkamaṃ anāgatakālakoṭṭhāsavācakataṃ sandhāyāha “anāgatakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhāta”nti. “Pubbantaṃ kappetvā”tiādīsu vuttanayena “aparantaṃ kappetvā”tiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Visesamattameva cettha vakkhāma.

Just as in phrases such as 'knowledge of the future' (Dhs. 1067) and 'those who hold views concerning the future' (Dī. Ni. 1.74), referring to the word 'aparanta' in each case as denoting the future-time-portion, the commentator says, 'designated as the future portion.' By the method stated in phrases such as 'having speculated about the past,' the meaning should also be understood in phrases such as 'having speculated about the future.' Here, we will state only the specific points.

Saññīvādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Doctrine of a Percipient Self

75. Āghātanā uddhanti uddhamāghātanaṃ, maraṇato uddhaṃ pavatto attāti attho. “Uddhamāghātana”nti pavatto vādo uddhamāghātano sahacaraṇavasena, taddhitavasena ca, antalopaniddeso vā esa. So etesanti uddhamāghātanikā. Evaṃ saddato nipphannaṃ atthato eva dassetuṃ “uddhamāghātanā attānaṃ vadantī”ti vuttaṃ, āghātanā uddhaṃ uparibhūtaṃ attabhāvanti attho. Te hi diṭṭhigatikā “uddhaṃ maraṇato attā nibbikāro”ti vadanti. “So etesa”ntiādinā assatthiyatthaṃ dasseti yathā “buddhamassa atthīti buddho”ti. Ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāto aparo nayo – saññīti pavatto vādo saññī sahacaraṇādinayena, saññī vādo etesanti saññīvādā samāsavasena. Saññīvādo eva vādo etesanti hi attho.

74. ‘After death’ (āghātanā uddhaṃ) is uddhamāghātanaṃ; the meaning is the self that exists after death. The doctrine that arises as ‘after death’ is uddhamāghātano, either by way of association or by way of derivation, or this is a designation with elision of the final word. ‘That [doctrine] is theirs,’ therefore they are uddhamāghātanikā. Thus, to show by way of meaning what is derived from the word, it is said, ‘they declare the self as existing after death,’ the meaning of which is the state of self that has come to be above, after death. For these holders of wrong view declare, ‘After death, the self is unchanging.’ By ‘That is theirs,’ etc., it shows the possessive meaning, just as in ‘He has enlightenment, therefore he is a Buddha.’ This is another method from the commentary: The doctrine that arises as ‘percipient’ is saññī by the method of association, etc. ‘The “percipient” doctrine is theirs,’ therefore they are saññīvādā by way of compounding. Indeed, the meaning is that their doctrine is precisely the ‘percipient doctrine’.

76-77. Rūpī [V 1.0386][M 1.0441] attāti ettha kasiṇarūpaṃ “attā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu rūpavinimuttena attanā bhavitabbaṃ “rūpamassa atthī”ti vutte saññāya viya rūpassāpi attaniyattā. Na hi “saññī attā”ti ettha saññā eva attā, atha kho “saññā assa atthī”ti atthena attaniyāva, tathā ca vuttaṃ “tattha pavattasaññañcassa ‘saññā’ti gahetvā”ti? Na kho panetamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “rūpamassa atthīti rūpī”ti, atha kho “ruppanasīlo rūpī”ti. Ruppanañcettha rūpasarikkhatāya kasiṇarūpassa vaḍḍhitāvaḍḍhitakālavasena visesāpatti. Sā hi “natthī”ti na sakkā vattuṃ parittavipulatādivisesasabbhāvato. Yadevaṃ siyā “ruppanasīlo rūpī”ti, atha imassa vādassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho na yujjati ruppanasīlassa bhedasabbhāvatoti? Yujjateva kāyabhedato uddhaṃ parikappitassa attano nibbikāratāya tena adhippetattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti. Atha vā “rūpamassa atthīti rūpī”ti vuttepi na koci doso kappanāsiddhena bhedena abhedassāpi niddesadassanato yathā “silāputtakassa sarīra”nti.

76-77. In the phrase ‘the self has form’ (rūpī attā), why is the kasiṇa-form called the ‘self’? Should not the self be separate from form? For when it is said ‘it has form,’ form, like perception, would be a property of the self. Indeed, in ‘the self is percipient,’ perception itself is not the self; rather, by the meaning ‘it has perception,’ it is merely a property of the self. And so it was said: ‘…having taken the perception that occurs there as its “perception”.’ This is the objection. However, it should not be understood thus: ‘it has form, therefore it is rūpī’; but rather, ‘it has the nature of being afflicted, therefore it is rūpī.’ And here, ‘affliction’ (ruppana) is the attainment of a special state by the kasiṇa-form, due to its similarity to material form, by way of periods of expansion and non-expansion. For it cannot be said that this special state ‘does not exist,’ due to the actual existence of distinctions such as being limited or extensive. If it were so, that ‘it has the nature of being afflicted, therefore it is rūpī,’ then would not the inclusion of this doctrine under the eternalist view be incorrect, due to the existence of destruction for that which has the nature of being afflicted? This is the objection. It is indeed correct, because it is intended by them that the self, conceived as existing after the breakup of the body, is unchanging. For thus it is said: ‘Without affliction after death.’ Alternatively, even when it is said ‘it has form, therefore it is rūpī,’ there is no fault, because the designation of the undivided by means of a conceptual division is seen, just as in ‘the body of a stone doll.’

Apica avayavavasena avayavino tathāniddesanidassanato yathā “kāye kāyānupassī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.390), ruppanaṃ vā rūpaṃ, rūpasabhāvo, tadassa atthīti rūpī, attā “rūpino dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 11.dukamātikā) viya, evañca katvā attano rūpasabhāvattā “rūpī attā”ti vacanaṃ ñāyāgatamevāti vuttaṃ “kasiṇarūpaṃ attā”ti. “Gahetvā”ti etena cetassa sambandho. Tatthāti kasiṇarūpe. Assāti parikappitassa attano, ājīvakādayo takkamattena paññapenti viyāti attho. Ājīvakā hi takkikāyeva, na lābhino. Niyatavāditāya hi kammaphalapaṭikkhepato natthi tesaṃ jhānasamāpattilābho. Tathā hikaṇhābhijātiādīsu kāḷakādirūpaṃ “attā”ti ekacce ājīvakā paṭijānanti. Purimanayena cettha lābhīnaṃ dasseti, pacchimanayena pana takkikaṃ. Evamīdisesu. Roga-saddo bhaṅgapariyāyo bhaṅgassāpi rujjanabhāvato, evañca katvā aroga-saddassa niccapariyāyatā upapannā hoti, tenāha “nicco”ti. Roga-saddo vā byādhipariyāyo. Arogoti pana rogarahitatāsīsena nibbikāratāya niccataṃ diṭṭhigatiko paṭijānātīti dassetuṃ “nicco”ti vuttaṃ[M 1.0442]. Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsapaṭhamāruppaviññāṇanatthibhāvākiñcaññāyatanāni yathārahamarūpasamāpattinimittaṃ nāma. Nimbapaṇṇe tapparimāṇo tittakaraso viya sarīrapparimāṇo arūpī attā sarīre tiṭṭhatīti takkamatteneva nigaṇṭhā “arūpī attā saññī”ti paññapentīti āha “nigaṇṭhādayo viyā”ti.

Furthermore, this is because the designation of the whole by way of the part is seen, just as in ‘contemplating the body in the body.’ Or, affliction is form, the nature of form; that exists for it, therefore it is rūpī, just as in ‘phenomena that have form,’ etc. And for this reason, because the self has the nature of form, the statement ‘the self has form’ is logically sound. Therefore, it is said, ‘the kasiṇa-form is the self.’ By this word ‘having taken,’ its connection is to be made. ‘There’ means in the kasiṇa-form. ‘Of it’ means of the conceived self. The meaning is that the Ājīvakas and others postulate this by mere reasoning. For the Ājīvakas are indeed mere reasoners, not attainers of meditative states. Due to their fatalism and their rejection of the fruit of kamma, there is no attainment of jhāna and absorption for them. Indeed, some Ājīvakas profess that in the dark birth, etc., the black form and so on is the ‘self.’ And here, by the former method, the view of the attainers is shown, but by the latter method, that of the reasoners. It should be understood thus in such cases. The word roga (affliction) is a synonym for destruction, because destruction also has the nature of affliction. For this reason, the synonymity of the word aroga (unafflicted) with ‘permanent’ is established. Therefore, he said ‘permanent.’ Alternatively, the word roga is a synonym for disease. But to show that the holder of the view professes permanence through immutability on the basis of being free from affliction (aroga), the commentator said ‘permanent.’ The concept of space obtained by removing the kasiṇa, the first formless consciousness, the concept of non-existence, and the base of nothingness are, respectively, the objects of the formless absorptions. Just as the bitter taste having the measure of a neem leaf exists in the neem leaf, so a formless self having the measure of the body exists in the body—thus the Nigaṇṭhas postulate by mere reasoning that ‘the formless self is percipient.’ Therefore, the commentator said, ‘like the Nigaṇṭhas and others.’

Tatiyā [V 1.0387] panāti “rūpī ca arūpī ca attā”ti laddhi. Missakagāhavasenāti rūpārūpasamāpattīnaṃ yathāvuttāni nimittāni ekajjhaṃ katvā ekova “attā”ti, tattha pavattasaññañcassa “saññā”ti gahaṇavasena. Ayañhi diṭṭhigatiko rūpārūpasamāpattilābhī tāsaṃ nimittaṃ rūpabhāvena, arūpabhāvena ca “attā”ti gahetvā “rūpī ca arūpī cā”ti abhinivesaṃ janesi athetavādino viya, takkamatteneva vā rūpārūpadhammānaṃ missakagahaṇavasena “rūpī ca arūpī ca attā”ti abhinivissa aṭṭhāsi. Catutthāti “neva arūpī ca nārūpī ca attā”ti laddhi. Takkagāhenevāti saṅkhārasesasukhumabhāvappattadhammā viya accantasukhumabhāvappattiyā sakiccasādhanāsamatthatāya khambhakucchi [thambhakuṭṭa (dī. ni. ṭī. 176-77)] hatthapādādisaṅghāto viya neva rūpī, rūpasabhāvānativattanato na ca arūpīti evaṃ pavattatakkagāheneva.

As for the third, it is the doctrine that ‘the self is both with form and without form.’ ‘By way of grasping a mixture’ means: by way of taking the aforementioned objects of the form and formless absorptions, having made them one, as ‘the one self,’ and taking the perception that occurs there as ‘its perception.’ For this holder of the view, an attainer of form and formless absorptions, having taken their objects as ‘the self’ by way of their nature as form and their nature as formlessness, generated the conviction that it is ‘both with form and without form,’ like one with an uncertain doctrine. Or, by mere reasoning, through grasping the mixture of form and formless phenomena, he became convinced and established in the view that ‘the self is both with form and without form.’ The fourth is the doctrine that ‘the self is neither with form nor without form.’ ‘Purely by grasping through reasoning’ means: just as phenomena that, being the remainder of formations, have reached a subtle state and are incapable of accomplishing their own function due to having reached an extremely subtle state; and just as a composite of a pillar, belly, hands, feet, etc., is neither ‘with form’ nor, because it does not transcend the nature of form, is it ‘without form’—it is purely by such grasping through reasoning that this view arises.

Ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – nevarūpī nārūpīti ettha hi antānantikacatutthavāde viya aññamaññapaṭikkhepavasena attho veditabbo. Satipi ca tatiyavādena imassa samānatthabhāve tattha desakālabhedavasena viya idha kālavatthubhedavasena tatiyacatutthavādānaṃ viseso daṭṭhabbo. Kālabhedavasena hi idha tatiyavādassa pavatti rūpārūpanimittānaṃ sahaanupaṭṭhānato. Catutthavādassa pana vatthubhedavasena pavatti rūpārūpadhammasamūhabhāvatoti. Dutiyacatukkaṃ antānantikavāde vuttanayena veditabbaṃ sabbathā saddatthato samānatthattā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, tampi “amati gacchati bhāvo osānametthā”tiādinā amhehi vuttameva, kevalaṃ pana tattha pubbantakappanāvasena pavatto, idha aparantakappanāvasenāti ayaṃ viseso pākaṭoyeva. Kāmañca nānattasaññī attāti ayampi vādo samāpannakavasena labbhati. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino diṭṭhigatikassa vasena saññābhedasambhavato. Tathāpi samāpattiyaṃ [M 1.0443] ekarūpeneva saññāya upaṭṭhānato lābhīvasena ekattasaññitā sātisayaṃ yuttāti āha “samāpannakavasena ekattasaññī”ti. Ekasamāpattilābhino eva vā vasena attho veditabbo. Satipi ca samāpattibhedato saññābhedasambhave bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇeyeva saññānānattassa oḷārikassa sambhavato takkīvaseneva nānattasaññitaṃ dassetuṃ “asamāpannakavasena nānattasaññī”ti vuttaṃ. Parittakasiṇavasenāti avaḍḍhitattā appakakasiṇavasena, kasiṇaggahaṇañcettha saññāya visayadassanaṃ. Visayavasena hi saññāya parittatā, iminā ca satipi saññāvinimuttadhamme “saññāyeva attā”ti vadatīti dasseti. Esa nayo vipulakasiṇavasenāti etthāpi. Evañca katvā antānantikavāde ceva idha ca antānantacatukke paṭhamadutiyavādesu saddatthamattato samānesupi sabhāvato tehi dvīhi vādehi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vādānaṃ viseso siddho hoti, aññathā [V 1.0388] vuttappakāresu vādesu satipi pubbantāparantakappanabhedamattena kehici visese kehici avisesoyeva siyāti.

This is a method independent of the commentary. Here, in the phrase 'neither with form nor without form,' the meaning should be understood by way of mutual exclusion, as in the fourth thesis of the finite and infinite views. And although this view has a similar meaning to the third thesis, the distinction between the third and fourth theses should be seen here by way of a difference in time and object, just as there is a distinction there by way of a difference in place and time. For here, the occurrence of the third thesis is by way of a difference in time, due to the non-simultaneous appearance of the signs of form and formlessness. The occurrence of the fourth thesis, however, is by way of a difference in object, due to its being a collection of phenomena of form and formlessness. The second and fourth theses should be understood according to the method stated in the finite and infinite views, since they are similar in every way in word and meaning. Whatever should be said here has already been stated by us with 'amati gacchati bhāvo osānametthā,' etc. However, there it occurred by way of speculation about the past, whereas here it occurs by way of speculation about the future—this distinction is indeed clear. Moreover, this thesis, 'the self has diverse perceptions,' is also obtained by way of one who has attained meditative absorption, because of the possibility of a difference in perception for one with wrong views who has obtained the eight attainments. Nevertheless, since perception arises in an attainment with a single form, it is exceedingly fitting that, for one who has obtained it, there is a perception of unity. Therefore, the Commentator said, 'one with a perception of unity by way of one who has attained absorption.' Alternatively, the meaning should be understood by way of one who has obtained only a single attainment. And although a difference in perception is possible due to a difference in attainments, since the gross diversity of perception is possible only externally with diverse objects, in order to show that having diverse perceptions is only by way of a mere reasoner, it was said, 'one with diverse perceptions by way of one who has not attained absorption.' 'By way of a limited kasiṇa' means by way of a small kasiṇa, because it has not been developed. And here, the term 'kasiṇa' indicates the object of perception. For the limitedness of perception is by way of its object, and by this, it shows that although there are phenomena apart from perception, one says, 'Perception itself is the self.' This same method should be seen also in the phrase 'by way of an extensive kasiṇa.' And for this reason, in both the finite and infinite views and here, although the first and second theses in the finite and infinite tetrad are similar merely in terms of word and meaning, the distinction of these two theses from those two views is established in terms of their intrinsic nature. Otherwise, if the meaning were taken in another way, among the theses of the kinds stated, although there might be a distinction from some merely due to the difference in speculation about the past and future, from others there would be no distinction at all.

Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo – “aṅguṭṭhappamāṇo attā, aṇumatto attā”tiādiladdhivasena paritto ca so saññī cāti parittasaññī kāpilakāṇādapabhutayo [kapilakaṇādādayo (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.76-77)] viya. Attano sabbagatabhāvapaṭijānanavasena appamāṇo ca so saññī cāti appamāṇasaññīti.

This, however, is a method independent of the commentary: by way of such views as, 'The self is the size of a thumb; the self is the size of an atom,' it is limited and it is percipient; therefore, it is called 'one with limited perception,' like the followers of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others. By way of professing its own all-pervading nature, it is unlimited and it is percipient; therefore, it is called 'one with unlimited perception.'

Dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍattā yathākammūpagañāṇassa dibbacakkhupabhāvajanitena yathākammūpagañāṇena dissamānāpi sattānaṃ sukhādisamaṅgitā dibbacakkhunāva diṭṭhā nāmāti āha “dibbena cakkhunā”tiādi. Catukkanayaṃ, pañcakanayañca sandhāya tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiya”nti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikavisayāsu hi pañcavokārajhānabhūmīsu vehapphalabhūmiṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā yathārahaṃ catukkanaye tikajjhānassa, pañcakanaye ca catukkajjhānassa vipākaṭṭhānattā tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiyo nāma. Suddhāvāsā pana tesamavisayā. Nibbattamānanti uppajjamānaṃ. Nanu ca “ekantasukhī attā”tiādinā pavattavādānaṃ aparantadiṭṭhibhāvato “nibbattamānaṃ disvā”ti paccuppannavacanaṃ anupapannameva siyā. Anāgatavisayā hi ete vādāti? Upapannameva anāgatassa ekantasukhībhāvādikassa pakappanāya [M 1.0444] paccuppannanibbattidassanena adhippetattā. Tenevāha “nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘ekantasukhī’ti gaṇhātī”ti. Ettha ca tassaṃ tassaṃ bhūmiyaṃ bāhullena sukhādisahitadhammappavattidassanaṃ paṭicca tesaṃ “ekantasukhī”tiādigahaṇato tadanurūpāyeva bhūmi vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddantarābhisambandhavasena viya hi atthapakaraṇādivasenapi atthaviseso labbhati. “Ekantasukhī”tiādīsu ca ekantabhāvo bahulaṃ pavattimattaṃ pati payutto. Tathāpavattimattadassanena tesaṃ evaṃ gahaṇato. Atha vā hatthidassakaandhā viya diṭṭhigatikā yaṃ yadeva passanti, taṃ tadeva abhinivissa voharanti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā udāne “aññatitthiyā bhikkhave, paribbājakā andhā acakkhukā”tiādi, (udā. 55) tasmā alamettha yuttimagganāti. “Dibbena cakkhunā disvā”ti vuttamatthaṃ samatthetuṃ “visesato hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because the knowledge of how beings fare according to their kamma has the divine eye as its accessory, although the state of beings being endowed with happiness and so forth is seen by the knowledge of how beings fare according to their kamma, which is generated by the power of the divine eye, it is called 'seen by the divine eye itself'. Therefore, the Commentator said, 'with the divine eye,' etc. Referring to the fourfold method and the fivefold method, it was said, 'the planes of the third and fourth jhānas.' For among the jhāna planes of the five-constituent existence that are the domain of those with wrong views, the remaining ones, after setting aside the Vehapphala plane, are called 'the planes of the third and fourth jhānas' because they are, respectively, the place of result for the third jhāna in the fourfold method and the fourth jhāna in the fivefold method. The Pure Abodes, however, are not their domain. 'Being reborn' (nibbattamānaṃ) means arising. Is it not so that since the theses of those who assert, 'The self is entirely happy,' etc., are views about the future (aparantadiṭṭhi), the present tense statement, 'having seen one being reborn,' would be inappropriate? For these theses have the future as their object. It is indeed appropriate, because what is intended is the speculation about the future state of being entirely happy, etc., by seeing the present arising. Therefore, the Commentator said, 'Having seen one being reborn, one grasps it as "entirely happy".' And here it should be understood that the plane mentioned is one that is suitable for that view, because their grasping of 'entirely happy,' etc., is dependent on seeing the frequent occurrence of phenomena accompanied by happiness, etc., in that particular plane. For just as a specific meaning is obtained by way of connection with another word, so too is a specific meaning obtained by way of the context of the meaning, etc. And in 'entirely happy,' etc., the state of being 'entirely' is applied mostly in dependence on the mere occurrence, because they grasp it thus by seeing the mere occurrence in that way. Alternatively, like the blind men who saw the elephant, those with wrong views adhere to and declare whatever they see. For this was stated by the Blessed One in the Udāna: 'Monks, the wanderers of other sects are blind, without eyes,' etc. Therefore, enough of searching for what is reasonable here. To establish the meaning stated as 'having seen with the divine eye,' the compiler said, 'Especially because,' etc.

Asaññīnevasaññīnāsaññīvādavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Theses on the Non-percipient and the Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient

78-83. Atha [V 1.0389] na koci viseso atthīti codanaṃ sodheti “kevalañhī”tiādinā. “Asaññī”ti ca “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti ca gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyoti sambandho. Kāraṇanti visesakāraṇaṃ, diṭṭhisamudāgamakāraṇaṃ vā. Satipi kiñci kāraṇapariyesanasambhave diṭṭhigatikavādānaṃ anādariyabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Kasmāti āha “diṭṭhigatikassā”tiādi, etena pariyesanakkhamābhāvatoti apariyesitabbakāraṇaṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – asaññīvāde asaññībhave nibbattasattavasena pavatto paṭhamavādo, “saññaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti ettha vuttanayena saññaṃyeva “attā”ti gahetvā tassa kiñcanabhāvena ṭhitāya aññāya saññāya abhāvato “asaññī”ti pavatto dutiyavādo, tathā saññāya saha rūpadhamme, sabbe eva vā rūpārūpadhamme “attā”ti gahetvā pavatto tatiyavādo, takkagāhavaseneva catutthavādo pavatto.

Then, he refutes the charge, 'There is no distinction,' with the passage beginning 'For it is merely...' The connection should be made thus: 'non-percipient' and 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' are the views of those who hold them. 'Reason' means a specific reason, or a reason for the arising of a view. Although there is some possibility of investigating a reason, to show that the doctrines of those who hold speculative views are unworthy of regard, it is said, 'A reason should not be sought absolutely.' Why? He says, 'For one who holds a speculative view...' and so on. By this, he shows the reason why it should not be investigated: because it is not amenable to investigation. This is what is meant: In the doctrine of the non-percipient, the first view arises by means of a being reborn in the non-percipient realm; by the method stated in 'he regards perception as self,' the second view arises by taking perception itself as 'self' and, due to the absence of any other perception apart from that which exists as a 'something,' holding the view 'non-percipient'; the third view arises by taking perception together with material phenomena, or all material and immaterial phenomena whatsoever, as 'self'; and the fourth view arises solely by the power of grasping through conjecture.

Dutiyacatukkepi kasiṇarūpassa asañjānanasabhāvatāya asaññīti katvā antānantikavāde vuttanayena cattāro vikappā pavattā. Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāde pana nevasaññīnāsaññībhave nibbattasattasseva cutipaṭisandhīsu[M 1.0445], sabbattha vā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthāya sukhumāya saññāya atthibhāvapaṭijānanavasena paṭhamavādo, asaññīvāde vuttanayena sukhumāya saññāya vasena, sañjānanasabhāvatāpaṭijānanavasena ca dutiyavādādayo pavattāti. Evaṃ kenaci pakārena satipi kāraṇapariyesanasambhave diṭṭhigatikavādānaṃ pariyesanakkhamābhāvato ādaraṃ katvā mahussāhena tesaṃ kāraṇaṃ na pariyesitabbanti. Etesaṃ pana saññīasaññīnevasaññīnāsaññīvādānaṃ sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho “arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti vacanato pākaṭoyeva.

In the second tetrad as well, due to the kasiṇa-form's nature of not knowing, having treated it as 'non-percipient,' four alternatives arise by the method stated in the doctrine of the finite and infinite. In the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, however, the first view arises by means of acknowledging the existence of a subtle perception—which is incapable of performing the function of gross perception either at death and rebirth-linking or in all circumstances—only for a being reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The second and subsequent views arise by the method stated in the doctrine of the non-percipient, by means of that subtle perception and by means of acknowledging the nature of knowing. Thus, although the investigation of a reason is possible in some way, because the doctrines of those who hold speculative views are not amenable to investigation, one should not, with respect and great effort, investigate their cause. Furthermore, the inclusion of these doctrines of the percipient, non-percipient, and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient in the eternalist view is indeed evident from the statement, 'He is healthy after death.'

Ucchedavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Annihilationist Doctrine

84. Avijjamānassa vināsāsambhavato atthibhāvahetuko ucchedoti dassetuṃ vijjamānavācakena santa-saddena “sato”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti āha “vijjamānassā”ti. Vijjamānatāpayutto cesa diṭṭhigatikavādavisayo sattoyeva idha adhippetoti dassanatthaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “sattassā”ti vuttaṃ, tena imamatthaṃ dasseti – yathā hetuphalabhāvena pavattamānānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ satipi ekasantānapariyāpannānaṃ bhinnasantatipatitehi visese hetuphalabhūtānaṃ paramatthato bhinnasabhāvattā [V 1.0390] bhinnasantānapatitānaṃ viya accantaṃ bhedasanniṭṭhānena nānattanayassa micchāgahaṇaṃ ucchedābhinivesassa kāraṇaṃ, evaṃ hetuphalabhūtānaṃ vijjamānepi sabhāvabhede ekasantatipariyāpannatāya ekattanayena accantamabhedagahaṇampi kāraṇamevāti. Santānavasena hi pavattamānesu khandhesu ghanavinibbhogābhāvena tesaṃ idha sattagāho, sattassa ca atthibhāvagāhahetuko ucchedavādo, anupubbanirodhavasena pana nirantaravināso idha “ucchedo”ti adhippeto yāvāyaṃ attā ucchijjamāno bhavati, tāvāyaṃ vijjatiyevāti gahaṇatoti āha “upaccheda”nti. U-saddo hi upa-saddapariyāyo, so ca upasaṅkamanattho, upasaṅkamanañcettha anupubbamuppajjitvā aparāparaṃ nirodhavasena nirantaratā. Apica punānuppajjamānavasena nirudayavināsoyeva ucchedo nāma yathāvuttanayena gahaṇatoti āha “upaccheda”nti. U-saddo, hi upa-saddo ca ettha uparibhāgattho. Niruddhato parabhāgo ca idha uparibhāgoti vuccati.

84. Because the destruction of what is non-existent is impossible, annihilation has existence as its cause. To show this, it is said 'sato' in the Pāḷi with the word 'santa' which expresses existence; therefore, he (the commentator) says 'vijjamānassa'. And to show that in this context, only a 'being' (satta) connected with the state of existence is intended as the subject of the doctrine of one who holds a speculative view, it is said 'sattassa' in the Pāḷi. By this, he shows the following meaning: Just as the mistaken grasp of the method of diversity is a cause for adherence to annihilationism—this grasp being an absolute determination of separateness, treating phenomena that are cause and effect as if they fall into different continua because they are ultimately of different natures, despite the fact that there is a distinction between these phenomena, which occur by way of cause and effect within a single continuum, and those that fall into different continua—so too, the grasping of absolute non-difference by the method of unity is also a cause, because although there is a difference in nature in things that are cause and effect, they are included in a single continuum. For, in the aggregates that occur by way of a continuum, due to the absence of analysis of the compact mass, there is in this context the grasping of a 'being', and the annihilationist doctrine is caused by grasping the existence of that 'being'. Furthermore, uninterrupted destruction by way of successive cessation is intended here as 'annihilation' (uccheda), because of the grasp that 'as long as this self is being annihilated, it still exists'. Therefore, he says 'upaccheda'. For the sound 'u' is a synonym for the prefix 'upa', and that has the meaning of 'approaching'. And 'approaching' here is the state of being uninterrupted by way of successively arising and ceasing again and again. Moreover, annihilation is simply destruction without re-arising, by means of not arising again, due to being grasped according to the aforementioned method; therefore, he says 'upaccheda'. For indeed, the sound 'u' and the prefix 'upa' here have the meaning of 'the part that is beyond'. And the part after what has ceased is here called 'the part that is beyond'.

Nirantaravasena[M 1.0446], nirudayavasena vā visesena nāso vināso, so pana maṃsacakkhupaññācakkhūnaṃ dassanapathātikkamanato adassanamevāti āha “adassana”nti. Adassane hi nāsa-saddo loke niruḷho “dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā”tiādīsu (kāsikā 6-3-109 suttaṃ passitabbaṃ) viya. Bhāvavigamanti sabhāvāpagamaṃ. Yathādhammaṃ bhavanaṃ bhāvoti hi atthena idha bhāva-saddo sabhāvavācako. Yo pana nirantaraṃ nirudayavināsavasena ucchijjati, so attano sabhāvena ṭhātumasakkuṇeyyatāya “bhāvāpagamo”ti vuccati. “Tatthā”tiādinā ucchedavādassa yathāpāṭhaṃ samudāgamaṃ nidassanamattena dasseti, tena vakkhati “tathā ca aññathā ca vikappetvāvā”ti. Tatthāti “sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapentī”ti vacane. Lābhīti dibbacakkhuñāṇalābhī. Tadavasesalābhī ceva sabbaso alābhī ca idha aparantakappikaṭṭhāne “alābhī” tveva vuccati.

Destruction (`nāsa`) in a specific sense—that is, by way of being uninterrupted or by way of non-arising—is `vināsa` (annihilation). But because that annihilation passes beyond the range of the physical eye and the wisdom eye, it is simply 'non-seeing' (`adassana`). Therefore, he says 'adassana'. For in common usage, the word 'destruction' (`nāsa`) is established in the sense of 'non-seeing', as in such cases as 'and two other alterations and destructions of a letter'. 'Disappearance of being' (`bhāvavigama`) means the departure from inherent nature (`sabhāvāpagama`). For in this context, the word 'being' (`bhāva`) signifies inherent nature (`sabhāva`) in the sense of 'becoming according to its nature' (`yathādhammaṃ bhavanaṃ`). Furthermore, that which is annihilated by means of uninterrupted, non-arising destruction is called 'disappearance of being' because it is unable to stand by its own inherent nature. With the passage beginning 'Therein...', he indicates the origin of the annihilationist doctrine according to the text merely by way of example; for that reason he will say, 'having conceived it thus and otherwise'. 'Therein' refers to the statement, 'they proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being'. 'One who has obtained' (`lābhī`) means one who has obtained the knowledge of the divine eye. Both one who has obtained the remaining (supernormal powers) and one who has not obtained them at all are, in this context of speculating on the future, called simply 'one who has not obtained'.

Cutinti sekkhaputhujjanānampi cutimeva. Esa nayo cutimattamevāti etthāpi. Upapattiṃ apassantoti daṭṭhuṃ samatthepi sati anolokanavasena apassanto. Na upapātanti pubbayogābhāvena, parikammākaraṇena vā upapattiṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkoti, evañca katvā nayadvaye viseso pākaṭo hoti. Ko paralokaṃ jānāti, na jānātiyevāti natthikavādavasena ucchedaṃ gaṇhātīti saha pāṭhasesena sambandho, natthikavādavasena mahāmūḷhabhāveneva “ito añño paraloko atthī”ti anavabodhanato imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhātīti adhippāyo. “Ettakoyeva visayo, yvāyaṃ indriyagocaro”ti attano dhītuyā hatthaggaṇhanakarājā viya kāmasukhābhirattatāyapi gaṇhātīti āha “kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā”ti. Vaṇṭato patitapaṇṇānaṃ vaṇṭena apaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ [V 1.0391] sandhāya “na puna viruhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Evameva sattāti yathā paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto puna na paṭisandhīyati, evameva sabbepi sattā appaṭisandhikā maraṇapariyosānā aponobbhavikā appaṭisandhikamaraṇameva nigacchantīti attho. Udakapubbuḷakūpamā hi sattā puna anuppajjamānatoti tassa laddhi. Tathāti “lābhī anussaranto”tiādinā [arahato (aṭṭha)] nidassanavasena vuttappakārena. Aññathāti takkanassa anekappakārasambhavato tato aññenapi pakārena. Lābhinopi cutito [M 1.0447] uddhaṃ upapātassa adassanamattaṃ pati takkaneneva imā diṭṭhiyo uppajjantīti vuttaṃ “vikappetvāvā”ti. Tathā ca vikappetvāva uppannā aññathā ca vikappetvāva uppannāti hi sambandho. Tattha “dve janā”tiādinā ucchedaggāhakappabhedadassanena imamatthaṃ dasseti. Yathā amarāvikkhepikavādā ekantaalābhīvaseneva desitā, yathā ca uddhamāghātanikasaññīvāde catutthacatukke saññīvādā ekantalābhīvaseneva desitā, nayime. Ime pana sassatekaccasassatavādādayo viya lābhīalābhīvaseneva desitāti. Yadevaṃ kasmā sassatavādādīsu viya lābhīvasena, takkīvasena ca paccekaṃ desanamakatvā sassatavādādidesanāhi aññathā idha desanā katāti? Vuccate – desanāvilāsappattito. Desanāvilāsappattā hi buddhā bhagavanto, te veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vividhenākārena dhammaṃ desenti, na aññathā. Yadi hi idhāpi ca tathādesanāya nibandhanabhūto veneyyajjhāsayo bhaveyya, tathārūpameva bhagavā vadeyya, kathaṃ? “Idha bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… yathā samāhite citte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti, so dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena arahato cuticittaṃ passati, puthūnaṃ vā parasattānaṃ, na heva kho taduddhaṃ upapattiṃ. So evamāha ‘yato kho bho ayaṃ attā rūpī cātumahābhūtiko mātāpettikasambhavo kāyassa bhado ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’tiādinā” visesalābhino, takkino ca visuṃ katvā. Yasmā pana tathādesanāya nibandhanabhūto veneyyajjhāsayo na idha bhavati, tasmā desanāvilāsena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ sassatavādādidesanāhi aññathāyevāyaṃ desanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

As for 'decease', it is just the decease of trainees and ordinary people as well. This is the method also in this passage 'mere decease'. 'Not seeing arising' means not seeing by way of not looking, even though one is capable of seeing. As for 'no arising', one is unable to see rebirth due to the absence of prior effort or due to not doing the preliminary practice; and for this reason, the distinction between the two methods becomes clear. 'Who knows the next world? One simply does not know.' Thus, by way of nihilism, one grasps annihilation; this is the connection with the remainder of the text. The intention is that by way of the nihilist view, through a state of great delusion, from not understanding that 'there is another world apart from this one,' one grasps this view. 'Whatever is the domain of the senses, that is the only domain'—thinking thus, like the king who took his own daughter's hand, one also grasps the annihilationist view due to being excessively attached to sensual pleasures. Therefore, the commentator said, 'or due to greed for sensual pleasure'. Referring to the state of non-reconnection with the stalk of leaves that have fallen from the stalk, it was said, 'they do not grow again'. As for 'just so are beings', the meaning is this: just as a yellow leaf, released from its bond, does not reconnect again, just so all beings do not have reconnection, have death as their end, have no further becoming, and go only to a death without reconnection. His doctrine is that beings, because of not arising again, are like a water bubble. As for 'thus', it is in the manner stated by way of example with the phrase beginning 'a gainer, recollecting'. As for 'otherwise', it is by a manner other than that, because of the possibility of many kinds of reasoning. Even for a gainer, these views arise by reasoning alone, based on the mere non-seeing of arising beyond decease. Therefore, it was stated, 'or having speculated'. Indeed, the connection to be made is that they arose only by speculating thus, and they arose only by speculating otherwise. Therein, with the passage beginning 'two people', he shows this meaning by showing the different types of those who grasp annihilation. Just as the doctrines of the eel-wrigglers were taught solely by way of non-gainers, and just as the doctrines of percipience in the fourth tetrad of the Uddhamāghātanika view were taught solely by way of gainers, these doctrines were not. But these doctrines, like the eternalist and partial eternalist doctrines and so on, were taught by way of both gainers and non-gainers. If so, why, unlike in the case of the eternalist doctrines and so on, was the teaching here not given separately for the gainer and for the reasoner, but was given by the Blessed One differently from the teachings on eternalism and so on? The reply is stated: It was done due to the attainment of elegance in teaching. The Blessed Buddhas have indeed attained elegance in teaching; they teach the Dhamma in various ways in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained, not otherwise. For if here also there were the disposition of those to be trained which is the basis for such a teaching, the Blessed One would speak in just such a way. How? 'Here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, relying on ardor... and so on... when his mind is concentrated, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the decease and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees the decease-consciousness of an Arahant, or of many other beings, but he does not see the arising beyond that. He says thus: "Sirs, because this self, which is material, made of the four great elements, born of mother and father, is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body, and does not exist after death," and so on'—he would speak, having made a distinction between the gainer of a special attainment and the reasoner. But since the disposition of those to be trained which is the basis for such a teaching does not exist here, therefore, through elegance in teaching, in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained, this teaching was given by the Blessed One in a manner different indeed from the teachings on eternalism and so on. Thus it should be understood.

Atha vā sassatekaccasassatavādādīsu viya na idha takkīvādato visesalābhīvādo bhinnākāro, atha kho samānappakāratāya samānākāroyevāti imassa visesassa pakāsanatthaṃ ayamucchedavādo bhagavatā purimavādehi visiṭṭhākārabhāvena desito. Sambhavati hi idha takkinopi anussavādivasena adhigamavato viya abhiniveso. Apica na imā diṭṭhiyo bhagavatā anāgate evaṃbhāvīvasena [M 1.0448] desitā, nāpi evamete bhaveyyunti parikappanāvasena, atha kho [V 1.0392] yathā yathā diṭṭhigatikehi “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 203, 427; 3.27, 28; udā. 55) maññitā, tathā tathāyeva ime diṭṭhigatā yathābhuccaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā pakāsitā, yehi gambhīrādippakārā aputhujjanagocarā buddhadhammā pakāsanti, yesañca parikittanena tathāgatā sammadeva thomitā honti.

Alternatively, unlike in the case of the eternalist and partial eternalist doctrines and so on, here the doctrine of the gainer of a special attainment is not different in form from the doctrine of the reasoner; but rather, due to being of a similar type, it is of a similar form indeed. Therefore, in order to make this distinction clear, this annihilationist doctrine was taught by the Blessed One in a form distinct from the previous doctrines. Indeed, here the adherence of even a reasoner is possible, like that of one who has attained understanding by way of oral tradition and so on. Furthermore, these views were not taught by the Blessed One on the basis of how things will be in the future, nor were they taught on the basis of speculation that 'thus they might be.' But rather, in whatever way these speculative views were held by those with such views as 'this alone is true, the other is false,' in just that way these speculative views were comprehended as they really are with the knowledge of omniscience and were declared, by which the Buddha-dhammas—profound and so on, not the domain of ordinary people—shine forth; and by the recounting of whom, the Tathāgatas are not rightly praised.

Aparo nayo – yathā ucchedavādīhi diṭṭhigatikehi uttaruttarabhavadassīhi aparabhavadassīnaṃ tesaṃ vādapaṭisedhavasena sakasakavādā patiṭṭhāpitā, tathāyevāyaṃ desanā katāti purimadesanāhi imissā desanāya pavattibhedo na codetabbo, evañca katvā arūpabhavabhedavasena ucchedavādo catudhā vibhajitvā viya kāmarūpabhavabhedavasenāpi anekadhā vibhajitvāyeva vattabbo, evaṃ sati bhagavatā vuttasattakato bahutarabhedo ucchedavādo āpajjatīti, atha vā paccekaṃ kāmarūpabhavabhedavasena viya arūpabhavavasenāpi na vibhajitvā vattabbo, evampi sati bhagavatā vuttasattakato appatarabhedova ucchedavādo āpajjatīti ca evaṃpakārāpi codanā anavakāsā eva hoti. Diṭṭhigatikānañhi yathābhimataṃ desanā pavattāti.

Another method: Just as the annihilationists, who hold wrong views and see ever higher existences, establish their own doctrines by refuting the doctrine of those who see another existence, so too has this teaching been set forth. Therefore, no objection should be raised regarding the difference in the presentation of this teaching from previous teachings. And for this reason, just as the annihilationist doctrine is taught as divided into four based on the distinctions of formless existence, so too it should be explained as being divided in many ways based on the distinctions of the sense-sphere and form existences. This being so, the annihilationist doctrine would have far more distinctions than the sevenfold classification taught by the Blessed One. Or alternatively, just as it is not explained by dividing it individually according to the distinctions of the sense-sphere and form existences, so too it should not be explained by dividing it according to the formless existence. Even so, the annihilationist doctrine would have fewer distinctions than the sevenfold classification taught by the Blessed One. Thus, an objection of this kind is also entirely without basis. For the teaching proceeds according to the inclination of those who hold wrong views.

85. Mātāpitūnaṃ etanti taṃsambandhanato etaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ santakanti attho. Sukkasoṇitanti pitu sukkaṃ, mātu soṇitañca, ubhinnaṃ vā sukkasaṅkhātaṃ soṇitaṃ. Mātāpettiketi nimitte cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Itīti imehi tīhi padehi. “Rūpakāyavasenā”ti avatvā “rūpakāyasīsenā”ti vadanto arūpampi tesaṃ “attā”ti gahaṇaṃ ñāpeti. Iminā pakārena itthanti āha “evameke”ti. Evaṃ-saddo hettha idamattho, iminā pakārenāti attho. Eketi ekacce, aññe vā.

85. 'This is of the mother and father' means: because of its connection to them, this is the possession of the mother and father; this is the meaning. 'Semen and blood' means: the father's semen and the mother's blood, or the blood of both, designated as semen. 'Mātāpettika' is a locative case in the sense of a cause. 'Iti' refers to these three terms. By not saying 'by way of the form-body,' but saying 'by way of the head of the form-body,' the commentator makes it known that they grasp even the formless as 'self.' Wishing to show that 'thus' (itthaṃ) means 'in this manner,' he said, 'thus some' (evam eke). Here, the word 'evaṃ' has the meaning of 'idaṃ' (this); the meaning is 'in this manner.' 'Eke' means some, or others.

86. Manussānaṃ pubbe gahitattā, aññesañca asambhavato “kāmāvacaro”ti ettha chakāmāvacaradevapariyāpannoti attho. Kabaḷīkāro cettha yathāvuttasudhāhāro.

86. Because humans were taken first, and because it is not possible for others, here in the phrase 'of the sense-sphere,' the meaning is 'included among the devas of the six sense-sphere realms.' And here, 'edible food' is the aforementioned divine food.

87. Jhānamanena [M 1.0449] nibbattoti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Mahāvayavo aṅgo, tattha visuṃ pavatto paccaṅgo, sabbehi aṅgapaccaṅgehi yutto tathā. Tesanti cakkhusotindriyānaṃ. Itaresanti ghānajivhākāyindriyānaṃ. Tesampi indriyānaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ purisavesavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ “samānepi tattha ubhayaliṅgābhāve purisasaṇṭhānāva tattha brahmāno, na itthisaṇṭhānā”ti.

87. Regarding 'born from this jhāna,' what needs to be said has already been stated below. A major limb is an 'aṅga,' and a distinct part that occurs therein is a 'paccaṅga'; thus, it is endowed with all major and minor limbs. 'Of those' refers to the faculties of eye and ear. 'Of the others' refers to the faculties of nose, tongue, and body. The form of these faculties, too, should be understood only by way of the male appearance. Indeed, it is stated in the commentaries: 'Even though there is an absence of both genders there, the Brahmās there have only a male form, not a female form.'

88-92. Ākāsānañcāyatana-saddo [V 1.0393] idha bhaveyevāti āha “ākāsānañcāyatanabhava”nti. Etthāha – yuttaṃ tāva purimesu tīsu vādesu “kāyassa bhedā”ti vattuṃ pañcavokārabhavapariyāpannaṃ attabhāvamārabbha pavattattā tesaṃ vādānaṃ, catuvokārabhavapariyāpannaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ nissāya pavattesu catutthādīsu catūsu vādesu kasmā “kāyassa bhedā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi arūpīnaṃ kāyo vijjati. Yo bhedoti vucceyyāti? Saccametaṃ, rūpattabhāve pana pavattavohāreneva diṭṭhigatiko arūpattabhāvepi kāyavohāraṃ āropetvā evamāha. Lokasmiñhi dissati aññatthabhūtopi vohāro tadaññatthasamāropito yathā taṃ “sasavisāṇaṃ, khaṃ puppha”nti. Yathā ca diṭṭhigatikā diṭṭhiyo paññapenti, tathāyeva bhagavāpi desetīti. Apica nāmakāyabhāvato phassādidhammasamūhabhūte arūpattabhāve kāyaniddeso daṭṭhabbo. Samūhaṭṭhenapi hi “kāyo”ti vuccati “hatthikāyo assakāyo”tiādīsu viya. Ettha ca kāmāvacaradevattabhāvādiniravasesavibhavapatiṭṭhāpakānaṃ dutiyādivādānaṃ aparantakappikabhāvo yutto hotu anāgataddhavisayattā tesaṃ vādānaṃ, kathaṃ pana diṭṭhigatikassa paccakkhabhūtamanussattabhāvāpagamapatiṭṭhāpakassa paṭhamavādassa aparantakappikabhāvo yujjeyya paccuppannaddhavisayattā tassa vādassa. Dutiyavādādīnañhi purimapurimavādasaṅgahitasseva attano anāgate taduttaribhavūpapannassa samucchedabodhanato yujjati aparantakappikatā, tathā ceva vuttaṃ “no ca kho bho ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hotī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.85) yaṃ pana tattha vuttaṃ “atthi kho bho añño attā”ti, (dī. ni. 1.87) taṃ manussattabhāvādiheṭṭhimattabhāvavisesāpekkhāya vuttaṃ, na sabbathā aññabhāvato. Paṭhamavādassa pana anāgate taduttaribhavūpapannassa attano samucchedabodhanābhāvato[M 1.0450], “atthi kho bho añño attā”ti ettha aññabhāvena aggahaṇato ca na yujjateva aparantakappikatāti?
