No na yujjati idhalokapariyāpannattepi paṭhamavādavisayassa anāgatakālikasseva tena adhippetattā. Paṭhamavādināpi hi idhalokapariyāpannassa attano paraṃ maraṇā ucchedo anāgatakālavaseneva adhippeto, tasmā cassa aparantakappikatāya na koci virodhoti.

88-92. The term 'base of infinite space' here refers only to existence; that is why the commentator says, 'the existence of the base of infinite space.' Here, an objector says: It is fitting to say 'upon the breakup of the body' in the first three views, because those views arise concerning an individual existence included in the five-aggregate existence. But why is 'upon the breakup of the body' said in the fourth and subsequent four views, which arise depending on an existence included in the four-aggregate existence? For formless beings have no body that could be said to break up. This is true. However, by means of the conventional usage that proceeds in the context of form-existence, the adherent of wrong views superimposes the term 'body' even onto formless existence and speaks in this way. Indeed, in the world, a term that has arisen in one context is seen to be applied to another, as in 'a hare's horn' or 'a sky-flower.' And just as those who hold wrong views propound their views, so too does the Blessed One teach; this is the refutation. Furthermore, because it is a 'mental body' (nāmakāya), the designation 'body' should be understood in the context of formless existence, which is a collection of mental phenomena such as contact. For 'body' is also used in the sense of a collection, as in 'a collection of elephants' or 'a collection of horses.' And here, let it be fitting that the second and subsequent views, which establish the complete annihilation of various states of existence, such as existence as a god in the sense-sphere, are considered to be speculations on the future, since those views concern the future. But how could the first view, which establishes the cessation of the directly perceived human existence for an adherent of wrong views, be considered a speculation on the future, since that view concerns the present? Indeed, for the second and subsequent views, the classification as 'speculation on the future' is fitting because they teach the annihilation in the future of one's self reborn in a higher existence than that included in the immediately preceding view. And so it was said: 'But, sir, this self is not thereby completely annihilated,' and so on. As for what was said there, 'There is, sir, another self,' that was said with reference to the distinction from a lower state of existence, such as the human existence, not because it is in every way another. But for the first view, since it does not teach the annihilation in the future of one's self reborn in a higher existence, and since in the statement 'There is, sir, another self,' another state is not grasped, its classification as 'speculation on the future' is not fitting at all. Is this the objection? No, it is not that it is unfitting. Even though the domain of the first view is included in this world, it is intended by that proponent to refer only to what is in the future. For the proponent of the first view also intends the annihilation of the self that is included in this world to be after death, by way of the future. Therefore, there is no contradiction in his being a speculator on the future.

Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Doctrine of Nibbāna in This Very Life

93. Ñāṇena daṭṭhabboti diṭṭho, diṭṭho ca so sabhāvaṭṭhena dhammo cāti diṭṭhadhammo, dassanabhūtena ñāṇena upaladdhasabhāvoti attho. So pana akkhānamindriyānaṃ abhimukhībhūto visayoyevāti vuttaṃ “paccakkhadhammo vuccatī”ti. Tattha yo anindriyavisayo, sopi supākaṭabhāvena indriyavisayo viya hotīti katvā tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tenevāha “tattha tattha [V 1.0394] paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacana”nti, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave yathākammaṃ paṭilabhitabbattabhāvassa vācakaṃ padaṃ, nāmanti vā attho. Nibbānañcettha dukkhavūpasamanameva, na aggaphalaṃ, na ca asaṅkhatadhātu tesamavisayattāti āha “dukkhavūpasamana”nti. Diṭṭhadhammanibbāne pavatto vādo etesanti diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādātipi yujjati.

93. Because it is to be seen by knowledge, it is diṭṭha (seen); and that which is seen is also a dhamma (phenomenon) in the sense of its own nature, therefore it is diṭṭhadhamma (a seen phenomenon). The meaning is that its own nature is apprehended by knowledge, which is the act of seeing. Moreover, because it is only the object that has come before the faculties called eyes, it was said: “It is called a paccakkhadhamma (directly perceived phenomenon).” Therein, even that individual existence which is not an object of the faculties becomes like an object of the faculties due to its extreme manifestation; it should be understood that it was spoken of thus for this reason. For that very reason, he said: “This is a designation for the individual existence obtained in this or that state of being.” The meaning is: it is a word, or a name, that expresses the individual existence to be obtained in this or that state of being according to kamma. And here, Nibbāna is only the pacification of suffering, not the supreme fruit, nor the unconditioned element, because these are not their domain. Therefore, he said: “the pacification of suffering.” It is also a suitable word-meaning that they are called diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā (proponents of the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life) because for them there is a doctrine that occurs regarding Nibbāna in this very life.

94. Kāmanīyattā kāmā ca te anekāvayavānaṃ samūhabhāvato sattānañca bandhanato guṇā cāti kāmaguṇāti atthaṃ sandhāyāha “manāpiyarūpādīhī”tiādi. Yāva phoṭṭhabbārammaṇañcettha ādi-saddena saṅgaṇhāti. Suṭṭhu appitoti sammā ṭhapito. Ṭhapanā cettha allīyanāti āha “allīno”ti. Parito tattha tattha kāmaguṇesu yathāsakaṃ indriyāni cāreti gocaraṃ gaṇhāpetīti atthaṃ dassetuṃ “tesū”tiādi vuttaṃ, tenāha “ito cito ca upanetī”ti. Pari-saddavisiṭṭho vā idha cara-saddo kīḷāyanti vuttaṃ “palaḷatī”tiādi [laḷati (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)]. Palaḷatīti hi pakārena laḷati, vilāsaṃ karotīti attho. “Ettha cā”tiādinā uttamakāmaguṇikānameva diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapentīti dasseti. Mandhātumahārājavasavattīdevarājakāmaguṇā hi uttamatāya nidassitā, kasmāti āha “evarūpe”tiādi.

94. Because they are desirable (kāmanīya), they are sensual pleasures (kāmā); and they are strands (guṇā) because they are a collection of many parts and because they bind beings; therefore, they are sensual strands (kāmaguṇā). With reference to this meaning, he said: “by pleasing and agreeable forms, etc.” And here, by the word ādi (etc.), he includes up to the tangible object. Suṭṭhu appito (well-applied) means properly established. And here, establishment is clinging; therefore, he said allīno (clinging). To show the meaning: “He causes the faculties to wander all around in those various sensual pleasures according to their own nature; he causes them to take the object,” it was said: “in those,” etc. Therefore, he said: “he brings it from here and there.” Alternatively, here the root car specified by the prefix pari occurs in the sense of “playing”; therefore, it was said: “he sports” (palaḷati), etc. Indeed, palaḷati means: he sports in various ways, he makes a display of charm. By “And here,” etc., he shows that those with wrong views declare as Nibbāna in this very life only that of those who possess the highest sensual pleasures. Indeed, the sensual pleasures of the great king Mandhātu and the deva-king Vasavattī were shown because of their supremacy. Why? He said: “in such a form,” etc.

95. Aññathābhāvāti [M 1.0451] kāraṇe nissakkavacanaṃ. Vuttanayenāti suttapadesu desitanayena, etena sokādīnamuppajjanākāraṃ dasseti. Ñātibhogarogasīladiṭṭhibyasanehi phuṭṭhassa cetaso abbhantaraṃ nijjhāyanaṃ socanaṃ antonijjhāyanaṃ, tadeva lakkhaṇametassāti antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo. Tasmiṃ soke samuṭṭhānahetubhūte nissitaṃ tannissitaṃ. Bhusaṃ vilapanaṃ lālappanaṃ, tannissitameva lālappanaṃ, tadeva lakkhaṇamassāti tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo. Pasādasaṅkhāte kāye nissitassa dukkhasahagatakāyaviññāṇassa paṭipīḷanaṃ kāyapaṭipīḷanaṃ, sasambhārakathanaṃ vā etaṃ yathā “dhanunā vijjhatī”ti tadupanissayassa vā aniṭṭharūpassa pacchā pavattanato “rūpakāyassa paṭipīḷana”ntipi vaṭṭati. Paṭighasampayuttassa manaso vihesanaṃ manovighātaṃ. Tadeva lakkhaṇamassāti sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Ñātibyasanādinā phuṭṭhassa paridevanāyapi asakkuṇantassa antogatasokasamuṭṭhito bhuso āyāso upāyāso. So pana cetaso appasannākāro evāti āha “visādalakkhaṇo”ti. Sādanaṃ pasādanaṃ sādo, pasannatā. Anupasaggopi hi saddo saupasaggo viya yathāvuttassa atthassa bodhako yathā “gotrabhū”ti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Tato vigamanaṃ visādo, appasannabhāvo.

95. The word aññathābhāvā (because of becoming otherwise) is a word in the ablative case in the sense of cause. Vuttanayena (by the stated method) means: by the method taught in the sutta passages; by this, he shows the mode of arising of sorrow and the like. The internal burning and sorrowing of a mind afflicted by the calamities of relatives, wealth, disease, virtue, and views is internal burning. Because this is its characteristic, that sorrow has the characteristic of internal burning. Dependent on that sorrow, which is the originating cause, is what is dependent on it. Intense lamentation is wailing; wailing is just that which is dependent on it. Because this is its characteristic, that lamentation has the characteristic of wailing dependent on that. The oppression of body-consciousness accompanied by pain, which is dependent on the body designated as sensitive, is bodily oppression. Alternatively, this word is a statement including its instrument, like “he shoots with a bow.” Or, because it occurs afterwards from an undesirable form which is the support for both of those, the meaning “oppression of the material body” is also suitable. The vexation of a mind conjoined with aversion is mental distress. “Because this is its characteristic”—this should be connected everywhere. For one afflicted by the calamity of relatives and so on, who is unable even to lament, the intense fatigue arisen from internalized sorrow is despair (upāyāso). Moreover, that is just a state of the mind's lack of clarity; therefore, he said, “it has the characteristic of dejection (visāda).” Sādanaṃ is clarifying; sādo is clarity, the state of being clear. Indeed, a word even without a prefix, like a word with a prefix, can be indicative of the aforesaid meaning, as in gotrabhū. Thus it should be known everywhere. Departure from that (clarity) is visādo (dejection), a state of lack of clarity.

96. Vitakkanaṃ [V 1.0395] vitakkitaṃ, taṃ panatthato vitakkova, tathā vicāritanti etthāpi, tena vuttaṃ “abhiniropanavasena pavatto vitakko”tiādi. Etenāti vitakkavicāre parāmasitvā karaṇaniddeso, hetuniddeso vā. Tenetamatthaṃ dīpeti “khobhakarasabhāvattā vitakkavicārānaṃ taṃsahitampi jhānaṃ tehi sauppīḷanaṃ viya hotī”ti, tenāha “sakaṇṭakaṃ [bhakaṇḍakaṃ (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ)] viya khāyatī”ti. Oḷārikabhāvo hi vitakkavicārasaṅkhātena kaṇṭakena saha pavattakathā. Kaṇṭakasahitabhāvo ca sauppīḷanatā eva, loke hi sakaṇṭakaṃ pharusakaṃ oḷārikanti vadanti.

96. Thinking (vitakkanaṃ) is what is thought (vitakkitaṃ); but that, in meaning, is just thinking (vitakka). It is the same here with vicāritaṃ (what is pondered). Therefore, it was said: “Thinking is that which proceeds by way of application,” etc. By this word etena, having referred to thinking and pondering, it is an indication of the instrument, or an indication of the cause. By that, he clarifies this meaning: “Because thinking and pondering have the nature of causing agitation, even the jhāna accompanied by them is as if oppressed by them.” Therefore, he said: “it is experienced as if with thorns.” For the state of coarseness is the state of being together with the thorn designated as thinking and pondering. And the state of being with a thorn is just oppressiveness. Indeed, in the world, they call what is thorny and harsh “coarse.”

97. Pītigataṃ pītiyeva “diṭṭhigata”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. 381; mahāni. 12) viya gata-saddassa tabbhāvavuttito. Ayañhi saṃvaṇṇakānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ anatthakapadaṃ, tulyādhikaraṇapadañca ṭhapetvā atthavaṇṇanā. Tathā hi tattha tattha dissati. “Yopanāti [M 1.0452] yo yādiso, (pārā. 45) nibbānadhātūti nibbāyanamatta”nti ca ādi. Yāya nimittabhūtāya ubbilāvanapītiyā uppannāya cittaṃ ubbilāvitaṃ nāma, sāyeva ubbilāvitattaṃ bhāvavācakassa nimitte pavattanato. Iti pītiyā uppannāya eva cittassa ubbilāvanato tassa ubbilāvitabhāvo pītiyā kato nāmāti āha “ubbilabhāvakaraṇa”nti.

97. Pītigataṃ is just pīti (joy), just as in diṭṭhigataṃ and so on, because the word gata is used to express that very state. Indeed, this is the nature of the commentators: to explain the meaning while setting aside meaningless words and words in apposition. Indeed, this is seen in various places: “Yo pana means yo yādiso (whoever, of whatever kind),” and “nibbānadhātu means mere extinguishing,” and so on. When that uplifting joy, which has become the cause, has arisen, the mind is called 'uplifted'. That very joy is itself the 'state of being uplifted' (ubbilāvitattaṃ), because the suffix expressing state occurs in the sense of cause. Thus, because the mind is uplifted only when joy has arisen, its state of being uplifted is said to be made by joy. Therefore, he said: “the making of the state of elation” (ubbilabhāvakaraṇaṃ).

98. Ābhujanaṃ manasikaraṇaṃ ābhogo. Sammā anukkamena, punappunaṃ vā ārammaṇassa āhāro samannāhāro. Ayaṃ pana ṭīkāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.98) vuttanayo – cittassa ābhuggabhāvo ārammaṇe abhinatabhāvo ābhogo. Sukhena hi cittaṃ ārammaṇe abhinataṃ hoti, na dukkhena viya apanataṃ, nāpi adukkhamasukhena viya anabhinataṃ, anapanatañcāti. Ettha ca “manuññabhojanādīsu khuppipāsādiabhibhūtassa viya kāmehi viveciyamānassa upādārammaṇapatthanāvisesato abhivaḍḍhati, manuññabhojanaṃ bhuttāvino viya pana uḷārakāmarasassa yāvadatthaṃ nicitassa sahitassa bhuttakāmatāya kāmesu pātabyatā na hoti, visayānabhigiddhanato visayehi dummociyehi jalūkā viya sayameva muccatī”ti ca ayoniso ummujjitvā kāmaguṇasantappitatāya saṃsāradukkhavūpasamaṃ byākāsi paṭhamavādī. Kāmādīnaṃ ādīnavadassitāya, paṭhamādijhānasukhassa santabhāvadassitāya ca paṭhamādijhānasukhatittiyā saṃsāradukkhupacchedaṃ byākaṃsu dutiyādivādino. Idhāpi ucchedavādeva vuttappakāro vicāro yathāsambhavaṃ ānetvā vattabbo. Ayaṃ panettha viseso – ekasmimpi attabhāve pañca vādā labbhanti. Paṭhamavāde yadi kāmaguṇasamappito attā, evaṃ so diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto. Dutiyādivādesu yadi paṭhamavādasaṅgahito soyeva attā paṭhamajjhānādisamaṅgī[V 1.0396], evaṃ sati diṭṭhadhammanibbānappattoti. Teneva hi ucchedavāde viya idha pāḷiyaṃ “añño attā”ti aññaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Kathaṃ pana accantanibbānapaññāpakassa attano diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādassa sassatadiṭṭhiyā saṅgaho, na ucchedadiṭṭhiyāti? Taṃtaṃsukhavisesasamaṅgitāpaṭiladdhena bandhavimokkhena suddhassa attano sakarūpeneva avaṭṭhānadīpanato. Tesañhi tathāpaṭiladdhena kammabandhavimokkhena suddho hutvā diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto attā sakarūpeneva avaṭṭhāsīti laddhi. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “ettāvatā kho bho [M 1.0453] ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī”ti sassatabhāvañāpakacchāyāya eva tesaṃ vādadassanaṃ katanti.

98. Bending the mind, directing the mind, is attention (ābhogo). By a proper sequence, or alternatively, the repeated bringing of the object is sustained attention (samannāhāro). This, however, is the method stated in the subcommentary: the state of the mind's attending, the state of inclining towards an object, is attention (ābhogo). For the mind inclines towards an object with pleasure; it is not as if it turns away with pain, nor is it as if it is neither inclined nor turned away with neither-pain-nor-pleasure. And here, the first proponent, having reflected unwisely due to being gratified by sensual pleasures, declared the calming of the suffering of saṃsāra, arguing: 'For one being secluded from sensual pleasures, the longing for a clinging-object especially increases, just as for one overcome by hunger, thirst, and so on, the longing for delightful food and so on increases. However, just as for one who has eaten delightful food there is no further desirability for consumption, so for one who is endowed with the sublime taste of sensual pleasure, having accumulated it as much as desired, due to having already consumed sensual pleasures, there is no further desirability for consumption in regard to sensual pleasures. Due to not being greedy for sense-objects, one is freed by oneself from sense-objects that are difficult to be freed from, like a leech.' Due to seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and so on, and due to seeing the peaceful nature of the bliss of the first jhāna and so on, and through satisfaction in the bliss of the first jhāna and so on, the second and subsequent proponents declared the cutting off of the suffering of saṃsāra. Here too, the investigation of the kind stated in the annihilationist view should be brought and applied as is suitable. This is the distinction here: in a single existence, five doctrines are found. In the first doctrine, if the self is devoted to sensual pleasures, in that case it has attained Nibbāna in the visible world. In the second and subsequent doctrines, if that same self, as included in the first doctrine, is endowed with the first jhāna and so on, in that case it has attained Nibbāna in the visible world. For that very reason, unlike in the annihilationist view, here in the Pāḷi the taking up of 'another' as in 'another self' was not done. How, then, is the doctrine of Nibbāna in the visible world, a doctrine of a self that declares ultimate Nibbāna, included under the eternalist view and not the annihilationist view? Because of showing the endurance of the purified self in its very own form, through the release from bondage obtained by being endowed with this or that special bliss. For their belief is: 'The self, having become purified through the release from the bondage of kamma thus obtained, having attained Nibbāna in the visible world, remained in its very own form.' For thus in the Pāḷi, the showing of their doctrine was done with the very semblance of indicating a state of permanence, with the words: 'To this extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the visible world.'

“Ettāvatā”tiādinā pāḷiyatthasampiṇḍanaṃ. Tattha yāsanti yathāvuttānaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ. Tassa imā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo kathitāti niyamanaṃ, niyatānapekkhavacanaṃ vā etaṃ “yaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti āgataṭṭhāne viya. Sesāti pañcapaññāsa diṭṭhiyo. Tāsu antānantikavādādīnaṃ sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgahabhāvo tattha tattha pakāsitoyeva. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ, pubbantāparantā eva diṭṭhābhinivesassa visayabhāvena dassitā, na pana tadubhayamekajjhanti? Asambhavo evettha kāraṇaṃ. Na hi pubbantāparantesu viya tadubhayavinimutte majjhante diṭṭhikappanā sambhavati tadubhayantaramattena ittarakālattā. Atha pana paccuppannattabhāvo tadubhayavemajjhaṃ, evaṃ sati diṭṭhikappanākkhamo tassa ubhayasabhāvo pubbantāparantesuyeva antogadhoti kathaṃ tadubhayamekajjhaṃ adassitaṃ siyā. Atha vā pubbantāparantavantatāya “pubbantāparanto”ti majjhanto vuccati, sopi “pubbantakappikā ca aparantakappikā ca pubbantāparantakappikā cā”ti upari vadantena bhagavatā pubbantāparantehi visuṃ katvā vuttoyevāti daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyampi “sabbepi te pubbantāparantakappike”ti etena sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesena vā saṅgahitoti veditabbaṃ. Aññathā hi saṅkaḍḍhitvā vuttavacanassa niravasesasaṅkaḍḍhanābhāvato anatthakatā āpajjeyyāti. Ke pana te pubbantāparantakappikāti? Ye antānantikā hutvā diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti evamādinā ubhayasambandhābhinivesino veditabbā.

With 'To this extent,' etc., is the summarizing of the meaning of the Pāḷi. Therein, 'of which' (yāsaṃ) is a word indicating the non-specification of the aforementioned views. That 'these sixty-two views have been taught' is a specification. Or, it is a word not requiring a specific referent, as in the place where it says 'with reference to which it was said.' 'The rest' refers to the fifty-five views. Among them, the inclusion of views such as the doctrine of finitude and infinitude under the eternalist view has been explained in the respective places. What is the reason here that only the past and future are shown as the domain of adherence to views, and not both together? The reason here is impossibility. For a speculative view does not arise in the middle period, which is free from both, unlike in the past and future, because it is of short duration, being merely the interval between the two. Or else, if the present existence is the middle between those two, then since its dual nature is capable of speculative views and is included in the past and future themselves, how could it be that both are not shown together? Alternatively, the middle is called 'past-and-future' because it possesses a past and a future. And it should be understood that this middle too was spoken of separately from the speculators on the past and future by the Blessed One who said above: 'Those who speculate on the past, those who speculate on the future, and those who speculate on the past and future.' In the commentary as well, it should be known that they are included by this general designation, 'all of them are speculators on the past and future,' or by way of ellipsis (ekasesa). Otherwise, for a statement spoken summarily, meaninglessness would result from the absence of an all-inclusive summary. Who, then, are those speculators on the past and future? They should be known as those who adhere to a connection with both, in the manner of: 'Those who, being holders of views of finitude and infinitude, are also proponents of Nibbāna in the visible world.'

100-104. “Idānī”tiādinā appanāvacanadvayassa visesaṃ dasseti. Tattha ekajjhanti rāsikaraṇatthe nipāto. Ekadhā karotīti ekajjhantipi neruttikā, bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ. Iti-saddo idamattho, iminā pakārena pucchitvā vissajjesīti attho. Ajjhāsayanti [V 1.0397] sassatucchedavasena diṭṭhijjhāsayaṃ. Tadubhayavasena hi sattānaṃ saṃkilesapakkhe duvidho ajjhāsayo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

100-104. With 'Now,' etc., he shows the distinction between the two concluding statements. Therein, 'ekajjhaṃ' is a particle in the sense of making a heap. Etymologists also say 'ekajjhaṃ' is from 'ekadhā karoti' (he makes into one), and this is an abstract neuter noun. The word 'iti' has the meaning of 'this'; the meaning is, 'having questioned in this manner, he answered.' 'Inclination' (ajjhāsayaṃ) means the inclination of views in terms of eternalism and annihilationism. For, on the side of defilement, the inclination of beings is twofold, based on both of these. Thus it is said:

“Sassatucchedadiṭṭhi ca, khanti cevānulomikā;

Yathābhūtañca yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, etaṃ āsayasaddita”nti. (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.136; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā, verajjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāpi passitabbaṃ);

“The view of eternalism and annihilationism, and conformity-patience, and whatever knowledge of things as they are—this is called 'inclination' (āsaya).”

Tañca [M 1.0454] bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ aparimāṇe eva ñeyyavisese uppajjanavasena anekabhedabhinnampi “cattāro janā sassatavādā”tiādinā dvāsaṭṭhiyā pabhedehi saṅgaṇhanavasena sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā dassento pamāṇabhūtāya tulāya dhārayamāno viya hotīti āha “tulāya tulayanto viyā”ti. Tathā hi vakkhati “antojālīkatā”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.146) “sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viyā”ti pana etena sabbaññutaññāṇato aññassa ñāṇassa imissā desanāya asakkuṇeyyataṃ dasseti paramagambhīratāvacanato.

And that disposition, although divided into many kinds by way of its arising in relation to immeasurable distinctions of knowable things for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One, while showing it, having delimited it with the knowledge of omniscience by encompassing it within sixty-two divisions, such as 'four persons are eternalists,' is as if weighing it with a standard scale. Therefore, the commentator said, 'as if weighing with a scale.' For that very reason, he will state, 'being caught in a net,' etc. Furthermore, by the phrase 'like one taking sand from the foot of Mount Sineru,' he shows the inability of any knowledge other than the knowledge of omniscience to expound this teaching, due to the statement of its supreme profundity.

Ettha ca “sabbe te imeheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā”ti vacanato, pubbantakappikādittayavinimuttassa ca kassaci diṭṭhigatikassa abhāvato yāni tāni sāmaññaphalādisuttantaresu vuttappakārāni akiriyāhetukanatthikavādādīni, yāni ca issarapakatipajāpatipurisakālasabhāvaniyatiyadicchāvādādippabhedāni diṭṭhigatāni (visuddhi. 1.160-162; vibha. anuṭī. 2.194-195 vākyakhandhesu passitabbaṃ) bahiddhāpi dissamānāni, tesaṃ ettheva saṅgahato antogadhatā veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Akiriyavādo tāva “vañjho kūṭaṭṭho”tiādinā kiriyābhāvadīpanato sassatavāde antogadho, tathā “sattime kāyā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.174) nayappavatto pakudhavādo, “natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.168) nayappavatto ahetukavādo ca adhiccasamuppannavāde. “Natthi paro loko”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.171) nayappavatto natthikavādo ucchedavāde. Tathā hi tattha “kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.85) vuttaṃ. Paṭhamena ādi-saddena nigaṇṭhavādādayo saṅgahitā.

And here, because of the teaching, 'All those recluses and brahmins proclaim by means of these very sixty-two grounds, or by one or another of them; there is none outside of these,' and because of the absence of any person holding a wrong view who is free from the triad beginning with speculators on the past, it should be understood that those wrong views with types spoken of in other suttas like the Sāmaññaphala Sutta—such as the doctrines of non-action, non-causality, and nihilism—and those wrong views with divisions such as the doctrines of a creator god (Issara), nature (pakati), Prajāpati, a soul (purisa), time (kāla), intrinsic nature (sabhāva), determinism (niyati), and chance (yadicchā), which are also seen externally, are included herein by way of being encompassed. How? The doctrine of non-action, for a start, is included in eternalism because it shows the absence of anything done, with phrases like 'barren, standing like a mountain peak.' Similarly, the doctrine of Pakudha, which proceeds by the method of 'these seven bodies,' etc., is included in eternalism. And the doctrine of non-causality, which proceeds by the method of 'there is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings,' etc., is included in the doctrine of accidental origination. The doctrine of nihilism, which proceeds by the method of 'there is no other world,' etc., is included in annihilationism. For indeed, it is said therein, 'with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated,' etc. By the first word 'etc.,' the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas and others are included.

Yadipi [V 1.0398] pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 1.177) nāṭaputtavādabhāvena cātuyāmasaṃvaro āgato, tathāpi sattavatātikkamena vikkhepavāditāya nāṭaputtavādopi sañcayavādo viya amarāvikkhepavādesu antogadho. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti (dī. ni. 1.377; ma. ni. 2.122; saṃ. ni. 2.35) evaṃpakārā vādā pana “rūpī attā hoti arogo [M 1.0455] paraṃ maraṇā”tiādivādesu saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. “Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, atthi sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃpakārā sassatavāde. “Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, natthi sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃpakārā ucchedavāde. “Hoti ca na hoti ca tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, atthi ca natthi ca sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃpakārā ekaccasassatavāde. “Neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, nevatthi na natthi sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃpakārā amarāvikkhepavāde. Issarapakatipajāpatipurisakālavādā ekaccasassatavāde. Kaṇādavādo, sabhāvaniyatiyadicchāvādā ca adhiccasamuppannavāde saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Iminā nayena suttantaresu, bahiddhā ca aññatitthiyasamaye dissamānānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ imāsuyeva dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu antogadhatā veditabbā. Te pana tattha tatthāgatanayena vuccamānā ganthavitthārakarā, atitthe ca pakkhandanamiva hotīti na vitthārayimha. Idha pāḷiyaṃ atthavicāraṇāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuttānatthapakāsanameva hi amhākaṃ bhāroti.

Although in the Pāḷi the fourfold restraint is presented as the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, nevertheless, because of its transgression of the seven practices and its nature as an equivocating doctrine, the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, like the doctrine of Sañjaya, is included among the doctrines of endless equivocation. Views of the type, 'That which is the life-principle is the body,' or 'The life-principle is one thing, the body is another,' are included in doctrines such as, 'The self is material and is healthy after death.' Views of the type, 'The Tathāgata exists after death; there are beings who are spontaneously arisen,' are included in eternalism. Views of the type, 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death; there are no beings who are spontaneously arisen,' are included in annihilationism. Views of the type, 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; there both are and are not beings who are spontaneously arisen,' are included in partial-eternalism. Views of the type, 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; there neither are nor are not beings who are spontaneously arisen,' are included in the doctrine of endless equivocation. The doctrines of Issara, Pakati, Pajāpati, Purisa, and Kāla are included in partial-eternalism. The doctrine of Kaṇāda, and the doctrines of intrinsic nature, determinism, and chance are included in the doctrine of accidental origination. By this method, the inclusion of wrong views seen in other suttas and outside in the doctrines of other sects within these very sixty-two views should be understood. However, were they to be discussed according to the way they appear in their respective contexts, they would make the book extensive and it would be like plunging into a non-ford; therefore, we have not elaborated. Indeed, in investigating the meaning of the Pāḷi here, our burden is only to clarify the meaning that is not obvious in the commentary.

“Evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā”ti vacanappasaṅgena suttassānusandhayo vibhajituṃ “tayo hī”tiādimāha. Atthantaranisedhanatthañhi visesaniddhāraṇaṃ. Tattha anusandhanaṃ anusandhi, sambandhamattaṃ, yaṃ desanāya kāraṇaṭṭhena “samuṭṭhāna”ntipi vuccati. Pucchādayo hi desanāya bāhirakāraṇaṃ tadanurūpena desanāpavattanato. Taṃsambandhopi tannissitattā kāraṇameva. Abbhantarakāraṇaṃ pana mahākaruṇādesanāñāṇādayo. Ayamattho upari āvi bhavissati. Pucchāya kato anusandhi pucchānusandhi, pucchaṃ anusandhiṃ katvā desitattā suttassa sambandho pucchāya kato nāma hoti. Pucchāsaṅkhāto anusandhi pucchānusandhītipi yujjati. Pucchānissitena hi anusandhinā tannissayabhūtā pucchāpi gahitāti. Atha vā anusandhahatīti anusandhi, pucchāsaṅkhāto anusandhi etassāti pucchānusandhi, taṃtaṃsuttapadeso. Pucchāya vā anusandhīyatīti pucchānusandhi, pucchaṃ vacanasambandhaṃ katvā desito taṃsamuṭṭhāniko taṃtaṃsuttapadesova. Ajjhāsayānusandhimhipi eseva nayo. Anusandhīyatīti anusandhi, yo yo anusandhi, anusandhino anurūpaṃ vā yathānusandhi.

On the occasion of the statement, 'Thus this teaching has come in accordance with its connection,' the commentator, in order to analyze the connections of the sutta, said, 'Three indeed,' and so on. For the determination of a specific point is for the purpose of precluding another meaning. Therein, 'connection' (anusandhi) is the act of connecting, merely a relationship, which, in the sense of being a cause for the teaching, is also called 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna). For questions and so on are an external cause of the teaching, because the teaching proceeds in accordance with them. That relationship, too, because it is dependent on them, is indeed a cause. The internal causes, however, are great compassion, the knowledge of teaching, and so on. This meaning will become clear later on. The connection made by a question is a pucchānusandhi. Because it is taught having made the question the connection, the relationship of the sutta is said to be made by the question. It is also suitable to say that the connection designated as a question is a pucchānusandhi. For by the connection that is dependent on the question, the question which is its basis is also taken. Alternatively, 'it connects' (anusandhahati), therefore it is a connection (anusandhi); 'this sutta passage has a connection designated as a question,' therefore it is a pucchānusandhi, referring to that particular sutta passage. Or, 'it is connected by a question' (pucchāya anusandhīyati), therefore it is a pucchānusandhi, referring to that particular sutta passage which is taught having made the question its verbal connection, and which originates from it. In the case of a connection by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi), this same method should be understood. 'It is connected' (anusandhīyati), therefore it is a connection (anusandhi). Yathānusandhi means whatever the connection may be; or, it means 'in accordance with the connection' (anusandhino anurūpaṃ).

Pucchāya, ajjhāsayena ca ananusandhiko ādimhi desitadhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā tappaṭipakkhadhammavasena [V 1.0399] vā pavatto uparisuttapadeso. Tathā [M 1.0456] hi so “yena pana dhammena…pe… kakacūpamā āgatā”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.100-104) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto, yathāpāḷimayaṃ vibhāgoti dasseti “tatthā”tiādinā. Tattha “evaṃ vutte nando gopālako bhagavantaṃ etadavocā”ti paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ sutte tathā abhāvato. “Evaṃ vutte nandagopālakasutte bhagavantaṃ etadavocā”ti pana paṭhitabbaṃ tasmiṃ sutte “aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavocā”ti atthassa upapattito. Idañhi saṃyuttāgamavare saḷāyatanavagge saṅgītasuttaṃ. Gaṅgāya vuyhamānaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ upamaṃ katvā saddhāpabbajite kulaputte desite nando gopālako “ahamimaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūressāmī”ti bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, upasampadañca gahetvā tathāpaṭipajjamāno nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto. Tasmā “nandagopālakasutta”nti paññāyittha. “Kiṃ nu kho bhante”tiādīni pana aññataroyeva bhikkhu avoca. Vuttañhi tattha “evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca ‘kiṃ nu kho bhante, orimaṃ tīra’ntiādi”.

By way of a question and by way of disposition, the subsequent passage of the sutta, which is not connected to the teaching given at the beginning, proceeds either by way of a corresponding teaching or by way of a teaching in opposition to it. For thus it is stated in the commentary with phrases like “by which teaching…pe… the simile of the saw has been given,” showing the division according to the Pāḷi text with “therein” and so forth. Therein, they recite, “When this was said, Nanda the cowherd said this to the Blessed One,” but that is not correct, as it is not found thus in the Sutta. Rather, it should be recited, “When this was said in the Nandagopālaka Sutta, he said this to the Blessed One,” because in that Sutta the meaning is established that “a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One.” For this is the Sutta that was chanted in the excellent Saṃyutta collection, in the Saḷāyatana Vagga. When the teaching was given to a clansman who had gone forth in faith, using the simile of a log being carried away by the Ganges, Nanda the cowherd, after saying, “I shall fulfill this practice,” took the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One, and practicing accordingly, he in no long time attained Arahantship. Therefore, it became known as the “Nandagopālaka Sutta.” However, it was a certain bhikkhu who spoke the words beginning with “What, venerable sir…?” For it is said therein: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: ‘What, venerable sir, is the near shore?’ and so on.”

Tatrāyamattho – evaṃ vutteti “sace kho bhikkhave, dārukkhandho na orimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchatī”tiādinā gaṅgāya vuyhamānaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ upamaṃ katvā saddhāpabbajite kulaputte desite. Bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti anusandhikusalatāya “kiṃ nu kho bhante”tiādivacanamavoca. Tathāgato hi “imissaṃ parisati nisinno anusandhi kusalo atthi, so maṃ pañhaṃ pucchissatī”ti ettakeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Orimaṃ tīranti orimabhūtaṃ tīraṃ. Tathā pārimaṃ tīranti. Majjhe saṃsīdoti vemajjhe saṃsīdanaṃ nimmujjanaṃ. Thale ussādoti jalamajjhe uṭṭhite thalasmiṃ ussārito āruḷho. Manussaggāhoti manussānaṃ sambandhībhūtānaṃ, manussehi vā gahaṇaṃ. Tathā amanussaggāhoti āvaṭṭaggāhoti udakāvaṭṭena gahaṇaṃ. Antopūtīti vakkahadayādīsu apūtikassāpi guṇānaṃ pūtibhāvena abbhantaraṃpūtīti.

Herein this is the meaning: “When this was said” means when the teaching was given to the clansmen who had gone forth in faith, using the simile of a log being carried away by the Ganges, beginning with “If, bhikkhus, a log does not approach the near shore.” “He said this to the Blessed One” means that due to his skill in making connections, he spoke the words beginning with “What, venerable sir?” For the Tathāgata, thinking, “There is one sitting in this assembly who is skilled in making connections; he will ask me a question,” concluded the teaching with just that much. “The near shore” means the shore that is on this side. Likewise, the far shore. “Sinking in the middle” means sinking and submerging in the middle. “Being cast up on high ground” means being cast up and having climbed onto high ground that has arisen in the midst of the water. “Seizing by humans” means seizing by related humans, or by humans. Likewise, seizing by non-humans. “Seizing by a whirlpool” means seizing by a water-whirlpool. “Rotten within” means that even if one is not rotten in the kidneys, heart, and so on, one is rotten within due to the rottenness of one's virtues.

“Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno”tiādi majjhimāgamavare uparipaṇṇāsake mahāpuṇṇamasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.88-90) tatrāyamattho – iti kirāti ettha kira-saddo aruciyaṃ, tena bhagavato yathādesitāya attasuññatāya attano aruciyabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Bhoti dhammālapanaṃ, ambho sabhāvadhammāti attho. Yadi rūpaṃ anattā…pe… viññāṇaṃ anattā. Evaṃ satīti [M 1.0457] sapāṭhasesayojanā. Anattakatānīti attanā na katāni, anattabhūtehi vā khandhehi katāni. Kamattānaṃ phusissantīti kīdisamattabhāvaṃ phusissanti. Asati attani khandhānañca khaṇikattā tāni kammāni kaṃ nāma attānaṃ attano phalena phusissanti, ko kammaphalaṃ [V 1.0400] paṭisaṃvedissatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa bhikkhuno cetoparivitakkaṃ attano cetasā ceto – pariyañāṇasampayuttena sabbaññutaññāṇasampayuttena vā aññāya jānitvāti sambandho.

“Then a certain bhikkhu,” and so forth, is the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta spoken in the Uparipaṇṇāsaka of the excellent Majjhima collection. Herein this is the meaning: In the phrase “iti kirā,” the particle “kira” is used in the sense of displeasure. By it, he shows his own displeasure with the emptiness of self as taught by the Blessed One. “Bho” is a term of address for the Dhamma; the meaning is “O, you of true nature!” “If form is non-self… pe… if consciousness is non-self. This being so…”—the connection with the remainder of the text should be made. “Done by non-self” means not done by a self, or done by the aggregates which are non-self. “What self will they affect?” means what kind of self-existence will they affect? When there is no self, and since the aggregates are momentary, what self will those actions affect with their result? Who will experience the fruit of the action? This is what is meant. The connection should be made thus: having known the mental reflection of that bhikkhu with His own mind—conjoined with the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others or with the knowledge of omniscience.

Avidvāti sutādivirahena ariyadhammassa akovidatāya apaṇḍito. Vidvāti hi paṇḍitādhivacanaṃ vidati jānātīti katvā. Avijjāgatoti avijjāya upagato, ariyadhamme avinītatāya appahīnāvijjoti attho. Taṇhādhipateyyena cetasāti “yadi ahaṃ nāma koci natthi, evaṃ sati mayā katassa kammassa phalaṃ ko paṭisaṃvedeti, sati pana tasmiṃ siyā kammaphalūpabhogo”ti taṇhādhipatito āgatena attavādupādānasahagatena cetasā. Atidhāvitabbanti atikkamitvā dhāvitabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – khaṇikattepi saṅkhārānaṃ yasmiṃ santāne kammaṃ kataṃ, tattheva phalūpapattito dhammapuñjamattasseva siddhe kammaphalasambandhe ekattanayaṃ micchā gahetvā ekena kārakavedakabhūtena bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā kammakammaphalānamasambandho siyāti attattaniyasuññatāpakāsanaṃ satthusāsanaṃ atikkamitabbaṃ maññeyyāti. Idāni anatidhāvitabbataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññathā”tiādimāha.

“Unlearned” means unwise, due to being unskilled in the noble Dhamma through the absence of learning and so forth. For “learned” is a term for the wise, because it means “one who knows.” “Gone to ignorance” means overcome by ignorance; the meaning is that due to not being trained in the noble Dhamma, ignorance has not been abandoned. “With a mind dominated by craving” means with a mind that has arisen from the dominance of craving, accompanied by clinging to a self-view, thinking: “If there is no one called ‘I,’ this being so, who experiences the result of the action done by me? But if there is such a one, there would be the enjoyment of the fruit of action.” “Should be overrun” means it should be transgressed. This is what is meant: even though conditioned formations are momentary, since the result arises in the very same continuity where the action was performed, and the connection between action and result is established for a mere heap of phenomena, one might wrongly grasp the principle of oneness and think that there must be a single agent and experiencer; otherwise, there would be no connection between action and its result. Thus, one might think that the teaching of the Teacher, which reveals the emptiness of self and what belongs to self, should be transgressed. Now, to clarify that it should not be overrun, he says, “What do you think?” and so forth.

Upari desanāti desanāsamuṭṭhānadhammadīpikāya heṭṭhimadesanāya upari pavattitā desanā. Desanāsamuṭṭhānadhammassa anurūpapaṭipakkhadhammappakāsanavasena duvidhesu yathānusandhīsu anurūpadhammappakāsanavasena yathānusandhidassanametaṃ “upari cha abhiññā āgatā”ti. Tadavasesaṃ pana sabbampi paṭipakkhadhammappakāsanavasena. Majjhimāgamavare mūlapaṇṇāsakeyeva cetāni suttāni. Kilesenāti “lobho cittassa upakkileso”tiādinā kilesavasena. Bhaṇḍanenāti vivādena. Akkhantiyāti kopena. Kakacūpamāti kharapantiupamā. Imasmimpīti pi-saddo apekkhāyaṃ “ayampi pārājiko”tiādīsu (vi. 1.72-73, 167, 171, 195, 197) viya, sampiṇḍane vā, tena yathā vatthasuttādīsu paṭipakkhadhammappakāsanavasena yathānusandhi[M 1.0458], evaṃ imasmimpi brahmajāleti apekkhanaṃ, sampiṇḍanaṃ vā karoti. Tathā hi niccasārādipaññāpakānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ vasena uṭṭhitāyaṃ desanā niccasārādisuññatāpakāsanena niṭṭhāpitāti. “Tenā”tiādinā yathāvuttasaṃvaṇṇanāya guṇaṃ dasseti.

“The higher teaching” means the teaching that is taught above the lower teaching, which illuminates the Dhamma that is the cause of the teaching. In the two kinds of sequential connections—by way of revealing suitable principles and opposing principles for the Dhamma that is the cause of the teaching—the statement, ‘Above, the six higher knowledges have come,’ is a display of the sequential connection by way of revealing suitable principles. All the rest, however, is by way of revealing opposing principles. These suttas are taught only in the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka of the excellent Majjhima Nikāya. “By defilements” means by way of defilements, as in “greed is a corruption of the mind,” and so forth. “By quarreling” means by dispute. “By intolerance” means by anger. “The simile of the saw” means the simile of a harsh row of teeth. In “Herein too,” the particle ‘pi’ is in the sense of expectation, as in “this too is a pārājika offense,” and so forth, or in the sense of conjunction. Therefore, it indicates expectation or conjunction, meaning: just as in the Vatthasutta and others, the sequential connection is by way of revealing opposing principles, so too in this Brahmajālasutta. Indeed, this teaching, which arose by way of the wrong views that proclaim permanence, substance, etc., is concluded by revealing the emptiness of permanence, substance, etc. By “Therefore,” etc., it shows the quality of the aforementioned explanation.

Paritassitavipphanditavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Craving and Agitation

105-117. Mariyādavibhāgadassanatthanti diṭṭhigatikānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiparāmāsassa tathāgatānaṃ jānanapassanena, sassatādimicchādassanassa ca sammādassanena saṅkarābhāva-vibhāgappakāsanatthaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhiparāmāsoyeva [V 1.0401] tesaṃ, na tu tathāgatānamiva yathābhūtaṃ jānanapassanaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhivipphandanamevetaṃ micchādassanavedayitaṃ, na tu sotāpannassa sammādassanavedayitamiva niccalanti ca hi imāya desanāya mariyādavibhāgaṃ dasseti. Tena vakkhati “yena diṭṭhiassādena…pe… taṃ vedayita”nti, “diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva…pe… dassetī”ti ca. “Tadapī”ti vuttattā yena somanassajātā paññapentīti attho labbhatīti dassetuṃ “yenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāmatthiyato hi avagatatthassevettha ta-saddena parāmasanaṃ. Diṭṭhiassādenāti diṭṭhiyā paccayabhūtena assādena. “Diṭṭhisukhenā”tiādi tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ tadapi vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ vedayitanti sambandho.

105-117. “For the purpose of showing the distinction of boundaries” means for the purpose of revealing the distinction and absence of confusion between the misapprehension through craving and views of those with wrong views and the knowing and seeing of the Tathāgatas, and between wrong seeing such as eternalism, etc., and right seeing. For them, there is only misapprehension through craving and views; it is not knowing and seeing as it really is, like that of the Tathāgatas. This feeling of wrong view is only the agitation of craving and view; it is not unmoving like the feeling of right seeing of a stream-enterer. And thus, by this teaching, it shows the distinction of boundaries. Therefore, it will be said: “by which delight in views… that feeling,” and “by that which is designated as view… it shows.” Because “that too” was said, in order to show that the meaning “by which, having become joyful, they proclaim” is obtained, “by which,” etc., was said. For, by the power of the context, here the word ‘ta’ (that) refers to that which is already understood. “By delight in views” means by the delight that has view as its condition. “By the pleasure of views,” etc., are synonyms of that very term. The connection is: that feeling of those venerable ascetics and brahmins who do not know, do not see, is the feeling of those who are subject to craving.

“Yathābhūtadhammānaṃ sabhāva”nti ca avisesena vuttaṃ. Na hi saṅkhatadhammasabhāvaṃ ajānanamattena micchā abhinivisanti. Sāmaññajotanā ca visese avatiṭṭhati. Tasmāyamettha visesayojanā kātabbā – “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti idaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ evaṃgahitaṃ evaṃparāmaṭṭhaṃ evaṃgatikaṃ hoti evaṃabhisamparāyanti yathābhūtamajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ atha vā yasmiṃ vedayite avītataṇhatāya evaṃdiṭṭhigataṃ upādīyati, taṃ vedayitaṃ samudayaatthaṅgamādito yathābhūtamajānantānaṃ apassantānanti. Evaṃ visesayojanāya hi yathā anāvaraṇañāṇasamantacakkhūhi tathāgatānaṃ yathābhūtamettha jānanaṃ, passanañca hoti, na evaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ, atha kho tesaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiparāmāsoyevāti imamatthaṃ imāya desanāya dassetīti pākaṭaṃ hoti. Evampi cāyaṃ desanā mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ jātā.

“The nature of things as they really are” is said without specification. For they do not wrongly adhere merely by not knowing the nature of conditioned things. And a general statement applies to specifics. Therefore, this specific application should be made here: For those who do not know or see as it really is that this ground for views, “the self and the world are eternal,” is thus grasped, thus misapprehended, has such a course, and has such a future destination; or, for those who, due to unabandoned craving with regard to some feeling, grasp such a wrong view, and do not know or see that feeling as it really is, from its arising, passing away, and so on. For by this specific application, it becomes clear that this teaching shows this meaning: just as there is for the Tathāgatas, with their unobstructed knowledge and all-seeing eye, a knowing and seeing here as it really is, it is not so for those with wrong views; rather, for them there is only misapprehension through craving and views. Thus too, this teaching has arisen for the purpose of showing the distinction of boundaries.

Vedayitanti [M 1.0459] “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti (dī. ni. 1.31) diṭṭhipaññāpanavasena pavattaṃ diṭṭhissādasukhapariyāyena vuttaṃ, tadapi anubhavanaṃ. Taṇhāgatānanti taṇhāya upagatānaṃ, pavattānaṃ vā tadeva vuttinayena vivarati “kevalaṃ…pe… vedayita”nti. Tañca kho panetanti ca yathāvuttaṃ vedayitameva paccāmasati, tenetaṃ dīpeti – “tadapi vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ vedayitamevā”ti vacchinditvā “tadapi vedayitaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevā”ti puna sambandho kātabboti. Tadapi tāva na sampāpuṇātīti heṭṭhimaparicchedena mariyādavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccala”nti vuttaṃ. Dassananti ca sammādassanasukhaṃ, maggaphalasukhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kuto cāyamattho labbhatīti eva-saddasāmatthiyato. “Paritassitavipphanditamevā”ti hi vuttena maggaphalasukhaṃ viya avipphanditaṃ hutvā ekarūpe avatiṭṭhati, atha kho taṃ vaṭṭāmisabhūtaṃ diṭṭhitaṇhāsallānuviddhatāya sauppīḷattā vipphanditamevāti [V 1.0402] attho āpanno hoti, tenevāha “paritassitenā”tiādi. Ayamettha aṭṭhakathāmuttako sasambandhanayo.

“Feeling” refers to that which occurs by way of proclaiming the view “the self and the world are eternal,” and is a term used as a synonym for the delight and pleasure in views; that too is an experience. “Of those who are subject to craving” means of those who are approached by or proceed from craving; that very term is explained in the same manner by “merely… feeling.” And the phrase “And this…” refers back to the aforementioned feeling. By this, it clarifies this meaning: having parsed it as “that feeling is merely the feeling of those who are subject to craving,” the connection should be made again as “that feeling is merely craving and agitation.” To show the distinction of boundaries by way of the lower limit—that it does not even attain that—it was said, “it is not unmoving like the seeing of a stream-enterer.” “Seeing” means the pleasure of right seeing, that is, the pleasure of path and fruition. And from where is this meaning obtained? From the force of the word ‘eva’ (merely). For when “merely craving and agitation” is said, this meaning is arrived at: it is not unagitated and established in a single state like the pleasure of path and fruition; rather, that pleasure in views, being the bait of the round of existence, is pierced by the dart of view and craving, and because it is accompanied by oppression, it is merely agitated. For that very reason, he said “by craving,” etc. This here is the method, independent of the commentary, with its connections.

Evaṃ visesakāraṇato dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni vibhajitvā idāni avisesakāraṇato tāni dassetuṃ “tatra bhikkhave”tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Sabbesañhi diṭṭhigatānaṃ vedanā, avijjā, taṇhā ca avisiṭṭhakāraṇaṃ. Tattha tadapīti “sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti ettha yadetaṃ “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti paññāpanahetubhūtaṃ sukhādibhedaṃ tividhampi vedayitaṃ, tadapi yathākkamaṃ dukkhasallāniccato, avisesena samudayatthaṅgamassādādīnavanissaraṇato vā yathābhūtamajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ hoti, tato eva ca sukhādipatthanāsambhavato, taṇhāya ca upagatattā taṇhāgatānaṃ taṇhāparitassitena diṭṭhivipphanditameva diṭṭhicalanameva. “Asati attani ko vedanaṃ anubhavatī”ti kāyavacīdvāresu diṭṭhiyā copanappattimattameva, na pana diṭṭhiyā paññapetabbo koci dhammo sassato atthīti adhippāyoti. Ekaccasassatādīsupi esa nayo.

Thus, having analyzed the sixty-two views by way of specific causes, now, in order to show them by way of a general cause, the discourse beginning, 'Therein, monks,' was commenced. For feeling, ignorance, and craving are the non-specific cause for all wrong views. Therein, as for 'that also': in the passage, 'they posit the self and the world as eternal,' whatever threefold feeling—distinguished as pleasant, etc.—is the cause for positing that 'the self and the world are eternal,' that feeling also occurs for those not knowing and not seeing it as it really is—in sequence, as a dart of suffering and impermanent, or, generally, from the perspective of its arising, ceasing, gratification, danger, and escape. And for that very reason, because of the possibility of desiring pleasure, etc., and because of being approached by craving, for those who have gone to craving, agitated by craving, it is merely the trembling of views, merely the stirring of views. In response to, 'If there is no self, who experiences feeling?', it is merely the attainment of agitation of the view at the doors of body and speech, but the intention is that there is no eternal phenomenon whatsoever to be posited by the view. This method also applies to the cases of partial-eternalism and so on.

Phassapaccayavāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Contact as a Condition

118. Paramparapaccayadassanatthanti yaṃ diṭṭhiyā mūlakāraṇaṃ, tassāpi kāraṇaṃ, puna tassapi kāraṇanti evaṃ paccayaparamparadassanatthaṃ. Yena hi taṇhāparitassitena [M 1.0460] etāni diṭṭhigatāni pavattanti, tassa vedayitaṃ paccayo, vedayitassāpi phasso paccayoti evaṃ paccayaparamparavibhāvinī ayaṃ desanā. Kimatthiyaṃ pana paccayaparamparadassananti ce? Atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ. Tena hi yathā diṭṭhisaṅkhāto paññāpanadhammo, tappaccayadhammā ca yathāsakaṃ paccayavaseneva uppajjanti, na paccayehi vinā, evaṃ paññapetabbadhammāpi rūpavedanādayo, na ettha koci sassato attā vā loko vāti evamatthantaraṃ viññāpitaṃ hoti. Taṇhādiṭṭhipariphanditaṃ tadapi vedayitaṃ diṭṭhikāraṇabhūtāya taṇhāya paccayabhūtaṃ phassapaccayā hotīti attho.

118. 'For the purpose of showing the sequence of conditions' means: for the purpose of showing the sequence of conditions thus: 'whatever is the root cause of the view, the cause of that, and again the cause of that.' For, by that agitation of craving these wrong views proceed. Feeling is the condition for that agitation, and for feeling, contact is the condition. Thus, this discourse is one that clarifies the sequence of conditions. But if it is asked, 'For what purpose is the showing of the sequence of conditions?' It is for the purpose of making known a different meaning. Indeed, just as the posited phenomenon, designated as 'view,' and the phenomena that are its conditions arise only by the power of their respective conditions and not without conditions, so too the phenomena to be posited, such as form, feeling, etc., do not arise without conditions. Herein, there is no eternal self or world whatsoever. Thus a different meaning is made known. The meaning is: that feeling, agitated by craving and views, which is the condition for craving, which is the cause of the view, is conditioned by contact.

131. Tassa paccayassāti tassa phassasaṅkhātassa paccayassa. Diṭṭhivedayite diṭṭhiyā paccayabhūte vedayite, phassapadhānehi attano paccayehi nipphādetabbe. Sādhetabbe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Balavabhāvadassanatthanti balavakāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tathā hi vināpi cakkhādivatthūhi, sampayuttadhammehi ca kehici vedanā uppajjati, na pana kadācipi phassena vinā, tasmā phasso [V 1.0403] vedanāya balavakāraṇaṃ. Na kevalaṃ vedanāya eva, atha kho sesasampayuttadhammānampi. Sannihitopi hi visayo sace cittuppādo phusanākāravirahito hoti, na tassa ārammaṇapaccayo bhavatīti phasso sabbesampi sampayuttadhammānaṃ visesapaccayo. Tathā hi bhagavatā dhammasaṅgaṇīpakaraṇe cittuppādaṃ vibhajantena “phasso hotī”ti phassasseva paṭhamamuddharaṇaṃ kataṃ, vedanāya pana sātisayamadhiṭṭhānapaccayo eva. “Paṭisaṃvedissantī”ti vuttattā “tadapī”ti etthādhikāroti āha “taṃ vedayita”nti. Gamyamānatthassa vā-saddassa payogaṃ pati kāmacārattā, lopattā, sesattāpi ca esa na payutto. Evamīdisesu. Hoti cettha –

131. 'Of that condition' means: of that condition designated as contact. 'In the feeling that is a view' means: in the feeling that is a condition for the view, which is to be produced by its own conditions with contact as primary. And this is a locative case in the sense of 'to be accomplished.' 'For the purpose of showing the state of being strong' means: for the purpose of showing the state of being a strong cause. Indeed, feeling arises even without the eye-base, etc., and some associated states, but it never arises without contact. Therefore, contact is the strong cause of feeling. It is a strong cause not only of feeling, but also of the remaining associated states. For even if an object is present, if a mind-moment is devoid of the mode of touching, it does not have an object-condition. Therefore, contact is the special condition for all associated states. Indeed, when analyzing a mind-moment in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the Blessed One first mentioned contact, saying, 'There is contact.' But for feeling, it is an exceedingly foundational condition. Because it was said, 'they will experience,' the commentator said, 'that feeling,' indicating that 'that also' is the governing word here. Or, this word is not used because of the freedom of choice regarding the usage of a word whose meaning is understood, because of elision, and also because of being a remainder. Thus it is in such cases. And here there is this:

“Gamyamānādhikārato, lopato sesato cāti;

Kāraṇehi catūhipi, na katthaci ravo yutto”ti.

Because the governing word is understood, because of elision, and because of being a remainder—thus by these four causes, a word is in some places not employed.

“Yathā hī”tiādinā phassassa balavakāraṇatādassanena tadatthaṃ samattheti. Tattha patatoti patantassa. Thūṇāti upatthambhakadārussetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

By the passage beginning, 'Just as,' he establishes that meaning by showing that contact is a strong cause. Therein, 'of the falling' means of that which is falling. 'Pillar' is a designation for a supporting timber.

Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānavaṭṭakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Cycle of Existence Based on Adherence to Views

144. Kiñcāpi [M 1.0461] imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāḷiyaṃ vedayitamanāgataṃ, heṭṭhā pana tīsupi vāresu adhikatattā, upari ca “phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentī”ti vakkhamānattā vedayitamevettha padhānanti āha “sabbadiṭṭhivedayitāni sampiṇḍetī”ti. “Yepi te”ti tattha tattha āgatassa ca pi-saddassa atthaṃ sandhāya “sampiṇḍetī”ti vuttaṃ. Ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sassatavādā…pe… sabbepi te chahi phassāyatanehi phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentīti hi vedayitakiriyāvasena taṃtaṃdiṭṭhigatikānaṃ sampiṇḍitattā vedayitasampiṇḍanameva jātaṃ. Sabbampi hi vākyaṃ kiriyāpadhānanti. Upari phasse pakkhipanatthāyāti “chahi phassāyatanehī”ti vutte upari phasse pakkhipanatthaṃ, pakkhipanañcettha vedayitassa phassapaccayatādassanameva. “Chahi phassāyatanehi phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentī”ti iminā hi chahi ajjhattikāyatanehi chaḷārammaṇapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ ekantato chaphassahetukamevāti dassitaṃ hoti, tena vuttaṃ “sabbe te”tiādi.

144. Although in this place in the Pāḷi, 'experiencing' has not come, yet because it is included in the three instances below, and because it will be stated later on, 'having touched again and again, they experience,' experiencing itself is primary here. Therefore, the commentator said, 'He summarizes all experiences of views.' It is said 'he summarizes' with reference to the meaning of the particle 'pi' which occurs in various places in the phrase 'Yepi te.' Indeed, 'Whatever ascetics and brahmins hold the eternalist view… and so on… all of them experience by touching again and again with the six bases of contact.' Therefore, because those of various views are summarized by means of the action of experiencing, it becomes a summarizing of experience itself. For indeed, any entire sentence has the action as primary. As for 'For the purpose of adding contact later on': when it is said 'by the six bases of contact,' it is for the purpose of adding 'contact' later on. And here, 'adding' is precisely the showing that experience has contact as its condition. Indeed, by this phrase, 'having touched again and again with the six bases of contact, they experience,' it is shown that the experiencing of the six sense-objects by means of the six internal sense-bases is exclusively caused by the six kinds of contact. Therefore, the passage beginning with 'sabbe te' was spoken.

Kambojoti evaṃnāmakaṃ raṭṭhaṃ. Tathā dakkhiṇāpatho. “Sañjātiṭṭhāne”ti iminā sañjāyanti etthāti adhikaraṇattho sañjāti-saddoti dasseti. Evaṃ samosaraṇa-saddo. Āyatana-saddopi tadubhayatthe. Āyataneti samosaraṇabhūte catumahāpathe. Nanti mahānigrodharukkhaṃ. Idañhi aṅguttarāgame [V 1.0404] pañcanipāte saddhānisaṃsasuttapadaṃ. Tattha ca seyyathāpi bhikkhave subhūmiyaṃ catumahāpathe mahānigrodho samantā pakkhīnaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.38) tanniddeso vutto. Sati satiāyataneti satisaṅkhāte kāraṇe vijjamāne, tatra tatreva sakkhitabbataṃ pāpuṇātīti attho. Āyatanti ettha phalāni tadāyattavuttitāya pavattanti, āyabhūtaṃ vā attano phalaṃ tanoti pavattetīti āyatanaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Sammantīti upasammanti assāsaṃ janenti. Āyatana-saddo aññesu viya na ettha atthantarāvabodhakoti āha “paṇṇattimatte”ti, tathā tathā paññattimatteti attho. Rukkhagacchasamūhe paṇṇattimatte hi araññavohāro, araññameva ca araññāyatananti. Atthattayepīti ettha pi-saddena ākaranivāsādhiṭṭhānatthe sampiṇḍeti. “Hiraññāyatanaṃ suvaṇṇāyatana”ntiādīsu [M 1.0462] hi ākare, “issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāse, “kammāyatanaṃ sippāyatana”ntiādīsu adhiṭṭhāne pavattati, nissayeti attho.

Kamboja is a country so named. Likewise, the Dakkhiṇāpatha. By 'sañjātiṭṭhāne' (at the place of birth), he shows that the word 'sañjāti' has a locative meaning, from 'they are born here.' The word 'samosaraṇa' (gathering place) is similar. The word 'āyatana' also occurs in both these meanings. 'Āyatane' means on a great road at a four-way junction which is a gathering place. 'Naṃ' means a great banyan tree. This is indeed a passage from the Saddhānisaṃsa Sutta in the Book of Fives of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. And there its explanation is given: 'Just as, monks, on good ground at a four-way junction, a great banyan tree becomes a refuge for birds from all around.' 'Sati satiāyatane' means: when the cause called 'sati' (mindfulness) is present, one attains the state of being able to witness in just those various spheres of higher knowledge, such as psychic powers; this is the meaning. Fruits proceed herein (āyatanti) because their existence is dependent on that, or it extends (tanoti) its own fruit which is a gain (āya); therefore, it is called 'āyatana' (cause). 'Sammanti' means they are pacified (upasammanti), they generate relief. The word 'āyatana' here does not, as in other cases, convey a different meaning such as 'place of birth'; therefore, he said 'paṇṇattimatte' (in a mere designation). The meaning is 'merely a designation in such and such a way.' Indeed, the term 'forest' (arañña) is used for what is merely a designation for a collection of trees and shrubs, and the forest itself is the 'araññāyatana'. In 'atthattayepi' (in the three meanings as well), by the particle 'pi', he summarizes the meanings of mine, dwelling, and foundation. Indeed, in 'hiraññāyatanaṃ suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ' (a mine of silver, a mine of gold) and so on, it occurs in the sense of a mine. In 'issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatanaṃ' (the abode of Issara, the abode of Vāsudeva) and so on, it occurs in the sense of a dwelling. In 'kammāyatanaṃ sippāyatanaṃ' (the basis of action, the basis of craft) and so on, it occurs in the sense of a foundation. The meaning is 'support'.

Āyatanti ettha ākaronti, nivasanti, adhiṭṭhahantīti yathākkamaṃ vacanattho. Cakkhādīsu ca phassādayo ākiṇṇā, tāni ca nesaṃ vāso, adhiṭṭhānañca nissayapaccayabhāvato. Tasmā tadetampi atthattayamidha yujjatiyeva. Kathaṃ yujjatīti āha “cakkhādīsu hī”tiādi. Phasso vedanā saññā cetanā cittanti ime phassapañcamakā dhammā upalakkhaṇavasena vuttā aññesampi taṃsampayuttadhammānaṃ āyatanabhāvato, padhānavasena vā. Tathā hi cittuppādaṃ vibhajantena bhagavatā teyeva “phasso hoti, vedanā, saññā, cetanā, cittaṃ hotī”ti paṭhamaṃ vibhattā. Sañjāyanti tannissayārammaṇabhāvena tattheva uppattito. Samosaranti tattha tattha vatthudvārārammaṇabhāvena samosaraṇato. Tāni ca nesaṃ kāraṇaṃ tesamabhāve abhāvato. Ayaṃ pana yathāvutto sañjātidesādiattho ruḷhivaseneva tattha tattha niruḷhatāya eva pavattattāti ācariyaānandattherena vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana padatthavivaraṇamukhena pavatto attho – āyatanato, āyānaṃ tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatanaṃ. Cakkhādīsu hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇā cittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādikiccena āyatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭenti vāyamanti, āyabhūte ca dhamme etāni tanonti vitthārenti, āyatañca saṃsāradukkhaṃ nayanti pavattentīti. Iti iminā nayenāti ettha ādiatthena iti saddena “sotaṃ paṭiccā”tiādipāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Herein, 'they abound (ākaronti), they dwell (nivasanti), they are established (adhiṭṭhahanti)'; this is the etymology in sequence. And in the eye and other bases, contact and so on are abundant. And these are their dwelling place, and also their foundation, because of being a support condition. Therefore, this threefold meaning is indeed suitable here. Since the question, 'How is it suitable?' may be asked, he stated the passage beginning with 'cakkhādīsu hi'. Contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—these five factors with contact as the fifth were spoken of by way of indication, because other associated states also have the nature of a basis; or they were spoken of by way of their prominence. For indeed, when analyzing a mind-moment, the Blessed One first distinguished these very states: 'There is contact, there is feeling, perception, volition, consciousness.' They are born (sañjāyanti) because of arising right there, through being the support and object. They gather (samosaranti) because of assembling there through being the physical basis, door, and object. And these bases are their cause, because in the absence of these, they are absent. But this aforesaid meaning of 'place of birth', etc., is simply by way of convention, because it proceeds in various places simply by being established in usage—thus it was said by the teacher, the Elder Ānanda. This, however, is the meaning that proceeds by way of explaining the word's meaning: it is 'āyatana' because of striving (āyatana), because of extending (tanana) the gains (āya), and because of leading to (nayana) the long-lasting (āyata) suffering of saṃsāra. For in the eye and other bases, mind and mental factors, which have their respective doors and objects, strive (āyatanti)—arise, endeavor, exert themselves—in their own respective functions of experiencing, etc. And these bases extend and expand those states which are gains. And they lead to and cause to proceed the long-lasting suffering of saṃsāra. In 'iti iminā nayena' (thus in this way), by the word 'iti' in the sense of 'and so on,' he includes the Pāḷi passage beginning with 'sotaṃ paṭicca'.

Tattha tiṇṇanti cakkhupasādarūpārammaṇacakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ visayindriyaviññāṇānaṃ. Tesaṃ samāgamanabhāvena gahetabbato “phasso saṅgatī”ti vutto. Tathā hi [V 1.0405] so “sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vuccati. Iminā nayena āropetvāti sambandho. Tena imamatthaṃ dasseti – yathā “cakkhuṃpaṭicca…pe… phasso”ti (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43, 45; 2.4.61; kathā. 465) etasmiṃ sutte vijjamānesupi saññādīsu sampayuttadhammesu vedanāya padhānakāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ phassasīsena desanā katā, evamidhāpi “phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādinā phassaṃ ādiṃ katvā [M 1.0463] aparantapaṭisandhānena paccayaparamparaṃ dassetuṃ “chahi phassāyatanehī”ti ca “phussa phussā”ti ca phassasīsena desanā katāti. Phassāyatanādīnīti ādi-saddena “phussa phussā”ti vacanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Herein, 'tiṇṇaṃ' refers to the three—eye-sensitivity, visible form as object, and eye-consciousness, etc.—that is, the three, namely, sense-object, sense-faculty, and consciousness. Because it is to be understood as the state of their coming together, 'contact is called a meeting.' Indeed, it is said to be 'manifested as a coming together.' The connection is to be made thus: 'by applying this method.' By this, he shows this meaning: just as in the sutta passage 'dependent on the eye... contact', where, despite the presence of perception and other associated mental states, the teaching is given with contact as the head to show that it is the principal cause of feeling, so too here, with 'dependent on contact, feeling arises' and so on, the teaching is given with contact as the starting point to show the sequence of conditions through a connection to the other end. The phrases 'with the six contact bases' and 'having contacted again and again' also present the teaching with contact as the head. In 'phassāyatanādīni' (contact bases and so on), the term 'ādi' (and so on) includes the expression 'having contacted again and again.'

“Kiñcāpī”tiādinā saddamattato codanālesaṃ dassetvā “tathāpī”tiādinā atthato taṃ pariharati. Na āyatanāni phusanti rūpānamanārammaṇabhāvato. Phasso arūpadhammo visamāno ekadesena ārammaṇaṃ analliyamānopi phusanākārena pavatto phusanto viya hotīti āha “phassova taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusatī”ti. Teneva so “phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti ca vuccati. “Chahi phassāyatanehi phussa phussā”ti aphusanakiccānipi nissitavohārena phusanakiccāni katvā dassanameva phasse upanikkhipanaṃ nāma yathā “mañcā ghosantī”ti. Upanikkhipitvāti hi phusanakiccāropanavasena phassasmiṃ pavesetvāti attho. Phassagatikāni katvā phassupacāraṃ āropetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upacāro nāma vohāramattaṃ, na tena atthasiddhi ataṃsabhāvato. Atthasijjhanako pana taṃsabhāvoyeva attho gahetabboti dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādimāha. Yathāhu –

With the passage beginning 'Kiñcāpi', having shown a hint of an objection merely by the word, he refutes it by way of meaning with the passage beginning 'tathāpi'. The sense bases do not make contact, because of the nature of material things to not take an object. It is said, 'It is contact itself that contacts that very object,' because contact, an immaterial state, though dissimilar and not adhering to the object with one part, occurs in the manner of contacting and is like one who contacts. For that very reason, it is called 'that which has the characteristic of contacting' and 'that which has the function of impinging.' In the phrase 'by the six bases of contact, having contacted again and again,' the showing of things that do not have the function of contacting as if they have the function of contacting by way of dependent designation is called 'attributing to contact,' as in 'the beds are shouting.' For 'upanikkhipitvā' (having attributed) means 'having introduced into contact by way of superimposing the function of contacting.' This means that having made them conform to the nature of contact, the metaphor of contact is superimposed. Metaphor is mere conventional usage; by it, the actual meaning is not established, because it is not their true nature. However, to show that the meaning to be taken is only that which has the true nature that accomplishes the meaning, he said the passage beginning with 'tasmā'. As it is said:

“Atthañhi nātho saraṇaṃ avoca,

Na byañjanaṃ lokahito mahesī”ti.

Indeed, the Protector, the Great Sage who acts for the welfare of the world, declared the meaning to be the refuge, not the letter.

Attano paccayabhūtānaṃ channaṃ phassānaṃ vasena cakkhusamphassajā yāva manosamphassajāti saṅkhepato chabbidhaṃ sandhāya “chaphassāyatanasambhavā vedanā”ti vuttaṃ. Vitthārato pana –

With reference to the sixfold feeling in brief—that is, from feeling born of eye-contact up to feeling born of mind-contact, by way of the six contacts that are its own conditions—it is said, 'feeling that arises from the six bases of contact.' But in detail:

“Phassato chabbidhāpetā, upavicārabhedato;

Tidhā nissitato dvīhi, tidhā kālena vaḍḍhitā”ti. –

This feeling, being sixfold by way of contact, threefold by way of the distinction of upavicāra, twofold by way of what is depended upon, and threefold by way of time, is thus augmented.

Aṭṭhasatapariyāye vuttanayena aṭṭhasatappabhedā. Mahāvihāravāsino cettha yathā viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ[V 1.0406], evaṃ phassaṃ, vedanañca paccayapaccayuppannampi sasantatipariyāpannaṃ dīpento vipākameva icchanti, aññe pana yathā tathā vā paccayabhāvo sati na sakkā vajjetunti sabbameva icchanti. Sāti yathāvuttappabhedā vedanā. Rūpataṇhādibhedāyāti “seṭṭhiputto [M 1.0464] brāhmaṇaputto”ti pitunāmavasena viya ārammaṇanāmavasena vuttāya rūpataṇhā yāva dhammataṇhāti saṅkhepato chabbidhāya. Vitthārato pana –

By the method stated in the 108 expositions, it becomes of 108 divisions. Herein, the residents of the Mahāvihāra, when explaining contact and feeling—just as with consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases—desire only the resultant that is included in one's own continuity, even though it is a condition and conditionally arisen. Other teachers, however, desire all of it, thinking that when the state of being a condition exists, it cannot be avoided. Sā (that) refers to feeling with the aforesaid divisions. The phrase rūpataṇhādibhedāya refers to the sixfold craving in brief—from craving for forms up to craving for dhammas—which is spoken of by way of the object's name, just as one is distinguished by the father's name in 'a merchant's son' or 'a brahmin's son.' But in detail:

“Rūpataṇhādikā kāma-taṇhādīhi tidhā puna;

Santānato dvidhā kāla-bhedena guṇitā siyu”nti. –

Cravings beginning with craving for forms are multiplied threefold by way of cravings beginning with sensual craving, again twofold by way of continuity, and threefold by way of the distinction of time.

Evaṃ vuttaaṭṭhasatappabhedāya. Upanissayakoṭiyāti upanissayasīsena. Kasmā panettha upanissayapaccayova uddhaṭo, nanu sukhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā ca taṇhāya ārammaṇamattaārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayapakatūpanissayavasena catudhā paccayo, dukkhā ca ārammaṇamattapakatūpanissayavasena dvidhāti? Saccametaṃ, upanissaye eva pana taṃ sabbampi antogadhanti evamuddhaṭo. Yuttaṃ tāva ārammaṇūpanissayassa upanissayasāmaññato upanissaye antogadhatā, kathaṃ pana ārammaṇamattaārammaṇādhipatīnaṃ tattha antogadhabhāvo siyāti? Tesampi ārammaṇasāmaññato ārammaṇūpanissayena saṅgahitattā ārammaṇūpanissayavasamodhānabhūteva upanissaye eva antogadhatā hoti. Etadatthameva hi sandhāya “upanissayenā”ti avatvā “upanissayakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Siddhe hi satyārambho niyamāya vā hoti atthantaraviññāpanāya vāti. Evamīdisesu.

For the craving with the 108 divisions thus stated. Upanissayakoṭiyā (by way of the decisive support category) means with decisive support as the principal. Why is only the decisive support condition singled out here? Is it not the case that pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are a condition for craving in four ways: as mere-object condition, object-dominance condition, object-decisive-support condition, and natural-decisive-support condition; and that painful feeling is a condition in two ways: as mere-object condition and natural-decisive-support condition? This is true. However, it is singled out thus because all of that is included in decisive support itself. It is fitting that the object-decisive-support condition is included in the decisive support condition by way of the generality of decisive support. But how could the mere-object and object-dominance conditions be included therein? Because they too are included by object-decisive-support by way of the generality of object, their inclusion in decisive support itself occurs only as they are comprised within the scope of object-decisive-support. It is with reference to this very meaning that, instead of saying upanissayena (by decisive support), the commentator said upanissayakoṭiyā (by way of the decisive support category). For when a point is established, a further statement is made either for the sake of determination or for making known another meaning. Thus it is in such cases.

Catubbidhassāti kāmupādānaṃ yāva attavādupādānanti catubbidhassa. Nanu ca taṇhāva kāmupādānaṃ, kathaṃ sāyeva tassa paccayo siyāti? Saccaṃ, purimataṇhāya pana upanissayapaccayena pacchimataṇhāya daḷhabhāvato purimāyeva taṇhā pacchimāya paccayo bhavati. Taṇhādaḷhattameva hi “kāmupādānaṃ upāyāso upakaṭṭhā”tiādīsu viya upa-saddassa daḷhatthe pavattanato. Apica dubbalā taṇhā taṇhāyeva, balavatī taṇhā kāmupādānaṃ. Atha vā apattavisayapatthanā taṇhā tamasi corānaṃ hatthapasāraṇaṃ viya, sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ kāmupādānaṃ corānaṃ hatthagatabhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ viya. Appicchatāpaṭipakkhā taṇhā. Santuṭṭhitāpaṭipakkhaṃ kāmupādānaṃ. Pariyesanadukkhamūlaṃ taṇhā, ārakkhadukkhamūlaṃ kāmupādānaṃ. Ayampi tesaṃ viseso kecivādavasena ācariyadhammapālattherena (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.144) dassito purimanayasseva visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.144) sakavādabhāvena vuttattā.

Of four kinds: from clinging to sensual pleasures up to clinging to the doctrine of self—thus, of four kinds. But is not craving itself clinging to sensual pleasures? How then can that very craving be its condition? True, but because a preceding craving, through the condition of decisive support, leads to the strengthening of a succeeding craving, the preceding craving itself becomes a condition for the succeeding one. For the very firmness of craving is 'clinging to sensual pleasures' (kāmupādāna), because the prefix 'upa-' functions in the sense of firmness, as in expressions like 'upāyāsa' (distress) and 'upakaṭṭha' (approached). Moreover, weak craving is just craving; strong craving is clinging to sensual pleasures. Alternatively, longing for an object not yet attained is craving, like thieves stretching out their hands in the darkness; grasping an object that has been attained is clinging to sensual pleasures, like thieves seizing goods that have come into their hands. Craving is the opposite of having few desires. Clinging to sensual pleasures is the opposite of contentment. Craving has the suffering of seeking as its root; clinging to sensual pleasures has the suffering of guarding as its root. This distinction between them has also been shown by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, in accordance with the 'some say' view, because the preceding method was stated in the Visuddhimagga as his own view.

Asahajātassa [V 1.0407][M 1.0465] upādānassa upanissayakoṭiyā, sahajātassa pana sahajātakoṭiyāti yathālābhamattho gahetabbo. Tattha asahajātā anantaraniruddhā anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanapaccayehi chadhā paccayo. Ārammaṇabhūtā pana ārammaṇamattaārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayehi tidhā, taṃ sabbampi vuttanayena upanissayeneva saṅgahetvā “upanissayakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca taṇhāya rūpādīni assādetvā kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjati, tasmā taṇhā kāmupādānassa upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo. Tathā rūpādibhede sammūḷho “natthi dinna”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.171; ma. ni. 1.445; 2.94-95, 225; 3.91, 116, 136; saṃ. ni. 3.210; a. ni. 10.176, 217; dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 907, 925, 971) micchādassanaṃ, saṃsārato muccitukāmo asuddhimagge suddhimaggaparāmasanaṃ, khandhesu attattaniyagāhabhūtaṃ sakkāyadassanañca gaṇhāti. Tasmā itaresampi tiṇṇaṃ taṇhā upanissayakoṭiyā paccayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahajātā pana sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetuvasena sattadhā sahajātānaṃ paccayo. Tampi sabbaṃ sahajātapaccayeneva saṅgahetvā “sahajātakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ.

For non-conascent clinging, craving is a condition by way of the decisive support category; for conascent clinging, however, by way of the conascent category. The meaning should be understood as is applicable. Therein, non-conascent craving that has just ceased is a condition in six ways by means of the proximity, contiguity, proximate decisive support, absence, disappearance, and repetition conditions. Craving that has become an object, however, is a condition in three ways by means of the mere object, object-dominance, and object-decisive support conditions.
