Having included all of that under the decisive support condition itself by the method stated, it is called 'the decisive support category'. And because, through craving, having savored forms and so on, one falls into a state of indulgence in sensual pleasures, craving is a condition for clinging to sensual pleasures by way of the decisive support category. Similarly, one who is deluded regarding the diversity of forms and so on grasps wrong view, such as 'There is nothing given'; one who desires to be liberated from saṃsāra grasps the impure path as the pure path; and one grasps personality view, which is the grasping of self and what belongs to a self in the aggregates. Therefore, it should be understood that craving is a condition for the other three clingings as well by way of the decisive support category. Conascent craving, however, is a condition for conascent clingings in seven ways by means of the conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root-condition. Having included all of that under the conascent condition itself, it is called 'the conascent category'.

Bhavassāti kammabhavassa ceva upapattibhavassa ca. Tattha cetanādisaṅkhātaṃ sabbaṃ bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo. Kāmabhavādinavavidho upapattibhavo. Tesu upapattibhavassa catubbidhampi upādānaṃ upapattibhavahetubhūtassa kammabhavassa kāraṇabhāvato, tassa ca sahāyabhāvūpagamanato pakatūpanissayavasena paccayo. Kammārammaṇakaraṇakāle pana kammasahajātamupādānaṃ upapattibhavassa ārammaṇavasena paccayo. Kammabhavassa pana sahajātassa sahajātamupādānaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena ceva hetumaggavasena ca anekadhā paccayo. Asahajātassa pana anantarassa asahajātamupādānaṃ anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanavasena, itarassa ca nānantarassa pakatūpanissayavasena, sammasanādikālesu ārammaṇādivasena ca paccayo. Tattha anantarādike upanissayapaccaye, sahajātādike ca sahajātapaccaye pakkhipitvā tathāti vuttaṃ, rūpūpahārattho vā hesa anukaḍḍhanattho vā. Tena hi upanissayakoṭiyā ceva sahajātakoṭiyā cāti atthaṃ dasseti.

For `bhava` (existence): this refers to both kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Therein, all kamma leading to existence, described as volition and so on, is kamma-existence. Rebirth-existence is of nine kinds, beginning with sense-sphere existence. Among these, the fourfold clinging is a condition for rebirth-existence and for the kamma-existence that is the cause of rebirth-existence—because it is a cause and because it acts as a helper—by way of natural decisive support condition. At the time of making kamma an object, however, the clinging conascent with kamma is a condition for rebirth-existence by way of object condition. For conascent kamma-existence, however, conascent clinging is a condition in many ways: by way of conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, and also by way of root and path conditions. Furthermore, for immediately preceding non-conascent kamma-existence, non-conascent clinging is a condition by way of the proximity, contiguity, proximate decisive support, absence, disappearance, and repetition conditions; and for other, non-proximate kamma-existence, it is a condition by way of natural decisive support; and at times of comprehension and so on, by way of object condition and so on. Therein, having included the proximity group under the decisive support condition, and the conascence group under the conascent condition, it is said 'thus' (`tathā`). Or this word `tathā` has the meaning of indicating the mode or the meaning of drawing in what was previously stated. For by that, it shows the meaning: 'it is a condition by way of the decisive support category and by way of the conascent category'.

Bhavo [M 1.0466] jātiyāti ettha bhavoti kammabhavo adhippeto. So hi jātiyā paccayo, na upapattibhavo. Jātiyeva hi upapattibhavoti, sā ca paṭhamābhinibbattakhandhā. Tena vuttaṃ “jātīti panettha savikārā pañcakkhandhā daṭṭhabbā”ti, tenāyaṃ codanā nivattitā “nanu jātipi [V 1.0408] bhavoyeva, kathaṃ so jātiyā paccayo”ti, kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “kammabhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti ce? Bāhirapaccayasamattepi kammavaseneva hīnapaṇītādivisesadassanato. Yathāha bhagavā “kammaṃ satte vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnapaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289) savikārāti nibbattivikārena savikārā, na aññehi, te ca atthato upapattibhavoyeva, so eva ca tassa kāraṇaṃ bhavitumayutto taṇhāya kāmupādānassa paccayabhāve viya purimapacchimādivisesānamasambhavato, tasmā kammabhavoyeva upapattibhavasaṅkhātāya jātiyā kammapaccayena ceva pakatūpanissayapaccayena ca paccayoti atthaṃ dassetuṃ “kammapaccayaṃ upanissayeneva saṅgahetvā upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana jātiyā sati jarāmaraṇaṃ, jarāmaraṇādinā phuṭṭhassa ca bālassa sokādayo sambhavanti, nāsati, tasmā jātijarāmaraṇādīnaṃ upanissayavasena paccayoti āha “jāti…pe… paccayo”ti vitthārato atthavinicchayassa akatattā, sahajātūpanissayasīseneva paccayavicāraṇāya ca, dassitattā, aṅgādividhānassa ca anāmaṭṭhattā “ayamettha saṅkhepo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mahāvisayattā paṭiccasamuppādavicāraṇāya niravasesā ayaṃ kuto laddhabbāti codanamapaneti “vitthārato”tiādinā. “Idha panassā”tiādinā pāḷiyampi paṭiccasamuppādakathā ekadeseneva kathitāti dasseti. Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ brahmajāle. Assāti paṭiccasamuppādassa. Payojanamattamevāti diṭṭhiyā kāraṇabhūtavedanāvasena ekadesamattaṃ payojanameva. “Mattamevā”ti hi avadhāraṇatthe pariyāyavacanaṃ “appaṃ vassasataṃ āyu, idānetarahi vijjatī”tiādīsu viya aññamaññatthāvabodhanavasena sapayojanattā, matta-saddo vā pamāṇe, payojanasaṅkhātaṃ pamāṇameva, na taduttarīti attho. “Matta-saddo avadhāraṇe eva-saddo sanniṭṭhāne”tipi vadanti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Hoti cettha –

Here, in 'existence is a condition for birth,' by 'existence' (`bhava`) is intended kamma-existence. For that is a condition for birth, not rebirth-existence. Indeed, birth itself is rebirth-existence, and it is the first-arisen aggregates. Therefore, it was said: 'Herein, birth is to be seen as the five aggregates with their alterations.' By this, the objection—'Is not birth itself existence? How then is it a condition for birth?'—is refuted. But how is this to be known: 'kamma-existence is a condition for birth'? Because even when external conditions are equal, the distinction of inferior, superior, and so on is seen solely through the power of kamma. As the Blessed One said: 'Kamma divides beings, that is to say, by way of inferiority and superiority' (MN 3.289). 'With their alterations' means with the alteration of arising, not with others. And these, in meaning, are rebirth-existence itself. And that very rebirth-existence is unsuitable to be the cause of that kamma-existence, because of the impossibility of distinctions such as prior and subsequent, as in the case of craving being a condition for sensual clinging. Therefore, to show the meaning that kamma-existence itself is a condition for birth—which is designated as rebirth-existence—by way of kamma-condition and also by way of natural decisive-support-condition, it was said, having included the kamma-condition under decisive-support-condition itself: 'it is a condition in the category of decisive support.' Furthermore, because when there is birth, aging-and-death occurs, and for the fool afflicted by aging-and-death and so on, sorrow and the like also arise, but do not arise when birth is absent; therefore, birth is a condition for aging-and-death and so on by way of decisive support. Thus, He said: 'Birth... is a condition...' Because a determination of the meaning has not been made in detail, and because the investigation of conditions has been shown only with conascent and decisive-support conditions as the main points, and because the arrangement of the factors and so on has not been touched upon, it was said: 'Herein, this is the summary,' etc. Because the investigation of dependent origination has a vast scope, the objection, 'From where is this exhaustive investigation to be obtained?' is dismissed with 'in detail,' etc. With 'But herein, of this...' etc., it is shown that even in the Pāḷi, the discourse on dependent origination is taught only in part. Therein, 'herein' means in this Brahmajāla Sutta. 'Of this' means of dependent origination. 'Only the purpose' means just a partial purpose, by way of feeling that is the cause of views. For `mattameva` is a synonymous expression in the sense of emphasis, as in 'A life of a hundred years is short; it exists now at this time,' etc., because it is purposeful by way of conveying a mutual meaning. Or, the word `matta` is in the sense of 'measure'; the meaning is that it is only the measure designated as 'purpose', nothing beyond that. Some also say: 'The word `matta` is in the sense of emphasis; the word `eva` is in the sense of determination.' Thus it should be understood in all cases. And here there is this:

“Mattamevāti [M 1.0467] ekatthaṃ, mattapadaṃ pamāṇake;

Mattāvadhāraṇe vā, sanniṭṭhānamhi cetara”nti.

'`Matta` and `eva` are of one meaning; the word `matta` is in the sense of 'measure'; or `matta` is for emphasis, and the other (`eva`) is for determination.'

Ekadesenevidha pāḷiyaṃ kathitattā paṭiccasamuppādassa tathā kathane saddhiṃ udāharaṇena kāraṇaṃ dassento “bhagavā hī”tiādimāha. Tena imamadhippāyaṃ dasseti “vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento bhagavā avijjā-taṇhā-diṭṭhīnamaññatarasīsena kathesi, tesu idha diṭṭhisīseneva kathento vedanāya diṭṭhiyā balavakāraṇattā vedanāmūlakaṃ ekadesameva paṭiccasamuppādaṃ kathesī”ti. Etāni ca suttāni aṅguttaranikāye dasanipāte (a. ni. 10.61 vākyakhandhe) tattha purimakoṭi na paññāyatīti asukassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa, cakkavattino vā kāle avijjā uppannā, na tato [V 1.0409] pubbeti evaṃ avijjāya purimo ādimariyādo appaṭihatassa mama sabbaññutaññāṇassāpi na paññāyati tatā mariyādassa avijjamānattāti attho. Evañcetanti iminā mariyādābhāvena ayaṃ avijjā kāmaṃ vuccati. Atha ca panāti evaṃ kālaniyamena mariyādābhāvena vuccamānāpi. Idappaccayāti imasmā pañcanīvaraṇasaṅkhātapaccayā avijjā sambhavatīti evaṃ dhammaniyāmena avijjāya koṭi paññāyatīti attho. “Ko cāhāro avijjāya, ‘pañca nīvaraṇā’ tissa vacanīya”nti (a. ni. 10.61) hi tattheva vuttaṃ, ṭīkāyaṃ pana “āsavapaccayā”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.144) āha, taṃ udāharaṇasuttena na sameti. Ayaṃ paccayo idappaccayo ma-kārassa da-kārādesavasena. Saddavidū pana “īdisassa payogassa dissanato ida-saddoyeva pakatī”ti vadanti, ayuttamevetaṃ vaṇṇavikārādivasena nānāpayogassa dissamānattā. Yathā hi vaṇṇavikārena “amū”ti vuttepi “asū”ti dissati, “imesū”ti vuttepi “esū”ti, evamidhāpi vaṇṇavikāro ca vākye viya samāsepi labbhateva yathā “jānipati tudampatī”ti. Kimettha vattabbaṃ, pabhinnapaṭisambhidena āyasmatā mahākaccāyanattherena vuttameva pamāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because dependent origination is taught only in part here in the Pāḷi, the commentator, wishing to show the reason for it being taught thus, together with an example, said, 'For the Blessed One...' etc. By that, he shows this intention: 'When teaching the discourse on the round of existence, the Blessed One taught with one of ignorance, craving, or views as the main point. Among those, herein, teaching with views itself as the main point, because feeling is a strong cause for views, the Blessed One taught only a partial aspect of dependent origination that is rooted in feeling.' And these suttas are in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, in the Book of Tens. Therein, 'the first point is not discerned' means: the first, initial limit of ignorance—such as 'Ignorance arose at the time of such-and-such a Sammāsambuddha or Cakkavatti monarch, and did not arise before that'—is not discerned even by my unobstructed omniscient knowledge, because such a limit does not exist. This is the meaning. And so, `Evañcetaṃ` means that by this absence of a limit, this ignorance is indeed spoken of as beginningless. `Atha ca pana` means that although it is spoken of thus as having no limit determined by time, `idappaccayā` ('conditioned by this') means that from this condition designated as the five hindrances, ignorance arises. Thus, by this fixed principle of the Dhamma, a point of ignorance is discerned. This is the meaning. For it was said right there: 'What is the nutriment for ignorance? "The five hindrances" should be said for it.' In the subcommentary, however, it says, 'with the taints as condition,' but that does not agree with the cited sutta. This condition, `ayaṃ paccayo`, becomes `idappaccayo` by way of substituting the letter `da` for the letter `ma`. Grammarians, however, say, 'Because such a usage is seen, the word `ida` itself is the original form.' That is indeed incorrect, because various usages are seen by way of letter alteration and so on. For just as by letter alteration, though `amū` is said, `asū` is seen, and though `imesu` is said, `esu` is seen, so too is it seen here. And letter alteration is found in compounds just as in a sentence, as for example in `jānipati tudampatī`. What is to be said here? It should be understood that what was said by the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana, who possessed the analytical knowledges, is itself the authority.

Bhavataṇhāyāti bhavasaññojanabhūtāya taṇhāya. Idappaccayāti imasmā avijjāpaccayā. “Ko cāhāro bhavataṇhāya, ‘avijjā’ tissa vacanīya”nti hi vuttaṃ. Bhavadiṭṭhiyāti sassatadiṭṭhiyā. Idappaccayāti idha pana [M 1.0468] vedanāpaccayātveva attho. Nanu diṭṭhiyo eva kathetabbā, kimatthiyaṃ pana paṭiccasamuppādakathananti anuyogenāha “tenā”tiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – anulomena paṭiccasamuppādakathā nāma vaṭṭakathā, taṃ kathaneneva bhagavā ete diṭṭhigatikā yāvidaṃ micchādassanaṃ na paṭinissajjanti, tāva iminā paccayaparamparena vaṭṭeyeva nimujjantīti dassesīti. Ito bhavādito. Ettha bhavādīsu. Esa nayo sesapadadvayepi. Iminā apariyantaṃ aparāparuppattiṃ dasseti. Vipannaṭṭhāti vividhena nāsitā.

'Craving for existence' means craving that is the fetter of existence. 'Conditioned by this' means conditioned by this ignorance. For it is said, "What is the nutriment for craving for existence? 'Ignorance' should be said." 'View of existence' means the eternalist view. 'Conditioned by this' here means conditioned by feeling. Should not only views be discussed? What then is the purpose of the discourse on dependent origination? In response to this inquiry, he said, 'Therefore,' and so on. This is what is meant: The discourse on dependent origination in forward order is a discourse on the cycle of existence. By that very teaching, the Blessed One showed that as long as those who hold such views do not relinquish this wrong view, they will continue to sink in the cycle of existence through this succession of conditions. 'From this' means from existence, etc. 'In this' means in existence, etc. This same method applies to the remaining two terms. Through this, he shows endless, successive arising. 'Ruined state' means destroyed in various ways.

Vivaṭṭakathādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Unfolding and so on

145. Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānanti diṭṭhigatikānaṃ micchāgāhadassanavasena adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, diṭṭhigatikavasena puggalādhiṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Puggalādhiṭṭhānadhammadesanā hesā. Yuttayogabhikkhuadhiṭṭhānanti yuttayogānaṃ bhikkhūnamadhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, bhikkhuvasena puggalādhiṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vivaṭṭanti vaṭṭato vigataṃ. “Yehī”tiādinā diṭṭhigatikānaṃ micchādassanassa kāraṇabhūtāya vedanāya paccayabhūtaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva phassāyatanamidha gahitaṃ desanākusalena bhagavatāti [V 1.0410] dasseti. Vedanākammaṭṭhāneti “vedanānaṃ samudaya”ntiādikaṃ imaṃ pāḷiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kiñcimattameva visesoti āha “yathā panā”tiādi. Nti “phassasamudayā, phassanirodhā”ti vuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ. “Āhārasamudayā”tiādīsu kabaḷīkāro āhāro veditabbo. So hi “kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa kāyassa āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 429) paṭṭhāne vacanato kammasamuṭṭhānānampi cakkhādīnaṃ upatthambhakapaccayo hotiyeva. “Nāmarūpasamudayā”tiādīsu vedanādikkhandhattayameva nāmaṃ. Nanu ca “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti vacanato sabbesu chasu phassāyatanesu “nāmarūpasamudayā nāmarūpanirodhā” icceva vattabbaṃ, atha kasmā cakkhāyatanādīsu “āhārasamudayā āhāranirodhā”ti vuttanti? Saccametaṃ avisesena, idha pana evampi cakkhādīsu sambhavatīti visesato dassetuṃ tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

145. 'The foundation for those holding views' means that which has become a foundation for those holding views by way of showing wrong grasping; it is said to be a foundation in persons by way of those holding views. For this is a Dhamma teaching founded on persons. 'The foundation for monks engaged in the practice' means that which has become a foundation for monks engaged in the practice; it is said to be a foundation in persons by way of the monks. 'Unfolding' means free from the cycle. By the passage beginning with 'By which...', he shows that the contact-base mentioned below—which is the condition for the feeling that is the cause of the wrong view of those holding views—is taken up here by the Blessed One, who is skilled in teaching. The phrase 'as a meditation subject on feeling' is stated in reference to this passage beginning 'the arising of feelings,' and so on. Because there is only a slight difference, he said the passage beginning 'Just as,' and so on. That is the cause stated as 'from the arising of contact, from the cessation of contact.' In 'from the arising of nutriment,' and so on, edible food should be understood. For, according to the Paṭṭhāna, 'Edible food is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment condition,' and so it is indeed a supporting condition even for the eye, etc., which are originated by kamma. In 'from the arising of name-and-form,' and so on, 'name' is the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Now, since it is said, 'Conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise,' should it not be said for all six contact bases, 'from the arising of name-and-form, from the cessation of name-and-form'? Why then is it said for the eye base, etc., 'from the arising of nutriment, from the cessation of nutriment'? This is true in a general sense, but it should be understood that it was stated thus in order to show specifically that here it can also occur in this way for the eye, etc.

Uttaritarajānaneneva diṭṭhigatassa jānanampi siddhanti katvā pāḷiyamanāgatepi “diṭṭhiñca jānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Sīlasamādhipaññāyo lokiyalokuttaramissakā, vimutti pana ida heṭṭhimā phalasamāpattiyo “yāva arahattā”ti [M 1.0469] aggaphalassa visuṃ vacanato. Paccakkhānumānena cettha pajānanā, tenevāha “bahussuto ganthadharo bhikkhu jānātī”tiādi, yathālābhaṃ vā yojetabbaṃ. Desanā panāti ettha pana-saddo aruciyattho, tenimaṃ dīpeti – yadipi anāgāmiādayo yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, tathāpi arahato ukkaṃsagativijānanavasena desanā arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpitāti. Suvaṇṇageho viya ratanamayakaṇṇikāya desanā arahattakaṇṇikāya niṭṭhāpitāti attho. Ettha ca “yato kho…pe… pajānātī”ti etena dhammassa niyyānikabhāvena saddhiṃ saṅghassa suppaṭipattiṃ dasseti, teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ko evaṃ jānātīti? Khīṇāsavo jānāti, yāva āraddhavipassako jānātī”ti paripuṇṇaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅgho dassito, tena yadetaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ “bhikkhusaṅghavasenāpi dīpetu”nti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8), taṃ yathārutavaseneva dīpitaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because the knowing of the view is accomplished only by a more superior knowing, the commentator said, 'and he knows the view,' even though this does not appear in the Pāli text. Morality, concentration, and wisdom are a mixture of mundane and supramundane. Here, however, liberation means the lower attainments of fruition, because the supreme fruit is mentioned separately with the words 'up to Arahantship.' And here the understanding is by direct perception and inference; for that very reason, the teacher said, 'A learned monk, a master of the texts, knows,' and so on, or it should be applied as is appropriate. In 'But the teaching...', the word 'pana' has the sense of disinclination. By this, it clarifies this meaning: although non-returners and others understand things as they truly are, nevertheless, by way of the Arahant's knowledge of the supreme state, the teaching is concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The meaning is: just as a golden house is completed with a jeweled pinnacle, so the teaching is completed with the pinnacle of Arahantship. And here, by this phrase 'When he... understands...', he shows the good practice of the Sangha together with the quality of the Dhamma as leading out. For that very reason, in the commentary, the community of monks is shown completely by asking, 'Who knows thus? The one whose cankers are destroyed knows, up to one who has begun insight practice.' Therefore, it should be understood that what was said below, 'to explain also by way of the community of monks,' is explained according to the text.

146. “Desanājālavimutto diṭṭigatiko nāma natthī”ti dassanaṃ desanāya kevalaparipuṇṇataṃ ñāpetunti veditabbaṃ. Anto jālassāti antojālaṃ, dabbapavesanavasena antojāle akatāpi tannissitavādappavesanavasena katāti antojālīkatā, anto jālassa tiṭṭhantīti vā antojālā, dabbavasena anantojālāpi tannissitavādavasena antojālā katāti antojālīkatā. Abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikāravācakato īpaccayo, antasarassa vā īkārādesoti saddavidū yathā “dhavalīkāro, kabaḷīkāro”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.181), imamatthaṃ [V 1.0411] dassetuṃ “imassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nissitā avasitāva hutvā ummujjamānā ummujjantīti attho. Māna-saddo cettha bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho appahīnena ummujjanabhāvena puna ummujjanabhāvassa lakkhitattā, tathā “osīdantā”tiādīsupi anta-saddo. Ummujjaneneva avuttassāpi nimujjanassa gahaṇanti dasseti “osīdantā”tiādinā. Tattha apāyūpapattivasena adho osīdanaṃ, sampattibhavavasena uddhamuggamanaṃ. Tathā parittabhūmimahaggatabhūmivasena, diṭṭhiyā olīnatātidhāvanavasena, pubbantānudiṭṭhiaparantānudiṭṭhivasena ca yathākkamaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Pariyāpannāti antogadhā. Tabbhāvo ca tadābaddhenāti vuttaṃ “etena ābaddhā”ti. “Na hetthā”tiādinā yathāvuttapāḷiyā āpannatthaṃ dasseti.

146. It should be understood that the demonstration, “There is no such person with a fixed view who is freed from the net of the teaching,” is to make known the complete perfection of the teaching. ‘Antojāla’ means “inside the net.” Even if not included inside the net by way of including the person or substance, they are made to be so by way of including the doctrine dependent on them; thus they are ‘antojālīkatā’ (made to be inside the net). Or, they stand inside the net, thus they are ‘antojālā.’ Even if not inside the net by way of substance, they are made to be inside the net by way of the doctrine dependent on them; thus they are ‘antojālīkatā.’ The suffix ‘ī’ occurs in the sense of ‘becoming what it was not before’ when joined with the roots ‘kar,’ ‘as,’ and ‘bhū,’ as it denotes transformation. Or, as grammarians say, it is a substitution of ‘ī’ for the final vowel, as in ‘dhavalīkāro’ (whitened) and ‘kabaḷīkāro’ (made into a lump). To show this meaning, “of this,” etc., was said. The meaning is: “Having become submerged and sunk, while emerging, they emerge.” And here, the suffix ‘-māna’ has the sense of a locative absolute construction, because the state of emerging again is marked by the unabandoned state of emerging. Likewise, in “sinking,” etc., is the suffix ‘-anta.’ By “emerging” alone, the inclusion of the unstated “sinking” is shown by “sinking,” etc. Therein, sinking down is by way of arising in a plane of misery; rising up is by way of a prosperous existence. Similarly, it should be applied respectively in terms of the limited and exalted planes; in terms of sluggishness and over-exertion with regard to views; and in terms of views about the past and views about the future. ‘Pariyāpannā’ means included within. And that state is due to being bound to that, hence it is said, “bound by this.” With “Not here,” etc., he shows the meaning that is included in the aforesaid Pāli.

Idāni [M 1.0470] upamāsaṃsandanamāha “kevaṭṭo viyā”tiādinā. Ke udake vaṭṭati paricaratīti kevaṭṭo, macchabandho. Kāmaṃ kevaṭṭantevāsīpi pāḷiyaṃ vutto, so pana tadanugatikovāti tathā vuttaṃ. Dasasahassilokadhātūti jātikkhettaṃ sandhāyāha tattheva paṭivedhasambhavato, aññesañca taggahaṇeneva gahitattā. Aññatthāpi hi diṭṭhigatikā ettha pariyāpannā antojālīkatāva. Oḷārikāti pākaṭabhāvena thūlā. Tassāti parittodakassa.

Now, he states the connection with the simile, beginning with “like a fisherman,” etc. ‘Kevaṭṭa’ is one who moves about or frequents the water (‘ke’); a fisherman. Although a fisherman’s apprentice is also mentioned in the Pāli, he is spoken of in that way because he is a follower of that one. “Ten-thousand world-system” is said in reference to the birth-field, because penetration of the truths is possible right there, and because the others are included by the very taking of that one. For elsewhere too, those with fixed views who are included herein are indeed made to be inside the net. ‘Oḷārikā’ means coarse because of being manifest. ‘Tassā’ means of the little water.

147. “Sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ saṅgahitattā”ti etena vādasaṅgahaṇena puggalasaṅgahoti dasseti. Attano…pe… dassentoti desanākusalatāya yathāvuttesu diṭṭhigatikānaṃ ummujjananimujjanaṭṭhānabhūtesu katthacipi bhavādīsu attano anavarodhabhāvaṃ dassento. Nayantīti satte icchitaṭṭhānamāvahanti, taṃ pana tathāākaḍḍhanavasenāti āha “gīvāyā”tiādi. “Nettisadisatāyā”ti iminā sadisavohāraṃ, upamātaddhitaṃ vā dasseti. “Sā hī”tiādi sadisatāvibhāvanā. Gīvāyāti ettha mahājanānanti sambandhīniddeso netīti etthāpi kammabhāvena sambajjhitabbo nī-saddassa dvikammikattā, ākhyātapayoge ca bahulaṃ sāmivacanassa kattukammatthajotakattā. Assāti anena bhagavatā, sā bhavanetti ucchinnāti sambandho. Puna appaṭisandhikabhāvāti sāmatthiyatthamāha. Jīvitapariyādāne vutteyeva hi puna appaṭisandhikabhāvo vutto nāma tasseva adassanassa padhānakāraṇattā. “Na dakkhantī”ti ettha anāgatavacanavasena padasiddhi “yatra hi nāma sāvako evarūpaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sakkhiṃ vā karissatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 228; saṃ. ni. 2.202) viyāti dasseti “na dakkhissantī”ti iminā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotīti āha “apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gamissantī”ti. Apaṇṇattikabhāvanti ca dharamānakapaṇṇattiyā eva apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ, atītapaṇṇattiyā pana tathāgatapaṇṇatti [V 1.0412] yāva sāsanantaradhānā, tato uddhampi aññabuddhuppādesu pavattati eva yathā adhunā vipassiādīnaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “vohāramattameva bhavissatī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.147) paññāya cettha paṇṇādesoti neruttikā.

147. By this, “because all views are included,” he shows that by the inclusion of doctrines, there is inclusion of persons. “Showing his own…” means: showing his own state of not descending into any of the states of existence, etc., which are the places of emerging and sinking for those with fixed views as mentioned, due to his skill in teaching. ‘Nayanti’ (they lead) means they bring beings to a desired place; but that is by way of dragging, so he said “by the neck,” etc. By “by its likeness to a guide-rope,” he shows a metaphorical expression or a comparative suffix. “For she…,” etc., is an explanation of the likeness. Here in 'gīvāya', 'of the great populace' is the indication of the genitive relation. In 'neti' also, it should be connected as the object, because the root 'nī' is ditransitive, and because in verbal constructions the genitive case often indicates the agent or the object. ‘Assa’ (of him) means: by this Blessed One, that guide-rope to existence is cut off—this is the connection. Again, “the state of no further linking” is stated for the implied meaning. For only when the ending of life is stated, is the state of no further linking said to be stated, because that very thing is the principal reason for not seeing him. Here in “na dakkhanti” (they will not see), the formation of the word is by way of the future tense, as in “For where indeed will a disciple know, or see, or personally witness such a thing?,” etc. He shows this with “na dakkhissanti” (they will not see). “What is meant?” he says: “They will go to a state of non-designation.” And “state of non-designation” means the non-designation of the presently existing designation. But as for past designation, the designation “Tathāgata” continues until the disappearance of the Dispensation, and even after that during the arising of other Buddhas, just as now with Vipassī, etc. Thus, he will say, “It will be mere convention.” And here, the etymologists say that ‘paṇṇa’ is a substitute for ‘paññā’.

Kāyoti attabhāvo, yo rūpārūpadhammasamūho. Evañhissa ambarukkhasadisatā, tadavayavānañca rūpakkhandhacakkhāyatanacakkhudhātādīnaṃ ambapakkasadisatā [M 1.0471] yujjati. Tanti kāyaṃ. Pañcapakkadvādasapakkaaṭṭhārasapakkaparimāṇāti pañcapakkaparimāṇā ekā, dvādasapakkaparimāṇā ekā, aṭṭhārasapakkaparimāṇā ekāti tividhā pakkambaphalapiṇḍī viya. Piṇḍo etassāti piṇḍī, thavako. Tadanvayānīti vaṇṭānugatāni, tenāha “taṃyeva vaṇṭaṃ anugatānī”ti.

‘Kāyo’ (body) means individual existence, which is the collection of material and immaterial phenomena. For thus, its likeness to a mango tree, and the likeness of its parts—the form aggregate, eye base, eye element, and so forth—to a ripe mango is fitting. ‘Taṃ’ means the body. “Measured by five ripe fruits, twelve ripe fruits, and eighteen ripe fruits” means: like a cluster of ripe mango fruits of three kinds: one measured by five ripe fruits, one by twelve ripe fruits, and one by eighteen ripe fruits. ‘Piṇḍī’ is so called because it has a mass (‘piṇḍo etassā’); it means a bunch or cluster. ‘Tadanvayāni’ means following the stalk. Therefore he said, “following that very stalk.”

Maṇḍūkakaṇṭakavisasamphassanti visavantassa bhekavisesassa kaṇṭakena, tadaññena ca visena samphassaṃ, maṇḍūkakaṇṭake vijjamānassa visassa samphassaṃ vā. Sakaṇṭako jalacārī satto idha maṇḍūko nāma, yo “pāsāṇakacchapo”ti voharanti, tassa naṅguṭṭhe aggakoṭiyaṃ ṭhito kaṇṭakotipi vadanti. Ekaṃ visamacchakaṇṭakantipi eke. Kirāti anussavanatthe nipāto. Ettha ca vaṇṭacchede vaṇṭūpanibandhānaṃ ambapakkānaṃ ambarukkhato vicchedo viya bhavanetticchede tadupanibandhānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ santānato vicchedoti ettāvatāva pāḷiyamāgataṃ opammaṃ, tadavasesaṃ pana atthato laddhamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“The touch of the poison of the frog’s thorn” means: contact with the thorn of a particular kind of poisonous frog, and with other poison; or, the contact of the poison existing in the frog’s thorn. Here, ‘maṇḍūko’ is a water-dwelling creature with a thorn, which they call a “stone-turtle.” They also say it is a thorn situated at the very tip of its tail. Some say it is the thorn of a poisonous fish. The particle ‘kira’ is in the sense of hearsay. And here, just as when the stalk is cut, there is a severance from the mango tree for the ripe mangoes bound to the stalk, so too, when the guide-rope to existence is cut, there is a severance from the continuity for the aggregates and so forth, bound to it. The simile that has come in the Pāḷi is only this much. The remainder, however, should be understood as obtained by meaning.

148. Buddhabalanti buddhānaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ. Kathitasuttassa nāmāti ettha nāma-saddo sambhāvane nipāto, tena “evampi nāma kathitasuttassā”ti vuttanayena suttassa guṇaṃ sambhāveti. Handāti vossaggatthe. Tena hi adhunāva gaṇhāpessāmi. Na papañcaṃ karissāmīti vossaggaṃ karoti.

148. “Buddhabalaṃ” means the knowledge-power of the Buddhas. In the phrase “Kathitasuttassa nāma,” the word “nāma” is a particle that occurs in the sense of esteem. By it, in the manner stated as “evampi nāma kathitasuttassa,” it praises the quality of the sutta. The word “handa” is used in the sense of relinquishment. By it, one expresses: “Indeed, I will now have the name of the sutta grasped. I will not cause a delay.” Thus, one makes a relinquishment.

Dhammapariyāyeti dhammadesanāsaṅkhātāya pāḷiyā. Idhatthoti diṭṭhadhammahitaṃ. Paratthoti samparāyahitaṃ, tadubhayattho vā. Bhāsitatthopi yujjati “dhammajāla”nti ettha tantidhammassa gahitattā. Ihāti idha sāsane. Nanti nipātamattaṃ “na naṃ suto samaṇo gotamo”tiādīsu viya. Nti dhammāti pāḷidhammā. Sabbena sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhanato atthasaṅkhātaṃ jālametthāti atthajālaṃ. Tathā dhammajālaṃ brahmajālaṃ diṭṭhijālanti etthāpi. Saṅgāmaṃ vijināti etenāti saṅgāmavijayo, saṅgāmo cettha pañcahi mārehi samāgamanaṃ abhiyujjhananti āha “devaputtamārampī”tiādi. Atthasampattiyā hi atthajālaṃ. Byañjanasampattiyā, sīlādianavajjadhammaniddesato [V 1.0413] ca dhammajālaṃ. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtānaṃ maggaphalanibbānānaṃ vibhattattā brahmajālaṃ. Diṭṭivivecanamukhena suññatāpakāsanena sammādiṭṭhiyā vibhattattā diṭṭhijālaṃ. Titthiyavādanimmaddanupāyattā anuttaro saṅgāmavijayoti evampettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

“In the Dhammapariyāya” means in the Pāḷi, which is called the Dhamma discourse. “Idhattho” means the benefit in the present life. “Parattho” means the benefit in the future life, or the benefit of both. The meaning of what was spoken is also suitable, because in the phrase “Dhammajāla,” the Pāḷi-Dhamma is taken. “Iha” means here, in this Dispensation. “Naṃ” is merely a particle, as in “na naṃ suto samaṇo gotamo,” and so forth. “Tantidhammā” means the Pāḷi-Dhammas. Because it gathers everything in every way, the net called 'meaning' exists in this Dhamma discourse; therefore, it is the Atthajāla (Net of Meaning). Likewise for Dhammajāla, Brahmajāla, and Diṭṭhijāla. “One conquers the battle by means of this,” thus it is Saṅgāmavijayo (Victory in Battle). And here, “battle” is the encounter and fight with the five Māras; thus, he said, “devaputtamārampi,” and so forth. Indeed, because of the accomplishment in meaning, it is Atthajāla. Because of the accomplishment in phrasing and the exposition of blameless dhammas such as virtue, it is Dhammajāla. Because it analyzes the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, which are supreme (brahmabhūta) in the sense of being excellent, it is Brahmajāla. Because it analyzes right view by means of resolving the tangle of views and by showing the state of being void of a self, it is Diṭṭhijāla. Because it is the means for crushing the doctrines of the sectarians, it is the Anuttaro Saṅgāmavijayo (Unsurpassed Victory in Battle). Thus, the application of the meaning here should be understood in this way.

Nidānāvasānatoti [M 1.0472] “atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti vacanasaṅkhātanidānapariyosānato. Mariyādāvadhivacanañhetaṃ. Apica nidānāvasānatoti nidānapariyosāne vuttattā nidānāvasānabhūtato “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādi (dī. ni. 1.5, 6) vacanato. Ābhividhiavadhivacanañhetaṃ. Idañca “avocā”ti kiriyāsambandhanena vuttaṃ. “Nidānena ādikalyāṇa”nti vacanato pana nidānampi nigamanaṃ viya suttapariyāpannameva. Alabbha…pe… gambhīranti sabbaññutaññāṇassa visesanaṃ.

“Nidānāvasānato” means from the end of the introduction, which is called the phrase “atha bhagavā anuppatto.” This is a term expressing a boundary-limit. Furthermore, another method: “Nidānāvasānato” means from the words beginning with “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ,” because it was spoken at the end of the introduction, being the end of the introduction. This is a term expressing an inclusive-limit. And this is stated in connection with the verb “avocā.” However, because of the statement “With the introduction, the beginning is auspicious,” the introduction itself, like the conclusion, is included within the sutta. The pair of words “Alabbhaneyyapaṭiṭṭhaṃ... paramagambhīraṃ” is a qualifier of the omniscient knowledge.

149. Yathā anattamanā attano anatthacaratāya paramanā verimanā nāma honti, yathāha dhammarājā dhammapade, udāne ca –

149. Just as, because of practicing for their own non-benefit, they become displeased, and just as other, unwholesome minds become what are called enemy minds, as the Dhammarājā said in the Dhammapada and the Udāna:

“Diso disaṃ yaṃ taṃ kayirā, verī vā pana verinaṃ;

Micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, pāpiyo naṃ tato kare”ti. (dha. pa. 42; udā. 33);

“Whatever harm a thief might do to a thief, or a foe to a foe, a wrongly directed mind can do one a worse harm than that.”

Na evamime anattamanā, ime pana attano atthacaratāya attamanā nāma hontīti āha “sakamanā”ti. Sakamanatā ca pītiyā gahitacittattāti dasseti “buddhagatāyā”tiādinā.

These monks are not displeased in that way; rather, because of practicing for their own welfare, they are what is called pleased. Therefore, the commentator said “sakamanā” (having their own minds). And he shows that the state of being ‘sakamanā’ is due to the mind being seized by joy, with the phrase beginning “buddhagatāya.”

Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāto aparo nayo – attamanāti samattamanā, imāya desanāya paripuṇṇamanasaṅkappāti attho. Desanāvilāso desanāya vijambhanaṃ, tañca desanākiccanipphādakaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇameva. Karavīkassa rutamiva mañjumadhurassaro yassāti karavīkarutamañjū, tena. Amatābhisekasadisenāti kāyacittadarathavūpasamakaṃ sabbasambhārābhisaṅkhataṃ udakaṃ dīghāyukatāsaṃvattanato amataṃ nāma. Tenābhisekasadisena. Brahmuno saro viya aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato saro yassātibrahmassaro, tena. Abhinandatīti taṇhāyati, tenāha “taṇhāyampi āgato”ti. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ abhinandantīti upagacchanti sevantīti atthoti āha “upagamanepī”ti.

This, however, is another method from the commentary: “Attamanā” means having a complete mind; the meaning is that their mental resolve is fulfilled by this discourse. The “splendor of the discourse” (desanāvilāso) is the flourishing of the discourse, and that is the omniscient knowledge itself, which accomplishes the task of teaching. “Karavīkarutamañjū” is one whose voice is lovely and sweet like the sound of the karavīka bird; by that voice. “Amatābhisekasadisena” means like an ambrosial consecration: water prepared with all ingredients that calms the distress of body and mind is called “ambrosia” (amata) because it leads to longevity. By that voice, which is like a consecration with ambrosia. “Brahmassaro” is one whose voice, endowed with the eight factors, is like the voice of Brahmā; by that voice. “Abhinandati” means “craves”; therefore, he said, “it also comes under craving.” Because verbal roots have many meanings, “abhinandanti” has the meaning of “they approach, they attend upon”; therefore, he said, “also in the sense of approaching.”

Tathā [V 1.0414] abhinandantīti sampaṭicchantīti atthamāha “sampaṭicchanepī”ti. Abhinanditvāti vuttoyevattho “anumoditvā”ti iminā pakāsitoti sandhāya “anumodanepī”ti vuttaṃ.

Likewise, he states the meaning of ‘abhinandanti’ as ‘sampaṭicchanti’ (they accept) with the word ‘sampaṭicchanepi’ (also in the sense of accepting). With reference to the fact that the meaning already stated as ‘abhinanditvā’ (having delighted) is clarified by ‘anumoditvā’ (having rejoiced), the word ‘anumodanepi’ (also in the sense of rejoicing) was stated.

Imamevatthaṃ [M 1.0473] gāthābandhavasena dassetuṃ “subhāsita”ntiādimāha. Tattha saddato subhāsitaṃ, atthato sulapitaṃ. Sīlappakāsanena vā subhāsitaṃ, suññatāpakāsanena sulapitaṃ. Diṭṭhivibhajanena vā subhāsitaṃ, tannibbedhakasabbaññutaññāṇavibhajanena sulapitaṃ. Evaṃ avaṇṇavaṇṇanisedhanādīhipi idha dassitappakārehi yojetabbaṃ. Tādinoti iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samapekkhanādīhi pañcahi kāraṇehi tādibhūtassa. Imassa padassa vitthāro “iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī, cattāvīti tādī, vantāvīti tādī”tiādinā (mahāni. 38) mahāniddese vutto, so upari aṭṭhakathāyampi āvibhavissati. Kiñcāpi “katamañca taṃ bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.7) tattha tattha pavattāya kathetukamyatāpucchāya vissajjanavasena vuttattā idaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ nāma bhavati. Byākaraṇameva hi veyyākaraṇaṃ, tathāpi pucchāvissajjanāvasena pavattaṃ suttaṃ sagāthakaṃ ce, geyyaṃ nāma bhavati. Niggāthakaṃ, ce aṅgantaraheturahitañca, veyyākaraṇaṃ nāma. Iti pucchāvissajjanāvasena pavattassāpi geyyasādhāraṇato, aṅgantaraheturahitassa ca niggāthakabhāvasseva anaññasādhāraṇato pucchāvissajjanabhāvamanapekkhitvā niggāthakabhāvameva veyyākaraṇahetutāya dassento “niggāthakattā hi idaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti āha.

To show this very meaning by way of a verse composition, the commentator said "subhāsita," etc. Therein, it is "subhāsitaṃ" (well-spoken) in terms of phrasing, and "sulapitaṃ" (well-uttered) in terms of meaning. Or, it is "subhāsitaṃ" through the exposition of virtue, and "sulapitaṃ" through the exposition of emptiness. Or, it is "subhāsitaṃ" through the analysis of views, and "sulapitaṃ" through the analysis of the omniscient knowledge that penetrates them. In this way, it should be connected with the methods shown here, such as the prohibition of dispraise and praise. The term 'Tādī' refers to one who has become "such" (`tādī`) for five reasons, beginning with looking equally upon the desirable and the undesirable. The detailed explanation of this term is given in the Mahāniddesa with phrases like "a tādī regarding the desirable and undesirable," "a tādī as one who has abandoned," "a tādī as one who has vomited," etc., and it will become clear later in the commentary as well. Although this sutta is called Veyyākaraṇa because it is spoken by way of answering a question of desire-to-explain that occurs in various places, beginning with "katamañca taṃ bhikkhave," for an exposition (`byākaraṇa`) is indeed a Veyyākaraṇa. Nevertheless, if a sutta that proceeds by way of question and answer has verses, it is called Geyya. If it is without verses and is without a cause for being another Aṅga, it is called Veyyākaraṇa. Thus, disregarding the fact that it is a question-and-answer discourse, because even for one that proceeds by way of question and answer there is a commonality with Geyya, and because for one without a cause for being another Aṅga, the very state of being without verses is not common to any other Aṅga, the commentator, showing that the very state of being without verses is the reason for it being a Veyyākaraṇa, said: "For because it is without verses, this is a Veyyākaraṇa."

Kasmāti codanaṃ sodheti “bhaññamāneti hi vutta”nti iminā. Ubhayasambandhapadañhetaṃ heṭṭhā, upari ca sambajjhanato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “bhaññamāne”ti vattamānakālavasena vuttattā na kevalaṃ suttapariyosāneyeva, atha kho dvāsaṭṭhiyā ṭhānesu akampitthāti veditabbāti. Yadevaṃ sakalepi imasmiṃ sutte bhaññamāne akampitthāti atthoyeva sambhavati, na pana tassa tassa diṭṭhigatassa pariyosāne pariyosāneti atthoti? Nāyamanuyogo katthacipi na pavisati sambhavamatteneva anuyuñjanato, ayaṃ pana attho na sambhavamatteneva vutto, atha kho desanākāle kampanākāreneva ācariyaparamparābhatena. Teneva hi ākārenāyamattho saṅgītimāruḷho, tathāruḷhanayeneva ca saṅgahakārena vuttoti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ, itarathā atakkāvacarassa imassatthassa takkapariyāhatakathanaṃ anupapannaṃ siyāti. Evamīdisesu. “Dhātukkhobhenā”tiādīsu attho mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanāya (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.171) gahetabbo.

He clarifies the objection 'Why?' with this phrase: 'for it is said, bhaññamāne (while being spoken).' This word is one that connects to what is before and after, due to its connection below and above. This is what is said: Because bhaññamāne is stated by way of the present tense, it should be understood that the ten-thousandfold world-system quaked not only at the conclusion of the sutta, but indeed at the sixty-two bases of views. [Objection:] 'If so, is it that only this meaning is possible: "it quaked while this entire sutta was being spoken," and not the meaning: "it quaked at the conclusion of each and every speculative view"?' This objection is not admissible anywhere, since it questions based on mere possibility. But this meaning was not stated based on mere possibility; rather, it was stated by the compiler through the very manner of the quaking at the time of the discourse, as brought down by the succession of teachers. Indeed, it was in that very manner that this meaning was raised to the level of the Communal Recitation (Saṅgīti), and it was stated by the compiler according to the method by which it was so raised. Thus, a conclusion should be reached in this matter. Otherwise, a statement based on conjecture about this meaning, which is beyond the sphere of conjecture, would be inappropriate. Thus it should be understood in such cases. In the passage beginning with 'by the disturbance of the elements,' the meaning should be taken from the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.

Aparesupīti [V 1.0415][M 1.0474] ettha pi-saddena pāramipavicayanaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Vuttañhi buddhavaṃse –

In the phrase aparesupi (in others too), with the particle pi, he includes the investigation of the perfections. For it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

“Ime dhamme sammasato, sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇe;

Dhammatejena vasudhā, dasasahassī pakampathā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 166);

“While he was comprehending these dhammas, with their intrinsic nature, function, and characteristic, the earth of the ten-thousandfold world-system quaked through the power of that Dhamma-comprehending wisdom.”

Tathā sāsanapatiṭṭhānantaradhānādayopi. Tattha sāsanapatiṭṭhāne tāva bhagavato veḷuvanapaṭiggahaṇe, mahāmahindattherassa mahāmeghavanapaṭiggahaṇe, mahāariṭṭhattherassa vinayapiṭakasajjhāyaneti evamādīsu sāsanassa mūlāni otiṇṇānīti pītivasaṃ gatā naccantā viya ayaṃ mahāpathavī kampittha. Sāsanantaradhāne pana “aho īdisassa saddhammassa antaradhāna”nti domanassappattā viya yathā taṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhāne. Vuttañhetamapadāne –

Likewise, he also includes the establishment of the Dispensation, its disappearance, and so on. In this regard, firstly, concerning the establishment of the Dispensation: at the Blessed One's acceptance of the Veḷuvana (Bamboo Grove), at the Elder Mahāmahinda's acceptance of the Mahāmeghavana (Great Cloud Forest), and at the Elder Mahāariṭṭha's recitation of the Vinaya Piṭaka—on these and other such occasions, thinking, 'The roots of the Dispensation have descended,' this great earth, having come under the sway of joy, quaked as if dancing. But at the disappearance of the Dispensation, thinking, 'Alas, the disappearance of such a good Dhamma!', this great earth quaked as if overcome with grief, just as it did at the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. For this is stated in the Apadāna:

“Tadāyaṃ pathavī sabbā, acalā sā calācalā;

Sāgaro ca sasokova, vinadī karuṇaṃ gira”nti. (apa. 2.54.131);

“Then this entire earth, though motionless, quaked and trembled; and the ocean, as if with sorrow, uttered a pitiful cry.”

Bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamaneti visākhāpuṇṇamadivase paṭhamaṃ bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamane. Paṃsukūlaggahaṇeti puṇṇaṃ nāma dāsiṃ pārupitvā āmakasusāne chaḍḍitassa sāṇamayapaṃsukūlassa tumbamatte pāṇe vidhunitvā mahāariyavaṃse ṭhatvā gahaṇe. Paṃsukūladhovaneti tasseva paṃsukūlassa dhovane. Kāḷakārāmasuttaṃ (a. ni. 4.24) aṅguttarāgame catukkanipāte. Gotamakasuttampi (a. ni. 3.176) tattheva tikanipāte. Vīriyabalenāti mahābhinikkhamane cakkavattisiripariccāgahetubhūtavīriyappabhāvena. Bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamane –

“At the approach to the Bodhi-maṇḍa” means: at the first approach to the Bodhi-maṇḍa on the full-moon day of Visākhā. “At the taking of the rag-robe” means: at the taking of a hempen rag-robe—which had been worn by a slave-girl named Puṇṇā and discarded in a charnel ground for the uncremated—after shaking off the worms, which were about the size of a tumba measure, while standing in the great lineage of the Noble Ones. “At the washing of the rag-robe” means: at the washing of that very rag-robe. The Kāḷakārāma Sutta is in the Catukkanipāta of the Aṅguttaranikāya. The Gotamaka Sutta is also there in the Tikanipāta. “By the power of energy” means: by the influence of the energy that was the cause for the renunciation of the glory of a wheel-turning monarch at the time of the Great Renunciation. At the approach to the Bodhi-maṇḍa—

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatu;

Upasussatu nissesaṃ, sarīre maṃsalohita”nti. (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22, 237; a. ni. 2.5; 8.13; mahāni. 196; avidūrenidānakathā);

“Indeed, let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up completely.”

Vuttacaturaṅgasamannāgatavīriyānubhāvenāti yathārahamattho veditabbo. Acchariyavegābhihatāti vimhayāvahakiriyānubhāvaghaṭṭitā. Paṃsukūladhovane bhagavato puññatejenāti vadanti. Paṃsukūlaggahaṇe yathā acchariyavegābhihatāti yuttaṃ viya dissati, taṃ pana kadāci pavattattā [M 1.0475] “akālakampanenā”ti [V 1.0416] vuttaṃ. Vessantarajātake (jā. 2.22.1655) pana pāramīpūraṇapuññatejena anekakkhattuṃ kampitattā akālakampanaṃ nāma bhavati. Sakkhinidassane kathetabbassa atthassānurūpato sakkhi viya bhavatīti vuttaṃ “sakkhibhāvenā”ti yathā taṃ māravijayakāle (jā. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā). Sādhukāradānenāti pakaraṇānurūpavasena vuttaṃ yathā taṃ dhammacakkappavattanasaṅgītikālādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 3.301).

The meaning of 'by the power of the energy endowed with the four factors thus stated' should be understood as is appropriate. 'Struck by a wondrous force' means struck by the power of an astonishing action. The teachers say: 'At the washing of the rag-robe, it was due to the Blessed One's power of merit.' Just as at the taking of the rag-robe, 'struck by a wondrous force' seems fitting. However, since that occurred on a certain occasion, it is called 'an untimely quaking.' But in the Vessantara Jātaka, because it quaked many times due to the power of merit from fulfilling the perfections, it is called an untimely quaking. In showing a witness: because it is suitable for the meaning to be stated, it is like a witness; therefore, it is said 'by way of being a witness,' as at the time of the victory over Māra. 'By giving cries of approval' is said according to the context, as at the time of the Turning of the Wheel of the Dhamma, the Communal Recitations, and so on.

“Na kevala”ntiādinā anekatthapathavīkampanadassanamukhena imassa suttassa mahānubhāvatāyeva dassitā. Tattha jotivaneti nandavane. Tañhi sāsanassa ñāṇālokasaṅkhātāya jotiyā pātubhūtaṭṭhānattā jotivananti vuccatīti vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Dhammanti anamataggasuttādidhammaṃ. Pācīnaambalaṭṭhikaṭṭhānanti pācīnadisābhāge taruṇambarukkhena lakkhitaṭṭhānaṃ.

By the passage beginning with 'Not only,' the great power of this sutta is shown by way of demonstrating the earth-quaking in its many meanings. Therein, 'in the Jotivana' means in the Nandavana. For it is said in the Vinayasaṃvaṇṇanā that it is called 'Jotivana' because it was the place where the light, known as the radiance of knowledge of the Dispensation, appeared. 'Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the Anamatagga Sutta and others. 'The place of the Pācīna-ambalaṭṭhikā' means the place in the eastern quarter marked by a young mango tree.

Evanti bhagavatā desitakālādīsu pathavīkampanamatidisati. Anekasoti anekadhā. Sayambhunā desitassa brahmajālassa yassa suttaseṭṭhassāti yojanā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Yonisoti micchādiṭṭhippahānasammādiṭṭhisamādānādinā ñāyena upāyena paṭipajjantūti attho. Ayaṃ tāvettha aṭṭhakathāya līnatthavibhāvanā.

With the word 'evaṃ,' he makes an extended application to the earth-quaking at the times of the Blessed One's discourses and so on. 'Anekaso' means in many ways. The syntactical connection is: '...of which excellent sutta, the Brahmajāla, taught by the Self-become One.' 'Idha' means in this Dispensation. 'Yonisoti' means: 'May they practice' by the right method, the means of abandoning wrong view, undertaking right view, and so on. This is the meaning. This, for a start, is the clarification of the hidden meaning of the commentary herein.

Pakaraṇanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Method of the Treatise

“Ito paraṃ ācariya-dhammapālena yā katā;

Samuṭṭhānādihārādi-vividhatthavibhāvanā.

Henceforth, that clear explanation of various meanings—of origin, method, and so on—which was made by the teacher Dhammapāla,

Na sā amhehupekkheyyā, ayañhi tabbisodhanā;

Tasmā tampi pavakkhāma, sotūnaṃ ñāṇavuḍḍhiyā.

That should not be disregarded by us, for this is its purification. Therefore, we shall also declare that, for the growth of wisdom in the listeners.

Ayañhi pakaraṇanayena pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanā – pakaraṇanayoti ca tambapaṇṇibhāsāya vaṇṇanānayo. “Nettipeṭakappakaraṇe dhammakathikānaṃ yojanānayotipi vadantī”ti abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā panāyaṃ desanāya samuṭṭhānapayojanabhājanesu, piṇḍatthesu ca paṭhamaṃ niddhāritesu sukarā, hoti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā –

Indeed, this is an explanation of the meaning of the Pāḷi by the method of the treatise. And 'the method of the treatise' means the method of explanation in the Sinhalese language. It is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: 'In the Netti and Peṭakopadesa treatises, it is also called the method of application for Dhamma-preachers.' Furthermore, because this explanation becomes easy to make and easy to understand when the origin, purpose, receptacle, and summarized meaning of the teaching are first determined, therefore—

Samuṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0417][M 1.0476] payojanaṃ, bhājanañcāpi piṇḍatthaṃ;

Niddhāretvāna paṇḍito, tato hārādayo saṃse.

A wise person, having first determined the origin, the purpose, the receptacle, and also the summarized meaning, should thereafter explain the methods and so on.

Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ nāma desanānidānaṃ, taṃ sādhāraṇamasādhāraṇanti duvidhaṃ, tathā sādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirato. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ ajjhattikasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhagavato mahākaruṇā. Tāya hi samussāhitassa lokanāthassa veneyyānaṃ dhammadesanāya cittaṃ udapādi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”tiādi. Ettha ca tividhāvatthāyapi mahākaruṇāya saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yāvadeva saddhammadesanāhatthadānehi saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇatthaṃ taduppattito. Yathā ca mahākaruṇā, evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇadasabalañāṇādayopi desanāya sādhāraṇamajjhattikasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Sabbañhi ñeyyadhammaṃ tesaṃ desetabbākāraṃ, sattānaṃ āsayānusayādikañca yāthāvato jānanto bhagavā ṭhānāṭṭhānādīsu kosallena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vicitranayadesanaṃ pavattesi. Bāhiraṃ pana sādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ dasasahassimahābrahmaparivārassa sahampatibrahmuno ajjhesanaṃ. Tadajjhesanañhi pati dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇājanitaṃ appossukkataṃ paṭippassambhetvā dhammassāmī dhammadesanāya ussāhajāto ahosi.

Therein, that called 'origin' is the cause of the teaching. It is twofold: common and uncommon. Likewise, the common is also twofold: internal and external. Therein, the common internal origin is the great compassion of the Blessed One. For, urged on by that, the mind of the Lord of the World arose to teach the Dhamma to those who are to be trained. With reference to that, it is said: 'Relying on compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,' and so on. And herein, the inclusion of great compassion in its threefold state should be understood, precisely because it arises for the purpose of ferrying beings across the great flood of saṃsāra by giving the hand of the true Dhamma teaching. And just as great compassion, so too omniscience, the ten powers of knowledge, and so on, are also called the common internal origin of the teaching. For the Blessed One, knowing perfectly all knowable phenomena, the manner in which they should be taught, and the dispositions, latent tendencies, and so on of beings, with skill in what is and is not a basis, set in motion a teaching with various methods in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained. The external common origin, however, is the request of the Brahmā Sahampati, accompanied by his retinue of ten thousand great Brahmās. For, on account of that request, having pacified the lack of eagerness generated by reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, the Master of the Dhamma became zealous to teach the Dhamma.

Asādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirato duvidhameva. Tattha ajjhattikaṃ yāya mahākaruṇāya, yena ca desanāñāṇena idaṃ suttaṃ pavattitaṃ, tadubhayameva. Sāmaññāvatthāya hi sādhāraṇampi samānaṃ mahākaruṇādivisesāvatthāya asādhāraṇaṃ bhavati, bāhiraṃ pana asādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇabhaṇananti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Apica nindāpasaṃsāsu sattānaṃ veneyyāghātānandādibhāvamanāpatti. Tattha ca anādīnavadassanaṃ bāhiramasādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānameva, tathā nindāpasaṃsāsu paṭipajjanakkamassa, pasaṃsāvisayassa ca khuddakādivasena anekavidhassa sīlassa, sabbaññutaññāṇassa ca sassatādidiṭṭhiṭṭhāne, taduttari ca appaṭihatacāratāya, tathāgatassa ca katthacipi bhavādīsu apariyāpannatāya sattānamanavabodhopi bāhiramasādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ.

The uncommon is also twofold: internal and external. Therein, the internal is that very pair: the great compassion by which, and the knowledge of teaching by which, this sutta was set forth. For although common in a general state, it becomes uncommon in a special state of great compassion, and so on. The external uncommon origin, however, is the speaking of praise and blame, as stated in the commentary. Furthermore, it is the non-falling of trainable beings into states of resentment, joy, and so on, with regard to blame and praise. And therein, the seeing of no fault is solely the external uncommon origin. Likewise, the non-comprehension by beings of the following is also the external uncommon origin: the order of practice with regard to blame and praise; the multifaceted virtue—beginning with the minor—which is the object of praise; omniscience; the Tathāgata's unimpeded movement in the domain of eternalist views and so on, and beyond; and his non-inclusion in any state of existence whatsoever.

Payojanampi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ anupādāparinibbānaṃ vimuttirasattā sabbāyapi bhagavato desanāya, tenevāha [M 1.0477] “etadatthā kathā, etadatthā mantanā”tiādi (pari. 366) asādhāraṇaṃ pana bāhirasamuṭṭhānato vipariyāyena veditabbaṃ. Nindāpasaṃsāsu hi sattānanveneyyāghātānandādibhāvappattiādikaṃ imissā desanāya phalabhūtaṃ kāraṇabhāvena [V 1.0418] imaṃ desanaṃ payojeti. Phalañhi taduppādakasattiyā kāraṇaṃ payojeti nāma phale satiyeva tāya sattiyā kāraṇabhāvappattito. Atha vā yathāvuttaṃ phalaṃ imāya desanāya bhagavantaṃ payojetīti ācariyasāriputtattherena vuttaṃ. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ phalaṃ, taṃ ākaṅkhitabbattā desanāya desakaṃ payojeti nāma. Apica kuhanalapanādinānāvidhamicchājīvaviddhaṃsanaṃ, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhijālaviniveṭhanaṃ, diṭṭhisīsena paccayākāravibhāvanaṃ, chaphassāyatanavasena catusaccakammaṭṭhānaniddeso, sabbadiṭṭhigatānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ, attano anupādāparinibbānadīpanañca payojanameva.

The purpose is also twofold: common and uncommon. Therein, the common purpose is final Nibbāna without clinging, because all of the Blessed One’s teachings have the taste of liberation. For that reason he said: 'For this purpose is the talk, for this purpose is the consultation,' and so on. The uncommon purpose, however, should be understood in reverse from the external origin. For the attainment by beings of states such as the dispelling of resentment and the arising of joy with regard to blame and praise—this being the fruit of this teaching—motivates this teaching by way of being its cause. For the fruit is said to motivate the cause by the power that produces it, because only when the fruit exists does that power attain the state of being a cause. Alternatively, as stated by the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta, the aforesaid fruit motivates the Blessed One with regard to this teaching. For whatever fruit is to be accomplished by the teaching, that fruit, because it is to be desired, is said to motivate the teacher of the teaching. Furthermore, the following are also the purpose: the destruction of various wrong livelihoods such as deception and flattery; the disentangling of the net of sixty-two views; the explanation of the causal structure headed by views; the instruction on the meditation subject of the Four Truths by way of the six sense bases; the complete comprehension of all speculative views without remainder; and the demonstration of one's own final Nibbāna without clinging.

Bhājanaṃ pana desanādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Ye hi vaṇṇāvaṇṇanimittaanurodhavirodhavantacittā kuhanādivividhamicchājīvaniratā sassatādidiṭṭhipaṅkanimuggā sīlakkhandhādīsu aparipūrakārino abuddhaguṇavisesañāṇā veneyyā, te imissā desanāya bhājanaṃ.

The receptacle, however, is the foundation of the teaching. For those trainable beings whose minds possess conformity and opposition regarding the signs of praise and blame, who delight in various wrong livelihoods such as deception, who are sunk in the mire of eternalist and other views, who do not fulfill the aggregates of virtue and so on, and who do not know the special qualities of the Buddha—they are the receptacle for this teaching.

Piṇḍattho pana idha labbhamānapadehi, samudāyena ca suttapadena yathāsambhavaṃ saṅgahito attho. Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇīyatāvacanena hi dassitaṃ paṭiññānurūpaṃ samaṇasaññāya niyojanaṃ, tathā khantisoraccānuṭṭhānaṃ, brahmavihārabhāvanānuyogo, saddhāpaññāsamāyogo, satisampajaññādhiṭṭhānaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalasiddhi, pariyuṭṭhānānusayappahānaṃ, ubhayahitapaṭipatti, lokadhammehi anupalepo ca –

The summarized meaning, however, is the meaning gathered here from the available words and from the sutta passage as a whole, as is appropriate. For by the words stating that resentment and so on should not be done, the following are shown: the application to the perception of a recluse in accordance with one's profession; likewise, persistence in patience and gentleness; devotion to the cultivation of the divine abidings; the proper balancing of faith and wisdom; the establishment of mindfulness and clear comprehension; the accomplishment of the power of the cultivation of reflective insight; the abandoning of active and latent defilements; the practice for the welfare of both oneself and others; and being unsullied by worldly conditions.

Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena dassitā sīlavisuddhi, tāya ca hirottappasampatti, mettākaruṇāsamaṅgitā, vītikkamappahānaṃ, tadaṅgappahānaṃ, duccaritasaṃkilesappahānaṃ, viratittayasiddhi, piyamanāpagarubhāvanīyatānipphatti, lābhasakkārasilokasamudāgamo, samathavipassanānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvo, akusalamūlatanukaraṇaṃ, kusalamūlaropanaṃ, ubhayānatthadūrīkaraṇaṃ, parisāsu visāradatā, appamādavihāro, parehi duppadhaṃsiyatā, avippaṭisārādisamaṅgitā ca –

By the words teaching abstinence from killing living beings and so on, is shown the purity of virtue; and by that, the attainment of shame and moral dread, being endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, the abandoning of transgression, the abandoning by substitution of opposites, the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct, the accomplishment of the three abstinences, the accomplishment of being dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed, the good arising of gain, honor, and fame, being a foundation for serenity and insight, the reduction of unwholesome roots, the planting of wholesome roots, the removal to a distance of both kinds of harm, confidence in assemblies, dwelling in heedfulness, being difficult to be overcome by others, and being endowed with non-remorse and so on.

“Gambhīrā”tiādivacanehi [M 1.0478] dassitaṃ gambhīradhammavibhāvanaṃ, alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhatā, kappānamasaṅkhyeyyenāpi dullabhapātubhāvatā, sukhumenapi ñāṇena paccakkhato paṭivijjhitumasakkuṇeyyatā, dhammanvayasaṅkhātena anumānañāṇenāpi duradhigamanīyatā, passaddhasabbadarathatā, santadhammavibhāvanaṃ, sobhanapariyosānatā, atittikarabhāvo, padhānabhāvappatti, yathābhūtañāṇagocaratā, sukhumasabhāvatā, mahāpaññāvibhāvanā ca. Diṭṭhidīpakapadehi dassitā samāsato sassataucchedadiṭṭhiyo līnatātidhāvanavibhāvanaṃ, ubhayavinibandhaniddeso[V 1.0419], micchābhinivesakittanaṃ, kummaggapaṭipattippakāsanaṃ, vipariyesaggāhañāpanaṃ, parāmāsapariggaho, pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhipatiṭṭhāpanā, bhavavibhavadiṭṭhivibhāgā, taṇhāvijjāpavatti, antavānantavādiṭṭhiniddeso, antadvayāvatāraṇaṃ, āsavoghayogakilesaganthasaṃyojanupādānavisesavibhajanañca –

By the words 'profound' and so on is shown: the elucidation of the profound Dhamma, its unobtainable standing, its rare manifestation even over countless eons, its inability to be directly penetrated even with subtle wisdom, its difficulty of attainment even by inferential knowledge known as 'in accordance with the Dhamma', its state of having all torment calmed, the elucidation of the peaceful Dhamma, its beautiful culmination, its insatiable quality, its attainment of the primary state, its state of being the domain for the knowledge of things as they truly are, its subtle nature, and the elucidation of great wisdom. By the terms that illuminate views are shown, in brief, the eternalist and annihilationist views; the elucidation of sluggishness and excessive haste, the explanation of dual bondage, the declaration of wrong adherence, the exposition of the practice of the wrong path, the making known of inverted grasping, the complete grasping of misapprehension, the establishment of views that follow after the past and the future, the analysis of the views of existence and non-existence, the occurrence of craving and ignorance, the explanation of the views of the finite and the infinite, the removal of the two extremes, and the analysis of the distinctions between cankers, floods, yokes, defilements, bonds, fetters, and clinging.

Tathā “vedanānaṃ samudaya”ntiādivacanehi dassitā catunnamariyasaccānaṃ anubodhapaṭibodhasiddhi, vikkhambhanasamucchedappahānaṃ taṇhāvijjāvigamo, saddhammaṭṭhitinimittapariggaho, āgamādhigamasampatti, ubhayahitapaṭipatti, tividhapaññāpariggaho, satisampajaññānuṭṭhānaṃ, saddhāpaññāsamāyogo, vīriyasamatānuyojanaṃ, samathavipassanānipphatti ca –

Likewise, by the words 'the arising of feelings' and so on, is shown: the accomplishment of the concordant and penetrative knowing of the Four Noble Truths, the abandoning by suppression and by eradication, the departure of craving and ignorance, the grasping of the cause for the establishment of the true Dhamma, the accomplishment of scripture and realization, the practice for the welfare of both, the grasping of the threefold wisdom, the proper establishment in mindfulness and clear comprehension, the balanced combination of faith and wisdom, the balanced application of energy and concentration, and the accomplishment of serenity and insight.

“Ajānataṃ apassata”nti padehi dassitā avijjāsiddhi, tathā “taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti padehi taṇhāsiddhi, tadubhayena ca nīvaraṇasaññojanadvayasiddhi, anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭānupacchedo, pubbantāharaṇāparantānusandhānāni, atītapaccuppannakālavasena hetuvibhāgo, avijjātaṇhānaṃ aññamaññānativattanaṃ, aññamaññūpakāritā, paññāvimutticetovimuttīnaṃ paṭipakkhaniddeso ca –

By the terms 'of those not knowing, not seeing' is shown the accomplishment of ignorance; likewise, by the terms 'the trembling and floundering of those who have gone to craving' is shown the accomplishment of craving; and by both of these, the accomplishment of the two, hindrances and fetters; the non-interruption of the cycle of saṃsāra with its unknown beginning; the bringing of the past portion and the connecting of the future portion; the analysis of cause by way of past and present time; the mutual non-transgression of ignorance and craving; their state of being mutually supportive; and the explanation of the opposite of liberation by wisdom and liberation of mind.

“Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti padena dassitā sassatādipaññāpanassa paccayādhīnavuttitā, tena ca dhammānaṃ niccatāpaṭisedho, aniccatāpatiṭṭhāpanaṃ, paramatthato kārakādipaṭikkhepo, evaṃdhammatāniddeso, suññatāpakāsanaṃ samatthanirīha paccayalakkhaṇavibhāvanañca –

By the term 'that too is conditioned by contact' is shown the state of being dependent on conditions for the designation of eternalism and so on; and by that, the denial of the permanence of phenomena, the establishment of impermanence, the rejection of an agent and so on in the ultimate sense, the explanation of the principle of 'thusness', the declaration of emptiness, and the elucidation of the characteristic of conditions as being capable and devoid of striving.

“Ucchinnabhavanettiko”tiādinā [M 1.0479] dassitā bhagavato pahānasampatti, vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo, sikkhattayanipphatti, nibbānadhātudvayavibhāgo, caturadhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ, bhavayoniādīsu apariyāpannatā ca –

By the text 'one for whom the guide to existence is cut off' and so on, is shown the Blessed One's accomplishment in abandonment, his mastery of knowledge and liberation, the accomplishment of the three trainings, the analysis of the two Nibbāna-elements, the complete fulfillment of the four resolutions, and his state of not being included in the wombs of existence and so on—

Sakalena pana suttapadena dassito iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu bhagavato tādibhāvo, tattha ca paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, kusaladhammānaṃ ādibhūtadhammadvayaniddeso sikkhattayūpadeso, attantapādipuggalacatukkasiddhi, kaṇhakaṇhavipākādikammacatukkavibhāgo, caturappamaññāvisayaniddeso, samudayatthaṅgamādipañcakassa yathābhūtāvabodho, chasāraṇīyadhammavibhāvanā, dasanāthakadhammapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādayo yathāsambhavaṃ saṅgahetvā dassetabbā atthā piṇḍattho.

Furthermore, by the entire sutta passage is shown: the Blessed One's state of being 'such' towards the desirable and undesirable, and the establishment of others therein; the explanation of the two dhammas that are the beginning of wholesome states; the instruction on the three trainings; the accomplishment of the four kinds of individuals, beginning with the self-tormentor; the analysis of the four kinds of kamma, beginning with dark with dark result; the explanation of the object of the four immeasurables; the true understanding of the fivefold group, beginning with arising and ceasing; the elucidation of the six qualities conducive to harmony; and the establishment in the ten qualities that make a refuge. These and other such meanings, which are to be shown after having been gathered together as is possible, constitute the condensed meaning.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Sixteen Hāras

Desanāhāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Desanā Hāra

Idāni [V 1.0420] nettiyā, peṭakopadese ca vuttanayavasena hārādīnaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ. Tattha “attā, loko”ti ca diṭṭhiyā adhiṭṭhānabhāvena, vedanāphassāyatanādimukhena ca gahitesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu taṇhāvajjitā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ. Taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ. Taṃ pana “paritassanāgahaṇena taṇhāgatāna”nti, “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti ca padehi samudayaggahaṇenañca pāḷiyaṃ sarūpena gahitameva. Ayaṃ tāva suttantanayo.

Now, in the Netti and the Peṭakopadesa, the ascertainment of the hāras and so forth proceeds by means of the method already stated. Therein, with regard to the five aggregates of clinging—which are grasped by means of the terms 'self' and 'world', by being the basis for wrong view, and through the portal of feeling, contact, sense bases, and so on—the five aggregates of clinging, exclusive of craving, are the truth of suffering. Craving is the truth of origination. Furthermore, that craving is indeed grasped in the Pāḷi in its own form by the grasping of 'agitation', by the phrase 'included in craving' (taṇhāgatānaṃ), by the phrase 'from feeling as condition, craving comes to be' (vedanāpaccayā taṇhā), and by the grasping of 'origination'. This, for now, is the Suttanta method.

Abhidhamme pana vibhaṅgappakaraṇe āgatanayena āghātānandādivacanehi, “ātappamanvāyā”tiādipadehi, cittapadosavacanena, sabbadiṭṭhigatikapadehi, kusalākusalaggahaṇena, bhavaggahaṇena, sokādiggahaṇena, diṭṭhiggahaṇena, tattha tattha samudayaggahaṇena cāti saṅkhepato sabbalokiyakusalākusaladhammavibhāvanapadehi gahitā dhammakilesā samudayasaccaṃ. Tadubhayesamappavatti nirodhasaccaṃ. Tassa pana tattha tattha vedanānaṃ atthaṅgamanissaraṇapariyāyehi paccattaṃ nibbutivacanena, anupādāvimuttivacanena ca pāḷiyaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Tassapi tattha tattha vedanānaṃ samudayādīni yathābhūtapaṭivedhanāpadesena channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayādīni yathābhūtapajānanapariyāyena, bhavanettiyā ucchedavacanena ca gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the Abhidhamma, however, according to the method found in the Vibhaṅga, the truth of origination comprises the kamma and defilements grasped, in brief, by terms that reveal all worldly wholesome and unwholesome states—such as the statements on 'hatred', 'delight', and so on; the terms 'with exertion' (ātappamanvāya) and so on; the statement on 'corruption of mind'; the terms for all that falls within the range of views; the grasping of 'wholesome and unwholesome'; the grasping of 'existence'; the grasping of 'sorrow' and so on; the grasping of 'view'; and, in various places, the grasping of 'origination'. The non-occurrence of both of these truths is the truth of cessation. Furthermore, its grasping in the Pāḷi should be understood through the synonymous terms for feelings, 'disappearance' and 'escape'; by the individual statement of 'extinguishment'; and by the statement of 'liberation through non-clinging'. The practice for knowing cessation is the truth of the path. Its grasping, too, should be understood in various places by the indication of the penetration of the origin and so on of feelings as they really are; by the method of knowing the origin and so on of the six sense bases as they really are; and by the statement on the cutting off of the craving that leads to becoming.

Tattha [M 1.0480] samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi nissaraṇanti evaṃ catusaccavasena, yāni pāḷiyaṃ sarūpeneva āgatāni assādādīnavanissaraṇāni, tesañca vasena idha assādādayo veditabbā. Veneyyānaṃ tādibhāvāpattiādi phalaṃ. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ payojanaṃ. Tadeva phalanti vuttovāyamattho. Tadatthañhi idaṃ suttaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ. Āghātādīnamakaraṇīyatā, āghātādiphalassa ca anaññasantānabhāvitā nindāpasaṃsāsu yathāsabhāvaṃ paṭijānananibbeṭhanānīti evaṃ taṃtaṃpayojanādhigamahetu upāyo. Āghātādīnaṃ karaṇapaṭisedhanādiapadesena atthakāmehi tato cittaṃ sādhukaṃ rakkhitabbanti ayaṃ āṇārahassa dhammarājassa āṇattīti. Ayaṃ assādādīnavanissaraṇaphalūpāyāṇattivasena chabbidhadhammasandassanalakkhaṇo desanāhāro nāma. Vuttañca –

Therein, gratification is shown by the truth of origination, danger by the truth of suffering, and escape by the truths of the path and cessation. Thus, by means of the four truths, and by means of those instances of gratification, danger, and escape that are found in the Pāḷi in their own form, gratification and so on should be understood here. For those to be trained, the fruit is the attainment of the state of equanimity (tādi), and so on. For whatever purpose, mentioned below, is to be accomplished by the teaching, that very purpose is called the fruit; this meaning has indeed been stated. It is for this purpose that this sutta was taught by the Blessed One. The means (upāya) is the cause for attaining each respective purpose, such as: the unsuitability of doing things like harboring hatred; the fact that the fruit of hatred and so on arises in one's own mental continuum and not another's; and the acknowledging and resolving of blame and praise according to their true nature. The command (āṇatti) of the Dhamma King, who is worthy of giving commands, is this: 'By those who desire their own welfare, the mind should be well guarded from that hatred and so on, by indicating the prohibition of doing such things as harboring hatred.' This, which has the characteristic of demonstrating the sixfold Dhamma by way of gratification, danger, escape, fruit, means, and command, is called the Desanā Hāra (the Hāra of Teaching). And it is said:

“Assādādīnavatā[V 1.0421], nissaraṇampi ca phalaṃ upāyo ca;

Āṇattī ca bhagavato, yogīnaṃ desanāhāro”ti.

Gratification and danger, escape, and also the fruit and the means, and the command of the Blessed One for yogis—this constitutes the Desanā Hāra.

Vicayahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Hāra of Analysis

Kappanābhāvepi vohāravasena, anuvādavasena ca “mama”nti vuttaṃ. Niyamābhāvato vikappanatthaṃ vāggahaṇaṃ. Taṃguṇasamaṅgitāya, abhimukhīkaraṇāya ca “bhikkhave”ti āmantanaṃ. Aññabhāvato, paṭiviruddhabhāvato ca “pare”ti vuttaṃ, vaṇṇapaṭipakkhato, avaṇṇanīyato ca “avaṇṇa”nti, byattivasena, vitthāravasena ca “bhāseyyu”nti, dhāraṇasabhāvato, adhammapaṭipakkhato ca “dhammassā”ti, diṭṭhisīlehi saṃhatabhāvato, kilesānaṃ saṅghātakaraṇato ca “saṅghassā”ti, vuttapaṭiniddesato, vacanupanyāsato ca “tatrā”ti, sammukhībhāvato, puthubhāvato ca “tumhehī”ti, cittassa hananato, ārammaṇābhighātato ca “āghāto”ti, ārammaṇe saṅkocavuttiyā anabhimukhatāya, atuṭṭhākāratāya ca “appaccayo”ti, ārammaṇacintanato, nissayato ca “cetaso”ti, atthassa asādhanato, anu anu anatthasādhanato ca “anabhiraddhī”ti, kāraṇānarahattā, satthusāsane

Even in the absence of conceiving, it is said 'mine' by way of conventional expression and by way of self-referential speech. Due to the absence of a fixed rule, the taking of the word 'vā' is for the purpose of expressing an alternative. The address 'bhikkhave' is due to their being endowed with those qualities and for the purpose of addressing them directly. 'Others' is said due to being different and being in opposition. 'Dispraise' is said due to being the opposite of praise and due to being unworthy of praise. 'They would speak' is said by way of distinctiveness and elaboration. 'Of the Dhamma' is said due to its nature of upholding and being the opposite of non-Dhamma. 'Of the Saṅgha' is said due to being united by view and virtue, and because it accomplishes the destruction of defilements. 'Therein' is said due to the restatement of what was said and the presentation of speech. 'By you' is said due to being face-to-face and being numerous. 'Resentment' is said due to the destruction of the mind and the striking of the object. 'Displeasure' is said due to a shrinking state towards the object, not facing it directly, and a state of dissatisfaction. 'Of the mind' is said due to thinking of the object and due to being a support. 'Lack of delight' is said due to not accomplishing the goal and repeatedly accomplishing what is unbeneficial. Due to not being worthy of a reason, and in the Teacher’s dispensation,

Ṭhitehi [M 1.0481] kātumasakkuṇeyyattā ca “na karaṇīyā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ adhippetatthe pavattatānidassanena, atthaso ca –

due to the impossibility of doing it by those established, it is said, “It should not be done.” Thus, by showing the occurrence in each intended meaning, and in terms of meaning—

Mamanti sāminiddiṭṭhaṃ sabbanāmapadaṃ. Vāti vikappananiddiṭṭhaṃ nipātapadaṃ. Bhikkhaveti ālapananiddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Pareti kattuniddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Avaṇṇanti kammaniddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Bhāseyyunti kiriyāniddiṭṭhaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ. Dhammassa, saṅghassāti ca sāminiddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Tatrāti ādhāraniddiṭṭhaṃ sabbanāmapadaṃ. Tumhehīti kattuniddiṭṭhaṃ sabbanāmapadaṃ. Na-iti paṭisedhaniddiṭṭhaṃ nipātapadaṃ. Āghāto, appaccayo, anabhiraddhīti ca kammaniddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Cetasoti sāminiddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Karaṇīyāti kiriyāniddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadanti. Evaṃ tassa tassa padassa visesatānidassanena, byañjanaso ca vicayanaṃ padavicayo. Ativitthārabhayena pana sakkāyeva aṭṭhakathaṃ, tassā ca līnatthavibhāvanaṃ anugantvā ayamattho viññunā vibhāvetunti na vitthārayimha.

'Mamaṃ' is a pronoun indicating ownership. 'Vā' is a particle indicating an alternative. 'Bhikkhave' is a noun indicating an address. 'Pare' is a noun indicating the agent. 'Avaṇṇaṃ' is a noun indicating the object. 'Bhāseyyuṃ' is a finite verb indicating an action. 'Dhammassa' and 'Saṅghassa' are nouns indicating ownership. 'Tatra' is a pronoun indicating location. 'Tumhehi' is a pronoun indicating the agent. 'Na' is a particle indicating negation. 'Āghāto,' 'appaccayo,' and 'anabhiraddhi' are nouns indicating the object. 'Cetaso' is a noun indicating ownership. 'Karaṇīyā' is a verbal noun indicating an action. Thus, by showing the distinction of each and every word, and by way of the phrasing, this is the analysis of words. However, due to fear of excessive elaboration, we have not elaborated, as it is possible for a wise person to clarify this meaning by following the commentary and the exposition of its hidden meaning.

“Tatra ce tumhe assatha kupitā vā anattamanā vā, api nu tumhe paresaṃ subhāsitaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ [V 1.0422] ājāneyyāthā”ti ayaṃ anumatipucchā.
