Sattādhiṭṭhānā, anekādhiṭṭhānā, paramatthavisayā, paccuppannavisayāti evaṃ sabbattha yathāsambhavaṃ pucchāvicayanaṃ pucchāvicayo. “No hetaṃ bhante”ti idaṃ vissajjanaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇaṃ, niravasesaṃ, sauttaraṃ, lokiyanti evaṃ sabbassāpi vissajjanassa yathārahaṃ vicayanaṃ vissajjanāvicayo.

‘If, in that case, you were angry or displeased, would you be able to distinguish between what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken by others?’ This is a question for assent. A question based on a being, a question based on multiple things, a question concerning the ultimate reality, a question concerning the present—thus, in all cases, the analysis of a question according to applicability is the 'analysis of questions'. ‘No, venerable sir.’ This answer is a categorical explanation, it is complete, it has a further point, it is mundane—thus, for every answer, the analysis according to what is fitting is the 'analysis of answers'.

“Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ…pe… na cetaso anabhiraddhi karaṇīyā”ti imāya paṭhamadesanāya “mamaṃ vā…pe… tumhaṃyevassa tena antarāyo”ti ayaṃ dutiyadesanā saṃsandati. Kasmā? Paṭhamāya manopadosaṃ nivāretvā dutiyāya tatthādīnavassa dassitattā. Tathā imāya dutiyadesanāya “mamaṃ vā…pe… api nu tumhe paresaṃ subhāsitaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ ājāneyyāthā”ti ayaṃ tatiyadesanā saṃsandati. Kasmā? Dutiyāya tatthādīnavaṃ dassetvā tatiyāya vacanatthasallakkhaṇamattepi asamatthabhāvassa dassitattā. Tathā imāya tatiyadesanāya “mamaṃ vā…pe… na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjatī”ti ayaṃ catutthadesanā saṃsandati. Kasmā? Tatiyāya manopadosaṃ sabbathā nivāretvā catutthāya avaṇṇaṭṭhāne paṭipajjitabbākārassa dassitattāti iminā nayena pubbena aparaṃ saṃsanditvā vicayanaṃ pubbāparavicayo. Assādavicayādayo vuttanayāva. Tesaṃ lakkhaṇasandassanamattameva hettha viseso.

“Monks, if others were to speak dispraise of me…pe… it should not cause mental displeasure.” This first teaching connects with the second teaching: “If others were to…pe… the obstacle lies within yourselves.” Why? Because the first prevents mental displeasure, while the second reveals the danger therein. Similarly, this second teaching connects with the third teaching: “If others were to…pe… would you be able to recognize what is well-spoken or ill-spoken by others?” Why? Because the second shows the danger therein, while the third reveals the inability to discern even the meaning of words. Likewise, this third teaching connects with the fourth teaching: “If others were to…pe… but such a thing is not found in us.” Why? Because the third completely prevents mental displeasure, while the fourth shows the proper way to act in the face of dispraise. In this way, by connecting the preceding with the subsequent, the analysis is the 'analysis of preceding and subsequent'. The analysis of gratification and so forth are as previously stated. Here, the only distinction is merely the demonstration of their characteristics.

“Api [M 1.0482] nu tumhe paresaṃ subhāsitaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ ājāneyyāthā”ti imāya pucchāya “no hetaṃ bhante”ti ayaṃ vissajjanā sameti. Kupito hi neva buddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakānaṃ na mātāpitūnaṃ na paccatthikānaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānāti. “Katamañca taṃ bhikkhave, appamattakaṃ…pe… tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyyā”ti imāya pucchāya “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādikā ayaṃ vissajjanā sameti. Bhagavā hi anuttarena pāṇātipātaviramaṇādiguṇena samannāgato, tañca kho samādhiṃ, paññañca upanidhāya appamattakaṃ oramattakaṃ sīlamattakaṃ. “Katame ca te bhikkhave, dhammā gambhīrā duddasā”tiādikāya pucchāya “santi bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā”tiādikā vissajjanā sameti. Sabbaññutaññāṇaguṇā hi aññatra tathāgatā aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhattā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā santā paṇītā atakkāvacarā nipuṇā paṇḍitavedanīyāti iminā nayena vissajjanāya pucchānurūpatāvicayanameva idha saṅgahagāthāya abhāvato anugītivicayoti. Ayaṃ padapañhādiekādasadhammavicayanalakkhaṇo vicayahāro nāma. Vuttañca “yaṃ pucchitañca vissajjitañcā”tiādi (netti. 4.2).

“Could you recognize the well-spoken and ill-spoken words of others?” To this question, the reply “No, venerable sir” is fitting. For an angry person does not know the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken words, whether from Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples, parents, or enemies. “And what, monks, is that trifling thing… when speaking the praise of the Tathāgata?” To this question, the reply beginning with “Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life” is fitting. For the Blessed One is endowed with the unsurpassed quality of abstaining from taking life and so on, yet that, in comparison to concentration and wisdom, is but a trifling thing, a minor thing, a mere matter of virtue. “And what, monks, are those dharmas that are profound, hard to see?” To this question, the reply beginning with “There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past” is fitting. For the qualities of the knowledge of omniscience, apart from the Tathāgata, are, for others, profound, hard to see, hard to penetrate, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of conjecture, subtle, and to be known only by the wise because they have a foundation that cannot be obtained by their knowledge. In this way, the very examination of the suitability of the answer to the question, here, due to the absence of a summary verse, is called the 'anugītivicaya'. This method of interpretation, which has the characteristic of investigating the eleven phenomena beginning with 'word' and 'question', is called the 'vicayahāra'. And it was said: “That which is asked and that which is answered,” and so on.

Yuttihārasaṃvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Method of Logical Analysis

Mamanti [V 1.0423] sāminiddeso yujjati sabhāvaniruttiyā tathāpayogadissanato, avaṇṇassa ca tadapekkhattā. Vāti vikappanatthaniddeso yujjati nepātikānamanekatthattā, ettha ca niyamābhāvato. Bhikkhaveti āmantananiddeso yujjati tadattheyeva etassa payogassa dissanato, desakassa ca paṭiggāhakāpekkhatoti evamādinā byañjanato ca –

The indication of ownership for ‘mamaṃ’ is suitable because of natural expression, because its usage is seen thus, and because dispraise is dependent on it. The indication of the meaning of alternation for ‘vā’ is suitable because particles have many meanings, and because here there is no fixed rule. The indication of address for ‘bhikkhave’ is suitable because the usage of this is seen for that very meaning, because of the speaker's dependence on a receiver, and by way of expression such as this, and so on.

Sabbena sabbaṃ āghātādīnamakaraṇaṃ tādibhāvāya saṃvattatīti yujjati iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samappavattisabbhāvato. Yasmiṃ santāne āghātādayo uppannā, tannimittakā antarāyā tasseva sampattivibandhāya saṃvattantīti yujjati kammānaṃ santānantaresu asaṅkamanato. Cittamabhibhavitvā uppannā āghātādayo subhāsitadubbhāsitasallakkhaṇepi asamatthatāya [M 1.0483] saṃvattantīti yujjati kodhalobhānaṃ andhatamasabhāvato. Pāṇātipātādidussīlyato veramaṇī sabbasattānaṃ pāmojjapāsaṃsāya saṃvattatīti yujjati sīlasampattiyā mahato kittisaddassa abbhuggatattā. Gambhīratādivisesayuttena guṇena tathāgatassa vaṇṇanā ekadesabhūtāpi sakalasabbaññuguṇaggahaṇāya saṃvattatīti yujjati anaññasādhāraṇattā. Tajjāayonisomanasikāraparikkhatāni adhigamatakkanāni sassatavādādiabhinivesāya saṃvattantīti yujjati kappanajālassa asamugghāṭitattā. Vedanādīnaṃ anavabodhena vedanāpaccayā taṇhā vaḍḍhatīti yujjati assādānupassanāsabbhāvato, sati ca vedayitabhāve (vedayitarāge (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.149) tattha attattaniyagāho, sassatādigāho ca viparipphandatīti yujjati kāraṇassa sannihitattā. Taṇhāpaccayā hi upādānaṃ sambhavati. Sassatādivāde paññapentānaṃ, tadanucchavikañca vedanaṃ vedayantānaṃ phasso hetūti yujjati visayindriyaviññāṇasaṅgatiyā vinā tadabhāvato. Chaphassāyatananimittaṃ vaṭṭassa anupacchedoti yujjati tattha avijjātaṇhānaṃ appahīnattā. Channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayatthaṅgamādipajānanā sabbadiṭṭhigatikasaññaṃ aticca tiṭṭhatīti yujjati catusaccapaṭivedhabhāvato. Imāhiyeva dvāsaṭṭhiyā sabbadiṭṭhigatānaṃ antojālīkatabhāvoti yujjati akiriyavādādīnaṃ, issaravādādīnañca tadantogadhattā, tathā ceva heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Ucchinnabhavanettiko tathāgatassa kāyoti yujjati bhagavato abhinīhārasampattiyā catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu ṭhatvā sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ bhāvitattā. Kāyassa bhedā parinibbutaṃ na dakkhantīti yujjati anupādisesanibbānappattiyaṃ rūpādīsu kassacipi anavasesatoti iminā nayena atthato ca sutte byañjanatthānaṃ yuttitāvibhāvanalakkhaṇo [V 1.0424] yuttihāro nāma yathāha “sabbesaṃ hārānaṃ, yā bhūmī”tiādi (netti. 4.3).

The complete non-doing of all hostility and the like leads to the state of one who is imperturbable—this is fitting, because of the existence of impartiality toward the pleasant and unpleasant. When hostility and similar states arise in a mental continuum, obstacles caused by them lead to the obstruction of that very person's attainment—this is fitting, because kamma does not transfer between different continuums. Hostility and similar states, having arisen and overwhelmed the mind, lead to an inability to discern well-spoken from ill-spoken words—this is fitting, because anger and greed are by nature blind and dark. Abstinence from immoral conduct such as taking life leads to the joy and praise of all beings—this is fitting, because the accomplishment in virtue gives rise to great renown. Praise of the Tathāgata by means of a quality endowed with profundity and other distinctions, even though it is only partial, leads to the comprehension of all the qualities of omniscience—this is fitting, because they are unparalleled. Speculations born from that wrong view and surrounded by unwise attention lead to adherence to eternalism and other such views—this is fitting, because the net of speculation remains un-uprooted. Through not understanding feeling and so on, craving grows conditioned by feeling—this is fitting, because of the existence of repeatedly contemplating gratification. And when there is the state of what is felt, the grasping at 'self' and 'what is mine', and at eternalism and other such views, is agitated—this is fitting, because the cause is present. For, conditioned by craving, clinging arises. For those who proclaim eternalist doctrines and experience corresponding feelings, contact is the cause—this is fitting, because without the convergence of sense object, sense faculty, and consciousness, it cannot arise. The cycle conditioned by the six sense bases for contact is uninterrupted—this is fitting, because therein ignorance and craving remain unabandoned. Understanding the arising, ceasing, and so on of the six sense bases for contact transcends all perceptions of those who hold speculative views—this is fitting, because of the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. By these very sixty-two views, all speculative views are enmeshed—this is fitting, because doctrines of non-action, a creator god, and the like are included within them, as it was explained thus previously. The Tathāgata’s body has the cord of becoming severed—this is fitting, because the Blessed One, through the fulfillment of his aspiration, having established himself in the four foundations of mindfulness, developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are. After the breakup of the body, the one who has attained Parinibbāna is not seen—this is fitting, because upon the attainment of Nibbāna without remainder, nothing whatsoever of form and the other aggregates remains. In this way, the method of interpretation characterized by clarifying the logical coherence of the meaning and the expression in the sutta is called the section on logical analysis (yuttihāra), as it is said: “Of all the sections, that which is the ground…” and so on.

Padaṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Proximate Cause

Vaṇṇārahāvaṇṇadubbaṇṇatānādeyyavacanatādi vipattīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇārahavaṇṇasubbaṇṇatāsaddheyyavacanatādi sampattīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā āghātādayo nirayādidukkhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Āghātādīnamakaraṇaṃ saggasampattiyādisabbasampattīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Pāṇātipātādipaṭivirati ariyassa sīlakkhandhassa [M 1.0484] padaṭṭhānaṃ, ariyo sīlakkhandho ariyassa samādhikkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ariyo samādhikkhandho ariyassa paññākkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ bhagavato paṭivedhappakārañāṇaṃ desanāñāṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Desanāñāṇaṃ veneyyānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbāyapi diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhupādānabhāvato sā yathārahaṃ navavidhassapi bhavassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Bhavo jātiyā. Jāti jarāmaraṇassa, sokādīnañca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samudayatthaṅgamādipaṭivedhanā catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ anubodhapaṭivedho hoti. Tattha anubodho paṭivedhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Paṭivedho catubbidhassa sāmaññaphalassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti avijjāgahaṇaṃ. Tattha avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārā viññāṇassa. Yāva vedanā taṇhāya padaṭṭhānanti netvā tesaṃ “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”tiādinā pāḷiyamāgatanayena sambajjhitabbaṃ. “Taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti ettha taṇhā upādānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ettha sassatādipaññāpanaṃ paresaṃ micchābhinivesassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Micchābhiniveso saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayayonisomanasikāradhammānudhammapaṭipattīhi vimukhatāya asaddhammassavanādīnañca padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Aññatra phassā”tiādīsu phasso vedanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Cha phassāyatanāni phassassa, sakalassa ca vaṭṭadukkhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samudayādipajānanaṃ nibbidāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, nibbidā virāgassātiādinā yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ netabbaṃ. Bhagavato bhavanettisamucchedo sabbaññutāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, tathā anupādāparinibbānassa cāti. Ayaṃ sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānadhammā, tesañca padaṭṭhānadhammāti yathāsambhavaṃ padaṭṭhānadhammaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo padaṭṭhānahāro nāma. Vuttañhi “dhammaṃ deseti jino, tassa ca dhammassa yaṃ padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi (netti. 4.4).

The proximate cause for failures such as dispraise for one worthy of praise, bad praise, and unacceptable speech. The proximate cause for successes such as praise for one worthy of praise, good praise, and credible speech. Similarly, ill will and the like are the proximate cause for suffering in hell and other such states. Abstaining from ill will and the like is the proximate cause for heavenly attainments and all other successes. Abstinence from killing living beings and other such transgressions is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of virtue. The noble aggregate of virtue is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of concentration. The noble aggregate of concentration is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of wisdom. The Blessed One’s knowledge of the mode of penetration, endowed with profundity and other distinctions, is the proximate cause for his teaching knowledge. Teaching knowledge is the proximate cause for the complete liberation of those to be trained from all suffering in the cycle of existence. All views, being forms of clinging to views, are, as appropriate, the proximate cause for the ninefold becoming. Becoming is the proximate cause for birth. Birth is the proximate cause for aging and death, as well as sorrow and the like. The penetration of feelings as they really are—their origin, cessation, and so on—is the understanding and penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Herein, understanding is the proximate cause for penetration. Penetration is the proximate cause for the fourfold fruit of recluseship. The phrase “not knowing, not seeing” refers to ignorance. Herein, ignorance is the proximate cause for formations; formations are the proximate cause for consciousness. This should be extended up to feeling being the proximate cause for craving, connecting them according to the scriptural passage: “With feeling as condition, craving arises.” In the phrase “for those overcome by craving, there is agitation and restlessness,” craving is the proximate cause for clinging. In the phrase “that too is conditioned by contact,” the assertion of eternalism and other views is the proximate cause for others’ wrong adherence. Wrong adherence is the proximate cause for listening to false teachings and the like, due to turning away from listening to the true Dhamma, associating with good persons, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. In the phrases “except through contact” and so on, contact is the proximate cause for feeling. The six sense bases are the proximate cause for contact and for all suffering in the cycle of existence. Clearly knowing the six sense bases as they really are—their origin and so on—is the proximate cause for disenchantment. Disenchantment is the proximate cause for dispassion, and so on, up to final Nibbāna without clinging. The Blessed One’s cutting off of the guide-rope of becoming is the proximate cause for his omniscience, and also for final Nibbāna without clinging. This is the method of proximate cause, characterized by the determination of the proximate cause phenomena for the phenomena mentioned in the sutta, and their respective proximate cause phenomena, as appropriate. For it is said: “The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and what is the proximate cause of that Dhamma…”—and so on (Netti. 4.4).

Lakkhaṇahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Characteristics

Āghātādiggahaṇena [V 1.0425] kodhūpanāhamakkhapalāsaissāmacchariyasārambhaparavambhanādīnaṃ saṅgaho paṭighacittuppādapariyāpannatāya ekalakkhaṇattā. Ānandādiggahaṇena abhijjhāvisamalobhamānātimānamadappamādānaṃ saṅgaho lobhacittuppādapariyāpannatāya ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā [M 1.0485] āghātaggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaganthanīvaraṇānaṃ saṅgaho kāyaganthanīvaraṇalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Ānandaggahaṇena phassādīnaṃ saṅgaho saṅkhārakkhandhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Sīlaggahaṇena adhicittādhipaññāsikkhānaṃ saṅgaho sikkhālakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Diṭṭhiggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaupādānānaṃ saṅgaho upādānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Vedanāna”nti ettha vedanāggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaupādānakkhandhānaṃ saṅgaho upādānakkhandhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā dhammāyatanadhammadhātupariyāpannavedanāggahaṇena sammasanupagānaṃ sabbesampi āyatanānaṃ, dhātūnañca saṅgaho āyatanalakkhaṇena, dhātulakkhaṇena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti ettha avijjāggahaṇena hetuāsavoghayoganīvaraṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho hetādilakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā, tathā “taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti ettha taṇhāggahaṇenapi. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ettha phassaggahaṇena saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ saṅgaho vipallāsahetubhāvena, khandhalakkhaṇena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. Chaphassāyatanaggahaṇena avasiṭṭhakhandhāyatanadhātindriyādīnaṃ saṅgaho phassuppattinimittatāya, sammasanīyabhāvena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. Bhavanettiggahaṇena avijjādīnaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ saṅgaho vaṭṭahetubhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti. Ayaṃ sutte anāgatepi dhamme ekalakkhaṇatādinā āgate viya niddhāraṇalakkhaṇo lakkhaṇahāro nāma. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “vuttamhi ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā”tiādi (netti. 4.5).

By taking up ill will and the like, there is an inclusion of anger, hostility, denigration, rivalry, envy, avarice, presumption, and disparagement of others, due to their single characteristic of being included in the arising of a mind of aversion. By taking up delight and the like, there is an inclusion of covetousness, unrighteous greed, conceit, excessive pride, intoxication, and heedlessness, due to their single characteristic of being included in the arising of a mind of greed. Similarly, by taking up ill will, there is an inclusion of the remaining ties and hindrances, due to their single characteristic of being a bodily tie and a hindrance. By taking up delight, there is an inclusion of contact and the like, due to their single characteristic of being the formations aggregate. By taking up virtue, there is an inclusion of the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom, due to their single characteristic of being a training. By taking up view, there is an inclusion of the remaining clingings, due to their single characteristic of being clinging. In the phrase “of feelings,” by taking up feeling, there is an inclusion of the remaining aggregates of clinging, due to their single characteristic of being aggregates of clinging. Likewise, by taking up feeling that is included in the phenomena-base and the phenomena-element, there is an inclusion of all sense-bases and elements suitable for contemplation, due to their single characteristic of being a sense-base and an element. In the phrase “of those who do not know, who do not see,” by taking up ignorance, there is an inclusion of roots, influxes, floods, yokes, hindrances, and the like, due to their single characteristic of being roots and so on. Similarly, also by taking up craving in the phrase “for those overcome by craving, there is trembling and agitation,” these same things are included. In the phrase “that too is conditioned by contact,” by taking up contact, there is an inclusion of perception, formations, and consciousness, due to their single characteristic of being causes of distortion and being an aggregate. By taking up the six sense bases, there is an inclusion of the remaining aggregates, sense-bases, elements, faculties, and the like, due to their single characteristic of being a sign for the arising of contact and being suitable for contemplation. By taking up the guide-rope of becoming, there is an inclusion of defiling phenomena such as ignorance, due to their single characteristic of being a cause of the round. This is the method of characteristics, characterized by the determination of phenomena, even those not mentioned in the sutta, as if they were, by virtue of their shared characteristic and so on. For so it is said: “When one thing is stated, whatever phenomena share the same characteristic…” (Netti 4.5).

Catubyūhahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of the Fourfold Array

Mamanti aneruttapadaṃ, tathā vāti ca. Bhikkhanasīlā bhikkhū. Parentiviruddhabhāvamupagacchantīti parā, aññatthe panetaṃ aneruttapadanti evamādinā neruttaṃ, taṃ pana “eva”ntiādinidānapadānaṃ, “mama”ntiādipāḷipadānañca aṭṭhakathāvasena, tassā līnatthavibhāvanīvasena ca suviññeyyattā ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha. Ye te nindāpasaṃsāhi sammākampitacetasā micchājīvato anoratā sassatādimicchābhinivesino sīlādidhammakkhandhesu appatiṭṭhitā sammāsambuddhaguṇarasassādavimukhā veneyyā, te kathaṃ nu kho yathāvuttadosavinimuttā [V 1.0426] sammāpaṭipattiyā ubhayahitaparā [M 1.0486] bhaveyyunti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Evamadhippetā puggalā, desanābhājanaṭṭhāne ca dassitā imissā desanāya nidānaṃ.

The word 'mamaṃ' is a term not to be etymologically analyzed, and so too is 'vā'. 'Bhikkhus' are those who have the characteristic of begging. 'Parā' (others) are those who approach a state of opposition. Furthermore, in another meaning, this term 'parā' is not to be etymologically analyzed. Thus, and so on, the etymology should be understood. However, that etymology, because it is easily understood by means of the Commentary on the introductory words such as 'evaṃ' and the Pāḷi words such as 'mamaṃ', and by means of its Sub-commentary which clarifies the hidden meaning, we have not elaborated for fear of excessive detail. Those trainable beings who exist—whose minds are greatly agitated by blame and praise, who do not abstain from wrong livelihood, who have wrong inclination towards wrong views such as eternalism, who are not established in the aggregates of qualities such as virtue, and who are averse to savoring the taste of the qualities of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—how could they, being freed from the aforementioned faults, through right practice, become devoted to the welfare of both? This is the Blessed One’s intention here. Thus have the intended persons and the receptacles for the teaching been shown, and the introduction to this discourse has also been shown.

Pubbāparānusandhi pana padasandhipadatthaniddesanikkhepasuttadesanāsandhivasena chabbidhā. Tattha “mama”nti etassa “avaṇṇa”nti iminā sambandhotiādinā padassa padantarena sambandho padasandhi. “Mama”nti vuttassa bhagavato “avaṇṇa”nti vuttena parehi upavaditena aguṇenasambandhotiādinā padatthassa padatthantarena sambandho padatthasandhi. “Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādidesanā suppiyena paribbājakena vuttaavaṇṇānusandhivasena pavattā. “Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādidesanā brahmadattena māṇavena vuttavaṇṇānusandhivasena pavattā. “Atthi bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā”tiādidesanā bhikkhūhi vuttavaṇṇānusandhivasena pavattāti evaṃ nānānusandhikassa suttassa taṃtadanusandhīhi, ekānusandhikassa ca pubbāparabhāgehi sambandho niddesasandhi. Nikkhepasandhi pana catubbidhasuttanikkhepavasena. Suttasandhi ca tividhasuttānusandhivasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ eva vicāritā, amhehi ca pubbe saṃvaṇṇitā. Ekissā desanāya desanāntarehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanaṃ desanāsandhi, sā panevaṃ veditabbā – “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave…pe… na cetaso anabhiraddhi karaṇīyā”ti ayaṃ desanā “ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ, tatrapi yo mano padūseñña, na me so tena sāsanakaro”ti (ma. ni. 1.232) imāya desanāya saddhiṃ saṃsandati. “Tumhaṃyevassa tena anantarāyo”ti ayaṃ “kammassakā māṇava sattā kammadāyādā kammayonī kammabandhū kammapaṭisaraṇā kammaṃ satte vibhajati, yadidaṃ hīnapaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289-297) imāya, “api nu tumhe…pe… ājāneyyāthā”ti ayaṃ –

Furthermore, the connection of preceding and following is sixfold by way of word-connection, meaning-connection, exposition-connection, summary-connection, sutta-connection, and teaching-connection. Among these, the connection of a word with another word, such as the connection of 'mamaṃ' with 'avaṇṇaṃ', is word-connection. The connection of the meaning of a word with the meaning of another word, such as the connection of the meaning of 'mamaṃ' spoken of the Blessed One with the dispraise spoken and blamed by others, is meaning-connection. The discourse beginning, 'Monks, should others speak disparagement of me...' proceeds by way of connection with the disparagement spoken by the wanderer Suppiya. The discourse beginning, 'Monks, should others speak praise of me...' proceeds by way of connection with the praise spoken by the young man Brahmadatta. The discourse beginning, 'Monks, there are other things that are deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand...' proceeds by way of connection with the praise spoken by the monks. Thus, the connection of a sutta with various connections by means of those respective connections, and of a sutta with a single connection by means of its preceding and following parts, is exposition-connection. Summary-connection, however, is investigated only in the Commentary by way of the fourfold sutta summary. And sutta-connection is investigated only in the Commentary by way of the threefold sutta connection, and has been explained by us before. The correlation of one discourse with other discourses is teaching-connection. And that should be understood thus: This discourse, 'Monks, should... of me... displeasure of mind is not to be made,' correlates with this discourse: 'Monks, even if lowly bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, whoever would corrupt their mind on that account would not be a doer of my teaching.' This discourse, 'For you, that would be an obstacle,' correlates with this discourse: 'Young man, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma, have kamma as their origin, kamma as their kin, kamma as their refuge. Kamma is what divides beings into inferior and superior.' This discourse, 'Would you now... know...?' correlates with:

“Kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ kodho sahate nara”nti. (a. ni. 7.64; mahāni. 5, 156, 195); –

“An angry person does not know the meaning, an angry person does not see the Dhamma; then there is blinding darkness, when anger overwhelms a person.”

Imāya, “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare vaṇṇaṃ…pe… na cetaso ubbilāvitattaṃ karaṇīya”nti ayaṃ “dhammāpi vo bhikkhave, pahātabbā, pageva adhammā”ti [M 1.0487] (ma. ni. 1.240), “kullūpamaṃ vo bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.240) ca imāya, “tatra ce tumhe…pe… tumhaṃyevassa tena antarāyo”ti ayaṃ –

With this, this discourse, 'Monks, should others speak praise of me... (etc.)... elation of mind is not to be made,' correlates with this discourse: 'Monks, even dhammas are to be abandoned by you, how much more so non-dhammas,' and with this discourse: 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.' This discourse, 'And if you there... (etc.)... for you, that would be an obstacle,' correlates with:

“Luddho [V 1.0427] atthaṃ na jānāti, luddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ lobho sahate nara”nti. (itivu. 88; mahāni. 5, 156; cūḷani. 128) ca –

“A greedy person does not know the meaning, a greedy person does not see the Dhamma; then there is blinding darkness, when greed overwhelms a person.”

“Kāmandhā jālasañchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā;

Pamattabandhunābaddhā, macchāva kumīnāmukhe;

Jarāmaraṇamanventi, vaccho khīrapakova mātara”nti. (udā. 64; netti. 27, 90; peṭako. 14) ca –

“Blinded by sensual desire, covered by the net, shrouded by the covering of craving, bound by the bond of heedlessness, like fish at the mouth of a fish-trap, they follow after aging and death, just as a suckling calf follows its mother.”

Imāya, “appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ sīlamattaka”nti ayaṃ “vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayampi kho brāhmaṇa yañño purimehi yaññehi appaṭṭhataro ca appasamārambhataro ca mahapphalataro ca mahānisaṃsataro cā”ti (dī. ni. 1.353) imāya paṭhamajjhānassa sīlato mahapphalamahānisaṃsataratāvacanena jhānato sīlassa appaphalaappānisaṃsatarabhāvadīpanato.

With this, this discourse, 'This is but a trifling thing, a mere matter of virtue,' correlates with this discourse spoken: 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... (etc.)... having attained the first jhāna, one abides therein. This sacrifice, too, O Brahmin, is indeed less costly and of less preparation, and of greater fruit and greater benefit than the previous sacrifices.' This is because of the statement that the first jhāna is of greater fruit and greater benefit than virtue, thereby showing that virtue is of lesser fruit and lesser benefit than jhāna.

“Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādidesanā “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo sīlavā ariyasīlena samannāgato”tiādidesanāya (dī. ni. 1.304), “aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”tiādidesanā “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho”tiādidesanāya, (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7, 8) gambhīratādivisesayuttadhammapaṭivedhena hi ñāṇassa gambhīrādibhāvo viññāyati.

The discourse beginning, 'Having abandoned the taking of life...' correlates with the discourse beginning, 'Indeed, good sirs, the ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with noble virtue.' The discourse beginning, 'There are other deep phenomena...' correlates with the discourse beginning, 'This Dhamma has been realized by me, which is deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand.' For it is through the penetration of the Dhamma endowed with special qualities such as profundity that the state of profundity, etc., of knowledge is known.

“Santi bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā”tiādidesanā “santi bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā…pe… abhivadanti sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadanti, asassato, sassato ca asassato ca, nevasassato ca nāsassato ca, antavā, anantavā, antavā ca anantavā ca, nevantavā ca nānantavā ca attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādidesanāya (ma. ni. 3.27).

The teaching beginning, “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of views about the past,” harmonizes with the teaching beginning, “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of views about the past… (pe)… they declare: ‘The self and the world are eternal. This alone is true, all else is worthless.’ Thus some declare. Others declare: ‘The self and the world are not eternal.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are both eternal and not eternal.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are finite.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are infinite.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are both finite and infinite.’ Others declare: ‘The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.’ ‘This alone is true, all else is worthless.’ Thus some declare.”

Tathā [M 1.0488] “santi bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā”tiādidesanā “santi bhikkhave [V 1.0428] …pe… abhivadanti saññī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā. Ittheke abhivadanti asaññī, saññī ca asaññī ca, nevasaññī ca nāsaññī ca attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā. Ittheke abhivadanti sato vā pana sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā paneke abhivadantī”ntiādidesanāya (ma. ni. 3.21), “vedanānaṃ samudayañca…pe… tathāgato”tiādidesanā “tadidaṃ saṅkhataṃ oḷārikaṃ, atthi kho pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodho, atthetanti iti viditvā tassa nissaraṇadassāvī tathāgato tadupātivatto”tiādidesanāya (ma. ni. 3.29), “tadapi tesaṃ…pe… vipphanditamevā”ti ayaṃ “idaṃ tesaṃ vata aññatreva saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ bhavissati parisuddhaṃ pariyodāta’nti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Paccattaṃ kho pana bhikkhave, ñāṇe asati parisuddhe pariyodāte yadapi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā tattha ñāṇabhāvamattameva pariyodāpenti, tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ upādānamakkhāyatī”tiādidesanāya (saṃ. ni. 2.43), “tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ayaṃ “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.45), “chandamūlakā ime āvuso dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā phassasamodhānā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti (pariyesitabbaṃ) ca ādidesanāya, “yato kho bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanāna”ntiādidesanā “yato kho bhikkhave, bhikkhu neva vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, na saññaṃ, na saṅkhāre, na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, so evaṃ asamanupassanto na kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatī”tiādidesanāya, “sabbete imeheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi antojālīkatā”tiādidesanā “ye hi keci bhikkhave…pe… abhivadanti, sabbete imāneva pañca kāyāni abhivadanti etesaṃ vā aññatara”ntiādidesanāya (ma. ni. 3.26), “kāyassa bhedā…pe… devamanussā”ti ayaṃ –

Likewise, the teaching beginning, “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the future,” harmonizes with the teaching beginning, “Monks, there are some… (pe)… who declare: ‘After death, the self is percipient and permanent.’ Some declare: ‘After death, the self is non-percipient.’ Some declare: ‘After death, the self is both percipient and non-percipient.’ Some declare: ‘After death, the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient.’ Some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of a being who exists. Some declare Nibbāna in this very life;” the teaching beginning, “the origin of feelings… (pe)… the Tathāgata,” harmonizes with the teaching, “This conditioned thing is gross. But there is the cessation of formations; there is this. Knowing this, the Tathāgata, who sees the escape from that, has transcended it;” this teaching, “that too for them… (pe)… is merely agitation,” harmonizes with the teaching, “It is not possible that, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from tradition, apart from reasoned speculation, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, they will have personal knowledge that is pure and bright. But when personal knowledge that is pure and bright is lacking, monks, whatever mere state of knowledge those venerable ascetics and brahmins purify there, that is spoken of as clinging for those venerable ascetics and brahmins;” this teaching, “that too is conditioned by contact,” harmonizes with the teachings, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving; with craving as condition, there is clinging,” and, “These things, friends, are rooted in desire, originate from attention, are produced by contact, and converge on feeling;” the teaching beginning, “When, monks, a monk of the six bases for contact,” harmonizes with the teaching, “When, monks, a monk does not regard feeling as self, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness as self, not regarding thus, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna;” the teaching, “All these are ensnared within these sixty-two grounds,” harmonizes with the teaching, “Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks… (pe)… declare anything, all declare these five aggregates or one among them;” and this teaching, “With the breakup of the body… (pe)… gods and humans.”

“Accī [M 1.0489] yathā vātavegena khittā (upasivāti bhagavā),

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ;

Evaṃ munī nāmakāyā vimutto,

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkha”nti. (su. ni. 1080) –

“Just as a flame tossed by the force of the wind (replied the Blessed One to Upasiva),

Goes to its end and cannot be reckoned;

So too the sage, freed from the mental group,

Goes to his end and cannot be reckoned.”

Ādidesanāya [V 1.0429] saddhiṃ saṃsandatīti. Ayaṃ neruttamadhippāyadesanānidānapubbāparānusandhīnaṃ catunnaṃ vibhāvanalakkhaṇo catubyūhahāro nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ “neruttamadhippāyo”tiādi (netti. 4.6).

Thus it connects with the teaching mentioned at the beginning. This is called the Fourfold Arrangement, which has the characteristic of clarifying four things: linguistic analysis, intended meaning, the origin of the teaching, and the connection of what precedes and what follows. And this has also been stated: “linguistic analysis and intended meaning,” etc.

Āvattahāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Method of Recurrence

Āghātādīnamakaraṇīyatāvacanena khantisoraccānuṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha khantiyā saddhāpaññāparāpakāradukkhasahagatānaṃ saṅgaho, tathā soraccena sīlassa. Saddhādiggahaṇena ca saddhindriyādisakalabodhipakkhiyadhammā āvattanti. Sīlaggahaṇena avippaṭisārādayo sabbepi sīlānisaṃsadhammā āvattanti. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena appamādavihāro, tena sakalaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ āvattati. Gambhīratādivisesayuttadhammaggahaṇena mahābodhipakittanaṃ. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ mahābodhīti vuccati, tena dasabalādayo sabbe buddhaguṇā āvattanti. Sassatādidiṭṭhiggahaṇena taṇhāvijjānaṃ saṅgaho, tāhi anamataggaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ āvattati. Vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samudayādipaṭivedhanena bhagavato pariññāttayavisuddhi, tāya paññāpāramimukhena sabbāpi pāramiyo āvattanti. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti ettha avijjāggahaṇena ayonisomanasikārapariggaho, tena ca nava ayonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā āvattanti. “Taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti ettha taṇhāggahaṇena nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā āvattanti. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”tiādi sassatādipaññāpanassa paccayādhīnavuttidassanaṃ, tena aniccatādilakkhaṇattayaṃ āvattati. Channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānanena vimuttisampadāniddeso, tena sattapi visuddhiyo āvattanti. “Ucchinnabhavanettiko tathāgatassa kāyo”ti taṇhāpahānaṃ vuttaṃ, tena bhagavato sakalasaṃkilesappahānaṃ āvattatīti ayaṃ desanāya gahitadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammavasena [M 1.0490] āvattanalakkhaṇo āvattahāro nāma. Yathāha “ekamhi padaṭṭhāne, pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi (netti. 4.7).

By the statement of the unsuitability of performing acts of resentment and so forth, patience, gentleness, and non-arising of defilements are included. Therein, by patience is included the endurance of suffering caused by the offenses of others, accompanied by faith and wisdom; likewise, by gentleness, virtue is included. And by taking up faith and so forth, all the factors of enlightenment, such as the faculty of faith, recur. By taking up virtue, all the dhammas that are benefits of virtue, such as non-remorse, recur. By the statement of abstention from killing living beings and so forth, there is dwelling in heedfulness, and by that, the entire holy life of the teaching recurs. By taking up the dhamma endowed with special qualities such as profundity, great enlightenment is proclaimed. Indeed, the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers, which has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge, which has the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers as its proximate cause, are called great enlightenment. By that, all the Buddha's qualities, such as the ten powers, recur. By taking up views such as eternalism, craving and ignorance are included; by them, the round of saṃsāra, which has an undiscoverable beginning, revolves. Through the penetration of the origin and so forth of feelings as they really are, there is the Blessed One's purity of the three kinds of full understanding; by means of that purity, with the perfection of wisdom as the principal, all the perfections recur. In the phrase 'of those not knowing, not seeing,' by taking up ignorance, unwise attention is comprehended; and by that, the nine dhammas rooted in unwise attention recur. In the phrase 'the agitation and trembling of those who have come to craving,' by taking up craving, the nine dhammas rooted in craving recur. The statement 'That too is conditioned by contact,' and so forth, shows the occurrence dependent on conditions for the declaration of eternalism and so forth; by that, the three characteristics, such as impermanence, recur. By understanding the six sense bases as they really are, the instruction on the accomplishment of liberation is given; by that, the seven purifications recur. By the statement 'The Tathāgata's body has the guide to existence cut off,' the abandonment of craving is stated; by that, the Blessed One's abandonment of all defilements recurs. Thus, this is the method of recurrence by name, characterized by recurrence by way of similar and dissimilar dhammas among the dhammas taken up in the discourse. As was said: 'When one proximate cause is found, one searches for the remaining proximate cause,' and so forth.

Vibhattihāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Method of Division

Āghātānandādayo akusalā dhammā, tesaṃ ayonisomanasikārādi padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yehi pana dhammehi āghātānandādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ appavatti, te abyāpādādayo kusalā dhammā, tesaṃ yonisomanasikārādi padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu āghātādayokāmāvacarāva, abyāpādādayo catubhūmakā, tathā [V 1.0430] pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirati kusalā vā abyākatā vā, tassā hirottappādayo dhammā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha kusalā siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā lokuttarā. Abyākatā lokuttarāva. “Atthi bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”ti vuttadhammā siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā. Tattha kusalānaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Abyākatānaṃ maggadhammā, vipassanā, āvajjanā vā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu kusalā lokuttarāva, abyākatā siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā lokuttarā, sabbāpi diṭṭhiyo akusalāva kāmāvacarāva, tāsaṃ avisesena micchābhinivese ayonisomanasikāro padaṭṭhānaṃ. Visesato pana santatighanavinibbhogābhāvato ekattanayassa micchāgāho atītajātianussaraṇatakkasahito sassatadiṭṭhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Hetuphalabhāvena sambandhabhāvassa aggahaṇato nānattanayassa micchāgāho tajjāsamannāhārasahito ucchedadiṭṭhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ sesadiṭṭhīnampi yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbaṃ.

Resentment, delight, and so forth are unwholesome dhammas; their proximate cause is unwise attention and so forth. But those dhammas by which there is the non-doing and non-occurrence of resentment, delight, and so forth—they are wholesome dhammas such as non-ill will; their proximate cause is wise attention and so forth. Among them, resentment and so forth are only of the sense sphere; non-ill will and so forth are of the four planes. Likewise, abstention from killing living beings and so forth is either wholesome or indeterminate; its proximate cause is dhammas such as moral shame and moral dread. Therein, the wholesome may be of the sense sphere, or it may be supramundane. The indeterminate is only supramundane. The dhammas spoken of as 'There are, monks, other dhammas that are profound' may be wholesome or may be indeterminate. Therein, the proximate cause of the wholesome is insight leading to emergence. The proximate cause of the indeterminate is the path dhammas, or adverting insight. Among them, the wholesome is only supramundane; the indeterminate may be of the sense sphere, or it may be supramundane. All views are only unwholesome and only of the sense sphere. Their proximate cause, generally, in wrong adherence, is unwise attention. Specifically, however, for the method of unity, due to the absence of analyzing the continuity and compactness, the wrong grasp accompanied by recollection of past lives and reasoning is the proximate cause of the eternalist view. For the method of diversity, due to not grasping the state of connection by way of cause and effect, the wrong grasp accompanied by suitable application of mind for that is the proximate cause of the annihilationist view. Thus, for the remaining views too, the proximate cause should be stated as is possible.

“Vedanāna”nti ettha vedanā siyā kusalā, siyā akusalā, siyā abyākatā, siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā rūpāvacarā, siyā arūpāvacarā, tāsaṃ phasso padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayādipaṭivedhanaṃ maggañāṇaṃ, anupādāvimutti ca phalañāṇaṃ, tesaṃ “aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”ti ettha vuttanayena dhammādivibhāgo netabbo. “Ajānataṃ apassata”ntiādīsu avijjātaṇhā akusalā kāmāvacarā, tāsu avijjāya āsavā, ayonisomanasikāro eva vā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṇhāya saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādadassanaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti [M 1.0491] ettha phassassa vedanāya viya dhammādivibhāgo veditabbo. Iminā nayena phassāyatanādīnampi yathārahaṃ dhammādivibhāgo netabboti ayaṃ saṃkilesadhamme, vodānadhamme ca sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato, padaṭṭhānato, bhūmito ca vibhajanalakkhaṇo vibhattihāro nāma. Yathāha “dhammañca padaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūmiñca vibhajjate ayaṃ hāro”tiādi (netti. 4.8).

Here in the text 'of feelings,' feeling may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate; may be of the sense sphere, may be of the form sphere, may be of the formless sphere. Their proximate cause is contact. The penetration of the origin and so forth of feelings as they really are is path-knowledge, and liberation without clinging is fruition-knowledge. For them, the division into dhamma and so forth should be understood by the method stated in 'other dhammas that are profound.' In the texts 'of one not knowing, not seeing,' and so forth, ignorance and craving are unwholesome and of the sense sphere. Among them, for ignorance, the cankers are the proximate cause, or unwise attention itself is the proximate cause. For craving, seeing gratification in things that fetter is the proximate cause. Here, in 'That too is conditioned by contact,' the division into dhamma and so forth for contact should be understood just as for feeling. By this method, the division into dhamma and so forth for the sense bases and so on should also be understood as is suitable. Thus, this, which has the characteristic of dividing the defiling dhammas and the purifying dhammas, both generally and specifically, by proximate cause, and by plane, is the method of division by name. As was said: 'This method divides the dhamma, the proximate cause, and the plane,' and so forth.

Parivattanahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Reversal

Āghātādīnamakaraṇaṃ khantisoraccāni anubrūhetvā paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalasiddhiyā ubhayahitapaṭipattimāvahati. Āghātādayo pana pavattiyamānā dubbaṇṇataṃ, dukkhaseyyaṃ, bhogahāniṃ, akittiṃ, parehi durupasaṅkamanatañca nipphādentā nirayādīsu mahādukkhamāvahanti. Pāṇātipātādipaṭivirati avippaṭisārādikalyāṇaṃ paramparamāvahati. Pāṇātipātādi pana vippaṭisārādiakalyāṇaṃ paramparamāvahati. Gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ veneyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ vijjābhiññādiguṇavisesamāvahati sabbaññeyyassa yathāsabhāvāvabodhato. Tathā gambhīratādivisesarahitaṃ [V 1.0431] pana ñāṇaṃ ñeyyesu sādhāraṇabhāvato yathāvuttaguṇavisesaṃ nāvahati. Sabbāpi cetā diṭṭhiyo yathārahaṃ sassatucchedabhāvato antadvayabhūtā sakkāyatīraṃ nātivattanti aniyyānikasabhāvattā. Sammādiṭṭhi pana saparikkhārā majjhimapaṭipadābhūtā sakkāyatīramatikkamma pāraṃ gacchati niyyānikasabhāvattā. Vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samudayādipaṭivedhanā anupādāvimuttimāvahati maggabhāvato. Vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samudayādiasampaṭivedho saṃsāracārakāvarodhamāvahati saṅkhārānaṃ paccayabhāvato. Vedayitasabhāvapaṭicchādako sammoho tadabhinandanamāvahati, yathābhūtāvabodho pana tattha nibbedhaṃ, virāgañca āvahati. Micchābhinivese ayonisomanasikārasahitā taṇhā anekavihitaṃ diṭṭhijālaṃ pasāreti. Yathāvuttataṇhāsamucchedo paṭhamamaggo taṃ diṭṭhijālaṃ saṅkoceti. Sassatavādādipaññāpanassa phasso paccayo asati phasse tadabhāvato. Diṭṭhibandhanabaddhānaṃ phassāyatanādīnamanirodhanena phassādianirodho saṃsāradukkhassa anivattiyeva yāthāvato phassāyatanādipariññā sabbadiṭṭhidassanāni ativattati, tesaṃ pana tathā apariññā [M 1.0492] diṭṭhidassanaṃ nātivattati. Bhavanettisamucchedo āyatiṃ attabhāvassa anibbattiyā saṃvattati, asamucchinnāya bhavanettiyā anāgate bhavappabandho parivattatiyevāti ayaṃ sutte niddiṭṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanalakkhaṇo parivattanahāro nāma. Kimāha “kusalākusale dhamme, niddiṭṭhe bhāvite pahīne cā”tiādi.

Refraining from ill will and the like, by cultivating patience and gentleness, brings about the practice for the welfare of both through the power achieved by the development of reflection. However, ill will and the like, when they arise, produce ugliness, painful sleep, loss of wealth, ill repute, and being difficult for others to approach, thereby bringing great suffering in hell and other realms. Abstinence from killing living beings and the like brings about non-remorse and other wholesome states in succession. However, killing living beings and the like brings about remorse and other unwholesome states in succession. Knowledge endowed with special qualities such as profundity brings, according to the suitability of those to be trained, special qualities such as higher knowledge and supernormal powers, due to the thorough understanding of all knowable things according to their intrinsic nature. However, knowledge lacking special qualities such as profundity does not bring the aforesaid special qualities, because of its commonality regarding knowable things. All these views, according to suitability, being the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, do not transcend the shore of personality-belief due to their non-liberating nature. Right view, however, with its requisites and being the middle path, crosses beyond the shore of personality-belief and goes to the further shore due to its liberating nature. The penetration of feelings as they really are—their arising and so on—brings about liberation through non-clinging, because it is the path. The non-penetration of feelings as they really are—their arising and so on—brings about confinement in the wandering of saṃsāra, because it is a condition for formations. Delusion, which conceals the nature of what is felt, brings about delight in it, while understanding as it really is brings disenchantment and dispassion toward it. In a state of wrong adherence, craving accompanied by unwise attention spreads the net of views of many kinds. The first path, which cuts off that aforesaid craving, contracts that net of views. Contact is the condition for positing eternalism and other doctrines; in the absence of contact, they are absent. Through the non-cessation of the contact-bases and so on of those bound by the fetter of views, the non-cessation of contact and so on is indeed the non-reversal of the suffering of cyclic existence. The full understanding of the contact-bases and so on as they really are transcends all views and perspectives; but the non-full understanding of them in that way does not transcend views and perspectives. The cutting off of the craving that guides to becoming leads to the non-arising of a future personal existence. If that craving is not cut off, the continuity of becoming will indeed revolve in the future. This is called the Method of Reversal, characterized by reversal from the opposite of the phenomena indicated in the Sutta. What did He say? 'Wholesome and unwholesome states, indicated, developed, and abandoned...' and so on.

Vevacanahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Synonyms

“Mamaṃ mama me”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. ‘Vā yadi cā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Bhikkhave samaṇā tapassino”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Pare aññe paṭiviruddhā”ti…pe… naṃ. “Avaṇṇaṃ akittiṃ ninda”nti…pe… naṃ. “Bhāseyyuṃ bhaṇeyyuṃ katheyyu”nti…pe… naṃ. “Dhammassa vinayassa satthusāsanassā”ti…pe… naṃ. “Saṅghassa samūhassa gaṇassā”ti…pe… naṃ. “Tatra tattha tesū”ti…pe… naṃ. “Tumhehi vo bhavantehī”ti…pe… naṃ. “Āghāto doso byāpādo”ti…pe… naṃ “appaccayo domanassaṃ cetasikadukkha”nti…pe… naṃ. “Cetaso cittassa manaso”ti…pe… naṃ. “Anabhiraddhi byāpatti manopadoso”ti…pe… naṃ. “Na no a mā”ti…pe… naṃ. “Karaṇīyā uppādetabbā pavattetabbā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu vevacanaṃ vattabbanti ayaṃ tassa tassa atthassa taṃtaṃpariyāyasaddayojanālakkhaṇo vevacanahāro nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ “vevacanāni bahūni tu, sutte vuttāni ekadhammassā”tiādi (netti. 4.10).

‘My, my, my’ are synonyms. ‘Or, and if’ are synonyms. ‘Bhikkhus, recluses, ascetics’ are synonyms. ‘Others, different, opposed’ are synonyms. ‘Disrepute, ill repute, blame’ are synonyms. ‘They might speak, say, declare’ are synonyms. ‘Of the Dhamma, of the Vinaya, of the Teacher's Dispensation’ are synonyms. ‘Of the Saṅgha, the assembly, the group’ are synonyms. ‘There, in that place, among them’ are synonyms. ‘By you, by you, by you venerable ones’ are synonyms. ‘Resentment, hatred, ill will’ are synonyms. ‘Displeasure, mental pain, mental suffering’ are synonyms. ‘Of the mind, of thought, of consciousness’ are synonyms. ‘Discontent, aversion, mental corruption’ are synonyms. ‘Not, not, un-, do not’ are synonyms. ‘To be done, to be produced, to be maintained’ are synonyms. In this way, synonyms should be stated for all terms. This is called the Method of Synonyms, characterized by the application of various synonymous words for each respective meaning. For this has been said: 'Many synonyms, indeed, are stated in the Sutta for a single thing,' and so on.

Paññattihāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Designation

Āghāto [V 1.0432] vatthuvasena dasavidhena, ekūnavīsatividhena vā paññatto. Apaccayo upavicāravasena chadhā paññatto. Ānando pītiādivasena vevacanena navadhā paññatto. Pīti sāmaññato pana khuddikādivasena pañcadhā paññatto. Somanassaṃ upavicāravasena chadhā, sīlaṃ vārittacārittādivasena anekadhā, gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ cittuppādavasena catudhā, dvādasadhā vā, visayabhedato anekadhā ca, diṭṭhisassatādivasena dvāsaṭṭhiyā bhedehi, tadantogadhavibhāgena anekadhā ca, vedanā chadhā, aṭṭhasatadhā, anekadhā ca, tassā samudayo pañcadhā, tathā atthaṅgamopi, assādo duvidhena, ādīnavo tividhena, nissaraṇaṃ ekadhā[M 1.0493], catudhā ca, anupādāvimutti duvidhena, “ajānataṃ apassata”nti vuttā avijjā visayabhedena catudhā, aṭṭhadhā ca, “taṇhāgatāna”ntiādinā vuttā taṇhā chadhā, aṭṭhasatadhā, anekadhā ca, phasso nissayavasena chadhā, upādānaṃ catudhā, bhavo dvidhā, anekadhā ca, jāti vevacanavasena chadhā, tathā jarā sattadhā, maraṇaṃ aṭṭhadhā, navadhā ca, soko pañcadhā, paridevo chadhā, dukkhaṃ catudhā, tathā domanassaṃ, upāyāso catudhā paññattoti ayaṃ pabhedapaññatti, samūhapaññatti ca.

Resentment is designated in ten ways by way of its basis, or in nineteen ways. Displeasure is designated in six ways by way of proximity. Joy is designated in nine ways by way of synonyms such as 'rapture'. Furthermore, in terms of general rapture, joy is designated in five ways by way of minor rapture and so on. Mental pleasure is designated in six ways by way of proximity. Virtue is designated in many ways by way of restraint and observance. Knowledge endowed with distinctions such as profundity is designated in four ways, or in twelve ways, by way of the arising of consciousness, and in many ways by way of the distinction of its object. View is designated by sixty-two kinds by way of eternalism and so on, and in many ways by way of the analysis included therein. Feeling is designated in six ways, in one hundred and eight ways, and in many ways. Its arising is designated in five ways, and likewise its cessation. Gratification is designated in two ways, danger in three ways, and escape in one way and in four ways. Liberation without clinging is designated in two ways. Ignorance, spoken of as 'for those not knowing, not seeing,' is designated in four ways and in eight ways by way of the distinction of its object. Craving, spoken of by the text beginning with 'for those who have gone to craving,' is designated in six ways, in one hundred and eight ways, and in many ways. Contact is designated in six ways by way of its support. Clinging is designated in four ways. Existence is designated in two ways and in many ways. Birth is designated in six ways by way of synonyms, and likewise aging in seven ways. Death is designated in eight ways and in nine ways. Sorrow is designated in five ways, lamentation in six ways. Suffering is designated in four ways, and likewise mental pain. Distress is designated in four ways. This is the designation of distinction and the designation of collection.

“Samudayo hotī”ti pabhavapaññatti, “yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti dukkhassa pariññāpaññatti, samudayassa pahānapaññatti, nirodhassa sacchikiriyāpaññatti, maggassa bhāvanāpaññatti. “Antojālīkatā”tiādisabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ saṅgahapaññatti. “Ucchinnabhavanettiko”tiādi duvidhena parinibbānapaññattīti evaṃ āghātādīnaṃ pabhavapaññattipariññāpaññattiādivasena. Tathā “āghāto”ti byāpādassa vevacanapaññatti. “Appaccayo”ti domanassassavevacanapaññattītiādivasena ca paññattibhedo vibhajjitabboti ayaṃ ekekassa dhammassa anekāhi paññattīhi paññapetabbākāravibhāvanalakkhaṇo paññattihāro nāma, tena vuttaṃ “ekaṃ bhagavā dhammaṃ, paṇṇattīhi vividhāhi desetī”tiādi (netti. 4.11).

‘It arises’ is the designation of origin; ‘one understands as it really is’ is the designation for the full understanding of suffering, the designation for abandoning the origin, the designation for realizing cessation, and the designation for developing the path. ‘Enmeshed within’ and so forth is the inclusive designation for all views. ‘One who has cut off the guide to existence’ and so forth is the twofold designation of final Nibbāna. In this way, the distinction of designations should be analyzed by way of the designation of origin, the designation of full understanding, and so on, for resentment and the like. Likewise, it should also be analyzed by way of such things as: ‘resentment’ is a synonymous designation for ill will; ‘displeasure’ is a synonymous designation for mental pain, and so on. This, which has the characteristic of clarifying the manner in which each single teaching is to be designated by many designations, is called the Mode of Designation. Therefore it is said: ‘The Blessed One teaches one Dhamma through various designations,’ and so forth.

Otaraṇahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Mode of Entry

Āghātaggahaṇena saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgaho, tathā anabhiraddhiggahaṇena. Appaccayaggahaṇena vedanākkhandhasaṅgahoti idaṃ khandhamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Tathā āghātādiggahaṇena dhammāyatanaṃ, dhammadhātu, dukkhasaccaṃ, samudayasaccaṃ vā gahitanti idaṃ āyatanamukhena, dhātumukhena, saccamukhena ca otaraṇaṃ[V 1.0433]. Tathā āghātādīnaṃ sahajātā avijjā hetusahajātaaññamaññanissasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo, asahajātā pana anantaraniruddhā anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanapaccayehi paccayo. Ananantarā pana upanissayavaseneva paccayo. Taṇhāupādānādi phassādīnampi tesaṃ sahajātānaṃ, asahajātānañca yathārahaṃ paccayabhāvo vattabbo. Koci panettha adhipativasena, koci kammavasena, koci āhāravasena, koci indriyavasena, koci jhānavasena koci [M 1.0494] maggavasenāpi paccayoti ayampi viseso veditabboti idaṃ paṭiccasamuppādamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Imināva nayena ānandādīnampi khandhādimukhena otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ.

By grasping resentment, the aggregate of formations is included; likewise by grasping dissatisfaction. By grasping displeasure, the aggregate of feeling is included—this is the entry by way of the aggregates. Similarly, by grasping resentment and the like, the phenomena-base, the phenomena-element, the truth of suffering, or the truth of the origin is grasped—this is the entry by way of the bases, elements, and truths. Furthermore, conascent ignorance is a condition for resentment and the like by way of root, conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. But non-conascent ignorance that has just ceased is a condition by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, decisive support by contiguity, absence, disappearance, and repetition conditions. However, ignorance that is not immediately preceding is a condition only by way of decisive support condition. It is stated that craving, clinging, and so on are conditions for contact and so on, as is appropriate, for both those that are conascent and those that are not. Here, some are a condition by way of dominance, some by way of kamma, some by way of nutriment, some by way of faculty, some by way of jhāna, and some even by way of the path—this distinction should also be understood. This is the entry by way of dependent origination. By this same method, the entry by way of the aggregates and so on should be clarified for joy and the like.

Tathā sīlaṃ pāṇātipātādīhi viraticetanā, abyāpādādicetasikadhammā ca, pāṇātipātādayo cetanāva, tesaṃ, tadupakārakadhammānañca lajjādayādīnaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhadhammāyatanādīsu saṅgahato purimanayeneva khandhādimukhena otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ. Esa nayo ñāṇadiṭṭhivedanāavijjātaṇhādiggahaṇesupi. Nissaraṇānupādāvimuttiggahaṇesu pana asaṅkhatadhātuvasenapi dhātumukhena otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ, tathā “vedanānaṃ…pe… anupādāvimutto”ti etena bhagavato sīlādayo pañcadhammakkhandhā, satipaṭṭhānādayo ca bodhipakkhiyadhammā pakāsitā hontīti taṃmukhenapi otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti sassatādipaññāpanassa paccayādhīnavuttitādīpanena aniccatāmukhena otaraṇaṃ, tathā evaṃdhammatāya paṭiccasamuppādamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Aniccassa dukkhānattabhāvato appaṇihitamukhena, suññatāmukhena otaraṇaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ paṭiccasamuppādādimukhehi suttatthassa otaraṇalakkhaṇo otaraṇahāro nāma. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “yo ca paṭiccuppādo, indriyakhandhā ca dhātuāyatanā”tiādi (netti. 4.12).

Likewise, virtue is the volition of abstinence from killing living beings and so on, and mental factors such as non-ill-will. Killing living beings and so on are volition itself. Because these states, and their supporting factors such as shame and compassion, are included in the aggregate of formations, the phenomena-base, and so on, the entry by way of the aggregates and so on should be clarified by the previous method. This is the method also for grasping knowledge, view, feeling, ignorance, craving, and so on. But in the case of grasping escape and liberation without clinging, the entry by way of the element should be clarified even by way of the unconditioned element. Likewise, by the text 'of feelings... liberated without clinging,' the Blessed One's five Dhamma aggregates beginning with virtue, and the factors of awakening beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, are revealed; thus, entry should also be known by way of these. By the text 'that too is conditioned by contact,' through showing that the designation of eternalism and so on is dependently arisen, entry should be known by way of impermanence. Likewise, because of the nature of things as such, entry should be known by way of dependent origination. Because what is impermanent is suffering and non-self, entry is made by way of the desireless and by way of emptiness. This same method applies to the remaining passages. This, which has the characteristic of entry into the meaning of the sutta by way of dependent origination and so on, is called the Mode of Entry. For so it is said: 'That which is dependent origination, and the faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases...' and so forth.

Sodhanahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Mode of Purification

“Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”nti ārambho. “Dhammassa vā avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ saṅghassa vā avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”nti padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. “Tatra tumhehi na āghāto, na appaccayo, na cetaso anabhiraddhi karaṇīyā”ti padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi ca. Dutiyanayādīsupi eseva nayo, tathā “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādi ārambho. “Katama”ntiādi pucchā. “Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādi padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. No ca pucchāsuddhi. “Idaṃ kho”tiādi pucchāsuddhi ceva padasuddhi ca, ārambhasuddhi.

“Monks, if others should speak disparagingly of me” is the opening statement. “Or if they should speak disparagingly of the Dhamma, or if they should speak disparagingly of the Saṅgha” is textual purity, but not purity of the opening statement. “In that case, you should not generate anger, resentment, or mental displeasure” is both textual purity and purity of the opening statement. This same method applies to the second method and so on. Similarly, “But this is insignificant…” and so on is an opening statement. “What?” and so on is a question. “Having abandoned the taking of life…” and so on is textual purity, but not purity of the opening statement, nor purity of the question. “This, indeed…” and so on is purity of the question, textual purity, and also purity of the opening statement.

Tathā [V 1.0434] “atthi bhikkhave”tiādi ārambho. “Katame ca te”tiādi pucchā. “Santi bhikkhave”tiādi ārambho. “Kimāgammā”tiādi ārambhapucchā[M 1.0495]. “Yathā samāhite”tiādi padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi, no ca pucchāsuddhi. “Ime kho”tiādi padasuddhi ceva pucchāsuddhi ca ārambhasuddhi ca. Iminā nayena sabbattha ārambhādayo veditabbā. Ayaṃ padārambhānaṃ sodhitāsodhitabhāvavicāraṇalakkhaṇo sodhanahāro nāma, vuttampi ca “vissajjitamhi pañhe, gāthāyaṃ pucchitāyamārabbhā”tiādi (netti. 4.13).

Similarly, “Monks, there is…” and so on is an opening statement. “And what are those?” and so on is a question. “Monks, there are…” and so on is an opening statement. “Relying on what?” and so on is an opening question. “Just as when one is concentrated…” and so on is textual purity, but not purity of the opening statement, nor purity of the question. “These, indeed…” and so on is textual purity, purity of the question, and also purity of the opening statement. By this method, the opening statements and so on should be understood everywhere. This, which is characterized by the examination of the state of being purified or unpurified of the textual openings, is called the Mode of Purification. And it was also said: “When the question has been answered, in the verse, when the question is asked, beginning with…” and so on.

Adhiṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Mode of Establishment

“Avaṇṇa”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tamavikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “mamaṃ vā”ti. Dhammassa vā saṅghassa vāti pakkhepi esa nayo. Tathā “sīla”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tamavikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādi. “Aññeva dhammā”tiādi sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tamavikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “tayidaṃ bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānātī”tiādi, tathā “pubbantakappikā”tiādi sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tamavikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “sassatavādā”tiādi. Iminā nayena sabbattha yathādesitameva sāmaññavisesā niddhāretabbā. Ayaṃ suttāgatānaṃ dhammānaṃ avikappanāvasena yathādesitameva sāmaññavisesaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo adhiṭṭhānahāro nāma, yathāha “ekattatāya dhammā, yepi ca vemattatāya niddiṭṭhā”tiādi (netti. 4.14).

“Dispraise” is a general basis. Without particularizing it, the specific statement is “of me, or…”. This same method applies in the case of “of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha.” Similarly, “virtue” is a general basis. Without particularizing it, the specific statement is “one abstains from the taking of life…” and so on. “There are other phenomena…” and so on is a general basis; without particularizing it, the specific statement is “This, monks, the Tathāgata understands…” and so on. Similarly, “those who speculate on the past…” and so on is a general basis. Without particularizing it, the specific statement is “the eternalists…” and so on. By this method, the general and the specific should be determined everywhere exactly as taught. This is called the Method of Establishment (adhiṭṭhānahāra), which is characterized by determining the general and the specific of the teachings found in the suttas exactly as they were taught, by way of non-particularization. As it is said: “Phenomena are for unity, and those which are also indicated for diversity…” and so on.

Parikkhārahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Method of Requisites

Āghātādīnaṃ “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādīni (dha. sa. 1237; vibha. 909) ekūnavīsati āghātavatthūni hetu. Ānandādīnaṃ ārammaṇābhisineho hetu. Sīlassa hiriottappaṃ, appicchatādayo ca hetu. “Gambhīrā”tiādinā vuttadhammassa sabbāpi pāramiyo hetu. Visesena paññāpāramī. Diṭṭhīnaṃ asappurisūpanissayo, asaddhammassavanaṃ micchābhinivesena ayonisomanasikāro ca avisesena hetu. Visesena pana sassatavādādīnaṃ atītajātianussaraṇādi hetu. Vedanānaṃ avijjā, taṇhā, kammādiphasso ca hetu. Anupādāvimuttiyā ariyamaggo hetu. Aññāṇassa ayonisomanasikāro hetu. Taṇhāya saṃyojaniyesu assādānupassanā hetu. Phassassa saḷāyatanāni hetu. Saḷāyatanassa nāmarūpaṃ hetu[M 1.0496]. Bhavanettisamucchedassa visuddhibhāvanā hetūti ayaṃ parikkhārasaṅkhāte hetupaccaye niddhāretvā [V 1.0435] saṃvaṇṇanālakkhaṇo parikkhārahāro nāma, tena vuttaṃ “ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ, janayantippaccayā paramparato”tiādi.

For anger and the like, the nineteen grounds for resentment, such as “He has done me wrong,” are the cause. For joy and the like, attachment to the object is the cause. For virtue, moral shame and moral dread, as well as fewness of wishes and so on, are the causes. For the Dhamma spoken of as “profound” and so on, all the perfections are the cause; specifically, the perfection of wisdom is the cause. For wrong views, association with an untrue person, listening to the dhamma of an untrue person, and unwise attention through wrong adherence are generally the cause. Specifically, however, for eternalism and the like, the recollection of past lives and so on is the cause. For feelings, ignorance, craving, kamma and so on, and contact are the causes. For liberation without clinging, the noble path is the cause. For ignorance, unwise attention is the cause. For craving, repeatedly seeing gratification in things that are objects of the fetters is the cause. For contact, the six sense bases are the cause. For the six sense bases, name-and-form is the cause. For the cutting off of the guide to becoming, the development of purification is the cause. This is called the Method of Requisites, which has the characteristic of exposition by determining the cause-condition designated as 'requisite'. Therefore, it is said: “Those phenomena which generate a [subsequent] phenomenon through conditions in succession,” and so on.

Samāropanahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Method of Imputation

Āghātādīnamakaraṇīyatāvacanena khantisampadā dassitā hoti. “Appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādinā soraccasampadā. “Atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā ñāṇasampadā. “Aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā”ti, “vedanānaṃ…pe… yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto”ti ca etehi samādhisampadāya saddhiṃ vijjāvimuttivasībhāvasampadā dassitā. Tattha khantisampadā paṭisaṅkhānabalasiddhito soraccasampadāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, soraccasampadā pana atthato sīlameva, sīlaṃ samādhisampadāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Samādhi ñāṇasampadāya padaṭṭhānanti ayaṃ padaṭṭhānasamāropanā.

By the teaching that things like anger are not to be done, the perfection of patience is shown. By the text beginning with “But this is a trifling matter,” the perfection of gentleness is shown. By the text beginning with “There is, monks,” the perfection of knowledge is shown. By the phrases “For one who does not grasp, Nibbāna is known for oneself,” and “having understood feelings… as they truly are, one is liberated without clinging,” the perfection of mastery in knowledge and liberation is shown, together with the perfection of concentration. Therein, the perfection of patience is the proximate cause of the perfection of gentleness due to the accomplishment of the power of reflection. The perfection of gentleness, however, is in essence virtue itself. Virtue is the proximate cause of the perfection of concentration. Concentration is the proximate cause of the perfection of knowledge. This is the imputation of the proximate cause.

Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanaṃ sīlassa pariyāyavibhāgadassanaṃ. Sassatavādādivibhāgadassanaṃ pana diṭṭhiyā pariyāyavacananti ayaṃ vevacanasamāropanā.

The statement of abstaining from the taking of life and so on is the showing of the analysis of synonyms for virtue. However, showing the analysis of eternalism and other views is a synonymous term for view. This is the imputation of synonyms.

Sīlena vītikkamappahānaṃ, tadaṅgappahānaṃ, duccaritasaṃkilesappahānañca sijjhati. Samādhinā pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, taṇhāsaṃkilesappahānañca sijjhati. Paññāya diṭṭhisaṃkilesappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, anusayappahānañca sijjhatīti ayaṃ pahānasamāropanā.

Through virtue, the abandoning of transgression, the abandoning by substitution of opposites, and the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct are accomplished. Through concentration, the abandoning of obsession, the abandoning by suppression, and the abandoning of the defilement of craving are accomplished. Through wisdom, the abandoning of the defilement of views, the abandoning by cutting off, and the abandoning of latent tendencies are accomplished. This is the imputation of abandonment.

Sīlādidhammakkhandhehi samathavipassanābhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchati pahānattayasiddhitoti ayaṃ bhāvanāsamāropanā. Ayaṃ sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānavevacanapahānabhāvanāsamāropanavicāraṇalakkhaṇo samāropanahāro nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ “ye dhammā yaṃ mūlā, ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā”tiādi, (netti. 4.16) ayaṃ soḷasahārayojanā.

Through the aggregates of qualities such as virtue, one reaches the complete fulfillment of the development of serenity and insight because of the accomplishment of the three abandonments. This is the imputation of development. This is called the Method of Imputation, which has the characteristic of examination by imputing the proximate cause, synonyms, abandonment, and development to the teachings that have come in the suttas. As it is said: “Those phenomena, rooted in what, and those of a single meaning explained by the Sage,” and so on. This is the application of the sixteen methods.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Sixteen Methods is completed.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Five Kinds of Methods

Nandiyāvaṭṭanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa Method

Āghātādīnamakaraṇavacanena [V 1.0436][M 1.0497] taṇhāvijjāsaṅkoco dassito. Sati hi attattaniyavatthūsu sinehe, sammohe ca “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinā āghāto jāyati, nāsati. Tathā “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādivacanehi “paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā, anupādāvimutto, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ…pe… yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādivacanehi ca taṇhāvijjānaṃ accantappahānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tāsaṃ pana pubbantakappikādipadehi, “ajānataṃ apassata”ntiādipadehi ca sarūpatopi dassitānaṃ taṇhāvijjānaṃ rūpadhammā, arūpadhammā ca adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yathākkamaṃ samatho ca vipassanā ca paṭipakkho, tesaṃ pana cetovimutti, paññāvimutti ca phalaṃ. Tattha taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, taṇhāvijjā vā, tadadhiṭṭhānabhūtā rūpārūpadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesamappavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā samathavipassanā maggasaccanti evaṃ, catusaccayojanā veditabbā.

Through the teaching of the non-doing of resentment and so on, the curtailment of craving and ignorance is shown. For when there is attachment and delusion regarding things pertaining to self and what is one's own, resentment arises with thoughts like, 'They have done me harm,' etc., but not when these are absent. Likewise, through statements such as, 'He abstains from killing living beings,' and through statements such as, 'The quenching is known individually,' 'liberated without clinging,' and 'of the six sense bases… one understands as they really are,' the complete abandonment of craving and ignorance is shown. Furthermore, for that craving and ignorance—whose nature is also indicated by terms such as 'speculating about the past' and 'of those not knowing, not seeing'—material and immaterial phenomena are the basis. Respectively, serenity and insight are their antidote, and for them, liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom are the fruit. Therein, craving is the truth of the origin, or craving and ignorance are; the material and immaterial phenomena that are their basis are the truth of suffering; their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation; and serenity and insight that fully know cessation are the truth of the path. Thus, the application to the four truths should be understood.

Taṇhāggahaṇena cettha māyāsāṭheyyamānātimānamadapamādapāpicchatāpāpamittatāahirikānottappādivasena sabbopi akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā avijjāggahaṇenapi viparītamanasikārakodhupanāhamakkhapaḷāsaissāmacchariyasārambha dovacassatā bhavadiṭṭhivibhavadiṭṭhādivasena. Vuttavipariyāyena pana amāyāasāṭheyyādivasena, aviparītamanasikārādivasena ca sabbopi kusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā samathapakkhiyānaṃ saddhindriyādīnaṃ, vipassanāpakkhiyānañca aniccasaññādīnaṃ vasenāti ayaṃ taṇhāvijjāhi saṃkilesapakkhaṃ suttatthaṃ samathavipassanāhi ca vodānapakkhaṃ catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇassa nandiyāvaṭṭanayassa bhūmi. Vuttañhi “taṇhañca avijjampi ca, samathena vipassanāya yo netī”tiādi.

Herein, by the taking up of craving, the entire unwholesome side is to be inferred by way of deceit, craftiness, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, evil desires, bad companionship, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and so forth. Similarly, by the taking up of ignorance, the entire unwholesome side is also to be inferred by way of perverted attention, anger, hostility, denigration of others' virtues, rivalry, envy, stinginess, contention, obstinacy, the view of eternalism, the view of annihilationism, and so forth. Conversely, by the opposite of what was said—through non-deceit, non-craftiness, and so forth, and through non-perverted attention, and so forth—the entire wholesome side is to be inferred. Likewise, the wholesome side is to be inferred by way of the faculties of faith and so forth, belonging to the serenity faction, and the perceptions of impermanence and so forth, belonging to the insight faction. Thus, this is the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, which has the characteristic of guiding, that by means of the application to the four truths, guides the meaning of the sutta concerning the defilement side through craving and ignorance, and the purification side through serenity and insight. For it was said: 'He who leads craving and ignorance by means of serenity and insight,' and so forth.

Tipukkhalanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Tipukkhala Method

Āghātādīnamakaraṇavacanena adosasiddhi, tathā pāṇātipātapharusavācāhi paṭivirativacanenāpi. Ānandādīnamakaraṇavacanena pana alobhasiddhi[M 1.0498], tathā abrahmacariyato paṭivirativacanenāpi. Adinnādānādīhi pana paṭivirativacanena tadubhayasiddhi. “Tayidaṃ bhikkhave[V 1.0437], tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā amohasiddhi. Iti tīhi akusalamūlehi gahitehi tappaṭipakkhato āghātādīnamakaraṇavacanena ca tīṇi kusalamūlāni siddhāniyeva honti.
