Tattha tīhi akusalamūlehi tividhaduccaritasaṃkilesamalavisamākusalasaññāvitakkapañcādivasena sabbopi akusalapakkho vitthāretabbo. Tathā tīhi kusalamūlehi tividhasucaritavodānasamakusalasaññāvitakkapaññāsaddhammasamādhi- vimokkhamukhavimokkhādivasena sabbopi kusalapakkho vibhāvetabbo.

By the statement of not doing resentment and so forth, the establishment of non-aversion occurs; similarly, also by the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and harsh speech. Furthermore, by the statement of not doing delight and so forth, the establishment of non-greed occurs. Through the passage beginning, 'This, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands,' the establishment of non-delusion occurs. Thus, with the three unwholesome roots being taken, by way of their opposite—that is, by the statement of not doing resentment and so forth—the three wholesome roots are indeed established. Therein, by means of the three unwholesome roots, the entire unwholesome side should be elaborated by way of threefold misconduct, threefold defilements, threefold stains, threefold uneven unwholesome perceptions, threefold thoughts, threefold conceptual proliferations, and so forth. Similarly, by means of the three wholesome roots, the entire wholesome side should be elucidated by way of threefold good conduct, threefold purity, threefold even wholesome perceptions, threefold wholesome thoughts, threefold wisdom, threefold true Dhamma, threefold concentration, threefold doors to liberation, threefold liberations, and so forth.

Ettha cāyaṃ saccayojanā – lobho samudayasaccaṃ, sabbāni vā kusalākusalamūlāni, tehi pana nibbattā tesamadhiṭṭhānagocarabhūtā upādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesamappavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā vimokkhādikā maggasaccanti. Ayaṃ akusalamūlehi saṃkilesapakkhaṃ, kusalamūlehi ca vodānapakkhaṃ catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇassa tipukkhalanayassa bhūmi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

And here, this is the application to the truths: Greed is the truth of the origin, or all wholesome and unwholesome roots are the truth of the origin. Furthermore, the aggregates of clinging, which are produced by them and have become their foundation and domain, are the truth of suffering. Their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation. The understanding of cessation, such as liberation and so forth, is the truth of the path. This is the ground of the Tipukkhala method, which has the characteristic of guiding, by means of applying the four truths to the defilement side through the unwholesome roots and to the purification side through the wholesome roots. For so it has been said:

“Yo akusale samūlehi,

Neti kusale ca kusalamūlehī”tiādi. (netti. 4.18);

“He who guides the unwholesome with its roots, and the wholesome with wholesome roots,” and so forth.

Sīhavikkīḷitanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Sīhavikkīḷita Method

Āghātānandādīnamakaraṇa-vacanena satisiddhi. Micchājīvāpaṭivirativacanena vīriyasiddhi. Vīriyena hi kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakke vinodeti, vīriyasādhanañca ājīvapārisuddhisīlanti. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena satisiddhi. Satiyā hi sāvajjānavajjo diṭṭho hoti. Tattha ca ādīnavānisaṃse sallakkhetvā sāvajjaṃ pahāya anavajjaṃ samādāya vattati. Tathā hi sā “niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti vuccati. “Tayidaṃ bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā samādhipaññāsiddhi. Paññavā hi yathābhūtāvabodho samāhito ca yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti.

By the statement of not doing resentment, delight, and so forth, the establishment of mindfulness occurs. By the statement of abstaining from wrong livelihood, the establishment of energy occurs. For by energy, one dispels thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty, and the virtue of purity of livelihood is also accomplished by energy. By the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, the establishment of mindfulness occurs. For by mindfulness, the blameworthy and the blameless are seen. And therein, having discerned the dangers and benefits, one lives, having abandoned the blameworthy and undertaken the blameless. For thus, it is called 'having deliverance as its manifestation.' Through the passage beginning, 'This, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands,' the establishment of concentration and wisdom occurs. For one with wisdom has comprehension of things as they really are, and one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.

Tathā “nicco dhuvo”tiādinā anicce “nicca”nti vipallāso, “arogo paraṃ maraṇā, ekantasukhī attā, diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto”ti ca evamādīhi asukhe “sukha”nti vipallāso. “Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito”tiādinā [M 1.0499] asubhe “subha”nti vipallāso. Sabbeheva diṭṭhippakāsanapadehi anattani “attā”ti vipallāsoti evamettha cattāro vipallāsā siddhā [V 1.0438] honti, tesaṃ paṭipakkhato cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni siddhāneva. Tattha catūhi yathāvuttehi indriyehi cattāro puggalā niddisitabbā. Kathaṃ duvidho hi taṇhācarito mudindriyo tikkhindriyoti, tathā diṭṭhicaritopi. Tesu paṭhamo asubhe “subha”nti vipallatthadiṭṭhiko satibalena yathābhūtaṃ kāyasabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Dutiyo asukhe “sukha”nti vipallatthadiṭṭhiko “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14; 6.58) vuttena vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vīriyabalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ vidhamati. Tatiyo anicce “nicca”nti vipallatthadiṭṭhiko samādhibalena samāhitabhāvato saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhati. Catuttho santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavicittattā phassādidhammapuñjamatte anattani “attā”ti vipallatthadiṭṭhiko catukoṭikasuññatāmanasikārena taṃ micchābhinivesaṃ viddhaṃseti. Catūhi cettha vipallāsehi caturāsavoghayogaganthaagatitaṇhuppādupādānasattaviññāṇaṭṭhitiapariññādivasena sabbopi akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi catubbidhajhānavihārādhiṭṭhānasukhabhāgiyadhammaappamaññāsammappadhānaiddhipādādivasena sabbopi vodānapakkho netabbo.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning ‘permanent, stable,’ the distortion of ‘permanent’ in what is impermanent is established. And by such passages as ‘healthy after death,’ ‘the self is completely happy,’ and ‘one has attained Nibbāna in this very life,’ the distortion of ‘happiness’ in what is not happiness is established. By the passage beginning ‘endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,’ the distortion of ‘beautiful’ in what is not beautiful is established. By all terms that express views, the distortion of ‘self’ in what is not-self is established. Thus, in this way, the four distortions are established here. By way of their opposite, the four foundations of mindfulness are indeed established. Therein, four persons should be designated by the four faculties as described. How so? For the person of craving temperament is twofold: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties; similarly, the person of speculative temperament is also twofold. Among them, the first, having the distorted view of ‘beautiful’ in the non-beautiful, discerns the true nature of the body by the power of mindfulness and enters the fixed course of rightness. The second, having the distorted view of ‘happiness’ in what is not happiness, destroys that distortion by the power of energy—which is called restraint by energy—spoken of in the passage beginning ‘one does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire.’ The third, having the distorted view of ‘permanent’ in the impermanent, penetrates the momentary nature of formations as it really is by the power of concentration, due to the state of being concentrated. The fourth, having the distorted view of ‘self’ in what is not-self—which is merely a collection of phenomena such as contact, etc., due to the diversity of continuity, collection, function, object, and compactness—destroys that wrong adherence by means of the mental application to emptiness with four sections. And here, by the four distortions, the entire unwholesome side should be led, by way of the four taints, four floods, four yokes, four bonds, four wrong courses, four origins of craving, four clingings, non-comprehension of the seven stations of consciousness, and so forth. Similarly, by the four foundations of mindfulness, the entire purification side should be led, by way of the four kinds of jhāna-abidings, four resolutions, four states partaking of happiness, four illimitables, four right strivings, four bases of psychic power, and so forth.

Ettha cāyaṃ saccayojanā – subhasaññāsukhasaññāhi, catūhipi vā vipallāsehi samudayasaccaṃ, tesamadhiṭṭhānārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesamappavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā satipaṭṭhānādikā maggasaccanti. Ayaṃ vipallāsehi saṃkilesapakkhaṃ, saddhindriyādīhi vodānapakkhaṃ catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇassa sīhavikkīḷitanayassa bhūmi, yathāha “yo neti vipallāsehi, kilese indriyehi saddhamme”tiādi (netti. 4.19).

And here, this is the application to the truths: Through the perceptions of the beautiful and of happiness, or through all four distortions, is the truth of the origin. The five aggregates of clinging, which have become their foundation and object, are the truth of suffering. Their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation. The understanding of cessation, such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, is the truth of the path. This is the ground of the Sīhavikkīḷita method, which has the characteristic of guiding, by means of applying the four truths to the defilement side through the distortions and to the purification side through the faculties such as faith and so forth, as it is said: ‘Who guides the defilements by means of the distortions, and the true Dhamma by means of the faculties,’ and so forth (Netti. 4.19).

Disālocanaaṅkusanayadvayavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Two Modes: Examining Directions and the Hook

Iti tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ siddhiyā vohāranayadvayampi siddhameva hoti. Tathā hi atthanayattayadisābhūtadhammānaṃ samālocanameva disālocananayo. Tesaṃ samānayanameva aṅkusanayo. Tasmā yathāvuttanayena [M 1.0500] atthanayānaṃ disābhūtadhammasamālokananayanavasena tampi nayadvayaṃ yojetabbanti, tena vuttaṃ “veyyākaraṇesu hi ye, kusalākusalā”tiādi (netti. 4.20). Ayaṃ pañcanayayojanā.

Thus, with the accomplishment of the three modes of meaning, the pair of modes of expression is also accomplished. Indeed, the thorough examination of phenomena that are the directions for the three modes of meaning is itself the mode of examining directions. The skillful guiding of them is itself the hook mode. Therefore, by the method as stated, that pair of modes should also be applied by way of the mode of thoroughly examining the phenomena that are the directions for the modes of meaning. For that reason, it was said: “For in explanations, those who are skilled and unskilled,” and so on. This is the application of the five modes.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Five Modes is concluded.

Sāsanapaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Establishment of the Dispensation

Idaṃ [V 1.0439] pana suttaṃ soḷasavidhe sāsanapaṭṭhāne saṃkilesavāsanāsekkhabhāgiyaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhādisaṃkilesānaṃ sīlādipuññakiriyassa, asekkhasīlādikkhandhassa ca vibhattattā, saṃkilesavāsanānibbedhāsekkhabhāgiyameva vā yathāvuttatthānaṃ sekkhasīlakkhandhādikassa ca vibhattattā. Aṭṭhavīsatividhe pana sāsanapaṭṭhāne lokiyalokuttaraṃ sattadhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇañeyyaṃ dassanabhāvanaṃ sakavacanaparavacanaṃ vissajjanīyāvissajjanīyaṃ kammavipākaṃ kusalākusalaṃ anuññātapaṭikkhittaṃ bhavo ca lokiyalokuttarādīnamatthānaṃ idha vibhattattāti. Ayaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānayojanā.

Furthermore, this Sutta, in the sixteenfold establishment of the dispensation, has the portion of defilement, the portion of latent tendencies, and the portion of the non-trainee, because of its analysis of defilements such as craving and views, of meritorious actions such as virtue, and of the group of qualities of the non-trainee such as virtue. Alternatively, it has the portion of defilement, the portion of latent tendencies, the portion of penetration, and the portion of the non-trainee, because of its analysis of the aforementioned matters and of the group of qualities of the trainee such as virtue. Moreover, in the twenty-eightfold establishment of the dispensation, this Sutta is mundane and supramundane; it is founded on beings and founded on the Dhamma; it is knowledge and the knowable; it is vision and cultivation; it is one's own statement and another's statement; it is what is to be explained and what is not to be explained; it is kamma and its result; it is wholesome and unwholesome; it is what is permitted and what is prohibited; and it is existence. This is because the meanings of the mundane, supramundane, and so on, are analyzed herein. This is the application to the establishment of the dispensation.

Pakaraṇanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Mode of the Treatise is concluded.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya paramasukhumagambhīraduranubodhatthaparidīpanāya suvimalavipulapaññāveyyattiyajananāya ajjavamaddavasoraccasaddhāsatidhitibuddhikhantivīriyādidhammasamaṅginā sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye asaṅgāsaṃhīravisāradañāṇacārinā anekappabhedasakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhinā mahāgaṇinā mahāveyyākaraṇena ñāṇābhivaṃsadhammasenāpatināmatherena mahādhammarājādhirājagarunā katāya sādhuvilāsiniyā nāma līnatthapakāsaniyā brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthavibhāvanā.

Thus ends the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta, which is the work named Sādhuvilāsinī, an Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. This work, for the purpose of illuminating the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-understand meaning, and for generating clear and vast wisdom and proficiency, was composed by the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, the teacher of the Great King of Kings of the Dhamma, a great leader of the monastic community, and a great grammarian; one endowed with qualities such as honesty, gentleness, amiability, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, intelligence, patience, and energy; one whose knowledge moves with expertise, unobstructed and unhindered through the Three Baskets with their commentaries; and one who plunges into the depths of the various kinds of his own and other doctrines.

Brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Brahmajāla Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is concluded.
